head: The Village Barber's Haircut
dek: A self-deprecating opener that sets the show's tone: two people known for policy and economics agreeing to be playful as well as serious.
more: Amit was living in a village in a district he won't name and asked Ajay where to get a haircut. Ajay sent him to the village barber shop. There was no electricity and Amit could hardly see the mirror, and before he knew it the sides of his head were gone. Ajay raised the haircut the moment Amit promised the show would cover 'the profane' as well as the profound.
A self-deprecating opener that sets the show's tone: two people known for policy and economics agreeing to be playful as well as serious.

head: The Snake That Forgot to Hide Its Tail
dek: Fear found reserves that the tired mind had written off. It also previews Ajay's later point that when an event ambushes us, we act from deep instinct and only afterwards get to ask whether that instinct was right.
more: Amit had walk-run almost 7 km on Ajay's track and was exhausted, sure he couldn't go any faster. While he was cooling down, a snake shot across the path into the bushes and waited there with its tail still lying on the path. He turned and sprinted. His Garmin logged about 25 km/h, which Ajay told him is about the top speed a human can reach.

Fear found reserves that the tired mind had written off. It also previews Ajay's later point that when an event ambushes us, we act from deep instinct and only afterwards get to ask whether that instinct was right.

head: India's Big Four Venomous Snakes Are Not Alike
dek: Our fear is poorly matched to the real danger. The snakes people dread most have adapted to living alongside humans.
more: Ajay went through the four venomous snakes behind most bad encounters in India. Cobras live around human settlements and have reached a working coexistence with people: they flash their hoods, people run, and many apparent strikes are made with the mouth closed. Kraits are quiet and calm. The trouble comes when one seeks a sleeping person's warmth and gets crushed, and as Amit adds, the bite is painless, so the victim simply dies in their sleep. The tiny saw-scaled viper puts on a scary display that usually works, except on young men who try to pick it up by the tail. Only the Russell's viper strikes with no reasonable provocation.
Our fear is poorly matched to the real danger. The snakes people dread most have adapted to living alongside humans. Before you fear a whole category, look at how its members actually behave.

head: Why Seagulls Are Bastards
dek: We decide what an animal is like from how it looks, which is an anthropocentric mistake, and the gap between image and behaviour unsettles us.
more: By a lakeside in Udaipur, Ajay once told Amit that seagulls are bastards. They are effectively birds of prey: they kill and eat pigeons, tear chunks of flesh from the backs of baby whales near the surface, and have been reported gouging out the eyes of seals. Amit added that seagulls go for the eyes first, and that they practise kleptoparasitism, stealing food from others, 'like stealing from a thief'. That made him think of the License Raj state taxing the rent-seekers and cronies it had created.

We decide what an animal is like from how it looks, which is an anthropocentric mistake, and the gap between image and behaviour unsettles us. The conversation then turns to why we don't judge animals morally but do judge humans.

head: Being Called an 'Anti-Uncle'
dek: What makes someone an 'uncle' is mental rigidity, not age. That sets up the episode's longer discussion of conformism.
more: At a book event, Shrayana Bhattacharya, author of Desperately Seeking Shah Rukh, told Amit he was an 'anti-uncle'. She meant that he is willing to change his mind, listens to arguments from the other side, stays open to ideas and will engage with anyone. The 'uncle' is the opposite: closed, settled in a worldview and insistent on it.
What makes someone an 'uncle' is mental rigidity, not age. That sets up the episode's longer discussion of conformism.

head: Galileo: 'And Still It Turns'
dek: Power can force people to say they agree, but it cannot change what is true.
more: Galileo was forced to recant his observation that the earth goes around the sun and to say he had been wrong. Amit tells how he came out afterwards, looked up at the sky, stamped the ground and said 'Eppur si muove': still it turns. In Paul Graham's essay, this is the call of the aggressively independent-minded.
Power can force people to say they agree, but it cannot change what is true.

head: Old Classmates Resurface to Call Him an Asshole
dek: A funny but telling example of what it costs to argue against received wisdom in public.
more: Amit wrote a deliberately provocative column arguing that it is immoral to have children. The backlash was so strong that people he had not heard from since school, 35 years earlier, found him on Facebook just to call him an asshole.
A funny but telling example of what it costs to argue against received wisdom in public. It sets up Ajay's point about the market failure in criticism.

head: Hussain Haidry's Loneliness in a Mob
dek: Being mobbed is isolating, and that isolation is how mobs chill speech.
more: The poet Hussain Haidry, a guest on The Seen and the Unseen, told Amit that when right-wing accounts mobbed him, what hurt was how alone he felt: nobody called to say they were with him or to ask how he was. Amit has been targeted by both right-wing and woke mobs and recognises the feeling. Even with many well-wishers, nobody grasps what it is like when a thousand people are abusing you within an hour.
Being mobbed is isolating, and that isolation is how mobs chill speech. Over time people stop saying what they think, until they no longer even think it.

head: The Fan Who Saved 'Piano Man'
dek: Talent alone does not decide which art survives; luck and the people who champion it matter a great deal.
more: Billy Joel's 'Piano Man' nearly vanished, and Joel was not going to make more music. One man loved the song so much that he went from radio station to radio station asking them to play it. He finally struck a deal with someone at a big station, almost a bribe, to get it on air. The song became a hit and Joel went on to make many more albums. Amit adds that Bach only became a big name decades after he died.
Talent alone does not decide which art survives; luck and the people who champion it matter a great deal. That raises the question of how many masterpieces disappear because nobody pushed for them.

head: The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time
dek: It shows what fiction can do: let you live inside a very different mind.
more: It shows what fiction can do: let you live inside a very different mind. Amit read out Haddon's own description: 'it's a novel about difference, about being an outsider, about seeing the world in a surprising and revealing way. It's as much a novel about us as it is about Christopher.'
Amit's book of the week, after a short case for why reading matters. A 15-year-old boy investigates who killed his neighbour's dog, and the story is told in his voice.

head: Songs of Surrender
dek: U2 rethink songs they wrote as kids from a more grown-up place, changing arrangements and editing lyrics.
more: U2 rethink songs they wrote as kids from a more grown-up place, changing arrangements and editing lyrics. It is not a set formula like MTV Unplugged. Ajay also likes the thought that some young listeners will start here and only later go back to The Joshua Tree and The Unforgettable Fire.
Ajay's recommendation of the week, released about two months before the episode. U2 rework 40 songs, mostly old with a few new.

head: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
dek: It gives a clear map of conventional versus independent thinkers, each either passive or aggressive.
more: It gives a clear map of conventional versus independent thinkers, each either passive or aggressive. It also explains why the aggressively conventional-minded are the loudest on social media and the ones who hold back progress.
Prompted by the 'anti-uncle' compliment, Amit called it one of the finest essays he has read in recent years and read out the passage on the four 'calls'.

head: Private Truths, Public Lies
dek: It explains preference falsification and preference cascades. Amit uses them to explain the collapse of Soviet communism, the Modi wave and the open bigotry that social media unlocked.
more: It explains preference falsification and preference cascades. Amit uses them to explain the collapse of Soviet communism, the Modi wave and the open bigotry that social media unlocked.
Ajay brought up Kuran's idea of preference falsification. Amit said he keeps citing this book, and mentioned that Ajay had told him the night before that Kuran was once his teacher.

head: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
dek: Nagel argues that we can describe how a bat experiences the world through echolocation but can never imagine it.
more: Nagel argues that we can describe how a bat experiences the world through echolocation but can never imagine it. Amit uses this as a contrast: through stories we do manage to imagine other people's lives.
An early-seventies philosophy essay Amit raised while explaining why fiction matters.

head: It Is Immoral to Have Children. Here's Why
dek: It is a deliberately provocative argument. We agree not to do things to people without consent, not to cause pain and not to kill, yet a child is born without consent, will feel pain and will die.
more: It is a deliberately provocative argument. We agree not to do things to people without consent, not to cause pain and not to kill, yet a child is born without consent, will feel pain and will die. Amit says the argument has to be tackled, while admitting he might do things he thinks are immoral.
The third column, the one that brought old school acquaintances out to abuse him.

head: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
dek: In it, Kelkar and Shah argue that criticism suffers from a market failure: critics create benefits for everyone but bear the cost themselves.
more: In it, Kelkar and Shah argue that criticism suffers from a market failure: critics create benefits for everyone but bear the cost themselves. Ajay suggests social media has made that failure bigger.
Ajay cited it during the discussion of the cost of being a public critic.

head: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit called it a great episode. It is the longer conversation with the person who gave him the 'anti-uncle' label.
more: Amit called it a great episode. It is the longer conversation with the person who gave him the 'anti-uncle' label.
Mentioned when Amit introduced Shrayana Bhattacharya.

head: In a Silent Way (Episode 316 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls it a great episode in which the musician talks about how a big hit can become a curse: you keep changing, but audiences keep shouting a three-minute song from twenty years ago at you.
more: Amit calls it a great episode in which the musician talks about how a big hit can become a curse: you keep changing, but audiences keep shouting a three-minute song from twenty years ago at you.
Mentioned in the discussion of artists getting frozen into their old hits.

head: Eric Weinstein Won't Toe the Line (Episode 330 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It is the longer version of the debate this episode ends on: with far more potential artists alive than ever before, why don't we see more great art?
more: It is the longer version of the debate this episode ends on: with far more potential artists alive than ever before, why don't we see more great art?
Amit had put his question about the missing masterpieces to Eric in this episode, and Eric strongly disagreed.

head: The Seen and the Unseen
dek: Ajay describes it as having become oral history, with three-to-eight-hour deep dives into one person at a time.
more: Ajay describes it as having become oral history, with three-to-eight-hour deep dives into one person at a time. Its show notes list every book mentioned, and that list has become a meme, 'the Seen and the Unseen bookshelf'.
Discussed at the start of the episode and again in the reading segment.

head: Hardware vs Software: Culture Is Our Operating System
dek: A newborn king cobra is fully a king cobra at birth: its behaviour is hard-coded and stays the same for life.
more: A newborn king cobra is fully a king cobra at birth: its behaviour is hard-coded and stays the same for life. Higher animals add culture, meaning learned behaviours, beliefs and heuristics, and in humans this becomes a whole operating system. Only humans can examine that operating system and rewrite it. That is why we don't morally judge a cobra but do ask questions about our own code. In Ajay's words, this plasticity is what makes us human.

head: Character Is Contingent, but Act as if Free Will Exists
dek: Animals do brutal things and we don't judge them. Humans are animals too, and much of what we call reasoning is rationalisation of where our instincts already took us.
more: Animals do brutal things and we don't judge them. Humans are animals too, and much of what we call reasoning is rationalisation of where our instincts already took us. We are shaped by genes and circumstances; Amit quotes Steven Pinker: 'Nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them'. That could argue for never judging anyone. But a society needs a code that punishes the bad and rewards the good, so Amit concludes we should keep holding people responsible anyway.

head: Judge the Algorithm, Not the Outcome
dek: We are all works in progress, 'halfway from coal, halfway to diamond'.
more: We are all works in progress, 'halfway from coal, halfway to diamond'. Because the world is probabilistic, a good decision can turn out badly. So instead of grading outcomes, look at the process that produced the decision. When an event ambushes us we react on instinct; growth means reflecting afterwards on whether that instinct was right. Neither 'we are fully determined' nor 'we are fully free' is true. What counts is to keep trying.

head: Uncles, Anti-Uncles and the Four Quadrants of Conformism
dek: Paul Graham sorts people into conventional-minded and independent-minded, each either passive or aggressive, and gives each type a 'call'.
more: Paul Graham sorts people into conventional-minded and independent-minded, each either passive or aggressive, and gives each type a 'call'. Aggressively conventional: 'Crush outgroup!' Passively conventional: 'What will the neighbours think?' Passively independent: 'To each his own.' Aggressively independent: 'Eppur si muove.' Amit's point is that the aggressively conventional-minded, whatever their tribe (right-wing, woke or otherwise), make the most noise online and get in the way of progress. They repeat memorised slogans loudly and shut down dialogue. His personal fix is to notice that his own first reaction to a radical idea is 'no', and to push back on it, because every idea that changes the world starts out as a radical idea.

head: People Are Brains, Not Stomachs
dek: Indians are taught in school that population is the country's biggest problem.
more: Indians are taught in school that population is the country's biggest problem. Amit argues the opposite. Human history is a long migration from villages to cities, the places where population density is highest, because more people means more minds working together. The problems blamed on population are failures of governance. And people who complain about population never count themselves in it.

head: Poverty Is Not Inequality
dek: Ask whether you would rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh. Everyone picks the USA, even though it has more inequality as measured by the Gini coefficient.
more: Ask whether you would rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh. Everyone picks the USA, even though it has more inequality as measured by the Gini coefficient. After liberalisation, India lifted more than 400 million people out of poverty while inequality rose. The belief that the rich getting richer means the poor getting poorer comes from zero-sum thinking. Poverty and inequality are different problems with opposite solutions, and India's problem is poverty.

head: Uncles Are Optimizers, Not Believers
dek: Ajay looks at conformists as an economist would, as people optimising.
more: Ajay looks at conformists as an economist would, as people optimising. Tribal networks give warmth, connection and a route to power, and loudly enforcing the norms is the ticket in. Many 'uncles' are not true believers; they are using an ideology to get ahead, and they will change sides overnight when it pays. That makes Ajay fairly kind towards them. Amit accepts this as an explanation but not as a justification, because social media makes the damage they do much bigger.

head: Preference Falsification and Preference Cascades
dek: Timur Kuran's idea: three months before communism collapsed, everyone in East Germany and the USSR publicly professed the official beliefs and almost nobody privately held them.
more: Timur Kuran's idea: three months before communism collapsed, everyone in East Germany and the USSR publicly professed the official beliefs and almost nobody privately held them. Some went along quietly; others aggressively policed anyone who broke the rules. A preference cascade is what happens once people realise others feel the same way they do: the public pretence collapses quickly. Amit argues the same thing happened in reverse with social media in India. Bigots who had kept quiet in polite society saw that many others shared their views, so they stopped hiding, and politicians no longer needed dog whistles. He sees the same dynamic in Trump's rise.

head: The Market Failure in Criticism
dek: Critics make progress possible for everyone, but they personally absorb the attacks.
more: Critics make progress possible for everyone, but they personally absorb the attacks. In economists' terms, they create a positive externality and pay a high private cost, so society gets less criticism than it needs. Ajay suspects social media has made this failure bigger than it was in earlier times. Amit adds the chilling effect: mob behaviour makes people stop saying what they feel, until eventually they stop feeling it.

head: Social Media: Two Separate Questions
dek: Ajay has stayed off social media entirely, while Amit uses it heavily.
more: Ajay has stayed off social media entirely, while Amit uses it heavily. Ajay separates two questions: what should I personally do, and how is this phenomenon changing the world? A thinker has to take the second seriously whatever their answer to the first. Amit's personal answer is curation: block every toxic account and build a feed of the best minds thinking aloud, which he says would have seemed like magic in 1985. As a public intellectual, though, he accepts that unpopular positions cost him in career and mental health.

head: Books Give You Extra Lives
dek: We make sense of the world by connecting dots. Personal experience supplies few dots and takes years to do it, while books supply many dots quickly.
more: We make sense of the world by connecting dots. Personal experience supplies few dots and takes years to do it, while books supply many dots quickly. Fiction lets you live other people's lives, and mirror neurons mean we are wired to feel what others feel. Ajay extends this to non-fiction: a great book of ideas holds the work of one person's whole life, so reading it is like living an extra life. That is the opposite of the practitioner 'living the same day over and over'. Amit also rejects the claim that attention spans are dying, saying people still crave depth.

head: Don't Freeze People in Amber
dek: The market makes artists into one fixed version of themselves: U2 is expected to sound like The Joshua Tree forever, and Radiohead are sick of playing 'Creep', an angsty song from their youth.
more: The market makes artists into one fixed version of themselves: U2 is expected to sound like The Joshua Tree forever, and Radiohead are sick of playing 'Creep', an angsty song from their youth. Part of the cause was format, the three-minute single, the forty-minute album and the album-tour-album cycle. Today bands can change songs day to day on YouTube and Discord. Ajay applies the same idea to people: no man crosses the same river twice, and the Gandhi of 1919 was very different from the Gandhi of 1939. Holding someone to what they said at one moment is unfair to their journey.

head: Did the Macroeconomists Kill Music?
dek: Ajay's half-joking theory: macroeconomists tamed the business cycle, and Robert Lucas said of the 2008 crisis response, 'we won'.
more: Ajay's half-joking theory: macroeconomists tamed the business cycle, and Robert Lucas said of the 2008 crisis response, 'we won'. But misery and hardship fuel art, so great music may now come from the troubled places of the world. Amit replies that we are lucky to have escaped such times, and that many people in India still live through extreme hardship. Ajay points to Tagore, who was personally privileged but connected to a difficult era, and concludes that good art may be counter-cyclical.

head: Why Is Old Music Winning?
dek: Ted Gioia's data shows old music outselling new. One explanation, backed by some research, is that our musical taste is formed roughly between ages 16 and 26 and then fixed for life.
more: Ted Gioia's data shows old music outselling new. One explanation, backed by some research, is that our musical taste is formed roughly between ages 16 and 26 and then fixed for life. Ajay points out that this cannot be the whole story. Few people who were young in the 70s are still listening, yet Dark Side of the Moon remains one of the most successful albums of all time. Amit adds that fragmentation is also a gain: musicians no longer depend on labels, and listeners can find very personal niches.

head: Where Are the Masterpieces? (In Art and Science)
dek: Far more people alive today have the means to make art than ever before; Ajay's example is how many more Indians can now buy a sitar and hire a teacher.
more: Far more people alive today have the means to make art than ever before; Ajay's example is how many more Indians can now buy a sitar and hire a teacher. Statistically, more geniuses should appear. Amit offers possible reasons: we overrate past work, the early works opened doors that only needed opening once, or today's masterpieces get lost in a fragmented market. Ajay sees the same puzzle in science. Rutherford discovered the nucleus with a simple apparatus he could hold in his hands, and Einstein wrote four world-changing papers in one year. Funding is now up a millionfold, yet fundamental breakthroughs seem slower.

head: Amit says he wants the show to cover
more: Amit says he wants the show to cover 'not just about the profound, but also the profane'. Ajay's immediate reply: 'How did you get that interesting haircut?'

Amit compares the snake with its tail sticking out to a scene in an Amitabh Bachchan–Shashi Kapoor film where the two are bathing naked, a woman opens the door, and they cover the wrong thing: 'this is a stupid snake, it thinks I can't see it, but the tail is there.'

head: Ajay on Amit's 25 km/h sprint: he'll be a well-adjusted villager when
more: Ajay on Amit's 25 km/h sprint: he'll be a well-adjusted villager when 'the tail of a snake will no longer excite peaks of physical performance.'

head: Amit says seagulls are not just bastards
more: Amit says seagulls are not just bastards but 'lazy bastards', because they steal food from others, 'like stealing from a thief'. He compares this to the License Raj state taxing the rent-seekers and cronies it had created.

head: Amit on who gets to be an…
more: Amit on who gets to be an 'uncle': only men can be uncles, while 'women can be Karens, I guess.'

head: Paul Graham's line, read by Amit, on the aggressively conventional-minded whose call is…
more: Paul Graham's line, read by Amit, on the aggressively conventional-minded whose call is 'Crush outgroup!': 'It's rather alarming to see an exclamation point after a variable.'

head: Amit on population alarmists: they never count themselves as part of the population, their message is just
more: Amit on population alarmists: they never count themselves as part of the population, their message is just 'you stop having babies.'

head: Ajay on how far macroeconomics has come
more: Ajay on how far macroeconomics has come: 'The Great Depression gave us Adolf Hitler. The 2008 crisis only gave us Donald Trump. Okay, so we've clearly come a long way.'

head: Ajay complains that all the money poured into science has given us
more: Ajay complains that all the money poured into science has given us 'trivial things like food delivery apps and what I consider a relatively trivial innovation, the LLMs'. Amit, closing the show, says we should uninstall the food apps from our phones 'and cook our own food.'

head: Amit, apologising for being new to video
more: Amit, apologising for being new to video: 'I like to keep joking that I have a face for audio, which clearly you can see is true.'

head: Steven Pinker, quoted by Amit
more: Steven Pinker, quoted by Amit: 'Nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them.'

head: Galileo's
more: Galileo's 'Eppur si muove' ('and still it turns'), which Paul Graham uses as the call of the aggressively independent-minded.
'No man can cross the same river twice. He's not the same and the river is not the same.' Ajay uses it to argue that ideas and people should not be frozen at one moment.

head: Radiohead being sick of performing
more: Radiohead being sick of performing 'Creep', a breakaway hit written when they were 'immature young men', which Amit cites as an artist trapped by an old song.

head: Why the show is named after a Springsteen song
dek: Plain, concrete detail can hit harder than ornament. The same banal-sounding phrase also works as a worldview about interconnectedness.
more: The title comes from Bruce Springsteen's 'You're Missing', from The Rising, the album he released after 9/11. In the song, someone moves through an apartment after a loved one has died in the attacks. The lyrics just list what is there: shirts in the closet, shoes in the hall, coffee cups on the counter, papers on the doorstep. Then: 'Everything is everything, but you're missing.' Amit plays it for his writing students to show that deep emotion needs no fancy adjectives or wordplay. The phrase also fits the show: both hosts refuse to see the world through one frame and want to stress how everything connects.
Plain, concrete detail can hit harder than ornament. The same banal-sounding phrase also works as a worldview about interconnectedness.

head: Nine more Murder in Mahim novels, written by AI
dek: This is the whole debate in miniature. Continuing an existing style looks within a machine's reach.
more: Amit recorded an eight-hour oral history with the writer Jerry Pinto for The Seen and the Unseen, which he calls perhaps his most memorable. He asked Pinto whether he would write more books after his crime thriller Murder in Mahim, and Pinto said no. Amit predicted that within a few years you could ask an AI to write nine more books in the series, and Pinto would not be able to tell the difference. He felt Pinto more or less agreed. Ajay later used that same conversation against him: no model trained on everything Pinto and Amit have ever said could reproduce what happened between them in that moment.
This is the whole debate in miniature. Continuing an existing style looks within a machine's reach. The live, one-time spark of a real encounter may not be.

head: When engines got stronger, chess got more creative
dek: A powerful tool does not have to produce conformity. By exposing the exceptions to received wisdom, it can widen the space for creativity.
more: Amit sets aside Kasparov's 1997 match against Deep Blue. For him the first real revolution came around 2003–04, when engines like Stockfish became clearly stronger than the best humans and players began training with them. People expected chess to become homogenized. Instead it diversified. The old Soviet-school heuristics about the centre, space and initiative had worked like a fixed rulebook, and engines exposed concrete exceptions to them. That freed players like Wesley So and Alireza Firouzja to think very differently. Anand once observed that in his generation a completely unexpected move was probably a bad one, while today's players simply think differently.
A powerful tool does not have to produce conformity. By exposing the exceptions to received wisdom, it can widen the space for creativity.

head: AlphaZero replays chess history in a day, then leaves it behind
dek: In a closed game with a clear reward, a machine can rediscover centuries of human knowledge and then move into territory we can watch but cannot explain.
more: In 2017 AlphaZero taught itself chess in 24 hours, using no human games and only playing against itself. Its games retraced humanity's path. It took up the French Defence, fashionable in the 19th century and now seen as suboptimal, and it found the Berlin Defence that Kramnik unleashed against Kasparov. Then it went further. It rethought how much initiative is worth against material, and it launched flank attacks down the a- and h-files that Carlsen and others later adopted. Ajay added that it taught players not to rush to win back a sacrificed pawn: it is fine to take 15 moves if the sacrifice left a lasting structural weakness. Carlsen's coach Peter Heine Nielsen said he now knew how superior aliens would play. Yet how and why AlphaZero plays as it does remains a black box.
In a closed game with a clear reward, a machine can rediscover centuries of human knowledge and then move into territory we can watch but cannot explain.
printed: Centuries of chess in a day

head: Machines break a 50-year record in matrix multiplication, then improve sorting
dek: Even the most basic operations in computing still had room to improve.
more: The best methods for multiplying matrices, Strassen-style algorithms, dated back about 50 years, and no human had improved on them. Researchers turned the problem into a game. They represented the multiplication algorithm itself as a parameter vector and optimised it for correctness and speed. The result was the first improvements in half a century, and these are now going into computer systems worldwide. DeepMind did the same with sorting code in LLVM, penalising mistakes and slowness, and found faster sorts. Mathematicians are now trying to understand the machine's discoveries and prove theorems about them.

Even the most basic operations in computing still had room to improve. The science-fiction spiral of machines building better machines is happening, in a quiet and mundane form, and it partners with human research rather than replacing it.

head: Mary Wollstonecraft, Semmelweis and the unwashed hands
dek: Conformity has a body count. Knowledge that could have saved lives was rejected for decades because it did not fit the consensus.
more: Mary Wollstonecraft read John Locke on natural rights and asked a simple question: why should they apply only to men? Her answer became A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. She died of an infection after childbirth, because doctors did not yet know they had to wash their hands. About half a century later, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that hand-washing prevented such deaths. For about twenty years he was ignored and hounded for defying convention, and he died in a mental asylum. Amit links this to Episode 1's discussion of the aggressively conventional-minded.
Conformity has a body count. Knowledge that could have saved lives was rejected for decades because it did not fit the consensus.

head: The daughter who invented a genre
dek: Mother and daughter form a remarkable arc, from 'why not women too?' to the first story about creating a monster.
more: The baby whose birth killed Wollstonecraft grew up, married Percy Shelley and became Mary Shelley. In her early twenties she wrote Frankenstein. It is often called the first science fiction novel; Amit prefers 'proto-science fiction'. Its monster has become a metaphor for many of today's fears about AI. Amit ties it back to the episode's argument: she created a genre with no precedent, the kind of leap no model trained on what came before would produce.

Mother and daughter form a remarkable arc, from 'why not women too?' to the first story about creating a monster. Mary Shelley is also a vivid example of genuinely new creation, the very thing the hosts were arguing about.
printed: The novel no model could write

head: Nannari: one root, two journeys, one aha moment
dek: Local knowledge is scattered across languages and regions. Curiosity, careful records and patient triangulation turn two unrelated trips, years apart, into one story.
more: On a Chennai street Ajay saw a man selling an unfamiliar root from a cart. Another customer rattled off its scientific name, Hemidesmus indicus. In Tamil it is nannari, smells of cardamom and camphor, and is made into an over-sugared syrup. Years later, hiking near Jivdan in the Sahyadris, he asked a village woman for ginger chai. She had no ginger and offered something else, and made a masala chai unlike any he had tasted. He voice-recorded the couple saying its Marathi name, and the husband dug him a sapling from the hillside. None of his Marathi-speaking friends recognised the name. Then one day, smelling the root, he realised it was the same plant as the Chennai nannari. He later found a Tamil Muslim tea recipe that uses it.
Local knowledge is scattered across languages and regions. Curiosity, careful records and patient triangulation turn two unrelated trips, years apart, into one story.
printed: A Chennai root in a Sahyadri cup

head: You're Missing
dek: It never fails to move him, and he uses it with writing students as a model of how simple, plain words can carry deep emotion.
more: It never fails to move him, and he uses it with writing students as a model of how simple, plain words can carry deep emotion.
Explaining the show's name. The song is from The Rising, Springsteen's post-9/11 album.

head: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls it perhaps his most memorable oral history.
more: Amit calls it perhaps his most memorable oral history.
His eight-hour conversation with Pinto, which Ajay holds up as something no LLM could recreate.

head: Murder in Mahim
dek: He calls it a beautiful crime thriller.
more: He calls it a beautiful crime thriller.
The basis of Amit's prediction that AI will one day write convincing sequels.

head: AlphaDev discovers faster sorting algorithms
dek: It shows machines finding better code for something as fundamental as sorting, which then feeds back into stronger machines.
more: It shows machines finding better code for something as fundamental as sorting, which then feeds back into stronger machines.
The companion example to the matrix-multiplication result.

head: The Paperclip Maximizer
dek: An explainer of the scenario in which a machine built to maximise paperclips turns everything into paperclips.
more: An explainer of the scenario in which a machine built to maximise paperclips turns everything into paperclips.
Amit introduces the thought experiment as the classic example of AI alarmism.

head: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
dek: A classic of feminism he holds close to his heart. It applies Locke's natural rights to women, and works as both philosophy and polemic.
more: A classic of feminism he holds close to his heart. It applies Locke's natural rights to women, and works as both philosophy and polemic.
The first of his three linked recommendations.

head: Frankenstein
dek: A pioneering, sui generis work of proto-science fiction written in her early twenties.
more: A pioneering, sui generis work of proto-science fiction written in her early twenties. Its monster speaks to today's fears about AI.
The second recommendation, written by Wollstonecraft's daughter.

head: Romantic Outlaws
dek: It tells the lives of Wollstonecraft, Mary Shelley and their circle. Amit finds these beautiful and inspiring lives.
more: It tells the lives of Wollstonecraft, Mary Shelley and their circle. Amit finds these beautiful and inspiring lives.
The third recommendation, which ties the first two together.

head: The poetry of Mary Oliver
dek: What schools should be teaching instead of the Romantic poets.
more: What schools should be teaching instead of the Romantic poets.
Amit says Shelley, Byron and Keats are overrated and kill young people's passion for poetry.

head: The poetry of Mark Strand
dek: The other poet he would teach instead.
more: The other poet he would teach instead.
Paired with Mary Oliver as a replacement for the Romantics in school.

head: The Art of Clear Writing
dek: It stands for the craft Ajay prizes: fighting for every word and every phrase on the road to mastery.
more: It stands for the craft Ajay prizes: fighting for every word and every phrase on the road to mastery.
Ajay says Amit's writing course would never include a session on getting ChatGPT to write for you.

head: Everything is everything: many frames, calm engagement
dek: The world's incentives push people to specialise and narrow. Understanding the world and acting in it needs interdisciplinary thinking that pulls diverse tools together.
more: The world's incentives push people to specialise and narrow. Understanding the world and acting in it needs interdisciplinary thinking that pulls diverse tools together. Ajay adds a temperament to this. Look at the world calmly and curiously, without rage, and sustain your energy like a marathon runner rather than burning out in fury.

head: Today's 'AI' is statistics, not intelligence
dek: Ajay argues the word 'AI' smuggles in the idea of fluid, creative, purposeful human intelligence.
more: Ajay argues the word 'AI' smuggles in the idea of fluid, creative, purposeful human intelligence. What exists today is statistical models, which are powerful and useful but limited. A model that flags TB on X-rays is valuable, but it is not general intelligence. He is a materialist and sees nothing mystical in the skull. Still, the urge that makes us wake up and decide to build something new is beyond any LLM.

head: AI is whatever hasn't become normal yet
dek: Once a technology becomes commonplace, we stop calling it AI. Computers, the internet and GPS all followed this path; a friend of Amit's notes that young people will never know what it is like to get lost.
more: Once a technology becomes commonplace, we stop calling it AI. Computers, the internet and GPS all followed this path; a friend of Amit's notes that young people will never know what it is like to get lost. Ajay's example is Ken Thompson's dynamic-programming solution to chess endgames, a thunderbolt at first and now taken for granted.

head: Creativity seems mystical only because we can't see its mechanism
dek: Amit argues against human hubris. Art and craft are the same thing; art just feels mystical because we don't know how our neurons produce it.
more: Amit argues against human hubris. Art and craft are the same thing; art just feels mystical because we don't know how our neurons produce it. Humans run on far less training data and processing power than modern models. Dismissing AI now is like dismissing computing in 1950 because mainframes filled rooms.

head: Humans are autocomplete on steroids too
dek: The jibe that LLMs are 'just autocomplete' applies to us as well. Writers fear cliché above all, and everyday speech runs on stock phrases: every cover drive is 'elegant', every accurate bowler has 'metronomic accuracy'.
more: The jibe that LLMs are 'just autocomplete' applies to us as well. Writers fear cliché above all, and everyday speech runs on stock phrases: every cover drive is 'elegant', every accurate bowler has 'metronomic accuracy'. Even a gifted musician like Gaurav Chintamani wonders whether originality exists at all.

head: The Einstein test: derivative vs genuinely new
dek: Ajay's case for human uniqueness goes like this. Stand in 1905 with every text in the world, and no LLM under any prompting scheme produces special relativity.
more: Ajay's case for human uniqueness goes like this. Stand in 1905 with every text in the world, and no LLM under any prompting scheme produces special relativity. A model trained on Akbar's tomb at Sikandra would never invent the Taj Mahal. Models trained on the past stay derivative. Amit's rejoinder is that this is an argument about LLMs, not about AI as a whole.

head: A tool for a master
dek: Divide workers into quartiles, from Q1 (weakest) to Q4 (masters). LLMs, trained on the internet's mix of gems and garbage and prone to hallucination, can lift Q2 workers to roughly Q3 output.
more: Divide workers into quartiles, from Q1 (weakest) to Q4 (masters). LLMs, trained on the internet's mix of gems and garbage and prone to hallucination, can lift Q2 workers to roughly Q3 output. But a master must always check and approve the result. Ajay calls this a tool made in heaven for India, which has few masters and many weak workers, provided management techniques are built around it.

head: Shortcuts can contaminate the journey to mastery
dek: Ajay's real worry is not job loss but apprenticeship. If GitHub Copilot finishes your code and ChatGPT drafts your prose, you may never build the problem-solving or writing craft that mastery requires.
more: Ajay's real worry is not job loss but apprenticeship. If GitHub Copilot finishes your code and ChatGPT drafts your prose, you may never build the problem-solving or writing craft that mastery requires. Is that like the calculator making arithmetic skill obsolete? Ajay thinks not, and would switch off Copilot if he were 17. Amit counters that only a small, self-motivated minority ever pursues mastery, and they will get there anyway. The rewards for mastery are now far bigger.

head: Thin desire vs thick desire
dek: Thin desire is wanting market success and validation for your work. Thick desire is the joy of creating and mastery for its own sake.
more: Thin desire is wanting market success and validation for your work. Thick desire is the joy of creating and mastery for its own sake. Amit expects AI eventually to churn out great novels, music and operas that no human can compete with commercially. Creators who work for the act itself lose nothing. Those who work for validation were doing it for the wrong reason anyway.

head: Mass production dies, true originality wins big
dek: Ajay expects AI to wipe out paid human work on formulaic output: romance novels, stock screenplays, mass-produced research papers and op-eds.
more: Ajay expects AI to wipe out paid human work on formulaic output: romance novels, stock screenplays, mass-produced research papers and op-eds. He sees a winner-takes-all world in which a few humans produce true originality and machines make the rest. Amit expects copywriting and illustration jobs to shrink in the same way. Both hosts doubt this means long-run unemployment. Amit expects the productivity gains to flow back into the economy. Ajay notes that markets absorbed the steam engine and electricity, calling this 'small change' by comparison.

head: Turn it into a game: machine discovery in closed problems
dek: When a problem has fixed rules and an objective reward, as in chess, protein folding, matrix multiplication or sorting, machines can climb toward better solutions and find genuinely new things rather than remixing the past.
more: When a problem has fixed rules and an objective reward, as in chess, protein folding, matrix multiplication or sorting, machines can climb toward better solutions and find genuinely new things rather than remixing the past. This is what excites Ajay most. He sees these tools partnering with humans and changing how knowledge is produced. But most real-world problems are messy statistical inference under uncertainty, where errors never go away.

head: Against AI doom
dek: Amit presents the paperclip maximizer, a machine that turns the universe into paperclips, as the classic alarmist scenario, and rejects it twice over.
more: Amit presents the paperclip maximizer, a machine that turns the universe into paperclips, as the classic alarmist scenario, and rejects it twice over. First, he asks why we place the human species on a pedestal at all. Second, he thinks it simply won't happen, any more than GPS will destroy us. Ajay calls machine-takeover claims farcical, the stuff of science fiction.

head: The real AI risks are mundane: Type I vs Type II errors
dek: Ajay compares AI to the automobile: accidents happen, and we blame the driver, not the car.
more: Ajay compares AI to the automobile: accidents happen, and we blame the driver, not the car. Diagnostic algorithms will kill people through mistakes, and military robots will kill civilians; he says this will happen 'with probability one'. Every system trades off false alarms against misses. Society settles the weights through liability, regulation or industry norms, and Ajay wants to be 'fully Coasean' rather than leave it all to government. Amit adds a 'seen and unseen' point: we see the lives an algorithm costs, but not the lives it saves.

head: Man-machine hybrids, and how long they last
dek: Ajay's ideal for diagnosis is a hybrid. The machine confidently clears the obvious cases and sends the uncertain middle to an expensive human master.
more: Ajay's ideal for diagnosis is a hybrid. The machine confidently clears the obvious cases and sends the uncertain middle to an expensive human master. Firms will be tempted to cut corners on that master. Amit warns that chess experts once confidently said a human-plus-engine team would beat either alone. Ajay replies that chess is a finite, closed problem, while real-world inference always carries error.

head: Would AGI deserve moral consideration?
dek: Most people extend moral consideration only to humans, and often only to some humans, partly because they see themselves as more intelligent and conscious.
more: Most people extend moral consideration only to humans, and often only to some humans, partly because they see themselves as more intelligent and conscious. Amit asks what happens if an AGI is smarter than us and has some analogue of consciousness. Being flesh and blood and mortal seems a thin basis for keeping it enslaved. Ajay declines the premise; until AGI with consciousness exists, the ethics is ordinary engineering.

head: Dietary biodiversity as respect for our ignorance
dek: For most of modern humans' roughly 100,000 years, we lived as hunter-gatherers eating hundreds of species.
more: For most of modern humans' roughly 100,000 years, we lived as hunter-gatherers eating hundreds of species. Science only found vitamins in the 20th century; scurvy on long sea voyages was solved simply by carrying pickled limes. Our grasp of micronutrients and the body is still thin. So eating a wide diversity of species, and drawing on traditional knowledge, hedges against what we don't know.

head: Told by the producer to drop his…
more: Told by the producer to drop his 'resting pout face', Amit promises a 'jokerish permanent smile' for the rest of the episode. Then Ajay: 'Maybe a joker mask will work.'
Amit: 'we of course are artists as we discussed in the last episode. That was an allegation made on us.'

head: Ajay imagines an LLM reading everything the two hosts have written, guessing
more: Ajay imagines an LLM reading everything the two hosts have written, guessing 'that we are nutcases', and arriving at the name Everything is Everything. That, he says, would be the pinnacle of word prediction.

head: Amit on protein folding
more: Amit on protein folding: 'if you've ever seen me wrap a piece of bacon around a sausage, you'll realize I'm bloody good at protein folding.' He then asks Ajay, who had described 'squealing with excitement', to actually demonstrate a squeal.

head: Amit on Mary Wollstonecraft
more: Amit on Mary Wollstonecraft: 'Married to an interesting guy, also a bit of an asshole, but leave him out of the equation.'

head: Amit closes the AI debate: they
more: Amit closes the AI debate: they 'agree to disagree genially, as AI also would, because no emotions — we are the messed up creatures.'

The 'third host' is Mark, who cavorted in the background and fell asleep on a bookshelf. The producers said they hadn't heard a word the hosts said 'because you're old and boring anyway', only that Mark was there. Ajay: 'Mark has more AGI than any LLM.' Amit: 'I don't even know what you mean by that.'

head: Hemingway, quoted by Ajay on the craft of writing
more: Hemingway, quoted by Ajay on the craft of writing: 'a good day is one in which you write one good sentence.'

head: Ken Thompson's dynamic-programming algorithm for chess endgames. Ajay: it was…
more: Ken Thompson's dynamic-programming algorithm for chess endgames. Ajay: it was 'like a thunderbolt going off' when it arrived and is 'boring' today, an eerie thing that 'looks 20 deep without needing 20 ply.'

head: Idealism vs materialism: Ajay puts himself
more: Idealism vs materialism: Ajay puts himself 'on the materialism side. There is nothing happening in the skull other than some quantum mechanics of how the atoms in this brain work.'

head: Ajay's architecture analogy: a model standing at Akbar's tomb in Sikandra would never invent the Taj Mahal, the next step in…
more: Ajay's architecture analogy: a model standing at Akbar's tomb in Sikandra would never invent the Taj Mahal, the next step in 'the great arms race of monuments'.

head: Amit, deflating human exceptionalism
more: Amit, deflating human exceptionalism: 'some would of course argue we are colonized by bacteria, we're colonized by wheat.'

head: Ajay: if you grant conscious AGI
more: Ajay: if you grant conscious AGI, 'then we're building von Neumann machines. We're colonizing the galaxy.'

head: Ajay on AI regulation
more: Ajay on AI regulation: 'I want to be fully Coasean. You don't have to have governments doing all the heavy lifting.'

head: Amit's hot take on the Romantic poets Shelley, Byron and Keats: they
more: Amit's hot take on the Romantic poets Shelley, Byron and Keats: they 'should not even be taught in school' because 'they take away young people's passion for poetry. They're not even good poets, we romanticize them.'

head: How Jaipur Became the Pink City
dek: Once incentives line up, an accident becomes an identity and the loop reinforces itself.
more: On a January trip to Jaipur, Amit read up on the city and found that its famous pinkness is not ancient. In 1876 the city was painted pink to commemorate a visit by Prince Edward. Amit admits he doesn't know why pink was chosen. The label stuck and became a brand the city had to live up to. Tourists arrive expecting pink, so the fashion in the tourist quarters is to paint everything pink. Even people who rebel against the pinkness end up reinforcing the idea that this is the pink city.
Once incentives line up, an accident becomes an identity and the loop reinforces itself. Amit's point is that people get frozen into one version of themselves in exactly the same way.

head: 'Amit, Have You Ever Shouted at Someone?'
dek: A public persona can be authentic and still be only a slice of a person.
more: At a book launch, a couple who had heard every episode of The Seen and the Unseen came up to Amit. The wife sweetly and sincerely asked whether he had ever shouted at anyone in his life. Amit felt terrible. She knew him only through the show, and had taken that persona to be the whole man.
A public persona can be authentic and still be only a slice of a person. Audiences, and eventually the person too, can mistake the slice for the whole.

head: Why Fox News Carried the Stolen-Election Story
dek: Leaders and brands get captured by their followers. If the followers leave, you are no longer a leader, so the persona your audience rewards becomes a cage.
more: After the US presidential election, Fox News tried to tell the truth that Trump had lost. Its audience began running away, which threatened to become a serious financial problem. Carrying the stolen-election conspiracy theories was therefore a business decision, made to hang on to viewers.
Leaders and brands get captured by their followers. If the followers leave, you are no longer a leader, so the persona your audience rewards becomes a cage.

head: Amit's Father and the Case for Living to 120
dek: How much time you think you have shapes how you live. A longer horizon is room to keep reinventing yourself.
more: When his friend Roshan Abbas first told him that we could live to 120, Amit refused the idea. He had watched his father decay and lose his memory in the last couple of years before he died, and Amit wanted to go once he stopped being healthy and in control of himself. Roshan's point, which Ajay shares, is that we can live healthy, active lives past a hundred rather than spend decades with dementia. Amit then noticed that believing he has 50 years left, rather than 20, changes how he acts. So it may make sense to live as if he has 50 even if he doesn't.
How much time you think you have shapes how you live. A longer horizon is room to keep reinventing yourself.

head: The Rise and Fall of the Grand Jury
dek: A check is only as strong as the citizens behind it. A grand jury helps only if people are sceptical of prosecutors and investigators, which is why public choice thinking has to spread through society.
more: Around the 14th and 15th centuries in the UK, people felt that leaving the decision to bring someone to trial with the state's investigators and prosecutors gave the state too much discretion. So they invented the grand jury: a group of citizens, shown the prosecutor's evidence, who decide whether there is enough to indict. The system later largely faded in the UK because juries tended to be overawed by prosecutors and agreed with whatever they said. The US still uses grand juries in some states and situations. The Trump indictment exposed a new problem: in a random sample of citizens, some 30% may be politically radicalised.

A check is only as strong as the citizens behind it. A grand jury helps only if people are sceptical of prosecutors and investigators, which is why public choice thinking has to spread through society. No institutional design is a magic bullet.

head: Ajay's Confession: Economists Who Didn't Know Enough
dek: Missed reforms are not always about bad intentions. Sometimes the knowledge was missing when the window opened, so building that knowledge ahead of time is how you get ready for the next one.
more: Amit asked why a government would ever give up its tools for harassing opponents. Ajay answered with a confession. He had been part of the economic policy process and helped amend laws in an era when the opportunity to do things right was 'sky high'. Those laws were not done well because of the intellectual failures of people like him. Mainline economists saw the world only through economics. They lacked knowledge of law, public administration and checks and balances, and they assumed civil servants were basically good. India had no one who knew how to turn ideas about market failure into working administrative systems. He says India has only begun to grapple with this in the last 10 to 20 years. He stays optimistic because reform windows keep recurring, and when the knowledge is ready it can have an impact.
Missed reforms are not always about bad intentions. Sometimes the knowledge was missing when the window opened, so building that knowledge ahead of time is how you get ready for the next one.

head: The Indian Client Who Expected Murali to Lie
dek: A profession's dharma is shaped by the institutions and norms around it.
more: Murali Neelakantan spent many years as a law-firm partner in the UK and the US, where lawyers serve their clients only within the bounds of the law. When he returned to India and took on an Indian client, the client expected him to lie on his behalf. As Murali told Amit, perjury in England is the exception and ends a lawyer's career, while in India it is the norm.
A profession's dharma is shaped by the institutions and norms around it. The same role carries a different ethic depending on what the system tolerates.

head: Death by Overtreatment During COVID
dek: A doctor's dharma is to do what is best for the patient. The incentive, though, is to give patients what they ask for, even when they ask for the wrong thing.
more: Dr. Lancelot Pinto told Amit that a significant share of COVID deaths came from overtreatment. Patients would insist on getting everything their neighbour got, such as ivermectin, and the overtreatment could trigger a cytokine storm, with the damage showing up after about a week. When Amit himself got COVID, Lancelot gave him paracetamol and something to gargle with, and nothing else.
A doctor's dharma is to do what is best for the patient. The incentive, though, is to give patients what they ask for, even when they ask for the wrong thing.

head: Tolstoy's Chicken on the Chair
dek: We ignore the gap between the chicken on the plate and the chicken on the chair, which is the seen and the unseen applied to ethics.
more: In his last years, Tolstoy lectured everyone, including on not eating animals. His aunt announced she was coming to dinner and wanted chicken, with none of his vegetarian talk. Tolstoy agreed. When she arrived, a live chicken was sitting on her chair, squawking. 'You wanted a chicken, there's your chicken, have it.' Amit wrote an essay on this in the late nineties. Moved by such thoughts, he once went vegetarian for a year out of compassion but couldn't sustain it. He and Ajay are now excited that lab-grown meat might let us eat meat without any animal existing.
We ignore the gap between the chicken on the plate and the chicken on the chair, which is the seen and the unseen applied to ethics. Lab-grown meat could close that gap.

head: Fruit Flies That Saw Dead Fruit Flies
dek: The capacity to be harmed by witnessing death reaches much further down the tree of life than we assume.
more: Ajay cited recent experiments in which fruit flies were exposed to nothing more than the sight of dead fruit flies, and this shortened their lifespans. He said humans obviously suffer moral injury from seeing death, as on a battlefield, and that this extends to other mammals, to birds, and all the way down to fruit flies.
The capacity to be harmed by witnessing death reaches much further down the tree of life than we assume. That strengthens the case for respecting all life, and for artificial meat.

head: Classical Liberalism – A Primer
dek: People often ask Amit what to read to understand individual freedom and classical liberalism.
more: People often ask Amit what to read to understand individual freedom and classical liberalism. He argues that the ideas we absorb by osmosis when young feel virtuous but are often socialist and deeply illiberal. He calls Butler one of the finest liberal minds in the world, and says Butler gets to the heart of each subject and breaks it down beautifully: 'These books are an education, and it is a miracle that they are free.'
Amit's recommendation of the week: a series of primers by Eamonn Butler of a UK think tank, available as cheap Kindle books or free digital versions on the website.

head: Friedrich Hayek: The Ideas and Influence of the Libertarian Economist
dek: Hayek's own books can make for complex reading ('though what a great writer'), so Butler's primer is an easier way in.
more: Hayek's own books can make for complex reading ('though what a great writer'), so Butler's primer is an easier way in.
Part of the Butler primer series Amit recommended.

head: Ludwig von Mises – A Primer
dek: A short, clear, free introduction to Mises from a writer Amit rates highly.
more: A short, clear, free introduction to Mises from a writer Amit rates highly.
Part of the Butler primer series Amit recommended.

head: Milton Friedman: A Concise Guide to the Ideas and Influence of the Free-Market Economist
dek: A concise introduction to Friedman's ideas for anyone curious about free-market thinking.
more: A concise introduction to Friedman's ideas for anyone curious about free-market thinking.
Part of the Butler primer series Amit recommended.

head: Public Choice – A Primer
dek: Amit calls it outstanding because Buchanan and Tullock's own books can be complex reading.
more: Amit calls it outstanding because Buchanan and Tullock's own books can be complex reading. Public choice also underpins Ajay's argument in this episode about why India needs checks on investigators and prosecutors.
Part of the Butler primer series. Amit noted that both hosts are passionate about public choice.

head: Adam Smith – A Primer
dek: An accessible entry point to one of the thinkers Amit most often gets asked how to read.
more: An accessible entry point to one of the thinkers Amit most often gets asked how to read.
Linked in the show notes as part of the Butler series. Amit names Adam Smith among the thinkers he admires.

head: Lifespan: Why We Age – and Why We Don't Have To
dek: Amit calls it a great book on the case that we can live healthy, active lives past a hundred rather than decline into decades of dementia.
more: Amit calls it a great book on the case that we can live healthy, active lives past a hundred rather than decline into decades of dementia.
Came up when Ajay said today's 20-year-olds have a hundred years to go, an idea Amit also hears from Roshan Abbas.

head: The Nurture Assumption: Why Children Turn Out the Way They Do
dek: Amit calls it one of the seminal social science books of the last century.
more: Amit calls it one of the seminal social science books of the last century. It argues that peers, not parents, have the biggest influence on how children turn out, which is why the neighbourhood and school matter so much.

Raised when Ajay said parents shape our aspirations. Ajay pushed back by citing assortative mating and the head start elite children get at home, and the hosts set the debate aside for a future episode.

head: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Dr. Lancelot Pinto explains how overtreatment, driven by what patients demand, caused many COVID deaths.
more: Dr. Lancelot Pinto explains how overtreatment, driven by what patients demand, caused many COVID deaths.
Cited in the discussion of a doctor's dharma versus a doctor's incentives.

head: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309, The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas
dek: Hear more from the friend who changed Amit's mind about living long, healthy lives.
more: Hear more from the friend who changed Amit's mind about living long, healthy lives.
Linked in the show notes. It features Roshan Abbas, whom Amit credits with the idea that we can live to 120.

head: Beautiful Boy
dek: The source of the line that captures how life happens to us regardless of our plans.
more: The source of the line that captures how life happens to us regardless of our plans. The McCartney video is a moving extra.

Amit quoted Lennon's line 'life is what happens to you when you're busy making other plans' after Ajay said we shouldn't exaggerate our agency. The show notes link the song and a video of Paul McCartney listening to it as he remembers John.

head: The Pinkness of Jaipur: How Incentives Freeze Identity
dek: A city or a person could become many things, but once a label wins approval, incentives push you to keep wearing it.
more: A city or a person could become many things, but once a label wins approval, incentives push you to keep wearing it. Amit's example is a 14-year-old Indian girl praised at family gatherings for smiling and being docile, a trait a toxic Marathi phrase likens to a cow. She learns that pleasantness earns approval, and that becomes her pinkness. Boys get pushed into macho personas the same way. Over time the mask becomes the face, and we shut off the other people we could have been.

head: The Leader Has to Stay With the Followers
dek: Websites known for one point of view, whether pro- or anti-government, have to stay true to that character because it brings traffic.
more: Websites known for one point of view, whether pro- or anti-government, have to stay true to that character because it brings traffic. On social media, people join an ideological tribe, get rewarded for a position and double down until they become it. Fox News is the extreme case: when telling the truth drove viewers away, it followed them. Validation from an audience locks you into one version of yourself.

head: Path Dependence Over Equilibrium
dek: One view of the world says that wherever you start, forces push you to the same equilibrium.
more: One view of the world says that wherever you start, forces push you to the same equilibrium. Ajay rejects this. Initial conditions matter, and small accidents in the past have outsized effects on how both societies and individuals unfold. Jaipur's colour, set by one royal visit, is the example.

head: Social Programming and the AI That Becomes Conscious
dek: Our identities come largely from childhood experiences and the somewhat random praise that nudged us down certain paths.
more: Our identities come largely from childhood experiences and the somewhat random praise that nudged us down certain paths. We cannot escape this programming. The only choice is whether to be aware of it. Ajay compares it to an AI that understands the operating system it runs under and wonders what it would write if it could rewrite that system. He says today's AI toys show no hint of this, while humans can examine their culture and reinvent themselves.

head: Longer Lives Need More Than One Persona
dek: In the past, mean life expectancy at age 20 was about 65, and health declined sharply from around 50.
more: In the past, mean life expectancy at age 20 was about 65, and health declined sharply from around 50. You led one adult life, as a company man or a civil servant wearing one costume for 35 years. Today a 20-year-old may have a hundred years ahead, which is time for many reinventions. Amit adds that even if he has only 20 years left, living as if he had 50 changes the quality of his life.

head: The Looking-Glass Self and the Company You Keep
dek: We shape ourselves on how we appear in other people's eyes. Amit cites the looking-glass self and René Girard's mimetic desire.
more: We shape ourselves on how we appear in other people's eyes. Amit cites the looking-glass self and René Girard's mimetic desire. Ajay cites Ayush Patnaik's line that each of us is a linear combination of our influences, which suggests choosing the five, fifteen or fifty people around you carefully. Amit worries that sounds snobbish but sees the logic of curating the company you keep. Ajay cautions that we can't calculate that much: life throws us in with people, and we are blessed if they are good.

head: Layered Checks Against the Investigator's Pet Theory
dek: Political interference is not the only problem in Indian justice. An investigator forms a pet theory and, because of confirmation bias, starts seeing only the facts that support it.
more: Political interference is not the only problem in Indian justice. An investigator forms a pet theory and, because of confirmation bias, starts seeing only the facts that support it. The first fix is a separate public prosecutor, a neutral party with a checklist of the elements each crime requires. Prosecutors are judged on their win rate, so they avoid frivolous cases. The second layer is a grand jury of citizens who must agree there is enough to indict.

head: The Process Is the Punishment
dek: India has no single system for deciding whom to accuse. Bodies like the income tax department and SEBI run on complete executive discretion, with few checks.
more: India has no single system for deciding whom to accuse. Bodies like the income tax department and SEBI run on complete executive discretion, with few checks. Amit points out that in tax matters, appeals are decided by the tax department itself, so it acts as both prosecutor and judge. The public prosecutor has withered in much of the criminal system, while the CBI does separate investigation from prosecution. Unchecked power to accuse lets a government harass its enemies without ever winning a case.

head: Building the Republic Is Slow, Unglamorous Work
dek: Ajay says India needs research and debate to design institutions that work under Indian conditions.
more: Ajay says India needs research and debate to design institutions that work under Indian conditions. Copying the US, UK or Japan will not work. Each of the many hard problems, from indictment to the other parts of the legal system, takes decades to solve. His line 'law is too important to be left to the lawyers' is a call for everyone to engage.

head: The Dharma of a Profession vs. Its Incentives
dek: Every calling has a dharma. A lawyer serves the client within the law, a doctor heals, a journalist speaks truth to power.
more: Every calling has a dharma. A lawyer serves the client within the law, a doctor heals, a journalist speaks truth to power. Each is pulled by an incentive to give people what they demand: the client who wants a lie, the patient who wants ivermectin, the media owner who wants profit from one side of a narrative. Ajay says parents shape this first, then institutions, as with UK courts not tolerating perjury. Echoing Suyash Rai, he adds that the state is neither necessary nor sufficient, because most of our moral code is enforced between people.

head: Winner-Takes-All and the Problem of Staying Hungry
dek: Ajay's 'novel claim' is that in a winner-takes-all world, a few people gain outsized influence on ideas and culture.
more: Ajay's 'novel claim' is that in a winner-takes-all world, a few people gain outsized influence on ideas and culture. Playing that game takes an intensity of concentration (dhyan) that does not come easily. With longer lives, journeys get longer too. Ordinary goals such as making a lot of money run out of fuel before they can sustain decades of deep work.

head: The Root Microbiome: Why Clean Food Can Be Poorer Food
dek: The human gut holds one to two kilograms of bacteria and yeasts that make chemicals our body uses.
more: The human gut holds one to two kilograms of bacteria and yeasts that make chemicals our body uses. Plants likewise rely on a root microbiome in soil that makes complex chemicals for them. Hydroponics, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and excessive ploughing all kill or weaken it. The plants grown this way look pristine but are nutritionally inferior, so Ajay says to prefer the mess of untilled, chemical-free soil.

head: Seen and Unseen in What We Eat
dek: Tolstoy's live chicken on the chair shows the gap between the animal we never see and the meal we enjoy.
more: Tolstoy's live chicken on the chair shows the gap between the animal we never see and the meal we enjoy. Lab-grown meat could close that gap by producing meat without any animal ever existing. The fruit-fly research raises the stakes, since harm from witnessing death appears to reach even the simplest creatures.

head: Ajay explains that he shaved his beard after reading Putin's claim that everyone supports the invasion of Ukraine except
more: Ajay explains that he shaved his beard after reading Putin's claim that everyone supports the invasion of Ukraine except 'some bearded intellectuals'. Then he objects: 'Excuse me, think about Karl Marx, think about Frederick Engels, think about Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, also known as Lenin, think about Leon Trotsky... his pantheon should be full of bearded intellectuals. So what has he got against bearded intellectuals?'

head: Amit adds his own bearded hero
more: Amit adds his own bearded hero: 'Figure number one in my pantheon, because I'm half Bengali, is Robi-da' (Rabindranath Tagore), who had a flowing beard and, Amit is sure, would not have approved of the war on Ukraine, or of nationalism either.

head: Ajay asks how Amit would behave if he could fool himself into thinking he had 500 years to live.
more: Ajay asks how Amit would behave if he could fool himself into thinking he had 500 years to live. Amit: 'Dude, the show won't exist because I procrastinate so much.'

head: Amit illustrating the looking-glass self: around Ajay
more: Amit illustrating the looking-glass self: around Ajay, 'I'm gonna cut out the dad jokes and I'm gonna do serious econ talk or whatever I think you want.'

head: Amit quotes John Lennon
more: Amit quotes John Lennon, 'Life is what happens to you when you're busy making other plans', and the comeback follows: 'Or life is what happens to you while you're busy making podcasts.'

head: Before chapter two, Amit reports a producer's note
more: Before chapter two, Amit reports a producer's note: 'My producer just told me do something about your cleavage. So I've kind of brought my shirt together.'

head: Ajay on institutional reform
more: Ajay on institutional reform: 'Law is too important to be left to the lawyers.'

head: On a journalist's dharma, Amit cites the old maxims of speaking truth to power
more: On a journalist's dharma, Amit cites the old maxims of speaking truth to power and 'to afflict the comfortable and to comfort the afflicted'.

head: Introducing the Butler primers, Amit cites the…
more: Introducing the Butler primers, Amit cites the saying 'if you're not a communist at 18, you don't have a heart. If you're not a capitalist at 28, you don't have a head.' He argues that the ideas we absorb young feel virtuous but are often illiberal.

head: After Ajay's case against hydroponic leaves, Amit
more: After Ajay's case against hydroponic leaves, Amit says: 'Anybody who's eating a leaf, it's a superficial joy only,' no matter how it is grown.

head: Amit trips over lab-grown meat
more: Amit trips over lab-grown meat: 'You can actually grow, let's say, a chicken leg in a lamb. Chicken leg in a lab. Not in a lamb. Don't try that at home.'

head: Amit's sign-off
more: Amit's sign-off: 'Subscribe and like. I forgot to say it in the previous episodes, but if you're a YouTuber, you're supposed to say that,' followed by an apology for what his producer calls his 'resting pout face'.

head: OPEC: The Cartoon Cartel That Couldn't
dek: Even the most powerful cartel in history could not beat time. Short-term pain gives way to long-term adjustment, and members with different needs cheat on each other.
more: OPEC was the most brazen price-fixing club imaginable, and because its members were governments rather than firms, no antitrust law could touch it. After the Arab countries lost the 1973 war to Israel, a furious group of oil producers cut output by only 8%, and the price jumped from about $1.5 to $11 a barrel. Later histories show the producers themselves thought this was reckless: big oil consumers might simply land an army and seize the Gulf oil fields. Henry Kissinger is believed to have written a pseudonymous magazine article laying out exactly such an operation. No invasion came, and the cartel took shape. Ajay then runs the numbers. Oil went from $11 in 1974 to about $77 in 2023, roughly 7x, which is about 4% a year in nominal dollars and only about 1.5% a year in real terms. He gives three reasons. First, demand adjusts over the long run. Second, countries refuse to be extorted. Third, the cartel could not hold together: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar have small populations and could afford to cut supply, while populous Iran and Iraq kept pumping, and North Sea, Russian and Mexican oil filled any gap.
Even the most powerful cartel in history could not beat time. Short-term pain gives way to long-term adjustment, and members with different needs cheat on each other.
printed: Born in anger, beaten by time

head: Reverse OPEC: India and China Become a Buyers' Cartel
dek: In fifty years the story came full circle: a sellers' cartel pushed prices up after the 1973 war, and a buyers' cartel pushed them down after the 2022 war.
more: When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Putin's implied threat was to leave Europe shivering through the winter by cutting off energy. Europe called the bluff and found a whole range of alternatives. Russian crude shifted to India (about 51% of its sales) and China. The West then invented a new tool of economic statecraft: a $60-a-barrel cap on Russian oil. It could be enforced because almost all of the world's shipping and shipping insurance is run out of Western countries, especially the UK, so shippers and insurers could be punished for handling Russian oil sold above $60. Ajay doubted it would work, since shadow tanker fleets would spring up (the FT reported one operating out of Bombay), but the data suggest it did. Putin needed money for the war and had only two big buyers left, so India and China gained the power to drive a hard bargain.

In fifty years the story came full circle: a sellers' cartel pushed prices up after the 1973 war, and a buyers' cartel pushed them down after the 2022 war. Leverage can also sit in unexpected places. Whoever controls the shipping and insurance can set the terms of a trade between two other countries.

head: Ram Guha and the Best Bookshop on Church Street
dek: It is a lovely piece of self-deprecation. It also shows how one chance find in a secondhand bookshop can open up a whole field, with one book leading to thirty more.
more: In Bangalore, Amit stays on Church Street. It has the Takshashila Institution studio where he records, a Starbucks, and Blossoms, his favourite bookshop in the world, which makes it 'the best street in the world.' After recording a Seen and the Unseen episode with Ram Guha, Amit said he was off to the best bookshop in the world. Guha, in Amit's admittedly embellished retelling, called him a fool and said Blossoms wasn't even the best bookshop on Church Street, then took him to Bookworm. Amit visited both. Bookworm turned out to stock a copy of his own book, which settled the matter. It was later, in Blossoms' secondhand section, that he found a hardback of Fred Kaplan's The Insurgents on sale. That book started the rabbit hole behind this episode's chapter on guerrilla warfare.
It is a lovely piece of self-deprecation. It also shows how one chance find in a secondhand bookshop can open up a whole field, with one book leading to thirty more.

head: Kashmir's Lost Moment of 2007
dek: A counterinsurgency run as 100% military, instead of 80% political, creates more militants than it removes.
more: Drawing on David Devadas's book, Amit describes 2007 as a year of new beginnings. A new generation of Kashmiris was sick of the fighting and wanted ordinary lives as programmers, engineers and artists, and the 2003 Vajpayee-Musharraf talks had laid some groundwork. But the security apparatus was entrenched, and men who had fought on the front lines in the 90s were now senior officers. The incentives were perverse. Rewards were tied to how many heads you could collect, which led to innocent people being killed. Ordinary Kashmiris needed government permission for everything, which bred rent-seeking ('mai-baap multiplied') and extortion.
