In one case a 19- or 20-year-old refused to hand over his Tata Indigo to a security man and was imprisoned. The window closed, Pakistan stepped in, and things got worse.

A counterinsurgency run as 100% military, instead of 80% political, creates more militants than it removes. Imagining yourself in a Kashmiri boy's shoes makes the cost of alienating your own citizens very concrete.

head: Decalogue I: The Father Who Calculated the Ice
dek: Amit insists the film is not anti-science but a lesson in humility. The world is deeply complex, and an engineer's confidence that everything can be figured out and calculated can go badly wrong.
more: The first film of Krzysztof Kieślowski's Dekalog is built on the commandment 'Thou shalt not have any other god than me.' A scientist father ('very much like you,' Amit tells Ajay) has a young son who is waiting for the lake to freeze so he can go skating. The father tracks temperatures, weather reports and every other piece of data, and finally concludes that today, within the margin of error, it is safe. The boy goes skating, the ice cracks, and he dies. In the last shot the father stands by the lake, and in the distance a homeless man has lit a fire to warm his hands.
Amit insists the film is not anti-science but a lesson in humility. The world is deeply complex, and an engineer's confidence that everything can be figured out and calculated can go badly wrong.

head: The Bicycle Shot: Show Don't Tell on Screen
dek: The strongest storytelling often leaves out the obvious beat and lets a single image carry the emotion, trusting the audience to fill in the rest.
more: In Kieślowski's A Short Film About Love, a young man in an apartment complex has a crush on a woman across the way and keeps creepily watching her through her window. He decides to go to her door, possibly while delivering the milk or papers, and ask her out. He rings the bell. A conventional film would show the door opening, the question and her answer. Instead the film cuts to a top-angle shot of him in the courtyard below, riding round and round on his cycle in sheer joy. Amit uses this scene to teach his writing students about show-don't-tell.
The strongest storytelling often leaves out the obvious beat and lets a single image carry the emotion, trusting the audience to fill in the rest.
printed: Round and round in sheer joy

head: The Wealth of Nations
dek: It is the source of the standard mental model of cartels as an ever-present threat, the very model the OPEC story then tests against the data.
more: It is the source of the standard mental model of cartels as an ever-present threat, the very model the OPEC story then tests against the data.
Ajay opens the cartel chapter with Smith's line that men of the same profession seldom meet without trying to rig the price. The book is linked in the show notes.

head: The Insurgents
dek: It is a recent book that covers Petraeus and later developments in counterinsurgency thinking.
more: It is a recent book that covers Petraeus and later developments in counterinsurgency thinking. It also has the clean summary of Galula's step-by-step method that Amit reads out on the show.
Amit found a discounted hardback in Blossoms' secondhand section, and it sent him down a rabbit hole on guerrilla warfare.

head: Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice
dek: Its central point is that fighting insurgents is completely different from conventional war, captured in the fly-versus-lion metaphor and the principle that you must keep the people on your side.
more: Its central point is that fighting insurgents is completely different from conventional war, captured in the fly-versus-lion metaphor and the principle that you must keep the people on your side.
Amit calls it 'the Bible' of counterinsurgency literature. Galula fought in China and Algeria, was once imprisoned by Mao's men, and wrote the book in the 60s.

head: Seven Pillars of Wisdom
dek: It is part of the early literature on guerrilla war that existed long before the US went into Vietnam and still failed to learn from it.
more: It is part of the early literature on guerrilla war that existed long before the US went into Vietnam and still failed to learn from it.
Cited as the origin of the description of this kind of warfare as 'eating soup with a knife'.

head: Learning to Eat Soup with a Knife
dek: It sits in the counterinsurgency canon Amit worked through after Kaplan and Galula, which convinced him that this kind of war is mostly a political problem.
more: It sits in the counterinsurgency canon Amit worked through after Kaplan and Galula, which convinced him that this kind of war is mostly a political problem.
Amit calls it 'a great book' whose title borrows T. E. Lawrence's image.

head: The Generation of Rage in Kashmir
dek: Devadas argues that 2007 was a moment of hope, with a new generation that wanted jobs and normal lives.
more: Devadas argues that 2007 was a moment of hope, with a new generation that wanted jobs and normal lives. He documents in detail how perverse incentives such as body-count rewards, rent-seeking and extortion wasted that moment and alienated people.
Amit's main source for how the Indian security apparatus mishandled Kashmir.

head: The Logic of Collective Action
dek: It offers a useful way to think about what a state is and why legitimacy matters in places like the Naxal belt.
more: It offers a useful way to think about what a state is and why legitimacy matters in places like the Naxal belt.
Amit names it as the source of the roving-bandit and stationary-bandit framework.

head: A Business History of India
dek: It tells the story of India's evolution through the lens of firms and markets.
more: It tells the story of India's evolution through the lens of firms and markets. Ajay urges even a businessperson who has never read a book to pick it up. What struck him most was how little has changed, and he came away with new respect for the people of a hundred and a hundred and fifty years ago.
Ajay's book of the week, by an economic historian he calls a deep thinker about India.

head: A Short Film About Love
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece. Its bicycle-in-the-courtyard scene is the example he uses to teach his writing students show-don't-tell.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece. Its bicycle-in-the-courtyard scene is the example he uses to teach his writing students show-don't-tell.
One of two Dekalog stories expanded into a roughly 90-minute film.

head: A Short Film About Killing
dek: Amit names it alongside A Short Film About Love, and calls both of them masterpieces.
more: Amit names it alongside A Short Film About Love, and calls both of them masterpieces.
The other Dekalog story expanded into a longer film.

head: Monopolies Need the State
dek: Amit's view is that cartels and monopolies can't last when anyone is free to enter the market, because someone will always come along and disrupt them.
more: Amit's view is that cartels and monopolies can't last when anyone is free to enter the market, because someone will always come along and disrupt them. Lasting monopolies exist only where the state restricts competition or hands someone an advantage. OPEC is the usual counterexample, but it is made up of state actors, not market players.

head: Stuck in the Short Run, Adaptive in the Long Run
dek: Demand barely responds to price in the short term: if petrol doubles tomorrow, you still have to drive to work.
more: Demand barely responds to price in the short term: if petrol doubles tomorrow, you still have to drive to work. Over time, though, people adjust dramatically. Higher prices pay for more exploration, more fuel-efficient cars and substitutes for oil. A price shock that looks like proof of cartel power is often just the short run talking.

head: Nobody Likes to Be Extorted
dek: Using a supply chokehold as hard power is short-sighted, whether it is OPEC with oil, China with rare earths against Japan in 2012, or Russia with energy against Europe.
more: Using a supply chokehold as hard power is short-sighted, whether it is OPEC with oil, China with rare earths against Japan in 2012, or Russia with energy against Europe. Ajay's thought experiment: suppose the Indian state made every call centre refuse to work for JP Morgan. JP Morgan would struggle for three weeks, and then the world would permanently route around a supplier that misbehaves. Victims respond by reducing their exposure.

head: The Missing Word Is 'Price'
dek: The 1972 Club of Rome report and the 'peak oil' scare both projected current consumption forward and predicted doom.
more: The 1972 Club of Rome report and the 'peak oil' scare both projected current consumption forward and predicted doom. Both left out the price system: scarcity raises prices, which spurs exploration, substitution and innovation. Lithium is not rare at all, since it is made in abundance in stars right after hydrogen and helium, and serious business plans for towing resource-rich asteroids back to Earth were nearly viable. Ajay never worries about running out of natural resources. The constraint he does worry about is global warming, because filling the air with CO2 is a real threat.

head: Counterinsurgency Is 20% Military, 80% Political
dek: One of Mao's generals put it this way, and it is the core of David Galula's method.
more: One of Mao's generals put it this way, and it is the core of David Galula's method. As summarised by Fred Kaplan: push the insurgents out, hold the area, win the people's trust and cut their ties to the insurgents, replace the insurgents' political organisation, then mop up. Petraeus boiled it down to one question to ask before any operation. Amit's verdict is that India's approach in Kashmir was close to 100% military and treated the people like an occupied population.

head: The Fly and the Lion
dek: Galula's metaphor for why conventional armies struggle against guerrillas.
more: Galula's metaphor for why conventional armies struggle against guerrillas. Each side is built for a different kind of fight, so conventional force against insurgents is like swatting at flies that keep coming back.

head: The R-Nought of Militancy
dek: Ajay recasts Petraeus's question in the maths of epidemics that COVID taught everyone.
more: Ajay recasts Petraeus's question in the maths of epidemics that COVID taught everyone. If each infected person infects more than one other person, the epidemic explodes. In the same way, if killing one militant creates even slightly more than one new militant, the insurgency grows without limit. Every operation should be judged by that ratio, not by body count.

head: Roving Bandits vs. Stationary Bandits
dek: Mancur Olson's model: a roving bandit robs a village and leaves for good.
more: Mancur Olson's model: a roving bandit robs a village and leaves for good. A stationary bandit settles in and taxes the village year after year, so he has reasons to build infrastructure and keep rival bandits out. A state is often a stationary bandit. In many Naxal areas the state was absent, so both it and the Naxalites behaved like roving bandits, and in some places the Naxals were the ones who settled in and provided services.

head: If Kashmir Is Integral, Kashmiris Are Your Citizens
dek: Amit is not arguing against fighting Pakistan-backed terrorists or defending borders.
more: Amit is not arguing against fighting Pakistan-backed terrorists or defending borders. His point is that claiming a territory means owning a duty to its people. A state's job is to serve its people, not rule over them, and alienating them hands the insurgency its next recruits.

head: Don't Turn the Military on Your Own People
dek: Armies are built to deliver overwhelming lethality against an enemy, and their training, manuals, equipment and tactics are designed for that job.
more: Armies are built to deliver overwhelming lethality against an enemy, and their training, manuals, equipment and tactics are designed for that job. Ajay is deeply uncomfortable when that machinery is used inside India against its own population.

head: Fear Ends Debate, and That Produces Bad Policy
dek: Ajay calls this the securitization of the Indian state. Once 'national security' is invoked, all questions are supposed to stop, in the same way that warnings of a crisis are used to shut down debate on financial policy.
more: Ajay calls this the securitization of the Indian state. Once 'national security' is invoked, all questions are supposed to stop, in the same way that warnings of a crisis are used to shut down debate on financial policy. He wants a debate led by civilians that engages with the complexity of these questions. In the French experience in Algeria and the American experience in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, criticism and soldier-intellectuals like Petraeus changed how the forces behaved. Per Ajay's book with Vijay Kelkar, this missing intellectual capacity is a weakness across the whole Indian state, not just in security.

head: Introspection Is How Institutions Learn
dek: The Western way of war produces diaries, logs and books in which people mourn their mistakes and study their wins, and that literature is how armies improve.
more: The Western way of war produces diaries, logs and books in which people mourn their mistakes and study their wins, and that literature is how armies improve. Big institutions change slowly. Ajay compares them to a battleship (Indian health) or a super tanker (financial regulation), and Amit worries that any existing army is an anachronism in fast-moving times. Ajay ties this to the middle-income trap: crude mobilisation of resources can lift a poor country to lower-middle income, but going further needs a culture of evidence, post-mortems and criticism.

head: Winning the War, Losing the Occupation
dek: Amit argues that even if Russia had captured Kyiv and killed Zelensky, it could never have won the counterinsurgency that followed, because Ukrainians clearly saw themselves as a separate people.
more: Amit argues that even if Russia had captured Kyiv and killed Zelensky, it could never have won the counterinsurgency that followed, because Ukrainians clearly saw themselves as a separate people. Ajay says this was his baseline from the start of the invasion. Any plan to invade should be tested by asking what happens after the conventional victory.

head: Everything Is a Gamble
dek: Amit spent five years as a professional poker player.
more: Amit spent five years as a professional poker player. He defines gambling as weighing up the probabilities and making a bet, and by that definition talking to someone in a bar, buying a 'haunted' house at a discount and launching this show are all gambles. Ajay agrees that taking risks is part of life, but calls lotteries (where you lose on average) and reckless derivatives positions decision mistakes. Amit replies that it is still the individual's right to make those mistakes, and that the state should stay out.
printed: All of life at the tables

head: The Eight Queens Problem opens the show. Amit solves it on the chessboard
more: The Eight Queens Problem opens the show. Amit solves it on the chessboard 'in one feverish attempt. So, like well done to me.' Ajay, who once wrote a program to solve it in Fortran, can't even see it as chess any more: 'for me it's an n-queens problem, and I have lost the ability to think of it as a chess problem.'

head: On whether the Saudi oil minister was imagining nuclear fusion replacing oil, Ajay notes that fusion
more: On whether the Saudi oil minister was imagining nuclear fusion replacing oil, Ajay notes that fusion 'is always the great technology of the next 20 years and has always been and will always be.'

head: Amit pitches a Bollywood film
more: Amit pitches a Bollywood film: Akshay Kumar flies a spaceship to an asteroid made of lithium and brings it back. Ajay objects that lithium is plentiful on Earth, so you'd need a heavy element. Tantalum gets suggested, and Ajay admits he just picked a name off the periodic table, which has 'all kinds of beautiful names' like yttrium.

head: Amit on his love for Blossoms' secondhand section
more: Amit on his love for Blossoms' secondhand section: 'if you want to go for a week to Bali, I'll go for a week to Blossoms.'

head: Amit's sign-off
more: Amit's sign-off: 'It's been a gamble on your part to watch it, and if you're still here, you've enjoyed it, right? So well done, you're a gambler.'

head: Adam Smith, as Ajay paraphrases him
more: Adam Smith, as Ajay paraphrases him: 'men of the same profession seldom get together in the same room without trying to rig the price.' Ajay uses it to state the standard mental model of cartels before showing how OPEC fell short of it.

head: Saudi oil minister Ahmed Zaki Yamani
more: Saudi oil minister Ahmed Zaki Yamani: 'the Stone Age did not end because the world ran out of stones.' The oil age will end through technological change, which Ajay says is now happening through decarbonisation. He adds that Siberian gas may still be sitting in the ground a thousand years from now.

head: Bob Dylan
more: Bob Dylan, 'one of our heroes': Amit quotes 'A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall' as rain pours down outside the recording.

head: A Visitor from the 20th Century
dek: Heroes are often handed down through family stories and childhood books.
more: Ajay explains that Oppenheimer died when he was one year old, so this history is not ancient to him. His father followed Oppenheimer closely and passed on many stories. Ajay read Robert Jungk's 1956 book Brighter Than a Thousand Suns several times, around age 10 to 12. As a PhD student he found Richard Rhodes' The Making of the Atomic Bomb. He adds that new archival material has emerged in recent years, so these histories can now be written better.
Heroes are often handed down through family stories and childhood books. Events that feel like textbook history are only one lifetime away.

head: The Poisoned Apple: How Oppenheimer Was Almost Lost
dek: Genius depends on finding the right environment. Amit uses the story to argue that one-size-fits-all education wastes the minds that don't fit its mould.
more: Before Göttingen, Oppenheimer was by most accounts a bad student. His physics tutor scolded him for not doing enough experimental work, and he told a friend, 'The lab work is a terrible bore, and it is impossible to feel that I am learning anything.' He was miserable enough to leave a poisoned apple on the tutor's table, which he later admitted. His wealthy parents got the university to drop expulsion on condition that he undergo psychiatric treatment. At Göttingen, studying under Max Born alongside classmates like Dirac and John von Neumann, he flourished.
Genius depends on finding the right environment. Amit uses the story to argue that one-size-fits-all education wastes the minds that don't fit its mould.
printed: An apple for the teacher, poisoned

head: Leo Szilard's Aha Moment Crossing a London Road
dek: Skepticism should be judged by when it was voiced. Big ideas stay curiosities until one missing piece makes them buildable, and then they change everything quickly.
more: Amit cites Rutherford calling atomic power 'moonshine' and an early Einstein saying nuclear energy would never be obtainable. Ajay asks him to look at the dates. For decades E=mc² was a curiosity with no engineering attached to it. Then Leo Szilard, crossing a road in London, suddenly saw that neutrons could set off a chain reaction. Fearing Hitler would get the bomb first, he reached Einstein, whose letter to Roosevelt led to the Manhattan Project.
Skepticism should be judged by when it was voiced. Big ideas stay curiosities until one missing piece makes them buildable, and then they change everything quickly.

head: Niels Bohr: 'You'll Have to Turn the US into a Factory'
dek: Even one of the greatest physicists misjudged the scale that inspired leadership and organisation could reach.
more: Niels Bohr was told about the Manhattan Project late. He first called it impossible, because it would require turning the whole United States into a factory. Later he conceded that they had done exactly that. The world's biggest factory was built for uranium enrichment, and an even bigger facility for plutonium processing. A team of a few thousand people, led by a 38-year-old Oppenheimer, saw it through.

Even one of the greatest physicists misjudged the scale that inspired leadership and organisation could reach. Ajay argues Oppenheimer's success was not inevitable: he was the right person in the right place at the right time.
printed: Turn America into a factory? Done

head: The Bohemian Who Learned Sanskrit
dek: Ajay argues that Oppenheimer's breadth and unconventional life were the source of his creative energy, not a side detail.
more: Oppenheimer was no narrow technician. About a hundred years ago he learned Sanskrit, and at the first bomb test in July 1945 he recalled the Gita's Vishwarup lines: 'I am become death, destroyer of the world.' He lived bohemian-style. He backed the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War, his brother was in the Communist Party, his wife was an eclectic character, and he had a lover deep inside the Communist Party.
Ajay argues that Oppenheimer's breadth and unconventional life were the source of his creative energy, not a side detail.

head: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished: Truman, Teller and McCarthyism
dek: The state used Oppenheimer when it needed him and destroyed him when he became inconvenient.
more: After the bomb, traditional power reasserted itself. Ajay believes that when Oppenheimer told Truman he felt he had blood on his hands over Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Truman bristled. Edward Teller pushed for the hydrogen bomb out of pure scientific curiosity. Oppenheimer asked what was gained by going from 20 kilotons to 200 or 2,000, and wanted to rein in what had been built. Having angered many bureaucrats, he became McCarthyism's most famous target. In a rigged process, his personal history, some of it dug out illegally, was made public, and he was pushed out of public policy and retired to Princeton.
The state used Oppenheimer when it needed him and destroyed him when he became inconvenient. Ajay calls the method character assassination, or in today's terms, information warfare.

head: The Rehabilitation: A State That Admitted Its Mistake
dek: A mature state is not one that never errs, but one that citizens can push into publicly admitting its errors.
more: In the last ten years, people used US freedom-of-information access to show that the legal process against Oppenheimer had been rigged and the rule of law violated. About two years before this episode, the US government officially admitted the mistake and reinstated his security clearance, decades after his death. Ajay was also struck that many of today's actors on both sides are children and grandchildren of that generation, who still carry its memories.
A mature state is not one that never errs, but one that citizens can push into publicly admitting its errors. Ajay says Indians don't even expect this of their state.

head: Roy Cohn: From McCarthy to Trump
dek: With enough historical distance, today's culture war looks like a long-running contest between the same two sides.
more: The chief counsel for Joe McCarthy who tried to subpoena Oppenheimer in the 1950s was Roy Cohn. Cohn later became Donald Trump's mentor and guide. Ajay traces one nationalist, power-hungry, unethical culture running from McCarthy and Cohn to Trump, with people like Oppenheimer on the other side.
With enough historical distance, today's culture war looks like a long-running contest between the same two sides. That is why Ajay rejects the claim that there are fine people on both sides.

head: Tim de Lisle: 'When in Doubt, Play Your Shots'
dek: Creative people should overreach while young and learn what not to do along the way.
more: When Amit joined Wisden in 2001, Tim de Lisle was his editor's editor; Tim later edited the Wisden Almanac and The Economist's Intelligent Life. Tim's tips were mostly about clarity, and Amit uses some of his examples in his own writing course. One rule stuck with him: 'when in doubt, play your shots.' Amit admits he was a terrible, show-offy writer back then.
Creative people should overreach while young and learn what not to do along the way. Amit applies this to Nolan's riskier films: better someone who tries too hard than someone who doesn't try.

head: Caro's Million Words and the Lost Book on Jane Jacobs
dek: Physical publishing limits cost us a book on Jane Jacobs by one of the greatest biographers.
more: Robert Caro told his publisher a Robert Moses biography would take a few months. It took twelve or thirteen years and ran to almost a million words. The publisher insisted it fit one bound volume, so it was cut to about 800,000 words. The cut included a book-length section, around 200,000 words, mostly on Jane Jacobs, which Amit says has never been made available. Caro then started on Lyndon Johnson; one volume is still left.

Physical publishing limits cost us a book on Jane Jacobs by one of the greatest biographers. Today an author could simply put the extra material online. Caro's thoroughness reminds Amit of Borges' map as big as the territory.

head: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
dek: It explains the science while carrying a lay reader along. Ajay says even people who think they aren't science-literate should read it, because all great acts of creation are human projects.
more: It explains the science while carrying a lay reader along. Ajay says even people who think they aren't science-literate should read it, because all great acts of creation are human projects. In his preface, Rhodes describes the early-20th-century physics community adopting him as their poet laureate.
Ajay's recommendation of the week. He found it as a PhD student and calls it the best book on the subject; he recalls Hans Bethe saying nobody can tell this story better.

head: Brighter Than a Thousand Suns
dek: It is the book that got Ajay deep into the Oppenheimer story and shaped how he thought about the world while growing up.
more: It is the book that got Ajay deep into the Oppenheimer story and shaped how he thought about the world while growing up.
A 1956 book Ajay read several times as a child, around age 10 to 12.

head: The Power Broker
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece that works on three levels: a biography of Moses, a biography of how New York was reshaped by top-down planning, and a study of how power corrupts an idealistic man.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece that works on three levels: a biography of Moses, a biography of how New York was reshaped by top-down planning, and a study of how power corrupts an idealistic man. He also praises the sweep of the storytelling. Ajay adds that it is a fundamental input for Indians thinking about urban planning.
Amit's recommendation of the week: Caro's Pulitzer-winning biography of New York bureaucrat Robert Moses.

head: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
dek: Jacobs is one of Amit's intellectual heroes. She argued that cities are about people, not buildings, and should grow organically.
more: Jacobs is one of Amit's intellectual heroes. She argued that cities are about people, not buildings, and should grow organically. Ajay separately invokes her phrase 'the ballet of the streets.'
Raised while discussing Moses' long running opposition to Jane Jacobs.

head: How to Write Well
dek: Amit calls it a lovely book on writing that focuses on clarity. He uses some of its examples in his own writing course.
more: Amit calls it a lovely book on writing that focuses on clarity. He uses some of its examples in his own writing course.
A book by Amit's editor's editor at Wisden.

head: Oppenheimer
dek: Amit admires Nolan for bringing artistic, intimate sensibility to big-screen spectacle.
more: Amit admires Nolan for bringing artistic, intimate sensibility to big-screen spectacle. Nolan left Warner Brothers for Universal because Warner was releasing films on HBO Max at the same time as in theatres. Ajay is anxious that the film may reduce Oppenheimer to caricature.
The opening topic; Amit hadn't seen it yet at recording time.

head: Dunkirk
dek: Amit calls it one of the greatest war films he has seen. Ajay knows that period deeply and felt the film told the story well.
more: Amit calls it one of the greatest war films he has seen. Ajay knows that period deeply and felt the film told the story well.
Raised by Ajay as the reason he has hope for Oppenheimer.

head: Blade Runner
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece and notes that Ridley Scott was one of Nolan's inspirations.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece and notes that Ridley Scott was one of Nolan's inspirations.
The original film, mentioned while praising its sequel.

head: Einstein's Letter to President Roosevelt (1939)
dek: It is the letter that, after Szilard reached Einstein, persuaded Roosevelt to start the bomb project before Hitler could get there.
more: It is the letter that, after Szilard reached Einstein, persuaded Roosevelt to start the bomb project before Hitler could get there.
Show-notes link tied to Ajay's account of how the Manhattan Project began.

head: On Exactitude in Science
dek: Amit uses Borges' idea of a map that must be as big as the world, and is out of date the next instant, to capture Caro's thoroughness.
more: Amit uses Borges' idea of a map that must be as big as the world, and is out of date the next instant, to capture Caro's thoroughness.
Invoked after describing Caro's endless Lyndon Johnson project.

head: The Auteur at Scale
dek: Many people assume intimate, artistic films belong on OTT and spectacle belongs in theatres.
more: Many people assume intimate, artistic films belong on OTT and spectacle belongs in theatres. Amit says Nolan, and Villeneuve too, straddle both, bringing intellectual concepts to big-budget screens. They earned enough studio trust to try new things instead of following proven templates.

head: America's Rise Was Imported Talent
dek: Ajay notes that the centre of early-20th-century science and mathematics was Göttingen in Germany, and that America was a backwater.
more: Ajay notes that the centre of early-20th-century science and mathematics was Göttingen in Germany, and that America was a backwater. The flight of Jewish and other European intellectuals made America take off. That also made home-grown builders of deep scientific communities, like Oppenheimer, disproportionately important.

head: Articulation as a Superpower
dek: Oppenheimer understood modern physics deeply and could also explain it clearly.
more: Oppenheimer understood modern physics deeply and could also explain it clearly. Ajay calls that rare combination unusually important in the modern world, and it was a large part of why he could lead and inspire others.

head: The Maverick Comes as a Package
dek: Oppenheimer's bohemian life, left-wing circles, Sanskrit and wide reading were not distractions from his genius.
more: Oppenheimer's bohemian life, left-wing circles, Sanskrit and wide reading were not distractions from his genius. Ajay sees them as the source of his energy and creativity. Institutions that want the brilliance but punish the unconventional life misunderstand where the brilliance comes from.

head: The Curse of the Smartest Person in the Room
dek: Oppenheimer usually knew more than anyone present and could persuade with elegance.
more: Oppenheimer usually knew more than anyone present and could persuade with elegance. Ajay says that kept humiliating the 'gray, bloodless, powerful people' who lost arguments to him, and their resentment later shaped his persecution.

head: Extraordinary Times Let Mavericks In, Then the System Takes Back Over
dek: Most power is held by dull, conventional people. Only in crises such as the Manhattan Project or Ukraine's war does the system hand control to mavericks, who then recruit the clever rather than the obedient.
more: Most power is held by dull, conventional people. Only in crises such as the Manhattan Project or Ukraine's war does the system hand control to mavericks, who then recruit the clever rather than the obedient. When the crisis passes, mediocrity returns and turns on them, as Oppenheimer found and as Jahnavi Phalkey's history of 1940s Indian science shows.

head: Education Sorts, It Doesn't Teach
dek: Markets offer 40 flavours of chips because people differ, yet education still uses a 19th-century factory model: same age, same subjects, same tests.
more: Markets offer 40 flavours of chips because people differ, yet education still uses a 19th-century factory model: same age, same subjects, same tests. India's version sorts out the already-bright for IITs and IIMs and passes that off as good teaching. Amit adds that most edtech startups just deliver the same syllabus through a new medium.

head: Renaissance Minds vs. Ever-Narrower Silos
dek: Oppenheimer was a generalist who was also a great theoretical physicist, so he could see the bigger picture, such as whether the world needed a hydrogen bomb at all.
more: Oppenheimer was a generalist who was also a great theoretical physicist, so he could see the bigger picture, such as whether the world needed a hydrogen bomb at all. Amit says modern academia pushes people into ever-narrower specialisations. Ajay adds that journal and funding incentives waste a vastly larger research workforce on incremental work.

head: Technician vs. Intellectual
dek: Ajay distinguishes technicians, who know one narrow procedure and don't engage with the wider world, from intellectuals, who think about the world on a larger scale.
more: Ajay distinguishes technicians, who know one narrow procedure and don't engage with the wider world, from intellectuals, who think about the world on a larger scale. He calls this a central feature of the modern world, and Oppenheimer was clearly the second kind.

head: The Universe Throws Darts; Culture Decides Which Land
dek: Ajay says we should not just admire 'the great J. Robert Oppenheimer'.
more: Ajay says we should not just admire 'the great J. Robert Oppenheimer'. Each of the world's seven billion people is a dart, so raw talent is plentiful. What shapes the world is the institutions and culture that do the sorting. A culture that protects mavericks produces truth and beauty, while one obsessed with order raises dull people to power.

head: A First-World State Can Be Made to Say 'We Were Wrong'
dek: All states are coercive and make mistakes. Ajay argues what marks a first-world country is that independent citizens can dig through archives, challenge the government, and get it to retract officially.
more: All states are coercive and make mistakes. Ajay argues what marks a first-world country is that independent citizens can dig through archives, challenge the government, and get it to retract officially. India, he says, does not even expect this.

head: The Cost of Being Ahistorical
dek: Ajay contrasts America, where descendants on both sides of the Oppenheimer affair still carry that memory, with India.
more: Ajay contrasts America, where descendants on both sides of the Oppenheimer affair still carry that memory, with India. There, he says, influential people often lack institutional memory across generations, which leaves the country without a deep understanding of the world.

head: We Shape Our Buildings, Then They Shape Us
dek: Robert Moses built flyovers and bridges without caring about the neighbourhoods underneath, while Jane Jacobs argued cities are about people.
more: Robert Moses built flyovers and bridges without caring about the neighbourhoods underneath, while Jane Jacobs argued cities are about people. Urban form changes how people live and what culture they have. So the choice between top-down planning and organic growth is not a technical side question.

head: Power Corrodes Even the Idealist
dek: In the 1920s and 30s Moses looked like a brilliant, idealistic visionary.
more: In the 1920s and 30s Moses looked like a brilliant, idealistic visionary. Amit says The Power Broker shows how bureaucratic power slowly inflated his ego, shaped his politics and hurt other people's lives, and that this is a lesson about all of us.

head: The Ballet of the Streets: India's Missing Middle Road
dek: Ajay borrows Jane Jacobs' phrase 'the ballet of the streets'. During COVID lockdowns the buildings were still there but that street ballet was gone.
more: Ajay borrows Jane Jacobs' phrase 'the ballet of the streets'. During COVID lockdowns the buildings were still there but that street ballet was gone. He says the Indian middle class wants an authoritarian planner to dictate parks and metros. India needs its own urban philosophy that neither romanticises unplanned growth nor copies Chandigarh-style master planning.

General Groves picked Oppenheimer because he was good at everything, including metallurgy, engineering and chemistry, except sports. Amit turns to Ajay: 'Kinda like you, you know everything except sports, right? Bollywood perhaps.'

head: Amit's caricature of academic hyper-specialisation: someone
more: Amit's caricature of academic hyper-specialisation: someone 'specializing in something like wheat production in Ukraine between the years 1836 to 1838', which he admits isn't far from real specialisations.

head: To show how rare Oppenheimer learning Sanskrit was, Ajay offers an analogy
more: To show how rare Oppenheimer learning Sanskrit was, Ajay offers an analogy: 'I'd challenge people in India to go learn Aramaic. Okay? We don't do that.'

head: The Freddy teaser: Amit's on-screen co-host is named after two of his heroes, a giant of the 19th century and one of the 20th. Ajay asks…
more: The Freddy teaser: Amit's on-screen co-host is named after two of his heroes, a giant of the 19th century and one of the 20th. Ajay asks, 'Was one of them born in Zanzibar?' Amit: 'None of them is Freddie Mercury. I'm sorry if that, you know, gets the temperature down immediately.'

head: Ajay names Chandigarh as the extreme of top-down planning.
more: Ajay names Chandigarh as the extreme of top-down planning. Amit: 'Well let me be clear about one thing. I was born in Chandigarh.' They swap in Brasilia as the example instead.

head: Amit calls this a golden age of cinema despite
more: Amit calls this a golden age of cinema despite 'a Marvel cinematic universe and other such garbage', then recalls his friend Madhu Menon complaining 15 minutes into Arrival: 'This is so slow. What is happening?'
'Trepidated' becomes the hosts' made-up word for their feelings about Nolan's film. Ajay explains: 'I'm scared of the movie being a mess. I'm scared of the movie hitting me too hard. I'm trepidated.'

head: Bhagavad Gita: at the first bomb test, Oppenheimer recalled the Vishwarup lines
more: Bhagavad Gita: at the first bomb test, Oppenheimer recalled the Vishwarup lines, 'I am become death, destroyer of the world', from a text he had read after learning Sanskrit.

head: Rutherford
more: Rutherford: 'Anyone who expects a source of power from these atoms is talking moonshine.' Early Einstein: 'there is not the slightest indication that nuclear energy will ever be obtainable.' Ajay's rejoinder: 'you gotta look at the dates of those things.'

head: Ajay on Oppenheimer's bohemian streak
more: Ajay on Oppenheimer's bohemian streak: 'in the language of the 60s, the line between hip and square, Oppenheimer was firmly hip.'

head: Winston Churchill's line, which Amit half-remembers and Ajay finishes
more: Winston Churchill's line, which Amit half-remembers and Ajay finishes: 'We shape our buildings and our buildings shape us.'

head: Right after tracing a line from McCarthy and Roy Cohn to Donald Trump, Ajay rejects the idea
more: Right after tracing a line from McCarthy and Roy Cohn to Donald Trump, Ajay rejects the idea that 'there are very fine people on both sides', saying historical distance shows that's 'not a fair statement.'

head: Ukraine's
more: Ukraine's 'Uber for artillery', which Ajay cites as maverick creativity that only wartime survival allows inside a military bureaucracy.

head: Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai, whom Ajay names as India's Oppenheimer-like figures: remarkable people given rare opportunities, next to whom…
more: Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai, whom Ajay names as India's Oppenheimer-like figures: remarkable people given rare opportunities, next to whom 'a lot of modern India seems dull in comparison.'

head: Bastiat Spent His Last Breath on His Ideas
dek: Bastiat was explaining ideas like opportunity cost before the terms were in common use.
more: Frédéric Bastiat, the 19th-century French writer, economist and parliamentarian, died at 49, the age Amit was when recording. He caught tuberculosis while travelling around France popularising his ideas. Knowing his lungs were failing, and referring to his book The Law, he wrote that he would proclaim his principle with all the force of his lungs, which were all too inadequate. Joseph Schumpeter called him the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived.
Bastiat was explaining ideas like opportunity cost before the terms were in common use. His early death leaves you wondering what he would have written with more time.

head: Two Candlesticks for a Satire
dek: The trophy carries the joke of its namesake's most famous satire, so the argument against protectionism sits on Amit's shelf.
more: Amit was the first person to win the Bastiat Prize twice. The prize goes to journalists who promote the values of a free society. Tim Harford later won it twice as well. The trophy is a candlestick, a nod to Bastiat's satirical Candlemakers' Petition, in which candlemakers ask the government to block out the sun.
The trophy carries the joke of its namesake's most famous satire, so the argument against protectionism sits on Amit's shelf.

head: Earthquake Bread at Four Times the Price
dek: In a crisis, moral intuition and economic logic can point in opposite directions.
more: As a student in the early-to-mid 90s, Amit volunteered after an earthquake in Gujarat and rode in an ambulance with paramedics. In one village almost every building had collapsed, but a couple of shops were open and had raised the price of bread three or four times. His first reaction was that this was evil. Later he understood that the high price stopped the first family from buying up all the bread. Families could pool money so everyone got a few slices.
In a crisis, moral intuition and economic logic can point in opposite directions. 'Gouging' prices ration a scarce good so it gets shared, while a capped price lets the first comer take everything.

head: The Friend Who Missed His Flight
dek: A price cap doesn't remove scarcity. It turns the scarcity into missing supply, and the person with an urgent need is the one left stranded.
more: About three years before the recording, the AAP government in Delhi tried a price cap on Uber, just a day before a friend of Amit's needed to get to the airport. With surge pricing gone, no cab was available and the friend missed his flight.
A price cap doesn't remove scarcity. It turns the scarcity into missing supply, and the person with an urgent need is the one left stranded.

head: Predicting That the Stent Price Cap Would Kill
dek: Economic first principles let you predict outcomes. 'Price controls always lead to shortages' is a forecast you can make in advance, not just an argument.
more: When the Indian government capped the price of stents because they were 'too expensive', Amit tweeted (or wrote in a column) that the cap would cause shortages and people would die. He says that is exactly what happened.
Economic first principles let you predict outcomes. 'Price controls always lead to shortages' is a forecast you can make in advance, not just an argument.

head: Raj Narain, Indira Gandhi and the Government Jeeps
dek: Separating party from state is a real protection, not a technicality. Ajay contrasts it with China, where party and state are the same thing.
more: Ajay recalls that Raj Narain took Indira Gandhi to Justice Sinha's courtroom in the Allahabad High Court over the 'sweet little problem' of using government jeeps for campaigning. Because the Congress party and the government were legally separate, her election was invalidated. That was India in 1975.
Separating party from state is a real protection, not a technicality. Ajay contrasts it with China, where party and state are the same thing.

head: How China's Makers Learned to Serve the Party
dek: Owning wealth means little unless it can stand up to the state. Entrepreneurs who agree to the 'fixing' are not thinking two moves ahead.
more: Ajay describes China in stages. First there was some real promise that founders could build businesses fairly. Then, again and again, party-connected 'takers' used state power to push innovators into distress sales or shut them down. Capitalists got the message: over the last 15 years, any significant business needs party members on the board or a 'princeling' (a child of party leaders) as a shareholder. That protection comes with unpredictable future demands, from 'give this guy a job' to 'run your product differently'. The result is a regime of uncodified taxation, as before the Magna Carta, and an investment slump. Russia is one step further, where Putin decides whether an oligarch is jailed, exiled or murdered.
Owning wealth means little unless it can stand up to the state. Entrepreneurs who agree to the 'fixing' are not thinking two moves ahead.

head: Jeff Bezos Takes On Donald Trump
dek: What keeps a society free is whether its institutions constrain the most powerful office, not whether its leaders are kind.
more: To offset the gloom about China and Russia, Ajay points to Jeff Bezos, who made his fortune building Amazon and bought the Washington Post. The Post did investigative journalism going after Donald Trump, and the President and the federal government could not shut it down or hit back at Bezos. In Russia, Ajay says, a billionaire who owns a critical newspaper would 'experience some accidents' and 'fall out of a window'.
What keeps a society free is whether its institutions constrain the most powerful office, not whether its leaders are kind.

head: Who Is the Greatest Human of the Last 30 Years?
dek: Your answer shows what you value most: consumer value, mass escape from poverty, or the invisible infrastructure of computing.
more: Amit sometimes asks people who has had the greatest positive impact on humanity in the last 30 years. His own top candidate was Jeff Bezos, until a friend argued for Deng Xiaoping, who lifted hundreds of millions of Chinese out of poverty. Ajay answers Ken Thompson, the main inventor of Unix. On Deng, Ajay quotes Zhou Enlai: 'it's too soon to tell'. His reason is that the intra-party democracy and term limits Deng built have peeled away.
Your answer shows what you value most: consumer value, mass escape from poverty, or the invisible infrastructure of computing.
printed: We didn’t start the fire, Ken did

head: The Economist Who Sneered at Hazlitt Readers
dek: Knowing basic economics thoroughly beats credentials that ignore it. Amit's comparison: you wouldn't trust a physicist who doesn't believe in gravity.
more: Amit recalls an economist both hosts know, one who had defended demonetisation or at least urged a wait-and-watch approach. This economist complained that too many people arguing with him had only read Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson. Amit's reaction was that this is enough, because those readers have the first principles.
Knowing basic economics thoroughly beats credentials that ignore it. Amit's comparison: you wouldn't trust a physicist who doesn't believe in gravity.

head: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
dek: It teaches you to look past a policy's visible effect to its unseen costs, the core habit of a good economist.
more: It teaches you to look past a policy's visible effect to its unseen costs, the core habit of a good economist.
Introduced as the essay that inspired the name of Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen; it opens with the parable of the broken window.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: Amit calls it the most important and seminal essay of the twentieth century.
more: Amit calls it the most important and seminal essay of the twentieth century. It explains how the price system, not central planning, coordinates an economy.
Hayek's reply to Oscar Lange's proposal for a central price committee.

head: The Fatal Conceit
dek: It argues that the knowledge society needs is spread across everyone, so a planner will always get it wrong.
more: It argues that the knowledge society needs is spread across everyone, so a planner will always get it wrong. Ajay says the computer revolution keeps reviving that conceit.
Ajay cites it while explaining Hayek's two-part insight on dispersed information and price coordination.

head: A primer on Hayek
dek: Hayek can be heavy going, and Butler's primer is a friendly way in.
more: Hayek can be heavy going, and Butler's primer is a friendly way in.
Mentioned while recommending everything by the two Freddies; Amit had recommended it in a previous episode.

head: I, Pencil
dek: A pencil narrates how its parts come from many countries, made by people who never talk to each other.
more: A pencil narrates how its parts come from many countries, made by people who never talk to each other. Prices do the coordinating, a small everyday miracle of spontaneous order.
Brought up after Adam Smith's 'man of system'; Amit says it's an essay he wants everyone to read.

head: The Evolution of Everything
dek: It shows how much of the world (language, economies, even natural selection) evolves without a designer.
more: It shows how much of the world (language, economies, even natural selection) evolves without a designer.
Mentioned while explaining spontaneous order in cities, economies and language.

head: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A long-form conversation about how order emerges without central design.
more: A long-form conversation about how order emerges without central design.
Amit mentions his early episode with Ridley on the book.

head: The Blind Watchmaker
dek: The greatest marvels of nature need no planner, the biological version of Hayek's point about economies.
more: The greatest marvels of nature need no planner, the biological version of Hayek's point about economies.
Raised as the answer to the watchmaker argument against natural selection; Ajay adds the example of the eye.

head: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A deep look at what GDP can and cannot measure, and the problems with how the number is built.
more: A deep look at what GDP can and cannot measure, and the problems with how the number is built.
Mentioned during Amit's critique of counting government spending in GDP.

head: What is Populism?
dek: Helps you recognise how populists work. Amit adds that the most important ingredient is simplistic narratives.
more: Helps you recognise how populists work. Amit adds that the most important ingredient is simplistic narratives.
Amit calls it a great book on populism while discussing how simplistic narratives win power.

head: Crowds and Power
dek: Useful for understanding how anger gets mobilised into an 'us vs them' route to power.
more: Useful for understanding how anger gets mobilised into an 'us vs them' route to power.
Ajay calls it a great book while discussing how political actors use rage and simple-minded economics to gain power.

head: Capitalism and Freedom
dek: Not an introductory book, but Ajay says each chapter was 'like an earthquake' that shakes you and makes you think about the world.
more: Not an introductory book, but Ajay says each chapter was 'like an earthquake' that shakes you and makes you think about the world.
Ajay's recommendation for the episode; Amit calls it a masterpiece.

head: Free to Choose
dek: Another Friedman classic on voluntary exchange. Amit uses it to make his point that capitalism equals consent and is the opposite of cronyism.
more: Another Friedman classic on voluntary exchange. Amit uses it to make his point that capitalism equals consent and is the opposite of cronyism.
Recommended alongside Capitalism and Freedom; Amit notes it also became a TV series, possibly on YouTube.

head: Economics in One Lesson
dek: It uses basic principles to clear up misconceptions about price controls, tariffs and inflation.
more: It uses basic principles to clear up misconceptions about price controls, tariffs and inflation. It has sold over a million copies in some 40-50 languages, and Amit thinks everyone should study economics because it is the study of human behaviour.
Amit's main recommendation for the episode, a book inspired by Bastiat's essay on the seen and the unseen.

head: The Seen and the Unseen (the Broken Window)
dek: A boy breaks a window and people say it's good for the economy because the glazier gets paid.
more: A boy breaks a window and people say it's good for the economy because the glazier gets paid. What is unseen is what the owner would have done with that money, such as buying a coat or a cake. The same fallacy drives claims that war is good for the economy. Unintended effects are often foreseeable once you understand economic laws.

head: GDP and Digging Ditches
dek: Amit objects to counting government spending in GDP, an argument he says Keynes and others won before the Second World War.
more: Amit objects to counting government spending in GDP, an argument he says Keynes and others won before the Second World War. The government could tax people to dig ditches and fill them, and GDP would rise without anyone being better off. A flawed number that becomes a target can be gamed.

head: Unintended Consequences and the Implausibility of Conspiracies
dek: Ajay credits Robert K. Merton (1936) with the idea that all purposeful social action has unintended consequences, because cause and effect are subtle, nonlinear and only dimly understood.
more: Ajay credits Robert K. Merton (1936) with the idea that all purposeful social action has unintended consequences, because cause and effect are subtle, nonlinear and only dimly understood. Karl Popper takes this further. If even 20 people struggle to achieve a goal together, conspiracy theories that require many secret actors to land a ball in a distant hole are hard to believe.

head: Populism Runs on Simplistic Narratives
dek: Populists and nationalists gain power by selling simple-minded economics that turns poor people's anger against elites.
more: Populists and nationalists gain power by selling simple-minded economics that turns poor people's anger against elites. Trump's 2016 story about lost jobs ('China bad', 'foreigners are taking your jobs') was appealing and mostly false. The real causes were many and complex, and a complex story can't become a slogan.

head: Interventions Redistribute From the Poor to the Rich
dek: Amit's teddy-bear example: a tariff of 20 rupees pushes a 90-rupee Chinese bear to 110, so consumers buy the local 100-rupee bear.
more: Amit's teddy-bear example: a tariff of 20 rupees pushes a 90-rupee Chinese bear to 110, so consumers buy the local 100-rupee bear. Ten rupees per buyer moves from consumers to local manufacturers, who also lose the incentive to improve. Public choice theory calls this diffuse costs and concentrated benefits: each consumer barely notices the loss, while an organised lobby collects the gain.

head: Why States Prefer Tariffs to Blowing Up the Railroad
dek: Bastiat's satirical 'negative railroad' and a tariff have the same effect on consumers.
more: Bastiat's satirical 'negative railroad' and a tariff have the same effect on consumers. Ajay's public-choice point is that blowing up a railroad or a port is a one-time decision. A tariff is discretionary: it can be granted, removed or reintroduced industry by industry. That hangs a sword of Damocles over the business class, which must keep funding those in power. Amit adds that following incentives explains party positions, such as AAP opposing FDI in retail because small retailers are among its biggest supporters.

head: Property vs. Plunder (Profit-Seeking vs. Rent-Seeking)
dek: Bastiat: you can prosper by applying your own faculties (property) or by seizing what others produce (plunder).
more: Bastiat: you can prosper by applying your own faculties (property) or by seizing what others produce (plunder). Today plunder usually runs through the coercive power of the state, as rent-seeking and cronyism. People choose whichever path is less burdensome. When the state makes honest trade too hard, as in India's early decades, a rent-seeking mentality takes hold.

head: Makers vs. Takers, and the Price of Refuge
dek: Makers build products and organisations that serve consumers. Takers grab what others built, and once the state has a monopoly on violence, they do it through regulations and rules.
more: Makers build products and organisations that serve consumers. Takers grab what others built, and once the state has a monopoly on violence, they do it through regulations and rules. Protection from the state comes with unpredictable demands later, which is in effect unpredictable taxation. So Ajay argues businesspeople must think philosophically about capital allocation and risk.

head: Counterfactual Histories as a Thinking Tool
dek: Ajay suggests imagining going back in a time machine to advise Deng Xiaoping in 1978, or Nehru.
more: Ajay suggests imagining going back in a time machine to advise Deng Xiaoping in 1978, or Nehru. These were people who meant well and tried to see the future, yet went wrong in many ways. Asking what you'd tell them sharpens your understanding of how the world works.

head: Safety and Freedom vs. Prosperity
dek: Ajay argues from a Maslow-style hierarchy that safety and freedom come first and prosperity second, so Deng's achievement is questionable when most people in China lack that safety.
more: Ajay argues from a Maslow-style hierarchy that safety and freedom come first and prosperity second, so Deng's achievement is questionable when most people in China lack that safety. He also points to Putin's Russia, an economy propped up by oil. Amit pushes back: safety and freedom partly come from having the means to secure them, so escaping poverty has value in itself.

head: Spontaneous Order / Self-Organising Systems
dek: Many beautiful things are, in Adam Ferguson's phrase, the product of human action but not human design.
more: Many beautiful things are, in Adam Ferguson's phrase, the product of human action but not human design. Bastiat's example is how Paris gets fed with no committee. Cities, languages and natural selection work the same way. Ajay prefers the mathematical term 'self-organising system': local decisions, no central control, remarkable results. The world should be a process of discovery, not design.

head: Hayek's Knowledge Problem and Price Coordination
dek: Knowledge about preferences and circumstances (your need for a taxi, a driver's willingness to work) is spread across society, so no planner can know it all.
more: Knowledge about preferences and circumstances (your need for a taxi, a driver's willingness to work) is spread across society, so no planner can know it all. Prices coordinate everyone without anyone needing to talk. Ajay calls the price system the heart and soul of economics, to the point of wanting COVID vaccines traded on free markets with futures contracts.

head: Prices Carry Information and Incentives (Uber Surge Pricing)
dek: Say 200 people want cabs and only 20 are available. Under a price cap, the first 20 get them, even if they're casually heading to the mall while someone else needs a hospital.
more: Say 200 people want cabs and only 20 are available. Under a price cap, the first 20 get them, even if they're casually heading to the mall while someone else needs a hospital. Surge pricing does two things. First, it lets those who value the ride most pay for it. Second, and more important, it signals an idle driver to come out and earn by serving others, which adds supply.
printed: The fare that finds a driver

head: Price Controls Always Lead to Shortages
dek: If cars were capped at ten thousand rupees, existing cars would be snapped up and production would stop.
more: If cars were capped at ten thousand rupees, existing cars would be snapped up and production would stop. The same logic applies to stents, Uber rides and earthquake bread. A cap doesn't change how scarce something is. It just removes the mechanism that rations it and calls forth more supply.

head: The Fatal Conceit Returns With Computers (and the Man of System)
dek: Ajay says the 20th century taught one bumper-sticker lesson: central planning brings stagnation, because people, not bureaucrats, are the source of innovation.
more: Ajay says the 20th century taught one bumper-sticker lesson: central planning brings stagnation, because people, not bureaucrats, are the source of innovation. Computers and AI keep reviving the planner's dream, a game of whack-a-mole. Amit links this to Adam Smith's 'man of system', who imagines he can move people like pieces on a chessboard. Ajay's counter is that humans are already intelligent agents acting on local knowledge.

head: Capitalism Equals Consent (Not Cronyism)
dek: Capitalism is many people acting voluntarily in positive-sum exchanges, the 'double thank you moment' where buyer and seller each value what they get more than what they give.
more: Capitalism is many people acting voluntarily in positive-sum exchanges, the 'double thank you moment' where buyer and seller each value what they get more than what they give. It is often confused with cronyism, its opposite. What is good for markets is not what is good for big businesses.

head: The episode is framed around Amit's
more: The episode is framed around Amit's 'friend Freddie', who must be kept in the frame and is named after his two heroes, Frédéric Bastiat and Friedrich Hayek. During his teddy-bear tariff example Amit adds, 'No one is better than my Freddy.' At the end he suggests Milton Friedman could be a Freddy too 'if you twist his surname around a bit.'

head: Ajay on conspiracy theories
more: Ajay on conspiracy theories: 'conspiracy theories are the opiate of the asses', because to believe one 'you have to be simple-minded.'

head: Amit on GDP: with government spending counted, you can keep
more: Amit on GDP: with government spending counted, you can keep 'digging up ditches, filling them, digging up ditches, filling them, and the GDP is just growing and growing.'

head: Asked about Deng Xiaoping's legacy, Ajay quotes Zhou Enlai
more: Asked about Deng Xiaoping's legacy, Ajay quotes Zhou Enlai: 'it's too soon to tell.'

head: Ajay names Ken Thompson, main inventor of Unix, as the greatest human of the last 30 years, riffing on the song line
more: Ajay names Ken Thompson, main inventor of Unix, as the greatest human of the last 30 years, riffing on the song line: 'we didn't start the fire, Ken did.'

head: Ajay explains that prices spare us explicit coordination (
more: Ajay explains that prices spare us explicit coordination ('you will play Hamlet and I will play Ophelia'). Amit replies: 'if you ever play Ophelia, I will be happy to play Hamlet. But don't blush.'

head: Ajay voices a pragmatic Chinese entrepreneur cutting deals with the party
more: Ajay voices a pragmatic Chinese entrepreneur cutting deals with the party: 'Chodo yaar, I have to get three party people as my board members. I'll do it... Anyway, I keep my 80%, no?' The fixing has been done. Meanwhile, a Russian billionaire who owns a critical newspaper 'will just experience some accidents, you'll fall out of a window.'

head: Amit on armchair economists: everybody gives gyan on economics, though nobody would give gyan on nuclear physics without studying it.
more: Amit on armchair economists: everybody gives gyan on economics, though nobody would give gyan on nuclear physics without studying it. And 'a physicist who does not believe in gravity is not a physicist I would trust.'

head: The sign-off
more: The sign-off: 'Please like and subscribe. It's a voluntary action. Double thank you moment if you've watched so far.'

head: Joseph Schumpeter called Bastiat
more: Joseph Schumpeter called Bastiat 'the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived'.

head: Oscar Lange's proposal for a central price committee was what Hayek's
more: Oscar Lange's proposal for a central price committee was what Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' argued against. Amit links it back to Bastiat's essay on how Paris gets fed without any central committee.

head: Adam Ferguson's phrase
more: Adam Ferguson's phrase 'the product of human action but not human design', and Adam Smith's 'man of system' who treats society like a chessboard.

head: Ajay calls himself part of the 19th-century tradition of economics, closer to the dreams of Ricardo, Adam Smith and Marx, and finds today's economics
more: Ajay calls himself part of the 19th-century tradition of economics, closer to the dreams of Ricardo, Adam Smith and Marx, and finds today's economics 'a pale shadow of what it can be.'

head: Tycho Brahe Hands His Life's Work to the Man He Detested
dek: Breakthroughs rest on unglamorous data work, and sometimes on a person putting the work above their pride.
more: Before Newton, astronomy ran on poor Greek data and muddled models: the sun circling the earth, and 'pure' circular orbits patched with epicycles. Copernicus put the sun at the centre but still assumed circles, so his model fit the data only slightly better. The breakthrough came from data. Tycho Brahe, a Danish lord at Uraniborg, spent his whole life building the world's best record of planetary movements. Near death, he realised the one person who could make sense of it was Johannes Kepler, whom he truly detested. He handed it over anyway, and Kepler found three simple laws in it: elliptical orbits, equal areas swept in equal times, and T² proportional to R³.
Breakthroughs rest on unglamorous data work, and sometimes on a person putting the work above their pride. Without Tycho's gift there are no Kepler's laws for Newton to explain.
printed: A gift for the man he detested

head: Newton's Plague-Year Lockdown
dek: Sustained focus on one question is the one trait the great breakthroughs seem to share.
more: The childhood version: plague shut down Cambridge, Newton went to live with his grandmother, and in one feverish year he built everything. That meant the three laws of motion, gravity as GMm/r², and calculus. With these first principles he showed that Kepler's laws follow as a consequence. Ajay notes that Newton, like Einstein (who worked on one question from age 16 until special relativity at 21), had an extraordinary ability to concentrate on a single problem. Beyond that, he says, we have little real insight into how genius happens.
Sustained focus on one question is the one trait the great breakthroughs seem to share. The 'lone genius' account is only the first layer of the story.

head: Keynes Opens Newton's Trunks
dek: The tidy textbook Newton lasted only because nobody had read his private papers.
more: When a descendant auctioned off Newton's papers, inherited from a great-grandfather, John Maynard Keynes turned up and paid £9,000 of his own money for a large share. He sniffed that the rest had 'doubtless ended up in America.' He was the first to study them properly and was aghast. Newton had spent his life on alchemy and the Bible, writing about a million words on alchemy and counting letters in scripture in search of the recipe for gold. Keynes's paper 'Newton, the Man' was meant for the 1942 tercentenary of Newton's birth. The war pushed the event to 1946, by which time Keynes had died, so his brother Geoffrey Keynes presented it.
The tidy textbook Newton lasted only because nobody had read his private papers. Primary sources can overturn a whole mythology.
printed: Reason in public, gold at home

head: The Illegal Alchemist Who Ran the Mint
dek: A neat illustration of how far the private person can sit from the public role.
more: In 1404 the British government banned alchemy. Nobody yet knew that base metals can't become gold, and the state couldn't risk anyone debasing the currency and wrecking the monetary system. So Newton's lifelong alchemy research was illegal. Late in life he became Master of the Mint, the equivalent of central bank governor. Amit's verdict: a poacher made gamekeeper.
A neat illustration of how far the private person can sit from the public role. It also shows that England's tolerance let a lawbreaking tinkerer work undisturbed.

head: Boris Hessen: The Marxist Who Explained Newton, Killed by Stalin
dek: A bitter irony: the scholar who showed that freedom and economic ferment produce genius was destroyed by a state that had abolished both.
more: In 1931 the Soviet physicist and philosopher Boris Hessen applied the Marxist approach to history to Newton, challenging the great man theory. He asked what social and economic conditions produce a Newton. Ajay notes that 1931 was still a time when Marxists held real intellectual leadership. Hessen was an outspoken free thinker, and in 1936 he was murdered in one of Stalin's purges, along with millions of others.
A bitter irony: the scholar who showed that freedom and economic ferment produce genius was destroyed by a state that had abolished both.

head: One Ramanujan, Fifty Lost
dek: Genius is common, but the conditions that let it come through are rare.
more: Amit suggests that a modern Newton would be a serial entrepreneur whose first few ventures fail. Ajay replies that the world can be cruel: such a person might simply fall by the wayside. Ramanujan made it only because something went right when he wrote to G. H. Hardy. Ajay suspects India produces about fifty such talents every year and loses most of them to the grind of coaching classes.
Genius is common, but the conditions that let it come through are rare. Every lucky break we celebrate stands for many talents that got no break.

head: Agarkar's Donkey God at Fergusson College
dek: Intellectual daring is not a ratchet. A provincial Indian college in the 1890s allowed irreverence that would be unthinkable there now.
more: In the 1890s, the reformer Gopal Ganesh Agarkar was teaching a biology class at Fergusson College in Pune. He asked: 'If donkeys had a god, what would that god look like?' After a few moments of silence he answered with a gesture. The college was then known as 'the hotbed of atheism.' Amit studied there a century later without knowing any of this, and doubts it could be that kind of place today.
Intellectual daring is not a ratchet. A provincial Indian college in the 1890s allowed irreverence that would be unthinkable there now.

head: Hind Swaraj: Wrong About Almost Everything, Right About One Thing
dek: A useful filter for any thinker: trust the views that come from what they have actually done over the views that are only pronouncements.
more: Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in his early forties. In it he attacks railways, lawyers ('the lawyers have enslaved India') and doctors ('Hospitals are institutions for propagating sin'), and claims that studying European medicine deepens our slavery. He later accepted treatment from European doctors himself. When Amit put these lines to Ramachandra Guha on The Seen and the Unseen and asked how Gandhi could be so wrong about so much yet right about nonviolent resistance, Guha's answer was simple. Gandhi was right about the one thing he had personal experience of, Satyagraha in South Africa.
A useful filter for any thinker: trust the views that come from what they have actually done over the views that are only pronouncements.

head: Gokhale's Parting Instruction: Don't Act, Just Look
dek: Sometimes the best mentoring is an instruction to wait and look before acting.
more: Gandhi first met his hero Gopal Krishna Gokhale in the early 1890s, on a walk around the grounds of Fergusson College. When Gandhi came back to India for good, the ailing Gokhale had read Hind Swaraj and was alarmed by its ideas. He saw a man of great conviction and energy who didn't yet know the country. So he made Gandhi promise to stay out of politics for a year and simply travel and observe. Gokhale died a month later. Gandhi kept the promise, and for reasons Amit can't explain, he did it barefoot.
Sometimes the best mentoring is an instruction to wait and look before acting. Gokhale's year of observation was a gift to a man who acted on instinct rather than study.

head: The Khilafat Alliance: An Accidental Masterstroke
dek: What history later calls strategy is often an accident that happened to work.
more: At the Congress session around 1918–19, nobody paid Gandhi much attention. After World War One the caliphate was abolished in Turkey, and the Ali brothers joined the Khilafat movement to restore it. Gandhi proposed an alliance: they would ask for the caliphate, he would ask for India's independence. Amit calls it utterly incoherent, pairing a demand for a nation-state with a call to restore a pan-Muslim caliphate. Yet at the 1920 session Gandhi went from marginal figure to leader of the Congress. In the movement around him emerged Sardar Patel, C. Rajagopalachari and the young Jawaharlal Nehru.
What history later calls strategy is often an accident that happened to work. Gandhi's rise is Amit's main evidence for calling him a black swan.

head: Jinnah: How a Wounded Ego Remade a Man
dek: Character and convictions are more contingent than we admit. A bruised ego and incentives we barely understand can turn a liberal into the architect of partition.
more: With Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta gone, Mohammed Ali Jinnah was the last great moderate, deeply educated and rational, and expected to lead the Congress. Ram Guha even tells how Jinnah once considered going to South Africa, where he and Gandhi might have become business partners. Gandhi's takeover in 1920 broke him. Jinnah said he was parting company with the Congress and Gandhi: 'I do not believe in working up mass hysteria. Politics is a gentleman's game.' His sense of self badly hurt, he moved towards the two-nation theory and became a different person. Amit traces the partition, and fissures India still struggles with, back to this moment.
Character and convictions are more contingent than we admit. A bruised ego and incentives we barely understand can turn a liberal into the architect of partition.

head: The Atlantic Charter: How Roosevelt Put a Clock on the Empire
dek: Indian independence was shaped as much in Anglo-American bargaining as in the freedom movement.
more: From 1939 Roosevelt knew America had to stand with Britain against Hitler, but isolationism held him back. It had three strands: racist nationalism that was happy to do business with Hitler; exhaustion after World War One and the Spanish flu; and a mistrust of empire going back to America's own revolt against Britain in 1776. Helping Britain could look like propping up Churchill's empire. Between September 1939 and December 1941 the two leaders argued it out, and the result was the Atlantic Charter. America would come to Britain's aid, but there had to be a post-colonial future. American support, including Lend-Lease, came with conditions about India.
Indian independence was shaped as much in Anglo-American bargaining as in the freedom movement. Ajay says this history is well established but badly under-taught in India.

head: The Ascent of Man
dek: Ajay thinks every literate adult in the world should read it.
more: Ajay thinks every literate adult in the world should read it.
What Ajay bought for Amit on their last visit to The White Crow.

head: Newton, the Man
dek: It is the source of the 'last of the magicians' view of Newton, showing the alchemist and Bible scholar behind the rational front.
more: It is the source of the 'last of the magicians' view of Newton, showing the alchemist and Bible scholar behind the rational front.
The paper behind Ajay's 'chapter two' on Newton, written after Keynes studied the papers he bought at auction. Available free as a PDF.

head: Essays in Persuasion
dek: Ajay disagrees with nearly all of Keynes's economics, but sees him as a master writer who knew the world.
more: Ajay disagrees with nearly all of Keynes's economics, but sees him as a master writer who knew the world. 'Everybody should dream of writing like that.'
One of the two Keynes collections Ajay recommends together, mentioned while pointing to the Newton essay.

head: Essays in Biography
dek: Read it as a model of beautiful writing and sharp insight into people, from an economist Ajay argues with but deeply admires.
more: Read it as a model of beautiful writing and sharp insight into people, from an economist Ajay argues with but deeply admires.
The other half of the Keynes pair Ajay recommends.

head: The social and economic roots of Newton's Principia
dek: It challenged the great man theory by tracing Newton to English conditions: freedom, sea power, tinkering.
more: It challenged the great man theory by tracing Newton to English conditions: freedom, sea power, tinkering. Its boldest move was linking capitalism to the world of ideas, which Ajay thinks was ahead of its time.
The 1931 paper behind Ajay's 'chapter three' on Newton, which applies Marxist historical analysis to Newton.

head: Epitaph on Sir Isaac Newton
dek: It sums up in one couplet the myth of the sudden lone genius, which the rest of the chapter complicates.
more: It sums up in one couplet the myth of the sudden lone genius, which the rest of the chapter complicates.
Ajay quotes it twice as the childhood version of Newton: 'God said, Let Newton be and all was light.'

head: The Discovery of India
dek: Ajay sees its picture of India as the story most of us still carry, and as an example of the synthesis that kept India away from a fundamentalist rejection of the West.
more: Ajay sees its picture of India as the story most of us still carry, and as an example of the synthesis that kept India away from a fundamentalist rejection of the West.
Ajay cites it when describing how Gandhi, Tagore, Nehru and Jinnah tried to reconcile the West's success with something at the core of being Indian.

head: The Essays of Paul Graham
dek: 'Just a treasure given to mankind.' They are free, full of insight, and written by someone who also builds things.
more: 'Just a treasure given to mankind.' They are free, full of insight, and written by someone who also builds things.
Amit's example that some of the best thinkers of the last 30 years are builders and capitalists, not only academics.

head: Keynes vs. Hayek rap battles: 'Fear the Boom and Bust' and 'Fight of the Century'
dek: Actors playing Keynes and Hayek rap about monetary policy, with lyrics by EconTalk host Russ Roberts.
more: Actors playing Keynes and Hayek rap about monetary policy, with lyrics by EconTalk host Russ Roberts. Amit calls them absolutely delightful.
Ajay's mention of Keynes reminded Amit of Keynes's great opponent, 'Freddie' Hayek. Ajay hadn't seen them.

head: Conversation and Society (Episode 182 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: An episode on the art of conversation that Amit remembers for its 'magical chemistry.'
more: An episode on the art of conversation that Amit remembers for its 'magical chemistry.'
Mentioned alongside the rap battles, which Russ Roberts wrote.

head: His Dark Materials trilogy
