dek: He calls the books masterpieces and asks people to trust him blindly. Years later, remembering them still makes him smile or tear up.
more: He calls the books masterpieces and asks people to trust him blindly. Years later, remembering them still makes him smile or tear up.
Amit bought it for Ajay at The White Crow, shocked that Ajay had never read Pullman. It came out around the same time as Harry Potter but never became as big.

head: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
dek: Dip in to watch a man engage with the world in writing every day, with unvarnished honesty, like a blogger of his time.
more: Dip in to watch a man engage with the world in writing every day, with unvarnished honesty, like a blogger of his time. Amit says this habit is how Gandhi kept evolving, whether you agree with him or not.
Amit's first Gandhi recommendation: all hundred volumes, free online.

head: Hind Swaraj
dek: Part of our history, and the best evidence for Amit's argument that Gandhi was incoherent on most things but right about nonviolent resistance.
more: Part of our history, and the best evidence for Amit's argument that Gandhi was incoherent on most things but right about nonviolent resistance.
'A thin booklet' that many talk about but few have read. Amit quotes its attacks on railways, lawyers and doctors.

head: The Mahatma and the Poet
dek: Tagore is more reasoned and principled, and right about things like the dangers of nationalism, yet he sees something special in Gandhi's force of will.
more: Tagore is more reasoned and principled, and right about things like the dangers of nationalism, yet he sees something special in Gandhi's force of will. Two great minds disagreeing well.
The letters and debates between Gandhi and Tagore, which Amit calls one of his favourite books about Gandhi.

head: Gandhi Before India
dek: Amit finds the South Africa years, when Gandhi was still forming, especially interesting, and calls Guha a phenomenal historian.
more: Amit finds the South Africa years, when Gandhi was still forming, especially interesting, and calls Guha a phenomenal historian.
The first of Guha's two Gandhi volumes. Amit read it alongside Lelyveld's Great Soul, which covers the same period.

head: Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World
dek: With the first volume, it gives the full arc. Amit calls both books 'just superb.'
more: With the first volume, it gives the full arc. Amit calls both books 'just superb.'
The second of Guha's two volumes on Gandhi.

head: Great Soul
dek: Lelyveld, a fine writer who has written widely for the New Yorker, hinted at a homosexual relationship, partly because the two called each other 'upper house' and 'lower house.' That was shocking enough to get the book banned.
more: Lelyveld, a fine writer who has written widely for the New Yorker, hinted at a homosexual relationship, partly because the two called each other 'upper house' and 'lower house.' That was shocking enough to get the book banned. Guha doesn't accept the theory, but Amit loves the book.
A biography covering Gandhi's South Africa years, including his friendship with Hermann Kallenbach, a German bodybuilder he lived with.

head: The Good Boatman
dek: 'A powerful book of ideas' for anyone who wants to engage with Gandhi's contradictions and multitudes, including themes like women and caste.
more: 'A powerful book of ideas' for anyone who wants to engage with Gandhi's contradictions and multitudes, including themes like women and caste.
At the end of Amit's conversations with Ram Guha, Guha recommended it as the one great book on Gandhi Amit hadn't read. He then read it.

head: Understanding Gandhi, Parts 1 and 2 (Episodes 104 and 105 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: The source of Guha's answer that Gandhi was right about what he had personally experienced.
more: The source of Guha's answer that Gandhi was right about what he had personally experienced. Amit says his other three episodes with Guha are also worth hearing.
The two episodes in which Amit asked Guha why Gandhi was wrong about so much yet right about nonviolence.

head: Luck is All Around
dek: A short, vivid case for how much luck lies behind your existence, and behind everything else's.
more: A short, vivid case for how much luck lies behind your existence, and behind everything else's.
Amit reads its opening paragraph aloud during the discussion of historical accident, calling it probably his favourite first paragraph out of hundreds of columns.

head: A Model That Fits the Data vs. Understanding Why It Works
dek: Kepler's laws fit Tycho's data beautifully but were statistical regularities, like an AI model that works without explaining itself.
more: Kepler's laws fit Tycho's data beautifully but were statistical regularities, like an AI model that works without explaining itself. Newton's achievement was to start from first principles (laws of motion, gravity, calculus) and derive Kepler's laws as a consequence. The same lens explains Copernicus: being right about the sun at the centre wasn't enough while he still assumed circles, so his model was only slightly better and his opponents weren't fools.
printed: First the data, then the why

head: Newton, the Last of the Magicians
dek: Keynes's verdict after reading Newton's papers. Newton stands where magic, superstition and religion give way to reason, and both lived uneasily in him.
more: Keynes's verdict after reading Newton's papers. Newton stands where magic, superstition and religion give way to reason, and both lived uneasily in him. In public he was clean and rational ('I do not make hypotheses'); in private he was a tormented alchemist. Ajay applies this to everyone: we are complicated, with old and new ideas fighting inside us, as in Nehru's line about being a battlefield of ideas.

head: Genius Is Expressed by Conditions
dek: Following Boris Hessen, Ajay argues that Newton grew out of 17th-century England.
more: Following Boris Hessen, Ajay argues that Newton grew out of 17th-century England. Protestant England allowed more free thought than Italy and Spain, where Bruno was burned and Galileo threatened. A century of sea power since the Armada drove optics, telescopes, navigation and machine-building, and the Magna Carta tradition meant Newton could break the alchemy law without ending up in a dungeon. Ajay's metaphor is gene expression: a society that protects mavericks lets its Newtons and Oppenheimers flourish.

head: Capitalism and Ideas Are One Continuum
dek: Hessen's radical point was not separating church and state, which was already accepted, but rejecting the 'Brahminical' view that ideas sit apart from making money.
more: Hessen's radical point was not separating church and state, which was already accepted, but rejecting the 'Brahminical' view that ideas sit apart from making money. Thinkers fuel business, and business brings thinkers hard problems. Researchers who only talk to each other are sterile, and a 'taker' economy run by a one-party state doesn't innovate. Amit adds that thinking and doing are not separate: Bezos, Jobs, Musk, Altman, Paul Graham and the Marginal Revolution economists are thinkers who build. Ajay calls today's regimented education and research business wasteful by comparison.

head: Black Swan or Lottery Winner? The Gandhi Debate
dek: Amit sees Gandhi as a black swan.
more: Amit sees Gandhi as a black swan. His influences (Tolstoy, Ruskin, a dogmatic vegetarian society in London) were random next to the Congress moderates, who read Mill, Bentham and Smith, and his rise came through an accident like Khilafat. Ajay counters that Gandhi drew on the best of Hindu and Jain philosophy and faced the great question of his age, how to reconcile India with the West, much as a child today grows up with AI regulation. In his view, conditions were ripe and someone was bound to emerge.

head: Losing the Battles, Winning the Masses
dek: Amit points out that almost every Satyagraha Gandhi led failed in its immediate aims; only his last one in South Africa was roughly half successful.
more: Amit points out that almost every Satyagraha Gandhi led failed in its immediate aims; only his last one in South Africa was roughly half successful. But each one mobilised ordinary people, which no moderate or extremist leader before him had managed. Judging a movement by its stated demands can miss what it actually achieved.

head: Hindsight Turns the Probabilistic into the Inevitable
dek: Before something happens, many outcomes are possible. Afterwards it is certain, so we invent neat narratives of influence and strategy.
more: Before something happens, many outcomes are possible. Afterwards it is certain, so we invent neat narratives of influence and strategy. Amit suspects even Gandhi's use of the Bhagavad Gita came after his ideas had formed, rather than shaping them.

head: Tacticians vs. System-Builders
dek: Ajay divides men of action into two kinds. Tacticians shift with the wind and judge only by results.
more: Ajay divides men of action into two kinds. Tacticians shift with the wind and judge only by results. System-builders look for a coherent framework, which is why they can admit being wrong. He calls Gandhi a do-it-yourself philosopher who built his system from experience. Amit disagrees: Gandhi was a tactician with a small, rigidly applied set of tactics, and Hind Swaraj is too incoherent to count as philosophy. The question is a good test to apply to any leader.

head: Indian Independence Was Coming Anyway
dek: Both hosts reject the simple story that the Congress fought the British and won freedom.
more: Both hosts reject the simple story that the Congress fought the British and won freedom. Their reasons: colonial empires were already devolving power step by step. 1913 marked the peak of British power and the end of the first globalisation; after it came Europe's 'Great Civil War' of two world wars and the Depression, which reached India within months of the 1929 crash and fed discontent. Britain was broke after WWII, and the Atlantic Charter tied American help to a post-colonial future. The freedom movement shaped the form independence took, not whether it came.

head: Nonviolence as a Strategy Matched to the Opponent
dek: Ajay argues that under French, Belgian or Japanese rule a freedom fighter would quickly have been jailed and killed.
more: Ajay argues that under French, Belgian or Japanese rule a freedom fighter would quickly have been jailed and killed. Gandhi understood that Britain was bound by liberal democracy and the rule of law, so appealing to its decency worked better than Bose's call to take up guns. Gandhi, Nehru and Patel stayed friendly with the British and never demonised them.

head: Be Analytical, Not Reverential
dek: Amit thinks of 'Mohandas Gandhi, not Mahatma Gandhi': a complex, tortured man with much to admire and much to dislike.
more: Amit thinks of 'Mohandas Gandhi, not Mahatma Gandhi': a complex, tortured man with much to admire and much to dislike. He has no patience for either the saint or the villain version. Ajay agrees that taking a great figure's ideas uncritically makes you a devotee, not someone who understands them.

head: Holding Two Opposing Judgments at Once
dek: Both hosts disagree with almost all of Keynes's economics (Hayek is Amit's man) and still consider him one of the most beautiful writers and people who ever lived.
more: Both hosts disagree with almost all of Keynes's economics (Hayek is Amit's man) and still consider him one of the most beautiful writers and people who ever lived. Judging someone's ideas and admiring the person are separate questions.

head: Read to Collect More Dots
dek: Amit is unimpressed by Gandhi's claim, reported by Ram Guha, that he didn't need to read because he could watch the world unfold.
more: Amit is unimpressed by Gandhi's claim, reported by Ram Guha, that he didn't need to read because he could watch the world unfold. Amit calls it a rationalisation. Reading gives you more data points to connect, and reading only one book turns its idea into a hammer for every nail.

head: Luck Is All Around
dek: Amit's column works through the odds against you existing: hundreds of millions of sperm, your parents' own improbable births and meeting, and our species evolving on one planet among trillions.
more: Amit's column works through the odds against you existing: hundreds of millions of sperm, your parents' own improbable births and meeting, and our species evolving on one planet among trillions. Every specific thing is wildly unlikely, yet something is bound to exist, so you are a miracle but not special. Ajay's twist: you are a unique string in DNA's four-letter alphabet, so wake up and do amazing things.

head: Amit opens by telling Ajay he looks like he
more: Amit opens by telling Ajay he looks like he 'escaped from a prison but forgot to take your pajamas.' Ajay's defence: it's getting cold, so he bumped up to a full sleeve.

Ajay's 'it's becoming evening' sets off The Rolling Stones' 'As Tears Go By': 'It is the evening of the day. What's the next line?' 'I want to hear the children play.' 'Brilliant. I'm so proud of you.'

Ajay: 'I'm a card-carrying economist, so in every episode you're gonna suffer some economics.' Amit reports the producer asking where the card is. Ajay: 'This is my card, that I will always play an economics card every time I speak with you.'

head: Ajay slips and
more: Ajay slips and says 'Newton showed up at the auction.' Amit corrects him to Keynes, and Ajay replies: 'Would be nice if Newton showed up.'

head: The papers were auctioned by some
more: The papers were auctioned by some 'nalayak bachcha' (good-for-nothing kid). Keynes complained the rest had 'doubtless ended up in America', which Ajay renders as 'America is like the backwaters where things go to die.'

head: Amit on an alchemist who had broken the law becoming Master of the Mint
more: Amit on an alchemist who had broken the law becoming Master of the Mint: 'like a poacher becoming a gamekeeper.'

head: Newton's million words on alchemy
more: Newton's million words on alchemy: 'That's like the Robert Caro book without the 200,000 words on Jane Jacobs taken out' — a nod to The Power Broker.

head: Epicycles, the…
more: Epicycles, the 'wheels within wheels' that kept orbits circular: Ajay notes this is where the phrase comes from.

head: Alexander Pope's epitaph, as quoted
more: Alexander Pope's epitaph, as quoted: 'Nature and her mysteries lay hidden in the night. God said, Let Newton be and all was light.'

head: Asked how gravity actually works, Newton replied
more: Asked how gravity actually works, Newton replied 'I do not make hypotheses' — which Ajay translates into modern English as 'I do not speculate.'

head: Amit recounts their dinner argument about free will: Amit said there can't be any, Ajay said of course there is, and Amit concluded
more: Amit recounts their dinner argument about free will: Amit said there can't be any, Ajay said of course there is, and Amit concluded 'we are having this argument because we can't help but have it.'

head: VS Naipaul's remark that Gandhi was…
more: VS Naipaul's remark that Gandhi was 'the least Indian of the Indian leaders.'

head: Gandhi, asked by a journalist what he thought of Western civilisation
more: Gandhi, asked by a journalist what he thought of Western civilisation: 'It would be a good idea.'

head: Einstein on Gandhi
more: Einstein on Gandhi: 'Generations to come will scarcely believe that such a man would walk this earth in flesh and blood.' Ajay uses it to focus on the man rather than the outcome.

head: Ajay's contemporary analogy for Europe's self-destruction helping Indian independence
more: Ajay's contemporary analogy for Europe's self-destruction helping Indian independence: 'If Wagner and Russian forces are going to fight it out with each other, it's easier for Ukraine to go free.'

head: Gandhi and Kallenbach called each other
more: Gandhi and Kallenbach called each other 'upper house' and 'lower house', possibly because one decided spending and the other had a veto. Cue the quip 'Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha', followed by the reminder that neither existed then.

head: Amit on Keynes's most famous line
more: Amit on Keynes's most famous line: 'In the long run, we are all dead. So, which of course is undoubtedly true as well.'

head: Ajay to the audience
more: Ajay to the audience: 'When there was a great pandemic, Newton was shipped off in the lockdown, and look what he did with his life. What do you have to show for your lockdown achievements?'

head: Amit's sign-off
more: Amit's sign-off: 'If you didn't like this episode, share this episode with everyone you didn't like, but please share it.'

head: Turning Down a Fresh Nobel Laureate
dek: A person is more than the one thing they are famous for, and you only reach that richer story if a conversation has room to wander.
more: When Abhijit Banerjee won the Nobel with Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer, his publishers at Juggernaut offered him for Amit's podcast that same week, but for only one hour. Amit asked for two or three hours and, when they refused, said no. One hour would have meant the standard questions about RCTs. With more time he could have gone back to the 1960s, when Amit's father studied at Presidency College under Abhijit's father, Deepak Banerjee, and traced Abhijit's path through Presidency, JNU and Harvard.

A person is more than the one thing they are famous for, and you only reach that richer story if a conversation has room to wander. The episode also led to Amit's column arguing that Harvard, the cluster, was what made Banerjee.

head: The $10 Part That Destroyed a $3.2 Billion Shuttle
dek: The lesson is not the cliché that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
more: Michael Kremer's 1993 paper takes its name from the 1986 Challenger disaster. The space shuttle was a $3.2 billion project, and it exploded because a flimsy $10 O-ring failed. Amit used Kremer's paper in a Times of India column to argue that Harvard, more than Presidency or JNU, was decisive in Banerjee's development.

The lesson is not the cliché that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. In interdependent work, small differences in quality multiply into huge differences in output, so excellent people need to be surrounded by other excellent people.

head: Oppenheimer Comes Alive at Göttingen
dek: The same talent can stall in one setting and soar in another. Being among peers of the highest calibre doesn't just teach you, it unlocks you.
more: In school and college Oppenheimer was unhappy and didn't fit in anywhere. He even tried to poison his physics teacher with an apple. Then he went to the University of Göttingen, where Max Born, who coined the term 'quantum mechanics', taught him and Dirac and John von Neumann were his classmates.
The same talent can stall in one setting and soar in another. Being among peers of the highest calibre doesn't just teach you, it unlocks you.

head: A Paper Written Before the Co-Authors Ever Met
dek: Internet-scale collaboration can produce serious work. Ajay still argues that remote teams need periodic in-person rapport, because without it humour gets misread and conversation turns robotic.
more: Ajay, Ila Patnaik and Achim Zeileis, a statistician in Vienna, got talking on mailing lists and realised they were chasing different pieces of a correlated puzzle. They wrote a paper together that Ajay counts among the nicest of his life, using only email and SVN, with no video calls. They met in person only afterwards.
Internet-scale collaboration can produce serious work. Ajay still argues that remote teams need periodic in-person rapport, because without it humour gets misread and conversation turns robotic.

head: Ramanujan Rebuilds 19th-Century Mathematics Alone
dek: Distance from the cluster is a handicap but not a death sentence. Being away from the mainstream can even breed originality.
more: Stuck in a remote corner of Tamil Nadu and cut off from the world's mathematics, Ramanujan did not despair about not being at Cambridge. He set about rebuilding 19th-century mathematics on his own. His breakthrough came when he reached Hardy and connected to the mathematics of the 20th century. Ajay pairs this with the early University of Chicago, whose distance from the East Coast universities fostered independent, unfashionable thinking.
Distance from the cluster is a handicap but not a death sentence. Being away from the mainstream can even breed originality.

head: Anand Versus the Soviet School of Chess
dek: A system that congregates and trains talent builds a knowledge base that lone geniuses must rebuild from scratch.
more: The Soviet Union made chess a state project. Functionary Nikolai Krylenko called for 'a five-year plan for chess' (Stalin later purged him in 1938). Chess was taught in schools like maths, and a shared body of heuristics was passed down by trainers. Devangshu Datta told Amit that Indian players facing East Europeans in the 1980s felt like self-taught HSC maths kids up against postgrads: 'in the post mortem, the opponent would say, oh, my trainer taught us that with this structure you have to play this way. And you'd be like, shit.' Viswanathan Anand grew up in the Philippines, where a TV chess programme set puzzles; he won so often that they asked him to stop entering and offered him all the chess books he wanted. Without Soviet training, he became world champion.

A system that congregates and trains talent builds a knowledge base that lone geniuses must rebuild from scratch. That makes Anand's achievement staggering, and also makes him an outlier rather than a model.
printed: The boy who skipped Soviet school

head: Where Dreams Come to Die and Art Comes to Be Corrupted
dek: Clusters don't only lift talent up. Their incentives and status games can also flatten it, and the homogenising pull of the city can strip away what made someone distinctive.
more: On a Seen and the Unseen episode, Vikram Sathaye told Amit about bright kids from small Maharashtra towns who arrive in Bombay steeped in Vijay Tendulkar and local art forms. Surrounded by shallow industry people, and insecure about being called 'vernie', a year later the same kid meets Vikram at a party and says, 'Dude, how are you doing? Let's go chill.'
Clusters don't only lift talent up. Their incentives and status games can also flatten it, and the homogenising pull of the city can strip away what made someone distinctive.

head: The Reverse Migration from Bollywood
dek: Urbanisation tends to erase dialects and subcultures. Technology and capitalism can now build new congregations that keep them alive.
more: Vinay Singhal built Stage.in as a 'Netflix for Bharat' that streams content in dialects such as Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and Rajasthani rather than in major languages. VCs told him it would never work. He charged Netflix rates, reached around 300,000 subscribers and raised a big funding round. Vinay described a 'reverse migration from Bollywood': Haryanvi creators who once headed to Bombay are coming home, and a Haryanvi industry of around 3,000 people now exists.
Urbanisation tends to erase dialects and subcultures. Technology and capitalism can now build new congregations that keep them alive.

head: Walking Through a Government in Exile
dek: Play-acting statehood is admirable and poignant, but it isn't training for the real thing.
more: In McLeod Ganj, Ajay visited the Tibet Museum, which sits inside the complex of the Central Tibetan Administration. The CTA has a Department of Finance, a Department of Home and other tidy structures. It is funded by donations, has no taxation and no coercive power. Ajay is proud that India has sheltered Tibetan refugees even when it was costly, but he wondered whether this 'wannabe state' could become the core of a future Tibetan government.

Play-acting statehood is admirable and poignant, but it isn't training for the real thing. He contrasts it with de Gaulle's Free French in London, who focused only on freeing France rather than on running ministries.

head: Warsaw's Communist HQ Becomes the Stock Exchange
dek: Having lived through communism, Eastern Europeans wanted to run as far from it as possible.
more: In Warsaw, Ajay heard how, after communism ended, Poland took the Communist Party office, the biggest and most powerful building in the city, and turned it into the stock exchange.
Having lived through communism, Eastern Europeans wanted to run as far from it as possible. That intent, combined with EU membership, helped them build capable liberal democracies.

head: The IBBI Plan That Was Shelved
dek: India knows how to build regulators properly. It hasn't yet learned to give that work the patience it gives to building a bridge.
more: When the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India was being set up, MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain led the writing of a project plan to build a high-quality bankruptcy regulator over two years. It was the closest India has come to building a coercive institution with care. In practice the law was notified anyway, and a handful of people were expected to deliver overnight.
India knows how to build regulators properly. It hasn't yet learned to give that work the patience it gives to building a bridge.

head: The Salt Tax After Freedom
dek: Swapping a foreign ruler for a domestic one doesn't remove the extractive state.
more: Before GST, Amit wrote an essay on Gandhi's Dandi Salt March. What surprises people is that the tax on salt was far higher in independent India than it had been under the British Empire, and Amit suspects it still is under GST.
Swapping a foreign ruler for a domestic one doesn't remove the extractive state. Amit sees India's state as a continuation of the colonial one, designed to rule rather than serve.

head: The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development
dek: It explains with simple multiplication why small differences in skill create huge differences in output and pay, and why the best people cluster together.
more: It explains with simple multiplication why small differences in skill create huge differences in output and pay, and why the best people cluster together.
Amit calls it a seminal 1993 paper and builds Chapter 1 around it.

head: The O-Ring Model (Marginal Revolution University video)
dek: He calls it fantastic and says it explains the model in detail, better than his own on-air summary.
more: He calls it fantastic and says it explains the model in detail, better than his own on-air summary.
Amit admits he may not explain Kremer's model eloquently and points listeners to this video.

head: The Rise of the Creative Class
dek: It argues that growth follows creative congregation: open, diverse cities draw entrepreneurs, artists and gay and lesbian communities, and capital then chases that talent.
more: It argues that growth follows creative congregation: open, diverse cities draw entrepreneurs, artists and gay and lesbian communities, and capital then chases that talent.
Introduced as a theory 'orthogonal' to Kremer's on why talent clusters.

head: What is the New Chinese Currency Regime?
by: Ajay Shah, Achim Zeileis and Ila Patnaik
dek: It is Ajay's example of serious research produced by a team spread across countries.
more: It is Ajay's example of serious research produced by a team spread across countries.
Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's story of collaborating with Zeileis and Patnaik over mailing lists and email.

head: Building the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
dek: Ajay calls it a milestone in India's journey: a real plan for building an organisation that will wield coercive power, even though it was largely ignored in practice.
more: Ajay calls it a milestone in India's journey: a real plan for building an organisation that will wield coercive power, even though it was largely ignored in practice.
The project plan for setting up the IBBI over two years.

head: Essays
dek: It is a chronological look at Orwell the thinker. It is also Amit's cure for writer's block: two or three pieces on any subject and the clarity and rhythm of Orwell's prose 'would free something within me'.
more: It is a chronological look at Orwell the thinker. It is also Amit's cure for writer's block: two or three pieces on any subject and the clarity and rhythm of Orwell's prose 'would free something within me'.
Amit's pick of the week: Orwell's collected essays, not his novels, in a volume arranged chronologically. Ajay seconds it, saying he wants 'to sell that book to everybody'.

head: Politics and the English Language
dek: He calls it 'such a primer on clear writing'.
more: He calls it 'such a primer on clear writing'.
The essay Amit asked every young writer he edited to read.

head: Why I Write
dek: A companion piece to Amit's segment on Orwell, clear writing and the link between writing and thinking.
more: A companion piece to Amit's segment on Orwell, clear writing and the link between writing and thinking.
Linked in the show notes alongside Amit's Orwell recommendation.

head: Reflections on Gandhi
dek: It shows what a beautiful writer and thinker Orwell was: sceptical of sainthood yet fair, and alert to the shrewd, able person inside Gandhi.
more: It shows what a beautiful writer and thinker Orwell was: sceptical of sainthood yet fair, and alert to the shrewd, able person inside Gandhi.
Amit reads aloud a long passage from this late Orwell book review, tying back to the previous episode's discussion of Gandhi.

head: Economical Writing
dek: It teaches how to write about economics, or any complex subject, in clear language for lay readers.
more: It teaches how to write about economics, or any complex subject, in clear language for lay readers. That's exactly what his writing students from sociology or anthropology need, since their fields reward jargon as an insider signal.
Added as a bonus recommendation; Amit calls McCloskey a great economist and great writer.

head: The Elusive Quest for Growth
dek: It's a bit dated but gets the basics right, knocking out the faddish ideas that have damaged development.
more: It's a bit dated but gets the basics right, knocking out the faddish ideas that have damaged development. It leaves you asking what your theory of growth really is, and most development and philanthropy are still gripped by those wrong ideas.
Ajay's pick of the week, building on the O-Ring discussion of development economics.

head: The White Man's Burden
dek: A classic on why the West's efforts to aid the rest have done so much ill and so little good, by a fantastic, clear writer and great thinker.
more: A classic on why the West's efforts to aid the rest have done so much ill and so little good, by a fantastic, clear writer and great thinker.
The one Easterly book Amit has read, mentioned after Ajay's pick.

head: Skeuomorphism and Sticky Conventions
dek: New technology often borrows the look of the old to put users at ease.
more: New technology often borrows the look of the old to put users at ease. Apple's reading app looked like a wooden bookshelf, and sound software shows virtual knobs. Words do the same: we still say 'rolling' with no film cans in sight. Conventions like the QWERTY keyboard stay long after their reason has vanished. Amit thinks there are more harmful versions of this, forms of the past we've outgrown but can't escape. Ajay adds that evolution tuned how fast the mind updates its models, so this stickiness runs deep.

head: The O-Ring Theory of Talent
dek: Kremer's insight is that in complex work, quality multiplies rather than adds.
more: Kremer's insight is that in complex work, quality multiplies rather than adds. In Amit's example, ten people performing at 0.99 produce 9.05; at 0.95, 5.99; at 0.90, just 3.49. A barely visible skill gap becomes a huge output gap, so a 0.99 person can earn two or three times a 0.95 person. The effect is strongest where quality beats quantity (one great novelist beats three mediocre ones) and where a task has thousands of links that must all hold. The result: the best people gain most by clustering with each other.

head: Plug Compatibility Tames Complexity
dek: Mass manufacturing found another answer to the O-Ring problem: precision standardisation.
more: Mass manufacturing found another answer to the O-Ring problem: precision standardisation. A car has 10,000 parts, yet it works because every ball bearing is within tight tolerances. Software does the same with APIs, testable black boxes that 'had better just work'. Where interfaces are defined, people can work apart without talking. Filmmaking is the opposite extreme, with fuzzy, personal relationships among hundreds of people, which is why it needs proximity.

head: Contracting Is Harder Than the Work
dek: Ajay splits creative collaboration into two stages. First comes agreeing who does what, how decisions get made and how resources are shared.
more: Ajay splits creative collaboration into two stages. First comes agreeing who does what, how decisions get made and how resources are shared. Then comes implementation. The first stage needs people who know and trust each other, which is the real magic of hubs like London, New York and Cambridge, Massachusetts. Implementation can then be done remotely, anywhere. Amit adds that meeting online comes with an agenda, while meeting in person allows digressions and banter where new thoughts emerge.

head: Capital Chases Talent: The Creative Class
dek: Richard Florida argues that growth follows creative congregation. Open, diverse cities attract entrepreneurs, artists and gay and lesbian communities.
more: Richard Florida argues that growth follows creative congregation. Open, diverse cities attract entrepreneurs, artists and gay and lesbian communities. Capital follows them, starting a virtuous cycle, or a vicious one where talent leaves. Network effects reinforce it: founders go where the best coders are, and coders go where the startups are. Amit ties this to the 'looking-glass self': we shape ourselves in the reflections of others, so the company we keep shapes who we become.

head: Outliers Don't Disprove the Rule
dek: Ajay argues that Indian middle-class parents overstate how make-or-break clusters are.
more: Ajay argues that Indian middle-class parents overstate how make-or-break clusters are. Books and the internet have changed how people acquire knowledge, and Ramanujan built greatness far from Cambridge. Amit agrees individuals should tell themselves this for morale. But geniuses like Ramanujan and Anand are rare, and many equally gifted people never reached a cluster and stayed invisible. Exceptions inspire; they shouldn't shape policy.

head: In the Humanities, Authenticity Is King
dek: In STEM, problems are universal and you can play a global game from anywhere.
more: In STEM, problems are universal and you can play a global game from anywhere. To understand human societies you have to be inside your subject. Every conversation and scene feeds intuition, so Indian economics is best studied in India. Ajay felt 'a certain emptiness' when abroad and away from his source material. The same logic explains why Hindi films get made in Bombay.

head: Brain Drain Is a Question About Home
dek: Amit reframes the old worry about IIT graduates leaving India. Each of them is making a rational choice and should.
more: Amit reframes the old worry about IIT graduates leaving India. Each of them is making a rational choice and should. The real question is why they have to leave, and what it would take to build centres of excellence here. Right now, he argues, India is chasing good people away, and those who stay do so despite the odds. Policymakers should create the conditions for talent to congregate.

head: The Depth of India's Bench
dek: Inside India, engineers stream from the Hindi heartland to hubs like Bangalore, Pune, Hyderabad and Madras.
more: Inside India, engineers stream from the Hindi heartland to hubs like Bangalore, Pune, Hyderabad and Madras. Ajay notes a remarkable claim he has heard: the US has the world's best engineering workforce and India is now second. The top end of a distribution multiplied by 1.4 billion people produces real critical mass.

head: Cities Homogenise, Technology Can Diversify
dek: Urbanisation is the engine of human progress, but it pressures newcomers to conform.
more: Urbanisation is the engine of human progress, but it pressures newcomers to conform. A Bhojpuri or Maithili speaker who moves to a Hindi-speaking city often drops their dialect so as not to seem 'vernie'. Technology and capitalism can now build virtual congregations, like Stage.in's dialect content, that keep subcultures alive. They can't fully replace in-person meeting, though.

head: Minimum Critical Mass
dek: You don't need a Bollywood-sized agglomeration, but some projects can't happen below a threshold: a movie needs a team of at least 10 to 20.
more: You don't need a Bollywood-sized agglomeration, but some projects can't happen below a threshold: a movie needs a team of at least 10 to 20. Bhopal may lack an engineering culture while Pune has one. Ajay takes the middle road: agglomerations matter and we need each other, but Silicon Valley isn't the only place where ideas can flourish.

head: Sturgeon's Law Versus Incentives for Mediocrity
dek: Ajay counters Amit's critique of Bollywood: 99% of everything is crass and shallow, including Indian and Silicon Valley startups.
more: Ajay counters Amit's critique of Bollywood: 99% of everything is crass and shallow, including Indian and Silicon Valley startups. Amit sharpens his point. The issue isn't that most output is bad. It's that a cluster's incentives can push a genuinely good person into producing bad work.

head: You Can't Rehearse Coercive Power
dek: The Central Tibetan Administration has the trappings of a state but runs on donations, so it is fundamentally a nice organisation.
more: The Central Tibetan Administration has the trappings of a state but runs on donations, so it is fundamentally a nice organisation. Ajay argues that no amount of play-acting prepares you for the poison of coercive power. It may even backfire through 'isomorphic mimicry', lulling people into thinking that departments with the right names mean they are ready to govern.

head: Violent Freedom Struggles Breed Bad States
dek: Most post-colonial states fared badly, and worst where freedom came through armed struggle.
more: Most post-colonial states fared badly, and worst where freedom came through armed struggle. Once unleashed, violence doesn't go away. It changes people and lifts the wrong kind of person to the top, when a decent state needs something like a philosopher king. Gandhi's ahimsa was the 'one simple piece of magic' India got right at the outset.

head: Why Eastern Europe Succeeded and Russia Failed
dek: East Germany inherited West Germany's whole institutional package overnight and flourished, though like north versus south Italy, the regional gap persists.
more: East Germany inherited West Germany's whole institutional package overnight and flourished, though like north versus south Italy, the regional gap persists. The rest of Eastern Europe and the Baltics built institutions from scratch. They wanted to flee communism, and the EU's 20,000 pages of draft laws and treaties kept them from certain mistakes, with Hungary and Poland the laggards. Russia privatised and created markets overnight, with Jeff Sachs among those pushing, but neglected the state. Liberal democracy means constitutionalism, rule of law and checks and balances, not just elections every five years.

head: Build Institutions Like Bridges
dek: India accepts that a bridge takes years of project management before the ribbon-cutting.
more: India accepts that a bridge takes years of project management before the ribbon-cutting. A new regulator like a food safety authority should be treated the same way. It needs organisational design, written processes, staff trained to work within them, IT systems and repeated review of checks and balances. Powers should then be notified in stages, starting with trivial transactions. Launching a coercive agency overnight sends it into permanent firefighting, invites lobbying for favours and attracts the wrong leaders.

head: An Institution's DNA Lives in Its Law
dek: Amit asks whether all institutions inevitably decay. Ajay says no.
more: Amit asks whether all institutions inevitably decay. Ajay says no. Laws either create arbitrary power or create checks and balances. Coercive power is like a nuclear reactor and needs enough 'cladding' around it, after which experience can feed back into steady improvement. Indian laws mostly assume people are good and recklessly confer discretion. Both hosts agree on the goal: a system where even the worst person in power can't do much harm.

head: Beyond the Great Man Theory
dek: When an Indian agency malfunctions, the reflex is to demand a better CEO.
more: When an Indian agency malfunctions, the reflex is to demand a better CEO. Ajay calls this primitive. The real debate, grounded in public choice theory, is about the right checks and balances for each organisation. Amit is gloomier: he sees India's state as designed to rule rather than serve, a continuation of the colonial state that is mighty hard to change.

head: Hope as an Intellectual Project
dek: A century ago, India's chattering classes argued about what free India would look like.
more: A century ago, India's chattering classes argued about what free India would look like. They got the state wrong, assuming it would be led by good people like Gandhi and Nehru, when coercive power attracts the most venal. Ajay sees today as a research and development phase: build the knowledge and community now, so that when the public demands to know why some agency is failing, the answers are ready.

head: Writing Forces Clear Thinking
dek: Clear thinkers tend to write clearly, but the reverse matters just as much.
more: Clear thinkers tend to write clearly, but the reverse matters just as much. Forcing yourself to write clearly exposes holes in your argument and gaps in your knowledge, and can change your mind. Didion said she didn't know what she thought until she wrote it down. Amit paraphrases McCloskey's view that writing is research, not something that follows it. Obscure prose is usually a sign of muddled thinking or insider signalling.

head: Ajay, explaining that some work needs a minimum team size, offers…
more: Ajay, explaining that some work needs a minimum team size, offers 'trivial production projects like some YouTube podcast with an eclectic name, everything is everything' as what you can make with essentially no team.

head: Amit scolds Ajay for hurting their producer Vartika's feelings with talk of tiny teams. Ajay protests
more: Amit scolds Ajay for hurting their producer Vartika's feelings with talk of tiny teams. Ajay protests: 'it's a three-man team and you know we couldn't have made a movie even if we wanted.'

head: On how much time he needs with a guest: Amit asked for two or three hours with Banerjee
more: On how much time he needs with a guest: Amit asked for two or three hours with Banerjee, 'and today of course I would insist on five hours or nothing.'

head: Amit notes that Orwell, like Bastiat, died at 49
more: Amit notes that Orwell, like Bastiat, died at 49, 'which is my age right now. So may I somehow reach the end of December, I'll be very happy.'

head: Young Anand kept winning the puzzle contests on a Philippine TV chess show until, as Amit remembers it, they called and
more: Young Anand kept winning the puzzle contests on a Philippine TV chess show until, as Amit remembers it, they called and said: 'Look, you're winning everything, just stop entering, we'll give you all the chess books you want once and for all.'

head: Devangshu Datta on facing Soviet-trained players: the opponent would explain in the post-mortem that his trainer taught him how to play that structure
more: Devangshu Datta on facing Soviet-trained players: the opponent would explain in the post-mortem that his trainer taught him how to play that structure, 'and you'd be like, shit.'

head: Amit's images for Anand's feat
more: Amit's images for Anand's feat: 'like someone taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and winning the damn thing', or 'winning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket.'

head: Amit's test for academic prose
more: Amit's test for academic prose: 'whenever I read something full of obfuscatory language, I know that person is full of shit.'

head: Ajay turns Orwell's dictum into…
more: Ajay turns Orwell's dictum into 'Podcasts should be like a windowpane.' Amit explains the source: Orwell's line that good prose should be like a windowpane.

head: Ajay: Orwell matters more
more: Ajay: Orwell matters more 'now that we know that history did not end', a nod to the 'end of history' idea. Amit: 'And now that nineteen eighty four is approaching.'

head: Freddy, the plush toy on the table, is named after Amit's hero Frédéric Bastiat and after Friedrich Hayek
more: Freddy, the plush toy on the table, is named after Amit's hero Frédéric Bastiat and after Friedrich Hayek: 'two Freddies, he carries both of them within him.'
'As every Russian schoolboy knows': Ajay's chess-world inside joke for things that seem deep to outsiders but are common knowledge to Soviet-trained kids. The phrase has spread far beyond chess.

head: Sturgeon's Law, cited by Amit
more: Sturgeon's Law, cited by Amit as 'ninety-eight percent of everything is crap'. Ajay's version: '99% of everything is crass, shallow bullshit', whether Bollywood, Indian startups or Silicon Valley.

head: Orwell lines recited from memory by Ajay, describing the mood of the 1930s
more: Orwell lines recited from memory by Ajay, describing the mood of the 1930s: 'It is forbidden to dream again; we maim our hopes or hide them. The horses are made of chromium steel, and little fat men shall ride them.' Amit's reaction: 'Insane memory.'

head: From Orwell's
more: From Orwell's 'Reflections on Gandhi', read by Amit: 'Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent', and that inside the saint 'there was a very shrewd, able person who could, if he had chosen, have been a brilliant success as a lawyer, an administrator, or perhaps even a businessman.'

head: The boss who made people cry, and why they kept coming back
dek: Demanding mentorship hurts at the time and transforms people later.
more: Amit opens by passing on what a former colleague of Ajay's told him. She had worked with Ajay for four years and has spent many years at the UN. She called him a monster who often made her weep, and said this happened to everyone. Yet they all kept returning to work with him, because they learned so much and, above all, learned how to learn. Ajay answered that the most interesting things in life are invisible spillovers that no market transaction captures.

Demanding mentorship hurts at the time and transforms people later. Ajay frames this kind of influence as a positive externality: we are each a linear combination of our influences, and most of the good in the world happens through these unpriced spillovers.

head: How sugar made cigarettes inhalable
dek: This is a hidden link between two great public-health villains. Sugar was more than a parallel addiction to tobacco; it helped make deep inhalation, and so lung cancer, possible at scale.
more: Drawing on Gary Taubes, Amit explains that cigarette smoke was alkaline until 1913, so trying to inhale it made you cough. That year the new Camel brand raised the tobacco's carbohydrate (sugar) content. The smoke turned acidic, became easy to inhale, and became more addictive.
This is a hidden link between two great public-health villains. Sugar was more than a parallel addiction to tobacco; it helped make deep inhalation, and so lung cancer, possible at scale.

head: When experts blamed automobiles instead of sugar
dek: Wrong ideas take hold through institutional silos. Physicians understood hormones but not diet, nutritionists understood diet but not hormones, and nobody yet grasped insulin resistance.
more: As early as 1907, the Bengali physician Kailas Chunder Bose linked rising diabetes to growing wealth under British rule, and early physicians tied diabetes to carbohydrates. Then Elliott Joslin, America's dominant diabetes physician, looked for other causes. In 1925 he claimed automobiles cause diabetes, because people stopped walking and got fat. His ally Harold Himsworth published a now-discredited paper blaming fat. Meanwhile Prohibition pushed Americans from alcohol toward candy, and sugar consumption soared.

Wrong ideas take hold through institutional silos. Physicians understood hormones but not diet, nutritionists understood diet but not hormones, and nobody yet grasped insulin resistance. Once a theory took root, careers were built on it and it became self-protecting.

head: Ancel Keys and the cherry-picked Seven Countries Study
dek: Science advances by testing your hypothesis against the evidence most likely to break it.
more: In the late 1950s, the University of Minnesota researcher Ancel Keys published his famous Seven Countries Study blaming saturated fat for heart disease. He left out countries that could have disproved him, such as France, with its high-fat diet and low heart disease, and Switzerland and Germany. He also ignored that his chosen countries ate a lot of sugar. The American Heart Association argued against him in 1957, but by 1960 he sat on its main panel, and in 1961 it issued low-fat guidelines. Amit says obesity rose from roughly one in seven to one in three Americans over the next forty years.

Science advances by testing your hypothesis against the evidence most likely to break it. When an influential researcher does the opposite and captures the institutions, a whole society can follow bad advice for decades.

head: How dissenters were silenced
dek: An orthodoxy enforced by industry money and social outrage can look like settled science.
more: In 1976 Jean Mayer wrote a New York Times piece on the bitter truth about sugar. Reader's Digest planned to run excerpts, but after the sugar lobby phoned the managing editor, the piece was spiked. Researcher David Kritchevsky, quoted in Nina Teicholz's book, described how fiercely anyone questioning official advice was attacked. In 1977 the US Senate's Dietary Goals recommended low fat and called sugar fine. Teicholz's chart shows the American obesity curve shooting up from around that time.
An orthodoxy enforced by industry money and social outrage can look like settled science. Amit thinks this scandal is bigger than the tobacco lobby's.

head: Chandra Bhan Prasad's pride in his diabetic village elders
dek: The same fact can mean very different things from different vantage points.
more: Ajay asked whether rising sugar consumption was just income elasticity. Amit agreed prosperity plays a part, but noted that Japan, France and Germany grew richer without the same outcome, so culture matters too. He then recalled the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad telling him that obese, diabetic village elders fill his heart with pride. Their grandparents could never have been prosperous enough to get diabetes. Prasad makes a similar point about the ghunghat. Lower-caste women were once barred from wearing it, so a Dalit bride wearing one is exercising a choice she was denied, even though Amit had always seen it as patriarchal oppression.
The same fact can mean very different things from different vantage points. What looks like a health crisis or oppression from one lens can be a marker of hard-won mobility and agency from another.
printed: Blame it on the motor car

head: Poker, COVID and reversing diabetes
dek: Knowing what to do is not the same as doing it. Amit had already gifted The Diabetes Code to friends but was too lazy to act.
more: Five years as a professional poker player, playing 15-hour sessions, took Amit to 105 kg. About five or six years ago he read the books, did keto plus intermittent fasting plus daily running, dropped to 85-86 kg, ran a 10k, and held that weight for a long time. COVID made him sedentary and comfort food took over, one biryani or pizza at a time, until he reached 107 kg. About 18 months before this episode he was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, with an HbA1c of 7.7. Three months on metformin changed little. Then Ajay suggested a continuous glucose monitor (CGM). A slice of toast sent him to 285, while eggs and bacon left a flat line. He moved to keto and then one meal a day, cooking two- or three-course dinners to music between six and eight, and brought his HbA1c down to 5.7.
Knowing what to do is not the same as doing it. Amit had already gifted The Diabetes Code to friends but was too lazy to act. Real-time feedback on his own body is what closed the gap.
printed: Dealt a bad hand at 107 kg

head: The doctor's embarrassed silence
dek: Medical advice is shaped both by outdated training and by the doctor's guess about your willpower.
more: After his diagnosis, Amit's doctor prescribed metformin and the usual drugs. When Amit asked about diet, the doctor looked embarrassed and said only, 'You're a smart man, you know what to do.' Ajay offered a reading of that moment: with non-communicable diseases, doctors act as amateur psychologists, judging a patient's discipline and tailoring advice to what they think the patient will actually do.
Medical advice is shaped both by outdated training and by the doctor's guess about your willpower. If you seem unlikely to change your lifestyle, the default is medication.

head: The friend who swore by oats
dek: Arguments rarely beat conventional wisdom, but seeing your own body's response does.
more: A friend kept insisting oats were healthy and called Amit crazy whenever he cited books and studies against them. Then she wore a CGM. Oats sent her glucose to 280, and eggs the next day left a flat line. She wore it for about a month, changed her lifestyle, and lost 25 kg.
Arguments rarely beat conventional wisdom, but seeing your own body's response does. Personal data persuaded her where citations could not.

head: Three spikes on a mountain
dek: Everyday life smears overlapping signals together and hides cause and effect.
more: While hiking in the hills near Dharamshala, Ajay reached a summit and had a 500 ml bottle of Gatorade, white rice and rajma. He then descended 1,000 metres while wearing a CGM. Normally such a meal produces one blurry, prolonged rise. Because he was burning energy so fast, he instead saw three distinct spikes, each burned off in turn. The Gatorade sugar came first, then the white rice as amylase converted it, and last the rajma's complex carbs.

Everyday life smears overlapping signals together and hides cause and effect. Under the right conditions, here an empty stomach and heavy exertion, the textbook account of how fast different carbs reach the blood becomes clearly visible.
printed: A summit meal in three acts

head: Chess rating as a brain-fog meter
dek: Sugar's cost to clear thinking is real and can be measured. Any consistent daily activity can serve as a personal gauge of how well your mind is working.
more: Amit plays bullet chess on chess.com under a pseudonym as an addict, not to improve, so his rating stays at a stable baseline. On keto it climbs about 150 points. After a cheat day with pizza it drops about 150, and more if he adds a biryani.
Sugar's cost to clear thinking is real and can be measured. Any consistent daily activity can serve as a personal gauge of how well your mind is working.

head: The Case Against Sugar
dek: In Amit's view it gives the best overarching account of the subject.
more: In Amit's view it gives the best overarching account of the subject. It argues that sugar causes diabetes and obesity in the same causal sense that smoking causes lung cancer, through its hormonal effects rather than overeating. It is also the source of the Camel-cigarette history.
The key book among the four Amit asks every viewer to read. He reads its mission statement aloud.

head: The Big Fat Surprise
dek: It shows how the low-fat dogma and the Ancel Keys era misled a generation, and how dissenters were silenced.
more: It shows how the low-fat dogma and the Ancel Keys era misled a generation, and how dissenters were silenced.
One of Amit's four essential books, called excellent and the source of the Kritchevsky quote and the obesity-epidemic chart.

head: The Obesity Code
dek: Part of the core reading that convinced Amit that the standard dietary wisdom on weight is wrong.
more: Part of the core reading that convinced Amit that the standard dietary wisdom on weight is wrong.
One of Amit's four essential books on sugar and nutrition.

head: The Diabetes Code
dek: It lays out how type 2 diabetes can be reversed through diet, which is the premise of the whole episode.
more: It lays out how type 2 diabetes can be reversed through diet, which is the premise of the whole episode.
Amit has gifted it to friends, who raved about it, and says it played a part in his own journey.

head: Sweetness and Power
dek: It provides the historical grounding for understanding sugar's hold on us.
more: It provides the historical grounding for understanding sugar's hold on us.
The first of Amit's four must-read books. He quotes it on refined sucrose's 'peculiar physiological effects'.

head: The Botany of Desire
dek: It captures, better than any statistic, how intoxicating and addictive sugar is from the very first taste.
more: It captures, better than any statistic, how intoxicating and addictive sugar is from the very first taste.
Amit reads Pollan's account of his son Isaac's first taste of cake icing.

head: The perfect treatment for diabetes and weight loss (Jason Fung interviewed by Diet Doctor)
dek: It explains why frequent eating means frequent insulin spikes and moves you toward insulin resistance.
more: It explains why frequent eating means frequent insulin spikes and moves you toward insulin resistance.
Linked while Amit attacks the dietitian advice that small, frequent meals are good.

head: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A 'great TIL' conversation that reframes diabetes and the ghunghat as markers of Dalit mobility and choice.
more: A 'great TIL' conversation that reframes diabetes and the ghunghat as markers of Dalit mobility and choice.
Brought up when Ajay asks whether rising sugar consumption is simply a matter of prosperity.

head: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
dek: It explains why some people defend received wisdom even when the evidence has moved on.
more: It explains why some people defend received wisdom even when the evidence has moved on.
Cited for the phrase 'aggressively conventional minded', one of the sources of resistance to the new nutrition science.

head: FreeStyle Libre Glucose Monitoring System (Reader & Sensor)
dek: It is the CGM that made this whole journey possible.
more: It is the CGM that made this whole journey possible. Ajay's tips: insert it and wait a full 24 hours before initialising for better accuracy, and expect it to differ from finger-prick readings because it tracks the average of the last 5-15 minutes. Amit's tips: calibrate with prick tests for a couple of days, and buy it directly, since services like Ultrahuman use the same sensor. Ajay also asks Abbott to open the API so readings can flow into a Google Sheet.
Ajay's recommendation for the week. He was wearing one on his arm during the episode.

head: The Emergency: A Personal History
dek: Too few people know this history. It shows how horrible the Emergency was, with half the opposition and hordes of journalists jailed, and why democracy must not be taken for granted.
more: Too few people know this history. It shows how horrible the Emergency was, with half the opposition and hordes of journalists jailed, and why democracy must not be taken for granted.
Amit's recommendation for the week. Kapoor is a journalist who lived through those years, and her husband was jailed.

head: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A companion conversation to her book, with someone Amit calls a 'really fine lady'.
more: A companion conversation to her book, with someone Amit calls a 'really fine lady'.
Amit mentions that Kapoor was on his show a few months earlier.

head: Gyan Prakash on the Emergency (Episode 103 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It frames the Emergency as part of the Indian state's centralising DNA, inherited from the colonial state.
more: It frames the Emergency as part of the Indian state's centralising DNA, inherited from the colonial state.
Raised while arguing that the Emergency was not an aberration. Prakash has written another great book on it.

head: Lenin's Tomb: The Last Days of the Soviet Empire
dek: It shows how a society struggles with an authoritarian state and how progress is damaged for a very long time.
more: It shows how a society struggles with an authoritarian state and how progress is damaged for a very long time. It is doubly interesting now because we know what Remnick didn't: Russia was headed back to hell under Putin.
Ajay's book recommendation for the week, on the dying days of the USSR.

head: The Bridge: The Life and Rise of Barack Obama
dek: Full of revealing detail, including the trivia that Obama played poker to network with Democratic Party insiders.
more: Full of revealing detail, including the trivia that Obama played poker to network with Democratic Party insiders.
Amit praises Remnick as one of the great journalists of our time and calls this a great book.

head: Sugar causes disease through hormones, not just overeating
dek: Taubes's argument is that sucrose and high-fructose corn syrup cause obesity and diabetes in the same causal sense that cigarettes cause lung cancer.
more: Taubes's argument is that sucrose and high-fructose corn syrup cause obesity and diabetes in the same causal sense that cigarettes cause lung cancer. The cause is their distinct metabolic and hormonal effects, and the damage builds over decades, possibly passing to the next generation through the womb. Amit links sugar to hypertension, heart disease and possibly cancer, and notes that some researchers call Alzheimer's 'type 3 diabetes'.

head: The addiction we never notice
dek: Sugar acts on the brain's reward centre the way nicotine and alcohol do.
more: Sugar acts on the brain's reward centre the way nicotine and alcohol do. Unlike coffee, which makes you jittery, it gives no warning when you've had too much. And since we are almost never without it, we never feel withdrawal and so never realise we are hooked.

head: Nutrition science lags medicine
dek: A consensus in medicine today is broadly reliable, but nutrition has stood on uncertain ground for a century.
more: A consensus in medicine today is broadly reliable, but nutrition has stood on uncertain ground for a century. Its history includes siloed experts, industry-funded studies and dogmas, such as 'fat causes heart disease' and 'obesity is just calories in versus calories out', that hardened into official guidelines.

head: Three forces keeping the old dogma alive
dek: The first is corporate interest: processed foods hide sugar behind labels like 'no added sugar' and ingredients like concentrated apple juice.
more: The first is corporate interest: processed foods hide sugar behind labels like 'no added sugar' and ingredients like concentrated apple juice. The second is Paul Graham's 'aggressively conventional minded'. The third is self-interested defenders of the status quo, including doctors trained on outdated science. Amit warns that in India, a doctor over forty is likely to give bad advice unless they have kept updating themselves.

head: Type 2 diabetes is reversible
dek: Amit is emphatic that type 2 diabetes is a disease of the diet, not a life sentence.
more: Amit is emphatic that type 2 diabetes is a disease of the diet, not a life sentence. His own HbA1c fell from 7.7 to 5.7 through keto and fasting.

head: Every meal is an insulin spike, so eat less often
dek: Every time you eat, insulin rises, and frequent spikes push you toward insulin resistance and eventually diabetes.
more: Every time you eat, insulin rises, and frequent spikes push you toward insulin resistance and eventually diabetes. That makes 'small frequent meals' bad advice and intermittent fasting a strong lifestyle. Amit suggests that is why fasting shows up in every major religion.

head: Eat the egg yolk
dek: Cholesterol in food is not the cholesterol in your blood. Amit calls the yolk perhaps the healthiest food known to man, and points to Time magazine covers that swung from 'cholesterol is bad' to 'butter is good'.
more: Cholesterol in food is not the cholesterol in your blood. Amit calls the yolk perhaps the healthiest food known to man, and points to Time magazine covers that swung from 'cholesterol is bad' to 'butter is good'.

head: Know thyself: adapt your diet rather than adopt one
dek: Ajay reframes the goal. Instead of following someone's book, start from your own tastes and food culture and adjust them until they work for your body.
more: Ajay reframes the goal. Instead of following someone's book, start from your own tastes and food culture and adjust them until they work for your body. Tools like the CGM make this do-it-yourself approach possible, because different people really are different.

head: Time in range beats a three-month average
dek: HbA1c smears three months of blood sugar into one weighted average. A CGM shows the moment-by-moment pattern, so you can watch for surges and volatility.
more: HbA1c smears three months of blood sugar into one weighted average. A CGM shows the moment-by-moment pattern, so you can watch for surges and volatility. Ajay's target is to stay between 70 and 160 for over 80% of the day, never going below 70.

head: Eating order matters
dek: Carbs on an empty stomach hit the blood fast, the way alcohol does.
more: Carbs on an empty stomach hit the blood fast, the way alcohol does. Eating fibre first, then protein and fat, then carbs slows absorption, so the classic Western meal of salad, main course, then dessert turns out to be ideal. A 20-minute walk after a meal also blunts the spike.

head: Sugar is not just sugar; it matters what it comes with
dek: Ajay tested the same dose of sugar three ways: alone, with fat, and with fat plus spices such as ginger, nutmeg and cinnamon.
more: Ajay tested the same dose of sugar three ways: alone, with fat, and with fat plus spices such as ginger, nutmeg and cinnamon. Each produced a visibly different surge. If you must have sugar, ice cream at the end of a meal, ideally spiced, is the least bad option.

head: White rice and maida are polymerised sugar
dek: Simple starches are one enzyme reaction, via amylase, away from sugar, so 100 g of white rice is not much better than 100 g of sugar.
more: Simple starches are one enzyme reaction, via amylase, away from sugar, so 100 g of white rice is not much better than 100 g of sugar. We have simply normalised them. Ajay says whole grains, dals and skins slow things down, and that oats vary with how heavily processed they are. Amit counters that ultimately all carbs are sugar at some level.

head: Treat the CGM as an annual habit-building project
dek: CGMs are expensive, but you don't need one all the time. Behavioural economics suggests habits form over two to three months.
more: CGMs are expensive, but you don't need one all the time. Behavioural economics suggests habits form over two to three months. So run a rigorous two-to-three-month experiment on yourself each year, then live on the habits it builds.

head: Food is social, so change what you buy
dek: Willpower usually loses to whatever is easy to reach, so change has to happen at the point of purchase.
more: Willpower usually loses to whatever is easy to reach, so change has to happen at the point of purchase. That means talking to the family and friends you eat with. Ajay says it is fine, even advisable, to be 'rude' about eating differently.

head: A calorie is not a calorie
dek: Calorie counts come from burning food in pure oxygen, which is not how the body processes it.
more: Calorie counts come from burning food in pure oxygen, which is not how the body processes it. Taubes argues carb calories drive insulin and fat storage differently from fat calories. The 2023 Corbin et al. study showed that complex carbs reach and feed the gut microbiome, with some measures 8x higher, and the microbes consume part of the energy. That amounted to roughly 200 calories a day of difference on identical-calorie diets.

head: The hydroponics parallel: starving your microbiome
dek: Plants fed simple chemical fertiliser underinvest in their root microbiome and lose nutritional quality and disease resistance.
more: Plants fed simple chemical fertiliser underinvest in their root microbiome and lose nutritional quality and disease resistance. Simple carbs do the same to humans: they are absorbed before reaching the gut, so the microbiome shrivels. Complex carbs travel all the way down and feed it.

head: Doctors as amateur psychologists
dek: For lifestyle diseases, doctors read your character and discipline and tailor their advice to what they think you will actually do.
more: For lifestyle diseases, doctors read your character and discipline and tailor their advice to what they think you will actually do. If they doubt you will change your lifestyle, they default to drugs.

head: The invisible spillovers that markets don't capture
dek: Ajay's answer to the 'you made people cry' charge.
more: Ajay's answer to the 'you made people cry' charge. Markets run on contracts and the 'double thank you' of a transaction, but much of what matters, like mentorship and influence, flows as unpriced positive or negative externalities between people.

head: Read nutrition studies sceptically
dek: Check who funded a study, since the sugar lobby is still powerful, and examine its methodology, starting from a critical default.
more: Check who funded a study, since the sugar lobby is still powerful, and examine its methodology, starting from a critical default. Trust meta-studies over single studies. Applying this to the claim that a glass of wine is good for the heart, Amit asks what it does to the liver, and Ajay adds that studies show the best amount of alcohol is zero.

head: Multivitamins are a five-star buffet
dek: Shruti Jahagirdar's advice, via Amit. Multivitamins give a little of everything but don't meet daily requirements, so work out exactly what you lack, especially on keto, and supplement that specifically.
more: Shruti Jahagirdar's advice, via Amit. Multivitamins give a little of everything but don't meet daily requirements, so work out exactly what you lack, especially on keto, and supplement that specifically.

head: Ajay's ideas for the food industry
dek: First, Indian sourdough makers should label clearly whether multigrain loaves are entirely whole grain.
more: First, Indian sourdough makers should label clearly whether multigrain loaves are entirely whole grain. Second, a product idea: separate whole wheat into maida and the rest, remove about 10 units of the maida, and recombine. The result would be a superior atta with a built-in 10% discount on refined flour.

head: Democracy is not to be taken for granted
dek: Amit argues that the Emergency was not an aberration. India's constitution centralised power enormously, and a dominant state is part of the Indian state's DNA, inherited from the colonial state.
more: Amit argues that the Emergency was not an aberration. India's constitution centralised power enormously, and a dominant state is part of the Indian state's DNA, inherited from the colonial state. Ajay's matching point from Lenin's Tomb is that the rule of law and democratic culture take a very long time to build and are easily damaged.

head: The naming joke that opens the show
more: The naming joke that opens the show: 'We just thought that we could call this show Amit and Shah. Because you know, Amit and Shah. But we're not gonna do that.' (The pun is on a prominent politician's name.)

head: After Ajay answers the…
more: After Ajay answers the 'you made people cry' charge in economics-speak about externalities, Amit says: 'You know, I keep telling my writing students, don't use jargon, don't use jargon. Look what you just did.'

head: On Ajay's line that cheesecake in the fridge ends up inside you, Amit adds…
more: On Ajay's line that cheesecake in the fridge ends up inside you, Amit adds: 'If there is a choice of the cheesecake being inside you and you being inside the cheesecake, please choose the second option. Even if it is hard to imagine and a little bit messy and you'll need a good shower later. Midjourney, here we come... Ajay Shah inside a cheesecake.'

head: Ajay warns that concentrated apple juice is a standard way to sneak sugar into…
more: Ajay warns that concentrated apple juice is a standard way to sneak sugar into '100% fruit' products. Amit: 'I feel jealous of that kind of apple juice because I find it so hard to stay concentrated.'

head: Amit on doctors who call type 2 diabetes irreversible
more: Amit on doctors who call type 2 diabetes irreversible: 'any doctor who tells you type 2 diabetes is a chronic disease and cannot be reversed is a lying quack. Treat him as no better than a homeopathic doctor or an Ayurvedic doctor.'

head: Amit trips over his Obama trivia
more: Amit trips over his Obama trivia: 'Barack Obama was also just like me.' Ajay: 'A basketball player.' Amit: 'I'm not a basketball player. Barack Obama, just like me, was also a poker player.' He then weighs the trade-off: 'You avoid sugar but you get gambling. I don't know which is a bigger evil... I didn't get type two diabetes by playing poker, so we know what the answer to that is.'

head: The sign-off pitch
more: The sign-off pitch: producer Vartika says Ajay needs patterned shirts, since he is down to the plain white ones he wears every day. So Ajay has been telling friends, 'guys, gift me shirts.' Amit: 'We want shirts, but like and subscribe.'

head: Michael Pollan once described Gary Taubes
more: Michael Pollan once described Gary Taubes as 'a Solzhenitsyn of the nutrition world', for taking on nutrition orthodoxy.

head: Pollan in The Botany of Desire, on his son Isaac's first taste of birthday-cake icing, imagined as…
more: Pollan in The Botany of Desire, on his son Isaac's first taste of birthday-cake icing, imagined as saying: 'Your world contains this. From this day onwards I shall dedicate my life to it.'

head: Kailas Chunder Bose, 1907
more: Kailas Chunder Bose, 1907: 'There is not the slightest shadow of a doubt that with the progress of civilization, of high education, and increased wealth and prosperity of the people under the British rule, the number of diabetic cases has enormously increased.'

head: Franklin Roosevelt called the sugar lobby the most powerful interest group he had seen.
more: Franklin Roosevelt called the sugar lobby the most powerful interest group he had seen. Amit: 'This is a man who won World War II in a sense, but couldn't beat the sugar lobby.'

head: Time magazine covers trace the swing in nutrition wisdom, from…
more: Time magazine covers trace the swing in nutrition wisdom, from 'cholesterol is bad news' to 'cholesterol is good news' to 'butter is good'.

head: Amit invokes The Insider, a film about the tobacco lobby, and calls what the sugar lobby did
more: Amit invokes The Insider, a film about the tobacco lobby, and calls what the sugar lobby did 'a far greater scandal'.

head: Amit closes with the ancient maxim
more: Amit closes with the ancient maxim 'know thyself', alongside 'sugar is poison', as the episode's two key messages.

head: 1869: The Year India Was Wired Into the World
dek: Modern India has an earlier birth date than 1947 or 1991: a burst of connectivity, technology and market institutions in the 1860s-70s.
more: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. Before it, ships from London went around the Cape of Good Hope, and having come that far they might as well continue to Calcutta. After it, the route ran through Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea straight to Bombay. In the same years the telegraph arrived, cutting a London-Bombay message to about four hours, and the railroad spread. Britain's Companies Act, Contract Act and Evidence Act reached Bombay within a couple of years of passing in London. The Bombay Stock Exchange opened in 1874. When the American Civil War cut US cotton supplies to Britain, a whole new cotton trade appeared: grown in Gujarat and Maharashtra, shipped through Bombay to London. This first modernisation, matching the first globalisation, lasted roughly from 1869 to 1913.

Modern India has an earlier birth date than 1947 or 1991: a burst of connectivity, technology and market institutions in the 1860s-70s. Ajay thinks Indian history undervalues this period because the nationalists oversold their case. He does not pine for colonial rule, but argues history should be read 'cold and clear.'

head: Malaria, Gin and Tonic, and American Ice
dek: A health problem in India created an industry on the other side of the world.
more: Malaria was a huge problem in India, and the defence was quinine. Quinine was too bitter to take on its own, so it was put into tonic water, and gin and tonic became a popular drink in India. A gin and tonic needs ice, and there were no fridges in the 19th century. So factories making ice sprang up in the American Midwest.
A health problem in India created an industry on the other side of the world. No planner arranged it; trade and prices connected the two. Amit tells it as a parallel to the Civil War cotton boom.

head: India in 1947 Was Freer Than You Think
dek: Good-looking growth numbers can hide deteriorating policy. Ajay's point is that the outcomes looked decent while the inputs were steadily getting worse.
more: Ajay argues that the 1947-62 growth was decent partly because social tension eased. The world war, the freedom-movement strife and Partition were over, and the new Republic, its Constitution and leaders like Nehru and Patel gave the private sector confidence. In 1947 the state intervened only modestly in the economy, the civil service was the best India has ever had, and for a while the current and capital accounts were fully convertible. Then, day after day, restrictions crept in and a vast repressive machinery was built. Amit adds that the roughly five percent growth of this period looks good only against the war years, and terrible against what Korea and Southeast Asia achieved.
Good-looking growth numbers can hide deteriorating policy. Ajay's point is that the outcomes looked decent while the inputs were steadily getting worse.

head: The World Before Passports
dek: Many controls we treat as permanent features of the world are emergency measures that never ended.
more: Before 1914 nobody needed a passport anywhere in the world. Royals wrote letters to each other asking for special treatment for their friends, but ordinary people could simply travel and migrate. Capital controls did not exist until Adolf Hitler introduced them in Germany. In India, restrictions on trade and capital flows began as a British wartime measure in 1939. The Treaty of Versailles included a clause restoring passport-free travel, and international conferences tried to bring it back into the 1960s.
