Soviet Russia blocked every attempt because it did not want its citizens leaving and never returning. Only the European Union has partly restored that old freedom.
Many controls we treat as permanent features of the world are emergency measures that never ended. 'Temporary' wartime losses of freedom tend to become normal.

head: 1962-1977: The Terrifying Years
dek: There was a real chance India would become 'another disgusting authoritarian third world country' or fall into civil war, and the skeptics of Indian democracy nearly looked right.
more: India in 1947 was a bold political experiment: universal suffrage in a country where women's literacy was six percent. Then came the 1962 China war, Nehru's death in 1964, the 1965 war with Pakistan, two droughts in a row, famine, and begging the US for PL 480 food aid. In 1969 the banks were nationalised. The 1971 war was a 'nationalist wet dream' but a huge economic burden. FERA followed in 1973. The glow of the Bangladesh war and Indira Gandhi's big election win soon gave way to double-digit inflation, the JP agitation and the Emergency. Ajay notes Indira was the first Indian prime minister whom political scientists classify as a populist.

There was a real chance India would become 'another disgusting authoritarian third world country' or fall into civil war, and the skeptics of Indian democracy nearly looked right. It is a reminder of how fragile the Indian project was.

head: Book a Scooter for Your Daughter's Wedding
dek: Amit's provocative claim is that Indira's economic regulations did more damage than the Emergency.
more: Amit reads from Shruti Rajagopalan's essay on the Indira years. The 14 largest banks were nationalised overnight by ordinance, along with coal, copper, general insurance and unprofitable textile firms. There were land ceilings and import tariffs above 350%, and the top income tax rate was 97.75%. The underground economy may have grown larger than the formal one. By the late 1970s it was almost impossible to start a business or close a failing one. The joke of the time was to book a scooter for a daughter early, so it would arrive by her wedding. Amit argues Indira did not even believe in this socialism and used it to tilt left against the Congress syndicate.

Amit's provocative claim is that Indira's economic regulations did more damage than the Emergency. They kept millions in poverty for decades longer than necessary and blocked the labour-intensive manufacturing boom that could have come before China's.
printed: The bride wore a waiting list

head: Nehru's Daughter Was Embarrassed to Be a Tyrant
dek: India 'lucked out.' What saved its democracy at the brink was partly one leader's sense of embarrassment, a reminder of how much rested on personal character rather than institutions.
more: Ajay says leaked diplomatic material from the Emergency shows Indira Gandhi was embarrassed about it, and elections were only a matter of time. The 1977 elections were genuinely free and fair, with no intimidation of the opposition and no booth tampering. Amit adds that she expected to win and that Sanjay Gandhi did not want her to call the elections. Ajay replies that it went deeper: Nehru's daughter could not bear becoming one more third-world tyrant.
India 'lucked out.' What saved its democracy at the brink was partly one leader's sense of embarrassment, a reminder of how much rested on personal character rather than institutions.

head: Three Gujaratis Turn the Ship in 1977
dek: 1991 did not come out of nowhere. Growth picked up more than a decade earlier, once the private sector began cautiously trusting the state again.
more: When the Janata Party came to power, three Gujaratis became the country's most powerful people: Morarji Desai as Prime Minister, H.M. Patel as Finance Minister and D.T. Lakdawala as Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission. They were not radical reformers, but they had a feel for how markets work. Lakdawala had always been at Bombay University, away from Delhi's leftist economics establishment. Patel had grown up near Amul and the cooperative movement. Through small measures and key staffing choices they began liberalising. Careful econometrics dates India's growth acceleration to 1979. Indira, on her return, carried these ideas further, and Rajiv Gandhi pushed them more.
1991 did not come out of nowhere. Growth picked up more than a decade earlier, once the private sector began cautiously trusting the state again.

head: The Reformers Who Came Home With No Promise
dek: Big reforms rest on years of unrewarded preparation by people who chose to stay and build knowledge and community without knowing whether it would ever pay off.
more: Ajay compares two dark periods, 1927-47 and 1962-77. In the first, the British Empire looked invincible, yet the best Indians wrote longhand letters and debated rival ideas of India, so that people and documents were ready in 1947. In the second, many gave up and emigrated. Ajay was born in 1966 and has heard these stories from his elders. Manmohan Singh came back after his PhD with no idea he would become finance minister or prime minister. Amit adds that Singh asked his young mentee Montek Singh Ahluwalia to come back and work for the country, and Montek left the World Bank. Vijay Kelkar 'felt obliged to say, Yes, sir, I will,' and packed his bags. Amit also notes that just as we remember those who fought, we should remember those who didn't. Ajay says most people were simply appeasers.
Big reforms rest on years of unrewarded preparation by people who chose to stay and build knowledge and community without knowing whether it would ever pay off.

head: Two Speeches a Week at the Finance Ministry
dek: Reform is partly a matter of signalling. The private sector invests when it can see a competent crew with a plan running the state.
more: When Ajay worked in the Ministry of Finance, every joint secretary in the Department of Economic Affairs gave two conference speeches every week. The aim was to show the private sector capable people, a way of thinking, a vision and a strategy that it would respect.
Reform is partly a matter of signalling. The private sector invests when it can see a competent crew with a plan running the state.

head: How 26/11 Emptied the Finance Ministry
dek: A chain of accidents can derail an economy only if the system depends on who happens to sit in which chair.
more: In 2008-09, with Manmohan Singh as PM and P. Chidambaram as Finance Minister, India was handling the global financial crisis well. Then came the Mumbai terror attacks. Home Minister Shivraj Patil could not cope, so Singh moved Chidambaram to Home, leaving Finance empty. Singh would have held it himself, but he needed an operation that January. Sonia Gandhi then installed Pranab Mukherjee, a socialist of the Indira-era 1970s, who brought in policies like retrospective taxation. Around 2013 he was 'kicked upstairs' to the presidency and Chidambaram returned. The Jaitley ministry after 2014 initially showed continuity, but from 2015 politics took over. Ajay rejects the bad-luck explanation. He argues the post-1991 reformers never rebuilt the oppressive laws and machinery of government, so everything depended on a few individuals.

A chain of accidents can derail an economy only if the system depends on who happens to sit in which chair. Ajay's lesson is to put freedom into laws and organisation design, not to rely on good people.

head: Sixteen Stormy Days
dek: It shows how India's First Amendment, unlike America's, was a blow against free speech.
more: It shows how India's First Amendment, unlike America's, was a blow against free speech. The Lok Sabha debates reveal Nehru taking illiberal positions to silence his communist rivals, a great statesman undone by hubris.
Amit's formal recommendation at the end of the episode; the author has been on The Seen and the Unseen twice.

head: Nehru: The Debates that Defined India
dek: Nehru's exchanges with Jinnah, Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Patel show fine minds disagreeing in good faith.
more: Nehru's exchanges with Jinnah, Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Patel show fine minds disagreeing in good faith. Amit finds this spirit of 'assume goodwill', lost in today's public discourse, deeply inspiring.
Amit's second end-of-episode recommendation.

head: The 1991 Project
dek: Its chronicles and oral histories of the reformers 'fill me with awe'.
more: Its chronicles and oral histories of the reformers 'fill me with awe'. They show that the reformers had worked for a decade and a half before 1991.
Mentioned while discussing the people who prepared the 1991 reforms over many years.

head: Planners vs. Searchers in Foreign Aid
dek: It frames the key contrast: planners impose top-down answers, while searchers find solutions by trial, error and feedback.
more: It frames the key contrast: planners impose top-down answers, while searchers find solutions by trial, error and feedback. Amit says poverty has only ever been ended by searchers.
Easterly's paper for the ADB, quoted at length to explain what went wrong after 1947.

head: India in the Persianate Age
dek: A 'magnificent book' adored by the Mughal historians on Amit's show. It suggests global trade shifted power to the port cities and weakened the centralised empire.
more: A 'magnificent book' adored by the Mughal historians on Amit's show. It suggests global trade shifted power to the port cities and weakened the centralised empire.
Cited via Vinay Sitapati's argument about pre-colonial India.

head: Half-Lion: How PV Narasimha Rao Transformed India
dek: Background on Narasimha Rao, who staked his political capital on the 1991 reforms.
more: Background on Narasimha Rao, who staked his political capital on the 1991 reforms.
Amit calls Sitapati's books great while introducing his idea that 1991 was a 're-liberalisation'.

head: Jugalbandi: The BJP Before Modi
dek: Same enthusiasm for Sitapati's work as an interpreter of post-Independence political history.
more: Same enthusiasm for Sitapati's work as an interpreter of post-Independence political history.
Named alongside Half-Lion as Sitapati's other great book.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: It sets out the first principles of state capacity, public administration, law, freedom, market failure and regulation.
more: It sets out the first principles of state capacity, public administration, law, freedom, market failure and regulation. Ajay says the 1991-2011 reformers lacked this knowledge, which left their reforms fragile.
Amit calls it a 'great book'; Ajay explains why he and Kelkar wrote it (first edition 2019, second 2022).

head: Manmohan Singh's PhD thesis
dek: One of the first works to challenge India's 'export pessimism'. It argued that exporting depends on incentives, prices and exchange rates, not on anything peculiar to India.
more: One of the first works to challenge India's 'export pessimism'. It argued that exporting depends on incentives, prices and exchange rates, not on anything peculiar to India.
Ajay on how Indian economic thinking began to change.

head: The End of History?
dek: Captures the post-Cold War sense that liberal democracy might be history's endpoint.
more: Captures the post-Cold War sense that liberal democracy might be history's endpoint. Amit warns that the 70% of Indians born after the Berlin Wall fell have forgotten those lessons.
Invoked when discussing the collapse of the Soviet Union.

head: Pandit's Mind (1951 Time magazine cover story on Nehru)
dek: A vivid portrait of how Fabian socialism and Brahminical contempt for the 'Banya' shaped Nehru's distrust of capitalism.
more: A vivid portrait of how Fabian socialism and Brahminical contempt for the 'Banya' shaped Nehru's distrust of capitalism.
Amit quotes it to trace Nehru's intellectual influences.

head: India's Founding Moment
dek: Helps explain the elite, top-down mindset of the founders, who felt they had to teach the nation how to think.
more: Helps explain the elite, top-down mindset of the founders, who felt they had to teach the nation how to think.
Cited for the idea that the Constitution was a pedagogic exercise.

head: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (Episode 283, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A deeper look at Rao and the reformers around him.
more: A deeper look at Rao and the reformers around him.
Mentioned while discussing the long preparation behind 1991.

head: Freedom as Consent
dek: Amit reframes freedom as consent. Two questions usually kept apart, 'how should I live?' and 'how should the state relate to society?', get the same answer: consent is everything and coercion is the ultimate evil.
more: Amit reframes freedom as consent. Two questions usually kept apart, 'how should I live?' and 'how should the state relate to society?', get the same answer: consent is everything and coercion is the ultimate evil. You can arrive at this from first principles (individual autonomy, John Locke's self-ownership) or from consequences (freedom produces the best outcomes). He also flags the 'grand liberal paradox': to protect our rights we need a state, and the state itself takes some of those rights through taxes and its monopoly on violence.

head: The World Is Positive-Sum
dek: Our brains evolved in scarce, tribal times, so we assume one person's gain is another's loss.
more: Our brains evolved in scarce, tribal times, so we assume one person's gain is another's loss. But in every voluntary exchange both sides gain, so more exchange means more total wealth. Angus Maddison's charts show world GDP exploding around 1800 with industrialisation and trade. Nitin Pai's estimate is that after 1991, each 1% of GDP growth lifted about three million Indians out of poverty, so 300-400 million in all. That makes freedom a humanitarian issue, not just an economic one.

head: Spontaneous Order
dek: We tend to assume anything complex and beautiful must have a designer.
more: We tend to assume anything complex and beautiful must have a designer. Amit suggests religion itself may be an example of this delusion. Yet languages, economies, societies and natural selection all emerge without a central planner. In Adam Ferguson's words, they are 'the products of human action and not human design.'

head: Planners vs. Searchers
dek: William Easterly's distinction. A planner thinks he already knows the answers and treats poverty as an engineering problem.
more: William Easterly's distinction. A planner thinks he already knows the answers and treats poverty as an engineering problem. A searcher admits ignorance, sees poverty as a tangle of political, social, historical and institutional factors, and finds solutions by trial, error and feedback. Firms in markets and politicians accountable to voters are searchers. Ajay sums it up as 'discovery, not design.'

head: Freedom Breeds Effervescence
dek: People can survive under unfreedom, even in a concentration camp. But once individual agency is taken away, a society stops thinking and creating, and art, science and business fall into dull despondency.
more: People can survive under unfreedom, even in a concentration camp. But once individual agency is taken away, a society stops thinking and creating, and art, science and business fall into dull despondency. A poor country needs the opposite: a bubbling of optimism, invention and new businesses, and that only comes from freedom.

head: India's 'Golden Age' GDP Was an Illusion
dek: Pre-industrial India had a large share of world GDP only because it had good weather, agriculture and a huge population.
more: Pre-industrial India had a large share of world GDP only because it had good weather, agriculture and a huge population. Output per person was abysmal everywhere then. Ajay warns against nostalgia: old India had extreme poverty and cruelty, little political development and no rule of law.

head: 1991 as Re-Liberalisation
dek: This is Vinay Sitapati's argument, relayed by Amit. Before 1947 the port cities were already plugged into global trade, and Richard Eaton suggests such trade shaped power in India even earlier.
more: This is Vinay Sitapati's argument, relayed by Amit. Before 1947 the port cities were already plugged into global trade, and Richard Eaton suggests such trade shaped power in India even earlier. So the real break with the past was Nehru's Fabian socialism and central planning, and 1991 was a return to openness rather than its invention.

head: The Three Centralising Impulses of 1947
dek: Amit sees a constant tug of war between state and society. In 1947 three forces pushed towards the centre.
more: Amit sees a constant tug of war between state and society. In 1947 three forces pushed towards the centre. Politically, the country seemed to be falling apart, so leaders wanted the centre to hold. Socially, Ambedkar saw villages as dens of localism and caste and wanted a transformative constitution; Madhav Khosla calls it a pedagogic exercise. Economically, Nehru distrusted profit and capitalists. Amit sympathises with all three, but thinks elites erred in believing a liberal society could be imposed from above.

head: Failure by Intensification
dek: The tragedy of Indian socialism was not being wrong but refusing to correct course.
more: The tragedy of Indian socialism was not being wrong but refusing to correct course. Some of the smartest people available met each failure with more controls. Ajay blames the Indian intellectual class as a whole, seduced by state power and the Soviet model, for creating the climate in which Nehru's and Indira's excesses could happen.

head: Export Pessimism Was About Incentives
dek: Indian elites once believed India could never export. Manmohan Singh's thesis argued that exports depend on prices, incentives and exchange rates.
more: Indian elites once believed India could never export. Manmohan Singh's thesis argued that exports depend on prices, incentives and exchange rates. Change came slowly. In 1947 India, with Gandhi, Tagore, Ramanujan and Nehru, had more intellectual capital than any other poor country, so East Asia racing ahead was deeply embarrassing. That shock pushed the best of the elite, like Vijay Kelkar who started out leftist, back to first principles.

head: Private Sector Confidence Drives Growth
dek: Growth comes from the private sector committing its time, its children's careers and its money to building firms.
more: Growth comes from the private sector committing its time, its children's careers and its money to building firms. That happens when business feels optimistic and safe about where India is heading. Growth follows changes in this mood, which is why small reforms in 1977 showed up as faster growth by 1979.

head: The Four Elites Compact
dek: Every country has four elites: political and bureaucratic, business, intellectual, and cultural.
more: Every country has four elites: political and bureaucratic, business, intellectual, and cultural. They need a working bargain. From 1991 to 2011 the bargain was this: the state was full of 'landmines', but when business hit one, someone competent listened and often fixed it. That fell apart as the state's deeds fell short of its words. Ajay's summary statistic: there was less freedom in 2010 than in 2000, and less in 2020 than in 2010.

head: Institutions Over Individuals
dek: The post-1991 reforms left the oppressive machinery of government intact.
more: The post-1991 reforms left the oppressive machinery of government intact. Ajay says the laws of 2008-09 were more oppressive than those of 1991. Good people ran an old apparatus better, but never rebuilt it, so one reshuffle could derail everything. His counterexample is the US under Donald Trump, where much of government carried on as usual because its institutions have quality of their own. Real reform means writing freedom into laws and designing better organisations.

head: Dig In Without Promise of Reward
dek: In both 1927-47 and 1962-77, India's prospects looked hopeless. The best people stayed, built knowledge and built community, without any guarantee of power or success.
more: In both 1927-47 and 1962-77, India's prospects looked hopeless. The best people stayed, built knowledge and built community, without any guarantee of power or success. When the openings came in 1947 and 1991, they were ready. Amit links this to Lincoln's line about spending most of your time sharpening the axe.

head: Freedom Is Not Inevitable, and Neither Is Despair
dek: Promising beginnings can turn ugly: Deng's 1978 opening led to today's China, the fall of the USSR led to today's Russia, and Weimar's freedom led to Nazi Germany.
more: Promising beginnings can turn ugly: Deng's 1978 opening led to today's China, the fall of the USSR led to today's Russia, and Weimar's freedom led to Nazi Germany. But the reverse also happens. Germany and Japan, once called inherently obedient or militaristic, became 'beautiful countries.' Be cautious, never complacent, and keep thinking and talking.

head: Why Scandinavia Doesn't Refute Free Markets
dek: People point to Nordic welfare states as proof that freedom isn't needed.
more: People point to Nordic welfare states as proof that freedom isn't needed. Amit's answer has two parts. First, these countries remain very free for starting and running businesses and for personal and social life. Second, they became rich while they were essentially free markets, and could afford welfare only after reaching a high standard of living.

head: Amit opens by explaining that a young cat is mewing in the background, because
more: Amit opens by explaining that a young cat is mewing in the background, because 'it sounds like the wailing of all the dispossessed and the hungry and the starving through these many, many years of India's tormented journey.'

head: Around 2008 Amit pitched a book called…
more: Around 2008 Amit pitched a book called 'Freedom After Midnight', a play on Lapierre and Collins's Freedom at Midnight, arguing that 1947 brought only political freedom. He never wrote it 'because I'm a lazy bum', and the New India Foundation rejected the proposal anyway.

head: Ajay lists the dangers of the 1940s, including
more: Ajay lists the dangers of the 1940s, including 'one minor character, Subhash Chandra Bose, threatening armed conflict in India.' Amit objects, and Ajay retracts: 'Fine. So scratch the Subhash Chandra Bose.'

head: Ajay praises the EU for restoring passport-free movement
more: Ajay praises the EU for restoring passport-free movement 'between France, Germany, and Belgium and UK. Oh, scratch that, not UK.'

head: On planners who answered every failure with more controls, Ajay says they insisted
more: On planners who answered every failure with more controls, Ajay says they insisted 'the floggings will continue until the morale improves.'

head: After a toilet break while recording with Amit, Vijay Kelkar pointed a finger and said he had one piece of advice. Amit braced for great wisdom
more: After a toilet break while recording with Amit, Vijay Kelkar pointed a finger and said he had one piece of advice. Amit braced for great wisdom: 'Every time you pass a toilet, enter it.' Amit: 'So that is, you know, the wise passing on their wisdom to younger folks.'

head: Amit, on the Janata reformers coming from outside Delhi
more: Amit, on the Janata reformers coming from outside Delhi: 'Maybe India's next intellectual revolution can happen far from Delhi in lonely Karjat.' Ajay: 'The further away you are from power, the more clearly you see.'

head: Ajay is pleased that viewers are often left wondering
more: Ajay is pleased that viewers are often left wondering, 'Do you guys agree on this or do you guys disagree on this?' Amit closes by telling him that since he brought no recommendations, he owes double next week.

head: Nehru to J.R.D.
more: Nehru to J.R.D. Tata: 'Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.'

head: Time magazine, 1951, on Nehru
more: Time magazine, 1951, on Nehru: 'Beatrice and Sidney Webb, the godparents of Fabian socialism, are in a truer sense his creators than Vishnu and Shiva.' The piece also describes his contempt for the 'Banya civilization' of the capitalist West.

head: Harold Laski's influence on Nehru
more: Harold Laski's influence on Nehru: John Kenneth Galbraith said Laski was at the centre of Nehru's thinking, and Ramachandra Guha quoted an unnamed wit saying that at every cabinet meeting 'there was an empty seat and Harold Laski sat on it.'

head: P. Chidambaram's verdict, quoted by Amit
more: P. Chidambaram's verdict, quoted by Amit: 'India suspected capitalists, it suspected the profit motive, and it tried to nail it down, block it, and thought that all growth would come from government planning.' By the late 1980s, Korea was a miracle economy and India 'a stagnant slow trot.'

head: Abraham Lincoln's line, as Amit quotes it
more: Abraham Lincoln's line, as Amit quotes it: 'If I have six hours to cut a tree, I'll spend the first five sharpening the axe.' Amit applies it to the reformers who prepared for years before 1991.

head: Adam Ferguson's description of spontaneous order
more: Adam Ferguson's description of spontaneous order: 'the products of human action and not human design.'

head: Abbé Faria and the whisper that unfroze him
dek: Big, frightening moments shrink when you treat them as a pile of vegetables to chop.
more: Amit retells a story Jerry Pinto told him on The Seen and the Unseen. José Custódio de Faria was born in 1756 in Candolim, when Goa was a Portuguese colony. His father was a priest and his mother a nun; they joined the church after having him and separated. A child prodigy famous for his sermons, he was invited as a teenager to speak before the Queen of Portugal in Lisbon. On stage, facing the queen, the royalty and his father, he froze. His father leaned forward and hissed in Konkani, 'Kaator re bhaaji': these are all vegetables, cut the vegetables. Faria later left India after getting caught up in a rebellion, took part in the French Revolution, and was jailed in solitary confinement on an island. There he remembered his father's words, built a mental framework and became one of the fathers of hypnotism. Dumas named a character in The Count of Monte Cristo after him.

Big, frightening moments shrink when you treat them as a pile of vegetables to chop. The same mantra got Faria through a royal hall and a prison cell. Ajay adds that Lisbon was then one of the great cities of the world, so the pressure on the boy would have been enormous.
printed: The boy who froze before a queen

head: The pottery experiment
dek: You get something right by getting it done repeatedly. Iteration beats planning, which is why Amit tells writers to treat the first draft as the block of stone they will later carve.
more: A group was split in two. One half had a week to make a single pot and could spend it researching and planning: reading books, taking courses, working out in theory what makes a perfect pot. The other half was told to make as many pots as they liked and just start. The best pots came from the second group.
You get something right by getting it done repeatedly. Iteration beats planning, which is why Amit tells writers to treat the first draft as the block of stone they will later carve.

head: Ali Abdaal's slow first 1,000 subscribers
dek: Creators overestimate the short term and underestimate the long term. Everyone is bad at the start, so anyone who needs early validation will quit before they ever get good.
more: When Ali Abdaal reached a million subscribers, he showed a graph of his growth. It took him half a year, 26 weeks of two videos a week, to reach his 50th video and his first thousand subscribers. His advice to new YouTubers is to make two videos a week for two years, about 200 videos, and not look at the metrics until then. Amit tells Ajay to listen carefully because this applies to their show.
Creators overestimate the short term and underestimate the long term. Everyone is bad at the start, so anyone who needs early validation will quit before they ever get good.

head: Why Everything is Everything took a year to launch
dek: It is easy to pass off procrastination as preparation. The hosts still disagree on this, and the disagreement is the lesson: you need both standards and momentum.
more: By August 2022 in Udaipur, Amit and Ajay were sure they would do the show and were debating names. Episode 1 arrived more than a year later. Ajay says the delay came from their dreams of quality: a messy, jugaad-style start didn't meet the bar. Amit disagrees. He grants Lincoln's line about spending most of your time sharpening the axe, but says they weren't sharpening anything. He was simply procrastinating. What got it moving was a chance brainstorm with their producer friend Vartika.
It is easy to pass off procrastination as preparation. The hosts still disagree on this, and the disagreement is the lesson: you need both standards and momentum.

head: India Uncut: 8,000 posts of thinking aloud
dek: Writing a lot in public, without fear of being imperfect, is how you build skill.
more: Around 2003-04 Amit started the blog India Uncut, which became hugely popular. He posted about five times a day and wrote around 8,000 posts in five active years. He never worried about getting any of them perfect. A lot of that writing would embarrass him now, but he says it was the journey that made him a better writer and thinker.
Writing a lot in public, without fear of being imperfect, is how you build skill. The embarrassing early work is part of the training, not a failure.

head: The athlete who ran in the rain
dek: Talent is not only an inborn gift. It can simply be the stubbornness to show up when every excuse is available.
more: Amit remembers an interview from the early 2000s with a top sportsperson. It sounded very Dravid-esque but wasn't Dravid, and Amit has failed to track it down. Asked about his greatest talent, the athlete said: he runs every day at five, and on the morning when he has a cold, has already met the year's goals, has a holiday coming up, it is raining and he doesn't feel like it, he still gets up and runs.
Talent is not only an inborn gift. It can simply be the stubbornness to show up when every excuse is available.

head: The trap of things coming easily
dek: Being labelled smart early can quietly stunt you. Effort is what drives improvement, so praise kids for how hard they try, not for how clever they are.
more: Amit admits, with some regret, that for much of his life he leaned on his supposed intelligence. Things came easily: an exam others studied 20 hours for, he could prepare for in 20 minutes. He calls this a trap. You never learn to put in effort, so you struggle when the harder task arrives, and the sense of entitlement means you don't work as hard as you should.
Being labelled smart early can quietly stunt you. Effort is what drives improvement, so praise kids for how hard they try, not for how clever they are.

head: A number painted on his forehead
dek: Early labelling hurts both groups. The 'talented' stop running as hard, and everyone else gets written off.
more: Ajay says India labels children smart or dumb at an early age, often based on mathematics. He was the lucky child who happened to blossom at the right age, and everyone started painting a number on his forehead. He has seen how harshly this sorting treats everyone else. He and Nitin Pai are planning to write 'heretical things' about the IIT JEE exam.
Early labelling hurts both groups. The 'talented' stop running as hard, and everyone else gets written off. Coming from someone who benefited from the label, the criticism carries weight.

head: The one habit Ajay is glad he built
dek: A focused life is mostly about cutting things out. Fewer decisions and less clutter leave room for what matters.
more: Asked by Amit which habit he is glad he built, Ajay says he has organised his whole life around one goal: more hours each day to read. He keeps getting rid of mundane tasks, avoids having to decide about unimportant things and lightens everyday chores, all to make time to read and think.
A focused life is mostly about cutting things out. Fewer decisions and less clutter leave room for what matters.

head: The notes behind the Ukraine episode
dek: Deep expertise isn't crammed in the week before. It comes from years of following your curiosity down rabbit holes and organising what you find.
more: During his Roam Research demo, Amit opens the page for his Seen and the Unseen episode with Ajay on Russia and Ukraine. Ajay had prepared it chapter by chapter, with detailed notes, links and a list of sources at the end, 'like a good academic'.
Deep expertise isn't crammed in the week before. It comes from years of following your curiosity down rabbit holes and organising what you find.

head: Gautam John's one-hour phone window
dek: You can choose how your attention is divided. Choppy scrolling makes for a choppy mind, so a hard boundary is a practical defence.
more: Amit's friend Gautam John once had a rule that he looked at his smartphone, for anything other than calls, only between five and six in the evening. Messages sent at other times would simply wait. He also uses only Signal, not WhatsApp.
You can choose how your attention is divided. Choppy scrolling makes for a choppy mind, so a hard boundary is a practical defence.

head: Dravid on Tendulkar
dek: Measuring yourself against others drains energy. A purpose aimed at becoming your own best self lasts longer.
more: Ajay attended a talk where Rahul Dravid said he never thought about Sachin Tendulkar and only tried to be the best Rahul Dravid he could be. Ajay uses it while arguing that a life built around showing off markers to others is a poor operating system.
Measuring yourself against others drains energy. A purpose aimed at becoming your own best self lasts longer.

head: Who will win the Nobel?
dek: Prizes reward people playing a particular game. Someone driven by curiosity rather than credentials may be brilliant and still choose not to play it.
more: Amit sometimes asks friends which Seen and the Unseen guest is most likely to win a Nobel Prize. The standard answer is Karthik Muralidharan, who is clearly on that track. Amit's own rule is to name the most brilliant person he knows, which is Ajay. When he told Ajay this, Ajay said it wouldn't happen because he isn't on that track. Amit sadly agrees: Ajay has defined his purpose differently and is playing a different game.
Prizes reward people playing a particular game. Someone driven by curiosity rather than credentials may be brilliant and still choose not to play it.

head: Donald Knuth's finished software
dek: Most software is 'rubbish layered on rubbish', always being torn up and rebuilt.
more: Donald Knuth spent his life polishing TeX, a professional typesetting system used to set many great books. Now old, he says TeX is finished: it needs no new features and has no recorded bugs. The code is open, and he asks only that anyone who builds on it after he's gone call it something else, because 'this is my Taj Mahal'. When someone does find a bug, Knuth sends them a cheque, and people frame it and hang it on the wall.
Most software is 'rubbish layered on rubbish', always being torn up and rebuilt. Knuth shows that a piece of software can actually be finished.
printed: A Taj Mahal made of code

head: Atomic Habits
dek: The best book on productivity he has read. Much of what he knows about productivity comes from it, and it led him to many other books.
more: The best book on productivity he has read. Much of what he knows about productivity comes from it, and it led him to many other books. If you read only one book on the subject, start here.
Amit's main recommendation of the episode. He also quotes it in the 'habits are everything' section.

head: Thomas Frank's YouTube channel
dek: Another creator who started small and built himself up by practising what he teaches.
more: Another creator who started small and built himself up by practising what he teaches. Good for working out which tools and ways of thinking suit you.
Recommended together with Ali Abdaal as the channels Amit followed while trying to understand productivity.

head: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
dek: Children praised for being intelligent did worse later and sometimes cheated.
more: Children praised for being intelligent did worse later and sometimes cheated. Children praised for effort kept improving. Useful for parents and for how you talk to yourself.
The study behind Amit's 'don't be it, just do it' section.

head: How to Enhance Performance & Learning by Applying a Growth Mindset
dek: Amit calls it a great episode of a podcast that is excellent on the whole.
more: Amit calls it a great episode of a podcast that is excellent on the whole. An accessible way into the growth-mindset research.
How Amit came across the Mueller and Dweck study.

head: Building a Second Brain
dek: The brain is a messy, impressionistic tool for retaining knowledge. Forte's idea of using technology as a second brain addresses the fact that we lose most of what we take in.
more: The brain is a messy, impressionistic tool for retaining knowledge. Forte's idea of using technology as a second brain addresses the fact that we lose most of what we take in.
Raised after Roam, as the bigger idea behind note-taking tools.

head: GNU Emacs
dek: A mature editor with a fully programmable interface. A few hundred lines of Lisp let you build your own productivity world on top of it, and thousands of existing extensions mean you don't start from scratch.
more: A mature editor with a fully programmable interface. A few hundred lines of Lisp let you build your own productivity world on top of it, and thousands of existing extensions mean you don't start from scratch.
Ajay's answer to Amit's wish for a do-everything Swiss army knife, and again in his Unix recommendation.

head: Unix and the command line
dek: After 40 years around computers, he considers it the most productive and powerful environment there is.
more: After 40 years around computers, he considers it the most productive and powerful environment there is. Small tools are strung together to do any task. Unix runs under Macs, Chromebooks, Android, Kindle and Linux, and he sees it as a philosophy as much as software.
Ajay's recommendation of the episode, making up for skipping one the week before.

head: TeX
dek: A professional typesetting system used for many great books. Its author considers it finished and it has no recorded bugs, a rare level of craftsmanship in software.
more: A professional typesetting system used for many great books. Its author considers it finished and it has no recorded bugs, a rare level of craftsmanship in software.
Ajay's example of how mature the Unix toolchain is.

head: Getting Things Done
dek: Named as the classic of the productivity-tools-and-procedures tradition, which Ajay questions as too managerial.
more: Named as the classic of the productivity-tools-and-procedures tradition, which Ajay questions as too managerial.
Ajay brings up GTD ('do, defer, delegate') as part of the productivity-techniques world. Amit recalls it is a David Allen book.

head: The Count of Monte Cristo
dek: It has a character named after Abbé Faria, which links the episode's mantra to classic literature.
more: It has a character named after Abbé Faria, which links the episode's mantra to classic literature.
Mentioned at the end of the Faria story.

head: Born a Muslim
dek: He points to her sentence about her grandfather shelling pine nuts all day to reward the children as a model of showing rather than telling.
more: He points to her sentence about her grandfather shelling pine nuts all day to reward the children as a model of showing rather than telling.
The book whose chapter-by-chapter notes Amit uses to demo Roam.

head: Being Muslim in India (Episode 216, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls it a great episode. It shows what his note-taking process produces.
more: Amit calls it a great episode. It shows what his note-taking process produces.
The episode with Ghazala Wahab that the Roam notes were prepared for.

head: Song of Myself, 51
dek: The source of 'we contain multitudes', Amit's excuse for offering advice that contradicts itself.
more: The source of 'we contain multitudes', Amit's excuse for offering advice that contradicts itself.
Amit invokes Whitman before contradicting his own first piece of advice.

head: The God Delusion
dek: It sets up Amit's argument that we are all stupid about almost everything.
more: It sets up Amit's argument that we are all stupid about almost everything.
Show-notes link for the line Amit attributes to either Hitchens or Dawkins, that believers are atheists about every religion but their own.

head: The Art of Clear Writing
dek: Many of the episode's habit and iteration ideas come from what he teaches his writing students.
more: Many of the episode's habit and iteration ideas come from what he teaches his writing students.
The writing course Amit keeps drawing on for examples: first drafts, 200 words a day, verbs over adjectives.

head: Kaator Re Bhaaji: cut the vegetables
dek: The episode's mantra. However grand or frightening a task is, it comes down to the next concrete piece of work, done routinely.
more: The episode's mantra. However grand or frightening a task is, it comes down to the next concrete piece of work, done routinely. Stop staring at the audience and start chopping.

head: Getting it done vs getting it right
dek: Every project involves a trade-off between finishing and perfecting. Amit leans towards finishing.
more: Every project involves a trade-off between finishing and perfecting. Amit leans towards finishing. The first draft is a brain-dump, like the block of stone Rodin started with before The Thinker. Getting it right comes from getting it done again and again, or as Vinay Sitapati puts it, never let perfection be the enemy of production.
printed: Get it done, then get it right

head: You suck at the start, so ignore validation
dek: Everyone begins badly. If you need early feedback to keep going, you will quit before you improve.
more: Everyone begins badly. If you need early feedback to keep going, you will quit before you improve. Creators overestimate what happens in the short term and underestimate the long term, so keep going without checking the numbers.

head: Your uniqueness is your edge
dek: Chasing gaps in the market, trends or the algorithm erases what makes you different.
more: Chasing gaps in the market, trends or the algorithm erases what makes you different. Do what you love and keep repeating it.

head: Iteration needs a sense of quality
dek: Ajay's counterpoint. Repetition only helps if you feel which way is uphill.
more: Ajay's counterpoint. Repetition only helps if you feel which way is uphill. Otherwise you can stay bad forever. He calls the celebration of 'jugaad' a fancy name for accepting shoddy work. Push standards ('no, this ain't good enough'), but don't let perfectionism paralyse you.

head: Don't do it, just be it
dek: A schedule-only habit ('read 7-8pm daily') breaks by day three and then damages your self-image ('I'm not a reader').
more: A schedule-only habit ('read 7-8pm daily') breaks by day three and then damages your self-image ('I'm not a reader'). Instead, decide who the best version of you is ('when I'm bored, I pick up a book, not the phone'). Once you own that identity, the habits follow, and one missed day means nothing.

head: Verbs matter, adjectives don't
dek: Praising traits ('you're so intelligent') creates entitlement and fragility, and in the Mueller-Dweck study such children did worse and sometimes cheated.
more: Praising traits ('you're so intelligent') creates entitlement and fragility, and in the Mueller-Dweck study such children did worse and sometimes cheated. Praising actions ('you tried, you persisted') keeps people improving. Talk to children about effort, persistence and habits, not cleverness or looks.

head: Show, don't tell
dek: In writing, a vague adjective like 'a loving grandfather' says little.
more: In writing, a vague adjective like 'a loving grandfather' says little. A concrete action brings the person to life. Amit's example from Ghazala Wahab's book is a grandfather who spends the day shelling pine nuts for his grandchildren.

head: Habits are the whole game
dek: Put a hundred writers in a room. Their goals won't tell you who is good, but their processes and habits will.
more: Put a hundred writers in a room. Their goals won't tell you who is good, but their processes and habits will. Habits compound like interest. Set targets small enough to survive a busy day, like 200 words a day rather than 1,000, because a missed big target starts a 'mujhse nahi hoga' (I can't do this) spiral. A gym membership doesn't build muscle; going does.

head: One habit at a time, two to three months each
dek: Ajay's method, drawn from his experience with a glucose monitor. Building a habit takes about two to three months of focused monitoring before it runs on autopilot.
more: Ajay's method, drawn from his experience with a glucose monitor. Building a habit takes about two to three months of focused monitoring before it runs on autopilot. You can't take on six at once. After that, keep half an eye on it to make sure it hasn't faded, then move to the next.

head: No one is watching you
dek: The deepest anxiety is what others think. Amit only realised in middle age that people are absorbed in their own lives.
more: The deepest anxiety is what others think. Amit only realised in middle age that people are absorbed in their own lives. Social media makes it worse by setting your real self against everyone else's projected self. Drop the comparison and work towards your own best version.

head: We are all stupid
dek: Borrowing the argument that believers are atheists about every religion but their own, Amit notes that each of us knows only a handful of things well.
more: Borrowing the argument that believers are atheists about every religion but their own, Amit notes that each of us knows only a handful of things well. That calls for humility about ourselves and for not judging others by the narrow skills we happen to value. As he puts it, you cannot test fish on climbing trees.

head: People blossom at different rates
dek: Ajay says age-sorted classrooms, where every child gets the same curriculum and exams at the same age, are an industrial-revolution idea.
more: Ajay says age-sorted classrooms, where every child gets the same curriculum and exams at the same age, are an industrial-revolution idea. Educators know people develop in different areas at different speeds. The aim should be to make the most of each person rather than attach a label and treat it as destiny.

head: Curiosity and endurance, not talent
dek: Ajay calls 'talent' one of the most harmful words. The real superpowers are curiosity and endurance, fuelled by purpose.
more: Ajay calls 'talent' one of the most harmful words. The real superpowers are curiosity and endurance, fuelled by purpose. Practical goals like a job, a paper or money are weak fuel because once you reach them you are left asking what next. Since the Greeks, we have known that meaning comes from being part of something bigger than yourself, and simple goals use only about ten percent of a person.

head: The Louis Vuitton bag of credentials
dek: Ajay's name for a life organised around status markers: the famous university, the top journal, the festival book talk, the Paris trip to show off.
more: Ajay's name for a life organised around status markers: the famous university, the top journal, the festival book talk, the Paris trip to show off. He calls this a poor operating system because it doesn't engage the mind. In research, he sees 'journal orientation', channelling curiosity into getting published, as toxic because it switches curiosity off. His own path has been dropping these distractions to stay connected to the core.

head: Thirty years of the same year
dek: Ajay argues that years alone don't build experience. Writing an eleventh paper like the first ten, or living the same life repeatedly, isn't growth.
more: Ajay argues that years alone don't build experience. Writing an eleventh paper like the first ten, or living the same life repeatedly, isn't growth. What changes a year is curiosity, endurance and willingness to challenge the status quo, which is why people who prefer to keep things as they are are at a disadvantage.

head: The form of your tools shapes your thinking
dek: A day of reading a physical book sets one rhythm of mind; a day of scrolling and swiping sets a choppier one, with shorter attention.
more: A day of reading a physical book sets one rhythm of mind; a day of scrolling and swiping sets a choppier one, with shorter attention. Roam's nested, linked structure made Amit think in a more structured way. How you take in and organise information is not neutral.

head: A second brain
dek: The brain is a messy, impressionistic tool and poor at holding knowledge.
more: The brain is a messy, impressionistic tool and poor at holding knowledge. Taking Tiago Forte's idea, Amit argues for using technology to store and organise what you learn, because otherwise most of it slips away. Whether you use Roam, Obsidian or Org Mode matters less than having the habit.

head: Old, mature tools are often the best
dek: Ajay rejects the fashion for the newest thing.
more: Ajay rejects the fashion for the newest thing. Tools that have kept passionate users for decades, like Emacs and TeX, built by great thinkers and polished over years, are usually higher quality than most current software.

head: The Unix philosophy
dek: Many small tools, each easy to chain together, combined to do any task.
more: Many small tools, each easy to chain together, combined to do any task. Ajay sees it as a way of thinking about computers and the world, not just a system. In his telling the same set of ideas led to TCP/IP, the internet and the web, which is why he names Ken Thompson, whose values and taste he credits for it, the greatest man of the last fifty years.

head: Ajay opens the episode
more: Ajay opens the episode: 'we are at the brink of a great moment in merchandising where the slogan just do it is going to be overpowered by the slogan Kaator Re Bhaaji.' The hosts are wearing Kaator Re Bhaaji t-shirts made by Amit's friend Narendra Shenoy.

head: Amit's dramatic scene-setting in Lisbon
more: Amit's dramatic scene-setting in Lisbon: 'an August gathering, though I don't know if it was August', with royalty 'in their breeches and their gowns, with magnificent smiles and frowns', plus a stern 'Don't interrupt the story' to Ajay.

head: Ajay dates Faria's birth in 1756
more: Ajay dates Faria's birth in 1756 as 'before the Battle of Plassey', and Amit replies, 'There you go.'

head: In the pottery experiment, the planning group gets to take online courses in…
more: In the pottery experiment, the planning group gets to take online courses in 'the art of clear pottery', a nod to Amit's writing course, The Art of Clear Writing.

head: Amit describing a dying reading habit
more: Amit describing a dying reading habit: 'somebody is wrong on the internet, and obviously I have to correct them', after which you decide you're 'a Netflix kind of person, or if I'm adequately gregarious... a Netflix and chill kind of person.'

head: Amit on owning your identity as a reader: at friends' houses
more: Amit on owning your identity as a reader: at friends' houses 'the first thing I will check out is their bookshelves. Only then will I say hello to them. I don't do this, by the way.'

head: Amit on no one watching you
more: Amit on no one watching you: 'No one is taking screenshots and waiting to put it on Twitter to shame you, or actually in my case, they are.'

head: After Amit's first slogan, Ajay
more: After Amit's first slogan, Ajay says: 'Very well, Amit. Now contradict yourself.' Amit replies, 'I will contradict myself for we contain multitudes, as the great Walt Whitman once said.'

head: Rodin and The Thinker: he didn't conjure it from thin air
more: Rodin and The Thinker: he didn't conjure it from thin air but 'edited the block of stone', which is Amit's picture of a first draft.
Ajay: 'the problem with practical goals is that you'll actually achieve them.' Amit: 'It's like the dog that chases a car and finally catches it and whatcha gonna do then.'

head: A line Amit attributes to either Christopher Hitchens or Richard Dawkins
more: A line Amit attributes to either Christopher Hitchens or Richard Dawkins: believers are atheists about the thousands of other religions, which he turns into 'we are all stupid'.

head: Ajay mentions GTD and Amit
more: Ajay mentions GTD and Amit replies, 'You're scaring the shit out of me. What is GTD?'

head: Ajay dislikes the word productivity because
more: Ajay dislikes the word productivity because 'it's too much of a managerial thing. It's too much Taylorism for me.'

head: After Ajay criticises academics chasing
more: After Ajay criticises academics chasing 'pubs', Amit says: 'it is not only academics who want pubs. I was once in Europe, it was a hot sunny day, beer peena tha, main pub dhoondh raha tha' (I wanted a beer, I was looking for a pub).

head: Amit's fantasy of building one app to replace Roam, Notion, Final Draft and Scrivener
more: Amit's fantasy of building one app to replace Roam, Notion, Final Draft and Scrivener: 'maybe I can do it one day and I'll get GPT-4 or GPT-5 to code it for me.'

head: Donald Knuth calls TeX
more: Donald Knuth calls TeX 'my Taj Mahal' and sends cheques to anyone who finds a bug. The finders frame them instead of cashing them.

head: Amit after Ajay's Unix tribute
more: Amit after Ajay's Unix tribute: 'What does a Marathi programmer say to another Marathi programmer when he finds a flaw in a computer program? Bug, bug. So anyway, bug is Marathi for see.'

head: Amit teasing Ajay for skipping last week's recommendation
more: Amit teasing Ajay for skipping last week's recommendation: 'You weren't prepared, which is a great flaw in your productivity processes, after all these things that you say.'

head: Amit calls the YouTube audience
more: Amit calls the YouTube audience 'gentle readers', and Ajay approves: 'Good old-fashioned 19th century speak.'

head: Norway Invented Salmon Sushi
dek: Dishes that feel ancient and authentic are often recent accidents of trade.
more: Salmon sushi did not exist until the 1980s. Norway was harvesting more salmon than it could store and needed export markets, so it sent Bjorn Erik Olsen to Japan. The Japanese objected that the salmon was too pink and not red enough, and local salmon was associated with parasites. An advertising campaign about Norway's pure waters failed. As a last resort, Olsen offered the food company Nichirei thousands of tons of salmon at a very cheap price on the condition that it be sold as sushi. It took off. Amit says this was the point at which sushi became a global dish, because mild salmon sushi suited Western palates. Ramen, he adds, is also relatively recent.
Dishes that feel ancient and authentic are often recent accidents of trade. Here a Norwegian storage problem ended up popularising Japanese food around the world.

head: Frederick the Great's Forbidden Potatoes
dek: A crop that is humble and hard to see can be a defence against plunder.
more: Ajay starts from James C. Scott: grain is calorie-dense, storable, transportable and easy to seize, so armies roaming Europe's wars stripped villages of it. The young Frederick the Great noticed that villages growing potatoes survived better. The crop grows underground, looks dirty and unimpressive, and peasants left it in the soil and dug it up as needed, so armies didn't bother taking it. As king, he pushed potato cultivation, which sometimes shaped the outcomes of his later wars. Peasants ignored his royal order to grow the suspect nightshade. In a story Ajay says may be apocryphal, Frederick then planted potatoes in heavily guarded royal gardens and told the soldiers to look away when people came to steal them.
A crop that is humble and hard to see can be a defence against plunder. And making something look forbidden can be a stronger incentive than ordering people to do it.
printed: Guard it, and they will steal

head: The Invasion of the Cavendish Banana
dek: Scale first flattens diversity. Mature markets and cheap technology can later make room for variety again.
more: Retelling Vikram Doctor: India, with hundreds of banana varieties, gave bananas to the world. In Latin America they were reduced to one dominant strain, the yellow Cavendish, which Amit calls dull and tasteless. It won on economies of scale and shelf life. Now it has been sent back to India, and Doc laments that indigenous bananas are dying out. Pushpesh Pant makes the same complaint about weddings, where every buffet has a Punjabi stall and a chowmein stall. Yet Amit says he no longer worries. Homogenisation comes with the first burst of markets, but deeper markets and technology now support a long tail, as Stage.in shows for Haryanvi and Bhojpuri.
Scale first flattens diversity. Mature markets and cheap technology can later make room for variety again.
printed: The banana that ate the rest

head: Semolina Upma Was a Wartime Compromise
dek: Dishes we call traditional often come out of a shock, here war, supply shortages and women's time.
more: Krish Ashok's theory: one of several reasons more women worked and more girls went to school in South India is that the South ate rice. Rice is cooked in one batch, while rotis demand hours of labour every day. During a rice shortage (Amit thinks around WWII and the Japanese invasion of Burma), orders came from above telling the South to eat more wheat, backed by promotion campaigns. Women who didn't want to spend all day making rotis found a compromise, a form of wheat that cooks like rice: semolina. That gave us upma.
Dishes we call traditional often come out of a shock, here war, supply shortages and women's time. Food choices are bound up with gender and labour economics.

head: Cow Dung Shaped Indian Cuisine
dek: Something as mundane as fuel can shape a whole cuisine. Even religious reverence can rest on material circumstances.
more: An insight from Vikram Doctor: the main cooking fuel in old India was cow dung, which gives a low, slow flame. So Indian cooking was built around boiling. Tandoors and frying arrived with the Mughals, and fried food in India is relatively recent. Amit adds that this fuel role is another reason the cow is venerated.
Something as mundane as fuel can shape a whole cuisine. Even religious reverence can rest on material circumstances.

head: Why Bombay Restaurants Were Bad (and FM Radio Too)
dek: High fixed costs push producers toward the median taste. When entry gets cheaper, the experimental and the niche can survive.
more: Five years earlier, Vikram Doctor told Amit that Bombay restaurants were bad because rents were so high that nobody could risk a niche or experimental menu. Everyone played safe with Udupi joints and paneer butter masala. Amit saw the same logic in Indian FM radio. Licences cost hundreds of crores and political news wasn't allowed, so stations had to play Bollywood to the lowest common denominator. No station would have aired The Seen and the Unseen or an economist chatting with an essayist. Podcasting changed that.
High fixed costs push producers toward the median taste. When entry gets cheaper, the experimental and the niche can survive.

head: His Mother's Osaman Isn't on the Internet
dek: Recipes that live only in someone's hands vanish unless captured. Ajay frames this as preservation, not nostalgia: save the knowledge, then keep innovating with it.
more: Ajay is half Kutchi and half Kathiawari, and notes that many Gujaratis wouldn't understand an authentic Kathiawari conversation. A small subset of Kutchis make a dal called Osaman. He has searched the whole internet for his mother's version and cannot find it. He and his sister plan to film her making it, and he asks producer Vartika on air to help. Some of the physical motions she makes while cooking can't be described in words.
Recipes that live only in someone's hands vanish unless captured. Ajay frames this as preservation, not nostalgia: save the knowledge, then keep innovating with it.

head: Vinay Singhal Had to Learn Two Languages
dek: Hindi has steamrolled dialects like Haryanvi, Maithili and Bhojpuri. Long-tail technology can restore dignity to them, not just preserve them.
more: Vinay Singhal grew up speaking Haryanvi in a Haryana village. When he moved to a town school in ninth standard, he had to learn English from scratch. When he moved to a big city, he had to learn Hindi. Today Stage, his platform for Haryanvi and other dialects, is reversing that pressure. Kids come to him with tears in their eyes saying they no longer feel ashamed of their language.
Hindi has steamrolled dialects like Haryanvi, Maithili and Bhojpuri. Long-tail technology can restore dignity to them, not just preserve them.

head: The Tagore Estate's Fly in Amber
dek: Freezing a creator's work cuts it off from the recombination that keeps culture alive.
more: Rajeswari Sengupta told Ajay that after Rabindranath Tagore's death, the heirs who controlled his intellectual property policed it strictly. They demanded that his works be performed exactly as they were in his time. Ajay calls this a tragedy. He adds that although he's no friend of rap, surely there should be a Rabindra rap sangeet. Amit replies there surely is, and points out that Shakespeare, never wrapped in cotton wool, has been reworked by everyone from David Gilmour to the rapper Akala.
Freezing a creator's work cuts it off from the recombination that keeps culture alive. Reverence that forbids reinterpretation slowly kills the thing it reveres.

head: The Indianness of Indian Food (Episode 95 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls Vikram Doctor the world's best food writer and describes the episode as tremendous.

more: Another of Amit's conversations on where Indian food comes from.

head: Against the Grain

more: Amit calls it a magnificent book and a masterpiece that everyone should read, along with every other book Scott has written.

head: Caesar and Cleopatra
dek: Source of the line about the barbarian who mistakes his tribe's customs for the law of nature.
more: Source of the line about the barbarian who mistakes his tribe's customs for the law of nature. It sums up the episode's case against ethnocentrism.
Ajay quotes Shaw's Caesar after the Bade Ghulam Ali Khan story.

head: Early Indians
dek: Uses genes of living people to reconstruct thousands of years of history, which Amit finds mind-blowing.
more: Uses genes of living people to reconstruct thousands of years of history, which Amit finds mind-blowing. It traces how we came from Africa, the migrations into India, and how caste endogamy set in about 2,000 years ago. Amit says it contains fundamental truths.
The first of Amit's three book recommendations for the episode.

head: Early Indians (Episode 112 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Source of his realisation that India's migrant groups mixed for thousands of years before endogamy locked in.
more: Source of his realisation that India's migrant groups mixed for thousands of years before endogamy locked in.
Amit's conversation with the author.

dek: Source of the contrast between the Han Chinese as one large population and India as thousands of small ones.
more: Source of the contrast between the Han Chinese as one large population and India as thousands of small ones.
Cited while discussing caste endogamy.

more: Explores how maintaining endogamy requires controlling female sexuality, which drives female seclusion.
Mentioned while explaining how caste endogamy affects women's lives.

head: Sonnet 18
dek: Shakespeare was never wrapped in cotton wool, so everyone has reworked him, which is how culture should work.
more: Shakespeare was never wrapped in cotton wool, so everyone has reworked him, which is how culture should work.
Amit's counterexample to the Tagore estate.

more: Shows Shakespeare turned into hip hop. Amit says culture is a party: mix karo, dance karo, enjoy karo.
A rap rendition of Sonnet 18 at about the five-minute mark of the linked video.

head: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants
dek: Reads India's past through living languages. Migrating men married local women, so a boy spoke his mother's tongue as a toddler and switched to the men's language later.
more: Reads India's past through living languages. Migrating men married local women, so a boy spoke his mother's tongue as a toddler and switched to the men's language later. Amit also cites its insights on the origins of Hindustani and Urdu and why Ghalib sometimes wrote obscurely. A must-read if you love language or India.
The second of Amit's three linked book recommendations; he pressed it on Varun Grover.

head: India Moving
dek: Amit calls it one of the great books of the last ten years, though not much written about.
more: Amit calls it one of the great books of the last ten years, though not much written about. Its big insight is that marriage is India's largest source of internal migration.
The third book, a history of internal migration in India over 2,000 years that zooms in where Tony Joseph zooms out.

head: Understanding India Through Its Languages (Episode 232 of The Seen and the Unseen)

more: A conversation companion to Wanderers, Kings, Merchants.

more: A conversation companion to India Moving.

more: Linked through that anecdote: Amit was flabbergasted that Grover hadn't read it.
Varun Grover recorded with Amit right after Peggy Mohan, and Amit gave him her book.

head: Whole-grain sourdough bread
dek: He calls it Pareto superior to industrial yeast bread on taste and especially on health.
more: He calls it Pareto superior to industrial yeast bread on taste and especially on health. It's fun to make, though you have to work to keep it near 20°C in India.
Ajay's first recommendation, a practice rather than a book.

head: Nothing Is Indian, Everything Is Indian
dek: Almost nothing we think of as quintessentially Indian started here: stitched clothes, the Patiala salwar, potatoes, chillies, tomatoes, guava, marigolds, saffron, possibly idli fermentation, rajma chawal, tandoori chicken, even English.
more: Almost nothing we think of as quintessentially Indian started here: stitched clothes, the Patiala salwar, potatoes, chillies, tomatoes, guava, marigolds, saffron, possibly idli fermentation, rajma chawal, tandoori chicken, even English. That is not a loss. Once influences arrive and are absorbed, they become ours.

head: Culture Is a Khichdi
dek: Food, language and clothes are best as mixtures. English borrows from Latin, Greek, Persian, Anglo-Saxon and Hindustani ('juggernaut' comes from Jagannath).
more: Food, language and clothes are best as mixtures. English borrows from Latin, Greek, Persian, Anglo-Saxon and Hindustani ('juggernaut' comes from Jagannath). So English is an Indian language, and arguably not even purely an English one. Purity is a myth; mixing is the joy.

head: Food Has Always Flowed Both Ways
dek: The Columbian Exchange brought New World crops such as potato, mirchi, tomato and amrood to India.
more: The Columbian Exchange brought New World crops such as potato, mirchi, tomato and amrood to India. The spice trade drew Europeans here, and trade flowed in both directions. Indian cuisine as we know it is a product of global exchange.

head: Grain Made States (and Plunder) Possible
dek: From James C. Scott: grain is calorie-dense, storable, transportable and easy to seize, which made early states and marauding armies possible.
more: From James C. Scott: grain is calorie-dense, storable, transportable and easy to seize, which made early states and marauding armies possible. Banana and papaya don't keep, so there is little to grab. The potato, growing out of sight underground, was a survival crop that armies overlooked.

head: Cuisine Is Contingent
dek: Amit's two-stage model: a cuisine starts from local conditions such as produce, climate, fuel, class and caste, then mixes with global influences shaped by mimetic desire.
more: Amit's two-stage model: a cuisine starts from local conditions such as produce, climate, fuel, class and caste, then mixes with global influences shaped by mimetic desire. Examples from the episode: US PL 480 wheat bringing rotis south; wartime rice shortages producing upma; a nawab's bad teeth producing the galouti kebab (by legend); Travancore's king promoting kappa (tapioca) during a 19th-century rice shortage; cow dung fuel making Indian food boiled rather than fried; Bombay rents killing experimental restaurants; caste separating Brahmin and Dalit kitchens in the same village.

head: Mass Media Homogenises, the Internet Diversifies
dek: Radio, TV and film flattened diversity. America converged on one standard accent, and state promotion of Hindi replaced the varied, bottom-up Hindustani of 75 years ago.
more: Radio, TV and film flattened diversity. America converged on one standard accent, and state promotion of Hindi replaced the varied, bottom-up Hindustani of 75 years ago. Ajay notes that Mussolini was the first to abuse radio on a large scale. The internet reverses this: YouTube, Stage and podcasts let Konkani (really many Konkanis), Haryanvi, regional cooking and niche talk shows survive.

head: Cultural Appropriation Is Incoherent
dek: Amit argues that if culture is a melding of influences, nobody can 'own' it.
more: Amit argues that if culture is a melding of influences, nobody can 'own' it. The Tagore estate's rules show what policing culture costs, and Shakespeare rapped by Akala shows what freedom gains.

head: Preserve Without Freezing: No Fly in Amber
dek: Ajay's balance: capture inherited knowledge, like his mother's Osaman, while it still exists.
more: Ajay's balance: capture inherited knowledge, like his mother's Osaman, while it still exists. But don't glorify the past or turn culture into a museum piece. Food, language and architecture should keep evolving with local conditions, new technology and creativity, without simply copying others.

head: Grand Architecture Is a Power Play
dek: Imposing buildings are usually built by the powerful to make people bow and to show off borrowed prestige.
more: Imposing buildings are usually built by the powerful to make people bow and to show off borrowed prestige. Thought through from first principles, architecture should fit local weather, materials and craftsmanship. Ajay argues food culture should be judged the same way.

head: Caste Endogamy Fragmented India
dek: Waves of migrants mixed freely for a couple of thousand years. Then, around 2,000 years ago, an ideology from the Gangetic belt won out and enforced caste endogamy.
more: Waves of migrants mixed freely for a couple of thousand years. Then, around 2,000 years ago, an ideology from the Gangetic belt won out and enforced caste endogamy. That required controlling women, which drove female seclusion. It also split India into thousands of small populations with separate cuisines. Ajay compares these to island ecosystems evolving in isolation.

head: Marriage Is India's Biggest Migration
dek: From Chinmay Tumbe: the largest source of internal migration in India is women moving at marriage.
more: From Chinmay Tumbe: the largest source of internal migration in India is women moving at marriage. Outside elite circles, these women leave their whole lives and friendships behind and start over. Men often keep the same friends all their lives.

head: Culture Is Humanity's Software
dek: Culture means all learned behaviour: language, customs, law, science, problem-solving.
more: Culture means all learned behaviour: language, customs, law, science, problem-solving. It sits on top of our biological hardware. Animals have it too: a Japanese monkey's rice-washing trick spread from band to band. Because culture is software, we can question and rewrite it. The obstacle is ethnocentrism, judging the world from your own tribe's point of view, which Ajay says is widely prevalent in India.

head: Health Depends on the Food System
dek: Homogenisation is often driven by big industrial food companies that want standardisation; McDonald's fries everywhere use a single Idaho Russet potato.
more: Homogenisation is often driven by big industrial food companies that want standardisation; McDonald's fries everywhere use a single Idaho Russet potato. Questioning processed food is self-preservation. The cultural case and the health case agree: more artisanal, local food would mean a new cuisine every 50 to 100 km.

head: Climate Decides What Ferments
dek: Dahi ferments best at about 36°C, which suits India. Sourdough and kefir need about 20°C, which rarely happens here.
more: Dahi ferments best at about 36°C, which suits India. Sourdough and kefir need about 20°C, which rarely happens here. All bread was once sourdough, until industrial yeast took over. India's climate is why it developed mainly unleavened breads like roti and naan, with khamiri roti in the cooler north as the exception.

head: Amit sneaks in proof that English is Indian: the word juggernaut comes from Jagannath
more: Amit sneaks in proof that English is Indian: the word juggernaut comes from Jagannath, 'and indeed the show, one could argue, is like a juggernaut blazing its way through the forests of YouTube.'

head: Ajay tells half-Bengali Amit that some say the rasgulla's geographical indicator belongs to Odisha and that the idea was brought by the Portuguese.
more: Ajay tells half-Bengali Amit that some say the rasgulla's geographical indicator belongs to Odisha and that the idea was brought by the Portuguese. Amit: 'Sugar is poison, colonialism is bad, now we know why. Carry on.'

head: Ajay's punchline to Frederick the Great's guarded potato gardens
more: Ajay's punchline to Frederick the Great's guarded potato gardens: 'This is the best way to make something work. It is to announce that it is illegal. So now you know why cryptocurrency has such a great future in India.'

head: Amit on bananas
more: Amit on bananas: 'in the best way possible, we are a banana republic.' The bananas we gave the world went, 'in the worst way possible', to the banana republics of Latin America.

head: Amit savours the…
more: Amit savours the 'Pushpesh Pant pet peeves': the tyranny of the tandoor, the curse of the curry and the myth of Mughlai. 'And if he wore Patiala pants like me, two more Ps.'

head: Ajay swears off basmati rice, calling it a tyranny. Amit, alliterating in Pushpesh Pant's honour, upgrades it to…
more: Ajay swears off basmati rice, calling it a tyranny. Amit, alliterating in Pushpesh Pant's honour, upgrades it to 'the barbarism of basmati', and Ajay to 'the brutality of basmati'.

head: As Ajay explains Kutchi pride, Amit butts in…
more: As Ajay explains Kutchi pride, Amit butts in: 'If Kutchis invented the underwear, the kachha, which is so impressive to me, but carry on.'

head: Bombay restaurants all serving paneer butter masala reminds Amit of Pratap Bhanu Mehta
more: Bombay restaurants all serving paneer butter masala reminds Amit of Pratap Bhanu Mehta, 'because he's called PBM'.

Ajay: 'I'm no friend of rap music, but surely there should be a Rabindra rap sangeet.' Amit admits that as a kid he thought rap was noise ('People are talking, why can't they sing?') but now loves it, and declares culture a party: 'mix karo, dance karo, enjoy karo.'

head: Amit's definition of culture, which he says they should rename the show after
more: Amit's definition of culture, which he says they should rename the show after: 'Everything is everything.'

head: Amit's sign-off after Ajay's sourdough and kefir sermon
more: Amit's sign-off after Ajay's sourdough and kefir sermon: 'May you have peace in your life, but ferment in your food.'

head: George Bernard Shaw's Caesar and Cleopatra, quoted by Ajay
more: George Bernard Shaw's Caesar and Cleopatra, quoted by Ajay: 'He is a barbarian who thinks that the customs of his tribe and island are the law of nature.'

head: Ajay uses the quip
more: Ajay uses the quip 'a language is a dialect with a navy' to argue that pre-Independence Hindustani was really many dialects, flattened later into standard Hindi.

head: Finding Springsteen through a stripped-down Born to Run
dek: The version you first meet can hide an artist. A bare live rendering of a song he hadn't liked on the album reframed it completely.
more: In his college hostel, seniors bought the vinyl of Born in the USA (1984), Springsteen's most accessible, pop-sounding album. At the time Ajay had ears only for Pink Floyd, so it didn't land. As a graduate student in the US, he and Susan stumbled on a mini-CD of a live 1988 performance at the Los Angeles Coliseum, right next to his university. He had skipped that show. On it was an acoustic Born to Run: just Springsteen, a guitar and a mouth organ. That led them to a three-CD live set (Racing in the Street, Thunder Road, Independence Day), though a long Led Zeppelin phase kept it a sideshow. Years later, at the Ministry of Finance in Delhi, he went back to Born to Run, Darkness on the Edge of Town and The River, and they came to life one by one.

The version you first meet can hide an artist. A bare live rendering of a song he hadn't liked on the album reframed it completely. Great work can also sit dormant in you for years before it switches on.

head: A critic watches Bonnie Raitt and sees rock and roll's future
dek: Life-changing partnerships can hinge on pure chance: a critic goes to see the headliner and finds the opener.
more: On May 9, 1974, Springsteen and the E Street Band opened for Bonnie Raitt. A young critic, Jon Landau, wrote a now-legendary review: 'Can anyone really be this good?… I saw rock and roll's future, and his name is Bruce Springsteen.' Landau, 27, then met Springsteen, 25. Springsteen had never really had a father and saw Landau as a father figure. He later wrote that Landau was the first person he met 'who had a language for discussing these ideas and the life of the mind'. Ajay was reminded of G. H. Hardy and Ramanujan: fascination with a genius, plus care not to disrupt it.

Life-changing partnerships can hinge on pure chance: a critic goes to see the headliner and finds the opener. What Landau brought was rare. He had a fan's pure love and a critic's ability to step back and analyse, and in him one impulse did not dampen the other.

head: The rented guitar and the untuned guitar
dek: Mastery starts with incompetence plus desire. Amit reads the untuned guitar as a metaphor for how, step by step, we discover how much of the craft we didn't know.
more: At seven, Springsteen badly wanted a guitar. His mother couldn't afford one, so she rented it. He couldn't figure it out. On the sunny morning it had to go back, he put on a show for half a dozen neighbourhood kids: shaking it, shouting at it, singing 'voodoo nonsense', doing everything but playing it, while they laughed. Later, with a guitar of his own, he wrote tunes on it without knowing how to tune it and felt cool in front of the mirror. Then someone tuned it for him, and he realised everything he'd done before was rubbish.
Mastery starts with incompetence plus desire. Amit reads the untuned guitar as a metaphor for how, step by step, we discover how much of the craft we didn't know.
