head: Steel Mill gets outplayed in San Francisco
dek: Losing to better people is useful information. Springsteen didn't think of himself as a natural genius, so he decided to outwork everyone.
more: In the early '70s, Springsteen's band Steel Mill went to an audition in San Francisco. After a couple of mediocre bands, they rocked the room and thought they had it. Then the next band showed far more sophisticated musicianship, and Steel Mill lost the gig. Springsteen wrote that it didn't sit well with him. Better talent didn't scare him. What worried him was not maximising his own abilities. He went home knowing 'there would have to be some changes made', and that began the slow road from Steel Mill to the E Street Band.

Losing to better people is useful information. Springsteen didn't think of himself as a natural genius, so he decided to outwork everyone. Amit ties this to the Beatles' years of shows in Hamburg and Mozart composing from age five: we see the success at 23, not the work since age seven.

head: Mike Appel dares John Hammond
dek: Breaks often come wrapped in awkwardness: a brash champion, a second-hand guitar, a cringing artist.
more: Springsteen's first manager and producer, Mike Appel, walked him into Columbia Records to audition for John Hammond, the man who had discovered Dylan. Springsteen hadn't brought his kit, so he bought a second-hand guitar and came in carrying it over his shoulder. Appel's opening line was a provocation, and Springsteen cringed inside, thinking 'shut the fuck up'. He played anyway and came out with a three-record deal.
Breaks often come wrapped in awkwardness: a brash champion, a second-hand guitar, a cringing artist. The talent still has to show up and play.

head: 'You want a hit? I'll write you a hit'
dek: Many artists answer a commercial demand with 'I must stay true to my art.' Springsteen treated it as a challenge, and the constraint produced some of his best songs.
more: When Springsteen turned in his debut, Greetings from Asbury Park, Clive Davis handed it back: no hits, nothing for radio. Springsteen went to the beach and wrote Spirit in the Night. Then he broke out his rhyming dictionary and wrote Blinded by the Light. These became two of the record's best songs, with Clarence Clemons's saxophone added. It happened again in 1984. Born in the USA was finished, and Jon Landau said they still needed a hit. Furious, Springsteen went to his room and turned how he felt into Dancing in the Dark ('I ain't nothing but tired… tired and bored with myself'). The lyrics are depressive; the tune is upbeat.

Many artists answer a commercial demand with 'I must stay true to my art.' Springsteen treated it as a challenge, and the constraint produced some of his best songs. Even irritation can be raw material.

head: Hungry Heart: ten minutes to write, thirty seconds to mix
dek: Speed and agonised slowness live in the same artist. The ten-minute song stands on decades of work, which is why Amit tells his writing students that great simplicity comes only after years of effort.
more: Springsteen wrote Hungry Heart in about ten minutes while doodling in a room, called the band in, and it was done. Bob Clearmountain mixed it in thirty seconds. Yet Springsteen wrote that they could never have worked with Clearmountain because he was too fast. The E Street way was to 'ruminate, contemplate, intellectualize', to do it the hard way, on 'an odyssey… searching for complicated answers to mystifying questions'. Making Born to Run included a 72-hour stretch running three studios side by side. Max Weinberg said he'd never seen anyone work as hard as Springsteen.

Speed and agonised slowness live in the same artist. The ten-minute song stands on decades of work, which is why Amit tells his writing students that great simplicity comes only after years of effort.

head: His sister's shotgun wedding becomes The River
dek: Springsteen didn't need myths or grand narratives; his family's ordinary drama was enough.
more: Springsteen's sister Virginia got pregnant at 17, dropped out of high school and married Mickey Shave. Mickey was a leather-jacketed, bull-riding greaser from Lakewood who worked in construction. A girl who had 'never boiled water' became a hardcore Irish working woman. Before Amit could name the song, Ajay guessed it: 'I got a job working construction.' That is The River, where Mary gets pregnant at seventeen and the narrator gets 'a union card and a wedding coat' for his 19th birthday.
Springsteen didn't need myths or grand narratives; his family's ordinary drama was enough. When writing students ask Amit 'what do I write about?', his answer is: look around you.

head: The boxing lesson and Independence Day
dek: The most painful personal material, worked honestly, becomes something strangers recognise as their own life.
more: Springsteen's father worked as a taxi driver, assembly-line worker, jail guard, and bus and truck driver, and slid into paranoia. At one point he believed love songs on the radio were a government ploy to get people married so they'd pay more taxes. In the memoir, a friendly boxing lesson in the living room turns when his father's open-palm punches land a little too hard. The boy understands he is seen as 'an intruder, a stranger, a competitor in our home, and a fearful disappointment'. That relationship flows into Independence Day ('Papa now I know the things you wanted that you could not say'). It also flows into Springsteen's later resolve to turn the ghosts that haunt him into ancestors.
The most painful personal material, worked honestly, becomes something strangers recognise as their own life.

head: Pitching Fire to Elvis's answering machine
dek: The ideas matter more than who owns them. In Ajay's view, the person is just the vehicle through which ideas go out into the world, so keep inventing and giving things away.
more: Springsteen wrote Fire and heard it as an Elvis Presley song. He got hold of Elvis's number and reached an answering machine, then sang the song and dictated the lyrics into it. Elvis ignored him. Springsteen gave the song to the Pointer Sisters, who made it a number-one hit; years later his own live versions are, to Ajay, the best. Ajay took a life rule from this: he freely gives his research ideas to others instead of writing them in a notebook to get to 'one day'.
The ideas matter more than who owns them. In Ajay's view, the person is just the vehicle through which ideas go out into the world, so keep inventing and giving things away.

head: Every live version of Jungleland, in order
dek: A song is not a fixed object; it records who the singer was each time he sang it.
more: Ajay sometimes takes one song, collects every live performance in chronological order, and listens straight through. Jungleland shows the effect most strongly: the 1976 version is brilliant, and the 2012 version is a grown man telling a different story. At the EV conference in Udaipur, the song's closing lines surfaced in his head: the poets around here 'don't write nothing at all, they just stand by and let it all be'. Every time he left a session, he went to his room and played versions of that one song over and over.
A song is not a fixed object; it records who the singer was each time he sang it. Listening across decades gives you an artist's autobiography that a single album never can.

head: Beethoven, the Ninth, and Devils and Dust
dek: Craft compounds. For people who keep working, the peak can come late, when a whole life's practice comes together in one effortless-seeming piece.
more: In S. Chandrasekhar's Truth and Beauty, Ajay found Beethoven writing to a friend at the end of his life, just before the Ninth Symphony, that he now knew how to write music. Ajay felt the same on first hearing Devils and Dust (2005), written in the context of the American invasion of Iraq. Springsteen said that after a lifetime in the craft some songs simply write themselves, as Dancing in the Dark, My Hometown and Downbound Train had, and that this one did too, in a very short time. Ajay was struck that he wrote it when he was no longer young.
Craft compounds. For people who keep working, the peak can come late, when a whole life's practice comes together in one effortless-seeming piece.

head: Famous, and broke until 1982
dek: Success can look like riches from outside long before it is. Ajay drew a wry lesson for Indians who complain about their own tax department: taxmen everywhere can be pretty cruel.
more: In 1975 Springsteen landed on the covers of Time and Newsweek, and then the tax authorities came for years of back taxes. Born to Run, Darkness on the Edge of Town and The River were all hits, but he didn't make a single paisa until 1982. Had Born in the USA flopped, he'd have been broke. The early hand-to-mouth years ran deep. Steel Mill once found a club nobody went to and talked the owner into letting them charge a dollar a head. Fifteen people came, and the five band members took home $3 each.
Success can look like riches from outside long before it is. Ajay drew a wry lesson for Indians who complain about their own tax department: taxmen everywhere can be pretty cruel.

head: The student who copied a novel by hand
dek: Copying great prose by hand forces you to read at the level of the sentence and absorb its rhythm.
more: A student in Amit's writing course, whose first language is Hindi, asked how to cope with writing in English. Her prose read like a second language but had flashes of real spark. Amit pointed her to Jhumpa Lahiri, who learned Italian as an adult and wrote a book in it. In a conversation with Tyler Cowen, Lahiri had named Agota Kristof as an inspiration. Kristof was a Hungarian writer who had to flee, learned French from scratch at 21, and wrote the Notebook Trilogy in it. The student then copied Kristof's sentences out by hand to get the book's rhythm into her head.
Copying great prose by hand forces you to read at the level of the sentence and absorb its rhythm. A learned language can also push a writer toward economy rather than ornament.

head: Born to Run (autobiography)
dek: Beautiful writing that takes you right into the man's mind. Amit says everyone should read it to understand artistic process, for example the passage on how Springsteen poured his whole life into the song Born to Run.
more: Beautiful writing that takes you right into the man's mind. Amit says everyone should read it to understand artistic process, for example the passage on how Springsteen poured his whole life into the song Born to Run.
Amit called it possibly his big recommendation of the episode and read from it throughout: the rented guitar, Meet the Beatles, Steel Mill, his sister, his father. He recommended it again at the end.

head: Bruce Springsteen: All the Songs
dek: It tells the story behind every single Springsteen song, and Amit pairs it with the memoir as two wonderful books.
more: It tells the story behind every single Springsteen song, and Amit pairs it with the memoir as two wonderful books.
Amit's formal recommendation at the end. It's a copy he gifted Ajay, whose cover arrived slightly torn; they kept it as 'part of the character of the book'.

head: The Notebook Trilogy (The Notebook, The Proof, The Third Lie)
dek: Amit calls it a benchmark for mastering a language learned late: spare, economical, elegant, every word doing a job.
more: Amit calls it a benchmark for mastering a language learned late: spare, economical, elegant, every word doing a job. Writers like Nabokov turn flamboyant in a new language; Kristof strips both language and life down to the essential, 'like Nebraska'. Available as an omnibus.
Ajay spotted the book and asked about its title. Amit told the story of his writing student and Jhumpa Lahiri.

head: Truth and Beauty
dek: A 'lovely slim book' that Ajay says everybody should read. It is about craft and the long journey of learning to do it, including Beethoven saying, just before the Ninth Symphony, that he now knew how to write music.
more: A 'lovely slim book' that Ajay says everybody should read. It is about craft and the long journey of learning to do it, including Beethoven saying, just before the Ninth Symphony, that he now knew how to write music.
Ajay's response to Amit's chapter on effort and craft.

head: Independence Day
dek: It's about fathers and sons, and Ajay sees in it the drama of small towns all over India: despair, the darkness at the edge of town, family conflict, the decision to leave, and the lost social network after you go.
more: It's about fathers and sons, and Ajay sees in it the drama of small towns all over India: despair, the darkness at the edge of town, family conflict, the decision to leave, and the lost social network after you go.
First of Ajay's father-son recommendations; Amit also read its lyrics in the father story.

head: Father and Son
dek: Ajay once found it a little clichéd, but twenty years on he thinks it's a really great song, so don't worry that it's too famous.
more: Ajay once found it a little clichéd, but twenty years on he thinks it's a really great song, so don't worry that it's too famous. The same singer voices both the father and the son.
Second of Ajay's father-son recommendations.

head: The Road
dek: A father and son try to walk the world in a post-apocalyptic landscape; Ajay says it takes you deep inside what it means to be a father and a son.
more: A father and son try to walk the world in a post-apocalyptic landscape; Ajay says it takes you deep inside what it means to be a father and a son.
Third of Ajay's father-son recommendations.

head: Self-Portrait
dek: A tiny poem on the same theme: the speaker resembles 'everyone but myself' and sees in shop windows the portrait of a stranger, 'often signed in a corner by my father'.
more: A tiny poem on the same theme: the speaker resembles 'everyone but myself' and sees in shop windows the portrait of a stranger, 'often signed in a corner by my father'.
Amit read it to close the episode after Ajay's father-son recommendations.

head: Born to Run (acoustic live version)
dek: The wall-of-sound album version didn't suit his taste at the time. Springsteen alone with guitar and mouth organ was an eye-opener that showed him a different way to understand the song.
more: The wall-of-sound album version didn't suit his taste at the time. Springsteen alone with guitar and mouth organ was an eye-opener that showed him a different way to understand the song.
The stripped-down live performance on a mini-CD that opened Springsteen up for Ajay.

head: The Promise (version on 18 Tracks)
dek: Ajay sees Born to Run, Thunder Road and The Promise as a triad: 'three windows into the same people, into the same life'.
more: Ajay sees Born to Run, Thunder Road and The Promise as a triad: 'three windows into the same people, into the same life'. He prefers the version on 18 Tracks.
A legal dispute with former producer Mike Appel, who claimed ownership of the song, upset Springsteen so much that it went unreleased for some 20-25 years.

head: Jungleland
dek: Stairway to Heaven starts with an alaap and builds.
more: Stairway to Heaven starts with an alaap and builds. Jungleland runs in reverse: wall of sound, guitar solo, what Springsteen calls the world's greatest saxophone solo, a little saxophone-and-piano jazz, then the alaap at the end. Ajay thinks they nailed it. Compare the 1976 and 2012 versions.
Ajay's example of the long-song form and of how songs change across live versions.

head: Racing in the Street
dek: It starts as a young-man-and-cars song about illegal street racing. Halfway through it turns into a psychological dive into a deeply sad person.
more: It starts as a young-man-and-cars song about illegal street racing. Halfway through it turns into a psychological dive into a deeply sad person. 'You never saw it coming.'
Ajay's example of Springsteen's writing.

head: Devils and Dust
dek: Springsteen said it wrote itself after a lifetime of craft; Ajay calls it 'one of those sweet and perfect songs'.
more: Springsteen said it wrote itself after a lifetime of craft; Ajay calls it 'one of those sweet and perfect songs'. It is his example of late-career mastery.
2005, written in the context of the American invasion of Iraq.

head: Dancing in the Dark
dek: A masterpiece with levels: depressive lyrics ('tired and bored with myself') set to an upbeat tune.
more: A masterpiece with levels: depressive lyrics ('tired and bored with myself') set to an upbeat tune. It shows Springsteen turning a commercial demand into real art.
Written in anger after Jon Landau said Born in the USA still needed a hit.

head: The River
dek: Amit calls it a great song whose opening section is brilliant. It shows Springsteen turning his family's ordinary life into a story with its own momentum.
more: Amit calls it a great song whose opening section is brilliant. It shows Springsteen turning his family's ordinary life into a story with its own momentum.
Rooted in his sister Virginia's teenage pregnancy and marriage.

head: Darkness on the Edge of Town
dek: 'Just beautiful, simple language, and everyone relates.' It is specific to his life, yet anyone anywhere can see themselves in it.
more: 'Just beautiful, simple language, and everyone relates.' It is specific to his life, yet anyone anywhere can see themselves in it.
Amit dates Springsteen's lyrical greatness from around this album onward.

head: I'm on Fire
dek: The approach works even on a 'non-metaphysical' subject like lust. Amit points to the image of waking with 'a sheet soaking wet and a freight train running through the middle of my head'.
more: The approach works even on a 'non-metaphysical' subject like lust. Amit points to the image of waking with 'a sheet soaking wet and a freight train running through the middle of my head'.
Example of Springsteen's specific-yet-universal writing.

head: Secret Garden
dek: It seems carnal at first, then turns into a song about how you can never truly know another person and the recesses in each of us no one else can reach.
more: It seems carnal at first, then turns into a song about how you can never truly know another person and the recesses in each of us no one else can reach.
Example of Springsteen going 'a level deeper than you expect'.

head: Brilliant Disguise
dek: It begins by asking whether the lover is wearing a mask and ends by turning the gaze on himself ('I damn sure don't trust myself').
more: It begins by asking whether the lover is wearing a mask and ends by turning the gaze on himself ('I damn sure don't trust myself'). Amit finds it stunning. The video is pure simplicity, the camera moving closer and closer.
From Tunnel of Love; Amit also praises its video.

head: Backstreets
dek: Greil Marcus wrote that it 'begins with music so stately, so heartbreaking that it might be the prelude to a rock and roll version of the Iliad'.
more: Greil Marcus wrote that it 'begins with music so stately, so heartbreaking that it might be the prelude to a rock and roll version of the Iliad'. Amit says Marcus put into words what he had always felt. The song is intimate and epic, and sometimes he wishes the piano went on forever.
Newly in love with crisp editing, Springsteen wanted to cut Roy Bittan's piano at the beginning and end. Landau talked him out of it.

head: Atlantic City (from Nebraska)
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece and Nebraska 'such a great stripped down album'.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece and Nebraska 'such a great stripped down album'. It shows Springsteen's willingness to keep changing direction.
Springsteen wrote to Landau that it was a song for the full band. The band takes didn't work, and what we hear is essentially just Springsteen and a guitar.

head: Growing Up (live)
dek: Before the song, Springsteen talked for what seemed like half an hour, and it was brilliant.
more: Before the song, Springsteen talked for what seemed like half an hour, and it was brilliant. It is proof that he never played 'cover versions of himself' and every show was new.
Amit's first time being truly entranced by Springsteen as a kid, in the '80s or early '90s.

head: You're Missing
dek: Amit cites it among his examples of Springsteen's great lyric writing.
more: Amit cites it among his examples of Springsteen's great lyric writing.
The song the show takes its name from, discussed in Episode 2.

head: TB Sheets
dek: Another great long song, by Van Morrison, a hero to both Springsteen and Amit.
more: Another great long song, by Van Morrison, a hero to both Springsteen and Amit.
Offered while Ajay discussed long songs as a genre; Ajay hadn't heard it yet.

head: Answering Machine
dek: One line, 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?', expresses so much.
more: One line, 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?', expresses so much.
Prompted by the Elvis answering-machine story. The Replacements are an '80s alternative rock band led by Paul Westerberg, whom Amit loves.

head: Like a Rolling Stone: Bob Dylan at the Crossroads
dek: Amit calls Marcus a genius music writer whose phrases capture what listeners feel but can't articulate.
more: Amit calls Marcus a genius music writer whose phrases capture what listeners feel but can't articulate.
Show-notes link. Amit quotes Marcus's review of Born to Run and mentions he wrote a book on Dylan.

head: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
dek: Amit loves its line 'What can be said at all can be said clearly, and whereof one cannot speak thereof one must be silent.' He uses it to argue that any one language is inadequate.
more: Amit loves its line 'What can be said at all can be said clearly, and whereof one cannot speak thereof one must be silent.' He uses it to argue that any one language is inadequate.
Opening segment on the limits of language.

head: On Exactitude in Science
dek: A short story about how an accurate map of the world would have to be as big as the world and would instantly be out of date.
more: A short story about how an accurate map of the world would have to be as big as the world and would instantly be out of date. It illustrates that no representation can fully capture reality.
Opening segment, alongside Wittgenstein.

head: Literature is words and storytelling, not books
dek: Books are just one form. Shakespeare wrote plays to be performed and read aloud, and the Nobel citation honoured Dylan for new poetic expressions in the great American song tradition.
more: Books are just one form. Shakespeare wrote plays to be performed and read aloud, and the Nobel citation honoured Dylan for new poetic expressions in the great American song tradition. Amit holds that anything that moves us through words is literature, which puts Springsteen's songs squarely in that category. Language alone is limited (Wittgenstein, Borges), but in storytelling it can still reach anyone.

head: The producer is a co-author
dek: Ajay's frame from academic research: if someone did for his papers what a producer does for a band, they'd get authorship.
more: Ajay's frame from academic research: if someone did for his papers what a producer does for a band, they'd get authorship. George Martin for the Beatles, Brian Eno for U2 and Jon Landau for Springsteen were first-class participants in the creative journey, not technicians.

head: The album as an architected whole
dek: In the LP era, each side had a first and last song, and the listener physically got up to flip the record.
more: In the LP era, each side had a first and last song, and the listener physically got up to flip the record. Springsteen designed around that. On Born to Run, the title track opens side one, Thunder Road closes it, and Jungleland comes on the next side. He recorded about 20 songs per album and kept 8-10. He wanted each record to be a statement of purpose, coherent without becoming a 'concept album'.

head: Long songs are their own genre
dek: Ajay ranks songs by complexity. Level one is simple, well-structured songs with clear meter and grammar (Geeta Dutt, Yesterday, Both Sides Now).
more: Ajay ranks songs by complexity. Level one is simple, well-structured songs with clear meter and grammar (Geeta Dutt, Yesterday, Both Sides Now). Next is early Springsteen, which rhymes only in snatches, 'a bit like modern art'. Then come long songs like Stairway to Heaven and November Rain, which must change style several times to sustain themselves. Jungleland inverts the usual build and ends on the alaap.

head: The ten-minute song that took thirty years
dek: Springsteen's apparent bursts of genius sit on huge, intentional effort: years of bar gigs, constant reworking, outworking better musicians.
more: Springsteen's apparent bursts of genius sit on huge, intentional effort: years of bar gigs, constant reworking, outworking better musicians. Ajay adds the principle of volume, borrowed from chess and poker. Produce a lot, because refinement comes from iteration, so build a hundred Taj Mahals, not one. Amit tells his writing students the same about simplicity.

head: Gift your ideas away
dek: From the Fire/Elvis story: don't hoard ideas in a notebook to claim 'one day'.
more: From the Fire/Elvis story: don't hoard ideas in a notebook to claim 'one day'. Keep inventing and let others run with your ideas. A full life produces plenty of ideas, and the person is just the vehicle through which they reach the world.

head: Write what's around you: the specific becomes universal
dek: Springsteen built his work from his sister's teenage marriage, his father's paranoia and his blue-collar town.
more: Springsteen built his work from his sister's teenage marriage, his father's paranoia and his blue-collar town. Writing about what is true to you makes it true for others too. Amit's advice to students who ask 'what do I write about?' is to look around them.

head: Plain words, a level deeper
dek: Shakespeare was both high art and the box-office star of his day because he wrote in the speech rhythms of his time.
more: Shakespeare was both high art and the box-office star of his day because he wrote in the speech rhythms of his time. Springsteen never uses a word you can't understand, yet his songs turn on you. Secret Garden moves from carnal to unknowable intimacy. Brilliant Disguise turns its suspicion on the singer. Racing in the Street goes from cars to a portrait of a sad woman.

head: Short snaps and strong endings
dek: Ajay looks for a short, four- or five-word sentence right after a long one.
more: Ajay looks for a short, four- or five-word sentence right after a long one. Amit notes that great poets know line endings matter. 'They are God giving you another shot' ends on a mute sound, as does 'The answer, my friend, is blowing in the wind.'

head: Don't play cover versions of yourself
dek: Springsteen refused to repeat his hits the same way. His live shows had long spoken passages, songs were reworked, and there were dozens of versions of The River.
more: Springsteen refused to repeat his hits the same way. His live shows had long spoken passages, songs were reworked, and there were dozens of versions of The River. Songs change meaning over time and with company. Ajay's practice of listening to every live version in chronological order mirrors this from the listener's side.

head: The right players, not the best players
dek: Springsteen rejected both one-man-one-vote band democracy ('a ticking time bomb… beginning and ending with the Beatles') and a faceless backing band.
more: Springsteen rejected both one-man-one-vote band democracy ('a ticking time bomb… beginning and ending with the Beatles') and a faceless backing band. He chose something in between, drawn from the neighbourhood. Ajay generalises it: success corrodes equal partnerships (Simon & Garfunkel), and bands, companies and teams need shared values and human connection more than the world's best drummer or technologist.

head: Turn ghosts into ancestors
dek: Springsteen chose not to let the worst of his relationship with his father be the final equation.
more: Springsteen chose not to let the worst of his relationship with his father be the final equation. He wrote 'I work to be an ancestor'. Amit reads this as seeing yourself as a character in a longer story. Ajay flips their earlier line, that we're each a linear combination of our influences: we are also adding to other people's, so we should be our best selves.

head: Scarcity made shared culture
dek: Springsteen left many outtakes unreleased that today might be streamed and live-jammed.
more: Springsteen left many outtakes unreleased that today might be streamed and live-jammed. Ajay notes that the old world's scarcity concentrated attention on a few works everyone shared. Fragmented attention would have made a different culture.

head: Great literature teaches you to see yourself in others
dek: Riffing on a Roger Waters line ('I see myself in every stranger's eyes'), Ajay says growing up means moving beyond self-centredness.
more: Riffing on a Roger Waters line ('I see myself in every stranger's eyes'), Ajay says growing up means moving beyond self-centredness. Springsteen's songs about ordinary people showed him the beauty and magic in everyone's lives. Amit adds that once art leaves the artist, each listener's journey with it is their own.

head: Ajay declares them
more: Ajay declares them 'a polyglot show' and counts: English, Amit fighting back in fluent Punjabi for Chandigarh, Bengali in another spat, a snatch of Konkani around 'Kaatar Re Bhaaji', and bits of Hindi. Five languages in one show.

head: Amit on the two kinds of BS in Ajay's life: Business Standard, where he's been a columnist
more: Amit on the two kinds of BS in Ajay's life: Business Standard, where he's been a columnist 'for the last sixty-three years or something like that', and Bruce Springsteen.

head: Ajay's origin story for the podcast
more: Ajay's origin story for the podcast: when Dylan won the Nobel, both of them instantly had the same two thoughts. Yes, that's literature; and Dylan before Springsteen? 'It should have been the other way around.'
Ajay: 'You're at episode thirteen of Everything is Everything… who knows where we'll be.' Amit: 'Are you comparing us to Springsteen? Don't you dare do that.'

head: On Springsteen's lyrical peak by his late 20s, Amit
more: On Springsteen's lyrical peak by his late 20s, Amit: 'What shit were we doing in our late 20s?' Ajay: 'We were writing really bad shit.'

head: Ajay, mid-Elvis story
more: Ajay, mid-Elvis story: 'Oh ye young reader, please go Google what is an answering machine.'

head: Springsteen's father thought love songs on the radio were a government ploy to get people married and paying more taxes.
more: Springsteen's father thought love songs on the radio were a government ploy to get people married and paying more taxes. Amit: 'I'm presuming there are greater taxes involved there.'

head: Ajay recalls Paul McCartney supposedly saying Ringo
more: Ajay recalls Paul McCartney supposedly saying Ringo 'was not even the best drummer in the Beatles' (Amit finds Paul too self-effacing for that). Amit then digresses into cricket: Mark Waugh said something similar about Steve, and Mark's nickname is 'Afghanistan', because he's the forgotten Waugh.

head: Ajay on success corroding partnerships, with Simon & Garfunkel torn apart at Bridge Over Troubled Water
more: Ajay on success corroding partnerships, with Simon & Garfunkel torn apart at Bridge Over Troubled Water: 'No, no, no, I did 53% of it and you did 47.' Then to Amit: 'Just you watch how much you're gonna hate me one day.'

head: Greetings from Asbury Park sold about 23,000 copies
more: Greetings from Asbury Park sold about 23,000 copies, 'a flop by record company standards, but a smash by mine. Who were all these strangers buying my music?' Ajay on the podcast: 'We get thousands of views. Who the hell are all these people watching us?' Amit: 'And don't they have anything better to do?'

head: Wittgenstein (
more: Wittgenstein ('whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent') and Borges's map as big as the world, which is out of date the moment it's drawn. Amit riffs on the old river saying: 'You do not step in the same map twice.' Later Ajay offers his own twist: 'no man can sing the same song twice.'

head: Born in the USA was a protest song, yet some people treated it as a flag-waving
more: Born in the USA was a protest song, yet some people treated it as a flag-waving 'yay, Born in the USA' MAGA anthem.

head: Springsteen on E Street organist Danny Federici: he had
more: Springsteen on E Street organist Danny Federici: he had 'the shortest highway between his fingers and his heart'.

head: Zelensky: 'I want ammunition, not a ride'
dek: Putin's whole plan rested on an assumption about will. One leader's refusal to run broke that assumption and changed the course of the war.
more: Russia's intelligence expected a replay of Afghanistan: the West would buckle, the leadership would flee and the army would melt away. The Americans did offer Zelensky a flight out of Kyiv, as they had in Afghanistan. He refused, asked for ammunition instead, stayed and rallied his people. After that, the West turned around and committed to backing Ukraine.
Putin's whole plan rested on an assumption about will. One leader's refusal to run broke that assumption and changed the course of the war.
printed: Offered a lift, he stayed put

head: How Europe beat Putin's energy blackmail
dek: Don't mistake the mild, self-effacing manner of advanced economies for weakness, because their intellectual, technological and financial depth is huge.
more: Putin bet that cutting gas to a Europe hooked on Russian pipelines would cause a deep recession and working-class anger. That anger, he hoped, would empower communists and Nazis and break the fragile centrist coalitions of Christian democrats and social democrats, a replay of the 1930s. Instead Europe tripled its work on renewables and imported LNG from all over the world. It built LNG terminals in six months when two to three years was thought necessary, and it subsidised poor households so nobody froze. Europe got through 2022 with difficulty but without a crisis.

Don't mistake the mild, self-effacing manner of advanced economies for weakness, because their intellectual, technological and financial depth is huge. Calling the bluff was also a strategic disaster for Russia: it lost its main gas buyer, and cheap gas sales to Europe were what its economy was built on.

head: Georgia, Crimea and the 'Poland moment'
dek: Aggression that goes unpunished teaches the aggressor the wrong lesson, and appeasement tends to end abruptly, with the aggressor miscalculating.
more: Russia invaded Georgia on 8 August 2008 and nobody helped. In February 2014 Putin grabbed Crimea and nobody did anything. Putin concluded the West had no stomach for a fight. Ajay compares this to Hitler taking Austria and Czechoslovakia unopposed until he invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Then Britain and France gave him an ultimatum and declared war. The 2022 invasion triggered a similar 'enough is enough' from the West.
Aggression that goes unpunished teaches the aggressor the wrong lesson, and appeasement tends to end abruptly, with the aggressor miscalculating.

head: The chess grandmasters who stood up to Putin
dek: Always separate the Russian state from the Russian people. Many Russians have protested at real personal cost.
more: About 40 Russian chess grandmasters, essentially the country's top players, signed a letter protesting the invasion. Many had to leave Russia and now play for other federations. The lone holdout Amit names is Sergey Karyakin, whom he calls a coward. Ajay adds that Garry Kasparov, who had warned about Putin for years, was what woke him up. Before that he had seen Putin as just another Russian strongman; Kasparov showed him this was a man yearning for the USSR.
Always separate the Russian state from the Russian people. Many Russians have protested at real personal cost.

head: Peter McIndoe and 'Birds Aren't Real'
dek: It is a delightful demonstration of how easily belief can be manufactured, and Amit brings it up while discussing drones as birds in a hostile sky.
more: At 23, Peter McIndoe deliberately invented a conspiracy theory as a public experiment. His claim was that the US government had killed all the birds decades ago and replaced them with surveillance robots. The 'proof': birds sit on power lines to recharge, you never see baby pigeons because factories only make adults, and birds poop on people to track them. He kept up the charade for three years, driving around in a van handing out flyers, and many people believed it.
It is a delightful demonstration of how easily belief can be manufactured, and Amit brings it up while discussing drones as birds in a hostile sky.

head: America built 100,000 tanks, then shut the factories
dek: This is what 'arsenal of democracy' really meant. The American way of war was designed around that manufacturing might and a large population, so it doesn't transfer neatly to a smaller country like Ukraine.
more: Until 1941 the American 'giant' was asleep. Then it started from scratch, built the world's biggest tank factories and turned out something like 100,000 tanks in roughly two years. By early 1944 field commanders were saying they didn't want any more, and factories started shutting down.

This is what 'arsenal of democracy' really meant. The American way of war was designed around that manufacturing might and a large population, so it doesn't transfer neatly to a smaller country like Ukraine.

head: Churchill holding the Americans back
dek: How many deaths a country can bear shapes its way of war. A smaller nation rationally fights more cautiously, which is the same logic behind Ukraine being frugal with its soldiers today.
more: With people and production to spare, the Americans were in a rush to launch Operation Torch in North Africa, then land in Sicily and on the beaches of Normandy. Churchill knew Britain's small population couldn't absorb heavy losses. He kept insisting they get it right and not let troops be mauled for almost nothing.
How many deaths a country can bear shapes its way of war. A smaller nation rationally fights more cautiously, which is the same logic behind Ukraine being frugal with its soldiers today.

head: Stalin's choice not to concentrate
dek: When the deeper resources are on your side, steady pressure everywhere can beat one concentrated thrust.
more: After Operation Barbarossa in June 1941, German Army Groups North, Centre and South were spread along a very long front, heading for St Petersburg, Moscow and later Stalingrad and the Baku oil fields. Stalin had to decide whether to mass his forces for one breakthrough. Ajay counts him, with Lenin and Trotsky, among the sophisticated intellectuals of the era. Stalin knew the USSR had the bigger population and that, backed by American industry, it would outproduce Germany, something the Germans were naive about. So he counter-attacked everywhere to grind down German men and industry. Germany couldn't be strong everywhere, which is part of why it lost Stalingrad.

When the deeper resources are on your side, steady pressure everywhere can beat one concentrated thrust. You don't need to know in advance where the enemy will crack. This is the intuition behind Ukraine's current strategy.

head: Bakhmut: losing a town to break Wagner
dek: In modern war, track the exchange rate of losses, not just territory. A place that has become a symbol can turn into a trap that drains the enemy.
more: Bakhmut, a small town of about 70,000, was taken by Wagner. Simplistic war thinking says Ukraine should have retreated early, but cities are where you defend, so Ukraine fought a long fighting retreat. It lost the town, but inflicted such losses on Wagner that a rift opened with the Russian MOD, leading to the Wagner mutiny and knocking out a key Russian fighting formation. Like Stalingrad, Bakhmut has become a symbol. The MOD cannot afford to lose ground that Prigozhin and Utkin conquered, so Ukraine keeps pressing there, locking up Russian forces at a disproportionate cost.
In modern war, track the exchange rate of losses, not just territory. A place that has become a symbol can turn into a trap that drains the enemy.

head: Kherson and Kharkiv looked like stalemate, until they didn't
dek: An attritional phase can hide an imminent collapse. Judging a campaign by visible kilometres gained can badly mislead.
more: Before Ukraine's big 2022 gains, its attacks looked fruitless day after day. Underneath, Russia's ability to supply Kherson was collapsing. One day Russia simply left, and Ukraine retook the whole province without a fight. The Russian redeployment left a chunk near Kharkiv undefended, and Ukraine used spare forces to seize another 10,000 to 15,000 square kilometres.
An attritional phase can hide an imminent collapse. Judging a campaign by visible kilometres gained can badly mislead.

head: The Finland tell
dek: Watch what a state does, not what it says. The emptied border exposes the NATO-threat story as propaganda and shows how stretched Russia is.
more: Russia loudly claims it is fighting NATO. When Finland was neutral, Russia kept about 100 units on the Finnish border. Now that Finland has joined NATO, that force has fallen to about 20, one-fifth of its traditional size, because everything is being poured into Ukraine.
Watch what a state does, not what it says. The emptied border exposes the NATO-threat story as propaganda and shows how stretched Russia is.

head: Tezuka: 'I'm begging you, let me work'
dek: A great master humble enough to learn from a young disciple, and a life of relentless devotion to craft right to the end.
more: Yoshihiro Tatsumi idolised Osamu Tezuka, then pioneered gekiga, a dark reaction against manga. Rather than resist, the master was taken by his admirer's form, championed it, and around 1970 wrote Ode to Kirihito in that spirit. Dying of stomach cancer in 1989, Tezuka kept drawing in hospital. When a nurse came to take his drawing equipment away, his last words were a plea to keep working. After his death his daughter found a drawer full of unfinished work.
A great master humble enough to learn from a young disciple, and a life of relentless devotion to craft right to the end.
printed: Let me work, said the master

head: How the War Was Won
dek: A recent book offering new insights on the grunt on the ground versus the high economic strategy of the Second World War.
more: A recent book offering new insights on the grunt on the ground versus the high economic strategy of the Second World War. Ajay has studied the subject all his life and still found it full of new knowledge.
Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode.

head: Ode to Kirihito
dek: One of the most powerful graphic novels he has read: an odyssey into the human condition and the moral decay circumstances can bring.
more: One of the most powerful graphic novels he has read: an odyssey into the human condition and the moral decay circumstances can bring. Tezuka wrote it after being inspired by his admirer Tatsumi's gekiga movement.

Amit's recommendation, held up on camera as a well-thumbed copy. It is a circa-1970 medical thriller about a doctor investigating a contagious disease in a remote area that turns people into dog-like creatures, which he eventually catches himself.

head: The Push Man and Other Stories
dek: Gekiga at its best: really dark urban stories that stare into the depths of the human soul and go where manga doesn't.
more: Gekiga at its best: really dark urban stories that stare into the depths of the human soul and go where manga doesn't.

A 1969 gekiga collection, later published in English by the Canadian house Drawn & Quarterly. Amit recounts 'Bedridden', in which a colleague sent to care for an injured worker's 'woman' finds a crippled sex slave and strangles the worker to become her ninth master.

head: Abandon the Old in Tokyo
dek: More bleak, unforgettable gekiga with endings you have to read for yourself.
more: More bleak, unforgettable gekiga with endings you have to read for yourself.

Tatsumi's collection from a year after The Push Man. Amit describes 'My Beloved Monkey', in which a man who loses his arm releases his pet monkey into a zoo enclosure and watches the other monkeys tear it to shreds.

head: The hard lessons from Ukraine's summer offensive
by: Christopher Miller and Ben Hall (Financial Times)
dek: It vividly describes the counteroffensive as 'a war of tree lines': small infantry groups advancing field by field under artillery and drones, slowly wearing down Russian defences.
more: It vividly describes the counteroffensive as 'a war of tree lines': small infantry groups advancing field by field under artillery and drones, slowly wearing down Russian defences.
Amit reads from this 'great piece' that Ajay had sent him.

head: The End of History?
dek: It captures the belief that history's arc had settled on liberal democracy, a belief the current wave of authoritarianism has shaken.
more: It captures the belief that history's arc had settled on liberal democracy, a belief the current wave of authoritarianism has shaken.
Invoked as the emblem of post-Cold War optimism when the Berlin Wall fell.

head: The Battle of Kursk
dek: Russia's defences today come straight from that Soviet playbook, and Ukraine has so far cut through only one to one-and-a-half of three or four lines.
more: Russia's defences today come straight from that Soviet playbook, and Ukraine has so far cut through only one to one-and-a-half of three or four lines.
Ajay suggests reading up on it while explaining Russia's fortified lines in Zaporizhzhia. At Kursk the Soviets built seven lines, and the Germans smashed through five before running out of juice.

head: Basic facts about the map (NYT interactive)
dek: A visual primer on the counteroffensive's geography.
more: A visual primer on the counteroffensive's geography.
Show-notes resource.

head: Why a faraway war matters
dek: Ajay sees the defeat of Nazi Germany and the collapse of the USSR as the great humanising milestones of the 20th century, ushering in freedom and democracy worldwide.
more: Ajay sees the defeat of Nazi Germany and the collapse of the USSR as the great humanising milestones of the 20th century, ushering in freedom and democracy worldwide. Putin wants to return to a world where big powers invade their neighbours. If he succeeds, Belarus and Poland come next, and China may make a play for Taiwan or India. With Trump, Xi, Putin and Erdogan in the picture, authoritarians prop each other up as Mussolini, Hitler and Imperial Japan once did. Just as the world couldn't ignore Spain in 1936, it can't ignore Ukraine now.

head: You don't invade your neighbours
dek: Ajay rejects the soft 'legitimate security interests' story.
more: Ajay rejects the soft 'legitimate security interests' story. Claiming Russia may invade Ukraine because Ukraine wants certain treaties is as preposterous as saying India may invade Bangladesh for signing treaties India dislikes. Sovereignty is black and white.
printed: A faraway war, close to home

head: The civilizational state
dek: Putin calls the USSR's collapse a geopolitical tragedy and is rebuilding an empire step by step.
more: Putin calls the USSR's collapse a geopolitical tragedy and is rebuilding an empire step by step. He grabs land, sets up fake republics like the DPR and LPR, then arms them in what is passed off as a civil war, which Ajay calls the standard Hitler-Stalin playbook. The underlying idea, the civilizational state, rejects borders altogether: it could justify invading Malaysia to 'protect' ethnic Chinese there.

head: Why the invasion failed: ossification and yes-men
dek: Following Michael Kofman, Amit notes that most people expected the invasion to succeed and the occupation to fail.
more: Following Michael Kofman, Amit notes that most people expected the invasion to succeed and the occupation to fail. The surprise was that the invasion itself failed. Big armies, like big companies, ossify and pass information upward slowly. An ageing autocrat with imperial delusions ends up surrounded by yes-men while the best minds disappear into exile, so his delusions go unchallenged.

head: Three levels of governance: why authoritarian militaries are the worst
dek: Level one is civilian government in a liberal democracy. You don't need the best people inside, because brilliant outside critics find the bugs and propose fixes.
more: Level one is civilian government in a liberal democracy. You don't need the best people inside, because brilliant outside critics find the bugs and propose fixes. Level two is a democracy's military, which is harder because secrecy and patriotism mute criticism, though America's greatness is that its best minds attacked its own Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq wars. Level three is an authoritarian military: critics are silenced, nothing is disclosed and there is no market test. Ajay notes the US publishes how many shells and Javelins it bought each year, while India's budget reveals so little that Japan's military is easier to study. As Amit adds, transparency drives accountability, and accountability drives efficiency. The Indian middle-class instinct that strongmen build strong militaries is backwards.

head: Patriotism is not standing with your government
dek: Separate the state from the people; a state's actions may not even serve its own people.
more: Separate the state from the people; a state's actions may not even serve its own people. When your country invades another, rallying around the flag is a basic intellectual blunder. Protest is the patriotic act.

head: Journalism vs content
dek: Ajay notes that Indian outlets such as Hindustan Times on YouTube swallow Russian propaganda.
more: Ajay notes that Indian outlets such as Hindustan Times on YouTube swallow Russian propaganda. Amit's diagnosis is that media companies have moved from journalism, with its rigour and pursuit of truth, to a content game of endlessly pumping out 'insight'. In that game the best propaganda machine wins.

head: Committed vs involved: morale as a weapon
dek: In bacon and eggs, the chicken is involved but the pig is committed. Russia fights for one man's grandeur; Ukraine fights for its existence.
more: In bacon and eggs, the chicken is involved but the pig is committed. Russia fights for one man's grandeur; Ukraine fights for its existence. Ajay adds that war is about money, men, material and morale, and morale can change the whole landscape. It guarantees nothing, though: Austria and Czechoslovakia were still overrun.

head: The revolution in military affairs has arrived
dek: Ajay's history runs in phases: Napoleonic warfare, the stalemate that ended with combined arms in WWI, the interwar integration of tanks and aircraft (Tukhachevsky and German thinkers), a nuclear detour, and the 'RMA' of the 80s and 90s.
more: Ajay's history runs in phases: Napoleonic warfare, the stalemate that ended with combined arms in WWI, the interwar integration of tanks and aircraft (Tukhachevsky and German thinkers), a nuclear detour, and the 'RMA' of the 80s and 90s. Ukraine is where that revolution finally plays out, built on two things. The first is near-total battlefield transparency from drones, satellites and electronic monitoring. The second is precision munitions accurate to 10 to 20 metres, versus WWII bombs landing kilometres away. Together they kill WWII doctrine of secretly massing force for a breakthrough.

head: The planning, not the plan
dek: Plans collapse on contact with reality. What modern militaries need is the ability to learn, improvise and adapt under fire, which depends on a culture of debate and criticism.
more: Plans collapse on contact with reality. What modern militaries need is the ability to learn, improvise and adapt under fire, which depends on a culture of debate and criticism. Macho, nationalist authoritarian armies lack that culture.

head: Combined arms has a team-size ceiling
dek: Western combined arms, where infantry, drones, electronic warfare, artillery and tanks act in concert so that 'two and two become twenty-two', needs years of training and life-or-death trust.
more: Western combined arms, where infantry, drones, electronic warfare, artillery and tanks act in concert so that 'two and two become twenty-two', needs years of training and life-or-death trust. It is undermined by ordinary human pettiness between specialists. A business rule of thumb says every doubling of headcount demands a redesigned organisation. In practice, Ukraine's hastily trained civilians manage combined arms at about 100 people, and larger operations fumble.

head: Ukraine is the lab for the next Western way of war
dek: Western doctrine assumes total air superiority, with the grunts only mopping up.
more: Western doctrine assumes total air superiority, with the grunts only mopping up. It has never had to deal with skies full of enemy drones, and since WWII it has only fought second- and third-rate opponents. Ukraine is fighting a peer without air superiority. Russia has three times the economy and population, but its incompetence makes the two sides roughly equal. So Ukraine now knows more about conventional war than anyone.
printed: Too obvious to be the plan

head: Attrition today means deep operations, not 1914
dek: 'Attritional' brings WWI trenches to mind. Ajay says today's version is Soviet-style deep operations.
more: 'Attritional' brings WWI trenches to mind. Ajay says today's version is Soviet-style deep operations. Using NATO intelligence, partisans and standoff weapons like Storm Shadow and HIMARS, Ukraine destroys ammunition dumps, command posts and supply lines day after day, choking Russia's fuel, food and troop rotation. Fronts like Bakhmut and Zaporizhzhia may be fixing operations. Nobody can tell in advance which will become the breakthrough.

head: Logistics, not the coastline, is the real target
dek: Crimea's only land link to Russia is the Kerch Bridge, which Ukraine can likely destroy, and the southern front is supplied out of Crimea.
more: Crimea's only land link to Russia is the Kerch Bridge, which Ukraine can likely destroy, and the southern front is supplied out of Crimea. Every armchair strategist imagined a 60 to 65 km armoured thrust to the Sea of Azov. The real aim was to cut logistics, such as the M14 highway, which sat beyond HIMARS's roughly 30 km range. Ukraine only needs to creep close enough, with better standoff weapons, to strangle supply.

head: War as positional chess
dek: Americans wanted Ukraine to play like Tal or Fischer, sacrificing material for a crushing breakthrough.
more: Americans wanted Ukraine to play like Tal or Fischer, sacrificing material for a crushing breakthrough. Ukraine is playing like Capablanca or Karpov, coordinating patiently and seizing tactical chances only when they appear. It is like Carlsen grinding equal endgames until his opponent cracks, as Nepomniachtchi did in their title match. Bakhmut's effect on Wagner couldn't have been predicted either.

head: Economies win wars
dek: Ukraine's real war economy is the combined advanced world: Europe, the US, Japan, South Korea (its top artillery-shell supplier), Australia and Canada.
more: Ukraine's real war economy is the combined advanced world: Europe, the US, Japan, South Korea (its top artillery-shell supplier), Australia and Canada. Russia, with a Spain-sized GDP, loses about 1,000 tanks a year while making about 200, and sanctions block any scale-up. So Ukraine can afford to waste equipment but stays frugal with lives. The open question is whether Russia can find Stalin-level resolve in the face of its losses.

head: Don't assume the mud season ends the fight
dek: Many expected the rasputitsa, the autumn mud season, to halt the fighting.
more: Many expected the rasputitsa, the autumn mud season, to halt the fighting. But the south, around Melitopol, is warmer than Kyiv, hundreds of kilometres away, and the sea moderates the weather. Winter also amplifies Russia's problems with fuel, materials and concealment. The war may well continue into winter, so the 'failed counteroffensive' verdict is premature.

head: After Amit relays how Gaurav Chintamani was mind-blown by Ajay's five-hour Ukraine masterclass, Ajay deflects
more: After Amit relays how Gaurav Chintamani was mind-blown by Ajay's five-hour Ukraine masterclass, Ajay deflects: 'I only know 16 things.'

head: On WWII bombs landing kilometres off target, Amit
more: On WWII bombs landing kilometres off target, Amit says: 'So if someone tries to bomb me in Andheri, they'll get you in Bandra.'

head: After quoting
more: After quoting 'The plan is useless. The planning is everything,' Ajay confesses: 'Gentle reader, if ever you think I'm eloquent, I'm actually just a database. I steal stuff.'

head: Ajay's war math: Russia has three times Ukraine's economy and population
more: Ajay's war math: Russia has three times Ukraine's economy and population, 'And Russian incompetence is like a 0.33 multiplication factor. So the two sides are roughly equal in battle.'

head: Ajay's one-line verdict on Russia's economy
more: Ajay's one-line verdict on Russia's economy: 'It is Saudi Arabia with nukes.'

head: Ajay on rivalry between specialists: the drone guy boasts that flying a drone is the greatest skill in the world, and the electronic warfare guy
more: Ajay on rivalry between specialists: the drone guy boasts that flying a drone is the greatest skill in the world, and the electronic warfare guy replies, 'Yeah, you guys, you just fly these birds. We, we shoot them down.'

head: On the dagger thrust to the Sea of Azov
more: On the dagger thrust to the Sea of Azov, 'dreamt up in public domain by every armchair military strategist in the whole world', Ajay remarks: 'if something is so obvious, you can't be doing that.'

head: Amit on Tezuka being called both the father and the godfather of manga
more: Amit on Tezuka being called both the father and the godfather of manga: 'So father and godfather at the same time.'

head: Two quotes on plans from Amit: von Moltke's
more: Two quotes on plans from Amit: von Moltke's 'no plan survives contact with the enemy' and Mike Tyson's 'Everyone has a plan till they get punched in the face.'

head: Ulysses S. Grant as the source of the American doctrine of concentrated force. Amit quotes a WWII historian
more: Ulysses S. Grant as the source of the American doctrine of concentrated force. Amit quotes a WWII historian: 'They built a powerful army when the need arose, attacked the enemy's strength as quickly as possible, and took and inflicted casualties until he stopped struggling. Anything less was a distraction.' He also cites Lawrence Freedman's summary of US doctrine as a 'main effort' on a single front.

head: America as the…
more: America as the 'arsenal of democracy', the WWII industrial colossus behind both its own way of war and Stalin's strategy.

head: Gekiga, the dark, adult, urban comics movement Yoshihiro Tatsumi pioneered against cheerier manga. Tatsumi wrote of Tezuka
more: Gekiga, the dark, adult, urban comics movement Yoshihiro Tatsumi pioneered against cheerier manga. Tatsumi wrote of Tezuka: 'Tezuka was like a god for me.'

head: The German Tank Problem: Statisticians vs the Brigadier's Girlfriend
dek: Careful reasoning about how data is generated can beat apparently privileged insider information.
more: Late in World War II the Allies needed to know whether Germany's new heavy tanks were a few showpieces or were being mass-produced. Spies, the people who 'knew the girlfriend of some brigadier', reported around 1,500 tanks a month. Statisticians used a different source: the serial numbers on tanks destroyed in battle. The methodical Germans numbered their tanks in sequence. So if you have seen, say, 24, 74 and 90, you should not conclude there are only 90 tanks. You take the average gap between the observed numbers and add it to the highest one. Their estimate was about 200 a month. When the Allies examined German production records after the war, the statisticians turned out to be right and the spies wrong.

Careful reasoning about how data is generated can beat apparently privileged insider information. A simple formula applied to the right structure outperformed gossip. Germany's orderly numbering itself became an intelligence leak; as Ajay notes, it would have been harder if every number had been randomized.

head: The Naive Question That Led to the Cramér-Rao Bound
dek: Admitting a gap in your knowledge is how you close it ('All gaps are overcomable').
more: Ajay began his PhD without ever having studied probability or statistics, so he was made to take a fourth-year undergraduate econometrics class taught by Dennis Aigner. Aigner opened with a 'helicopter tour' of all of statistics that swept Ajay away. As Aigner showed how one estimator could be improved, and then improved again, Ajay asked whether there had to be a theoretical limit. Aigner replied that an Indian had asked exactly that question and answered it. The answer is the Cramér-Rao lower bound.

Admitting a gap in your knowledge is how you close it ('All gaps are overcomable'). A beginner's obvious question can lead straight to a field's foundational result, and in this case that result was proved by a young Indian in Calcutta.

head: CR Rao in Calcutta, and Fisher's Decency
dek: World-class work can come from an isolated outpost, but recognition depends on the decency of the people who control the field.
more: CR Rao was born in 1920. He came from Andhra Pradesh to Calcutta as an ordinary student at PC Mahalanobis's Indian Statistical Institute (ISI). This was before independence, so there was no government money, and Mahalanobis often funded the institute himself. Cut off from the European mainstream, Rao produced two of the handful of greatest results in 20th-century statistics: the Cramér-Rao lower bound in 1943, and the Rao-Blackwell theorem, which is a technique for making an estimator one step better. Each was discovered independently of the other person named in it. Ajay asked the mathematician Rajeeva Karandikar how Rao's name survived, given how easily Indian work gets ignored. The answer was Ronald Fisher. Fisher visited ISI, understood the results and started calling them by the joint names. Ajay compares this to the Royal Society presenting Darwin and Wallace together.

World-class work can come from an isolated outpost, but recognition depends on the decency of the people who control the field. Without Fisher, work done in Calcutta in 1943, with no internet, could simply have disappeared. Ajay says Indian work is still routinely ignored and later claimed by others, and that this has happened to him.

head: How ISI's Head Start Was Squandered
dek: Being at the frontier once guarantees nothing. Fields reinvent themselves, and communities that don't follow get left behind.
more: Having one CR Rao convinced a whole generation at ISI that 'this is a game we can play'. ISI was world-class, and its journal Sankhya was respected internationally and stocked by libraries everywhere. That early lead did not build into anything larger. In the 1970s and 80s the frontier moved from mathematical statistics, which proves theorems about closed-form estimators, to computational statistics. Bradley Efron's bootstrap in 1979 was one of the key innovations. In computational statistics an estimator can be an algorithm, which requires combining statistics with computer science. India's statistics community stuck to theorem-proving and missed the shift that grew into today's data-science revolution.

Being at the frontier once guarantees nothing. Fields reinvent themselves, and communities that don't follow get left behind. Ajay also sees a deeper problem: the way Indian state-funded research institutions are managed seems incompatible with excellence.

head: CRRao.jl: A Name as a Commitment Device
dek: Naming your work after a hero is a public promise to meet his standard.
more: At XKDR Forum and the Chennai Mathematical Institute, Ajay's colleague Sourish Das leads a Julia package. It gives one uniform way to call many kinds of estimators, from linear regression to random forests, in either frequentist or Bayesian form. While names were being debated, Sourish proposed calling it CRRao.jl as a 'commitment device', a way to kick themselves into doing it well. Later CR Rao's daughter emailed to say she had shown her father the package and he had smiled.
Naming your work after a hero is a public promise to meet his standard. That smile was, in Ajay's words, the closest he ever came to the greatness of CR Rao.

head: Abraham Wald and the Missing Bullets
dek: The data you can see has been filtered by survival, and the most important evidence is often what is absent.
more: Around 1942 Abraham Wald was drafted into a wartime research group so brilliant that someone quipped Milton Friedman was the fourth smartest person in the room. Wald did not have security clearance. The joke went that a secretary stood beside him and took away each sheet as soon as he finished writing it. The group was asked how to strengthen planes that came back riddled with bullets. Returning planes had more holes in the fuselage than in the engine, so the obvious plan was to reinforce the fuselage. Wald asked where the missing bullets were. If hits are spread fairly evenly, the missing ones struck the planes that never came back. So the engine, the part with the fewest holes on returning planes, was the part to protect.

The data you can see has been filtered by survival, and the most important evidence is often what is absent. Amit connects this to Ricky Ponting, who said he carried a map of the gaps in the field rather than of the fielders.

head: The Cricket Tipster Scam
dek: A great track record means nothing until you know how many attempts failed and vanished.
more: Amit once wrote a column built on this scam. You contact 1,000 cricket bettors and offer free tips. You tell 500 of them India will win the next India–Sri Lanka match and tell the other 500 that Sri Lanka will. Whatever happens, you then split the group you got right in half and repeat. After a few rounds, a dozen or so people have seen you call five or six results in a row, and they will gladly pay you. Mutual funds can work the same way: run a family of funds following random strategies, and by sheer luck one of them will show a brilliant five- or six-year record.
A great track record means nothing until you know how many attempts failed and vanished. Selection can look exactly like skill.

head: How Many Lives Does It Take to Kill a Factory?
dek: Choosing the right thing to measure can overturn intuition. The option that looks deadlier for each flight can cost fewer lives overall.
more: Allied bombers flew from Britain to hit German factories and refineries, facing German fighters and 88mm anti-aircraft guns. Pilots wanted to fly at 20,000 feet, above the guns. But WWII bombs, falling under gravity, could land kilometres off target, so very few hit from that height. At 6,000 feet more crews would be shot down, but far more bombs would hit. The statisticians, including a young Robert McNamara, ignored how frightening each altitude felt. They calculated how many airmen died for each factory destroyed, and the answer was 6,000 feet. When the pilots were told, they were in uproar. Along the way Ajay explains that the phrase 'a wing and a prayer' comes from crippled bombers gliding home with their engines shot out.

Choosing the right thing to measure can overturn intuition. The option that looks deadlier for each flight can cost fewer lives overall. Refusing to put numbers on a hard trade-off does not make it go away.

head: Wald's Death in India
dek: The story comes full circle: the wartime statisticians and the ISI world of Mahalanobis and Rao were closely connected, and Calcutta was then a stop for the world's best statisticians.
more: Amit adds a sad coda. Abraham Wald died in 1950, aged 48, in an Air India crash in India, along with his wife. He had just given a talk at ISI in Calcutta and was travelling to a statistics congress in Bangalore.
The story comes full circle: the wartime statisticians and the ISI world of Mahalanobis and Rao were closely connected, and Calcutta was then a stop for the world's best statisticians.

head: Mahalanobis: Genius Trapped by His Own Genius
dek: The certainty and control that make a brilliant scientist and institution-builder can turn into hubris when applied to a messy society.
more: Mahalanobis trained in physics. On the voyage back to India he was given volumes of the statistics journal Biometrika, and he arrived home in love with statistics. He taught physics at Presidency College before founding ISI. Reading from Nikhil Menon's Planning Democracy, Amit describes a stern, prim workaholic with coconut-oiled hair who showed affection only to his pets. He was a proud polymath, 'a physicist by training, statistician by intellect, and planner by conviction', who 'thought he knew best in practically every matter'. He made staff and students record their daily activities in a diary. Milton Friedman warned that able mathematicians, used to a field of absolutes, become dangerous when they turn to economic planning. Another account, which Amit attributes to Hannah Arendt, calls him domineering and vain, a Bengali aristocrat moving towards Stalinist-style authoritarianism.

The certainty and control that make a brilliant scientist and institution-builder can turn into hubris when applied to a messy society. Ajay calls this a recurring theme: the precision of science and engineering leaves many successful people unprepared for the real world.
printed: The man who thought he knew

head: The 1944 Jute Showdown: Sampling vs Counting
dek: A well-designed sample can beat a brute-force count on accuracy and cost at the same time.
more: In 1944 random sample surveys were not yet widely accepted anywhere in the world, and there were calls to abandon them. The Bengal government settled the dispute with a contest over jute. Traditional plot-by-plot counting and ISI's random sample survey were run at the same time, and both were checked against official jute sales figures. The count was off by 16.6%. The sample survey was off by only 0.3%, and it cost a tenth as much.
A well-designed sample can beat a brute-force count on accuracy and cost at the same time. A clean head-to-head test was what finally won the argument for ISI.

head: The Bharat Sadhu Samaaj: Licensing Holy Men
dek: The planning era's ambition reached as far as certifying holy men and recruiting them to sell the Plan.
more: In the mid-1950s there were an estimated 75 lakh sadhus in India, and the worry was that many were frauds. A sadhu registration bill was brought in 1956. To be recognised as a sadhu you would apply for a government licence and join the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj. President Rajendra Prasad then addressed the gathered sadhus. He told them nothing could be achieved in the other world without first setting this world in order, which was a pitch for their support of the Five-Year Plan. Amit found the story in Nikhil Menon's Planning Democracy.
The planning era's ambition reached as far as certifying holy men and recruiting them to sell the Plan. It is a vivid, comic picture of how far the planning state tried to extend.

head: Haldane Moved to India to Stop Wearing Socks
dek: This is Amit's favourite example of the writing principle 'show, don't tell': one concrete detail conveys a whole philosophy of life.
more: JBS Haldane came to work at ISI in the mid-1950s, when he was in his sixties. He quipped that Mahalanobis's constant travels 'define a novel random vector'. Asked why he had left England for India, he didn't talk about simple living or escaping convention. He said he didn't want to wear socks anymore. Photos from the rest of his life show him in banyan, dhoti and pyjama, and never in socks.
This is Amit's favourite example of the writing principle 'show, don't tell': one concrete detail conveys a whole philosophy of life.

head: Chintaman Deshmukh's Proposal on a Tree
dek: The official who saved the institute was also a romantic. As Amit puts it, even people who care about statistics and math have hearts.
more: Around 1944 Chintaman Deshmukh, a senior official who later became finance minister, approved funding that practically guaranteed ISI's survival. Nikhil Menon describes him as a Cambridge-educated man who topped the Indian Civil Service, recited Vedic shlokas for pleasure, translated Kalidasa's Meghaduta and quoted scripture in support of economic policy. Widowed in the early 1950s, he married Durgabai Deshmukh. She was a feisty, outspoken woman who had been married off as a child at eight and, at 14, refused to go through with the marriage. Her autobiography, Chintaman and I, opens with his proposal.
The official who saved the institute was also a romantic. As Amit puts it, even people who care about statistics and math have hearts.

head: The Great Mental Models (three-volume set)
dek: Formal education rarely teaches how to think about the world. These books supply the frames for finding connections across fields, which is the 'everything is everything' idea in practice.
more: Formal education rarely teaches how to think about the world. These books supply the frames for finding connections across fields, which is the 'everything is everything' idea in practice. Amit calls them a treasure everyone should own, and notes the Kindle copies are cheap.
Amit's recommendation for the episode. A friend, Gautam John, gave him the set in Bangalore. Volume one covers general thinking models, and later volumes cover physics, chemistry and mathematics.

head: The Knowledge Project Podcast

more: Amit calls it 'the excellent Knowledge Project podcast'.
Mentioned while recommending The Great Mental Models, written by the same author.

A Julia statistical modelling package led by Sourish Das and named after CR Rao. The show notes link its GitHub page, its documentation and Sourish's write-up, 'CRRao: A Julia Statistical Modeling Package for All'.

dek: A visual walk-through of the estimation idea Ajay describes, in which serial numbers reveal how many tanks were made.
more: A visual walk-through of the estimation idea Ajay describes, in which serial numbers reveal how many tanks were made.
A YouTube explainer linked in the show notes for the opening story.

head: Tyrannies Leak: HUMINT and SIGINT
dek: Intelligence comes from people (HUMINT) or from intercepted signals and communications (SIGINT).
more: Intelligence comes from people (HUMINT) or from intercepted signals and communications (SIGINT). Authoritarian regimes are especially exposed to human sources, because their obedient staff are often full of people who privately hate the ruler.

head: Estimators and Their Limit: Cramér-Rao and Rao-Blackwell
dek: Statistics is the craft of designing, analysing and comparing estimators, which are formulas that infer unknowns like the total number of German tanks.
more: Statistics is the craft of designing, analysing and comparing estimators, which are formulas that infer unknowns like the total number of German tanks. The Cramér-Rao lower bound shows there is a theoretical limit on how good an estimator can be for a given model and data set. The Rao-Blackwell theorem is a method for making an estimator one step better. CR Rao worked out both in Calcutta, the first in 1943.

head: Survivorship Bias
dek: A data set usually contains only the survivors: planes that made it home, funds that weren't shut down, tips that happened to be right.
more: A data set usually contains only the survivors: planes that made it home, funds that weren't shut down, tips that happened to be right. The units that died along the way are invisible. Before trusting the data, ask how it was generated and what is missing. Wald's armour advice and the cricket-tipster scam are two versions of the same trap.

head: Statistics Is Thinking, Not Button-Pushing
dek: Ajay warns that data analysis is too often treated as feeding data into software and reading off answers.
more: Ajay warns that data analysis is too often treated as feeding data into software and reading off answers. Stories like the tank and bomber problems show that real insight comes from understanding the problem, using intuition and common sense.

head: From Theorems to Algorithms: Mathematical vs Computational Statistics
dek: Mid-century statistics was mathematical statistics: estimators were closed-form formulas, analysed by proving theorems.
more: Mid-century statistics was mathematical statistics: estimators were closed-form formulas, analysed by proving theorems. From the 1970s, with innovations like Bradley Efron's bootstrap in 1979, an estimator could be an algorithm. That merged statistics with computer science and led to today's data science. India's statistics community, so strong in the old style, missed this shift.

head: Ramanujan vs Anand: Two Models of Indian Genius
dek: Ramanujan was a self-taught prodigy who appeared despite deprivation, but Cambridge and GH Hardy turned him into a great mathematician, so that achievement belongs to Cambridge's ecosystem.
more: Ramanujan was a self-taught prodigy who appeared despite deprivation, but Cambridge and GH Hardy turned him into a great mathematician, so that achievement belongs to Cambridge's ecosystem. Anand was largely built by an Indian chess ecosystem, and he then helped nurture the next generation, so that India's teenagers are now among the best in the world. CR Rao fits the Anand model: an ordinary student who flourished inside the ecosystem Mahalanobis built.

head: Excellence Comes From Founders, Not Bureaucracies
dek: ISI reached the world frontier before independence, with no government funding, because of one eccentric, driven founder.
more: ISI reached the world frontier before independence, with no government funding, because of one eccentric, driven founder. Ajay is sceptical of calls for more public-sector universities. In his view, India's state-funded research and teaching institutions, IITs included, have management problems that seem incompatible with quality. What creates excellence is individuals who build isolated centres of excellence.

head: Credit Depends on the Decency of Gatekeepers
dek: Work done in India, then and now, is easily ignored or later claimed by others in the global mainstream.
more: Work done in India, then and now, is easily ignored or later claimed by others in the global mainstream. Rao's 1943 results entered the canon only because Ronald Fisher chose to recognise them, just as the Royal Society chose to give Wallace credit alongside Darwin. Recognition is not automatic. It depends on the fairness of the people who shape a field.

head: High Modernism
dek: High modernism is a two-part belief. First, scientists and engineers know what should be done.
more: High modernism is a two-part belief. First, scientists and engineers know what should be done. Second, that special claim on truth entitles them to coercive power over everyone else. Minds trained on controlled systems such as a mathematical model, an engineering project or one piece of software are unprepared for societies, which are full of the unknowable. Milton Friedman made the same point about mathematicians like Mahalanobis who turn to economic planning.

head: Measure the Right Thing: Lives per Factory Destroyed
