dek: The bombing problem flips once you change what you measure. Instead of asking how risky each flight is, you ask how many lives each factory destroyed costs.
more: The bombing problem flips once you change what you measure. Instead of asking how risky each flight is, you ask how many lives each factory destroyed costs. Flying low is deadlier per flight but far more accurate, so fewer crews die in total. Choosing the right objective turns a gut fear into a solvable estimation problem.

head: Random Sampling Beats Brute-Force Counting
dek: Mahalanobis and ISI were early champions of the random sample survey.
more: Mahalanobis and ISI were early champions of the random sample survey. In the 1944 Bengal jute contest, a sample survey came within 0.3% of the truth, while plot-by-plot counting was off by 16.6%, and the survey cost a tenth as much. A well-designed sample can be both more accurate and cheaper than counting everything.

head: Show, Don't Tell
dek: A core writing principle: rather than stating a point in abstract words, convey it through a concrete detail.
more: A core writing principle: rather than stating a point in abstract words, convey it through a concrete detail. Haldane could have said he wanted a simple life free of convention. Instead he said he didn't want to wear socks anymore, and everyone instantly understood.

head: After the German Tank Problem, Amit offers the moral
more: After the German Tank Problem, Amit offers the moral: 'The moral of the story is brigadiers lie to their girlfriends.' Ajay adds: 'Or that tanks don't lie.'

head: Ajay brings the gag back in the bombing story, listing the ways to check bomb damage
more: Ajay brings the gag back in the bombing story, listing the ways to check bomb damage: 'You have a spotter plane, you have local intelligence, you have the brigadier's girlfriend.'

head: Amit on Wald's wartime group: it was so brilliant that someone quipped
more: Amit on Wald's wartime group: it was so brilliant that someone quipped 'Milton Friedman is the fourth smartest person in the room'. And because Wald lacked security clearance, the joke went that a secretary took away each sheet the moment he finished writing it.

head: After telling how Wald died in a plane crash in India, Amit adds…
more: After telling how Wald died in a plane crash in India, Amit adds: 'Milton Friedman would now be the third smartest man in the room, but not in a way he would have liked.'

head: Poker banter between the stories.
more: Poker banter between the stories. Amit: 'You had a German tank story. I call you and I raise you with a British airplane story.' After Ajay's bombing story, Amit says: 'You raised me, so I will just fold.'

head: On Sourish Das naming the package after CR Rao, Amit
more: On Sourish Das naming the package after CR Rao, Amit says: 'We should have called the show CR Rao. Everything is CR Rao.'

head: When Ajay starts talking about Julia, Amit riffs on the famous lyric
more: When Ajay starts talking about Julia, Amit riffs on the famous lyric: 'As another Julia would say, the hills are alive with the sound of coding.'

head: After the story of India missing the boat on computational statistics, Amit
more: After the story of India missing the boat on computational statistics, Amit says: 'We missed the boat on algorithms and what I'm worried about is that you and I will miss the boat on the YouTube algorithm.' He follows with a pun on going viral and Viral Shah, the Julia co-creator Ajay had just mentioned.

head: When cats start fighting off-camera, Amit tells viewers it is the…
more: When cats start fighting off-camera, Amit tells viewers it is the 'ghosts of statisticians past who have worked at the ISI wailing to see the condition'.

head: Amit happily accepts Ajay's claim that CR Rao, from Andhra Pradesh, is the Bengal Renaissance's greatest achievement
more: Amit happily accepts Ajay's claim that CR Rao, from Andhra Pradesh, is the Bengal Renaissance's greatest achievement: 'You know the whole world is Bengali.' He mentions a fantasy novel in which Bengal colonizes the world, quotes the American Statistical Association's praise of Rao as a 'Bengal Renaissance man', and later declares: 'All Bengali geniuses are belong to me, Dada.'

After reading Nikhil Menon's portrait of a stern, prim Mahalanobis who showed affection only to dogs, cats and cows, Amit tells Ajay that apart from the dogs and cows, 'the rest of this seems to fit you'. Ajay replies: 'Cows also.'

head: On Mahalanobis making staff log their daily activities, Amit says to Ajay, the privacy advocate
more: On Mahalanobis making staff log their daily activities, Amit says to Ajay, the privacy advocate: 'he would have loved Aadhaar'.

head: On the government licensing sadhus, Ajay asks…
more: On the government licensing sadhus, Ajay asks: 'Was there a certification examination? Was there a UID?' Amit trips over his words: 'Once the Bharat Sadhu Samaaj was farmed, formed, not farmed, you could farm them', with sadhus' 'documentation in triplicate'.

head: On Haldane and socks, Amit says nobody likes wearing socks
more: On Haldane and socks, Amit says nobody likes wearing socks 'unless they're kind of kinky and, you know, they wear it on their heads while doing unspeakable things. Look up autoerotic asphyxiation.' The show notes link the topic with the warning: '(Do not try this at home.)'

head: After the eucalyptus-tree proposal
more: After the eucalyptus-tree proposal: 'when men were men and inscribed Sanskrit shlokas into barks of trees. Have you ever done that?' The answer: 'No, no such luck.'

head: Amit, a self-described man of the right, introduces his recommendation
more: Amit, a self-described man of the right, introduces his recommendation: 'I want to turn to my right because I'm always turning to the right.'

head: Amit quotes Haldane's line that Mahalanobis's constant travels
more: Amit quotes Haldane's line that Mahalanobis's constant travels 'define a novel random vector', then admits: 'I have no idea what that phrase means, but I'm sure you do.'

'Coming back on a wing and a prayer': Ajay calls it one of the most beautiful phrases in English and traces it to WWII bombers whose engines were shot out, gliding home on just a wing and hoping to make it.

head: Ricky Ponting on becoming a great batsman, quoted by Amit as an intuitive version of Wald's insight
more: Ricky Ponting on becoming a great batsman, quoted by Amit as an intuitive version of Wald's insight: 'Most batsmen have a map of the fielders in their head. I had a map of the gaps.'

head: Darwin and Wallace: Ajay compares the joint names on Rao's theorems to the…
more: Darwin and Wallace: Ajay compares the joint names on Rao's theorems to the 'Darwin-Wallace theory of evolution'. The Royal Society gave both men credit, even though Wallace had his idea in a malaria fever dream weeks earlier while Darwin had been working on it for decades.

head: Sankhya, the journal ISI built in its golden age, was respected as world-class
more: Sankhya, the journal ISI built in its golden age, was respected as world-class, and 'libraries all over the world would get Sankhya'.

head: The American Statistical Association on CR Rao, quoted by Amit
more: The American Statistical Association on CR Rao, quoted by Amit: 'Rao is a living legend whose work has influenced not just statistics, but has far-reaching implications for fields as varied as economics, genetics, anthropology, geology, national planning, demography, biometry, and medicine.'

head: Milton Friedman on Mahalanobis, quoted by Amit: able mathematicians
more: Milton Friedman on Mahalanobis, quoted by Amit: able mathematicians, 'working in a field of absolutes', become dangerous in economic planning because 'they produce specific and detailed plans in which they have confidence without perhaps realizing that economic planning is not the absolute science that mathematics is.'

head: The tycoon's question: can we grow rich and still beat our wives?
dek: The question sets up the whole episode. It asks whether freedom is a package you must take whole, or a menu you can pick from.
more: Over dinner abroad, a friend of Amit's who runs one of Asia's biggest businesses (and holds degrees in philosophy and anthropology) posed a question. He let Amit use the question but not his name: can a society grow rich while keeping its illiberal habits, or must it give them up to prosper? Amit guessed that the median Indian male would say yes, you can grow rich and keep beating your wife. Amit's own view is that in the long run, true prosperity, even in the material sense, is impossible without modern liberal values. Ajay added two lenses. The answer may differ for an individual and for a society. And if the answer were 'no', some people might choose to give up prosperity rather than accept enlightenment values.
The question sets up the whole episode. It asks whether freedom is a package you must take whole, or a menu you can pick from. China bet on the menu.

head: Samuelson's dotted line: when the USSR looked like the future
dek: Even the best economists can mistake a coercive sprint for a durable growth model.
more: After 1917 the Soviets forced industrialisation through central planning and enormous cruelty. By 1945 they were the great land power, though Ajay notes they won the war with heavy Western help. They had a nuclear bomb by 1949, helped by knowledge stolen from the Manhattan Project. In edition after edition, Paul Samuelson's hugely influential economics textbook carried a GDP chart on its inside cover with a dotted projection showing the USSR overtaking the US. Orwell, Koestler and Nehru rejected the regime's cruelty, but many still thought it would 'work' in purely instrumental terms. In 1989 it collapsed under its own contradictions. Ajay says Russia has never recovered: today it has a Spain-sized GDP.
Even the best economists can mistake a coercive sprint for a durable growth model. The instrumental case for unfreedom failed on its own terms, not just on ethical ones.

head: Four flavours of yogurt: what China learned from the Soviet collapse
dek: China was not a copy of the Soviet model. It was a deliberate update: give people economic abundance and keep political control.
more: The Chinese Communist Party studied the fall of the USSR closely and swore to do whatever it took to survive. One lesson it drew was that consumer shortages kill regimes. So China opened up to a private consumer economy with '400 kinds of yogurt', to trade, and to FDI, while keeping one-party rule, state direction and limits on personal freedom.
China was not a copy of the Soviet model. It was a deliberate update: give people economic abundance and keep political control. The episode argues this update is now breaking too.

head: 'Our way is right': the 2008 meeting with Wang Qishan
dek: The 2008 crisis gave the 'China model' its moment of confidence. Western capitalists started to doubt their own system, and global firms went all in on China.
more: Richard McGregor's The Party describes a 2008 meeting, just after the financial crisis hit America. A group of American businessmen met Wang Qishan, China's vice premier in charge of the financial sector. Wang told them that America has its way, China has its way, and China's way is right. Amit says the Americans could be forgiven for thinking there might be something to it.
The 2008 crisis gave the 'China model' its moment of confidence. Western capitalists started to doubt their own system, and global firms went all in on China.

head: Deng Xiaoping's crippled son
dek: Deng's reforms came from someone who had felt the regime's cruelty in his own family.
more: During the Cultural Revolution, Red Guards threw Deng Xiaoping's son, then about 11 or 14 years old, out of a first-floor window. The fall broke his bones and crippled him for life. When Deng came to power in 1978, he built guardrails against a repeat of Maoism. He introduced term limits of ten years for the head of state and a succession system that neither Mao nor the Soviet Union ever had. He also set a non-confrontational 'bide our time' stance toward the West. Ajay explains that Xi Jinping later dismantled all of this.
Deng's reforms came from someone who had felt the regime's cruelty in his own family. This explains why he spread power out, and why Xi concentrating it again matters so much.
printed: A son, a window, and term limits

head: Mao's war on sparrows
dek: This is the 'man of system' delusion in its purest form: a leader who thinks he can redesign a whole society, or an ecosystem, to fit a master plan.
more: Amit reads from his 2016 demonetisation column. In 1958 Mao ordered every sparrow in China killed because sparrows ate farmers' grain. Countless sparrows died. But sparrows also ate locusts, and once they were gone, locusts multiplied and destroyed the crops. Famine followed, and no fewer than 45 million people died in the three years after Mao's orders. This was part of the wider Great Leap Forward.

This is the 'man of system' delusion in its purest form: a leader who thinks he can redesign a whole society, or an ecosystem, to fit a master plan. Amit wrote the piece to warn that we do not learn from such cautionary tales.

head: China's red phone
dek: This is the hidden wiring of a Leninist state. Real authority runs through party channels that sit outside the formal, legal state.
more: McGregor describes the 'red phone' sitting on the desks of the heads of a few hundred state-owned organisations. Each had its own four-digit number. When it rang, it was the party high command and you had to pick up. You could also use it to call others on the network. It became a symbol of power, corruption and decadence.
This is the hidden wiring of a Leninist state. Real authority runs through party channels that sit outside the formal, legal state.

head: From father's bicycle to two cars
dek: Whatever its sins, China delivered huge generational mobility and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty.
more: In Smoke and Mirrors, her 2007-08 book on China, Pallavi Aiyar recounts a student telling her that a generation ago his father cycled many miles to work, and now he owns two cars. When Amit asked Aiyar about it on his podcast, she said this was not one student's story. Everybody told her some version of it.

Whatever its sins, China delivered huge generational mobility and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Amit admits India still hasn't matched this. Any honest critique of the China model has to start by acknowledging it.

head: Songbirds on the expressway, and Lahore's two faces
dek: This is Amit's lament. We like to think bottom-up culture always outlasts top-down rule.
more: Aiyar describes Beijing as surreal. Old men in Mao suits walked their caged songbirds along expressways, and elderly women practised tai chi surrounded by bulldozers. What struck her most was that people showed no visible trauma or resistance. Amit connects this to his 2006 trip to Pakistan, where he covered the Indian cricket team for The Guardian, the Wall Street Journal and Cricinfo. In Lahore, where his father was born but felt no nostalgia for, Amit found a warm, effusive Punjabi culture living alongside a darkness coming from the regime's ideology.
This is Amit's lament. We like to think bottom-up culture always outlasts top-down rule. But the longer an oppressive regime lasts, the more it can reshape the culture itself.

head: Vaccine nationalism and the made-in-China milk problem
dek: Authoritarianism fails in practical terms, not just moral ones. Past coercion destroys the trust a state needs when it finally asks citizens to cooperate.
more: India made no pretence of building its own COVID vaccine. The Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine (Covishield) came to India with help from the Gates Foundation, and a private Indian company built huge manufacturing capacity with no help from the state. China, driven by nationalism and an insistence that it had 'arrived', pushed its own vaccines, which gave poor protection. Decades of coercion also meant that many older Chinese, the people most vulnerable to COVID, refused a government vaccine. Ajay notes that many Chinese won't even drink made-in-China milk.
Authoritarianism fails in practical terms, not just moral ones. Past coercion destroys the trust a state needs when it finally asks citizens to cooperate.

head: The app that screams: China's lockdown nightmare
dek: Digital tools that look like conveniences in a free society can become instruments for crushing individuals in an authoritarian one.
more: China ran some of the world's most extreme lockdowns and presented them as proof that the Chinese way was better. Month after month, people were trapped in their homes. Phones, digital identity and tracking were used so that if you stepped into the next street, an app raised an alarm and an official came after you. Production stopped, global supply chains broke, and protests broke out, which is rare in China. Eventually the regime gave up, COVID surged, and many people died.
Digital tools that look like conveniences in a free society can become instruments for crushing individuals in an authoritarian one.

head: The Essential Dykes To Watch Out For
dek: The comic strip ran for roughly 1985 to 2008 and became iconic. It captured, and arguably helped create, a lesbian counterculture.
more: The comic strip ran for roughly 1985 to 2008 and became iconic. It captured, and arguably helped create, a lesbian counterculture. Its strip 'The Rule' gave the world the Bechdel test. It is also a model of steady, week-after-week craft.
Amit's second closing recommendation, taken from the pile of books on set that viewers had asked about.

head: Blankets
dek: One of the graphic novels Amit calls a masterpiece. He says he may someday do a full list of the comics he loves.
more: One of the graphic novels Amit calls a masterpiece. He says he may someday do a full list of the comics he loves.
Listed alongside Fun Home as proof of what comics can do.

head: The Party: The Secret World of China's Communist Rulers
dek: He calls it a great book on how the party really works.
more: He calls it a great book on how the party really works. It shows the Leninist machinery under China's reforms: control of personnel, propaganda and the army, a party above the law, the red phone, and the 'take it or leave it' compact.
Amit quotes it throughout his history of China.

head: Smoke And Mirrors
dek: Amit calls Aiyar a fantastic writer and a sharp analyst, not just a travel writer.
more: Amit calls Aiyar a fantastic writer and a sharp analyst, not just a travel writer. The book gives a ground-level view of China's transformation and how people absorbed it.
Her first book on China, from around 2007-08, quoted for the bicycle-to-two-cars story and the passage about Beijing's surreal cityscapes.

head: How China Escaped the Poverty Trap
dek: He calls it a really interesting book. Its framing of the poverty trap provokes debate, and Amit says he even has a problem with the framing itself.
more: He calls it a really interesting book. Its framing of the poverty trap provokes debate, and Amit says he even has a problem with the framing itself.
Amit reads its parable of the pauper and two finance gurus to set up a question on how poor countries escape poverty.

head: The End of History?
dek: It captured the post-1989 sense that liberal democracy had won the argument.
more: It captured the post-1989 sense that liberal democracy had won the argument. The China model later revived that very debate.
Mentioned as 'that famous essay' written as the Soviet Union fell.

head: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
dek: He calls it a great book that is often overlooked. It coined the 'man of system', the planner who treats people like chess pieces, which is the best warning against Maoist-style grand designs.
more: He calls it a great book that is often overlooked. It coined the 'man of system', the planner who treats people like chess pieces, which is the best warning against Maoist-style grand designs.
Amit reads the full 'man of system' passage from it.

head: The Fatal Conceit
dek: Amit says Hayek's phrase 'the fatal conceit' aptly expresses the same idea: the belief that planners can design a society.
more: Amit says Hayek's phrase 'the fatal conceit' aptly expresses the same idea: the belief that planners can design a society.
Cited right after Smith's 'man of system' passage.

head: The Road to Serfdom
dek: Amit calls Thatcher one of his heroes of the 20th century and Hayek his favourite 'Freddie'.
more: Amit calls Thatcher one of his heroes of the 20th century and Hayek his favourite 'Freddie'. It is the classic argument for freedom against state planning.
Amit tells how Margaret Thatcher slammed it on the table at her first cabinet meeting and said it would guide them.

head: The Constitution of Liberty
dek: Rounds out the Hayek reading behind the episode's case for freedom.
more: Rounds out the Hayek reading behind the episode's case for freedom.
Show-notes link, listed with Hayek's other books.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: Ajay says it would have been a very good book for Deng Xiaoping as well, because its message is to fix the freedom side first.
more: Ajay says it would have been a very good book for Deng Xiaoping as well, because its message is to fix the freedom side first. Amit calls it 'the greatest plug I've ever seen somebody give for their own freaking book.'
Asked what he would do in Deng's place, Ajay recalls the question behind the book: if a time machine could carry one book to Nehru, which should it be?

head: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It covers his long-standing problem with GDP. Because government spending counts in GDP, a state can inflate the number with make-work and roads to nowhere.
more: It covers his long-standing problem with GDP. Because government spending counts in GDP, a state can inflate the number with make-work and roads to nowhere.
Mentioned when Amit asks whether China's GDP growth was hollow.

head: Freedom comes as a package
dek: Amit's thesis is that economic, political and personal freedoms rise and fall together, and real prosperity needs all of them.
more: Amit's thesis is that economic, political and personal freedoms rise and fall together, and real prosperity needs all of them. The Soviet Union bet that it needed none. China bet that limited economic freedom alone was enough. Ajay adds two lenses. The answer may differ for an individual and a society. And if freedom really is indivisible, some people may choose to give up prosperity rather than accept enlightenment values.

head: Authoritarian sprints run up 'technical debt'
dek: Coercive regimes can mobilise resources and sprint for a while. But they pile up distortions, much like technical debt in software, and eventually the bill comes due.
more: Coercive regimes can mobilise resources and sprint for a while. But they pile up distortions, much like technical debt in software, and eventually the bill comes due. The old argument goes: 'be thuggish first, get rich, then add democracy'. Some made it about India in 1947, when female literacy was only 6-7%. Ajay's answer is that a society built on coercion cannot easily switch into freedom. Chile, Taiwan and South Korea managed the transition, but it is hard.

head: Coordination by coercion looks like success
dek: Free markets coordinate messily through prices and private bargains, and nobody can tell where they will lead.
more: Free markets coordinate messily through prices and private bargains, and nobody can tell where they will lead. A state can force everyone onto one standard, as China did with a single payment system, much like UPI. That produces fast, visible wins. Such short-term wins are why so many admirers took China as proof that industrial policy and wise officials could guide an economy.

head: The permanent anti-freedom camp
dek: In every free country there are thinkers who want less freedom. Some are social conservatives who see free people as degenerate.
more: In every free country there are thinkers who want less freedom. Some are social conservatives who see free people as degenerate. Some are would-be rulers hungry for power without checks and balances. Some are fans of industrial policy. They admired the USSR, then turned to China. Global business followed along, partly because, as Ajay says, practitioners inside firms tend to follow the prevailing consensus.

head: Ideas rule the world
dek: Ajay frames the whole story as a history of ideas. The Soviet Union's achievements and horrors both came from one scholar's thinking.
more: Ajay frames the whole story as a history of ideas. The Soviet Union's achievements and horrors both came from one scholar's thinking. So the most important debate is over which ideas societies adopt, and freedom is the central one.

head: Preference falsification and preference cascades
dek: This is Timur Kuran's framework. Under repression, everyone hides what they really think, so the regime looks universally supported.
more: This is Timur Kuran's framework. Under repression, everyone hides what they really think, so the regime looks universally supported. Once people realise others share their discontent, the silence turns into a cascade and the regime collapses suddenly. Amit uses this to explain the fall of the USSR.

head: The man of system
dek: Adam Smith's warning: the planner falls in love with his own ideal plan and imagines he can move people around like chess pieces.
more: Adam Smith's warning: the planner falls in love with his own ideal plan and imagines he can move people around like chess pieces. Hayek called the same error 'the fatal conceit'. Mao's sparrow campaign and demonetisation are Amit's examples. Each person has their own reasons for acting, and plans that ignore this end in disaster.
printed: Pawns with minds of their own

head: Under the hood, still Leninist
dek: Even after Deng's reforms, McGregor and the historian Robert Service both find China still recognisably communist.
more: Even after Deng's reforms, McGregor and the historian Robert Service both find China still recognisably communist. The party controls personnel, propaganda and the army, along with the cadres and the news. It sits above the law and is not even registered as an organisation that could be sued.

head: The take-it-or-leave-it compact
dek: McGregor's description of the post-Mao bargain: stay out of politics, and you and your family can get on with life and maybe get rich.
more: McGregor's description of the post-Mao bargain: stay out of politics, and you and your family can get on with life and maybe get rich. Propaganda backs it up by telling people that only the party stands between China and chaos. Read the other way, the compact says 'get rich or else'. It holds only while growth delivers.

head: The illusion of 'macroeconomic management'
dek: In a free economy, business cycles are normal. Policy can soften them, but no one can 'manage' an economy.
more: In a free economy, business cycles are normal. Policy can soften them, but no one can 'manage' an economy. China pulled four levers year after year to hit GDP targets: land rules, construction, infrastructure and credit. On paper it seemed to have beaten the business cycle. In reality the credit turned into bad loans within two or three years. As the economy grew, the levers became too weak for problems worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

head: Roads to nowhere: GDP versus return on equity
dek: Government spending counts in GDP. So a state can boost the headline number with make-work, roads to nowhere and empty cities.
more: Government spending counts in GDP. So a state can boost the headline number with make-work, roads to nowhere and empty cities. Amit calls such growth 'a shadow, a chimera'. Ajay's test is return on equity. A private developer won't build a road to nowhere because they worry about getting paid. The state will.

head: Capitalism needs busts
dek: Marx was right that capitalism swings between booms and busts, and wrong that the swings would keep worsening.
more: Marx was right that capitalism swings between booms and busts, and wrong that the swings would keep worsening. Ajay argues the busts are necessary because they create the right incentives. China's endless pump-priming produced a generation of 50-year-old business leaders who had never seen a downturn and didn't understand risk. Capital went to whoever borrowed most and got closest to the party.

head: The four elites and the populist playbook
dek: Every society has four elites: the state (officials and politicians), business, intellectuals and culture.
more: Every society has four elites: the state (officials and politicians), business, intellectuals and culture. Populists capture the state and turn it on the other three, often under the banner of anti-corruption. Under Xi, the threatened families responded by sending their children and money abroad, and that loss of confidence hit the economy hard.

head: Why people distrust authoritarian states
dek: Amit's point is that the distrust is practical, not moral. Authoritarian rulers face no pressure to perform, so they tend to be incompetent.
more: Amit's point is that the distrust is practical, not moral. Authoritarian rulers face no pressure to perform, so they tend to be incompetent. Ajay adds that every act of state cruelty teaches the victim's hundred friends and family that the regime cannot be trusted. That built-up distrust came due during COVID.

head: Authoritarianism breeds a culture of obedience
dek: Decades of authoritarian rule kill initiative, creativity and the willingness to be a maverick.
more: Decades of authoritarian rule kill initiative, creativity and the willingness to be a maverick. People learn to look up and wait for orders. Culture lives in instinct, and so do the habits of freedom. That is why a country cannot flip from communism to liberal democracy overnight: the institutions and the know-how of being free can't be switched on at will.

head: India's rent-seeking streak is institutional, not cultural
dek: Amit offers this as an open-source idea he once planned to write up with a friend.
more: Amit offers this as an open-source idea he once planned to write up with a friend. The habit of making money by exploiting others or colluding with the state is not part of Indian or Hindu culture. It grew out of the all-powerful state built from the 1940s to the 1970s, which suppressed private enterprise. Under it, the best way to make money was to work for the state or collude with it in zero-sum games.

head: Ends, means, and the limits of money
dek: Asked whether China's prosperity justified its methods, Ajay answers on two levels.
more: Asked whether China's prosperity justified its methods, Ajay answers on two levels. Ethically, state murder and cruelty are beyond the pale, and income gains add less to happiness than people assume. Instrumentally, coercive growth stalls badly. A stuck China with many young men and few prospects is fertile ground for nationalism and military aggression, including against India.

head: The elite as a bridge to globalisation
dek: Ajay is an optimist. Following Adam Smith, he sees growth as the natural state of affairs wherever there is a tolerable level of justice, and state oppression as what holds it back.
more: Ajay is an optimist. Following Adam Smith, he sees growth as the natural state of affairs wherever there is a tolerable level of justice, and state oppression as what holds it back. A poor country with a capable elite can plug into the world economy through export-led growth and FDI once it has freedom. A country with equally low human capital everywhere must first build that small capable pool, which takes much longer. Either way, full transformation takes generations, not 50 years.

head: Judging Deng
dek: Ajay's verdict: Deng kept a high-modernist class of bureaucrats and technocrats steering the country, and that was the core flaw.
more: Ajay's verdict: Deng kept a high-modernist class of bureaucrats and technocrats steering the country, and that was the core flaw. The lesson is to fix freedom first. Amit pushes back: if Deng's goal was simply to lift hundreds of millions out of poverty within tight constraints, he succeeded. Ajay replies that great statesmen play for 50 to 100 years. Measured that way, Taiwan, not China, is the success story.

head: Xi's perfect storm
dek: Ajay names five forces breaking the China model. First, a return to Maoist and Leninist politics: term limits scrapped, power concentrated, grievance-driven nationalism.
more: Ajay names five forces breaking the China model. First, a return to Maoist and Leninist politics: term limits scrapped, power concentrated, grievance-driven nationalism. Second, COVID mismanagement. Third, confrontation with the advanced economies, which make up 60-70% of world GDP, plus debt diplomacy with countries like Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Fourth, unsustainable economic management. Fifth, the populist attack on the other elites. The regime and the borders are intact. But like the USSR in 1989, the model has lost credibility, and global firms see they bet too much on it.

head: The Patnaik-Shah-Varma discount
dek: Ayush Patnaik asked Ajay a question. Take an Indian woman at any percentile of income and move her to the same percentile in China, where she would also earn more.
more: Ayush Patnaik asked Ajay a question. Take an Indian woman at any percentile of income and move her to the same percentile in China, where she would also earn more. Would she prefer China? Patnaik's view is yes everywhere except the elite, because Chinese society is fundamentally better for women. Amit coins a name for how much income an Indian woman would give up just to have China's greater social freedoms.

head: The Bechdel test
dek: This comes from Alison Bechdel's strip 'The Rule'. It is a simple frame that exposes how male-centred cinema, and history itself, have been.
more: This comes from Alison Bechdel's strip 'The Rule'. It is a simple frame that exposes how male-centred cinema, and history itself, have been. Amit guesses almost every Bollywood film fails it.

head: Ajay on post-Soviet Russia
more: Ajay on post-Soviet Russia: 'It's a Spain sized GDP. Frankly, it's just Saudi Arabia with nukes.' Amit imagines listeners from Spain and Saudi Arabia protesting in Hindi: why drag us into this?

head: While Ajay is explaining roads to nowhere, Amit
more: While Ajay is explaining roads to nowhere, Amit: 'we are private capitalists and Everything is Everything is like a road to nowhere. Where are the returns? We are just spending on it. It's a labor of love, no returns.' Ajay: 'we are socialists in our personal life.'

head: After Ajay compares the thrill of a first bicycle with a first car, Amit
more: After Ajay compares the thrill of a first bicycle with a first car, Amit: 'Can I make a shameful confession? I love my car, but I don't know how to ride a cycle.'

head: Ajay suggests his own book, In Service of the Republic, for Deng Xiaoping.
more: Ajay suggests his own book, In Service of the Republic, for Deng Xiaoping. Amit: 'That is the greatest plug I've ever seen somebody give for their own freaking book.'

head: On Shambaugh's China's Future, Amit
more: On Shambaugh's China's Future, Amit: 'I hadn't heard of this book till 30 seconds ago, boss. If you had told me, I would have read it and taken notes and seemed more knowledgeable than I am.'
Amit: 'you're a card-carrying economist as you have described yourself. I've never seen your card.'

head: Amit calls Hayek
more: Amit calls Hayek 'one of our favorite Freddies'. After the Thatcher story he adds: 'So she had the same favorite Freddie as I do.'

head: As Ajay describes Xi stoking grievance, nationalism and hatred of elites, Amit says drily
more: As Ajay describes Xi stoking grievance, nationalism and hatred of elites, Amit says drily: 'I was thinking all of this sounds familiar, but carry on.'

head: Ajay declares…
more: Ajay declares that 'the blushes of the China model rose'. Amit: 'What a line. I would urge my writing students to not learn from this and do things like this.'

head: Ajay calls Karl Marx
more: Ajay calls Karl Marx 'an academic scribbler' who 'never saw the outside of the world other than sitting inside the British Library', and says his ideas still shaped the whole Soviet experiment.

head: Deng Xiaoping's foreign-policy maxim
more: Deng Xiaoping's foreign-policy maxim, 'bide our time'. Xi Jinping abandoned it.

head: A Chinese professor quoted by McGregor
more: A Chinese professor quoted by McGregor: 'the party is like God. He is everywhere. You just can't see him.' Law professor He Weifang adds that the party 'is not even registered as an organization'.

head: Before the 2007 Party Congress, Edict 19 of the propaganda department told editors to strictly control coverage of the October Revolution anniversary
more: Before the 2007 Party Congress, Edict 19 of the propaganda department told editors to strictly control coverage of the October Revolution anniversary and 'not play up the disintegration of the Soviet Union'.

head: A Chinese state office named
more: A Chinese state office named 'Measures for Internment and Deportation of Urban Vagrants and Beggars'. Amit says it is self-explanatory. Shanghai lawyer Zheng Enchong lists what people faced: surveillance, home searches, detention, re-education through labour, and being locked in psychiatric asylums.

head: Margaret Thatcher at her first cabinet meeting, slamming Hayek's The Road to Serfdom on the table
more: Margaret Thatcher at her first cabinet meeting, slamming Hayek's The Road to Serfdom on the table: 'Gentlemen. This is what will guide us.'

head: Amit on how authoritarian regimes reshape culture over time
more: Amit on how authoritarian regimes reshape culture over time: 'as they say paradigms change one funeral at a time.'

head: How Amul beat Polson by making its butter rancid on purpose
dek: A wartime supply chain shaped a market for half a century, and what people called 'taste' was really a side effect of bad old refrigeration.
more: During World War One the British Army wanted huge amounts of butter. Polson, a British company that grew up in India, built the first milk supply chain out of Gujarat and sent butter by train to Bombay and on to the UK. After the war Polson turned to the Indian market and dominated butter into the 1960s and early 70s; Ajay ate it as a child. Then Kurien's cooperative movement in Gujarat, backed by Danish technical and financial aid, built Amul with chilling plants and refrigerated vans and sent clean, high-quality butter to Bombay. It flopped, because Bombay found it bland. On investigation, the cause was Polson's poor refrigeration: its butter always arrived slightly rancid after the train journey, and Bombay had learned to expect that taste. Scientists identified the chemicals that form when butter goes rancid and added them to Amul. Amul then took off and drove Polson out of business.

A wartime supply chain shaped a market for half a century, and what people called 'taste' was really a side effect of bad old refrigeration. A better product can lose until it reproduces the flaws customers have learned to expect.
printed: A butter too fresh for Bombay

head: The Churchill Cigar Assistant that outlived Churchill
dek: A supply chain created by a wartime shortage outlived its only customer by decades.
more: In the 1980s a Tamil Nadu government department called the CCA asked for a bigger budget, saying its allocation had been stagnant for a long time. A curious bureaucrat traced its origins to World War Two. Churchill could no longer get his favourite Cuban cigars because supply lines were cut, and the world's second-best cigars came from a town in Tamil Nadu. With India still under British rule, a department was set up to supply them to him: the Churchill Cigar Assistant. The war ended, Churchill died and India became independent, yet the department survived for decades and finally asked for more money. Amit credits the story to a book by Bibek Debroy.
A supply chain created by a wartime shortage outlived its only customer by decades. Once a government body exists, it keeps justifying itself long after anyone remembers why it was created.

head: Apple made the iPod shuffle less random so it would feel random
dek: Like Bombay's rancid butter, this is a company bending reality to fit what customers expect.
more: Amit offered this as a counterpart to the Amul story. The early iPod shuffle played songs truly at random, and users complained when it served up six Bruce Springsteen songs in a row, insisting that couldn't be random. Apple responded by adding an algorithm that broke up such streaks, so the shuffle would appear random without actually being random. Ajay added the statistician's view: the runs test checks randomness by looking at how often streaks of different lengths occur, so data from the original iPod would have shown that Apple's shuffle wasn't random.
Like Bombay's rancid butter, this is a company bending reality to fit what customers expect. People don't understand randomness: true randomness produces streaks that feel rigged.

head: Hiroo Onoda kept fighting for 29 years after the war ended
dek: People act on the picture in their heads, not on the world outside.
more: Amit read the opening of Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion. In 1914, on an island reached by a mail steamer only once in sixty days, English, French and German residents went on living as friends for six weeks without knowing their countries were at war. Amit noted that the same thing happened when World War One ended, with soldiers still killing each other while leaders shook hands. It reminded him of Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese soldier posted to an island in the Philippines around 1944 with orders to defend it to the death. Nobody told him the war was over, and he went on defending it for twenty-nine years. Amit first heard the story in Dan Carlin's 'Supernova in the East'.

People act on the picture in their heads, not on the world outside. Without information, a person can spend decades fighting a war that has already ended, which shows both the cost of information gaps and the folly of nation states.
printed: On guard for a finished war

head: Weeping in the rain to Blueprint for Armageddon
dek: There are no sound effects and no script, just one man thinking aloud, and it moved Amit more than almost anything.
more: Amit started Dan Carlin's World War One series on a run. When his one-hour workout ended he couldn't go back up to his apartment and stood downstairs, still listening. On another run it began to rain and he stayed outside. That day Carlin read out the letters a group of soldiers wrote to their wives and girlfriends the night before a battle in which they all died, not knowing it would be their last night. Amit wept in the rain.

There are no sound effects and no script, just one man thinking aloud, and it moved Amit more than almost anything. That convinced him a story told well needs nothing else, and that audio is the most primal and powerful medium.

head: The book that kept him in an Irani cafe until 9 pm
dek: A great book can override every plan you had for the day. Amit's verdict: this is the good life.
more: Ajay was at Strand Book Stall in Bombay, needing to head home to Bandra before rush hour got worse. He came across 'Seizing the Enigma' at random, read the first page or two and bought it. Outside, the opening had so gripped him that he wandered aimlessly for a while, gave up on going home, sat down in a local Irani cafe and read the whole book until 9 pm.
A great book can override every plan you had for the day. Amit's verdict: this is the good life.

head: The scholar who quit to 'stand by his country'
dek: Patriotism and obedience to the state are different things, and sometimes loving your country means opposing its government.
more: A good friend told Ajay about a scholar at a Western think tank in Moscow who resigned when the Ukraine war began because he wanted to stand by his country. Ajay didn't have the wit to disagree in the moment, but on the show he says loyalty to a country is not loyalty to its state. Amit offered the opposite example: a group of top Russian chess players who published a letter against Putin right after the invasion. Many of them can no longer enter Russia and now play for other countries, and Amit calls that real bravery and patriotism.
Patriotism and obedience to the state are different things, and sometimes loving your country means opposing its government.

head: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
dek: Dunbar's finding that we are wired for about 150 relationships, in tiers of 5, 15, 50 and 150, supports Ajay's view that our few close bonds make or break a life and deserve deliberate effort.
more: Dunbar's finding that we are wired for about 150 relationships, in tiers of 5, 15, 50 and 150, supports Ajay's view that our few close bonds make or break a life and deserve deliberate effort.
Came up when Amit asked Ajay how he thinks about friendship, and Ajay cited Dunbar's number.

head: History of European Morals
dek: It is the source of the 'expanding circle', the idea that through history we extend moral consideration from family to tribe to nation and beyond.
more: It is the source of the 'expanding circle', the idea that through history we extend moral consideration from family to tribe to nation and beyond. Amit uses it to explain past horrors like slavery and to worry that today's circles are shrinking.
Amit's detour from Dunbar's number to the idea of the expanding circle.

head: The Expanding Circle
dek: Singer argues the circle should include animals. Amit thinks people two hundred years from now may judge us for eating animals the way we now judge Jefferson for keeping slaves.
more: Singer argues the circle should include animals. Amit thinks people two hundred years from now may judge us for eating animals the way we now judge Jefferson for keeping slaves.
Amit credited Singer with extending Lecky's circle to animals. He wasn't sure which Singer book makes the case; the show notes link this one.

head: Unlikely is Inevitable
dek: Explains why poker players who lose several hands in a row as 80% favourites are wrong to call the game rigged: over a large enough sample, unlikely runs are bound to happen.
more: Explains why poker players who lose several hands in a row as 80% favourites are wrong to call the game rigged: over a large enough sample, unlikely runs are bound to happen.
A piece from Range Rover, Amit's poker column for the Economic Times, which he recalled during the randomness tangent.

head: A trade deficit with a babysitter
dek: Harford always pays his babysitter and she buys nothing from him, yet both are better off.
more: Harford always pays his babysitter and she buys nothing from him, yet both are better off. It shows why worrying about bilateral trade deficits makes no sense.
Amit's 'Bravo, Babysitters!' chapter, based on Harford's Financial Times column of December 2005.

head: Public Opinion
dek: A masterpiece for understanding how the media shapes what we believe and what to watch out for.
more: A masterpiece for understanding how the media shapes what we believe and what to watch out for. Over a century old, it hasn't been made obsolete by any technological change.
Amit's first recommendation. He held up the physical book and read from its first chapter, 'The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads'.

head: Hardcore History
dek: Just one man talking conversationally, with no script and no sound effects, and it taught Amit about history, humanity and the power of audio storytelling.
more: Just one man talking conversationally, with no script and no sound effects, and it taught Amit about history, humanity and the power of audio storytelling.
Amit's second recommendation, which he called perhaps the greatest podcast of all time.

head: Supernova in the East
dek: It is the source of the story of the soldier who defended a Philippine island for 29 years because nobody told him the war was over.
more: It is the source of the story of the soldier who defended a Philippine island for 29 years because nobody told him the war was over.
The Hardcore History episode (part one) where Amit first heard of Hiroo Onoda.

head: Blueprint for Armageddon
dek: It kept Amit outside his building after runs and made him weep in the rain.
more: It kept Amit outside his building after runs and made him weep in the rain. He says it taught him about resilience, character, tragedy and the folly of nation states.
The Hardcore History series on World War One: six episodes of about five hours each.

head: Seizing the Enigma
dek: Its first two pages gripped him so completely that he skipped his commute and read the whole book in an Irani cafe until 9 pm.
more: Its first two pages gripped him so completely that he skipped his commute and read the whole book in an Irani cafe until 9 pm.
Ajay's recommendation, a book he picked up at random at Strand Book Stall.

head: Friendship is finite and deserves deliberate effort
dek: Robin Dunbar observed that we are wired for about 150 relationships, roughly the size of a hunter-gatherer band, in tiers of about 5 very close people, then 15, 50 and 150.
more: Robin Dunbar observed that we are wired for about 150 relationships, roughly the size of a hunter-gatherer band, in tiers of about 5 very close people, then 15, 50 and 150. Ajay prioritises these few bonds because they make or break a life. He adds two points. Age is irrelevant to friendship: there are petty, power-hungry old people and wise young ones. And friendships have their moments: a time and state of mind clicks and may never recur. That is fine; be grateful for it rather than blaming anyone.

head: The expanding circle, and how it can shrink
dek: Lecky's idea, which Amit loves: humans extend moral consideration to a circle that starts with family and widens to tribe, nation and beyond.
more: Lecky's idea, which Amit loves: humans extend moral consideration to a circle that starts with family and widens to tribe, nation and beyond. Everyone outside the circle might as well be an animal, which explains horrors like slavery and the treatment of women. Peter Singer argues the circle should reach animals. Amit's worry is that the circle can also contract, and rising nationalism and identity politics are shrinking it. Ajay adds that Mahavir and Jainism emerged in a protein-starved, far-from-golden society. Amit sees this as an early 'globalization' of the mind, before people could physically connect.

head: Progress is not guaranteed
dek: Many of us grow up assuming the world will keep getting better. Ajay thinks technology and GDP probably will improve, but a society's overall progress is far more complex.
more: Many of us grow up assuming the world will keep getting better. Ajay thinks technology and GDP probably will improve, but a society's overall progress is far more complex. Many countries have gone terribly wrong, and a child's state could well get worse even as their technology improves.
printed: Who counts as one of us

head: What globalization actually means
dek: Ajay defines globalization by five cross-border flows: ideas, people, goods, services and capital.
more: Ajay defines globalization by five cross-border flows: ideas, people, goods, services and capital. It measures how far these flows, arising from voluntary transactions, are not shaped by national borders. Two forces drive it up and down. One is the state, which bans books, issues passports, levies customs duties and imposes capital controls. The other is technology, such as container ships, air freight and telecom, which keeps shrinking the cost of distance.

head: The First Globalization: capital flows downhill
dek: Steamships, the Suez Canal and the telegraph set off the first globalization.
more: Steamships, the Suez Canal and the telegraph set off the first globalization. States stayed out of the way: people travelled without passports, capital moved freely, and a lawyer could go practise in London. The only constraint was technology. Capital flowed downhill: projects in the US, Argentina and India raised money in London, where returns on extra capital were low, and invested it where returns were high. Keynes described a world around 1912 in which goods from everywhere arrived at your doorstep.

head: The long dark chapter, 1914 to 1982
dek: Nationalism destroyed the first globalization. World War One brought passports, naval blockades and submarine attacks on shipping.
more: Nationalism destroyed the first globalization. World War One brought passports, naval blockades and submarine attacks on shipping. Nazi Germany, wanting to go after the Jews, imposed the world's first capital controls. After 1945 Keynes and Harry Dexter White built the Bretton Woods order of GATT, the World Bank and the IMF, choosing fixed exchange rates. Keynes intuitively understood that you can't manage the exchange rate and also keep capital flowing freely, a point later formalised in Nobel-winning work. So capital controls were part of the deal. As a result, the world trade-to-GDP ratio only returned to its 1913 level in 1982.

head: The Second Globalization: the unconditional welcome
dek: From about 1982 to 2016–17, container ships, wide-body aircraft, computers and telecom cut the cost of distance.
more: From about 1982 to 2016–17, container ships, wide-body aircraft, computers and telecom cut the cost of distance. Fixed exchange rates and capital controls were dismantled, and the EU restored visa-free movement. India's software and services boom came from plugging into this world. Everyone was let in without conditions, on the assumption that prosperity would liberalise them. Instead, Deng's China became more authoritarian and Gorbachev's Russia became Putin's Russia.

head: Comparative advantage
dek: Ricardo showed that cross-border trade raises welfare even when one party is better at everything.
more: Ricardo showed that cross-border trade raises welfare even when one party is better at everything. What matters is a difference in the ratio of how much better each side is at two different things. Amit's version: even if he were better at both podcasting and economics, he would still do the podcasting and leave the economics to Ajay.

head: Freedom works unless there's a market failure
dek: Ajay's public-economics test is that state intervention is justified only when there is a market failure, such as asymmetric information, an externality or a public good.
more: Ajay's public-economics test is that state intervention is justified only when there is a market failure, such as asymmetric information, an externality or a public good. Buying ball bearings from Mozambique involves none of these, so blocking or taxing it harms welfare and GDP. Amit adds two points. A tariff redistributes from the poor consumers at large to rich interest groups. And voluntary trade is consent, a positive-sum game, while state coercion destroys the gains.

head: Economic statecraft
dek: Economic statecraft means using state power on the economy to coerce other countries.

head: The Third Globalization
dek: Ajay coined this term. Many people read the new restrictions as 'globalization RIP', but Ajay disagrees.
more: Ajay coined this term. Many people read the new restrictions as 'globalization RIP', but Ajay disagrees. The advanced economies, which include Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, have made basic good behaviour a condition of entry, starting with not invading your neighbour. Rogue states such as Russia, China, Iran and North Korea face the toolkit; for everyone else, globalization is deepening. One sign is the post-COVID boom in Indian services exports, as companies realised remote workers could just as well be in India. Ajay also argues that no coalition can realistically build a currency or payment system to rival the dollar and the euro.

head: Country versus state
dek: The state is the community that holds a monopoly of physical violence in a territory.
more: The state is the community that holds a monopoly of physical violence in a territory. The country is its people. Ajay repeatedly separates the wonderful Chinese people from the saber-rattling Chinese state. Amit's concern about the third globalization is that the roughly 15% of the world being shut out consists of ordinary people who happen to live under rogue regimes, not rogue people.

head: Trade deficits are a non-problem: the double thank-you moment
dek: Countries don't trade; individuals and firms do. Every voluntary cross-border deal is a 'double thank-you moment' where both sides think they got a great deal.
more: Countries don't trade; individuals and firms do. Every voluntary cross-border deal is a 'double thank-you moment' where both sides think they got a great deal. So a bilateral deficit, such as India's with China, is just the sum of millions of mutually beneficial transactions, like Tim Harford's one-way spending on his babysitter. Thinking at the level of nations instead of individuals is the core mistake.

head: Current account deficits mean capital is coming in
dek: Ajay's two points of economics geekery. First, count goods and services together, because a widget, a potato and a haircut are all things you sell.
more: Ajay's two points of economics geekery. First, count goods and services together, because a widget, a potato and a haircut are all things you sell. India's standard data counts goods only. Second, the goods-and-services balance equals the current account deficit, which by an accounting identity is matched by capital inflow funding investment above domestic savings. Ajay's high-growth dream for India borrows from the first globalization: let capital flow downhill from advanced economies, where it earns poor returns, at 10–20% of GDP a year.

head: Bide your time: India as a status quo power
dek: Ajay doesn't resent the limits that come with the third globalization.
more: Ajay doesn't resent the limits that come with the third globalization. India has no wish to conquer Bangladesh, so rules like 'don't invade your neighbour' cost it nothing, and the club is an open invitation that India uses every day. Borrowing Deng Xiaoping's advice, he says India should spend the next hundred years becoming an advanced economy and democracy, and rethink the world order only then.

head: Unlikely is inevitable
dek: People misread streaks as evidence of rigging, whether it is six Springsteen songs in a row or five lost poker hands as an 80% favourite.
more: People misread streaks as evidence of rigging, whether it is six Springsteen songs in a row or five lost poker hands as an 80% favourite. Given enough repetitions, improbable sequences are certain to occur, and statisticians test real randomness with tools like the runs test.

head: The world outside and the pictures in our heads
dek: Lippmann's framing: we act on our mental picture of the world, which can lag reality badly.
more: Lippmann's framing: we act on our mental picture of the world, which can lag reality badly. Examples are islanders who stayed friends for six weeks after their nations went to war, soldiers who kept killing after the armistice, and Hiroo Onoda's 29 years on guard. Amit sees this as the key to understanding how the media shapes us, and says no technological change has made it obsolete.

head: Audio is the most primal medium
dek: Hardcore History convinced Amit that you need nothing but a story and a voice.
more: Hardcore History convinced Amit that you need nothing but a story and a voice. Storytelling was humanity's first entertainment, before music, television or binge-watching, and audio still carries the most emotional power.

head: Ajay explains that Indian capital controls let only poultry farms and nanotechnology firms borrow abroad.
more: Ajay explains that Indian capital controls let only poultry farms and nanotechnology firms borrow abroad. Amit: 'So if you're a really small chicken, you have the best of both worlds, poultry farms and nano chicken.'

head: Amit's version of comparative advantage
more: Amit's version of comparative advantage: 'I am a better podcaster than you. I am also a better economist than you. However, I do the podcasting and I let you do the economics because hey, I can't spend all my time doing economics.'
After Ajay explains that ASML's machines make chip tracks about ten silicon atoms wide, Amit asks what the sensual organic sound is called when these atoms brush against each other: 'ASMR by ASML.'

Ajay describes an Indian importer telling his girlfriend he got a great deal on Chinese goods, while the Chinese exporter tells her boyfriend she got a great price from India. Amit: 'Everyone has a good romantic life in your stories.'

head: Pleased by Ajay's words, Amit refuses to say the traditional blessing
more: Pleased by Ajay's words, Amit refuses to say the traditional blessing 'aapke muh mein ghee shakkar' because he reversed his diabetes (Episode 9). He keeps the ghee, 'a superfood', and drops the sugar: 'Avoid shakkar, it is poison.'

head: Amit's Churchill cigar timeline
more: Amit's Churchill cigar timeline: 'World War II ended, Winston Churchill died, India gained independence, not in that order.'

After a run of tangents (cigars, butter, iPods, runs tests), Ajay admits they're playing antakshari with stories: one person tells a story and the next picks up its last syllable. Amit suggests a whole episode like that and begs: 'Gentle reader, kindly don't unsubscribe right now.'

head: Ajay on the optimism of the second globalization, when the West welcomed everyone unconditionally
more: Ajay on the optimism of the second globalization, when the West welcomed everyone unconditionally: 'We felt confident that as you become rich, you will inevitably stop beating your wife.'

head: Ajay on a worn-out word
more: Ajay on a worn-out word: 'By the time a word graduates into the airport books, you know, it surely stops making much sense.'

head: An American Tail: to debunk myths of a lost golden age, Ajay quotes the fable told to the mice in Russia
more: An American Tail: to debunk myths of a lost golden age, Ajay quotes the fable told to the mice in Russia: 'there are no cats in America and the streets are filled with cheese.'

Chintaman Deshmukh took part in the Bretton Woods negotiations. Amit adds that Keynes wanted him as the IMF's first managing director, but the Americans objected: 'What Indian fellow, what are you talking about?'

head: Ajay on why Nazi Germany introduced the world's first capital controls
more: Ajay on why Nazi Germany introduced the world's first capital controls: 'Nazi is German for nationalist socialist,' and Hitler brought in the controls when he wanted to go after the Jews.

head: Amit compares future judgement of meat-eaters to how we view slavery
more: Amit compares future judgement of meat-eaters to how we view slavery: just as Jefferson kept slaves and thought it morally fine, people two hundred years from now may look back and say 'oh they ate animals.'

head: The BT Cotton Satyagraha
dek: Farmers are often talked about as if they have no agency, yet here they saved themselves by defying the state out of plain self-interest.
more: By the 1990s Indian cotton was being ravaged by bollworms, and farmers were stuck in an escalating race of ever more pesticide. Genetically modified BT cotton, which bollworms don't attack, was available around the world, but the Indian government invoked the precautionary principle and banned all GM crops. Farmers in Gujarat got BT seed through the black market and planted it anyway. In 2002 cotton failed across Gujarat, except on the BT farms. The government's response was to declare the only surviving crops illegal and order them destroyed. Sharad Joshi's Shetkari Sanghatana gathered farmers from Maharashtra and elsewhere, marched to Gujarat, stood on those fields and said 'over our dead bodies', then marched to Delhi with bales of cotton. Barun Mitra spoke at the press conference. The Vajpayee government relented and lifted the ban. When Amit last checked, over 90% of India's cotton was BT and India had passed China as the world's biggest cotton producer and exporter. The sequel: India stalled at two generations of GM cotton while the world moved further ahead, so farmers turned to the black market again for HTBT cotton, and some were arrested for it.

Farmers are often talked about as if they have no agency, yet here they saved themselves by defying the state out of plain self-interest. Satyagraha is not only a pre-Independence word. One of independent India's most inspiring campaigns of civil disobedience was fought for the freedom to plant a better seed.

head: Sharad Joshi: From Bern to a Farm in Ambethan
dek: Amit's answer to the lament that independent India produced no great leaders is that it did, and we didn't pay attention.
more: Sharad Joshi was born on 3 September 1935 and studied commerce at Sydenham College. He taught economics and statistics around 1957, then became a civil servant, and from 1968 to 1977 worked in informatics in Bern, Switzerland, and with the UN. In 1977, in his forties, he came back to India, bought 23 acres in Ambethan village in Pune district and became a full-time farmer. He soon saw that everything was broken. He looked past the usual answer of government handouts and traced the problem to state overreach. He also rejected the pessimism that such ideas are too counterintuitive for ordinary people. He built the Shetkari Sanghatana, drew lakhs of farmers to his rallies, and coined phrases like 'negative subsidy'. He also saw a point Mrinal Pande later made in a Pragati symposium Amit edited: behind every Indian crisis lies a further crisis of the women in it. So around the mid-1980s he founded the women's wing Shetkari Mahila Aghadi, whose legendary rally drew two lakh women farmers and no men. Later he spent years in the Rajya Sabha, where nobody listened.

Amit's answer to the lament that independent India produced no great leaders is that it did, and we didn't pay attention. Joshi showed that liberal economic ideas can become mass politics. He did not dilute the diagnosis; he trusted farmers to recognise it from their own lives.
printed: From Bern to a farm in Ambethan

head: The Farmers Who Had Lived Hayek
dek: Grassroots politics need not be only populism and handouts. People can see and clearly describe what is being done to them.
more: About five or six years before this recording, Barun Mitra took Amit to a gathering near Nashik where farmer leaders from across Maharashtra, including Shetkari Sanghatana people, were meeting. The visit produced Amit's only Hindi episode of The Seen and the Unseen, with Gunvant Patil. What moved Amit was a contrast. His own beliefs about liberty and the parasitic state came from books and frameworks, at a distance. Farmer after farmer there held exactly the same beliefs, but had reached them through lived experience.
Grassroots politics need not be only populism and handouts. People can see and clearly describe what is being done to them. The idea that farmers can't understand markets is the real condescension.

head: The CPMC for Columnists
dek: Apply a restriction to your own life and its absurdity becomes obvious.
more: To show what an APMC means to a farmer, Amit applies it to his own trade. Imagine a 'CPMC' for columnists: he and Ajay could legally sell their columns to only one central party. It would pay them perhaps a tenth of what they earn now, anyone who wanted the column would pay a crazy markup, and the whole thing would run on committee politics. No city dweller would tolerate being told to buy groceries from one place at twenty times the price. Yet comfortable urban elites dismiss freeing farmers with 'farmers will get exploited', even though the recent farm bills left APMCs in place and only added the choice to sell elsewhere.
Apply a restriction to your own life and its absurdity becomes obvious. The loudest defenders of 'protecting' farmers usually enjoy the very freedoms they would deny them.

head: From Punjab's Paddy Fields to Delhi's Smog
dek: One well-meant subsidy can spread into groundwater collapse, a diabetes-friendly diet and a capital city's air.
more: Punjab is relatively arid and has limited groundwater, so it should not be growing water-hungry rice. But the state guarantees an MSP for rice and gives farmers free electricity. Farmers use that electricity to run bore wells and tube wells, pump out far more groundwater than the ecosystem can bear, and grow rice. After the harvest, the cheapest way to clear the stubble is to burn it, and the wind carries the smoke to Delhi in its worst smog months. No Delhi chief minister can fix this, because the cause lies outside his jurisdiction. Ajay totals up the damage. Each rupee raised in taxes costs society roughly three rupees in GDP. That money subsidises rice and wheat in Punjab and Haryana, and the cheap grain harms people's health, drains groundwater, strains the electricity system and fills the Hindi heartland's air with particulate matter. Amit adds that during Tamil Nadu's water crisis, social media urged people to take bucket baths instead of showers, while most of the water was going to crops that should never have been grown there.

One well-meant subsidy can spread into groundwater collapse, a diabetes-friendly diet and a capital city's air. The costs of a policy often land far away from where it was made, on people who had no say in it.
printed: Rice in Punjab, smoke in Delhi

head: Down to Earth
dek: Joshi was a great thinker and politician who also took the role of public intellectual seriously and worked hard to get his thinking out.
more: Joshi was a great thinker and politician who also took the role of public intellectual seriously and worked hard to get his thinking out. If you want to understand agriculture from the view of a farmer who lived it and led a great farmers' movement, this is the book to read.
Amit's main recommendation, held up on camera. It is a collection of Joshi's columns.

head: Talking to an Empty Room
dek: The title breaks Amit's heart. Joshi spent years in Parliament with great ideas that nobody paid attention to, and the country would have gained a lot by listening.
more: The title breaks Amit's heart. Joshi spent years in Parliament with great ideas that nobody paid attention to, and the country would have gained a lot by listening.
Amit's second recommendation, a collection of Joshi's speeches in the Rajya Sabha.

head: The Wizard and the Prophet
dek: It covers the tension between the scientific and industrial revolution in agriculture and concerns about sustainability.
more: It covers the tension between the scientific and industrial revolution in agriculture and concerns about sustainability. Ajay calls this the great food-system question of the next 25 years: how to feed 1.4 billion people sustainably, in a way that also fits with public health.
Ajay's recommendation, about Norman Borlaug and William Vogt (Amit helped with the pronunciation of Vogt).

head: The Mystery of Capital
dek: Amit calls it one of the greatest books he has read, one that opened his mind about economics and gave him many 'today I learned' moments.
more: Amit calls it one of the greatest books he has read, one that opened his mind about economics and gave him many 'today I learned' moments. Its key idea is 'dead capital': assets such as untitled slum homes or land with restricted use that are worth something but can't be turned into capital.
An unplanned 'random reco' in the middle of the land discussion, while Amit explains why farmers can't raise credit on their land.

head: The Price of Onions
dek: Tomatoes swinging between Rs 200 and Rs 2 a kg is the same story the book tells, with tomatoes in place of onions.
more: Tomatoes swinging between Rs 200 and Rs 2 a kg is the same story the book tells, with tomatoes in place of onions. India has been through this before.
Ajay brings it up at the start, when asked about the tomato price drama.

head: Entry and Exit in Agriculture (Episode 1 of The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Pavan Srinath and Karthik Shashidhar
dek: His guests argued that small farmers are forced to master two skills, farming and entrepreneurship, when they might prefer to specialise in one, and that tiny holdings make scale impossible.
more: His guests argued that small farmers are forced to master two skills, farming and entrepreneurship, when they might prefer to specialise in one, and that tiny holdings make scale impossible.
Amit's very first episode, which was about scale and corporatisation in agriculture.

head: Futures Markets in Agriculture (Episode 12 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit once thought futures were arcane finance that didn't concern ordinary people.
more: Amit once thought futures were arcane finance that didn't concern ordinary people. This conversation showed him they can be a powerful tool for removing a farmer's uncertainty.
Mentioned when discussing the absence of agricultural futures markets in India.

head: The Right to Property (Episode 26 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Rajagopalan explains at length what this restriction leads to: depressed land prices, land-use-change scams, and farmers who can't exit agriculture.
more: Rajagopalan explains at length what this restriction leads to: depressed land prices, land-use-change scams, and farmers who can't exit agriculture.
Cited during the discussion of the ban on selling farmland for non-agricultural use.

head: CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey (CPHS) data
dek: If you ask whether people primarily rely on agriculture for their income, CPHS data gives about 35%, which Ajay considers a truer picture than surveys that count anyone doing some farm work.
more: If you ask whether people primarily rely on agriculture for their income, CPHS data gives about 35%, which Ajay considers a truer picture than surveys that count anyone doing some farm work.
Ajay uses it to question the standard claim that 50-60% of Indians depend on agriculture.

head: The Price System Is a Rationing Mechanism
dek: If 90 units of tomatoes arrive instead of 100, the price must rise until enough buyers walk away, whether by switching to puree, changing recipes or doing without.
more: If 90 units of tomatoes arrive instead of 100, the price must rise until enough buyers walk away, whether by switching to puree, changing recipes or doing without. How far it has to rise depends on how flexible people are. Staples like wheat and rice, which people buy without watching the price, need huge price swings to close a small gap. Discretionary luxuries like avocados need only a small rise. This is not the market malfunctioning; it is how the market works.

head: Samuelson's Cobweb Model and the Three Decisions
dek: In Paul Samuelson's cobweb model, farmers look at today's high tomato price, all plant more, the price crashes, and they pull back, so the boom-and-bust repeats forever.
more: In Paul Samuelson's cobweb model, farmers look at today's high tomato price, all plant more, the price crashes, and they pull back, so the boom-and-bust repeats forever. The model only works if three decisions go wrong. Farmers must choose what to sow by looking backward, the inputs they invest must be fixed, and there must be no storage technology. In healthy markets, people look ahead, adjust their inputs and store produce, so the cycle doesn't happen. A swing from Rs 2 to Rs 200 is a peculiarly Indian problem, not a normal feature of food markets.

head: Four Mechanisms That Stabilise Food Markets
dek: Food markets elsewhere are calm because of four mechanisms. (1) Futures markets show everyone the expected price at harvest, so even farmers who never trade can make better sowing decisions. (2) Storage: cold chains and also processing into paste, puree or dehydrated onions, which moves food from now into the future. (3) Domestic trade moves surplus from one state to a shortage in another. (4) International trade treats the world market as an effectively infinite buffer stock.
more: Food markets elsewhere are calm because of four mechanisms. (1) Futures markets show everyone the expected price at harvest, so even farmers who never trade can make better sowing decisions. (2) Storage: cold chains and also processing into paste, puree or dehydrated onions, which moves food from now into the future. (3) Domestic trade moves surplus from one state to a shortage in another. (4) International trade treats the world market as an effectively infinite buffer stock. India has hobbled all four. For example, the Forward Markets Commission was mostly a game of banning things, and moving commodity futures under SEBI hasn't changed much. Whenever prices rise, policymakers want to shoot the messenger.

head: Storage Is a Service, Not 'Hoarding'
dek: Farming means understanding the land up to the farm gate.
more: Farming means understanding the land up to the farm gate. Storage and speculation are a separate skill: forecasting shortages, sourcing cheaply and putting your own money at risk to carry goods into a future where releasing them pushes prices down. Ajay calls this God's own work. But Indian cinema turned it into the villainous 'hoarding', and laws like the Essential Commodities Act discourage the private storage that would smooth out tomato price swings.

head: Speculation as Insurance: The Once-a-Decade Windfall
dek: Running storage is a dull business most years, but once in ten or twenty years prices spike and the operator makes 'like a bandit'.
more: Running storage is a dull business most years, but once in ten or twenty years prices spike and the operator makes 'like a bandit'. That windfall is what pays for the decades of standing ready, like an option or an insurance premium. When the state seizes the upside at exactly that moment, it destroys the incentive to build the capacity in the first place. The same logic applies to vaccine makers whose pandemic-time pricing the state crushed: why would anyone invest in that capacity next time?

head: The APMC Monopsony
dek: Farmers are legally required to sell at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee, which makes it a state-created monopsony (a single buyer, the opposite of a monopoly).
more: Farmers are legally required to sell at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee, which makes it a state-created monopsony (a single buyer, the opposite of a monopoly). A few traders there collect rent. In an old study Amit recalls, farmers got Rs 2 for tomatoes that consumers paid Rs 20 for. With competing middlemen it might be Rs 10 and Rs 12, leaving both farmer and consumer Rs 8 better off. This is a negative-sum game for everyone except the rent-seekers, captured in Sharad Joshi's lines: 'I sell my produce cheap and die. You pay so much that you die too.'

head: Negative Subsidy
dek: Sharad Joshi's term turns a common urban belief upside down. City people think farmers live off subsidies such as free electricity.
more: Sharad Joshi's term turns a common urban belief upside down. City people think farmers live off subsidies such as free electricity. But export bans, trade restrictions and controlled markets mean farmers routinely get less than the world price for what they grow. Added up, Joshi calculated, this comes to billions.
