In net terms farmers are paying, not being paid, and the money is simply wasted.

head: Farmers Are Rational Economic Agents
dek: Ajay credits the economist B.S. Minhas with persuading his generation to drop the image of the farmer as a fool.
more: Ajay credits the economist B.S. Minhas with persuading his generation to drop the image of the farmer as a fool. Farmers understand incentives and act on them as well as anyone. Policies built on the assumption that farmers can't choose wisely, such as forbidding them to sell outside the APMC or to plant BT cotton, are both wrong and condescending.

head: Trade Is Between Individuals, Not Nations
dek: Nobody would stop a sale between Andheri and Bandra, or Bombay and Pune.
more: Nobody would stop a sale between Andheri and Bandra, or Bombay and Pune. Most people would agree a farmer in Maharashtra should be able to sell to someone in Tamil Nadu, even though the Indian state restricts it. Amit asks why it should be any different when the buyer is in Georgia, Azerbaijan or Arkansas. Thinking in terms of nation-states hides the fact that every trade is a voluntary deal between two people who both gain.

head: Farming Is a Business, and One or Two Acres Is Subscale
dek: Ajay has changed his mind on this. On one or two acres a farm lacks technology and choices, and slips into near-feudal dependence on one local person who lends money, sells inputs and buys the crop.
more: Ajay has changed his mind on this. On one or two acres a farm lacks technology and choices, and slips into near-feudal dependence on one local person who lends money, sells inputs and buys the crop. Farming should be treated as a business, with a P&L, a balance sheet and risks. The way out is consolidating land into 20-, 200- or 2,000-acre operations through leasing and land markets, not romanticised cooperatives. Being a 'landless labourer' should simply mean supplying labour in a labour market. As Amit puts it, asking every farmer to also be an entrepreneur is like asking every banker to own his own little bank. Let the arrangements evolve on their own, like Sikh farmers from Punjab who farm land in Madhya Pradesh and Ukraine.

head: Land-Use Restrictions Create Dead Capital and Trap Farmers
dek: Agricultural land can only be sold to another farmer for farming, so its price stays artificially low.
more: Agricultural land can only be sold to another farmer for farming, so its price stays artificially low. Changing the land-use certificate can raise its value 40 times, which is why a common scam is to buy farmland through connections and get it reclassified. Real farmers can't exit at fair value and can't borrow against their land. Holdings shrink with each generation as land is divided among children, which feeds agitations for reservations among landowning communities like the Jats, Patidars and Marathas. This is Hernando de Soto's 'dead capital', and Amit sees the same thing in untitled slums, idle government land and FSI limits.

head: Liquid Land Markets as Climate Adaptation
dek: Through his work at XKDR Forum, Ajay has concluded that the world is not holding back carbon emissions, and that warming will hit hardest above the Vindhyas.
more: Through his work at XKDR Forum, Ajay has concluded that the world is not holding back carbon emissions, and that warming will hit hardest above the Vindhyas. A sensible response would be for households to sell their land and start new lives south of the Vindhyas, in farming or something else. That requires working land markets at both ends. Without them, families cling to land that climate change is slowly ruining.

head: The Missing Structural Transformation
dek: As countries grow they move people out of agriculture and from villages to cities.
more: As countries grow they move people out of agriculture and from villages to cities. India liberalised the rest of its economy in 1991 but left agriculture out. Apart from strong growth from 1991 to 2011, India's growth has been weak and modern-sector jobs have not appeared. The commonly quoted figure is that 50-60% of people depend on agriculture, which produces about 14% of GDP. Ajay notes that this depends on how survey questions are worded. Counting only those who primarily earn from agriculture gives about 35% (CMIE CPHS data), still eight to nine times the level in advanced economies. Small plots also block mechanisation, so more people are needed to work the same land.

head: MSPs Distort What India Grows and Eats
dek: Minimum support prices began with good intentions, but they skew incentives.
more: Minimum support prices began with good intentions, but they skew incentives. When cereals got an MSP, farmers moved out of pulses, and for decades India grew too few pulses, the main source of protein for people who don't eat animals. That is an unseen nutritional cost. Cereals became the subsidised crop and pulses were left to the market, so the state ended up encouraging the very carbohydrates that drive India's diabetes epidemic. And as Barun Mitra found, MSPs promised for 24 commodities were actually paid for only six.

head: India Exports Water
dek: Amit credits the agricultural economist Ashok Gulati with this shift in perspective.
more: Amit credits the agricultural economist Ashok Gulati with this shift in perspective. Rice and sugarcane are extremely water-intensive, and India exports both, so in effect India is one of the world's biggest exporters of water. It does this in a country with droughts and chronic shortages, because MSPs and free power make these crops artificially attractive.

head: Don't Hate the Middleman, Fix the Rules
dek: Anger at the gap between the farm-gate price and the consumer price often turns into populist hatred of middlemen, who in India often belong to particular occupational castes or are rich.
more: Anger at the gap between the farm-gate price and the consumer price often turns into populist hatred of middlemen, who in India often belong to particular occupational castes or are rich. Ajay sees in this an old, Prussian-style love-of-the-land feeling. His warning is that individuals who make the most of the constraints they are given are not the villains. The fault lies with a state that stops voluntary bargains from solving the problem.

head: GMOs: Settled Science vs. Respect for Complexity
dek: Amit says GM crops are as close to scientific consensus as anything gets.
more: Amit says GM crops are as close to scientific consensus as anything gets. Billions of meals have been eaten, BT brinjal is widely used in Bangladesh, golden rice helped children in the Philippines avoid blindness, and the precautionary principle taken too far stops all progress. He adds that opposition often comes from interested parties, such as the pesticide lobby and NGOs whose funding depends on alarm. Ajay takes a middle position: editing DNA is harder than editing code, and we know how badly code goes wrong. So we shouldn't ban gene editing, but we should approach it with caution.

head: Bad Policy Is Downstream of Bad Ideas
dek: India's agricultural controls did not come from nowhere. They came from the leading agricultural economics of an earlier generation.
more: India's agricultural controls did not come from nowhere. They came from the leading agricultural economics of an earlier generation. Echoing Keynes, Ajay argues that the bottleneck is knowledge. India needs a new generation of thinkers to build new ideas and research and change the climate of opinion, and policy will follow.

head: Amit opens with a limerick called…
more: Amit opens with a limerick called 'Tomato' about Ajay blushing at YouTube praise: 'My good friend Ajay sat in his bed / reading YouTube comments in his head. / He was all aglow, like a tomato. / The fulsome praise made his cheeks go red.'

head: Ajay admits that as a…
more: Ajay admits that as a 'callow immature youth' he produced a limerick every ten minutes, so the mathematician Meena Mahajan, a year senior at college, nicknamed him 'Limya' in the Maharashtrian style. Amit replies that he may be the world's only professional limerick writer, having written a weekly limerick for the Sunday Times of India until it got too political.

head: Ajay on the tomato price spike: people flying in from abroad were asked to fill the rest of their bags with tomatoes. Amit follows
more: Ajay on the tomato price spike: people flying in from abroad were asked to fill the rest of their bags with tomatoes. Amit follows with: 'Are you hiding tomatoes in your cheeks or are you happy to see me?'

head: Ajay calls storage
more: Ajay calls storage 'God's own work' and blames Bengalis: 'because there were so many Bengali movies around hoarders,' storage got a bad name and the state outlawed it. Amit, who is half Bengali, replies: 'For the purpose of this episode, Ajay, I'm half Punjabi. We shall not refer to the other half... there is plenty to blame us Punjabis also for, as we shall find out.' That sets up the later Punjab rice and stubble-burning story.

head: During the CPMC-for-columnists thought experiment, Amit tells Ajay
more: During the CPMC-for-columnists thought experiment, Amit tells Ajay: 'I hope you're the best paid columnist in India, but perhaps not.'

head: After Ajay's sobering point about climate change and frozen land markets, Amit offers what he calls…
more: After Ajay's sobering point about climate change and frozen land markets, Amit offers what he calls 'probably an inappropriate joke': if the state won't let land markets be liquid, maybe climate change will.

head: Amit, on behalf of a viewer, sets Ajay a quota of at least one book recommendation per episode instead of masala tea. Ajay defends himself
more: Amit, on behalf of a viewer, sets Ajay a quota of at least one book recommendation per episode instead of masala tea. Ajay defends himself: 'books are very nerdy and I'm very nerdy. So I thought it'd be hazaar cool to go beyond books and talk about fun things like kefir and masala tea.' Amit closes the show: 'Books are hazaar cool.'

head: Sharad Joshi's couplet, spoken by a farmer to a consumer
more: Sharad Joshi's couplet, spoken by a farmer to a consumer: 'Marte tum bhi ho, marte hum bhi hain.' Amit translates: 'I die my friend and so do you. I sell my produce cheap and die. You pay so much that you die too.'

head: Amit borrows the Hotel California line to describe farmers who can't sell their land at fair value
more: Amit borrows the Hotel California line to describe farmers who can't sell their land at fair value: 'you can check out but you can never leave.'

head: Alex Tabarrok on Mumbai's FSI limits, as Amit recalls it
more: Alex Tabarrok on Mumbai's FSI limits, as Amit recalls it: 'in Bombay you reclaim the sea. You need to reclaim the sky.'

head: The Bookshop Romeo
dek: Expected-value thinking is not only for gamblers. When the downside is tiny and the upside is huge, you should take the shot every time.
more: The first column of Amit's 'Range Rover' poker column for the Economic Times imagined a young man whose favourite author is Milan Kundera. He walks into a bookshop and sees a pretty girl in a distant aisle reading Kundera. Should he go up and introduce himself? Even if he is diffident and puts the odds of a date at 10% and of finding a soulmate at 1%, those outcomes are worth so much that the approach is massively plus EV. A 90% rejection rate costs him only a moment of embarrassment.

Expected-value thinking is not only for gamblers. When the downside is tiny and the upside is huge, you should take the shot every time. Most of us already sense this intuitively, and naming it helps fear stop disguising itself as prudence.

head: Just Bet on the Side Batting Second
dek: When the rules of a game change, people keep playing by the old mental model, and that creates a big, systematic edge for anyone who has updated. (Amit adds that cricket betting is illegal in India and he doesn't advise it.)
more: Before the 2016 IPL, a friend who dabbled in cricket betting asked Amit, by then retired from poker, for a tip. Amit's advice was to bet on the side batting second in every match. The friend expected deep nuance, ignored him, and called back after the 14th match. The chasing side had won 13 of the 14, comfortably, losing about 3.4 wickets on average and finishing in around 17 overs. Chasing gives a small informational edge worth perhaps 55-45 or 60-40, nothing like that. The real cause was that teams batting first kept underestimating the par score. Virat Kohli, captaining Bangalore, lost at least three games batting first and implied his bowlers were to blame because 'we got the par score'.

When the rules of a game change, people keep playing by the old mental model, and that creates a big, systematic edge for anyone who has updated. (Amit adds that cricket betting is illegal in India and he doesn't advise it.)

head: Amla and de Villiers Refuse to Score
dek: Aggressive cricket and aggressive batting are not the same thing. The same EV logic that demands attack in T20 demands total defence when there is no reward for risk.
more: On 6 December 2015, the fourth day of a Delhi Test, South Africa came out needing about 431 runs to win in a day and a half against India. They judged that a win was impossible on that pitch against those bowlers. Hashim Amla made 25 off roughly 244 balls, and AB de Villiers, one of the most aggressive batsmen ever, made 43 off about 293. People couldn't believe natural stroke-players were batting like this.

Aggressive cricket and aggressive batting are not the same thing. The same EV logic that demands attack in T20 demands total defence when there is no reward for risk. Doing the correct thing can look stupid to an audience judging by style.

head: From Gavaskar's 36 Not Out to Bazball
dek: An entire sport can play a format suboptimally for decades because everyone inherits the previous format's habits.
more: When ODIs arrived, teams played them like Test cricket. In the 1975 World Cup, Sunil Gavaskar batted all 60 overs for 36 not out, defending himself with 'I didn't play every ball'. The ODI game updated slowly. New Zealand sent Mark Greatbatch out as an early pinch-hitter, and in the 1996 World Cup Jayasuriya and Kaluwitharana attacked from the start, but the middle overs stayed a period of consolidation. About seven or eight years ago England front-loaded their ODI batting, made 300-plus scores routine outside the subcontinent, and won the 2019 World Cup, with some luck in the final. Under Brendan McCullum ('Baz') they then took this into Tests. Amit's ex-Cricinfo colleague Andrew Miller coined the term 'Bazball', which McCullum dislikes because 'it's not just all crash and burn'.

An entire sport can play a format suboptimally for decades because everyone inherits the previous format's habits. England's edge was not raw aggression. They were finally getting expected value right by looking at the data.

head: Johnny von Neumann vs the Coin Toss
dek: Much of what we call randomness is really our inability to compute.
more: At the time of the great debates between Einstein and others about probability in physics, John von Neumann asked whether a coin toss is truly random or merely Newtonian mechanics we haven't bothered to compute. He worked out formulas and heuristics that, given some initial facts about the coin, predicted the outcome at roughly 0.66 to 0.33. More recently, Ajay recalls, a project associated with Persi Diaconis had researchers around the world toss physical coins millions of times. They found that a coin starting heads-up lands heads about 51% of the time.

Much of what we call randomness is really our inability to compute. Even the textbook 50-50 event carries a tiny exploitable edge, and Ajay jokes that you can use it whenever you want to cheat at an important life decision.

head: Messi's Numbers and Guardiola's Goalkeeper
dek: A tactic can look ridiculous in the moment, like a misplaced pass that gifts the opponent the ball, and still be right on average.
more: Football is broken down to a science. When Amit wrote 'What Cricket Can Learn From Poker', Messi had a 12.1% chance of scoring when shooting from outside the box and 8% from a direct free kick. Coaches drill these numbers into players, so they know the EV of shooting versus passing to a striker. The data-driven 'playing out from the back' approach, from the Cruyff school and adopted by Pep Guardiola, led Guardiola on arriving at Manchester City to get rid of a goalkeeper good enough to play for England, because he couldn't play out from the back.

A tactic can look ridiculous in the moment, like a misplaced pass that gifts the opponent the ball, and still be right on average. Elite teams value players for what is plus EV, not for traditional skills done beautifully.

head: Steel or Software? The Bet Everyone Makes Leaving College
dek: People who think they are too risk-averse to touch the stock market are already making a concentrated, undiversifiable bet with their most important asset.
more: When Ajay was leaving college, he would put a question to people his age. If you bought shares in a few industries and held them for 30 years, betting on whether steel or software would do well, everyone would call it speculative. Yet choosing an industry or a company is exactly that bet, made with your human capital. In the 1980s nobody could have known Indian pharma or Indian software would boom. Those who happened to choose them look brilliant, and the media then lionises them as geniuses.

People who think they are too risk-averse to touch the stock market are already making a concentrated, undiversifiable bet with their most important asset. Much celebrated success is luck that we retell as genius.

head: A First Course in Probability
dek: The classic probability textbook behind the episode's expected-value reasoning, for anyone who wants the rigorous maths beneath the intuitions.
more: The classic probability textbook behind the episode's expected-value reasoning, for anyone who wants the rigorous maths beneath the intuitions.
Ajay names it as the probability 'wing' of his brain and asks Amit to connect it with cricket.

head: What Cricket Can Learn From Poker
dek: Amit's foundational case for applying expected value to cricket. It includes the football data example (Messi's 12.1% from outside the box versus 8% from free kicks) showing how far other sports had moved towards data.
more: Amit's foundational case for applying expected value to cricket. It includes the football data example (Messi's 12.1% from outside the box versus 8% from free kicks) showing how far other sports had moved towards data.
Amit's 2016 Cricket Monthly piece, cited in the episode and listed as essential reading.

head: What Cricket Can Learn From Economics
dek: Applies the economist's idea of opportunity cost to cricket. This is the lens behind the episode's claim that T20's scarcity of deliveries makes dot balls costlier and wickets cheaper.
more: Applies the economist's idea of opportunity cost to cricket. This is the lens behind the episode's claim that T20's scarcity of deliveries makes dot balls costlier and wickets cheaper.
Essential reading in the show notes, the companion to the episode's opportunity-cost argument.

head: Unlikely is Inevitable
dek: Explains the law of truly large numbers: given a big enough sample, any unlikely event is bound to happen, so streaks are not evidence of a bad decision.
more: Explains the law of truly large numbers: given a big enough sample, any unlikely event is bound to happen, so streaks are not evidence of a bad decision.
Amit mentions the column while explaining why ten tails in a row needn't mean a weighted coin.

head: We Are All Gamblers
dek: Every action involves probabilities, from real estate versus other investments to software versus television as a career.
more: Every action involves probabilities, from real estate versus other investments to software versus television as a career. We are all implicitly making probabilistic judgments, so 'gambler' shouldn't be an insult.
Amit cites this 2010 column while arguing that traders aren't uniquely gambling.

head: The Bookshop Romeo
dek: The Milan Kundera bookshop example: a high-reward, near-zero-cost approach is massively plus EV.
more: The Milan Kundera bookshop example: a high-reward, near-zero-cost approach is massively plus EV. It is a portable illustration of expected value in everyday life.
The first column in Amit's Range Rover poker column, retold in the episode.

head: Expected Value: Judge the Decision, Not the Outcome
dek: Take a bet that pays 51 paise on heads and costs 49 on tails: its EV is +1 paisa a flip, so you should take it.
more: Take a bet that pays 51 paise on heads and costs 49 on tails: its EV is +1 paisa a flip, so you should take it. Yet you'll lose half the single flips, and even over a hundred flips you can still end up behind. Observers will call the right decision a blunder because of the result. Poker players are trained not to be results-oriented. Ajay calls judging policy by outcome a widespread analytical flaw, because many good decisions go wrong through dumb luck.

head: Parallel Universes of Possibility
dek: Imagine every coin flip splitting the world into parallel universes: H or T, then HH, HT, TH, TT, and so on.
more: Imagine every coin flip splitting the world into parallel universes: H or T, then HH, HT, TH, TT, and so on. Which universe you land in is pure luck. Given enough trials, even a hundred heads in a row will occur somewhere, which is the law of truly large numbers. So you can't evaluate your actions by how they worked out. Live by a good set of rules and don't sweat results.

head: Luck Is Bigger Than We Think (Against the Great Man Theory)
dek: Play Nadal at tennis or Magnus Carlsen at chess a hundred times and you lose every game.
more: Play Nadal at tennis or Magnus Carlsen at chess a hundred times and you lose every game. The best poker player against a beginner is closer to 51-49 per hand, because skill needs a long sample to show. Life works similarly. Lucky breaks such as where you were born can make you arrogant, and bad luck can make you defeatist, so sweat only what you control. Ajay adds that this runs opposite to the great man theory: celebrated CEOs often just happened to be in the right industry at the right time.

head: Rehabilitating Speculation
dek: In polite Indian company, wise grown-ups supposedly don't speculate.
more: In polite Indian company, wise grown-ups supposedly don't speculate. Ajay argues that everything significant involves judgment under uncertainty: a surgeon choosing a diagnostic path, a financier allocating money, two people deciding whether to launch a new YouTube show. Only the most controlled, predictable work is free of speculation.

head: Above the API vs Below the API
dek: An API call takes an instruction and reliably returns a predictable answer every time.
more: An API call takes an instruction and reliably returns a predictable answer every time. The Uber driver lives below the API: code tells him to take this customer from here to there, and he has no agency. The people who design and decide, embracing risk, complexity and probabilistic thinking, live above it. Most interesting things happen above the API, and it is where one should aim to be.

head: T20 Opportunity Cost: Scarce Balls, Cheap Wickets
dek: ODIs give you 11 resources across 50 overs; T20 gives the same 11 resources across only 20.
more: ODIs give you 11 resources across 50 overs; T20 gives the same 11 resources across only 20. Deliveries become scarcer, so each dot ball costs more, each wicket is worth less, and the EV of aggression rises. Teams nonetheless carried over the ODI grammar of pinch-hitting, consolidating and slogging. Amit's prescription is to front-load: attack throughout and send hitters first, keeping 'builders' for when wickets fall. Finishing an innings with only two or three wickets down signals you weren't aggressive enough. As Ajay put it, 'You left money on the table.'

head: Strike Rate Minus Required Strike Rate
dek: In T20, averages and aggregates no longer matter; strike rate does. Amit's proposed metric is a batsman's strike rate minus the strike rate his team needed to reach the par score.
more: In T20, averages and aggregates no longer matter; strike rate does. Amit's proposed metric is a batsman's strike rate minus the strike rate his team needed to reach the par score. If it's negative, he made the rest of the team carry his slowness, and the more runs he scores the bigger the liability. During a match the calculation shifts ball by ball. For example, losing three wickets in the first over raises the value of the remaining wickets and makes caution more valuable.

head: Fix the Metrics, Fix the Incentives
dek: Ajay calls this the quintessential problem of all organisations: personal objectives (looking good) diverge from team objectives (winning).
more: Ajay calls this the quintessential problem of all organisations: personal objectives (looking good) diverge from team objectives (winning). Judge batsmen on averages and you push them towards suboptimal play. They should instead be judged against a hurdle rate, the rate needed to win. The fix must go upstream to selectors, just as hiring a star trader in a dumb way is management's fault. Amit adds the Indian history behind this. In eras when India usually lost abroad, Gavaskar-style chasing of personal landmarks made sense and stuck around. Selectors also find it safer to pick the guy with a good average than one who correctly risks his wicket and gets unlucky.

head: Experts Shouldn't Sell Certainty
dek: Experts on TV and Twitter are incentivised to exude certainty, but a complex world allows only probabilistic answers such as 70% this, 20% that.
more: Experts on TV and Twitter are incentivised to exude certainty, but a complex world allows only probabilistic answers such as 70% this, 20% that. Forecasters who gave Trump a low chance in 2016 weren't necessarily wrong just because he won. Ajay says the conversation between economists and the real world is dysfunctional: people want a super-forecaster, and an honest economist must often say 'I don't know.' Better to talk about the forces at work than play the forecasting game.

head: Ajay's improvised intro paints Amit as a…
more: Ajay's improvised intro paints Amit as a 'serious philosopher' who spends his nights reading complex books by German philosophers. Amit: 'I did, I confess, read German philosophers, but that is not something that one admits in public.' The show notes title the chapter 'What? He Reads German Philosophers? Scoundrel!'

head: Amit specifies a perfectly fair coin
more: Amit specifies a perfectly fair coin, 'not like the Sholay coin, but a proper legit coin', a nod to the famous coin in the film Sholay.

head: Ajay on von Neumann
more: Ajay on von Neumann: 'Johnny to all his good friends. There's only one Johnny in the world, and that's Johnny von Neumann.'

head: Ajay's practical takeaway from the 51% coin-toss finding
more: Ajay's practical takeaway from the 51% coin-toss finding: 'whenever you want to cheat at important life decisions, offer to the blokes around you, let's toss the coin, and I've given you a slight edge.'

head: After Ajay's lecture on living above the API, Amit asks…
more: After Ajay's lecture on living above the API, Amit asks: 'I might get kicked out from your circle of friends for asking this question, but I have to. On behalf of our gentle listeners as well. What the fuck is an API?'

head: Amit's three possible outcomes of a skied shot: a six, a catch, or
more: Amit's three possible outcomes of a skied shot: a six, a catch, or 'the ball hits a bird in the sky and then drops down on a fielder's head and the bird and the fielder die', which he calls 'incredibly unlikely, but nevertheless a non-zero possibility.'
Ajay: 'now shut up and give us cricket.' Amit: 'I can't shut up and give you cricket, I have to talk.'

head: Ajay recalls watching Sunil Gavaskar bat at Wankhede as a child and says Sachin Tendulkar grew up about fifty metres from him in Bandra East.
more: Ajay recalls watching Sunil Gavaskar bat at Wankhede as a child and says Sachin Tendulkar grew up about fifty metres from him in Bandra East. Amit: 'A day should come when Sachin Tendulkar says, You know, I grew up in the same neighborhood as Ajay Shah. I would like that day to come.'

head: Harry Truman's plea for…
more: Harry Truman's plea for 'a one-handed economist', made because his advisers kept saying 'on one hand this, on the other hand that.' Amit sympathises with both Truman, who had to decide, and the economists, because the world is not simple.

head: Ajay recalls Churchill's lament that one economist gives you two views
more: Ajay recalls Churchill's lament that one economist gives you two views, 'and three if it's John Maynard Keynes.'

head: Amit's sign-off to the audience
more: Amit's sign-off to the audience: 'you were taking a gamble when you started watching this episode. But it is very clear now that you have reached the end, that the gamble was worth it. So congratulations.'

head: The Canard Taught in School
dek: Ideas absorbed in childhood feel like common sense because nobody ever asks us to check them.
more: As a schoolboy in the 'Hum Do Hamare Do' era of family planning, Amit was taught that India was poor because it had too many people. It felt intuitive: a poor country, not enough to go around. Only as he came into adulthood did he realise the opposite was true. He grew angrier as he saw most people still holding the belief and refusing to adjust their views to the facts.

Ideas absorbed in childhood feel like common sense because nobody ever asks us to check them. The intuitive story of a fixed pie and too many mouths can be the exact reverse of what the evidence shows.

head: Paul Ehrlich's Taxi Ride Through Delhi
dek: The most influential population panic of its era rested on a visceral recoil from crowds of poor people, not on evidence.
more: Amit reads the passage from The Population Bomb in which Paul Ehrlich says he had long understood the population explosion 'intellectually' but only came to understand it 'emotionally' in an ancient taxi crawling through a crowded Delhi slum: fleas on the seats, over a hundred degrees, dust and smoke, and 'people, people, people, people.' Ehrlich wondered whether they would ever reach the hotel. He also wrote that he couldn't see how India could feed 200 million more people by 1980. Amit notes that Delhi's population has since grown about five times, and argues Ehrlich was embellishing because mid-60s Delhi wasn't that crowded.
The most influential population panic of its era rested on a visceral recoil from crowds of poor people, not on evidence. The city that horrified Ehrlich went on to absorb many times more people.
printed: Fleas, dust and a doomsday book

head: Sanjay Gandhi's Sterilisation Quotas
dek: Once a policy becomes a numerical target passed down a hierarchy, every link in the chain has a reason to coerce the next one.
more: Reading from Coomi Kapoor's The Emergency, Amit describes how Sanjay Gandhi, acting as an extra-constitutional authority, pushed family planning, which also earned international credibility because bodies like the Ford Foundation were pressing for it. He bypassed the nodal ministry and went straight to chief ministers eager to please him, Bansi Lal of Haryana most notoriously. Sterilisations rose from 26.24 lakh in 1975-76 to 81.32 lakh in 1976-77, and Haryana hit four times its target. Every district and officer had quotas, and missing them meant withheld salaries, suspensions and transfers. The pressure flowed down to police and junior staff. Teachers had to 'motivate' at least five sterilisations to get paid, and some offered half their salaries to find volunteers. A third or fourth child could be refused admission to government school without a sterilisation certificate. Loans, land and jobs were tied to certificates, and some Delhi government hospitals refused treatment until the patient agreed to be sterilised. Police opened fire at least eight times between August and December 1976.

Once a policy becomes a numerical target passed down a hierarchy, every link in the chain has a reason to coerce the next one. The cruelty comes from how the incentives are designed, not from a few bad apples.

head: The Siege of Pipli
dek: Even if you believe population is a problem, coercive family planning tells citizens that the state, not they, owns their bodies.
more: In Pipli, a Haryana village 45 km north of Delhi, a widower named Hawa Singh was forcibly taken for sterilisation. His incision turned septic and he bled to death. The block development officer still came back for more 'volunteers' and picked up a man repairing shoes by the roadside. Villagers drove the officials out. Several hundred policemen then besieged the village overnight. At 6 am they opened fire, killing two women making cow-dung cakes outside their huts, and threatened to send an aircraft to bomb the area. Out of a population of 2,761, between 400 and 500 men were rounded up and sterilised. Amit adds that sterilisation incentives continue across rural India today, and that it is always women who suffer most.

Even if you believe population is a problem, coercive family planning tells citizens that the state, not they, owns their bodies. Amit calls this worse than slavery, and notes how normalised it became.
printed: The night they came for Pipli

head: The Simon–Ehrlich Wager
dek: Betting on a prediction exposes doom narratives to reality. Scarcity sets off human ingenuity and price adjustment, so resources don't simply run out as people multiply.
more: Paul Ehrlich once declared that if he were a gambler, he'd take even money that England would not exist in the year 2000. Economist Julian Simon noticed the word 'bet' and publicly challenged him. Ehrlich could choose five resources and any period longer than a year. Simon would bet (around $10,000, as Amit recalls) that their prices would fall instead of rising with scarcity. Ehrlich picked copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten. The bet was made in 1980, and by 1990 all five were cheaper. Ehrlich nonetheless remains a major figure and, Amit says, 'a hero of the left even today.'

Betting on a prediction exposes doom narratives to reality. Scarcity sets off human ingenuity and price adjustment, so resources don't simply run out as people multiply. Being spectacularly wrong rarely costs a public intellectual his standing.

head: A PhD on Fertility, and Poland's Birth Strike
dek: Fertility tracks how people see the future. Dread alone can make a society stop having children, with no pill required.
more: Offering what he calls 'an amusing fact', Ajay reveals that his PhD thesis was on fertility, specifically women in Malaysia having babies, which took him deep into the fertility literature. His favourite story from it is about Poland. A young country carved out by the Treaty of Versailles, it was immediately invaded by the Soviets, with Leon Trotsky stopped at its edges. It then lived precariously between Germany and the Soviet Union, neither of which could be trusted as a neighbour. Under that constant sense that something would go wrong, birth rates collapsed, and this happened without any modern reproductive technology.
Fertility tracks how people see the future. Dread alone can make a society stop having children, with no pill required.

head: The Idle Young Men of Bihar
dek: A demographic dividend without jobs turns into a demographic disaster.
more: Amit's friend Kumar Anand described travelling through semi-urban Bihar near Saharsa, where he lives, and seeing streets full of young men standing around. They weren't waiting for a bus, smoking at a katta, or waiting for a contractor's truck to take them to work. They were just standing, idle. Kumar Anand and Mohit Satyanand later did a road-trip episode on Bihar for The Seen and the Unseen, and much of what they described was young people who either have no jobs or no longer care.
A demographic dividend without jobs turns into a demographic disaster. Hopeless young men don't dream of building families, which feeds the very fertility and social problems Ajay warns about.

head: Julian Simon's 'I Told You So' to Milton Friedman
dek: Two great minds disagreed and then settled it with no ego involved: the senior figure openly conceded and credited the junior one.
more: In December 1976, a young Julian Simon wrote to Milton Friedman about his plan for airline overbooking. When a flight is oversold, passengers write sealed bids of the lowest amount they'd accept to take the next flight, and the low bidders are paid and rebooked. He asked Friedman to vouch to the Civil Aeronautics Board that it wasn't the work of a crank. Friedman replied that the plan made sense to every economist, but he declined to write. He reasoned that if it were that good, airlines would already be doing it, so 'we must be overlooking something.' Then Alfred E. Kahn, an economist, was appointed head of the CAB, and airlines adopted the scheme. In 1979 Simon sent Friedman American Airlines' glowing report on it. Friedman replied with a short, gracious letter.

Two great minds disagreed and then settled it with no ego involved: the senior figure openly conceded and credited the junior one. In a polarised age where people dread being seen to be wrong in public, that grace is rare and worth copying.
printed: I told you so, by post

head: The Ultimate Resource
dek: Its thesis that human beings are the ultimate resource is the root of the 'people are brains, not stomachs' worldview.
more: Its thesis that human beings are the ultimate resource is the root of the 'people are brains, not stomachs' worldview.
Amit cites Simon's 1981 book (later released in a second edition) as the best phrasing of what he believes.

head: Too Many People?
dek: It finds no correlation between population density and poverty, with striking counterexamples: Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer, and Bahrain is three times as dense as India and far richer.
more: It finds no correlation between population density and poverty, with striking counterexamples: Monaco is forty times as dense as Bangladesh and far richer, and Bahrain is three times as dense as India and far richer.
Amit opens his case with this 2007 study.

head: The Great Breakthrough and Its Cause
dek: It extends Simon's argument that the industrial revolution and productivity booms happened because population rose.
more: It extends Simon's argument that the industrial revolution and productivity booms happened because population rose. More people multiply the opportunities for free trade and voluntary exchange, and everyone benefits.
Amit mentions Simon's last book, edited and finished by Timur Kuran, Ajay's former professor.

head: An Essay on the Principle of Population
dek: Read it to see where the idea began: Malthus claimed people grow exponentially while resources grow arithmetically, so mass starvation was inevitable.
more: Read it to see where the idea began: Malthus claimed people grow exponentially while resources grow arithmetically, so mass starvation was inevitable.
Amit traces modern population pessimism back to this 1798 essay.

head: The Population Bomb
dek: A case study in confident doom. It declared the battle to feed humanity already lost and predicted hundreds of millions would starve in the 1970s and 80s, which never happened.
more: A case study in confident doom. It declared the battle to feed humanity already lost and predicted hundreds of millions would starve in the 1970s and 80s, which never happened.
Amit reads its opening lines and Ehrlich's Delhi taxi passage.

head: The Book That Incited a Worldwide Fear of Overpopulation
dek: It shows the global scale of the coercion: health workers paid per IUD inserted, birth-control pills pitched out of helicopters over villages in the Philippines, and millions sterilised, often coercively, from Mexico to Bangladesh.
more: It shows the global scale of the coercion: health workers paid per IUD inserted, birth-control pills pitched out of helicopters over villages in the Philippines, and millions sterilised, often coercively, from Mexico to Bangladesh.
Amit quotes Mann on the population-control movements of the 1950s–70s, led by bodies like the Rockefeller and Ford Foundations.

head: The Emergency: A Personal History
dek: A great journalist's first-hand account of how the sterilisation drive spun out of control: quotas, withheld salaries, denied medical care, police firings and the siege of Pipli.
more: A great journalist's first-hand account of how the sterilisation drive spun out of control: quotas, withheld salaries, denied medical care, police firings and the siege of Pipli.
Amit names it as one of his recommendations for the episode and reads at length from its chapter on Sanjay Gandhi and family planning.

head: Triumph of the City
dek: It explains that cities are great because they pack large numbers of clever people close together.
more: It explains that cities are great because they pack large numbers of clever people close together. It also admits dense cities can be terrible (crime, slums, public health), which makes good governance the real challenge.
Ajay says he built his intuition about density from this book.

head: The Skeptical Environmentalist
dek: It taught him that cities follow an arc: London around the turn of the 19th century was as polluted and overrun as any Indian city today, and it later became much cleaner.
more: It taught him that cities follow an arc: London around the turn of the 19th century was as polluted and overrun as any Indian city today, and it later became much cleaner.
Amit cites it while discussing how messy cities improve over time.

head: The Origins of Totalitarianism
dek: Arendt was among the first to show how much Nazi Germany and Stalin's Russia had in common, which makes her an essential guide to authoritarian regimes.
more: Arendt was among the first to show how much Nazi Germany and Stalin's Russia had in common, which makes her an essential guide to authoritarian regimes. Amit adds that it is not a book of history but 'a book of the present moment.'
Ajay's book recommendation for the episode. He had earlier drawn on Arendt to argue that totalitarian regimes depopulate.

head: Yuganta
dek: He calls it a masterpiece that made him understand his society and culture far better.
more: He calls it a masterpiece that made him understand his society and culture far better. It is literary criticism of our epics and the role of women in them, sometimes disquieting to read. It is also an analysis of a society we still live in, not of another time and place.
Amit's book recommendation for the episode.

head: People Are Brains, Not Stomachs
dek: A person is not just a mouth to feed but a mind that creates. More people mean bigger networks, more positive-sum games and more mutually beneficial trades.
more: A person is not just a mouth to feed but a mind that creates. More people mean bigger networks, more positive-sum games and more mutually beneficial trades. Amit also sees a moral problem in population pessimism: calling population a problem means calling other people the problem while placing yourself above it.

head: Voting With Your Feet Toward Density
dek: If density caused poverty, people would flee crowded places. Instead, all of human history is migration from sparse villages to dense cities: people go from Bihar to Mumbai, not the reverse.
more: If density caused poverty, people would flee crowded places. Instead, all of human history is migration from sparse villages to dense cities: people go from Bihar to Mumbai, not the reverse. Even a Mumbai slum beats the village for those who choose it. Amit's challenge to the listener: if you're in a city, why are you there? And if you're in a village, you either made your money in a city or want to go to one.

head: Urban Agglomeration Is the Engine of Modernity
dek: Ajay argues a city's greatness is the number of clever people living within 20 minutes of you, and the combined human capital that challenges and drives you.
more: Ajay argues a city's greatness is the number of clever people living within 20 minutes of you, and the combined human capital that challenges and drives you. We are each creatures of the people around us. Scatter everyone onto a 100-metre grid and that flowering dies. Modern culture is urban, created in dense collections of people, not in the landowner machismo of rural life.

head: Population Problems Are Governance Problems
dek: The poverty, slums, crime and pollution we blame on population are really failures of governance.
more: The poverty, slums, crime and pollution we blame on population are really failures of governance. Glaeser shows dense cities can be terrible, and New York in the 70s was famous for crime, rats and cockroaches. Lomborg shows London was once as polluted as any Indian city today. Ajay cautions that improvement is not inevitable and takes purposeful action, but cities around the world have fixed these problems and the know-how exists.

head: Never Extrapolate a Trend Forever
dek: Malthusian doom comes from projecting a growth curve into infinity, as with Malthus's claim that people grow exponentially while resources grow arithmetically, or the doomsayers' vision of 70 billion people visiting each other by elevator because there are no roads.
more: Malthusian doom comes from projecting a growth curve into infinity, as with Malthus's claim that people grow exponentially while resources grow arithmetically, or the doomsayers' vision of 70 billion people visiting each other by elevator because there are no roads. Julian Simon mocked this by noting that if the recent growth of university buildings continued, one day the earth would be nothing but university buildings. We think in zero-sum terms, but human ingenuity and the price system respond to scarcity by finding alternatives.

head: Why the Poor Have More Children
dek: Poor families treat children as resources, which is itself evidence that people are assets.
more: Poor families treat children as resources, which is itself evidence that people are assets. High child mortality made extra children a form of insurance. Yet even with child mortality far lower today, the poor still have more children and the rich fewer.

head: Three Worlds of Coercion
dek: Ajay compares family planning in pre-Emergency India (modest coercion), Emergency India (terrible, subject to the whims of one or two people) and communist China (the one-child policy, draconian beyond belief).
more: Ajay compares family planning in pre-Emergency India (modest coercion), Emergency India (terrible, subject to the whims of one or two people) and communist China (the one-child policy, draconian beyond belief). The more concentrated the power, the further a mistaken idea escalates into disaster. That is the case for dispersing power and making such state intrusion illegitimate.

head: Not All Coercion Is Equal
dek: Coercion comes in degrees of intrusiveness. Stopping a Punjab farmer from burning his field is mild.
more: Coercion comes in degrees of intrusiveness. Stopping a Punjab farmer from burning his field is mild. Telling a single woman she cannot use surrogacy is a different order of evil, because it reaches into personal life. Amit makes the same point about forced sterilisation: the state tells you that you do not own your body. Whether to have children should be the business of individuals alone.

head: There Is No Budget Constraint on Coercion
dek: Government spending has a built-in brake: extracting taxes is hard, and people resist, move money abroad or hide it, so even a half-witted government weighs what it spends.
more: Government spending has a built-in brake: extracting taxes is hard, and people resist, move money abroad or hide it, so even a half-witted government weighs what it spends. Coercion has no such limit. Governments can pile one coercive rule on another with no cap on the total and little sense of degree. So citizens must push back much harder against intrusive coercion.

head: Having a Child Is an Act of Hope
dek: Drawing on Hannah Arendt's point that totalitarians run out of people to oppress, Ajay argues that tyranny breeds hopelessness and stagnation, and men and women respond by going on a birth strike.
more: Drawing on Hannah Arendt's point that totalitarians run out of people to oppress, Ajay argues that tyranny breeds hopelessness and stagnation, and men and women respond by going on a birth strike. Russia shows it now: about 300,000 men of reproductive age have died in Ukraine and about a million of the best and brightest have left, about 1.3 million people, and with them a future stream of children. Such collapses happened long before modern contraception existed.

head: Fear the Population Bust, Not the Boom
dek: The real danger is a sharp fall in fertility. The US and UK declined slowly, giving society generations to adjust.
more: The real danger is a sharp fall in fertility. The US and UK declined slowly, giving society generations to adjust. In China and Russia the children vanished suddenly, leaving few young people and many old ones, which is wrenching for a society.

head: The Arithmetic of an Ageing Society
dek: Set pensions and financial wealth aside and look only at people. The elderly need nursing, cooking, cleaning and personal care, which only the young can provide.
more: Set pensions and financial wealth aside and look only at people. The elderly need nursing, cooking, cleaning and personal care, which only the young can provide. If 10 old people need the services of 15 young people, that works. When the old share balloons and they need 60 young people's services, it becomes impossible, because the young must also produce everything else. These services can't be imported, so their prices shoot towards infinity and few elderly can afford dignity.

head: India's Quiet Fertility Decline
dek: India's last census was in 2011, with no 2021 census in sight, and its statistics are weak across the board: census data has even been manipulated to draw electoral maps, and GDP, industrial production, NSSO and ASI figures are poorly measured.
more: India's last census was in 2011, with no 2021 census in sight, and its statistics are weak across the board: census data has even been manipulated to draw electoral maps, and GDP, industrial production, NSSO and ASI figures are poorly measured. Even so, alternative sources point to a rapid fall in fertility over the last 10–15 years. Ajay attributes it to how would-be parents read their world: cramped urban housing, long commutes, a skewed sex ratio, the norm of needing a job before marriage amid poor employment, and an ever-interfering state.

head: Loosen the Rules on Who Can Raise Children
dek: Ajay argues that having more children should be a good thing for those who choose it, that government should never limit that choice, and that society shouldn't insist only a father and mother can raise a child.
more: Ajay argues that having more children should be a good thing for those who choose it, that government should never limit that choice, and that society shouldn't insist only a father and mother can raise a child. Opening up to single parents and other unconventional arrangements would reflect the blossoming of human freedom. It would also be practical in a country facing a fertility problem.

head: Bare Branches: When the Dividend Becomes a Disaster
dek: The Chinese 'bare branches' problem refers to young men who never find their feet, never learn a trade, earn an income, move out or build a family.
more: The Chinese 'bare branches' problem refers to young men who never find their feet, never learn a trade, earn an income, move out or build a family. Renuka Sane and her co-authors find that more men relative to women means more crime. Amit adds a neuroscience point he recalls (possibly from Robert Sapolsky): the brain region responsible for socialisation in males fully develops only around 25, which is why most violence comes from males aged 18–25. Ajay adds that raising boys without talking to girls is 'a dagger wound on the soul.' Without jobs, Amit concludes, the demographic dividend becomes a demographic disaster.

head: Noticing that the hosts are wearing matching shirts, Ajay asks…
more: Noticing that the hosts are wearing matching shirts, Ajay asks: 'What spontaneous banter can we do about this spontaneous order?'

head: Amit says the design on Ajay's shirt reminds him of…
more: Amit says the design on Ajay's shirt reminds him of 'maggots on a dead cow,' then reveals the source: twentieth-century population pessimist Harrison Brown, who wrote that humanity 'will not rest content until the earth is covered completely and to a considerable depth with a writhing mass of human beings, much as a dead cow is covered with a pulsating mass of maggots.'

head: After reading Ehrlich's anguished
more: After reading Ehrlich's anguished 'Would we ever get to our hotel?', Amit deadpans: 'And I'm pleased to report he did get to his hotel.' Later he adds that Ehrlich is still a hero of the left even though 'he has been wrong about everything in his life.'

head: Ajay on botched sterilisation camps
more: Ajay on botched sterilisation camps: 'the autoclave will not be working, the instruments will be contaminated. That's garden variety incompetence of the Indian state. That's unsurprising.'

head: Ajay on India's statistics
more: Ajay on India's statistics: 'The bad news to you, Virginia, if you believed that the Indian census was gospel truth. It's not.' He adds that Indian-style gerrymandering works by manipulating the census rather than by redrawing constituencies.
Amit: 'I sometimes provocatively say that most Urdu poetry is a whining of incels, but you know, that is just a provocation, but the whining of incels could kinda become a problem.'

head: Amit on gender segregation
more: Amit on gender segregation: 'I went to a boys' school. I learned how to talk to girls by watching Bollywood, which is not quite the best thing, is it?'

head: Julian Simon's gloat-without-gloating letter to Milton Friedman
more: Julian Simon's gloat-without-gloating letter to Milton Friedman: 'I'm one of your great fans, and I'm not an I told you so type. Still, you may find it interesting to compare your second and third paragraphs...'

head: Amit on Alfred E. Kahn, the economist whose appointment to the Civil Aeronautics Board let Simon's overbooking auction happen
more: Amit on Alfred E. Kahn, the economist whose appointment to the Civil Aeronautics Board let Simon's overbooking auction happen: 'he's a good economist because not all economists get economics, but he's a good economist. He gets it.'

head: Malthus's notorious line from his 1798 essay
more: Malthus's notorious line from his 1798 essay: 'Instead of recommending cleanliness to the poor, we should encourage contrary habits and court the return of the plague,' because for him the plague would be deliverance.

head: Robert Sapolsky, probably on an episode of Sam Harris's podcast (
more: Robert Sapolsky, probably on an episode of Sam Harris's podcast ('I might be misremembering'), is Amit's source for the claim that the socialising part of the male brain matures only around 25.

head: Why Europe Risked Death for Pepper
dek: Behaviour that looks irrational from the outside is often a sensible answer to a life-or-death constraint.
more: As a child, Ajay couldn't see why Europeans would board ships with a 25% chance of dying just to get pepper; he could have lived with salt on his omelette. The answer: Europe's population had grown to the limit of its agricultural carrying capacity, so people could only survive winter on meat stored from summer. Stored meat rots. The choice was to eat rotten meat and fall ill, or to preserve it with spices. When the Ottomans took Istanbul in 1453 and cut the land route for spices from India, Europe had to find a sea route. The Portuguese worked their way around the Cape of Good Hope to Madagascar, where they met a Malay navigator who knew how to ride the monsoon currents to Calicut.
Behaviour that looks irrational from the outside is often a sensible answer to a life-or-death constraint. History makes sense once you rebuild the problem people actually faced.
printed: A matter of life and pepper

head: When My Ship Comes In
dek: Financial institutions are not abstract designs. They are answers to concrete, felt problems in the real economy.
more: Fitting out a ship, hiring a crew and sending it to Calicut for pepper and cardamom was a huge bet in a Europe that was not yet rich. About one voyage in four was lost to cyclones, pirates or something else. The English phrase 'when my ship comes in' comes from this all-or-nothing gamble. No single person could afford a bet that size, and that pressure produced the first great financial innovations: the joint stock company and the limited liability company.
Financial institutions are not abstract designs. They are answers to concrete, felt problems in the real economy. Even the idioms we still use preserve the shape of those old risks.

head: The Factory on Fire
dek: This is the price system at work. A decentralised, voluntary network gives anyone who stumbles on information a reason to push it into the price, with no coercion and no central authority involved.
more: While teaching near Coimbatore in the early years of NSE, Ajay heard a man describe riding his two-wheeler past a factory and seeing it on fire. His response was to speed to the nearest NSE broker and sell all his shares in that company.
This is the price system at work. A decentralised, voluntary network gives anyone who stumbles on information a reason to push it into the price, with no coercion and no central authority involved.

head: Reuters and the Pigeons of Waterloo
dek: Building a faster channel for information is a real contribution, not cheating.
more: Reuters made its name by using pigeons to be first to carry news of the Battle of Waterloo to London. Whether Britain won or lost decided fortunes, and Reuters was the first to get that information to a trading venue. Ajay notes that in India people would complain about 'unfair access to information'.
Building a faster channel for information is a real contribution, not cheating. It is how news gets into prices.

head: Satellite Trading as a Railway Line
dek: Financial plumbing is real infrastructure. Connecting people to markets changes their opportunities as much as roads and railways do.
more: Ravi Narayan, part of NSE's founding team, used to say that when satellite communications for NSE trading first reached a small Indian town, it was like a railway line arriving there for the first time. Investors in that town no longer had to book long-distance trunk calls to a Bombay broker. They became equal, first-class participants in the national market. NSE was a global pioneer in electronic trading over satellite.
Financial plumbing is real infrastructure. Connecting people to markets changes their opportunities as much as roads and railways do.

head: Options Traders of 19th-Century Bombay
dek: Derivatives have been around in some form for a very long time, including in India.
more: Ajay recalls a speech at the Bombay Stock Exchange in which a Western speaker described the late 19th century and said the local traders were as good as anyone in the world at trading put and call options. He adds that there are stories of derivatives-like contracts on olive oil in sixth-century Greece.

Derivatives have been around in some form for a very long time, including in India. Today's hostility to them comes from a gap in knowledge, not from anything inherent in the instruments or the culture.

head: The Caravanserai and the Fountains: When Charity Freezes
dek: The rule that made the waqf trustworthy at the start, that its purpose could never change, turned into dead weight centuries later.
more: Amit retells Timur Kuran's examples of the waqf, an endowment locked to a fixed public purpose forever. One waqf funded a caravanserai (a roadside inn) on the Silk Route in the mid-1200s. By the 1600s nobody used that route, but the funds could not be moved out of the caravanserai. Another waqf built water fountains, about thirty a year. Once piped water became common, the real need was better pipes, but the money could only go to fountains.

The rule that made the waqf trustworthy at the start, that its purpose could never change, turned into dead weight centuries later. Capital that cannot be reallocated becomes what Hernando de Soto calls dead capital.

head: A Question That Keeps You Awake at Night
dek: Good scholarship starts with a question you can't let go of. And patient fieldwork can overturn a stereotype that everyone takes for granted.
more: In the late 1980s, Mukulika Banerjee asked someone whether she should do a PhD. The advice was to do one only if a question kept her awake at night. Her question: Pathans are stereotyped as violent, so how did the nonviolent Khudai Khidmatgar movement led by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the 'Frontier Gandhi', come out of them? She spent ten years on it, going from village to village in the North-West Frontier Province to find elderly former members. Her conclusion was that the Pathans' nonviolence was not borrowed from Gandhi or the West. It grew from within their own society.
Good scholarship starts with a question you can't let go of. And patient fieldwork can overturn a stereotype that everyone takes for granted.
printed: The question that kept her up

head: The Guest's Chicken and the Hindu Mother
dek: Hospitality and accommodation run deep in both cultures. Amit sees this as part of something in our own tradition that he worries we might lose today.
more: On Mukulika Banerjee's travels in the North-West Frontier, beef was the cheap staple and every household kept one expensive chicken for special guests. Out of mehmaan-nawazi (hospitality), even the poorest households served her that chicken. Feeling guilty about it, she started eating beef for the rest of the trip, although she is Hindu. Back in India she told her devout mother, who thought for a while and accepted it.
Hospitality and accommodation run deep in both cultures. Amit sees this as part of something in our own tradition that he worries we might lose today.

head: Capital Ideas
dek: It is a bit dated, but it tells the story of how modern finance emerged once models and computers came in.
more: It is a bit dated, but it tells the story of how modern finance emerged once models and computers came in. That is the layer of finance Ajay described in the episode.
Ajay's book recommendation at the end of the episode.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece and perhaps the most important essay of the last century.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece and perhaps the most important essay of the last century. It explains that prices carry information, and that central planners can never gather the knowledge that society expresses through prices.
A mid-episode recommendation while discussing prices as a public signal.

head: When Genius Failed
dek: It tells the story of the collapse of Long-Term Capital Management, a firm with several Nobel Prize-winning academics.
more: It tells the story of the collapse of Long-Term Capital Management, a firm with several Nobel Prize-winning academics. It shows how badly finance can go wrong.
A mid-episode recommendation after the discussion of how academic economics feeds into finance.

head: Inventing Money
dek: Ajay thinks Dunbar's LTCM book, which came out a year later, is the better of the two.
more: Ajay thinks Dunbar's LTCM book, which came out a year later, is the better of the two.
Ajay adds it when Amit recommends When Genius Failed.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: A good way to think about when the state should step in and when it should not.
more: A good way to think about when the state should step in and when it should not. Amit's view is that overreach is a far bigger problem than inaction.
Amit recommends it mid-episode, teasingly calling it an 'obscure book', after Ajay explains market failures and the role of the state.

head: Private Truths, Public Lies
dek: A seminal book on preference falsification and preference cascades.
more: A seminal book on preference falsification and preference cascades.
Amit introduces Timur Kuran and recommends all three of his books at the end.

head: The Long Divergence
dek: It knocks down the usual explanations for the Middle East's economic stagnation and shows how inheritance law and the waqf held it back.
more: It knocks down the usual explanations for the Middle East's economic stagnation and shows how inheritance law and the waqf held it back. Amit says it is worth reading even if you have no interest in Islam or the Middle East, because it shows how incentives shape societies.
The basis of the chapter on why the Middle East fell behind Europe.

head: Freedoms Delayed
dek: It follows the same institutional story into its political consequences and is rich in history.
more: It follows the same institutional story into its political consequences and is rich in history.
Described as a kind of part two of The Long Divergence.

head: The Mystery of Capital
dek: Source of the idea of 'dead capital', meaning wealth locked up where it cannot be put to productive use.
more: Source of the idea of 'dead capital', meaning wealth locked up where it cannot be put to productive use.
A mid-episode recommendation while explaining how waqf funds became stuck.

head: The Pathan Unarmed
dek: Ten years of fieldwork showing that the Khudai Khidmatgar's nonviolence grew from within Pathan society rather than being imported.
more: Ten years of fieldwork showing that the Khudai Khidmatgar's nonviolence grew from within Pathan society rather than being imported. Amit calls the finding profound and says the book, published around 2001, deserved far more readers.
Amit's main recommendation, tied to the theme of Kuran's work challenging stereotypes about Islam.

head: Understand Anything Through Its History
dek: Ajay calls this a general way of learning. A field like physics or finance makes sense when you trace it through time: what problem people faced, and how they solved it.
more: Ajay calls this a general way of learning. A field like physics or finance makes sense when you trace it through time: what problem people faced, and how they solved it. Modern finance is built up in layers, each one a solution to a real need of its time, and none of it was designed in advance. It evolved the way the eye did.

head: Wall Street Tells Main Street What to Do
dek: We admire the visible economy of chairs, cameras and coffee shops.
more: We admire the visible economy of chairs, cameras and coffee shops. Behind it, the financial system processes information and sends out the incentives that decide what gets built, which is why Ajay says finance occupies the 'commanding heights' of the economy. Mahalanobis would have hated that framing.

head: Finance as the Selector
dek: The real economy produces many competing bets, such as EVs versus combustion engines, or headphones versus biscuits.
more: The real economy produces many competing bets, such as EVs versus combustion engines, or headphones versus biscuits. All of them ask finance for money, and finance chooses, like a cricket selector judging who will deliver. Finance is speculative by nature, so it can back new people, new technologies and product categories that don't exist yet.

head: Joint Stock Companies and Limited Liability Go Together
dek: Pre-modern finance meant lending only to people you knew, with unlimited liability and debtors' prisons for those who failed.
more: Pre-modern finance meant lending only to people you knew, with unlimited liability and debtors' prisons for those who failed. The joint stock company spread a big risky bet across thousands of people, each putting in a small amount they could afford to lose. Limited liability capped each investor's loss at what they put in, so lenders get only what is left of a failed company. You can't attract thousands of investors without that cap, so the two ideas depend on each other.

head: Failure Is Normal and Healthy
dek: Shares going to zero and lenders taking losses are part of how capitalism works.
more: Shares going to zero and lenders taking losses are part of how capitalism works. Ajay criticises the Indian populist reflexes that treat these as scandals: misusing 'consumer protection' to mean investors should never lose money, and chasing 'rich promoters' to repay a limited liability company's debts. He finds it striking that 17th-century UK commercial concepts are still missing in India.

head: Separate the Money from the Ideas
dek: Without finance, a good idea without inherited wealth goes nowhere.
more: Without finance, a good idea without inherited wealth goes nowhere. Modern finance lets people with knowledge raise equity and debt from people with money, so the people who know, not the people who inherited, end up shaping resource allocation and prices. This sped up capitalism. John Hicks made the point that the stock market was as essential to the Industrial Revolution as the steam engine.

head: Liquidity from Fungible Shares
dek: Real estate is a messy market because no two flats are alike, and even gold has purity problems and steep resale discounts.
more: Real estate is a messy market because no two flats are alike, and even gold has purity problems and steep resale discounts. Cut a company like Infosys into a billion identical shares and you get standardised units that can be traded. For the first time, an owner could be sure of selling tomorrow, backed by institutions like exchanges and clearinghouses that made trading between strangers safe.

head: The Price as a Public Good
dek: Trading produces a public price that anyone can see almost for free. It combines everyone's information and works like a dashboard for entrepreneurs: high valuations say 'come build here', poor ones say 'stay away'.
more: Trading produces a public price that anyone can see almost for free. It combines everyone's information and works like a dashboard for entrepreneurs: high valuations say 'come build here', poor ones say 'stay away'. Self-organising price signals coordinate the economy better than a planning commission could.

head: Short Selling as Freedom of Speech
dek: If you think a share is overpriced but don't own it, you can borrow it, sell it, and buy it back later.
more: If you think a share is overpriced but don't own it, you can borrow it, sell it, and buy it back later. That lets bearish views enter the price as well as bullish ones. Blaming short sellers when things go wrong is shooting the messenger.

head: The Double Thank-You Moment
dek: Every speculative trade is voluntary, and both sides walk away thinking they got a good deal.
more: Every speculative trade is voluntary, and both sides walk away thinking they got a good deal. Short selling involves more of these moments: the long-term holder earns a rental fee for lending the share, and then the borrower makes a second voluntary trade on the market. None of it requires coercion.

head: Bubbles Look Obvious Only in Hindsight
dek: Markets sometimes go crazy, and Ajay knows no way to stop that entirely.
more: Markets sometimes go crazy, and Ajay knows no way to stop that entirely. But during something like the early internet, nobody could know whether a stock was worth 10x or 10,000x. In the moment, a huge upside was a reasonable view.

head: Banking Is Magical but Fragile
dek: Banks take on heavy leverage and create, out of thin air, an appearance of liquidity and the ability to fund long-term assets with short-term deposits.
more: Banks take on heavy leverage and create, out of thin air, an appearance of liquidity and the ability to fund long-term assets with short-term deposits. That is very useful in good times but weak at the core. Because politicians won't let grandmothers and dentists lose their deposits, banking becomes political, and every banking system goes through a crisis every 20 or 30 years.

head: The Three Pillars of Modern Finance
dek: After 1947, three things transformed finance. Telecommunications connected markets everywhere.
more: After 1947, three things transformed finance. Telecommunications connected markets everywhere. Computation took over the bookkeeping, settlement and calculation. Academic economics produced knowledge about portfolios, risk and diversification that now runs in real-world models. Ajay sees finance as the place where advanced economic theory has most directly become working real-world systems.
printed: Side bets on the main bets

head: From Relationship Banking to Model-Based Banking
dek: Bank managers used to lend based on personal knowledge of you and your family over chai.
more: Bank managers used to lend based on personal knowledge of you and your family over chai. That was expensive and discriminated against women, Muslims and lower-caste people. Credit bureaus and statistical models that predict the probability of default are cheap, evidence-based and work for small loans, so credit can reach people who have no relationship with a banker.

head: Derivatives as Side Bets
dek: Derivatives are bets placed alongside the main bets on shares, currencies and bonds.
more: Derivatives are bets placed alongside the main bets on shares, currencies and bonds. They let people who have knowledge but not much capital take part in price discovery. Bonds, currencies and their derivatives move together as one market, the 'bond-currency-derivatives nexus', which Indian policy often fails to see as connected.

head: Live Above the API
dek: An algorithm is just a trading rule a human designs. Carrying it out is clerical work that should go to code rather than a person.
more: An algorithm is just a trading rule a human designs. Carrying it out is clerical work that should go to code rather than a person. The computer wants nothing and decides nothing on its own. It is a tireless, millisecond-precise clerk, while humans keep the intellectual work.

head: Two Ways Finance Goes Wrong
dek: The first is a society hostile to finance, using state power to stifle it.
more: The first is a society hostile to finance, using state power to stifle it. Ajay calls this a Luddite vision and says it is where India largely is. The second is pure laissez-faire, which ignores real market failures in finance: public goods, asymmetric information and externalities. The state is needed, but it needs knowledgeable regulators who won't slide into banning things or into populism.

head: The Long Divergence: Debunking the Usual Explanations
dek: Around 1000 AD the Middle East's economy resembled Europe's. Then it stagnated until the mid-19th century while Europe surged ahead.
more: Around 1000 AD the Middle East's economy resembled Europe's. Then it stagnated until the mid-19th century while Europe surged ahead. Kuran rejects three common explanations. Islam was not hostile to commerce, since Muslim traders dominated trade hubs. The region did innovate, in government institutions and taxation. And it was not incurious, as Bernard Lewis argued: it kept up with military textbooks but never took up economic ones.

head: Progressive Laws, Backward Outcomes
dek: Islamic inheritance law was fairer than Northern Europe's primogeniture.
more: Islamic inheritance law was fairer than Northern Europe's primogeniture. Two-thirds went to the extended family, and daughters received a share (half of what sons got). But when a partner died, his share was split among many heirs, so partnerships stayed small, short and simple. Without lasting partnerships, joint stock companies never formed, and nor did the legal and accounting systems that grow around them. Europe's unfair eldest-son rule gave certainty about succession and so allowed lasting firms. Amit draws no prescriptive lesson, only an appreciation of how accidents of history create path dependence.

head: The Waqf: Private Public Goods That Ossified
dek: A waqf was a private endowment for a fixed public purpose, which Amit admires as public goods provided voluntarily, without taxes.
more: A waqf was a private endowment for a fixed public purpose, which Amit admires as public goods provided voluntarily, without taxes. Because the purpose could never change, waqfs became tied to needs that had disappeared, and their capital sat idle instead of being redirected as it would have been in other societies.

head: Isomorphic Mimicry in Indian Finance
dek: India copies the form of modern finance by using the word 'company', but the Companies Act, the way it is enforced, the appetite for unlimited liability and the populist actions of investigation agencies suggest the substance is missing.
more: India copies the form of modern finance by using the word 'company', but the Companies Act, the way it is enforced, the appetite for unlimited liability and the populist actions of investigation agencies suggest the substance is missing. Ajay worries this failure of institution building could hold India back disproportionately.

head: Amit's opener: someone asked what Ajay is good at, Amit
more: Amit's opener: someone asked what Ajay is good at, Amit said 'Finance,' and they replied 'Finance and fun? What are you talking about?' Amit says his defence of finance as fun 'was attributed to bias.'
Ajay: 'economics is the second most important thing in the world.' Amit: 'Wait, wait, wait. What is first? This is a family show.'
Amit: 'If a history of the world is written, it could easily be called From Pepper to Peppa Pig.' Ajay has never heard of Peppa Pig, and Amit promises to send links 'and introduce you to that magic.'

head: After invoking Mahalanobis's phrase
more: After invoking Mahalanobis's phrase 'commanding heights of the economy' for finance, Ajay adds that Mahalanobis 'would, of course, turn in his metaphorical grave when it was put like this.'

head: Amit on central planners
more: Amit on central planners 'like Prashant-da': 'never say anything against Bengalis unless they are planners.'

head: Amit recommends
more: Amit recommends 'an obscure book' by 'Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah' and asks Ajay if he's heard of it. Ajay: 'Some obscure blokes. I think at one point Sachin Tendulkar told me that he's heard of this guy.' Amit: 'That's well played, sir.'

head: Ajay calls Amit a…
more: Ajay calls Amit a 'genius poker intellectual' in his algorithmic trading example. Amit says he 'started purring peacefully' at being called a GPI, which 'fills my heart with gladness.'

Ajay, 'politically incorrect': straight-through processing (STP) in finance was long humorously called 'sack the peasants'. Amit clarifies: 'you don't literally mean put the peasants out of a job. You mean end the peasantry... the peasants... will be writing symphonies.'

head: Ajay on the AI as a clerk
more: Ajay on the AI as a clerk: 'It won't take a break to have chai, it won't have a bad hair day, it will be millisecond, split second, precision.'
'Wall Street tells Main Street what to do', the famous line Ajay uses to frame finance as the brain that guides the real economy.

head: John Hicks: the Industrial Revolution
