more: John Hicks: the Industrial Revolution 'was as much about the stock market as it was about the steam engine', the invisible machine alongside James Watt's visible one.

head: Merton Miller's description of banking
more: Merton Miller's description of banking as 'a disaster-prone 19th century industry.'

head: Chess player Levon Aronian called a chess game a conversation. Amit applies this to markets
more: Chess player Levon Aronian called a chess game a conversation. Amit applies this to markets as 'a symphony of voices expressing opinions.'

head: Ajay's evolution analogy for finance
more: Ajay's evolution analogy for finance: 'Mother evolution did not design the eye, the eye evolved incrementally.'

head: Sun Microsystems Decides to Make Its Own CPUs
dek: Several things had to come together for this leap. There was a real threat, a supplier strangling Sun's future.
more: In the late 1980s Sun Microsystems built workstations from off-the-shelf parts, using CPUs from Motorola. Its real innovation was the operating system, a BSD Unix variant from UC Berkeley brought in by co-founder Bill Joy. Then Motorola hit a wall and could not make its CPUs faster, which choked Sun's growth. At the same time, labs at Stanford and Berkeley were working on a controversial idea called reduced instruction set computing (RISC): make the CPU radically simple and it goes much faster. That challenged the complex-instruction-set chips made by the two giant incumbents, Intel and Motorola. Sun put the two together and leapt into designing CPUs, inventing a whole new architecture called SPARC. Ajay believes Texas Instruments served as its fab for a time. Sun was successful and influential in CPUs for about ten years. It made a similar leap with Java, even though no corporation usually makes money from a programming language.

Several things had to come together for this leap. There was a real threat, a supplier strangling Sun's future. There was a technological opening in RISC. There was cash and the backing of financial markets. And there were two revered engineers, Bill Joy and Andreas Bechtolsheim, who gave the firm the nerve to try and the pull to recruit almost anyone in the world.

head: Google, Android, and Andy Rubin's Late-Evening Call
dek: The normal next steps for a search company would have been economies of scope: search for movies or music, or a search box for a company's private data.
more: Google began as a search engine built on Larry Page's PageRank. Downloading and indexing the entire internet pushed its infrastructure so hard that Google came to see itself as an infrastructure company, one that knew how to handle more CPUs than anyone. Then came Android. Andy Rubin had been building Android, but it wasn't working well, partly because phones of that era lacked the CPU power and battery life to do much. He ran out of steam. In the version Ajay read in the press, Rubin was due to sign a term sheet the next morning selling Android to a Canadian telecom company. Late that evening he reached out to Google instead, saying the project belonged there and he would go with it. The deal was thrashed out overnight. Google turned a flaky early Android into one of the world's most important operating systems.

The normal next steps for a search company would have been economies of scope: search for movies or music, or a search box for a company's private data. Google instead set out to 'organize the whole world's information' and leapt into writing an operating system, the most complex software there is. Rubin chose Google because of its engineering reputation. Ajay traces a Unix culture that formed at Sun and passed through Netscape to Google: Eric Schmidt was chief scientist at Sun, and Bell Labs Unix legend Rob Pike worked at Google. A strong culture is what makes great engineers want to bring their best work to you.

head: How a Bookshop's Christmas Problem Became AWS
dek: A cost headache, idle servers, became a world-changing business because Amazon didn't let its self-image as an e-commerce shop limit what it attempted.
more: Ajay describes early Amazon as doing 'the dullest thing in the world': an online bookshop putting lots of SKUs on a screen and grinding out deliveries, much like Flipkart or Myntra. Shopping surged before Christmas, and since you never want to turn away a customer, Amazon sized its computers for that peak. The result was that it paid the cost of capital 365 days a year for equipment really needed only 10 to 15 days a year. The aha moment was to package that spare capacity, wrap it in an API, and rent it to other people. Doing this meant building something as complex as an operating system, which a typical e-commerce firm would dismiss as 'not our capability.' Amazon did it anyway and effectively invented cloud computing, an industry it continues to dominate.

A cost headache, idle servers, became a world-changing business because Amazon didn't let its self-image as an e-commerce shop limit what it attempted. Amit pushed back on calling Amazon 'just a bookshop': imagining a bookshop on the internet was itself a spectacular leap. By contrast, Flipkart and Myntra were me-toos that never innovated.
printed: Christmas comes but once a year

head: Damodaran, Gurley, and the Story of Uber
dek: A valuation follows from the story you tell about a firm, and something truly new can't be sized by looking at what already exists.
more: Around 2014, valuation expert Aswath Damodaran wrote a skeptical post on Uber. His story was that Uber was in the taxi and car-service business, a total addressable market of about $100 billion, of which Uber would get at most 10%. Bill Gurley, a legendary investor and an early backer of Uber, replied that Damodaran had the wrong story. Uber was out to replace car ownership, a far bigger market, and Gurley laid out the numbers. Damodaran publicly agreed that Gurley was right and that he had missed it, and redid his valuation. As Amit remembers it, the estimate went from about $5 billion to about $28 billion.

A valuation follows from the story you tell about a firm, and something truly new can't be sized by looking at what already exists. Damodaran's public change of mind is also a model of intellectual humility.

head: Netflix Refuses to Be Kodak
dek: Reimagining yourself is hardest at the peak of success in your old story, and that is exactly when it matters most.
more: Reed Hastings's Netflix began in 1997 as a DVD rental business. In 2007 it shipped its billionth DVD; the film was Babel. At that point it seemed to have cornered the market, and it could have made Kodak's mistake with film by refusing to accept that the world was changing. Instead it started a streaming service. Amit thinks it began by making season three of Breaking Bad big, then went on to commission House of Cards.
Reimagining yourself is hardest at the peak of success in your old story, and that is exactly when it matters most.

head: Writing In Service of the Republic: From Chore to Creative Act
dek: Many projects begin as drudgery, like laying the foundations of a house.
more: When Ajay and Vijay Kelkar started their book, the aim was modest: a primer of public economics and public administration, carrying ideas each field didn't know to the other. It was exposition done as a responsibility, and frankly a bit boring. At around 20 chapters, Ajay was not having fun. Their method was to revise repeatedly, then Ajay would take a physical hard copy to Pune. The two would spend a half day or a full day walking through every page, and 20 new ideas would come up. As the book grew, each innovation fed the next and it turned into a genuinely creative project. Ajay finds that on the first draft the language is always bad, and that it becomes good only around the 15th rewrite, after repeated head-to-toe scrubs.

Many projects begin as drudgery, like laying the foundations of a house. With enough iteration and collaborative brainstorming they come alive, and the joy arrives late. Ajay recommends this kind of in-person, page-by-page working session for collaborative projects.

head: Robert Lucas and the Ten Complete Rewrites
dek: Knowing that a master's early drafts are also bad frees you from despair about your own.
more: The economist Robert Lucas, who had died recently, is one of Ajay's heroes. Ajay puts Lucas in Milton Friedman's league for beautiful writing and spent a lot of time studying how both men wrote. Then he came across Lucas saying that any article required 10 complete rewrites, meaning he would literally throw a draft away and start from scratch.

Knowing that a master's early drafts are also bad frees you from despair about your own. All work starts out bad, and you have to keep improving it until it comes alive. That is when the hard-work phase ends and the fun begins.

head: The Soul of a New Machine
dek: When Ajay was young, this book was his first glimpse of what it means to do engineering with all your heart and soul.
more: When Ajay was young, this book was his first glimpse of what it means to do engineering with all your heart and soul. He felt the passion in it. In his words, it shows there are still some men who know how to love desperately.

Ajay's recommendation of the episode. He says he is unsatisfied by most books about the tech era he lived through, and similarly by books on the 2008 crisis, which he followed by reading five hours a day. So he reached back to an older period. In this book, a journalist was embedded in a project to design a microprocessor equivalent at the now-defunct Data General in the late 70s and early 80s.

head: The Creative Act
dek: Amit recommends it to all businessmen. Succeeding at anything takes imagination and thinking like a creator, so the book holds lessons for anyone starting a firm.
more: Amit recommends it to all businessmen. Succeeding at anything takes imagination and thinking like a creator, so the book holds lessons for anyone starting a firm.

Amit's recommendation of the episode. His hard copy was a gift from Gaurav Chintamani, who helps with the show's sound. Amit read out a passage: 'Turning something from an idea into a reality can make it seem smaller. It changes from unearthly to earthly. The imagination has no limits. The physical world does. The work exists in both.'

head: Narrative and Numbers
dek: Amit says it makes a profound point that goes beyond valuation, into what firms are about and the stories they tell themselves.
more: Amit says it makes a profound point that goes beyond valuation, into what firms are about and the stories they tell themselves. It is also a beautiful story of intellectual humility.
Source of Amit's account of how Damodaran revalued Uber after Bill Gurley challenged his story about the company.

head: How to Miss By a Mile: An Alternative Look at Uber's Potential Market Size
dek: Gurley argued that Uber was out to replace car ownership, not just compete with taxis.
more: Gurley argued that Uber was out to replace car ownership, not just compete with taxis. That shows why you can't size a disruptor by looking at what already exists.
Gurley's response to Damodaran.

head: The Innovator's Dilemma
dek: It explains why big companies tend to get ossified while disruption comes from small upstarts.
more: It explains why big companies tend to get ossified while disruption comes from small upstarts. That makes Sun's leap into an adjacent, far harder industry all the more remarkable.
Amit cited it when asking what impressed Ajay about Sun's audacity.

head: Essays
dek: It collects Orwell's nonfiction. He would just bang out three or four columns a week, and they were all brilliant.
more: It collects Orwell's nonfiction. He would just bang out three or four columns a week, and they were all brilliant. Amit says he loves Orwell so much.
Raised in the discussion of writing processes, as a contrast to slow, many-draft writers like Robert Lucas and Paul Graham. Amit has recommended it before.

head: Paul Graham's essays
dek: Amit calls Graham one of the finest essayists of the century. Graham takes a couple of months over each essay, workshopping it and getting feedback from friends.
more: Amit calls Graham one of the finest essayists of the century. Graham takes a couple of months over each essay, workshopping it and getting feedback from friends.
Raised to support the Lucas story about rewriting.

head: Economies of Scale, Economies of Scope
dek: Explains the two textbook growth paths (doing more of the same, or moving into adjacencies) against which Sun, Google and Amazon look so audacious.
more: Explains the two textbook growth paths (doing more of the same, or moving into adjacencies) against which Sun, Google and Amazon look so audacious.
Linked in the show notes for Ajay's framing of the standard ways firms expand.

head: Scale, Scope, and the Great Leap
dek: Firms usually grow in two ways. Economies of scale means doing what you already know at 10x or 100x volume.
more: Firms usually grow in two ways. Economies of scale means doing what you already know at 10x or 100x volume. That is hard because the knowledge of a few artisans doesn't transfer easily to big teams, and at scale rare events become commonplace, so process manuals have to grow complicated. Economies of scope means moving into adjacencies, serving customers who already trust you with things close to what you know. A great leap is neither. It is a jump into something far more complex: Sun from assembling computers to designing CPUs, Google from search to an operating system, Amazon from a bookshop to operating-system-level cloud infrastructure.

head: What Makes an Audacious Leap Possible
dek: Ajay's ingredients are internal cash flows and the support of financial markets (as he puts it, 'Wall Street tells Main Street what to do'), people inside asking hard questions about threats, and leaders with deep engineering credibility.
more: Ajay's ingredients are internal cash flows and the support of financial markets (as he puts it, 'Wall Street tells Main Street what to do'), people inside asking hard questions about threats, and leaders with deep engineering credibility. Revered engineers give the firm the confidence that 'we can do anything,' push people past ordinary answers, and act as a magnet for talent.

head: Side Projects as a Plus-EV Culture Bet
dek: Amit notes that Larry Page and Sergey Brin started Google straight out of college, before conventional corporate thinking could indoctrinate them.
more: Amit notes that Larry Page and Sergey Brin started Google straight out of college, before conventional corporate thinking could indoctrinate them. They let employees spend some hours each week on funded side projects. Judged one project at a time, this looks like a distraction with negative expected value. Judged as an investment in a culture where everyone can innovate and chase what excites them, it pays off hugely.

head: Engineering Aesthetics and Managing Above vs Below the API
dek: Engineers see a real difference between clean and bad design even when two products look the same from outside, and that difference matters.
more: Engineers see a real difference between clean and bad design even when two products look the same from outside, and that difference matters. A 'shut up and get it done' execution mindset forces compromises inside the product. Those may be wise in the short term, but they create bad products in the medium term and drive away the best people. Routine work can be run with instructions and hard-driving bosses. Creative work above the API, where people must dream, imagine and strategize, cannot.

head: Execution Is Commoditized; Imagination Is Scarce
dek: Almost all important firms today play a knowledge game. Execution is necessary but easy to buy.
more: Almost all important firms today play a knowledge game. Execution is necessary but easy to buy. What is scarce is the great leap of ideas. Ajay argues that mainstream Indian firm culture obsesses over execution, regimented organizations and obedient people, and is weak in strategic thinking and innovation. He sees this as part of what keeps India poor.

head: People Respond to Incentives, Great People Volunteer
dek: This is a line Nachiket Mor once said to Ajay, and it appears in Ajay's book with Vijay Kelkar.
more: This is a line Nachiket Mor once said to Ajay, and it appears in Ajay's book with Vijay Kelkar. Drive an ordinary person with KRAs, piece rates or a profit share and they will run hard for you. But they won't imagine, create, solve problems on their own, or deliver great leaps. Great people are moved by something deeper: commitment and a passion for excellence, beauty and imagination. The best engineers are there to build something beautiful, not to meet a KRA.

head: Checking Yourself for Survivorship Bias
dek: Ajay questions his own thesis. Maybe many firms tried audacious leaps and failed, and a few succeeded by dumb luck.
more: Ajay questions his own thesis. Maybe many firms tried audacious leaps and failed, and a few succeeded by dumb luck. That is why the show will never do an episode on great fund managers, where results are mostly survivorship bias. Having watched these three firms over many years, he still believes they were special. He invites listeners to argue the point.

head: You Can't Size a Disruptor by the Incumbent's Market
dek: New services change how people behave, so today's market is the wrong yardstick.
more: New services change how people behave, so today's market is the wrong yardstick. Amit's example: ten years ago, a food delivery market sized by how many people phoned restaurants would have looked tiny. Delivery then reshaped daily life for nuclear families where both partners work, and gave rise to cloud kitchens serving home-like food. Amit also showed a tweet by Aaron Levie making the same point.

head: The Great Business Leader Is a Storyteller
dek: Execution and incentives can make you a good leader. Greatness needs the imagination of an artist who can tell a new story about what the firm really is.
more: Execution and incentives can make you a good leader. Greatness needs the imagination of an artist who can tell a new story about what the firm really is. Amit offers examples. Is Starbucks a coffee vendor, or in the real estate business because people need a place to sit and work? Is Walmart a retailer, or leasing space to brands? Are tech giants monopolies, or rivals all fighting for our attention? The show notes turn this on the listener: what is your story about yourself, and how could you reimagine it?

head: Idea vs Reality: Shrinkage or an Exponential?
dek: Rick Rubin observes that turning an idea into reality makes it seem smaller.
more: Rick Rubin observes that turning an idea into reality makes it seem smaller. Amit recognizes this in writing, where the first draft disappoints and business plans hit trouble and pivots. Ajay sees it the opposite way: work starts workmanlike and gets more beautiful with each pass, until it comes alive and becomes a joy. Amit reconciles the two views with kaator re bhaaji: keep putting in the work, and magic can happen.

head: Many Writing Processes, One Requirement
dek: Lucas did ten complete rewrites per article, and Paul Graham spends months workshopping each essay with friends.
more: Lucas did ten complete rewrites per article, and Paul Graham spends months workshopping each essay with friends. Orwell banged out three or four brilliant columns a week. There is no single correct method. Find what works for you, but there is no substitute for sitting down and doing the work.

head: One True Sentence
dek: Hemingway's cure for writer's block was to sit down, write one true sentence, then one more.
more: Hemingway's cure for writer's block was to sit down, write one true sentence, then one more. Amit reads 'true' not as factually correct but as authentic to that moment and to what you are trying to say. That shrinks an overwhelming project down to a single honest step.

head: The opening
more: The opening 'mystery hunt': Ajay had once claimed to be an expert in sixteen things, and Amit reports that 'the internet is abuzz, matters have gone viral, hashtags have been formed. Tell me at least one more of those sixteen things.' Ajay's answer: firms.

head: Amit's pun
more: Amit's pun: 'I see that you have made a firm resolve to talk about firms today.'

head: Amit after the Sun story
more: Amit after the Sun story: 'Also, what a great name, Bill Joy, who cannot like a guy with a name like that.'

head: Ajay's portrait of retail Amazon
more: Ajay's portrait of retail Amazon as 'the biggest recruiter in the whole world of PhDs in economics who will find every behavioral economics bug in your behavior and con you out of 35 more paise for the shirt.'

head: Ajay on survivorship bias
more: Ajay on survivorship bias: 'we're never going to do a show here saying three great fund managers.'
Ajay: 'I may be ancient, but there are periods where I was not around.' Amit: 'Is it true you took part in the 1857 rebellion?' Ajay: 'Not quite.'
Ajay: 'I always love my babies much better at the end than at the beginning.' Amit: 'Because young babies are a pain.'

head: Amit's sign-off asks viewers what they think of the firms discussed, and
more: Amit's sign-off asks viewers what they think of the firms discussed, and then 'the most important thing, what do you think of Ajay's shirt?'

head: Ajay's aside while explaining how Sun funded its CPU leap
more: Ajay's aside while explaining how Sun funded its CPU leap: 'Wall Street tells Main Street what to do.'

head: Ajay paraphrased Hemingway as getting one sentence right to light up your day. Amit corrected it to…
more: Ajay paraphrased Hemingway as getting one sentence right to light up your day. Amit corrected it to 'one true sentence,' from Hemingway's Paris Review interview about writer's block.

head: The Funeral That Raised a Question: Bacha Khan's Servants of God
dek: A state can erase a movement from politics and still fail to erase it from people's memory.
more: In 1988, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, known as Bacha Khan or the 'Sarhadi Gandhi', died in Peshawar. Tens of thousands of people, joined by the Afghan president, followed his body to Jalalabad for burial. He had founded the Khudai Khidmatgar ('servants of God') in 1930. It grew from about a thousand members to 25,000 a year later, and eventually to lakhs of red-kurta-wearing marchers, the 'Red Shirts'. They met every provocation with principled nonviolence. Gandhi first saw in him a kindred soul and later an inspiration. The movement opposed Partition, then asked for a Pashtun homeland, then chose to stay in Pakistan, where the state crushed it: members were jailed or killed and the movement faded away. Bacha Khan died a lonely old man, yet ordinary people still turned out in huge numbers to mourn him.

A state can erase a movement from politics and still fail to erase it from people's memory. Amit's broader point is that once a state decides the direction everyone must go in, free thinkers become its first casualties.

head: Underwear and Turbans: The Akalis Who Inspired a Pathan
dek: Courage spreads across communities. A Muslim Pathan learned something about principled defiance from Sikh prisoners, which is one small example of how India's freedom movements drew inspiration from each other.
more: In the 1920s, Bacha Khan was in a British jail alongside Akali prisoners. The jailers ordered the Akalis to take off their turbans, which their faith forbade. Instead they stripped down to their underwear, kept only their turbans on, and chanted 'Sar jaave taan jaave, mera Sikhi dharam na jaave' ('let my head go, but not my Sikh faith'). Bacha Khan watched this and was deeply moved. In jail he also met figures like Baba Kharak Singh of the Akali Dal.

Courage spreads across communities. A Muslim Pathan learned something about principled defiance from Sikh prisoners, which is one small example of how India's freedom movements drew inspiration from each other.

head: Mukulika Banerjee's Question That Kept Her Up at Night
dek: The best research starts from a burning question that contradicts received wisdom.
more: As a PhD student in India in the late 1980s, Mukulika Banerjee was puzzled. Academic convention held that peasants don't do mass politics and that Pathans are a violent frontier people. So how did a Pathan who grew up among peasants lead the subcontinent's greatest nonviolent movement? An advisor told her to do a PhD only if she had a question that kept her up at night. She did. Indian institutions repeatedly refused to back a woman going to the North-West Frontier Province, and she spent two years hunting for funding before some came, partly from abroad. She then learned Pashto, wore a chador, went village to village looking for surviving Khudai Khidmatgars, and took ten years to write 'The Pathan Unarmed'.
The best research starts from a burning question that contradicts received wisdom. The obstacles thrown up by gatekeepers are part of the price of answering it.

head: The Expensive Chicken and the Beef
dek: Real respect for another culture can mean giving up a taboo of your own so that you don't impose costs on your hosts.
more: During her fieldwork, Mukulika found that beef was the everyday staple in Pashtun villages, but every household kept one expensive chicken to serve honoured guests as an act of hospitality. She didn't want families to sacrifice that chicken everywhere she went, so she started eating beef with them. Much later she told her devout Hindu mother. Amit calls her mother's response a beautiful story that moves him deeply.
Real respect for another culture can mean giving up a taboo of your own so that you don't impose costs on your hosts. It also shows that people back home can be more open-minded than we expect.

head: The Street of Storytellers, Visited Unknowingly
dek: We often walk through places without knowing the history in them. Knowing it turns a pretty bazaar into a site of memory.
more: In 2006 Amit visited Kissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar, loved its look and its people, took photographs, and wrote a blog post called 'Twilight in the Street of Storytellers'. Only later did he learn that around 200 people had been killed in a massacre there, the Khudai Khidmatgar movement's equivalent of Jallianwala Bagh.
We often walk through places without knowing the history in them. Knowing it turns a pretty bazaar into a site of memory.

head: The Fat Frogs of Tatsinskaya
dek: Huge outcomes can turn on a small, clever blow against logistics.
more: About 250,000 German troops were encircled at Stalingrad. They needed 700 to 900 tons of supplies a day, 300 tons was the bare survival minimum, and the airlift actually delivered only 100 to 150 tons. A year earlier, roughly 100,000 men trapped near Leningrad had been kept alive by air, so Hitler's team tried the same thing. Transports carrying about 2.5 tons each flew 1.5-hour sorties out of Tatsinskaya, the airfield closest to the action, about 80 km inside German-held territory. Following their doctrine of hitting the enemy's logistics, the Soviets sent a near-suicidal tank raid through thin German lines. Scouts gave only ten minutes' warning. Planes tried to take off with too little fuel and crashed into each other. T-34s parked at the edge of the runway and shot planes down one by one as they lifted off. Of roughly 200 planes, about 70 were destroyed. The surviving planes had to fly from a farther airfield, the airlift collapsed, and weeks later Paulus surrendered.

Huge outcomes can turn on a small, clever blow against logistics. Ajay sees the planners behind the raid as the real heroes, and he thinks a film should match Dunkirk's restraint and let the events themselves supply the drama.
printed: Tanks at the edge of the runway

head: The Bridge: When Military Police Shot Their Own
dek: A chokepoint under pressure is an operations problem, and the panic of the people in it can destroy the very capacity they need to escape.
more: The Red Army covered roughly 2,500 km from Stalingrad to Berlin in about 500 days, about the distance from Ludhiana to Kanyakumari. About ten times along the way, a retreating German army, with all its men, equipment and stores, had to squeeze across a single bridge. Artillery then was too imprecise to easily destroy such bridges, so they held, but each crossing was a brutal planning problem: what to abandon, and how many vehicles of what kind could get across per day. Tired, frightened men under fire tended to break ranks and turn into a mob, and then the crossing collapsed. At several of these crossings, German military police killed German soldiers to keep order.

A chokepoint under pressure is an operations problem, and the panic of the people in it can destroy the very capacity they need to escape. Holding discipline there can become a matter of life and death.

head: Haimabati Sen: Child Widow to Doctor
dek: Child marriage, huge age gaps and short life expectancy together made child widowhood common.
more: Haimabati was born in 1866 in a poor family in Khulna, then part of Bengal and now in Bangladesh, to a father who was progressive for his time. During the 1872 famine, aged six, she was caught stealing rice from the family store to give to the starving poor outside. A visiting sub-inspector found that she was the only child in her school who could answer his question, and told her that so much learning was a sure route to widowhood. Her relatives were appalled when she read the Ramayana. At nine she was married to a 45-year-old widower who had two children her own age. She played with their dolls by day and was traumatised at night. Her husband died when she was ten. By twelve her parents and in-laws were dead too, and an uncle took the money left for her. Many child widows of that era ended up in prostitution; one 1853 Kolkata study counted more than 12,000 prostitutes, many of them child widows. Haimabati instead made her way to Benares, educated herself, became a doctor, remarried and had children. As Amit recalls, she later became a prominent figure among doctors, and something of a sharp-tongued one.
Child marriage, huge age gaps and short life expectancy together made child widowhood common. Her escape from that system was nearly impossible, which is what makes her story so extraordinary.

head: The Memoir Locked in a Trunk for Eighty Years
dek: Much of history survives by luck, and an extraordinary woman's voice can almost be lost to a forgotten trunk.
more: Haimabati began writing her memoirs in the 1920s and died in 1933. The papers sat locked in a trunk for about eighty years. When they surfaced, her family didn't grasp their importance until Tapan Raychaudhuri persuaded them, and the memoir was edited, translated and published. Amit pictures the opening shot of his web series as a woman's hand opening that dusty trunk, intercut with a little girl's feet running and stumbling. He would add a fictional parallel story about a modern descendant who finds the papers.
Much of history survives by luck, and an extraordinary woman's voice can almost be lost to a forgotten trunk. Amit is baffled that stories like this aren't already being filmed.

head: Indira's Letter to Sanjay
dek: Policies that hurt millions can come from political tactics rather than conviction.
more: Coomi Kapoor's book reproduces a private letter Indira Gandhi wrote to Sanjay in the late 1960s, in which she essentially says they care only about power, not left or right. Amit reads the Congress's leftward turn of that period, including bank nationalisation, as a tactic to set her apart from her rivals in the Syndicate, such as Morarji Desai, rather than as ideology. He contrasts her with Nehru, who acted on conviction. Still, he declines to simply judge her: at 13, her aunt Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit called her ugly and stupid, which reportedly left a deep mark.
Policies that hurt millions can come from political tactics rather than conviction. And even people who wield power ruthlessly are shaped by old wounds.

head: Vidya Charan Shukla and the Editors Who Crawled
dek: Compliant media and opportunistic hypocrites show up under every authoritarian turn.
more: As Information and Broadcasting minister during the Emergency, Vidya Charan Shukla called Delhi's editors to his office and told them: not one bad word against Indira Gandhi. Apart from exceptions like Ramnath Goenka's Indian Express, most complied. Simon Jenkins said he had seen Franco's Spain and Mao's China but never a press crackdown like this one. S. Nihal Singh described a Times of India editor who followed every order during the Emergency and then, once it ended, wrote a two-page piece attacking Indira. Shukla was a sycophant who wanted her made ruler for life with no further elections, and he was accused of harassing actresses. Amit compares him to Gollum, enslaved by his lust for power. In 2013, old and long irrelevant, Shukla was killed in a Naxal attack on his way to a Congress rally. Amit admits he found it hard to feel sad.
Compliant media and opportunistic hypocrites show up under every authoritarian turn. Amit leaves it to viewers to draw the parallels with today.

head: Peepli, 1976: The Women Making Cow-Dung Cakes
dek: Quotas enforced by a coercive state turn into atrocities. Amit would tell this story by first showing the victims as full human beings, so that the viewer feels their deaths as lives cut short and not as statistics.
more: During Sanjay Gandhi's sterilisation drive, some hospitals refused to admit pregnant women unless they could show a nasbandi certificate. In Peepli, a Haryana village under Bansi Lal (who elsewhere had a protesting elderly advocate stripped and paraded through town), an ageing widower named Hawa Lal was taken away to meet sterilisation quotas and died during the operation. The village erupted. Officials came back with soldiers and grabbed the first man they saw, a cobbler, for forced sterilisation. People from neighbouring villages joined the protests, and hundreds of police laid siege to the village. At 6 AM shots were fired, killing two women who were making cow-dung cakes outside. The rest of the village then submitted to the nasbandi.

Quotas enforced by a coercive state turn into atrocities. Amit would tell this story by first showing the victims as full human beings, so that the viewer feels their deaths as lives cut short and not as statistics.

head: Snehalata Reddy's Crime Was Friendship
dek: Authoritarian regimes punish people for who they know, not just what they do.
more: Snehalata Reddy was a cultured actress in theatre and film with a deep love of poetry. Her husband, as Amit recalls, was a poet and filmmaker. Her only crime was being a friend of George Fernandes, who was on the run. She was arrested and treated badly, and she was not allowed treatment for her asthma. By one account she went in a young beautiful woman and came out looking old and haggard. Shortly after her release at the end of the Emergency, she died of a heart attack.
Authoritarian regimes punish people for who they know, not just what they do. Artists in particular must either sing the regime's tune or pay the price.

head: Babu Beats Bobby
dek: Distracting people with entertainment fails once people are angry enough.
more: In 1977, the government was nervous about a JP Narayan rally where Jagjivan Ram, nicknamed 'Babu', was to speak. It told Doordarshan to broadcast the blockbuster 'Bobby' (1973) to keep people at home. The rally was packed anyway, and the next day's headline read 'Babu Beats Bobby'. Amit would open his Emergency web series by intercutting a nervous, portly politician putting on his cap backstage with a family huddled around a 1970s TV watching Dimple Kapadia.
Distracting people with entertainment fails once people are angry enough. A single headline can capture the moment a regime loses its hold.

head: A Note Dropped From a Prison Van
dek: Small acts of decency by strangers kept people connected under repression.
more: Journalist Virendra Kapoor, Coomi Kapoor's husband, was being moved between jails in a police van. He scribbled a note (a parchi) for Coomi with her landline number, saying which station he'd be at so she could see him, and dropped it out of the back. A man on a scooter behind the van saw it, waited until the van was out of sight, picked it up, and got the message to her. She went to Bareilly to see him being put on a train with three other prisoners, not knowing if she'd ever see him again. At the other end of the same platform, a crowd was chanting slogans for a Congress politician boarding the train.
Small acts of decency by strangers kept people connected under repression. In the same scene, the powerful carried on celebrating a few metres away.
printed: A note falls from a van

head: Subramanian Swamy's Disguise and the Young Karyakarta
dek: The Emergency was a crucible for much of today's political class.
more: While on the run during the Emergency, Subramanian Swamy disguised himself as a Sardar, with a pagri and kara. One of his hideouts was Ahmedabad, since Gujarat did not have a Congress government then. He stayed with Makarand Desai, and the RSS karyakarta who met him at the station and escorted him to the house was Narendra Modi. Other dissenters of the time also went on to big political careers: Arun Jaitley, then a young law student, went to jail, and Lalu Prasad Yadav and Nitish Kumar were young activists in JP's movement.

The Emergency was a crucible for much of today's political class. Amit says that if he had been one of those young dissenters, he would have resolved to treat the opposition and the press with dignity if he ever held power, and he is not sure that lesson has been learned.

head: Govind Nihalani, My Friend Sancho, and an Accidental Ghosting
dek: Creative energy moves between film industries over time. On the personal side, ghosting someone often comes from embarrassment rather than malice, and it gets harder to undo the longer it lasts.
more: After Amit's 2009 novel 'My Friend Sancho' came out, filmmaker Govind Nihalani, director of 'Ardh Satya' and 'Party', wanted to make a film of it. Amit wrote a treatment note, but nobody in Bollywood bit. Around 2010, Nihalani told him that nothing would happen in the Hindi film industry, but the Marathi industry reminded him of Hindi alternative cinema in the early 1980s, when Shyam Benegal and others were at their peak. He suggested moving the story to Pune. Amit wrote a two-pager, the project stalled, and out of embarrassment he stopped meeting Nihalani. He apologises on air.
Creative energy moves between film industries over time. On the personal side, ghosting someone often comes from embarrassment rather than malice, and it gets harder to undo the longer it lasts.

head: A Mad Love Story: Ajay's Parents
dek: Behind many settled lives is an earlier generation that took real risks.
more: Ajay's parents had an inter-caste marriage. They eloped three times, and the first two attempts ended in terrible, violent events. On the third, they kept running until they reached Banaras, where they secretly married in an Arya Samaj ceremony. Their story was once optioned for a film but never made.
Behind many settled lives is an earlier generation that took real risks. Some of the most dramatic stories sit inside our own families.

head: Writing Darkness at Noon as France Fell
dek: A book that changed the world came close to being lost, and its survival depended on luck and on one person's courage.
more: In 1940 Arthur Koestler, a Hungarian who wrote in German, was living in a dingy part of Paris with his girlfriend Daphne Hardy, a 21-year-old British art student. He wrote the novel page by page in German and she translated it into English as he went. Her German was shaky and she knew little about Soviet communism, so she softened things: for example, she rendered 'interrogation' as 'hearing'. But she was living with him, talking with him, and had a feel for the book. Then the Germans reached Paris, France surrendered, and Koestler, wanted in many countries, was interned. He survived only because the Germans never worked out who he was. Before they split up, he posted the German manuscript to his editor in Switzerland. Hardy, a British citizen, hid the dangerous English manuscript and was evacuated from Marseille. Koestler escaped, Ajay thinks by walking across the Pyrenees into Spain.

A book that changed the world came close to being lost, and its survival depended on luck and on one person's courage. Ajay adds a wry policy point: the absence of good identity systems saved a dissident's life.
printed: Page by page, as Paris fell

head: Daphne Hardy Names the Book
dek: A translator's bold call on a title helped shape one of the 20th century's most consequential books, and a novel helped shift a country's election.
more: Koestler's working title was a dull 'Rubashov: A Novel'. In England, with a war on, no phones and Koestler out of reach, Hardy sold the English manuscript to a publisher and retitled it herself: 'Darkness at Noon'. The book became hugely influential. Ajay argues it tipped the 1946 French election, which the Communist Party lost because readers finally understood what Soviet Russia really was.
A translator's bold call on a title helped shape one of the 20th century's most consequential books, and a novel helped shift a country's election.

head: The German Original Resurfaces in 2015
dek: Rediscovered manuscripts and newly opened archives together can give us a clearer version of a classic.
more: For 75 years the world had only Hardy's translation. In 2015 the German manuscript turned up in Switzerland, and the graduate student who found it immediately understood what it was. A new translation followed, informed by the Kremlin archives that were briefly open before Putin's Russia closed up again, so the new translator could check Koestler's insider knowledge of Stalin's interrogations against the archival record. Ajay holds up his two most prized possessions: a 1941 edition that came from his father, and the 2015 edition.
Rediscovered manuscripts and newly opened archives together can give us a clearer version of a classic. Comparing the two translations shows what the first one got right and what it softened.

head: My Life and Struggle
dek: Amit calls it a great autobiography. It shows a period when the finest minds were in jail rather than in universities, and how those encounters shaped Bacha Khan.
more: Amit calls it a great autobiography. It shows a period when the finest minds were in jail rather than in universities, and how those encounters shaped Bacha Khan.
Mentioned while describing Bacha Khan's years in jail with Akali prisoners and Baba Kharak Singh.

head: Twilight in the Street of Storytellers
dek: A record of a place he loved before he knew it had been the scene of a massacre on the scale of Jallianwala Bagh.
more: A record of a place he loved before he knew it had been the scene of a massacre on the scale of Jallianwala Bagh.
Amit's 2006 blog post and photographs from Peshawar's Kissa Khwani Bazaar.

head: The Memoirs of Dr Haimabati Sen
dek: It tells, in her own words, how a destitute child widow became a doctor.
more: It tells, in her own words, how a destitute child widow became a doctor. It is now available in print and on Kindle.
The memoir that sat in a trunk for eighty years before it was translated and published.

head: The Emergency: A Personal History
dek: Amit adores it and thinks everyone should read it, both for this period and to understand the fundamental nature of the Indian state and the damage its power can do, because history rhymes in disturbing ways.
more: Amit adores it and thinks everyone should read it, both for this period and to understand the fundamental nature of the Indian state and the damage its power can do, because history rhymes in disturbing ways.
The source for Amit's Emergency web-series pitch and most of its characters and stories.

head: The Looking-Glass Self
dek: It frames the question of who we are once there is no one left to reflect us back.
more: It frames the question of who we are once there is no one left to reflect us back.
The idea behind Amit's novel concept 'Missing', about a boy who wakes up to find all of humanity gone.

head: My Friend Sancho
dek: Amit dismisses it as slight. It comes up as the start of his story about Nihalani, Marathi cinema, and the apology he owes.
more: Amit dismisses it as slight. It comes up as the start of his story about Nihalani, Marathi cinema, and the apology he owes.
Amit's 2009 novel, which Govind Nihalani wanted to adapt into a film.

head: Dunkirk
dek: Amit, who says he is no Nolan fanboy, calls it the best war film ever made.
more: Amit, who says he is no Nolan fanboy, calls it the best war film ever made. Ajay sees it as the model for letting real events carry the drama.
Ajay explains that this episode began with Dunkirk: watching it felt like being taken back in a time machine.

head: Darkness at Noon
dek: It goes inside the minds of Soviet leaders confessing at show trials. Ajay says it changed the world, including the 1946 French election.
more: It goes inside the minds of Soviet leaders confessing at show trials. Ajay says it changed the world, including the 1946 French election. He urges reading both Daphne Hardy's original translation and the 2015 translation of the rediscovered German manuscript.
The subject of Ajay's final chapter, about how the book was written, lost and rediscovered.

head: The World of Yesterday
dek: Zweig's memoir of living through Europe's collapse into fascism, Bolshevism and nationalism.
more: Zweig's memoir of living through Europe's collapse into fascism, Bolshevism and nationalism. Amit reads out its 'pale horses of the apocalypse' passage.
Amit's closing recommendation, prompted by Ajay's Koestler story.

head: Nonviolence Built From Local Materials
dek: Mukulika Banerjee found that Bacha Khan didn't import nonviolence.
more: Mukulika Banerjee found that Bacha Khan didn't import nonviolence. He reframed ideas his people already held: patience in Islam, the 'greater jihad' (Jihad-e-Akbar) as an inner struggle against fear and anger, and the Pashtun codes of ghairat (courage), melmastia (hospitality), badal (revenge) and nanawatai (refuge even for enemies). The British became unwanted guests who had broken the code of hospitality and had to be evicted politely but firmly. Because the ideology came from his followers' own culture, it was easy for them to understand and spread.

head: India Contains Multitudes
dek: Indian freedom fighters are often said to have borrowed Western Enlightenment values.
more: Indian freedom fighters are often said to have borrowed Western Enlightenment values. Amit argues that Indian culture holds opposite values side by side and can feed our worst instincts or our best ones. Liberal values also grow locally, if we look for them.

head: When the Best Minds Are in Jail
dek: Under colonial rule, and later during the Emergency, prison was where leaders met, argued and were shaped.
more: Under colonial rule, and later during the Emergency, prison was where leaders met, argued and were shaped. A government that jails its dissenters ends up locking away its best thinkers.

head: Deep Battle: Hit the Logistics
dek: Soviet doctrine held that you defeat a modern army by choking its supplies, not by meeting it head-on.
more: Soviet doctrine held that you defeat a modern army by choking its supplies, not by meeting it head-on. Tatsinskaya is the textbook case. Ajay notes that Ukraine is doing the same to Russian invaders today.

head: Owning a Plane vs. Having an Airworthy Plane
dek: Planes must be light, so many parts are designed to wear out quickly and need frequent replacement.
more: Planes must be light, so many parts are designed to wear out quickly and need frequent replacement. Flying more sorties means more maintenance and more downtime, so the number of aircraft you own overstates what you can actually fly.

head: Laminar vs. Turbulent Flow at a Chokepoint
dek: A bridge is a pipe with fixed capacity. The most gets through when the flow is smooth and planned, with hard decisions made in advance about what to leave behind.
more: A bridge is a pipe with fixed capacity. The most gets through when the flow is smooth and planned, with hard decisions made in advance about what to leave behind. Once desperate people turn into a mob, the flow becomes turbulent and the whole crossing breaks down.

head: Populism Isn't Left or Right
dek: Ajay argues that labels like left and right hide what is really going on.
more: Ajay argues that labels like left and right hide what is really going on. Populism is a tactic of grabbing power by stirring up hatred of elites, and it looks the same whichever side uses it. Indira's power-first letter to Sanjay fits this pattern.

head: History Rhymes, Disturbingly
dek: Amit says the Emergency should be studied as a lesson in the oppressive power of the Indian state, not just as a closed chapter.
more: Amit says the Emergency should be studied as a lesson in the oppressive power of the Indian state, not just as a closed chapter. The same patterns of pliant media, sycophantic ministers, jailed opponents and coercive targets can come back in new forms.

head: The Lesson Persecution Should Teach
dek: Anyone who suffered under, or resisted, abuse of power has the clearest reason to never repeat it: treat the opposition with dignity and let the press speak freely.
more: Anyone who suffered under, or resisted, abuse of power has the clearest reason to never repeat it: treat the opposition with dignity and let the press speak freely. Amit asks whether today's leaders, many of whom were Emergency-era dissenters, learned this.

head: The Looking-Glass Self
dek: Our sense of self is built from how others see us and how we want them to see us.
more: Our sense of self is built from how others see us and how we want them to see us. Amit's novel idea 'Missing' runs two stories side by side. In one, a family finds that a missing person's absence becomes a strong presence in their lives. In the other, the missing boy wakes to find everyone else gone, which asks what a self is when there is no one left to mirror it.

head: Inertia vs. Remarkableness
dek: When the path is already laid out for you, you can arrive just by following it.
more: When the path is already laid out for you, you can arrive just by following it. When every barrier is against you, only exceptional people get through. That is why every 19th-century Indian woman doctor was remarkable.

head: Books in the Battle of Ideas
dek: Ajay places Koestler and Orwell alongside Milton Friedman, Hayek and George Stigler in the 20th century's battle between liberal democracy and authoritarian or populist ideas.
more: Ajay places Koestler and Orwell alongside Milton Friedman, Hayek and George Stigler in the 20th century's battle between liberal democracy and authoritarian or populist ideas. A novel like 'Darkness at Noon' could change how voters understood a regime. He thinks that battle is still not won.

head: Ajay claims Amit will
more: Ajay claims Amit will 'become one of the world's great movie makers, and we're actually giving away some of his concepts'. Amit: 'you left me speechless for a moment'.

head: After Amit's cinematic trunk-opening pitch, Ajay
more: After Amit's cinematic trunk-opening pitch, Ajay says: 'You see, I tell stories from history. This is the real thing. He's a movie maker.' Amit: 'No, no, I'm not a movie maker. I'm a lafunga.'

head: Ajay on the Bacha Khan pitch
more: Ajay on the Bacha Khan pitch: 'I will sign up to watch this web series, even though I don't have a Netflix subscription.'

head: Amit, offering to be a showrunner
more: Amit, offering to be a showrunner: 'why do you just want to be a card carrying economist so boring?' Ajay: 'I am a happy customer.'

head: Amit on Ajay calling the tanks fat frogs
more: Amit on Ajay calling the tanks fat frogs: 'the last time you used that phrase fat frogs, you were asking me to lose weight. So I'm happier in this context.'

head: After hearing that Ajay's parents eloped three times
more: After hearing that Ajay's parents eloped three times: 'And out of that great romantic, courageous affair emerges a boring card carrying economist. What a waste. What a waste.'

head: Amit wore a red kurta in honour of the Khudai Khidmatgar
more: Amit wore a red kurta in honour of the Khudai Khidmatgar 'Red Shirts' and asked Ajay to wear red, but Ajay had no red shirt. Amit's closing line: 'may some of these movies and web series get made, and we can also be celebrities and walk red carpets... You couldn't even wear a red shirt.'
On the 'Babu Beats Bobby' headline, Amit: 'it is just greatest fucking headline in independent India's history.'

head: Amit stumbles over Devangshu Datta's
more: Amit stumbles over Devangshu Datta's 'four grandfathers'. Ajay corrects him: 'Two grandfathers and four great grandfathers.' Then Amit muses about getting Devangshu to write down the memoirs of his river-pirate ancestor: 'Like how does one do that? What am I even saying?'

head: Ajay, Aadhaar-era policy wonk, on Koestler escaping because the Germans couldn't identify him
more: Ajay, Aadhaar-era policy wonk, on Koestler escaping because the Germans couldn't identify him: 'So, gentle reader, if you ever think that digital identity is such a great thing. Think twice.'

head: Amit's self-deprecation
more: Amit's self-deprecation: 'I did write one shitty novel', and on his publisher V.K. Karthika of Westland, who agrees to publish every idea he pitches: 'I think she's kinda given up on me.'

head: Gandhi called Bacha Khan's movement the practical form of the idealistic nonviolence he believed in. Amit says Bacha Khan's
more: Gandhi called Bacha Khan's movement the practical form of the idealistic nonviolence he believed in. Amit says Bacha Khan's 'God' in 'servants of God' is best read as a set of higher principles.

head: L.K. Advani on the press during the Emergency
more: L.K. Advani on the press during the Emergency: 'when asked to bend, they chose to crawl.' Simon Jenkins said he had seen Franco's Spain and Mao's China but never such a press crackdown.

head: Amit compares Vidya Charan Shukla to Gollum from…
more: Amit compares Vidya Charan Shukla to Gollum from 'The Lord of the Rings', enslaved by his lust for power and ending up a pitiful figure.

head: Ajay quotes Lionel Trilling: Koestler, Orwell and Camus
more: Ajay quotes Lionel Trilling: Koestler, Orwell and Camus 'lived at the dark crossroads of literature and politics'.

head: Vajpayee's Speech on the Knowledge Economy
dek: The power-and-coercion view of the state has a germ of truth, but settling for it is 'a royal road to ruin', and it is what underdevelopment looks like.
more: Ajay recalls a speech by Vajpayee from around 2002 or 2003 with some beautiful paragraphs on the knowledge economy. Vajpayee argued that knowledge should not stay inside universities. It should cast aside superstition in individual lives, feed into firms so they become high-productivity firms, and feed into the state so it practises evidence-based policy. Ajay contrasts this with the cynical Indian view that politics is just winning elections and then sending agencies after your rivals.

The power-and-coercion view of the state has a germ of truth, but settling for it is 'a royal road to ruin', and it is what underdevelopment looks like. A real knowledge society is one where ideas leave the campus and change homes, firms and governments.

head: Einstein, the Patent Clerk
dek: Breakthroughs come from curiosity and passion, not from incentive structures.
more: Ajay holds up Albert Einstein as the ideal of how knowledge should be made. Einstein was a full-time clerk in a patent office, probably poorly paid, with zero budget and no research funding, and he became one of the most influential scientists ever. Ajay pairs him with Ramanujan: supremely brilliant people driven by their own inner hunger.

Breakthroughs come from curiosity and passion, not from incentive structures. Modern academia runs on career ladders, journal publications and funding chases, and it tends to filter out exactly this kind of person.

head: Why Adam Smith's Prose Can Be Turgid
dek: Judge thinkers by the inputs they had. Smith worked from a tiny sample of knowledge and still produced remarkable ideas, which makes his achievement greater.
more: Amit's writing students ask why their hero Adam Smith sometimes writes heavy prose. Amit's answer is to think about what Smith had available to read. Even after Gutenberg, only a small elite read, the models of good writing were few, and there were no writing courses or the body of craft knowledge we take for granted today.

Judge thinkers by the inputs they had. Smith worked from a tiny sample of knowledge and still produced remarkable ideas, which makes his achievement greater. It also shows how much richer the raw material is for any learner today.

head: From Newspaper Gatekeepers to an Eight-Hour Podcast
dek: Creators now own the means of production for ideas. Niche formats nobody imagined can find their audience without permission from a gatekeeper.
more: Amit contrasts writing in the 1990s with today. Back then you sent an article to the Times of India or the Hindustan Times. Gatekeepers with their own biases, news cycles and 800-word limits decided whether it ran, and the paper sold readers' eyeballs to advertisers while you got a tiny cut. As an early blogger he could write about anything at any length and talk directly with readers. Now, as a professional podcaster, all his income comes directly from listeners and viewers. He says that pitching long-form podcasts to a radio company thirty years ago would have got him laughed out of the room.
Creators now own the means of production for ideas. Niche formats nobody imagined can find their audience without permission from a gatekeeper.

head: Grigori Perelman Says No to Journals and a Million Dollars
dek: Perelman cut out both middlemen of academic credit, the journal and the prize.
more: Ajay tells the story of the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who lives with his mother and walks in the forest gathering mushrooms. After doing great work, Perelman simply posted his paper on arXiv. Asked why he wouldn't publish in a journal, he said a proof is either right or wrong, and a journal's brand name changes nothing. When the Clay million-dollar award came, the organisers quietly asked whether he would come and collect it. He refused. He said prizes give disproportionate rewards to one person, damage the collaborative DNA of the community, and ignore the many shoulders he stood on. Besides, what would he do with a million dollars?
Perelman cut out both middlemen of academic credit, the journal and the prize. Ajay says it was Perelman who opened his eyes to how winner-takes-all credit distorts everyone else's incentives.

head: Winning the Bastiat Prize, Twice
dek: A prize can sustain a lonely contrarian instead of rewarding conformity.
more: Amit pushes back on Ajay's case against prizes. The Bastiat Prize is named after his hero Frédéric Bastiat and goes to journalists who uphold the ideals of a free society. Amit won it in 2007, when he was nearly alone in India writing about freedom and was abused for it. He later left writing for five years to play poker, came back to find he had been forgotten, and won it again in 2015, becoming, he says, the first person to win it twice. Both times the recognition and the $10,000 helped keep him going, and the prize rewarded the opposite of conventional thinking.
A prize can sustain a lonely contrarian instead of rewarding conformity. Amit still refuses government and elite-club awards. His answer is many competing prizes, not none.

head: The Missionary Position: Mother Teresa in Theory and Practice
dek: It is about Mother Teresa and why one should always be suspicious of sanctimony.
more: It is about Mother Teresa and why one should always be suspicious of sanctimony. Amit wants people to read it and make up their own minds. He calls Hitchens a great writer who died too young and who called out the bullshit on both left and right.
Amit's recommendation segment. He thought of it after Ajay's line that James Watt did more for India's poor than Mother Teresa.

head: The Case Against Education
dek: It matches the episode's argument. Amit thinks the whole paradigm of schooling is broken: a system designed in the early 19th century to produce industrial workers, with same-age kids studying the same subjects.
more: It matches the episode's argument. Amit thinks the whole paradigm of schooling is broken: a system designed in the early 19th century to produce industrial workers, with same-age kids studying the same subjects. He sees a huge opportunity for whoever replaces it.
Amit's second recommendation. He cites the subtitle as 'Why the Education System Is a Waste of Time and Money'.

head: Unelected Power
dek: It covers the softer, advanced-economy version of the problem: power wielded by unelected officials, with checks and balances weakening.
more: It covers the softer, advanced-economy version of the problem: power wielded by unelected officials, with checks and balances weakening. You could call these 'first world problems', but Ajay says thinking about them sharpens thinking about the same problems in underdeveloped countries.
Ajay's recommendation, on the problem of the administrative state.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: India has an extreme form of the problem, where officials wield coercion and the rule of law breaks down.
more: India has an extreme form of the problem, where officials wield coercion and the rule of law breaks down. This book addresses that directly.
Mentioned alongside Unelected Power as the book about India's version of the administrative-state problem.

head: Publish and Perish
dek: Callard uses an economist's tool, incentives, to explain turgid academic writing.
more: Callard uses an economist's tool, incentives, to explain turgid academic writing. Tenure needs publications in particular journals, and those journals reward their conventions and the fashions of the day. Amit calls Callard the best kind of intellectual because she is always engaging with people on Twitter.
What Amit points his writing students to when academics ask how to write clearly in a world that rewards turgid prose.

head: Politics and the English Language
dek: Orwell shows the link runs both ways: forcing yourself to write clearly forces you to think clearly, and jargon is where muddled thinking hides.
more: Orwell shows the link runs both ways: forcing yourself to write clearly forces you to think clearly, and jargon is where muddled thinking hides.
Cited for the link between clear writing and clear thinking.

head: Social conformity despite individual preferences for distinctiveness
dek: The title captures what happens on campus. Young people arrive convinced they are independent rebels and end up conforming to the fashion of the day anyway.
more: The title captures what happens on campus. Young people arrive convinced they are independent rebels and end up conforming to the fashion of the day anyway.
Part of Amit's complaint that academia is gripped by conformity.

head: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
dek: It gives a name to the people who turn toxic intellectual fashions into enforced orthodoxy.
more: It gives a name to the people who turn toxic intellectual fashions into enforced orthodoxy.
Amit borrows Graham's phrase 'aggressively conventional-minded' to describe who fills academia.

head: The Three Pillars of a Knowledge Society
dek: Ajay's frame for the episode is that knowledge is the nuclear reactor running the modern world.
more: Ajay's frame for the episode is that knowledge is the nuclear reactor running the modern world. Any knowledge institution has three jobs: make new knowledge, diffuse it through society, and translate it into a better world through firms and the state. This should be the mission statement in the mind of every university trustee. Ajay thinks all three pillars are currently somewhat broken.

head: The Journal Game Has Replaced the Hunger to Know
dek: Academics now climb career ladders by gaming journals.
more: Academics now climb career ladders by gaming journals. The question has shifted from 'what important problem can I solve?' to 'how do I get into journal X?' Researchers chase editors' and referees' fashions like lemmings. A one-week idea becomes a five-to-eight-year publication slog that adds no creativity, and most published papers are never cited. The irony is that top journals can carry weaker papers, because the most effort goes into hacking them. Ajay calls economics the most broken journal process of all.
printed: Shut up and get the pub

head: Who Should Fund Research: Corporations Beat Governments and Philanthropies
dek: Corporate funding works because firms are meritocratic and pose concrete problems, such as making a widget survive at 256 degrees instead of 123.
more: Corporate funding works because firms are meritocratic and pose concrete problems, such as making a widget survive at 256 degrees instead of 123. Finance is a healthy example within economics, and Ajay rejects the Indian discomfort with profit-motivated research. Government funding is a state-capacity problem: America's DARPA works fantastically well, while in poor countries the money flows to cronies. Philanthropy is distorted in two ways. Feel-good humanitarian goals crowd out abstract research, and risk-averse bureaucracies run it when they should behave like venture capitalists.

head: Credentialism Has Hollowed Out the Diffusion of Knowledge
dek: Universities have become brand-name factories. Students want the degree to get a job at Google, not the knowledge.
more: Universities have become brand-name factories. Students want the degree to get a job at Google, not the knowledge. Universities raise prices, build resort-like campuses, and regiment students for 12 hours a day, which breeds mediocrity. The real bargain is that parents get four years of daycare, kids get a stamp, and employers get a signal. Economists separate a person's intrinsic capability from the brand's incremental value, and the evidence suggests the brand adds little. In the end, your curiosity and hard work will out.

head: Learning Is Lifelong, and the University Is an Industrial-Era Construct
dek: The idea that four years of college finishes your learning dates from an era when people stopped working at 55 or 60.
more: The idea that four years of college finishes your learning dates from an era when people stopped working at 55 or 60. With rising longevity (Ajay jokes their young cameraman Vaishnav has 100 years to go), the world, your values and your trade will change several times. Real understanding is slow. You must keep unlearning, relearning and reinventing yourself, the way two veterans learned to make a YouTube show. Society needs institutions and a culture built around lifelong learning.

head: Organisations Must Think Strategically, Not Just Execute
dek: For knowledge to improve the world, firms and governments must look at themselves critically and keep asking who they are, what they are doing wrong, and where they will be in five or ten years.
more: For knowledge to improve the world, firms and governments must look at themselves critically and keep asking who they are, what they are doing wrong, and where they will be in five or ten years. That means using strategy, operations and tactics, not only execution. The common failure is that organisations become contests for power, and those in charge shut down criticism to protect themselves, which leads to mediocrity and stagnation.

head: The Selectors Are the Root Cause
dek: In cricket, a player's true value only matters once it reaches the selectors.
more: In cricket, a player's true value only matters once it reaches the selectors. In academia, the deepest failures lie in who gets selected, promoted and funded, because those incentives shape everyone else's behaviour. Admissions demand regimentation and good grades, and India's populist insistence on 'objective' exams makes it worse. The result is safe, bureaucratic people instead of curious ones, which wastes the seed corn. Fix the management decisions and the organisation follows.

head: Credit Is Dispersed, So Prizes Damage Collaboration
dek: Ideas emerge from countless conversations and influences. Picasso didn't conjure cubism out of thin air, and whoever crosses the finish line is only the last runner in a relay.
more: Ideas emerge from countless conversations and influences. Picasso didn't conjure cubism out of thin air, and whoever crosses the finish line is only the last runner in a relay. Winner-takes-all prizes and narrow authorship make people hoard ideas instead of sharing them. Ajay wants much broader authorship, extending even to someone you met once at a bicycle repair shop whose conversation shaped your paper, and a world of low-powered rather than high-powered incentives.

head: A Free Market in Prizes
dek: Amit agrees that elite-controlled prizes mean the elites rewarding the elites, and he would never take a government award.
more: Amit agrees that elite-controlled prizes mean the elites rewarding the elites, and he would never take a government award. His answer is competition, not abolition. Anyone should be able to fund a prize for whatever they value, so lonely contrarians can be recognised and others inspired, instead of a few monopolistic gatekeepers deciding.

head: Why Academic Prose Is Turgid, and What to Do About It
dek: Following Agnes Callard, Amit sees turgid writing as an incentive problem: tenure depends on journals whose conventions demand it.
more: Following Agnes Callard, Amit sees turgid writing as an incentive problem: tenure depends on journals whose conventions demand it. His two-part advice is this. First, clear academic writing is possible, so find models like Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok. Second, if your career forces you into that style, do it knowingly and keep the habit out of everything else. He adds that every intellectual has a duty to be a public intellectual, writing clearly for everyone.

head: Clear Writing Forces Clear Thinking
dek: Borrowing from Orwell, Amit argues the link runs both ways: clear thinkers write clearly, and writing clearly forces you to think clearly.
more: Borrowing from Orwell, Amit argues the link runs both ways: clear thinkers write clearly, and writing clearly forces you to think clearly. Abstract jargon often exists to obscure rather than illuminate. As editor of the policy magazine Pragati, he constantly had to wrestle academics' prose into clarity. His rule of thumb is that hard-to-read academic writing is usually nonsense.

head: Silos and Conformity Kill Knowledge
dek: Amit's two big complaints about academia. Silos push scholars ever deeper into trivia that matters neither to the world nor to the body of knowledge.
more: Amit's two big complaints about academia. Silos push scholars ever deeper into trivia that matters neither to the world nor to the body of knowledge. Conformity means that even self-styled rebels adopt the fashion of the day. Knowledge needs multiple frames and a multidisciplinary outlook, which is the motto behind the show's name.

head: Universities as Modern Waqfs
dek: Following Timur Kuran's insight on waqfs in the Middle East, Amit notes that an endowment set up to build water fountains keeps its capital long after piped water makes the mission pointless.
more: Following Timur Kuran's insight on waqfs in the Middle East, Amit notes that an endowment set up to build water fountains keeps its capital long after piped water makes the mission pointless. Universities like Harvard and Stanford sit on massive endowments. There is also an unseen cost: the world still assumes the best and brightest are there and that whatever comes out of them is the holy grail.

head: Communities of Choice Replace Communities of Circumstance
dek: For most of history your knowledge was limited to the people around you, and even after the printing press only elites read.
more: For most of history your knowledge was limited to the people around you, and even after the printing press only elites read. Universities made sense as places to gather knowledge and bright minds. Today anyone with hunger can learn anything from YouTube, podcasts and books; Amit says he wishes he were fifteen today. For all its toxicity, Twitter lets you watch the world's best minds think aloud every morning. Most of Amit's friends are people he met because of the internet.

head: Creators Now Own the Means of Production
dek: Gatekeepers used to control distribution, along with their biases, scarce space and budgets.
more: Gatekeepers used to control distribution, along with their biases, scarce space and budgets. Now anyone can publish, build niches nobody knew existed, and earn money directly from their audience. Most content is bad, as Sturgeon's Law says it always was, but the right response is no longer to complain. It is to make something better yourself.

head: Playing the Long Game
dek: Amit sees creators as the new agents of knowledge changing the world. They build a repository and a community that reaches across geography, which no campus professor can, and across time.
more: Amit sees creators as the new agents of knowledge changing the world. They build a repository and a community that reaches across geography, which no campus professor can, and across time. He started The Seen and the Unseen hoping someone would listen thirty years later. His imagined audience is a fifteen-year-old girl in a remote Indian town, learning from YouTube and podcasts, who will be prime minister in thirty years.

head: The opening: Amit says Ajay keeps teasing him
more: The opening: Amit says Ajay keeps teasing him, 'Amit, I'm a card-carrying economist. I've done a PhD and all of that. You've studied nothing, you're a fool', yet here he is agreeing that degrees mean nothing. Ajay concedes: 'Across twenty short episodes, Amit has changed my views.'

head: Amit's verdict on Ajay's opening rant
more: Amit's verdict on Ajay's opening rant: 'Truly wise words. And the reason I say they're truly wise words is because I agree with all of them. If I did not agree with all of them, they would not be truly wise. They would be partly wise.'

head: Ajay quotes Edison
more: Ajay quotes Edison: 'genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration.' Amit: 'Edison didn't have air conditioning in his time.' Ajay, sweating through the shoot: 'And his cameras did not overheat in the Indian heat.'

head: Josh Felman's line, relayed by Ajay: putting one child through college in America
more: Josh Felman's line, relayed by Ajay: putting one child through college in America 'involves buying one brand new BMW car every year and rolling it off the edge of a cliff.'

head: Ajay on the credential as a luxury good
more: Ajay on the credential as a luxury good: 'You get a Louis Vuitton bag, it is some IIT degree, and then you're supposed to be done.'

head: Ajay turns the…
more: Ajay turns the 'publication orientation' bullying on Amit: 'Captain Varma, when are you giving us your great books? When are you going to produce a movie for us? I will say, you know, shut up and get me the movie.'

head: Amit on academic silos
more: Amit on academic silos: 'you'll be writing about wheat production in Arizona between the years 1863 to 1865.'

head: Ajay on the human condition
more: Ajay on the human condition: 'we fragile, frail bags of wetware, are actually not finished with learning over any finite horizon.'

head: Amit, unfiltered
more: Amit, unfiltered: 'I think academics is utterly irrelevant. It's a circle jerk. It's pompous old farts talking to other pompous old farts.'

head: Ajay on what the internet would have meant for a self-taught genius
more: Ajay on what the internet would have meant for a self-taught genius: 'Today, Ramanujan would have been doling out his gems, one blog article at a time.'

head: Amit on elite awards
more: Amit on elite awards: 'oh you government bureaucrat, you want to give me your Padma Shri, fuck off' and 'the Khan Market Liberal Award will never be accepted by me.'

head: Amit, clinging to his two Bastiat Prizes against Ajay's anti-prize stance
more: Amit, clinging to his two Bastiat Prizes against Ajay's anti-prize stance: 'But do not take my two candlesticks away from me.'

head: Amit on industrial-era schooling
more: Amit on industrial-era schooling: 'monkeys can climb trees, but you're also putting fish through an exam of how to climb trees. It's not fair, it's crazy.'
'Publication orientation': the dreaded phrase older academics use to beat idealism out of young researchers. In Ajay's words, 'you're supposed to organize your life around shut up and get the pub.'

head: Ajay quotes…
more: Ajay quotes 'a beautiful quotation': 'the process of education is not filling a pail, the process of education is kindling a fire.'

head: Ajay quotes a songwriter on how slowly understanding arrives
more: Ajay quotes a songwriter on how slowly understanding arrives: 'and if you listen very hard, the tune will come to you at last.'

head: Ajay quotes lines from a songwriter both hosts think a lot about, to argue against winner-takes-all prizes
more: Ajay quotes lines from a songwriter both hosts think a lot about, to argue against winner-takes-all prizes: 'and I won and I won big once. And I paid the cost. Inside I felt like I was carrying the broken spirits of all the other ones who lost.'

head: Sturgeon's Law, invoked by Amit against sniffiness about YouTube creators
more: Sturgeon's Law, invoked by Amit against sniffiness about YouTube creators: 'Ninety five percent of everything is crap', and it always has been.

head: Walking Into an Invisible Glass Wall
dek: We have normalised the state so completely that we stop seeing it until we collide with it.
more: In a very well-maintained office, Ajay was mid-sentence when he took an abrupt right turn to fetch his computer from a room. He walked straight into a glass wall that had been wiped so clean nothing showed it was there, and hurt himself a little. Amit teased him about it, then used it as the episode's opening metaphor: the state is like an invisible fist that gets in your way when you least expect it. Ajay agreed that the state invisibly reshapes our lives and now and then slams into us.
We have normalised the state so completely that we stop seeing it until we collide with it. The episode's project is to make that invisible wall visible.

head: The Poker Stable: Memorisers vs. Askers of Why
dek: Memorised mechanics let you play correctly in situations someone has already solved for you.
more: In Amit's years as a professional poker player, many pros started out in a 'stable'. A successful player who could only play so many hands himself would stake a group of players and coach them in mechanics: with twenty big blinds, here is your reshove range; in this spot, this is your equity against that range. Most players learned these by rote and played correctly. Only a small fraction of winning players, who were already a small fraction of all players, worked things out from first principles. Amit says he was always asking why.
