Memorised mechanics let you play correctly in situations someone has already solved for you. Asking why gives you an understanding you can carry into any field. It is more cumbersome, but it is what separates the rare masters.

head: Where Your Taxes Go: Moustache Allowances and Sandstone Elephants
dek: Each of these comes out of money collected under coercion, and that cost falls even on the poorest.
more: On his old blog India Uncut, Amit ran a series called 'Where Your Taxes Go' that passed number eighty and kept going. He read out examples of state spending: moustache allowances, educating and rehabilitating monkeys, overpaying for condoms, policing parrots, salaries for fake municipal employees who don't exist, golf buggies for the army, countless statues, sixty-two sandstone elephants, and the regulation of skirt hemlines.
Each of these comes out of money collected under coercion, and that cost falls even on the poorest. Seen that way, an absurd line item is a moral question as well as a waste.

head: The Restaurant That Must Break the Law
dek: A state with too much scope produces rules that cannot all be obeyed. That turns every business into a lawbreaker by default and stops society from solving its own problems.
more: In an early episode of The Seen and the Unseen, restaurateur Madhu Menon described the many licences a restaurant in Bangalore needed. The excise department, wanting to track alcohol coming in and going out, allowed only one door. The fire safety department required multiple doors. No restaurant could satisfy both rules, and restaurateurs across India end up paying thirty or forty bribes a month just to operate.
A state with too much scope produces rules that cannot all be obeyed. That turns every business into a lawbreaker by default and stops society from solving its own problems.
printed: One door, many doors, no way out

head: America Was Built by Mad Religious Sects
dek: The secular state started as an arrangement for letting religious oddballs alone.
more: Ajay gives the history behind early American political thinking. Many of the people who settled America belonged to fringe religious sects persecuted by Europe's Catholic and Protestant establishments. These were not atheists but groups more eccentric than mainline European religion would tolerate. Separation of church and state was meant to give such sects space to practise as they liked, not to lead toward secularism, which is how the 20th century actually turned out. From this came a lasting American question: if 20 or 200 people wall themselves into a commune, which of the state's rules can they suspend, and which, like the ban on murder, must still apply? America's answer was to let people found new cities and townships with many of their own rules.

The secular state started as an arrangement for letting religious oddballs alone. The question of how far a community can set its own rules has been a source of energy for the American project, and Ajay thinks India would benefit from taking it seriously.
printed: Mad sects and the secular state

head: The UAE Official Who Could Pass a Law by the Day After
dek: Frictionless lawmaking destroys legal certainty. The slow, consultative, many-veto process of a liberal democracy is what makes a law worth something.
more: Ajay was once discussing securities law with a policymaker in the UAE. The official waved his fist and declared that if Ajay handed him the correct securities law tomorrow, he would have it enacted by the day after. He meant it as a boast about decisiveness. Ajay heard the opposite: if a law can be enacted that fast, it can be changed just as fast, so nobody has any protection.
Frictionless lawmaking destroys legal certainty. The slow, consultative, many-veto process of a liberal democracy is what makes a law worth something.

head: Tiger, Elephant or Tortoise?
dek: The magic is sustained growth. Decency, consultation and fewer mistakes, kept up over decades, beat a heroic sprint.
more: At the Orange City Literature Festival, an audience member asked Ajay whether he wanted India to be a tiger or an elephant. He said he wanted India to be the tortoise, chipping away for many years at sustained growth. He contrasts this with India's hare-like run of roughly 20 years of high growth from 1991 to 2011, followed by weaker years, and with the UK and the US, which grew at modest rates for a century.
The magic is sustained growth. Decency, consultation and fewer mistakes, kept up over decades, beat a heroic sprint.
printed: Not a tiger, not an elephant

head: The policy questions around airlines
dek: It is a deep dive into a single industry. He uses it to raise the episode's opening question: is it better to work through one practical case at a time or to learn the general principles in their own right?
more: It is a deep dive into a single industry. He uses it to raise the episode's opening question: is it better to work through one practical case at a time or to learn the general principles in their own right?
Ajay opens the first chapter with his recent article on public policy in the airline industry.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: Amit calls it Ajay's 'masterpiece of a book'. It treats in detail the questions the follow-up episode will cover.
more: Amit calls it Ajay's 'masterpiece of a book'. It treats in detail the questions the follow-up episode will cover.
Amit previews the next episode, on when the state should make policy and what public policy even means.

head: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
dek: It sets out his core claim that the existence of the state is itself violence.
more: It sets out his core claim that the existence of the state is itself violence. Every state action therefore carries a moral cost that has to be justified.
Amit mentions writing this piece for the Times of India while making the episode's central argument.

head: Where Your Taxes Go (India Uncut series)
dek: A memorable catalogue, from moustache allowances to sixty-two sandstone elephants, of what coerced money ends up paying for.
more: A memorable catalogue, from moustache allowances to sixty-two sandstone elephants, of what coerced money ends up paying for.
Amit reads examples aloud from his old blog's long-running list of wasteful state spending.

head: Anarchy, State, and Utopia
dek: He calls it a 'great book' and recommends it as the place to engage seriously with the question of anarchy versus the state.
more: He calls it a 'great book' and recommends it as the place to engage seriously with the question of anarchy versus the state.

After calling the state an act of violence, Amit clarifies that he is not arguing for abolishing it. He mentions 'marvelous books' on how such questions can lead to a good equilibrium and recommends Nozick's.

head: State Building
dek: It is a slim book, and Amit recommends everyone read it. It replaces the vague 'big state vs small state' debate with two separate dimensions: how much a state tries to do and how well it does it.
more: It is a slim book, and Amit recommends everyone read it. It replaces the vague 'big state vs small state' debate with two separate dimensions: how much a state tries to do and how well it does it.
Amit introduces it as the source of the scope-and-strength framework at the heart of Chapter 3.

head: Restaurant Regulations in India (Episode 18 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A concrete account of how an overreaching state makes honest business impossible and bribes unavoidable.
more: A concrete account of how an overreaching state makes honest business impossible and bribes unavoidable.
The source of the excise-versus-fire-safety door contradiction Amit describes.

head: Essays on Nationalism
dek: He calls it one of the most beautiful books in the world and Tagore one of the most beautiful writers of the English language.
more: He calls it one of the most beautiful books in the world and Tagore one of the most beautiful writers of the English language. The ideas are deep, powerful and timeless, and the book is slim enough that a lazy reader has no excuse.
Ajay's recommendation for the episode. He says it is not directly on the topic, 'and yet everything is interconnected.'

head: The Libertarian Reader
dek: It collects essays by liberal thinkers such as Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek, a good distillation of many strands of thought.
more: It collects essays by liberal thinkers such as Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek, a good distillation of many strands of thought. Amit asks readers not to be put off by the label in the title.
Amit's recommendation, introduced after he reads out a Boaz quote about the state.

head: The Origins of Political Order
dek: He calls the two volumes magisterial. Over a long sweep of history they show how the state evolved, which you need in order to understand the interplay between state and society.
more: He calls the two volumes magisterial. Over a long sweep of history they show how the state evolved, which you need in order to understand the interplay between state and society.
The first of a two-part work Amit recommends after State Building.

head: Political Order and Political Decay
dek: It completes Fukuyama's history of the state's evolution and helps you see the state-society relationship more clearly.
more: It completes Fukuyama's history of the state's evolution and helps you see the state-society relationship more clearly.
The second volume of the same work.

head: Pune Public Policy Festival (January 19-20, 2024)
dek: Pune, once called the 'Oxford of the East', may be pulling some of the policy conversation away from Delhi.
more: Pune, once called the 'Oxford of the East', may be pulling some of the policy conversation away from Delhi. The festival brings young professionals together with policy experts, bureaucrats, economists and thinkers to debate tradeoffs such as environment vs growth, growth vs equality, and technology vs privacy.
The episode's sponsor. This year's theme is 'Tradeoffs'.

head: Mechanics vs. First Principles
dek: You can learn the mechanics of a field or keep asking why. Amit's poker players memorised ranges without understanding them.
more: You can learn the mechanics of a field or keep asking why. Amit's poker players memorised ranges without understanding them. Ajay's example is engineering: a technician trained on one air conditioner can repair it, but without thermodynamics and advanced physics they cannot invent the next one or follow developments like solid-state heat pumps. Ajay thinks India over-values job-ready vocational training. A liberal arts education is in one sense useless, but its general principles prepare a 20-year-old for a world that will keep changing over their working life.

head: Stories vs. Frameworks
dek: Amit's view on explaining ideas. A story grabs attention, but the principle it teaches often floats free and gets forgotten.
more: Amit's view on explaining ideas. A story grabs attention, but the principle it teaches often floats free and gets forgotten. A framework of first principles and root causes can be applied to anything, and its flaws are out in the open where people can argue with them. Hence his love of economics, which he sees as the study of human behaviour: scarcity and incentives show up in policy, literature, art and music.

head: The Great Liberal Paradox
dek: Liberalism says everyone has rights that no one should infringe. But rights only mean something if they are defended, and defending them requires a state with a monopoly on violence.
more: Liberalism says everyone has rights that no one should infringe. But rights only mean something if they are defended, and defending them requires a state with a monopoly on violence. So we have to give up some of our rights to protect the rest.

head: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
dek: Amit's claim is that the state itself is violence, not just some of what it does.
more: Amit's claim is that the state itself is violence, not just some of what it does. It is funded by taxes that nobody would pay unless forced, under threat of imprisonment, much like a monopoly mafia. That doesn't make the state illegitimate, since we need it. But every ideology, whether communist, libertarian or social democrat, has to answer one central question: for what purposes is this violence justified, and why?

head: Part-Time Slavery
dek: Add up direct and indirect taxes and perhaps a third of your income goes to the state.
more: Add up direct and indirect taxes and perhaps a third of your income goes to the state. That means you spend roughly January to April each year working for the state rather than for yourself. Amit offers this as a way to see the real cost of the state: we are not completely free.

head: Everyone Is a Taxpayer
dek: The claim that only about 3% of Indians pay taxes confuses income tax with all taxes.
more: The claim that only about 3% of Indians pay taxes confuses income tax with all taxes. The domestic help buying salt and the beggar buying tea or milk for a baby both pay indirect taxes. Inflation, caused by the government expanding the money supply, works as a tax on the poor. So every state expense, from a space programme to a statue, is partly paid for by the poorest people.

head: Normalised Taxation: The Dandi March Benchmark
dek: Ajay points out that the British tax levels that provoked Gandhi's Dandi March were modest compared with the taxes independent India levies.
more: Ajay points out that the British tax levels that provoked Gandhi's Dandi March were modest compared with the taxes independent India levies. What once set off a mass movement is now accepted without much thought.

head: Coercion Has No Budget Constraint
dek: Ajay's distinction: the state's monopoly on violence works through two channels.
more: Ajay's distinction: the state's monopoly on violence works through two channels. One is taxation, which raises money to spend. That channel has a natural check: raising revenue is hard, rupees are fungible, people hate paying, and budgets force some discipline. The other channel is direct coercion, rules saying 'thou shalt not' backed by punishment. Nobody keeps a single ledger of these, so hundreds of agencies add new restrictions every year unchecked. Ajay thinks this may be the bigger problem for public administration.

head: Constitutions Are Contextual
dek: From Subhashish Bhadra's Caged Tiger. America's constitution came out of people fleeing persecution, so it protects the people from the state.
more: From Subhashish Bhadra's Caged Tiger. America's constitution came out of people fleeing persecution, so it protects the people from the state. India's was written amid Partition's violence, when it was unclear whether the centre would hold, so it centralised power and protects the state from the people. Amit argues this inversion still shapes a mindset in which citizens exist to serve the state and the state's reach keeps growing.

head: Scope and Strength
dek: Fukuyama's framework replaces the vague 'big state vs small state' debate with two dimensions.
more: Fukuyama's framework replaces the vague 'big state vs small state' debate with two dimensions. Scope is how many things the state tries to do, from defence and law and order up to roads, temples, pilgrimage subsidies and space programmes. Strength is state capacity, how well it does those things. Sierra Leone is low on both, close to anarchy. The USSR had huge scope and middling strength. Amit's ideal is limited scope with great strength. India is the reverse: it meddles in bedrooms and businesses, and Amit has read that setting up a business in Delhi takes more licences than getting a gun. Meanwhile it fails at its core jobs. In Amit's view there is effectively no rule of law in India except for the privileged.
printed: Do less, but do it well

head: Strong as Capable, Not Strong as Scary
dek: Ajay criticises two ideas of 'strong' popular with India's middle class.
more: Ajay criticises two ideas of 'strong' popular with India's middle class. One is a state that can grab the most powerful people and put them in jail. The other is a leader who can announce a new law or policy overnight. He rejects both. A strong state should mean a competent one: handling COVID vaccination policy so that as few people as possible die in a second wave, or reaching every child with a polio vaccine within a year or two.

head: Slowness Is a Feature, Not a Bug
dek: Liberal democracy disperses power: no single decision-maker, checks and balances, many people able to veto.
more: Liberal democracy disperses power: no single decision-maker, checks and balances, many people able to veto. That makes it look slow and shambolic, and that is the point. Amit adds that the rules should be designed so the system is robust: even the worst strongman you can imagine should be able to do only limited damage. Ajay sees the admiration for strongmen as a symptom of India's failure to teach the humanities.

head: Liberal Ends, Conservative Means
dek: Amit's heroes of the freedom struggle are the 19th-century classical liberals: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, Ranade and Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
more: Amit's heroes of the freedom struggle are the 19th-century classical liberals: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, Ranade and Gopal Krishna Gokhale. They wanted a freer, more just society but pursued it through engagement, discourse and dialogue rather than overnight revolution. Hoping for someone to seize power and impose liberalism is not liberal, because whoever can impose it can just as easily impose its opposite.

head: The Thirty-Year Sprint Fallacy
dek: India's per capita GDP in PPP terms is about one-ninth of America's, which is a little over three doublings.
more: India's per capita GDP in PPP terms is about one-ninth of America's, which is a little over three doublings. At 7% real per capita growth, income doubles every 10 years, so 30 years would bring India within reach of today's United States. But Ajay notes that 7% per capita growth sustained for 30 years has essentially never happened in world history. Forcing it through dictatorship brings short-lived, Hitler- or Stalin-style mobilisation and then disaster. Ajay calls catching up in 30 years the wrong goal.

head: Discover, Not Design
dek: Ajay's phrase, which Amit links to Adam Ferguson's observation that much social progress comes from human action but not human design.
more: Ajay's phrase, which Amit links to Adam Ferguson's observation that much social progress comes from human action but not human design. The growth after 1991 came from freeing parts of the economy so people could discover positive-sum trades, not from government programmes aiming at 7% or 8%. India didn't free up enough, and growth targets imposed from above are bound to backfire.

head: Two Reasons to Seek Knowledge
dek: Ajay distinguishes two motives for learning. One is instrumental: if you want to work in business or government, you need to understand the world.
more: Ajay distinguishes two motives for learning. One is instrumental: if you want to work in business or government, you need to understand the world. The other is amusement: even if you have shut yourself off behind high walls, you'll enjoy the spectacle more if you understand it, the way a chess game is more fun to watch the more chess you know.

head: Amit, after Ajay's crash into a spotless glass wall
more: Amit, after Ajay's crash into a spotless glass wall: 'in terms of clarity, there is something that is out there that can match the clarity of your prose. So, you know, compliment to both you and the glass wall.'

head: Ajay to a commenter who said he was too lazy to work things out himself
more: Ajay to a commenter who said he was too lazy to work things out himself: 'So you, gentle reader, how dare you be lazy? Your immortal soul deserves better. Get off your butt and start by reading a slim book.'

head: Amit, when Ajay recommends Tagore
more: Amit, when Ajay recommends Tagore: 'my heart fills with joy that you named my fellow Bengali Robida, and I almost feel like you're flirting with me.'

head: Amit finally understands Ajay's
more: Amit finally understands Ajay's 'thirty-year sprint': tortoises live for centuries, so for them 30 years really is a sprint. The tortoise, he imagines, listens to Hindustani classical. Ajay adds The Seen and the Unseen, and Amit runs with it: 'which is often heard by hares at double speed, which is also perfectly fine. We cater to hares, we cater to tortoises, and we cater to some human beings.'

head: David Boaz, read out by Amit
more: David Boaz, read out by Amit: 'Conservatives want to be your dad, telling you what to do and what not to do. Liberals want to be your mommy, feeding you, tucking you in and wiping your nose. Libertarians want to treat you as an adult.' Amit clarifies that Boaz means American welfare-state liberals, and urges listeners to drop labels and think about principles.

head: Ajay interjects with a line he attributes to Churchill
more: Ajay interjects with a line he attributes to Churchill: 'Dogs look up to us. Cats look down on us. Pigs treat us as equals.' Amit: 'Beautifully said.'

head: Adam Ferguson's idea of social progress as the result of…
more: Adam Ferguson's idea of social progress as the result of 'human action, but not human design', which Amit uses to back Ajay's 'discover, not design'.

Amit's 'family-friendly version' of a Banarasi line: 'Bharme jaaye duniya, hum bajaayein harmonia' (let the world go to hell, I'll play my harmonium). He admits he is sometimes in 'harmonia mode'. The show notes link Kashinath Singh's Kashi Ka Assi.
Pune as 'the Oxford of the East', an intellectual hub of India whose influence shifted to Delhi after Independence. Amit raises it in the sponsor message for the Pune Public Policy Festival.

head: Ajay's sign-off
more: Ajay's sign-off: 'Did you ever think that there would be an episode of Everything Is Everything in which seven different animals would be mentioned? We've had a cat, a dog, a pig, a tiger, elephant, tortoise, and a hare.'

head: Amit's closing line
more: Amit's closing line: 'We are all turtles on the march of knowledge towards the end of history.'

head: When colour grading cost $800,000
dek: In about a decade, tools that only a few studios could afford became consumer-grade and nearly free.
more: DaVinci Resolve is now one of the big three editing programs, and anyone can download it free and get state-of-the-art editing and colour grading. Amit points out that in 2010, when it only did colour grading, it cost $800,000. India had no copy at all, so Bollywood films were sent to Hollywood for colour grading and shipped back, with the rental added to the film's costs.

In about a decade, tools that only a few studios could afford became consumer-grade and nearly free. The means of production now sit with individual creators, which is what lets two people run their own show.

head: How Europe learned to be a state
dek: State capacity is learned slowly, through narrow and repeated practice over generations.
more: Ajay asks whether the large Swedish state appeared fully formed, and answers that it did not. Through the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, European states did essentially two things. They ran a fiscal system to raise taxes (the 'fiscus'), and they waged war, along with the contracting and technology that arms required. Over centuries of doing these narrow jobs they learned HR, contracting, checks and balances, how to control corruption, how to solve principal-agent problems, and how to keep the military in its barracks within a liberal democracy. Only after that was the capability applied to new problems such as vaccines.

State capacity is learned slowly, through narrow and repeated practice over generations. Taking on a wide scope before the capability exists invites failure. This is why Ajay wants India to spend 25 to 50 years mastering the basics.

head: Parades that hid rot
dek: Secrecy removes the scrutiny that exposes malfeasance, so the most opaque parts of the state tend to hide the most failure.
more: Ajay is explaining why secrecy makes a state function harder to run well. He notes that the military is admired and respected but shrouded in secrecy. Once the shooting started in Putin's war, the world discovered mind-blowing failures inside the Russian military. These had been hidden behind pompous parades, nationalism and militarism.

Secrecy removes the scrutiny that exposes malfeasance, so the most opaque parts of the state tend to hide the most failure. A grand spectacle tells you nothing about whether the institution actually works.

head: Kerala's diabetes, Bihar's hunger, Delhi's schemes
dek: A single scheme designed for a country this diverse solves the designer's local problem, not the citizen's.
more: Amit draws on two Seen and the Unseen episodes: one with Pranay Kotasthane on centrally sponsored schemes, and one with RS Nilakantan on his book about South India. Kerala's health problem is diabetes and obesity, while Bihar and other parts of north and central India face malnourishment. Ideally each state would get a health budget and decide locally how to tackle its own problem. Instead, central schemes are designed in Delhi around nearby northern priorities and miss local needs.
A single scheme designed for a country this diverse solves the designer's local problem, not the citizen's. This is a concrete case for the subsidiarity principle.

head: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
dek: The book examines how hard it is for states and bureaucracies to 'see' society, and how often the state inflicts cruelty and violence on people when it does see them.
more: The book examines how hard it is for states and bureaucracies to 'see' society, and how often the state inflicts cruelty and violence on people when it does see them. Ajay calls it a great cautionary book on the fraught relationship between the individual and the state. He and Kelkar borrowed its idea of 'state legibility' to coin 'premature state legibility' for the debates over India's digital systems.
Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode, after the toolkit for thinking about state intervention.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece. It is the source of the toolkit used in this episode: market failure, the extended complexity test for state intervention, and the principle of choosing the least intrusive intervention.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece. It is the source of the toolkit used in this episode: market failure, the extended complexity test for state intervention, and the principle of choosing the least intrusive intervention.
Amit plugs it right after Ajay lays out the four buckets of market failure, and again before the book recommendations.

head: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
dek: It supplies the first two dimensions of the test. Interventions involving many transactions, or a lot of discretion for frontline staff, are harder to deliver.
more: It supplies the first two dimensions of the test. Interventions involving many transactions, or a lot of discretion for frontline staff, are harder to deliver. Kelkar and Shah later added stakes and secrecy.
Ajay cites this 2004 paper while building the 'chai conversation' test for how hard a state intervention will be.

head: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 20 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: This is where Amit learned how schemes designed in Delhi fail to fit the very different needs of different states.
more: This is where Amit learned how schemes designed in Delhi fail to fit the very different needs of different states.
Cited when Amit argues that government should be as local as possible.

head: Johan Norberg's writings on Sweden's free-market rise
dek: Amit says Norberg shows in detail that the Nordic countries were model free-market economies that got rich before they became welfare states.
more: Amit says Norberg shows in detail that the Nordic countries were model free-market economies that got rich before they became welfare states.
Amit's reply to people who cite Scandinavian welfare states against the case for freedom.

head: $800,000 to Zero - The FASCINATING History of DaVinci Resolve
dek: Amit calls it a great video on how a once-unaffordable professional tool became free.
more: Amit calls it a great video on how a once-unaffordable professional tool became free.
The video where Amit learned the DaVinci Resolve story, linked in the show notes.

head: RODE Wireless PRO
dek: They record in 32-bit float, so there is no fight over levels while recording and no clipping.
more: They record in 32-bit float, so there is no fight over levels while recording and no clipping. Everything can be fixed afterwards, much like shooting RAW in photography.
The new mics that replaced the hosts' boom arms in this episode.

head: Pune Public Policy Festival (January 19-20, 2024)
dek: Young professionals meet bureaucrats, economists and thinkers around the theme of trade-offs: environment versus growth, growth versus equality, technology versus privacy.
more: Young professionals meet bureaucrats, economists and thinkers around the theme of trade-offs: environment versus growth, growth versus equality, technology versus privacy. Amit also likes that it pulls policy discussion back to Pune, once called the Oxford of the East, and away from Delhi.
The episode's sponsor.

head: Every state action is justified violence
dek: The state is always coercive, and it pays for everything through taxes it collects by force.
more: The state is always coercive, and it pays for everything through taxes it collects by force. We accept this because we need it to protect our rights. So every time someone says 'the state should do X', they are proposing violence and owe a justification. The state is not a benevolent beast whose actions are free.

head: Strong state, narrow scope
dek: This follows Fukuyama's two axes. Scope is how much the state meddles in.
more: This follows Fukuyama's two axes. Scope is how much the state meddles in. Strength is how well it does those things. The ideal is a strong state with limited scope. 'Strong' means robust democratic systems that resist radical swings and can enforce the rule of law. It does not mean a strongman.

head: Market failure is a free lunch, not Robin Hood
dek: Freedom is the baseline, and people should be left alone by default. Economists have identified a narrow class of problems where the right intervention can make some people better off without hurting anyone.
more: Freedom is the baseline, and people should be left alone by default. Economists have identified a narrow class of problems where the right intervention can make some people better off without hurting anyone. That makes it something everyone can agree on, unlike populist redistribution or class warfare. Even a monopoly should be regulated in ways the monopolist could accept, not out of envy of the rich. A natural monopoly may only need its prices regulated, not to be broken up.

head: The four buckets of market failure
dek: 1. Market power: monopolies and oligopolies. 2.
more: 1. Market power: monopolies and oligopolies. 2. Externalities, meaning uncontracted spillovers. Positive ones include your education or vaccination benefiting me, which leads people to underinvest in them. Negative ones include smoking, loudspeakers and crime. 3. Asymmetric information: grandmothers and dentists cannot test medicine purity, check a restaurant's kitchen, or judge whether their bank is sound. 4. Public goods. Outside these four, freedom stays the default.

head: A public good is not 'something good for the public'
dek: Technically, a public good is non-rival and non-excludable. Non-rival means my use doesn't reduce yours: one woman walking safely doesn't use up the street's safety.
more: Technically, a public good is non-rival and non-excludable. Non-rival means my use doesn't reduce yours: one woman walking safely doesn't use up the street's safety. Non-excludable means you couldn't even in theory exclude a newborn, as with clean air. North India's air pollution is therefore a true public-goods problem. Ajay would back taxing people to fly 10,000 drones over the Hindi heartland, spot every fire, and ticket whoever lit it. India's 'digital public goods', by contrast, are mostly rival and excludable.

head: Economics hides technical terms in plain English
dek: Unlike science, economics reuses ordinary words such as market failure, public good, adverse selection and moral hazard.
more: Unlike science, economics reuses ordinary words such as market failure, public good, adverse selection and moral hazard. They sound accessible but have precise meanings. A shop having only blue cushions when you wanted green is not a market failure. Amit adds that words like rights versus entitlements, or liberal and progressive, have drifted far from their original meanings.

head: Utilitarian claims assume knowledge is easy, so demand a high bar of proof
dek: 'Freedom doesn't work here' is a claim about consequences. Amit warns that such claims often rest on engineering-style assumptions that 'if we do this, that will happen', and that rarely comes true.
more: 'Freedom doesn't work here' is a claim about consequences. Amit warns that such claims often rest on engineering-style assumptions that 'if we do this, that will happen', and that rarely comes true. Consequences matter, but anyone who wants to override freedom should face a very high burden of proof. Otherwise market failure becomes a convenient excuse to crush freedom. Amit also notes that nobody talks about state failure, which public choice theory shows is everywhere.

head: Freedom wins even if you don't value freedom
dek: Ajay offers a second, value-neutral argument. Suppose you are a conservative who prizes order or tradition over liberty.
more: Ajay offers a second, value-neutral argument. Suppose you are a conservative who prizes order or tradition over liberty. Even so, defaulting to freedom and limiting the state to market failures it can actually fix is the objective path to prosperity. You don't need to share the moral premise to accept the economic one.

head: Business-friendly is the opposite of market-friendly
dek: Market-friendly means competition and free entry, which benefits consumers.
more: Market-friendly means competition and free entry, which benefits consumers. Business-friendly means protecting incumbents, who lobby for tariffs and regulations to keep rivals out. Amit argues that genuine monopolies are very rare in competitive markets. Most real monopolies trace back to cronyism or a state-created barrier to entry, or turn out to be defined wrongly.

head: 'Where is the coercion?'
dek: Amit's four-word diagnostic question for any problem in society: trace it to the act of coercion.
more: Amit's four-word diagnostic question for any problem in society: trace it to the act of coercion. In his experience, that is where the root of the problem always turns out to be.

head: Market failure doesn't license intervention: implementation failure
dek: Spotting a market failure only opens the question. Ajay's rule is not to rush in where angels fear to tread.
more: Spotting a market failure only opens the question. Ajay's rule is not to rush in where angels fear to tread. Ask whether the state can actually succeed, and cheaply. Otherwise you create a corrupt bureaucracy that kicks private people around. Be willing to walk away, or to back out when an intervention isn't working.

head: The four-question 'chai conversation' test of difficulty
dek: Pritchett and Woolcock (2004) supplied two questions, and Kelkar and Shah added two more. (1) Are there many transactions? (2) Do frontline staff have discretion? (3) Are the stakes high? (4) Is there secrecy?
more: Pritchett and Woolcock (2004) supplied two questions, and Kelkar and Shah added two more. (1) Are there many transactions? (2) Do frontline staff have discretion? (3) Are the stakes high? (4) Is there secrecy? A polio drive has many transactions but no discretion, since staff just follow a manual, so it is easy to roll out. A truant teacher steals about ₹15,000 a month, so the effort put into misbehaviour is limited. In criminal justice the accused faces jail, so the pressure toward corruption goes to infinity. Secrecy, as in the military, hides failure. Four yes/no answers tell you whether you face an easy problem or a hard one.

head: Pick the least intrusive intervention, and go to the root cause
dek: Most market failures can be addressed in several ways, and each brings different winners and losers.
more: Most market failures can be addressed in several ways, and each brings different winners and losers. Choose the one that intrudes least on people's lives, in line with the liberal dream of living on your own terms without thinking about the state. An intervention that touches your body is worse than one that doesn't. Knocking on your door is worse than not knocking, and entering your house is worse than standing at the door. The cheapest fix is usually at the root cause: clean the air rather than build hospitals, and build good roads rather than trauma centres at every highway exit.

head: The subsidiarity principle
dek: Each government function belongs at the lowest level of government that can handle it.
more: Each government function belongs at the lowest level of government that can handle it. Local governments understand local problems, as with Kerala's diabetes versus Bihar's malnourishment. A scheme designed centrally imposes one region's priorities on everyone.

head: You don't always have to do something
dek: State capacity, money and bandwidth are limited, so every intervention has an opportunity cost.
more: State capacity, money and bandwidth are limited, so every intervention has an opportunity cost. Before acting, ask whether this is the right thing to do and whether the state needs to do it at all. India hasn't yet solved basics like the rule of law, so spreading the state thinner carries a real cost.

head: Learning by doing: start with narrow scope
dek: Every advanced economy took hundreds of years to learn to run a state.
more: Every advanced economy took hundreds of years to learn to run a state. Ajay's advice for India is to master a few things first, such as police and judiciary, for 25 to 50 years. Only then should society debate widening the state's scope. Arguing over more or less welfare is premature while those basic problems remain unsolved.
printed: Sweden wasn’t built in a day

head: Rich first, welfare later; Swedish results need Swedish foundations
dek: Amit makes two points about the Nordic countries. Behind their welfare states they keep great individual liberty, and starting a business there is far easier than in India.
more: Amit makes two points about the Nordic countries. Behind their welfare states they keep great individual liberty, and starting a business there is far easier than in India. They also became rich as free-market economies before building welfare states, once state capacity existed. Ajay adds that you cannot copy one Swedish outcome without the surrounding environment that supports it.

head: Opening on Ajay's big smile after the clunky boom arms were removed
more: Opening on Ajay's big smile after the clunky boom arms were removed: 'I have the feeling one day I will disappear and you will be even happier.' (Amit)

The German philosopher mix-up. Amit is told he missed a chance to plug a German philosopher and asks what Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative has to do with it. Ajay means the proletariat owning the means of production: 'So you and I, humble slaves and producers, are no longer the subjects of the giant media companies.' The exchange lands on the pun that names the chapter: 'Who says Immanuel can't? Now Immanuel can.'

head: The boom-arm running gag. Ajay says the new mics give
more: The boom-arm running gag. Ajay says the new mics give 'a new level of human freedom. We can wave our arms around.' He then builds it into the economics: by default people should 'swing their arms wildly and not be constrained by a boom arm required by a government regulator.' On externalities: 'my freedom to move my fist should be limited not just by the absence of the boom arm, but by the proximity of your nose.'

head: Ajay keeps casting Amit
more: Ajay keeps casting Amit as 'the great dictator Amit Bhai' running the country over chai. Amit fires back: 'Mr. Shah is a great dictator. Mr. Shah with his authoritarian command over facts. Mr. Shah with his oppression of bad ideas. You are the problem here, let me tell you that.'

head: Ajay on food safety
more: Ajay on food safety: 'Gentle reader, please Google gutter oil. It will blow your mind.' Amit, judging only from Ajay's face: 'I suspect it will blow your guts as well. ... don't tell me, don't tell me, continue.'

head: Amit teases Ajay's habit of calling things
more: Amit teases Ajay's habit of calling things 'one of the great ideas in economics': 'how many are there? One of the greatest means kitne?' He closes the episode on the same note, calling Ajay 'one of the greatest hosts of Everything is Everything', a show that has two hosts.

head: Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister (Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay), quoted for the policymaker's fallacy
more: Yes Minister / Yes Prime Minister (Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay), quoted for the policymaker's fallacy: 'we must do something, this is something, therefore we must do this.'

head: Marx, unnamed: Ajay sets the market-failure worldview against
more: Marx, unnamed: Ajay sets the market-failure worldview against 'the great German philosopher who claimed that the history of mankind is a history of class warfare'. He also invokes Robin Hood: 'We're not doing Robin Hood.'
Pune as 'the Oxford of the East', an intellectual hub whose centre of gravity shifted to Delhi after independence. Amit uses it to explain why the Pune Public Policy Festival matters.

head: Inoculation: The Gruesome Ancestor of Vaccines
dek: People understood the principle of immunity long before they understood the biology.
more: Smallpox killed about 25% of the children who caught it, and nearly everyone met it within the first ten or twenty years of life. People worked out that mild exposure protects. The method was to break a pustule on an infected person, cut a small wound in a healthy child's skin, and smear the white pus into it. About 10% of inoculated kids still caught smallpox and died, but 10% is less than 25%. Ajay says there is fair evidence the practice was invented in India, though it may have come from the Ottoman Empire. It likely travelled from India to the Ottomans and then to imperial courts in Europe.

People understood the principle of immunity long before they understood the biology. Without a way to control the dose, though, the protection came at a terrible price. Smallpox is so virulent that using a tenth or a hundredth as much pus barely changed the risk.
printed: A little pus, a lot of nerve

head: Edward Jenner and the Cowpox Breakthrough
dek: The real leap was not knowing that exposure protects, since inoculators already knew that.
more: Edward Jenner noticed that women who worked with cows often caught cowpox, a mild relative of smallpox. Once they had it, they were completely protected against smallpox. Cowpox is close enough to smallpox to train the immune system but different enough not to kill. That gap is the idea behind modern vaccines, which use weakened (attenuated) pathogens, engineered carriers or synthetic molecules.
The real leap was not knowing that exposure protects, since inoculators already knew that. It was finding a way to get the protection without killing a large share of the people treated.

head: A Vaccine Designed by Software in a Day
dek: Vaccine design has become partly an information problem. During COVID the bottlenecks were regulation and manufacturing, not the science.
more: Amit recalls that when COVID broke out, experts warned we might never find a vaccine. Vaccines traditionally took years or decades, and the search for an HIV vaccine is still going on. Instead, researchers in China sequenced SARS-CoV-2 and uploaded the file. A piece of software read it and printed out the design of an mRNA vaccine practically the same day. Ajay says all the remaining delay came from US FDA testing and building factories to scale up production.
Vaccine design has become partly an information problem. During COVID the bottlenecks were regulation and manufacturing, not the science.

head: Larry Brilliant, Neem Karoli Baba and India's Smallpox Fight
dek: One of the great achievements of public health in India turned partly on chance: a guru's dream and a penniless hippie sleeping at a gate.
more: In the early 1970s, smallpox had been wiped out almost everywhere except India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Ethiopia and Somalia. Those holdouts were a reservoir that could reinfect the world. Larry Brilliant was an American hippie living near Rishikesh with the spiritual guide Neem Karoli Baba. One day the Baba said a goddess had told him in a dream that Larry must go down to the plains and fight smallpox, and he ordered him out. Larry took an overnight bus to Delhi and reached the WHO compound at 4 a.m., with nobody there but barking dogs. He had nowhere else to go, so he slept at the gate. In the morning the staff found he had a medical degree and signed him on as a junior flunky in the smallpox programme. He eventually became one of the top people leading India's smallpox eradication programme.
One of the great achievements of public health in India turned partly on chance: a guru's dream and a penniless hippie sleeping at a gate. Small, odd events can have huge consequences.
printed: Sent down the hill by a goddess

head: How the Show Got Its Name
dek: In the song, the phrase points at everything the world offers while noting that the one person who matters is absent.
more: The two finalists for the show's name were 'Watching the Wheels' and 'Everything is Everything'. 'Watching the Wheels' is John Lennon's song: contemplative and humble, about a universe bigger than us that trundles along while we watch with amusement. Everyone would recognise it. 'Everything is Everything' comes from Bruce Springsteen's 'You're Missing', on The Rising, the album he wrote after the 9/11 attacks. The song matters deeply to both hosts. They tested both names on many people and chose 'Everything is Everything', judging that it could stand on its own even though most people don't know the song. Their young friend Ishaan Chintamani later sang 'Watching the Wheels' for them, and his version opens the episode.
In the song, the phrase points at everything the world offers while noting that the one person who matters is absent. That gives the show's title a bittersweet undertone.

head: Smallpox Town: A Novel That Never Got Written
dek: Reading non-fiction about a disease can spark surreal fiction, and old ideas can resurface years later when a conversation touches the right nerve.
more: In his early twenties, Amit read a great book on smallpox (he has forgotten the title) and a detailed New Yorker essay on the disease. That gave him an idea for a novel called 'Smallpox Town', written as one word. In it, the city itself catches smallpox, not its people. Buildings break out in pustules, the ground scabs over, and the whole course of the disease plays out on the city. He forgot the idea until Ajay's smallpox story brought it back.
Reading non-fiction about a disease can spark surreal fiction, and old ideas can resurface years later when a conversation touches the right nerve.

head: Why We Sleep
dek: From it he learned that sleep-deprived drivers cause more accidents than drunk drivers.
more: From it he learned that sleep-deprived drivers cause more accidents than drunk drivers. Drunk driving is dangerous, but driving while sleep deprived is even more so.
Amit's only recommendation of the episode. It came up after the hosts joked about the government policing people's sleep.

head: Beggars in Spain (Sleepless series)
dek: He calls it a phenomenal science fiction book. Its premise is a world with two kinds of humans: those who need to sleep and those who don't.
more: He calls it a phenomenal science fiction book. Its premise is a world with two kinds of humans: those who need to sleep and those who don't.
Ajay's first recommendation, following the sleep discussion. He misremembers the title on air; the show notes link the Sleepless series and Beggars in Spain.

head: A History of Global Health: Interventions into the Lives of Other Peoples
dek: It is one of the great books in public health, a field Ajay says is practically absent in India.
more: It is one of the great books in public health, a field Ajay says is practically absent in India. India has healthcare, plus doctors trying to make health policy without having read this book. Amit adds that public health and healthcare are completely different things.
Ajay's second recommendation, which he calls one of the fundamental books on health.

head: Watching the Wheels
dek: Ajay describes its mood as contemplative and humble: the universe trundles along while we watch it, curious and amused.
more: Ajay describes its mood as contemplative and humble: the universe trundles along while we watch it, curious and amused.
One of the two finalist names for the show. Ishaan Chintamani's cover opens the episode.

head: Watching the Wheels (Chris Cornell version)
dek: Amit says Chris Cornell's is his favourite version of the song.
more: Amit says Chris Cornell's is his favourite version of the song.
Ishaan's first take had a grungy angst, and Amit asked Gaurav Chintamani whether Ishaan was copying Cornell.

head: You're Missing
dek: Ajay says the song is immensely interesting and important to both hosts.
more: Ajay says the song is immensely interesting and important to both hosts. Its line 'everything is everything' points at all the world's wonders while marking someone's absence.
From The Rising, the album Springsteen wrote after 9/11, and the source of the show's name.

head: A Vaccine Is First a Private Good
dek: When you get vaccinated, you are the main beneficiary. It is like eating a chocolate or getting a toothache fixed, not something distant like clean air or foreign affairs.
more: When you get vaccinated, you are the main beneficiary. It is like eating a chocolate or getting a toothache fixed, not something distant like clean air or foreign affairs. Self-interest alone gives people every reason to pay for vaccines. So the analysis should start from freedom and assume no state at all, then ask what, if anything, actually fails.

head: Positive Externality and the Voucher Response
dek: Your vaccination also protects the people around you, which is a positive externality and therefore a market failure.
more: Your vaccination also protects the people around you, which is a positive externality and therefore a market failure. The failure only matters for people who decline to pay for a vaccine. For everyone who buys one out of self-interest, there is no problem to solve. The standard fix is a voucher: the government tops up a person's own willingness to pay to reflect the benefit to everyone else. For a disease frightening enough, even that may be unnecessary, while for something like flu there are shades of grey. A positive externality justifies funding help. It does not justify state production, import bans, central planning or coercion.

head: Integer-Valued vs Real-Valued Decisions
dek: Education is a 'how much' decision. Because some benefits spill over to others, every single person underinvests in it, so the market failure is universal.
more: Education is a 'how much' decision. Because some benefits spill over to others, every single person underinvests in it, so the market failure is universal. A vaccine is a yes-or-no decision. Anyone who takes it has no market failure; the problem exists only for those who say no. That makes vaccines a much narrower case for state action than education.

head: Only Eradication Is a Public Good
dek: Most diseases can never be eradicated. The common cold moves in and out of many species, including pigs, and rabies survives in dogs and foxes.
more: Most diseases can never be eradicated. The common cold moves in and out of many species, including pigs, and rabies survives in dogs and foxes. A few pathogens, such as smallpox and polio, live only in humans, so they can be wiped out. A world without smallpox meets the test of a public good. It is non-rival: one person's enjoyment doesn't reduce anyone else's. It is non-excludable: no newborn can be shut out of it. Routine vaccination only creates an externality. Eradication clears the higher bar of a public good.
printed: Wiped out, and good for all

head: Touching the Body Is Among the Highest Forms of State Intrusion
dek: Ajay places a state touching your body on the same scale as the death penalty, torture and incarceration.
more: Ajay places a state touching your body on the same scale as the death penalty, torture and incarceration. That raises a moral puzzle: what if a few thousand people refuse a smallpox vaccine for religious or personal reasons? Ajay would accept significant coercion only for genuine eradication projects like smallpox and polio. Even then he calls it debatable and stresses that each person must make up their own mind.

head: Judge Coercion by Principle, Not by Whether You Like the Cause
dek: Amit is strongly pro-vaccine and strongly pro-freedom.
more: Amit is strongly pro-vaccine and strongly pro-freedom. He argues that the coercion he cheers today could tomorrow be used for something he opposes, so the question must be whether the forcing itself is justified, and the bar should be very high. Ajay adds that future biotechnology could give governments vaccines that make people more docile and controllable. Amit calls coercion a more widespread disease than any other.

head: Price Controls Backfire
dek: Capping vaccine prices to help the poor discourages producers and innovators and always creates scarcity.
more: Capping vaccine prices to help the poor discourages producers and innovators and always creates scarcity. The poor end up worse off, because a cheap vaccine you cannot find does you no good. This is coercion with good intentions and bad outcomes.

head: Let Private Supply Run Alongside the State
dek: Restricting supply to the government in the name of protecting people only slows vaccination.
more: Restricting supply to the government in the name of protecting people only slows vaccination. The government can run its own programme, but private players should operate too. When richer people pay full price for privately supplied vaccines, more of the scarce cheap supply is left for people who can't afford it. Mechanisms can even be built so they subsidise others. Shutting out prices, information and incentives is what does the damage.

head: Three Ways to Build a Vaccine
dek: 1. Attenuated vaccines take the pathogen and weaken it with heat, acid or other techniques, leaving just enough for the immune system to learn from. 2.
more: 1. Attenuated vaccines take the pathogen and weaken it with heat, acid or other techniques, leaving just enough for the immune system to learn from. 2. Engineered carriers are the second route. The AstraZeneca vaccine, sold in India as Covishield, puts the SARS-CoV-2 spike into a chimpanzee virus that is harmless to humans and injects about a trillion particles. The body learns the spike's protein surface, so it is ready when the real virus arrives. 3. Synthetic vaccines build a new molecule that looks like the virus, and mRNA vaccines belong to this frontier. Manufactured vaccines like these carry essentially no risk of infection, whereas some attenuated vaccines sicken about one person in ten thousand.

head: Vaccines as Everyday Health-Seeking Behaviour
dek: Vaccines are not just for children, and they are not something only the government does.
more: Vaccines are not just for children, and they are not something only the government does. Treat them like sleep hygiene, nutrition and exercise. A whole range of adult vaccines exists. Talk about them, post them on Instagram and give others FOMO. Their friend Rajeshwari Sengupta paid for 42 vaccines for her child. Paying upfront to rule out diseases is, in Ajay's words, a free lunch.

head: FDA Approval as a Global Public Good
dek: The US FDA does the expensive testing and publishes the results, so every country can benefit for free.
more: The US FDA does the expensive testing and publishes the results, so every country can benefit for free. Ajay thinks the FDA is too conservative and slow, which makes its approval a high bar. Countries like India and Bangladesh should simply import approved vaccines from global manufacturers instead of chasing self-reliance.

head: Amit on the bureaucratic mind
more: Amit on the bureaucratic mind: 'there's nothing as attractive to a bureaucrat as the thought of a government program.' Whisper 'government program, committee, budget' in their ear before bed, and 'they'll go to sleep with a beatific smile on their face and their wife will think they're having an affair.'

head: Amit on Ajay's mumbling: Ajay once told him to take
more: Amit on Ajay's mumbling: Ajay once told him to take 'the influencer vaccine'. Amit replied: 'There's a vaccine that protects me from influencers. I'm signing up, give it to me. You had me at hello.' Ajay had actually said influenza.

head: After listing the popular myths about state-run vaccination, Amit
more: After listing the popular myths about state-run vaccination, Amit says: 'My blood is already boiling. It's a good time to inject me with pus.'

head: Ajay pictures state officials
more: Ajay pictures state officials 'strapping down Amit Bhai' as he hollers and screams, 'a scene straight out of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.' Amit: 'which Amit Bhai are you talking about? It better not be me.' Later Amit adds: 'You really want to strap me down, don't you?'

head: On Larry Brilliant landing a job at the WHO
more: On Larry Brilliant landing a job at the WHO: 'He was brilliant. He was very brilliant. He was not just brilliant, he was very brilliant.'

head: Amit's alternative explanation for the guru's dream
more: Amit's alternative explanation for the guru's dream: perhaps Larry Brilliant hadn't bathed in three days and Neem Karoli Baba simply made up the goddess to get rid of him. Ajay: 'Enough is enough.'

head: Amit clarifies
more: Amit clarifies that 'adult vaccines' doesn't mean 'vaccines that have grown up.' Ajay: 'Or a vaccine that makes sure that you'll never be an adult.' Amit: 'That would be an excellent vaccine as well.'

head: The sleep nanny state. Amit imagines the government scolding him
more: The sleep nanny state. Amit imagines the government scolding him: 'Ajay Shah you slept seven hours, thirty five minutes... You need to get your two hours of REM.' Ajay goes further: sleepy drivers impose a negative externality, so your phone tells your sleep tracker, which tells your car not to start. Amit: 'What have you done, Ajay Shah, this is the beginning of the end.'
'You are never too old to have a happy childhood.' Amit credits the line to Ajay, who admits it's 'stolen'. Ajay's joke that follows is a vaccine that makes sure you'll never be an adult.

head: Ajay explains the intuition behind inoculation
more: Ajay explains the intuition behind inoculation with 'as the old Greek saying goes, that which does not destroy you makes you stronger.'

head: Albert Camus's L'Etranger: Amit recites its opening
more: Albert Camus's L'Etranger: Amit recites its opening, 'my mother died today, or was it yesterday', while admitting he hasn't read The Plague.

head: Ishaan Chintamani, son of Gaurav Chintamani, covers Lennon's
more: Ishaan Chintamani, son of Gaurav Chintamani, covers Lennon's 'Watching the Wheels' at the top of the episode, and two more takes play at the end. Amit thought Ishaan's grungy chorus was borrowed from Chris Cornell's version, his favourite. Gaurav explained that Ishaan had heard both Lennon and Cornell and made the song his own.

head: Tyler Cowen's
more: Tyler Cowen's 'self-recommending': Amit borrows it to plug his own Seen and the Unseen episode, adding, 'but I don't think he means this.'

head: The swimmer who opens and closes the series
dek: Amit sees the habit as conviction applied to small routines as well as big causes.
more: Amit's proposed web series, The Reformers, opens with an overhead shot of a tiny glistening blue speck surrounded by land. The camera zooms down until the speck becomes a large swimming pool with a man doing laps. The scene recurs in quiet moments across nine or ten seasons: someone comes to speak to him, he answers, they leave, and he keeps swimming. It is also the very last scene. The swimmer is KP Krishnan, for whom swimming is non-negotiable. He once asked to step out of a long cabinet meeting for an hour just to swim. Amit's eight-hour interview with him took four sessions instead of three because one session, at a conference in Kochi, ran into his 6 pm swimming time.
Amit sees the habit as conviction applied to small routines as well as big causes. It also works as a metaphor for the reformer's life: you keep going alone, and interruptions come and go.

head: A Rhodes Scholarship and a handshake
dek: Montek doesn't dwell on the scene, but Amit says Indian men will recognise why it is moving: a generation's restraint, where the most important feelings go unspoken.
more: In his memoir Backstage, Montek Singh Ahluwalia describes winning a Rhodes Scholarship. There were no mobile phones, so he got word to his mother and told his father in person. His father simply shook his hand and said 'congratulations', and that was all. Ajay adds that Montek travelled to Britain by ship, going first by train to Bombay. Amit observes that a voyage gives you time to gather your thoughts.
Montek doesn't dwell on the scene, but Amit says Indian men will recognise why it is moving: a generation's restraint, where the most important feelings go unspoken.

head: Narayana Murthy's licence for an obsolete computer
dek: The licence raj did more than slow businesses down. It locked them into worse, more expensive technology just as the world was moving ahead.
more: In 1983 Narayana Murthy of Infosys wanted to import state-of-the-art Data General computers with three removable 200 MB drives. He spent months travelling to the ministry in Delhi for an import licence. The licence came through just as Data General released a newer machine with 300 MB drives that was 30% cheaper. Because the licence was tied to the specific model number, he had to buy the older, costlier machine or start another months-long licence chase.
The licence raj did more than slow businesses down. It locked them into worse, more expensive technology just as the world was moving ahead.

head: The satellite dish that started a software revolution
dek: Turning points can depend on an insider clearing one absurd permission.
more: As Ajay recalls it, with the caveat that he may be slightly off, the first important software development centre in India set up by a global company was Texas Instruments'. It needed a satellite dish, and the state had to permit it. In the mid-to-late 1980s, Montek was one of the key people who pushed through permission to install the dish.
Turning points can depend on an insider clearing one absurd permission. A single dish approval marks the start of India's software story.

head: Eighty people locked in the finance ministry basement
dek: The 1991 reforms read like a grand political moment. On the ground they were drafted by people who gave up their freedom for a week so the work could be done before the budget.
more: After the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis hit (Montek had already drafted a secret reform roadmap, the 'M document', around 1990), the reform budget had to be prepared in total secrecy. Eighty people were taken to the basement of the Ministry of Finance and kept there for eight days, senior officers included. Dormitory beds were set up and food was brought in. Only the most senior people, such as the finance minister or finance secretary, could come and go.
The 1991 reforms read like a grand political moment. On the ground they were drafted by people who gave up their freedom for a week so the work could be done before the budget.

head: The suit that smelled of India
dek: Protectionism leaves physical traces on ordinary life. Ajay later calls such humiliations the 'psychic dynamite' that pushed India's elite toward reform.
more: NK Singh once told Ajay this story. In an elevator at the IMF, one man turned around without looking and asked the person behind him, 'You're from India, aren't you?' The reason he knew: India had banned imports of the proper dry-cleaning fluids as luxuries. Indian dry cleaners used bad petrochemicals that left a distinctive stink on suits, so anyone in a suit with that smell had to be from India.
Protectionism leaves physical traces on ordinary life. Ajay later calls such humiliations the 'psychic dynamite' that pushed India's elite toward reform.

head: The prime minister who coded in COBOL
dek: What Amit admires more than learning is the capacity to keep learning and reinventing yourself.
more: PV Narasimha Rao, born around 1920, knew about ten languages, including Telugu, Hindi, Marathi, Kannada, Urdu and Persian. When computers arrived in India in the 1980s, he was a minister, and he taught himself computer languages: he could code fluently in COBOL and BASIC and wrote for Unix. Delhi still never took him seriously, partly because it doesn't take the South seriously and partly because its idea of refinement was skin-deep. Vinay Sitapati's chapter titles in Half-Lion ('Andhra's Socialist', 'Puppet Chief Minister', 'Delhi Darbar') trace his many reinventions.
What Amit admires more than learning is the capacity to keep learning and reinventing yourself. Delhi's markers of sophistication missed exactly that.

head: How Narasimha Rao got the job by not wanting it
dek: History turns on accidents, and on the odd advantage of being the person who isn't scheming.
more: After Rajiv Gandhi's death, the Congress fought over who would lead. The post was first offered to Vice President Shankar Dayal Sharma, who declined because he would rather become President later, as he did. Narasimha Rao got the top job because he was seen as not trying for it, which made him acceptable to everyone. Vinay Sitapati argues that his greatest quality was his loneliness: his ideal evening was reading or learning something new, not politicking.
History turns on accidents, and on the odd advantage of being the person who isn't scheming. Rao could play the power game, but his detachment is what made him the consensus choice.

head: 'You just apply. Leave the rest to me.'
dek: Rao was not merely managing the politics while others did the reforms.
more: Narasimha Rao met Akio Morita, chairman of Sony. He leaned over and almost whispered that millions of Indians dreamed of nothing more than owning a Sony television, so why not set up a factory in India? Morita gently replied that he would need so many licences that he would never get them. Rao leaned in further and answered in an even softer voice.
Rao was not merely managing the politics while others did the reforms. He was a true believer who personally pushed investment past the licence raj.

head: A half-burnt pyre for a reforming prime minister
dek: Amit argues the Congress should proudly claim the 1991 liberalisation.
more: When Narasimha Rao died in 2004 he was already an outcast in his own party, and the Congress did not let his body be brought to Delhi for a state funeral. As Vinay Sitapati describes in Half-Lion, television channels that night showed his half-burnt pyre in Hyderabad, with his skull partly exposed and stray dogs coming at the remains.
Amit argues the Congress should proudly claim the 1991 liberalisation. Instead, petty politics disowned the man whose actions lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, which makes Amit angry.

head: 'Saamagri taiyaar hai': a nuclear handover
dek: This was grace across party lines: Rao did the groundwork and left the credit to a successor.
more: In his tribute after Narasimha Rao's death, Atal Bihari Vajpayee revealed a private exchange from May 1996. As Rao handed over power, he told Vajpayee that the material was ready, meaning the nuclear test. Rao's government had prepared it, but with elections underway it left the decision to the next government.
This was grace across party lines: Rao did the groundwork and left the credit to a successor.

head: Chidambaram's note on file: leave it to my successor
dek: Complex, multi-year reforms survive when outgoing governments refuse to rush them and incoming ones refuse to bin them.
more: Ajay explains that when the RBI was created in 1934, its Act called it a temporary measure; in his telling, the British had no idea what they were doing. The real framework only arrived in 2015 with the monetary policy framework agreement signed by Rajiv Mehrishi and Raghuram Rajan. The inflation-targeting work was hatched in 2013 and agreed at file level by Montek, Manmohan Singh and P Chidambaram. With elections coming, Chidambaram wrote on file that such a momentous change should not be rushed through by a lame-duck administration, and left it to his successor. Arun Jaitley then implemented it.
Complex, multi-year reforms survive when outgoing governments refuse to rush them and incoming ones refuse to bin them.

head: Arun Jaitley: 'Who am I to disagree?'
dek: It is unusual and admirable for a minister to defer openly to the judgement of political rivals on a technical question.
more: From Amit's interview with KP Krishnan: in the 2000s, Krishnan and 'a certain young man called Ajay Shah' were seen as heretics for constantly pushing inflation targeting. When the new government came in, Krishnan gave the document to Arun Jaitley, who said the next morning, 'Let's go with it.' Krishnan urged him to think about the ramifications of something so radical. Jaitley felt insulted, as if he were being called unthoughtful, and then explained why he was confident.
It is unusual and admirable for a minister to defer openly to the judgement of political rivals on a technical question.

head: Isher Judge's Hindi-medium climb
dek: The reformers shared a restless curiosity about the world. For Isher, getting into the conversation at all meant first conquering a language barrier.
more: Isher Judge came from a conservative Sikh family and went to an all-girls, Hindi-medium Marwari school in Calcutta, in a world where higher education abroad was unthinkable. She went to Presidency College and then moved to Delhi, where she initially struggled with English, the language all the economics was written in. She was suspicious of slick Delhi boys with accents, but Montek's sense of humour won her over. They courted by watching Godard, Truffaut and Bresson films, and she became a fine economist in her own right. Amit regrets keeping her memoir, Breaking Through, unread and never inviting her on his show before she died.
The reformers shared a restless curiosity about the world. For Isher, getting into the conversation at all meant first conquering a language barrier.

head: Padma Desai, erased by alphabetical order
dek: The women among the reformers fought the same intellectual battles as the men while also fighting for recognition and for basic control over their own lives.
more: Padma Desai co-wrote a seminal 1968 book with Jagdish Bhagwati that argued against India's state-controlled system. His name comes first only because of alphabetical order, yet search results credit the book to him alone. She studied the Soviet Union for years and wrote a respected 1989 book on perestroika. Trapped in an abusive first marriage and denied a divorce, she used one of the legal grounds available, change of religion, and converted to Christianity so she could marry Bhagwati. Her memoir is Breaking Out.
The women among the reformers fought the same intellectual battles as the men while also fighting for recognition and for basic control over their own lives.

head: The panel that vanished during the Lehman collapse
dek: When a crisis breaks, the people actually running the system disappear from public view.
more: Amit imagines the season on the 2008 crisis opening in a dimly lit Delhi basement with no phone signal. Ajay is moderating a panel with KP Krishnan of the finance ministry, RBI governor Subbarao and SEBI chief Bhave. One by one, someone walks up and whispers to each of them, and they get up and leave. Finance Minister Chidambaram, unable to reach any of their phones after Lehman Brothers collapsed, had got through to their drivers instead.
When a crisis breaks, the people actually running the system disappear from public view. Amit says the story of how they handled 2008 deserves one or two seasons of its own.

head: Watching one stock price through the night
dek: In a crisis, situational awareness is hard, because the loudest voices often have an axe to grind.
more: Ajay had planned a conference months in advance for 14–15 September 2008. On the 13th, as Lehman was filing for bankruptcy, Indian markets were turbulent and a small run seemed to be forming on ICICI Bank. ICICI's stock was only slightly down when the NSE closed at 3:30 pm. Ajay stayed up for hours watching the price of ICICI's ADR in New York, since all the evening's news would show up there. It barely moved, so he went to sleep. By the time his conference began in a basement at the IHC, Lehman had collapsed and Bombay's money market was choking.
In a crisis, situational awareness is hard, because the loudest voices often have an axe to grind. A market price can be a cleaner signal than the rumours.

head: Sushma Swaraj's plan to oppose in public
dek: Adversarial politics in public can sit alongside private cooperation on what's good for the country, a quiet kind of statesmanship that fills Amit's heart with joy.
more: KP Krishnan told Amit about the New Pension Scheme, which was prepared under the Vajpayee government and handed to the Manmohan Singh government, which embraced it. Sitting across the table from Sushma Swaraj, then in opposition, the government side explained the scheme. She said it was wonderful and good for the country, warned that she would have to oppose it publicly in Parliament, and then laid out a step-by-step strategy for getting it passed anyway.
Adversarial politics in public can sit alongside private cooperation on what's good for the country, a quiet kind of statesmanship that fills Amit's heart with joy.

head: How a terror attack reshuffled economic policy
dek: Economic trajectories can turn on personnel shuffles caused by unrelated events.
more: Drawing on Puja Mehra's The Lost Decade, Amit traces a chain of accidents. After the 2008 Bombay attacks, Home Minister Shivraj Patil proved inadequate, so Manmohan Singh moved his best man, Chidambaram, to the home ministry. Sonia Gandhi got Pranab Mukherjee installed at finance, and when Manmohan went in for an operation, Pranab stayed on. He was a disaster as finance minister, bringing in retrospective taxation among other things, and was later 'kicked upstairs' to the presidency.
Economic trajectories can turn on personnel shuffles caused by unrelated events. A security crisis ended up derailing the reform momentum.

head: The postcard that won over Pranab Mukherjee
dek: Financial reform bores most audiences, so reformers have to show its effect on one real, named person to get it through.
more: KP Krishnan needed a financial-sector reform that Pranab Mukherjee's 1970s socialist instincts would reject. He prepared a two-slide presentation. The first slide was a postcard to Pranab from a constituent in Bengal, Sharmishtha Bandopadhyay, describing how her life savings had been wiped out and asking him to do something. Pranab had it read aloud and grew furious, demanding to know what Krishnan wanted. Krishnan explained that the current system was ruining ordinary people like her and proposed the reform. Seen that way, Pranab approved it on the spot.
Financial reform bores most audiences, so reformers have to show its effect on one real, named person to get it through.

head: Recruitment by Jedi hand wave
dek: Much of India's reform talent arrived through personal pulls from people with conviction rather than formal hiring.
more: Vijay Kelkar, then working in Geneva, ran into Manmohan Singh in a corridor at a Kathmandu conference around 1974. Manmohan simply said Kelkar would come and work with them; Kelkar felt obliged to say yes, an offer letter followed, and he moved to India. Kirit Parikh took two years to relocate: he worked first at the Atomic Energy Commission, and after Vikram Sarabhai died, he asked his recruiter whether the offer still stood and was told to come whenever he liked. Ajay introduced Viral Shah to Nandan Nilekani at an NCAER conference, and by that evening Nandan had offered Viral a job at UIDAI. Rakesh Mohan once phoned Ajay on a Thursday evening asking him to fly to Delhi the next morning to discuss joining the finance ministry, and Ajay said yes.
Much of India's reform talent arrived through personal pulls from people with conviction rather than formal hiring. There's a small recruitment story behind each of these careers.

head: Krishnan's first day was Ajay's last
dek: A bittersweet near-miss: two people who would later be linked on reforms like inflation targeting crossed paths on the day one of them was leaving.
more: In 2005, KP Krishnan, who had been a legend in the world of water supply and whom Ajay knew from a water conference, burst into Ajay's office at the Ministry of Finance to announce he had just joined as a joint secretary. Ajay had to tell him it was his last day; he was packing his boxes. It was also the day Ajay's mother died.
A bittersweet near-miss: two people who would later be linked on reforms like inflation targeting crossed paths on the day one of them was leaving.

head: Opening up petroleum, one piece at a time
dek: Reform takes years of teamwork between strategic economists and skilled bureaucrats, plus a system that lets them stay on across governments.
more: When Vijay Kelkar became an adviser to the petroleum ministry, the state had a complete monopoly over exploration, extraction, refining, distribution and petrochemicals. Kelkar, the economist, worked closely with Secretary Lavraj Kumar, who knew how to work the bureaucratic and political machine. Both believed state monopolies made no sense. When Lavraj Kumar's tenure ended, Kelkar, though not from the IAS, became petroleum secretary and held the post for six years across governments. Over that time exploration, extraction, refining and petrochemicals were opened to the private sector; distribution fumbled.

Reform takes years of teamwork between strategic economists and skilled bureaucrats, plus a system that lets them stay on across governments. Ajay says this capability is no longer working the way it used to.

head: Manmohan's whisper to Naushad Forbes
dek: Even the finance minister driving the reforms had to recruit public advocates one at a time, because almost nobody outside understood or backed them.
