more: Around 1991–92, Manmohan Singh explained his reform ideas at a meeting with industry leaders. Naushad Forbes sat between Ambani and JRD Tata (or so Amit recalls), producing a famous photograph that left everyone asking who the man in the middle was. Forbes had spoken in support of reform during the meeting. As they shook hands afterwards, Manmohan held on, pulled him a little closer, and whispered a request.
Even the finance minister driving the reforms had to recruit public advocates one at a time, because almost nobody outside understood or backed them.

head: Breaking Out
dek: The story of a remarkable economist and a strong woman who often goes uncredited.
more: The story of a remarkable economist and a strong woman who often goes uncredited. Amit says everyone should read it.
Padma Desai's autobiography, discussed alongside Isher's.

head: The Lost Decade
dek: Details the reshuffle that put Pranab Mukherjee in the finance ministry and decisions like retrospective taxation.
more: Details the reshuffle that put Pranab Mukherjee in the finance ministry and decisions like retrospective taxation.
Cited for how reform stalled after the 2008 Bombay attacks.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: Amit calls it brilliant, a book on how economic policy should be made, by two people who were inside the reform story.
more: Amit calls it brilliant, a book on how economic policy should be made, by two people who were inside the reform story.
Mentioned while introducing Vijay Kelkar as Ajay's mentor and co-author.

head: The Struggle and the Promise
dek: Written by a business leader who backed reform publicly when few others did.
more: Written by a business leader who backed reform publicly when few others did.
Amit isn't sure whether Manmohan Singh's 'tell the world' whisper appears in this book or came up in his podcast with Forbes.

head: The Logic of Collective Action
dek: The classic account of concentrated interests beating dispersed beneficiaries.
more: The classic account of concentrated interests beating dispersed beneficiaries. Ajay uses it to show what a purely political-economy view would predict, and why India defied that prediction.
Ajay invokes Olson's logic while explaining how India escaped 300% customs duties.

head: Kohrra
dek: Amit calls it a marvellous series and was so impressed by Suvinder Vicky's lead performance that he wants him to play Montek.
more: Amit calls it a marvellous series and was so impressed by Suvinder Vicky's lead performance that he wants him to play Montek.
Amit's casting pitch for the series: Suvinder Vicky as Montek.

head: The Seen and the Unseen
dek: India hasn't yet done its economic history well, and Amit's long conversations with people like KP Krishnan and Montek are oral history, entry points into 'conversations with greatness'.
more: India hasn't yet done its economic history well, and Amit's long conversations with people like KP Krishnan and Montek are oral history, entry points into 'conversations with greatness'.
Ajay's closing recommendation, given in place of the usual book pick.

head: The 1991 Project
dek: A great website on 1991 that reproduces the legendary M document.
more: A great website on 1991 that reproduces the legendary M document.
Mentioned while describing Montek's secret pre-crisis reform roadmap, the 'M document'.

head: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls it an epic piece of oral history, made possible by Ajay, and urges everyone to listen.
more: Amit calls it an epic piece of oral history, made possible by Ajay, and urges everyone to listen. It covers the reform process and the handling of the 2008 crisis in detail.
The eight-hour, four-session conversation behind the swimming motif and several anecdotes in this episode.

head: Naushad Forbes Wants to Fix India (Episode 282, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A conversation with a business leader who supported reform when there was almost no public support.
more: A conversation with a business leader who supported reform when there was almost no public support.
Where Amit heard, on or off the record, about Manmohan Singh's whisper to Forbes.

head: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
dek: Despite its 'enigmatic title', it is an economic-history episode on India's bad years from the 1962 China war to the Emergency, while East Asia took off.
more: Despite its 'enigmatic title', it is an economic-history episode on India's bad years from the 1962 China war to the Emergency, while East Asia took off.
Cited while explaining why India's elite turned toward reform.

head: The reforms as a second, silent freedom movement
dek: India did not become fully free in 1947.
more: India did not become fully free in 1947. For decades afterwards, economists and bureaucrats worked behind the scenes against their own incentives to dismantle an oppressive state, much as freedom fighters worked for principles with no immediate reward. The result lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Amit wants to tell it through human stories rather than policy, because every good story is a human story.

head: Sharpen the axe before the crisis
dek: Amit cites the Abraham Lincoln line about spending five of six hours sharpening the axe before chopping a tree.
more: Amit cites the Abraham Lincoln line about spending five of six hours sharpening the axe before chopping a tree. People like Montek came back from lucrative jobs abroad to unglamorous advisory posts in the late 1970s and spent years preparing. When the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis opened a window, the ideas, the people and even a written roadmap (the M document) were ready.

head: Wounded pride as the engine of reform
dek: After 1947, India's elite believed India was the post-colonial country most certain to succeed: the land of Tagore, Ramanujan, Nehru and Gandhi.
more: After 1947, India's elite believed India was the post-colonial country most certain to succeed: the land of Tagore, Ramanujan, Nehru and Gandhi. The bad years from the 1962 China war to the Emergency, while Korea, Taiwan and Southeast Asia grew rich through openness, felt like a personal affront. That dissonance made former Marxists, including many Bengalis raised on land reform, rethink their views.

head: Ideas, interests and institutions beat simple political economy
dek: A pure Mancur Olson reading predicts that incumbents protected by 300% tariffs, with concentrated gains and the power to pay bribes, would never let tariffs fall.
more: A pure Mancur Olson reading predicts that incumbents protected by 300% tariffs, with concentrated gains and the power to pay bribes, would never let tariffs fall. Yet India cut customs duties year after year until 2007–08. Ajay says this happened because the reformers read, argued and debated ideas, so policy didn't collapse into a contest between factions. Interests matter, but ideas and institutions can outplay them.

head: Decency and grace across elections
dek: Big reforms outlast single governments only when politicians act with restraint.
more: Big reforms outlast single governments only when politicians act with restraint. Examples from this episode: Narasimha Rao left the nuclear test to Vajpayee; Chidambaram deferred inflation targeting to his successor; Jaitley adopted it; the pension scheme passed from Vajpayee's government to Manmohan's; Sushma Swaraj privately helped pass a reform she would publicly oppose.

head: A stable professional elite as institutional memory
dek: Ministers are temporary.
more: Ministers are temporary. Long reforms like opening up petroleum needed a professional elite of people such as Lavraj Kumar and Vijay Kelkar who could think, mentor and protect one another, and carry knowledge across changes of government. Ajay warns this capability is no longer working the way it used to.

head: Counterintuitive ideas need a long game
dek: The reformers' core ideas, positive-sum games and spontaneous order, are hard to explain and easy to caricature: 'the state shouldn't do this' gets heard as 'he's anti-poor, pro-business'.
more: The reformers' core ideas, positive-sum games and spontaneous order, are hard to explain and easy to caricature: 'the state shouldn't do this' gets heard as 'he's anti-poor, pro-business'. With almost no public support, as shown when Manmohan Singh privately asked Naushad Forbes to speak up, these people still spent decades on the cause. Amit contrasts that with armchair columnists like himself.

head: Put a human face on boring reforms
dek: Financial reforms put audiences to sleep but shape everyone's life. KP Krishnan's postcard tactic with Pranab Mukherjee shows how to convert them: start with one named person whose savings the current system destroyed.
more: Financial reforms put audiences to sleep but shape everyone's life. KP Krishnan's postcard tactic with Pranab Mukherjee shows how to convert them: start with one named person whose savings the current system destroyed. Amit says reformers and storytellers both need to find ways to tell these stories.

head: Curiosity and constant reinvention
dek: Amit sees a common trait in the reformers: refusing to accept the world as it is and wanting to understand it.
more: Amit sees a common trait in the reformers: refusing to accept the world as it is and wanting to understand it. Rao learned programming in middle age, and Isher and Montek courted by discovering European cinema together. What impresses Amit most is the ability to keep learning, more than learning itself.

head: The doubly remarkable women
dek: The male reformers swam against the tide. Women like Isher Judge Ahluwalia and Padma Desai first had to break into ministries and academic departments run almost entirely by men.
more: The male reformers swam against the tide. Women like Isher Judge Ahluwalia and Padma Desai first had to break into ministries and academic departments run almost entirely by men. Amit sees a leftover of this today: almost every accomplished woman he invites on his podcast asks 'Why me?', while the men never do.

head: Prices cut through the fog of war
dek: During the Lehman weekend, rumours were everywhere and the loudest voices had agendas.
more: During the Lehman weekend, rumours were everywhere and the loudest voices had agendas. Ajay relied on one signal, the ICICI ADR price in New York, because everything that had happened since the Indian market closed would be reflected in it. A traded price combines dispersed information better than any single person's opinion.

head: After Ajay admits his taste in films is a 13-year-old's love of spectacle, Amit sums up the pair
more: After Ajay admits his taste in films is a 13-year-old's love of spectacle, Amit sums up the pair: 'You are the kind of person who likes to blow things up, and I'm the kind of person who wants to curl up in a corner and cry.'

The pilot's opening shot looks like a violent clash of colours until the camera pulls back to show someone spreading Marmite on toast. Ajay admits he hates Marmite, and Amit says 'So does the protagonist of this particular chapter.'

head: Ajay on the Texas Instruments satellite-dish saga
more: Ajay on the Texas Instruments satellite-dish saga: 'Voluntary transactions by consenting adults were very complicated.'

head: On the 80 officials locked in the finance ministry basement for eight days, Amit borrows the Hotel California line
more: On the 80 officials locked in the finance ministry basement for eight days, Amit borrows the Hotel California line: 'you can check out but you can never leave.'

head: Ajay sets up the dry-cleaning story
more: Ajay sets up the dry-cleaning story with 'if you are a male who is an unfortunate owner of a thing called a suit', noting that dry cleaning is how you signal class, since poor people can't afford it.

head: On Shankar Dayal Sharma turning down the top job to become President later, Amit paraphrases
more: On Shankar Dayal Sharma turning down the top job to become President later, Amit paraphrases: 'I can chill and be in the Rashtrapati Bhavan. Not in so many words, obviously, because I don't think Mr. Sharma would have said I can chill.'

head: Ajay on the RBI's origins: the 1934 Act called it a temporary measure because the British
more: Ajay on the RBI's origins: the 1934 Act called it a temporary measure because the British 'had no idea what they were doing', so 'the concept of the Reserve Bank of India really only began in 2015.'

head: Ajay recalls Jagdish Bhagwati telling a dinner table that his brother, PN Bhagwati, found out Jagdish and Padma Desai were…
more: Ajay recalls Jagdish Bhagwati telling a dinner table that his brother, PN Bhagwati, found out Jagdish and Padma Desai were 'living in sin' and grumbled that it was a crime under the IPC, 'so just be careful.'

head: Ajay calls Isher telling him his articulation was like young Montek's
more: Ajay calls Isher telling him his articulation was like young Montek's 'the sweetest thing that anybody ever said to me.' Amit: 'I'm sure young Montek's humour was better than yours.' Ajay: 'No doubt.'

head: Ajay announces
more: Ajay announces 'Chapter three.' Amit: 'it's not actually chapter three. You're losing count. What kind of card carrying economist are you when you can't even count?'

head: As the panellists vanish one by one during the Lehman crisis, Amit says the audience doesn't mind
more: As the panellists vanish one by one during the Lehman crisis, Amit says the audience doesn't mind 'because you're on stage and you're so beautiful and they're just looking at you lost in rapture.'

head: Ajay describes Manmohan Singh recruiting Vijay Kelkar in a Kathmandu corridor
more: Ajay describes Manmohan Singh recruiting Vijay Kelkar in a Kathmandu corridor with 'a Jedi hand wave', the Star Wars mind trick, after which Kelkar simply felt obliged to say yes.

head: Amit calls In Service of the Republic
more: Amit calls In Service of the Republic 'the brilliant book' and wonders, 'Have we mentioned it before?' The answer: 'A couple of hundred times.'

head: Asked who should play him, Ajay recalls a student at ISB who once said he looked like someone from Hollywood
more: Asked who should play him, Ajay recalls a student at ISB who once said he looked like someone from Hollywood, 'and I've forgotten the name.'

head: Ajay refers to the episode
more: Ajay refers to the episode 'for which you have the enigmatic title, Why Freedom Matters, but it's actually an economic history piece', a dig at Amit's titling.

head: Ending his recommendation of Amit's podcast, Ajay signs off
more: Ending his recommendation of Amit's podcast, Ajay signs off with 'we're at the end of this episode of The Seen and the Unseen.' Amit: 'We won't edit that out. It's a very nice fumble.'

head: Churchill's Hardest Call: Sinking the French Fleet at Mers-el-Kébir
dek: Some of history's most consequential choices have no clean moral answer.
more: Summer 1940: Rommel's tanks punch through the Ardennes, France loses the battle and signs an armistice. That leaves the French Navy, which by default could fall into German hands. For Britain, whose entire way of war rested on total naval domination, that was intolerable. Britain had just sent a 300,000-strong expeditionary force to fight alongside France, so it urged French commanders through informal channels to bring their ships over and join the Allies. The French were pulled the other way by three things: orders from Pétain's Vichy regime, a military culture of blind obedience, and a lingering belief that France was a first-class power equal to Britain and America. Some French officers promised to scuttle the ships if the Germans came for them, but that was only a promise about the future. At the Algerian port of Mers-el-Kébir the Royal Navy pleaded until the very end. The French refused, Churchill gave the order, and about 1,300 French sailors died. Churchill later wrote that it was one of the worst decisions he had to make in the war. Some historians call it a mistake; Ajay sides with Churchill.

Some of history's most consequential choices have no clean moral answer. Amit points out that the story suits blockbuster scale but has no Hollywood resolution: no victory for anyone, only a moral dilemma and unease. Judging it in hindsight is easy. Standing in Churchill's shoes, or the French commanders', is not.

head: Silence of the Heart: ERP's Sound Evangelists and the Couple Who Heard Differently
dek: Films often show couples drifting apart because they see the world differently.
more: In 1926, as sound came to cinema, AT&T set up Electrical Research Products Inc. (ERP) to spread 'good sound' in theatres around the world. Its trained men carried kits, listened intently for echoes, and fixed rooms with padding and drapes. The devil was silence and its sidekick was reverberation. They treated it as a cultural and almost moral mission, and grew from about 1,000 screens at the start of 1929 to about 4,000 by its end. They boasted of creating 'ERP widows' and later hired only bachelors. The backlash came: the French burned a theatre down, and the Indian film industry mastered sound and told them it didn't need them. Onto this true history Amit lays a fiction: a couple who join ERP together as equal zealots. Slowly the woman starts hearing rooms differently from her husband and everyone else. At first she gaslights herself and assumes something is wrong with her ears. Later she owns it: why is he right and she wrong?

Films often show couples drifting apart because they see the world differently. Almost none show them drifting apart because they hear it differently. Listening becomes a metaphor for how we quietly force ourselves to conform to someone else's perception, and for the moment we stop.

head: You Could Learn to Echolocate Like a Bat
dek: The brain is far more plastic than we assume. When one faculty is lost, it adapts and finds creative new ways to read the world, which suggests most of us carry abilities we never discover.
more: Ajay's digression: take people who lost their sight after about age five, once they had already learned to see. With careful training, about two-thirds of them learn to orient themselves by echolocation, whistling and listening for the reflections the way bats do. Some get good enough to ride a bicycle outdoors, sensing traffic and houses. Amit counters with Thomas Nagel's essay arguing we can never know what it is like to be a bat. He then concedes a data point on Ajay's side: Krish Ashok told him about a visually impaired colleague who listens to everything at 6x speed. Amit tops out at about 3.5x.
The brain is far more plastic than we assume. When one faculty is lost, it adapts and finds creative new ways to read the world, which suggests most of us carry abilities we never discover.
printed: Ride a bike like a bat

head: The Doolittle Raid: Hacked Bombers and a One-Way Mission
dek: Bold outcomes come from people who understand their tools well enough to rebuild them.
more: After Pearl Harbor (December 1941) the US wanted to strike Japan itself, both to disrupt its formidable production and to puncture Japanese complacency. But Japan was out of reach of existing equipment. Engineers hacked the B-25 bomber in sixteen different ways, including extra fuel tanks for roughly 80–90% more range and new de-icing gear. The plan was for a carrier group to sail toward Japan and launch bombers that could take off from a carrier but not land on one. They would bomb Japan and fly on to China. Stalin refused landing rights at Vladivostok because of his peace treaty with Japan, so Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang prepared airfields. A Japanese ship spotted the group and radioed home before being destroyed. Japan, unable to imagine carrier-launched bombers, prepared for a naval fight instead. The Americans launched early from the wrong spot. The planes hit targets with reasonable success but fell short of China: crews crash-landed or bailed out, and most were rescued by the Kuomintang. One damaged plane landed at Vladivostok, its crew was interned in Central Asia, and the NKVD staged a fake escape into Iran. Japan's reprisal killed roughly 70,000 Chinese soldiers and 250,000 civilians. Coming in April 1942, just four months after Pearl Harbor, the raid shattered Japan's sense of ease.

Bold outcomes come from people who understand their tools well enough to rebuild them. The defender's worst weakness can be a failure of imagination. The story also shows the terrible costs carried by bystanders.

head: The Boy Who Burned Down His School: VP Menon's Origin Story
dek: History hinges on tiny accidents: no ten rupees, perhaps no Menon at Patel's side, perhaps a different India.
more: Amit pitches this as a story told across scattered scenes. A schoolboy in the early 1900s is failed for poor attendance despite explaining how far he must travel. He runs out in tears, clutching his lunchbox. He sits shaking at a railway station, walks by the river, eats his cold lunch under a tree, sleeps, and wakes at dusk beside an empty liquor bottle. At a liquor store he buys a bottle, saying his mother will pay later, and asks for a matchbox. The last scene: the school is on fire. This is VP Menon. He fled by train to Kolar and, decades later, could still recite every station on that journey. He worked in the mines, giving orders to men twice his age, then sold towels on Bombay's streets. In Delhi he arrived to find his pocket picked, and a Sardarji stranger gave him ten rupees, a fortune then; Menon forgot to ask his name. He joined government as a clerk, nearly quit after the Rowlatt Act, and decided some people must stay within the system to change it. He went on to become Sardar Patel's executor in integrating the princely states. He was also a difficult husband and father.

History hinges on tiny accidents: no ten rupees, perhaps no Menon at Patel's side, perhaps a different India. Behind the 'expressionless bureaucrat' is a messy, complex human being. People contain multitudes.

head: The Maharaja of Jodhpur's Pen-Gun
dek: India's map was not drawn calmly. It was negotiated through bluff, coercion, nerve and charm, one prince at a time.
more: Hanwant Singh, the Maharaja of Jodhpur, was being courted by Jinnah, who offered him a blank cheque to choose Pakistan. VP Menon and Mountbatten persuaded him to sign with India. Mountbatten left the room, and as Hanwant Singh was about to sign, he pointed his pen at Menon: it was also a gun. In Amit's cinematic imagining, Menon simply raises an eyebrow and smiles, and the Maharaja signs. Years later, Hanwant Singh called Menon and offered to make him MP from Jodhpur; Menon declined.
India's map was not drawn calmly. It was negotiated through bluff, coercion, nerve and charm, one prince at a time. With 500-plus princely states, there are 500-plus such stories.
printed: The pen was also a gun

head: The Nawab of Junagadh Counts His Dogs
dek: Behind the solemn history of Partition and integration lie absurd, darkly comic human moments that reveal priorities better than any treaty.
more: Realising he must leave rather than stay in India, the Nawab of Junagadh chartered a plane. He loaded the treasury, the jewellery, his dogs, his begums and his children. As the plane was about to take off, one begum cried that she had left her child behind in the palace. The Nawab looked around, counted his dogs, confirmed they were all aboard, and told her to get off. The plane left for Karachi without her.
Behind the solemn history of Partition and integration lie absurd, darkly comic human moments that reveal priorities better than any treaty.

head: The Battle of Kiev: The Comedian Who Wouldn't Leave
dek: It is an underdog story with world-historical stakes. Ordinary people, including a comedian president, improvised their way to stopping a superpower.
more: In 2022 the supposedly second-most powerful army in the world invaded Ukraine. Ajay sees Ukraine as institutionally weak and messy, much like India. Its president, Zelensky, was a former TV comedian who had once starred in a show where Russia invades Ukraine and he plays the president. Many expected an Afghanistan-style collapse. Russian-compromised hit squads made an assassination attempt on him almost daily, yet he stayed, later saying he was no hero, just a terrified man who knew that leaving meant collapse. Russian cyber and electronic warfare blinded government communications, so officials resorted to WhatsApp. But Russian insiders had leaked the invasion plans to Western intelligence. Zelensky's team didn't fully believe the warnings, but did move key defence assets, so the first Russian strikes hit empty sites. As CIA Director Burns had predicted, Russian paratroopers seized Hostomel airport. Then the Ukrainians caught their breath and mounted a scrappy underdog defence, including blowing up a bridge to flood an attack route. They did this while facing Western disdain: European appeasement, memories of Obama's inaction over Crimea in 2014, and Trump's 'perfect phone call' over Javelin missiles. Russia eventually withdrew from the Kiev region. Amit adds Zelensky's line rejecting evacuation and Ukraine's 'Uber for artillery'.

It is an underdog story with world-historical stakes. Ordinary people, including a comedian president, improvised their way to stopping a superpower. The decisive early fight was almost entirely Ukrainian.

head: How Music Works
dek: The best book he has read about music. It is deeply meta, digs into the 'whys', and explores his obsession with how form shapes the world.
more: The best book he has read about music. It is deeply meta, digs into the 'whys', and explores his obsession with how form shapes the world. He says to read it even if you don't care about music.

head: Every military has a foundational 'way of war'

more: Ajay argues that armed forces build their doctrine on a non-negotiable precondition. For Britain it was overwhelming naval domination; for the US and NATO today it is air superiority, which Russia never achieved over Ukraine. Threats to that foundation, like the French fleet passing to Germany, get treated as existential, which explains otherwise shocking decisions.

head: Hindsight is easy; standing there is hard
dek: Both hosts resist tidy verdicts on wartime choices. Amit says the world and people are complex, and sometimes there is no clear line to draw.
more: Both hosts resist tidy verdicts on wartime choices. Amit says the world and people are complex, and sometimes there is no clear line to draw. Ajay adds that the real test is imagining yourself in the moment as Churchill or the French commander, deciding with incomplete information.

head: Hackers vs. users
dek: Ajay's meta-lesson from the Doolittle Raid: one level of the world buys equipment and uses it as intended.
more: Ajay's meta-lesson from the Doolittle Raid: one level of the world buys equipment and uses it as intended. Real excellence comes from understanding tools well enough to take them apart and rebuild them for uses nobody imagined, as with the B-25 modified in sixteen ways.

head: Failure of imagination
dek: Japan had warning that an American carrier group was near. But because no carrier plane could reach Japan in their mental model, they prepared for a naval fight and missed the air raid.
more: Japan had warning that an American carrier group was near. But because no carrier plane could reach Japan in their mental model, they prepared for a naval fight and missed the air raid. Ajay calls this 'fighting the last war': the gravest defensive blind spot is the attack you cannot conceive of.

head: Latent capacities and brain plasticity
dek: Two-thirds of people who lose their sight after childhood can learn echolocation, and a blind listener can process speech at 6x.
more: Two-thirds of people who lose their sight after childhood can learn echolocation, and a blind listener can process speech at 6x. When one channel closes, the brain rewires to find new ways of reading the world, so we likely carry untapped abilities.

head: We hear (and perceive) the world differently
dek: Amit argues that people in the same room experience its sound differently without being able to articulate it.
more: Amit argues that people in the same room experience its sound differently without being able to articulate it. Hearing becomes a metaphor for perception generally: we often override our own perception to conform to someone else's, and owning your way of perceiving can be an act of self-respect.

head: Grand canvas, intimate story
dek: The episode's storytelling principle: epic events matter on screen when you zoom into one person facing one problem.
more: The episode's storytelling principle: epic events matter on screen when you zoom into one person facing one problem. A macrocosm, like ERP's ideological zeal rising and falling, can contain a microcosm, like a marriage, that mirrors it.

head: Stakes make the drama
dek: Ajay explains why the Second World War is endlessly compelling: individual life-and-death decisions coincide with the fate of the world.
more: Ajay explains why the Second World War is endlessly compelling: individual life-and-death decisions coincide with the fate of the world. The Falklands War had dramatic moments but low stakes, so nobody wants that movie. He makes the point with the quip that academic politics is vicious because the stakes are so low. Amit gently disagrees: any story with humans in it has high stakes.

head: The means matter, not just the ends
dek: Amit loves India but feels deep disquiet that it was assembled from 500-plus princely states through coercion and broken promises.
more: Amit loves India but feels deep disquiet that it was assembled from 500-plus princely states through coercion and broken promises. He calls it 'fast-track colonization': what the British did over centuries, Patel and Menon did in a couple of years. Once you accept that the end justifies the means, any imagined end can license brutality. He suggests Americans may feel similar dissonance about Native Americans.

head: Counterfactuals: Goa, Surat and five hundred Indias
dek: Ajay asks what if Goa had stayed European and inherited first-world institutions, or the British had kept Surat as a 'Hong Kong of India', the way Hong Kong at China's doorstep helped Deng Xiaoping's reforms.
more: Ajay asks what if Goa had stayed European and inherited first-world institutions, or the British had kept Surat as a 'Hong Kong of India', the way Hong Kong at China's doorstep helped Deng Xiaoping's reforms. Amit imagines many small states, too weak to fight but competing to govern well, in line with their shared belief in decentralisation. Ajay pushes back: India's princely states had very poor political development, unlike England's long path from the Magna Carta in 1215 to checks and balances. The deeper point is that the world is shaped by accidents and could have been otherwise.

head: The paratrooper playbook
dek: Airborne troops drop behind enemy lines, seize a critical asset such as an airfield, fly in heavy equipment, and sow confusion while the main force pushes to link up.
more: Airborne troops drop behind enemy lines, seize a critical asset such as an airfield, fly in heavy equipment, and sow confusion while the main force pushes to link up. It worked in Crete in 1941 with about 6,000 paratroopers. It failed at Arnhem ('A Bridge Too Far') because paratroopers can only hold for a limited time. Russia's capture of Hostomel airport in 2022 followed the same template.

head: First draft of history and sense-making, at once
dek: Journalists traditionally write history's first draft and scholars write the considered account later.
more: Journalists traditionally write history's first draft and scholars write the considered account later. Amit observes that today both happen simultaneously, with analysts like William Spaniel making real-time videos while writing slower books.

head: Amit's mic kept making noises and flipped out of his kurta. Ajay told the cinematographers
more: Amit's mic kept making noises and flipped out of his kurta. head: Ajay describes 1940 France's delusions of grandeur as believing it was a…
more: Ajay describes 1940 France's delusions of grandeur as believing it was a 'Vishwaguru' with novel philosophy to give the world, a sly dig using the Indian nationalist buzzword. Amit later reuses it while mocking the Jodhpur negotiation: 'we'll be Vishwaguru one day.'

head: On the Doolittle Raid crews obeying orders on a near-suicidal mission
more: On the Doolittle Raid crews obeying orders on a near-suicidal mission: 'even though your commander is a guy called Doolittle.'

more: Amit on Japan's misreading of the carrier sighting: someone's fatal sin was that he was naval gazing and not navel gazing. Ajay: 'He was fighting the last war, so to speak.'

head: Ajay dismisses the Falklands as low-stakes
more: Ajay dismisses the Falklands as low-stakes, 'like academic politics', and Amit refuses to let the aside slip by unnoticed. Ajay finishes it: 'Why is academic politics so vicious? The answer is because the stakes are so low.'

more: On Zelensky's comedy-to-presidency path, Amit: 'the difference is that India did not make Kapil Sharma the president.'

more: Ajay on old war movies: they were made so badly, Soviet propaganda films included, 'that you could see the cardboard tanks being blown up.'

more: Zelensky's legendary reply when the Americans offered to evacuate him: 'I don't want a ride, I want ammo.' It inspired this episode's fifth chapter title.

more: David Byrne in How Music Works imagines ERP's engineers as uniformed men communicating in silence, 'like some acoustic Sherlock Holmes', able to survey a room with their ears.

more: Amit likens ERP's evangelising of its sound values to 'an American version of Macaulay', cultural imperialism through acoustics. ERP arrived just before Al Jolson's The Jazz Singer ushered in sound cinema.

head: Amit frames the making of India as not just
more: Amit frames the making of India as not just 'the discovery of India', as Nehru put it, but its invention: a vision imposed on people who may not have wanted it.
Trump's 'perfect phone call' with Zelensky, in which, per Ajay, Javelin anti-tank missiles were held up to pressure Zelensky into launching a fake investigation against Biden's son.

head: Amit recalls Ukraine's wartime innovation, an…
more: Amit recalls Ukraine's wartime innovation, an 'Uber for artillery', and the death in combat of the vice president of the Ukraine Chess Federation as emblems of ordinary people's heroism.

head: Clearing out his father's house
dek: The house became a mirror. Amit realised his mind had the same problem: years of accumulated preoccupations taking up the real estate that should go to what matters.
more: Amit's father died during the second wave of Covid, and Amit had to clear his big house in Chandigarh. It was full of thousands of books, trunks, furniture and curios. Despite living in a huge bungalow with many rooms, his father had effectively been living in half a room, because everything else was full of things. Amit had no space for the books, so he brought three friends to take what they wanted. His own rule was to keep only books he wanted to read that were so rare they weren't available anywhere, not even as a downloadable PDF. He chucked the rest. The one exception was a 50-volume Great Books of the Western World set that his father had urged him to take for ten years. Amit keeps it purely for sentiment and admits he'll never read it.

The house became a mirror. Amit realised his mind had the same problem: years of accumulated preoccupations taking up the real estate that should go to what matters. That is what turned physical decluttering into a resolution about mental decluttering.
printed: Half a room in a big bungalow

head: 'Every time a friend of mine does well, a part of me dies'
dek: Decluttering applies to people too. Amit now cuts out negativity on purpose.
more: In the late 1990s, Amit and a friend (now a celebrated and controversial novelist) walked out of dinner at Oh! Calcutta in Tardeo, Bombay. The friend said, 'You know, Amit, every time a friend of mine does well, a part of me dies.' He was trying to be clever, but Amit stopped in the street, stunned. He came to see that many people are like this: they smile and pretend to wish you well, but they don't.

Decluttering applies to people too. Amit now cuts out negativity on purpose. He has curated his Twitter feed, left gossipy WhatsApp groups, and avoids people who snark at others instead of trying to do better themselves.

head: Keith Jarrett and the broken piano in Cologne
dek: Harford's thesis is that being thrown out of your comfort zone can unlock creativity that autopilot never would.
more: Amit retells the story that opens Tim Harford's book Messy. In January 1975, 17-year-old Vera Brandes, the youngest concert organiser in Europe, booked the legendary Keith Jarrett for a sold-out show in Cologne. The hall couldn't get the Bösendorfer he needed and supplied a small, inferior piano instead. Its sound didn't reach the balcony and some keys didn't work. In the pouring rain a replacement couldn't be moved, so Jarrett sat in his car, ready to leave. Brandes knocked on his window in tears, and he agreed to play for her sake. Forced to pound the keys and work within a narrow range on an instrument he had never played, he improvised. The resulting album, The Köln Concert, sold about 3.5 million copies and, as Amit recalls it, became the best-selling solo jazz and piano album ever.
Harford's thesis is that being thrown out of your comfort zone can unlock creativity that autopilot never would. A life curated into perfect comfort risks losing exactly that.

head: The nephew in a tiny New York flat
dek: A hard constraint can build the habit of intentional buying that willpower alone rarely sustains.
more: Ajay's nephew Hemen lives in a very small flat in New York. The lack of space has pushed him to extremes of decluttering. By default he doesn't own things, and he buys something only if it really fits his life and his tiny 'budget' of space. Ajay adds a jab at Indian debates that set a minimum size for affordable housing: go visit New York sometime.
A hard constraint can build the habit of intentional buying that willpower alone rarely sustains. Amit reads Hemen as 'dancing in chains', with space as his chains.

head: Where is your Gangauli?
dek: It is a beautiful way to separate the place you face from the place you belong.
more: On The Seen and the Unseen, Amitava Kumar once told Amit about a scene from Rahi Masoom Raza's novel Aadha Gaon, set at Partition. Activists urge a Muslim villager to go to Pakistan. He replies that when he prays he turns towards Mecca, but when he thinks of home he thinks of his village, Gangauli. Amit now asks guests, 'Where is your Gangauli?' Max Rodenbeck, who grew up in Cairo, said his Gangauli is the Cairo of his childhood, which no longer exists. Amit admits he has no answer of his own. He laments being cosmopolitan but not rooted, and settles on home being whatever surrounds him: his books, his room, the vibe.

It is a beautiful way to separate the place you face from the place you belong. In an age when everything lives in the cloud, it raises the question of whether home is a place at all or something we carry around with us.

head: 365 sprints, not a marathon
dek: Steady output can hide a destructive process. The healthier model is a steady daily baseline that makes sprinting easy when it's genuinely needed, rather than sprinting as the only way of working.
more: Ajay asks how Amit ships both The Seen and the Unseen and Everything is Everything every week. Amit answers: 'Badly.' The weekly deadline is the only reason he gets them done. And his 365 episodes look like a marathon but are really 365 sprints. He doesn't sleep for two days before each recording, then spends two days recovering. His resolution for his 'second half century' is to replace this with a real marathon of daily habits: an hour of writing, two hours of reading, every day.
Steady output can hide a destructive process. The healthier model is a steady daily baseline that makes sprinting easy when it's genuinely needed, rather than sprinting as the only way of working.

head: To Have or To Be?
dek: Fromm's 1976 book was a pioneer on these questions: how to move beyond the simple consumerism many Indians discovered only in the last 20–30 years, towards a better sense of why we are here and what gives life meaning.
more: Fromm's 1976 book was a pioneer on these questions: how to move beyond the simple consumerism many Indians discovered only in the last 20–30 years, towards a better sense of why we are here and what gives life meaning.
Ajay's recommendation of the day, right after Amit jokes that listeners aren't allowed to buy anything because this is a decluttering episode.

head: The Köln Concert
dek: A celebrated masterpiece improvised on a substandard piano Jarrett had never played.
more: A celebrated masterpiece improvised on a substandard piano Jarrett had never played. It is the best illustration of creativity coming from mess.

dek: A beautiful lyric about our place in the natural order, with the lines 'like every sparrow falling, like every grain of sand'.
more: A beautiful lyric about our place in the natural order, with the lines 'like every sparrow falling, like every grain of sand'.

head: Biophilia
dek: Wilson's idea of biophilia, the wonder at every leaf, fungus and virus as something magical, is where Ajay's reverence for 'statistically improbable' arrangements of atoms begins.
more: Wilson's idea of biophilia, the wonder at every leaf, fungus and virus as something magical, is where Ajay's reverence for 'statistically improbable' arrangements of atoms begins.

head: The Blind Watchmaker
dek: Dawkins shows the eye is improbable yet has no designer. Ajay turns this around: a fabricated watch is also a miraculous arrangement of atoms, so things deserve to be used rather than left idle.
more: Dawkins shows the eye is improbable yet has no designer. Ajay turns this around: a fabricated watch is also a miraculous arrangement of atoms, so things deserve to be used rather than left idle.
Ajay cites the watch-on-the-beach versus the human eye argument, then flips it.

head: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
dek: Dunbar's research shows we can sustain only about 150 meaningful connections, and most of our emotional energy goes to roughly 5 and then 15 people.
more: Dunbar's research shows we can sustain only about 150 meaningful connections, and most of our emotional energy goes to roughly 5 and then 15 people.
Behind Ajay's argument for decluttering your social life.

head: Great Books of the Western World
dek: Not a reading recommendation (he admits he'll never read it). It is the one artifact he kept for sentiment, an example of what is worth keeping and why.
more: Not a reading recommendation (he admits he'll never read it). It is the one artifact he kept for sentiment, an example of what is worth keeping and why.
The 50-volume set Amit kept from his father's house, linked in the show notes.

head: The things you own end up owning you
dek: Amit's summary of decluttering, borrowing Chuck Palahniuk's line. Every possession becomes baggage.
more: Amit's summary of decluttering, borrowing Chuck Palahniuk's line. Every possession becomes baggage. Joshua Fields Millburn's version: a happy life comes from subtracting, not adding. Strip life down and the mind becomes uncluttered too.

head: Two roots of decluttering: the monk and the tech bro
dek: Ajay sees two strands merging. One is the ancient spiritual ideal of the monk who owns nothing.
more: Ajay sees two strands merging. One is the ancient spiritual ideal of the monk who owns nothing. The other is the modern tech bro's wish to protect his brain and work with intensity on a few things.

head: Live in the micro: one thing today
dek: Taking Annie Dillard's 'How we live our days is how we live our lives', Amit argues that we obsess over grand goals while life is just an accumulation of days.
more: Taking Annie Dillard's 'How we live our days is how we live our lives', Amit argues that we obsess over grand goals while life is just an accumulation of days. Instead of a panic-inducing ten-item to-do list, commit to one thing a day. Everything after that is a bonus.
printed: A mind like his father’s house

head: Declutter the mind: preoccupations and toxic people
dek: The clutter that matters most is mental. That means unimportant preoccupations crowding out what matters, and toxic, envious or gossipy people who drain energy.
more: The clutter that matters most is mental. That means unimportant preoccupations crowding out what matters, and toxic, envious or gossipy people who drain energy. Keep people who make you want to become a better version of yourself.

head: Things are replaceable; time is not
dek: With everything in the cloud, Amit enjoys objects (thirteen shower gels!) but isn't attached to any of them.
more: With everything in the cloud, Amit enjoys objects (thirteen shower gels!) but isn't attached to any of them. He also sees a 'false virtue' in performatively renouncing things. The real wealth is experiences and relationships, and the real scarcity is time.

head: Embrace productive mess
dek: Routines and discipline are good, but a fully curated life of familiar voices and comfort breeds autopilot.
more: Routines and discipline are good, but a fully curated life of familiar voices and comfort breeds autopilot. Creative people, Darwin among them, tend to work on several projects at once (per research by Howard Gruber and Sara Davis, cited in Harford's Messy). Amit's own experiment is writing by hand in a paper diary every day, because the medium makes the mind work differently.

head: Tsundoku as a surface area of serendipity
dek: Owning more books than you'll read isn't necessarily clutter. Unread books surround you with possibilities you haven't discovered yet.
more: Owning more books than you'll read isn't necessarily clutter. Unread books surround you with possibilities you haven't discovered yet.

head: Dancing in chains
dek: Ranjit Hoskote's phrase, adopted by Amit. Everyone lives within constraints of space, money or time, and the task is to dance as well as you can within them.
more: Ranjit Hoskote's phrase, adopted by Amit. Everyone lives within constraints of space, money or time, and the task is to dance as well as you can within them.
printed: In praise of a little chaos

head: Rooted cosmopolitanism and the portable home
dek: Sugata Srinivasaraju's ideal of being both rooted and cosmopolitan. Amit has only the cosmopolitan half, and so locates home in whatever surrounds him rather than in a place.
more: Sugata Srinivasaraju's ideal of being both rooted and cosmopolitan. Amit has only the cosmopolitan half, and so locates home in whatever surrounds him rather than in a place.

head: India's abundance shock broke our thumb rules
dek: Between roughly 1991 and 2011, trade barriers fell and incomes rose at the same time.
more: Between roughly 1991 and 2011, trade barriers fell and incomes rose at the same time. India went from scarcity to plenty within one generation. Habits about what to buy and what to keep, built for scarcity, are now miscalibrated, which makes India's clutter problem especially big.

head: Consumer surplus pays for experiments
dek: Reviews can't tell you whether a gadget fits your life; only trying it can.
more: Reviews can't tell you whether a gadget fits your life; only trying it can. When you find the right fit, the gap between what you'd pay and what you paid is so large that it covers many failed purchases. So buy cheap gadgets boldly, learn from them, and be a 'grim reaper' about the misses.

head: Never buy to impress
dek: Buying to flaunt is a waste of life. Ajay's rules for clothes: start with cheap, functional basics.
more: Buying to flaunt is a waste of life. Ajay's rules for clothes: start with cheap, functional basics. Respect genuine fashion knowledge, since it isn't all a con. Value technical gear (merino inners, hiking pants) and things that last; he still wears 30-year-old pants because his body size hasn't changed since college.

head: One in, one out
dek: Their friend Vishal Nevatia owns exactly twelve shirts, and if a thirteenth arrives, one must go.
more: Their friend Vishal Nevatia owns exactly twelve shirts, and if a thirteenth arrives, one must go. Capping inventory ties what comes in to what goes out, so junk can never pile up.

head: Respect the atoms: gift away what you don't use
dek: Every fabricated object is a statistically improbable arrangement of atoms, a miracle by historical standards.
more: Every fabricated object is a statistically improbable arrangement of atoms, a miracle by historical standards. What you paid is a sunk cost and irrelevant. The only question is whether you're using it. If not, give it to someone who will rather than letting it idle or end up in a landfill.

head: Don't gift what you think is bad
dek: Amit's caveat to Ajay. By Sturgeon's Law most human-made things are crap, and following Tyler Cowen, he won't pass on books he dislikes.
more: Amit's caveat to Ajay. By Sturgeon's Law most human-made things are crap, and following Tyler Cowen, he won't pass on books he dislikes. Someone who reads only one or two books a year shouldn't have one of them be bad.

head: The superpower of living in a pigsty
dek: Needing a neat environment before you can think is itself a cognitive burden.
more: Needing a neat environment before you can think is itself a cognitive burden. Ajay trains himself to work anywhere, on a floor or a railway platform, so his thinking has no preconditions.

head: Declutter people: the 5 and the 15
dek: Per Robin Dunbar, we can sustain about 150 meaningful connections. About 40% of our emotional energy goes to 5 people and another 20% to 15 more.
more: Per Robin Dunbar, we can sustain about 150 meaningful connections. About 40% of our emotional energy goes to 5 people and another 20% to 15 more. Rather than spreading ourselves thin on shallow interactions and FOMO, accept that circle and lavish attention on it.

head: The innovation funnel
dek: Like a sales funnel: generate many wild ideas freely, triage instinctively, and carry only a few through to completion.
more: Like a sales funnel: generate many wild ideas freely, triage instinctively, and carry only a few through to completion. Unfinished projects are not failures; they are the cost of finding the good ones. Feeling obliged to finish everything you start produces B- and C-grade work.

head: Two gears: triage, then tunnel
dek: With 150 unfinished papers, Ajay works in two modes. First he triages to pick the one thing for now.
more: With 150 unfinished papers, Ajay works in two modes. First he triages to pick the one thing for now. Then he blocks hours to do it with full intensity while ignoring everything else clamouring for attention. Then he comes out, triages again, and goes back in.

head: Say no to things you love
dek: Saying no to what you dislike is trivial. Focus means turning down the many things you'd madly love to do so you can actually commit to one.
more: Saying no to what you dislike is trivial. Focus means turning down the many things you'd madly love to do so you can actually commit to one.

head: Bias towards action
dek: Amit's warning about the innovation funnel: procrastinators can use 'marinating ideas' as an excuse never to execute.
more: Amit's warning about the innovation funnel: procrastinators can use 'marinating ideas' as an excuse never to execute. Ideas sound good and implementation is hard. Pick any one, do it, mess it up, and learn by doing.

head: Perun: The Anonymous PowerPoint Sense-Maker
dek: Depth and substance can build an audience without credentials, production budgets or the backing of the media establishment.
more: Ajay introduced Amit to Perun while they prepared their five-and-a-half-hour Ukraine episode for The Seen and the Unseen. Perun is a pseudonymous economist whose YouTube videos are just PowerPoint slides with him talking over them. He never shows his face, has no bestselling books and no TV channel behind him, and his slides are crammed with words, against every presentation rule. He still has close to half a million subscribers, and many videos pass a million views. Amit draws four lessons. Real expertise shows nuance and data rather than certainty. Gatekeepers are no longer needed. Anyone with PowerPoint can do it. And what audiences crave is sense-making.
Depth and substance can build an audience without credentials, production budgets or the backing of the media establishment. People are hungry for understanding, not just noise.

head: Perun Passes the Gell-Mann Amnesia Test
dek: Check a source against the subject you know best. A creator who survives that test has earned a measure of trust on the subjects you can't verify.
more: Amit explains Gell-Mann amnesia, a term Michael Crichton coined after his friend, the physicist Murray Gell-Mann. You read a newspaper, spot rubbish in the one field you know, and still trust everything else in it. Amit often feels let down when experts he admires talk about a subject he knows, and he wonders whether they bluff elsewhere too. Having done several episodes on Indian defence, he expected Perun to slip. Instead he found no elementary errors, and Perun understood the Indian defence industry better than many people whose job it is to know it.
Check a source against the subject you know best. A creator who survives that test has earned a measure of trust on the subjects you can't verify.

head: The Township That Must Fly to Space: Perun's Procurement Parable
dek: When tiny budgets, fantasy specifications, forced indigenisation and red tape all pile up, the best vendors walk away.
more: Amit retells Perun's critique of Indian defence procurement in his own metaphor, admitting Perun did it better. Imagine you are a foreign defence firm. India gives you the budget for a single room and asks you to build a super-advanced township that can fly to space. You must work with an Indian partner, own only 49%, transfer all your technology and know-how, and take 100% of the blame if anything goes wrong. Meanwhile the requirements may keep changing. Perun's summary: the army asks for 2030 technology, is told it can have 2010 technology, says no, and stays stuck with 1940 technology. As Perun puts it, this calls for a slow clap.
When tiny budgets, fantasy specifications, forced indigenisation and red tape all pile up, the best vendors walk away. The buyer then ends up with the oldest equipment of all.
printed: A township on a room’s budget

head: MiG-21s, a Retired Rifle and a Fighter on Foreign Engines
dek: Path dependence is real, but it does not excuse failing to plan a platform's replacement.
more: Amit lists Perun's examples of dysfunction. Ten years ago India rejected foreign assault-rifle designs to build its own, and is now retiring that rifle and going back to foreign designs. India spent some thirty years trying to build an indigenous fighter, the Tejas, while costs ballooned, and it now flies with foreign engines. Worst of all, MiG-21s, aircraft of the 1960s, are still in service when they should have been retired thirty years ago. Search 'MiG-21 crash' and you find experienced pilots, scarce human capital, dying in them.
Path dependence is real, but it does not excuse failing to plan a platform's replacement. Here the planning failure is paid for in pilots' lives.

head: How Ajay's College Lab Dates the LCA
dek: A country that tries to build frontier equipment alone can spend decades on it, and by the time it is ready the world has moved on.
more: When Ajay started college in 1983, he benefited greatly from a computational fluid dynamics lab funded as part of the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) project. The money came through the Aeronautical Development Agency, which was set up to do the deep R&D for the LCA. He uses this to show how old the LCA project is: its research was already running when he was a first-year student.
A country that tries to build frontier equipment alone can spend decades on it, and by the time it is ready the world has moved on.

head: The Military Pension Deal That Vanished
dek: Reform agreements can evaporate through changes of government and bureaucratic reshuffles.
more: In the early days of the National Pension System (NPS), S. Narayan in the Finance Ministry sent Ajay to hold careful meetings with the Army, Navy and Air Force on how NPS would be brought to the military. The senior leadership of all three services agreed orally. Then the UPA came to power in 2004. The CPI(M) blocked NPS for years, and pensions were moved, wrongly in Ajay's view, from the Department of Economic Affairs to the Department of Financial Services. All institutional memory was lost, and when NPS finally rolled out, the military link was gone.

Reform agreements can evaporate through changes of government and bureaucratic reshuffles. The result here was One Rank One Pension (OROP), which is why pensions now swallow so much of the defence budget.
printed: The pension deal that went AWOL

head: The Health Expert Who Envied Finance
dek: Specialists who stay in their own field think its problems are unique.
more: For years, a health-expert friend of Ajay's believed Indian healthcare worked badly because economists kept all the best people in finance. Ajay took years to convince her that finance has huge problems too. The same failures run across health, finance, defence, intelligence and monetary policy.
Specialists who stay in their own field think its problems are unique. With some breadth you see that the underlying problems are the same everywhere.

head: From the Free Corps to the Brownshirts
dek: Militarism flows both ways between an army and its society. Civilian control and a professional, apolitical army are institutional achievements, not accidents.
more: After the First World War, German veterans formed an informal organisation called the Free Corps, which became home to toxic right-wing nationalism. They brought back strongman values, intolerance and a readiness for street violence. That was the raw material for the Nazi Party, and many brownshirts came from the Free Corps. Hitler's society then fed back into a military project to conquer the world, which ended terribly for Germany. Ajay contrasts this with Nehru's achievement of keeping the Indian army in its barracks as a professional force. Amit adds Pakistan, where the military came to dominate society.
Militarism flows both ways between an army and its society. Civilian control and a professional, apolitical army are institutional achievements, not accidents.

head: 'Saamagri Taiyaar Hai': Narasimha Rao's Handover to Vajpayee
dek: Strategic shifts survive when leaders across party lines share a vision.
more: After Narasimha Rao died, Vajpayee told this story. When Rao handed over power in 1996, he told Vajpayee 'Saamagri taiyaar hai': the material is ready, the nuclear tests can be carried out. Rao had not run the tests himself because elections had brought in a new government, and he left them to it as a courtesy. Amit adds that Manmohan Singh continued the turn away from the Soviet Union. During UPA-1 he pushed the nuclear deal with the US against opposition from the Left, even within his own party, and was ready to give up being Prime Minister over it.
Strategic shifts survive when leaders across party lines share a vision. Ajay's caveat is that this realignment came from the top, not from the bureaucracy, and so remained incomplete.

head: France and Germany: From Four Wars to a Passport-Free Commute
dek: Even the bitterest enemies can build a lasting peace through institutions.
more: France and Germany killed each other in the Napoleonic Wars, in 1870, in 1914 and again up to 1945. After that they were fully at peace. Today people living in France wake up, drive to work in Germany and never show a passport at the border.
Even the bitterest enemies can build a lasting peace through institutions. Diplomacy aims to make war unnecessary, and killing fewer people is a high virtue worth sacrificing other things for.

head: A Heretical Thought Experiment on 1971
dek: Indians tend to blame the US for 1971. Ajay instead treats it as a diplomatic failure that India could have handled differently, a useful habit of looking at one's own agency.
more: Ajay asks what would have happened if the United States had not backed Pakistan so deeply in 1971. Perhaps Bangladesh could have broken away anyway. He argues that Indian foreign policy itself left the US solidly aligned with Pakistan and against India. Pakistan then felt strong enough to commit atrocities in Bangladesh and get away with them.
Indians tend to blame the US for 1971. Ajay instead treats it as a diplomatic failure that India could have handled differently, a useful habit of looking at one's own agency.

head: Selecting Soldiers by a 15-Kilometre Run
dek: Selecting for the trait that is easy to train, and ignoring the one that isn't, skews the whole pipeline away from what modern war demands.
more: Ajay says he is depressed by newspaper reports about how Indian military hiring filters candidates. Thousands of young men gather at a village and run 15 kilometres, and roughly the fastest one percent get shortlisted. His response: almost anyone can be trained to military fitness, but not to the brainpower a modern army needs.
Selecting for the trait that is easy to train, and ignoring the one that isn't, skews the whole pipeline away from what modern war demands.

head: Poland Buys a Korean Tank
dek: A country with limited money is better off buying one notch below the frontier at scale, through partnerships, than chasing the best equipment or self-reliance.
more: Poland is preparing for a possible Russian invasion if Ukraine falls and wants thousands of tanks. It did not buy the German Leopard or the American Abrams. It chose a very good South Korean tank, a notch below those, that fits its budget. It also signed deep contracts with the Koreans: partnering in R&D and manufacturing, taking equity and earning royalties on future global sales.
A country with limited money is better off buying one notch below the frontier at scale, through partnerships, than chasing the best equipment or self-reliance.

more: Perun is a model sense-maker. He goes deep, lays out all the data and viewpoints, writes excellent show notes, claims no false certainty, and was Amit's guide to the Russia-Ukraine war.

more: It is detailed and accurate on the Indian defence industry, with no elementary errors, and Amit found it better informed than many people whose job is to know this.

more: It is a history of how the Indian Army evolved, including the debates in the 40s, 50s and 60s over what role it should play in society. Amit says it gave him a really nuanced understanding of the subject.

more: It is very hard to write a genuinely new book on WWII, and Ajay says Hanson has done it, with deeper ideas, a more meta-level analysis and implications for today's world.
Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode. He first tells everyone to read any twenty books on the Second World War, then suggests this one.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: Its framework of four cross-cutting failures (HR, contracting, budgeting and checks on coercive power) explains defence as well as health or finance.
more: Its framework of four cross-cutting failures (HR, contracting, budgeting and checks on coercive power) explains defence as well as health or finance. Amit calls it an eye-opener.
Amit cites the book's chapter on 'foundational processes' to set up Ajay's explanation of why the same failures recur across Indian public policy.

head: 'Wet Streets Cause Rain': Michael Crichton explains Gell-Mann Amnesia
dek: It is Crichton's own explanation of why we trust media on topics we can't check after catching it out on the ones we can.
more: It is Crichton's own explanation of why we trust media on topics we can't check after catching it out on the ones we can.
Linked after Amit explains Gell-Mann amnesia in praising Perun's accuracy.
