dek: It gives more background on Indian national security.
more: It gives more background on Indian national security.
Another of Amit's earlier episodes on Indian defence, linked in the show notes.

head: Sense-Makers Over Credentials
dek: Amit argues that real expertise means depth, data and nuance, not TV-style certainty.
more: Amit argues that real expertise means depth, data and nuance, not TV-style certainty. In a world flooded with information, we need trusted curators or 'sense-makers', and Amit uses social media mainly to follow such people across different fields. Ajay adds that Perun disproves two stereotypes: that you need elite credentials, and that online platforms reward only shallow content.

head: Wars Are Won by Brains, Not Machismo
dek: Ajay argues that bellicosity and fanaticism belong to the Middle Ages, and fanatics don't win wars.
more: Ajay argues that bellicosity and fanaticism belong to the Middle Ages, and fanatics don't win wars. Modern war is a complex thinking project of strategy, logistics, tactics, training, teamwork and adaptation under fire, like chess. The 1971 army of Sam Manekshaw, Y. B. Chavan and Indira Gandhi was quiet, clinical and professional. Ajay sees today's macho image of the army as a recent populist turn that should be questioned.

head: Military Strategy in Three Steps: Threats, Cost-Efficient Force Design, Incremental Evolution
dek: First, write down the threats you face, which change over time; China's economy growing to five times India's is one example.
more: First, write down the threats you face, which change over time; China's economy growing to five times India's is one example. Second, design a force that meets those threats cost-efficiently. With an infinite budget anything is possible, but democracies can't spend like North Korea or Russia. Third, move toward that design step by step. India spends about half a percent of GDP a year on equipment that lasts about 20 years, so replacing everything at once is unaffordable. Instead, upgrade what you have, such as fitting old T-72 and T-90 tanks with new weapons and electronics.

head: The Missing Long-Horizon Strategy Community
dek: Ajay says Indian government organisations can't think strategically because officials plan only for their own tenure.
more: Ajay says Indian government organisations can't think strategically because officials plan only for their own tenure. In the UK, US and Germany, informal national-security and economic-strategy communities persist across elections and hold the 25-year view. India had this briefly in economics from about 1977 to 2011, and in foreign policy under Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee and Jaswant Singh after the USSR collapsed. Both efforts stayed incomplete, and a pro-Soviet, pro-Russian strain of thinking persists, even though India's business, education and economic ties now run to the West.

head: Foundational Processes: The Same Plumbing Breaks Everywhere
dek: Ajay and Vijay Kelkar identify four failures that hit every area of Indian policy: HR (hiring, firing, promotion, measuring performance), government contracting, budgeting and finance (including paying vendors on time), and checks and balances on coercive power.
more: Ajay and Vijay Kelkar identify four failures that hit every area of Indian policy: HR (hiring, firing, promotion, measuring performance), government contracting, budgeting and finance (including paying vendors on time), and checks and balances on coercive power. Experts who stay in their own silo miss this. Within health, people narrow further to 'polio' or 'HIV'. They also treat these processes as beyond their pay grade; a military officer can't change the General Financial Rules (GFR) that govern government contracting. Amit draws the lesson in the show's name: everything is everything, so don't let your vision get compartmentalised.

head: Build Capability by Narrowing Scope First
dek: Early European states did only two things, raising taxes and waging wars, and through them learned HR, contracting and public financial management.
more: Early European states did only two things, raising taxes and waging wars, and through them learned HR, contracting and public financial management. They did not run ordnance factories. Arms came from private vendors and mercenaries, who even sold arms to Indian kings, so states had to become good at contracting. India did the reverse. As one of the poorest and least capable states, it expanded in a socialist frenzy into almost everything, and now does everything at small scale and badly.

head: Diplomacy Is the Outer Layer; War Is What Happens When It Fails
dek: Military power is the big stick that must exist but should be used as little as possible, because it is costly and killing is morally wrong.
more: Military power is the big stick that must exist but should be used as little as possible, because it is costly and killing is morally wrong. Ajay cites the First World War, Hitler's invasion of Poland and Putin's invasion of Ukraine as failures of diplomacy. Diplomacy means countries negotiating changes to their domestic policies to suit each other. India's opening position of 'strategic autonomy' rules that out, and in 1947 India inherited a strong military but no foreign-policy capability. Treaties and coalitions let countries insure each other against risk, which lowers defence costs. Going it alone against China, whose economy is about as much bigger than India's as Russia's is than Ukraine's, would be very expensive.

head: Only the US Can Go It Alone, and It Doesn't
dek: The US can develop frontier weapons by itself at a sensible cost for three reasons.
more: The US can develop frontier weapons by itself at a sensible cost for three reasons. It has the deepest private defence-research ecosystem, funded by DARPA and others. It builds thousands of fighters for export rather than hundreds. And it doesn't actually insist on self-reliance, since contracts flow to Japan, Israel and Europe. Everyone else builds in partnerships: Germany with Britain, Korea with Poland, Japan with many countries. Supply chains also depend on foreign policy. If a tank's laser range finder comes from Sweden, being prickly with Sweden puts that supply at risk. India's Arjun tank and LCA show what going it alone produces: equipment that arrives twenty years too late.

head: Perun's Diagnosis: Four Horsemen and a Pension Squeeze
dek: As Amit relays it, Perun names four horsemen of the defence procurement apocalypse: tiny budgets, fantastical requirements, demands for indigenisation, and bureaucratic procedure.
more: As Amit relays it, Perun names four horsemen of the defence procurement apocalypse: tiny budgets, fantastical requirements, demands for indigenisation, and bureaucratic procedure. The US budget is about ten times India's and China's about five times. Of India's budget, 53% goes on salaries and pensions, with pensions alone at 23%, up from 12% in 2008. Of roughly $47 billion in 2023, only about $3.7 billion went on modernisation. Amit cautions that some figures may be slightly off.

head: A Young Country With an Old Army
dek: India's large young population should give it a young army, but the hiring model makes soldiering a career.
more: India's large young population should give it a young army, but the hiring model makes soldiering a career. Long service contracts take soldiers into their 30s, followed by decades of pensions. Foreign armies use fixed-term contracts and keep on only some soldiers. The Agnipath scheme tried that model, with short initial contracts, longer terms for a minority, and a one-time tax-free severance instead of pensions. It triggered protests across the country because Indians see the army as a job for life.

head: Hire for Brainpower, Train the Biceps
dek: Ajay argues that the bottleneck in a modern army is brainpower, not fitness.
more: Ajay argues that the bottleneck in a modern army is brainpower, not fitness. Half-jokingly, his recruitment exam would be a chess.com Elo rating plus poker, because on a battlefield the board is not fully visible. He wants small, highly trained, empowered, even subversive teams, in the spirit of the Marines' 'adapt, improvise, overcome'. Ukrainians are rewriting the software of Western equipment and finding uses its makers never imagined. Women make up 10% of Ukraine's army and make excellent snipers because they are calm, patient and clinical.

head: Defence Economics: One Notch Behind the Frontier, Then Scale
dek: Ajay's prescription for a poor country is to specify equipment one notch below the global frontier and get unit costs down through scale.
more: Ajay's prescription for a poor country is to specify equipment one notch below the global frontier and get unit costs down through scale. That means fewer types of equipment (flying a mix of Rafales, MiG-21s and Sukhois is confused), integration into global supply chains, and exports, as in India's car industry. He compares counting equipment to judging a chess position by adding up piece values, which tells you little: Israel was outgunned in 1967 and still won the Six-Day War, and Ukraine has held off a better-equipped Russia. Accept limited resources, don't blame your tools, and focus on the human brain.

head: Build a New Army Beside the Old One
dek: The Navy and Air Force are already small, technical and English-speaking, while the army is still largely an agricultural workforce.
more: The Navy and Air Force are already small, technical and English-speaking, while the army is still largely an agricultural workforce. Merging them now into theatre commands could smother the better culture, as happens when a small firm merges into a giant one. Ajay suggests copying Russia's battalion tactical groups: new formations of about a thousand people with new manuals, modern equipment and deep integration with the Air Force and Navy. Meanwhile the old army would be slowly downsized, the way an old pension system is phased out. China's PLA, once a mass force much like India's army, laid off about half its personnel to modernise.

head: Nuclear Deterrence Has Broken the Reform-Through-Failure Loop
dek: Historically, states that performed badly got beaten, and defeat forced reform.
more: Historically, states that performed badly got beaten, and defeat forced reform. India's 1962 defeat led Nehru and others to deep army reforms that paid off in 1965 and 1971. Economic policy works the same way: India adopted inflation targeting only after a great inflation crisis. Nuclear deterrence between India, China and Pakistan has largely stopped such wars, so there has been no major test of the military since 1999. Weaknesses could be piling up unseen until a conventional war, like Ukraine's, exposes them.

head: Ideas Come Before Implementation
dek: Ajay's counterweight to the pessimism is that India is building, for the first time, a body of knowledge and a new generation of people who understand law, public administration and state capacity.
more: Ajay's counterweight to the pessimism is that India is building, for the first time, a body of knowledge and a new generation of people who understand law, public administration and state capacity. Many reforms discussed in this episode never happened because neither the knowledge nor the people existed. In an open society ideas matter, and that groundwork comes before change.

head: Ajay: Perun is…
more: Ajay: Perun is 'not a Harvard MIT New York Times.' Amit: 'As far as we know.'

head: Ajay calls Perun
more: Ajay calls Perun 'emboldening for the boring old fogies like you and me, who are the purveyors of this kind of dreary multi-hour content.' Amit: 'Speak for yourself, Ajay Shah. You know, I am not boring and dreary and old, at least compared to you.'

head: Amit's pun on Y. B.
more: Amit's pun on Y. B. Chavan: 'Mr. Chavan was a man also given not just to military affairs but metaphysics, because he would always be thinking, why be Chavan?'

head: Perun's dry humour, as Amit relays it: when India and Pakistan inherited their shares of the British Indian Army
more: Perun's dry humour, as Amit relays it: when India and Pakistan inherited their shares of the British Indian Army, 'the guns immediately turned at each other.' And when asked whose side India is on, Perun answers: 'India is on India's side.'

head: A former defence minister, per Perun's video, said the army's weapon requirements read like something
more: A former defence minister, per Perun's video, said the army's weapon requirements read like something 'straight out of a Marvel Comics superhero movie.'

head: Asked for the way out, Ajay answers
more: Asked for the way out, Ajay answers: 'Intellectualism, everything is everything.' Amit: 'As usual, you're giving glib answers to serious questions.'

head: Ajay on the brains a military needs
more: Ajay on the brains a military needs: 'You want Vaishnav levels of brain power in the military. I mean, he's a wimp, he doesn't have any biceps. Adding biceps is trivial.' Vaishnav Vyas shot the episode.

head: Ajay on the Indian elite's ties to the West
more: Ajay on the Indian elite's ties to the West: 'When is the last time you met anybody who went to Russia to get an education? Okay, that's like not a thing that happens anymore. Not that it ever did.'

head: When Amit doubts that the army could ever be cut down politically, Ajay
more: When Amit doubts that the army could ever be cut down politically, Ajay replies: 'This is a country where customs duties went from three fifty percent to fifteen percent. Anything is possible.'
Amit: 'It's so sad that none of us know much about the Indian Navy given the amount of naval gazing we do.'

head: After Ajay's optimistic long view, Amit
more: After Ajay's optimistic long view, Amit says: 'both of us are playing a long game, but as your hero John Maynard Keynes once said, in the long run, we are all dead.'

head: Ajay's recommendation
more: Ajay's recommendation: 'I have 20 recommendations, which is that everybody... should read books on the second world war. It doesn't matter which books you read.' Only after twenty does he offer Hanson's book.

head: Amit's sign-off
more: Amit's sign-off: 'Watch all our previous videos, watch Perun's video, just watch videos all day, right? The world is going to hell. Just watch videos.'

head: Clausewitz's
more: Clausewitz's 'war is politics by other means', with Amit's twist: 'which means if you're doing politics well, you don't need the war.'
Ajay: 'ever since Joan of Arc, the fanatics don't really win wars.' He contrasts this with the toxic masculinity of Telugu and Bollywood films' portrayal of the army.
'Adapt, improvise, overcome', the US Marines saying Ajay uses to describe the brainy force India needs.

head: Ukraine's
more: Ukraine's 'Uber for artillery', which the hosts discussed in their Ukraine episode as an example of improvisation that slow, rule-bound organisations can't manage.

head: Bell Labs: The Monopoly That Could Afford the Long Game
dek: The decisive ingredient was a long time horizon, not a giant budget. A small slice of money, freed from the pressure to ship a feature by January, built much of the modern world.
more: Asked where he would go in a time machine, Bill Gates picked Bell Labs in December 1947, the month the transistor was created. Bell Labs was AT&T's R&D arm, and by the 1960s it employed more than 15,000 people, over 1,200 of them PhDs. Telephony was a natural monopoly with enormous entry barriers, so AT&T had a guaranteed revenue stream and could fund work that did not have to pay off by next quarter. Amit says the figures are often overstated: about 2.8% of revenue went to R&D, and only around 0.3% went to the basic research that produced semiconductors and Unix. Arthur C. Clarke said the New Jersey site looked like a large, modern factory, and it was one: a factory for ideas whose production lines are invisible.
The decisive ingredient was a long time horizon, not a giant budget. A small slice of money, freed from the pressure to ship a feature by January, built much of the modern world.

head: 'Hey, I'm Dick, Let's Go for Lunch'
dek: Great minds multiply each other when they bump into each other casually.
more: In his memoir, Brian Kernighan recalls settling into his new Bell Labs office when a stranger walked in, said 'Hey, I'm Dick, let's go for lunch,' and took him out. Only later did Kernighan realise this was the great Richard Hamming, whose textbook he had learned from. Thompson, Ritchie and the other giants were just across the hall. No single boss controlled your career, there were no departmental walls, and hierarchy was set mostly by whom people respected.

Great minds multiply each other when they bump into each other casually. Kernighan sums it up as 'geography is destiny.' Amit uses this to argue that in-person interaction matters more than performative office attendance does.

head: The Professor Who Forged Ken Thompson's Signature
dek: Good institutions trust people to use judgement about people. Ajay argues that India's turn toward cutoffs and rigid black-and-white rules, and its suspicion of all discretion, has lost something essential.
more: As a Berkeley undergrad, Ken Thompson worked on the university computer from midnight to 8 a.m., calling it 'my personal computer' because nobody else was around. When a professor asked whether he would apply to graduate school, Thompson said no, believing he was just a regular guy. Without telling him, the professor filled in the application, forged his signature and sent it in, and Thompson was admitted. Ajay adds a parallel from his own family. His father, who returned to education late through night school, got poor marks in his Bombay University master's and assumed a PhD was out of reach. The department's elders, who knew him personally, talked it over and took him into the PhD anyway.

Good institutions trust people to use judgement about people. Ajay argues that India's turn toward cutoffs and rigid black-and-white rules, and its suspicion of all discretion, has lost something essential.

head: How the Telephone Company Tracked Down Ken Thompson
dek: Talent clusters pull in more talent: the names on the doors did the recruiting.
more: Thompson told Bell Labs he would never work for a corporation. They kept after him and flew him east to give a talk. Walking down the corridor and reading the names on the doors, he thought how amazing it would be to work near these people. Afterwards he drove to a friend's house, where a printed offer reached him, and then went on to a motel without having decided. Bell Labs reached him there too. When he asked how they had found him, they said they had called every motel in New Jersey. He accepted.
Talent clusters pull in more talent: the names on the doors did the recruiting. The story also shows an organisation using its own particular strengths to win.

head: Unix Was Born on a Junked PDP-7 in Three Weeks
dek: Junk hardware, no funding and a few weeks alone produced one of the most important pieces of software ever written.
more: Multics, a joint project of MIT, Bell Labs and (Ajay thinks) General Electric, failed, and Bell Labs management swore off funding operating-systems research. Ken Thompson found an obsolete PDP-7 with about 16 to 32 kilobytes of memory and a disk that was too fast for the computer. He wrote a Space Travel game on it, where you landed a craft on Jupiter. Fighting with that disk, he built a disk-scheduling algorithm, a file system and a device driver, and realised he was three weeks from a complete operating system. His wife and child left to visit his parents in California, and he planned exactly one week each for an editor, an assembler and a kernel. It worked out that way, and Unix booted.
Junk hardware, no funding and a few weeks alone produced one of the most important pieces of software ever written. Playing with a game led to the foundation of modern computing.

head: Smuggling an Operating System In as Patent Software
dek: When managers won't back the bet you believe in, find a problem they will pay for where your bet is the cheapest solution.
more: Management still would not fund operating-systems work. Bell Labs was filing roughly one patent a day, and patent applications needed strict formatting, diagrams and equations, so management was about to buy a specialised typesetting system from an outside vendor. The Unix group offered to build it in-house for the same money. Privately they knew they would deliver a full document-processing system (roff, then nroff, then troff) running on Unix, and that the deal would let them build Unix out on modern hardware. Management approved.
When managers won't back the bet you believe in, find a problem they will pay for where your bet is the cheapest solution. The term 'markup' in HTML traces back to this typesetting work.

head: Inventing C in Order to Rewrite Unix
dek: Sometimes you have to build the tool that lets you build the thing. Ajay calls C the most important programming language in the world today, and it exists because of Unix.
more: Every operating system of the era was written in assembly language, so it took someone like Ken Thompson to write one at all. Dennis Ritchie asked whether Unix could be written in a high-level language. None of the existing languages were good enough, so he and others created C. Then Thompson and Ritchie rewrote the whole of Unix in C, and Unix became portable to more and more machines.
Sometimes you have to build the tool that lets you build the thing. Ajay calls C the most important programming language in the world today, and it exists because of Unix.

head: How Antitrust Pressure Set Unix Free
dek: Ajay claims some credit for the economists: the commercial path not taken produced a global commons.
more: Unix was far ahead of everything else, and AT&T could have launched its own computers and operating system and become a monopoly in computing too. Ajay's view is that AT&T, already fighting antitrust authorities, feared such a move would look like an extension of its telecom monopoly. It compromised by sending Unix to universities under an academic licence that allowed reading and tinkering but not commercialisation. Source code spread worldwide, along with a famous book that printed the kernel with a line-by-line commentary. At Berkeley, Bill Joy connected Unix to networking, and Unix became the vehicle for TCP/IP and the internet.

Ajay claims some credit for the economists: the commercial path not taken produced a global commons. Unix became the shared language of operating-systems education, and that is where open source comes from.

head: Ajay's 1991 Email to Linus Torvalds
dek: A word of encouragement to a young builder facing a famous critic can matter.
more: In 1991 a young student in Finland posted on Net News that, while fooling around with Minix code, he had written a new operating system, and asked what people thought. The eminent computer scientist Andy Tanenbaum replied with a harsh critique. Ajay, older than Linus, felt Tanenbaum was being unfair and emailed Linus not to be disheartened because his work was very important. Ajay booted Linux around version 0.1, and apart from seven or eight years on Mac OS X, it has been his only system since.
A word of encouragement to a young builder facing a famous critic can matter. Ajay was present at the founding of the system that now runs most of the world's computers.

head: Steve Jobs 'Got Religion' When iTunes Took a Week
dek: A single concrete result can turn a decision taken on trust into conviction.
more: At NeXT, Steve Jobs chose BSD Unix, and when he returned to Apple he brought the NeXT team with him; that became Mac OS X and later the foundation of Apple's phones and tablets. Until then Jobs had relied on the advice of people he trusted that BSD Unix was the path. The turning point came when iTunes was written in roughly a week on Apple's new Unix environment.
A single concrete result can turn a decision taken on trust into conviction. Ajay credits that speed to Unix's design.

head: Ken Thompson's 'Useless' Chess Program
dek: Good research management protects play from outsiders who demand immediate usefulness.
more: During a tour of Bell Labs for a powerful visitor, Ken Thompson demonstrated a chess program. The visitor called it cute but asked how it was useful. Thompson had applied dynamic programming, developed by Richard Bellman and Robert Kalaba at RAND, to the endgame by working backwards from every mating position. Ajay notes that Kalaba was his teacher and that his own PhD on women in Malaysia rested on dynamic programming. The president of Bell Labs defended Thompson, saying algorithms developed along the way helped schedule phone calls in the Bell system. Amit adds that endgames with up to seven pieces are now essentially solved through tablebases.
Good research management protects play from outsiders who demand immediate usefulness. Bell Labs would not fund an operating system, but it never stopped people from writing one.

head: Aadhaar's 'Impossible' De-duplication Problem
dek: This is the Unix method applied to a national project. Identify the hardest component and solve it first, and the rest becomes ordinary execution on confident ground.
more: Building Aadhaar, Nandan Nilekani, Sanjay Jain and others singled out one hard piece: matching any person against 1.4 billion records, so that a second fake ID, or a fraudulent claim for PDS rations, is caught. They took the algorithm to the world's biggest computer companies and top research groups. The presentations that came back said it could not be done. The team built it themselves and it worked.
This is the Unix method applied to a national project. Identify the hardest component and solve it first, and the rest becomes ordinary execution on confident ground.

head: What awk Revealed About the Show's Audience
dek: A tiny command-line program turns raw numbers into an insight. Ajay reads the trend as the early information problem fading: people who now know what the show is keep coming back.
more: In his screencast, Ajay ran a one-line awk program on the show's monthly viewing data: hours times 60, divided by unique viewers. In June 2023 about 300 hours went to 1,947 viewers, an average of about nine minutes each, mostly curious drop-ins. By November, about 14,000 viewers were averaging around 45 minutes.
A tiny command-line program turns raw numbers into an insight. Ajay reads the trend as the early information problem fading: people who now know what the show is keep coming back.

head: The Idea Factory: Bell Labs and the Great Age of American Innovation
dek: It explains how a lab that played the long game produced ideas that became the foundation of the modern world.
more: It explains how a lab that played the long game produced ideas that became the foundation of the modern world.
Amit's 'first recommendation of today' while setting the stage at Bell Labs. The title comes from Arthur C. Clarke's description of the lab.

head: The Design of Everyday Things
dek: It teaches that everything beautiful is also beautifully functional, and otherwise is not beautiful.
more: It teaches that everything beautiful is also beautifully functional, and otherwise is not beautiful. The same applies to engineering.
Amit's quick mid-episode recommendation during the discussion of elegance.

head: The Elements of Programming Style
dek: It carries the values of good prose into code: simplicity, elegance, being easy to understand, and not a word out of place.
more: It carries the values of good prose into code: simplicity, elegance, being easy to understand, and not a word out of place.
Amit brings up Kernighan's early programming book as modelled on Strunk and White, and Ajay cites the pairing as proof that engineering and culture belong together.

head: The Elements of Style
dek: It is the classic statement of the clarity-and-brevity values that Bell Labs carried into programming.
more: It is the classic statement of the clarity-and-brevity values that Bell Labs carried into programming.
Named as the model for Kernighan and Plauger's programming book.

head: Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers
dek: It is by one of Bell Labs' great figures, the man Amit quotes as saying that the purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.
more: It is by one of Bell Labs' great figures, the man Amit quotes as saying that the purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.
The textbook Kernighan had learned from before Hamming casually invited him to lunch.

head: In the Beginning...Was the Command Line
dek: It is not an engineering book. Stephenson 'gets the dream, he gets the philosophy' of this world and tells it in an instinctive, passionate way.
more: It is not an engineering book. Stephenson 'gets the dream, he gets the philosophy' of this world and tells it in an instinctive, passionate way.
The first of Ajay's three closing recommendations.

head: The Cathedral & the Bazaar
dek: Ajay considers Raymond the first to grasp the sociology of why Unix works.
more: Ajay considers Raymond the first to grasp the sociology of why Unix works. It contrasts a few great people building a cathedral with the teeming, arguing bazaar that produces something beautiful, and explains how unpaid volunteers end up building the world's best software.
The second of Ajay's closing recommendations.

head: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Episode 23 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It shows the energy two people generate face to face, the same effect Bell Labs relied on.
more: It shows the energy two people generate face to face, the same effect Bell Labs relied on.
Cited as one of their most fun episodes, which came about on the fly while shooting in person.

head: The Magic Was Culture, Not Money
dek: Murray Hill had about 3,000 employees, around 1,000 of them PhDs. Ajay points out that many organisations today, including private players in India, could fund something that size.
more: Murray Hill had about 3,000 employees, around 1,000 of them PhDs. Ajay points out that many organisations today, including private players in India, could fund something that size. Many labs had comparable talent. Bell Labs stood out because of its management and culture: a federated, self-organising structure, little top-down control, and the post-war American mood of optimism and willingness to question authority. The same spirit later appeared in Berkeley's counterculture.

head: Eccentrics, Not Dreamers
dek: Bell Labs welcomed unconventional people but not those who only built castles in the air.
more: Bell Labs welcomed unconventional people but not those who only built castles in the air. You could take a long view, but ideas had to become things and every project had a purpose. Long horizons were combined with a demand that the work eventually ship.

head: Geography Is Destiny
dek: Kernighan's line explains why the Bell Labs corridor mattered: creativity comes from casual, repeated contact with brilliant people.
more: Kernighan's line explains why the Bell Labs corridor mattered: creativity comes from casual, repeated contact with brilliant people. Amit argues this isn't about bureaucratic office attendance. Ideas are sparked by real people in the same place, which is also how many of this show's best episodes came about.

head: The Second System Problem
dek: This is a phrase from the Bell Labs community. A first system, like MIT's CTSS, is built in isolation by nervous mavericks, so it comes out spare, elegant and coherent.
more: This is a phrase from the Bell Labs community. A first system, like MIT's CTSS, is built in isolation by nervous mavericks, so it comes out spare, elegant and coherent. After it succeeds, arrogance and overreach set in, power-seekers join the project, and it becomes hard to refuse weak feature requests from powerful people. The second system collapses under its own ambition. Multics was the classic case, and Amit cites a description of it as trying to climb many trees at the same time.

head: Look at the Person, Not the Procedure
dek: Thompson's forged application and Ajay's father's PhD admission both depended on trusted people using judgement.
more: Thompson's forged application and Ajay's father's PhD admission both depended on trusted people using judgement. Ajay warns that India has turned everything into mechanical rules and cutoffs and opposes all discretion, and so loses the ability to recognise talent that doesn't fit the form.

head: Dancing With Chains
dek: Amit's motif from their previous episode: Thompson's junked computer, the borrowed typesetting budget and the too-fast disk were constraints that pushed creativity.
more: Amit's motif from their previous episode: Thompson's junked computer, the borrowed typesetting budget and the too-fast disk were constraints that pushed creativity. Ajay turns this into a challenge for Indians who imagine places like IBM's labs as free of politics and constraints. CR Rao, an obscure graduate student at ISI Calcutta before email, had no 'right to win' and still reached the frontier. Recognise the constraints and try to ease them, but don't use them as an excuse.

head: Engineering and Philosophy Sit on the Same Shelf
dek: Unix shows the close connection between technical excellence and the 'soft' world of culture, aesthetics and writing.
more: Unix shows the close connection between technical excellence and the 'soft' world of culture, aesthetics and writing. Examples include Strunk and White leading to The Elements of Programming Style, and Steve Jobs being driven by the aesthetics of typesetting and fonts. Ajay sees the separation of these two cultures in India's 'doctor-engineer' world as a reason engineers lose their sense of what good engineering is.

head: Simplicity and Beauty Are the User Interface of the Mind
dek: Systems built from a few simple components, with many features deliberately left out, work better because humans can understand them.
more: Systems built from a few simple components, with many features deliberately left out, work better because humans can understand them. Ajay quotes David Gelernter: when faced with complexity, our only defence is beauty. Aesthetics here is a working necessity for minds shaped by evolution, not decoration.

head: Small Tools, Hardest Part First
dek: Unix builds one small tool at a time, limited in function but thoroughly tested and fast, and makes it easy to combine tools like Lego.
more: Unix builds one small tool at a time, limited in function but thoroughly tested and fast, and makes it easy to combine tools like Lego. This contrasts with top-down enterprise IT projects that throw thousands of people at one giant system. Ajay's own method is to 'upload' a problem into his mind and let it sit without writing code, then isolate the two or three hardest components and grind on them with tunnel vision. Once those are solved, the overall design falls into place. Aadhaar's de-duplication is an example.

head: Writing, Thinking and Coding Are One Skill
dek: Bell Labs wrote terse, precise man pages and slim, excellent books, and its members spent real time improving each other's drafts.
more: Bell Labs wrote terse, precise man pages and slim, excellent books, and its members spent real time improving each other's drafts. Amit adds that the link between writing and thinking runs both ways, citing Deirdre McCloskey (writing is part of research) and Joan Didion (I don't know what I think till I write it down). Ajay agrees that good programmers become better thinkers, unless they code like grunts through Red Bull nights without applying their minds.

head: The Man Page Drives the Program
dek: Writing good documentation forces clear thinking about what a program should and should not do.
more: Writing good documentation forces clear thinking about what a program should and should not do. It also invites readers to criticise the design, which poor documentation doesn't. Documentation is a design tool, not an afterthought.

head: Write for Humans, Tend a Fifty-Year Garden
dek: Following Donald Knuth, code should be written as if explaining the algorithm to a person sitting beside you.
more: Following Donald Knuth, code should be written as if explaining the algorithm to a person sitting beside you. Knuth went further by writing programs as essays mixed with code, which tools split into a compiled program and a typeset book. Hastily written code gets thrown away within a year, so much of the software world keeps tearing houses down and rebuilding them. Unix won partly because its community keeps improving mature fifty-year-old codebases. That takes devotion over decades, not short sprints.

head: Open Source Is Just Science Continued
dek: Bell Labs shared code naturally, in the same way mathematicians publish proofs and as Newton published his demonstrations.
more: Bell Labs shared code naturally, in the same way mathematicians publish proofs and as Newton published his demonstrations. In the mid-1970s Bill Gates argued for secret commercial software and Richard Stallman for software open like mathematics and physics. Microsoft once earned most of the industry's profits yet produced no new ideas, while the open camp kept winning. Open code also lowers the cost of competing: anyone can fork and try a different idea. Amit frames this as markets in the broad sense, meaning voluntary cooperation, whether through contracts and IP or through freely swapping code.

head: Real Digital Public Goods
dek: Source code posted for download is non-rival (my download doesn't reduce yours) and non-excludable.
more: Source code posted for download is non-rival (my download doesn't reduce yours) and non-excludable. Unix and the internet were funded partly by AT&T salaries and by the US Department of Defense for TCP/IP. Yet no government controls them, nobody was coerced, and they belong to no nation. Ajay contrasts this with loose use of the term 'digital public goods'.

head: Stubborn Frugality
dek: Clever people working for decades on underpowered machines with small budgets have refined Unix's algorithms to a high level, so it gets more out of less hardware than well-funded corporate code does.
more: Clever people working for decades on underpowered machines with small budgets have refined Unix's algorithms to a high level, so it gets more out of less hardware than well-funded corporate code does. Old computers that would otherwise be discarded can be revived with Unix. For developers, quick-and-dirty work falls short of the community's standard.

head: Freedom Built Into the Architecture
dek: An operating system can easily impose harsh control, and computing could have become a straitjacket.
more: An operating system can easily impose harsh control, and computing could have become a straitjacket. Unix and the internet instead accepted a degree of anarchism: anonymous use, encryption and VPNs. Spam is a cost of that openness, but Ajay argues the alternative would be worse: a world where Microsoft or governments authenticate and meter every message. The way computing is built determines how much freedom its users have.

head: The Frontier Is Open to Anyone
dek: The Linux kernel is maintained by 10,000 to 20,000 programmers worldwide, coordinated openly through Git, which Linus Torvalds wrote.
more: The Linux kernel is maintained by 10,000 to 20,000 programmers worldwide, coordinated openly through Git, which Linus Torvalds wrote. Anyone in India, Bangladesh or Vietnam can watch the work happen and join in at whatever level suits them: a bug report, a feature request, documentation or code. You no longer need to be physically present at a place like Bell Labs.

head: Good File Names Are a Superpower
dek: Ajay's working habits include lowercase names for ordinary files, uppercase for directories and special files like README, underscores instead of spaces, and a README in every directory as a note to his future self.
more: Ajay's working habits include lowercase names for ordinary files, uppercase for directories and special files like README, underscores instead of spaces, and a README in every directory as a note to his future self. With files that are thirty or forty years old, careful naming and structure are his defence against a forgetful mind.

head: Plain Text Plus Pipes
dek: Keep data in plain text, never in formats only one program can read, so every tool can read every other tool's output.
more: Keep data in plain text, never in formats only one program can read, so every tool can read every other tool's output. The pipe passes one command's output to the next, so sort, tail, grep, wc and awk combine into answers in a single line. A few dozen commands combined this way cover a great deal of work.

head: Programming Is for Everybody
dek: Unix blurs the line between users and programmers. Chaining commands, writing a one-line awk program or saving a two-step script as a new command already counts as programming.
more: Unix blurs the line between users and programmers. Chaining commands, writing a one-line awk program or saving a two-step script as a new command already counts as programming. Ajay says that is how Unix users automate their own work, and that he can get a newcomer writing real code within 15 minutes without making it intimidating.

head: After listing Amit's research, Ajay
more: After listing Amit's research, Ajay says: 'This boy is not a Bengali dreamer. Look at the number of books he has read for this one episode. Get off your butt and read some books.' Amit replies: 'I am Bengali in the sense that I would urge my gentle readers, don't get off your butt. It's a very comfortable place. God gave you a butt for a reason, right? Actually God gave you a butt for two reasons.'

head: Ajay demands practicality
more: Ajay demands practicality: 'show me where is the beef, or show me where is the rasgulla?' Amit responds: 'What you said was firstly anti-national and secondly unhealthy. No rasgullas, too much sugar.'

head: On the PDP-7 found in a corner, Ajay says every office has a supply of unused rubbish
more: On the PDP-7 found in a corner, Ajay says every office has a supply of unused rubbish, and 'this story runs contrary to any declutter manifesto that you do want to keep your PDP 7s', a jab at their own Declutter episode.

head: Ajay on Hamming's prediction that computation would take over science: every sad graduate student learns it.
more: Ajay on Hamming's prediction that computation would take over science: every sad graduate student learns it. 'You may think you're doing biology, you may think you're doing political science. Ghoom phir ke, it's just programming.'

head: Ajay's WhatsApp-uncle dystopia: an uncle insisting on an Aadhaar iris scan every time you switch on your phone
more: Ajay's WhatsApp-uncle dystopia: an uncle insisting on an Aadhaar iris scan every time you switch on your phone 'because otherwise terrorists will use phones'. He adds a world where you must scan your iris before emailing and are 'charged four rupees for each email'.

head: A jab at India Stack nationalism
more: A jab at India Stack nationalism: 'for all the Indian nationalists, Nobody called it America Stack, they just called it Unix and the Internet.'

head: Ajay, a market-loving economist, before making a public-goods case for open source
more: Ajay, a market-loving economist, before making a public-goods case for open source: 'So unaccustomed as I am to questioning some of the fundamentals of how modern capitalism works.'

head: Richard Hamming
more: Richard Hamming: 'The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.' He also predicted in the early sixties that more than half of Bell Labs' work would turn out to be computation.

head: David Gelernter
more: David Gelernter: 'When faced with complexity, our only defense is beauty.'

head: Amit on writing as thinking: Deirdre McCloskey's view that writing is part of research rather than something done after it, and Joan Didion's
more: Amit on writing as thinking: Deirdre McCloskey's view that writing is part of research rather than something done after it, and Joan Didion's 'I don't know what I think till I write it down.'

head: The Restaurant That Could Never Have the Right Number of Doors
dek: This is rent-seeking in miniature. When the state controls permissions and its rules contradict each other, compliance becomes impossible, and that impossibility is what officials can charge for.
more: A friend of Amit's ran a restaurant in Bangalore. The fire department told him he needed multiple entrances. The excise department told him he could have only one, so that it could track alcohol going in and out. Officials from all of these departments took bribes from him, whatever number of doors he had.
This is rent-seeking in miniature. When the state controls permissions and its rules contradict each other, compliance becomes impossible, and that impossibility is what officials can charge for.
printed: Too many doors, too few doors

head: Sheldon Adelson vs Online Poker
dek: Special interests lobby based on what they believe will protect them, not on what is true.
more: Amit was a professional poker player, so he watched this from the inside. Sheldon Adelson owned physical casinos, including the Sands and the Venetian. He was a big funder of the Republican Party and spent years lobbying to keep online poker banned, which made him widely hated among poker professionals. He believed online poker threatened his casinos. Amit points out the irony: it didn't. The overall gambling ecosystem grew, and live casinos were not hurt.
Special interests lobby based on what they believe will protect them, not on what is true. Consumers can lose out even when the threat the lobbyist fears is imaginary.
printed: A bad bet on online poker

head: Why Raees Gets Public Choice Wrong
dek: Moral crusaders and the people who profit from a ban are often quiet allies.
more: Amit set Ajay a quiz: what does Shah Rukh Khan's film Raees have to do with public choice theory? In the film, SRK plays a macho bootlegger in Gujarat, where alcohol is banned. He tries to stop a politician who is leading a Darubandi Yatra, a rally demanding that alcohol be banned. Amit says this makes no sense. Under Bruce Yandle's 'bootleggers and Baptists' idea, the prohibitionist and the bootlegger are on the same side: the Baptist gets alcohol banned, and the bootlegger then profits by selling it.
Moral crusaders and the people who profit from a ban are often quiet allies. Before trusting a pious-sounding regulation, ask who gains from it.

head: Why Newton Gets Voting Right
dek: Voter indifference is not stupidity. It is a reasonable response when one vote almost never changes the outcome.
more: In a Housefull Economics column, Amit wrote about the film Newton. Rajkummar Rao plays an election officer who sets up polling booths in Chhattisgarh and tries to teach people their civic duty. The voters who turn up have no interest in who is on the ballot; they came only because they had to. Amit says that, unlike Raees, this film understands the economics: it shows Anthony Downs's idea of rational ignorance.
Voter indifference is not stupidity. It is a reasonable response when one vote almost never changes the outcome. A good film can teach an economic idea better than a lecture.

head: The Election Lost by One Vote
dek: Rational ignorance holds for the typical voter. But rare cases exist where a single vote really does decide the result, and sometimes they happen close to home.
more: Amit once said on The Seen and the Unseen that a single vote never decides an election. A listener corrected him: a local election in India had been decided by exactly one vote, and the losing candidate's wife had not gone to vote.
Rational ignorance holds for the typical voter. But rare cases exist where a single vote really does decide the result, and sometimes they happen close to home.

head: How India Nearly Got Proportional Representation
dek: People who block a reform because they assume their power is permanent often end up harmed by that choice.
more: In Amit's Seen and the Unseen episode with Jayaprakash Narayan, JP describes how he almost got proportional representation adopted. He had friends in high places and spoke to the different parties, and when the UPA was in power all the principal players had nearly agreed. Then Sonia Gandhi said no, believing Congress would stay in power under first-past-the-post and that PR would hurt it. Amit notes the irony: under PR, the BJP would not be as dominant today and Congress would hold many more seats. When Amit raised PR with Pratap Bhanu Mehta, PBM said it would be an absolute disaster that would tear the country apart. These are two of the people Amit considers the tallest intellectuals in India, and they hold opposite views.
People who block a reform because they assume their power is permanent often end up harmed by that choice. And the design of an electoral system is genuinely contested, even among the wisest people.
printed: The reform that almost got through

head: An Honest Father in the IAS
dek: Public choice theory is about systems, not villains. If outcomes are bad, look at the incentives before blaming the people.
more: Before discussing bureaucrats, Amit mentions that his father was an IAS officer and a good man, 'unfortunately for me' perhaps a little too honest, or completely honest. He uses this to reject the lazy stereotype that all babus are corrupt. In his view most bureaucrats are essentially good people who are responding to the incentives in front of them.
Public choice theory is about systems, not villains. If outcomes are bad, look at the incentives before blaming the people.

head: Germany Designed Its Constitution Against Another Hitler
dek: Electoral rules are design choices made in response to specific dangers.
more: Ajay has been strongly influenced by the history behind the modern German constitution. Hitler's Nazi party won the 1933 elections with something like 32% of the vote and went on to destroy the country (Amit adds: an entire continent). After the Second World War, Germany's central design goal was to build checks and balances so that a small, passionate base could never again install an extremist. After much debate, they chose proportional representation. Ajay says he is not an expert and offers this as a thought for listeners to explore.
Electoral rules are design choices made in response to specific dangers. First-past-the-post is not the natural or only form of democracy.

head: Vitalik Buterin and the Basti Auction
dek: Elections can be bought wholesale. The weak point of democracy is not only the ignorant voter but also the voter who can be bought.
more: Ajay recalls the conversation he and Amit had with Vitalik Buterin. Vitalik argued that the core problem with voting systems is that it is too easy to bribe a person to vote against their own interest. Ajay says this happens all the time in India. Frontline electoral politics often means going to one community elder or one basti at a time, and whoever bids highest gets those votes. This greatly increases the influence of money in politics.
Elections can be bought wholesale. The weak point of democracy is not only the ignorant voter but also the voter who can be bought.

head: No Shirt Worth Buying: Not Voting as a Signal
dek: Staying away from the polls is also information. Gaps in the political market get filled by new entrants, for better or worse.
more: Amit once skipped an election because no party seemed worth voting for, and he didn't want to vote tactically for the least evil. Someone told him that if he hadn't voted, he had no right to an opinion on the result. He disagreed. If you go to a mall and every shirt is bad, you don't have to buy one, and your not buying tells the market there is a gap. Likewise, the many Indians who don't vote signal to political entrepreneurs that existing parties aren't meeting demand. Amit says the Aam Aadmi Party did exactly this. He did not like AAP and criticised them from the Anna movement days onward, but he calls them a remarkably successful piece of political entrepreneurship: they offered disaffected middle-class voters someone who looked like them and talked about corruption, which Amit notes is the first rallying cry of populist movements.
Staying away from the polls is also information. Gaps in the political market get filled by new entrants, for better or worse.
printed: Nothing on the rack worth buying

head: Public Choice – A Primer
dek: It was the first public choice book Amit read and his 'gateway drug' into the field.
more: It was the first public choice book Amit read and his 'gateway drug' into the field. It is short enough to read in under an hour, and he calls it masterful.
Recommended first in the reading list at the start of the episode; available as a free PDF from the IEA.

head: The Calculus of Consent
by: James M Buchanan and Gordon Tullock
dek: It is the founding text of the field. It also frames the constitution as the 'rules of the game', which ideally should rest on consensus.
more: It is the founding text of the field. It also frames the constitution as the 'rules of the game', which ideally should rest on consensus.
Named as the 1962 book that many regard as the start of public choice theory; returned to in the constitution chapter.

head: The Logic of Collective Action
dek: It is the source of 'concentrated benefits and diffuse costs', which explains why small organised interest groups beat the large unorganised public.
more: It is the source of 'concentrated benefits and diffuse costs', which explains why small organised interest groups beat the large unorganised public.
Part of the 1965 entry in Amit's reading list; Amit believes Ajay owns a first edition.

head: An Economic Theory of Democracy
dek: Amit first learned about rational ignorance from this book: the idea that voters sensibly don't spend scarce attention on a vote that almost never decides anything.
more: Amit first learned about rational ignorance from this book: the idea that voters sensibly don't spend scarce attention on a vote that almost never decides anything.
Listed among the seminal books, then cited in the voting chapter.

head: Books by William A Niskanen
dek: Amit says Niskanen has great books on the incentives of bureaucrats.
more: Amit says Niskanen has great books on the incentives of bureaucrats.
Mentioned in the reading list and again when discussing bureaucrats.

head: Government's End: Why Washington Stopped Working
dek: A scary read on how far special interests have captured the state in the US.
more: A scary read on how far special interests have captured the state in the US. India isn't there yet, Amit says, but could easily get there.
Recommended twice in the special interests chapter.

head: Parkinson's Law
dek: Amit calls it a classic book of comedy that is also a public choice book.
more: Amit calls it a classic book of comedy that is also a public choice book. It covers how work expands to fill the time available, how officials multiply subordinates rather than rivals, and how they grow budgets and turf.
Brought up while discussing the incentives of bureaucrats.

head: A Life in Indian Politics — Episode 149 of The Seen and the Unseen
dek: Jayaprakash Narayan tells how India almost adopted proportional representation, until Sonia Gandhi said no.
more: Jayaprakash Narayan tells how India almost adopted proportional representation, until Sonia Gandhi said no.
Cited in the discussion of first-past-the-post versus proportional representation.

head: The Anti-Defection Law — Episode 13 of The Seen and the Unseen
dek: Amit sees the anti-defection law as another thing that gets in the way of Indian democracy.
more: Amit sees the anti-defection law as another thing that gets in the way of Indian democracy.
Mentioned after the discussion of tactical voting and Arrow's theorem.

head: The First Assault on Our Constitution — Episode 194 of The Seen and the Unseen
dek: Amit calls it a great episode on the First Amendment, which badly harmed free speech in India.
more: Amit calls it a great episode on the First Amendment, which badly harmed free speech in India.
Cited in the constitution chapter.

head: Public Choice Theory: Governments Are People
dek: Public choice applies economics, the study of how people respond to incentives under scarcity, to politics: politicians, bureaucrats, voters and the state.
more: Public choice applies economics, the study of how people respond to incentives under scarcity, to politics: politicians, bureaucrats, voters and the state. The government is not a benevolent being. It is made up of fallible people pursuing their own interests. Amit argues that there is no single aggregated 'public interest', because different people want different things. This matters especially in India, where he says the biggest religion is the religion of government, the 'Mai Baap Sarkar' expected to fix every problem.

head: The State as a Community Holding a Monopoly on Violence
dek: Ajay cites Max Weber: the state is not a set of institutions but a community of people who achieve and maintain a monopoly of physical violence over a territory.
more: Ajay cites Max Weber: the state is not a set of institutions but a community of people who achieve and maintain a monopoly of physical violence over a territory. Rule-bound, predictable institutions are something to aspire to, and countries achieve them to very different degrees. So we should ask what the people inside the state want and what they are trying to maximise. Amit adds a caution: even 'community' is too collective. Only individuals have values and interests, so keep thinking in terms of individuals.

head: Politicians Think Until the Next Election
dek: A politician's main incentive is to get elected, so the time horizon is always the next election.
more: A politician's main incentive is to get elected, so the time horizon is always the next election. A party leader is always facing some local election somewhere. Many good policies depend on counterintuitive truths: life is positive-sum, not zero-sum, and order emerges bottom-up in markets, languages and natural selection. People instinctively prefer a strong leader who will simply 'fix the price', so politicians cater to popular sentiment and neglect policies that only pay off in the long run. Amit adds the old cartoon of two wolves and a sheep voting on what to have for dinner as a reminder of the dangers of majority rule.

head: Why Today's Politics Attracts Different People
dek: Amit uses public choice to answer the lament that India no longer has leaders like its freedom fighters.
more: Amit uses public choice to answer the lament that India no longer has leaders like its freedom fighters. Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and Rajaji were not competing for power, because power was not on offer, so politics attracted people driven by principle. Today's highly centralised state offers enormous power, so it attracts people who want power.

head: Milton Friedman's Four Ways to Spend Money
dek: Spending your own money on yourself makes you both economise and seek value.
more: Spending your own money on yourself makes you both economise and seek value. Spending your own money on a stranger makes you economise but not care much about value. Spending someone else's money on yourself makes you seek value but not economise. Spending someone else's money on someone else gives you no reason to do either, and that is government. Ajay adds PJ O'Rourke's line comparing giving money and power to politicians with giving whiskey and car keys to teenagers.

head: Maybe the State Would Do More Good With Less Money
dek: If you believe in the Mai Baap state, you will accept a higher tax-to-GDP ratio.
more: If you believe in the Mai Baap state, you will accept a higher tax-to-GDP ratio. If you are sceptical of how governments use coercion and spending, a lower ratio may be better. Ajay notes that this thought is almost absent among Indian economists, who generally favour bigger government.

head: Rent-Seeking
dek: Rent-seeking has nothing to do with renting out property. It is what happens when the state controls something or creates artificial scarcity and then profits from it.
more: Rent-seeking has nothing to do with renting out property. It is what happens when the state controls something or creates artificial scarcity and then profits from it. Amit's hypothetical: the government decides podcasters need a licence, renewable every six months, and he has to pay a bribe for each renewal.

head: Concentrated Benefits, Diffuse Costs
dek: Politicians need money, and special interests supply it as an investment that will need a return, usually through policies that shield them from competition or redistribute wealth to them.
more: Politicians need money, and special interests supply it as an investment that will need a return, usually through policies that shield them from competition or redistribute wealth to them. The public doesn't notice because each person's loss is tiny and invisible, while the gain to the beneficiary is large. Amit's illustration: the government takes one rupee from everyone and hands it all to Ajay. Another example: small traders, who matter to some parties both as voters and as funders, push to keep FDI out of retail, and consumers quietly pay more for less.

head: Market Interventions Redistribute From Poor to Rich
dek: Amit's strong claim: whether it is protection from competition, a tariff on Chinese goods or a ban on FDI in retail, intervening in free markets takes money from the many and gives it to a well-organised few.
more: Amit's strong claim: whether it is protection from competition, a tariff on Chinese goods or a ban on FDI in retail, intervening in free markets takes money from the many and gives it to a well-organised few. Many regulations sound pious, so you have to dig into why they really exist.

head: Bootleggers and Baptists
dek: This idea, coined by the regulatory economist Bruce Yandle, describes how a prohibition brings together the moralist (the Baptist, who says alcohol breaks families and must be banned) and the profiteer (the bootlegger, who sells the banned good).
more: This idea, coined by the regulatory economist Bruce Yandle, describes how a prohibition brings together the moralist (the Baptist, who says alcohol breaks families and must be banned) and the profiteer (the bootlegger, who sells the banned good). They look like enemies but want the same policy, and sometimes they literally work together.

head: Worse Than Lobbying Is a World Without It
dek: Ajay complicates the anti-lobbying instinct. In London, New York or Tokyo, firms can openly criticise policy and lobby for their interests, which means power is spread out.
more: Ajay complicates the anti-lobbying instinct. In London, New York or Tokyo, firms can openly criticise policy and lobby for their interests, which means power is spread out. In India, the rule of law has declined and regulators hold arbitrary power, so industry has been frightened into silence. In the same way, firms funding parties in exchange for favourable policy is bad, but a protection racket is worse: there, firms that don't pay face coercive state agencies. Amit adds that the deeper problem is a state with too much power to interfere in markets at all, which makes elections 'a battle to be the one legal mafia for five years'.

head: Bureaucrats Protect and Expand Their Turf
dek: Using Parkinson's Law and William A Niskanen, Amit describes bureaucratic incentives.
more: Using Parkinson's Law and William A Niskanen, Amit describes bureaucratic incentives. Officials want more subordinates rather than rivals, bigger budgets and wider power. They resist any change with unpredictable consequences, which creates a status quo bias. Someone who would agree from the outside that a ministry should be abolished will defend it once inside.

head: The Administrative State
dek: A healthy liberal democracy spreads power across the legislature, the judiciary and the executive, and also across journalists, intellectuals, businesses, NGOs and citizens.
more: A healthy liberal democracy spreads power across the legislature, the judiciary and the executive, and also across journalists, intellectuals, businesses, NGOs and citizens. In an administrative state, the legislature and judiciary stop acting as checks. Officials run the country, with ministers making the big calls and officers the small ones, and citizens become subjects. Ajay says this describes what India is becoming. Indians who apply Western ideas of liberal democracy misread their own situation. His remedy is more democracy: real checks and balances, and many sources of power outside government, so that officials feel the consequences when things go wrong.

head: Corruption Is More Than Suitcases of Cash
dek: Ajay blames Bollywood for reducing corruption to suitcases of cash. His definition is broader: corruption is acting against the organisation's professional purpose for personal gain.
more: Ajay blames Bollywood for reducing corruption to suitcases of cash. His definition is broader: corruption is acting against the organisation's professional purpose for personal gain. That includes doing favours for friends and family, not enforcing the law against them, taking expedient career-boosting actions you don't believe in, maximising your own power, and laziness, meaning holding a civil servant's power while doing no work.

head: When in Doubt, Ban It
dek: Ajay says Indian officials' urge to shut down parts of the economy no longer comes from Nehru-Mahalanobis-style central planning, which faded long ago.
more: Ajay says Indian officials' urge to shut down parts of the economy no longer comes from Nehru-Mahalanobis-style central planning, which faded long ago. It comes from personal incentives: understanding cryptocurrency or complex derivatives is hard, so ban them. Closing restaurants at 10 pm prevents the occasional crime headline that could embarrass the official, who never sees the cost to the city's vitality and economy.

head: Rational Ignorance
dek: Anthony Downs's idea: one vote almost never decides an election, and even if it did, it probably wouldn't change your life much.
more: Anthony Downs's idea: one vote almost never decides an election, and even if it did, it probably wouldn't change your life much. Time and attention are scarce, so it is rational not to study manifestos, track records and policy trade-offs.

head: Why People Vote Anyway
dek: If voting rarely matters, why do people vote? One reason is a norm: you see yourself as a good citizen, just as you signal a left turn on an empty road.
more: If voting rarely matters, why do people vote? One reason is a norm: you see yourself as a good citizen, just as you signal a left turn on an empty road. Another is tribal affiliation: voting is like wearing your club's red shirt to a Manchester United game.

head: The State Cannot Demand Duties
dek: Asked about a citizen's duty to vote, Ajay answers from first principles.
more: Asked about a citizen's duty to vote, Ajay answers from first principles. The state has no right to demand duties of the people. Their fundamental right is to be left alone. He has never voted, because the cost-benefit calculation never made sense to him.

head: First-Past-the-Post vs Proportional Representation
dek: Under first-past-the-post, a party can win 35% of the votes and 80% of the seats, or swing from power to nowhere on small shifts in vote share.
more: Under first-past-the-post, a party can win 35% of the votes and 80% of the seats, or swing from power to nowhere on small shifts in vote share. Proportional representation gives seats in proportion to votes, so smaller parties and minority interests get a voice in Parliament. Amit avoids taking a side, noting that wise people disagree. His larger point is that elections alone don't make a democracy: a republic also needs rules of the game.

head: Tactical Voting Hides True Preferences
dek: Voters often back the candidate who can beat the one they dislike most, rather than the one they actually prefer.
more: Voters often back the candidate who can beat the one they dislike most, rather than the one they actually prefer. Amit cites Kenneth Arrow's impossibility theorem to argue that a political marketplace cannot fully satisfy people's true preferences.

head: Booth-Level Results Enable Collective Punishment
dek: Ajay points out that results are visible booth by booth, and a booth covers about 2,000 people.
more: Ajay points out that results are visible booth by booth, and a booth covers about 2,000 people. A winning party therefore knows how each basti voted and can reward or punish the whole community. He calls this a fundamental negation of liberal democracy, and a key enabler of vote-buying.

head: The Rules of the Game Matter Most
dek: Incentives come from how the state is designed, and the constitution sets the rules of the game.
more: Incentives come from how the state is designed, and the constitution sets the rules of the game. A good constitution limits the state and protects citizens. The test of a good system is whether a terrible person could gain power and still do little harm, because the state simply doesn't have that much power. Buchanan and Tullock argued that a constitution should contain only what everyone agrees on.

head: India's Constitution Protects the State More Than the Citizen
dek: The Constitution was written when the country was falling apart and it was unclear whether the princely states would join.
more: The Constitution was written when the country was falling apart and it was unclear whether the princely states would join. For understandable reasons, it centralised power and copied the colonial setup in which the state rules and the people are subjects. Free speech gets lip service but is hedged by caveats such as public order and decency. Amit sees a dilemma: the Constitution is less liberal than he would like but more liberal than Indian society. Every government since Nehru has amended it whenever it wanted to do something unconstitutional.
printed: A state too weak to harm

head: Constitutions Are Elite Projects
dek: Ajay argues that successful constitutions rarely reflect broad consensus.
more: Ajay argues that successful constitutions rarely reflect broad consensus. They are written by elites at a 'constitutional moment', and the German and Japanese ones were partly imposed by an outside power. In India, the real constitution is effectively the basic structure, which the judiciary has mostly though not always defended against amendments. The rest functions like an ordinary law that keeps getting amended. That pushes India toward something like the British unwritten tradition, where the work lies in wisely applying the basic structure doctrine.

head: Amit claims to have written the first public choice limerick ever, for his weekly Times of India slot
more: Amit claims to have written the first public choice limerick ever, for his weekly Times of India slot: 'A neta who loves currency notes / told me what his line of work denotes. / It is kind of funny, / we steal people's money / and use some of it to buy their votes.'
Ajay: 'This is even before ChatGPT?' Amit: ChatGPT 'can't write limericks because it can't count, it can't do math', and a good limerick needs a 9-9-6-6-9 syllable count, not just rhymes.

head: Amit's rent-seeking hypothetical: the government decides people like Amit Varma and Ajay Shah can't podcast without a licence
more: Amit's rent-seeking hypothetical: the government decides people like Amit Varma and Ajay Shah can't podcast without a licence, 'renewable every six months. And of course I have to pay a bribe for it.'

head: Amit sets Ajay a quiz on what Raees has to do with public choice theory. Ajay doesn't know and hasn't seen the film.
more: Amit sets Ajay a quiz on what Raees has to do with public choice theory. Ajay doesn't know and hasn't seen the film. Amit: 'Good.' His verdict on the plot: SRK's bootlegger should be backing the prohibitionist politician: 'Yatra karo, I will dance at your wedding also.'

head: Quote duel: Ajay cites PJ O'Rourke (
more: Quote duel: Ajay cites PJ O'Rourke ('giving money and power to politicians is like giving whiskey and car keys to teenagers'). Amit replies: 'You throw a PJ O'Rourke quote at me, I will raise you with HL Mencken': every election is 'a sort of an advanced auction sale of stolen goods.'

head: Amit on what Indian elections really decide
more: Amit on what Indian elections really decide: 'I really think of the elections as a battle to be the one legal mafia for five years.'

head: Ajay on why Indians think corruption means suitcases of cash
more: Ajay on why Indians think corruption means suitcases of cash: 'I blame Bollywood for this.'

head: Listing the many voices that should matter in a liberal democracy (journalists, intellectuals, businesses, NGOs), Ajay adds…
more: Listing the many voices that should matter in a liberal democracy (journalists, intellectuals, businesses, NGOs), Ajay adds: 'Podcasters should matter. Podcasters should matter above all.'

head: Ajay calls elections
more: Ajay calls elections 'the great temple of the Amar Chitra Katha version of democracy', where the people vote and all problems are solved. Amit replies that first he wants to talk about 'the great temple of Indian entertainment, which is Bollywood.'

head: Amit says people signal left turns even on an empty road because it is a habit
more: Amit says people signal left turns even on an empty road because it is a habit, 'unless you're in Bombay and you drive like me.'

head: Ajay's confession
more: Ajay's confession: 'I am very sad to say, but I have not voted because I never felt the cost benefit analysis made sense and it has been a mystery to me why people vote.'

head: Amit recalls an old cartoon: someone asks the Parliament bookshop for the Constitution and is told
more: Amit recalls an old cartoon: someone asks the Parliament bookshop for the Constitution and is told, 'we only stock books here, not periodicals.'

head: Ajay on India's constitutional moment
more: Ajay on India's constitutional moment: 'some people wrote a United States Constitution, some people wrote the Constitution of India, and we lucked out and got a fairly bad document.' Earlier, Amit corrected him mid-sentence: 'Elite rather than elitist.'
Ajay: 'There's no Mahalanobis and Nehru anymore. Nobody is dreaming what the country wants to be.' Amit: 'And in a sense, thank God that's gone.'

head: Mai Baap Sarkar: Amit's name for India's
more: Mai Baap Sarkar: Amit's name for India's 'religion of government', the belief that a parental state should solve every problem.

head: A thank-you note, two decades late
dek: Small acts of intellectual generosity can shape someone for decades without the giver ever knowing.
more: Amit plays a video message from one of his writing students, Uja Sharma. Around 2000–2001, as a final-year student at the College of Business Studies in Delhi University, she was doing a project on futures and options and found that 90% of her research material carried Ajay's name. She emailed him without expecting a reply. He answered promptly and spent more than an hour on a video call explaining how derivatives worked, how the policy was coming together and what NSE was doing. She aced the subject. The memory had faded on Ajay's side, but Amit says it 'clearly happened' and is exactly the kind of thing Ajay does.
Small acts of intellectual generosity can shape someone for decades without the giver ever knowing. The person who was helped remembers, and passes it on.

head: Ajay discovers his dharma as a help desk
dek: When the same kind of request keeps arriving at your door, it may be telling you where you are most useful.
more: In the late 1990s, derivatives trading was taking off in India. Ajay did seminars across the country and a series of tutorial-style TV conversations that were replayed twice a day, so people came to see him as the teacher of derivatives. Then strangers began emailing him their plans and their problems and asking him to fix them. At first he was taken aback, since he was not going to debug other people's work. By the fifth email he decided this was his calling. He has replied carefully to such emails ever since, and makes time for PhD students and early-career academics too.
When the same kind of request keeps arriving at your door, it may be telling you where you are most useful. Accepting that role can quietly do a lot of public good.
printed: A help desk by divine decree

head: Amit Varma as a Design One firm
dek: The episode's ideas about firm design apply to individual careers too.
more: Hearing Ajay describe the firm where one person owns 100% and is also the CEO, Amit recognises his own life. He thinks of every creator as an entrepreneur running their own brand, both shareholder and CEO, and compares himself to Travis Bickle talking to the mirror in Taxi Driver. The upside is total alignment: he follows his own vision and has passed up big opportunities to do what he loves. The downsides are that he cannot scale and is limited by his own imagination and knowledge, with no advisors to see further ahead.

The episode's ideas about firm design apply to individual careers too. A solo creator gets perfect alignment but pays for it in scale and blind spots. Ajay adds that employees wouldn't fix this, because people rarely challenge a 100% owner.

head: Tom Watson Jr's giant gamble at IBM
dek: Family heirs are not always timid caretakers. A successor with hunger and skin in the game can take bet-the-company risks, which is exactly what Ajay says owner-run firms usually fail to do.
more: Tom Watson Jr inherited IBM from his father, its founder. At the time IBM was a feudal sort of company where employees sang the company anthem every morning. The son bet on the world's most expensive operating system project, OS/360, which in inflation-adjusted dollars cost more than the Manhattan Project. He led IBM through it.
Family heirs are not always timid caretakers. A successor with hunger and skin in the game can take bet-the-company risks, which is exactly what Ajay says owner-run firms usually fail to do.
printed: The son who bet the house

head: Shamin Desai's film class at Channel V
dek: Amit links the memory back to the episode's theme: a senior person taking time to teach juniors is what good corporate culture looks like.
more: Amit worked at Channel V from 1995 to 1997, his second job. There a filmmaker named Shamin Desai, who sadly died a few years ago, gathered five or six people from the promos department for an informal film-appreciation session. He explained that Coppola made Rumblefish at the same time as The Outsiders, with almost the same cast. He argued that Rumblefish was a masterpiece, then played it for them. Amit remembers it as a masterclass in film appreciation.
Amit links the memory back to the episode's theme: a senior person taking time to teach juniors is what good corporate culture looks like. It echoes Ajay's help-desk story.

dek: A masterpiece about a family enterprise, and Coppola at his absolute peak.
more: A masterpiece about a family enterprise, and Coppola at his absolute peak.
Part of Amit's recommendation: a legendary 1970s film that won many Oscars.
