dek: Amit says both films are masterpieces and that together they are Coppola at his peak.
more: Amit says both films are masterpieces and that together they are Coppola at his peak.
Recommended with the first film. Amit notes it also won Oscars.

head: Rumblefish
dek: Amit loved it, and Desai convinced that small room it was a masterpiece.

Came up while Amit was praising Coppola. It triggered his memory of Shamin Desai's film-appreciation session at Channel V.

head: What You Can Learn from Family Business
by: Nicolas Kachaner, George Stalk Jr, and Alain Bloch
dek: It counters the stereotype with evidence from family firms worldwide. Professionally run firms do better in good times, but family firms do less badly in bad times.
more: It counters the stereotype with evidence from family firms worldwide. Professionally run firms do better in good times, but family firms do less badly in bad times. Family firms are frugal, keep a high bar for capital expenditure and carry little debt. They make fewer and smaller acquisitions, are surprisingly diversified and international, and retain talent better. Ajay says he agrees with all of it.
A Harvard Business Review piece Amit cites. He notes that Indians look down on family firms but look up to Western media that give gyan.

head: Think in incentives, not class stereotypes
dek: Ajay argues that India has a kind of caste system in business. People look down on traditional business families and revere the IIT-certified professional.
more: Ajay argues that India has a kind of caste system in business. People look down on traditional business families and revere the IIT-certified professional. They assume family managers are second-rate and that hiring a professional will solve everything. His thesis is that this is the wrong lens. The right one looks at the forces that produce good and bad decisions inside a firm: alignment, skin in the game, time horizons, risk appetite and how power is spread. On those terms a family CEO can beat a professional CEO, or lose to one.

head: Design One: the founder as 'little deity'
dek: The founder owns 100% and is also the CEO. Incentives are perfectly aligned, and the owner will work flat out.
more: The founder owns 100% and is also the CEO. Incentives are perfectly aligned, and the owner will work flat out. The cost is that nobody can check the founder. No one disagrees or forces a debate, so bad projects get picked and money gets wasted. Having employees doesn't fix this, because people rarely challenge someone who owns 100% of the firm.

head: Under-diversification breeds timid firms
dek: When most of an owner's wealth, ego and social standing is tied up in one firm, they become risk-averse.
more: When most of an owner's wealth, ego and social standing is tied up in one firm, they become risk-averse. They make only small, incremental changes and avoid the big bets that transform a business. Capitalism needs those gambles: some firms succeed wildly and many die, and that creative destruction is healthy. Owner-run firms that won't take such bets fall behind as markets and technology change. The flaw is the structure, not the person.

head: Design Two: minority shareholders and the narrow Indian debate
dek: The founder keeps 60% and stays CEO, while outside investors hold 40%, possibly through an IPO.
more: The founder keeps 60% and stays CEO, while outside investors hold 40%, possibly through an IPO. This is common among listed Indian family firms. Alignment stays high and the founder is slightly more diversified, but power is just as concentrated and the founder remains risk-averse. A new problem appears: a 60% owner can take more than 60% of the cash, so minority investors pay less for the shares. Ajay says most Indian company law and SEBI rules for listed firms target this one issue, and miss the bigger flaws of under-diversification and excessive power.

head: Design Three: the professional-CEO trap
dek: The family keeps 60% and hires a salaried 'professional' CEO with no equity, a move the Indian elite tends to applaud.
more: The family keeps 60% and hires a salaried 'professional' CEO with no equity, a move the Indian elite tends to applaud. But that CEO has no skin in the game, and their career incentives push toward caution. In a typical five-year term, the first three years go into avoiding the sack through cost control and small improvements. They then squeak through to a second term and coast to year ten without rocking the boat. The 60% chairman, who hires them and can fire them, also nudges them away from risk and is unlikely to be stopped from taking extra cash. Meanwhile the CEO consolidates power inside the firm with no one to question them.

head: Design Four: dispersed shareholding plus a strong board
dek: This is how mature firms around the world work. There is no promoter.
more: This is how mature firms around the world work. There is no promoter. Shares are spread across institutions and the public, which has only started happening in India in the last 10–15 years. Shareholders pick a board of about seven people: the CEO, roughly three shareholder directors whose 5–15% stakes matter to them, and roughly three independent directors. The board sets strategy and organisation design, hires the CEO, decides their pay and holds them accountable. Sometimes the board makes things so hot that the CEO leaves, and Ajay calls that healthy. Stock options give the CEO a reason to chase upside, and diversified shareholders can accept that some firms fail. Ajay stresses that this is culture, not law, and takes decades to build.

head: Concentrated power and the great-man myth
dek: The business world credits success to a visionary CEO and blames failure on a bad one.
more: The business world credits success to a visionary CEO and blames failure on a bad one. Ajay says much of the outcome is luck and forces outside the firm, such as being in the right industry at the right time, or the world suddenly changing. The world is too complicated for any single mind. Better decisions, and the ability to admit and fix mistakes, come only from many minds debating. People also tend to behave worse when they hold concentrated power. Indian business, he says, is still stuck in a 'primitive great man theory'.

head: Build the board before you hire the outsider
dek: For a family firm moving toward Design Four, Ajay suggests an order. First spread out the shareholding and build the board as a real institution, with about three shareholder directors and three independents.
more: For a family firm moving toward Design Four, Ajay suggests an order. First spread out the shareholding and build the board as a real institution, with about three shareholder directors and three independents. Only after that bring in a professional CEO. Power in the hands of an aligned family member is relatively safe. Power in the hands of an unchecked hired manager is the real worry. Outside strategy advisors help by challenging the existing management. All this requires the current CEO to give up power, which is rare: Ajay has sat on more than 20 boards and seen 'disgusting levels of arrogance' in CEOs.

head: Execution is management's comfort zone; strategy is the hard part
dek: Indian managements retreat into execution because strategy means facing an unpredictable world and making difficult calls.
more: Indian managements retreat into execution because strategy means facing an unpredictable world and making difficult calls. A board and strategy advisors exist to pull management out of that comfort zone. They push for transformation, such as demanding growth of five times, rather than small step-by-step improvements.

head: Family wealth fades across generations, so plan the path to Design Four
dek: Amit cites a worldwide pattern: when a family becomes wealthy, about 70% of that wealth is lost by the next generation and about 90% by the one after.
more: Amit cites a worldwide pattern: when a family becomes wealthy, about 70% of that wealth is lost by the next generation and about 90% by the one after. Ajay's answer is that if a family member has the hunger and ability, a family-led path toward Design Four beats handing the firm to a professional. Many families lack such a successor, though. Others are pushed into dispersed shareholding by their history, for example when venture capital and private equity investors exit after an IPO. Then making Design Four work is the only option.

head: Rich countries are built of sophisticated firms
dek: Ajay says India's path from poor to rich runs through its firms. Public policy can only create the right conditions and nudge a little.
more: Ajay says India's path from poor to rich runs through its firms. Public policy can only create the right conditions and nudge a little. The real change is cultural: norms, how power works in the boardroom, and how the seven people in that room behave. That journey has to be made by the Indian elite.

head: Ajay on becoming the nation's derivatives help desk
more: Ajay on becoming the nation's derivatives help desk: 'by the fifth email, I got the message that the good Lord had intended for me to be a help desk. So I decided to discharge my dharma.'

head: Ajay's running example is the fictional
more: Ajay's running example is the fictional 'Amitbhai Media Limited'. After Designs Two and Three each make things worse, Amit pleads: 'And now we need to get to design four, please save Amitbhai Media Limited.'

head: Ajay mocking Indian reverence for entrance exams: there is…
more: Ajay mocking Indian reverence for entrance exams: there is 'the instinctive respect that somebody who could solve maths problems in 12th standard is a cool guy.'

head: Amit, as Ajay takes apart the professional CEO
more: Amit, as Ajay takes apart the professional CEO: 'At this point, I must point out to gentle readers that our good friend Ajay Bhai Shah is from IIT, right? So he is a professional, and he's coming to my family firm... This is most insidious, but continue.'

head: After a cat-like scream is heard in the background, Amit tells listeners it wasn't a cat
more: After a cat-like scream is heard in the background, Amit tells listeners it wasn't a cat: 'It was a wailing of a CEO who had been ejected by the animal behavior of an unruly board.'

head: When Ajay instantly produces a copy of The Godfather, Amit is stunned
more: When Ajay instantly produces a copy of The Godfather, Amit is stunned: 'Oh you have it. What the fuck? You have everything here.' He wonders whether Ajay owns something that looks like a book but has a screen, so any book Amit names just appears on it.

head: Taxi Driver: Amit compares himself, as both shareholder and CEO of his own one-person firm, to Travis Bickle in front of the mirror (
more: Taxi Driver: Amit compares himself, as both shareholder and CEO of his own one-person firm, to Travis Bickle in front of the mirror ('You're talking to me?'), adding 'I can't act, of course.'

head: Steve Jobs as the poster child of the visionary-CEO myth. Ajay's rebuttal
more: Steve Jobs as the poster child of the visionary-CEO myth. Ajay's rebuttal: 'Steve Jobs made many, many wrong decisions. He almost took Apple into bankruptcy.'

head: The Nehrus as an example of decline across generations
more: The Nehrus as an example of decline across generations: 'Motilal Nehru downwards, they just kind of got lesser and lesser as people.'

head: Dhirubhai and Mukesh Ambani
more: Dhirubhai and Mukesh Ambani: 'every Dhirubhai is not going to have a Mukesh. You know, that was just getting extraordinarily lucky.'

head: How Ajay got hooked: Corbett, Everest books and the IIT Bombay mountaineering club
dek: Lifelong passions are often seeded by childhood reading and kept alive by a community that hands down know-how you can't easily learn alone.
more: Ajay grew up on Jim Corbett's books and accounts of the first ascent of Everest, and has gone into the mountains since age 13. At IIT Bombay in the early 80s he joined a community that already existed. A physics professor, Professor Mahajan, had led the building of a mountaineering and rock-climbing culture there in the late 70s and early 80s. Gear was scarce and expensive, so the club pooled it. Members passed down how to run an overnight trek, a week-long trek, or a two-week trek in the Himalayas. Today the same knowledge comes from the internet and GPS, and good, cheap gear is easy to buy.

Lifelong passions are often seeded by childhood reading and kept alive by a community that hands down know-how you can't easily learn alone. Those barriers have mostly fallen. The main thing left is to not quit, as most people do in their teens and twenties.
printed: A boy, a book and a mountain

head: Goechala: the night that was too cold to sleep, and the decision to turn back
dek: The hardest call in the mountains is when to stop. A reason that feels 'stupid', like aching fingers, may have been early frostbite.
more: On the Goechala trek, the Sikkim-side approach to Kanchenjunga, Ajay slept in a one-person tent at the last campsite, Lamuney, at roughly 4,500-4,800 metres. The wind came up. Even in merino inners, fleece, a full-sleeve shirt and a jacket, inside a sleeping bag, he was kept awake all night by the cold. Wind chill, he explains, makes felt cold depend on wind speed, not just the thermometer. At 4 a.m. they started walking in ghostly moonlight, with so little oxygen that he took two or three breaths for every step. Other trekkers had given up after days of bad weather. His group got a clear day and reached Goechala 1, with Kanchenjunga in front of them. His guide said he could make Goechala 2, though not Goechala 3. Ajay said no: his gloves were bad, it was perhaps minus 10 or minus 20, and his fingertips hurt too much. He still wishes he had gone on.

The hardest call in the mountains is when to stop. A reason that feels 'stupid', like aching fingers, may have been early frostbite. You rarely know in the moment, and turning back with lifelong regret beats pressing on into damage.

head: Porter on the first IIT Bombay climb of Konkan Kada
dek: You don't have to be the star climber to be part of something historic.
more: In his third year at IIT Bombay, Ajay was a 'coolie' on the first successful climb of Konkan Kada from IIT Bombay. Konkan Kada is the cobra-shaped overhanging west face of Harishchandragad, looking down into the Konkan almost to the sea. He made two long ferries up and down the face carrying 20 kg of food, water and climbing stores tied to his hip. On the last day he was the first person out. He rappelled about 1,800 feet through sheer overhang, and at each stop the rope's natural twist spun him 360 degrees while he took photographs all around.
You don't have to be the star climber to be part of something historic. Carrying loads for someone else's ambitious project can give you one of the great experiences of your life.
printed: The coolie who came down first

head: Edward Weston and the rise and fall of pedestrianism
dek: An activity done for love can turn competitive, then a spectacle, then toxic.
more: Amit retells the story from Matthew Algeo's book. In 1860 Edward Weston bet a friend that Lincoln would lose. If Lincoln won, Weston would walk from the State House in Boston to the Capitol in Washington in ten days. Lincoln won. Weston walked, took a little longer, and missed the inauguration, but the whole country followed his progress, much as it later followed Lindbergh. Weston decided walking should be a competitive sport. For about twenty years 'pedestrianism' was America's biggest spectator sport. Crowds paid to watch men circle tracks for six days a week, Sundays excepted. Weston, in hunting boots and breeches, was its Federer. The Irish working-man Dan O'Leary was its Nadal. The African American Frank Hart, O'Leary's protege known as 'Black Dan', was a third pillar. Early on, fans analysed technique: Weston's long strides against O'Leary's shorter, lighter steps. Later it became an ugly contest of who could stay awake for six days.
An activity done for love can turn competitive, then a spectacle, then toxic. Amit imagines the old champions, once the sport died, going out to walk alone again and rediscovering why they loved it.

head: Tigran Petrosian: 'I'm playing to play'
dek: The purest stance toward any pursuit is to do it for itself, not for the result or anyone's approval: hiking to hike, walking to walk.
more: Petrosian, the great grandmaster and pioneer of the exchange sacrifice, went partly deaf. Once, in a losing position, a young opponent who revered him offered a draw. Petrosian didn't hear it and went on to lose. In the main story, an opponent who badly wanted a draw tested the waters. He asked, 'Are you playing to win?' Petrosian said no. 'Are you playing to draw?' No. 'Then why are you playing?' Petrosian answered: 'I'm playing to play.'
The purest stance toward any pursuit is to do it for itself, not for the result or anyone's approval: hiking to hike, walking to walk. Amit offers it as a philosophy for life.

head: How Ajay broke his ankle coming down from Tung
dek: The fall itself was bad luck, but the conditions for it were his own doing: no homework and a relaxed guard just when the day felt finished.
more: In the Sahyadris, Ajay's group did two up-and-down climbs in one day, the second being Tung, about a thousand metres up and five hundred down in all. From the top they could see the lake where they would camp. Back at the base there was a chai shop. Thinking the day was basically over, they had a fresh lime soda while the sun went down. He hadn't checked Google Earth, so he didn't realise there were still about 300 metres of descent to the lake. The view from the top had flattened the terrain. They set off late in failing light, got a little lost, and followed a pipe down toward the lake. A pipe takes the shortest, and so the steepest, line. Then came the bit of bad luck: he fell and broke his ankle. It was his first accident in 45 years of hiking.

The fall itself was bad luck, but the conditions for it were his own doing: no homework and a relaxed guard just when the day felt finished. Amit links it to Tom Vanderbilt's finding that most road accidents happen close to home, and to writing projects whose last stretch looks flat from above.
printed: A lime soda before the fall

head: Outpaced by nobody: the Bangalore teenagers at Panchachuli
dek: Youth no longer guarantees fitness. Ajay notes elsewhere that our grandparents had strength from agricultural work.
more: Ajay and his friend KP Krishnan went hiking to Panchachuli, near the India-China border in Uttarakhand, with a band of teenage boys and girls from Bangalore. The two older men assumed they would be the weakest link. Instead they were among the strongest. The teenagers, used to video games and Netflix, were strikingly unfit.
Youth no longer guarantees fitness. Ajay notes elsewhere that our grandparents had strength from agricultural work. Today, fitness is a habit you build, not something that comes with your age.

head: Man-eaters of Kumaon
dek: Part of the reading that made mountains and forests seem like 'the greatest thing in the world' to him.
more: Part of the reading that made mountains and forests seem like 'the greatest thing in the world' to him. He calls Corbett's three best books 'really wonderful' and says everybody will enjoy them.
Ajay grew up on Corbett's books and names this first in his recommendations segment.

head: The Man-eating Leopard of Rudraprayag
dek: One of the three Corbett books he considers great.
more: One of the three Corbett books he considers great.
The second of the three Corbett books Ajay suggests reading in sequence.

head: Jungle Lore
dek: Completes his recommended Corbett sequence.
more: Completes his recommended Corbett sequence.
The third of the Corbett books Ajay singles out.

head: Into Thin Air
dek: It is about one summer on Everest when many bad things happened, and it shows the go/no-go call on the final summit day.
more: It is about one summer on Everest when many bad things happened, and it shows the go/no-go call on the final summit day. Ajay says every Everest accident comes down to that judgment.
Raised right after the Goechala story, in the discussion of knowing when to stop. Ajay says it is a great book he would recommend to everybody.

head: Into the Wild
dek: Ajay says Krakauer has 'some really good books' and this is another one.
more: Ajay says Krakauer has 'some really good books' and this is another one.
Added alongside Into Thin Air in the recommendations segment.

head: For Whom the Bell Tolls
dek: He calls it one of the great books of the world. Move its story to a purely urban setting and 'the oomph is lost', which shows how much wild landscapes add to a story and to life.
more: He calls it one of the great books of the world. Move its story to a purely urban setting and 'the oomph is lost', which shows how much wild landscapes add to a story and to life.
Ajay's thought experiment on why mountains and forests matter.

head: Biophilia
dek: 'Biophilia', a perception of and presence with all forms of nature, names what Ajay feels hiking gives him.
more: 'Biophilia', a perception of and presence with all forms of nature, names what Ajay feels hiking gives him.
Ajay cites Wilson's term when Amit asks if his love of hiking is part of a turn toward nature.

head: Father Returning Home
dek: Its phrase 'man's estrangement from a man-made world' stuck with him, and he uses it to ask whether embracing nature makes you a different person.
more: Its phrase 'man's estrangement from a man-made world' stuck with him, and he uses it to ask whether embracing nature makes you a different person.
Quoted in Amit's newsletter post. He calls it a great poem.

head: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
dek: Its line 'the Zen you find in the mountain is the Zen that you take up there' captures his point: what you get from the mountains depends on the mind you bring.
more: Its line 'the Zen you find in the mountain is the Zen that you take up there' captures his point: what you get from the mountains depends on the mind you bring.
Ajay quotes it while explaining why he hikes.

head: Traffic
dek: His takeaway: most accidents happen close to home, because familiar ground makes the brain switch off.
more: His takeaway: most accidents happen close to home, because familiar ground makes the brain switch off. That is exactly what happened to Ajay below Tung.
Raised after Ajay's ankle story. Amit calls it a great book.

head: Google Earth (desktop version)
dek: Check the elevation of the summit, the base of the climb and your campsite before you go, so you know the whole day's work.
more: Check the elevation of the summit, the base of the climb and your campsite before you go, so you know the whole day's work. He says the desktop version beats the browser one.
The main lesson from his ankle injury, and his research tool for every trek.

head: We are monkeys: city life leaves a hole
dek: Ajay extends Marx's idea of alienation beyond the assembly-line worker.
more: Ajay extends Marx's idea of alienation beyond the assembly-line worker. Biologically we are one more branch of the tree of life, built to live among trees. A life spent among concrete, coffee shops and bars leaves something missing. Amit frames the same idea with Dilip Chitre's phrase 'man's estrangement from a man-made world'.

head: Marx: right on the diagnosis, wrong on the cure
dek: Ajay credits Marx with being first to see how capitalism, globalisation and the market economy act like a 'wild west wind' that tears down feudalism and old social customs and brings modernity.
more: Ajay credits Marx with being first to see how capitalism, globalisation and the market economy act like a 'wild west wind' that tears down feudalism and old social customs and brings modernity. He says Marx was wrong on essentially every remedy. Amit adds that getting the description right and the prescription wrong is practically a feature of leftist thought.

head: The principle of the greatest problem
dek: On a long climb, the body always complains about whatever is scarcest at that point.
more: On a long climb, the body always complains about whatever is scarcest at that point. When oxygen is plentiful, your thighs complain. When your legs are strong, your lungs do. The constraint you must fight keeps moving, so you focus on whichever one binds now.

head: Know when to stop: no sunk costs, no performance
dek: Above roughly 7,500 metres, the 'dead zone', you are beyond the design spec of the human body, and your judgment degrades along with everything else.
more: Above roughly 7,500 metres, the 'dead zone', you are beyond the design spec of the human body, and your judgment degrades along with everything else. Ajay says every Everest accident comes down to the go/turn-back call. Years of training (sunk cost) and wanting to post the summit photo both push people to continue. Amit adds that, as with drinking, judgment fails just when you need it, and risk-takers start out biased toward going on.

head: Movement, business, racket
dek: Ajay's summary of the pedestrianism story. Great ideas start as something done for love, get monetised, and end as a racket.
more: Ajay's summary of the pedestrianism story. Great ideas start as something done for love, get monetised, and end as a racket. He applies it to rock climbing, which he sees as a solitary puzzle like a crossword, now turned into speed competitions, and to people who climb mountains to brag on social media. The antidote is Petrosian's 'playing to play': keep the activity free of competition and performance.

head: The demand is in the mind: hiking as moving meditation
dek: A day of hiking can burn two to four thousand calories, but it is spread over hours of gentle slopes in 30-60 minute stints with breaks.
more: A day of hiking can burn two to four thousand calories, but it is spread over hours of gentle slopes in 30-60 minute stints with breaks. If you can row or run for 10-20 minutes, your body is ready. The real challenge is mental: settling into a meditative zone where you watch your breathing, heart and calves. People fill the zone differently. KP Krishnan recites thousands of Sanskrit shlokas as he walks. Short bursts of speed followed by panting don't work.

head: Don't go casually: modest fitness, basic kit, real preparation
dek: On easy tourist routes like Triund behind Dharamshala, and on pilgrimages like Gangotri, Ajay sees people suffering because they arrive unfit, in party clothes, after watching miraculous YouTube clips.
more: On easy tourist routes like Triund behind Dharamshala, and on pilgrimages like Gangotri, Ajay sees people suffering because they arrive unfit, in party clothes, after watching miraculous YouTube clips. Their grandparents had farm-work strength. People who sit watching Netflix and eating processed food don't. Basic fitness, proper footwear, some kit and mental preparation turn the trip from torture into joy. Separately, real danger begins with technical climbing: if you're not using your hands, trekking itself is not truly dangerous.

head: Day hike → overnight → indefinitely
dek: Ajay's path for beginners. Start with day hikes, ideally with people who know the route.
more: Ajay's path for beginners. Start with day hikes, ideally with people who know the route. If you find yourself at a summit wishing you didn't have to go back, pitch a tent: one night, then two, seven, ten. In India today, tents beat the caves and temples people once slept in. Long routes mean learning to live off the land by buying food in villages. Once you can do that, there's no natural stopping point. On a north-south route in Maharashtra, he and Ayush Patnaik have looked at each other around day seven and realised they could just walk on to Kanyakumari.

head: Leave no trace, respect the silence
dek: There is no one to clean up the mountains, so don't litter and bring your plastic back.
more: There is no one to clean up the mountains, so don't litter and bring your plastic back. Wet wipes made with nylon or polyester are plastic and pollute for a thousand years, so buy all-cotton, biodegradable ones. Bluetooth speakers and loud talk carry for hundreds of metres in mountain silence and spoil the experience for everyone. Speak in whispers and you will see more birds and wildlife.

head: Treat the mountain crew as teammates, not hotel staff
dek: India's elite are used to demanding service from hotels. In the mountains the crew is carrying your load, cooking and washing dishes at altitude, and their means are limited.
more: India's elite are used to demanding service from hotels. In the mountains the crew is carrying your load, cooking and washing dishes at altitude, and their means are limited. Ask for things, take no for an answer with a smile (black coffee when the creamer runs out), and do your own small tasks. Amit notes this is good advice for everyday life too, since we only need it because we behave badly at home.

head: Character is how you behave under stress
dek: On real adventures, especially in the Sahyadris, which are less 'corseted' than standard Himalayan routes, you will run short of water, get lost, or have someone fall ill.
more: On real adventures, especially in the Sahyadris, which are less 'corseted' than standard Himalayan routes, you will run short of water, get lost, or have someone fall ill. Arul Menezes once got kidney stones at the top of Harishchandragad. These setbacks become good stories later. What matters is staying calm, solving problems, and not taking it out on others.

head: Never relax until the tent is up
dek: The lesson of Ajay's broken ankle. Danger peaks when you think the job is done.
more: The lesson of Ajay's broken ankle. Danger peaks when you think the job is done. Do your homework (Google Earth elevations of summit, base and campsite), stay fully present until the end of the day, and avoid shortcuts like following pipes, which take the steepest line. Amit connects it to Tom Vanderbilt's finding that accidents cluster near home, and to writing: from high up, the last stretch always looks flat.

head: Eat carefully on the trail, especially at dinner
dek: Ajay assumed burning thousands of calories gave him licence to eat anything.
more: Ajay assumed burning thousands of calories gave him licence to eat anything. Hiking with a CGM showed him that Maggi, white rice and maida still spike your blood sugar. Dinner matters most because you burn almost nothing afterwards. Include some protein, such as dal and eggs, and look for micronutrients, since trail food is all cooked.

head: Walking as a pastime depends on technology
dek: Drawing on Adam Gopnik's essay, Amit argues that walking for pleasure was never simply natural.
more: Drawing on Adam Gopnik's essay, Amit argues that walking for pleasure was never simply natural. Gaslight let Londoners walk after dark. The rule of law made streets safe, especially for women. From the 1980s, the Walkman and cushioned sneakers made walking easier still. Each layer removes drudgery so we can attend to the experience itself.

head: Amit's opening
more: Amit's opening: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged that that which we love the most hurts us the most. And today you will see my fellow cast member in a cast.' Then, on Ajay saying the worst is behind him: 'though at that time I was standing behind you.'

head: Amit on Ajay's message mid-hike: Ajay had
more: Amit on Ajay's message mid-hike: Ajay had said 'Amit, you won't hear from me for a week', and 'in the middle of that blissful period of mental peace and calm' came the news that he'd broken his ankle. Amit also calls him a hiking evangelist, meaning 'a person who evangelises hiking and not that while hiking you evangelise.'

head: Amit, looking at each camera in turn, warns viewers that Ajay's
more: Amit, looking at each camera in turn, warns viewers that Ajay's 'great German philosopher' (Marx) and 'the good Lord intended' are ironic: 'we are not actually fans of Marx... at least I am certain there is no good lord. However, monkeys do exist and we are monkeys.'

head: Ajay's call to action
more: Ajay's call to action: 'We said to gentle reader, get off your butt and read some books. Today we're saying, gentle reader, get off your butt and go take a hike.' Amit hopes listeners are getting up to walk 'not because they're sick of the show.'

head: After Ajay says you should be able to…
more: After Ajay says you should be able to 'row or run' for 20 minutes, Amit clarifies: 'by row we mean the English row', a bilingual pun on the Hindi for crying.

head: Told hikers should carry 5-15% of body weight, Amit
more: Told hikers should carry 5-15% of body weight, Amit says: 'This is why, Ajay, you should be overweight like me, because then you're carrying a lower percentage.' Ajay: 'I don't recommend it.'

head: Amit, stung by the Netflix jibe
more: Amit, stung by the Netflix jibe: 'My question for you is on whose butt should I sit. I'll sit on my butt only, no?'

head: Ajay explains the zo, a yak-cow cross
more: Ajay explains the zo, a yak-cow cross with 'the strength of the yak and the domesticity of a cow'. Amit: 'Jimi Hendrix has a song called Hazo. I wonder whether he was thinking of it.'

head: After Ajay recalls Arul Menezes howling with kidney stones atop Harishchandragad, Amit asks…
more: After Ajay recalls Arul Menezes howling with kidney stones atop Harishchandragad, Amit asks: 'Have you asked Arul before sharing this anecdote?'

head: Amit on turning mishaps into stories
more: Amit on turning mishaps into stories: 'That is how YouTubers think of content. So what if I broke my ankle? Content mila.'

head: Ajay calls Google Earth
more: Ajay calls Google Earth 'the greatest joy in the world'. Amit: 'Google Earth is not the greatest joy on earth. It's bacon.' He later closes the lesson: 'even after you do switch off, don't eat too much for dinner.'

head: On the five apples for a day hike, Amit
more: On the five apples for a day hike, Amit: 'And by apples you mean the fruit, not iPad and MacBook.'

head: Ajay's closing self-portrait
more: Ajay's closing self-portrait: 'if I had not been an economist, I would be a biologist.'

head: The 1991 trade reforms were 30 years in the making
dek: Reforms that look overnight are usually the visible tip of decades of data, research and argument.
more: Amit argues that the 1991 reforms happened quickly, with no public consultation, so perhaps change can skip the slow pipeline. Ajay disagrees using customs duties. From the 1960s, through the work of Bhagwati, Srinivasan and Manmohan Singh's PhD thesis, economists argued fiercely about trade barriers against 'the lefties and the nationalists'. The data and research piled up, and the reformers won the debates conference after conference. By 1991, cutting duties from 350% to 5% was a settled question for many people. The only open question was how to sequence it. Ajay adds that the reforms that skipped this groundwork tended to work out less well.

Reforms that look overnight are usually the visible tip of decades of data, research and argument. That groundwork also produces the people who carry the knowledge, because 'the joint secretaries don't know much'.

head: From clueless about pension law to drafting inflation targeting
dek: Turning a good idea into reality needs very different skills at each stage.
more: While describing the implementation stage of policy, Ajay offers a personal aside. When the New Pension System was being turned into law, he understood the idea but knew nothing about its legal scaffolding, so he could only watch as a spectator. By the time inflation targeting came along, he had learned enough to follow the whole path himself: from monetary economics, to drafting an agreement, to drafting a law.

Turning a good idea into reality needs very different skills at each stage. Even an expert economist had to learn the craft of legal drafting, which Ajay calls an 'exotic skill in India' because most laws here are poorly drafted.

head: Turning down Kirit Parikh: Ajay's biggest mistake
dek: Close apprenticeship with a great mind can beat the prestige of credentials.
more: On another podcast, a friend asked Ajay without warning to name one mistake he had made in his life. He went back to age 21. Fresh out of IIT, the economist Kirit Parikh invited him to apprentice with him for a couple of years before doing a PhD. Ajay was dazzled by the idea of a PhD in the United States, so he declined and went abroad. He now calls it the dumbest decision imaginable.
Close apprenticeship with a great mind can beat the prestige of credentials. The glamour of a famous path can hide a better opportunity sitting right in front of you.

head: The hunter-gatherer paradise and the curse of agriculture
dek: Progress is not a straight line, and the story we grow up with can be badly wrong.
more: As children we are told that savage hunter-gatherers progressed to agriculture and then to industry. Ajay says modern thinking has turned this around. Hunter-gatherers were free, women were free, and health was good: male skeletons reached six feet and female skeletons five feet seven, heights not seen again until the 20th century. Agriculture brought disease, shrinking heights, social control and women treated as property. Grain also enabled early states, whose main dealings with the people were taxation and conscription. He describes the stretch from agriculture in Babylon about 5,000 years ago to liberal democracy in 19th-century UK as a long 'dark regress'.
Progress is not a straight line, and the story we grow up with can be badly wrong. For most of history the state was something to escape, not something that served you.

head: The 20th century as a stress test of progress
dek: Catastrophe is always possible, so you should never assume progress is locked in.
more: Ajay suggests judging progress over the span of one life. Pick 20-year-olds and 60-year-olds at random from the 20th century, and for large numbers of them the rest of life went terribly: two world wars, the Russian Revolution, Nazi rule, the threat of communism and nuclear war. Weimar Germany's flowering of freedom in 1918 became Hitler in 1933. The hope of 1989 gave way to Putin's Russia, a near-miss in Poland and Hungary's decline. Deng Xiaoping's program from 1978 ended in Xi Jinping's one-man rule from 2012. Large-scale land war returned in 2022. India too began in 1947 with Gandhiji, Nehru, Tagore and Ramanujan, 'the star pupil' of the post-colonial world, and he asks the listener to look at where we've come.
Catastrophe is always possible, so you should never assume progress is locked in. Strive for it, but stay 'cold and careful and nervous' about the world.
printed: A century that broke its promises

head: Three stages of Ajay's belief about persuasion
dek: Persuasion is real but slow, partial and hidden by ego. Expecting visible surrender sets you up for despair, while a 10% shift in ten people is a big win.
more: As a child, Ajay believed that showing someone how Kepler's laws follow from Newton's laws would instantly change the world and banish superstition. Then came decades of gloom, when he believed people only talk past each other, avoid conflict, and never change their minds. Now he holds a middle view. In a zone of truth and trust, people do hear each other. Nobody admits defeat, not even privately, but over time the mind mulls things over and shifts by about 10%.
Persuasion is real but slow, partial and hidden by ego. Expecting visible surrender sets you up for despair, while a 10% shift in ten people is a big win.

head: Choosing knowledge over action
dek: Find the place where you are most useful, even if a respected mentor sees a different path for you.
more: A mentor and boss at the Ministry of Finance had a clear career track mapped out for Ajay and was sure it was right. Ajay felt his real place was in the world of knowledge: reading and writing books, doing research, working with data and statistics. He followed that path and is surprised to have ended up in front of a camera on this show. He has also lived through the 'crushing humiliation and misery' of seeing his areas of work go horribly wrong, again and again.
Find the place where you are most useful, even if a respected mentor sees a different path for you. Then accept that the world owes you nothing, and keep building anyway.

head: Weapons of the Weak
dek: It develops the view that states emerged to tax and conscript, and that many people sensibly tried to keep the state out of their lives.
more: It develops the view that states emerged to tax and conscript, and that many people sensibly tried to keep the state out of their lives. Ajay sees 'more than a shadow' of this in Indian society, where many people want to stay far away from the government.
Ajay's recommendation for the episode, building on his argument that the move from hunter-gatherer life to agriculture was a decline.

head: Against the Grain
dek: It explains why agriculture and grain-based early states made life worse for ordinary people, which overturns the childhood story of steady progress.
more: It explains why agriculture and grain-based early states made life worse for ordinary people, which overturns the childhood story of steady progress.
Mentioned in Ajay's recommendation as an earlier show recommendation and a source of his argument about agriculture and early states.

head: Seeing Like a State
dek: It is another James C Scott book the hosts value for understanding the state.
more: It is another James C Scott book the hosts value for understanding the state.
Amit notes that the show has recommended both Against the Grain and Seeing Like a State, making it 'very much a James C Scott fantasy'.

head: The Bear Came Over the Mountain
dek: It is perhaps Amit's favourite short story of all time, and he calls it 'just magnificent'.
more: It is perhaps Amit's favourite short story of all time, and he calls it 'just magnificent'.
A short story published in The New Yorker, linked in the show notes and free to read.

head: The Solution
dek: In a few lines it skewers a state that blames its people instead of serving them.
more: In a few lines it skewers a state that blames its people instead of serving them.
Amit reads it aloud after Ajay says the state should be the agent of the people but often becomes their ruler.

head: Kashi Ka Assi
dek: Its line about playing your harmonium while the world goes to hell captures the temptation to withdraw, which Ajay then answers.
more: Its line about playing your harmonium while the world goes to hell captures the temptation to withdraw, which Ajay then answers.
Amit quotes a line from it, in its family-friendly version, to frame the cynic's question: why care about the world at all?

head: The End of History?
dek: It captures the moment when liberal democracy seemed to have won for good.
more: It captures the moment when liberal democracy seemed to have won for good. That assumption has since reversed, which Amit uses to question whether progress is inevitable.
Amit cites it, noting the question mark, as the symbol of the optimism of 1989.

head: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It explains why the academy has stepped away from real-world problem solving.
more: It explains why the academy has stepped away from real-world problem solving.
Ajay mentions it when noting that universities don't do the work of imagining policy solutions.

head: Separate the state from the people
dek: Indians tend to be 'excessively statist' and blur the state, the people, and individuals into one thing, as in saying 'India won the World Cup'.
more: Indians tend to be 'excessively statist' and blur the state, the people, and individuals into one thing, as in saying 'India won the World Cup'. Ajay argues the people matter more. Almost all wealth, truth, beauty and creativity comes from society, and so does most of the rot, such as the crushing of freedom. The basic question should be how people can build culture, associations, firms and clubs themselves, instead of always running to the mai-baap sarkar.

head: Change from below and from above: you need both
dek: Amit once believed policy people would achieve nothing. His view was that you should work on the demand side of the political marketplace, the people, because the supply side, the state, responds to demand.
more: Amit once believed policy people would achieve nothing. His view was that you should work on the demand side of the political marketplace, the people, because the supply side, the state, responds to demand. He now thinks small changes on the supply side can have a massive impact, and that both are needed. Ajay gives two templates. Decriminalising homosexuality and recognising gay marriage were people-led: states followed opinion polls. Globalization in India was an elite, top-down project, because anti-foreigner feeling comes easily and the case for openness was clear mainly to thinkers and leaders like Vajpayee, Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Manmohan Singh, Chidambaram and Narasimha Rao.

head: A liberal constitution as 'topsoil' cannot change society from the top
dek: Ambedkar called the constitution a mere topsoil: a liberal document laid over a deeply illiberal society to keep it in check.
more: Ambedkar called the constitution a mere topsoil: a liberal document laid over a deeply illiberal society to keep it in check. Later scholars, such as Madhav Khosla with his idea of its 'pedagogic' effect, kept this top-down view. Amit argues it cannot work. Many people stopped trying to build a better society after independence, expecting the constitution and the state to do the job.
printed: India didn’t win the World Cup

head: Right description, wrong prescription
dek: Critics of Big Tech are right about the problems: addiction machines, data harvesting, tribalism, echo chambers and polarization.
more: Critics of Big Tech are right about the problems: addiction machines, data harvesting, tribalism, echo chambers and polarization. But their usual answer, state regulation of algorithms, is dangerous. Once the state can tell companies what to do, that power will eventually be held by the worst possible person. Amit argues social problems must be solved socially.

head: Progress is not guaranteed
dek: Amit notes that belief in progress rests on a tiny sample of centuries.
more: Amit notes that belief in progress rests on a tiny sample of centuries. Ajay suggests the timescale of one life. Much of the 20th century was catastrophic, the hopes of 1989 were betrayed, and democratic backsliding is now happening in country after country. Dream of progress and work for it, but don't fall into a 'millennial fervour' that assumes it is locked in.

head: Tyrants want people, not territory
dek: Drawing on James C Scott, Ajay argues that early states existed mainly to tax and conscript.
more: Drawing on James C Scott, Ajay argues that early states existed mainly to tax and conscript. Their rulers wanted more people to control, so 'lines on maps' are a silly modern idea. People voted with their feet and ran away from states. Being stateless was better than living under a tyrannical state.

head: The policy pipeline: left to right, no skipping steps
dek: Ajay describes how the state changes as a sequence of stages. (1) Data and measurement. (2) Research: refining 'crude oil' data into knowledge. (3) Imagining low-coercion solutions to genuine market failures, with several rival ideas, because 'when there is only one game in town, you have surely a bad thing going'. (4) A vigorous public debate that widens the Overton window, which needs free speech. (5) Expert committees that legitimize radical ideas. (6) Decisions, encoded in laws. (7) Implementation: drafting good laws and designing accountable organizations.
more: Ajay describes how the state changes as a sequence of stages. (1) Data and measurement. (2) Research: refining 'crude oil' data into knowledge. (3) Imagining low-coercion solutions to genuine market failures, with several rival ideas, because 'when there is only one game in town, you have surely a bad thing going'. (4) A vigorous public debate that widens the Overton window, which needs free speech. (5) Expert committees that legitimize radical ideas. (6) Decisions, encoded in laws. (7) Implementation: drafting good laws and designing accountable organizations. Each stage needs very different knowledge, failure at any stage kills the reform, and the whole journey can take about 25 years.

head: No data, game over
dek: Without measurement, you are left with opinion and spectacle, and 'the guy with the biggest megaphone will win'.
more: Without measurement, you are left with opinion and spectacle, and 'the guy with the biggest megaphone will win'. Building a measurement system, for example for air quality, takes about a generation. Ajay warns of a bait-and-switch: in a moral panic ('there is a crisis. Something must be done. X is something.'), frightened people accept authority, and the state rushes through its most oppressive measures.

head: Satellites can measure what weak states won't
dek: In poorer countries, government data suffers from incompetence and from suppression of unflattering numbers.
more: In poorer countries, government data suffers from incompetence and from suppression of unflattering numbers. Satellite imagery gets around both problems. For example, lights photographed at 1:30 a.m. come from street lights, petrol stations and commercial complexes. That gives a monthly map of prosperity at half-kilometre resolution. India's ISRO doesn't release such data freely, but other providers do.

head: Fame is a curse; common knowledge is usually wrong
dek: When you put any field under the microscope, what famous people say loudly usually turns out to be wrong.
more: When you put any field under the microscope, what famous people say loudly usually turns out to be wrong. Ajay also defends correlations, which parts of the economics profession look down on. Interpreted with care, they are a powerful path to insight.

head: Coercion is the poison
dek: Ajay judges every state intervention by its cost in money or coercion, and since all tax money is raised through coercion, the two are really the same thing.
more: Ajay judges every state intervention by its cost in money or coercion, and since all tax money is raised through coercion, the two are really the same thing. A good solution gets the job done substantively, even if only 60%, with the least coercion. It should assume realistic state capacity, which Ajay says is a euphemism for state incapacity.

head: Society changes one conversation at a time
dek: Megaphone advocacy on social media 'gets precisely nothing done'. What changes minds is quiet, face-to-face conversation in a zone of truth and trust, and living as an example, because people do as we do, not as we say.
more: Megaphone advocacy on social media 'gets precisely nothing done'. What changes minds is quiet, face-to-face conversation in a zone of truth and trust, and living as an example, because people do as we do, not as we say. Each good conversation shifts both sides by about 10%, and that adds up: persuading ten people by 10% on a couple of important things is a real achievement.
printed: One WhatsApp uncle at a time

head: The world is interested in you, even if you aren't interested in it
dek: Ajay answers the cynic who says 'let the world burn, I'll enjoy my life'.
more: Ajay answers the cynic who says 'let the world burn, I'll enjoy my life'. Even with zero altruism, self-interest demands that you understand politics and society. If you were in Weimar Germany, your job in 1918 was to hold off the nationalists, and in 1933 to take your loved ones and leave. Without a theory of the world, you get crushed when catastrophe comes.

head: Endurance is the highest superpower
dek: Idealists burn out by smashing their heads against 'some mad bugger's wall', often because they believe the world will be fixed quickly.
more: Idealists burn out by smashing their heads against 'some mad bugger's wall', often because they believe the world will be fixed quickly. The other extreme, apathy, is just as wrong. Ajay's alternative is to pace yourself, keep realistic expectations, treat the work as your dharma, and ask for no reward or success. We are pebbles in an avalanche. Accept defeat without becoming bitter or quitting.

head: Honest post-mortems among fellow travelers
dek: Ajay says the Indian elite is still at a 'crude credentialist transactional stage' of community.
more: Ajay says the Indian elite is still at a 'crude credentialist transactional stage' of community. Real community means bonds of values and trust. Its members practise 'the Western way of war': write up the war diaries, celebrate successes, criticize failures harshly, cry together, and keep going. This avoids both collapse and the 'childish triumphalism' Ajay sees as common in India. Doing, failing and debating in this way is how knowledge builds up.

head: The time-machine letter
dek: Ajay's exercise for looking honestly at yourself. Our ego insists we did everything right and the world did everything wrong.
more: Ajay's exercise for looking honestly at yourself. Our ego insists we did everything right and the world did everything wrong. Imagining a letter to your younger self forces you to list what you would do differently, and with hindsight you find that almost everything could have been done better.

head: Right after Ajay defends the value of correlations, Amit offers one
more: Right after Ajay defends the value of correlations, Amit offers one: total hours watched of Everything is Everything have been rising along with India's GDP, so 'the prosperity of our nation relies upon us.'

Amit's 'naughty thought': it's good that the world is going backwards, 'Because the creator economy is booming. And Ajay Shah, we need content.' Ajay replies: 'Like if there had been no war in Ukraine, what episode would you make?'

Ajay: 'In a good country, elected legislators write laws. In a bad country, the joint secretary writes the law.' Amit then pictures this episode playing on a giant screen to a hall full of protesting joint secretaries, adding: 'And you of all people with a broken ankle, you don't even have all your joints.'

head: Amit applies Ajay's 10% theory of persuasion
more: Amit applies Ajay's 10% theory of persuasion: 'right after this recording, I am going to ask you for ten Diet Cokes. So you change your views by ten percent and give me one. Isn't that cunning of me?'

head: Ajay on Nazism
more: Ajay on Nazism: 'Nazi stands for nationalist socialism', calling it two bad ideas fused into one.

head: When Ajay says the art and beauty all come from the people, Amit interjects that the state
more: When Ajay says the art and beauty all come from the people, Amit interjects that the state 'can set up a commission to compose a sonata. They can set up a commission to come up with a new raga which is nationalistic.'

head: Amit claims he shifted the Overton window of podcast duration. His five- and six-hour episodes made two or three hours normal: when he started
more: Amit claims he shifted the Overton window of podcast duration. His five- and six-hour episodes made two or three hours normal: when he started, 'one hour was considered a deep dive', and now 'one hour is like a miniature.'

head: Riffing on…
more: Riffing on 'paradigms change one funeral at a time', Amit recalls Ajay's line that 'society changes one WhatsApp uncle at a time'.

Ajay opens with a line about the dialectic being interested in you even if you aren't interested in it. Amit asks him to explain it in simple English, and Ajay obliges: 'You may not be interested in the world, but the world is interested in you. There you go.'

head: Ajay on raw data without analysis
more: Ajay on raw data without analysis: 'there is data, data everywhere, but not a thought to think.'

head: Bertolt Brecht's
more: Bertolt Brecht's 'The Solution', read by Amit: after the 17 June uprising, leaflets on the Stalinallee said the people had lost the government's confidence. Brecht's reply: 'Would it not in that case be simpler for the government to dissolve the people and elect another?'

head: Martin Luther King's
more: Martin Luther King's 'the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends towards justice', and the saying that 'paradigms change one funeral at a time'. Amit uses both to question the assumption that progress is inevitable.

head: Francis Fukuyama's
more: Francis Fukuyama's 'The End of History?' (1989, 'with the question mark'), along with the fall of the Berlin Wall and the Soviet Union, as the high point of liberal optimism.

head: Steven Pinker's
more: Steven Pinker's 'the better angels of our nature', cited by Amit for the good side of our hardwiring that culture can amplify. Social media, by contrast, amplifies our 'worse demons' of tribalism.

head: Ajay's tribute to the scientific revolution
more: Ajay's tribute to the scientific revolution: 'nature and her mysteries lay hidden in the night. God said let Newton be and all was light', followed by Maxwell's equations, relativity and Darwin.
'A republic, if you can keep it': Ajay recalls this answer from a framer of the US constitution but can't remember who said it. His point is that every generation has to fight for its freedom.

head: Gandhiji's
more: Gandhiji's 'be the change that you want to see in the world', which Ajay invokes for why change must start with us.

head: Amit quizzes Ajay on who said that he wasn't so smart, he just stayed with problems longer. Even with the clue
more: Amit quizzes Ajay on who said that he wasn't so smart, he just stayed with problems longer. Even with the clue 'he's one of your heroes', Ajay can't guess. The answer is Albert Einstein. Ajay adds that at 16 Einstein wondered what the world would look like riding a beam of light, and stayed with that question for years until it led to special relativity.

head: Amit's two perseverance quotes: Confucius
more: Amit's two perseverance quotes: Confucius, 'It doesn't matter how slowly you go, as long as you don't stop', and Vivian Greene, 'don't wait for the storms to pass, learn to dance in the rain'.

head: From Kashinath Singh's Kashi Ka Assi, in its…
more: From Kashinath Singh's Kashi Ka Assi, in its 'family friendly version': 'Bhaad mein jaaye duniya, hum bajaayein harmonium'. The world is going to hell, but I'm going to play my harmonium.

head: Amit's running gag of crediting
more: Amit's running gag of crediting 'Robi-da, my favourite philosopher'. He cites Robi-da's song about treading a path of 'ekla cholo', and later says 'Shob kichu, shob kichu. Everything is everything, as a great Robi-da would say.'

head: Mera Joota Hai Japani, which Amit plays
more: Mera Joota Hai Japani, which Amit plays as 'a famous song that is about the glory of globalization'.

head: Robert Clive Without Email
dek: How far authority can be centralised depends on the communication technology of the day.
more: Ajay explains the old Indian 'national' firm through the East India Company. Clive did his own thing because no email could reach him, and Indian branch managers until the 1980s were the same: regional satraps who had to be empowered because they couldn't check back with HQ. Once computers and telecom arrived, Robert Clive was under daily surveillance from HQ.

How far authority can be centralised depends on the communication technology of the day. Without connectivity, decentralisation is forced on a firm, along with discretion, sloppy process and petty corruption. With connectivity, central control becomes possible.

head: Pleading With Indian Airlines Staff and the Demigod Branch Manager
dek: Whom you bother persuading shows you where power sits inside an organisation.
more: Ajay's defining image of the old era is a customer earnestly arguing with an Indian Airlines frontline employee. It made sense, because those employees really did have discretion. In banks, the teller had little power, but the branch manager was 'like a demigod' who made genuinely important decisions, so it was worth arguing with him.

Whom you bother persuading shows you where power sits inside an organisation. In the old Indian firm it sat at the local front line, which allowed sensible local adaptation and also local bias and corruption.

head: The Customer Yelling at Amazon Customer Care
dek: Habits formed under one organisational design outlive it. Customers still try to argue with frontline staff who no longer have any discretion.
more: While working at a Starbucks, Amit overheard a woman at the next table lose her temper with Amazon customer care and declare she would never buy from the company again. He thought it was pointless, since the agent was following a script and couldn't help her. Ajay's story then gave him the explanation: the habit dates from an era when frontline staff could actually change outcomes.
Habits formed under one organisational design outlive it. Customers still try to argue with frontline staff who no longer have any discretion.

head: Maggi and Kit Kat Taste Different in Every Country
dek: Global firms already treat each country as its own product market. Ajay asks why Indian firms then sell one Maggi, or run one home-loan algorithm, across a country as diverse as India.
more: Ajay noticed that Maggi noodles taste different in Indonesia, India and the UK. Nestle runs focus groups and R&D to tune the flavour for each country, such as Thailand versus Indonesia versus India. Kit Kat varies the same way. Kit Kat fans revere the British original. Americans are stuck with a sugar-loaded version pushed by Hershey's. Japanese Kit Kats are legendary, and travellers carry bagfuls home.
Global firms already treat each country as its own product market. Ajay asks why Indian firms then sell one Maggi, or run one home-loan algorithm, across a country as diverse as India.

head: Kerala Is Three Places
dek: Even a small, seemingly uniform state contains several distinct markets.
more: When CMIE's algorithm divided India into homogeneous regions, Kerala came out as three: North, Central and South. Ajay discussed this with many people who know Kerala, and they agreed. The three parts really do differ in important ways, and three is the right level of detail, not ten.
Even a small, seemingly uniform state contains several distinct markets. The useful level of detail is a judgement call: fine enough to show real differences, coarse enough to stay usable.

head: 5x Income, 18x Phones: Homework for the Kelkar–Shah Book
dek: A single well-chosen indicator can reveal how far apart India's regions are socially, which an all-India average hides completely.
more: For the decentralisation chapter of In Service of the Republic, Ajay compared CMIE's 100 homogeneous regions. The richest region is about 5.3 times richer than the poorest. The number that stayed with him was the share of women who own a mobile phone, which captures household prosperity, social progressiveness and willingness to give a teenage girl a phone. That share is about 18 times higher in the top regions than in the bottom ones.
A single well-chosen indicator can reveal how far apart India's regions are socially, which an all-India average hides completely.

head: Bank of America's Tiny India in 1991
dek: Tailoring a product or process to a region has fixed costs, and a small market can't pay them.
more: In 1991 Bank of America took more interest in India than it does today. Even so, its entire Indian operation was about the size of its business in some small US state, because India was too poor to support much.

Tailoring a product or process to a region has fixed costs, and a small market can't pay them. As Indian markets for loans, noodles and chocolate grow, the case for regional customisation gets stronger.

head: South Indian Firms Cursing the North
dek: When a firm calls a market 'too difficult', it is often describing the limits of its own understanding.
more: Ajay knows firms that are comfortable operating in South India and dismiss North India as a wasteland they can't and won't operate in. His answer is to hire people who understand the North and work out how to compete there. The upside is real, even if the tidy, calm southern playbook won't work.
When a firm calls a market 'too difficult', it is often describing the limits of its own understanding. Those gaps are where other firms find room.

head: Credit Scores From Caps Lock and Battery Levels
dek: Behavioural data lets firms make predictions about one person, which is Amit's case for 'a market of one'.
more: Amit recalls his episode with Rahul Matthan and Matthan's book. Lenders are using big data to judge an individual's creditworthiness from odd signals: whether you type in all caps, or whether you anxiously keep your phone near 100% charge or let it run down to 3–4%.

Behavioural data lets firms make predictions about one person, which is Amit's case for 'a market of one'. Ajay's reply is that such models are still trained on a pooled group, so someone has to choose which group.

The clip that opens the episode.

head: Local → National → Adaptive: The Arc of the Indian Firm
dek: Until the 1980s, Indian firms were national only in name. Branch managers ran their own operations because they couldn't be monitored.
more: Until the 1980s, Indian firms were national only in name. Branch managers ran their own operations because they couldn't be monitored. From the 1990s, IT and telecom produced the true national firm, with central processes and controls. Ajay argues the next stage must bring local responsiveness back, this time with central controls intact.

head: The Brain With Severed Nerves
dek: Lant Pritchett describes the Indian state as a brain whose nerves to the fingers have been cut.
more: Lant Pritchett describes the Indian state as a brain whose nerves to the fingers have been cut. Ajay applies this to the old Indian firm. HQ may have had a strategy, but each branch did its own thing, so the firm was really a coalition of individuals and couldn't carry out a strategy, manage risk or stop local corruption.
printed: When the branch was a kingdom

head: The Unnoticed Engine of India's Boom
dek: The binding constraint on Indian business into the 1990s was telecom, which was either unavailable or absurdly expensive.
more: The binding constraint on Indian business into the 1990s was telecom, which was either unavailable or absurdly expensive. Then trade barriers fell, computers got cheap and the Vajpayee-era reforms ended the Department of Telecom's stranglehold. A generation of managers used this to build national firms with central data, ERP systems, Andersen Consulting/Accenture-style process engineering and operational audits. Firms grew in scale and productivity without adding much labour. Ajay counts this as a core driver of GDP growth from 1991 to 2011 that hardly anyone talks about.

head: Isomorphic Mimicry
dek: Amit borrows the biologists' term for copying a practice simply because it worked elsewhere.
more: Amit borrows the biologists' term for copying a practice simply because it worked elsewhere. Imported best practice made Indian firms more efficient but also more alike. Ajay agrees, but says the main channel was global firms' practices, not Indian business schools. In banking, for example, the template of a well-run foreign bank came in through foreign banks and people who had worked in them.

head: India as ~100 Homogeneous Regions
dek: CMIE groups India's roughly 700 districts into about 100 regions.
more: CMIE groups India's roughly 700 districts into about 100 regions. Each is a contiguous cluster of about seven districts within one state, with similar women's literacy and agroclimatic zone, and holds about 14 million people. Ajay says state boundaries are 'kinda random', so this is the more useful unit. Measured this way, India is more diverse than Europe or Africa. Lant Pritchett once told Ajay that by some measures India's spread is wider than that of Latin America and Africa merged together.

head: Localise Once the Market Can Pay for It
dek: Global firms reformulate products country by country.
more: Global firms reformulate products country by country. As India grows towards the market size of an Indonesia or Thailand, it becomes worth customising within India too: first North versus South, then by state, then by homogeneous region. This applies to software, such as home-loan algorithms, as much as to food. How far to go is a strategy choice, but one design for the whole country is hard to justify.

head: No Customer of One Without a Pool
dek: Amit argues Amazon and YouTube already personalise for each individual.
more: Amit argues Amazon and YouTube already personalise for each individual. Ajay replies that even a personal prediction comes from a model trained on many people's data. The real decision is which pool to train on: the world, India, South India, Tamil Nadu or one homogeneous region. Indian firms habitually choose all-India.
printed: A data set of one won’t do

head: Seeing Like a Firm
dek: Like James C Scott's state, the big national firm can't perceive local reality.
more: Like James C Scott's state, the big national firm can't perceive local reality. Despite trillion-rupee valuations, it serves only some income bands in each region and leaves much of the country unserved. That leaves room for well-adapted local firms, like a deeply optimised Rajasthan firm, even though the national firms have a cost of capital no one can match.

head: The Federated Firm: HQ as Treasury, Regions as Mini-CEOs
dek: Multinationals already know Poland differs from France. Ajay proposes Indian firms borrow that approach.
more: Multinationals already know Poland differs from France. Ajay proposes Indian firms borrow that approach. HQ keeps strategy, capital allocation, governance, the board and HR, plus non-negotiables like anti-money-laundering. Regional units own their P&L and adapt products, processes and models such as home-loan scoring. They compete for HQ capital on ROE. Firms range from Casio, which changes only local ads and distribution, to fully flexible designs. Whether to use 5, 20 or 100 regions depends on the firm's management capability relative to the diversity it faces.

head: Coase Reopened: Must the Inside of a Firm Be Stalinist?
dek: Coase asked why firms are centrally run internally while the outside world runs on prices and contracts, which raises the question of where a firm's boundary should be.
more: Coase asked why firms are centrally run internally while the outside world runs on prices and contracts, which raises the question of where a firm's boundary should be. Ajay's modern question is whether the inside needs that much central control at all. Amit frames it as: if bottom-up order works for societies, how much of it can large firms copy?

head: India Is a Smaller Market Than 1.4 Billion
dek: Amit summarises Sajith Pai's income tiers, giving rough figures. About 1–2 crore Indians are at the top, of whom 20–30 lakh are fully 'first world'.
more: Amit summarises Sajith Pai's income tiers, giving rough figures. About 1–2 crore Indians are at the top, of whom 20–30 lakh are fully 'first world'. About 10 crore are middle class, living like people in middle-income countries; Amit says domestic workers and drivers belong here. The rest live like sub-Saharan Africa and often cannot even afford to migrate to a city for work. For some products, the real market is tiny.

head: Profit Dispersion Reveals a Firm's Blind Spots
dek: Ajay's reply to the 'small market' view is to compute revenue or profit per capita, or ROE, for each homogeneous region.
more: Ajay's reply to the 'small market' view is to compute revenue or profit per capita, or ROE, for each homogeneous region. A wide interquartile range suggests a failure of the firm, not of the market. People in the weakest regions have some disposable income too, and serving them means dropping the one-product-for-all-India mindset.

head: Tastes Travel With People
dek: Amit points out that tastes are not tied to places: Tamils and Bengalis live all over India.
more: Amit points out that tastes are not tied to places: Tamils and Bengalis live all over India. He suggests firms could make many variants, ship all of them everywhere, and let local shopkeepers decide what to stock. Ajay agrees this is a real problem and compares it to travellers bringing back British or Japanese Kit Kats, or a Tamilian stocking up on podi in Chennai.

head: Why Bad Players Bet on Poker but Never on Chess
dek: Noise hides ability. Wherever luck is loud and feedback is slow, people mistake good fortune for skill.
more: Ajay once asked Amit why weak players happily put money on poker but never on chess. Amit's answer: chess gives you feedback after every game, and Elo ratings on chess sites and in competitive chess are accurate, so everyone knows their level and a bad player won't bet against a better one. Poker is also a game of skill, but its variance is far higher. Every bad player gets lucky hands, lucky sessions, even lucky months, and many conclude they are good when they aren't.

Noise hides ability. Wherever luck is loud and feedback is slow, people mistake good fortune for skill. Good players guard against this by judging themselves on expected value rather than on short-term results.

head: Entitlement Tilt: When Doing It Right Makes You Play Wrong
dek: Knowing the correct play doesn't protect you from how you react to bad outcomes.
more: The kind of tilt Amit was personally prone to was 'entitlement tilt'. He would sit down armed with math, game theory and a knowledge of ranges. Then a player who knew none of it, playing as if it were a festive card game, would hand him bad beats on hands he had played correctly. Amit would start fuming, play badly and lose money.

Knowing the correct play doesn't protect you from how you react to bad outcomes. Believing you deserve to win because you're doing things right is a trap of its own. The mental game is a separate skill from the math.

head: Why the Winners Leave Poker and the Losers Stay
dek: This is adverse selection over time. The people who can leave do, and the ecosystem fills up with those who can't.
more: Amit played poker seriously from 2010 to 2015 and wrote a regular poker column for the Economic Times. When he started, he saw that only about 5% of players were long-term winners, and he assumed the winners would stay while the losers rotated out. By the time he left, he had realised the opposite was true. Winners leave because what makes them good at poker also makes them good at other things. Losers stay because they're addicted. He has seen lives destroyed by gambling addiction, and he warns anyone with an addictive personality not to play.

This is adverse selection over time. The people who can leave do, and the ecosystem fills up with those who can't. It also suggests that disciplined probabilistic thinking is a skill that carries over to other fields.

head: Why I Loved and Left Poker

more: It explains the law of truly large numbers: with enough iterations, the most unlikely things will happen. That is why bad luck shouldn't be read as fate.

more: The full body of his poker writing, for readers who want to go deeper than the stripped-down presentation.
