head: Expected Value: Separate the Decision from the Outcome
dek: Amit starts with a fair coin. Heads, you win 51 paise; tails, you pay 49.
more: Amit starts with a fair coin. Heads, you win 51 paise; tails, you pay 49. Over 100 flips you'd expect to be up 100 paise, which is +1 paisa per flip, so taking the bet is 'plus-EV'. If it lands tails, you didn't decide badly; you got unlucky. The poker version: you hold ace-ten of hearts with a flush draw, which is about 38% to hit by the river. Your opponent shoves 10,000 into a 10,000 pot. You must call 10,000 to win 20,000, so you need to be right 33.3% of the time. That makes it an easy call. If he had bet 20,000 instead, you'd need 40%, and the right play is just about a fold. Keep making plus-EV decisions and you win in the long run.

head: Pot Equity, Fold Equity, and Why Aggression Pays
dek: Pot equity is your chance of winning multiplied by the size of the pot.
more: Pot equity is your chance of winning multiplied by the size of the pot. Fold equity is what you collect when your raise makes the opponent give up. An all-in that loses money on raw winning chances can become plus-EV if the opponent folds half the time. So there are two reasons to bet: for value (to make a worse hand call) or as a bluff (to make a better hand fold). Implied odds stretch the same logic forward in time. Calling with a small pair can be worth it, even though you'll hit your third six only about one time in eight, if hitting it lets you extract much more money later. Since you never know an opponent's exact cards, all of this is calculated against the range of hands they might hold.
printed: The coin that pays a paisa

head: Position Is Information
dek: The dealer button moves one seat every hand, and the player on the button acts last.
more: The dealer button moves one seat every hand, and the player on the button acts last. Acting later means you have already seen what everyone else did before you choose. That informational edge is so valuable that you can profitably play weaker and weaker hands the later your position. Part of a hand's value lies in when you get to decide, not just in the cards.

head: Game Theory Optimal vs Exploitative Play
dek: Suppose you bet 100 into a 200 pot on the river. Your opponent gets 3-to-1 on a call and needs to be right 25% of the time.
more: Suppose you bet 100 into a 200 pot on the river. Your opponent gets 3-to-1 on a call and needs to be right 25% of the time. If your betting range is exactly 25% bluffs and 75% value hands, you can't lose in the long run, whatever they hold or do. If they call too much or fold too much, you profit; if they play perfectly, you break even. For a pot-sized bet, the balanced mix is one-third bluffs. Real humans can't play this way consistently, so real poker is exploitative. You spot opponents' deviations: if they fold too much, you bluff more; if they call too much, you bet more for value. The same logic explains why the optimal strategy in rock-paper-scissors is pure randomness, and why both penalty-takers and goalkeepers must randomise.

head: Tilt: Mastering the Math Isn't Enough
dek: Tilt is a loss of composure, usually triggered by anger, that leads to bad decisions and lost money.
more: Tilt is a loss of composure, usually triggered by anger, that leads to bad decisions and lost money. Poker's emotional load is unusual. A bad day on March 15 can wipe out everything you won in January and February, especially since most players don't manage their bankroll. That can be devastating for men whose ego is tied to money as status and to winning. Loss aversion makes it worse, because a loss hurts more than an equal win pleases. There are many kinds of tilt, and you need to know which ones you're prone to.

head: Acknowledge Luck, Then Control the Controllable
dek: This is Amit's first life lesson from poker. Poker is a game of skill, but the amount of luck in it is so large that the skill lies in managing that luck.
more: This is Amit's first life lesson from poker. Poker is a game of skill, but the amount of luck in it is so large that the skill lies in managing that luck. Life is the same. Misreading luck has costs in both directions. Good fortune can make us arrogant and complacent, while bad fortune can make us defeatist or give us imposter syndrome. The answer is not fatalism. Accept what you can't control, focus only on what you can, and play the cards you're dealt as well as possible.

head: Don't Be Results-Oriented: Poker as a Route to Equanimity
dek: Poker players are taught not to judge themselves by short-term results but by the quality of their process.
more: Poker players are taught not to judge themselves by short-term results but by the quality of their process. Amit links this to the Gita: your dharma is to work hard and do the right thing, not to chase validation or the rewards you feel you're owed. Much of our unhappiness comes from not accepting consequences we don't control. Fully absorbing this produces a peaceful, almost Buddhist detachment from outcomes.

head: Think Probabilistically and Beat Hindsight Bias
dek: This is Amit's second life lesson. Hindsight bias makes everything in the past look inevitable.
more: This is Amit's second life lesson. Hindsight bias makes everything in the past look inevitable. Once an event is over it either happened or it didn't. But beforehand, like a die still in the air, it was a set of probabilities. Seeing past decisions this way stops us blaming ourselves for good bets that went wrong. Putting rough numbers on important decisions also gives us clarity about what we are doing and why.
printed: The die is still in the air

head: We Are All Gambling Already
dek: When people dismiss poker as gambling, Amit gives two answers. First, it's a game of skill.
more: When people dismiss poker as gambling, Amit gives two answers. First, it's a game of skill. Second, what's wrong with gambling? If gambling means acting on probabilistic judgements, we do it all day. Crossing the road carries a risk of being hit by a truck that is greater than the risk of an air accident. Approaching someone at a bar, buying a house and making a friend are all bets. Every action, with its opportunity costs, is a gamble. Most of us think probabilistically without admitting it; doing it openly helps us do it better.

head: The Law of Truly Large Numbers
dek: In his column 'Unlikely is Inevitable', Amit explains that with enough iterations, the most unlikely things will happen.
more: In his column 'Unlikely is Inevitable', Amit explains that with enough iterations, the most unlikely things will happen. So when terrible things happen to us, it isn't fate or the universe conspiring against us; it is how probability works over a long life. Ajay gives a personal version from years of walking in the mountains.

head: Many Small 51% Bets Beat One Big Conviction Bet
dek: Ajay applies this to finance, citing what he believes is Mark Twain's line: 'if you must forecast, forecast often'.
more: Ajay applies this to finance, citing what he believes is Mark Twain's line: 'if you must forecast, forecast often'. The common mistake is to stay cautious and only commit when you feel absolutely sure, which he calls a delusion. Efficient markets theory says markets know a lot and pricing mistakes are small, so even reaching 51% accuracy is hard. Many small positions, each with a 51% chance, will work out better than one giant position held with full conviction.

head: Independence and the Illusion of Diversification
dek: Ajay points out a hidden requirement. The law of large numbers only works if the draws are independent.
more: Ajay points out a hidden requirement. The law of large numbers only works if the draws are independent. In poker, shuffling guarantees that. In finance it does not, because a single mindset can make a hundred apparently separate bets all flow from one correlated idea. You then believe you're diversified when you aren't. So you need many genuinely different ideas, each with a 51% edge.

head: Put In Volume
dek: This is Amit's third life lesson. A single hand between the world's best player and a beginner is roughly 51-49, so the edge only shows up over a large sample.
more: This is Amit's third life lesson. A single hand between the world's best player and a beginner is roughly 51-49, so the edge only shows up over a large sample. Poker players call building that sample 'putting in volume'. Every decision should aim to be plus-EV, and you must stay self-critical, because your assumptions or math may be wrong. For creators, volume pays twice. Constant iteration makes you better, and each new piece is another chance at a breakthrough idea or a viral hit. This doesn't mean spreading yourself across everything, which Amit calls daft; it means putting volume into what you're passionate about.

head: The Tragic Asymmetry: Life Doesn't Give You a Million Hands
dek: In poker you can play a million hands; Amit used to play several tables at once online.
more: In poker you can play a million hands; Amit used to play several tables at once online. In many areas of life you can't build that kind of sample. Amit notes that he and Ajay were dealt incredibly good starting hands, and that their dharma is to make the most of them and help others. Ajay's response: where a large sample isn't an option, be zen. Don't beat yourself up, don't rage against the world, accept those lotteries and make the best of them.

head: The opening spar. Ajay says listeners think
more: The opening spar. Ajay says listeners think 'we're some dull people that keep trying to feed you one obscure episode after another', and that 'one of us is a genius' at poker. Amit replies: 'I object to this. First of all, nobody thinks we're dull people... at least everybody in the comments seems to love us.' Then: 'the golden rule is that you underpromise and overdeliver. You are over promising by saying I'm a genius.'

head: On entitlement tilt, Amit describes the opponent who ruins his math-perfect game
more: On entitlement tilt, Amit describes the opponent who ruins his math-perfect game: 'some idiot who knows none of this and is playing it like Teen Patti on Diwali'. Teen Patti is the casual card game played at Diwali.

head: Amit on not being results-oriented
more: Amit on not being results-oriented: 'Lord Krishna and Spike Lee would be in agreement over this. Do the right thing, don't worry about the fruits of your action.' The line pairs the Gita's teaching on action with Spike Lee's film title.

head: Ajay cites Mark Twain (
more: Ajay cites Mark Twain ('I think') as saying 'if you must forecast, forecast often', and uses it to argue for many small bets over rare high-conviction ones.

But a hand of poker between the world's best player and 'someone who just learned the rules, maybe someone who just watched my presentation' is about 51-49.

head: Amit says films and popular culture
more: Amit says films and popular culture 'completely get it wrong'. They make poker look like a game of spotting tells and bluffs, when the foundation is math and game theory.

head: The deadpan ending. Picking up on Ajay's advice not to beat yourself up, Amit muses aloud
more: The deadpan ending. Picking up on Ajay's advice not to beat yourself up, Amit muses aloud: 'How does somebody beat themselves up?' After a pause from Ajay, he signs off: 'next time.'

head: The Luckiest Thing: Being There When NSE Was Built
dek: Ajay calls it dumb luck, but he made it possible by choosing the riskier, more interesting place to be.
more: Ajay finished his PhD in the US in 1993, two years after India's reforms began in 1991. He could have stayed in America, but he had a gut instinct that India was entering a dramatic period, so he moved back without knowing what would come of it. At that moment a team including R.H. Patil, Ravi Narayan and Chitra Ramakrishna was building the National Stock Exchange. Ajay got to be a bit player in it, and calls it one of the most exciting times of his life.

Ajay calls it dumb luck, but he made it possible by choosing the riskier, more interesting place to be. That one choice put him where the luck could find him, which is the episode's theme in a single life decision.
printed: A walk-on part in a war

head: The Biggest Mistake: Floating Instead of Working
dek: Talent praised as an identity becomes a trap. Effort and habit compound over time, and a few minutes of honest self-reflection each day is how you catch yourself drifting before decades slip by.
more: Asked for his biggest mistake, Amit says he didn't work hard enough through most of his life. He daydreamed about grand plans and never built the processes and habits he now teaches his writing students. Behind this was a deeper mistake: he came to self-reflection late. He doesn't like who he was twenty years ago. He was arrogant because he could learn in one hour what took others ten. He links this to the study on praise: children praised for being smart grew entitled, while those praised for effort kept trying. Still, he doubts he could have avoided the mistake, because he had to live and change before he could even see it.
Talent praised as an identity becomes a trap. Effort and habit compound over time, and a few minutes of honest self-reflection each day is how you catch yourself drifting before decades slip by.
printed: The perils of the quick study

head: Tracy Chapman, Fast Car and Stevie Wonder's Missing Disc
dek: Chance only paid off because both pieces were already in place. She had thousands of hours of craft behind her, and she happened to be there, ready.
more: At the 1988 Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert, Stevie Wonder found that a computer disc with programmed music he needed was missing. He refused to go on and reportedly left in tears. Tens of thousands of people were waiting. Tracy Chapman had played an earlier set to a smaller crowd and was still around with her acoustic guitar. The organisers asked her to fill in. She sang a couple of songs, including Fast Car. Her album had sold about 200,000 copies before the concert and about two million in the two weeks after. Amit, for whom Fast Car has been his favourite song since the late 80s, remembered this story when Chapman sang it at the Grammys recently. That memory is what brought the phrase 'surface area of serendipity' to his mind.

Chance only paid off because both pieces were already in place. She had thousands of hours of craft behind her, and she happened to be there, ready. Without the songs, nobody would have asked her. Without being there, the songs would never have reached that crowd.
printed: A missing disc and a fast car

head: Charati Charato Bhaga: Ajay's Father Building CMIE
dek: Increasing your surface area of serendipity is not a modern networking trick.
more: When Ajay's father started CMIE in 1976, it was his first project of that kind. He made a point of leaving the house every day to meet people, explain his project and get them to join in. This was before email and smartphones, so he set up a stream of meetings every day. He often quoted a Sanskrit proverb to Ajay: Charati Charato Bhaga, good things happen to those who walk.

Increasing your surface area of serendipity is not a modern networking trick. It is an old, deliberate discipline: if you are building something new, you have to go out every day and tell the world about it.

head: The Starbucks Hello That Built This Show's Crew
dek: Amit is a self-described introvert who has never marketed his shows. Here he got lucky on a day he happened to go out, partly because someone else, a natural connector, took the initiative.
more: A few months earlier, Amit was sitting in a Starbucks in Versova when a bearded man a couple of tables away said, 'Hi, you're Amit, right?' It was Vaibhav, who runs Chalchitra Talks. They had worked together online but never met. As they were parting, Amit realised the show might soon need a new crew, so he took Vaibhav's number. When the time came, he messaged Vaibhav, who sent him Nomsita's number. That is how the show got the crew Amit calls a blessing.

Amit is a self-described introvert who has never marketed his shows. Here he got lucky on a day he happened to go out, partly because someone else, a natural connector, took the initiative. Even a small increase in exposure can change your life in ways you can't plan.

head: How Ajay Rationed His Own Exposure
dek: Exposure doesn't have to mean being everywhere. You can put your ideas into lasting outlets that reach people without you, and spend the time you save on the craft itself.
more: Early in his career Ajay was invited into a good circuit of Indian economics conferences and is grateful for it. As the economics community declined, many of those conferences stopped working, so he became choosier about which ones to attend. He also helped build conferences where knowledge, not fame, is what counts. For years he accepted guest lectures because teaching in India works so badly. Then he built ongoing outlets: co-editing the Leap Blog, Everything is Everything, the XKDR YouTube channel, a flow of working papers and a fortnightly column. After that he began declining most speaking and teaching invitations because the opportunity cost was too high.
Exposure doesn't have to mean being everywhere. You can put your ideas into lasting outlets that reach people without you, and spend the time you save on the craft itself.

head: Fast Car (live at the Nelson Mandela Tribute Concert, 1988)
dek: It has been Amit's all-time favourite song since the late 80s and still moves him deeply.
more: It has been Amit's all-time favourite song since the late 80s and still moves him deeply. This performance made Chapman famous and is his main example of the surface area of serendipity.
The story that opens the episode's main theme: Chapman filling in for Stevie Wonder in 1988.

head: Surface Area of Luck
dek: It gives the episode's central formula: your chance of being lucky equals the action you take on your passion multiplied by the number of people you effectively tell about it.
more: It gives the episode's central formula: your chance of being lucky equals the action you take on your passion multiplied by the number of people you effectively tell about it.
Amit credits the idea to Jason Roberts and reads a definition from this essay, linked in the show notes.

head: The UNIX Episode (Episode 32)
dek: It tells the fuller story of free software and Unix, Ajay's model of people working for decades on something with no promised reward.
more: It tells the fuller story of free software and Unix, Ajay's model of people working for decades on something with no promised reward.
Ajay refers to it while lamenting how little open-source work happens in India.

head: The Tipping Point
dek: It helps you ask whether you are a deep specialist or someone who links people, and whether you should deliberately stretch toward the other.
more: It helps you ask whether you are a deep specialist or someone who links people, and whether you should deliberately stretch toward the other.
Amit uses the book's types of mavens, connectors and salesmen to describe himself and others.

head: Even Cowgirls Get the Blues
dek: The line reminds Ajay that people who seem brusque and prickly from a distance are usually fine once you get going, which helps him with his own difficulty meeting new people.
more: The line reminds Ajay that people who seem brusque and prickly from a distance are usually fine once you get going, which helps him with his own difficulty meeting new people.
Named as the source of the line 'There are no strangers, there are just friends you don't have yet.'

head: To Kill a Mockingbird
dek: It anchors his argument that if we looked for the good in each other instead of resenting each other, ideas would travel better through India's elite networks.
more: It anchors his argument that if we looked for the good in each other instead of resenting each other, ideas would travel better through India's elite networks.
Ajay recalls the ending, where Scout says Boo Radley turned out to be nice and Atticus says most people are, once you get to know them.

head: Six Degrees
dek: It explains how connected the world is, which is the science behind Ajay's model of transmission loss in human networks.
more: It explains how connected the world is, which is the science behind Ajay's model of transmission loss in human networks.
Amit calls it his 'mid-episode recommendation' during Ajay's discussion of networks and six degrees of separation.

head: Anatomy of a Fall
dek: It won the Palme d'Or at Cannes and several Oscar nominations.
more: It won the Palme d'Or at Cannes and several Oscar nominations. Amit calls it a masterpiece about the tension between telling a simple, explainable story and respecting how complex the world is, and says it proves we are in a golden age of cinema.
Amit's second recommendation, covering for Ajay, who drew a blank.

head: Anatomy of a Folly
dek: It is the longer version of his argument about how great films balance simplifying a story with honouring complexity.
more: It is the longer version of his argument about how great films balance simplifying a story with honouring complexity.
Amit's newsletter post on Anatomy of a Fall, linked in the show notes.

head: MAMI Film Festival
dek: It is his annual vacation: four films a day for about ten days.
more: It is his annual vacation: four films a day for about ten days. He counts living in Mumbai near its theatres as a lucky boost to his own surface area of serendipity, and says it reminds him how good world cinema is today.
Amit describes Mumbai's annual festival of the best films from Cannes, Venice, Berlin and elsewhere, plus great Indian films.

head: The Leap Blog
dek: It is where his ideas are available to anyone, all the time, instead of in one-off lectures.
more: It is where his ideas are available to anyone, all the time, instead of in one-off lectures.
Ajay names it, which he co-edits, among the outlets that let him decline most teaching and speaking invitations.

head: Surface Area of Serendipity = Excellence × Exposure
dek: Luck is not pure chance. You can widen the area it can hit.
more: Luck is not pure chance. You can widen the area it can hit. The idea is credited to Jason Roberts: your luck equals the passionate action you take multiplied by how many people you effectively tell about it. Amit restates it as excellence and exposure. Neither works alone. Without great songs, Tracy Chapman being backstage means nothing, and great songs that never reach anyone are wasted. Ajay sets out the two failures: the Jimi Hendrix who practises only in the bathroom, and the 'content-free hustler' who networks but knows nothing.

head: Exposure Runs Both Ways: You to the World, the World to You
dek: Amit widens the idea beyond networking. Reading, watching films and thinking about ideas also increase your surface area, because each one is a chance for something to change you.
more: Amit widens the idea beyond networking. Reading, watching films and thinking about ideas also increase your surface area, because each one is a chance for something to change you. Making things counts too. Every podcast, newsletter or essay leads to lucky connections, can change something in the world, and sharpens your own thinking.

head: Focus on Verbs, Not Adjectives
dek: Amit takes his writing advice and applies it to life. Praise for traits ('you're so smart') breeds entitlement and less effort, as the Mueller and Dweck study showed.
more: Amit takes his writing advice and applies it to life. Praise for traits ('you're so smart') breeds entitlement and less effort, as the Mueller and Dweck study showed. Praise for effort keeps people working. So build habits and processes rather than an identity of being talented, and make a daily habit of honest self-reflection, which most people never practise.

head: Don't Demand the Lollipop Before the Work
dek: Ajay sees a common pattern among young Indians: they want a guaranteed reward, a contract or a clear career path, before they commit years of effort.
more: Ajay sees a common pattern among young Indians: they want a guaranteed reward, a contract or a clear career path, before they commit years of effort. Great work doesn't come that way. Linus Torvalds wrote the Linux kernel as a young man with no salary, prize or fame in sight. Ajay thinks demanding a direct payoff for effort leads to weakness and mediocrity. Amit adds that this isn't individuals' fault: generations of scarcity built a goal-driven 'IIT, IIM, Citibank VP' culture that leaves little room for anything higher.

head: Greatness Is Way More Than 10,000 Hours
dek: Ajay pushes back on the popular 10,000-hour rule. That much practice might get you to play Für Elise reasonably well, but creating something genuinely new is different.
more: Ajay pushes back on the popular 10,000-hour rule. That much practice might get you to play Für Elise reasonably well, but creating something genuinely new is different. Torvalds, Ken Thompson, Tracy Chapman, Jimi Hendrix and Jimmy Page devoted entire lives to their work at extreme intensity. Real excellence is a lifelong devotion, not a number of hours you can finish.

head: Virtuous and Vicious Cycles of Excellence
dek: Amit builds on Nomsita's line, 'I am happy when I am doing things well, and I do things well when I'm happy.' If you do work for its own sake, the joy pushes you deeper, and going deeper brings more joy.
more: Amit builds on Nomsita's line, 'I am happy when I am doing things well, and I do things well when I'm happy.' If you do work for its own sake, the joy pushes you deeper, and going deeper brings more joy. The opposite is the entitled credential-holder: denied validation, they become bitter; given it, they decide they never needed to work. Ajay adds that the most dangerous thing about being an IITian is the feeling that 'I have arrived,' which lets people stop trying for years. You can slide into a vicious cycle without noticing, so self-reflection is how you get out.
printed: Round and round, up or down

head: The Hybrid Life: A Day Job Plus a Lifelong Craft
dek: Ajay borrows Richard Stallman's line, 'a good programmer will never starve.' A day job doesn't have to be your whole life.
more: Ajay borrows Richard Stallman's line, 'a good programmer will never starve.' A day job doesn't have to be your whole life. Ten to twenty hours a week on a personal project, kept up for decades, builds a large body of expertise. It also gives you a coherence that careers rarely do, since jobs move you between roles while your own project lets you chase one thing for years. India's economy now allows this kind of life, but the culture hasn't caught up.

head: Mavens and Connectors: Personality and Intention
dek: Using Gladwell's terms, Amit calls himself a maven, someone who goes deep, rather than a connector who naturally links people.
more: Using Gladwell's terms, Amit calls himself a maven, someone who goes deep, rather than a connector who naturally links people. His instinct has always been 'main marketing nahi karunga' (I won't do marketing): build something good and trust it to find its audience. He admits this is idealistic and wonders whether he should deliberately become more of a connector. Ajay, also a natural introvert, admits he struggles to meet new people too, but has learned to do it.

head: Superconnecting: Ideas Over Credentials, Across Disciplines
dek: Mentors like Rakesh Mohan, Suman Bery, Vijay Kelkar and Montek brought Ajay into India's economics community when he was new, and he tries to do the same for others.
more: Mentors like Rakesh Mohan, Suman Bery, Vijay Kelkar and Montek brought Ajay into India's economics community when he was new, and he tries to do the same for others. He follows two rules. First, ignore credentials such as Harvard, MIT, IIT or journal names, and judge people by whether their questions and ideas are interesting. Second, connect people across fields like economics, finance, public policy, software and statistics, who would never meet by chance at a conference.

head: The Inverse Law of Conference Panels
dek: Ajay argues that famous and powerful people are so constrained in public that on stage they say only bland, safe things, however interesting they are one-on-one.
more: Ajay argues that famous and powerful people are so constrained in public that on stage they say only bland, safe things, however interesting they are one-on-one. Gatherings meant to produce ideas should run on ideas, not big names. He leaves star-studded lineups to industry bodies like CII and FICCI.

head: Six Degrees and Transmission Loss
dek: Ajay's thought experiment: if ideas passed between people with no loss, six degrees of separation would mean you could play for one person and the whole world, Putin included, would soon know.
more: Ajay's thought experiment: if ideas passed between people with no loss, six degrees of separation would mean you could play for one person and the whole world, Putin included, would soon know. Then everyone could focus purely on their craft. In reality every link weakens the message, and only long-built trust lets a few sentences land with full force. Amit adds a twist: famous people are only about two degrees away from most of us, and it is the unknown person in Wisconsin who is hard to reach.

head: Culture as Network Infrastructure
dek: Ajay moves from the individual to the culture. If people were less envious, resentful and competitive, and more willing to see what is valuable in each other, ideas would travel through elite networks with less loss.
more: Ajay moves from the individual to the culture. If people were less envious, resentful and competitive, and more willing to see what is valuable in each other, ideas would travel through elite networks with less loss. Then everyone would need less self-promotion and fewer conferences. Modern India's elite culture is still young and being formed, and it is made of everyday behaviours, so each person can help improve it.

head: Great Art Edits Reality Yet Honours Its Complexity
dek: Every story simplifies the world, because telling a story means editing reality.
more: Every story simplifies the world, because telling a story means editing reality. Great art still manages to respect how complex the world is, and Amit finds that tension fascinating. Anatomy of a Fall is literally about it. More broadly, Amit argues that films like it show world cinema is in a golden age, whatever the Marvel and Bollywood mainstream suggests.

head: Amit's opening thank-you: there are…
more: Amit's opening thank-you: there are 'eighty-four trillion videos on YouTube' and 'eight billion people on this earth, constantly increasing that number because we are a horny species. And yet you're watching Ajay Shah and me.'

head: Ajay on famous panellists: once they go on a conference stage
more: Ajay on famous panellists: once they go on a conference stage, 'you end up having to say world peace.' Such star-studded events, he says, 'are for CII and FICCI to do, but not for the Indian intellectual community.'

head: Ajay on youngsters who want to join an open-source project for three months to put GitHub on their résumé
more: Ajay on youngsters who want to join an open-source project for three months to put GitHub on their résumé: 'And I just want to kick them out of the office that nothing works like that.'

head: Ajay on the…
more: Ajay on the 'content-free hustlers who are just trying to go out and schmooze and actually know nothing.'

head: Ajay's zero-transmission-loss world: Jimi Hendrix steps out of his bathroom, plays for one person and runs back in…
more: Ajay's zero-transmission-loss world: Jimi Hendrix steps out of his bathroom, plays for one person and runs back in, 'because then you're done, then Putin knows.' Amit later adds that Ajay is surely two degrees from Putin, 'though why you should want that kind of proximity...'

head: After Ajay says Amit knows when he's speaking with dead intent
more: After Ajay says Amit knows when he's speaking with dead intent: 'You are always dead serious with me, as I'm sure. And I'm never dead serious with you. So I'm glad we got that sorted out.'

head: Ajay credits Amit with…
more: Ajay credits Amit with saying 'every time another person succeeds a little part of me dies.' Amit: 'I didn't say that. I quoted a friend. My sentiment is the opposite.' Ajay: 'I withdraw my statement.'

head: Amit roasts his co-host: watch world cinema even
more: Amit roasts his co-host: watch world cinema even 'if you watch one film every three years like Ajay Shah here.' Later: 'Increase your surface area of serendipity, Ajay Shah, by watching as many films as you can, don't go to boring conferences. All these economists say the same damn things.'

head: Amit calls the young crew on camera
more: Amit calls the young crew on camera, 'Run, run. Run faster... Stop running,' then credits them for everything good about the show: 'All the credit goes here, some of it to me, none of it to Ajay.'

head: Amit's pitch for Magic Fruit: watch it so
more: Amit's pitch for Magic Fruit: watch it so that 'thirty years later, forty years later, perhaps ninety years later, if you're thirty and you live till one twenty, you'll be able to tell people I was there.'

head: Ajay explains moving back to India in 1993 with the lyric
more: Ajay explains moving back to India in 1993 with the lyric: 'Would you exchange a walk on part in a war for a lead role in a cage?'
'Youth is wasted on the young,' says Ajay. 'Indeed, and wisdom is wasted on the old,' replies Amit. At the end Amit returns to it: Magic Fruit shows the young sometimes have both.

head: Richard Stallman's line
more: Richard Stallman's line 'a good programmer will never starve,' which Ajay uses to argue that a day job can coexist with a serious craft.

head: Ajay accepts the role of luck with a song lyric
more: Ajay accepts the role of luck with a song lyric: 'I don't know why fortune smiles on some and lets the rest go free.'

head: Amit explains his introvert reluctance with Sartre
more: Amit explains his introvert reluctance with Sartre: 'hell is other people.'
'There are no strangers, there are just friends you don't have yet,' attributed to Tom Robbins's Even Cowgirls Get the Blues.

head: What's Water? The Plug Point as the Unseen
dek: The systems that matter most are often the ones we have stopped seeing.
more: Amit explains that the name of his podcast, The Seen and the Unseen, began with Bastiat's idea of the unintended consequences of public policy. Over time it came to mean the hidden layers behind society and our own minds, including the things we stop noticing. He recalls David Foster Wallace's story of one fish asking another 'how's the water today?' and the second replying 'what's water?' For us, electricity is that water: we plug in and it simply works. He invites the listener to dive into the plug point and travel down the wire to see what lies at the other end.
The systems that matter most are often the ones we have stopped seeing. Curiosity starts by treating the ordinary as strange.

head: Telling Akbar About the Switch
dek: By historical standards, an ordinary person today commands powers no emperor ever had, and we barely notice.
more: Ajay imagines taking a time machine to Akbar, the most powerful ruler of the Middle Ages, and telling him that you can plug something in, flick a switch, and magic happens. Electricity is technology so advanced it is indistinguishable from magic. Yet we have become 'dumb users' who flick switches and get a bill at month's end (or, in parts of India, steal the power).
By historical standards, an ordinary person today commands powers no emperor ever had, and we barely notice.

head: Routing Around the Shockley Limit
dek: A physical limit binds a particular design, not the goal. Ingenuity gets past it by changing the approach.
more: Solar panel costs have fallen at a compound rate of roughly 20–25% a year for 30 years. Ajay recalls that Shockley, one of the three Bell Labs scientists who invented the transistor, derived from quantum mechanics a ceiling on how much sunlight a silicon cell can turn into electricity. Ajay remembers the figure as about twelve percent. Engineers didn't accept defeat. They tried other materials and stacked layers, so that light passing through one layer is captured by the next.
A physical limit binds a particular design, not the goal. Ingenuity gets past it by changing the approach.

head: The Windmill That Kept Climbing
dek: Big engineering leaps are usually a sequence of solved sub-problems, each one unlocking the next.
more: A windmill sounds simple, but its progress has been a chain of ambitions. First, go higher, because winds are stronger aloft, as any kite flier knows. Then build giant blades that are light and strong and last 25 years. Then go offshore, where the flat sea gives stronger winds and allows even bigger machines: roughly 100-metre blades on each side, mounted on steel pylons driven into India's shallow coastal shelf, with the power carried back to land.
Big engineering leaps are usually a sequence of solved sub-problems, each one unlocking the next.
printed: Up, up and out to sea

head: From Heater-Bulbs to LEDs
dek: The energy revolution is not only about new power sources. Demand-side efficiency is a miracle in its own right.
more: Ajay remembers when the big puzzle was making tungsten bulbs last longer by filling them with a noble gas so the filament wouldn't oxidize. Tube lights then improved efficiency. But a tungsten bulb puts out 10% of its energy as light and 90% as heat, so it is really a heater. LEDs reached about 90% efficiency. White LED light required cracking blue LEDs, which Japanese scientists at UC Santa Barbara achieved. The exotic technology was then mass-produced and is now everywhere in India.
The energy revolution is not only about new power sources. Demand-side efficiency is a miracle in its own right.
printed: The bulb that was a heater

head: Zero-Priced Afternoons in Germany
dek: Renewables create stretches of near-free energy. The big opportunity is to reorganise life and business around them.
more: On many summer days in Germany, the price of electricity falls to zero because there is so much solar capacity, and Germany isn't even very sunny. India has perhaps 250–275 days of bright sun. If it got the economics right, afternoon power could be free there too. Ajay's favourite consequence is charging your EV, and a backup battery pack, for free every afternoon, so that personal transport costs only the price of the vehicle.
Renewables create stretches of near-free energy. The big opportunity is to reorganise life and business around them.

head: Killing the 1971 Oil Embargo Rumour
dek: Don't let convenient national myths settle in your head as facts. Trace them to a source, and especially those that feed a 'toxic brew' in foreign policy.
more: Growing up, Ajay heard vague claims that Middle Eastern states cut off oil to India during the 1971 Bangladesh war. The story supposedly didn't matter only because the war lasted 14 days and the Pakistani army surrendered. It nagged at him: had Saudi Arabia been colluding with the US? He felt something that big couldn't be left as a vague allegation. So he reached a personal friend of a former Indian ambassador to Saudi Arabia, and learned it never happened. It was a made-up rumour meant to paint those states as hostile to India.
Don't let convenient national myths settle in your head as facts. Trace them to a source, and especially those that feed a 'toxic brew' in foreign policy.

head: Kalpakkam Seen from the Finance Ministry
dek: Proving you can build something and building it competitively are different games.
more: While at the Ministry of Finance, before the Indo-US nuclear deal, Ajay realised that private firms in the US and France were building commercially competitive reactors. India's reactors were science projects. Once the Kalpakkam facility's costs were reckoned correctly, it simply wasn't competitive. Private outfits like Westinghouse are cost-conscious and risk-taking. Meanwhile, the era when Homi Bhabha, India's best and brightest, worked for the state (at an institution funded first by the Tatas, then by the government) is gone. The modern Indian state no longer attracts that level of talent.
Proving you can build something and building it competitively are different games. Pride in the first shouldn't block buying the second.

head: Manmohan Singh Stakes His Job on the Nuclear Deal
dek: Leaders can break institutional inertia, but a downstream rule can quietly cancel a historic win.
more: Amit praises Manmohan Singh for pushing through the Indo-US nuclear deal with George W. Bush despite opposition from the Left parties and Sonia Gandhi's reluctance. Singh said he would not stay prime minister if he couldn't do it. Ajay adds the backdrop: India's military and foreign-policy establishment leaned towards the USSR. The rapprochement with the US came from the imagination of leaders like Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee, Jaswant Singh and Manmohan Singh, not from the bureaucracy. The sour coda is that India's nuclear liability rules mean not one American or French reactor has arrived since.
Leaders can break institutional inertia, but a downstream rule can quietly cancel a historic win.

head: Bhutan Works, Nepal Doesn't
dek: Unemotional 'who has the skill, who has the site, who has the demand' deals beat nationalism.
more: India spends military and diplomatic effort protecting Bhutan from Chinese incursions, as Doklam in 2017 showed. In return, Indian companies build and run hydel plants in Bhutan, send the power back to India, and pay Bhutan rent for the sites. Indian engineering, Indian utilities, Indian demand and a Bhutanese site add up to a pragmatic deal. Nepal has vast hydel potential that fits perfectly: glaciers melt in summer just when North India runs its ACs. But the relationship is broken by toxic fights over its constitution and the idea of a Hindu state, so the deals never happen.
Unemotional 'who has the skill, who has the site, who has the demand' deals beat nationalism. The gap between Bhutan and Nepal shows what bad foreign policy costs.

head: Tamil Nadu's North Sea
dek: Natural endowments are only potential. Institutions and diplomacy decide whether a region cashes them in.
more: Ajay likens offshore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka to the UK's North Sea oil and gas: a bounty only a government with policy muscle can reap. Electricity is a state subject, so Tamil Nadu must first fix its own system. Evening peak prices, not flat-priced 25-year power purchase agreements, are what make offshore wind pay, so builders should be risk-takers who can go bankrupt. Then India must mend ties with Sri Lanka so Indian firms can build on Sri Lankan sites and bring the power ashore in Tamil Nadu. That would make Tamil Nadu a renewable-energy paradise for exporters facing carbon taxes. Amit pegs the needed investment at around 14 lakh crore rupees.
Natural endowments are only potential. Institutions and diplomacy decide whether a region cashes them in.

head: Why Amit Takes an Uber Despite Owning a Car
dek: A zero price on a scarce resource doesn't make it free. It makes it unavailable, and everyone pays in other ways.
more: Looking for other uses of the price system, Amit messaged his Takshashila friends, and Nitin Pai suggested car parking. On one side of a wall, real estate (especially Mumbai rent) is exorbitant. On the other side, the road, parking is free. So whoever gets there first takes the spot, need doesn't matter, and there are parking shortages everywhere. That is why Amit, who owns a small car he likes, often takes an Uber or public transport in Bombay.
A zero price on a scarce resource doesn't make it free. It makes it unavailable, and everyone pays in other ways.

head: World Energy Outlook 2023
dek: He admits people flee from reports as boring official platitudes, but calls this one unputdownable.
more: He admits people flee from reports as boring official platitudes, but calls this one unputdownable. Energy is 'pure drama' right now, and the report's facts, graphs and stories make that vivid. Never read a report, he says, but make an exception for this one.
Ajay's recommendation of the week: the IEA's October 2023 energy report.

head: Midnight in Chernobyl
dek: Gripping non-fiction reportage on what happened behind the scenes at Chernobyl.
more: Gripping non-fiction reportage on what happened behind the scenes at Chernobyl. Amit finds the TV series pretty good, but prefers the book. It shows the disaster as a failure of the Soviet state, rooted in the system's structure and incentives so that it seems bound to happen. It also reminds Indian readers that their own state was then a 'fax copy' of the Soviet model. Above all, it's a crackling read.
Amit's recommendation of the week, tied to the nuclear chapter.

head: Nuclear Power Can Save the World
by: Joshua S Goldstein, Staffan A Qvist & Steven Pinker
dek: It puts nuclear safety in perspective. Sixty years of nuclear deaths, Chernobyl included, roughly equal one month of coal-related deaths.
more: It puts nuclear safety in perspective. Sixty years of nuclear deaths, Chernobyl included, roughly equal one month of coal-related deaths. And 60 years of American nuclear waste could fit in a single Walmart.
The New York Times essay Amit reads from while making the case for nuclear power.

head: Anupam Manur's piece on the Bangalore water crisis
dek: Amit urges everyone to read it because it is so counterintuitive. Pricing water helps the poor, since the current system effectively redistributes from the poor to the rich who use far more water.
more: Amit urges everyone to read it because it is so counterintuitive. Pricing water helps the poor, since the current system effectively redistributes from the poor to the rich who use far more water.
Brought up while discussing other uses of the price system, amid Bangalore's water shortage.

head: Sell the Tiger to Save It
dek: It argues that legalising the sale of tigers would make people breed them, as they breed cows or chickens, and so save the species.
more: It argues that legalising the sale of tigers would make people breed them, as they breed cows or chickens, and so save the species. That runs against the reflex to ban everything.
Recalled as an old example of counterintuitive price-system thinking, written for the New York Times.

head: India's Agriculture Crisis (Episode 140, The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra & Kumar Anand
dek: A deeper dive into agriculture as a field where the state controls everything and farmers suffer.
more: A deeper dive into agriculture as a field where the state controls everything and farmers suffer.
One of the agriculture episodes Amit promised to link.

head: Aggregation Turns Randomness into Predictability
dek: One person switching a TV on or off is random, but thousands of households cancel each other out.
more: One person switching a TV on or off is random, but thousands of households cancel each other out. That makes demand smooth and forecastable, just as an insurer can predict daily car crashes even though each crash surprises the driver. Grid managers forecast demand in 15-minute slots using weather, cricket matches and other variables, then choose the cheapest way to meet it.

head: The Old World: Planners, Slow Coal and Canteen Contractors
dek: In the old system, government grid managers work like air traffic controllers, frantically matching supply to demand slot by slot.
more: In the old system, government grid managers work like air traffic controllers, frantically matching supply to demand slot by slot. Coal plants take hours to spin up or down, so sudden swings must be met by fast gas and hydel. Private generators are not real businesses. They sit on 25-year contracts with fixed returns, take no risk and do no thinking. The government does all the business thinking, and the waste shows up as expensive electricity.

head: Never Count Out Human Ingenuity
dek: Twenty-five years ago, net zero looked impossible because civilisation runs on fossil fuels, and many thought the planet was headed to become Venus.
more: Twenty-five years ago, net zero looked impossible because civilisation runs on fossil fuels, and many thought the planet was headed to become Venus. Then came a run of miracles: solar costs falling 20–25% a year for 30 years, giant offshore wind, and LEDs jumping lighting efficiency from 10% to 90%. Geothermal and geologic hydrogen are now on the horizon.

head: The Cruel Mismatch: Sun at Noon, Demand at Dusk
dek: Solar floods the grid in the afternoon, but demand spikes in the evening.
more: Solar floods the grid in the afternoon, but demand spikes in the evening. People come home and switch on lights, ACs and TVs, and fridge compressors kick in, all at once. Gas and hydel can't cover the gap, and coal can't run flat-out all day. The old grid has no good answer, and the renewable revolution has made the planners' lives harder.

head: Technology Races Ahead, Institutions Lag
dek: Ajay argues the bottleneck is no longer science but human institutions that 'did not get the memo' that the world has changed.
more: Ajay argues the bottleneck is no longer science but human institutions that 'did not get the memo' that the world has changed. Amit's image for this is the 'tube light' state, the Indian slang for someone slow on the uptake. Reality changes, and the state struggles to catch up 10–20 years later.

head: A Gap Between Supply and Demand Calls for Prices
dek: Whenever you hear 'reconcile supply and demand', the answer is the price system, which goes back to Adam Smith in 1776.
more: Whenever you hear 'reconcile supply and demand', the answer is the price system, which goes back to Adam Smith in 1776. Grid engineers can only order suppliers around because consumers face a fixed price. The efficient route is for both sides to adjust. Let prices fall to near zero on sunny afternoons and rise to 15, 25 or 50 rupees a unit in the evening, and nobody should cry profiteering.

head: Three Adjustments Flexible Prices Unleash
dek: First, demand: people check spot prices on their phones, AC remotes adjust temperature to price, ice is made in the free afternoon, and firms run a daytime shift plus a late-night one while skipping the expensive evening.
more: First, demand: people check spot prices on their phones, AC remotes adjust temperature to price, ice is made in the free afternoon, and firms run a daytime shift plus a late-night one while skipping the expensive evening. Second, wind: it keeps blowing after sunset, so it earns the evening premium and attracts investment. Third, storage: batteries, and water pumped from the Konkan up to the Sahyadris by day and released as hydel power at night. Storage operators are simply businesses that buy cheap and sell dear, with no central planner needed.

head: Let Markets, Not Engineers, Pick the Technology Mix
dek: Ajay rejects the engineer-led, centrally planned vision of the 'right' energy mix.
more: Ajay rejects the engineer-led, centrally planned vision of the 'right' energy mix. Investors should bet on wind, storage or offshore projects themselves and go bankrupt if they guess wrong. Failure has to be possible, which a 25-year fixed contract never allows.

head: Price Fluctuation Is Pro-Poor
dek: Without prices you get shortages, and the poor already live with them.
more: Without prices you get shortages, and the poor already live with them. Under flexible prices, average costs fall thanks to near-free solar afternoons. A poor household could charge an electric two-wheeler at noon, while the rich pay extra to top up their cars in the evening. Amit adds that supply-side innovation lowers prices over time. Ajay's analogy is airfares: red-eye and midday flights are cheap, 8 a.m. flights are dear, and people self-select instead of facing one flat government price.

head: Nuclear Is the Safest Energy, and Tribalism Hides It
dek: Coal smoke alone kills more than half a million people a year.
more: Coal smoke alone kills more than half a million people a year. In 60 years of nuclear power, only three accidents raised alarm: Three Mile Island killed no one, Fukushima's deaths came from the tsunami and a panicked evacuation, and Chernobyl was the result of Soviet bungling. Twenty-four countries run nuclear power without going on to build bombs. France gets about 71% of its electricity from nuclear, and its grid's carbon per kilowatt-hour is a tenth of the rest of the world's. Amit argues that the 'no nukes' movement of the 70s became green dogma because people think in tribes rather than judging each idea on its merits.

head: Decouple Nuclear Weapons from Nuclear Energy
dek: India's nuclear journey, from Homi Bhabha to Indira Gandhi and Pokhran, was a nationalist, self-reliant weapons project, and Ajay sees that story as done.
more: India's nuclear journey, from Homi Bhabha to Indira Gandhi and Pokhran, was a nationalist, self-reliant weapons project, and Ajay sees that story as done. Nuclear energy is a different game. It should belong to private, competitive, global capitalism, which means buying the best and cheapest reactors from whoever makes them.

head: The Liability Trap and the Promise of SMRs
dek: India's liability rules hold foreign reactor makers liable forever for any accident, whoever was at fault, so no vendor will sell.
more: India's liability rules hold foreign reactor makers liable forever for any accident, whoever was at fault, so no vendor will sell. This has negated the essence of the Indo-US nuclear deal. The same wall awaits small modular reactors: 50-megawatt 'black boxes' that could sit in a factory corner. They could let, say, an aluminium plant make zero-carbon metal and export to Europe without facing carbon border taxes.

head: Foreign Policy Is About Interests, and Energy Runs Through It
dek: Amit notes that markets gain from larger networks, and nationalism shrinks them.
more: Amit notes that markets gain from larger networks, and nationalism shrinks them. Ajay argues foreign policy should be deal-making for citizens' welfare, not propaganda or scoring debating points at the UN. Energy shows the stakes: Bhutan's hydel deal is a success, Nepal's untapped hydel is a failure, and the Sri Lanka offshore-wind bounty is waiting. India has failed to give its neighbours a stake in its prosperity, as a European Union-style approach would.

head: Prices in 'Sacred' Domains
dek: The logic that fixes electricity applies elsewhere. Price water, which helps the poor.
more: The logic that fixes electricity applies elsewhere. Price water, which helps the poor. Price parking, since free roadside parking next to exorbitant real estate makes no sense. Privatise garbage collection. Allow organ sales. Legalise selling tigers so people breed them. Pay vaccine makers in line with the trillions of dollars they add to world GDP. Allow a market for surrogacy. Amit adds that every interference with the price system effectively redistributes from the poor to the rich.

head: Conservative and Liberal at Once: the Universal Outlaw
dek: Ajay calls himself conservative because he opposes social engineering by the state, and liberal because he treats the world as a blank slate to rethink from first principles.
more: Ajay calls himself conservative because he opposes social engineering by the state, and liberal because he treats the world as a blank slate to rethink from first principles. That offends both traditionalists and progressives who want the state as a big stick. Amit describes himself as having 'liberal ends but conservative means', in the tradition of Gokhale, Ranade and Agarkar.

head: After Ajay describes asking a coal plant to spin up, Amit deadpans
more: After Ajay describes asking a coal plant to spin up, Amit deadpans: 'I went to a coal power plant and I said, Hey dude, I need you to spin up and you're right, it was very slow in responding. I didn't hang around for a couple of hours to see if it started responding.'

head: Ajay on consumers who think power just appears
more: Ajay on consumers who think power just appears: 'we the fat, indolent, lazy ingrates of the world get this illusion that we just throw a switch and magically the electricity just happens.'

head: Amit points out that Ajay unknowingly used two slang words
more: Amit points out that Ajay unknowingly used two slang words, 'blade' (windmill blades) and 'tube light'. 'Blade' is Chennai slang for damn boring, learned from Anand Ramachandran, 'the funniest man in Indian history'. Ajay is the opposite of blade, making engineering so fun Amit would have wanted to be one: 'Thank God I wasn't.' And when it comes to Amit's bad jokes, Ajay is a tube light: 'You get them the next day.'

head: Ajay on markets
more: Ajay on markets: 'every trivial 300 parameter LLM knows that when you say reconcile a gap between supply and demand, that's what the price system does.'

head: Ajay daydreaming of free afternoon power in India
more: Ajay daydreaming of free afternoon power in India: 'imagine there are no policy mistakes. It's easy if you try.'

head: Ajay on solar's evening disappearance
more: Ajay on solar's evening disappearance: 'the sun is a fickle friend. He like misbehaves on you when you need him the most.'

head: Amit, after Ajay mocks government canteen contractors
more: Amit, after Ajay mocks government canteen contractors: 'some of my closest friends are government canteen contractors. You know, they make great medu vadas. They will be very offended at seeing this episode.'

head: Amit borrows Ajay's
more: Amit borrows Ajay's 'Hey, Mr. Gas' for TV news: 'every time I watch news television and I see some random expert spouting yarn on something, I feel like saying to him, Hey, Mr. Gas. Shut the fuck up.'

head: After Ajay describes small modular reactors as black boxes in a factory corner, Amit
more: After Ajay describes small modular reactors as black boxes in a factory corner, Amit says: 'I've been in your dinky little Mumbai flat, and one third of the flat is taken up by this big black box. Is it a reactor?'

head: Ajay casts the offshore wind opportunity as divine exasperation: the good Lord putting a bounty off the coast and
more: Ajay casts the offshore wind opportunity as divine exasperation: the good Lord putting a bounty off the coast and saying 'India, Sri Lanka, get your shit together. I'm giving you such a big prize, if only you will understand how to work together.'

head: Ajay's report recommendation
more: Ajay's report recommendation: 'So never ever read a report, but this time make an exception.' Amit: 'I'll make an exception just for you.' Then Amit on Midnight in Chernobyl: 'You can't put it down. Though you should at some point put it down because how long can you carry a book around?'

head: Ajay channels the line
more: Ajay channels the line 'sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic', imagining showing a light switch to Akbar.

head: Adam Smith
more: Adam Smith: 'the amazing solution, the remarkable solution, was in the pages of Adam Smith in 1776', namely let prices move.

head: G.K. Gokhale, Ranade and Agarkar, the freedom-struggle liberals Amit claims as heroes of…
more: G.K. Gokhale, Ranade and Agarkar, the freedom-struggle liberals Amit claims as heroes of 'liberal ends but conservative means'.

head: Amit on the Indian state of the Chernobyl era
more: Amit on the Indian state of the Chernobyl era: 'in many ways was a fax copy of what the Soviet state was'.

head: Friedman's 1968 speech that reset macroeconomics
dek: A clearly argued idea, delivered just before events vindicate it, can redirect a whole discipline.
more: In the 1950s, Keynesian economists were confident that government could tame the business cycle with fiscal policy. Through the 1960s that confidence cracked; the famous 1964 Kennedy tax cut, for example, did not deliver what the models forecast. In 1968 Milton Friedman became president of the American Economic Association and used the platform for a plain-English speech on what monetary policy can and cannot do. He treated people as agents who react to government actions, and he introduced the natural rate of unemployment. The inflation-ridden 1970s then unfolded much as he had warned. Robert Lucas, Tom Sargent, Ed Prescott and others turned his ideas into formal models that became modern macroeconomics.

A clearly argued idea, delivered just before events vindicate it, can redirect a whole discipline. Decades later it can reshape institutions too: Ajay traces today's inflation targeting, including India's adoption in 2015, back to this article.

head: The lone warriors of Indian inflation targeting
dek: Reforms that look obvious in hindsight often begin as lonely, mocked causes kept alive by a handful of people over many years.
more: Amit plays a behind-the-scenes clip in which someone off camera is coaxed into shouting 'Inflation targeting is nonsense', and adds, 'you see what Ajay has to go through.' He then turns serious. Ajay and K. P. Krishnan argued for inflation targeting in India about a decade before it was adopted in 2015. Ajay says the regime has since made a huge difference in simplifying and stabilizing the Indian economy.
Reforms that look obvious in hindsight often begin as lonely, mocked causes kept alive by a handful of people over many years.

head: Hayek: shaped by war, flu, and one book
dek: Great thinkers are formed by trauma and by chance encounters with books.
more: Friedrich Hayek was born around 1899. He fought in World War I, where an attack in 1917 damaged the hearing in his left ear, and in 1918 he survived the Spanish flu. Amit contrasts this with his own generation, for whom Partition and the Emergency feel distant. At the London School of Economics Hayek drifted into democratic socialism and Marxism. Reading Ludwig von Mises's book Socialism turned him into a classical liberal, and he became Keynes's great intellectual opponent.
Great thinkers are formed by trauma and by chance encounters with books. A single book can turn a socialist into one of the twentieth century's leading defenders of markets.

head: What Wittgenstein actually wrote in the trenches
dek: Great minds are still young bodies in a war. The gap between the legend and the diary is a useful corrective to hero-worship.
more: Hayek was Wittgenstein's second cousin and read the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus before it was published, and both men served in World War I. Amit once came across Wittgenstein's wartime diaries on Twitter and expected profound philosophy written under fire. Instead the diaries were mostly about wanting sex.
Great minds are still young bodies in a war. The gap between the legend and the diary is a useful corrective to hero-worship.

head: Hayek was personally closer to Keynes than to Friedman
dek: Intellectual disagreement and personal friendship can coexist, and often do among serious thinkers.
more: Hayek and Keynes were the great intellectual rivals of their era, while Hayek and Friedman were broadly on the same side, though Amit recalls they disagreed on monetary policy. Even so, the biographer of both Hayek and Keynes observed that Hayek was personally closer to Keynes than to Friedman.
Intellectual disagreement and personal friendship can coexist, and often do among serious thinkers.

head: Armen Alchian stopping people in hallways
dek: A paper's real influence shows in how urgently smart people press it on others.
more: When Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' came out, the economist Armen Alchian was so struck by it that he would stop colleagues in university hallways and urge them to read it.
A paper's real influence shows in how urgently smart people press it on others. Some ideas get passed hand to hand.

head: Coase, the outsider who won the economics Nobel
dek: Outsiders who don't take a field's assumptions for granted can see puzzles that insiders have stopped noticing.
more: Ronald Coase was a law thinker, not even an economist, yet he won the Nobel Prize in Economics. Ajay argues that being an outsider helped him. He did not simply adopt economists' vocabulary and modelling habits. Instead he asked a naive-sounding question: why does commerce run on prices and bargaining outside the firm, but on obedience and organisation charts inside it?
Outsiders who don't take a field's assumptions for granted can see puzzles that insiders have stopped noticing.

head: Bastiat's tuberculosis-lunged vow
dek: Bastiat is a model of the public intellectual: he stated, in plain language, ideas that scholars formalized decades later, and he treated those ideas as commitments worth his last breath.
more: Frédéric Bastiat (1801–1850) was an essayist, for a time a member of parliament, and a tireless popularizer who travelled to spread his ideas. In Amit's telling, Bastiat caught tuberculosis on a book tour in the US. Realizing he was dying, he vowed to keep proclaiming his principles to his last breath. He died at 49.
Bastiat is a model of the public intellectual: he stated, in plain language, ideas that scholars formalized decades later, and he treated those ideas as commitments worth his last breath.

head: Winning the Bastiat Prize twice
dek: Being claimed by a tradition you admire can mean more than the money or the validation of a prize.
more: Amit won the Bastiat Prize, a global journalism award for writers who promote the free society, in 2007 and again in 2015. He believes Tim Harford is the only other two-time winner. The money helped at the time, but what mattered more was the prize's namesake. Amit sees Bastiat as a Renaissance man with interests across everything, no credentialism, never part of the system, and an outsider whose ideas went against convention.
Being claimed by a tradition you admire can mean more than the money or the validation of a prize. Bastiat offers a template for thinking independently without credentials.
printed: Six francs and a missing shoe

head: The Role of Monetary Policy
dek: Of the thousands of macro papers Ajay has read, this is the one he sees as the turning point of twentieth-century macroeconomics, both in ideas and in policy.
more: Of the thousands of macro papers Ajay has read, this is the one he sees as the turning point of twentieth-century macroeconomics, both in ideas and in policy. It treats people as optimizers, introduces the natural rate of unemployment, confines monetary policy to keeping prices stable, and is written in plain English.
Ajay's first pick: Friedman's 1968 American Economic Association presidential address.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: Amit admits his bias but considers it the greatest work of the twentieth century.
more: Amit admits his bias but considers it the greatest work of the twentieth century. It shows that knowledge is too dispersed for any central planner to gather, and that prices solve the coordination problem. It had a huge impact on him and on economics.
Amit's first pick: Hayek's 1945 rebuttal of Oscar Lange's proposal for a Central Pricing Board.

head: The Nature of the Firm
dek: It opened Ajay's mind to thinking about the market economy. It explains why firms exist: contracting is costly.
more: It opened Ajay's mind to thinking about the market economy. It explains why firms exist: contracting is costly. It treats the firm as a complicated thing to be understood rather than a profit-maximizing black box.
Ajay's second pick: Coase's 1937 article.

head: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
dek: Through the broken-window parable it introduces opportunity cost, roughly sixty years before the term was coined, in language anyone can follow.
more: Through the broken-window parable it introduces opportunity cost, roughly sixty years before the term was coined, in language anyone can follow. The lesson applies to taxes, state funding of the arts, and how you spend your own hour.
Amit's second pick, and the source of the name of his podcast The Seen and the Unseen.

head: Economics in One Lesson
dek: One of the seminal books from which many people learn economics for the first time.
more: One of the seminal books from which many people learn economics for the first time.
Cited as a book directly inspired by Bastiat's seen-and-unseen essay.

head: I, Pencil
dek: It combines Adam Smith's invisible hand with Hayek's insight about knowledge.
more: It combines Adam Smith's invisible hand with Hayek's insight about knowledge. Told by a pencil, it shows millions of scattered know-hows combining to make it with no one in charge.
Brought up as another essay Amit loves, while explaining how prices coordinate society.

head: The Road to Serfdom
dek: Amit calls it brilliant. It lays out how central planning and its authoritarianism lead to serfdom.
more: Amit calls it brilliant. It lays out how central planning and its authoritarianism lead to serfdom.
Part of Hayek's backstory: a 1944 bestseller so scarce, partly because of wartime paper shortages, that Hayek himself couldn't get a copy.

head: Socialism: An Economic and Sociological Analysis
dek: This is the book that turned the young Hayek from democratic socialism and Marxism into a classical liberal.
more: This is the book that turned the young Hayek from democratic socialism and Marxism into a classical liberal.
Mentioned in Hayek's biography.

head: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
dek: Amit calls it Wittgenstein's great book, and it is a link between two giants of 20th-century thought.
more: Amit calls it Wittgenstein's great book, and it is a link between two giants of 20th-century thought.
Mentioned in passing: Hayek, Wittgenstein's second cousin, read it before it was published.

head: Keynes vs. Hayek rap battles ('Fear the Boom and Bust' and 'Fight of the Century')
dek: Amit calls them great: a fun way into the clash between the two dominant schools of thought of that era.
more: Amit calls them great: a fun way into the clash between the two dominant schools of thought of that era.
Linked in the show notes while describing the long Hayek–Keynes rivalry; co-written by Russ Roberts of EconTalk.

head: The Evolution of Everything
dek: A great book showing that almost everything beautiful in the world, from language to life itself, emerges from the bottom up rather than by design.
more: A great book showing that almost everything beautiful in the world, from language to life itself, emerges from the bottom up rather than by design.
Raised while explaining spontaneous order.

head: Matt Ridley on The Seen and the Unseen
dek: Amit calls it a great episode, and a longer conversation on bottom-up order.
more: Amit calls it a great episode, and a longer conversation on bottom-up order.
Amit's episode with Ridley, mentioned alongside his book.

head: Marginal Revolution University
dek: Amit calls it the best way to understand concepts like the price system and opportunity cost clearly.
more: Amit calls it the best way to understand concepts like the price system and opportunity cost clearly. The videos are essentially recorded PowerPoints with no fancy production, and the knowledge is brilliant.
Amit's closing recommendation.

head: Keynes invented macroeconomics
dek: Before Keynes, nobody meaningfully treated a whole economy as a unit to study.
more: Before Keynes, nobody meaningfully treated a whole economy as a unit to study. He built that toolkit in the fires of the Great Depression. The resulting Keynesian package had several parts: government manages the business cycle mainly through fiscal policy, monetary policy matters little, and wise policymakers act on a public assumed to be 'more or less dumb'. Ajay thinks those Depression-era ideas didn't carry over well to later decades.

head: People are optimizers, not passive subjects (the Lucas program)
dek: Friedman insisted that when government acts, people change their behavior in response.
more: Friedman insisted that when government acts, people change their behavior in response. A pattern fitted to past data therefore can't be assumed to hold once policy changes. Robert Lucas and collaborators formalized this into models of optimizing individuals and firms. Change the interest rate or the tax rate and they respond. This became the machinery of modern economics.

head: The natural rate of unemployment
dek: Some unemployment always exists: people switch jobs, get laid off, or leave the labor force.
more: Some unemployment always exists: people switch jobs, get laid off, or leave the labor force. There is a floor consistent with stable inflation. Policy that tries to push unemployment below it only stokes inflation.

head: Monetary policy as a boring, accountable utility
dek: A central bank creates money out of thin air. Because it stands ready to borrow or lend unlimited amounts overnight, it sets the short-term interest rate, and that one decision is monetary policy.
more: A central bank creates money out of thin air. Because it stands ready to borrow or lend unlimited amounts overnight, it sets the short-term interest rate, and that one decision is monetary policy. Modern macro says this is the only thing it can do and the only thing it should do: deliver a stable, predictable inflation target. In India that target is 4%, and citizens should hold the RBI accountable for hitting it. Friedman's 1968 version focused on money supply. Modern financial systems made money supply too volatile to measure and control, so central banks switched to steering interest rates, but the rest of Friedman's package survives.

head: Boring fiscal policy that saves room for emergencies
dek: Fiscal policy is about the deficit the government runs. Ajay's rule: run a small, non-discretionary primary balance every year.
more: Fiscal policy is about the deficit the government runs. Ajay's rule: run a small, non-discretionary primary balance every year. Then, when a 2008-style crisis or a pandemic hits, run a large deficit. Small surpluses in normal years buy the space for those rare big deficits.

head: The second pillar: finance can sink economies
dek: Friedman's analysis of the Great Depression showed that a collapsing banking system can drag a whole economy down with it.
more: Friedman's analysis of the Great Depression showed that a collapsing banking system can drag a whole economy down with it. Ben Bernanke worked out the details and was running the Fed when 2008 hit. Ajay credits the two pillars together, inflation targeting and an understanding of finance, for the world getting through 2008 relatively mildly.

head: The knowledge problem
dek: Central planners treat running an economy as a problem of logic, like running an algorithm on all the data.
more: Central planners treat running an economy as a problem of logic, like running an algorithm on all the data. Hayek argued the data can never be gathered. Knowledge is scattered across millions of people and places, changes constantly, and is often unknown even to its holders: you may not know what you'll want tomorrow. Ajay's example from the earlier episode on power: on a cloudy day people switch off their ACs and use them at night instead, which no one can forecast. So decisions must be decentralized.

head: Prices are a miracle of coordination
dek: Suppose an earthquake disrupts a tin factory. You never hear about it, but the price of tin rises and you economize.
more: Suppose an earthquake disrupts a tin factory. You never hear about it, but the price of tin rises and you economize. Prices carry information that no one could otherwise communicate. Bastiat asked how Paris gets fed every morning without a planner; the answer is prices. Amit argues that if one person had invented prices, he would be ranked among the greatest thinkers in history. Cowen and Tabarrok compress it as 'a price is a signal wrapped in an incentive'.

head: Spontaneous order
dek: We instinctively assume things must be designed from the top down. Yet languages evolve from millions of people using words, and natural selection produced both humans and trees with no planner.
more: We instinctively assume things must be designed from the top down. Yet languages evolve from millions of people using words, and natural selection produced both humans and trees with no planner. People drunk on power often have an 'engineering mindset' that they can design and coordinate everything. Often the state just needs to get out of the way.

head: Why firms exist: contracting is costly
dek: Coase asked why the economy runs on prices and bargaining outside firms but on organisation charts and obedience inside them.
more: Coase asked why the economy runs on prices and bargaining outside firms but on organisation charts and obedience inside them. His answer is transaction costs. Negotiating, lawyering and endless renegotiation take time, effort and emotional energy. Inside a firm the boss simply says 'do this', which is efficient but sacrifices the flexibility of markets. A firm's optimal size is where these trade-offs balance out.

head: Firm boundaries shift as technology changes
dek: Coase treats the firm as a rational solution to a problem, so when the costs of collaboration change, the best solution changes too.
more: Coase treats the firm as a rational solution to a problem, so when the costs of collaboration change, the best solution changes too. Open-source software lets loose coalitions of individuals build what companies used to build, without the burden of being inside a firm. Firms themselves needn't be Stalinist. Great firms like Hindustan Lever are institutions with dispersed power and many autonomous decision-makers, so they survive changes of CEO.

head: Working in a firm is voluntary, not slavery
dek: Some argue that if you accept autocratic firms, you should accept autocratic rulers.
more: Some argue that if you accept autocratic firms, you should accept autocratic rulers. Amit rejects this. You join a firm voluntarily, sign a contract, and can leave under its terms. Calling corporate work 'modern slavery' gets it wrong, because the job is the best option available to the person who took it.

head: The seen and the unseen: opportunity cost
dek: In Bastiat's parable, someone breaks a window and onlookers say it's good for the economy because the glazier earns six francs.
more: In Bastiat's parable, someone breaks a window and onlookers say it's good for the economy because the glazier earns six francs. What is unseen is the shoe or book the owner would have bought with that money. Bastiat applies the same logic to taxes, state sponsorship of the arts and conscription. Look past first-order effects to what the money would otherwise have done.

head: Your future self is the unseen
dek: Amit teaches Bastiat's line that when the immediate consequence is favorable, the later consequences are often disastrous.
more: Amit teaches Bastiat's line that when the immediate consequence is favorable, the later consequences are often disastrous. Example: you sit down to write, play 'one game' of Candy Crush, and lose the hour. The dopamine is what is seen. A less-informed future self is what is not seen.

head: Great papers teach frames, not just conclusions
dek: Firms may one day look completely different, and a specific paper's conclusion may date.
more: Firms may one day look completely different, and a specific paper's conclusion may date. What lasts is the way of thinking: foundational principles you can bring to any question.
