head: Ideas outlast their authors
dek: Bastiat, Hayek and Friedman are gone, but their ideas still shape policy and how millions think.
more: Bastiat, Hayek and Friedman are gone, but their ideas still shape policy and how millions think. Amit's closing reminder is that people are temporary and ideas are what shape civilization. That includes the hosts themselves.

head: In a behind-the-scenes clip, Amit gets someone off camera to shout
more: In a behind-the-scenes clip, Amit gets someone off camera to shout 'Inflation targeting is nonsense!' at Ajay, the man who spent a decade fighting for it, then turns to the audience: 'You see what Ajay has to go through.'

head: Amit's public service announcement
more: Amit's public service announcement: 'When people think of Hayek, they think Salma Hayek. When people think of Lange, they think Jessica Lange. No, you do not need to think about those figures.' Think of Friedrich Hayek, and ignore Oscar Lange completely.

head: After noting that Hayek was personally closer to his rival Keynes than to his ally Friedman, Amit
more: After noting that Hayek was personally closer to his rival Keynes than to his ally Friedman, Amit says: 'So the few times you and I disagree, Ajay Shah, I don't worry about our friendship at all.'

head: Ajay notes that Coase was a law thinker, not even an economist, yet won the Nobel Prize in Economics. Amit cuts in with the show's title
more: Ajay notes that Coase was a law thinker, not even an economist, yet won the Nobel Prize in Economics. Amit cuts in with the show's title: 'Everything is everything.'

head: On why the five promised papers became four
more: On why the five promised papers became four: 'Because the light is going down.' That reminds Amit of Bastiat's Candlemaker's Petition, in which candlemakers ask the government to block the sun.

head: Shooting outdoors, Amit clarifies
more: Shooting outdoors, Amit clarifies that 'in the show notes below' means below the YouTube screen, 'not below where I am sitting because there is grass and there is fresh earth.'

head: On Bastiat's question of how a planner could feed Paris
more: On Bastiat's question of how a planner could feed Paris: 'And where are we going to grow upma? Though I don't think anyone in Paris has upma.'

head: Amit has Bastiat silence the broken-window optimists by borrowing a phrase of Ajay's from an earlier episode
more: Amit has Bastiat silence the broken-window optimists by borrowing a phrase of Ajay's from an earlier episode: 'Hey Mr. Gas, keep quiet.'

head: Ajay explaining central banks
more: Ajay explaining central banks: 'A central bank invents money. Okay, it makes money out of thin air. Okay, just like the Bitcoin and Ethereum folk do.'

head: Amit, listing products of natural selection
more: Amit, listing products of natural selection: 'There's no planner. There's no God, though that is the subject for another day.'

The 'disappearance': Amit says one day he and Ajay will be gone, 'why someday, we could be gone now?' Next, a little girl hosts a parody channel, 'Nothing Is Nothing', about how the world 'is not related to anything.' Ajay's verdict: 'this little girl is very dangerous. Once you go below the surface, you understand that she's actually playing with us all the time.'

head: Amit half-remembers Friedman's line
more: Amit half-remembers Friedman's line 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.' Ajay replies 'It's complicated': Friedman was wrong to emphasize money supply, which central banks gave up trying to control in the early 1980s, though the rest of his philosophy holds.

head: Oscar Lange's proposal for a Central Pricing Board (
more: Oscar Lange's proposal for a Central Pricing Board ('CPB, lovely acronym') to set the price of everything. Hayek's 1945 essay was written to rebut it.

head: Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen takes its name from Bastiat's essay
more: Amit's podcast The Seen and the Unseen takes its name from Bastiat's essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen'.

head: Trump's Own Agencies Said No
dek: A populist's real limit is the culture inside the state's coercive arms.
more: In office, Donald Trump asked the IRS and the FBI to investigate and torment his political rivals. By and large they refused, saying the requests were illegal and broke their rules. Trump also could not stop the Democrats from raising money, hiring advisors, holding rallies and getting out the vote in 2020. Even so, Biden only squeaked through, and because the court cases against Trump have not played out in time, he remains viable in 2024.

A populist's real limit is the culture inside the state's coercive arms. When career officials serve rules rather than rulers, the leader cannot capture them. The thin 2020 margin is the sobering coda: even with free speech, a working media and working intellectuals, institutions buy time but do not decide the outcome.

head: The Richest Man Who Dared Oppose the President
dek: Whether the rich feel safe enough to criticise the government is a barometer of a country's institutional quality.
more: Jeff Bezos, the richest person in the US, openly took an anti-Trump position. He also owned the Washington Post, which exposed the misdeeds of the Trump years. Ajay notes that rich people are usually the most timid, because they have the most to lose. Amit adds that under Bezos the Post kept running anti-Amazon and anti-Bezos stories.

Whether the rich feel safe enough to criticise the government is a barometer of a country's institutional quality. Amit's addition: strong institutions breed values that become part of the culture, strong enough that an owner cannot bend his own newsroom.

head: The War for Israel's Soul
dek: A democracy's character depends on the values its citizens carry, and large shifts in who those citizens are can reshape electoral politics within a generation.
more: Ajay says up front that he is sympathetic to Israel. It came out of nothing and a war in 1948, and was built by European Jews who carried enormous human capital. As a sign of its liberal decency, he notes that gay people cross illegally from neighbouring Arab countries every day because homosexuality is legal in Israel. After the USSR fell, a large wave of Jewish immigrants arrived from Eastern Europe, notably Russia. They brought conservative values on religion, women and personal freedom, which opened the way for hardline religious-nationalist politics.

A democracy's character depends on the values its citizens carry, and large shifts in who those citizens are can reshape electoral politics within a generation. Even a great success story can slide back into fighting the demons of the twentieth century.

head: Israel's Soldiers Defend the Judges
dek: Military people usually suffer most from strongman machismo and are often the first to back the destruction of institutions.
more: Benjamin Netanyahu tried to give the executive veto power over the selection of judges. The public poured into the streets, and the movement was strikingly led by people from elite military formations. They said they had given blood for the country but would not let the executive ride roughshod over the judiciary. The protests won about 75%, though not 100%, of what they fought for.

Military people usually suffer most from strongman machismo and are often the first to back the destruction of institutions. Here they championed separation of powers, which reveals how deep Israel's liberal core runs.

head: Hungary: Von Neumann's Country Goes Thuggish
dek: Climbing out of a thuggish regime and building sound institutions is extremely hard.
more: Hungary, the country of John von Neumann, was expected to flourish after communism, as Czechoslovakia did. Instead it became a thuggish right-wing state despite being in the EU and NATO. Elections still happen, but police go after the opposition, the press is gone, and fundraising and mobilising are impossible. The Central European University was driven out and relocated to a free country. Viktor Orbán has won five times.

Climbing out of a thuggish regime and building sound institutions is extremely hard. Even membership of Europe's civilising clubs does not guarantee it, and Ajay sees no sign yet of how Hungary's slide ends.

head: Stalin's List of 40,000
dek: Culture is transmitted by people. Killing a country's intellectual, business and cultural elite destroys its foundations, and it takes generations to rebuild that knowledge and those norms.
more: Poland was invaded by Nazi Germany on 1 September 1939 and by Russia on 16 September 1939. After the war it was swallowed by the Russians, who installed a communist party. Stalin had a careful list drawn up of 40,000 members of the Polish elite, and they were murdered. Ajay asks listeners to imagine the same happening to any country they love.
Culture is transmitted by people. Killing a country's intellectual, business and cultural elite destroys its foundations, and it takes generations to rebuild that knowledge and those norms.

head: The EU as a Rough Working Draft
dek: Institution-building is far easier when you can copy a working model and are anchored inside a stable club.
more: Around 2005, Ajay visited Poland and talked at length with the builders of the new post-1989 state. They told him the EU was their stabilising force: instead of designing every law and institution from scratch, they got a rough template from the EU. Poland and Ukraine started at similar levels after communism. Poland, inside the EU and NATO, took off; Ukraine, outside them and subject to constant Russian meddling, did not.
Institution-building is far easier when you can copy a working model and are anchored inside a stable club. External anchors act as ballast that carries a young democracy forward.

head: Poland's Fall and Redemption
dek: Populism can be reversed, especially in a country that has not been hollowed out too far and is anchored in the EU and NATO.
more: Poland was the post-communist star pupil, then spent ten years under the Law and Justice Party (PiS). Ajay describes PiS as an alliance of farmers, Christians and thugs that opposed women's freedom, Western influence and foreigners, and monopolised power. Yet Poland's Freedom House score stayed at 80/100. In the October 2023 election, the centre-left party led by Donald Tusk won. Poland now faces the messy task of undoing institutional damage without itself breaking the rule of law.

Populism can be reversed, especially in a country that has not been hollowed out too far and is anchored in the EU and NATO. But the cure has to respect due process, which makes repair slow and difficult.

head: Three Days Weeping in Warsaw
dek: Knowing the history of a place turns sightseeing into an emotional encounter with human civilisation.
more: Ajay recalls spending three days visiting historical sites in Warsaw, weeping like a baby. Amit reflects that a tourist with no background sees only buildings, streets and weather, but the deeper you go, everything takes on meaning. Ajay sums it up: learning makes travel come alive; otherwise just go to the beach in Goa.
Knowing the history of a place turns sightseeing into an emotional encounter with human civilisation. The preparation is the travel.

head: Ideas Load Like Dial-Up Photos
dek: Good concepts don't just add information; they bring a blurry picture of the world into focus.
more: Amit remembers downloading photographs over 90s dial-up: the image first appeared as a pixelated blur, then slowly sharpened into high definition, and the sharpening itself was thrilling. Learning what 'populism' really means felt the same way. A vague notion of 'popular' resolved into a clear frame for seeing the world.
Good concepts don't just add information; they bring a blurry picture of the world into focus. That moment of seeing clearly is one of the great pleasures of learning.

head: Why They Stayed Silent on Hamas and Israel
dek: In a black-and-white discourse even a carefully nuanced position draws attacks from both sides.
more: After the Hamas attacks and Israel's retaliation, many commenters asked the hosts to discuss it. They declined because they lacked enough knowledge. Amit still states his position: he is against Hamas, which he calls evil and the worst thing that happened to Palestine, and against the Israeli state as it currently is. He cares for the Palestinian people and sympathises with the Israeli people.
In a black-and-white discourse even a carefully nuanced position draws attacks from both sides. Knowing the limits of your knowledge, and saying so, is itself an intellectual virtue.
printed: Nuance draws fire from both sides

head: What Is Populism?
dek: It taught Amit most of what he knows about populism. It replaces the naive 'populism = popular' with a precise checklist for spotting populists anywhere, which he says 'everyone should read.'
more: It taught Amit most of what he knows about populism. It replaces the naive 'populism = popular' with a precise checklist for spotting populists anywhere, which he says 'everyone should read.'
The backbone of the episode. Amit walks through Müller's seven traits of populists and three ways populists consolidate power, and names it again as his closing recommendation.

head: Lord of the Flies
dek: Ajay spent his life worrying about 1984, but feels we have stumbled into Lord of the Flies instead.
more: Ajay spent his life worrying about 1984, but feels we have stumbled into Lord of the Flies instead. The social media dystopia is people bullying and tormenting each other, and 'you don't even need the state to make you miserable.'
Ajay's response to Amit's Orwell recommendations.

head: On Tyranny
dek: Ajay thinks it is important enough to recommend a second time in an episode about the populist threat to democracy.
more: Ajay thinks it is important enough to recommend a second time in an episode about the populist threat to democracy.
Ajay's recommendation of the week, which he says repeats one he has made before.

head: Republic
dek: Plato was clear-eyed about democracy's weaknesses long before radio, rallies, TV and social media made it easy to blast simplistic messages to the masses.
more: Plato was clear-eyed about democracy's weaknesses long before radio, rallies, TV and social media made it easy to blast simplistic messages to the masses.
Ajay cites it while discussing why simplistic messages win in mass democracies.

head: Freedom House
dek: A decent, easy-to-use democracy measure. Rival measures disagree somewhat but agree quite a bit.
more: A decent, easy-to-use democracy measure. Rival measures disagree somewhat but agree quite a bit.
Ajay uses its democracy scores to compare Poland (80/100), Israel (74/100) and Hungary (65/100) around October 2023.

head: Beauty and the Beast (1991)
dek: Its scene of the male character flipping through Belle's book, complaining it has no pictures, and Belle replying that some people can use their imagination.
more: Its scene of the male character flipping through Belle's book, complaining it has no pictures, and Belle replying that some people can use their imagination.
The setup for Ajay's On Tyranny recommendation.

head: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It is the backdrop to Amit's point that elite complacency, entitlement and condescension are real problems, even though anti-elitism is dangerous.
more: It is the backdrop to Amit's point that elite complacency, entitlement and condescension are real problems, even though anti-elitism is dangerous.
Amit cites it while admitting his own frustration with elites and how academia is broken.

head: Fields Hijack Common Words
dek: Words like 'nationalism' and 'populism' mean something quite different to political scientists than to ordinary speakers.
more: Words like 'nationalism' and 'populism' mean something quite different to political scientists than to ordinary speakers. Populism is not 'what is popular'; it is toxic. Every field appropriates everyday English words, and if you read technical writing with the everyday meaning in mind, you will misunderstand it. Mastering a field's handful of core terms is half the battle.

head: Only Some of the People Are 'The People'
dek: Müller's core insight is that populism is anti-pluralist. Populists define 'the people' as those who support them and treat everyone else as illegitimate.
more: Müller's core insight is that populism is anti-pluralist. Populists define 'the people' as those who support them and treat everyone else as illegitimate. Trump said the other people don't matter and called the press 'the enemies of the people.' The same move appears when supporters are 'patriots' and critics are 'anti-national.'

head: The Seven-Point Populist Playbook
dek: Müller's checklist of what populists share: (1) defining the people as their supporters; (2) anti-elite rhetoric; (3) acting like victims, with majorities nursing invented historical grievances; (4) monolithic parties that turn into personality cults; (5) performed proximity to the people ('I worked in the mills'); (6) simplistic narratives; (7) conspiracy theories, which grow naturally out of the rest.
more: Müller's checklist of what populists share: (1) defining the people as their supporters; (2) anti-elite rhetoric; (3) acting like victims, with majorities nursing invented historical grievances; (4) monolithic parties that turn into personality cults; (5) performed proximity to the people ('I worked in the mills'); (6) simplistic narratives; (7) conspiracy theories, which grow naturally out of the rest. Ajay urges listeners to keep it as a mental toolkit.

head: Politics Needs an Enemy
dek: Carl Schmitt argued that having an enemy, an 'other', is essential to politics.
more: Carl Schmitt argued that having an enemy, an 'other', is essential to politics. If there is no external invader to rally against, populists manufacture internal enemies. They also pose as outsiders while being hardcore insiders: Amit points to Trump as a crony capitalist embedded in lobbying for forty years.

head: Simplistic Narratives and Rational Ignorance
dek: Amit's favourite of Müller's seven points. The world is complex and we understand it through stories simpler than reality.
more: Amit's favourite of Müller's seven points. The world is complex and we understand it through stories simpler than reality. Voters are 'rationally ignorant': they have livings to earn. So 'your jobs went overseas, immigrants took the rest' beats an honest, multifactorial explanation, and it supplies an 'other' to rail against. People with integrity stay with the nuanced truth; populists don't care. Ajay adds that hatred is the simplest narrative of all.

head: Great Leaders Bring Out Our Best; Populists Our Worst
dek: Ajay's test for a leader is which part of us they appeal to. Populists reduce us to our identity and fan resentment.
more: Ajay's test for a leader is which part of us they appeal to. Populists reduce us to our identity and fan resentment. Amit adds a grim mechanic: love and solidarity don't make people rush out to vote, but anger and hatred do.

head: Populism Cuts Across Left and Right
dek: Hitler, Mao, Lenin and Trump were all populists, operating under very different systems, and both left and right populism are equally toxic.
more: Hitler, Mao, Lenin and Trump were all populists, operating under very different systems, and both left and right populism are equally toxic. Neither the left/right binary nor democracy/totalitarianism classifies them correctly. Amit's preferred lens is consent versus coercion. By that lens, every Indian party is left on economics, right on social issues, and statist throughout.

head: The Populist Engine: Underclass Against the Elites
dek: Ajay's reading of the field is that the central engine of populism is rousing the underclass to hate the elite.
more: Ajay's reading of the field is that the central engine of populism is rousing the underclass to hate the elite. He traces it through the French Revolution, Marx, Hitler, Lenin and Mao. A movement mobilises against the cultural, business and intellectual elites, captures the political elite (the state), and then destroys the other three, gutting the country's capability.

head: Rehabilitate 'Elite', but Elites Must Look in the Mirror
dek: Ajay argues that truth, beauty and wealth creation come from elites, and that treating 'elite' as a dirty word is populism of the left.
more: Ajay argues that truth, beauty and wealth creation come from elites, and that treating 'elite' as a dirty word is populism of the left. Amit agrees that anti-elitism becomes anti-knowledge and anti-expertise, so leaders end up taking advice from quacks. He adds a corrective: elites are often complacent, entitled and condescending. When people vote against your values, the first job is introspection.

head: Tribes Over Principles
dek: Within eight years Trump turned the Republican Party into the opposite of what it stood for.
more: Within eight years Trump turned the Republican Party into the opposite of what it stood for. He became an enemy of free markets, with 2016 trade policies identical to Bernie Sanders'. Amit's disillusioning conclusion is that many people hold principles only because their tribe does, and switch when the tribe switches.

head: Parties Need to Be Institutions Too
dek: Political theory says the state should be depersonalised, with power dispersed.
more: Political theory says the state should be depersonalised, with power dispersed. Ajay argues political parties need the same. America's glory years rested on two institutionalised parties with recognisable character, bureaucratic capability and the capacity to nurture ideas. Populism hollows the party out from inside, and the gutting of the Republican Party will matter for the next 25 years.

head: The Consolidation Playbook
dek: Müller describes three things populists do once in power. They colonise the state, placing loyalists in independent institutions and discrediting the rest, sometimes by brute force and sometimes slowly.
more: Müller describes three things populists do once in power. They colonise the state, placing loyalists in independent institutions and discrediting the rest, sometimes by brute force and sometimes slowly. They practise mass clientelism: cronyism, contracts, and protection from especially foreign competition. And they shut down dissent in civil society, with NGOs among the first targets. Ajay links this to China, where the Communist Party has a cell inside every company.

head: The Chilling Effect
dek: Regimes don't need to jail everyone. Make an example of a couple of people and everyone else starts self-censoring.
more: Regimes don't need to jail everyone. Make an example of a couple of people and everyone else starts self-censoring. Over time people stop noticing their own silence, which makes this kind of repression invisible and hard to call out.

head: Bread and Circus
dek: Ajay borrows the Roman phrase. 'Bread' is subsidies and transfers that placate the people; he calls one subsidy programme after another a crude form of clientelism that has become normalised.
more: Ajay borrows the Roman phrase. 'Bread' is subsidies and transfers that placate the people; he calls one subsidy programme after another a crude form of clientelism that has become normalised. 'Circus' was gladiators in the Colosseum; today it is the drumbeat of noise on TV and social media that stops people thinking about real issues.

head: A Fair Election Is More Than a Fair Count
dek: Votes being counted correctly is not enough. The opposition must be free to fundraise, have advisors, use a free press, organise without coercion and rally in the streets.
more: Votes being counted correctly is not enough. The opposition must be free to fundraise, have advisors, use a free press, organise without coercion and rally in the streets. The right question is how many percentage points state pressure on the opposition shifted the vote. Ajay calibrates with Freedom House: Hungary scores 65/100 yet has effectively lost democracy, so even a respectable-looking score can hide its sustained loss.

head: Democracy Needs a Republic and a Healthy Discourse
dek: Power in the people's hands is good. But it needs a republic, with a constitution and safeguards that protect individual rights and constrain the state, and a public discourse where simplistic narratives don't win.
more: Power in the people's hands is good. But it needs a republic, with a constitution and safeguards that protect individual rights and constrain the state, and a public discourse where simplistic narratives don't win. Amit says the weak discourse is partly the failure of people like them, who must wade into the mess instead of just complaining.

head: Eternal Vigilance
dek: Hungary shows that even in the heart of Europe, liberal values can collapse completely.
more: Hungary shows that even in the heart of Europe, liberal values can collapse completely. Amit invokes Jefferson's 'eternal vigilance': civilisation and liberalism are never permanently achieved. Without constant defence, our baser instincts take over.

head: Social Media Pulls Toward the Extremes
dek: On social media, people join ideological tribes, and status within them comes from signalling, attacking the other side and cancelling insufficiently pure insiders.
more: On social media, people join ideological tribes, and status within them comes from signalling, attacking the other side and cancelling insufficiently pure insiders. A vocal minority drags discourse to the extremes even if the silent majority is moderate. Kuran-style preference cascades get amplified. The median voter theorem predicted near-identical centrist candidates (Jeb Bush vs Hillary Clinton), but Trump broke it and won.

head: Wokeism Begins Where Liberalism Ends
dek: Liberalism is about individual freedom, rights and the autonomy of each person, who 'contains multitudes'.
more: Liberalism is about individual freedom, rights and the autonomy of each person, who 'contains multitudes'. Amit sees wokeism as thinking only in groups. It imposes an identity with a ready-made narrative of victimhood or oppression, a version of old class warfare. Amit worries we are left with a contest between left and right populisms, both of which led to disaster in the 20th century.

head: The Vulgar Familiarity of Social Media Knowledge
dek: Ajay argues social media creates a counterfeit of knowledge: 140 characters make people cocky, and clueless people confidently mouth 'truths' at the dinner table.
more: Ajay argues social media creates a counterfeit of knowledge: 140 characters make people cocky, and clueless people confidently mouth 'truths' at the dinner table. In his father's world, people spoke with care and nuance and would humbly say, 'I have only read four books on this subject.' He sees no easy way out except our own striving.

head: Amit, after his point on conspiracy theories
more: Amit, after his point on conspiracy theories: 'Religion is the opiate of the masses.' Ajay: 'Conspiracy theories are the opiate of the asses.'

head: Amit the writing teacher polices Ajay's mixed metaphors all episode.
more: Amit the writing teacher polices Ajay's mixed metaphors all episode. First: 'You can pour salt on a wound and you can pour oil on a fire. Why would you pour salt on a fire, Ajay Shah?' ('My mistake.'). Then 'a black eye in the heart of Europe. What is this?' Finally, 'the spinal cord of the foundation. My brain is going to hell,' and the two settle on calling it 'the structural engineering of this episode.'

head: On Trump's junk-food photo ops, Amit
more: On Trump's junk-food photo ops, Amit: 'I can completely understand why someone says a hamburger is tasty. Yes, some hamburgers are tasty. But if you tell me a hamburger is good for you, you know, there's a serious kind of problem with that.'

head: Ajay, deliberately
more: Ajay, deliberately: 'Gentle reader, you will be noticing my explicit use of the word elite, because I want to torment the wokes in the audience as well.'

head: When Ajay says even star pupil Poland collapsed into populism, Amit coins a…
more: When Ajay says even star pupil Poland collapsed into populism, Amit coins a 'T-shirt line': 'You are my Poland.' He imagines the genteel, nuanced Ajay suddenly 'burning trucks and beating people up,' with hope that he too can be brought back.

head: Ajay asks listeners to correct him where he's wrong.
more: Ajay asks listeners to correct him where he's wrong. Amit: 'They'll correct you if you're right also.' Ajay: 'Please correct me if you think I'm right.'

head: Amit's 90s nostalgia: downloading photographs over dial-up
more: Amit's 90s nostalgia: downloading photographs over dial-up 'of Samantha Fox or otherwise' and watching them sharpen from pixels. 'Whatever the objectives, you get a thrill.'

head: Ajay sets up his recommendation with Beauty and the Beast: the male character (
more: Ajay sets up his recommendation with Beauty and the Beast: the male character ('conservative, toxic masculinity, all that stuff') flips through Belle's book and complains there are no pictures. Hence the illustrated On Tyranny, 'that you should give every WhatsApp uncle in your life.'

head: The episode opens with Amit holding a prop
more: The episode opens with Amit holding a prop: 'an ancient manuscript that we have found, which looks like a leaf' covered in 'mysterious words in a mysterious language.' Later, when Ajay says events in faraway countries matter to all of us, Amit brings the leaf back with a play on 'for whom the bell tolls': 'not for whom the leaf turns, the leaf turns for thee.'

head: Ajay pivots to defining populism with the Bee Gees'
more: Ajay pivots to defining populism with the Bee Gees' 'Words': 'It's only words and words are all we have.' Amit: 'I never thought you're gonna quote the Bee Gees at me, but well done.'

head: Asked what is driving today's polarisation, Ajay quotes…
more: Asked what is driving today's polarisation, Ajay quotes 'a poet': 'somebody shout, somebody scream, what happened to the post-war dream?' His answer to the lyric's question is social media.

head: The frog in slowly boiling water: Amit uses the parable for gradual institutional capture, then debunks it.
more: The frog in slowly boiling water: Amit uses the parable for gradual institutional capture, then debunks it. 'It's a myth. If you heat the water and a frog is in it, the frog will at some point jump out. But it's a great metaphor.'
'History may not repeat, but it rhymes.' Amit invokes the line to ask what is genuinely new this time, and answers: the pace of technology and the incentives of social media.
'It's the country of John von Neumann.' Ajay on why the world expected great things from post-communist Hungary.

head: Getting Into IIT by Swimming
dek: Any test for a deeper quality soon gets gamed until it measures only itself.
more: Amit retells a thought experiment from Deepak VS, whom he had recently interviewed on The Seen and the Unseen: replace the IIT entrance exam with a swimming test. Deepak argued the engineers would be just as good. Amit got carried away and said they would be better, since the exam really selects for hunger, passion and initiative. Deepak corrected him: by the second year the system would be gamed again, with Kota running swimming classes and billboards of coaches in Speedos. Amit builds a film on this. A boy who genuinely loves engineering is stuck on a treadmill of IIT-sized pools. He is beaten by kids who don't care about engineering, and the person he is falling for hits him from the next lane to get ahead. He escapes to the open sea, where he finally loves swimming, the fishermen and the sea creatures. His coaching grades collapse, he fails, and his mother stops talking to him. He swims out past the danger marker into a storm and disappears.
Any test for a deeper quality soon gets gamed until it measures only itself. The real joy of learning lies outside the lane, but the system rewards only racing from this point to that point.

head: The Lost Plutonium of Nanda Devi
dek: Real history can be stranger than any pitch room would allow.
more: In the 1950s China was building nuclear weapons, and spy satellites could not yet watch the Tibetan plateau. The CIA approached India with a plan. An Indian Army team had just climbed Kanchenjunga, so the idea was to put a permanent listening station on its summit, at around 28,000 feet, looking down on Tibet. It would be powered by a plutonium battery that would run for years. The Indian climbers flatly refused: no one could carry a 70 kg battery up Kanchenjunga. They proposed Nanda Devi instead. The CIA quietly recruited elite American climbers, swearing them to secrecy with all expenses paid. On the second attempt a storm hit, so the team lashed the equipment to rocks at a memorised spot (there was no GPS) and retreated. When they returned, the place was unrecognisable and the device was gone. It was never found. One theory is that the Chinese climbed up from their side and took it. Another is that the always-warm plutonium melted its way hundreds of metres into the glacier. If it ever reaches the Ganga, tens of millions could die. India's cover story was that hikers and hippies were damaging a precious reserve, so Nanda Devi was shut and searched with Geiger counters for years.

Real history can be stranger than any pitch room would allow. Ajay notes that a Cold War spy plan and an environmental closure turn out to be the same story, and the danger is still up there, with a half-life of thousands of years.

head: The Soviet Guard Who Held Plutonium in the Snow
dek: A neat piece of physics, the constant warmth of radioactive decay, appears here as a survival tactic under terror.
more: During the Soviet atom bomb project, NKVD jailers under Beria watched over physicists they did not trust. The guards had orders to shoot all the physicists if the first test failed. One guard burst in on a physicist holding a piece of metal and accused him of being a malingerer passing off stainless steel as plutonium. The physicist remembered that plutonium is always warm from radioactive decay. He told the guard to hold it outside at minus twenty degrees. The guard stood out for half an hour and got frostbite on his earlobes, but the metal stayed warm.
A neat piece of physics, the constant warmth of radioactive decay, appears here as a survival tactic under terror. In Stalin's system, winning the argument only bought you a day.

head: Delhi College and a City in Churn (1803–1857)
dek: Early 19th-century Delhi was a living experiment in colliding worlds: language, knowledge, print and politics all changing at once.
more: Drawing on Swapna Liddle's The Broken Script, Amit pitches a web series set in Delhi between the East India Company's win in the second Anglo-Maratha war (1803) and 1857. The Mughals rule in name while the Company holds real power. Princes scheme against each other, and Bahadur Shah Zafar was a plotter, not the weak poet of popular depiction. Persian, the language of power, vanishes in fifty years. Printing presses arrive, and newspapers and poetry flourish. At the centre is Delhi College. Its endowment came from one Fazal Ali on the condition that teaching be in local languages, so Western knowledge ended up being taught in Hindustani, which had no technical terms for it. The cast includes Ghalib, a cultural legend who was also dodging moneylenders and flattering the British, and Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who wrote obsequiously as a Mughal emperor's emissary. 1857 ends it all. The British see the revolt as Muslim-led and deepen a Hindu-Muslim divide. The college dissolves into nothingness.
Early 19th-century Delhi was a living experiment in colliding worlds: language, knowledge, print and politics all changing at once. It was ended by violence rather than by its own failure.

head: Ramchandra, the Forgotten Mathematician
dek: Genius alone doesn't decide who becomes famous. Patronage and historical rupture do too.
more: Ramchandra, born in 1821 and a teacher at Delhi College, tried to explain the rules of calculus using algebra in a treatise on maxima and minima. It reached the British mathematician Augustus De Morgan, who was blown away and tried hard to promote him. Someone later called the pair the Hardy and Ramanujan of their age, except that Hardy succeeded and De Morgan couldn't. Ramchandra was also a fearless rationalist who attacked traditional medicine and every religion, local and Western. He started journal after journal to be a public intellectual. Then, around thirty, in 1852, he converted to Christianity, which nothing in his writing explains. After 1857 he became headmaster of some random school.
Genius alone doesn't decide who becomes famous. Patronage and historical rupture do too. People also remain mysteries; we can't fully explain even well-documented lives.
printed: The Ramanujan who missed his Hardy

head: Sayyid Ahmad Khan Goes Back to School at Thirty
dek: It takes real humility for an accomplished person to admit their gaps and start learning again.
more: Sayyid Ahmad Khan, who founded Aligarh Muslim University, was taught by private tutors until about twenty, then went out and made a name for himself. At thirty, which was middle-aged given life expectancy then, he decided he didn't know enough. He hired six private tutors for six subjects and educated himself all over again.
It takes real humility for an accomplished person to admit their gaps and start learning again. That is the mark of a serious mind.

head: When Poetry Sold Newspapers
dek: A mass audience once paid for verse and serious debate. What a public consumes is not fixed.
more: In this period, the star attraction that every Delhi newspaper needed was not gossip but poetry. The Delhi Urdu Akhbar carried news from Afghanistan, Herat, France, Russia, Gwalior, Nagpur and more, and in 1841 ran an editorial arguing for widow remarriage. Mushairas were everywhere, and their verses were printed as tazkiras that sold so well that one Karimuddin, who didn't care for poetry, began holding regular mushairas just so he could publish them. Another tazkira opened with essays teaching readers about meter and metaphor.
A mass audience once paid for verse and serious debate. What a public consumes is not fixed. Even commercial greed can end up funding a cultural scene.
printed: All the news fit to rhyme

head: The German Navy Scuttles Itself at Scapa Flow
dek: Treaties are signed by governments but carried out by people, and people can refuse.
more: Germany built a navy to challenge the Royal Navy, but it was not ready when the First World War began in 1914. Its shiny new ships, about half the size of the British fleet, mostly sat out the war in dock. The Treaty of Versailles capped the German army at 100,000 men, allowed no tanks and no navy, and ordered the fleet handed to Britain at Scapa Flow in the far north of Scotland. That meant more than a hundred ships and more than a hundred submarines. During the handover the German sailors were treated pettily, without enough food or sanitation. Instead of surrendering, they had mounted explosives, and some seventy or eighty warships blew up and sank one by one. Many died because evacuations weren't planned.

Treaties are signed by governments but carried out by people, and people can refuse. Amit raises the hard question: a soldier should obey orders, yet we would cheer the same defiance had the sides been reversed.

head: Pre-Nuclear Steel from Scapa Flow
dek: Seemingly separate stories, a scuttled fleet in Scotland and lost plutonium in the Himalayas, turn out to be physically linked.
more: Since the first nuclear tests, radioactive dust has spread everywhere, contaminating iron ore, coal and steel mills. Geiger counters need steel that isn't radioactive to begin with, or they lose their discriminating power. The source of clean, pre-bomb steel is the scuttled German fleet. Divers cut pieces off the wrecks at Scapa Flow and bring them up. The Geiger counters used to hunt for the Nanda Devi plutonium were made from this steel.

Seemingly separate stories, a scuttled fleet in Scotland and lost plutonium in the Himalayas, turn out to be physically linked. As Amit observes, the ships became more useful underwater than they ever were afloat.

head: Vlogging in Love
dek: Social media promises authenticity, but you can be sincere without knowing yourself.
more: Amit pitches a low-budget film told entirely through naturalistic vlogs, with no third-person camera. At a vloggers' meetup, cameras replace guns in a Mexican standoff. Each vlogger films themselves with others in the background, and the camera pulls back into a hall of mirrors. The heart of the film is love. A likable everyday-Joe vlogger falls for a new vlogger who seems completely constructed: beautiful, androgynous, impossible to read. Love shocks him in two ways. Someone else becomes real to him, and he must ask whether his love depends on the other person's genitals. The arc Amit wants is that this androgynous person turns out to be the one being true to themselves. Everyone else, including the hero in gentle ways, is performing.
Social media promises authenticity, but you can be sincere without knowing yourself. Sometimes the person who looks most artificial is the most honest one.

head: Parachuting Sheep into Ethiopia
dek: Armies march on their stomachs. A near-mutiny was averted by solving a food problem, and the solution was absurd but workable.
more: In 1935 Mussolini, dreaming of a new Roman Empire, invaded what is now Ethiopia and Somalia. His soldiers were unwarlike men who mostly wanted a good time, and their hearts, and stomachs, weren't in the fight. Groups of soldiers in the boondocks rebelled over bad military food. The fix: sheep from Italy were loaded onto planes, strapped to parachutes and dropped one by one over the army camps. Live sheep rather than meat made sense because, with refrigeration limited, the live animal kept the meat fresh. At least one blurry black-and-white photo exists. Ajay offers it as a scene for writers to build a story around.
Armies march on their stomachs. A near-mutiny was averted by solving a food problem, and the solution was absurd but workable.

head: The Broken Script
dek: He calls it one of the finest history books he has read in recent years and the best book of quasi-Mughal history he has come across.
more: He calls it one of the finest history books he has read in recent years and the best book of quasi-Mughal history he has come across. It brings alive the collapse of Persian, the print and poetry boom, Ramchandra, and the end of it all in 1857.
The source of Amit's Delhi College story, covering Delhi from about 1803 to 1857.

head: Not Waving but Drowning
dek: One of Amit's favourite poems. It is about a man whose lifelong distress was mistaken for waving, which mirrors his drowning IIT aspirant.
more: One of Amit's favourite poems. It is about a man whose lifelong distress was mistaken for waving, which mirrors his drowning IIT aspirant.
Read aloud in full to close the swimming story.

head: Seven Stories That Should Be Films (Episode 23, Everything is Everything)
dek: The first episode in the series this episode continues.
more: The first episode in the series this episode continues.
One of the two earlier mixed-bag episodes of stories that should be films.

head: Every Selection Test Gets Gamed
dek: An entrance exam is really a filter for hunger, passion and initiative, not for the subject itself.
more: An entrance exam is really a filter for hunger, passion and initiative, not for the subject itself. That is why even swimming might work in year one. But once a test becomes the gate, a coaching industry rebuilds itself around it, and the test stops measuring what you wanted.

head: Reality Is Not Obliged to Be Reasonable
dek: Fiction must be plausible, and reality doesn't have to be. Ajay's elevator pitch for Nanda Devi (CIA, China, plutonium, hippies, tens of millions dead in UP) sounds like word soup, yet every word is true.
more: Fiction must be plausible, and reality doesn't have to be. Ajay's elevator pitch for Nanda Devi (CIA, China, plutonium, hippies, tens of millions dead in UP) sounds like word soup, yet every word is true. Non-fiction is often the richest source of stories.

head: When a Lingua Franca Disappears
dek: In early 19th-century Delhi, Persian held the place English holds in India today: nobody's mother tongue, but the language of power and of every official document.
more: In early 19th-century Delhi, Persian held the place English holds in India today: nobody's mother tongue, but the language of power and of every official document. Within fifty years it was gone, and parents' whole stock of learning became useless in front of their children. Amit contrasts this with today's supposedly unprecedented change: he still speaks the language he spoke as a child, under the same government and maps.

head: Writing Ossifies Language
dek: Before print, language evolves through a fluid, spontaneous order. When printing presses spread, writing a word down fixes it in one form and one usage.
more: Before print, language evolves through a fluid, spontaneous order. When printing presses spread, writing a word down fixes it in one form and one usage. That brings stability but also loses much of the flux.

head: Knowledge Needs a Language Ready to Carry It
dek: Delhi College taught Western knowledge in Hindustani because its endower insisted on local languages.
more: Delhi College taught Western knowledge in Hindustani because its endower insisted on local languages. The British ignored the local knowledge systems, though, and the language had no technical terms for the new content. Amit notes this mismatch is a problem to this day.

head: The Many Currents We Swim In
dek: Ghalib was a legend who also ran from moneylenders and flattered the British.
more: Ghalib was a legend who also ran from moneylenders and flattered the British. Ram Mohan Roy was a fearless reformer who also wrote obsequiously to a Mughal emperor. People are pulled at once by history, by society and by personal need, so no single act defines them.

head: Orders vs Conscience
dek: A soldier is supposed to follow orders, and if everyone rationalises disobedience, things fall apart.
more: A soldier is supposed to follow orders, and if everyone rationalises disobedience, things fall apart. Yet our verdict on Scapa Flow depends on whose side we're on: had Britain lost and Nazis been taking its navy, we would cheer the sailors who blew it up. Ajay sets it beside Mers-el-Kébir. There French sailors chose to obey orders rather than join the British, who then opened fire and killed thousands.

head: The Tapestry of the World
dek: Since nuclear testing began, nearly all newly made steel carries radioactive contamination, so sensitive Geiger counters need pre-bomb steel salvaged from the Scapa Flow wrecks.
more: Since nuclear testing began, nearly all newly made steel carries radioactive contamination, so sensitive Geiger counters need pre-bomb steel salvaged from the Scapa Flow wrecks. That links a 1919-era naval mutiny to a Cold War spy mission in the Himalayas. Seemingly separate histories are physically woven together.

head: Authenticity as the Laziest Pose
dek: Ajay's definition: we are all lazy, so we can fake a persona only briefly, and the one self we can sustain without effort is our own.
more: Ajay's definition: we are all lazy, so we can fake a persona only briefly, and the one self we can sustain without effort is our own. Online, audiences sense contrivance and performers tire of it. Amit adds that a pose you keep working at becomes yours, and the mask often becomes the face.

head: Character Is a River, Not a Rock
dek: Character is contingent. Skip breakfast and your brain chemistry, and your behaviour, shift by evening.
more: Character is contingent. Skip breakfast and your brain chemistry, and your behaviour, shift by evening. We may be sincere yet not know ourselves, so a fixed, authentic self is harder to define than we assume.
printed: When the mask becomes the face

head: Love as Realising Someone Else Is Real
dek: Using Iris Murdoch's line, Amit argues that we all live with main character syndrome, treating everyone else as a prop.
more: Using Iris Murdoch's line, Amit argues that we all live with main character syndrome, treating everyone else as a prop. Love shatters this by making another person undeniably real.

head: Lust Is Honest, Love Can Be a Cover
dek: Amit says he prefers lust to love because lust is what it is. 'Love' can be an evolutionary adaptation or a cover for wanting status, social acceptance or a certain companion.
more: Amit says he prefers lust to love because lust is what it is. 'Love' can be an evolutionary adaptation or a cover for wanting status, social acceptance or a certain companion. Science suggests we mostly act for reasons other than those we tell ourselves, and rationalise after the fact.

head: Ajay asks for a redemptive ending after the drowning story, and Amit
more: Ajay asks for a redemptive ending after the drowning story, and Amit replies: 'Redemption, you want a happy story. We all die.' Then Ajay delivers a tale of lost plutonium that could poison the Gangetic plain, and Amit retorts: 'This is your redemptive story.'

head: Amit proposes merchandise for their joint production: a T-shirt reading
more: Amit proposes merchandise for their joint production: a T-shirt reading 'Okay, fine, I'll kill you tomorrow,' the Soviet guard's verdict after the plutonium proved itself. He calls it 'the best T-shirt line ever.'

head: Ajay pitches the Nanda Devi story to Amit as a movie mogul in two minutes
more: Ajay pitches the Nanda Devi story to Amit as a movie mogul in two minutes: 'America, India, cooperation, CIA, intelligence, China, nuclear proliferation, plutonium... tens of millions of people in UP could die. Hippies at Nanda Devi.' He says Amit would call it 'word soup.'
Ajay: 'Gentle reader, you should tell your great great grandchildren don't live in the Gangetic plain.' Amit: 'Gentle reader don't have great great grandchildren.'

head: Ajay on Soviet vocabulary
more: Ajay on Soviet vocabulary: 'You got to be a communist to know the phrase malingerer. It's used in Russian to basically kill people.'

head: Ajay sums up the Delhi College mismatch
more: Ajay sums up the Delhi College mismatch: 'It's like we're teaching the Magna Carta, but we're doing it in Urdu.'

head: Ajay on the Treaty of Versailles handover
more: Ajay on the Treaty of Versailles handover: 'You've got an Amazon delivery happening. Think of a delivery of a navy.'

head: Amit on the wrecks becoming Geiger-counter steel
more: Amit on the wrecks becoming Geiger-counter steel: 'in a perverse way, the ships were more useful under the water than they would have been over the water.'

head: Amit makes Ajay say
more: Amit makes Ajay say 'vlogging' before starting his story: 'Well done. I'm proud of you. Many people can't do this. So already, achievement unlocked.'

head: Amit insists he won't give spoilers about how the vlogging film ends, then admits
more: Amit insists he won't give spoilers about how the vlogging film ends, then admits: 'But actually the truth is I haven't thought of that yet.'

head: Ajay voices the Italian soldiers in Ethiopia
more: Ajay voices the Italian soldiers in Ethiopia: 'Mamma Mia... I'll go out to far away countries and I'll kill strangers, but you gotta feed me.' When Amit asks why not drop boxes of meat, Ajay explains the sheep is 'a life support system,' and Amit adds that 'it can keep the soldiers company in other ways.'

head: Stevie Smith's
more: Stevie Smith's 'Not Waving but Drowning' ('I was much too far out all my life, and not waving but drowning'), read as the coda to the IIT-swimmer story.

head: Iris Murdoch
more: Iris Murdoch: 'Love is the extremely difficult realization that someone other than oneself is real,' used to frame the vlogger who falls in love.

head: The Mexican standoff (
more: The Mexican standoff ('I have a gun to your head, you have a gun to her head, she has a gun to my head,' as Ajay puts it), Reservoir Dogs and Tarantino, reimagined with vloggers pointing cameras instead of guns.

'A ship is safe in the harbor, but that's not what ships are for.' Ajay applies the saying to the German fleet that sat out the First World War in dock, and Amit chimes in with Otis Redding's 'Sittin' on the Dock of the Bay.'

head: Ajay contrasts the IIT-swimmer allegory
more: Ajay contrasts the IIT-swimmer allegory with 'silly TV serials about children preparing in Kota.'

head: The sign-off
more: The sign-off: 'everything, my friends, is stories. Everything, my friends, is everything.'

head: George Everest's House in Mussoorie
dek: Some places carry history best when left alone. Restoring heritage takes taste as well as money, and an official makeover can destroy the very atmosphere that made a place worth visiting.
more: When George Everest chose a place to live, he picked a stunning spot in Mussoorie overlooking a forested valley where, Ajay recalls, tigers once roamed. Over the years Everest House became a run-down white marble building, caught in legal disputes but open to anyone who wandered in. Ajay loved sitting there and imagining Everest's life after mapping the country. On his last visit, government agencies were doing ugly, tasteless construction to turn it into a museum.
Some places carry history best when left alone. Restoring heritage takes taste as well as money, and an official makeover can destroy the very atmosphere that made a place worth visiting.

head: The Maps India Wouldn't Sell Its Own People
dek: Security rules can take a public good away from the citizens who paid for it while barely slowing down a real adversary.
more: When Ajay grew old enough to want serious maps, he found that the Survey of India's sheets were often decades out of date (some regions last surveyed around 1934). They came only at a coarse 1:200,000 scale, not the 1:10,000 or 1:20,000 a hiker needs. Worse, maps within about 100 km of the border, including the whole coastline, could not be sold, on the grounds that terrorists might use them. Living in Bombay, he was cut off from coastal maps, and hiking in the Himalayas he was cut off from border maps. The same maps sit in a museum in London.
Security rules can take a public good away from the citizens who paid for it while barely slowing down a real adversary. The cost of the rule falls on the people, and the threat is untouched.
printed: Wanted in Bombay, kept in London

head: Barun Mitra, Tribal Land Rights and Google Earth
dek: Secure property rights change incentives. People invest in the land under them once they know it is theirs, and satellite imagery from a private company became the evidence that made those rights possible.
more: Barun Mitra and fellow activists were fighting for the land rights of tribals, in Gujarat as Amit remembers it. The tribals had no proof that they had occupied the land long enough to qualify. The activists used historical Google Earth satellite images to go back in time and presented them as evidence in court, and the tribals won. Ajay adds that this was before Android phones, so the team walked the ground with Garmin handheld GPS units and fed the coordinates into Google Earth. Afterwards the tribals, who had lived there for years without building anything pakka or adding toilets, began building toilets.

Secure property rights change incentives. People invest in the land under them once they know it is theirs, and satellite imagery from a private company became the evidence that made those rights possible.

head: His Father's Wall-Sized Map of India
dek: A small act by a parent can start a lifelong passion. And even now, something as simple as a good wall map of India is hard to buy.
more: In Ajay's childhood home there was a map twice his height. His father had taken the four Survey of India sheets that together made up the country, pasted them onto a wooden board and fixed it to the wall. Young Ajay stared at it constantly, learning rivers, memorising district and place names, and working out the best routes between places. As an adult he has never found a modern wall map of India of National Geographic or Rand McNally quality, and he asks listeners to point him to one.
A small act by a parent can start a lifelong passion. And even now, something as simple as a good wall map of India is hard to buy.
printed: Four sheets, one country, one boy

head: A Generation That Will Never Be Lost
dek: Technologies quietly remove whole experiences from human life. Something every earlier generation knew can vanish within one generation without anyone noticing.
more: Amit recalls a friend's remark that stopped him in his tracks. Because of GPS and phone maps, people born today will never know what it feels like to be lost. Amit adds that this is also a loss of a kind, but leaves it there.
Technologies quietly remove whole experiences from human life. Something every earlier generation knew can vanish within one generation without anyone noticing.

head: How Google Decided to Map the Whole World from Hyderabad
dek: When the state fails to provide a public good, a private firm with enough ambition can build it, and in this case the work is done from India itself.
more: Google first assumed that where governments, as in the US and UK, released map data, the job was done. That approach failed in countries like India, where the government either doesn't have the data or won't release it. Ajay credits Sanjay Jain as a pioneer who pushed Google to raise its ambition. Jain and others wrote software called MapMaker, and a large facility in Hyderabad, which Ajay estimates at 5,000 to 10,000 people, now traces roads, bridges, buildings and rivers from satellite imagery to build Google's map of the entire world.
When the state fails to provide a public good, a private firm with enough ambition can build it, and in this case the work is done from India itself.
printed: Made in Hyderabad, for the world

head: Apple, iPods and How MP3 Won
dek: Dominance creates its own opposition. When one firm gets too powerful, its rivals have a reason to cooperate on open standards, which ends up benefiting everyone.
more: In the early iPod and iTunes era, Ajay says, Apple sold music in a proprietary format that only worked on Apple devices, even though you had paid for the file. The rest of the industry saw the threat of an Apple monopoly over the world's music and agreed to build rival systems on MP3, an open format anyone can read and write. Consumers got angry and Apple backed off. Ajay sees the same pattern in maps: Microsoft, Amazon and others, alarmed by Google's lead, now use OpenStreetMap and feed it corporate data, including GPS traces from Amazon deliveries.
Dominance creates its own opposition. When one firm gets too powerful, its rivals have a reason to cooperate on open standards, which ends up benefiting everyone.

head: Going From Tall to Short Without Shrinking
dek: Economic development shows up in people's bodies. One person's position in the height distribution can track a country's progress over a lifetime.
more: At college Ajay was tall for his generation. Today he is short compared with 20- and 25-year-olds. His height hasn't changed; the people around him have grown taller as India has developed.
Economic development shows up in people's bodies. One person's position in the height distribution can track a country's progress over a lifetime.

head: Taller in First Class, Shorter in Second
dek: Inequality can literally be seen in people's height, shaped by childhood nutrition and illness, not just in their incomes.
more: When Amit first came to Bombay in the mid-1990s, he noticed something on the local trains that disturbed him: people in first class were generally taller than people in second class. He admits this is anecdotal and not backed by data. Separately, he notes that a cousin of almost the same age who grew up in the US turned out much stronger than him. He also wonders whether, among four brothers, the youngest ends up tallest because the family has prospered by the time he grows up.
Inequality can literally be seen in people's height, shaped by childhood nutrition and illness, not just in their incomes.

head: Taking the Hands
dek: It is a great poem, and it shows how a whole universe can fit into something small, which sets up an episode about maps.
more: It is a great poem, and it shows how a whole universe can fit into something small, which sets up an episode about maps.
Amit reads this short poem aloud to open the episode.

head: The Book of Love
dek: Its idea of something old and mysterious leads into how mysterious the world once was before maps.
more: Its idea of something old and mysterious leads into how mysterious the world once was before maps. Ajay adds that love is still a mystery, but our understanding of space has been transformed.
A song by Stephen Merritt that Amit had just discovered. He reads its lyrics about a book 'full of charts and facts and figures and instructions for dancing.'

head: Thelma and Louise
dek: It is one of his favourite films of all time. It comes with a story he says 'should be true' even if it isn't: Saudi censors cut every shot of women driving, leaving a four-minute film.
more: It is one of his favourite films of all time. It comes with a story he says 'should be true' even if it isn't: Saudi censors cut every shot of women driving, leaving a four-minute film.
Amit's recommendation of the day: an early-nineties road movie, chosen because it is about travelling rather than maps.

head: On Exactitude in Science
dek: It is a short parable about cartographers who make a map as large as the empire itself, and it shows the limits of any static map.
more: It is a short parable about cartographers who make a map as large as the empire itself, and it shows the limits of any static map. A perfectly accurate map would be as big as the world and out of date the next moment.
Amit reads the full one-paragraph story aloud while discussing Google Maps.

head: India Awakes
by: Free To Choose Network (presented by Johan Norberg)
dek: It covers an inspiring real case in which satellite data, used as court evidence, secured property rights and changed incentives on the ground.
more: It covers an inspiring real case in which satellite data, used as court evidence, secured property rights and changed incentives on the ground.
A documentary Amit cites for the story of Barun Mitra using historical Google Earth images to win land rights for tribals.

head: Google Maps
dek: He calls it 'a madly great map.' It is free to users and routes you on foot, by car or by public transport through any city.
more: He calls it 'a madly great map.' It is free to users and routes you on foot, by car or by public transport through any city. Ajay himself regularly contributes corrections and missing places.
The first of three systems Ajay says have given Indians a 'map paradise.'

head: Google Earth (desktop version)
dek: On a big screen in terrain mode, its 3D views and aerial flybys are 'a delight' and 'paradise.' He thinks people should be willing to pay a lot for it, though it is currently free.
more: On a big screen in terrain mode, its 3D views and aerial flybys are 'a delight' and 'paradise.' He thinks people should be willing to pay a lot for it, though it is currently free.
Ajay urges listeners to install the desktop version rather than only using the web version.

head: Maps Take You From Darkness to Light
dek: Ajay asks you to picture Akbar or Aurangzeb ruling a country they couldn't see.
more: Ajay asks you to picture Akbar or Aurangzeb ruling a country they couldn't see. Without maps, rulers had only local knowledge held in local languages and passed along through Chinese whispers. Locals might want a payment for information or mislead travellers on purpose. You could solve local problems but never see the whole picture, plan routes, assess revenue or decide where to build. A good map makes local guides unnecessary: anyone, from anywhere, can see the land and make plans.
printed: Water for horses, or a ford?

head: Maps Are Data, Not Paintings
dek: A printed map is only one way of showing the underlying data, which is a list of coordinates with properties attached.
more: A printed map is only one way of showing the underlying data, which is a list of coordinates with properties attached. Thinking of maps as data explains how one survey can produce topo sheets, road maps and national maps. It also explains why releasing the database matters more than printing sheets.

head: Maps as a Public Good That Belongs to the People
dek: Surveying a country is enormously costly, but once it is done, each extra copy of a map costs almost nothing.
more: Surveying a country is enormously costly, but once it is done, each extra copy of a map costs almost nothing. Maps are non-rival (my use doesn't reduce yours) and non-excludable, which makes them a classic public good and one of the British administration's early achievements in India. Ajay argues that a public good the state keeps to itself is worthless. Rich countries release such data freely, for example the US TIGER database, which anyone can download without registering. Indian agencies like ISRO and the Survey of India keep theirs locked away.

head: Every Map Is a Model of the World
dek: No single map does everything. Topo sheets, transport maps and political maps each simplify reality for a particular purpose.
more: No single map does everything. Topo sheets, transport maps and political maps each simplify reality for a particular purpose. Google Maps is superb for navigation but won't show district boundaries, so if your unit of interest is a district, it's the wrong model. Choose the map that suits the question you are asking.

head: Driving by the Headlights: Mundane Work Adds Up
dek: Amit sees George Everest as both dreamer and doer. The individual surveyor noting hill heights never saw the big picture and might not live to see the finished map; he did his small task as his dharma.
more: Amit sees George Everest as both dreamer and doer. The individual surveyor noting hill heights never saw the big picture and might not live to see the finished map; he did his small task as his dharma. Amit borrows the novelist E.L. Doctorow's image: you can drive the whole distance seeing only as far as your headlights. Ajay adds that gathering data and building statistics take decades of patient work without immediate reward, and the effort eventually adds up to something spectacular.

head: The Technologies That Replaced the Theodolite
dek: Accurate maps once required thousands of people walking the country with theodolites, which only a state as capable as British India could manage.
more: Accurate maps once required thousands of people walking the country with theodolites, which only a state as capable as British India could manage. Four technologies changed this. GPS gives roughly 10-metre precision using US Department of Defense satellites that only broadcast while the handset works out its own position. Satellite photographs can be traced over like translucent paper. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) reveals buildings in 3D, and digital elevation maps capture terrain. On top of these come GPS traces from millions of Android phones, which reveal where roads exist and how fast traffic moves on them. Ajay also urges listeners to switch off location tracking on their phones.

head: An End Run Around Low State Capacity
dek: Ajay sees India's failures as a general pattern of underdevelopment rather than the fault of any one agency: monetary policy, police, courts, the military and the Survey of India all work badly.
more: Ajay sees India's failures as a general pattern of underdevelopment rather than the fault of any one agency: monetary policy, police, courts, the military and the Survey of India all work badly. Reforming the Survey of India would take a generation of visionary leaders. Instead, Google Maps, Google Earth and OpenStreetMap, all built on public goods paid for by rich-country taxpayers, have given Indians better maps than George Everest ever had, without using Indian tax money or Indian state capacity.

head: Borges's Map and the Live Map
dek: Borges's parable of a map as big as the empire shows that a perfectly accurate map would be as large as the world and out of date the moment it was finished.
more: Borges's parable of a map as big as the empire shows that a perfectly accurate map would be as large as the world and out of date the moment it was finished. Amit's point is that Google Maps gets around this by updating continuously, rerouting you as traffic changes. Even with every resource he could want, George Everest could only have produced a static map.

head: OSM: What a Digital Public Good Really Means
dek: Ajay complains that the phrase 'digital public good' is widely misused.
more: Ajay complains that the phrase 'digital public good' is widely misused. A true one is non-rival and non-excludable, like the Linux source code or OpenStreetMap data. OSM began with map databases released by rich countries, then grew through volunteers who map their own neighbourhoods, and is now strengthened by corporations wary of Google. No coercion or taxation was involved; it is the energy of the people.

head: When One Firm Gets Too Powerful, Rivals Cooperate
dek: Monopoly threats produce counter-coalitions. The music industry backed the open MP3 format against Apple's lock-in, and Microsoft, Amazon and others now back OSM against Google.
more: Monopoly threats produce counter-coalitions. The music industry backed the open MP3 format against Apple's lock-in, and Microsoft, Amazon and others now back OSM against Google. As a side benefit, sophisticated corporate users improve open systems through complaints, bug reports and feature demands.

head: Terrorism as an All-Purpose Excuse
dek: Ajay argues that the Indian state's first reaction to citizens making their own maps has been to ban them: restricting private mapping, resisting Google Street View, and blocking purchases of foreign satellite imagery.
more: Ajay argues that the Indian state's first reaction to citizens making their own maps has been to ban them: restricting private mapping, resisting Google Street View, and blocking purchases of foreign satellite imagery. As with neglecting coal deaths while fixating on terrorism, invoking security can justify banning almost anything. Technology alone isn't enough; it has to be paired with a liberal pushback against the coercive state.

head: Technology as the Source of Liberal Hope
dek: Amit takes a cautionary point from the story: we tend to assume the world is fixed, that only the state can provide certain things and that the state is moribund.
more: Amit takes a cautionary point from the story: we tend to assume the world is fixed, that only the state can provide certain things and that the state is moribund. He says he is full of despair about the world, but technology gives him hope because it empowers individuals in ways political movements have not. Even the smartphone, despite being a surveillance and distraction machine, is full of tools that give people freedom.

head: Lines on a Map Are Temporary
dek: Amit sees a 'crumbling of the mainstream' across media and entertainment, and wonders whether nation-states might be next.
more: Amit sees a 'crumbling of the mainstream' across media and entertainment, and wonders whether nation-states might be next. Political borders are man-made and history shows they don't last. Maps of languages, dialects or cuisines can be just as revealing, and on the ground the borders simply aren't visible. Ajay has walked to the edge of the India-China border in Ladakh and Uttarakhand and found only the Himalaya.

head: Height Measures Development, Not Genes
dek: Average height mostly reflects childhood nutrition and illness rather than genetics.
more: Average height mostly reflects childhood nutrition and illness rather than genetics. Ajay notes that people of Indian descent raised in advanced economies reach the same average height as people there. Each childhood illness interrupts the use of growth hormone for a while. That is why a quiz map of 19-year-old men's heights puts India near the bottom.

head: Ajay on mistranslation in a world without maps
more: Ajay on mistranslation in a world without maps: 'There will be all kinds of confusion when Tulu is translated into Persian... The person says, I want to find a good place to get water for my horses. And the person thinks the question was, Where can the horses ford the river?'

head: Ajay recalls a traveller's account that Shah Jahan was…
more: Ajay recalls a traveller's account that Shah Jahan was 'more or less convinced that most of the world is ruled by him.' Amit: 'That's the main character syndrome in a geographical sense.'

head: Ajay on the ban on selling border-area maps
more: Ajay on the ban on selling border-area maps: 'All the survey of India maps are there in the museum in London. So any self-respecting terrorist will go to London and get those maps.'

head: Amit's pun
more: Amit's pun: 'And since we all stand on the shoulders of giants, it could well be said that Indian map makers since Everest have climbed Mount Everest.'
Amit: 'if Uber was using Survey of India data, if they had access to it, you know, you and I would be traveling by train. So you know thank God for that.'

head: Ajay on the joys of Google Earth
more: Ajay on the joys of Google Earth: 'You can be rotating around Nanda Devi, visualizing where the plutonium might be hiding.'

head: Following up last week's
more: Following up last week's 'stories that should be films' episode, Amit pitches a new film: two OSM volunteers meet at a mapping meetup and go map-making together. Things go wrong, but they come back together in the end, because what is the movie called? 'It's called Awesome. I just told you.'

head: Ajay imagines his pre-satellite self
more: Ajay imagines his pre-satellite self: 'I would be this old guy with white hair pontificating that the journey to economic development generally takes about 100 years. So we can hope that in 2125 India will have a good quality survey of India.'
Ajay: 'Our equipment is better than Satyajit Ray. It is our imaginations that are the constraint.' Amit agrees about the equipment, then adds: 'You know, no one is better than Satyajit Ray.'

head: When Amit announces a quiz, Ajay squeals
more: When Amit announces a quiz, Ajay squeals: 'An exam. An exam. I love exams.' Amit: 'I have rarely seen you so excited.' Ajay: 'Even if I get zero on five.'

head: Amit's map quiz: Ajay recognises Tolkien's Middle-earth at once (
more: Amit's map quiz: Ajay recognises Tolkien's Middle-earth at once ('the land of Mordor where the shadows lie'). He mistakes George Orwell's 1984 map of Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia for a map of malaria or yellow fever. He guesses fertility rate for a map of linguistic diversity, on which India leads the world, even after Amit gives the clue by speaking three languages. The last two maps show how mothers are treated (India does badly) and the heights of 19-year-old men.

head: Amit on the possibly apocryphal Saudi censorship of a road movie with every shot of women driving removed
more: Amit on the possibly apocryphal Saudi censorship of a road movie with every shot of women driving removed: 'therefore Thelma and Louise in Saudi Arabia was four minutes.'

head: Ajay defining a true public good
more: Ajay defining a true public good: 'you cannot even theoretically exclude a newborn child from the glories of Linux.'

head: Amit opens by promising
more: Amit opens by promising 'instructions for dancing,' a phrase from the Magnetic Fields lyric 'It's full of charts and facts and figures and instructions for dancing,' which he reads out later.

head: Robert Clive and the Battle of Plassey: Ajay dates British map-making in India to 1767
more: Robert Clive and the Battle of Plassey: Ajay dates British map-making in India to 1767, 'a scant ten years after the Battle of Plassey,' starting in the parts of Bengal and Bihar the British controlled.

head: Novelist E.L. Doctorow's line, quoted by Amit as advice for writers
more: Novelist E.L. Doctorow's line, quoted by Amit as advice for writers: 'If you can see the light from your headlights, you can make the whole distance that way.'

head: Ryan, the push-ups, and a deliberate post-hoc fallacy
dek: This is post hoc ergo propter hoc in its purest form. One thing happened, then another, so the first must have caused the second.
more: In the late 1980s and early 1990s at Ferguson College, Pune, Amit was so thin you could count his ribs. Fresh from a boys' school and in an arts class that was about 80% girls, he chose between the canteen and the tapri based on the wind, so his shirt would not blow against his ribs. Gyms were not yet part of the culture. His consolation was Ryan, a devout Christian who was just as thin. Then one day, through Ryan's open hostel door, Amit saw him doing push-ups. Ryan explained that masturbation was a sin, and he had set himself 25 push-ups as the penance for each time. Six months later Ryan was buff, a 'Greek god', and Amit was the only one left with visible ribs. When another hostel friend (Amit gives him a pseudonym, Varun) quietly asked how to get a body like Ryan's, Amit told him, deliberately and as a joke: you have to masturbate.

This is post hoc ergo propter hoc in its purest form. One thing happened, then another, so the first must have caused the second. The joke works because the real cause, the push-ups, was hidden inside the sequence. Many of our causal stories leave out the hidden middle step in the same way.
printed: The penance that built a Greek god

head: The witch doctor's coat and the flooding Nile
dek: Our sense of causality was built for a simple world of tigers and deer, where effects follow causes quickly.
more: A witch doctor claims that every spring he takes off his coat, and then the Nile floods, so the river must be responding to his coat. The sequence is real: spring, then coat, then flood. The causal claim is absurd. Ajay adds a thought experiment. If pressing a button gives you a biscuit one second later, two or three tries convince you that you caused it. Stretch the delay to 10 seconds and it gets harder. At 10 hours the mind can no longer connect the two.

Our sense of causality was built for a simple world of tigers and deer, where effects follow causes quickly. Today's information environment is far more complex, and many important processes play out over long timescales. So we have to lean on evidence and data rather than gut feel.

head: The coin in the crowded swimming pool
dek: Social science happens in the swimming pool, not the beaker. Real controlled experiments are rare, and confirmation bias fills the gap.
more: Amit recalls a metaphor from his friend Shruti Rajagopalan, who he thinks may have been quoting Don Boudreaux. Does dropping a coin into water raise the water level? In a lab, with a beaker and everything controlled, the answer is easy. Now try it in a huge, crowded swimming pool where people are splashing, it is windy and it is raining. The data will mostly be garbage. Amit says this is why economists love the post-war splits of North and South Korea and East and West Germany.
