They come close to a controlled experiment on free markets, and 'spoiler alert, free markets won'.
Social science happens in the swimming pool, not the beaker. Real controlled experiments are rare, and confirmation bias fills the gap. So claims that X caused Y deserve humility and caution.
printed: Signal lost in the deep end

head: What really caused the Great Depression?
dek: A dramatic event followed by a disaster makes an easy causal story. The less visible chain of policy decisions in between can matter far more.
more: The standard story is that the 1929 stock market crash caused the Great Depression. Drawing on Thomas Sowell, Amit points out that unemployment in the months after the crash peaked at about 9% and was down to around 6.5% by June 1930. Then the government began to intervene, starting with the Smoot-Hawley tariff and followed by a series of other interventions, and things exploded. Sowell also notes a later stock market crash that was followed by decades of strong growth. Amit adds that he thinks Amity Shlaes has a book making a similar case.

A dramatic event followed by a disaster makes an easy causal story. The less visible chain of policy decisions in between can matter far more. Blaming the obvious trigger is a post-hoc fallacy at the scale of history.

head: The tomato glut and the coming chip glut
dek: This is the fallacy of composition in action. What is rational for one actor can be ruinous when everyone does it.
more: When tomatoes are scarce, a farmer reasons that he should plant tomatoes, spend heavily on inputs and make a killing. That is sensible for one farmer. But a million farmers respond to the same prices, the market floods, prices collapse to zero, and angry farmers dump truckloads of tomatoes on the roadside because transporting them isn't worth it. Ajay sees the same pattern with semiconductors: after the chip shortage, 'every idiot in the world' decided to build a fab. He predicts a glut and bankruptcies among chipmakers within a year or two.
This is the fallacy of composition in action. What is rational for one actor can be ruinous when everyone does it. The disciplined question is always: what happens if everybody does this?
printed: Too many tomatoes spoil the price

head: The dart-throwing monkey and the Infosys IPO
dek: Much of 'success' comes from the luck of being in software rather than seafood.
more: In finance it is well accepted that a monkey throwing darts builds a decent portfolio, and that nearly all clever humans picking stocks underperform it. Yet each of us thinks we are in the elite 0.01%. Ajay extends this to careers. Nobody could have predicted the software boom from the mid-90s, and the Infosys IPO was mostly undersubscribed. Insiders in a booming industry then credit their success to their own decisions. The honest test is to ask how you would have done if you had simply bought shares in 10 companies in your industry and done nothing. Only the outperformance over that baseline is yours.
Much of 'success' comes from the luck of being in software rather than seafood. Separate the industry tailwind from your own contribution before crediting the CEO, or yourself.

head: Economic Facts and Fallacies
dek: Sowell is one of Amit's intellectual heroes, 'still going strong at ninety plus'.
more: Sowell is one of Amit's intellectual heroes, 'still going strong at ninety plus'. The book names fallacies that are foundational, in that many other errors grow out of them. Understanding these frailties makes our thinking clearer.
The framework for the whole episode. Its opening chapters lay out the five foundational fallacies the hosts discuss.

head: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
dek: When you buy coffee, both you and the seller say thank you because both are better off.
more: When you buy coffee, both you and the seller say thank you because both are better off. It is the simplest illustration that voluntary exchange is positive-sum.
Used to rebut the zero-sum fallacy. Stossel is 'one of my favorite columnists ever'.

head: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It shows that as industrialisation, travel and free markets multiplied double thank-you moments, value and innovation exploded.
more: It shows that as industrialisation, travel and free markets multiplied double thank-you moments, value and innovation exploded. This is the economic history behind the positive-sum world.
Cited for its chart of world GDP, flat for centuries and then shooting up.

head: Profit = Philanthropy
dek: In a world of voluntary exchange, the only way to profit is by making someone else better off.
more: In a world of voluntary exchange, the only way to profit is by making someone else better off. Profit is therefore an incentive to do good for others.
The column behind Amit's line that the pursuit of profit is the greatest form of philanthropy.

head: The Great Redistribution
dek: It uses tariffs to show that interfering with free markets usually redistributes wealth from poor consumers to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the interference.
more: It uses tariffs to show that interfering with free markets usually redistributes wealth from poor consumers to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the interference.
The column Amit links when he jokingly names a law of economics after himself.

head: The Evolution of Cooperation
dek: Ajay calls it 'a fabulous book'. It formalises the optimal response to being wronged: strike back once, but not twice, not thrice, not forever.
more: Ajay calls it 'a fabulous book'. It formalises the optimal response to being wronged: strike back once, but not twice, not thrice, not forever. Some punishment is optimal, grudges are not. That is very different from the behaviour of warlike tribes.
Raised after Amit argued for generosity over crabby, zero-sum behaviour in personal life.

head: Tim Urban's tweet on getting to know people
dek: 'Whenever I get to know someone who seems perfect, I end up disappointed.
more: 'Whenever I get to know someone who seems perfect, I end up disappointed. Whenever I get to know someone who I think is the worst of the worst, I'm pleasantly surprised. Angels and demons aren't real.' It is a reminder to judge people less and stay open to them.
Read out while discussing the danger of judging individuals by their group, or by one opinion.

head: 'Wet streets cause rain' (Michael Crichton on Gell-Mann Amnesia)
dek: It is a memorable label for reverse causation: you see wet streets and rain together and conclude the streets caused the rain.
more: It is a memorable label for reverse causation: you see wet streets and rain together and conclude the streets caused the rain.
Amit borrows Crichton's phrase for getting causation backwards.

head: The Forgotten Man
dek: It supports Sowell's case that government interventions, not the stock market crash, turned a downturn into a depression.
more: It supports Sowell's case that government interventions, not the stock market crash, turned a downturn into a depression.
Mentioned ('if I remember correctly') as also arguing that the 1929 crash alone did not cause the Great Depression.

head: Poker and Life (Episode 38 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Most of what happens to us is sheer dumb luck. Don't let success go to your head or failure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.
more: Most of what happens to us is sheer dumb luck. Don't let success go to your head or failure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.
Recalled while drawing the personal lesson from the post-hoc fallacy.

head: The Man of System (excerpted from The Theory of Moral Sentiments)
dek: It is the classic statement of the arrogance of imagining society as pieces on a chessboard that a planner can move at will.
more: It is the classic statement of the arrogance of imagining society as pieces on a chessboard that a planner can move at will.
Amit calls it a 'brilliant passage' and the origin of the chess-pieces fallacy.

head: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
dek: Hayek's 'fatal conceit' is the belief that we can control a complex world from the top down.
more: Hayek's 'fatal conceit' is the belief that we can control a complex world from the top down. Beyond a certain level of complexity, no one has the information to do so.
Cited as Hayek's name for the chess-pieces fallacy.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: It is the foundation for understanding why order can emerge without a top-down plan, and why central planners can never gather all the knowledge they need.
more: It is the foundation for understanding why order can emerge without a top-down plan, and why central planners can never gather all the knowledge they need.
Referred to as 'Hayek's great essay' while explaining spontaneous order.

head: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41 of Everything is Everything)
dek: A deeper dive into the ideas behind the chess-pieces fallacy.
more: A deeper dive into the ideas behind the chess-pieces fallacy.
'An episode I really love', where the hosts discussed Hayek's essay and spontaneous order.

head: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18 of Everything is Everything)
dek: The earlier episode covered how farmers chasing the same high prices produce gluts and collapsing prices.
more: The earlier episode covered how farmers chasing the same high prices produce gluts and collapsing prices.
Mentioned by Ajay while giving the tomato-glut example of the fallacy of composition.

head: The Selfish Gene
dek: Every organism optimises for itself, so you can never suppress each person's drive to pursue their own life, liberty and happiness.
more: Every organism optimises for itself, so you can never suppress each person's drive to pursue their own life, liberty and happiness. That is why top-down control keeps failing.
Ajay says the chess-pieces fallacy 'goes all the way to selfish gene'.

head: Untitled
dek: It is a slave speaking, saying that any system you design without us will not work.
more: It is a slave speaking, saying that any system you design without us will not work. A poetic version of why top-down designs fail.
'I can't resist recommending' it. Ajay used it as an epigraph at the end of the technology-policy chapter of his book with Vijay Kelkar.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: It is Ajay's own treatment of economic policy, in which the limits of top-down system design are a recurring theme.
more: It is Ajay's own treatment of economic policy, in which the limits of top-down system design are a recurring theme.
Mentioned as 'the Kelkar and Shah book', where the Leonard Cohen poem serves as an epigraph to the technology-policy chapter.

head: Understanding the State (Episode 25 of Everything is Everything)
dek: The state acts through coercion, starting with taxation. That makes every government rupee carry an opportunity cost.
more: The state acts through coercion, starting with taxation. That makes every government rupee carry an opportunity cost.
Recalled during the open-ended fallacy: 'we have done an episode in the past' on how every act of government is an act of violence.

head: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It brings two big ideas to policy: the no-free-lunch budget constraint, and the fact that coercive power has no such constraint.
more: It brings two big ideas to policy: the no-free-lunch budget constraint, and the fact that coercive power has no such constraint.
Ajay points to 'our pair of episodes' on when the state should act and what it should do.

head: Declutter (Episode 30 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It covers recognising the constraints in our own lives, especially time, and prioritising accordingly.
more: It covers recognising the constraints in our own lives, especially time, and prioritising accordingly.
Amit thinks they discussed the personal side of the open-ended fallacy there.

head: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
dek: Ajay is glad an economist has 'opened the box of violence'. Taming violence, both between citizens and between state and citizens, is central to the development story, and economists usually stick to money and markets.
more: Ajay is glad an economist has 'opened the box of violence'. Taming violence, both between citizens and between state and citizens, is central to the development story, and economists usually stick to money and markets.
Ajay's recommendation for the week, prompted by Amit opening the episode by asking why we fight.

head: The Three Languages of Politics
dek: It is a slim book you can read in an hour.
more: It is a slim book you can read in an hour. Kling shows that ideological tribes talk past each other because they start from different core values: equality for left-liberals, tradition for conservatives, freedom for libertarians. Recognising the other side's value is the way to find common ground.
Amit's recommendation for the week, on the theme of why we fight.

head: In My Tribe
dek: It continues Kling's thinking, and Amit recalls a follow-up there or elsewhere that adds nuance to the three-languages framework.
more: It continues Kling's thinking, and Amit recalls a follow-up there or elsewhere that adds nuance to the three-languages framework.
Mentioned alongside the book. Kling 'used to be a great blogger' and now has a newsletter 'you must subscribe to'.

head: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42 of Everything is Everything)
dek: The sheep come in three flocks with different values, but all of them share an overarching interest in not being trampled by the wolves.
more: The sheep come in three flocks with different values, but all of them share an overarching interest in not being trampled by the wolves.
Ajay connects Kling's framework to the 'wolves and sheep' theme of that episode.

head: Stone Age brains in a modern world
dek: The world is too complex to grasp, so we make sense of it through simple stories.
more: The world is too complex to grasp, so we make sense of it through simple stories. Those stories clash with each other, and sometimes all of them clash with reality. Our instincts were forged for small hunter-gatherer tribes. Ajay adds that the roughly 4,000 generations of modern humans are too few to change that 'hardware'. Many fallacies are instincts that once worked and now misfire.

head: Why we disagree: facts, values and the reasoning engine
dek: Ajay's triad. We reason from facts (skewed by overweighting personal experience), from values (partly our birthright, often muddled), and through a reasoning engine.
more: Ajay's triad. We reason from facts (skewed by overweighting personal experience), from values (partly our birthright, often muddled), and through a reasoning engine. Disagreement comes from a difference in one of the three. The hope is that the reasoning engine, meaning logic, argument and proof, can be common ground for a shared notion of truth.

head: The zero-sum fallacy
dek: When a tribe splits a deer, every chunk I take is one you can't have. Modern exchange is different: voluntary transactions leave both sides better off.
more: When a tribe splits a deer, every chunk I take is one you can't have. Modern exchange is different: voluntary transactions leave both sides better off. Zero-sum thinking drives statism and the confusion of inequality with poverty. Since 1991, hundreds of millions of Indians have left poverty even as inequality rose. Treating the economy as a fixed pie favours redistribution over growth and wrecks incentives. On a personal level, Amit argues against crabby scarcity thinking and for generosity, because someone else's success is not your loss.

head: Knowledge is the greatest positive-sum game
dek: Ajay's extension of the zero-sum argument. Newton, the Magna Carta and the transistor were created in some corner, and everyone got better off.
more: Ajay's extension of the zero-sum argument. Newton, the Magna Carta and the transistor were created in some corner, and everyone got better off. The inventors of the transistor did not gain at our expense. Accumulated human knowledge is a public good whose spillovers transform everything.

head: Intervention redistributes from the poor to the rich
dek: Amit's self-named 'law'. Interfering with free markets usually transfers wealth upward.
more: Amit's self-named 'law'. Interfering with free markets usually transfers wealth upward. With tariffs, competition shrinks and ordinary consumers pay more or get less. The value they lose goes to the narrow interest groups that lobbied for the tariff.

head: The fallacy of composition
dek: This is the belief that what is true of a part is true of the whole. Politicians help one group and present its gains as gains for society, which is really robbing Peter to pay Paul.
more: This is the belief that what is true of a part is true of the whole. Politicians help one group and present its gains as gains for society, which is really robbing Peter to pay Paul. Ajay sees it as the core difference between thinking like a firm and thinking about an economy. Exporting more makes sense for one company, but using state power to subsidise land, electricity or the exchange rate so that every company exports can unbalance the economy. The test to always apply is: what if everyone does it?

head: The flip side: don't judge individuals by their group
dek: Amit inverts the fallacy of composition. Stereotyping takes a trait attributed to a group, or seen in one member, and paints every individual with it.
more: Amit inverts the fallacy of composition. Stereotyping takes a trait attributed to a group, or seen in one member, and paints every individual with it. One sociopathic economist doesn't make all economists sociopaths. The same applies to condemning someone as evil over a single disagreement on social media. People regress to the mean: neither angels nor demons.

head: A country is not a company
dek: Ajay previews a future episode. Successful businesspeople assume their skills carry over to government, but they mostly don't, for two reasons.
more: Ajay previews a future episode. Successful businesspeople assume their skills carry over to government, but they mostly don't, for two reasons. First, economy-wide actions trigger composition effects that a single firm never faces. Second, government wields coercive power, which firms largely lack.

head: The post-hoc fallacy and its cousins
dek: The post-hoc fallacy assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Its cousin, cum hoc ergo propter hoc, assumes that two simultaneous events must be causally linked.
more: The post-hoc fallacy assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Its cousin, cum hoc ergo propter hoc, assumes that two simultaneous events must be causally linked. Michael Crichton's 'wet streets cause rain' gets the arrow backwards. These made sense in a simple world where a rustle in the bush meant a tiger. Amit argues that religion and ritual grew from such simple causal stories, for example about what causes rain. In a complex world they mislead us constantly, especially in economics.

head: Our causal radar has a short range
dek: If the biscuit arrives one second after the button press, we see causality instantly.
more: If the biscuit arrives one second after the button press, we see causality instantly. If it arrives 10 hours later, we are lost. Many processes in the universe play out over long timescales, exactly where our intuition fails. So we must push harder to be evidence-based before making causal claims.

head: Luck dominates, so judge yourself against the baseline
dek: Amit's personal lesson: most of what happens to us is luck. Don't build stories like 'I am good, so good things happened' or 'I am bad, so bad things happened'.
more: Amit's personal lesson: most of what happens to us is luck. Don't build stories like 'I am good, so good things happened' or 'I am bad, so bad things happened'. Keep doing the right thing, your dharma. Ajay's version for firms is to compare your results with simply holding your industry's stocks. Only the outperformance is your contribution.

head: The chess pieces fallacy
dek: Adam Smith's 'man of system' and Hayek's 'fatal conceit' describe the belief that society is a static chessboard a planner can arrange.
more: Adam Smith's 'man of system' and Hayek's 'fatal conceit' describe the belief that society is a static chessboard a planner can arrange. Top-down control works for a tribe or a 10-person family firm. At scale, no one has the information, and spontaneous order emerges from 'human action, but not human design'. Amit says millions of Indians stayed poor longer than they should have because planners did not trust people's ingenuity. Ajay is less sure the lesson has been learned. For individuals, the lesson is to focus on processes and habits, not grand goals.

head: The open-ended fallacy and no free lunch
dek: Health, safety and open space are open-ended desires, but resources are limited and have alternative uses.
more: Health, safety and open space are open-ended desires, but resources are limited and have alternative uses. Amit says India's biggest religion is government: we assume 'mai-baap sarkar' will pay for everything, as if money were unlimited and costless. Yet every government rupee is extracted through taxation, which is coercive and costly, so it has an opportunity cost. Ajay invokes Milton Friedman's 'no free lunch'. A responsible policy thinker should pair every proposal for more spending with matching cuts elsewhere.

head: The sophisticated health expert asks for less government healthcare spending
dek: Ajay offers a contrarian test of expertise. The Indian government spends poorly, and prevention is better than cure.
more: Ajay offers a contrarian test of expertise. The Indian government spends poorly, and prevention is better than cure. So the right plea is to reorient the system away from healthcare and towards public health, meaning preventive measures, rather than to demand more money for the same things.

head: Coercion has no budget constraint
dek: Spending is at least capped by what the state can raise. Coercion has no such cap.
more: Spending is at least capped by what the state can raise. Coercion has no such cap. A government can ban one thing after another and whittle away freedoms day by day with nothing to stop it. So actions that reduce freedom deserve even more scrutiny than actions that cost money.

head: Your time is the open-ended fallacy you live with
dek: Amit's personal version. With age, the binding constraint shifts from money to time.
more: Amit's personal version. With age, the binding constraint shifts from money to time. We act under an illusion of immortality and try to give our minds to everything. He cites Steve Jobs's advice to his designer Jonathan Ive: pick a couple of things, say no to the rest, even the ones you love. This is not about a productivity fetish, since time to relax and chill out is useful too.

head: The three languages of politics
dek: Arnold Kling argues that political tribes talk past each other because their core values differ: equality for left-liberals, tradition for conservatives, freedom for libertarians and classical liberals.
more: Arnold Kling argues that political tribes talk past each other because their core values differ: equality for left-liberals, tradition for conservatives, freedom for libertarians and classical liberals. Arguing in your own value's language is pointless. Amit gives an example: with a left-winger, he argues that a statist intervention hurts the poor rather than that it reduces freedom. Ajay adds that the sheep come in three flocks, but all share an interest in not being trampled by the wolves.

head: India's crisis of thinking
dek: Ajay's closing plea. Knowing these fallacies is easy, but internalising them takes a long time.
more: Ajay's closing plea. Knowing these fallacies is easy, but internalising them takes a long time. Exam-driven, credential-focused India has a sterile idea of knowledge as a trade you apply, and real reasoning has been pushed out of most people's consciousness. Thinking about thinking is a skill, and it can be learned.

head: The episode opens with both hosts fumbling over who should speak first. Amit turns it into the thesis
more: The episode opens with both hosts fumbling over who should speak first. Amit turns it into the thesis: 'both of us wanted the other one to go first, and we ended up kind of fighting over it. Not really a fight, but it's a good question. Why do we keep fighting?'

head: Amit scripts his own cue and Ajay obliges.
more: Amit scripts his own cue and Ajay obliges. Amit: 'How does your first fallacy involve hunting? I love it how you follow my instructions and ask me all the questions I want.'

head: On catching Ryan doing push-ups
more: On catching Ryan doing push-ups: 'this goes against the ethical code... thin boys whose bones are visible don't do push-ups.' After hearing the penance explanation: 'in my mind, I did sashtang pranam and I just left.'

head: Six months later the girls are…
more: Six months later the girls are 'giggling at the improbable presence of a Greek god in their midst... and now I am the only person whose bones are visible.'

head: Explaining cum hoc ergo propter hoc, Amit admits
more: Explaining cum hoc ergo propter hoc, Amit admits: 'I love the name because of the main activity in the story.'

head: On Ajay's biscuit experiment
more: On Ajay's biscuit experiment: 'I'm on keto diet, so if I press a button, I don't want a biscuit to come ever. Bacon strips, another matter.' He later reveals his keto plus one-meal-a-day plan: 'because I want to be like Ryan. Which Ryan do I want to be like? Any of the two.'

head: Amit, on not generalising about economists
more: Amit, on not generalising about economists: 'we know many economists who are sociopaths, Ajay, I want to tell you that, but I know you're not one of them. You're a deeply emotional and empathetic person.'

head: Amit points to a graph and then corrects himself
more: Amit points to a graph and then corrects himself: 'when I say as you can see, I mean you, gentle reader. He can't see any graph on the screen. There's no screen, there's only me.'

head: Amit, unabashed
more: Amit, unabashed: 'I'm gonna be a little vain. I'm gonna name a law of economics after myself because I keep talking about it and no one seems to get it.'

head: Ajay on investor hubris: the dart-throwing monkey beats nearly all stock pickers
more: Ajay on investor hubris: the dart-throwing monkey beats nearly all stock pickers, 'Of course, hope springs eternal. We each of us think that I'm in that 0.01% of the cool people that know what to do.'

head: Ajay teases Amit's claim that India has learned to distrust top-down planning
more: Ajay teases Amit's claim that India has learned to distrust top-down planning: 'Gentle readers, see how optimistic Amit is.'

head: In an episode about why we fight, Ajay says Amit opened by…
more: In an episode about why we fight, Ajay says Amit opened by 'whining'. Amit: 'I wasn't whining and we will fight over the use of your word whining. I don't whine.'
'PPP: perpetually planned poverty', a phrase coined by the hosts' mutual friend Kumar Anand for what statism and zero-sum thinking produce.
'Mai-baap sarkar kar degi' (the parent-government will provide). Amit says India's 'biggest religion is government', the mindset that powers the open-ended fallacy.

head: Adam Ferguson's phrase that things happen through
more: Adam Ferguson's phrase that things happen through 'human action, but not human design', invoked with Hayek to describe spontaneous order.

head: Milton Friedman's
more: Milton Friedman's 'no free lunch', Ajay's shorthand for the fact that government money is neither free nor infinite.
Robert Trivers's work on altruism and self-interest, cited by Amit to argue that we are hardwired for both, and that being altruistic indirectly serves our self-interest.

'Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will', the phrase Amit uses to answer the gloom: we see what is wrong but keep fighting. He followed it with 'Everything is everything' and then admitted it 'was a dramatic way to end the chapter'.

head: How Spotify Led Amit to Shoegaze and Back to an Old Love
dek: If you let an algorithm's random playlist run and follow whatever strikes you, it can pull you out of a musical comfort zone.
more: While Amit was listening to a lot of Yo La Tengo, Spotify suggested a 'shoegaze' playlist, a word he had never heard. He let it play, and a band called Galaxie 500 grabbed him. That set off a flashback. In the early-to-mid 90s, one of his favourite alternative-rock bands was Luna, fronted by Dean Wareham, and he had a vague sense that Wareham had an earlier band. In an India where the shops sold Deep Purple and Michael Jackson, he had no way of finding it. That earlier band was Galaxie 500. Amit then explains the genre: guitar-heavy, feedback-drenched bands with indistinct vocals, whose guitarists stood still on stage staring at their effects pedals.

If you let an algorithm's random playlist run and follow whatever strikes you, it can pull you out of a musical comfort zone. It can also close loops that scarcity once left open, and the old music you couldn't get can return as a new passion.

head: What Are the Two Most Recent Songs You Know?
dek: It is a quick, funny self-audit of how musical taste freezes at a certain age, and a reminder that newer artists can be very good if you give them a chance.
more: Ajay and a friend put a question to themselves: what are the two most recent songs you know? His instinctive answer was 'November Rain' from 1992. After thinking carefully, he found one song he knows and loves from 2017, Harry Styles' 'Sign of the Times', and one from 2018, which he couldn't name until Amit supplied it: 'Shallow' by Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper. He credits YouTube Music for bringing him new music.
It is a quick, funny self-audit of how musical taste freezes at a certain age, and a reminder that newer artists can be very good if you give them a chance.

head: Boris, Igor and the Goat
dek: Equality can be reached by making everyone poorer. This is why Amit insists that poverty, not inequality, is the problem worth solving.
more: Amit retells a parable from Steven Pinker's Enlightenment Now. Two Russian farmers: Boris has a goat and Igor doesn't. Igor complains to the authority that this isn't fair. Asked what he wants done, he says: kill Boris's goat. Inequality is solved, and now neither of them has a goat.

Equality can be reached by making everyone poorer. This is why Amit insists that poverty, not inequality, is the problem worth solving. Redistribution feels virtuous, but it can leave everyone worse off.

head: Indira's Preamble vs Ambedkar's Preamble
dek: Great thinkers contain multitudes and change their minds, so judge them by their full body of work.
more: Amit supported the CAA protests, and he was heartened to see young people across India on the streets holding up the Preamble of the Constitution. What filled him with despair was that they held up Indira's version, which contains the word 'socialist'. When the words 'secular' and 'socialist' were debated in Ambedkar's time, he said no to both. On 'secular', his view was that if the value runs through every article, stating it is mere signalling. On 'socialist', his view was that the choice of economic system is for politics to decide, not the Constitution. Ambedkar himself then favoured a socialistic organisation, but he changed his mind by the 1950s. Amit notes that Chandra Bhan Prasad's two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith.

Great thinkers contain multitudes and change their minds, so judge them by their full body of work. The fashionable reading of the Constitution quietly carries a word that, Amit argues, kept India poor.

head: Sex Workers Push Back on a TV Panel
dek: Elite moralising about other people's choices removes their agency. Criminalisation pushes the trade into the underworld, where trafficking and coercion flourish and victims cannot turn to the police.
more: Amit recalls a talk show hosted by Barkha Dutt where Kiran Bedi took a moralistic line on prostitution. Actual sex workers on the show pushed back. They said they had entered the work willingly, that it was the best option open to them, and they asked who she was to patronise them.

Elite moralising about other people's choices removes their agency. Criminalisation pushes the trade into the underworld, where trafficking and coercion flourish and victims cannot turn to the police.
printed: Ban it, and the mob moves in

head: The Matunga Racket
dek: Laws against victimless crimes don't just fail. They hand the state's own enforcers a tool for extortion against harmless people.
more: While Section 377 still effectively criminalised homosexuality, cops placed ads on online bulletin boards asking gay men to meet them. When the men turned up at a railway station, often Matunga, plainclothes cops met them and extorted them, threatening to tell their wives or fathers. They then walked the victims to an ATM and emptied their accounts. Amit wrote a column about this racket years ago.
Laws against victimless crimes don't just fail. They hand the state's own enforcers a tool for extortion against harmless people.

head: When Banning Child Labour Pushed Children Into Worse Lives
dek: No parent wants their child in a factory. They send children to work because every other option is worse.
more: Amit cites two follow-up studies. In Bangladesh, Oxfam found that 30,000 children were laid off from alleged sweatshops after Western activists complained, and many girls went into prostitution while many boys turned to crime. In Nepal, after a scandal over children making carpets, UNICEF found that 5,000 to 7,000 children were laid off and the girls almost uniformly went into prostitution. Amit notes that the journalists behind such stories never follow up. Only these studies did.

No parent wants their child in a factory. They send children to work because every other option is worse. A ban that feels virtuous can destroy the lives it claims to save, and the real cure is growth that lifts family incomes.
printed: Saved from work, lost to worse

head: The Degrowth Advocate With a Single Malt
dek: Degrowth is a textbook luxury belief: fashionable for those who have already escaped poverty, devastating for those who haven't.
more: At a recent party, a very successful professional from Hyderabad, sipping a single malt, told Amit he found the word 'degrowth' very attractive and that India had had enough growth. Amit told him that free speech is fine, but what he was saying was deeply immoral, because degrowth hurts the poor. He adds that every one percent rise in GDP gets about two million Indians out of poverty.
Degrowth is a textbook luxury belief: fashionable for those who have already escaped poverty, devastating for those who haven't. Two million people are real human beings, not a statistic.

head: The Strongman Eventually Turns on His Rich Backers
dek: Populist leaders have often been bad for growth and for the very businesspeople who backed them.
more: Ajay argues that business elites who have skimped on understanding society often back the strongman, expecting favours. He gives examples. In Saudi Arabia, MBS led a shakedown of hundreds of rich people and seized their wealth. In China, Xi Jinping attacked the rich, partly destroying and partly expropriating them. In Russia, Putin went after the rich. Each billionaire believed he was the insider who would get special treatment, and for a while it seemed to work.
Populist leaders have often been bad for growth and for the very businesspeople who backed them. The only sustainable path for building firms is rule of law and liberal democracy.

head: Lunapark
dek: He calls it a great album from a band he loved.
more: He calls it a great album from a band he loved.
Luna was one of Amit's favourite alternative-rock bands of the early-to-mid 90s.

head: Sign of the Times
dek: A song he genuinely loves, and Harry Styles is called 'bloody good'. A reason not to look down on new music.
more: A song he genuinely loves, and Harry Styles is called 'bloody good'. A reason not to look down on new music.
One of the two most recent songs Ajay knows and loves, from 2017.

head: Troubled: A Memoir of Foster Care, Family, and Social Class
dek: Highly recommended. Henderson, whom Amit calls a very fine thinker worth following, coined 'luxury beliefs', the idea behind this episode.
more: Highly recommended. Henderson, whom Amit calls a very fine thinker worth following, coined 'luxury beliefs', the idea behind this episode.
Henderson's new book about growing up in foster homes, which Tyler Cowen also discussed on Marginal Revolution.

head: Luxury Beliefs are Status Symbols
dek: Gives the original framing: beliefs that confer status on the upper class while inflicting costs on the lower classes.
more: Gives the original framing: beliefs that confer status on the upper class while inflicting costs on the lower classes.
Linked in the show notes as the source of the term Amit defines at the start of the episode.

head: On Inequality
dek: A slim, great book that sets out the 'doctrine of sufficiency': define what is enough to live on and get everyone there.
more: A slim, great book that sets out the 'doctrine of sufficiency': define what is enough to live on and get everyone there. A philosopher's case for why that matters more than equality.
Cited while arguing that poverty, not inequality, is the problem.

head: The Communist Manifesto
dek: The book ends with a checklist program for action, and you'll be astonished how much of it exists in modern India, which in many ways is the communist paradise Marx and Engels wanted.
more: The book ends with a checklist program for action, and you'll be astonished how much of it exists in modern India, which in many ways is the communist paradise Marx and Engels wanted.
Ajay suggests it as an exercise during the discussion of socialism.

head: Defending the Undefendable
dek: Block, an Austrian economist, defends ideas considered beyond the pale, much as Amit has just defended sweatshops and legal prostitution.
more: Block, an Austrian economist, defends ideas considered beyond the pale, much as Amit has just defended sweatshops and legal prostitution. You don't have to agree, but it makes you think in different ways instead of swallowing a tribe's dogma.
Amit's closing reading recommendation. He says he might one day borrow the title for an episode.

head: The Matunga Racket
dek: Shows concretely how criminalising consenting adults breeds extortion.
more: Shows concretely how criminalising consenting adults breeds extortion.
His old column on cops extorting gay men while Section 377 was in force.

head: Luxury Beliefs
dek: Rob Henderson's term for fashionable opinions that give elites status while their costs fall on the poor.
more: Rob Henderson's term for fashionable opinions that give elites status while their costs fall on the poor. Amit pictures elites in air-conditioned rooms typing on MacBooks, choosing a fourth pair of luxury headphones, and proposing policies that hurt the poor. His antidote is Gandhi's test: before any policy, ask what it does to the poor. In a poor country like India, that is a moral question.

head: Socialism Means Coercion, Not 'Good for Society'
dek: Many people hear 'socialism' as 'caring for society', just as populism is confused with 'popular'.
more: Many people hear 'socialism' as 'caring for society', just as populism is confused with 'popular'. Amit's definition: the state owns much of the property and regulates the rest, so you are a subject rather than a citizen, and freedom is something the state grants. His lens is consent versus coercion. The 20th century was the history of socialism's failure, and in India socialism kept hundreds of millions poor for decades longer than necessary.

head: Poverty, Not Inequality, Is the Problem
dek: In a zero-sum world, poverty and inequality would move together. In a positive-sum world, growth makes the poor richer and the rich richer still, so inequality can rise as poverty falls, as it did after 1991.
more: In a zero-sum world, poverty and inequality would move together. In a positive-sum world, growth makes the poor richer and the rich richer still, so inequality can rise as poverty falls, as it did after 1991. The thought experiment: would you rather be poor in the USA, which is more unequal, or in Bangladesh, which is poorer? Tackling inequality calls for redistribution, which is easy to sell and makes you feel virtuous. Tackling poverty calls for growth, which in a poor country will inevitably raise inequality, and that is fine.

head: The Doctrine of Sufficiency
dek: Harry Frankfurt argues that what matters morally is not equality but whether everyone has enough.
more: Harry Frankfurt argues that what matters morally is not equality but whether everyone has enough. Define the level a person needs to live on and get everyone there. This works as a proxy for ending poverty, a goal Amit says every Indian government has failed to reach.
printed: Mind the poverty, not the gap

head: 200 Basis Points and the Power of Compounding
dek: Ajay's response to people who say a little inequality-chasing won't hurt growth much.
more: Ajay's response to people who say a little inequality-chasing won't hurt growth much. He uses illustrative numbers: a growth-hostile Indian policy setup yields about 2% per capita growth, and a pro-growth one about 4%. By the rule of 70, 2% means 35 years to double and 70 to quadruple. 4% means about 16 years to double and 32 to quadruple. Thirty-two years is within a young person's planning horizon, such as the show's editor Nomsita's. Seventy years is beyond imagining.

head: Banning Victimless Crimes Feeds the Underworld
dek: This luxury belief comes from the right: ban prostitution, betting, alcohol and, formerly, homosexuality.
more: This luxury belief comes from the right: ban prostitution, betting, alcohol and, formerly, homosexuality. Bans don't end these activities. They push them to the underworld, where the cops are paid off, the rule of law doesn't reach, and trafficking, match-fixing and spurious liquor thrive. In the Netherlands, legal and regulated brothels mean sex workers have rights, pay taxes and face little crime. England legalises betting and taxes the houses, not the gamblers' winnings. Amit wants banks to offer betting the way they offer demat accounts. His line is that the left should accept freedom in the marketplace and the right freedom in the bedroom.

head: Bootleggers and Baptists
dek: Bruce Yandle's insight is that the moralist calling for a ban and the bootlegger profiting from it want the same thing: the activity stays illegal.
more: Bruce Yandle's insight is that the moralist calling for a ban and the bootlegger profiting from it want the same thing: the activity stays illegal. So in the real world, the bootlegger funds the prohibitionist politician rather than fighting him.

head: Pro-Business vs Pro-Market
dek: Capitalism turns ugly when allied with state power. That is cronyism, where businesses use the state to keep competitors out.
more: Capitalism turns ugly when allied with state power. That is cronyism, where businesses use the state to keep competitors out. True free markets need the rule of law and little else, so the only way to get rich is to serve people, which makes every trade a 'double thank you' moment. Anti-capitalist elites attack the system while tweeting on capitalist platforms and ordering next-day delivery from Amazon.

head: Respect the Agency of the Poor (Sweatshops and Child Labour)
dek: People work in sweatshops because it is the best option open to them. Banning it removes that option and leaves worse ones.
more: People work in sweatshops because it is the best option open to them. Banning it removes that option and leaves worse ones. Child labour is horrible, but blunt bans pushed by Western activists have sent laid-off children into prostitution and crime. Studies estimate the family income above which children stop being sent to work. The long-term solution is growth.

head: Price Controls Destroy Information
dek: Prices signal scarcities and constraints and encourage people to produce more.
more: Prices signal scarcities and constraints and encourage people to produce more. In Amit's thought experiment, capping cars at Rs 10,000 would kill the industry and push the few remaining cars onto the black market. In real life, he tweeted that the price control on stents would cause scarcity, and it did, and people died. Banning Uber surge pricing means no car when you urgently need one to get to a hospital or catch a flight. These controls are the Yes Minister instinct at work: we must do something, this is something, let's do it.

head: Why Elites Hold Luxury Beliefs
dek: Ajay, a card-carrying economist, asks what the elites are optimising for.
more: Ajay, a card-carrying economist, asks what the elites are optimising for. His hypotheses: it costs nothing once you are already rich. Pious views are old-style philanthropy that buys safety from pitchforks and a populist state. Moral fervour makes you look caring, so others want to work with you. These beliefs are cheap talk that signals club membership. Timur Kuran's preference falsification means people say what helps them get ahead. All of this needs intellectual soft-headedness: a broad doctor-engineer class with little social science or humanities, where few can call out the claims.

head: We Signal Virtue to Ourselves, and Social Media Locks It In
dek: Amit argues that most holders of luxury beliefs mean well. They lie to themselves as much as to others, and holding the right opinion stands in for doing good.
more: Amit argues that most holders of luxury beliefs mean well. They lie to themselves as much as to others, and holding the right opinion stands in for doing good. Social media makes it worse. You join a tribe for belonging, accept its dogmas, attack outsiders, then attack insiders for impurity, which is why most cancellation comes from your own side. Once you have said something publicly, ego makes you double down. Amit read Marx and Engels at 17 and said silly things. With screenshots following him forever, he might never have grown out of them.

head: The Anointed and the Benighted
dek: Thomas Sowell's diagnosis, which Amit reads aloud. The prevailing vision offers believers a state of grace.
more: Thomas Sowell's diagnosis, which Amit reads aloud. The prevailing vision offers believers a state of grace. Agreeing makes you morally superior, and disagreeing is treated as sin to be exposed, not error to be argued with. Amit's takeaway is that this is old and hardwired, not just a social media problem: we want to belong to a tribe and keep displaying our virtue.

head: Be Firm on Values, Open on Facts
dek: Amit's closing advice. Don't swallow any tribe's dogma from A to Z, and you don't need an opinion on everything after 30 seconds of thought.
more: Amit's closing advice. Don't swallow any tribe's dogma from A to Z, and you don't need an opinion on everything after 30 seconds of thought. Hold your values firmly, but treat the facts of a complex world with humility and listen to people who disagree.

head: Ajay asks why they are colour-coordinated in shades of blue.
more: Ajay asks why they are colour-coordinated in shades of blue. Amit: 'Well, you know, maybe we both love the blues.'

head: Ajay turns Amit's Spotify discovery into a Bayes' theorem problem (working back from track to genre). Amit protests
more: Ajay turns Amit's Spotify discovery into a Bayes' theorem problem (working back from track to genre). Amit protests: 'Ajay, I'm talking about art, I'm talking about music, I'm talking about the soul.'

head: Ajay introduces the topic
more: Ajay introduces the topic: 'there's an English word luxury like Louis Vuitton and Indian hotels, and there is a word like beliefs, which is like Bayes theorem and trigonometry.'

head: After Ajay picks
more: After Ajay picks 'Shallow' as his 2018 song, Amit: 'You and I should perform Shallow sometime. I'll do the high parts.'

head: Ajay says 32 years out is a practical horizon for their editor Nomsita.
more: Ajay says 32 years out is a practical horizon for their editor Nomsita. Amit: 'Thirty-two years later she'll be younger than you are now.'

head: Amit corrects himself from…
more: Amit corrects himself from 'prostitutes' to 'sex workers', then takes it back: 'You and I are prostitutes, we're selling our services for money... I do a lot of things free even. So I'm even worse.'

head: In the price-control thought experiment, Amit tells viewers to pause the video and think, then freezes on camera
more: In the price-control thought experiment, Amit tells viewers to pause the video and think, then freezes on camera: 'Have you paused? I just did statue...'

head: The running
more: The running 'under my chair' gag: Amit keeps saying links are in the show notes 'under my chair', and finally wonders aloud what else is down there.

head: Amit, after a long tirade
more: Amit, after a long tirade: 'Ajay, I have ranted and raved, which is my elite privilege. It is a luxury that I get to enjoy.'

head: Ajay begins his analysis
more: Ajay begins his analysis: 'I'm a card-carrying economist, okay, and here is my card.'
Amit: 'Those who signal the most virtue possess the least. You know, and I have found this to be true especially of men, so watch out.'
The 'gentle reader' running joke. Amit mid-sentence: 'dear listener, dear reader. We are not listeners, we are readers.'

head: Amit on instant opinions
more: Amit on instant opinions: 'You've thought about that for thirty seconds. I have read about it for thirty years... and we are supposed to, on Twitter, be on equal ground.'

head: Yes Minister: Amit invokes the line
more: Yes Minister: Amit invokes the line 'we must do something, this is something, let's do it' to describe intellectually lazy elite policymaking.

head: Amit's twist on…
more: Amit's twist on 'the better angels of our nature': social media 'plays to the worst demons of our nature, as it were, instead of the better angels.'

head: India's Founding Leaders Learned Governance as City Bosses
dek: The freedom movement's leaders were not only activists. Running cities was their training ground in governance and public finance.
more: Amit points out that under the British, Indian local governments had real powers over local tasks the colonial state couldn't be bothered with. C. Rajagopalachari was effectively mayor of Salem in 1917 as chairman of the municipal board. Jawaharlal Nehru held a similar post in Allahabad in 1923. Chittaranjan Das and then Subhas Chandra Bose held it in Calcutta, and Sardar Patel was prominent in municipal politics. After independence, India kept the colonial coercive superstructure and lost this empowered local layer.

The freedom movement's leaders were not only activists. Running cities was their training ground in governance and public finance. Modern India dismantled the very crucible that produced its first prime minister and home minister.

head: Uttar Pradesh Is Four European Countries
dek: We call these units 'states' and 'districts', but they are country-sized.
more: From his conversations with Karthik Muralidharan, Amit relays that India's 15 biggest states would each rank among the world's top 42 countries by population. By his own calculation, Uttar Pradesh is as big as France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined, all run by one state government. Karthik also notes that the average Indian district is bigger than 85 countries. Yet only 3% of India's budget is spent at the local level, against about 50% in supposedly centralised China.

We call these units 'states' and 'districts', but they are country-sized. Each of those 85 countries would demand its own democracy, while an Indian district gets almost no say and almost no money of its own.

head: Kerala Was Three Steps Ahead on COVID
dek: Where a state has built real capability, instructions from New Delhi are a downgrade.
more: Malayali students studying in China brought COVID home, so Kerala faced the first surge before almost anyone else in India. Its capable health system was already running quarantines and isolation. The Union government first did nothing and then announced nationwide lockdowns. Kerala's health authorities pushed back, saying they knew what they were doing.
Where a state has built real capability, instructions from New Delhi are a downgrade. Whoever holds the local knowledge should be making the decisions.

head: Susan Thomas, a Dog Bite, and a Kerala Government Clinic
dek: One-size-fits-all policy fails because state capacity itself differs hugely across India.
more: Susan Thomas was bitten by a family dog. She insists it was her fault because she was troubling the dog. Ajay lists the surprises that followed. First, her family took her to a government clinic without a second thought, which people like them rarely do elsewhere in India. Second, the doctor was actually present and competent. Third, he asked the right questions: is it a family dog, is it healthy, will it be under observation? He then gave only antiseptic, since a rabid dog would collapse first and that would be the moment to start vaccinating. Most Indian doctors, public or private, would have 'blasted' a full course of rabies injections.

One-size-fits-all policy fails because state capacity itself differs hugely across India. Someone who favours radical health reform for most of the country should still respect and keep what Kerala has built.
printed: A bite, and no needless needles

head: Lancelot Pinto's Paracetamol-First COVID Treatment
dek: Good practice can mean doing less. That takes courage, because a doctor who goes by the defensive playbook is protected from blame when random bad outcomes happen.
more: Dr Lancelot Pinto treated Amit through COVID twice. His approach was to avoid over-medication. Many deaths, he believed, came from demanding patients being overmedicated, which made their immune systems overreact. He started Amit on paracetamol and escalated step by step, and Amit never needed more than paracetamol and cough syrup.
Good practice can mean doing less. That takes courage, because a doctor who goes by the defensive playbook is protected from blame when random bad outcomes happen.

head: The Catholic Church's Secret Sauce Was Subsidiarity
dek: Decentralisation is a proven design for institutions that last. Empires that centralised tended to crash, while a decentralised Church lasted more than 1,500 years.
more: Economists parrot the subsidiarity principle as their own, but Ajay traces it to the Catholic Church. From around 380 to about 1950, the Church was a major world power. The Vatican controlled armies, took part in international treaties, and outlived most empires. Churches everywhere had their own autonomy, and central control was kept to the bare minimum.
Decentralisation is a proven design for institutions that last. Empires that centralised tended to crash, while a decentralised Church lasted more than 1,500 years.

head: The Dutch Tanks Run by the German Army
dek: This is the European Union's design philosophy in miniature. Instead of defining the state by lines on maps, each function goes to the scale where it works: one currency, shared defence, and local personal law.
more: After World War II the Netherlands went back to buying German tanks. As a small NATO member with perhaps twenty tanks, it found that maintaining its own logistics tail and fixed costs made no sense at that scale. So the Dutch paid for the tanks but placed them under German army command, with Dutch soldiers serving inside fully integrated German units.

This is the European Union's design philosophy in miniature. Instead of defining the state by lines on maps, each function goes to the scale where it works: one currency, shared defence, and local personal law.

head: The Monkey and the Two Cats
dek: The loud debate between states, such as the South complaining it subsidises the North, distracts from the bigger issue: the centre keeps most of the bread.
more: Amit retells Pranay Kotasthane's fable. Two cats fight over a piece of bread, and a monkey offers to split it fairly. Each time one half is bigger, he eats a bit of it, overshoots, and eats from the other half. When only two tiny equal crumbs remain, he takes those too as payment for his labour. Pranay uses it to show that Indian states fight over horizontal devolution (which state gets what share) while ignoring vertical devolution (how much the centre passes down at all, about 42% to states).
The loud debate between states, such as the South complaining it subsidises the North, distracts from the bigger issue: the centre keeps most of the bread.
printed: Split the bread, keep the bread

head: Nehru's Trick of Amending Away Unconstitutionality
dek: A constitution that the government of the day can rewrite at will stops restraining power and starts serving it.
more: Drawing on a talk by Shruti Rajagopalan, Amit explains that Nehru began the practice of amending the Constitution whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional, so the courts couldn't stop him. It happened so often that an early cartoon showed a reader asking the parliament bookshop for a copy of the Constitution and being told the shop doesn't stock periodicals.
A constitution that the government of the day can rewrite at will stops restraining power and starts serving it.

head: CMIE Consumer Pyramids dx
dek: It makes India's heterogeneity measurable. Average income differs about 5x between the richest and poorest regions, and young women's mobile phone ownership differs 10-15x.
more: It makes India's heterogeneity measurable. Average income differs about 5x between the richest and poorest regions, and young women's mobile phone ownership differs 10-15x.
Ajay's go-to household survey data, which divides India into about 100 homogeneous regions of roughly seven districts each.

head: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
dek: Three 'phenomenal thinkers' propose unconventional measures of women's empowerment, such as who orders the groceries in a household.
more: Three 'phenomenal thinkers' propose unconventional measures of women's empowerment, such as who orders the groceries in a household.
Amit brings it up after Ajay's metric of women owning mobile phones.

head: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Pinto, 'one of the great doctors in this country', explains his don't-overmedicate approach, the same one that saw Amit through COVID twice on paracetamol and cough syrup.
more: Pinto, 'one of the great doctors in this country', explains his don't-overmedicate approach, the same one that saw Amit through COVID twice on paracetamol and cough syrup.
An aside prompted by Ajay's story of the sensible Kerala doctor.

head: Brave New World
dek: Amit calls it a great podcast and asks listeners to check it out.
more: Amit calls it a great podcast and asks listeners to check it out.
Amit plugs the show he produces before retelling Vasant's joke about Bubba.

head: The Fable of the Monkey and the Two Cats
dek: Amit calls it a 'great newsletter post'. It shows why the vertical question (how much the centre passes down) matters more than states squabbling over their shares.
more: Amit calls it a 'great newsletter post'. It shows why the vertical question (how much the centre passes down) matters more than states squabbling over their shares.
Amit retells it while asking how money flows between India's levels of government.

head: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
dek: Its framework shows what India underuses. Indians rely on loyalty or a little voice, while Americans use exit: if you dislike your city or state, you move.
more: Its framework shows what India underuses. Indians rely on loyalty or a little voice, while Americans use exit: if you dislike your city or state, you move.
Ajay cites 'the great Hirschman book' when explaining migration's role in American federalism.

head: Seeing Like a State
dek: Scott's insight that early states competed for people rather than land.
more: Scott's insight that early states competed for people rather than land. Bad governments lose their people, so migration works as a verdict on governance.
Ajay links Scott's ideas on the state to his case for celebrating migration.

head: The Power Broker
dek: Its central figure, Robert Moses, embodied the top-down planning philosophy that Jane Jacobs fought.
more: Its central figure, Robert Moses, embodied the top-down planning philosophy that Jane Jacobs fought.
One of the books Amit says he'd naturally recommend on this topic but has recommended before.

head: Triumph of the City
dek: A book Amit would recommend on cities; he names it rather than re-pitching it in detail.
more: A book Amit would recommend on cities; he names it rather than re-pitching it in detail.
Named with The Power Broker as a natural, previously recommended pick for a cities episode.

head: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
dek: He calls it 'an absolute masterpiece'. Jacobs argued that cities grow bottom-up and are people more than buildings and highways, and Amit counts her among the great thinkers of the 20th century.
more: He calls it 'an absolute masterpiece'. Jacobs argued that cities grow bottom-up and are people more than buildings and highways, and Amit counts her among the great thinkers of the 20th century. Everyone who lives in a city has skin in the game.
Amit's main recommendation of the episode.

head: Bimal Patel's forthcoming book
dek: Patel is India's pre-eminent urban thinker and understands town planning like almost nobody else in India.
more: Patel is India's pre-eminent urban thinker and understands town planning like almost nobody else in India. Ajay says to run, not walk, when it comes out, and Amit calls him one of the great thinkers of modern India.
Ajay's recommendation, revealed as a 'great secret' because the book isn't out yet.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: It argues that economic growth comes from dispersing power and building a genuine republic, and that India's failures stem from an overbearing, concentrated state.
more: It argues that economic growth comes from dispersing power and building a genuine republic, and that India's failures stem from an overbearing, concentrated state.
Ajay cites his book with Kelkar when discussing the concentration of power.

head: Nation-States Grew Top-Down, Cities Grew Bottom-Up
dek: Nation-states arose coercively. Their first needs were taxes and conscripts for war, with little owed in return.
more: Nation-states arose coercively. Their first needs were taxes and conscripts for war, with little owed in return. City governments arose organically: once enough people lived together, they needed order, rule of law and basic services, which made them responsive and nimble by nature. India inherited only the coercive nation-state structure and never let responsive government grow from below. This reframes federalism as a matter of where governments come from, not just how power is handed down.

head: Heterogeneity Is a First-Order Policy Problem
dek: India's internal gaps are continental in scale. Lant Pritchett told Ajay that India's richest-to-poorest ratio resembles that of Latin America's richest place versus Africa's poorest.
more: India's internal gaps are continental in scale. Lant Pritchett told Ajay that India's richest-to-poorest ratio resembles that of Latin America's richest place versus Africa's poorest. CMIE regions differ 5x in income and 10-15x in young women's phone ownership. Kerala has a life expectancy of 75, like Argentina, while UP's is 64, like Liberia. Kerala's infant mortality is 7 (the USA's is 6), while Madhya Pradesh's is 48. Every question about policy and the state has to start from this diversity.

head: Both the 'What' and the 'How' of Government Vary by Place
dek: Heterogeneity changes two things.
more: Heterogeneity changes two things. First, what problems the state should tackle: air quality in North India, Arabian Sea cyclones eating Kerala's coastline, diabetes and obesity in Kerala, malnutrition and stunting in the heartland. Second, how it should tackle them, through local technologies, organisation designs and management. A single central policy sends the wrong prescription to half the country.

head: Uniform Civil Service Pay Is a Distortion
dek: Ajay calls it a 'mad idea' that civil servants across India are paid essentially the same.
more: Ajay calls it a 'mad idea' that civil servants across India are paid essentially the same. Pay should reflect local conditions, so a civil servant in Bombay should earn more than one in Calcutta. Flattening pay means officials in rich regions are underpaid and those in poor regions overpaid, which distorts the whole design of the state.

head: Mosquitoes Can Be Controlled, but Only Locally
dek: Indians have fatalistically accepted malaria, but deliberate public health action can control mosquitoes.
more: Indians have fatalistically accepted malaria, but deliberate public health action can control mosquitoes. Mosquito populations change every 100-200 km because natural selection adapts them to local weather and to the behaviour of the people they bite. So control programmes must be designed neighbourhood by neighbourhood, by local governments. Some places, such as Ladakh, may not need one at all.

head: The Subsidiarity Principle
dek: Place every government function at the lowest level that can handle it.
more: Place every government function at the lowest level that can handle it. Currency belongs at the top, because changing money at the Maharashtra-Gujarat border would be absurd. Mosquito control belongs at the village or city level. Start at the bottom, move up only when that fails, and centralise only where decentralisation is truly infeasible.

head: Federalism Decided Question by Question, Not by Map
dek: The European Union is deliberately not a country. It pools what makes sense to pool: the euro through the European Central Bank, defence through NATO, and small armies merged into larger ones.
more: The European Union is deliberately not a country. It pools what makes sense to pool: the euro through the European Central Bank, defence through NATO, and small armies merged into larger ones. It leaves the rest local, such as personal law that reflects Catholic thinking in Portugal and Spain and more secular norms in Northern Europe. The right scale is chosen separately for each function.

head: The Concurrent List Is a Fantasy
dek: The Constitution's framers imagined the concurrent list as a space where a wise chief minister and Nehru would work things out together.
more: The Constitution's framers imagined the concurrent list as a space where a wise chief minister and Nehru would work things out together. The fine print says that once the Union legislates on a concurrent subject, it wins, so in practice the list belongs to the Union. Planners then went after the state list too, through centrally sponsored schemes: 'run education my way and I'll pay 65%'. That hijacks the state's 35% and imposes a central design on it. Ajay notes that much of the Constitution's federal structure echoes the Government of India Act of 1935.

head: Cities and Villages Are Different Problems
dek: The 73rd and 74th Amendments, pushed under Rajiv Gandhi with Mani Shankar Aiyar as a key thinker, treated village and city government as twin projects.
more: The 73rd and 74th Amendments, pushed under Rajiv Gandhi with Mani Shankar Aiyar as a key thinker, treated village and city government as twin projects. A village of about 150 households, or 600 people, lacks the economies of scale for enough civil servants, politicians, competition, and checks and balances. Research finds only weak gains from village-level decentralisation. Cities, some bigger than whole countries (greater Bombay outnumbers Australia), clearly have the scale to run serious governments.

head: A GST Slice for Cities
dek: Unlike income tax, GST can be traced to where each transaction happens, the shop, and so to a city.
more: Unlike income tax, GST can be traced to where each transaction happens, the shop, and so to a city. The blueprint drawn up in 2003 by Vijay Kelkar, Arvind Modi and Ajay for the FRBM implementation task force imagined cities as a level of government. Ajay proposes a single-rate GST of about 10%, split roughly 3% to the Union, 2% to the state and 5% to the city. Today cities depend on two finance commissions for their money. State finance commissions are often never constituted, lack data and are not neutral, and property tax can only raise so much. A direct GST share would end this dependence.

head: Migration Is Exit, and It Should Be Celebrated
dek: In American federalism, unhappy citizens move, which is Hirschman's 'exit'.
more: In American federalism, unhappy citizens move, which is Hirschman's 'exit'. People sort themselves into places that match their values, and governments that drive people away lose their tax base. James C. Scott's insight is that early states competed for people, not land. Ajay calls the lament for migrants who left village 'paradise' for city slums a luxury belief. People choose, and urban slums usually beat villages. Migration also offsets falling birth rates in prosperous states. Amit's caveat is that Indian states feel this pressure only weakly, because most tax money flows to the centre.

head: Power and Accountability Are Unlinked in Indian Cities
dek: From Shruti Rajagopalan: city residents can vote for municipal officials who have little real power.
more: From Shruti Rajagopalan: city residents can vote for municipal officials who have little real power. The state-level politicians who do hold power have their vote banks elsewhere, so they don't answer to city residents. City governance stays bad because of this structural mismatch.

head: A Choice Between Bad and Bad
dek: Decentralisation enthusiasts can forget that Indian chief ministers act almost like dictators.
more: Decentralisation enthusiasts can forget that Indian chief ministers act almost like dictators. Legislatures provide little check, there is nothing like the Rajya Sabha at the state level to force negotiation, and state judiciaries are often cowed. Centralised power produces distant officials who don't know the city, while local power is held in too few hands. Advocates of decentralisation must also push for political reform at the state and city level, and Amit adds that this means reasoning from first principles rather than chanting slogans.

head: Growth Follows the Republic
dek: The thesis of In Service of the Republic is that development is about dispersing power.
more: The thesis of In Service of the Republic is that development is about dispersing power. That means co-equal executive, legislative and judicial branches that check each other. India's poverty and weak growth trace back to concentrated power and an overbearing Union. The same logic applies further down: states and cities also need to become genuine republics, not personal fiefdoms.

head: A Hundred States, Many of Them Cities
dek: Ajay notes that very little is best done at the state level; most of the important work happens in cities.
more: Ajay notes that very little is best done at the state level; most of the important work happens in cities. His thumb rule is that India should have about a hundred states, with big cities as states of their own. West Bengal, for example, could be two or three states, one of them Calcutta. A city-state would deal with the Finance Commission directly and could get both a GST slice and direct transfers. This works within the existing constitutional scheme and avoids risky amendments at a time when drafting skill is poor.

head: Every Government Needs Its Own Intellectual Community
dek: Decentralising power without decentralising knowledge reduces government to a raw power game.
more: Decentralising power without decentralising knowledge reduces government to a raw power game. Each state and city needs its own data, researchers, public debate and critics. Janaagraha argues that India's cities fall into about 63 groups of similar cities (Bombay, New Bombay and Thane being one), and each group could share data, research and municipal services.

head: Ajay opens the show with a riff on Julius Caesar's
more: Ajay opens the show with a riff on Julius Caesar's 'lean and hungry look': "Your Amit has a hungry look. Such men are dangerous. Amit, what dangerous ideas do you have to offer us?"

head: After Ajay's mosquito obsession and his line about there perhaps being no mosquitoes in Ladakh, Amit
more: After Ajay's mosquito obsession and his line about there perhaps being no mosquitoes in Ladakh, Amit says: "Mosquitoes and Ladakh would be an incredible title for a rock album, a heavy metal album in fact."

head: The tank running gag. When Ajay says he can't resist bringing something up, Amit groans
more: The tank running gag. When Ajay says he can't resist bringing something up, Amit groans, "You can never resist talking about tanks. Fine, Ajay Shah, one more time let's talk about tanks." He then pictures a thumbnail of Ajay peering out of a tank and signs off the episode with "Ajay in a tank."

head: Ajay voices the Dutch attitude to Germany after WWII
more: Ajay voices the Dutch attitude to Germany after WWII: "Okay, fine, we forgive you, you know, we know you invaded us a couple of times, but we let it go", and then they went back to buying German tanks.

Amit retells a joke from Vasant Dhar. Vasant's friend Bubba claims to know everyone. At Trump Tower the secretary says Donald will be so happy to see him. At the White House, Biden spots him, rushes out, and falls over a couple of times on the way. At the Vatican, Vasant loses Bubba in the crowd, and then the Pope appears on the balcony with Bubba beside him. The man next to Vasant taps him and asks: "Excuse me, who's that guy with Bubba?"

head: Amit on the awkward middle tier of government
more: Amit on the awkward middle tier of government: "When T20 cricket became popular, people said Test cricket rahega, T20 rahega, we don't need ODIs anymore. So I think states are kinda like ODIs."

head: Amit: the population of Iceland equals that of Mumbai's Versova. Ajay: about 300,000
more: Amit: the population of Iceland equals that of Mumbai's Versova. Ajay: about 300,000, "and half of them are fishermen." Amit: "Iceland or Versova?" Ajay: "Iceland." Amit: "But yeah, we have fishermen too and we are proud of them."

head: As animals pile up in the episode, Ajay
more: As animals pile up in the episode, Ajay says, "In this episode we've got a dog, a cat, a monkey." Amit adds: "And tanks, many, many tanks."

head: Ajay on how much of India's Constitution was carried over from colonial law
more: Ajay on how much of India's Constitution was carried over from colonial law: "It is remarkable how much plagiarism test would pick up things in the constitution of India that come from the Government of India Act."

head: Amit says there are two Ajay Shahs: a sober, analytical man of history
more: Amit says there are two Ajay Shahs: a sober, analytical man of history, and "a heretic who thinks mad ideas and all of those mad ideas make sense." He demands that the heretic present himself.

head: A bee keeps circling Amit's head
more: A bee keeps circling Amit's head: "It seems to have fallen in love with me, and while my charms are undoubted, I would not welcome this particular attention." Ajay links it to the song lyric behind the title of the show's first episode, and Amit supplies the line: "Dragonflies are busy buzzing me."

head: When Ajay proposes splitting West Bengal into two or three states, one of them Calcutta, Amit offers…
more: When Ajay proposes splitting West Bengal into two or three states, one of them Calcutta, Amit offers: "I have names for the three states. Calcutta, West and Bengal."

head: Amit on Ajay's odd verb choices
more: Amit on Ajay's odd verb choices: "I love the way you combine unexpected verbs and nouns, like in a previous episode you said solving a mountain. And over here you're like building a book."

head: Amit quotes B.R. Ambedkar's famous verdict
more: Amit quotes B.R. Ambedkar's famous verdict, "What is a village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance and narrow mindedness". He calls it Ambedkar's argument for centralising power, given caste and the treatment of women in villages. It raises the real puzzle of how far local government should go.

head: The Schoolboy Who Timed Firecrackers Floor by Floor
dek: Amit sees mischief like this as raw initiative and creativity. Given real opportunity in the economy, the same kind of person can do amazing things.
more: At breakfast, Amit's friend Vaishnav told him about a boy at his school. On a festival day (Amit thinks it was Diwali), the boy went to the fifth floor with a homemade chain of strings and delayed-fuse firecrackers. He dangled one firecracker into the toilet on each floor below and timed them to go off in sequence. The fourth floor went off and the teachers ran up. When they got there, the third floor went off, so they ran there, then the second, and so on.

Amit sees mischief like this as raw initiative and creativity. Given real opportunity in the economy, the same kind of person can do amazing things. The question the episode keeps returning to is how India channels that energy into productive firms.

head: They Stole a Bridge in Bihar
dek: Amit says these stories are bad on one hand and good on the other, because they show potential.
more: Amit recalls his Seen and the Unseen episode on Bihar with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand. Thieves stole an entire bridge: one day it was there, the next it was gone. The show notes link a report on a 60-foot bridge stolen in broad daylight. Before that, a patch of water had been stolen too; Amit calls it a river, and the show notes link a stolen pond. He adds that many big telemarketing scams are run out of a couple of towns in Bihar.

Amit says these stories are bad on one hand and good on the other, because they show potential. India has the imagination and the sheer numbers of inventive people to compete with anyone, and it is constraining itself. Ajay's reply is that the task is to channel this energy into firms.

head: Sundar Pichai's Infosys Test
dek: Amit's twist: so many American firms having Indian CEOs speaks to the greatness of America, not India.
more: Ajay recalls Sundar Pichai saying it will be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi immigrant becomes CEO of Infosys, just as Pichai, an Indian immigrant, became CEO of Google. Ajay argues India is too insular for that today: people would culturally resent a foreigner running a beloved company like Infosys or TCS. In the US, Satya Nadella at Microsoft and Pichai at Google were ordinary appointments that nobody protested as anti-foreign.

Amit's twist: so many American firms having Indian CEOs speaks to the greatness of America, not India. Being open to foreign talent at the very top shows whether a country puts building a great firm ahead of identity.

head: The Korean Chaebol Bargain
dek: Even a cosy state-business deal can drive productivity if the measure of success is one the state cannot fake.
