more: Ajay retells a story Lant Pritchett often tells about South Korea's chaebols. It looked like crony capitalism: the government struck a political bargain with eight or ten big business houses and promised to create conditions for them to export. Because the goal was exporting, the Korean state had no way to rig the outcome. It could not make the American market easier, could not hurt American competitors, and could not help through protectionism.

Even a cosy state-business deal can drive productivity if the measure of success is one the state cannot fake. Making exports the goal pushed all of Korean public policy towards pro-productivity, pro-social behaviour.
printed: Korea’s cosy deal, with a catch

head: Indian Software Didn't Wait for the State
dek: There is enough hunger and opportunity in India to make huge progress without waiting for the state to fix everything.
more: Ajay concedes that better education, health and electricity policy are good goals, but each is a 25-year journey that won't move the needle soon. TCS, Infosys and the other heroes of Indian software did not wait for the government to build colleges that would train a million programmers a year. They solved their own problems and kept their dealings with the Indian state to a minimum.

There is enough hunger and opportunity in India to make huge progress without waiting for the state to fix everything. The software industry's playbook is a can-do one: compete abroad, stay away from the state.
printed: They didn’t wait for the state

head: In Defense of Globalization
dek: Amit calls it a great, magnificent book that everyone should read. It is the natural companion to Ajay's case for globalisation.
more: Amit calls it a great, magnificent book that everyone should read. It is the natural companion to Ajay's case for globalisation.
Amit's recommendation for the episode. It came up right after Ajay credited Bhagwati and others with showing that exporting creates a healthier political economy.

head: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Covers how Indian firms should keep evolving to suit a diverse country.
more: Covers how Indian firms should keep evolving to suit a diverse country. Amit says it combines big-picture thinking with granular detail.
The other firms episode Amit singles out as significant.

head: Development Is the Emergence of High-Productivity Firms
dek: Every country has labour; the puzzle is getting more done per working hour, and that mostly happens inside firms.
more: Every country has labour; the puzzle is getting more done per working hour, and that mostly happens inside firms. A firm brings together capital, labour, governance, technology, management and contracts. If a quarter of Indians worked in firms at the global frontier of productivity, India would be an advanced economy (though only a third of working-age Indians work today). Saudi Arabia and Qatar show the contrast: high income from selling gas, but without the firms, the knowledge or the changed society. Ajay calls real development a human story.

head: Development Economics Has Lost the Plot
dek: Ajay argues the field got absorbed in philanthropy, aid, poverty and redistribution.
more: Ajay argues the field got absorbed in philanthropy, aid, poverty and redistribution. It says surprisingly little about the world's great development successes: Taiwan, South Korea, Israel and Chile, poor in 1945 and advanced today. He wants researchers to study firm productivity, domestic political economy, and the causes and consequences of internationalisation. These questions can't be answered with randomised controlled trials, and he is proud of working on them anyway.

head: Internationalisation (I18N) Comes in Interlocking Modes
dek: A firm internationalises through imported inputs, exports, foreign capital (equity, from portfolio investment up to FDI, and debt), foreign employees, and building operations abroad.
more: A firm internationalises through imported inputs, exports, foreign capital (equity, from portfolio investment up to FDI, and debt), foreign employees, and building operations abroad. Policy economists often treat these as a menu to pick from. Ajay says they feed each other. Foreign workers know cheap vendors back home, and foreign shareholders and board members open doors to FDI in places like Brazil. Even imports reveal something: because local inputs are easier, firms import only highly specialised things.

head: Exporting Is a Market Test, Not a Revenue Game
dek: Business people see exports as extra sales, but that is a fallacy of composition.
more: Business people see exports as extra sales, but that is a fallacy of composition. When a whole country exports more, its currency strengthens, imports get cheaper and some domestic producers die. India's software exports pushed up the rupee and hurt manufacturing exports, which economists call Dutch disease. That is just Ricardian specialisation, and since imports and exports move together, the gap between them isn't a meaningful target. Exporting matters because passing a global market test proves a firm is world-class. It also opens a bigger market and economies of scale; for a global firm size signals quality, while for a local monopoly like Coal India it means nothing.

head: Exporting Cleans Up a Toxic Political Economy
dek: Domestic firms compete by turning a weak developing-country state against each other: favourable regulations, tax raids, and joint lobbying to keep foreigners out.
more: Domestic firms compete by turning a weak developing-country state against each other: favourable regulations, tax raids, and joint lobbying to keep foreigners out. The worst players can win, and they make the state worse. Ajay credits Jagdish Bhagwati, T. N. Srinivasan and Anne Krueger with seeing that exporting changes this game. No amount of lobbying in Delhi helps Infosys sell to Germany; only productivity does. Exporting firms also stop talking nationalism, because they want cheap foreign inputs.

head: Fake Exports: Subsidies and a Rigged Exchange Rate
dek: A government can create the motions of exporting without the substance in two ways.
more: A government can create the motions of exporting without the substance in two ways. It can hand out subsidies, such as PLI, or it can weaken the currency; at 100 rupees a dollar instead of 80, even inefficient firms can export. Either way the country confuses means with ends. The goal was never a billion dollars of exports; it was high-quality firms.

head: You Can't Love Exports and Hate Multinationals
dek: Modern production is spread across countries. An engine made in Brazil can be shipped to Madras, assembled into a car and sold in America.
more: Modern production is spread across countries. An engine made in Brazil can be shipped to Madras, assembled into a car and sold in America. About 50% of global trade happens within firms, and smart firms ignore borders, choosing locations for low cost and for diversification. Harnessing exports means being deep inside the world of multinationals, both foreign firms coming in and Indian firms going out. George Fernandes-style irritation with multinationals, plus tax and rules-of-origin harassment, works directly against exporting.

head: Mr. Capital: The Invisible Biggest Input
dek: An engineer sees a steel mill as iron ore, coal, labour and imported machines.
more: An engineer sees a steel mill as iron ore, coal, labour and imported machines. An economist notices the elephant in the room: capital. Its cost per ton of steel is bigger than any of those inputs. To compete with the best mills in Korea, Japan or America, an Indian mill must match their cost of capital. Foreign equity and debt are cheaper, partly because India is poor and partly because its financial system is bad. So openness to foreign capital is about competitiveness, not ideology.

head: Competition Punishes Prejudice, So Hire Nationality-Blind
dek: Ajay cites George Stigler: a capitalist who discriminates against a minority is hurting herself.
more: Ajay cites George Stigler: a capitalist who discriminates against a minority is hurting herself. Successful firms care about getting things done, which gives capitalism a progressive social character. It brings people into voluntary contracts and 'double thank you' moments that are immune to prejudice. Amit adds that discrimination is costly only in a truly competitive market, and Ajay replies that exporting is that market. Refusing to hire foreigners is as wrong as refusing to hire Muslims or Dalits. Sometimes nationality is even an asset, such as Korean networks for selling into Korea.

head: Policymakers Should Kick Subsidy-Seekers Out of the Room
dek: Every location has some cheap and some expensive inputs. Labour costs more in Brazil, and electricity is cheaper in Germany.
more: Every location has some cheap and some expensive inputs. Labour costs more in Brazil, and electricity is cheaper in Germany. India's bad electricity policy needs fixing, but that is a 25-year journey and no excuse for subsidies today. A factory with 20 workers using 20 megawatt hours of electricity a day probably belongs in Germany, because there is no Indian edge. The state should let firms choose where and what to produce. As Amit notes, most of what Ajay asks of the state is to get out of the way.

head: The Indian State's Anti-Foreign Reflex
dek: Indian civil servants and regulators, more so under populism, treat foreign engagement as bad by default.
more: Indian civil servants and regulators, more so under populism, treat foreign engagement as bad by default. This covers foreign bank accounts, travel abroad, overseas subsidiaries, tax havens and running a business through Dubai. The reflex runs through SEBI, RBI, the ED, company affairs, income tax and GST. Only the largest firms can afford the compliance nightmare; smaller ones just give up. Ajay calls this the Indian state actively harming India's emergence.

head: Is Your Skill Fixing India, or Being a Competent Firm?
dek: Ajay's strategic question for managers. A competent firm should look outward and keep dealings with the Indian state to a minimum, as the software industry did.
more: Ajay's strategic question for managers. A competent firm should look outward and keep dealings with the Indian state to a minimum, as the software industry did. Even if you are clean, competitors will turn the state against you. The world market is effectively infinite, so you can keep growing for 25 years, and it insulates you from India's ups and downs.

head: Internationalisation as a Hard-to-Fake Metric for Boards and Investors
dek: Boards can use internationalisation metrics to hold managers to account and look past quarter-to-quarter profit.
more: Boards can use internationalisation metrics to hold managers to account and look past quarter-to-quarter profit. These include export share and growth, assets abroad, access to global capital, foreign hires, specialised imports and the number of countries a firm operates in. Investors use the same test. A firm selling in the EU, UK or US has proved it is good, while a domestic winner might have won through state power. Amit calls this a 'fast and frugal heuristic'. Ajay applies it to Nitin Pai's three types of Indian IT firm: services exporters like TCS and Wipro and SaaS exporters are safe bets, domestic firms need more scrutiny.

head: India's Quirky Rules Create Dwarf Firms
dek: There is a subtler harm too. India's unusual web of SEBI and RBI rules, a government-monopoly identity system and UPI shapes firms around Indian peculiarities.
more: There is a subtler harm too. India's unusual web of SEBI and RBI rules, a government-monopoly identity system and UPI shapes firms around Indian peculiarities. Their systems and software then don't work in Bangladesh, Japan or America. Ajay also asks whether UPI is actually good, or whether it won because PayPal was blocked. You can't tell when success came behind protection.

head: Patriotism vs Nationalism
dek: Amit draws on a distinction Ram Guha once made to him. Patriotism is loving your country.
more: Amit draws on a distinction Ram Guha once made to him. Patriotism is loving your country. Nationalism is toxic, exclusionary, chest-thumping and macho, and it powers the demands for tariffs, subsidies and currency manipulation that keep firms mediocre. A patriot wants India to compete and win. Ajay adds a nuance: the import substitution of the 1960s and 70s wasn't toxic nationalism but analytical failure by deluded economists. Firms, though, always stand ready to ask for protection.

head: Amit, deadpan, on Bihar's crime wave
more: Amit, deadpan, on Bihar's crime wave: "Like an entire bridge has been stolen from Bihar. You know, think of the innovation. People just stole a bridge... Only in Bihar." He adds that the bridge went only after a patch of water had already been stolen.

head: Amit in role-play mode
more: Amit in role-play mode: "I'm a podcaster, what do I do? I'm kidding. Don't look at me like that... I'm a podcaster, I will podcast."

head: On RCTs: Ajay says you don't have to be an…
more: On RCTs: Ajay says you don't have to be an "RCT Nazi" to study big questions. Amit piles on: "I wouldn't be surprised if there's an RCT somewhere. That do people perceive a yellow shirt to be brighter than a black shirt? That's the kind of rubbish they are doing."

head: Amit on Ajay's personified economic inputs
more: Amit on Ajay's personified economic inputs: "In a previous episode, gentle reader, you met Mr. Gas. Today you have met Mr. Capital." He says these characters reveal Ajay's "interior landscape".

head: Ajay's summary of what exporting demands of Infosys, since lobbying Delhi can't win German customers
more: Ajay's summary of what exporting demands of Infosys, since lobbying Delhi can't win German customers: "Like shut up and do your goddamn job better."

head: Ajay mocking economists who treat modes of internationalisation as a menu
more: Ajay mocking economists who treat modes of internationalisation as a menu: "Do I want this, do I not want this? He loves me, he loves me not."

head: I18N: Ajay explains that early computing ran in English on 127 ASCII characters. When software had to support Korean, Japanese and other languages
more: I18N: Ajay explains that early computing ran in English on 127 ASCII characters. When software had to support Korean, Japanese and other languages, "computer scientists were very lazy in typing", so 'internationalization' became I + 18 letters + N.

head: George Fernandes, whom Ajay describes…
more: George Fernandes, whom Ajay describes as "obsessively irritated about multinational corporations operating in India", a stance modern trade theory rejects.

head: Dutch disease: Indian software exports pushed up the rupee and hurt manufacturing exports. Ajay calls it Ricardian trade theory at work
more: Dutch disease: Indian software exports pushed up the rupee and hurt manufacturing exports. Ajay calls it Ricardian trade theory at work and "part of life".

head: ASML, TSMC and Sony as firms to admire and study
more: ASML, TSMC and Sony as firms to admire and study: "What is the magic of ASML? What is the magic of TSMC? What is the magic of Sony?"

head: China under Xi Jinping: global firms realised they were overexposed to China and rushed to diversify.
more: China under Xi Jinping: global firms realised they were overexposed to China and rushed to diversify. Ajay: "Sadly, not much has happened in terms of Indian gains out of this process."
Taiwan, South Korea, Israel and Chile, poor in 1945 and advanced today, as the great development stories. Ajay notes the OECD hasn't admitted Taiwan, yet it is "a first-class advanced economy".

head: Amit borrows the idea of…
more: Amit borrows the idea of 'fast and frugal heuristics' (one or two simple rules for a complex problem) and proposes a firm's level of internationalisation as one.

head: Wrong About Everything He 'Knew' About Podcasting
dek: Conventional wisdom about a new medium is often carried over from old media.
more: The Seen and the Unseen began seven years ago as an experiment. Amit assumed attention spans were short: grab listeners in the first fifteen seconds and keep episodes to fifteen or twenty minutes. The show went the other way. Short episodes became three- and four-hour deep dives into subjects, then seven- and eight-hour oral histories of people. The longer it got, the more love it received. His conservative estimate is twenty million hours of listening. Thirteen of the last seventeen times he was at an airport, someone stopped him to thank him. The YouTube version brings in under one percent of listens.
Conventional wisdom about a new medium is often carried over from old media. Amit's audience showed him that what they wanted was depth, not brevity.

head: Krish Ashok's Colleague Who Listens at 6x
dek: The brain adapts to listening speed far more than we assume. Pauses speed up along with the words, so nuance survives.
more: Amit listens to most things at 2x and goes up to 3x when researching an episode. He raises the speed in steps so that each one starts to feel normal. On an episode of The Seen and the Unseen, Krish Ashok told him about a blind colleague who listens at 6x, a speed at which audio becomes mush for Amit.
The brain adapts to listening speed far more than we assume. Pauses speed up along with the words, so nuance survives. The speed that feels comfortable to you is simply where you stopped pushing.

head: The Listener Who Interrupted a Recording
dek: This is what podcast intimacy means: the listener feels part of a conversation rather than an audience at a broadcast.
more: After hearing Amit's episode with Abhinandan Sekhri, a listener told Amit he had felt so much like he was sitting in a living room with two friends that at one point he interrupted them, speaking out loud to a recording.

This is what podcast intimacy means: the listener feels part of a conversation rather than an audience at a broadcast. It is also why strangers approach Amit in public, which he welcomes as his greatest reward.
printed: Not radio with a pause button

head: Fifteen Years of Friendship, One Podcast
dek: A long, attentive conversation opens a space that years of casual friendship never do.
more: Their friend Anjali Sharma told Ajay that she had known Josh Felman for fifteen years, yet his Seen and the Unseen episode revealed things that were completely new to her. Josh replied that she had simply never asked. Amit added his own experience: recording with friends of fifteen or twenty years, he realised mid-episode that he didn't really know them. Friendships skim the surface, and nobody asks about your parents or what makes you cry at night.
A long, attentive conversation opens a space that years of casual friendship never do. Much of what people would tell you, they are just waiting to be asked.

head: Ramachandra Guha in a Dark Room
dek: A YouTube search on any expert turns up dozens of talks and panels, none of which shows you who the person is.
more: Ramachandra Guha has been caricatured by both left and right, and has come on The Seen and the Unseen six times. In one conversation he described lying on his bed in a dark room listening to Hindustani classical music, losing all track of time, until his wife came home in the evening and found him there. The show notes link the exact ragas and performances, so listeners can hear what he heard.

A YouTube search on any expert turns up dozens of talks and panels, none of which shows you who the person is. Long-form audio can, and linking the music turns his anecdote into an experience the listener shares.

head: Paul Simon on Poems vs Songs
dek: Audio, like song, is consumed in a line by distracted people. Don't build in prerequisites that only work if the listener caught every earlier moment.
more: Ajay recalled an interview in which Paul Simon was asked how writing poetry differs from writing songs. A poem, Simon said, is like a painting the mind goes over many times. A song is linear, so there is no second take. Attention is also uncontrolled: a driver ignoring the radio may get hooked midway by a sound or a phrase. So a good song can't require you to have been there from the start.
Audio, like song, is consumed in a line by distracted people. Don't build in prerequisites that only work if the listener caught every earlier moment.

head: The Ballad of John Axon
dek: This is 'show, don't tell' in audio. Hearing the people who knew a man talk about him says far more than a narrator announcing that his villagers thought well of him.
more: John Axon was a railway driver who realised his train was going out of control. He could jump and save himself, or stay on board and try to save lives further down the line. He stayed and died. A group of people wrote songs about him. They also went to his village and recorded interviews with people who knew him, train sounds, his family, even someone crying in the background, without planning to use any of it. Their masterstroke was putting all of it into the 1957 work.
This is 'show, don't tell' in audio. Hearing the people who knew a man talk about him says far more than a narrator announcing that his villagers thought well of him.
printed: The driver who stayed on board

head: Turning Down a Nobel Laureate
dek: The format decides what a conversation can reach. Knowing what you want lets you say no even to a celebrity guest, since fifty other people will happily do the one-hour version.
more: A publisher offered to fly Amit to Delhi to record with Abhijit Banerjee in the same week he won the Nobel Prize. Amit asked for three hours; they offered one, and he declined. One hour would have meant talking only about the RCT work behind the prize. With three, he wanted to begin in 1963, when Banerjee's father taught Amit's father at Presidency College, Calcutta, and build a prehistory of the man.
The format decides what a conversation can reach. Knowing what you want lets you say no even to a celebrity guest, since fifty other people will happily do the one-hour version.

head: Five and a Half Hours, Book Never Mentioned
dek: You don't prepare in order to show off what you know. Preparation gives you the freedom to follow a better conversation.
more: During a Bangalore trip with about six recordings in seven days, Amit stayed up all night writing several thousand words of notes on Sugata Srinivasaraju's massive new book on Deve Gowda. The next day they recorded for five and a half hours and never mentioned the book. Sugata's life, the milieu he grew up in and how he watched the city transform were fascinating enough on their own.

You don't prepare in order to show off what you know. Preparation gives you the freedom to follow a better conversation. Being his own boss, with no producer demanding 45 minutes on the book, let Amit go where nobody else goes.
printed: Notes for a book never mentioned

head: When Tyler Cowen Came On
dek: There's no single right way to interview, but the host's and guest's styles have to mesh.
more: Amit admires Tyler Cowen, whose interviewing style is the opposite of his own: a list of brilliant prepared questions taken one after another without digressions. Cowen joined The Seen and the Unseen in a remote recording. Amit would ask a question, Cowen would answer crisply and stop, then the next question, and so on. Amit never found his usual flow. Neither of them was at fault; each was simply being himself.
There's no single right way to interview, but the host's and guest's styles have to mesh. Amit says he would approach a five-hour conversation with Cowen very differently today.

head: Jerry Pinto Sends a Fan to Shanta Gokhale
dek: Guests recommending one another's episodes is the strongest validation long-form work can get.
more: At a book event in mid-April, Jerry Pinto and Shanta Gokhale were signing books in adjoining queues. A reader told Jerry that his eight-hour Seen and the Unseen episode had been transformational. Jerry answered by asking whether she had heard Amit's episode with Shanta. In his own episode, Amit and Jerry had teared up together while talking about their mothers.
Guests recommending one another's episodes is the strongest validation long-form work can get. It also shows that when a host is vulnerable, guests open up in return.
printed: Have you heard the other one?

head: Mrinal Pande's Hour-Long First Answer
dek: Interruptions keep a conversation shallow, and silence lets people go deep.
more: Amit asked Mrinal Pande his first question. She then spoke for more than an hour, in a mix of Hindi and English, while he said nothing. She took listeners from her childhood in the 1950s to the end of the 1970s: her parents, her mother, her sisters, her coming of age as a woman. Amit says a younger, callower version of himself might have cut in after two minutes.
Interruptions keep a conversation shallow, and silence lets people go deep. The magic came entirely from not stepping in.
printed: Not a word from the host

head: Shruti's Present-Tense History
dek: Clarity includes tense. Ajay's rule is past tense for the past, present for the present and future for the future, which matters most when the listener can't rewind.
more: Before the Seen and the Unseen episode on the 1991 reforms, Amit worried that Shruti Rajagopalan, who is professorial and explains everything in detail, would dominate Ajay, whom Amit calls the crispest thinker he knows. The conversation went well. But Ajay kept getting thrown because Shruti narrated historical events in the present tense, and he couldn't tell whether she meant now or long ago.
Clarity includes tense. Ajay's rule is past tense for the past, present for the present and future for the future, which matters most when the listener can't rewind.

head: The 'Gobbledygook' Edit
dek: Experts can't see their own jargon. Part of a co-host's job is to speak up for the listener who is confused.
more: In Everything is Everything's Four Papers episode, Ajay talked about monetary and fiscal policy as easily as breathing, and Amit kept stopping him for lapsing into jargon. The released video is a cleaned-up version as a result. Amit's caveat is that this was the only time. Normally EIE is the organic conversation, only lightly cleaned up.
Experts can't see their own jargon. Part of a co-host's job is to speak up for the listener who is confused.

head: Ali Abdaal's Thousandth Subscriber at Video Fifty
dek: Exponential growth looks like failure for a long time. Someone who needs validation quits around video thirty.
more: Amit points to YouTuber Ali Abdaal's subscriber graph, an exponential curve: a long flat stretch, then a line that turns almost vertical. Abdaal made two videos a week and only reached his thousandth subscriber around video fifty. His later advice to new creators: make two videos a week for two years and don't look at the numbers.
Exponential growth looks like failure for a long time. Someone who needs validation quits around video thirty. Someone who loves the work keeps iterating until they become good, and then great.

head: Two Years Without Looking at the Numbers
dek: The hosts follow their own advice: during the early learning phase, keep the work separate from the metrics.
more: When they started Everything is Everything, Amit asked Ajay not to look at the numbers for two years, about 104 episodes, and simply keep making the show. EIE is tiny next to The Seen and the Unseen, yet a loyal audience that turns up every Friday is already forming.
The hosts follow their own advice: during the early learning phase, keep the work separate from the metrics.

head: The Fan Who Caught a Missing Show Note
dek: People who love your work feel that they own a piece of it. An audience like that is worth more than any number of shallow likes.
more: Before he and Amit became friends, Sudhir Sarnobat listened to a Seen and the Unseen episode with around 114 show-note links. He wrote to Amit to point out one book that hadn't been linked.
People who love your work feel that they own a piece of it. An audience like that is worth more than any number of shallow likes.

head: Hardcore History
dek: Carlin reads about forty books per episode and then simply talks, with no sound effects and no dramatised delivery, and it is riveting.
more: Carlin reads about forty books per episode and then simply talks, with no sound effects and no dramatised delivery, and it is riveting. It proves you need neither a co-host nor production to tell a great audio story.
Amit's first podcast as a listener, cited for his tip that one person is enough to tell a story.

head: Blueprint for Armageddon
dek: Carlin reads letters that soldiers wrote to their wives and girlfriends the night before a reckless mission in which they all died.
more: Carlin reads letters that soldiers wrote to their wives and girlfriends the night before a reckless mission in which they all died. That was the moment Amit understood the power of audio storytelling.
The roughly 26–27 hour Hardcore History series on World War One that first hooked Amit.

head: The Ballad of John Axon
dek: A landmark in audio history. Interviews and background sound recorded in Axon's village went into the final piece, making it a masterclass in show, don't tell.
more: A landmark in audio history. Interviews and background sound recorded in Axon's village went into the final piece, making it a masterclass in show, don't tell.
A 1957 work, which Amit isn't sure whether to call a play or an album, about a railway driver who died staying on his runaway train.

head: Sun of the Family
dek: The producers interviewed his parents, brother and girlfriend, and a whole person comes alive through the inflections in their voices and their particular memories.
more: The producers interviewed his parents, brother and girlfriend, and a whole person comes alive through the inflections in their voices and their particular memories. Amit calls it heartbreaking and a second landmark of show, don't tell.
A Danish radio show from around 1997 about a young musician who killed himself. Amit asks listeners to post a link in the comments if it's available online.

head: EconTalk
dek: It is the closest to his own approach: relaxed and conversational, with no fixed structure, going deep.
more: It is the closest to his own approach: relaxed and conversational, with no fixed structure, going deep. It focuses on ideas rather than the guest's life.
Amit studied many podcasters' styles while building his course, and calls EconTalk legendary and the OG podcast.

head: A Meditation on Form
dek: It explains how form dictates content: what a five-minute conversation demands of a host compared with an eight-hour one.
more: It explains how form dictates content: what a five-minute conversation demands of a host compared with an eight-hour one.
Linked when Amit urges podcasters not to be trapped by conventions about length.

head: 1000 True Fans
dek: Kelly argued that creators don't need scale: a thousand true fans paying $100 a year comes to $100,000.
more: Kelly argued that creators don't need scale: a thousand true fans paying $100 a year comes to $100,000. It was theoretical when written, and Amit says subscription models like Substack have since made it real.
Cited for the principle that it is better to be loved by a few than liked by many.

head: Sinocism
dek: Bishop isn't a mainstream name, and he writes about China in a way so specialised that mainstream outlets might never commission him.
more: Bishop isn't a mainstream name, and he writes about China in a way so specialised that mainstream outlets might never commission him. Yet he is a superstar among his subscribers.
Amit's example of a creator who succeeds in a deep niche.

head: Furrows in a Field
dek: Amit calls it a great book, even though their five-and-a-half-hour conversation never got to it.
more: Amit calls it a great book, even though their five-and-a-half-hour conversation never got to it.
Sugata's massive book on Deve Gowda, which Amit took thousands of words of notes on before their recording.

head: The Rooted Cosmopolitanism of Sugata Srinivasaraju (Episode 277, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Five and a half hours on Sugata's life, the milieu he grew up in and how he watched his city transform, which is material no panel discussion about the book would produce.
more: Five and a half hours on Sugata's life, the milieu he grew up in and how he watched his city transform, which is material no panel discussion about the book would produce.
The episode that never mentioned the book.

head: Playwright at the Centre
dek: Amit calls it a great book on the history of Marathi theatre. Their conversation never even reached the subject.
more: Amit calls it a great book on the history of Marathi theatre. Their conversation never even reached the subject.
Mentioned while describing his eight-and-a-half-hour episode with Gokhale, an authority on the subject.

head: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit and Jerry teared up together while talking about their mothers. It is his example of how a host's vulnerability draws guests out of rehearsed sound bites.
more: Amit and Jerry teared up together while talking about their mothers. It is his example of how a host's vulnerability draws guests out of rehearsed sound bites.
An eight-hour episode that people still bring up to Amit.

head: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (Episode 321, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It revealed things about Josh that even a friend of fifteen years had never heard.
more: It revealed things about Josh that even a friend of fifteen years had never heard.
Raised by Ajay as an example of what a podcast conversation draws out of a guest.

head: Episode of The Seen and the Unseen with Ramachandra Guha
dek: They show the person behind the caricatures, down to the ragas he listens to alone in a dark room, which are linked in the show notes.
more: They show the person behind the caricatures, down to the ragas he listens to alone in a dark room, which are linked in the show notes.
Guha has been on the show six times. The first two episodes were on Gandhi, and Amit read thirty books to prepare.

head: Long As I Can See The Light
dek: A musical wink that fits an episode literally recorded until the daylight ran out.
more: A musical wink that fits an episode literally recorded until the daylight ran out.
Amit said he would talk 'as long as the light lasts' and Ajay quipped 'As long as you can see the light.' The show notes link Chris Cornell's version.

head: ATR2100x microphone
dek: It is a dynamic mic, so it picks up only what is close to it, which suits a home setup better than a studio condenser mic.
more: It is a dynamic mic, so it picks up only what is close to it, which suits a home setup better than a studio condenser mic. It costs about ₹7,000 and has both USB and regular connections, so you can plug it into a laptop and also use it for Zoom calls.
Amit's microphone recommendation for beginners.

head: The Art of Clear Writing
dek: His full method for clear writing, including rules like putting the verb soon after the subject, avoiding 'the latter', and making every sentence go forward or deeper.
more: His full method for clear writing, including rules like putting the verb soon after the subject, avoiding 'the latter', and making every sentence go forward or deeper.
He has taught it to more than 2,600 people, and several of the episode's writing-for-audio tips come from it.

head: Why Audio Can Go Long: When, How and Why We Listen
dek: When: people listen while commuting, working out or doing chores, so they are a captive audience who won't switch tabs.
more: When: people listen while commuting, working out or doing chores, so they are a captive audience who won't switch tabs. How: many listen at higher speeds and lose no nuance. Why: most media is a mile wide and an inch deep, while audio is the most efficient way to go deep. Binge-watching shows that attention spans aren't the real problem. Ajay pushes back that only a small fraction of people crave depth and most want diversion, which is still enough to sustain a show. Amit replies that everyone has the capacity for depth and only needs a trigger.

head: Try Higher Listening Speeds
dek: The brain can comprehend up to about 500 words a minute, while people speak at 160–200.
more: The brain can comprehend up to about 500 words a minute, while people speak at 160–200. That spare capacity may be why we sometimes get bored listening to someone. Raise the speed in steps, to 1.2x and then 1.5x: each step starts to feel normal, until one stops feeling normal, and that is your natural level. The silences speed up too, so nuance survives. Don't judge anyone's speed. Ajay adds that this was a new discovery for him and is worth trying.

head: Podcasting Is Not Time-Shifted Radio
dek: Ajay first thought of podcasts as radio on demand. Amit says they are fundamentally different.
more: Ajay first thought of podcasts as radio on demand. Amit says they are fundamentally different. In India, high FM licence fees push radio towards the lowest common denominator, and FM isn't even allowed to do news. Podcasting costs nothing but time, needs no licence, and allows both depth and intimacy. Because anyone can make anything, it uncovers niches nobody suspected existed, such as audiences for eight-hour conversations. Even a small niche in India, or across the world, is large in absolute numbers.

head: A Voice in Your Head: The Distance Metaphor
dek: Think about distance. Cinema is a big screen far away, filmed from far away, which suits westerns and car chases.
more: Think about distance. Cinema is a big screen far away, filmed from far away, which suits westerns and car chases. Television is two or three metres away, which suits sitcoms. YouTube is half a metre away, with closer framing. Radio is like four people in a car, being broadcast to. A podcast is a voice inside your head. So you don't need a radio announcer's voice modulation, and putting one on would be a bug, not a feature, because listeners expect intimacy.

head: The Two Imperatives: Respect the Listener, Be Yourself
dek: Old media had the few talking down to the many. An intimate medium doesn't allow that, because listeners are accomplished people who often know more than you do, so respect their time and intelligence.
more: Old media had the few talking down to the many. An intimate medium doesn't allow that, because listeners are accomplished people who often know more than you do, so respect their time and intelligence. Second, be authentic. When a student in his course asked what gap in the market he should fill, Amit said that thinking this way is a mistake. Among seven billion people and a million podcasts, the only thing that sets you apart is that you are you. Treat the show as your own journey, and people at any point on a similar journey will come along.

head: Write for the Ear: One Thing at a Time
dek: A reader can go back over a sentence; a listener washing dishes can't.
more: A reader can go back over a sentence; a listener washing dishes can't. So give one piece of information at a time. Don't put a dependent clause between the subject and the verb, as in 'Amit Varma, while...'. Avoid 'the latter' and passive constructions, which force the mind backward. When a story changes setting, signal the switch, and repeat who is speaking or where things are happening if needed. Repetition that would be bad in print can help in audio.

head: Why Listeners Stay: Wanting and Structure
dek: Don't be dogmatic about structure, but at every moment ask why the listener would keep listening.
more: Don't be dogmatic about structure, but at every moment ask why the listener would keep listening. Usually it is empathy for a character plus curiosity about how their conflict resolves. Margaret Atwood warned that you can't take the reader for granted. Kurt Vonnegut said every character must want something, even if it is only a glass of water. Write the first draft as a brain dump, then restructure it with the listener in mind.
printed: One thing at a time, please

head: Show, Don't Tell: Verbs Over Adjectives
dek: 'Show, don't tell' doesn't mean describing a scene. It means conveying something through action instead of abstraction: fewer adjectives, more verbs.
more: 'Show, don't tell' doesn't mean describing a scene. It means conveying something through action instead of abstraction: fewer adjectives, more verbs. The film cliché of the 'pet the dog' scene shows a character's warmth instead of announcing it, and words like 'nice' mean little anyway. In audio, you can show a person through the voices and memories of the people who knew them, as The Ballad of John Axon does.

head: Forward or Deeper: Every Element Must Earn Its Place
dek: Amit's rule for writing is that every sentence must either move the story forward or take it deeper, through context, detail or colour.
more: Amit's rule for writing is that every sentence must either move the story forward or take it deeper, through context, detail or colour. The same goes for sound effects: footsteps on gravel can announce that someone is arriving, but effects added because they sound cool become intrusive. EIE learned this with on-screen inserts. They used to add too many; now there is no photo of Karl Marx just because his name comes up. Every extra element costs the audience some attention.

head: The Curse of Knowledge
dek: When you know a subject well, you assume the audience shares your baseline.
more: When you know a subject well, you assume the audience shares your baseline. Crew member Vaishnav told Amit that a recent EIE episode skimmed over technical points he had wanted explained. In audio the listener can't go back, so introduce new voices quickly and set scenes clearly. In conversation, the host must keep one eye on the listener. Amit's technique is to say 'let me state this as I understand it' and restate the guest's point simply, so the guest can correct him if needed.

head: Form Dictates Content, Content Shapes Character
dek: Don't be trapped by conventions about length; Amit credits himself with shifting India's Overton window on how long a podcast can be.
more: Don't be trapped by conventions about length; Amit credits himself with shifting India's Overton window on how long a podcast can be. For a five-minute show you needn't read the guest's book. For half an hour, a ChatGPT summary will do. For an hour you must read the book. For eight hours you must read everything they've written, read around the subject and care about their life. First define your purpose: are you a fox or a hedgehog, interested in the subject or the person, their knowledge or their journey? Long form changes the host, because it teaches you to listen and to sink into another person's life.

head: Take Guests Out of Autocomplete Mode
dek: Authors arrive with prepared sound bites and can talk about their book on autopilot, like ChatGPT.
more: Authors arrive with prepared sound bites and can talk about their book on autopilot, like ChatGPT. Amit sincerely asks about their childhood and home, and makes himself vulnerable too. Guests then tend to open up in return. After they have talked about things they haven't discussed in forty years, they talk about their actual subject more naturally as well.

head: Over-Prepare, Then Let It Go
dek: You will never know as much as your guest, but you need enough knowledge to follow their digressions.
more: You will never know as much as your guest, but you need enough knowledge to follow their digressions. For his first episodes with Ramachandra Guha on Gandhi, Amit read thirty books. He usually ends up using only a fraction of his preparation, and that is fine, because it was never meant for showing off.

head: Respect the Guest: Don't Interrupt, Listen to Understand
dek: For Amit, not interrupting is an article of faith. Interruptions stop guests from going deep.
more: For Amit, not interrupting is an article of faith. Interruptions stop guests from going deep. Once guests expect them, they speak in half-sentences and can't make nuanced points. Most of us listen in order to reply or to look smart. Instead, put your ego aside and treat yourself as a bystander in the guest's story rather than its main character. Amit says this habit has made him more self-reflective and a better listener.

head: Follow the Flow, Not the Question List
dek: Panel moderators are often already thinking about question seven while the guest answers question six, and they miss the interesting digression in the answer.
more: Panel moderators are often already thinking about question seven while the guest answers question six, and they miss the interesting digression in the answer. Amit prepares themes in depth but in no fixed order, and follows whatever thread comes up. Ajay notes this is a high bar. It separates real fluid intelligence from media that is about appearances and diction, because you have to understand what the guest said in real time and build on it.

head: The Three Scaffoldings of a Long Conversation
dek: Amit's own theory for eight-hour episodes, which he is still developing.
more: Amit's own theory for eight-hour episodes, which he is still developing. There are three overlapping frameworks: the guest's life story, their work, and the themes and ideas he wants to explore, many of which come up during the conversation. He moves between them in no fixed order and without breaking the flow. Too much on ideas feels abstract, and too much on life can also put listeners off. The Natasha Badhwar episode is his model of balance. The Nilanjana Roy episode leaned towards ideas but became a top-ten hit anyway.

head: Bias for Action: Get It Done Over Getting It Right
dek: In policy, Lincoln's line about spending most of your time sharpening the axe makes sense, but creators should do the opposite.
more: In policy, Lincoln's line about spending most of your time sharpening the axe makes sense, but creators should do the opposite. The brain is wired to procrastinate, and you only learn by doing. Everyone is bad at first. Amit tells people to listen to The Seen and the Unseen in reverse order, and expects the hosts to see flaws in today's EIE episodes in two years. Vinay Sitapati once told him that perfection is the enemy of production.

head: Life Is Not a Spectator Sport — Judge People by Their Best
dek: Ajay's motto since childhood is that playing cricket himself matters more than watching Sachin Tendulkar play.
more: Ajay's motto since childhood is that playing cricket himself matters more than watching Sachin Tendulkar play. He argues that a culture which values people's best work and forgives their worst would lower everyone's fear of starting. Amit adds that creators should do instead of whining: if you don't like someone's work, make something better. And remove negative people from your life where you can.

head: Play the Long Game
dek: Creators overestimate what they can achieve in the short term and underestimate the long term, because organic growth is exponential.
more: Creators overestimate what they can achieve in the short term and underestimate the long term, because organic growth is exponential. If you chase the numbers and reshape your work around them, you lose your soul. If you make the work out of love, you keep improving through iteration. Ajay adds that putting on an inauthentic show can last only so long before you lose interest, while authenticity lets you keep going long enough to get better.

head: Better to Be Loved by a Few Than Liked by Many
dek: Amit credits the line to Paul Graham, as quoted by Sam Altman, and says he practised it long before he saw it put into words.
more: Amit credits the line to Paul Graham, as quoted by Sam Altman, and says he practised it long before he saw it put into words. People who love your work feel they own part of it and support it. Amit would rather have a hundred thousand people listen to an episode than get ten million YouTube likes. He contrasts many channels' average view time of about fifteen seconds with his own average listening session of about forty minutes. Kevin Kelly's and Li Jin's 'true fans' essays show the economics can work.

head: Think Out of the Box — Including Language
dek: When a show like Serial succeeds, everyone copies its structure, tone and voice; don't.
more: When a show like Serial succeeds, everyone copies its structure, tone and voice; don't. In India, English-language podcasts are saturated with shows from around the world, while Hindi, Malayalam and other language audiences are underserved. If you can be authentic in another language, don't think of it as beneath you, because that audience needs you more and will love you more.

head: Start Alone, Start Free
dek: For storytelling, one person is enough. Dan Carlin proves it, and his first-ever episode would probably make him cringe today.
more: For storytelling, one person is enough. Dan Carlin proves it, and his first-ever episode would probably make him cringe today. Hosting is free and early episodes can be recorded on a phone. For a mic, choose a dynamic one over a condenser: studio condenser mics capture every nuance but also the room, while a dynamic mic, like the one a rock star holds at a concert, picks up only what is close to it. Imposter syndrome shouldn't stop you.

head: Ajay's introduction
more: Ajay's introduction: 'before Amit Varma became a world famous inventor and producer of a YouTube show, he in his previous incarnation pioneered the format of the podcast in India.' This is a gentle tease, given that EIE is tiny next to Amit's audio show.

head: To show what not to do in audio, Amit writes a sentence about his own arrest
more: To show what not to do in audio, Amit writes a sentence about his own arrest: 'The famous podcaster Amit Varma, while conducting a webinar on writing from his home office in Andheri, Mumbai, was arrested by the Delhi police for the crime of making Delhi more polluted by broadcasting his convoluted classes there.' The sequel: he 'protested his innocence before the officers in khaki, one of whom he berated for using an adverb.' The version rewritten for audio begins: 'The famous podcaster Amit Varma is behind bars.'

head: On why the verb should come straight after the subject: rather than…
more: On why the verb should come straight after the subject: rather than 'Ajay Shah, while sipping from his herbal tea that he made with the seventy four herbs he had gathered in his garden...', Amit suggests 'Ajay Shah stabbed his co-host Amit with a knife', which he calls a much more dramatic way to put it.

head: Amit mimes jogging while describing a typical listener, Ajay smiles, and Amit demands
more: Amit mimes jogging while describing a typical listener, Ajay smiles, and Amit demands, 'Why did you smile when I did this?' He drops the jogger for someone washing dishes. When he gestures again, the listener ends up 'washing dishes on an elevated platform.'

head: Defending the eight-and-a-half-hour episode with 83-year-old Shanta Gokhale
more: Defending the eight-and-a-half-hour episode with 83-year-old Shanta Gokhale: 'One hour for each decade of her life. Are you telling me that is sufficient?'

head: Amit's sign-off as the daylight fades
more: Amit's sign-off as the daylight fades: 'one piece of technology that you and I cannot control, Ajay Shah, even in these modern times, is the sun... the sun is kind of setting on us, but literally, not metaphorically, and not even literally because the sun isn't setting, the earth is turning.'

head: At the XKDR Forum anniversary party, Bhargav Zaveri asked guests to complete
more: At the XKDR Forum anniversary party, Bhargav Zaveri asked guests to complete 'There are two kinds of people in the world...'. Amit's answer: 'the doers and the whiners.' On air he tells Ajay, 'And you have described the whiners.'

head: Amit promises to talk
more: Amit promises to talk 'as long as the light lasts' and Ajay replies, 'As long as you can see the light.' The show notes link Chris Cornell's 'Long As I Can See The Light'.

head: Robert McKee, whom Amit describes as the author of many great books on storytelling
more: Robert McKee, whom Amit describes as the author of many great books on storytelling: 'story is a natural form of thought.' Amit uses it to argue that audio is the oldest form of storytelling.

head: Margaret Atwood
more: Margaret Atwood: 'A word after a word after a word is power.' Kurt Vonnegut: 'every character must want something, even if it is only a glass of water.' Amit pairs them on why you can never take the listener's attention for granted.

head: After Ajay's Paul Simon story, Amit's tribute
more: After Ajay's Paul Simon story, Amit's tribute: 'in the clearing stands a songwriter or a poet by his side', praising Simon as a remarkable songwriter and, in his own way, a great poet.

head: Neil Simon, from what Amit recalls as Barefoot in the Park
more: Neil Simon, from what Amit recalls as Barefoot in the Park: 'There are two kinds of people in the world, the watchers and the doers, and the watchers sit around watching the doers do.'

head: Abraham Lincoln's
more: Abraham Lincoln's 'Give me six hours to chop down a tree and I'll spend the first five sharpening the axe', reversed for creators: 'You have to cut the tree to learn how to cut the tree.'

head: Asked whether he designs for loyal fans or occasional listeners, Amit says he doesn't think about the audience at all, quoting
more: Asked whether he designs for loyal fans or occasional listeners, Amit says he doesn't think about the audience at all, quoting 'Ekla chalo re' (walk alone) and adding 'whoever comes comes along.'

head: Why dehydration makes cardio harder, and how to use it
dek: Knowing the mechanism (blood viscosity and pump load) explains a familiar feeling and suggests a training tool.
more: An adult has about six litres of blood. Sweat out a litre during exercise and you have lost roughly a sixth of that base, so the blood thickens and the heart works harder to pump it. That is why dehydrated exercise feels so draining and why a drink of water brings quick relief. Ajay's twist: on a treadmill with a fridge of water nearby, you could train slightly under-hydrated on purpose to raise the load on your heart. Amit, who once read 20 to 40 running books in a couple of months, added that marathon runners have died from drinking too much water.
Knowing the mechanism (blood viscosity and pump load) explains a familiar feeling and suggests a training tool. The marathon point is the counterweight: more water is not always better.
printed: Thin on water, thick in blood

head: The CPAP machine that fixed the wrong problem
dek: Interventions have second-order effects. The biggest benefit of a treatment can turn up somewhere you weren't looking.
more: Amit tested positive for mild sleep apnea and began using a CPAP machine. Poor sleep had never really troubled him, but chronic acid reflux had: for years he woke most mornings with a cold or a sore throat. The pressurised air from a nasal mask stopped the acid from rising at night, and the morning sore throats disappeared. He also urges anyone who snores to get tested for sleep apnea.
Interventions have second-order effects. The biggest benefit of a treatment can turn up somewhere you weren't looking.

head: Escaping a perfect home office for Starbucks
dek: Discipline is often about designing your environment, not summoning willpower.
more: Amit records episodes in batches (eight episodes in nine days in Delhi, for instance), which leaves him weeks of free time. He admits he wastes much of it on online bullet chess, even in a home office he loves, with a sit-stand desk and all the tech. His fix is to work from Starbucks, where sitting among other people with laptops makes him too sheepish to play chess for an hour.
Discipline is often about designing your environment, not summoning willpower. Even people who look very productive are fighting the same battle.

head: A chess rating as a gauge of mental sharpness
dek: A skill you practise every day can double as a personal experiment that shows how diet and other factors affect your thinking.
more: Amit has been prescribed modafinil for sleep apnea and uses it, with caveats, during long recording runs. He noticed that on keto, or on days he takes modafinil, his Chess.com bullet rating rises about 100 points, and falls back when he stops. He isn't trying to improve at chess, so the swing works as a fairly clean measure of his cognitive state.
A skill you practise every day can double as a personal experiment that shows how diet and other factors affect your thinking.

head: Two books from Lant Pritchett that changed Ajay's thinking
dek: Good books often reach you through trusted people. Spend time with people who know great books, and when someone you respect recommends one, give it a proper chance.
more: Lant Pritchett pointed Ajay to Seeing Like a State and to The Functions of the Executive, a 1938 management book that reshaped how he thinks about organisations, both firms and government bodies. Ajay took the suggestions seriously because he respected Lant. Seeing Like a State led him to read everything by James C. Scott, including Against the Grain, which he considers a near-perfect book.
Good books often reach you through trusted people. Spend time with people who know great books, and when someone you respect recommends one, give it a proper chance.

head: 'When are you most happy?' at a café in Bir
dek: Tie happiness to small processes you can reach every day, not to big goals.
more: Sitting in a café in Bir with Ajay, Vaishnav, Nomsita and friends, Amit asked everyone when they were happiest. One said in the mountains, another said with her dog, and Ajay said when he has a new idea. Amit noticed that every answer was easy to achieve.
Tie happiness to small processes you can reach every day, not to big goals. Big goals are elusive, and even reaching them may not satisfy you.

head: Vinay Singhal's two language struggles, and STAGE
dek: Two forces pull on Indian languages. A 'great flattening' pushes dialects toward Hindi and English, while the internet lets niche languages survive on small, devoted audiences.
more: Vinay Singhal grew up in a Haryana village speaking Haryanvi. He had to work hard twice: once to learn English after joining an English-medium school in the eighth standard (he rose to the top of his class), and again to master Hindi when he moved to a city. His venture STAGE now makes content in dialects like Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and Maithili.

Two forces pull on Indian languages. A 'great flattening' pushes dialects toward Hindi and English, while the internet lets niche languages survive on small, devoted audiences. Amit's advice to new podcasters: if your other language is nearly as good as your English, use it, because that audience is underserved.
printed: A thousand true fans for Haryanvi

head: Hanging off a mountain: 'Let's solve this'
dek: This is Ajay's crisis rule in action, which he states elsewhere in the episode: the bigger the crisis, the calmer you need to be, so that you can actually think.
more: On the hike where Ajay broke his leg, he slipped off an edge and was left hanging while his friend Ayush held his hand. Ajay was soaked in panic sweat. For about thirty seconds, neither said a word. Then Ajay looked up and said, 'Let's solve this.'
This is Ajay's crisis rule in action, which he states elsewhere in the episode: the bigger the crisis, the calmer you need to be, so that you can actually think.

head: Why coming back from America was his best decision
dek: Early-stage environments offer outsized purpose. Being a bit player in a big story can matter more than being a star in a mature one.
more: Asked whether he regrets leaving the US, Ajay calls returning to India one of the best decisions of his life. In America he would have worked on second-order problems. In India he got to take on the big founding questions of a developing country and play a small part in important national stories.
Early-stage environments offer outsized purpose. Being a bit player in a big story can matter more than being a star in a mature one.

head: The story behind Ajay's shirts
dek: A small story about letting go of convention and experimenting late. Signature styles can come about by accident.
more: For years Ajay wore a uniform copied from economists Kirit Parikh and Shekhar Shah: plain white or off-white Khadi Emporium shirts, half-sleeved because India is too hot for full sleeves. He has never worn a suit and tie in India. Later he found printed shirts in Udaipur, tried them on Everything is Everything, liked how they looked, and now most of his shirts are gifts. Many are silk shirts from Indian Colours printed with contemporary Indian art.
A small story about letting go of convention and experimenting late. Signature styles can come about by accident.
printed: From khadi white to silk prints

head: How long-form conversations made Amit a better listener
dek: Form shapes the person doing the work. Long conversation demands humility and real attention, and over time it builds both.
more: The Seen and the Unseen evolved from short takes on single subjects, to three- and four-hour dives into whole fields, to deep dives into people that sometimes run six to eight hours. Amit says this change in form changed him. He listens to understand rather than to respond, keeps his ego out, and enjoys learning what shaped his guests, including their dreams and fears.
Form shapes the person doing the work. Long conversation demands humility and real attention, and over time it builds both.

head: From Amul Tetra Paks to protein powder
dek: When the state fails at waste management, small personal choices are a way of living by your values, even if you are a drop in the ocean.
more: Having seen how badly Bombay handles its trash, and knowing that plastic breaks down into microplastics that end up in our stomachs, Ajay changed small habits. He buys milk in pouches rather than Tetra Paks, because a pouch uses fewer grams of plastic per litre. After about ten Amul Tetra Pak protein drinks he felt bad about so much packaging for 200 ml, and switched to protein powder.
When the state fails at waste management, small personal choices are a way of living by your values, even if you are a drop in the ocean.

head: Wild Strawberries
dek: Amit thinks it is the best way into Bergman, who can feel inaccessible.
more: Amit thinks it is the best way into Bergman, who can feel inaccessible. It is a masterpiece about old age and growing old gracefully.
Mid-episode pick, right after Ajay's joke that a country's films get better as its median age rises.

head: Primers on public choice, classical liberalism, Hayek and Friedman
dek: Excellent short introductions to great thinkers he believes everyone should read.
more: Excellent short introductions to great thinkers he believes everyone should read.
Part of Amit's answer to a request for his top-ten bookshelf. He laments that there is no single primer on classical liberalism.

head: Seeing Like a State
dek: It chipped away at Ajay's belief in technological high modernism. In his words, it showed him 'what a book can do'.
more: It chipped away at Ajay's belief in technological high modernism. In his words, it showed him 'what a book can do'.
Listed by Amit on his bookshelf and named by Ajay as one of the books that arrived at exactly the right time, via Lant Pritchett.

head: Against the Grain
dek: He calls it one of the most perfect executions of a book. Anyone who wants to learn the craft of writing a book should study it.
more: He calls it one of the most perfect executions of a book. Anyone who wants to learn the craft of writing a book should study it.
After Seeing Like a State, Ajay read everything else Scott wrote.

head: The Functions of the Executive
dek: It opened up his thinking on organisational behaviour and on what goes wrong in large, complex organisations, both firms and government.
more: It opened up his thinking on organisational behaviour and on what goes wrong in large, complex organisations, both firms and government.
A 1938 management book that Lant Pritchett recommended to Ajay.

head: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
dek: It makes clear that a minimum wage prices the poorest workers out of jobs entirely, hurting the people it claims to protect.
more: It makes clear that a minimum wage prices the poorest workers out of jobs entirely, hurting the people it claims to protect.
A video Amit links while explaining why India lost the garment industry to Bangladesh.

head: The Skeptical Environmentalist
dek: Lomborg traces how great Western cities like London were filthy and unhealthy about a hundred years ago and cleaned up as they got richer.
more: Lomborg traces how great Western cities like London were filthy and unhealthy about a hundred years ago and cleaned up as they got richer. Amit's takeaway: growth helps sustainability.
Cited in the answer on degrowth and sustainability, along with Lomborg's work in general.

head: Hardcore History
dek: He calls it quite amazing.
more: He calls it quite amazing.
A listener asked for his favourite podcasts.

dek: He thinks she does an incredible job.
more: He thinks she does an incredible job.
His top Indian podcast pick.

head: Grand Tamasha
dek: Vaishnav is a fine thinker, and the podcast is a good way to follow Indian politics.
more: Vaishnav is a fine thinker, and the podcast is a good way to follow Indian politics.
Favourite podcasts. Vaishnav had been especially active during the elections.

head: When Crime Pays
dek: A must-read on crime in Indian politics.
more: A must-read on crime in Indian politics.
Mentioned along with Vaishnav's podcast.

head: EconTalk
dek: A long-time favourite of Amit's.
more: A long-time favourite of Amit's.
Roberts is another favourite and came on The Seen and the Unseen to talk about conversation.

head: Who We Are and How We Got Here
dek: Source of Amit's favourite line: India is not one large population like the Han Chinese but a collection of thousands of small ones.
more: Source of Amit's favourite line: India is not one large population like the Han Chinese but a collection of thousands of small ones.
Paired with Early Indians in the caste answer.

head: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants
dek: A great book on the history of India's languages.
more: A great book on the history of India's languages.
A pointer for the question on how Indian languages will evolve. Amit also recorded an episode with her.

head: A Meditation on Form
dek: His account of how moving to very long conversations changed the show and made him a better listener.
more: His account of how moving to very long conversations changed the show and made him a better listener.
Asked which Seen and the Unseen conversations changed him most.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: In the second edition, each of the 45 chapters comes with a reading list, which makes it a good starting point for further study.
more: In the second edition, each of the 45 chapters comes with a reading list, which makes it a good starting point for further study.
Asked for a step-by-step guide to learning India.

head: Blue
dek: He calls Joni Mitchell absolutely incredible, and Blue is one of his favourite albums.
more: He calls Joni Mitchell absolutely incredible, and Blue is one of his favourite albums.
Asked which songwriters besides Springsteen he admires.

head: New York
dek: Where to start with Lou Reed. He calls it a masterpiece.
more: Where to start with Lou Reed. He calls it a masterpiece.
Songwriters he admires.

dek: One of his two specific favourites, from different phases of Dylan's life.
more: One of his two specific favourites, from different phases of Dylan's life.
Songwriters he admires. He loves everything by Dylan.

dek: His other specific Dylan favourite, from a later phase.

Songwriters he admires.

more: A great album he urges listeners to check out.
Van Morrison is a recurring favourite.

head: Moondance
dek: Another Van Morrison album he recommends.
more: Another Van Morrison album he recommends.
Mentioned alongside Astral Weeks.

head: People are brains, not stomachs
dek: Amit rejects the idea of overpopulation outright. The right population is whatever arises through consent and without coercion.
more: Amit rejects the idea of overpopulation outright. The right population is whatever arises through consent and without coercion. People move from low-density places to high-density cities, which are also the most prosperous places, so they are voting with their feet. Treating people as mouths to feed is condescending. They are minds that create value.

head: Low fertility, pension traps, and India's north-south buffer
dek: Young people bring energy, risk-taking and dynamism. Ageing societies make better films but face more social problems.
more: Young people bring energy, risk-taking and dynamism. Ageing societies make better films but face more social problems. The deeper danger is badly designed state pension systems that go bankrupt when the ratio of young to old shifts. India has a temporary cushion: free migration from the north supports the ageing south. When the north and east age too, the gap with the south and west will become a much bigger problem. Amit adds that immigration is the ultimate fix for ageing.

head: How India lost garment exports to Bangladesh
dek: Only about 35% of working-age Indians are employed, one of the worst rates in the world.
more: Only about 35% of working-age Indians are employed, one of the worst rates in the world. With so many idle workers, wages should fall, but high minimum wages and dense labour laws make large workforces risky to employ, so firms stay small. Bangladesh avoided this, has lower wages, and attracts factories from all over the world. West Bengal's trade-union troubles add to the contrast. Garment work is low-end and labour-intensive, so this was India's game to lose.

head: Growth for poverty, market-failure tools for the environment
dek: India's PPP-adjusted income per person is about a tenth of America's, so degrowth is morally wrong here.
more: India's PPP-adjusted income per person is about a tenth of America's, so degrowth is morally wrong here. Amit calls it a classic luxury belief. Ajay separates the problems blamed on capitalism. Low wages and poor working conditions get fixed by growth: a poor factory is hot, a richer one adds fans, and a richer one still adds air conditioning. Pollution, carbon emissions and the loss of biodiversity are externalities. They call for taxes, Coasean bargains or state action, not for slower growth.

head: Funding should follow the child
dek: There is no single Indian education template. Kerala, Himachal and UP are on different paths.
more: There is no single Indian education template. Kerala, Himachal and UP are on different paths. Large parts of India have already moved to private schools, yet public money flows only to pupils in state schools. Ajay calls that mean and unfair, and argues the state's job is to route public money fairly, for example through vouchers.

head: The one price a market economy lets the central bank set
dek: Asked how a believer in prices for everything can accept a central bank fixing short-term interest rates, Ajay answers from first principles.
more: Asked how a believer in prices for everything can accept a central bank fixing short-term interest rates, Ajay answers from first principles. Money solves the double-coincidence-of-wants problem that makes barter hopeless at scale. In a fiat system, the only known way to create money requires the central bank to pick that short rate. Crypto offers a possible route to money without the state, which he takes seriously.

head: Organisations versus institutions
dek: In India, 'institution' is used too loosely. An institution behaves predictably and consistently no matter who is in charge, which brings it close to the rule of law.
more: In India, 'institution' is used too loosely. An institution behaves predictably and consistently no matter who is in charge, which brings it close to the rule of law. Hindustan Lever qualifies. Most Indian state bodies are personalised organisations. RBI had to have inflation targeting written into law before it could become an institution. Organisations should be analysed sceptically, using public choice theory: people respond to incentives and seek ease, money and power.

head: Why Indian infrastructure is slow: good delays and bad ones
dek: Some delay is healthy. Public debate about trade-offs and due process in land acquisition are what civilised countries do.
more: Some delay is healthy. Public debate about trade-offs and due process in land acquisition are what civilised countries do. The bad delay comes from incompetence, especially the government's weak contract management: market surveys, bid preparation, disputes and design changes. Private builders have improved a lot. A Bombay building that once took five to ten years now takes about two, and L&T builds airports abroad.

head: Reach and revenue
dek: Amit's framework for the creator economy. Some work builds reach, which builds credibility, and revenue eventually comes from somewhere.
more: Amit's framework for the creator economy. Some work builds reach, which builds credibility, and revenue eventually comes from somewhere. For him the podcast is reach and the writing course pays. Early students came because of his podcast and blog; now they come through word of mouth. That only works if you put your heart into everything, not just the paid parts.

head: Own your readers: start a newsletter
dek: Waiting for newspapers to publish you means writing rarely, within fixed word counts and news cycles, with your readers scattered.
more: Waiting for newspapers to publish you means writing rarely, within fixed word counts and news cycles, with your readers scattered. A newsletter lets you write more often, iterate toward excellence and choose your own form. Every reader who likes a piece subscribes, so you build a community you own. Amit gives this advice to any writer, especially in India, where outlets for long-form journalism are scarce.

head: There is no objectively great book, only the right book at the right time
dek: Ajay argues that we change over time, so a book's impact depends on when it reaches us.
more: Ajay argues that we change over time, so a book's impact depends on when it reaches us. The skill is to engage lightly with many books and keep a mental index of what each one covers, so the right one can land when you are ready. Amit agrees: reading a hundred books indiscriminately beats reading ten selected ones, and you should reach for a book, not your phone, when you're bored.

head: Your hours build your future self
dek: Amit's recipe for breadth: cut distractions with hard limits (his phone greys out Twitter and Instagram after half an hour each), read a lot, take notes, and file Twitter bookmarks into folders to revisit later.
more: Amit's recipe for breadth: cut distractions with hard limits (his phone greys out Twitter and Instagram after half an hour each), read a lot, take notes, and file Twitter bookmarks into folders to revisit later. Every hour either makes your future self smarter or duller. Willpower is a muscle that strengthens with use. He also defends rest: John Lennon's line that no time is wasted unless you feel it is wasted.

head: Purpose, community and adjacencies: the engine of a life of knowledge
dek: Ajay adds four points. Deliberately step back from mass culture like cricket, Bollywood and TV.
more: Ajay adds four points. Deliberately step back from mass culture like cricket, Bollywood and TV. Invest in your five, fifteen or fifty people, because conversation fuels learning. Avoid running on mid-level goals like getting a job or becoming famous. Treat everything as relevant instead of becoming a narrow specialist. Memory works by connection, so the more your knowledge links up, the more you retain, and you move into new fields one adjacent step at a time. His own purpose, which he can control even when the wider world goes wrong, is to build knowledge and community.

head: Learn India by looking out of the window
dek: India is not a subject you learn from a single textbook, the way you might learn physics.
more: India is not a subject you learn from a single textbook, the way you might learn physics. You are surrounded by the source material, so observe it with curiosity. Ajay's example is how the gender mix of flights changes with the time of day. Keep asking why things are the way they are.

head: Spontaneous order produces bad things too, and also fixes them
dek: A listener argues that patriarchy and caste also emerged through spontaneous order.
more: A listener argues that patriarchy and caste also emerged through spontaneous order. Amit agrees the term is descriptive, not a claim that the outcome is good. Ajay says not to expect utopia: global warming is a market failure that calls for state action, while social evils have to be changed from the bottom up by society itself. Amit adds that the world has become far better for women over a century, through changing values and markets, not through lazy calls to pass another law.

head: National development versus 'kinky' development
dek: Asked about intellectual dishonesty in economics, Amit draws on Lant Pritchett's distinction.
more: Asked about intellectual dishonesty in economics, Amit draws on Lant Pritchett's distinction. National development asks the hard, messy question of how to end poverty. 'Kinky' development tackles small questions with neat answers that advance careers but barely touch the problem. Amit names RCTs as the classic example.

head: Profit is philanthropy, within limits
dek: Amit says Nehru was wrong to tell J.R.D. Tata that profit is a dirty word.
more: Amit says Nehru was wrong to tell J.R.D. Tata that profit is a dirty word. In a competitive market, every trade leaves both sides better off, a 'double thank you'. Like individuals under Mill's harm principle, firms may do as they please unless they harm others, for example by colluding with the state. Ajay adds that in India, where a malfunctioning state lets firms legally impose costs on others, an ethical business is one that stays aware of the market failures it causes.

head: Freedom feels unintuitive
dek: Our minds were shaped in prehistoric times, so we think tribally and top-down, and our first reaction to behaviour we dislike is to ban it, even when it harms no one.
more: Our minds were shaped in prehistoric times, so we think tribally and top-down, and our first reaction to behaviour we dislike is to ban it, even when it harms no one. We see the world as zero-sum and miss that trade is positive-sum. That is why freedom is undervalued as a core value in India.

head: Market failure is rare; government failure is everywhere
dek: The one place Amit and Ajay part ways. Ajay often justifies state action by pointing to market failure.
more: The one place Amit and Ajay part ways. Ajay often justifies state action by pointing to market failure. Amit worries that people hear this as 'market failure is everywhere', when in fact it is rare and government failure is built into the state's incentives. Their values on freedom, autonomy and consent are fully aligned. Amit also notes that friendship rests on shared values, not identical views.
