head: Praise effort, not attributes
dek: Based on the Mueller and Dweck experiment, Amit's top parenting advice is to praise children for trying, not for being clever.
more: Based on the Mueller and Dweck experiment, Amit's top parenting advice is to praise children for trying, not for being clever. Children told they are smart came to feel entitled, eased off and even cheated. Amit thinks it happened to him: as a young man he was full of himself and didn't try hard enough.

head: Technology adds magnitude to whatever you already are
dek: Ajay's biggest change of mind. He used to believe Moore's Law, Unix and the internet would make the world better by spreading knowledge.
more: Ajay's biggest change of mind. He used to believe Moore's Law, Unix and the internet would make the world better by spreading knowledge. Now he sees them as amplifiers. Power makes you more of what you already are, so for some people technology helps and for others it makes things more toxic. Amit thinks the dark side is real but that technology, including AI, is still a large net positive.

head: Three behaviours to denormalise
dek: Ajay names three. First, careless noise: motorcycles, construction, speakerphones, wedding parties you can hear a kilometre away.
more: Ajay names three. First, careless noise: motorcycles, construction, speakerphones, wedding parties you can hear a kilometre away. Second, celebrity culture, which reveres people famous for being famous. Third, populist contempt for expertise: fifty years ago people knew less but respected knowledge. Amit adds a fourth: judge people's virtue by what they do, not what they say. He notes that feminists who have worked in the field for decades complain about younger activists who win status on Twitter through slogans without doing the work.

head: Mimetic desire, communities of choice, and rooted cosmopolitanism
dek: Before marrying or having children, ask whether you want it or just copy others (René Girard's mimetic desire).
more: Before marrying or having children, ask whether you want it or just copy others (René Girard's mimetic desire). Choose your community by values and interests, not by the circumstances of your birth. Amit's own regret, using a phrase from Sugata Srinivasaraju: he became cosmopolitan without staying rooted in his own culture, and not everything about where we come from is toxic. In the end, what matters is the people you collect.

head: Two traps to drop: competition and performance
dek: Ajay's answer to how a young person should find meaning. Stop trying to outdo classmates and neighbours, and stop living for social media or your résumé.
more: Ajay's answer to how a young person should find meaning. Stop trying to outdo classmates and neighbours, and stop living for social media or your résumé. Once both are gone, you are left doing what you actually value. He links this to his calm: someone who isn't competing or performing doesn't rattle easily.

head: Pick one, and find a master
dek: Many young people are paralysed by possibilities and end up doing nothing.
more: Many young people are paralysed by possibilities and end up doing nothing. Amit's cure is Steve Jobs's advice to Jony Ive: learn to say no even to things you love, then commit to one and let flow come. Ajay adds that apprenticing with a passionate master, not chasing credentials, teaches the craft and gives you energy.

head: Be the best you can be at time T
dek: Amit's new rule is to end every year fitter than the last and with more work done.
more: Amit's new rule is to end every year fitter than the last and with more work done. Ajay pushes back: ageing is certain, so that target sets you up for sadness. A better aim is to be the best version of yourself at each point in time, without raging against the limits age brings.

head: 1947 came at an unlucky moment
dek: Ajay's single wish from a genie: India's founding generation was formed between 1927 and 1947, when freedom was in retreat worldwide and war economies made full state mobilisation look normal.
more: Ajay's single wish from a genie: India's founding generation was formed between 1927 and 1947, when freedom was in retreat worldwide and war economies made full state mobilisation look normal. He would send Nehru, Gandhi, Rajagopalachari and others a bag of books. Ideally, the new state would have spent about 10% of GDP on basic public goods: rule of law, courts and a fair tax system. Amit doubts books alone would have changed minds formed over decades.

head: Caste: thousands of small populations, slowly dissolved by markets
dek: Caste endogamy, enforced for about 2,000 years, turned India into many small, closed gene pools.
more: Caste endogamy, enforced for about 2,000 years, turned India into many small, closed gene pools. That shrinks economic networks, limits mobility, and causes diseases found nowhere else. Amit's answer, echoing Chandra Bhan Prasad, whose two heroes are Babasaheb Ambedkar and Adam Smith, is growth and cities. When firms compete for workers and customers, discrimination becomes costly. The 1991 reforms freed many lower-caste people from old constraints, though Amit admits the fight is far from over.

head: Metcalfe's law and the rise of English
dek: Among the elite, English has become India's common language. By Metcalfe's law, a network's value grows with the square of its nodes, so every new English speaker makes the network more valuable, and parents know it.
more: Among the elite, English has become India's common language. By Metcalfe's law, a network's value grows with the square of its nodes, so every new English speaker makes the network more valuable, and parents know it. On the street, Hinglish has won. Against this flattening, the long tail of dialects survives online.

head: Universal suffrage is non-negotiable
dek: Asked whether voting could be limited to people who pass a test, Amit says no.
more: Asked whether voting could be limited to people who pass a test, Amit says no. Education doesn't guarantee good judgement, and whoever sets the bar decides who is left out. India gave women the vote before many rich nations did, and he counts universal suffrage among the things the republic got right.

head: After Ajay explains how dehydration makes the heart work harder, Amit
more: After Ajay explains how dehydration makes the heart work harder, Amit says: 'The Bengali in me is freaking delighted because I'm just thinking that I don't need to go running anymore. I can just stay away from water and walk around gently and the heart is still working for you.' Ajay replies: 'More challenging than walking around gently when well hydrated.'

head: Ajay's theory of cinema
more: Ajay's theory of cinema: 'the quality of movies in a country is basically proportional to the median age. So when India was a very young country, the quality of the movies was atrocious.' He later concludes that young people 'give us bad movies' but are great for society. Amit responds by recommending Wild Strawberries.

head: Ajay asks whether, once he has made Amit a master programmer, Amit would cry at a beautiful algorithm.
more: Ajay asks whether, once he has made Amit a master programmer, Amit would cry at a beautiful algorithm. Amit: 'Tears are coming to my eyes thinking of the amount of brute coercion that would be required to make me a master of computer programming.'

head: Ajay's rental tip in his rant against noise
more: Ajay's rental tip in his rant against noise: 'never rent a house that is close to a temple or a mosque because they'll just make so much noise.'

head: Ajay says power makes you more of what you already are. Amit cuts in…
more: Ajay says power makes you more of what you already are. Amit cuts in: 'Since power corrupts, then that means we're all inherently...'

head: Reading out a listener question from Vaishnav Vyas, who shoots the show
more: Reading out a listener question from Vaishnav Vyas, who shoots the show: 'Vaishnav Vyas. I wonder who that is.' Amit: 'I wonder who that is.'

head: Nehru's remark to J.R.D.
more: Nehru's remark to J.R.D. Tata, 'Do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word', which Amit says Nehru got completely wrong.

head: Amit quotes Prem Panicker, a friend and Seen and the Unseen guest, who said that with beat reporters gone, Indian journalism is…
more: Amit quotes Prem Panicker, a friend and Seen and the Unseen guest, who said that with beat reporters gone, Indian journalism is 'a mile wide and an inch deep'.
'No man can cross the same river twice': Ajay's line for why the same book can transform you at one age and fall flat at another.
'If you're not busy being born, you're busy dying': Amit applies it to the specialist who stops engaging with the world.

head: Annie Dillard
more: Annie Dillard: 'How you spend your days is, of course, how you spend your life.' Amit's answer to what his aim in life is.
printed: Drop the race, skip the show

head: Richard Bach
more: Richard Bach: 'What a caterpillar calls the end of the world, the master calls a butterfly.' Amit adds it after Ajay's point about apprenticing with a master.
'There will be no Ram Rajya': Ajay's reminder that no system, including spontaneous order, will deliver paradise.

head: Ajay loves Ramanujan as much as Einstein and Gandhi as much as Nehru, because for him
more: Ajay loves Ramanujan as much as Einstein and Gandhi as much as Nehru, because for him 'it's the ascent of man', not ethnicity or a line on a map. Amit notes the phrase comes from Bronowski's book and suggests 'the Ascent of Humans' instead.

head: Pushpesh Pant's Maps of Souring Agents
dek: Political borders are only one way to divide a landscape, and often not the most meaningful one.
more: Opening the episode, Amit recalls his Seen and the Unseen conversation with food writer Pushpesh Pant. Pant said he carries imagined maps in his head that have nothing to do with political boundaries. One is drawn by which souring agent a region cooks with: tamarind or kokum, and so on.
Political borders are only one way to divide a landscape, and often not the most meaningful one. Food, language and ecology draw their own lines, and those lines follow how people actually live.

head: Aanchal Malhotra and the Rant That Stopped Mid-Sentence
dek: Prejudice survives on abstractions such as 'Hindus', 'foreigners' and the nation.
more: While researching her book on Partition, Aanchal Malhotra sat with a Pakistani family that had lived through it. One family member began ranting that Hindus are this and Hindus are that, then suddenly remembered that Aanchal was sitting right there. The woman turned to her and reassured her that she wasn't included.

Prejudice survives on abstractions such as 'Hindus', 'foreigners' and the nation. It struggles when the abstraction becomes a real person sitting across the table. Amit's lesson is that the concrete human connection is real and the line on the map is the fiction.

head: The Border Town 300 Metres From Mexico
dek: The nation is an imagined community that is strongest far from the border.
more: The idea for this episode came alive for Ajay while he was reading human stories about the Texas–Mexico border. One interviewee lived in a border town with a Mexican city 300 metres away. They said the people across the line were their friends and neighbours. To them, the national debate about two countries and keeping migrants out felt like something that belonged to people far away.
The nation is an imagined community that is strongest far from the border. Up close, life follows the gravity law: your people are simply the people near you.

head: Border Haats: Rupees Only, Then Barter
dek: The urge to trade keeps finding ways around bureaucratic rules.
more: India has built eight border haats on the India–Bangladesh border, which Ajay calls pitifully few for a border that long. These are controlled marketplaces where people from both sides meet to trade. The rule was that all transactions must be in Indian rupees. The other side pointed out that they had no rupees, so the rule was relaxed to allow barter. Ajay also mentions the free movement zone on the Burma border near Nagaland and the easy India–Nepal border.

The urge to trade keeps finding ways around bureaucratic rules. Ajay calls these half-open arrangements a healthy step away from a 'Stalinist' total cutoff and wants them amplified, because both countries gain from trade.

head: Two Lahores at Three in the Morning
dek: A society's lived culture and its state ideology are separate layers, and the culture often has far more in common with the supposed enemy than the state admits.
more: In 2006 Amit spent a few weeks travelling through Pakistan to follow an Indian cricket tour, live-blogging as he went. At 3 AM in Lahore he posted a photo of kids playing cricket in the street. Food could be ordered from anywhere, and despite the Islamic Republic, alcohol and recreational drugs were easy to get. Apart from one or two stray incidents, he met warmth everywhere. He saw two layers sitting uneasily together: the effusive Punjabiyat of kite-flying festivals that Indians know well, and the shrill harshness of the Islamic Republic state. He also notes that well into the 1950s the India–Pakistan border was porous, and people crossed freely to visit relatives.

A society's lived culture and its state ideology are separate layers, and the culture often has far more in common with the supposed enemy than the state admits. The closed border we take for granted today is a recent normal.

head: Learning English by Copying Agota Kristof
dek: Copying a stylist's sentences is an old way to absorb how a language moves.
more: A participant in Amit's writing course told him that Hindi was her first language, she was only now learning English, and asked what she should do. Amit pointed her to Agota Kristof, who learned French as an adult and wrote in pared-down prose. She later told him she had sat with the Notebook Trilogy and copied its sentences out herself.
Copying a stylist's sentences is an old way to absorb how a language moves. Spare prose by someone who also came to the language late is an especially good model for a learner.

head: A Trade Deficit With a Babysitter
dek: Harford keeps paying his babysitter and she never pays him back, so he runs a 'deficit' with her that is plainly good for both of them.
more: Harford keeps paying his babysitter and she never pays him back, so he runs a 'deficit' with her that is plainly good for both of them. It is a neat demolition of trade-deficit panic.
Amit cites it when arguing that worry over trade deficits is misplaced nationalist rhetoric.

head: History of European Morals
dek: It is the source of the idea that the circle of people we grant moral consideration widens over history, from family to tribe to nation, and is destined to include all of humanity.
more: It is the source of the idea that the circle of people we grant moral consideration widens over history, from family to tribe to nation, and is destined to include all of humanity.
Amit introduces Lecky's 'expanding circle' as a moral framework he thinks about a lot.

head: The Expanding Circle
dek: Singer argued that the circle will expand beyond humans to include animals.
more: Singer argued that the circle will expand beyond humans to include animals.
Mentioned as Singer's extension of Lecky's thesis.

head: 1000 True Fans
dek: A creator doesn't need a mass audience, only a thousand true fans. Once geography stops mattering, those fans can be scattered anywhere in the world and still make the work viable.
more: A creator doesn't need a mass audience, only a thousand true fans. Once geography stops mattering, those fans can be scattered anywhere in the world and still make the work viable.
Amit invokes it while explaining how the internet freed him from communities of circumstance.

head: The Lives of Others
dek: He calls it a masterpiece and possibly one of the finest debut films he has seen.
more: He calls it a masterpiece and possibly one of the finest debut films he has seen. It brings out the full tragedy of what Germany's separation did to people.
Amit's mid-episode recommendation after the discussion of East and West Germany.

head: The Notebook Trilogy
dek: Kristof was a Hungarian writer who fled during the twentieth century, learned French as an adult and wrote these books in it.
more: Kristof was a Hungarian writer who fled during the twentieth century, learned French as an adult and wrote these books in it. Late-arriving writers like Nabokov can revel in florid language, but Kristof stripped both prose and narrative to the bone, with enormous power. It is set in a constantly shifting borderland during an unnamed war, with children trying to make sense of the world, so it fits the episode's theme too.
Amit's main end-of-episode recommendation.

head: The Gravity Model of Human Interaction
dek: Economists found that trade between two countries is roughly proportional to the product of their GDPs divided by the square of the distance between them, which mirrors Newton's law of gravitation.
more: Economists found that trade between two countries is roughly proportional to the product of their GDPs divided by the square of the distance between them, which mirrors Newton's law of gravitation. 'Distance' has to be read broadly: two English-speaking countries are effectively closer than an anglophone and a francophone one. Ajay generalises the model to all human interaction. Double the distance and interaction falls by four times, not two. This is the logic behind dense cities, and he suggests that even the length of a lift ride between floors changes how often neighbours meet.

head: Borders Hurt Most the People Who Live On Them
dek: Ajay's thought experiment is to zoom into a border such as the one between West Bengal and Bangladesh.
more: Ajay's thought experiment is to zoom into a border such as the one between West Bengal and Bangladesh. There is no demilitarised zone, just a field with a house on each side. The families talk, party, marry, trade and send their kids to play together. Draw a hard line through that and a person at the centre of the circle loses half their social network. Fifty or sixty kilometres away, the border barely matters. The cost of a border falls hardest on exactly the people who are each other's closest circle.

head: Abstract Categories vs Concrete Connection
dek: Lines on maps, nationalism and ideas of purity are abstractions. People eating, drinking, marrying and being friends with each other is the concrete reality.
more: Lines on maps, nationalism and ideas of purity are abstractions. People eating, drinking, marrying and being friends with each other is the concrete reality. Amit worries that the smartphone age keeps us lost in toxic abstractions that blind us to how much we already share, a shared culture he describes as a khichdi of food and dress.

head: Borders Can't Really Be Sealed
dek: Borders behave like fractals: the closer you look, the longer they get, so fencing and patrolling them properly is close to impossible.
more: Borders behave like fractals: the closer you look, the longer they get, so fencing and patrolling them properly is close to impossible. The incentive to trade forest honey for rice is strong, fences get wire-cut, and walls can be climbed or blown open. Ajay argues that sealing efforts, including Trump's wall, are largely political posturing. In practice India's borders with Nepal and Bangladesh are open, and he considers that a decent state of affairs.

head: The European Union as a Civilising Project
dek: Europe was the champion of nationalist cruelty: Germany invaded France in 1870, 1914 and 1940, and millions died.
more: Europe was the champion of nationalist cruelty: Germany invaded France in 1870, 1914 and 1940, and millions died. From the ashes of the Second World War came the EU. Today people drive across the French–German border with no papers and no checkpoints and work freely on the other side, as full participants rather than immigrants. Ajay sees this as the height of civilisation. The state keeps its legitimate job, such as protecting people from violence, but stays out of their natural dealings with each other. Amit sums it up as society coming first and the state being subsidiary.

head: Hybrid Cultures at the Edges
dek: Open borders produce blended cultures where people speak each other's languages.
more: Open borders produce blended cultures where people speak each other's languages. Ajay points to the hybrid Gujarati–Marathi culture on the Gujarat–Maharashtra border and the Marathi–Kannada culture on the Maharashtra–Karnataka border. At the French–German border the culture is neither French nor German but a mix of both. People at an edge identify with their neighbours, not with a distant capital.

head: Countries Don't Trade, People Do
dek: Fiscal deficits deserve worry; bilateral trade deficits do not. A trade deficit with China just means Indians bought more from Chinese people than the reverse, and every voluntary trade benefits both sides.
more: Fiscal deficits deserve worry; bilateral trade deficits do not. A trade deficit with China just means Indians bought more from Chinese people than the reverse, and every voluntary trade benefits both sides. Thinking about trade in terms of nation states is nationalist framing. If Amit wants to trade with someone in Canada or in Pune, it should be nobody's business.

head: South Asia's Missing Trade
dek: Globally, the gravity model predicts trade between countries reasonably well.
more: Globally, the gravity model predicts trade between countries reasonably well. Its biggest misses are in South Asia, where it predicts far more trade than actually happens between India and Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal or Sri Lanka, because nation states have distorted the natural flow. Amit calls this the seen and the unseen at work. The trade we see is small, and the unseen trade that politics prevented would have left people on both sides better off. That makes the region one of the world's great untapped sources of welfare.

head: The Expanding Circle — and Why It Isn't Guaranteed
dek: Lecky's thesis is that moral consideration starts with immediate family and widens to the tribe, the town and the nation, to women, to other races, and eventually to all of humanity.
more: Lecky's thesis is that moral consideration starts with immediate family and widens to the tribe, the town and the nation, to women, to other races, and eventually to all of humanity. Peter Singer argued it would extend to animals. Amit warns against taking this for granted, since recent decades have brought more polarisation and more 'othering'. Labels like 'foreigner' and 'another country', which quickly becomes 'an evil country', are barriers to the circle widening.

head: Communities of Circumstance vs Communities of Choice
dek: For most of history, your community was decided for you by geography, caste, class, school and workplace, so you mostly met people like yourself and had little room to grow.
more: For most of history, your community was decided for you by geography, caste, class, school and workplace, so you mostly met people like yourself and had little room to grow. The internet lets people form communities around shared interests, values and passions instead. For creators, this means a thousand true fans scattered across the world can sustain the work, and the long tail can thrive as mainstream media and entertainment crumble. Amit says that if he had been born twenty years earlier he would have been a much sadder person, with no audience and no growth.

head: The Tyranny of Distance Persists for Atoms and Hugs
dek: Ajay's caution is that distance has died only for electrons. Information moves almost free of cost, but physical goods like pots of honey and sacks of rice are heavy, so borders still matter for them.
more: Ajay's caution is that distance has died only for electrons. Information moves almost free of cost, but physical goods like pots of honey and sacks of rice are heavy, so borders still matter for them. Human relationships also need physical presence: sharing chai, touching. That keeps the physical movement of people across borders important.

head: Borders Can Break a People, If the State Goes All the Way
dek: Ajay offers a counterpoint to his own argument. Add electrified fences, dogs and machine guns and keep them up for fifty to seventy-five years, and one people can be turned into two.
more: Ajay offers a counterpoint to his own argument. Add electrified fences, dogs and machine guns and keep them up for fifty to seventy-five years, and one people can be turned into two. North and South Koreans today can barely talk to each other, and the North has no idea what to make of K-pop. East Germans still carry psychic wounds decades after the Wall fell. Culture is built from daily interaction, and cutting that interaction off for long enough changes it.

head: Divided Nations as Natural Experiments in Freedom
dek: Economics and political science rarely get controlled experiments. Korea and Germany came close: essentially the same people were split in two, and only one half was given freedom.
more: Economics and political science rarely get controlled experiments. Korea and Germany came close: essentially the same people were split in two, and only one half was given freedom. South Korea and West Germany show what free markets and individual liberty can do, while North Korea and East Germany show the tragic alternative.

head: Metaphorical Walls
dek: Walls can also be built with words. Rhetoric and ways of seeing the world can split neighbours living side by side, and Amit sees this happening in India and elsewhere.
more: Walls can also be built with words. Rhetoric and ways of seeing the world can split neighbours living side by side, and Amit sees this happening in India and elsewhere. Ajay asks whether these divisions can override the large gains from trade, friendship and love. Amit answers that the divisions grow sharper under scarcity, missing markets and an oppressive state, because the gains from trade need freedom to flourish.

head: Ajay's opening parable
more: Ajay's opening parable: the Lord holds an accountability session and asks every profession to prove it has added value. The economists include the gravity model on their résumé. The Lord replies, 'Gravity? But that's what the physicists do.' Ajay adds that economists 'all suffer from physics envy, just like me,' and that, 'being imperialists,' they then claimed a general gravity law in the affairs of men.

head: Ajay suggests that the number of floors between neighbours in a tall building changes how often they meet.
more: Ajay suggests that the number of floors between neighbours in a tall building changes how often they meet. Amit replies: 'The secretary of my building is a famous astrologer, apparently. We haven't had anything to do with each other. I don't know which floor he lives on.'

head: Amit tells Ajay he is…
more: Amit tells Ajay he is 'an economist who has a poet's heart.' Later, after Ajay's line about a border putting 'a line through their heart,' Amit adds: 'In this field right now, there is no border between economists and poets.'

head: Ajay to Indian nationalists
more: Ajay to Indian nationalists: 'you ain't seen anything yet. If you think of the ferocity, the hatred, the cruelty of nationalism, Europe gets gold medals galore.'

head: After explaining that fully militarised borders really can split one people into two, Ajay deadpans
more: After explaining that fully militarised borders really can split one people into two, Ajay deadpans: 'Not that I'm recommending this to anybody who's watching the show.'

head: Amit struggling with the director of The Lives of Others
more: Amit struggling with the director of The Lives of Others: 'Forgive me for the pronunciation. Florian, if you're watching, I'm sorry.'

head: John le Carré: Ajay says we imagine borders as a one-kilometre demilitarised zone with men holding machine guns
more: John le Carré: Ajay says we imagine borders as a one-kilometre demilitarised zone with men holding machine guns, 'like all of us have read in John le Carré novels.' In reality a border is usually just a field.

head: Amit interrupts Ajay's point about trade across porous borders to mention
more: Amit interrupts Ajay's point about trade across porous borders to mention 'a song from the film Border about this,' then says, 'Anyway, carry on.'

head: Ronald Reagan's
more: Ronald Reagan's 'tear down this wall' speech, which Amit sets against Donald Trump's promise to build a wall on the Mexican border: from one Republican president saying 'Tear down this wall' to another who wants to build one.

head: Paul Graham's
more: Paul Graham's 'it's better to be loved by a few than liked by many,' quoted by Amit alongside Kevin Kelly's thousand true fans.

head: Sport beyond borders: Amit says he cheers for the way Pep Guardiola's teams play
more: Sport beyond borders: Amit says he cheers for the way Pep Guardiola's teams play, 'from Barcelona to Manchester City,' without any tribal loyalty to those clubs, and for Levon Aronian when he plays chess.

head: Retiring at Nineteen Because He Couldn't Be Anand
dek: Loving something and making a career of it are separate decisions. In winner-take-all fields with thin markets, the sensible move can be to keep the passion and change the profession.
more: Amit played serious chess in college but stopped at nineteen, in the early '90s. His reasoning was simple: back then, unless you reached Vishy Anand's level, you could not make a living from the game. He left competitive play but kept following chess closely, and it remains one of the three sports he tracks most keenly.
Loving something and making a career of it are separate decisions. In winner-take-all fields with thin markets, the sensible move can be to keep the passion and change the profession.

head: Whoever Pays, Plays: The Early World Championship
dek: For decades, the 'best player in the world' was partly whoever could find sponsors, and champions wrote rules that favoured themselves.
more: Wilhelm Steinitz became the first widely accepted world champion in 1886 by beating Johannes Zukertort, who had finished three points ahead of him at a great London tournament in 1883. There was no governing body, so as Steinitz aged the rule became that any strong challenger who could raise the funding got a match. Siegbert Tarrasch had slightly better results but couldn't find the money. Emanuel Lasker could, beat Steinitz in the 1890s, and held the title for 27 years. Rubinstein and Nimzowitsch also failed to fund challenges. When Capablanca finally negotiated, Lasker demanded that the challenger win by two points, or the match would count as a draw and Lasker would keep the title. In 1920 Lasker offered to simply hand over the crown. Other players protested, so he played Capablanca in 1921 and lost.

For decades, the 'best player in the world' was partly whoever could find sponsors, and champions wrote rules that favoured themselves. The institutions around a contest quietly shape who gets remembered as the genius.

head: How Botvinnik's Rules Protected Botvinnik
dek: Rules that look equitable can be quietly designed to protect incumbents.
more: After Alekhine died in 1945, FIDE took over the world championship, and Mikhail Botvinnik won the tournament that launched the Soviet era. FIDE's qualifying cycle ran through national championships, zonals and interzonals, and it capped how many players any one country could send. That looked fair, since the Soviets held most of the top spots. Amit points out that Botvinnik was close to the rule-makers, and limiting Soviet entrants limited the number of strong compatriots who could threaten him. Two more rules helped him: a drawn match let the champion keep the title, and a deposed champion got an automatic rematch. Botvinnik kept his crown after drawing with Bronstein, and won it back from both Smyslov and Tal before the rematch rule was scrapped.
Rules that look equitable can be quietly designed to protect incumbents. It is always worth asking who wrote them.

head: Fischer's Path to the Crown, and His Vanishing Act
dek: Even a lone genius needed three peers to step aside. And once he reached the summit, his exit echoed the self-serving conditions of an earlier champion half a century before.
more: As a teenager, Bobby Fischer struggled in interzonals against strong Soviets like Keres, Geller and Tal. Later, as a rebel, he skipped the zonals and then decided he wanted to play after all. One by one, the top three American qualifiers gave up their places for him. He won two candidates matches 6-0 (one against Taimanov), destroyed former champion Petrosian, and beat Spassky in Reykjavik after forfeiting the first game. When Karpov qualified to challenge him in 1975, Fischer set bizarre conditions reminiscent of Lasker's, effectively refused to play, and disappeared from chess as a bearded recluse.
Even a lone genius needed three peers to step aside. And once he reached the summit, his exit echoed the self-serving conditions of an earlier champion half a century before.

head: The Soviet State Picks Its Champion
dek: Even a supposedly pure contest of intellect was bent by politics: the state preferred loyalty to brilliance.
more: The Soviet system chose its own national heroes. Anatoly Karpov, a positional genius, young and a loyal party man, was perfect for them. They were biased against Viktor Korchnoi even though he was also Soviet and played Karpov in several title matches. They didn't much want the young, aggressive, outspoken Garry Kasparov either. Karpov and Kasparov then played a match with no game limit, the winner being the first to six wins. Karpov pulled ahead, Kasparov clawed back, and then came draw after draw while both players' health collapsed, until the match was cancelled. They played again, Kasparov won, and he beat Karpov again later.
Even a supposedly pure contest of intellect was bent by politics: the state preferred loyalty to brilliance. Badly designed formats can also grind down the best players in the world.

head: Kasparov Breaks Away from FIDE
dek: A century after Steinitz, the world title still depended on who could fund a match.
more: In the 1990s a dispute over money for Kasparov's title match against Nigel Short led Kasparov to break with FIDE and form the PCA. He questioned where FIDE's legitimacy came from in the first place. The PCA staged the Short match, which Kasparov won easily. FIDE ran a rival cycle, but its champions, crowned in one-off tournaments, weren't seen as legitimate. The PCA cycle had its own farce: around 1997 Alexei Shirov beat Vladimir Kramnik for the right to challenge Kasparov, but nobody could raise the money for the match and the cycle fell apart. Kramnik emerged in the next cycle and beat Kasparov in the early 2000s. The titles were later reunified, and Vishy Anand went on to win the crown.
A century after Steinitz, the world title still depended on who could fund a match. Legitimacy in chess has always been contested and somewhat arbitrary.

head: 'They Teach Us This in Nursery'
dek: Systematised knowledge compounds. What one player agonises over for forty minutes, another simply recognises, so the Soviet edge was pedagogy rather than raw brainpower.
more: Devangshu Datta is a friend of both hosts who played seriously in the 1980s and knows Vishy Anand well. He told Amit what it was like to face Soviet players as a young man. He would sweat through the opening and middlegame, spend 40 minutes on a single move, and still lose. Afterwards the Soviet player would ask what he'd been calculating, because Soviet children were simply taught what to play in such formations. With no internet or databases, players elsewhere had to work it all out for themselves.
Systematised knowledge compounds. What one player agonises over for forty minutes, another simply recognises, so the Soviet edge was pedagogy rather than raw brainpower.

head: A Maruti 800 in a Formula One Race
dek: Anand's greatness is best measured against the infrastructure he didn't have.
more: Amit frames Vishy Anand's achievement against the training machine he lacked. Anand had brilliant tactical sense and learned everything else on the fly. Even so, in his teens he was beating the world's best and became one of the top players. Amit remembers the race, when he himself was a teenager, to become India's first grandmaster. Pravin Thipsay earned norms but got stuck, and Dibyendu Barua had famously beaten Korchnoi at age twelve, but the younger Anand got there first. Behind his gentlemanly image, Amit adds, Anand was a ferocious, aggressive player. India has since gone from zero grandmasters to 84.
Anand's greatness is best measured against the infrastructure he didn't have. Having succeeded without that system, he went on to inspire the generation that followed.

head: Turing's Chess Engine That Couldn't Run
dek: Ideas can arrive decades before the hardware that can run them. Computer chess began as pure theory waiting for the machines to exist.
more: In 1948 Alan Turing and David Champernowne designed a chess program called Turochamp. It was an algorithm on paper, and no computer of the time could actually process it, so it could never be tested. Turing died young and tragically, Champernowne abandoned the project, and it went nowhere. Only after Moore's Law kicked in did processing power catch up with such ideas.
Ideas can arrive decades before the hardware that can run them. Computer chess began as pure theory waiting for the machines to exist.

head: AlphaZero Replays Chess History in a Day
dek: Centuries of accumulated human wisdom were rediscovered and then surpassed in a day.
more: Inspired by AlphaGo, AlphaZero was given no human principles or heuristics. It simply played itself for 24 hours. In that time it retraced chess history: it fell for the French Defence, then decided it was slightly inferior, and it discovered the Berlin Defence, which Kramnik revived to beat Kasparov in the early 2000s. Then it went beyond human knowledge. In a match against Stockfish, the strongest brute-force engine, it calculated a tenth or a hundredth as much and still destroyed it, purely through principles it had found for itself.
Centuries of accumulated human wisdom were rediscovered and then surpassed in a day. Long-held principles in any field can be locally right but globally miscalibrated.
printed: Centuries of chess in a day

head: Correspondence Chess in the Engine Age
dek: 'Computers have solved it' is often an overstatement. Different machines have different blind spots, and judgement about which one to trust is still a human skill.
more: Correspondence chess is played by letter: you post a move, your opponent replies, and a game can take years. Devangshu Datta still competes in correspondence world championship cycles even though everyone has engines. It remains meaningful because engines like Stockfish and Houdini think differently and handle different kinds of positions differently, so human judgement in choosing between them still matters.
'Computers have solved it' is often an overstatement. Different machines have different blind spots, and judgement about which one to trust is still a human skill.

head: The Secret Army of Seconds
dek: At the top, preparation is itself intelligence warfare. Even who you hire leaks information.
more: Before a world championship match, each player studies for months with a team of 'seconds', and the members are kept secret. If you learn that your rival has hired someone known for a particular Sicilian line, you can work out their preparation. Peter Heine Nielsen was Anand's main second and later Carlsen's for a long time. He captained about four others whom most people never heard of, distilled all their analysis, and discussed the likely lines with Carlsen.
At the top, preparation is itself intelligence warfare. Even who you hire leaks information.

head: Carlsen Walks Away from the Throne
dek: When the best player in a field rejects its format, he exposes how stale that format has become.
more: Magnus Carlsen tired of the world championship ritual. The champion waits while challengers grind through a qualifying marathon, and then both players give up six months of their lives to dreary study. He told the chess world to find another way and asked why it should even be classical chess. He now plays more rapid, blitz and Chess960 (Fischer Random), where the pieces behind the pawns are randomised identically for both sides, wiping out opening theory while the principles still apply. Amit thinks his abdication devalued the title, since Carlsen is 20 to 40 rating points clear of the field. He predicts there will never be another dominant player like Magnus.
When the best player in a field rejects its format, he exposes how stale that format has become. Chess's centre of gravity may be shifting away from classical play.

head: Cheating: Phones in Toilets and the Niemann Affair
dek: Cheating and detection form an arms race. With the right safeguards and high reputational costs, it becomes manageable rather than existential.
more: Some players, including grandmasters, have been caught checking engine analysis on a phone during toilet breaks. Hans Niemann, a brash American who has admitted to cheating online, beat Carlsen over the board. Carlsen withdrew from the tournament, and Nakamura also alleged cheating, though nothing was proved. Ajay asked why anyone would cheat online at all, and Amit answered that prestige and rating count for a lot. Amit considers the threat real but overblown. Chess.com's detection algorithms are winning the arms race, and top events use metal detectors, closed playing halls and 20-minute broadcast delays.
Cheating and detection form an arms race. With the right safeguards and high reputational costs, it becomes manageable rather than existential.

head: Every Phone Beats the World Champion
dek: Compounding progress becomes invisible once it's mundane. We carry superhuman intelligence in our pockets and mostly waste it.
more: Ajay recalls being startled when their friend Ayush told him that mobile phones now play chess well enough that any of them can beat the world champion. Ajay had followed computing all along, but this still amazed him. It also saddened him to think about what people actually do with phones.
Compounding progress becomes invisible once it's mundane. We carry superhuman intelligence in our pockets and mostly waste it.

head: Gukesh: Human-Trained and Unshakeable
dek: In an engine-saturated era, deep grounding in principles can be an edge: you don't have to out-prepare opponents if you can take them out of their preparation and outplay them.
more: Before the Candidates, Carlsen ranked Gukesh fairly low. Amit broadly agreed, but saw Gukesh as high-variance because his rating had swung from a great Olympiad to a poor Grand Swiss, so he could win or finish near the bottom. Amit admits he was partly wrong. Gukesh showed remarkable stability, was never outplayed, and lost only once, to Firouzja, after a blunder in time trouble. One explanation: until he became a grandmaster, Gukesh didn't use computers and learned only from humans and books, which made him rock-solid on principles. His coach Grzegorz Gajewski, formerly Anand's second, marvels at how calm he is.

In an engine-saturated era, deep grounding in principles can be an edge: you don't have to out-prepare opponents if you can take them out of their preparation and outplay them. Amit's willingness to admit he misread the variance is a small lesson in itself.

head: The Philippine Accident That Made Anand
dek: Hubs of excellence often start with a lucky accident in one person's life.
more: Anand spent his formative years in the Philippines, where there was a regular chess programme on TV. He watched it and kept cracking its puzzle of the week. At one point the programme told him they had already sent him all the books and he should stop entering. Amit believes that exposure kept Anand ahead of his Indian contemporaries. Anand then became a cultural figure, and Tamil Nadu became the hub of Indian chess as parents began hoping their kid could be the next Anand.
Hubs of excellence often start with a lucky accident in one person's life. That person's success then makes the path visible and aspirational for thousands of others.

head: Aronian Enjoyed the Conversation
dek: Reframing competition as conversation lets you value the exchange of ideas even when you lose.
more: Levon Aronian, a player of deep culture and one of Amit's favourites, had just lost a game but came out smiling. Asked about it, he said he had really enjoyed the conversation. Amit loves the idea that every chess game is an exchange of competing ideas, and he sums up his own attitude as 'I play to play'.
Reframing competition as conversation lets you value the exchange of ideas even when you lose. The result matters, but the dialogue is the enduring reward.

head: How Haryana Got Its Women Wrestlers
dek: Clusters of excellence often come from historical accidents rather than regional virtue.
more: Haryana is notoriously bad for women, yet it produces many women wrestlers. In the late 1970s the wrestler Chandgi Ram wanted sons to train, as wrestlers did, but had a daughter, Sonika Kaliraman. When the Olympics opened up women's wrestling, he trained her. His assistant Mahavir Singh Phogat then trained his three daughters, whose story became the film Dangal, and a cluster of women wrestlers was born.
Clusters of excellence often come from historical accidents rather than regional virtue. One person's circumstance can coincide with a rule change and tip the first domino.

head: Women Who Insisted on Playing the Men
dek: Choosing the harder field on principle both signals and builds belief that women can compete at the very top.
more: Hou Yifan refuses on principle to play the women's world championship and wants to compete only against men. Alexandra Goryachkina won the women's world junior championship in her mid-teens and then declared she would play in the open category instead. She did so for the next three years while still a junior, finishing mid-pack. Amit admires both for blazing a path.
Choosing the harder field on principle both signals and builds belief that women can compete at the very top. Amit's message to parents is to treat daughters' potential as equal.

head: Briefly No. 1 at Atomic Chess
dek: Variants restore the beginner's thrill of reasoning from first principles.
more: Amit plays bullet and blitz purely for the dopamine, under an anonymous handle, and unlike in his professional poker days he makes no effort to improve. His real intellectual stimulation now comes from chess.com variants like Atomic Chess and Fog of War, where the usual heuristics and pattern recognition stop working. In a couple of them he was briefly number one on chess.com before falling off the charts.
Variants restore the beginner's thrill of reasoning from first principles. Nobody has an advantage the first time a game is new, which makes them a playground for fresh thinking.

head: How Life Imitates Chess
dek: Amit considers Kasparov a great mind, and hopes he succeeds in 'the larger game that he is playing'.
more: Amit considers Kasparov a great mind, and hopes he succeeds in 'the larger game that he is playing'.
Recalled while praising Kasparov's introduction to Game Changer. Kasparov is described as a hero of both hosts for more than his chess.

head: Hikaru Nakamura's channel
dek: He plays bullet game after game for five or six hours while explaining his thinking, which is fantastic and instructive.
more: He plays bullet game after game for five or six hours while explaining his thinking, which is fantastic and instructive. Amit thinks streaming may even have revitalised Nakamura's own love for chess before his strong showings in the last two Candidates.
Streaming by one of the world's best players, which took off during Covid.

head: Atomic Chess and Fog of War
dek: Your usual heuristics, instincts and even pattern recognition stop working, so you have to work out how to play from first principles.
more: Your usual heuristics, instincts and even pattern recognition stop working, so you have to work out how to play from first principles. That gives you a fresh intellectual thrill on a level playing field.
Chess variants on chess.com that Amit plays. He was briefly number one in a couple of them.

head: I Play to Play
dek: It captures the idea that the game itself, not just winning, is the reward.
more: It captures the idea that the game itself, not just winning, is the reward.
Linked to Amit's line 'I play to play' in the discussion of Aronian's 'I really enjoyed the conversation'.

head: Experts See Patterns, Not More Moves
dek: Adriaan de Groot's study (which Amit dates to 1942) found that elite players don't calculate further ahead than amateurs.
more: Adriaan de Groot's study (which Amit dates to 1942) found that elite players don't calculate further ahead than amateurs. Through vast experience they read whole formations at a glance. Playing a lot builds this, but the Soviet school went further and formalised pattern knowledge into a pedagogy taught from first principles from childhood, while players elsewhere had to discover it game by game. Ajay recalls the classic chess-book phrase that captures this: 'as every Russian schoolboy knows'.

head: Chess Glory Doesn't Prove a Great Nation, but How It's Built Matters
dek: The Soviets went after chess because Lenin, Trotsky and others played it and saw it as pure human intelligence, so dominance would prove the system's superiority.
more: The Soviets went after chess because Lenin, Trotsky and others played it and saw it as pure human intelligence, so dominance would prove the system's superiority. Ajay's counter is that the USSR ruled chess from Botvinnik to Kasparov and still collapsed as a broken regime. Even so, he respects India's rise more because it wasn't state-manufactured. The Soviets filtered millions of children with heavy incentives, whereas India's grandmasters bubbled up organically from families and communities while the state did nothing.

head: The Tank vs the Climbing Robot
dek: Early computer chess was brute force: Minimax plus ever more processing power.
more: Early computer chess was brute force: Minimax plus ever more processing power. In his introduction to Game Changer, Kasparov explains why this left programmers and players cold. The dream was an elegant ascent, and what arrived was raw power. Demis Hassabis notes that even superhuman engines like early Stockfish and Houdini were stuffed with thousands of human-made heuristics. Reaching the summit is not the same as understanding the mountain.

head: Computers Diversified Chess Instead of Flattening It
dek: Many expected universal access to engines to homogenise chess, with everyone playing the same computer moves.
more: Many expected universal access to engines to homogenise chess, with everyone playing the same computer moves. The opposite happened. The real homogeniser had been the Soviet school, where everyone trained on the same principles and played alike. Engines supplied concrete exceptions to those principles, such as moves rejected by rule of thumb that turn out to win. Once players began learning from computers in the 2000s, they developed distinct individual styles.

head: AlphaZero Rewrote the Price of Material
dek: Learning only by playing itself, AlphaZero showed that humans had been overvaluing material relative to initiative.
more: Learning only by playing itself, AlphaZero showed that humans had been overvaluing material relative to initiative. Ideas once dismissed as reckless, like pushing an a- or h-pawn up the flank, can create real possibilities. Ajay highlights the change in how compensation is understood. Nineteenth-century sacrifices were precise combinations repaid within a few moves, whereas AlphaZero gives up material for position and waits ten or fifteen moves for a structural payoff. Amit adds that humans had positional sacrifices before, notably Petrosian's exchange sacrifice, but AlphaZero pushed the idea much further.

head: Chess Isn't Solved, and the Human Connection Matters
dek: Asked whether engines have killed chess, Amit offers an analogy: even if AI could perfectly mimic an Amit–Ajay conversation, Ajay wouldn't stop talking to him.
more: Asked whether engines have killed chess, Amit offers an analogy: even if AI could perfectly mimic an Amit–Ajay conversation, Ajay wouldn't stop talking to him. Chess is also far from solved. Endgame tablebases give perfect answers only with seven or fewer pieces, engines disagree with one another, and there is no single memorisable line that draws every game. Players like Carlsen deliberately steer toward 'playable' positions where both sides must think for themselves.

head: Play Moves That Are Only Bad Against Computers
dek: Elite preparation covers the best engine lines, so the edge comes from deviating.
more: Elite preparation covers the best engine lines, so the edge comes from deviating. A move that is slightly suboptimal against perfect play can be excellent against a human whose preparation doesn't cover it. The refutation may be too counterintuitive to find over the board, and the surprise breeds second-guessing. Changing the move order alone can force an opponent to start thinking and wondering about hidden preparation. Surprise can be worth more than optimality.

head: Volume Is the New Coach
dek: Online multi-tabling let poker players accumulate in thirty months the number of hands an old-school player like Doyle Brunson took thirty years to play, and youth took over the game.
more: Online multi-tabling let poker players accumulate in thirty months the number of hands an old-school player like Doyle Brunson took thirty years to play, and youth took over the game. Chess followed the same path. Top players are online constantly, and young players sharpen their skills through enormous numbers of games. Bigger samples mean faster pattern recognition, which, together with engine study, is why teenagers now reach the elite.

head: Making the Invisible Visible Turns Games into Spectator Sports
dek: Poker exploded when broadcasts showed players' hole cards. Chess has done something similar.
more: Poker exploded when broadcasts showed players' hole cards. Chess has done something similar. Engine evaluation bars and grandmaster commentators reveal what is really happening, some events show audiences both players' heart rates (which the players can't see), and confession booths let players narrate their thinking mid-game. Opening up the inner state of a cerebral game lets newcomers follow the drama.

head: Testing a Pure-Nature Theory of Grandmasters
dek: Ajay plays out a deliberately extreme model in which each person's maximum Elo is fixed at conception.
more: Ajay plays out a deliberately extreme model in which each person's maximum Elo is fixed at conception. If that were true, grandmaster counts should simply track population. Because the grandmaster title is an objective threshold rather than a relative ranking, you can build cross-country panel data and test this. The data reject it. India has about 84 grandmasters with roughly 1.44 billion people, the US has 101 with roughly 330 million, and Russia has 236 with about 140 million, while populous Bangladesh and Pakistan have little chess success. Most of the explanation must lie in nurture, culture and community.

head: Nature Gives You Knobs, Nurture Turns Them
dek: Talent only shows up when a series of filters is passed.
more: Talent only shows up when a series of filters is passed. Their friend Ayush's rule of thumb is that a family needs about $5,000 per head, or roughly 10–20 lakh rupees a year for a family of five, to afford the 'silliness' of chess. Ajay adds that it helps to have chess in the household, and that a child must start before age ten with a computer, internet and coaching. Parents also need to be able to travel to tournaments, sometimes giving up work, rather than pushing the child toward the JEE. Amit argues that India's 1.4 billion is a misleading number. Most Indians live in conditions like sub-Saharan Africa, and perhaps only 10–20 million live where children get open-ended leisure time, which is where non-instrumental mastery grows.

head: Clusters Help, but Online Networks May Matter More
dek: Ajay wonders whether Mylapur works like an urban agglomeration.
more: Ajay wonders whether Mylapur works like an urban agglomeration. There, coaches, clubs and articulate masters keep a research conversation going in concepts and language, beyond what an engine can compute, and families might relocate to be part of it. Amit agrees that hubs help but says they are neither necessary nor sufficient. Vidit Gujrathi is from Nagpur, Erigaisi from Hyderabad, and Firouzja emerged from Iran without any chess renaissance there. In his view the bigger force is the network effect of online play, since conversations happen through games, supplemented by training camps such as those Anand now runs. His advice to small-town parents is not to relocate but to support the child and let her immerse herself online.

head: Clusters Are Born from Accidents, So 'India' Is the Wrong Unit
dek: Amit is uneasy with treating 'India' as one unit.
more: Amit is uneasy with treating 'India' as one unit. Excellence comes in small clusters, often seeded by accident: Anand's Philippine childhood made Tamil Nadu a chess hub, and Chandgi Ram's lack of a son created Haryana's women wrestlers. India's chess boom is really one cluster of educated, aspirational families with computers, supportive parents and Anand as a hero. Ajay agrees and predicts that India's path to excellence will run through many such little cultures, of physicists, podcasters and others, each of which can 'explode'.

head: 84 Grandmasters Don't Make 84 Poets
dek: Ajay lays out a spectrum of cognitive and cultural complexity. Cricket and the IPL need a simpler package of skills, and chess requires somewhat more culture and community.
more: Ajay lays out a spectrum of cognitive and cultural complexity. Cricket and the IPL need a simpler package of skills, and chess requires somewhat more culture and community. Leadership, innovation, particle physics and literature need a far richer mix of books, debate, general intelligence and organisational capital. India's services-export success mostly fills narrow roles where a global firm supplies the culture and strategy, and the worker can 'shut up and turn the wrench'. Few Indian organisations act as talent factories, as Ajay sees NIPFP and XKDR Forum doing. Success at the simpler end shouldn't be mistaken for having reached the richer one.

head: Listen to the Lunchroom
dek: Ajay's test of an organisation's intellectual health is to overhear its lunch conversations.
more: Ajay's test of an organisation's intellectual health is to overhear its lunch conversations. Where work is just a job, lunch is a break and people discuss Bollywood. As capability grows and the work becomes a passion, ideas take over the lunch table. He has watched this happen in lunchrooms at the Ministry of Finance and at NIPFP.

head: Women in Chess: Structure and Nurture, Not Destiny
dek: Chess has no men's category, only an open category plus a women's category created because far fewer women played.
more: Chess has no men's category, only an open category plus a women's category created because far fewer women played. The distinction matters mainly for world championships. Judit Polgar reached the world top ten. Nigel Short argued that men show higher variance, producing more geniuses and more imbeciles, but Amit declines that debate. He points to nurture instead: Indian parents are far likelier to take a son around the tournament circuit than a daughter. Unlike poker, whose drunk, sexist tables drive women away, chess offers a civilised environment and no reason women can't rise to the top.

head: After Ajay's lavish introduction, Amit opens
more: After Ajay's lavish introduction, Amit opens with: 'Ajay, I have told you in the past, you have to undersell and overdeliver. Now you have oversold and we will definitely underdeliver.'

head: Amit describes Anand
more: Amit describes Anand as 'an aggressive, ferocious player' in the past tense, catches himself, and corrects course: 'And is, in fact... I apologize, Vishy, if you're watching this.'

head: Ajay on the household conditions chess requires: enough income for…
more: Ajay on the household conditions chess requires: enough income for 'the silliness', since 'this is a pure waste of time and life to play chess'. Then comes the moment parents get hooked: 'it's so cool that my little seven-year-old snotty little brat actually beats me in chess.'

Ajay's 'trivial debating point' against treating chess as proof of national greatness: the USSR dominated the game and collapsed anyway, and 'if there is one thing that Russia is good at, it is at exporting all its talent.'

head: Ajay contrasts India's organic chess rise with the Soviet programme, a project where
more: Ajay contrasts India's organic chess rise with the Soviet programme, a project where 'some hormones were injected and some creature was produced'.

head: Before revealing his lunchroom test of an organisation's quality, Ajay issues a mock warning to his own colleagues
more: Before revealing his lunchroom test of an organisation's quality, Ajay issues a mock warning to his own colleagues: 'If you are in XKDR Forum, now please shut up.'

head: Ajay's favourite chess-book phrase
more: Ajay's favourite chess-book phrase, 'as every Russian schoolboy knows', used to preface a deep insight as though it were nursery knowledge, for example: 'the king is an attacking piece'.

head: Kasparov's verdict on Carlsen
more: Kasparov's verdict on Carlsen: he combines the best of Fischer and Karpov, Fischer's dynamic creativity with Karpov's boa-constrictor squeeze. Carlsen takes equal positions and squeezes for 40 or 50 moves until 'you lose, and you don't know how you lost'.

head: Ken Thompson
more: Ken Thompson, 'another of your heroes' as Amit tells Ajay, built Belle, the world computer chess champion of the early 1980s at roughly 2200 Elo, which Amit admits is 'stronger than me today'.

head: Clean-bowling Rahul Dravid in office cricket
dek: Amit offers this as his entire 'action' record in cricket. It sets up the episode's premise: he is a spectator-analyst, not a practitioner, and is cheerfully honest about it.
more: When Amit was managing editor at Cricinfo, Rahul Dravid visited the office. The staff played office cricket with a ball halfway between a squeezy ball and a plastic ball, which you could spin forwards or backwards to make it zip through the air. Amit persuaded Dravid to bat. His first ball was a wide, and then he clean-bowled Dravid with the next two. Dravid called him Shoaib Akhtar, refused to play on and threw the bat away.
Amit offers this as his entire 'action' record in cricket. It sets up the episode's premise: he is a spectator-analyst, not a practitioner, and is cheerfully honest about it.

head: The cycling fan who can't ride a cycle
dek: Deep appreciation of a sport can be entirely intellectual. Ajay's line 'you don't have to be a hen to know about eggs' becomes the license for the whole episode.
more: Ajay asks Amit for his 'thought to action ratio' in each sport. For poker it is high, since he played professionally for years. For cycling it is literally zero, because he never learned to ride. He grew up privileged (his father was in the IAS and there was always a car), and his working life in Bombay was local trains and buses until he bought a car.
Deep appreciation of a sport can be entirely intellectual. Ajay's line 'you don't have to be a hen to know about eggs' becomes the license for the whole episode.

head: Oscar Pereiro, the accidental Tour de France champion
dek: Letting a 'harmless' breakaway go is a calculated risk. When every rival is focused on one threat, the person nobody is watching can walk off with the prize, and luck can finish the job.
more: In a mid-2000s Tour (Amit doesn't recall the exact year), the favourites let a breakaway go that included Oscar Pereiro, who was not considered a serious contender. He gained enough time to lead for a while. The other contenders were busy fighting Floyd Landis and ignored him, so Pereiro finished second overall. Then Landis was disqualified for drug use, and Pereiro became Tour de France champion.
Letting a 'harmless' breakaway go is a calculated risk. When every rival is focused on one threat, the person nobody is watching can walk off with the prize, and luck can finish the job.

head: Tour of Flanders 2022: Pogačar stalls himself out of the race
dek: Cat-and-mouse games have a hidden cost. While two rivals optimise against each other, third parties can catch up, and the cleverest move becomes self-defeating.
more: Tadej Pogačar (about 65 kg, a superb climber) attacked on the hills. Only Mathieu van der Poel (about 75 kg, a far better sprinter) managed to stay with him. Pogačar knew he could only win the sprint by coming out of Van der Poel's slipstream, so he refused to lead. Both slowed almost to a standstill, eyeing each other. Meanwhile three chasers, cooperating because they had nothing to lose, caught up. Van der Poel won, Dylan van Baarle was second, Valentin Madouas third, and Pogačar, the dominant rider all day, finished fourth.
Cat-and-mouse games have a hidden cost. While two rivals optimise against each other, third parties can catch up, and the cleverest move becomes self-defeating.

head: Paris-Roubaix: Van Aert trapped by a two-man team
dek: Two teammates against one rival is a near-checkmate. Whatever the lone rider does, he spends his energy for someone else's benefit.
more: In last year's Paris-Roubaix, three riders were heading for the finish: the great rivals Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert, plus Van der Poel's teammate Jasper Philipsen, a strong sprinter. Van der Poel attacked. Van Aert also punctured, so he had to chase with Philipsen sitting on his wheel. If he caught Van der Poel, Philipsen would beat him in the sprint; if he didn't, Van der Poel would win. Van der Poel won, Philipsen came out of Van Aert's slipstream to take second, and Van Aert was third.
Two teammates against one rival is a near-checkmate. Whatever the lone rider does, he spends his energy for someone else's benefit.

head: The 2023 Vuelta: the decoy who won
dek: Team roles are fixed in theory but dynamic in practice. When the plan succeeds too well, loyalty, ambition and public sentiment collide, and the result can break a team.
more: Jumbo-Visma had both Primož Roglič (who had won that year's Giro and three straight Vueltas) and Jonas Vingegaard (who had just won the Tour). They sent their star mountain domestique Sepp Kuss into a breakaway. The idea was to put him in the leader's jersey so that Remco Evenepoel's team would exhaust itself chasing him. Instead Evenepoel collapsed. Kuss now led with Roglič and Vingegaard second and third. Roglič wanted to race for the win, but there was outrage on social media: after years of helping others win, Kuss deserved a gift. Vingegaard was fine with that. The team let Kuss win and finished 1-2-3, and an angry Roglič left for Bora-Hansgrohe.
Team roles are fixed in theory but dynamic in practice. When the plan succeeds too well, loyalty, ambition and public sentiment collide, and the result can break a team.
printed: The domestique who kept the jersey

head: Armstrong to Landis: 'Run like you stole something'
dek: Leaders do reward their domestiques, but only when the race allows it.
more: In what Amit recalls as Lance Armstrong's last Tour win, his domestique Floyd Landis paced him up the final mountain. Only four riders were left: Landis, Armstrong, Jan Ullrich and (Amit thinks) Ivan Basso. Having secured his time gains, Armstrong wanted Landis to take the stage and told him to 'run like you stole something.' The rivals wouldn't let Landis get away, so Armstrong said 'Fuck it, if he won't win, I will win' and took the stage himself.
Leaders do reward their domestiques, but only when the race allows it. The gift is conditional on tactics.

head: Tour de France 2022: Pogačar against two Jumbo-Visma leaders
dek: Even the strongest individual is in a bad spot against a coordinated pair.
more: On a brutal mountain stage over the Col du Galibier to the Col du Granon, Jumbo-Visma put Wout van Aert in the breakaway so he could drop back and help their two leaders, Roglič and Vingegaard. Rivals didn't know Roglič was injured from an earlier crash. The front group thinned to Pogačar, Roglič, Vingegaard and a struggling Geraint Thomas. The two Jumbo riders attacked Pogačar in turn, and he had to close every gap. Then Pogačar launched his own attack. He failed to drop Vingegaard and burned so much energy that Vingegaard took about three minutes on the final climb and went on to win the Tour.
Even the strongest individual is in a bad spot against a coordinated pair. Some call Pogačar's attack stupid; Amit also floats the theory that he simply 'bonked', meaning he ran out of calories.

head: How Carapaz won Olympic gold
dek: Being the clear favourite makes you everyone's target. Weaker rivals can tacitly coordinate to tire out the strongest rider, and the winner may simply be the attacker nobody bothered to follow.
more: Wout van Aert is so powerful that if he reaches the finish with a small group, he wins. So without any explicit collusion, rivals attack one after another and wait for him to chase, because chasing would cost them their own 'bullet.' The same used to happen to Peter Sagan. In the last Olympic road race, Van Aert, tired of chasing, let Richard Carapaz go. Nobody else chased either, and Carapaz took gold. Van Aert got silver and Pogačar bronze.
Being the clear favourite makes you everyone's target. Weaker rivals can tacitly coordinate to tire out the strongest rider, and the winner may simply be the attacker nobody bothered to follow.

head: Evenepoel, Van Aert and the Belgian team
dek: Team obligations work in both directions. The same rules that once forced Evenepoel to sacrifice himself later stopped Van Aert from chasing him down.
more: At world championships and Olympics, riders race for national teams. A young Remco Evenepoel was told to work for Belgian favourite Wout van Aert. Van Aert didn't have the legs that day, and Evenepoel was furious, feeling he could have won. The next year Evenepoel broke away alone. Van Aert couldn't chase his own teammate and had to sit with the others, and Evenepoel won the world title.
Team obligations work in both directions. The same rules that once forced Evenepoel to sacrifice himself later stopped Van Aert from chasing him down.

head: Roglič: from skiing crash to cycling great
dek: A forced pivot, made late, can still lead to greatness when the underlying drive is intact.
more: As a Slovenian teenager, Primož Roglič had a horrific crash at a junior skiing world championship, around 2007–08. Amit still rewatches the footage. Roglič skied again but realised he wouldn't be among the world's best, perhaps because the injury cost him a developmental phase, perhaps for mental reasons. He loved sport, so he took up cycling relatively late. Some say he's not a great bike handler because of that, yet he became one of the great riders of his generation and won the Vuelta three times.
A forced pivot, made late, can still lead to greatness when the underlying drive is intact.
printed: From the piste to the peloton

head: Tour 2020: the time trial that wasn't a collapse
dek: The popular story that 'Roglič collapsed' is false. He finished fifth out of about 150.
more: In the Covid year, Roglič led the Tour going into the decisive second-last stage, a time trial. He was the current Olympic time trial champion and hadn't bothered attacking his 21-year-old compatriot Pogačar, who was about 30 seconds behind. As the last rider to start, Roglič heard radio updates that Pogačar had caught up with and then passed his time. On the final climb he looked close to tears, and his teammates, including Van Aert, knew the dream was over. Amit tweeted live that it was a seminal moment in world sport. Afterwards the 30-year-old Roglič hugged and congratulated Pogačar.
The popular story that 'Roglič collapsed' is false. He finished fifth out of about 150. Sometimes a loser didn't choke; the winner was simply extraordinary.

head: The doping arms race and the erased decade
dek: When everyone in a competitive system cheats, punishing one villain makes little sense.
more: Amit recalls that Greg LeMond, or possibly another top rider, took a few months off around the late 1980s and on returning could barely keep up because the pace had become absurdly high. Through the 1990s cycling became a drugs arms race, with EPO giving altitude-training-like effects. Tour winners from 1996 onwards (Riis, Ullrich, Pantani, Armstrong for seven years, then Landis, who was disqualified) were all on drugs. Rather than hand titles to runners-up, the authorities declared that the results of a whole period, including all seven of Armstrong's wins, don't count.
When everyone in a competitive system cheats, punishing one villain makes little sense. The honest fix is to void the era, and an outsider's return can be what reveals the new normal.

head: Van Aert's sacrifice, undone by a crash
dek: Elite preparation is now highly optimised, but it only improves your odds.
more: Wout van Aert, also a cyclocross champion, skipped this year's cyclocross world championship so he could spend weeks at altitude preparing for the cobbled classics, the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix. As the cobbled monuments arrived, he crashed badly through no fault of his own and was out for weeks. Similarly, a crash at Liège-Bastogne-Liège last year disrupted Pogačar's preparation, and he couldn't truly compete at the Tour.
Elite preparation is now highly optimised, but it only improves your odds. One wheel touch can wipe out months of sacrifice.

head: Chris Horner's YouTube channel
dek: After every stage of a major race, Horner breaks down what happened and calls teams 'knuckleheads' for wasted energy or pointless breakaways.
more: After every stage of a major race, Horner breaks down what happened and calls teams 'knuckleheads' for wasted energy or pointless breakaways. Along the way he teaches real tactical and strategic thinking, and Amit says it makes you a better thinker.
Amit's main recommendation. Horner was a top rider himself and became the oldest man to win a Grand Tour when he took the Vuelta at 41.

head: The BIGGEST Day of My Career (Chris Horner on his Vuelta a España win)
dek: A first-hand account of how the oldest Grand Tour winner pulled it off.
more: A first-hand account of how the oldest Grand Tour winner pulled it off.
Amit mentions Horner has videos on how he won the Vuelta at 41 and links them in the show notes.

head: The Lanterne Rouge Cycling Podcast
dek: Hour-long deep dives after races and great previews from two young, deeply involved enthusiasts.
more: Hour-long deep dives after races and great previews from two young, deeply involved enthusiasts. Amit says they add a different dimension from Chris Horner.
The second YouTube channel Amit follows. He believes Patrick also consults on strategy for Visma | Lease a Bike.

dek: A ready-made primer before watching the 2024 Tour, which started the weekend this episode was released.
more: A ready-made primer before watching the 2024 Tour, which started the weekend this episode was released.
Amit guessed their Tour preview would already be up and promised to link it.

dek: A primer for anyone who wants to start watching the Tour.
more: A primer for anyone who wants to start watching the Tour.
Show-notes link. The episode was timed to the start of the 2024 Tour.

head: You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs
dek: Ajay asks Amit for his 'thought to action ratio' in each sport, and for cycling it is zero.
more: Ajay asks Amit for his 'thought to action ratio' in each sport, and for cycling it is zero. Ajay's line, which Amit credits to him, is that practice isn't required for understanding, and being inside the game can even get in the way of seeing it whole.

head: A test of body and character
dek: Unlike Formula One, where the car matters enormously, road cycling is one rider's body against another's on nearly identical machines.
more: Unlike Formula One, where the car matters enormously, road cycling is one rider's body against another's on nearly identical machines. Over a three-week Grand Tour the toll shows on riders' faces, and the race becomes a test of character as much as fitness.

head: Slipstream: the physics that makes cycling a team sport
dek: The lead rider cuts through the air and leaves a low-pressure pocket behind him.
more: The lead rider cuts through the air and leaves a low-pressure pocket behind him. A rider tucked in that pocket saves about 30% of his effort. Almost every tactic follows from this: domestiques shielding leaders, breakaways rotating turns, sprinters hiding until the last moment, and time trials that space riders out so no one can draft.

head: Weight is destiny: climbers, punchers, sprinters, domestiques
dek: Body weight, which a rider can control only partly, sorts riders into roles.
more: Body weight, which a rider can control only partly, sorts riders into roles. Grand Tour winners are light climbers (around 61–65 kg) because power-to-weight dominates on long mountains. Heavier punchers (around 75–78 kg, such as Van Aert, Van der Poel and Sagan) have explosive power for flats, cobbles and short steep climbs, so they suit one-day classics. Sprinters save everything for the last stretch. Riders who don't excel at any of these often become domestiques, who work for the team's stars. Lance Armstrong was a heavier exception, but that was the doping era.

head: Different jerseys, different games on the same road
dek: In a Grand Tour the general classification (the Tour's yellow jersey) goes to the lowest total time over three weeks.
more: In a Grand Tour the general classification (the Tour's yellow jersey) goes to the lowest total time over three weeks. Separate competitions reward sprint points (green jersey), mountain points and the best young rider. A sprinter happily loses an hour on a mountain day because he is only chasing points, so riders around him may be playing completely different games.

head: The breakaway–peloton game
dek: Early in a race a small group breaks away from the main bunch (the peloton).
more: Early in a race a small group breaks away from the main bunch (the peloton). Teams that want to win the stage don't catch it immediately, or another breakaway forms and drains them. They hold the gap at around three minutes and time the catch for the closing kilometres. The peloton has an edge because a domestique told to ride flat out for only 20 km can go harder than breakaway riders who must last 100 km. Sprint teams sometimes play chicken, each refusing to chase so the other burns its riders, and the breakaway survives.

head: Cooperate, then defect
dek: Strangers in a breakaway share the work silently, each taking a turn in the wind, because a lone rider can't stay away.
