more: Strangers in a breakaway share the work silently, each taking a turn in the wind, because a lone rider can't stay away. Sitting in without working is 'desperately uncool', unless there is a tactical reason such as your team leader chasing behind. Near the finish the cooperation collapses: all else equal, the rider in front loses the sprint, so everyone slows and watches everyone else.

head: Limited bullets: why two beats one
dek: Every rider has only so many hard efforts, or 'bullets', in a race. When someone attacks, the others wait for someone else to chase so they can sit on his wheel.
more: Every rider has only so many hard efforts, or 'bullets', in a race. When someone attacks, the others wait for someone else to chase so they can sit on his wheel. Two teammates can take turns attacking a lone rival, who must close every gap until he is empty. The same logic lets rivals wear down a dominant favourite without ever talking to each other.

head: Controlling a race with relentless pace (the Sky Train)
dek: US Postal under Armstrong, and later Team Sky for Chris Froome, used domestiques to set a pace so high that nobody could attack.
more: US Postal under Armstrong, and later Team Sky for Chris Froome, used domestiques to set a pace so high that nobody could attack. Rouleurs drove the flat sections, then mountain domestiques took over one by one until the peloton was strung out in a single line. Rivals lost their teammates while the team leader still had helpers.

head: Strategy before the race, tactics during it, run from the team car
dek: Plans are set before a race, but a directeur sportif in the team car, with a TV feed and live power data, radios instructions as it unfolds.
more: Plans are set before a race, but a directeur sportif in the team car, with a TV feed and live power data, radios instructions as it unfolds. That includes reminding riders to eat, because 'bonking' (running out of calories) can end a campaign. Domestiques ferry food and drinks from the car to their leaders.

head: The aggregation of marginal gains
dek: Dave Brailsford took British cycling from the bottom of the heap to Team Sky winning the Tour seven times in eight years.
more: Dave Brailsford took British cycling from the bottom of the heap to Team Sky winning the Tour seven times in eight years. There was no single breakthrough. Instead the team looked for 1% improvements in diet, training plans, riding position, helmet aerodynamics and more, and let them add up. Amit teaches the idea to his writing students. Brailsford is now working to turn Manchester United around.

head: How doping was cleaned up: better testing and team incentives
dek: From the late 1990s, doping was an arms race in which you had to dope just to compete.
more: From the late 1990s, doping was an arms race in which you had to dope just to compete. It ended because testing technology caught up and because teams, which suffer when a rider is caught, now monitor their own riders. Amit argues today's sport is by and large clean, and that today's high speeds come from better training science, such as altitude camps, so fans can watch in good faith.

head: Crashes are the great equaliser
dek: One touched wheel can bring down a whole group, as when Vingegaard, Roglič and Evenepoel all crashed together at this year's Tour of the Basque Country weeks before the Tour.
more: One touched wheel can bring down a whole group, as when Vingegaard, Roglič and Evenepoel all crashed together at this year's Tour of the Basque Country weeks before the Tour. Teams try to keep their leaders near the front of the peloton to reduce the risk, but luck remains a huge factor.

head: We follow sport for its stories
dek: The physical spectacle draws us in, but rivalries and redemption arcs keep us watching.
more: The physical spectacle draws us in, but rivalries and redemption arcs keep us watching. Examples include Roglič's unfinished quest for the Tour, Pogačar against Vingegaard, the Belgian tension between Evenepoel and Van Aert, and the Van Aert versus Van der Poel rivalry that began in cyclocross.

head: Ajay's opening jab
more: Ajay's opening jab: 'Amit, tell me, you look like a guy who would be very fast on a cycle.' Amit: 'This is really a low blow. And the Bengali in me does not appreciate this low blow.'

head: Amit on learning to drive late
more: Amit on learning to drive late: 'I am now the best driver in Bombay. Because driving in Bombay is not about driving, it is about Bombay. But that is a subject for another episode.'

head: Right after the hen-and-eggs line about knowing a sport without playing it, the episode is christened
more: Right after the hen-and-eggs line about knowing a sport without playing it, the episode is christened: 'Welcome to a scrambled eggs episode on cycling.'

head: A running gag casts Ajay as a…
more: A running gag casts Ajay as a 'card-carrying physicist' and aeronautical engineer, invoked as Amit explains the physics of the slipstream.

head: Amit explaining a breakaway
more: Amit explaining a breakaway: 'In a sense, when it comes to mainstream economics, you are a breakaway, and the peloton is far, far, far behind you.'

head: Ajay claims childhood cycling glory: riding up a slope and round a curve with both hands off. Amit: had he been French or Belgian
more: Ajay claims childhood cycling glory: riding up a slope and round a curve with both hands off. Amit: had he been French or Belgian, 'the loss of economics could have been the gain of cycling.' Ajay: 'This is why economic development matters.'

head: Amit's VPN advisory
more: Amit's VPN advisory: 'Young men watching this for porn, okay? Do not do that. It is sinful, save your energy for studying economics and physics and aeronautical engineering.'
Cycling's vocabulary is largely French because the French were pioneers of European cycling: domestique, directeur sportif, puncheur, and rouleurs (who 'just roll through these flat stages').

head: Amit compares cycling's clean-up to cricket
more: Amit compares cycling's clean-up to cricket: 'Just as there is no more match fixing in cricket, I would like to believe, after a dark age, it's a similar thing in cycling.'

head: Alpe d'Huez, the iconic Tour de France mountaintop finish
more: Alpe d'Huez, the iconic Tour de France mountaintop finish that 'really separates the great climbers from the not so great climbers.'

head: 2.5 Million Applicants for 368 Peon Jobs
dek: Mass unemployment and a skills shortage exist side by side because degrees are being handed out without the abilities they claim to certify.
more: Citing a statistic he got from Karthik Muralidharan, Amit describes a government advertisement for 368 peon posts that drew about two and a half million applicants, roughly 250 of them PhDs. That works out to around 6,500 applicants per job (his figures, 'something to that effect'). He sets this beside entrepreneur friends who say they can't find skilled people, which is why job-hopping is rampant in Bangalore.

Mass unemployment and a skills shortage exist side by side because degrees are being handed out without the abilities they claim to certify. The gap isn't only vocational. Many graduates can't really read, understand text, or make sense of the world.
printed: The peon jobs PhDs queued for

head: Heights in Bombay's Local Trains
dek: Deprivation in childhood leaves marks. Stunted height is visible.
more: After moving to Bombay in the 1990s, Amit commuted by local train. He found it heartbreaking that first-class passengers were, on average, significantly taller than those in second class. A lifetime of different nutrition had written social class onto people's bodies.
Deprivation in childhood leaves marks. Stunted height is visible. The stunting that bad education does to minds is just as real but unseen, so we rarely reckon with it.
printed: First class, and a head taller

head: India's PISA Experiment That Backfired
dek: A state that controls money and power but avoids accountability would rather not know than measure.
more: India's education bureaucracy long resisted the OECD's PISA test. Under international pressure it allowed a limited round, and it handpicked Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu in the hope of looking good. Their 15-year-olds instead ranked among the worst in the world. Ajay recalls that the bureaucracy then ran away from the project and stopped measuring, and he isn't sure much of the micro data was ever released.
A state that controls money and power but avoids accountability would rather not know than measure. The cover-up tells you what the system is really optimising for.

head: The Upper-Tail Bump: India's Hidden Talent Pool
dek: India tells two stories at once: a tiny core at the top that is outrageously good, and a mainline that is horrible.
more: India's PISA score distribution has a small bump at the top, meaning an unusual number of 15-year-olds with remarkably high scores. Someone took that percentage and multiplied it by India's cohort of 15-year-olds. Ajay can't recall whether it was him or Lant Pritchett. The answer was that India has perhaps the second- or third-largest plausible scientific and engineering workforce in the world.
India tells two stories at once: a tiny core at the top that is outrageously good, and a mainline that is horrible. Pointing to the IITs says nothing about the typical child.

head: When Even an IAS Family Couldn't Afford to Fly
dek: Where India allowed markets, access exploded. In education, which matters most, it didn't.
more: Amit, son of an IAS officer, can't recall taking a domestic flight as a child in the 1980s. It was too expensive even for his family, who flew only on a foreign holiday every three years or so. Getting a telephone line took five or six years. After the 1991 reforms let markets into airlines and telecom, both became cheap and widely accessible, and state operators like MTNL and BSNL became essentially irrelevant.
Where India allowed markets, access exploded. In education, which matters most, it didn't. Amit's plea is not to privatise everything, only to stop constraining private players and see what happens.

head: Karthik vs Lant: Does Education Cause Development?
dek: Smart experts genuinely disagree on whether schooling drives growth. Amit's own reversal shows a deeply held, intuitive belief giving way to evidence.
more: Amit once assumed that a country educates its people first and develops afterwards. When first told otherwise he resisted, until the data changed his mind more than a decade ago. On his show, Karthik Muralidharan had implied that development follows education. Lant Pritchett, in a later episode, said there is no evidence for that and that causality runs the other way. After the Lant episode, Amit's friend Murali Neelakantan tweeted that it might be a two-way virtuous cycle. Amit says the cold hard data backs Lant.
Smart experts genuinely disagree on whether schooling drives growth. Amit's own reversal shows a deeply held, intuitive belief giving way to evidence.

head: Nehru in a Time Machine
dek: India ran the 'educate first, prosperity follows' experiment for decades.
more: Nehru's generation saw Britain, with near-universal schooling and Oxford and Cambridge, as the model. At independence India's female literacy was about 6%. Ajay imagines bringing Nehru to 2024 and telling him literacy is now around 75%. Nehru would assume India must be at 60–70% of UK per capita GDP. We would have to hang our heads and admit India is a lower-middle-income country at about a tenth of the global frontier.
India ran the 'educate first, prosperity follows' experiment for decades. The literacy arrived and the prosperity didn't, which is a homegrown version of Pritchett's finding.

head: Heckman's Starving Grad Students
dek: Much of a child's cognitive development comes from hearing rich, complex adult conversation.
more: Ajay recalls an interview in which James Heckman, he thinks only half kidding, said the world has two problems. Graduate students are starving for money, and children in disadvantaged families lack exposure to ideas. Pay the grad students to sit with the kids and talk to them about ideas and the world, and you solve both.

Much of a child's cognitive development comes from hearing rich, complex adult conversation. That is cheap to provide and enormously valuable, yet affluent homes now drown it out with mass media and test prep.

head: Josh Felman's Theory of Jewish Achievement
dek: When a culture makes every ordinary member regularly synthesise ideas and say them out loud, it builds intellectual capability at scale.
more: Ajay asked Josh Felman why Jews have such outsized intellectual achievements, including the most Nobel laureates per capita. The standard answer is selection. Repeated pogroms meant people with portable human capital fled and flourished, while those holding land and physical businesses didn't. Felman offered another answer. In the religious gathering, held at home rather than in a formal institution, it isn't a priest who speaks. Each person takes a turn delivering a 10–15 minute oration that weaves the religious text into their own life.
When a culture makes every ordinary member regularly synthesise ideas and say them out loud, it builds intellectual capability at scale. Book clubs and learning circles can recreate this.

head: Takshashila's Thursday Show-and-Tell
dek: Rituals of sharing what you learned turn learning into something social and multidisciplinary.
more: Amit recalls that he and Ajay first had meaningful interactions at a book club run by a friend. Ajay's story reminds him of a weekly Thursday ritual at the Takshashila Institution in Bangalore. One by one, researchers such as Nitin Pai plug their laptops into the projector and present what they learned that week, often outside their own field.
Rituals of sharing what you learned turn learning into something social and multidisciplinary. 'Everything is everything' becomes an institutional habit.

head: The IIT Director and the JEE
dek: Reforms that look impossible from inside often have a working precedent next door.
more: Ajay asked a wise, good director of IIT Tirupati how the JEE's role in IIT admissions could be reduced. The director said it would be a nightmare, hard to do, and would bring litigation. Ajay pointed out that the IIMs had already done it by adding interviews and group discussions and reducing the weight of the exam.
Reforms that look impossible from inside often have a working precedent next door. The real obstacle is a centralised mindset, not feasibility.

head: Why a Former Cricket Writer Skips the IPL
dek: Deep learning needs protected time. Every shallow distraction has an opportunity cost, so Amit advises young people to immerse in subjects instead of flitting between them.
more: Amit was a cricket journalist for years and followed the game deeply. He has stopped following it completely. Asked why he doesn't watch the IPL, he said it would eat his evenings for a month and a half.
Deep learning needs protected time. Every shallow distraction has an opportunity cost, so Amit advises young people to immerse in subjects instead of flitting between them.

head: The Collected Stories of Lydia Davis
dek: Fiction lets you enter the minds of others and live their lives. Davis is 'one of the great modern writers', and many of her stories are a paragraph or less.
more: Fiction lets you enter the minds of others and live their lives. Davis is 'one of the great modern writers', and many of her stories are a paragraph or less. Literature keeps you learning without feeling like you are in learning mode.
Amit's end-of-episode pick, which he calls both unrelated and related to education.

head: Essays
dek: Davis writing about her own craft and literature, 'and much more besides'.
more: Davis writing about her own craft and literature, 'and much more besides'.
Recommended as a companion to her collected stories.

head: To Kill a Mockingbird
dek: Growing up, he read it as a masterpiece about the minds of a parent and a child facing bigotry he assumed was in the past.
more: Growing up, he read it as a masterpiece about the minds of a parent and a child facing bigotry he assumed was in the past. Now he finds it a hundred times more relevant, because history never ended and that darkness is still around us.
Ajay's pick, following Amit's lead in recommending literature.

head: The Beautiful Tree
dek: A 'wonderful book' on budget private schools serving the poor, grounded in work among poor families and how they actually choose.
more: A 'wonderful book' on budget private schools serving the poor, grounded in work among poor families and how they actually choose. 'Do read that as well.'
Mentioned in the chapter on private enterprise in education.

head: Private Education Is Good for the Poor
dek: Their Hyderabad study found many slum dwellers chose to pay for budget private schools over free government ones.
more: Their Hyderabad study found many slum dwellers chose to pay for budget private schools over free government ones.
Cited to challenge the idea that private schools are only for the rich.

head: How Much Does Free Education Cost?
dek: A Delhi survey of households earning under Rs 5,000 a month found the same thing: a large share send their kids to budget private schools.
more: A Delhi survey of households earning under Rs 5,000 a month found the same thing: a large share send their kids to budget private schools.
Cited alongside the Tooley–Dixon study.

head: Where Has All the Education Gone?
dek: Ajay calls it one of the most important papers in the history of development economics.
more: Ajay calls it one of the most important papers in the history of development economics. It is a cold cross-country statistical analysis finding that expanding schooling produced essentially zero growth.
Ajay introduces this 2001 paper in the chapter on education and development. Amit later urges listeners to read it in full and follow its citations.

head: The first PISA results for India: The end of the beginning
dek: Pritchett on what India's first PISA results revealed.
more: Pritchett on what India's first PISA results revealed.
Linked with Ajay's account of India's limited PISA round in Himachal Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

head: PISA
dek: It tests a household-based random sample of 15-year-olds, not just those in school, on applying science and maths rather than rote memory.
more: It tests a household-based random sample of 15-year-olds, not just those in school, on applying science and maths rather than rote memory. You need a rough sense of its scores to take part in any serious education debate.
Ajay presents it as one of the two numbers anyone in the field must know.

head: James Heckman's work on early childhood / The Heckman Equation
dek: Hard-nosed return-on-investment evidence that the biggest payoffs come from interventions at ages 0–3 or 0–5, especially for disadvantaged children.
more: Hard-nosed return-on-investment evidence that the biggest payoffs come from interventions at ages 0–3 or 0–5, especially for disadvantaged children. That includes cognitive basics, social-emotional learning, and what kids overhear.
Ajay introduces Heckman's research in the early-childhood chapter. Amit says it shook him when he first heard of it.

head: The Seen and the Unseen
dek: He suggests every parent consider it 'a soundtrack of the child's life'.
more: He suggests every parent consider it 'a soundtrack of the child's life'. The serious point is that children gain a lot from overhearing rich adult conversations about ideas.
Half in jest, Ajay proposes it to Heckman as an experiment for children aged 0–5 and 5–17.

head: Education in India (Episode 77, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: An earlier long-form conversation with Amit Chandra on the state of Indian education.
more: An earlier long-form conversation with Amit Chandra on the state of Indian education.
One of the many education episodes Amit says he has done and links in the show notes.

head: We Are Brains, Not Stomachs (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
dek: A growing population is good because people are brains, not stomachs. That only pays off if those brains are trained to think, and India isn't doing that.
more: A growing population is good because people are brains, not stomachs. That only pays off if those brains are trained to think, and India isn't doing that.
Amit invokes its idea while discussing India's potential.

head: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
dek: It sets out the policy pipeline, where change starts with information and research.
more: It sets out the policy pipeline, where change starts with information and research. That is where Ajay thinks philanthropy should put its money.
Ajay links it when explaining why Aser mattered so much.

head: Fund Schooling, Not Schools
dek: The core voucher idea: public money should follow the child to whatever school the parent chooses.
more: The core voucher idea: public money should follow the child to whatever school the parent chooses.
A 2007 column whose title names this episode's third chapter.

head: It is immoral to have children. Here's why
dek: A provocative column, which Amit says is not the standard antinatalist argument.
more: A provocative column, which Amit says is not the standard antinatalist argument. It backs his point that having children is a huge responsibility that goes beyond material comfort and a school seat.
Mentioned while arguing that too many people jump into parenthood unprepared.

head: Not More, But Better
dek: The near-universal consensus says more money, teachers and schools.
more: The near-universal consensus says more money, teachers and schools. Yet Aser shows 57% of class five children can't read a class two text, and among 14–18-year-olds one in four can't read a class two text and half can't do class-three division. Karthik Muralidharan's findings show that spending on buildings, on hiring 'better' teachers, or on student inputs doesn't move outcomes. The real problem is design and incentives: a teacher works hard until made permanent, then stops showing up.

head: Data First: Juxtapose Spend (PPE) Against Outcomes (Aser/PISA)
dek: Every debate on education spending should put two numbers side by side.
more: Every debate on education spending should put two numbers side by side. One is per pupil expense: government education spending divided by the number of children actually in government schools. The other is an outcome measure like Aser or PISA. PPE has doubled and quadrupled while outcomes have stagnated or fallen. Measurement is where change starts; without it you thrash around for decades.

head: Most of India Is Sub-Saharan Africa
dek: Elites look around their cafés and see startups and potential. Amit's point is that most Indians live in conditions comparable to sub-Saharan Africa.
more: Elites look around their cafés and see startups and potential. Amit's point is that most Indians live in conditions comparable to sub-Saharan Africa. The people the elite think of as service staff are the actual middle class, and only a tiny sliver sits above them. Add a broken education system and the country's potential is being wasted on a huge scale.

head: The Misunderstood Profit Motive
dek: Nehru-era hostility to profit led to rules banning for-profit schools, piles of licences (Amit recalls something like 42 to open a school in Delhi), and utopian regulations on playground size and toilet ratios.
more: Nehru-era hostility to profit led to rules banning for-profit schools, piles of licences (Amit recalls something like 42 to open a school in Delhi), and utopian regulations on playground size and toilet ratios. These choke supply. In competitive markets profit comes from serving people well. Airlines and telecom were opened up after 1991 and access boomed; education never was.

head: Parents Vote With Their Feet
dek: Poor parents choose to pay perhaps Rs 4,000 a year for a budget private school over a free government school that spends around Rs 10,000 per pupil.
more: Poor parents choose to pay perhaps Rs 4,000 a year for a budget private school over a free government school that spends around Rs 10,000 per pupil. Studies suggest private schools get similar or slightly better outcomes at about a third of the cost, and parents can hold them accountable. Parents also weigh things researchers miss, such as how safely a child can get to school.

head: Fund Schooling, Not Schools (Vouchers)
dek: An idea first proposed by Milton Friedman. Keep public spending, but give the per-child amount to parents as a voucher they can cash at any school, government or private.
more: An idea first proposed by Milton Friedman. Keep public spending, but give the per-child amount to parents as a voucher they can cash at any school, government or private. Schools then have to compete for students, and absentee teachers face consequences. Amit says not to let the perfect be the enemy of the good: if the money will be spent anyway, let parents direct it.
printed: Let the money follow the child

head: Symmetric Spending Per Child (Article 14)
dek: Ajay takes a milder but sharper position: leave government schools as they are, but stop abandoning children who leave them.
more: Ajay takes a milder but sharper position: leave government schools as they are, but stop abandoning children who leave them. Today the state spends on a child only if they stay in the government system. Fairness, and the Article 14 idea of equality, demands equal spending per child in India, not per child enrolled in public schools.

head: English as India's Master Network
dek: Parents pushed for English-medium education even when government schools insisted on vernacular first languages.
more: Parents pushed for English-medium education even when government schools insisted on vernacular first languages. They understood that English is the link language and the ticket to progress. Educationists note the switch to an English-speaking household takes about three generations and hurts learning along the way. Ajay still sees private schools as the exit valve that let families start that journey.

head: Schooling Doesn't Cause Development (Pritchett's Paradox)
dek: Across countries and decades, more schooling produced essentially no growth.
more: Across countries and decades, more schooling produced essentially no growth. Haiti today has France's 1970 education numbers but none of its prosperity. Ajay offers three rival explanations. First, implementation failed, which fits India but not the global data. Second, education is mostly signalling, a Louis Vuitton bag that sorts people rather than teaching them. Third, we've defined education wrongly. The truth may be some of each. Counting learning outcomes instead of inputs explains part of the paradox, but not all of it.

head: The Industrial School Rewards Only Conscientiousness
dek: Age-sorted classrooms, fixed curricula and rote procedures are a 19th-century design meant to produce factory workers and babus.
more: Age-sorted classrooms, fixed curricula and rote procedures are a 19th-century design meant to produce factory workers and babus. Of the five big personality traits, this system measures and nurtures only conscientiousness, so obedient children thrive. What actually matters is flexible general intelligence: being able to look at rain falling on a roof and apply quadratic equations to a real question. In Ajay's words, education should kindle a fire, not fill a pail.

head: Learning How to Learn
dek: Amit argues the defining skill of the next twenty or thirty years is learning how to learn, which means thinking independently.
more: Amit argues the defining skill of the next twenty or thirty years is learning how to learn, which means thinking independently. His schooling taught him nothing; life taught him numeracy, probabilistic thinking and clear writing. He and Ajay are considering a 'Life Lessons' course to teach such things to people of any age.

head: The Heckman Window and the Power of Overhearing
dek: James Heckman's return-on-investment research points to early childhood, ages 0–3 or 0–5, especially for disadvantaged children, as the best place to intervene.
more: James Heckman's return-on-investment research points to early childhood, ages 0–3 or 0–5, especially for disadvantaged children, as the best place to intervene. The basics of reading and arithmetic matter, and so do social-emotional learning and regulating behaviour. Talking with a child and making eye contact matters, but a lot of learning comes from overhearing adults discuss ideas with a rich vocabulary. Amit adds that what is missed in those years can't be made up later.

head: The Family Is Where Education Really Happens
dek: Denmark has a rich welfare state and the US a thin one, yet family background predicts outcomes equally strongly in both.
more: Denmark has a rich welfare state and the US a thin one, yet family background predicts outcomes equally strongly in both. Knowledge moves through families almost without anyone noticing, through conversations, books that actually get discussed, and informal apprenticeships. Amit calls this an extra layer of privilege beyond money. Populist sneering at 'nepo babies' misses this, and schools can't replace it. Heckman's interventions therefore aim to improve the home itself.

head: Age Heterogeneity
dek: Ajay argues there's little a 10-year-old can teach another 10-year-old.
more: Ajay argues there's little a 10-year-old can teach another 10-year-old. In hunter-gatherer bands, children of mixed ages roamed as a pack, played, and gradually joined the real work. Adults benefit the same way. Ajay, at 58, counts a 25-year-old among the most important people in his life. Groups of the same age share one view of the world, which limits everyone in them.

head: School Is Daycare: Don't Confuse It With Education
dek: Amit warns parents not to treat school as daycare and consider their job done.
more: Amit warns parents not to treat school as daycare and consider their job done. Ajay goes further and says parents would be better off seeing that school really is just daycare. Real knowledge-building happens elsewhere: at home, through books, conversation and attention, and without piling on pressure.

head: The Integrated Mind vs the Technician
dek: Some people are engineers at work and medieval in the rest of their lives, or they design chips all day and then watch Netflix.
more: Some people are engineers at work and medieval in the rest of their lives, or they design chips all day and then watch Netflix. Ajay calls that a hole in the heart. A full person reads about everything and brings general intelligence to every part of life, from making dahi to starting a business to relationships.

head: The Ladder of Changing Your Mind
dek: At the bottom are people who never change their minds. The attainable minimum is to dig in during the argument but shift your views 5–10% after a week of reflection, which Ajay calls gold.
more: At the bottom are people who never change their minds. The attainable minimum is to dig in during the argument but shift your views 5–10% after a week of reflection, which Ajay calls gold. Higher up is thanking the person who changed your mind. Higher still is saying 'you're right' in the moment, and the greatest statement of all is 'I was wrong.' Surround yourself with smart people and serious book clubs where everyone has actually read the chapter.

head: Credentialism's Two Victims
dek: The first victim is yourself: 'I'm from IIT, so I've arrived.' The second is how you judge others, dismissing people without degrees, as lazy HR departments do.
more: The first victim is yourself: 'I'm from IIT, so I've arrived.' The second is how you judge others, dismissing people without degrees, as lazy HR departments do. Amit adds a nuance. Signalling and networks are real, so take the IIT track if it's rational. Just don't be single-track. Go deep into subjects instead of flirting with them.

head: Let a Thousand Flowers Bloom
dek: Policy people should be far more skeptical of education spending and of competitive exams like UPSC, JEE and the boards.
more: Policy people should be far more skeptical of education spending and of competitive exams like UPSC, JEE and the boards. They should also resist central control from New Delhi, which makes every IIT and IIM the same, much like public sector banks. Each institution should have local autonomy and its own vision. Educators, too, should doubt their paradigm and stop measuring themselves by how many students cleared the IIT JEE.

head: Philanthropy Belongs at the Start of the Policy Pipeline
dek: Ajay says funding Aser was the most effective use of philanthropic capital ever, because data and research change how thinking people see a problem.
more: Ajay says funding Aser was the most effective use of philanthropic capital ever, because data and research change how thinking people see a problem. A poor use of money is putting an ERP system on a broken government paradigm or lending staff to a joint secretary for small incremental fixes. Philanthropies also suffer a principal-agent problem: staff want visible wins they can claim credit for.

head: Bias for Action: Good for Individuals, Bad for States
dek: For a creator, acting first is how you learn. Amit admits the show's first episodes weren't great, but episode 50 beats episode one and episode 250 will beat episode 50.
more: For a creator, acting first is how you learn. Amit admits the show's first episodes weren't great, but episode 50 beats episode one and episode 250 will beat episode 50. The state, though, wields coercive power over millions, so Ajay wants it slow, careful and doing less. Act in haste, repent at leisure.

head: Right after Ajay explains the…
more: Right after Ajay explains the 'upper tail bump' in India's PISA distribution, Amit says: 'You're looking very hot today. Can I give you an upper tail bump?'

head: Ajay introducing per pupil expense
more: Ajay introducing per pupil expense: 'The second number I would like to introduce for this field is called PPE. And no, that does not mean personal protective equipment.'
Ajay's 'orthodox ex-Ministry of Finance' view of education spending: 'the counterfactual that I would always ask is we would have done better by taking all that money and paying down debt.'

head: Ajay's plan for government schools
more: Ajay's plan for government schools: turn them into canteens. Kids study at private schools, a bell rings at noon, they run to the government school for the midday meal, and at 12:45 another bell sends them running back. 'So this is a great harmonious coexistence.'

head: Amit recalling the joke from the era of long waiting lists
more: Amit recalling the joke from the era of long waiting lists: 'when your daughter is born you book a scooter so that for her marriage it'll be ready.'

head: Ajay on education as pure signalling: it's a Louis Vuitton bag, or
more: Ajay on education as pure signalling: it's a Louis Vuitton bag, or 'the up and coming North Indian business person who buys a used Mercedes to try to signal that she is so successful.'

head: Ajay on age-segregated schooling: being
more: Ajay on age-segregated schooling: being 'herded into a factory where you are a ten year old with other dumb ten year olds just like yourself.'

head: As rain falls during the outdoor shoot, Amit
more: As rain falls during the outdoor shoot, Amit says 'the skies are crying at the state of the world.' After Ajay describes middle-class homes 'drenched in mass culture,' Amit adds: 'Right now we are getting drenched, but we will continue this episode.'
Ajay: 'it's easy to get a book accepted at a publisher, it's easy to sell 10,000 copies of a book. It is truly hard to get people to actually read a book.'

head: Ajay imitating a credential snob
more: Ajay imitating a credential snob: 'Oh, this Amit guy, he doesn't particularly have any degrees. He doesn't have that Louis Vuitton bag. So he must be a clueless bugger.' Amit later: 'this man here went to IIT, this man here went abroad and got fancy PhD. This man here has no credentials whatsoever. We can still be friends, right?'

head: Ajay on philanthropists tinkering with a broken system
more: Ajay on philanthropists tinkering with a broken system: 'putting lipstick on a pig, of putting an ERP system on top of a broken government policy paradigm.'

head: Nehru's famous line to JRD Tata
more: Nehru's famous line to JRD Tata, 'do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word', cited by Amit as the root of the ban on for-profit education.

head: Lant Pritchett
more: Lant Pritchett as 'the child saying that the emperor has no clothes' about the post-war global schooling enterprise. He likes to note that Haiti's education measures today match France's in 1970.

head: Amit on one-size-fits-all schooling
more: Amit on one-size-fits-all schooling: 'If you're going to test a monkey on how to climb a tree, you're also testing a fish on how to climb a tree.' He contrasts it with supermarkets offering forty types of ketchup and thirty types of ghee.

head: Ajay on what education should be…
more: Ajay on what education should be: 'kindling the fire and not filling the pail.'

head: Ajay attributes
more: Ajay attributes 'do not confuse school with your education' to an old Unix fortune.

head: ERNET: A Whole Country on 1.54 Megabits
dek: Small, well-placed investments in knowledge can have huge effects. ERNET built the human capital for the services boom before the bandwidth existed.
more: When Ajay first came back to India in the early 1990s, the only internet connectivity in the country was at the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST). Its head, S. Ramani, led a project called ERNET, a single T1 line running at 1.54 megabits per second for all of India. On a tiny budget it seeded hundreds of people with UNIX and internet knowledge, including people the hosts know personally. By the time telecom opened up, that knowledge had already spread across the country.
Small, well-placed investments in knowledge can have huge effects. ERNET built the human capital for the services boom before the bandwidth existed.

head: How Breaking a Monopoly Built India's Biggest Industry
dek: India's cleanest infrastructure success came from the state stepping aside, not from the state spending money.
more: In the late 1990s the Vajpayee government broke the Department of Telecom's stranglehold on telecom policy and opened the sector to private and foreign investment. It also privatised VSNL and ended its monopoly on international telephony. Private firms then laid fibre optic cables into India, with landing stations linking the Middle East to Bombay and Madras to Singapore, until India had effectively infinite bandwidth. Users paid for it, not the government. Ajay's one regret is that this happened in 1999 instead of alongside the early-90s customs duty cuts, which cost India about eight years. Amit recalls the objections of that time: telecom was too important and national security was at stake.
India's cleanest infrastructure success came from the state stepping aside, not from the state spending money. The 'too important to open up' arguments were forgotten once the reform worked.

head: Crawling Up the Coast: Mphasis Finds Cheap Talent
dek: This is the 'equalising differences' theory working as designed. Labour in Vijayawada is cheaper than in Bangalore, so once connectivity exists, work flows to wherever the cheap labour lives.
more: The founder of Mphasis told Ajay how the firm was expanding along the coast of Andhra Pradesh and Orissa. It would pick a town of five to ten lakh people, put up a building, hire 2,000 people and start work. It begins with call centres, where the firm polishes recruits' English accent and grammar, and moves up to software. Workers stay near home instead of migrating, and fibre connects them to global production.
This is the 'equalising differences' theory working as designed. Labour in Vijayawada is cheaper than in Bangalore, so once connectivity exists, work flows to wherever the cheap labour lives.

head: JNPT: Three Competing Terminals in One Port
dek: Careful policy design can create competition where a monopoly would otherwise form.
more: In the 1990s the government did not hand JNPT to a single private operator. It set the port up as three competing terminals. One stayed with the government so that costs could be measured and prices benchmarked, and the other two were contracted to different private vendors. The result was vigorous competition inside a single port.
Careful policy design can create competition where a monopoly would otherwise form. Ajay notes that this level of design brilliance was rarely repeated in later Indian infrastructure.

head: Hoping Against the Data
dek: This is the episode's opening theme in action. The hardest belief to update is one you championed yourself, and measuring honestly over a window chosen to favour your side makes the conclusion hard to dodge.
more: Ajay calls himself an enthusiast for India and supported the 1990s infrastructure paradigm. Year after year he watched the goods export data, hoping manufacturing exports would take off as ports, highways, airports and railways were built. For this episode he chose a ten-year window (FY2012-13 to FY2022-23) that deliberately flatters India because it includes the post-pandemic goods boom. Even then, growth was negligible. He openly says his views have shifted.

This is the episode's opening theme in action. The hardest belief to update is one you championed yourself, and measuring honestly over a window chosen to favour your side makes the conclusion hard to dodge.

head: China's Roads to Nowhere
dek: By any reasonable account China built too much infrastructure and wasted trillions of dollars of poor people's money.
more: Central planners and optimistic economists in China drove a gigantic infrastructure build. Over time, political decisions led to roads with nothing at the other end. In the short run everyone was happy: there were construction contracts, announcements and ribbon cuttings. Yet each extra unit of investment bought less and less GDP.
By any reasonable account China built too much infrastructure and wasted trillions of dollars of poor people's money. India should ask whether it is heading down a smaller version of the same road.

head: Two Days Inside a World-Class Jeans Factory
dek: A factory floor shows how India's labour rules shape firms. High mandated labour costs push even labour-intensive industries toward machines that microeconomics calls inefficiently capital-intensive.
more: Arvind showed Ajay 'one bad factory and one good factory', and the good one was, by their account, the best blue jeans factory in India. It sits on the outskirts of Bangalore, employs about 2,500 blue-collar workers and exports everything it makes. Because India's minimum wages and mandatory benefits are high, the factory constantly adds machines, each justified by a hard-nosed internal rate of return calculation, to compete with Bangladesh and Vietnam. Even the process of making new jeans look old and faded is now done by robots. The day shift is almost entirely women, while 24-hour operations are 100% men because of safety, transport and regulatory hurdles. Ajay called it one of the greatest two days of his life and asked listeners to suggest more factory visits.

A factory floor shows how India's labour rules shape firms. High mandated labour costs push even labour-intensive industries toward machines that microeconomics calls inefficiently capital-intensive. Amit adds that this hurts the very workers the minimum wage is meant to protect.
printed: The robot that fades your jeans

head: Lonavala Chikki Is Made in Ulhasnagar
dek: A small, memorable example of capitalism equalising differences. Lonavala's real estate is expensive, so production moves somewhere cheaper and the finished product travels back.
more: Ajay was explaining that you would rather make a product where costs are low and sell it where they are high. Amit asked whether Lonavala chikki was made in China. Ajay said it wasn't, but it was made in Ulhasnagar: he had gone on a field trip to find out. When he asked, the man told him they don't make it in Lonavala, they make it in Ulhasnagar.
A small, memorable example of capitalism equalising differences. Lonavala's real estate is expensive, so production moves somewhere cheaper and the finished product travels back.

head: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit says it is his most popular Seen and the Unseen episode to date.
more: Amit says it is his most popular Seen and the Unseen episode to date.
Mentioned as the episode, with Shrayana Bhattacharya, that led Amit to Vivian Gornick.

head: Where Has All the Education Gone?
dek: Pritchett was the child who said the emperor has no clothes. He showed that piling on years of schooling did not deliver development, and Ajay now applies the same scepticism to infrastructure.
more: Pritchett was the child who said the emperor has no clothes. He showed that piling on years of schooling did not deliver development, and Ajay now applies the same scepticism to infrastructure.
Ajay connects the infrastructure puzzle to the previous episode's education debate, and the paper's title inspires this episode's own title.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: It is the source of the argument that every rupee of government spending costs about three rupees of GDP, so public money needs strong reasons.
more: It is the source of the argument that every rupee of government spending costs about three rupees of GDP, so public money needs strong reasons.
Amit cites 'your great book' while arguing that even infrastructure spending must justify itself.

head: Public Finance at XKDR Forum
dek: He sees building state capability in government contracting as a high priority now that the state has retreated from PPPs.
more: He sees building state capability in government contracting as a high priority now that the state has retreated from PPPs.
Ajay mentions that his organisation runs a research programme on how governments can contract better.

head: Two Barriers to Updating Your Beliefs
dek: Ajay names two traps. The first is social: conventional wisdom, the mainstream, famous people and Nobel laureates.
more: Ajay names two traps. The first is social: conventional wisdom, the mainstream, famous people and Nobel laureates. He says he has resisted this since childhood by treating great thinkers as the kick-off for an argument rather than an authority. The second is arrogance, which he finds harder: refusing to revise conclusions you worked hard to reach. He admits he changes his mind too slowly, and that we are all less Bayesian than we should be.

head: Lower Tariffs Mean More Exports
dek: Cutting customs duties makes imported raw materials and inputs cheaper, so Indian exports become more competitive.
more: Cutting customs duties makes imported raw materials and inputs cheaper, so Indian exports become more competitive. The 1990s tariff cuts produced an export surge. The common belief that a country needs more protectionism to export is backwards.

head: Development Means Hosting Global Value Chains
dek: Half or more of global trade happens inside firms. Multinationals place each stage of production wherever it is cheapest: a ball bearing goes to Brazil, an engine is made there, and the car is assembled in Madras.
more: Half or more of global trade happens inside firms. Multinationals place each stage of production wherever it is cheapest: a ball bearing goes to Brazil, an engine is made there, and the car is assembled in Madras. A country prospers by becoming host to these production chains, whether the firms are Indian or foreign. That requires moving intermediate goods cheaply to remote low-wage places, which is why infrastructure was given top priority in Indian development strategy.

head: Capitalism Works by Equalising Differences
dek: Any gap in wages, land or raw material costs is a business opportunity: produce where it is cheap and sell where prices are high.
more: Any gap in wages, land or raw material costs is a business opportunity: produce where it is cheap and sell where prices are high. Low-end garment work does not belong in Bombay. The chikki sold in Lonavala gets made in Ulhasnagar. Looking for such differences is a simple trick for understanding where economic activity goes.

head: Foreign Firms Seed Domestic Industries Through Their Alumni
dek: Foreign firms often lead because they already have global production systems and customer relationships.
more: Foreign firms often lead because they already have global production systems and customer relationships. People who worked in them then leave to start domestic firms. Bangladesh's garment industry grew this way from a few pioneers, and Indian software grew from early firms like Datamatics and TCS. This is one reason FDI matters beyond the capital it brings.

head: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? Services Yes, Goods No
dek: Telecom infrastructure delivered a services revolution: IT-ITES is now India's biggest industry, with roughly $300-400 billion a year of fast-growing exports.
more: Telecom infrastructure delivered a services revolution: IT-ITES is now India's biggest industry, with roughly $300-400 billion a year of fast-growing exports. Ports, highways, airports and railways were meant to do the same for goods, and they did not. From FY2012-13 to FY2022-23, a window that flatters India, goods exports grew about 4% a year in nominal dollars and about 1.3% in real dollars, which means doubling only every half-century or so. FDI grew about 4% a year in real terms. Ajay insists on measuring in constant US dollars so exchange rates and inflation cannot create a money illusion. Global firms have not chosen India as a manufacturing platform.

head: ICOR: Why Infrastructure Gives Less Bang for the Buck
dek: The incremental capital output ratio (ICOR) compares extra capital invested with the extra output it produces.
more: The incremental capital output ratio (ICOR) compares extra capital invested with the extra output it produces. Ajay gives four reasons it has worsened for Indian infrastructure. First, diminishing returns: the best projects, such as the Golden Quadrilateral, JNPT and the Delhi metro, get done first, and a metro in Nagpur costs about as much but is worth far less. Second, the shift from PPPs to government projects, which cost more and are maintained worse. Third, project choice becomes political, favouring powerful constituencies, religious sites or swing seats. Fourth, public choice incentives favour launching projects over running them.

head: The Hard Part of Being a State Is the Humdrum Part
dek: Politicians and civil servants enjoy announcements, contracts and inaugurations.
more: Politicians and civil servants enjoy announcements, contracts and inaugurations. The unglamorous work of operating assets, regulating private players and overseeing projects wins no applause, and this is where the Indian state is weakest. Weak infrastructure regulation and poorly run airports are the result.

head: Contracting Is a Core State Capability
dek: From 1991 to 2011, India made a heroic attempt at public-private partnership (PPP) infrastructure.
more: From 1991 to 2011, India made a heroic attempt at public-private partnership (PPP) infrastructure. Many contracts went badly because the state's contracting skills were poor. The right response was to research those failures and improve step by step. Instead the government retreated to building things itself, which costs more and maintains worse. Ajay argues states should do complex contracts with private players in defence, innovation, vaccines and infrastructure rather than build. Amit draws the wider lesson: don't run from hard problems just because they're hard.

head: Viability Gap Funding: Subsidise Externalities Without Losing Discipline
dek: In a PPP, private investors check the traffic projections before committing money, so roads to nowhere get filtered out.
more: In a PPP, private investors check the traffic projections before committing money, so roads to nowhere get filtered out. Some roads also bring wider benefits that tolls alone can't capture. Ashok Lahiri's idea at the Ministry of Finance was viability gap funding: the government specifies the road, bidders compete in a reverse auction on how little subsidy they need, and the subsidy is then fixed. The private builder keeps the incentive to build well and maintain the asset.

head: Find the Binding Constraint Before You Spend
dek: The central question in development economics is what most holds back firms, Indian or foreign, from producing across India.
more: The central question in development economics is what most holds back firms, Indian or foreign, from producing across India. Infrastructure is probably not that choke point today. Ajay offers capital controls or hostile taxation as a hypothetical alternative. If fixing those brought a surge of FDI, jammed ports and roads would make infrastructure the constraint again. As with education, stop putting public money into what isn't working until you have diagnosed why.

head: The Unseen Cost of Public Spending
dek: Each rupee the government spends costs the economy about three rupees, and the coercion of taxation carries a moral cost as well.
more: Each rupee the government spends costs the economy about three rupees, and the coercion of taxation carries a moral cost as well. GDP counts state spending as output whether or not it creates value, so pointless work still raises GDP. Bastiat's lesson is to ask what the money would have done if left with the taxpayers it was taken from.

head: Minimum Wages Push Firms Toward Machines
dek: High minimum wages and mandatory benefits push Indian factories into inefficient capital intensity, replacing workers with machines one investment at a time to compete with Bangladesh and Vietnam.
more: High minimum wages and mandatory benefits push Indian factories into inefficient capital intensity, replacing workers with machines one investment at a time to compete with Bangladesh and Vietnam. Amit puts it bluntly: anyone whose work is valued below the legal minimum is not paid more. They lose the job.

head: Amit opens by noting that Ajay is wearing a sparkling white kurta (
more: Amit opens by noting that Ajay is wearing a sparkling white kurta ('the Sanskari look') with an ant climbing up his collar. Later he interrupts Ajay's account of being a lifelong free thinker to report that the ant is now on his neck, then says: 'Anyway, continue.'

head: Ajay says the Lonavala chikki is made in Ulhasnagar.
more: Ajay says the Lonavala chikki is made in Ulhasnagar. Amit: 'So you could actually write on it made in USA. USA standing for Ulhasnagar Sweets Association.'

head: Ajay mocking the old schooling paradigm
more: Ajay mocking the old schooling paradigm: 'if only India will develop years of schooling comparable to the UK of 1947, then India will become like the UK of 1947.'

head: Ajay on diminishing returns: a Delhi metro is valuable
more: Ajay on diminishing returns: a Delhi metro is valuable, but 'by the time you're doing a metro in Nagpur, you know, frankly, there's very little use of a metro in Nagpur.'

head: After describing infrastructure climbing onto the…
more: After describing infrastructure climbing onto the 'high table of development strategy' and declaring itself top priority, Ajay catches himself: 'Now I'm anthropomorphizing a block named infrastructure.'

head: John Maynard Keynes
more: John Maynard Keynes: 'When the facts change, I change my mind, and what do you do, sir?' Ajay holds this up as the ideal and admits he changes his mind too slowly.

head: Ajay lists the economists he admires but argues with…
more: Ajay lists the economists he admires but argues with: Larry Summers, Marty Feldstein, Lant Pritchett and Jeff Hammer. He treats them as a kick-off for an argument: 'Puny little me is going to argue about this with a great person.'

head: Paul Graham's phrase
more: Paul Graham's phrase 'aggressively conventional-minded', from The Four Quadrants of Conformism, which Amit uses for the people who push back on anyone questioning a consensus.

head: The Emperor's New Clothes: Ajay casts Lant Pritchett
more: The Emperor's New Clothes: Ajay casts Lant Pritchett as 'the little child saying that the emperor has no clothes' with his paper 'Where Has All the Education Gone?', which gives this episode its title.

head: Frédéric Bastiat
more: Frédéric Bastiat and 'the seen and the unseen': Amit invokes Bastiat to argue that state spending hides a large opportunity cost.

head: The wallet that never comes out
dek: The convenience of UPI is real and immediate. Its costs to freedom are abstract and come later, which is why it gets praised without much examination.
more: Amit describes the habit many Indian men have of patting one pocket for the wallet and another for the phone before leaving. He still carries his wallet, but since arriving at the shoot location a few days earlier he has not used it once, because he pays for everything by phone. That bothers him, since he and Ajay have always argued that cash is freedom and that demonetisation was an attack on it.
The convenience of UPI is real and immediate. Its costs to freedom are abstract and come later, which is why it gets praised without much examination. That tension frames the whole episode.

head: Six failed UPI payments at a Delhi red light
dek: A system pushed from the top, with the state forcing its use, has nobody on the hook for the moments it fails.
more: A Delhi cop stopped Ajay for going through a red light. The cop refused cash and insisted on electronic payment of the fine. Despite perfect internet connectivity, the UPI transaction failed six times in a row and only went through on the seventh attempt, while Ajay sat grumbling about the state of modern India.
A system pushed from the top, with the state forcing its use, has nobody on the hook for the moments it fails. The user is compelled to use it and has nowhere to go when it breaks.
printed: Fined in Delhi, failed six times

head: Even a computer-savvy friend got conned
dek: Systems that grow organically develop consumer-protection and fraud-handling machinery as they go.
more: Ajay's very tech-savvy friend Ayush Patnaik lost 15,000 rupees to UPI fraud. Ajay explains that UPI was designed top-down and never settled who takes responsibility or how consumer complaints get resolved. So when a payer and payee disagree about whether money arrived, there is no real recourse, and fraud has grown at scale.
Systems that grow organically develop consumer-protection and fraud-handling machinery as they go. A designed 'science project' leaves those messy details for later, and ordinary users pay for it.

head: How the internet beat a government standard (X.25 vs TCP/IP)
dek: The internet itself is the clearest historical case of bottom-up, decentralised engineering defeating a top-down standard backed by governments.
more: Global telecom monopolies, many of them state-owned even in rich countries, jointly designed a networking standard called X.25 and pushed it as the new global standard, and equipment makers fell in line. Meanwhile DARPA contracted researchers, including Vint Cerf, to build a protocol that could survive battlefield conditions by rerouting dynamically when lines went down. Bill Joy and others put TCP/IP into Unix, academics and hobbyists built BSD and later Linux, and TCP/IP beat X.25 as well as the corporate standards from Microsoft and Novell.

The internet itself is the clearest historical case of bottom-up, decentralised engineering defeating a top-down standard backed by governments. India's push for 'digital public goods' replays the losing side of that story.

head: PayPal knocked, RBI said no
dek: The fair comparison for UPI is not cash-only India. It is an India where private and foreign payment players were allowed in.
more: In the late 90s and early 2000s, PayPal already offered a payment handle like 'Amit at PayPal' with a backend for sending and receiving money, which is essentially the UPI idea. Many Indian exporters receive large sums through PayPal from customers abroad. When PayPal asked the Reserve Bank of India to let it run domestic payments in India, RBI refused. Ajay notes that even today UPI is open to banks only.
The fair comparison for UPI is not cash-only India. It is an India where private and foreign payment players were allowed in. That alternative never existed, so its cost stays invisible.

head: Holding out against Aadhaar, and the one-word answer
dek: The real distinction is not how much data an entity holds but whether you agreed to give it and whether you can walk away.
more: Amit refused Aadhaar for as long as he could, but eventually had to link it in order to pay his taxes. People often asked him why he minded giving data to the government when Google and Facebook already had it. His answer was always one word: consent. With a private company he accepts terms of use and can delete his account. With Aadhaar he had no choice.
The real distinction is not how much data an entity holds but whether you agreed to give it and whether you can walk away.

head: Teesta Setalvad's credit card bills
dek: The state could always snoop. The question is friction, and what changes when a common identifier makes linking databases cheap for a state of low capability.
more: Amit recalls that in the case against activist Teesta Setalvad, the state went through her credit card bills, found she had once bought alcohol, and used it against her at a press conference. He raises this to support Rahul Matthan's argument that the state could always gather such data through older channels without Aadhaar. Ajay replies that before Aadhaar the state had to query some twenty separate databases, which at Indian levels of state capability was a real barrier. The two leave open a disagreement on whether Aadhaar lets the state find your bank details.
The state could always snoop. The question is friction, and what changes when a common identifier makes linking databases cheap for a state of low capability.

head: From dismissive outsider to wanting insiders inside
dek: Outside criticism and inside engagement can coexist. The useful skill is telling which issues demand that insiders speak up and which reward staying in the room.
more: Amit has always seen himself as an outsider who speaks truth to power and offends every party equally. Partly through conversations with Ajay, which fed into his newsletter post 'Insiders and Outsiders', he concluded he had sometimes been unfairly harsh on people working inside the system. He still draws a hard line at demonetisation, which he once wrote in the Times of India was the largest assault on property rights in human history. Any economist who backed it, he says, failed a permanent litmus test. DPI is different: if it is getting built anyway, he wants good people shaping it.
Outside criticism and inside engagement can coexist. The useful skill is telling which issues demand that insiders speak up and which reward staying in the room.
printed: The outsider who wants insiders in

head: Gordon Lish and the hidden hand in Raymond Carver
dek: A distinctive literary voice is often partly a collaboration, and good editing can be invisible until it is gone.
more: While recommending Raymond Carver, Amit notes that much of Carver's writing was done for Esquire under the editor Gordon Lish, who was given a lot of credit for Carver's work. When the two stopped working together, readers could see how much Lish had contributed.
A distinctive literary voice is often partly a collaboration, and good editing can be invisible until it is gone.

head: In Service of the Republic (chapters 27 and 28)
dek: They showed him that the problem with India's digital infrastructure goes beyond isolated issues like Aadhaar coercion: the whole design logic behind the apparatus is flawed.
more: They showed him that the problem with India's digital infrastructure goes beyond isolated issues like Aadhaar coercion: the whole design logic behind the apparatus is flawed. The book also introduces the phrase 'premature state legibility'.
Amit opens the episode by saying these chapters prompted it.

head: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
dek: Ajay calls it critical reading for every advocate of technology monopolies.
more: Ajay calls it critical reading for every advocate of technology monopolies. It explains why progress comes from many competing minds rather than one designed system.

Ajay cites it while describing the messy, competitive 'bazaar' of technology, such as rival electronic health record standards in the US. He urges the engineers behind DPI to read it, and Amit seconds it in the recommendations segment.

head: Cathedral
dek: He calls it a masterpiece that 'just kinda blows me away', and says it is free to read online.
more: He calls it a masterpiece that 'just kinda blows me away', and says it is free to read online.
A short story Amit remembered because its title echoes Raymond's essay. He says the connection is verbal, not conceptual.

head: The Collected Stories of Raymond Carver
dek: He ranks Carver among the great short-story writers: minimal, easy and elegant, in some ways a successor to Ernest Hemingway.
more: He ranks Carver among the great short-story writers: minimal, easy and elegant, in some ways a successor to Ernest Hemingway.
Amit recommends Carver's whole body of work after recommending 'Cathedral'.

head: Short Cuts
dek: Amit was excited because its structure echoed Altman's Nashville. He admits he was a little disappointed, perhaps because of anchoring, since he was comparing it with Nashville and with Carver's original stories.
more: Amit was excited because its structure echoed Altman's Nashville. He admits he was a little disappointed, perhaps because of anchoring, since he was comparing it with Nashville and with Carver's original stories.
Altman's film built from a set of Raymond Carver short stories.

head: Nashville
dek: It is one of his favourite films of all time, and he calls it 'just a masterpiece'.
more: It is one of his favourite films of all time, and he calls it 'just a masterpiece'.
Mentioned as the 1975 Altman film that Short Cuts reminded him of.

head: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma, with Ajay Shah as co-host
dek: All three of them had a long conversation in it, so it is a way into Vitalik's thinking on politics and identity.
more: All three of them had a long conversation in it, so it is a way into Vitalik's thinking on politics and identity.
Amit mentions it after Ajay recommends Vitalik.

head: Seeing Like a State
dek: 'Please go read' it, Ajay urges. It shows how state schemes to improve the human condition have failed.
more: 'Please go read' it, Ajay urges. It shows how state schemes to improve the human condition have failed. He offers an alternative subtitle: 'the unintended consequences of state legibility projects'.
The source of the two concepts Ajay leans on most, 'high modernism' and 'state legibility'.

head: The Narrow Corridor
dek: It argues that liberty and prosperity depend on a rare balance between state power and a society that pushes back, and that countries can easily fall out of that corridor.
more: It argues that liberty and prosperity depend on a rare balance between state power and a society that pushes back, and that countries can easily fall out of that corridor.
Ajay cites it while warning that surveillance technology may tip the balance of power toward the Indian state.

head: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Ajay explains in more depth there how economists define public goods and market failure.
more: Ajay explains in more depth there how economists define public goods and market failure.
Amit points listeners to it during the discussion of the term 'public good'.

head: Ajay Shah on the Dangers of Digital Public Infrastructure (Episode 72 of Brave New World)
dek: Ajay making the same argument about the dangers of DPI on another podcast.
more: Ajay making the same argument about the dangers of DPI on another podcast.
Show-notes further reading.

head: Exploring Digital Public Goods
dek: A resource on the digital public goods idea whose terminology the episode questions.
more: A resource on the digital public goods idea whose terminology the episode questions.
A website linked in the show notes.

head: What a public good really is, and why UPI and Aadhaar aren't
dek: Economists define a public good as non-rival and non-excludable. Clean air is the classic case: your breathing doesn't reduce mine, and nobody can stop a newborn from breathing it.
more: Economists define a public good as non-rival and non-excludable. Clean air is the classic case: your breathing doesn't reduce mine, and nobody can stop a newborn from breathing it. Ajay credits Paul Samuelson with the basic theory. Linux and OpenStreetMap qualify as digital public goods. UPI is the property of one corporation, has finite capacity, and is highly excludable, since even non-banks cannot join as full participants. Aadhaar is a government monopoly. Governments are supposed to provide public goods, but something does not become a public good just because the government provides it.
printed: A monopoly by any other name

head: Greenwashing with good-sounding words
dek: Calling these systems 'public goods' or 'infrastructure' borrows the moral glow of words that middle-class India cheers for automatically, which makes criticism sound perverse.
more: Calling these systems 'public goods' or 'infrastructure' borrows the moral glow of words that middle-class India cheers for automatically, which makes criticism sound perverse. Ajay calls this Orwellian. He insists on protecting the meaning of technical terms. Amit's position is that everyday language can evolve on its own, but technical terms like 'market failure' or 'public good' must not slide into 'the market didn't give me a red shirt' or 'good for the public'.

head: High modernism
dek: This is James C Scott's term for the belief that powerful scientists, engineers, bureaucrats and politicians can design society on a whiteboard and impose the design, either through deference or coercion.
more: This is James C Scott's term for the belief that powerful scientists, engineers, bureaucrats and politicians can design society on a whiteboard and impose the design, either through deference or coercion. The real world is a complicated mix of asymmetric information, fraud, crime and consumers with real problems, and designed systems handle that richness poorly. In plain terms, the label sounds attractive but describes coercion from the top down.

head: No business model makes a 'science project'
dek: UPI has no revenue model, so every participant is supposed to take part out of nation-building spirit.
more: UPI has no revenue model, so every participant is supposed to take part out of nation-building spirit. Private firms will put on a demo and attend the ribbon-cutting, but they won't invest seriously in teams, equipment, consumer protection or continuing improvement without profit. The results are chronic transaction failures, unresolved disputes and widespread fraud.

head: Single standards are the silence of a graveyard
dek: Amit puts it simply: the core problem is monopoly, whether state or private, because competition forces a system to adapt or go bust.
more: Amit puts it simply: the core problem is monopoly, whether state or private, because competition forces a system to adapt or go bust. Ajay adds that standards wars like Betamax vs VHS or TCP/IP vs X.25 are signs of a healthy field, not something to fix. Linux has ten rival file systems, the US has 13 or 14 rival electronic health record systems, and messaging is split across Signal, WhatsApp and Google Chat. Incompatibility is annoying, but private connectors appear to bridge it, and the squabbling drives continuous improvement.

head: Discovery, not design
dek: The modern world is too complex for even the brightest engineers to design.
more: The modern world is too complex for even the brightest engineers to design. Consumer protection, fraud prevention and the 'hundreds of pages of manuals' have to evolve inside a self-organising system where people pursue their own interests every day. Ajay sees regulation that imposes one central plan as the core flaw. Society's job is to unleash many people searching for solutions, not to have a 'pointy-headed guy at the top' design the Republic.

head: State legibility, and premature state legibility
dek: State legibility, another of Scott's terms, is the state's ability to see its people.
more: State legibility, another of Scott's terms, is the state's ability to see its people. Historically, states that gathered information about their people have repeatedly abused it, so every increase in what the state can see needs a matching increase in checks and balances. India issued its first Aadhaar number in 2009 and still has no privacy law in 2024. Unlike countries that carried common-law privacy traditions forward (a policeman can't open my letter, so he can't read my email), India has neither those traditions nor a modern law. Ajay and Kelkar's book calls this 'premature state legibility'. Amit adds that Indians are already 'subjects and not citizens'.
printed: The state can see you now

head: Friction was the privacy
dek: Defenders say the state could always piece together your profile from many databases.
more: Defenders say the state could always piece together your profile from many databases. Ajay says that is true in principle, but given how weak India's state capability is, linking twenty databases was a real barrier in practice. A universal ID removes that friction, so database linkage actually happens for the first time. Amit had taken comfort in the state's incompetence, and this argument takes that comfort away.

head: The narrow corridor
dek: Drawing on Acemoglu and Robinson, Ajay argues that the freedom and prosperity of advanced economies come from a rare balance: a capable state held in check by a society that tells it to 'buzz off'.
more: Drawing on Acemoglu and Robinson, Ajay argues that the freedom and prosperity of advanced economies come from a rare balance: a capable state held in check by a society that tells it to 'buzz off'. That balance is not the natural state of affairs. Where the state wins decisively, as in China or Russia, modern technology can keep it on top for good. Ajay and Kelkar ask whether India's surge in state legibility has tipped the balance and created new obstacles to becoming a republic.

head: Why the state is not Google
dek: Google has no coercive power over you. You can spread your digital life across 20 firms, none of which can subpoena the others.
more: Google has no coercive power over you. You can spread your digital life across 20 firms, none of which can subpoena the others. The worst outcomes are a security breach or manipulative targeted ads, and in advanced economies breaches cost companies hundreds of millions of dollars, which pushes them to protect data. The Indian state has coercive power, is not accountable, has weak capability, and is already leaking sensitive datasets. Amit reduces the difference to one word: consent.

head: Credit the technology, not the monopoly
dek: The cheers for UPI give a state monopoly the credit for what Moore's Law would have delivered anyway.
more: The cheers for UPI give a state monopoly the credit for what Moore's Law would have delivered anyway. Ajay's analogy is Air India: early air travel felt miraculous, but that was the magic of aviation, and service improved once rival airlines were allowed in. Had India opened payments to private and foreign players in the 90s, it would have had several rival systems. They would have been somewhat inconvenient, but they would have kept improving.

head: Short-term wins, long-term sins
dek: Many policies feel great to consumers in the short run and turn out to be toxic.
more: Many policies feel great to consumers in the short run and turn out to be toxic. India celebrated the Green Revolution, but the means it used, MSP and wheat and rice in Punjab and Haryana, created costs the country is still paying. A thinker's job is to ask whether the strategic path is right, not just whether it works today.

head: In public life, engineers must also be philosophers
dek: Ajay respects the idealists who built these systems at great personal cost, but he rejects the defence 'I'm just a plumber, the philosophers failed us'.
more: Ajay respects the idealists who built these systems at great personal cost, but he rejects the defence 'I'm just a plumber, the philosophers failed us'. He blames India's weak tradition of political philosophy, law and thinking about liberty for making silver bullets look exciting. Anyone acting in public space still has to think through how their work affects welfare. Amit extends the duty to everyone with a voice.

head: DPI is not a development silver bullet
dek: Ajay's closing point: the popular idea that digital payments and identity mark a transformative moment for Indian economic development is mistaken.
more: Ajay's closing point: the popular idea that digital payments and identity mark a transformative moment for Indian economic development is mistaken. India's development problems lie elsewhere, and the hype itself shows how weak economic thinking in India is.

head: When the crew calls…
more: When the crew calls 'Amit rolling' before the take, Amit says: 'it's very easy to get a Bengali like me rolling because an essential condition for that is roundness. And I have a lot of that. I'm trying to lose some of it.'

head: Ajay uses the old line twice in the episode
more: Ajay uses the old line twice in the episode: 'An economist is someone who, when something works in practice, wonders whether it works in theory.'

head: Ajay declares…
more: Ajay declares 'I'm a Nazi on language... no plebeian evolution of language' and lodges his protest 'in triplicate': 'the Guild of Economists shall not accept such terminology.'

head: Amit on how technical terms get diluted
more: Amit on how technical terms get diluted: 'Oh, the market failed to give me a red shirt, it's a market failure.'

head: The running card joke. Ajay calls himself a…
more: The running card joke. Ajay calls himself a 'card carrying engineer, in addition to being an economist', and Amit asks how many cards he has ('I carry a couple'). Amit later wants him to become a card-carrying political philosopher too, and Ajay sums up Vitalik Buterin as 'the card carrying engineer that turned into a card carrying political philosopher.'
Amit: 'my philosophy is let a thousand flowers bloom, which is why we are wearing these shirts' and adds 'Dil garden garden hoya.'

head: Amit justifies wandering off to Raymond Carver and Robert Altman in an episode about DPI
more: Amit justifies wandering off to Raymond Carver and Robert Altman in an episode about DPI: 'these are payments for the soul.'

head: Tower of Babel: Ajay warns that if everyone uses technical words in their own way
more: Tower of Babel: Ajay warns that if everyone uses technical words in their own way, 'we will get a tower of Babel.'
