head: Paul Samuelson, credited by Ajay with the basic theory of clean air as a public good, which he calls…
more: Paul Samuelson, credited by Ajay with the basic theory of clean air as a public good, which he calls 'one of the great milestones in history.'

head: A Country Without Highways
dek: The capital shortage that Solow-inspired planners worried about was real and visible.
more: Explaining why early development thinkers fixated on capital stock, Ajay recalls that before he first went abroad to do his PhD, he had never seen a highway in India. The country had no highways and no metro systems at all.

The capital shortage that Solow-inspired planners worried about was real and visible. The rest of the episode shows why piling on capital still didn't deliver development, and that is the central puzzle.

head: His Father on the 'Technology Transfer' Myth
dek: Poverty is not caused by rich countries hoarding knowledge. The bottleneck lies at home, which points the search for the cause away from technology and toward firms and institutions.
more: When Ajay was a child, UN bodies (UNIDO or UNCTAD, he can't recall which) obsessed over formal state-to-state frameworks for rich countries to hand their 'secret runes' of technology to poor ones. His father told him this was completely wrong. The knowledge is all in books, papers and machine manuals, and patents put it in the public domain. The job is to go and learn it, not to ask for it.
Poverty is not caused by rich countries hoarding knowledge. The bottleneck lies at home, which points the search for the cause away from technology and toward firms and institutions.

head: The Blue Jeans Factory Outside Bangalore
dek: Indian firms can already operate at the global technological frontier.
more: One of Ajay's happiest recent moments was visiting a blue jeans factory on the outskirts of Bangalore. Its people track every machine available worldwide, work out the ROI carefully, buy equipment from China, Taiwan and Europe, read the manuals and deploy it in India.
Indian firms can already operate at the global technological frontier. So India is not poor because it lacks knowledge. The answer has to lie elsewhere.

head: Is Our YouTube Show World-Class?
dek: Their own studio shows the point in miniature. Equipment and manuals are globally available and Indians can use them to the hilt, so a 'technology gap' cannot explain a 10x income gap.
more: On the ride up the mountain, Ajay asked Amit a blunt question. Was their show, shot by Nomsita and Vaishnav on Sony equipment, inferior to the global state of the art in any way? Amit said he saw no important aspect of their production values that lagged. Even their microphone was the best available anywhere.
Their own studio shows the point in miniature. Equipment and manuals are globally available and Indians can use them to the hilt, so a 'technology gap' cannot explain a 10x income gap.
printed: Not for want of a manual

head: The Terrible Starts of Taiwan, Korea and Israel
dek: Where a country starts does not decide where it ends up. Countries that once looked up to India have overtaken it, and countries with devastated beginnings clawed their way to prosperity.
more: Each of the rare success stories began badly. Taiwan was a minor island that had suffered a cruel Japanese occupation and then took in people fleeing mainland China under Chiang Kai-shek, whom Ajay calls 'a pretty rotten person'. Seoul changed hands six times in the Korean War and was destroyed on the scale of Berlin, Stalingrad or Dresden, and early South Korean officials looked up to India's civil service practices. Israel fought a war in 1948 and was surrounded by hostile states.
Where a country starts does not decide where it ends up. Countries that once looked up to India have overtaken it, and countries with devastated beginnings clawed their way to prosperity.

head: Why 1947 India Fell for the Big State
dek: Nehru's choice is easier to understand when you see that the whole world seemed to prove state command worked.
more: Ajay reconstructs the mood of the time. Russia had lost a war to Japan in 1905, been beaten at Tannenberg, and fought a civil war until 1921 after the communists 'kicked in the door'. Yet by 1945 it was the greatest land power in the world. By the end of the Second World War every major combatant had become a big-state, commanded economy: the USSR, Nazi Germany, a UK war economy largely managed by Keynes, and a US that passed laws to order private firms around.

Nehru's choice is easier to understand when you see that the whole world seemed to prove state command worked. That intellectual fog persists today, since most Indian businesspeople still want the government to do more, not less.
printed: All the world’s a war economy

head: The Book for Nehru's Time Machine
dek: Policy failure often reflects the ideas available at the time rather than bad intentions.
more: Ajay describes how long it took him, as an economist raised on the Solow model, to accept that it wasn't working. He slowly moved toward state capability, rule of law, checks and balances and public choice theory. When he and Vijay Kelkar wrote In Service of the Republic after years in the Ministry of Finance, their private brief was to write the one book they would send back in time to Nehru. Amit adds that this assumes Nehru was a brilliant, well-meaning man who lacked the ideas that came later: public choice theory didn't yet exist, and Hayek wasn't taken seriously.
Policy failure often reflects the ideas available at the time rather than bad intentions. That is why Ajay sees development as 'first and foremost a journey of ideas'.
printed: A book for Nehru’s time machine

head: The Controversial Divorce-Rate Column
dek: Read a number by what it reveals, not by how it looks. More divorces can mean more women can leave bad marriages.
more: When Ajay suggested the rate of single mothers as a good indicator of social progress, Amit recalled a column of his that drew a lot of heat. In it he argued that a rising divorce rate is one of the great indicators of women's empowerment in India.
Read a number by what it reveals, not by how it looks. More divorces can mean more women can leave bad marriages. Social freedom is part of the development package, not separate from it.

head: Envy After the Cycling Episode
dek: Prosperity is about having choices, not just survival. The dream is for every Indian to have such options, and what they then do with them is their birthright.
more: After Amit recorded an episode on cycling, Ajay came away envious of the advanced commercial and organisational culture in Europe that supports the whole world of cycling. For him it showed the kind of life experience that only a rich country makes widely available.
Prosperity is about having choices, not just survival. The dream is for every Indian to have such options, and what they then do with them is their birthright.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: Amit calls it 'a masterful book' and the first to lay out a fundamental framework for state capability, checks and balances and public choice.
more: Amit calls it 'a masterful book' and the first to lay out a fundamental framework for state capability, checks and balances and public choice. He says it reads like a textbook, only far more readable. Read it, gift it, and dip into it often.
Amit's first recommendation at the end. Earlier, Ajay explained that it grew out of his and Kelkar's years in the Ministry of Finance, written as the book they would send back to Nehru.

head: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit recommends listening to it, but says engaging with Pritchett's work itself matters even more.
more: Amit recommends listening to it, but says engaging with Pritchett's work itself matters even more. It is where he learned the national-versus-kinky-development frame, which changed how he sees the field.
Raised while discussing Pritchett's finding that growth, not redistribution, explains poverty reduction, and again among the joint recommendations.

dek: Amit says Pritchett's papers are eye-opening and seminal because they are built on hard data and look at outcomes.
more: Amit says Pritchett's papers are eye-opening and seminal because they are built on hard data and look at outcomes.
One of the key Pritchett papers linked as part of the joint recommendation of 'all of Lant Pritchett's works'.

head: What I, as a development economist, have been actively "for"
dek: Part of the body of work Amit wants every listener to engage with directly, not just through podcast conversations.
more: Part of the body of work Amit wants every listener to engage with directly, not just through podcast conversations.
Linked among the Pritchett blog posts and papers Amit recommends together with Ajay.

head: On the Mechanics of Economic Development
dek: He calls it 'a beautiful paper'. Its key line is that once you start thinking about this question, it's hard to think about anything else.
more: He calls it 'a beautiful paper'. Its key line is that once you start thinking about this question, it's hard to think about anything else.
Ajay cites it while framing the 10x gap between India and the US.

by: Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and co-authors
dek: It does careful measurement of state capability and finds that Indian state capability got worse during the 1991-2011 boom.
more: It does careful measurement of state capability and finds that Indian state capability got worse during the 1991-2011 boom.
Cited when Ajay argues that GDP growth does not mean the state improved.

head: Missing In Action
dek: A great book on the Indian state by friends of the show, worth reading even if, like Amit, you think markets belong inside society rather than as a third pillar.
more: A great book on the Indian state by friends of the show, worth reading even if, like Amit, you think markets belong inside society rather than as a third pillar.
Mentioned as a 'great book' that uses the state-society-market framing Amit pushes back on.

head: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: One of Amit's two most popular episodes, and it speaks directly to the gulf between the genders that Ajay sees as a failure of India's social capital.
more: One of Amit's two most popular episodes, and it speaks directly to the gulf between the genders that Ajay sees as a failure of India's social capital.
Plugged after Ajay says Indian boys and girls don't know how to talk to each other.

dek: The male side of the same story: half the country can't talk to the other half.
more: The male side of the same story: half the country can't talk to the other half.
Plugged together with The Loneliness of the Indian Woman.

head: Walk around an IKEA and admire the company
dek: He urges listeners not just to shop there but to admire 'the audacity of conception': how the furniture is designed and manufactured and how the stores and global marketing are built.
more: He urges listeners not just to shop there but to admire 'the audacity of conception': how the furniture is designed and manufactured and how the stores and global marketing are built. It shows the deep capability that sits inside great firms.
Ajay's example of what world-class firms in advanced economies look like.

head: The Poverty of Development Economics
dek: Further reading for anyone who wants to dig into the episode's main theme of where development economics went astray.
more: Further reading for anyone who wants to dig into the episode's main theme of where development economics went astray. It is not discussed in the conversation itself.
Listed in the show notes among the episode's joint reading recommendations.

head: The 10x Gap Is the Defining Question
dek: Even after adjusting for purchasing power, Indian per capita GDP is one-tenth that of the US.
more: Even after adjusting for purchasing power, Indian per capita GDP is one-tenth that of the US. That is a tenfold difference, not 10% or 20%. Development economics is the study of why that gap exists and what can close it. Most of the world's countries are poor, so the question goes far beyond India.

head: 'Money Isn't Everything' Is a Luxury Belief
dek: People may decide money matters little in their own lives, but at national level income is the difference between deprivation and dignity.
more: People may decide money matters little in their own lives, but at national level income is the difference between deprivation and dignity. It means protein for growing children, a hot bath in a North Indian winter, mosquito screens on windows, and surviving a medical emergency. Prosperity gives people choices, and what they do with those choices is their birthright. Elites who downplay money feel virtuous while the poor bear the cost.

head: Why the Solow Model Failed as a Theory of Development
dek: Post-war development thinking took the Solow-Swan growth model, in which output depends on capital per person and productivity (seen as machines and manuals), and concluded that poor countries should save, build capital and import technology.
more: Post-war development thinking took the Solow-Swan growth model, in which output depends on capital per person and productivity (seen as machines and manuals), and concluded that poor countries should save, build capital and import technology. India refutes this. Only about a third of working-age people are employed. The global capital market has trillions available. Every manual is readable by India's English-speaking elite. If the model were right, India would already be rich, so the real constraints lie elsewhere.

head: Failure Is the Norm, Success the Exception
dek: Early optimists treated development like a puppy growing into a dog: inevitable, needing only nutrients such as aid and technology transfer.
more: Early optimists treated development like a puppy growing into a dog: inevitable, needing only nutrients such as aid and technology transfer. In fact, of the countries poor in 1945, only South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile have become rich, while more than a hundred have not. Ajay compares this to climbing Everest. Told it's just a matter of protein bars, you fail. Told it's statistically hard, you train properly. The development community's habitual cheerleading obscures this.

head: Rich Countries Are Alike; Poor Countries Are Poor in Their Own Ways
dek: In an echo of Anna Karenina, poor countries differ so much that Ajay had to 'zero base' his thinking each time he worked outside India.
more: In an echo of Anna Karenina, poor countries differ so much that Ajay had to 'zero base' his thinking each time he worked outside India. Advanced economies, by contrast, share a package. They are liberal democracies with free speech, a free press and rule of law. Their states act as agents of the people. They have world-class firms, separation of church and state, falling religiosity, and marriages formed by choice rather than tribe. Amit adds that tribalism thrives on scarcity and zero-sum thinking. Development is a full package of freedom: of the mind, in the bedroom, in the public square.

head: A Windfall Is Not Development
dek: Oil-rich states like Saudi Arabia got wealth from under the ground without the package of development, so most people still live what most would consider a terrible life.
more: Oil-rich states like Saudi Arabia got wealth from under the ground without the package of development, so most people still live what most would consider a terrible life. The goal is flourishing people, not a rich treasury. That is why Ajay hopes India never strikes such a windfall.

head: Fix the Middle: Growth Explains Almost All of Poverty
dek: Lant Pritchett shows that median income alone explains 99% of the variation in poverty rates across countries.
more: Lant Pritchett shows that median income alone explains 99% of the variation in poverty rates across countries. Inequality, welfare schemes and redistribution account for roughly 1%. A separate Pritchett paper argues growth is both necessary and sufficient for development. So helping the poor directly is a humanitarian impulse, not development economics. The real lever is lifting the mean and median income of the whole economy.

head: The Three Pillars of Development
dek: Ajay's framework has three parts. First, high-productivity firms that approach the US frontier.
more: Ajay's framework has three parts. First, high-productivity firms that approach the US frontier. Second, a capable state, which in Amit's words should 'do a few things well instead of many things badly'. Third, a political system in which the state is the people's agent, not a feared mai-baap ruler. Unlike Pritchett, Ajay doesn't treat rule of law as a separate pillar, because it is what makes the second and third possible. The hosts say they are libertarians, not anarchists: they want a state that is small but capable.

head: Society and Trust Capital
dek: Behind firms and the state stands society: its norms, communities and ability to collaborate.
more: Behind firms and the state stands society: its norms, communities and ability to collaborate. In the World Values Survey, 50-90% of people in advanced economies say most people can be trusted, against about 15% in India. Low trust means neighbours can't settle problems like loud loudspeakers or local public goods between themselves, so everything is pushed onto a weak state. That causes a premature expansion of the state's scope and then its organisational collapse. The starkest sign of the deficit is that Indian boys and girls don't know how to talk to each other.

head: Output Is Made in Firms
dek: What makes the US great is Google, Microsoft and JP Morgan, not its government.
more: What makes the US great is Google, Microsoft and JP Morgan, not its government. Firms are where labour, capital and know-how become output, and that process is far from trivial. Development economics neglects firms because they are seen as 'rich people' and funders and journals aren't interested. Yet studying firms is also how you find the policy failures that hold them back. Amit's 'seen and unseen' point applies: we see what firms achieved, not what bad laws such as well-meant labour laws stopped them from achieving.

head: Markets Are Society in Action, Not a Third Pillar
dek: Amit rejects the popular 'state, society, market' trio used by Raghuram Rajan, Rohini Nilekani, and Pranay Kotasthane and Raghu S Jaitley.
more: Amit rejects the popular 'state, society, market' trio used by Raghuram Rajan, Rohini Nilekani, and Pranay Kotasthane and Raghu S Jaitley. There are only the state and society. Markets are simply how members of society voluntarily do things for one another in positive-sum ways. Firms make money by solving people's problems, so hostility to markets is hostility to ordinary cooperation.

head: GDP Growth Doesn't Mean the State Got Better
dek: Building State Capability found that Indian state capability worsened during the 1991-2011 boom.
more: Building State Capability found that Indian state capability worsened during the 1991-2011 boom. As the economy grows, larger sums tempt the same judges, regulators and officials, and checks built for a smaller economy break down. Meanwhile good growth numbers breed complacency, so the pressure to reform the state fades. Amit adds that money flowing in makes the state a self-feeding, bloated beast. This mismatch helps explain why developing countries grow in hare-like spurts, while the UK and US grew at 3% for 200 years without faltering.

head: The Big Developmental State Delusion
dek: The Nehru-Mahalanobis vision, in Ajay's slightly exaggerated words, was that the state would 'grab the people by the scruff of the neck and drag the people into development', with no respect for private enterprise.
more: The Nehru-Mahalanobis vision, in Ajay's slightly exaggerated words, was that the state would 'grab the people by the scruff of the neck and drag the people into development', with no respect for private enterprise. Keynes's corrective is that the state should do what the private sector won't do at all, not slightly improve on it. Ajay asks why, for example, a government monopoly was needed in payments with UPI. Since the obstacle is a mindset, Ajay argues development is first a journey of ideas: knowledge must change before firms, the state and society can.

head: Public Health Is Not Health Care
dek: Development thinking has long equated health with building hospitals and village health centres.
more: Development thinking has long equated health with building hospitals and village health centres. Ajay calls this deluded. The state's job is population-scale prevention: clean water, sanitation, air quality, mosquito control, fighting antimicrobial resistance and reducing road crashes. Amit puts the distinction simply: getting your own malaria treated is private health care, while eradicating the mosquitoes so malaria never happens is a public good the state should provide.

head: Clad the State's Coercive Power Like a Nuclear Reactor
dek: Coercive power is poison. The state is meant to turn it into welfare, which requires heavy cladding: limited powers, checks and balances, careful organisational design and well-drafted laws.
more: Coercive power is poison. The state is meant to turn it into welfare, which requires heavy cladding: limited powers, checks and balances, careful organisational design and well-drafted laws. Every new power or new data stream given to the state needs matching cladding. Without it you get premature state legibility, which sets up state failure.

head: National Development vs Kinky Development
dek: Pritchett separates the big task of raising a nation's median income, which is what ends poverty, from 'kinky development', which retreats into narrow problems that can be solved and credited.
more: Pritchett separates the big task of raising a nation's median income, which is what ends poverty, from 'kinky development', which retreats into narrow problems that can be solved and credited. Amit compares it to the drunk who searches for his keys under a lamppost not because he dropped them there but because that's where the light is. RCTs on questions like whether treated mosquito nets help are the lamppost: easy career wins that barely move national development.

head: Three Incentives That Distorted Development Economics
dek: First, philanthropies, and especially their staff, crave attributable wins, so they fund trivial interventions and consultants who handle a joint secretary's daily office work.
more: First, philanthropies, and especially their staff, crave attributable wins, so they fund trivial interventions and consultants who handle a joint secretary's daily office work. Second, populist politics rewards visible handouts ('I gave you 2000 rupees') over building conditions for growth. Third, the 'frat boy world' of US economics journals prizes rigour and causal identification over important questions, so careers are built on narrow RCTs. Together these pulled the field away from its core question.

head: Think Independently; Judge Outcomes, Not Intentions
dek: Amit's opening and closing plea. Don't adopt your tribe's package of beliefs as part of your identity.
more: Amit's opening and closing plea. Don't adopt your tribe's package of beliefs as part of your identity. Keep returning to the question that first motivated you, which is how to make India better for everyone. Policies meant to help the poor often hurt them, and the data is there for anyone to check. That includes checking the hosts.

head: The episode is shot on a mountaintop. Amit calls the backdrop
more: The episode is shot on a mountaintop. Amit calls the backdrop 'the best green screen known to man. It is a natural green screen.' Ajay, the tech geek, shows off his hair light: 'A hundred and fifty million kilometers behind me', meaning the sun.

head: When Ajay compares development to a child growing up or a puppy becoming a dog, Amit cuts in…
more: When Ajay compares development to a child growing up or a puppy becoming a dog, Amit cuts in: 'The philosopher in me wants to argue with the economist in you and say that growth from a child to an adult and from a puppy to a dog is actually deeply tragic.'

The 'Bengali economist' running gag. Amit says: 'between us we are a Bengali economist. We don't like Bengali economists. But between us, like I'm Bengali, he's an economist.' His proof of being Bengali: 'I put on the jacket first.' Earlier, Ajay mentions that Amit has promised a YouTube short explaining PPP 'in English and in Bengali'.

head: Explaining why the location changed, Amit says a leopard almost attacked them and announced
more: Explaining why the location changed, Amit says a leopard almost attacked them and announced, 'I smell a Bengali economist.' He raised a finger in reply: 'No, you smell a Bengali and you smell an economist.' The real reason was that the light was fading, so they watched the sunset and finished the next morning, because 'development is a long journey, so are episodes.'

head: Mocking philanthropy's hunger for credit, Ajay imagines a staffer's career claim
more: Mocking philanthropy's hunger for credit, Ajay imagines a staffer's career claim: 'I contributed to this policy that got 73.4 people out of poverty.'
Ajay on 'the peculiar frat boy world of the economics journals', where referees join in as if they were co-authors, demand twenty changes, and the author can't say no.

head: Amit's closing note of humility after an hour and a half of strong opinions
more: Amit's closing note of humility after an hour and a half of strong opinions: 'We could also be full of shit, right?'

head: Robert Solow, the MIT economist and Nobel laureate, and the Solow-Swan growth model. Ajay calls it the hidden
more: Robert Solow, the MIT economist and Nobel laureate, and the Solow-Swan growth model. Ajay calls it the hidden 'theory of development' behind decades of capital-first planning.
'We are all Macaulay's children': Ajay on India's English-speaking elite, who were expected to bring in the manuals that would make the country rich.

head: Amit inverts Tolstoy's opening line of Anna Karenina (
more: Amit inverts Tolstoy's opening line of Anna Karenina ('all happy families are alike'): poor countries are poor in different ways, but successful ones share a recognisable package.

head: K-pop as a sign of advanced-economy flourishing. Ajay says it doesn't surprise him that South Korea is home to…
more: K-pop as a sign of advanced-economy flourishing. Ajay says it doesn't surprise him that South Korea is home to 'a remarkable cultural phenomenon across the whole world'.

head: The World Values Survey question
more: The World Values Survey question 'Do you believe that people can generally be trusted?' Advanced economies score 50-90%; India scores about 15%.

head: Keynes on the role of the state
more: Keynes on the role of the state: 'the job of the state is not to do things a little bit better than what private people will do. The job of the state is to do the things that the private sector will not do at all.' Ajay regrets not quoting it in their UPI episode.

head: The drunk looking for his keys under the lamppost
more: The drunk looking for his keys under the lamppost 'because the light is here', retold by Amit with a polite Mumbai cop, as a picture of mainstream development economics.
'A long arc from the French Revolution to Thomas Piketty': Ajay's shorthand for the enduring political obsession with inequality.

head: The young man who wants to stay in Himachal
dek: The scarce input for local development is curious, policy-literate people who choose to stay.
more: The crew held an Everything is Everything viewers' meetup in Bir, and only a couple of people came at short notice. One was Shubham Dhiman, who drove three hours from his village near Hamirpur. He had done the public policy course at Takshashila and was full of curiosity about policy, yet rooted in the place: he didn't want a city job, he wanted to do something for Himachal. His conversation with Ajay raised the question of how to develop such places without destroying them, and that question became this episode.
The scarce input for local development is curious, policy-literate people who choose to stay. The episode is partly a toolkit addressed to them.

head: How Udaipur bet on its lakes over farming
dek: One deliberate trade-off, based on which use of a scarce resource creates more value, can change a region's destiny.
more: Udaipur's lakes used to depend on the monsoon. In good years the city was staggeringly beautiful. In other years the water evaporated, and people would check with each other whether 'the lakes are nice' before deciding to go. Vasundhara Raje, Rajiv Mehrishi and others then changed Rajasthan's rules for prioritising irrigation water: whatever the scarcity, Udaipur's lakes get water first. Farmers lower in the queue lost out in the short term. But Udaipur became a high-value tourism engine, the 'Venice of the East', and lakhs of livelihoods now connect to its economy.

One deliberate trade-off, based on which use of a scarce resource creates more value, can change a region's destiny. Rajasthan is not great farmland, so it stopped playing a B-grade agriculture game and went world-class on the asset it uniquely had.

head: Abandoned villages, from Uttarakhand to the Sahyadris
dek: The old picture of Himalayan development as a fight between too many people and the forests is out of date.
more: Uttarakhand has more than 3,000 abandoned villages. On the way up to Panchachuli, Ajay stayed in a village of about 200 houses with only three families left, and each hiker was offered an entire empty house for the night. On the Pindari Glacier trek he heard about a pregnant woman whom four men carried 20 km on a stretcher to reach the nearest health facility. Leaving such places is rational. He now sees the same thing in the deep Sahyadris: on a nine-day trek in January (the one where he broke his ankle on day five), he reached a village on day three with about twenty houses and just one old man and one old woman still living there.

The old picture of Himalayan development as a fight between too many people and the forests is out of date. Low fertility and out-migration mean remote India is emptying out, and policy has to start from that fact.

head: Dharamshala's staircase of decline
dek: Without urban governance, decline repeats as a series of steps. Each place enjoys a 20–30 year bloom, gets ruined by negative externalities, and the high-value visitors move further uphill.
more: Dharamshala began with the Dalai Lama's arrival in 1959 and an airport soon after. Its fame spread slowly, by word of mouth and the Lonely Planet. By the 1980s it had become overcrowded, with all the failures of a bad Indian city. High-value tourists moved up to McLeod Ganj, which worked for about twenty years before it too went bad. They then moved to Lower Dharamkot, which degraded in turn, and then to Upper Dharamkot. Now Dharamshala has become a cricket venue, and Ajay predicts the low-value crowds that come with cricket will soon destroy Upper Dharamkot too.

Without urban governance, decline repeats as a series of steps. Each place enjoys a 20–30 year bloom, gets ruined by negative externalities, and the high-value visitors move further uphill. For Ajay, watching this happen was the moment he understood the problem.

head: Looking down at Bir through smoke from Billing
dek: Clean air and a clear view are public goods, and a bonfire is a textbook negative externality.
more: The day before recording, the crew stood at Billing, 2,500 metres up, and looked down at Bir 800 metres below. The town was covered in a haze of particulate matter from fires, including tourists' bonfires. From the landing ground below, you could barely see Billing. Ajay's fix: drones with thermal cameras to spot every fire, and a policeman sent to fine whoever lit it ten thousand rupees.
Clean air and a clear view are public goods, and a bonfire is a textbook negative externality. No individual can fix it, so this is exactly where even a freedom-first thinker says the state must act.
printed: Where there’s smoke, send a drone

head: The book fair that made a hiker
dek: One book found by chance at the right age can shape a whole life. Amit then turns this around and suggests Ajay can now be that spark for young people.
more: At about eleven, Ajay wandered into a book fair in Bombay and found Harish Kapadia's Trek the Sahyadris. He read it a hundred times. Then, with no help and no knowledge, he and a group of other kids from Bandra East started hiking in the Sahyadris on their own.
One book found by chance at the right age can shape a whole life. Amit then turns this around and suggests Ajay can now be that spark for young people.
printed: A book fair, then the Sahyadris

head: Order Without Design
dek: He calls it a masterpiece and a desert-island book. It is about more than town planning: it shows how urban planning and economics come together, with many good frameworks for thinking about cities.
more: He calls it a masterpiece and a desert-island book. It is about more than town planning: it shows how urban planning and economics come together, with many good frameworks for thinking about cities.
Amit's first pick in the closing recommendations, tied to the episode's discussion of town planning.

head: Horizon
dek: Lopez is one of the great travel writers and a beautiful, introspective writer.
more: Lopez is one of the great travel writers and a beautiful, introspective writer. Amit says a journey becomes truly beautiful when it is also a journey inside you.
Amit's second pick, prompted by being surrounded by the landscape around Bir.

head: Autumn Passage to the Himalaya
dek: Ajay calls it a lovely book and essential if you take an interest in the Himalayas.
more: Ajay calls it a lovely book and essential if you take an interest in the Himalayas.
Kapadia's new book from 2023, recommended right after Ajay's tribute to him.

head: Development for the locals, not scenery for the visitors
dek: Ajay rejects the outsider's wish that hill people stay poor so their places stay pretty.
more: Ajay rejects the outsider's wish that hill people stay poor so their places stay pretty. The goal is sustained economic growth for the people of the Himalayan states, and the only question is which strategy delivers it. Amit adds that worrying about 'low-value tourism' is not snobbery. The test is whether locals prosper while the place keeps what makes it good, and the low-level equilibrium fails both: locals earn less and the beauty is destroyed.

head: The plains recipe fails in the mountains
dek: The usual path for states like Gujarat or Haryana is infrastructure, factories and modern agriculture.
more: The usual path for states like Gujarat or Haryana is infrastructure, factories and modern agriculture. It doesn't transfer to the Himalayas. These states are landlocked, so they lack the coastline that gives cheap access to container ships and world trade. Mountain airports, railways and highways are hugely expensive and would need very high user charges. Following the standard recipe means always doing it worse than the plains. In line with the subsidiarity principle, the local political system should pick its own priorities.

head: Build on your one-of-a-kind asset
dek: Udaipur has its lakes; the Himalayan states have the Himalayas. Switzerland, Colorado and Japan show that a beautiful place can support a high-value tourism economy and first-world incomes for locals over generations.
more: Udaipur has its lakes; the Himalayan states have the Himalayas. Switzerland, Colorado and Japan show that a beautiful place can support a high-value tourism economy and first-world incomes for locals over generations. The strategy should be built around that unique asset.

head: The demographic transition has turned
dek: Fertility rates in Himachal and Uttarakhand are around 1.6–1.7, with similar levels in Sikkim and Bhutan.
more: Fertility rates in Himachal and Uttarakhand are around 1.6–1.7, with similar levels in Sikkim and Bhutan. Together with out-migration, this points to gently declining populations and thousands of abandoned villages. The 1950s–60s worry about people clearing forests for farms and houses no longer applies, and tourism's low use of labour is no longer a problem.

head: Freedom first, then market failure, then the state
dek: The disciplined public-economics method: start by imagining the world where people do whatever they want, and respect the creativity and bottom-up energy in society.
more: The disciplined public-economics method: start by imagining the world where people do whatever they want, and respect the creativity and bottom-up energy in society. Then find what goes wrong, classify it as a market failure, and only then ask whether the state can uniquely add value.

head: Tourism GDP = N × P, and externalities wreck P
dek: A region's tourism income is the number of tourists (N) times their daily spend (P).
more: A region's tourism income is the number of tourists (N) times their daily spend (P). Left alone, each establishment rationally adds disco lights, loudspeakers and bonfires to attract customers, but each one spoils the area around it. These uncoordinated choices push out high-spending visitors. Chasing N lowers P.

head: The boom-bust trap and the hundred-year view
dek: A place gets 20–30 good years, then collapses into a stable low-income equilibrium.
more: A place gets 20–30 good years, then collapses into a stable low-income equilibrium. Low-value tourists don't require high human capital to serve them, and they degrade the place further, a vicious cycle. Sustainability here means an economic arc that keeps rising over a century, the timescale on which human capital and a 'Switzerland of India' get built. There are no quick fixes.

head: Town planning as lines on maps, not micromanagement
dek: Following Bimal Patel, about 40–50% of land should be marked for streets and parks before unplanned construction makes that impossible.
more: Following Bimal Patel, about 40–50% of land should be marked for streets and parks before unplanned construction makes that impossible. This answers Amit's worry about high modernism. Ajay rejects the Indian style of planning that specifies every school and petrol pump, but argues that basic rule of law alone can't handle urban market failures. In Bir, he imagines a vehicle-free walking zone with cafés across from the paragliding landing ground.

head: Why Bir is a better bet than Bangalore
dek: This is Ajay's answer to Amit's worry about isomorphic mimicry. First, small towns are easier to fix, so urban reformers should learn there before taking on big cities.
more: This is Ajay's answer to Amit's worry about isomorphic mimicry. First, small towns are easier to fix, so urban reformers should learn there before taking on big cities. Second, incentives line up. Bangalore sells software, so residents complain about the city but tolerate it, and the state becomes predatory, extracting money from the software makers. Bir sells the place itself, so good governance and income move together. Udaipur shows the effect: locals keep it clean, and police treat a woman's safety at 2 AM as make-or-break. He also says the knowledge comes first: reach out to the frontier experts instead of accepting normal Indian town planning, and learn from community successes he cites in Meghalaya, Bhutan and Nepal.

head: Airports filter for high-value tourists
dek: Kangra's runway is around 1,300 m and Kullu's around 1,100 m, too short for big aircraft.
more: Kangra's runway is around 1,300 m and Kullu's around 1,100 m, too short for big aircraft. Ladakh shows the logic: because you must fly to Delhi and then to Leh, the effort involved selects for a different, higher-value tourist than easy road access does. Longer runways would shift Himachal's visitor mix upward.

head: National parks as economic engines
dek: Indian parks stop poaching and commercial development, which is good, but they contribute almost nothing to GDP.
more: Indian parks stop poaching and commercial development, which is good, but they contribute almost nothing to GDP. Yellowstone gets about four million visitors a year spending $1,000–2,000 each, which Ajay puts at $4–8 billion in revenue, and it has about 900 miles of trails. The model for places like the Great Himalayan National Park: attractive gateway villages like Bir on the edge, hundreds of kilometres of walking trails, campgrounds, and a little high-end lodging run by private operators under strict biodiversity contracts. He adds that Sikkim's Kangchenjunga reserve, about 2,000 of the state's 7,000 sq km, could be run jointly with Nepal's matching reserve.

head: Amit on the hypocrisy of complaining about crowds
more: Amit on the hypocrisy of complaining about crowds: 'the definition of too many tourists is a tourist who comes after me.'

head: Amit admits that while listening to Ajay talk with Shubham, his first thought was…
more: Amit admits that while listening to Ajay talk with Shubham, his first thought was 'episode!' Then he corrects himself: the proper phrase is 'knowledge to the world', not talk of churning out content.

head: Ajay's picture of an unmanaged Bir: five restaurants competing
more: Ajay's picture of an unmanaged Bir: five restaurants competing with 'five thousand watts and ten thousand watts' and lights 'blinking so that the aliens can see us from Alpha Centauri.'

more: Steven Pinker's 'nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them', which Amit applies to regions: each place has different natural knobs, so policy has to fit them.

more: John Maynard Keynes: after starting from freedom and identifying market failures, Ajay says, 'we would start like John Maynard Keynes and wonder' whether the state can add value.

head: The show's origin: at the Emergent Ventures conference in Udaipur, by a lake a year before launch, the hosts came up with two names
more: The show's origin: at the Emergent Ventures conference in Udaipur, by a lake a year before launch, the hosts came up with two names: 'Watching the Wheels', after a John Lennon song, and 'Everything is Everything', which Amit attributes to a Bruce Springsteen song.

head: Malini Goyal's line on Bangalore
more: Malini Goyal's line on Bangalore: 'the software is 5G, but the hardware is 2G.' Amit adds that in Bir the software is the hardware and needs to be made 5G.

head: Ajay calls Udaipur
more: Ajay calls Udaipur 'the Venice of the East', one of the most beautiful cities in the world, built on high-value tourism.
'You must learn to walk before you can run', a chapter title from Kelkar and Shah's In Service of the Republic, used to argue that urban reformers should start with small towns.

head: TIFR and BARC Began as Tata Projects
dek: State-run Indian science was a choice made after 1947, not a law of nature.
more: Ajay points out that two flagship institutions of post-independence Indian science, TIFR and BARC, started as private projects of the Tata group. After independence they were handed to the Union government, which funded them entirely and made their staff civil servants. That 'make' template was then repeated across ICMR, ICAR, DRDO, CSIR and ISRO: vertical government organisations, often sited away from economic centres, building things in-house.

State-run Indian science was a choice made after 1947, not a law of nature. Some of its most iconic public institutions were born private, which makes it easier to ask whether today's India needs a different model.

head: Israel's Blabbermouth Engineers vs Apple's Sealed Lips
dek: Knowledge spillovers are simply how human communities work. Unless you lock people in a vault in the desert, ideas leak.
more: Ajay contrasts two cultures. In Silicon Valley, NDAs and a commercial culture keep employees silent, so nobody outside knows what product Apple will announce next. Israel is the opposite: its scientists and engineers are said to be blabbermouths. Nearly all of them went through conscription, often including real fighting, and the bonds formed there cut across company lines. Every firm's knowledge quietly leaks to others through networks of army buddies.

Knowledge spillovers are simply how human communities work. Unless you lock people in a vault in the desert, ideas leak. That is why firms capture only part of what their research is worth, and why they underinvest in it.

head: NASA's 80/20 Pitch to Lawmakers
dek: NASA's greatness is largely a contracting machine. Sending most of the money out builds capability across the whole country, and it also makes the budget easier to defend politically.
more: NASA's founding paragraphs warned against building an in-house army and told the agency to contract out. It defends its budget by telling lawmakers that of every 100 it receives, 80 goes out to universities and private firms. It also contracts in stages by Technology Readiness Level. First come early concept documents from rival universities and firms, then design documents, then working demos tested in NASA's office, and finally production orders, such as 'build me five of these engines'.
NASA's greatness is largely a contracting machine. Sending most of the money out builds capability across the whole country, and it also makes the budget easier to defend politically.

head: How NASA Fathered the Semiconductor Industry
dek: Contracted-out public research by a demanding buyer can pull entire civilian industries into existence.
more: When integrated circuits first appeared, NASA was effectively the only buyer. On Earth, bulky circuit boards were fine, but spacecraft desperately needed miniaturisation. NASA 'smelled blood', and all the early IC firms ran on NASA contracts.

Contracted-out public research by a demanding buyer can pull entire civilian industries into existence. Today's CPUs trace back to NASA contracts, which shows how large the spillovers from the 'buy' model can be.

head: NASA's Control Room Sits Inside a Private University
dek: Contracting out is not just about outsourcing the canteen. The US hands even the crown jewels of space exploration to a university, and that scale of ambition is the hidden source of NASA's success.
more: The Jet Propulsion Laboratory is the nerve centre for all of NASA's interplanetary missions, the 'control room' for craft flying to Mars and Jupiter. It is not a government facility. It is a long-term NASA contract housed at Caltech, a private university, and it has been there since the 60s. Thousands of JPL staff sit physically next to Caltech's researchers, and coffee-table conversations benefit both sides.
Contracting out is not just about outsourcing the canteen. The US hands even the crown jewels of space exploration to a university, and that scale of ambition is the hidden source of NASA's success.

head: The Rafale Is a Private-Sector Fighter
dek: Even defence, the most state-centric domain, can run on a buy model, provided the legal instruments for sharing risk exist.
more: India does military R&D the 'make' way, through DRDO. France does most of its military R&D and production through corporations. The military sets a challenge ('I want ABCD capabilities') and private firms do the R&D under government contracts. Cost-plus contracts effectively pay for the private firm's risk-taking without being grants. The Rafale was designed and built this way.
Even defence, the most state-centric domain, can run on a buy model, provided the legal instruments for sharing risk exist.

head: NHAI: India Has Already Done Make-to-Buy Once
dek: Structural reform of the state is possible in India once leadership grasps the idea.
more: Asked why entrenched bureaucrats would ever give up their budgets and staff, Ajay offers the National Highways Authority of India. Highways used to be built by the Public Works Department. In the Vajpayee period, the leadership decided the government should instead give out contracts to private builders. NHAI was designed from day one as a 'buy' organisation, staffed with engineers and lawyers who write contracts rather than build roads. It still has not mastered PPP highways, but the shift happened.
Structural reform of the state is possible in India once leadership grasps the idea. It takes generations, but there is a working Indian precedent for exactly this transition.

head: How 200 Nazis Turned a Cow Town into an R&D Capital
dek: Talent compounds when planted in one place. Seed a town with a few remarkable people, give it generations, and the effect on local capability is enormous.
more: After World War II, the Americans and Soviets raced across occupied Europe for the German scientists behind the V-1 and V-2 missiles, and many scientists tried hard to end up in the West. But many were diehard Nazis who could not be trusted loose in society. So the US military dumped them in Huntsville, Alabama, an obscure town of cows and peasants, kept them in semi-imprisonment and built them a lab. Ajay notes this was 'make, not buy'. They put down roots and raised families, and their children competed in the local schools and drove up standards. Over a couple of generations Huntsville became one of the world's great scientific and engineering R&D capitals.
Talent compounds when planted in one place. Seed a town with a few remarkable people, give it generations, and the effect on local capability is enormous.

head: The Gandhians Who Chose One Village
dek: This is the Huntsville lesson from the opposite direction. A few committed people in one place, playing the long game, change outcomes for generations.
more: Ajay's father told him that after the British left, many people joined Nehru and others in building the Indian state. Others refused, saying they wanted to do good at the ground level instead. Individuals, or pairs of them, went to a single village each and dug in. Generations later those villages still show better hygiene, better education and a better status for women.
This is the Huntsville lesson from the opposite direction. A few committed people in one place, playing the long game, change outcomes for generations.

head: Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
by: RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
dek: It is clear, readable and rigorous, unlike most turgid academic papers.
more: It is clear, readable and rigorous, unlike most turgid academic papers. It lays out why the state should 'buy' rather than 'make' innovation and offers a concrete 20-year blueprint. Amit says that once you read it, the logic makes a lot of sense, even if you share his doubts about the 'why'.
The paper the whole episode is built around. Amit recommends it himself so Ajay can't 'cop out' by recommending his own paper.

head: How Innovation Works: And Why It Flourishes in Freedom
dek: Ridley shows innovation as a bottom-up process emerging from within society.
more: Ridley shows innovation as a bottom-up process emerging from within society. Amit thinks Ridley would share much of his skepticism about top-down innovation policy, so it is a good counterweight to the paper.
Amit's second end-of-episode recommendation.

dek: Ajay calls it 'stirring' and 'goosebumps material': a dream of building India on rationalism, beyond superstition, with science as a way of life.
more: Ajay calls it 'stirring' and 'goosebumps material': a dream of building India on rationalism, beyond superstition, with science as a way of life. Its dream remains worth honouring even if the 1947-era methods need rethinking.
Ajay opens with it as the founding charter of India's post-independence scientific project. The paper quotes it at length in its conclusion.

head: When Ideas Have Sex
dek: Contracting research out to universities and firms gets ideas mixing across society, which is exactly the recombination Ridley describes and exactly what you want.
more: Contracting research out to universities and firms gets ideas mixing across society, which is exactly the recombination Ridley describes and exactly what you want.

head: Knowledge Spillovers: The Market Failure Behind Innovation Policy
dek: By default, a free society innovates on its own.
more: By default, a free society innovates on its own. But innovators capture only part of the gains, because knowledge leaks through publications, patents (which are disclosure documents), reverse-engineered machines and people talking to friends. If society gains 100 and the innovator keeps 40, private actors underinvest. The case for the state is to tax and then spend in ways that maximise spillovers, closing the gap: for example, from roughly 60 in private spending up to the socially right level of 100.

head: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
dek: Amit's framework: the state exists on taxes extracted by coercion, so every action has a moral cost.
more: Amit's framework: the state exists on taxes extracted by coercion, so every action has a moral cost. Ceding some rights to the state so it can protect our rights is the 'great liberal paradox'. Political philosophies differ mainly on when that coercion is justified. Positive externalities exist almost everywhere, so pointing to one is not enough to justify state action.

head: Reduce the Scope, Increase the Strength
dek: Amit wants a state that does a few things well, like rule of law, defence and city management, rather than many things badly.
more: Amit wants a state that does a few things well, like rule of law, defence and city management, rather than many things badly. A space programme beats building statues, but it ranks below the basics. Ajay agrees on focus: leadership attention is finite, and spreading it across many projects degrades all of them.

head: One Rupee Spent Costs Three
dek: Kelkar and Shah estimate that every rupee the government raises costs about three rupees of GDP.
more: Kelkar and Shah estimate that every rupee the government raises costs about three rupees of GDP. The cost comes from collection, compliance (lawyers, accountants) and above all from people distorting their behaviour to avoid taxes. So spending should stop when the last rupee no longer returns three rupees to society. Amit adds a caveat: a 3x return is not sufficient on its own, because the people who pay and the people who benefit differ. Taking a rupee from him to make three for someone else is not acceptable to him.

head: The Seen and the Unseen of Nehruvian Science
dek: Ajay argues that post-independence investment in science and higher education (IIT Bombay in 1957) seeded India's IT industry, now its greatest industry.
more: Ajay argues that post-independence investment in science and higher education (IIT Bombay in 1957) seeded India's IT industry, now its greatest industry. Amit, borrowing Bastiat, accepts that this is the seen effect. The unseen effects are what that money would have done if left with the poor it was taken from, and the cost of the top-down technocratic mindset that kept hundreds of millions in poverty for decades.

head: Free-Ride Gratefully; Fund Only What Is Uniquely Indian
dek: India should free-ride shamelessly on the trillions the West spends on R&D: the transistor, Unix, thermodynamics, cheap solar panels, the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine (Covishield).
more: India should free-ride shamelessly on the trillions the West spends on R&D: the transistor, Unix, thermodynamics, cheap solar panels, the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine (Covishield). State money belongs on problems nobody else will solve. Examples are COVID transmission in hot, humid, open Indian homes, drones that fly in Ladakh's thin air, vaccines for tropical diseases like malaria and chikungunya, and most of the humanities and social sciences. Amit notes this is the converse of subsidiarity: take everything you can from the world, and build locally only what the world won't.

head: Social Science Requires Detachment from Your Tribe
dek: Ajay quotes Heisenberg: every electron is the same, but every love is different.
more: Ajay quotes Heisenberg: every electron is the same, but every love is different. The humanities and social sciences are contextual, so India must grow its own scholars. The hard part is studying your own society coldly, without advocacy or tribal loyalty.

head: Make vs Buy in State R&D
dek: Like a firm deciding between running its own canteen and hiring a caterer (and then policing the contract), the state can do research in-house in vertical organisations like ISRO, DRDO and CSIR, or contract it out to universities, public or private, and firms.
more: Like a firm deciding between running its own canteen and hiring a caterer (and then policing the contract), the state can do research in-house in vertical organisations like ISRO, DRDO and CSIR, or contract it out to universities, public or private, and firms. Since the market failure is about spillovers, 'make' defeats the purpose: knowledge stays sealed inside the state. 'Buy' plants labs in universities and firms, where PhD students carry knowledge out, teaching spreads it, and firms find civilian uses.

head: Research Means Risk, and Governments Hate Risk
dek: If failure is impossible, it is development, not research. Research needs many rival pathways, some of which will fail.
more: If failure is impossible, it is development, not research. Research needs many rival pathways, some of which will fail. Inside government, approval processes lock onto one path, insiders snuff out rivals, and auditors treat failure as wrongdoing. Contracting out lets the state fund, say, six rival COVID vaccine teams and double down on the two that work. Even if the only goal were landing a craft on the moon, 'buy' would get there cheaper and faster.

head: Invisible Infrastructure
dek: Amit's worry is that US examples work because of contracting capability and rule of law; NASA and NIH see remarkably few fraud cases.
more: Amit's worry is that US examples work because of contracting capability and rule of law; NASA and NIH see remarkably few fraud cases. In India, research scholars wait years for grants, and contracting out could become a crony gravy train. Ajay agrees this needs a multi-generation build, and argues that space excellence is really contracting excellence: the US equivalents of the GFR made NASA possible.

head: Politicians Are the Entrepreneurs
dek: Officials who control budgets and subordinates have every reason to resist giving work away.
more: Officials who control budgets and subordinates have every reason to resist giving work away. Citing Kelkar, Ajay argues change must come from political leadership: ideas circulate in public discourse, bubble up to leaders, and leaders drive gradual change. NHAI under Vajpayee is the proof of concept.

head: A 20-Year Blueprint for Contracting Out Science
dek: The paper writes 'drafting instructions' for three pillars. First, add chapters to the General Financial Rules, which today assume risk-free purchases, to allow grants and cost-plus contracts.
more: The paper writes 'drafting instructions' for three pillars. First, add chapters to the General Financial Rules, which today assume risk-free purchases, to allow grants and cost-plus contracts. Second, write contracting out into each organisation's founding document, so auditors can't ask 'why did you contract out?'. Third, build manuals and teams that combine scientific, engineering and legal skills. Since only about five big organisations matter, reform one or two of them and create one or two new ones: an Indian NIH for health research financing and a DARPA-like agency. ISRO could then move gradually toward NASA-like levels of 60-80% contracted out.

head: The opener.
more: The opener. Amit: 'I am an organic human being... Organic matter, it's a great weakness, I know, but that's who I am.' Ajay, by contrast, is a 'bionic man' with a metal rod in his bone since a crash at nineteen and a new titanium jaw implant. Ajay: 'Sadly, no batteries and no CPUs.' The metal sets airport security screaming, so he prefers half-sleeve shirts when flying.

head: Ajay on risk-taking under audit
more: Ajay on risk-taking under audit: 'How will you explain to the CAG, we tried this and it did not work? ... You paid salaries, you purchased so many parts... and in the end nothing worked. Okay, how can it be? We should have a CBI investigation.' He blames the 'Stalinist idea in government' that everything always works correctly.

head: Amit on research scholars waiting years for grant money
more: Amit on research scholars waiting years for grant money: 'our invisible infrastructure is invisible because it is non-existent.'

head: Ajay's Huntsville moral: 200 Nazis dropped into a…
more: Ajay's Huntsville moral: 200 Nazis dropped into a 'tiny hick town filled with cows and peasants, in three generations, it turns into magic.' Amit replies: 'I hope it's not leading to a normative place. Let's find 200 Nazis and round them up, though it won't be as difficult as it seems in the current day.'

head: Amit recommends Ajay's paper himself
more: Amit recommends Ajay's paper himself: 'this paper by these three people. I don't know if you've heard of them.' He explains he did it so Ajay can't 'do the cop out of saying my recommendation is my paper.'

head: Rain starts mid-recording and Amit launches a pop quiz
more: Rain starts mid-recording and Amit launches a pop quiz: 'Why does it always rain on me?' Ajay: 'I don't know.' Amit supplies Travis and his favourite line, 'Is it because I lied when I was seventeen?', then follows with 'I'm only happy when it rains' (Garbage).

head: The NASA section ends with a twist on the familiar
more: The NASA section ends with a twist on the familiar 'what happens here stays here' line: 'What happens in NASA doesn't stay in NASA.'

head: Frédéric Bastiat's
more: Frédéric Bastiat's 'the seen and the unseen': Amit borrows the phrase to argue that the IT boom seeded by Nehru-era science is the seen effect, while the coerced money and the top-down mindset are the unseen costs.

head: Heisenberg, as quoted by Ajay
more: Heisenberg, as quoted by Ajay: 'every electron is the same and every love is different.' He uses it to explain why physics travels across borders but the humanities and social sciences must be built at home.

head: Matt Ridley's
more: Matt Ridley's 'When Ideas Have Sex', which Amit invokes for what happens when research is spread across universities and firms instead of sealed inside the state.

head: Why stock prices rose during the COVID catastrophe
dek: Stock prices carry real information, but much of what moves an index is the discount rate, not the health of the economy.
more: Ajay warns against reading the stock market index as a report card on the economy or the government. His example is COVID. It was a terrible catastrophe, yet when the US Fed and the RBI cut rates sharply, stock prices went up. Firms were not suddenly better run. Markets were simply discounting future cash flows at a new, lower interest rate.

Stock prices carry real information, but much of what moves an index is the discount rate, not the health of the economy. A country therefore has no clean daily scorecard the way a firm does. Policymakers are partly flying blind.

head: Amit's personal rules (rules vs deals, applied to life)
dek: Deciding in advance how you'll handle a whole class of situations saves mental energy and prevents mistakes, just as a state should run on rules rather than case-by-case bargains.
more: Taking Ajay's rules-vs-deals frame down to the individual, Amit shares two rules he lives by. First, he avoids negativity: people who complain about others and take a victimhood attitude instead of a can-do one are best avoided, in real life and on Twitter. Second, when he is with someone, he tries to listen and understand their story instead of making himself the centre of it. He admits he doesn't always succeed.
Deciding in advance how you'll handle a whole class of situations saves mental energy and prevents mistakes, just as a state should run on rules rather than case-by-case bargains.

head: The Warhol: a quiz question you can work out
dek: Amit's philosophy of quizzing: a good question rewards reasoning rather than recall, which makes it fun even for people who aren't trivia buffs.
more: Prompted by talk of celebrity culture, Amit reads out a question he set about 15 years ago and later used in a column on quizzing: 'X is a unit of hype. One kilo X is equal to 10.42 days. One mega X is equal to 28.5 years. What is X?' Ajay works it out live. One X is about 0.01 days, roughly 864 seconds. Amit nudges him to round up to fifteen minutes, and Ajay gets it: Andy Warhol, who said everyone will be famous for fifteen minutes. So X is a Warhol. Ajay then counters with his own puzzle, the millihelen.
Amit's philosophy of quizzing: a good question rewards reasoning rather than recall, which makes it fun even for people who aren't trivia buffs.

head: The essay-length test for opinions
dek: A practical filter against the halo effect and Twitter-style hot takes: speak only on what you have actually studied well enough to argue at length.
more: While discussing the halo effect, Amit recalls a group conversation from earlier that day. Someone kept offering half-baked opinions, and Amit spontaneously laid down a rule: if you state an opinion, you should be able to defend it with an essay-length argument. He admits it sounds extreme, but says there is too much cheap opinion around, much of it received wisdom or tribal allegiance.
A practical filter against the halo effect and Twitter-style hot takes: speak only on what you have actually studied well enough to argue at length.
printed: Argue it at length or hush

head: Withholding judgment on Alice Munro
dek: We usually know only one version of a messy human story. Honest suspension of judgment, without excusing the wrong, is often wiser than a rush to condemn or defend.
more: News broke that Alice Munro's daughter had said Munro's second husband abused her when she was nine, and that Munro turned a blind eye. Before Amit's flight to DC, Shruti Rajagopalan, a fellow Munro fan, messaged him, disturbed. On the flight he was reading David Brooks's How to Know a Person, which discusses Vivian Gornick's Fierce Attachments: a mother and daughter who understand each other completely and yet not at all. Amit decided to keep loving Munro's work and withhold judgment on her. He still says she clearly did something wrong in minimising her daughter's grief. He separates art from artist, though he adds there are some writers, like Pablo Neruda, he will never read because he knows too much about them.
We usually know only one version of a messy human story. Honest suspension of judgment, without excusing the wrong, is often wiser than a rush to condemn or defend.
printed: The other stories we don’t know

Ajay recalls Amit shaking his head at how it could ever be done.

more: It describes three designs of a firm and how maturing means dispersed shareholding, a powerful board, and a management team accountable to it.
Ajay on dispersion of power within firms.

more: The source of his starfish-vs-octopus image: a diverse country needs many thinking people spread around, not one central brain.
Ajay on decentralised power in firms operating in a heterogeneous India.

more: Part of the show's body of work on firms, the first F of the light triad.
Among the 'many episodes on firms' Amit promises to link in the intro.
