dek: A deeper treatment of subsidiarity: each city knows best what it should do for itself.
more: A deeper treatment of subsidiarity: each city knows best what it should do for itself.
Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's argument for splitting the state into union, state, city and village governments.

head: The Art of Podcasting (Episode 49)
dek: It covers the lessons about conversation and listening that made How to Know a Person resonate with him.
more: It covers the lessons about conversation and listening that made How to Know a Person resonate with him.
Linked when Amit says Brooks's book echoes what he learned from long-form podcasting.

head: A country is not a company
dek: Firms are the source of prosperity, so it feels intuitive that a successful CEO or consultant could run a country.
more: Firms are the source of prosperity, so it feels intuitive that a successful CEO or consultant could run a country. That is a fallacy rooted in top-down instincts that evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes. Running a state differs in its feedback loops, guaranteed survival, coercive power, complexity, rules vs deals, dispersion of power and time horizons.

head: Firms are cells, the economy is the organism
dek: An analogy a friend gave Ajay. The economy is the sum of its firms' productivity, so there is no prosperity without high-productivity firms, just as a body needs healthy cells.
more: An analogy a friend gave Ajay. The economy is the sum of its firms' productivity, so there is no prosperity without high-productivity firms, just as a body needs healthy cells. But understanding the whole organism is a different body of knowledge from studying one cell at a time.

head: Firms get slapped into shape; governments fly blind
dek: Firms see daily stock prices, weekly production numbers, monthly profits and market share, so mistakes show up within months and managers can keep debugging.
more: Firms see daily stock prices, weekly production numbers, monthly profits and market share, so mistakes show up within months and managers can keep debugging. Government has no such loop. The stock index isn't a report card, GDP arrives quarterly with a lag and is badly measured in India, and elections come every five years and turn on base passions. Political feedback also rewards the wrong things: a farm loan waiver wins votes now and can be 'a necessary anesthetic, but it is not the structural change you need.' Constant state and local elections push towards short-termism.

head: Social science is a coin in a stormy swimming pool
dek: Shruti Rajagopalan's analogy, which Amit thinks may come from Don Boudreaux.
more: Shruti Rajagopalan's analogy, which Amit thinks may come from Don Boudreaux. Testing whether a coin displaces water is easy in a lab beaker. Social science is like dropping the coin into a giant crowded pool in a storm, with forty people swimming and throwing things. Everything is multicausal, so governments can't run clean A/B tests the way a business choosing between polyester blends can.
printed: A penny in a stormy pool

head: The state can't go bankrupt
dek: The threat of bankruptcy disciplines every firm. A CBI, RBI, SEBI or ministry is guaranteed to exist however badly it performs.
more: The threat of bankruptcy disciplines every firm. A CBI, RBI, SEBI or ministry is guaranteed to exist however badly it performs. For many state bodies the right metaphor for monopoly power is not supernormal profits but unquestioned access to coercive power. Losing the fear of death breeds complacence and misbehaviour.

head: Monopoly and failure are state problems, not market problems
dek: Amit argues that monopolies don't arise under genuine free-market competition.
more: Amit argues that monopolies don't arise under genuine free-market competition. They come either from state interference that shields a crony, or from the state itself: violence, money, and the many monopolies it sets up. Likewise, market failure is rare while government failure is ubiquitous, because of the state's incentives and structure. Meanwhile, competing private firms deliver Schumpeter's creative destruction.

head: Coercion is core to the state
dek: A firm is a bundle of voluntary contracts with customers, employees and other firms; firms that hire goons are a scummy minority who belong in jail.
more: A firm is a bundle of voluntary contracts with customers, employees and other firms; firms that hire goons are a scummy minority who belong in jail. Following Max Weber's definition of the state as a monopoly of physical violence in a territory, the state is inherently coercive. So lessons from running firms don't carry over, and as Lord Acton warned, the same person will face very different incentives at the head of government.

head: Voluntary exchange: the double thank you and the market as conversation
dek: Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off, which is how economies grow.
more: Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off, which is how economies grow. Amit also pictures the market as a vast conversation: firms pitch to customers, rivals offer to serve them better, and teams inside firms tweak designs, all of which helps people serve others and understand themselves better. The state has no need to hold that conversation; it can simply take.

head: The complexity gap
dek: Even a large firm is simple next to a government spread across countless departments and offices, often with conflicting objectives, all interacting with society.
more: Even a large firm is simple next to a government spread across countless departments and offices, often with conflicting objectives, all interacting with society. Ajay, who has worked in both worlds, says you must scale back your ambition of even measuring and understanding government, let alone changing it.

head: Don't trade the real target for easy wins
dek: Because big problems are complex and progress can't be attributed quickly, many in development and policy retreat to small problems they can solve with an RCT and claim credit for.
more: Because big problems are complex and progress can't be attributed quickly, many in development and policy retreat to small problems they can solve with an RCT and claim credit for. These don't move the needle on poverty. Amit's advice to young people in the ideas and policy world: resist easy wins pursued for career advancement or self-gratification.

head: Bias for action: an open disagreement
dek: Ajay is uneasy with the startup slogan even for firms: thinking is precious, and shooting first is superficial.
more: Ajay is uneasy with the startup slogan even for firms: thinking is precious, and shooting first is superficial. In government it is 'truly dangerous'. You must identify the market failure, find the lowest-cost intervention, reshape incentives and negotiate the political economy. Amit agrees about the state but insists firms need a bias for action, since great companies iterate and pivot, and thinkers like Jeff Bezos combined action with deep thought. They agree it's not a binary; the real enemy is reflexive short-termism.

head: Rules, not deals
dek: A small firm can live deal to deal as a hustler. A large one like McDonald's must move to standard contracts with franchisees, or it collapses into complexity and corruption.
more: A small firm can live deal to deal as a hustler. A large one like McDonald's must move to standard contracts with franchisees, or it collapses into complexity and corruption. The state, the most complex organisation of all, must run on rules. That gives policy coherence across its many arms and over time, and it lets private actors plan for the long term. Article 14 also requires equal treatment. The state's job is to set stable rules that reshape incentives, not to make steel or cut individual bargains.

head: Dispersion of power
dek: A friend's image: a tiny firm is cooking, with one cook choosing every ingredient.
more: A friend's image: a tiny firm is cooking, with one cook choosing every ingredient. A growing firm is gardening: you create conditions, culture, incentives and checks, and run a portfolio of bets. In a country as diverse as India, a firm should be an octopus with many thinking nodes, not a starfish with one brain. For the state there is no option. Power is deliberately split into legislature, executive and judiciary, and into union, state, city and village governments under the subsidiarity principle.

head: The personalisation fallacy
dek: An autocratic firm costs society little, since fifty rivals will serve customers and the firm learns or dies.
more: An autocratic firm costs society little, since fifty rivals will serve customers and the firm learns or dies. But we wrongly credit a superstar CEO like Jack Welch for what a large, dispersed organisation achieved. We do the same with heads of government, praising or opposing a leader for outcomes that came from the wider policy ecosystem.

head: Time horizons and the inexorable policy pipeline
dek: High cost of capital in India's weak financial system makes firms short-sighted: in a net present value calculation with a high rate, the future barely counts, and owners expect to sell within three years.
more: High cost of capital in India's weak financial system makes firms short-sighted: in a net present value calculation with a high rate, the future barely counts, and owners expect to sell within three years. Government must play a hundred-year game to close the 9x per-capita GDP gap with America. Reform moves through a pipeline: data, research, theories of change, public debate, expert committees, drafting laws, then building state capacity. It takes 10 to 20 years, a rhythm most private-sector people aren't used to.

head: Live by the longest and shortest time horizons
dek: Amit's personal application. Think about your life as a whole rather than chasing one immediate gratification after another, but recognise that life is a succession of days.
more: Amit's personal application. Think about your life as a whole rather than chasing one immediate gratification after another, but recognise that life is a succession of days. He used to fixate on awards to win and books to write. Grand goals are toxic, because achieving them only reveals grander ones. Echoing Annie Dillard, a day is your life: build the best possible day and a great life follows.

head: Politics, governance and policy are different games
dek: Running a firm well doesn't disqualify someone from governing. Flexible thinkers like Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant or Jeff Bezos could retool, but must change how they think.
more: Running a firm well doesn't disqualify someone from governing. Flexible thinkers like Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant or Jeff Bezos could retool, but must change how they think. Equally, politicians who have mastered the game of retail politics often arrive in government with no feel for governance (substance over narrative, working with people, understanding institutions) or for the economy. Citizens should hold everyone to high standards.

head: The halo effect
dek: Ajay admires India's post-1990s business, consulting and finance talent as world-class, yet warns against assuming it transfers to public policy.
more: Ajay admires India's post-1990s business, consulting and finance talent as world-class, yet warns against assuming it transfers to public policy. Amit names the bias: excellence in one field creates a halo, so people assume you're expert elsewhere, like a microbiologist dispensing wisdom on all of medicine. His antidote is to opine only on what you've studied.

head: Democracy is not a marketplace
dek: At a restaurant, everyone orders what they like from the menu. In a democracy, if three vote for seafood, the fourth eats it or goes hungry, even if allergic to prawns.
more: At a restaurant, everyone orders what they like from the menu. In a democracy, if three vote for seafood, the fourth eats it or goes hungry, even if allergic to prawns. The 'political marketplace' metaphor breaks down because democracy risks majoritarianism. Hence the need for a republic, with a constitution protecting individuals and minorities from the state.

head: Amit opens by contrasting the dark triad (
more: Amit opens by contrasting the dark triad ('the three characteristics that make up serial killers') with a 'light triad' of three Fs: 'firms, finance, and freedom'. He then nominates a bad F: 'Fallacy should be part of the dark triad of bad economic thinking. We'll figure out the other two Fs later.'

head: Ajay on a government-created monopoly that blocks private and foreign competitors
more: Ajay on a government-created monopoly that blocks private and foreign competitors: 'this is the new Air India. It will sit here, it will lord over the society and people will clap saying, Oh, it is so great India now has planes.' Amit notes that it sounds dystopian, except it's real.

head: Ajay, deflating the…
more: Ajay, deflating the 'China model' buzz: 'There is nothing a Fortune 500 company CEO wants to do more than to fly into a third world country, shake hands with a strong man, and make a deal.' People call this decisive government; he says it should embarrass us.

head: Ajay's dry aside on India's layers of government
more: Ajay's dry aside on India's layers of government: 'a union government and a little confused creature called a state government and a city government or a village government.'

head: After the hosts can't settle the bias-for-action debate, Amit invites viewers to ask for a full episode on it
more: After the hosts can't settle the bias-for-action debate, Amit invites viewers to ask for a full episode on it: 'Though Ajay might say, Let us not do it. That will be bias for action.'

head: Amit's jab at development economists who pick easy problems: they run an RCT, declare
more: Amit's jab at development economists who pick easy problems: they run an RCT, declare 'I have solved it', and say 'give me credit for it, give me a Nobel prize', while poverty doesn't budge.

head: The celebrity exchange.
more: The celebrity exchange. Ajay: 'In the modern celebrity culture, a company is like a country.' Amit: 'Are you a celebrity? Of course not. You're not a celebrity. Readers kindly comment and let us know if that is true.' Ajay: 'A celebrity is one who is famous for being famous. A celebrity is one whose name is worth more than her services.'

head: Ajay's counter-puzzle to Amit's Warhol quiz
more: Ajay's counter-puzzle to Amit's Warhol quiz: 'What is a millihelen?' Helen's was 'the beauty that launched a thousand ships. So millihelen is the beauty that will launch one ship.' Amit: 'Nice one.'

head: Amit says a flexible-minded business leader could learn to govern
more: Amit says a flexible-minded business leader could learn to govern, 'But your standard issue McKinsey consultant will just fuck it up.'

head: Amit on his rule of listening rather than making himself the centre
more: Amit on his rule of listening rather than making himself the centre: 'one is male and hardwired like a male, we are the center of the universe, but one can make an effort.'

head: Andy Warhol's line that everyone in the world will be famous for fifteen minutes: the basis of Amit's
more: Andy Warhol's line that everyone in the world will be famous for fifteen minutes: the basis of Amit's 'unit of hype', the Warhol, in which a kilo-Warhol is 10.42 days.

head: Lord Acton's
more: Lord Acton's 'power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely', which Amit uses to explain why the same person behaves differently at the head of a firm and of a government.

head: Annie Dillard
more: Annie Dillard: 'How you spend your days is, of course, how you spend your life', Amit's corrective to chasing grand goals.

head: Pablo Neruda: Amit separates art from artist, but names Neruda as someone he will never read
more: Pablo Neruda: Amit separates art from artist, but names Neruda as someone he will never read 'because I know too much about them.'

head: The girl who learned to write on her mother's gravestone
dek: The image sets up the episode: two outlaws, mother and daughter, linked by loss and by books, each radical in an age that wasn't ready for her.
more: Amit opens with a quiz, reading a passage he wrote. In early-nineteenth-century London, a man walks his young daughter to the churchyard at St Pancras, to the grave of her mother, who died of an infection days after giving birth to her. The girl traces the inscribed letters with her finger and learns to write that way. For years afterwards she returns alone to read beside the grave, carrying guilt that her birth killed her mother. Ajay guesses Mary Wollstonecraft, who is the mother. The girl is Mary Shelley. Amit admits the scene may be romanticised, but both women wrote books that changed the world.
The image sets up the episode: two outlaws, mother and daughter, linked by loss and by books, each radical in an age that wasn't ready for her.

head: Wollstonecraft meets Locke next door, and the backlash
dek: One chance encounter with the right book can redirect a life.
more: Wollstonecraft was born in 1759 into a world where wives couldn't own property or initiate divorce and husbands could legally beat them. She was one of seven children of an alcoholic, violent father. Her escape came through a neighbour, Reverend Henry Clare, who introduced her to John Locke. There was no internet and few bookshops then, so you stumbled on such ideas by accident. Locke's language of equal rights for 'all men' made her ask where women stood. She answered Burke's defence of tradition and aristocracy with A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790), then wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792). The reaction was scathing. Thomas Taylor mocked it with 'A Vindication of the Rights of Brutes', arguing that if women could have rights, so could animals. Horace Walpole called her a 'hyena in petticoats'.

One chance encounter with the right book can redirect a life. A principle's logic can also run further than its authors intended: Wollstonecraft simply took Locke's equality at face value, and that alone made her an outlaw.

head: Walking in the rain before jumping into the Thames
dek: Behind the famous treatise was a life of real torment, because being ahead of your time meant living without social cover.
more: After an affair with a lover who proved unfaithful, and a child born outside marriage, a despairing Wollstonecraft decided to drown herself in the Thames. It was raining. She walked up and down for half an hour first so that her clothes would grow heavy and she would sink. Her suicide letter to the lover, reproduced in her collected letters, says she chose the Thames because no one who goes in comes out alive. A bystander saw her and rescued her. She later married the philosopher William Godwin and died eleven days after giving birth to their daughter. The cause was an infection Amit traces to a doctor who did not wash his hands.

Behind the famous treatise was a life of real torment, because being ahead of your time meant living without social cover. Her death also starts the thread of unwashed hands that the episode later pulls through Semmelweis.

head: An eighteen-year-old invents science fiction with no template
dek: Inventing without a template is a different order of achievement. The clumsiness and clichés modern readers notice are the marks of someone building the road as she walked it.
more: Mary Godwin grew up in her father's intellectual salon and ran away with the already-married Percy Shelley. Around 1816 she sat by a fire with Shelley, Lord Byron and John Polidori, trading ideas for books. Polidori described the anatomist William Lawrence's lectures arguing there is no soul, only the body's organs. Percy, obsessed with Promethean themes, wondered whether humans had created God. Mary had grown up on Milton's Paradise Lost, and she fused these influences into Frankenstein. She was eighteen. Science fiction did not exist as a genre and she had no craft models, yet she told the story through three nested voices (a ship's captain, Frankenstein and the monster) in an age of omniscient narrators. The book was ignored, and people assumed her husband had written it. Percy contributed perhaps 4,000 of its 78,000 words, and Amit says those passages stand out as the bad writing.
Inventing without a template is a different order of achievement. The clumsiness and clichés modern readers notice are the marks of someone building the road as she walked it.

head: Semmelweis: the man who solved childbed fever and died in an asylum
dek: Being right without a mechanism, in a way that insults the status of the people you must persuade, is a near-fatal combination.
more: Ignaz Semmelweis was born in 1818, the year of Frankenstein. He switched from law to medicine and in 1846 joined Vienna General Hospital as an obstetric assistant. One maternity ward had 10% mortality and the other 4%, and women begged to be kept out of the first. He ruled out overcrowding, since the safer ward was more crowded, and weather, since the wards were next to each other. The clue came when a colleague died after a scalpel nick with the same symptoms as childbed fever. Staff in Ward One also worked on corpses before examining mothers. Semmelweis made them wash in a chlorinated solution. Deaths fell from 18% in one recorded month to two percent, then one, and to zero within two years. But germ theory did not yet exist, so he could not explain why it worked, and he never published. Doctors took offence at being called unclean. He was sacked over departmental politics and had to move countries. In 1865 he was lured into an asylum, beaten by guards and locked in a straitjacket in a dark cell. He died two weeks later of a gangrenous arm.
Being right without a mechanism, in a way that insults the status of the people you must persuade, is a near-fatal combination. The story comes full circle: unwashed hands killed Wollstonecraft too.

head: The doctor who believed Semmelweis
dek: Some true ideas are resisted because accepting them means accepting guilt for past harm.
more: One German physician Semmelweis reached actually accepted the handwashing finding. He then realised that a loved one, a cousin or similar, had died after he attended her without washing his hands. Understanding that he had unknowingly killed her, he took his own life. Ajay voices the reflex of the doctors who refused to listen: 'Am I being blamed for all the deaths that came before?'
Some true ideas are resisted because accepting them means accepting guilt for past harm.

head: Scurvy and the decades-long gap
dek: Discovery is often not the bottleneck; adoption is. Even a cheap, proven fix can sit unused for a generation.
more: Ajay recalls the tidy childhood version of scurvy. Sailors died in agony until it turned out that carrying preserved lime fixed the problem, because all they lacked was vitamin C. But when you check the dates, decades passed between the discovery and its wider adoption.
Discovery is often not the bottleneck; adoption is. Even a cheap, proven fix can sit unused for a generation.

head: Wegener stares at a map until the continents move
dek: The evidence was in front of everyone; it took one person to look and decades for the field to catch up.
more: Alfred Wegener got his idea by looking at a map. The east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa fit like jigsaw pieces. He turned this into testable claims: the same fossils and the same rock formations should appear on both sides. He found both, then similar matches elsewhere, and proposed that a single supercontinent, Pangaea, had split apart. His peers asked what force could possibly move continents. His 1912 book was met with derision, and he died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. Only in the 1960s did plate tectonics win acceptance. Ajay remembers his father treating it as hot new science, including the idea that India broke off near Madagascar and smashed into Eurasia, pushing up the Himalayas.

The evidence was in front of everyone; it took one person to look and decades for the field to catch up. Amit adds that Wegener was no outsider but a working geologist, punished for stepping past convention.

head: Boltzmann misses his vindication by a few years
dek: Vindication can arrive just after the person is gone. Ajay's broader point: being a maverick is a lonely psycho-social battle against jobs, careers and an establishment, while the warm comfort is to go with the flow.
more: In the 1860s and 1870s Boltzmann helped move physics from the kinetic theory of gases, where molecules are deterministic hard dots, to statistical mechanics. It used probability throughout to link microscopic states to measurable quantities like temperature and entropy. The theory predicted well, but no microscope of the day could show an atom, so sceptics asked whether anyone had ever seen one. He struggled for jobs, was thrown out of his home university in Vienna, and killed himself in 1906. That was a couple of years before the world accepted he was right. Ajay says these stories come from Jacob Bronowski's The Ascent of Man.

Vindication can arrive just after the person is gone. Ajay's broader point: being a maverick is a lonely psycho-social battle against jobs, careers and an establishment, while the warm comfort is to go with the flow.

head: Mendel's print run of forty
dek: The economics of distribution once decided which ideas spread. A world-changing result could be stuck at forty copies, read by people who couldn't see its importance.
more: Mendel was an obscure monk in Austria who tried to turn breeders' intuitions about inheritance into laws. He was lucky to choose a simple plant, the pea, and his results marked one of the great moments in science. But printing was expensive: the run for his paper was 40 copies, all he could afford, and he mailed them to a few people. Those who read it shrugged that plant breeding was nothing new, and missed what it meant.
The economics of distribution once decided which ideas spread. A world-changing result could be stuck at forty copies, read by people who couldn't see its importance.

head: Darwin's 22-year delay and Wallace's malaria
dek: Caution and boldness both have costs: Darwin's perfectionism nearly cost him priority, as with Newton and Leibniz.
more: Darwin sailed on the Beagle collecting specimens, and by 1837, thinking about the creatures of the Galapagos, he grasped evolution. He immediately saw it as a personal disaster, because telling the world God did not create us would bring everyone down on him. So he spent some 22 years polishing his book. Meanwhile Alfred Russel Wallace, delirious with malaria in the jungles of Indonesia, cracked the same theory from scratch. Having a bias for action, he came home ready to present. Friends who knew of Darwin's secret project arranged a simultaneous presentation in 1859. Even then evolution lacked a mechanism, as critics demanded to be shown where the code of the finch was written. Only near the end of the century did people join it to Mendel's genetics, giving biology its first real theory.

Caution and boldness both have costs: Darwin's perfectionism nearly cost him priority, as with Newton and Leibniz. Big theories sometimes need two outlaws' halves, separated by decades, to fit together.

head: Cholera, a well and caste
dek: Data can expose a society's structure as sharply as a disease's route.
more: In mid-nineteenth-century London, John Snow worked out that cholera spreads through water. The finding met resistance for decades, especially in India. Near the end of the century another investigator mapped cholera deaths in an Indian village and found that most victims were upper caste. They drew from a contaminated well that lower castes were barred from using. The only lower-caste victim was the washerman who washed their clothes. Amit credits Chinmay Tumbe's Age of Pandemics for the story.
Data can expose a society's structure as sharply as a disease's route. Here exclusion ironically protected the excluded, and even so clear a link took decades to be accepted.

head: Karikó's years of 'no, no, no'
dek: Amit then turns the story around. We only hear about the outlaws who were eventually vindicated, while many others were right, ignored and never redeemed.
more: Katalin Karikó's early mRNA research was treated as a fringe joke. She applied for grant after grant and was rejected every time. The University of Pennsylvania told her she was not of faculty quality. Years later, as Amit puts it, the moment met the woman: mRNA vaccines proved a miracle, and in a sense she saved the planet.
Amit then turns the story around. We only hear about the outlaws who were eventually vindicated, while many others were right, ignored and never redeemed.

head: The population column and reflexive rage
dek: Once a belief becomes part of the self, disagreement feels like aggression.
more: When Amit wrote a column arguing that population is a strength rather than a problem, many readers reacted with instant anger and abuse instead of engaging with the argument. His reading is that school had taught them population is India's problem. They had folded that belief into their identity, so they experienced his argument as an attack on themselves.
Once a belief becomes part of the self, disagreement feels like aggression. That is one answer to why the conventional-minded turn aggressive.

head: Romantic Outlaws
dek: A joint biography of mother and daughter that vividly shows how hostile their world was to women.
more: A joint biography of mother and daughter that vividly shows how hostile their world was to women. Animals gained legal protection in 1824, twenty years before the first law limiting violence against women.
Amit calls it the first recommendation of the day; it supplied most of his material on Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley, and he reads passages from it.

head: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
dek: The founding protofeminist text, written with no role models. It argues that a false education makes women slaves of the male gaze, and it grounds virtue in reason rather than religion or tradition.
more: The founding protofeminist text, written with no role models. It argues that a false education makes women slaves of the male gaze, and it grounds virtue in reason rather than religion or tradition. It may read tame today, so read it against its time.
Discussed at length; Amit reads passages and notes the show has recommended it before.

head: Frankenstein
dek: An eighteen-year-old wrote it with no genre and no craft models. Brian Aldiss called it the first science fiction book.
more: An eighteen-year-old wrote it with no genre and no craft models. Brian Aldiss called it the first science fiction book. Its three-narrator nested structure was innovative, and its question, whether the beings we create have rights, is live again with AI.
The centre of the second chapter.

head: The Collected Letters of Mary Wollstonecraft
dek: Amit calls it 'a beautiful book': Wollstonecraft's inner life in her own words.
more: Amit calls it 'a beautiful book': Wollstonecraft's inner life in her own words.
Mentioned while telling the story of her suicide attempt; her suicide letter is reproduced there.

head: Age of Pandemics
dek: Amit calls it a wonderful book that tells, fascinatingly, how cholera's link to water was found and then resisted for decades, especially in India.
more: Amit calls it a wonderful book that tells, fascinatingly, how cholera's link to water was found and then resisted for decades, especially in India.
Source for the John Snow and caste-cholera-map stories.

head: The Ascent of Man (TV series)
dek: A sweeping history of scientific thought that has shaped Ajay since childhood and is full of stories like these.
more: A sweeping history of scientific thought that has shaped Ajay since childhood and is full of stories like these.
Ajay says the Wegener, Boltzmann, Mendel and Darwin stories all come from it; he watched it as a child and has recommended it before.

head: The Ascent of Man (book)
dek: The written companion to the series that fed Ajay's stories of scientific outlaws.
more: The written companion to the series that fed Ajay's stories of scientific outlaws.
Recommended together with the BBC series.

head: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
dek: A two-axis frame (passive vs aggressive, conventional vs independent) that identifies the aggressively conventional-minded as the real threat to new ideas.
more: A two-axis frame (passive vs aggressive, conventional vs independent) that identifies the aggressively conventional-minded as the real threat to new ideas. Amit calls it 'such a great frame'.
Amit opens the chapter on the aggressively conventional-minded with it, noting it came up in the very first episode of the show.

head: Who's Got the Guts to Go to the Moon?
dek: Argues that most research today is super safe and nobody chases moonshots.
more: Argues that most research today is super safe and nobody chases moonshots. It sets out the life cycle of new ideas: a weirdo outsider proposes one, experts ignore or suppress it, and eventually it wins because it's better.
Amit's second essay recommendation; he had shared it on Twitter and sent it to Ajay.

head: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24, Everything is Everything)
dek: The fuller argument for why the academic system filters out creative mavericks.
more: The fuller argument for why the academic system filters out creative mavericks.
Ajay says his selection-bias argument here is 'essentially the same story we told in our Knowledge Society episode', where he discussed the five personality traits.

head: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
dek: It shows in great detail how Gandhi was 'quite a weirdo', a reminder of how unconventional great free thinkers look up close.
more: It shows in great detail how Gandhi was 'quite a weirdo', a reminder of how unconventional great free thinkers look up close.
Ajay's example of a great dissident who documented his own strangeness.

head: The Outlaws
dek: Progress is slow. In every age some people think things that will later seem completely normal but are radical at the time, and they are often shunned, despised or destroyed for it.
more: Progress is slow. In every age some people think things that will later seem completely normal but are radical at the time, and they are often shunned, despised or destroyed for it. Seen in hindsight, their stories are deeply moving.

head: Locke's self-ownership
dek: Amit's intellectual hero John Locke grounded liberalism in one premise: you own yourself.
more: Amit's intellectual hero John Locke grounded liberalism in one premise: you own yourself. Every other right follows from it. Free speech follows because you own your thoughts, property because you mix your labour with unowned things, and life follows too. Locke himself was treated as an outlaw in his time, yet his ideas inspired the American Declaration of Independence and, through it, Wollstonecraft.

head: Virtue from reason, not tradition
dek: Wollstonecraft argued that humans are special because we can reason, and that virtue, which only our species has, must therefore flow from reason.
more: Wollstonecraft argued that humans are special because we can reason, and that virtue, which only our species has, must therefore flow from reason. It sounds bland now, but it was radical: virtue was then assumed to come from religion, tradition and convention, so her argument challenged every construct of society, not just relations between the sexes.

head: Radicals must first speak their audience's language
dek: Because Wollstonecraft's only readers were men who read political philosophy, she couldn't argue that women would be autonomous and fulfilled.
more: Because Wollstonecraft's only readers were men who read political philosophy, she couldn't argue that women would be autonomous and fulfilled. She had to argue that freed women would be better daughters, sisters, wives, mothers and citizens. Amit finds this tragic, but it is how the first version of a radical idea gets through the door.

head: Don't blame pioneers for clichés
dek: Frankenstein looks clichéd today only because so much later work copied it.
more: Frankenstein looks clichéd today only because so much later work copied it. The same is true of Fritz Lang's Metropolis in cinema and of much that came from Shakespeare. When reading an originator, remember that the clichés started there.

head: Science fiction carries the biggest questions
dek: Amit resists treating science fiction as a niche subgenre and counts some of the greatest writers, like Margaret Atwood and Ursula K.
more: Amit resists treating science fiction as a niche subgenre and counts some of the greatest writers, like Margaret Atwood and Ursula K. Le Guin, among its practitioners. Frankenstein's question was live in 1818 and is live again with AI: if we create a being that surpasses us cognitively and differs only in not being mortal or organic, why should it be our moral inferior?

head: The missing mechanism
dek: The recurring reason true ideas get rejected is that they work without a known 'how'.
more: The recurring reason true ideas get rejected is that they work without a known 'how'. Semmelweis had no germ theory, Wegener no force to move continents, Darwin no genetics, and Boltzmann no microscope able to show an atom. Good predictions were not enough; the establishment waited, sometimes for decades, until the last-mile explanation arrived.

head: Science advances one funeral at a time
dek: Amit invokes the Planck principle: new ideas win not by converting their opponents but as those opponents die off.
more: Amit invokes the Planck principle: new ideas win not by converting their opponents but as those opponents die off. Playing the long game is cold comfort when, as Keynes said, in the long run we're all dead. Amit's open question is why science has to progress by funerals.

head: Survivorship bias in outlaw stories
dek: We celebrate Semmelweis, Wegener and Karikó because they were eventually vindicated, even if only after death.
more: We celebrate Semmelweis, Wegener and Karikó because they were eventually vindicated, even if only after death. For each of them, countless others were right, ignored and never redeemed, so hero stories hide the true cost of being early. Amit guesses only one in a million make it that way.

head: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
dek: Paul Graham sorts people on two axes, conventional versus independent-minded and passive versus aggressive.
more: Paul Graham sorts people on two axes, conventional versus independent-minded and passive versus aggressive. The passively conventional are most common and the aggressively independent rarest. Amit sees Wallace as aggressively independent and Darwin as passively independent. Being conventional-minded is understandable, as cognitive economy or even rationality. What puzzles Amit is the aggression, which he sees as the real danger to progress.

head: Ridicule at scale kills moonshots
dek: Social media amplifies aggressively conventional behaviour, especially in ideological tribes where attacking heretics raises your status.
more: Social media amplifies aggressively conventional behaviour, especially in ideological tribes where attacking heretics raises your status. People get cancelled and outcast far faster than Semmelweis was. Echoing Mastroianni, Amit argues that where Wegener faced disdain only from fellow professionals, a modern Wegener would face the whole world, so few propose such ideas and research stays safe.

head: Why the conventional get aggressive: defending the system
dek: Ajay's answer to Amit's puzzle: people are tacitly upholding an establishment of institutions, credentials, journals, universities, jobs and funding.
more: Ajay's answer to Amit's puzzle: people are tacitly upholding an establishment of institutions, credentials, journals, universities, jobs and funding. An idea that disrupts it threatens their own lives, so they defend it like any bureaucracy. Amit's population story adds an identity angle: when beliefs fuse with the self, challenges feel like attacks.

head: The $500 bill on the ground
dek: Since most people ignore mavericks, taking them seriously is a personal arbitrage opportunity.
more: Since most people ignore mavericks, taking them seriously is a personal arbitrage opportunity. Many of their ideas will be wrong, but that is where the innovation lies. Ajay suggests spending an hour with a 'mad person' over a sane one and changing our conformist filters (clean shirt, right jokes, one of the gang). Amit adds the caveat: don't listen blindly, but do take them seriously.

head: Creativity and weirdness are causally linked
dek: Ajay argues that a well-socialised person absorbs their elders' programming.
more: Ajay argues that a well-socialised person absorbs their elders' programming. The kind of imagination that produces a Boltzmann probably requires being somewhat badly adjusted, so not every oddball is a genius, but a disproportionate share of geniuses are oddballs. That makes them hard to accept in a society whose structures are quiet, tame and conventional.

head: The career pipeline selects for conscientiousness alone
dek: Every rung of an intellectual career rewards keeping your head down and playing the game: board exams, college grades, a PhD with three safe papers, an academic job, then papers and grants for tenure.
more: Every rung of an intellectual career rewards keeping your head down and playing the game: board exams, college grades, a PhD with three safe papers, an academic job, then papers and grants for tenure. Of the five personality traits, only conscientiousness gets selected. This helps explain why knowledge resourcing has grown by millions of times while progress feels underwhelming.

head: Sugar-coated heroes and the modern microscope
dek: We admire Newton or Solzhenitsyn through their highlights. A WikiLeaks-style dump of their lives would reveal the reckless, imprudent behaviour that comes with free thinking.
more: We admire Newton or Solzhenitsyn through their highlights. A WikiLeaks-style dump of their lives would reveal the reckless, imprudent behaviour that comes with free thinking. Today social media and surveillance put that microscope on every living maverick, making it easy to dismiss them as madmen and damaging the innovation process.

head: Hindsight admiration is cheap
dek: In Graham's essay, Princeton's Robert George asks his students whether, as white people in the pre-abolition South, they would have been abolitionists.
more: In Graham's essay, Princeton's Robert George asks his students whether, as white people in the pre-abolition South, they would have been abolitionists. They all say yes, which simply isn't true. Admiring Semmelweis or Darwin now costs nothing. The real test is whether we take today's oddballs seriously.

head: Ajay on Darwin spending 22 years on his book
more: Ajay on Darwin spending 22 years on his book: 'Amitbhai, you'll be pleased to know he was as great a book writer as you.' Amit: 'He took a long time, you mean.' Ajay: 'He just plodded and plodded and plodded, and he didn't even have a word processor.' Later, at '22 years', Amit: 'I have time, I have time.'

head: Ajay on Darwin's theory
more: Ajay on Darwin's theory: 'One day we were told God created man. Next day we are told we came out of monkeys. I mean it's quite a fall.' On cartoonists drawing Darwin as a monkey: 'he had a face for that.'

head: Ajay on Newton sitting on the calculus while Leibniz rushed to publish
more: Ajay on Newton sitting on the calculus while Leibniz rushed to publish: 'It's like I'm Newton. Once I understand it, how can humans understand it?'

head: In Washington DC, Amit's history-obsessed friend Vikram Raghavan points to a building where John Maynard Keynes had a heart attack under a staircase.
more: In Washington DC, Amit's history-obsessed friend Vikram Raghavan points to a building where John Maynard Keynes had a heart attack under a staircase. Amit: 'So did he say in the short run we are all dead?' Keynes survived that one.

head: After Ajay says it's better to spend an hour with a mad person than a sane one, Amit
more: After Ajay says it's better to spend an hour with a mad person than a sane one, Amit: 'That's why I do the show with you.'

head: Amit, pulling Ajay back to his question
more: Amit, pulling Ajay back to his question: 'But that five hundred dollar bill as five hundred dollar bills tend to do distracted you.'
Ajay: 'If biology has to be more than stamp collecting, then it is the child of Mendel and Darwin.'

head: Thomas Taylor's mocking reply to Wollstonecraft
more: Thomas Taylor's mocking reply to Wollstonecraft, 'A Vindication of the Rights of Brutes': if women get rights, why not animals? Amit notes that Peter Singer would later make the animal case seriously in Animal Liberation.

Fritz Lang's Metropolis, cited as the origin of many cinematic clichés, just as Frankenstein originated literary ones; Ajay adds the Shakespeare example 'All that glisters is not gold' (not 'glitters').

head: From Letters to the Royal Society, and Back Again
dek: Institutions outlive their original purpose and turn into credential machines.
more: Ajay traces how research communication began. Scientists wrote a letter to the Secretary of the Royal Society in London describing their new work. The Secretary gathered these into a publication sent to all members, and modern journals grew out of that habit. Journals existed to disseminate research. Today that job has vanished: mature working papers, blog posts and newspaper pieces carry high-quality novel knowledge, and nobody needs a journal website to read a paper. What journals still provide is a brand name that helps you get a job or a grant.

Institutions outlive their original purpose and turn into credential machines. Once you see that journals now certify careers rather than spread knowledge, you can judge a paper on its merits instead of by where it was published. We are back to an everyone-to-everyone model, minus the Secretary.

head: SEC Trivia Gets Published, SEBI Drama Gets Rejected
dek: Universalism can be provincialism in disguise. Ajay's alternative is to find the important questions in the reality you actually live in.
more: Ajay describes the nightmare Indian social scientists face with global journals: 'this is not an interesting question.' Any obscure regulation change at the US SEC is thought worthy of the top finance journals. The dramatic regulatory moves of SEBI, arguably the world's most activist financial regulator, are dismissed because it is India. Indian researchers end up contorting their work to show it sheds light on 'the grand questions of the age as seen in Germany.'

Universalism can be provincialism in disguise. Ajay's alternative is to find the important questions in the reality you actually live in. That is where the energy and emotional resilience come from to survive setbacks and produce real discoveries.

head: Mendel's Forty Copies
dek: The bottleneck has moved from printing copies to winning attention. Pushing your work out after it is written (videos, blog posts, op-eds, talks) is part of the craft, not vanity.
more: Recalling a fact from the Outlaws episode, Ajay notes that Mendel ordered forty copies of his paper from the press. Today there is no limit on copies because everything is electronic, but the world is now flooded with rubbish. A researcher who puts a finished paper on a website finds that nobody is waiting to read it.

The bottleneck has moved from printing copies to winning attention. Pushing your work out after it is written (videos, blog posts, op-eds, talks) is part of the craft, not vanity. Without it, Ajay jokes, YouTubers a hundred years from now will celebrate the paper nobody read in your lifetime.

head: The Cute Title That Kept Luring Ajay Back
dek: The title is the one sentence most people will ever read of your paper.
more: Ajay admits that one paper's title (he won't name it or its authors) stuck in his head for years and pulled him back to read the paper several times. Each time, the paper turned out to be unrelated to the title. He thinks academia has overdone cute titles. Two that get the balance right: Vijayendra Rao's dowry paper 'The Rising Price of Husbands', which Amit loves, and Ajay's own paper with Ayush and Susan, 'But Clouds Got in My Way', about clouds blocking infrared radiation on its way to satellites.
The title is the one sentence most people will ever read of your paper. A literary flourish helps, but a title that doesn't describe the paper wastes the reader's attention and your credibility.

head: Why It's 'Shah and Thomas'
dek: A good convention removes a fight people would otherwise have, here over status among co-authors.
more: Amit points out that Ajay's most frequent co-author is Susan Thomas. Ajay explains that people assume 'Shah and Thomas' means he is the lead author. In fact the papers list authors alphabetically, and her role is in no way smaller. He notes that alphabetical ordering is not universal and conventions differ by community. He likes it because the only real question becomes whether you get authorship at all. Once you do, everyone is equal, which avoids endless fights over the n-factorial possible orderings.
A good convention removes a fight people would otherwise have, here over status among co-authors. It also means you shouldn't read hierarchy into author order without knowing the field's rules.

head: Ajay Underestimated How Hard This Would Be
dek: Reading a thing well does not mean you can make it. Learning a craft takes years, honest review of your old work, and studying how masters did it, not just what they concluded.
more: Looking back, Ajay says he started reading papers early. He assumed he would slide naturally from reading papers to writing them, and he was wrong. He has since learned by reviewing his own work from a year or two earlier. He also reverse-engineers papers that leave him 'shocked at how perfect' they are, asking how the authors pulled it off.
Reading a thing well does not mean you can make it. Learning a craft takes years, honest review of your old work, and studying how masters did it, not just what they concluded.

head: The World Didn't Pick Ajay's Best Papers
dek: You can't control how your work is received, but you can stay detached and keep moving.
more: Amit asks how a creator handles work that gets ignored. He says he finishes an episode with full intensity, then forgets it and moves on. Ajay says his Google Scholar page shows that some papers got cited and many did not, and he doesn't think the world chose his best work. He accepts it: the archive exists and someone may find it in a hundred years. His enthusiasm for any paper decays exponentially, so he talks about a paper only while he is still excited by it. Right now that is his innovation-policy paper with Mashelkar and Susan Thomas.
You can't control how your work is received, but you can stay detached and keep moving. Let your own excitement decide what you promote, and never give a talk you don't want to give.

head: The Clash of Economic Ideas
dek: Amit calls it a fantastic book. The passage gives a clear picture of the idea pipeline: abstract research to applied policy ideas to journalists to the public.
more: Amit calls it a fantastic book. The passage gives a clear picture of the idea pipeline: abstract research to applied policy ideas to journalists to the public.
Amit opens the episode by reading a passage from it about how ideas travel from abstract researchers to the public.

head: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
dek: That episode argued that much of academia has become a circle game of academics writing for each other on fashionable, obscure topics.
more: That episode argued that much of academia has become a circle game of academics writing for each other on fashionable, obscure topics. This episode builds on that critique.
Cited when Amit asks whether the academic idea pipeline is broken.

head: The Leap Blog
dek: Much of what appears there fits the Introduction-Methods-Results-Discussion structure, which Ajay calls a low-bullshit way to do scientific communication.
more: Much of what appears there fits the Introduction-Methods-Results-Discussion structure, which Ajay calls a low-bullshit way to do scientific communication.
Mentioned while explaining the IMRD structure; Ajay describes it as a peer-reviewed research outlet he co-edits.

head: The Rising Price of Husbands
dek: One of Amit's favourite titles: clever and also accurately about the paper.
more: One of Amit's favourite titles: clever and also accurately about the paper.
Amit's example during the discussion of paper titles; an early-90s study of how dowry was changing.

head: But Clouds Got In My Way: Bias And Bias Correction Of VIIRS Nighttime Lights Data In The Presence Of Clouds
by: Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Anshul Tayal and Susan Thomas
dek: About how clouds interfere with infrared radiation reaching satellites.
more: About how clouds interfere with infrared radiation reaching satellites. The title is witty and still describes the work, and Amit called it a great title.
Ajay's own example of a good title; also on his list of favourite papers in the show notes.

head: Both Sides Now
dek: Amit calls it 'the great song'; it is the source of the paper's title.
more: Amit calls it 'the great song'; it is the source of the paper's title.
Amit imagines Ajay finishing the clouds paper, putting on Joni Mitchell, and finding the title in a line from the song.

head: Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
by: RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
dek: Ajay says he is 'full of that idea' right now, which by his own rule is exactly when he will talk about a paper.
more: Ajay says he is 'full of that idea' right now, which by his own rule is exactly when he will talk about a paper.
Mentioned as the paper Ajay is currently most excited about; it was discussed in Episode 59, Rethinking Innovation Policy.

head: The Elements of Style
by: William Strunk Jr and EB White
dek: Researchers greatly underrate the craft of writing, and Ajay says 'the simple Strunk and White' should be universal knowledge for everyone doing research.
more: Researchers greatly underrate the craft of writing, and Ajay says 'the simple Strunk and White' should be universal knowledge for everyone doing research.
Ajay's first recommendation at the end of the episode.

head: The Art of Clear Writing
dek: Researchers absorbed in econometrics or computer science have missed the core of writing, and this course addresses it directly.
more: Researchers absorbed in econometrics or computer science have missed the core of writing, and this course addresses it directly.
Ajay's second recommendation.

head: The Idea Supply Chain
dek: Following Hayek and Keynes, Larry White compares ideas to timber.
more: Following Hayek and Keynes, Larry White compares ideas to timber. Abstract researchers grow the trees, applied researchers mill them into policy ideas, and journalists and intellectuals build the furniture (books, op-eds, commentary) that policymakers and the public use. Amit uses this as the starting picture and asks where today's pipeline has broken.

head: The End of the Physics Illusion
dek: Social science once hoped for grand unifying theories that hold everywhere, the way physics does.
more: Social science once hoped for grand unifying theories that hold everywhere, the way physics does. The data revolution changed that. There are now roughly 10,000 important datasets, each its own universe with its own logic and its own small community of specialists (for example, the people who work on the CMIE household survey). Economics has become solving one puzzle at a time, loosely held together rather than loyal to one framework.

head: The Spectrum of Universality
dek: Fields differ in how far their findings travel. Physics and mathematics are fully universal.
more: Fields differ in how far their findings travel. Physics and mathematics are fully universal. The humanities are fully contextual. Social science sits in between, needing deep local context while drawing on general theory. Even STEM can turn local: diabetes in India might differ from diabetes in China if genetics matter.

head: A Paper Is a Unit of Knowledge, Not a Journal Credential
dek: Ajay defines a 'paper' broadly: any piece of new insight, whether a blog post, op-ed, working paper or journal article.
more: Ajay defines a 'paper' broadly: any piece of new insight, whether a blog post, op-ed, working paper or journal article. Knowledge is a graph of such papers feeding into each other, used by three kinds of decision-makers: individuals, firms and governments. Journals no longer spread knowledge; they hand out credentials. A mature reader can judge a paper directly: did it give me a new idea, did it change my mind?

head: Question, Answer, Novelty
dek: Every STEM or social-science paper needs three things. It needs a clearly stated question, a persuasive and well-supported answer, and novelty.
more: Every STEM or social-science paper needs three things. It needs a clearly stated question, a persuasive and well-supported answer, and novelty. A summary of twenty existing papers, which an LLM could write, is useful but is not a paper. The same tests make a good referee report: the reviewer restates the question and the answer in their own words, then judges whether the claims are supported and whether the work is new. In a confused paper, neither the question nor the answer can be pulled out easily.
printed: Is it new? Is it true?

head: Importance Is in the Eye of the Beholder
dek: Gatekeepers claim to know which questions matter. Global warming does; the headgear of tribals in Chandrapur doesn't.
more: Gatekeepers claim to know which questions matter. Global warming does; the headgear of tribals in Chandrapur doesn't. Ajay rejects this snobbery. Researchers guard their time carefully, so if someone has put serious effort into a question, outsiders should assume there are people and situations for which it matters. The establishment said the same dismissive thing to every maverick in history.

head: How to Play the International Journals Game
dek: If you want to publish in international journals, Ajay offers two pieces of advice.
more: If you want to publish in international journals, Ajay offers two pieces of advice. First, position your work around questions those journals already find interesting, for example a natural experiment in your country that sheds light on their world. Second, avoid big breaks with the past, because peer review rewards small, incremental improvements. Amit is blunter: in peer review the excellent are always judged by the mediocre. Both agree this has nothing to do with writing a good paper for its own sake.

head: Communication Has Two Variables
dek: In his writing course, Amit asks why people who master difficult subjects still fail to communicate, even with friends or partners.
more: In his writing course, Amit asks why people who master difficult subjects still fail to communicate, even with friends or partners. His answer: learning involves one variable, yourself, while communication involves two, you and the other person. Writing is not transferring what's in your head onto a screen. It succeeds only when it has the intended effect on the intended reader.

head: Research Writing Is Writing
dek: Researchers like to think writing is for creative-writing people and cut corners on it.
more: Researchers like to think writing is for creative-writing people and cut corners on it. Ajay says the purpose of a paper is to change a skeptical reader's mind. That needs passion and prose that is lively and engaging; being an academic is no excuse for dullness. Most papers sink without a trace, partly because too little care went into writing them. In the old adage he quotes, if it was not hard to write, it will not be easy to read.

head: The Paper Is Not the Journey
dek: Doing research is like climbing a mountain, with fumbling, dead ends, months away and sudden aha moments.
more: Doing research is like climbing a mountain, with fumbling, dead ends, months away and sudden aha moments. The paper should leave all of that out and present only the question, the approach, what was done and what was found. The journey can also change the destination: you may set out for India and arrive in America, and then you write about the route to America. Amit's summary: while doing the work, it's the journey; when presenting it, it's the destination.

head: Learn the Structures, Then Break Them
dek: Beginners should stick to standard structures and break them only once they have found their powers.
more: Beginners should stick to standard structures and break them only once they have found their powers. The STEM default is IMRD. The Introduction reviews what is known and ends with your questions. Methods must be detailed enough for anyone to replicate the work. Results report the findings with little interpretation. Discussion explains what they mean and where research should go next. Ajay's economics version has a title and abstract, then an 'introduction' that is really a 1,000-word executive summary, often published separately. After that come the setting and questions, the methods and results, robustness checks against alternative explanations, and a conclusion that asks 'so what?'

head: The Readership Funnel
dek: Ajay's rule of thumb: about 100,000 people see the title, 10,000 read the abstract, 1,000 start the paper and 100 finish it.
more: Ajay's rule of thumb: about 100,000 people see the title, 10,000 read the abstract, 1,000 start the paper and 100 finish it. Better writing widens every stage. So the title, a one-sentence summary, and the 100-word abstract deserve the most care.

head: Write Inside Out, and Be Ready to Throw It Away
dek: Writing changes what you think, so planning from the title down rarely works.
more: Writing changes what you think, so planning from the title down rarely works. Ajay writes the body first (setting, questions, methods, results), then the conclusions, then the 1,000-word introduction, then the abstract, and the title last. Writing is expensive, but don't hold on to text just because you produced it, since that is a sunk-cost trap. Ajay often deletes a weak chunk and rewrites it from scratch rather than patching old prose.

head: The Slideshow as a Development Platform
dek: Ajay's teams build the paper first as a dense internal slideshow of 40 to 50 slides, containing every table, graph and citation in the order the argument runs.
more: Ajay's teams build the paper first as a dense internal slideshow of 40 to 50 slides, containing every table, graph and citation in the order the argument runs. Each meeting walks through it and produces errors to fix and new ideas. Assistants, who are apprentices, implement the changes and must come back with something they believe is flawless and are ready to defend. When meetings stop producing changes, the work has converged and is turned into prose. Amit separates this from Jeff Bezos's ban on simplifying PowerPoints: this deck holds everything and is never shown to an outside audience. Ajay also distinguishes the roles: authors invent, assistants implement and are thanked rather than credited as authors.

head: Small Rooms Beat Big Conferences
dek: Finished work still needs pushing: blog posts, newspaper pieces, a video of the paper, and talks.
more: Finished work still needs pushing: blog posts, newspaper pieces, a video of the paper, and talks. Ten minutes in front of 200 people leaves no impression; 30 to 50 minutes with ten focused people actually changes minds. So Ajay avoids big conferences and goes to small ones. Amit links this to a line he borrowed from Paul Graham: it's better to be loved by a few than liked by many.

head: Writing Papers Takes a Long Apprenticeship
dek: Paper-writing is a craft, and you get better through practice, honest review of your past work, and studying how excellent papers were built.
more: Paper-writing is a craft, and you get better through practice, honest review of your past work, and studying how excellent papers were built. A PhD doesn't make you good at it. Being able to conceive a research project and lead it to completion takes many years after the PhD.

head: Ajay opens by promising that after his masterclass
more: Ajay opens by promising that after his masterclass, 'gentle readers will become gentle writers.'

head: Ajay on research guiding individual choices: to decide whether to go to college
more: Ajay on research guiding individual choices: to decide whether to go to college, 'first you should get a PhD and learn to read the papers about the gains from college... Because if you haven't read those papers, how can you make a decision about whether or not it's worth going to college?' Amit: 'This is a trap.'

head: Amit, on Ajay's Chandrapur example
more: Amit, on Ajay's Chandrapur example: 'There is also the radical possibility that the headgear of the Chandrapur tribals causes global warming.' Ajay plays along with a straight face, suggesting obscure chemicals in the headgear could trigger reactions in the upper atmosphere. Amit: 'I didn't expect you to riff off my immature quip, but continue.'
Amit: 'I will say this as gently as I can. I think the peer review system makes me want to puke.'

head: Amit, after Ajay says journals only reward small incremental moves
more: Amit, after Ajay says journals only reward small incremental moves: 'You and I should throw a party where we call every academic we know and we get them completely drunk, and then we gather a bunch of journals and we have a bonfire of the journals.'

head: Asked why we fail to communicate, Ajay brings up Broca's area, the part of the brain that handles speech.
more: Asked why we fail to communicate, Ajay brings up Broca's area, the part of the brain that handles speech. Amit: 'That's a deeply technical answer and it is absolutely correct.'

head: Ajay mentions the Leap Blog without explaining it, and Amit catches him
more: Ajay mentions the Leap Blog without explaining it, and Amit catches him: 'You just committed the curse of knowledge.'

head: Amit pictures Ajay, Ayush and Susan finishing their exhausting paper, putting on Joni Mitchell, and finding the title

head: Paul Graham's line, which Amit has adopted
more: Paul Graham's line, which Amit has adopted: 'It's better to be loved by a few than liked by many.'

head: The Wicked Witch and the iPhone
dek: What we call 'our knowledge' is mostly unusable without the huge web of materials, machines and specialised people that carries it.
more: A friend shared a post by Tim Urban in a WhatsApp group, and it set up the episode. In Urban's thought experiment, a powerful witch makes every material good on Earth vanish. That leaves about 7.3 billion naked people, but all their knowledge stays in their heads. She leaves a note: build one working iPhone 6S and everything comes back. How many years would that take? Amit liked how Urban built up to it on Lex Fridman's podcast. He started from the fact that no human being knows how to make a pencil. Fridman assumed metals would be on hand and a thousand people could manage it. Urban pushed back: what about the materials, the mining, and the cranes?
What we call 'our knowledge' is mostly unusable without the huge web of materials, machines and specialised people that carries it. Knowledge in heads is not the same as a working civilisation.

head: Never: First Comes Barbarism
dek: Modern abundance rests on institutions and physical capital, not just on what individuals know.
more: Ajay's answer to Urban's question is 'Never. It's impossible.' Without markets, laws, institutions and food-processing machines, there is no way to feed seven and a half billion people. Humanity would first sink into the world of a post-apocalyptic novel like Cormac McCarthy's The Road, with people eating each other. The witch would be forgotten and the population would crash to about 10 million. A new scientific civilisation would eventually emerge, but it would not retrace the exact path to semiconductors, integrated circuits and touch screens.
Modern abundance rests on institutions and physical capital, not just on what individuals know. History's particular path cannot simply be replayed.

head: Solitary Confinement With Only Pen and Paper
dek: Much of what we 'know' is borrowed trust in books and proofs we have never worked through ourselves.
more: Ajay's personal thought experiment: you are thrown into solitary confinement with paper and pen but no books. He notes this is worse than how the British treated Nehru. What would get you into a flow state? His answer is a Whitehead-and-Russell-style project. He would start from axioms and try to rebuild all the mathematics he knows, beginning with whether he can prove Pythagoras' theorem. He knows many results but always looks them up. Without books or proofs, he says, his theorems are 'mere beliefs'.

Much of what we 'know' is borrowed trust in books and proofs we have never worked through ourselves. Trying to rebuild it is a way to respect our shared inheritance of five hundred years of mathematics, and to find out how much of it we actually own.

head: Silphium: The Roman Super-Herb That Vanished
dek: Written records can keep a lost thing alive as a target long after the thing itself is gone.
more: The Romans wrote a great deal down, including recipes, and they praised a herb called silphium as food of the gods. It grew in what they called Carthage, modern Libya. They used its flowers, stalk and resinous gum. Nobody could cultivate it, so foragers gathered it from the wild and it fetched the highest prices. Within a couple of hundred years it was gone. Legend says the last plant was given to Emperor Nero, and Amit adds that Pliny the Elder recorded this in his Natural History. Expeditions into Libya's mountains found nothing. In recent years a Turkish scientist found a matching Ferula plant in remote parts of Greece and Turkey. He cooked old recipes for food connoisseurs, who rave about the results. He has kept the find quiet so foragers and eBay sellers do not wipe it out again, and has learned to grow it in a greenhouse. The Roman texts also name a cheap, harsh substitute for silphium resin: hing (asafoetida), itself a Ferula.

Written records can keep a lost thing alive as a target long after the thing itself is gone. Modern tools like greenhouse cultivation can then do what the ancients could not. The hing link ties a lost Roman luxury to the Indian kitchen and opens possibilities like Roman-inspired curd rice.

head: Dhaka Muslin: 1,200 Threads and Sixteen Villages
dek: Knowledge spread across many specialised hands, with nobody writing the process down, can vanish in a single generation.
more: At the end of the 18th century, European fashion moved to clinging, see-through gowns made of muslin, and it caused a scandal. The finest was Dhaka muslin, made from a plant found on the banks of the Meghna in Bengal. Making it took sixteen villages, each doing one stage of the work. Ordinary muslin has 20 to 40 threads per square inch; Dhaka muslin had around 1,200. Once the trade died, the know-how vanished within a generation and the plant could not be found. A revival project used a 19th-century leaf for DNA analysis, then satellite imagery along the Meghna, and found a plant sharing 70% of the original's DNA. Weavers across Bangladesh refused to attempt 1,200 threads. One agreed, worked in a temperature-controlled hut, and produced a 300-thread version. Dresses made from it have sold for thousands of dollars.

Knowledge spread across many specialised hands, with nobody writing the process down, can vanish in a single generation. Getting it back takes surviving samples plus modern science, and even then recovery is partial: 300 is a long way from 1,200.

head: Fogbank: When America Forgot How to Make Part of Its Own Bomb
dek: Even with military-grade bureaucracy and record-keeping, and with the original people still alive, tacit knowledge disappears once the work stops being done.
more: Aerogels are the lightest materials known; a litre might weigh two or three grams. For one kind of US atomic bomb, a special aerogel code-named Fogbank was developed 40 to 50 years ago. Nuclear weapons need complex maintenance, and during a recent overhaul the US found it had run out of Fogbank. Today's scientists worked from the archives, including project reports, papers and experiment logs, and could not make it. Retired scientists were brought back and handed their own documents ('You bloody now deliver'), and they failed too. With auditors screaming, about $70 million went into a fresh research project to reach the same material from scratch. Ajay adds a related hypothesis: maintenance know-how may have evaporated when the Soviet Union collapsed, so Russia may not have a single working nuclear bomb today.
Even with military-grade bureaucracy and record-keeping, and with the original people still alive, tacit knowledge disappears once the work stops being done. Documents alone do not preserve know-how.

head: The Guard and the Bench
dek: Organisations keep the ritual long after they lose the reason for it. Recording why we do things matters as much as recording what we do.
more: An army camp keeps a guard beside a random bench in a garden 24 hours a day, changing shifts every eight hours. A new commandant asks why. The guard, the deputy and the previous commandants all say it has always been this way. He becomes obsessed and tracks down the camp's founder, now 93 and bedridden on a farm. He flies out in economy and gets past the worried wife. When he asks why a guard stands beside the bench, the old man replies that the paint hasn't dried yet.
Organisations keep the ritual long after they lose the reason for it. Recording why we do things matters as much as recording what we do.

head: Tu Youyou and the Cold Extraction of Wormwood
dek: A breakthrough can come from empathy for suffering plus close reading, with no credentials required.
more: In 1974, during the Vietnam War, Tu Youyou was sent to help Vietnam. Its people asked for help with one thing: malaria. The plasmodium parasite was becoming resistant to quinine. Moved by what she saw, she remembered claims in ancient Chinese texts about malaria cures. Around two thousand plants from those texts had already been tested and failed, and papers said wormwood did not work. She was not a PhD, but she was a master of classical Chinese. She read one passage as saying the plant should be soaked in water without heating, a cold extraction rather than the usual hot one. She tried it on twenty patients and all twenty recovered. Scientists later found the part of the molecule that attacks the parasite and built stronger derivatives. The result, artemisinin, is now the mainstay of malaria treatment worldwide.
A breakthrough can come from empathy for suffering plus close reading, with no credentials required. Ancient texts mostly fail testing, but a rare careful reading can save millions of lives.

head: Frisky Goats and a Gorilla's Medicine Walk
dek: A great deal of human knowledge was gathered by observing nature, not invented in labs.
more: Coffee was discovered when a shepherd in Ethiopia noticed his goats became unusually frisky after eating the plant's berries. He tried chewing them himself, and centuries of trial and error later people arrived at roasting. Scientists have also observed that a gorilla with an upset stomach will walk 15 kilometres to find one particular plant and eat it. Indigenous peoples learn exactly this kind of knowledge by watching animals.
A great deal of human knowledge was gathered by observing nature, not invented in labs. That knowledge, held by forest peoples, is now vanishing quickly.

head: Why Homeopathy Took Off
dek: Quackery thrives when the mainstream option is actively harmful. Its popularity says more about how bad the alternatives were than about whether it works.
more: Homeopathy became popular in the 19th century, when mainstream medicine was dangerous. There was no germ theory and bloodletting was the cure for most things. As the show discussed in its Semmelweis episode, ten percent of people who entered maternity wards died, so nobody wanted to go there. An alternative made of sugar pills at least would not kill you, so it caught on.
Quackery thrives when the mainstream option is actively harmful. Its popularity says more about how bad the alternatives were than about whether it works.

head: Germany and Japan Rise Like a Phoenix
dek: Physical ruin can be reversed fast when knowledge, records, property rights and good institutions survive or are restored.
more: By 1945 both countries were devastated. Factories were destroyed and Tokyo's wooden houses had been firebombed. Germany's institutions were first taken over by the Nazis and then wrecked in the war. From 1945 to 1948 Europe also saw horrific ethnic cleansing, with Germans expelled from countries such as Czechoslovakia and Poland. Yet in 1933 Germany had had more Nobel laureates than the UK, and the knowledge of the Weimar era was still in people's heads. West Germany recovered with three advantages. The Marshall Plan brought money, and books and manuals could be printed abroad and brought back. Records were kept, so pre-war shareholders were honoured and Volkswagen returned. An old Weimar constitutional draft, with pacifism added, became the new constitution. Japan recovered under a successful period of American rule and a pacifist constitution. Both countries turned their backs on nationalism and militarism. East Germany, under communist rule, never quite recovered.

Physical ruin can be reversed fast when knowledge, records, property rights and good institutions survive or are restored. East Germany, with the same people under different institutions, shows the reverse case. Ajay admits that in 1945 he would not have predicted the recovery.

head: Ludwig Erhard, the Right Man in the Right Place
dek: After a catastrophe, knowing how prosperity actually works (free markets, property rights, rule of law) may be the most important knowledge a society can hold on to.
more: Amit gives much of West Germany's revival to Ludwig Erhard, Adenauer's finance minister from about 1949 to 1962. Having lived through the Weimar years, Erhard understood the value of freedom and property rights. His Germany combined a strong rule of law with free markets in which individuals and firms could flourish, which carried the country up from a base of massive destruction. Amit counts Erhard among the great men of the 20th century.
After a catastrophe, knowing how prosperity actually works (free markets, property rights, rule of law) may be the most important knowledge a society can hold on to.

head: The iPhone Thought Experiment
dek: Shows how much of what we know depends on a material and social web that no single person, or even all of humanity, could quickly rebuild.
more: Shows how much of what we know depends on a material and social web that no single person, or even all of humanity, could quickly rebuild.
Amit's friend shared it in a WhatsApp group, and it frames the whole episode.
