more: A pencil narrates its own making, across many countries, materials and kinds of knowledge. It shows that self-sufficiency is a myth and that specialisation works miracles.

more: Explains how prices carry information and incentives, a remarkable form of communication between people who never meet.

head: Knowledge Builds Like a Coastal Shelf, and Erodes Like One
dek: We like to picture knowledge as layers of sediment, each generation standing on the shoulders of giants.
more: We like to picture knowledge as layers of sediment, each generation standing on the shoulders of giants. Amit points out that the ocean of time also washes layers away. Much of what was once known is lost; some is regained and some never comes back. That is the theme of the episode.

head: Self-Sufficiency Is a Myth
dek: No one person can make a pencil, let alone a phone. Civilisation runs on a web of specialised people and knowledge coordinated through prices.
more: No one person can make a pencil, let alone a phone. Civilisation runs on a web of specialised people and knowledge coordinated through prices. Bastiat made the same point about feeding Paris: nobody plans it, yet the food arrives.

head: Social Technology
dek: Progress depends on social inventions as well as engineering. Prices, for instance, carry information and incentives across millions of strangers, as Hayek explained.
more: Progress depends on social inventions as well as engineering. Prices, for instance, carry information and incentives across millions of strangers, as Hayek explained. Rebuilding after a collapse means rebuilding these institutions, not just machines.

head: Reboot Civilisation: What Is Essential and What Is Accidental
dek: Amit's recurring thought experiment: keep human hardware and genetic wiring, erase everything else, and ask what would evolve again.
more: Amit's recurring thought experiment: keep human hardware and genetic wiring, erase everything else, and ask what would evolve again. Money probably would; football probably would, since kicking a round object is primal; cricket almost certainly wouldn't. The exercise separates what comes from human nature from what is historical accident.

head: Tacit Knowledge Dies Without Practice
dek: Fogbank and Dhaka muslin teach the same lesson. Much know-how lives in people's hands and habits, not on paper.
more: Fogbank and Dhaka muslin teach the same lesson. Much know-how lives in people's hands and habits, not on paper. Stop doing something for a generation and even excellent records cannot bring it back.

head: Watch for Records
dek: Whether lost knowledge can be recovered depends on what survived: written accounts, physical samples (plants kept in a London herbarium) and finished products (Dhaka muslin in the Victoria and Albert Museum) that can be reverse-engineered.
more: Whether lost knowledge can be recovered depends on what survived: written accounts, physical samples (plants kept in a London herbarium) and finished products (Dhaka muslin in the Victoria and Albert Museum) that can be reverse-engineered. Modern tools like DNA analysis and greenhouses then work from those clues.

head: Ancient Texts: Mostly Rubbish, Occasionally Mind-Blowing
dek: About two thousand plants from traditional Chinese texts were tested against malaria and failed before artemisinin worked.
more: About two thousand plants from traditional Chinese texts were tested against malaria and failed before artemisinin worked. Ancient texts have a low hit rate, but the rare hits can change the world. Only rigorous testing tells them apart.

head: Modern Arrogance About Where Knowledge Comes From
dek: We assume we make everything, but about half of the 20 most important drugs (quinine, artemisinin, metformin) began as traditional plant knowledge.
more: We assume we make everything, but about half of the 20 most important drugs (quinine, artemisinin, metformin) began as traditional plant knowledge. Modern science refined and standardised them, for example into precise slow-release doses. The forest knowledge of indigenous peoples is disappearing fast and deserves protection.

head: Be Deeply Skeptical of Tradition, but Never Dismissive
dek: Traditions hold the results of millions of trial-and-error experiments, so some of them work.
more: Traditions hold the results of millions of trial-and-error experiments, so some of them work. Focusing only on the successes is survivor bias: the two thousand failed plants matter too. Old knowledge systems also built theories on first principles that were simply wrong. Accept a traditional remedy only once it passes the scientific method.

head: Why Quackery Seems to Work, and Why Drugs Must Beat Placebo
dek: Three effects make useless remedies look effective. Reversion to the mean: a cold clears up in the same time with or without medicine.
more: Three effects make useless remedies look effective. Reversion to the mean: a cold clears up in the same time with or without medicine. Confirmation bias: we remember the hits and explain away the misses. The placebo effect is powerful; in one World War II story, a patient told he had been given anaesthetic felt nothing during surgery. That is why proper trials compare a medicine against a placebo, not against nothing.

head: Mastery Needs Conversation
dek: Zweig's prisoner taught himself chess in isolation, but Amit argues a human playing only himself hits a ceiling.
more: Zweig's prisoner taught himself chess in isolation, but Amit argues a human playing only himself hits a ceiling. AlphaZero can improve that way; the human brain can't. People improve by absorbing ideas and patterns from others, and every game against an opponent is a dialogue.

more: A satire from around 1801 on see-through muslin: a milliner gets a lady to remove her bonnet, tunic, petticoat and corset, then announces, 'In these days, if you want to be well dressed, you have to be well undressed.' Amit calls it a very male-gaze joke about a very male-gaze society.

head: From Smuggled Chess Computers to Smuggled Nvidia Chips
dek: Trade barriers don't make technology vanish. They push it underground.
more: Ajay remembers pre-1991 India, when protectionism made modern electronics almost impossible to buy. People relied on informal, black-market chains and on friends travelling abroad. His most prized purchase was an early chess computer whose LEDs blinked to show the next move, brought back by a neighbour flying to Singapore. Amit had the same one. You would expect this to be a distant memory. Instead, in Shanghai today you nudge, hint and wink to find the dealer with the right Nvidia A100. In Kazakhstan there is a bigger black market, where people fly in from New Delhi with suitcases of chips to sell at a profit.

Trade barriers don't make technology vanish. They push it underground. The world thought it was done with this kind of protectionism, yet the same back-channel economy has returned, this time created by export controls aimed at China.

head: When a Used Car Cost More Than a New One
dek: When shortages get bad enough, price stops reflecting quality and starts reflecting availability.
more: For listeners born after 1991, Amit gives one fact that captures the old closed economy. A secondhand car cost more than a new one, because a new car had a seven-year waiting list while a used car was available immediately, whatever its condition. He points listeners to his Seen and the Unseen episode on the 1991 reforms with Ajay and Shruti Rajagopalan.

When shortages get bad enough, price stops reflecting quality and starts reflecting availability. Amit tells the story as a warning, since tariffs, industrial policy and protectionism are back and the world 'almost feels as if' it is going backwards.

head: When India Was on the Wrong Side of Export Controls
dek: Export controls are not a new weapon invented for China. India lived under them, and the Cold War blockade of the USSR is the template.
more: In the late 1980s, the latest Sun SPARCstation workstations were not licensed for export to India, so you simply could not buy one here. Ajay calls them pitifully weak machines by modern standards. Until Manmohan Singh and George W. Bush signed the nuclear deal, US export controls on Indian buyers were extensive, and some remain even now.

Export controls are not a new weapon invented for China. India lived under them, and the Cold War blockade of the USSR is the template. What is new is the scale: the Bureau of Industry and Security, once fading in importance, has been revived into something bigger than it was even in the Cold War.

head: How NSE Built Its Risk System From Cheap CPUs
dek: If a problem can be split into independent pieces, many cheap processors can match a few elite ones.
more: In the early 1990s, NSE wanted something never done before: derivatives risk management that ran in real time and covered every single participant, not just clearing members. Ashish Chauhan (now NSE's CEO) and Susan Thomas were sent to Chicago to pick between the CME's and CBOT's systems. Susan came back and told the leadership, Ravi Narayan and Chitra Ramakrishna, that both were dull 1970s technology. She proposed a Beowulf cluster instead: many cheap Intel CPUs computing in parallel. Each participant's risk could be calculated separately, so the work splits cleanly across CPUs. NSE's IT leadership thought the idea was crazy and that real time was impossible. Tempers flared, and Ravi Narayan split the difference by funding a proof of concept at IGIDR. The target was 100 calculations a second, beyond what the incumbents thought possible. Built with Shovam Mishra, the system, called PRISM, succeeded and, reworked over the years, still runs NSE's derivatives risk management today.

If a problem can be split into independent pieces, many cheap processors can match a few elite ones. Ajay uses this to argue that blocking top-end chips mostly makes a determined country's work slower and more painful, not impossible.

head: When the Chips Are Down
dek: Together with Chip War, it demystifies the semiconductor wars and what is really going on beneath the headlines.
more: Together with Chip War, it demystifies the semiconductor wars and what is really going on beneath the headlines.
Amit's first pick in the recommendations segment. Pranay is a dear friend of both hosts.

more: It is critical for understanding what has actually happened in China. It backs Amit's refusal to take a caricatured, good-versus-evil Cold War view of a deeply complex country, even while he largely agrees about the damage Xi Jinping is doing.
