Ajay refers to it while explaining how Xi Jinping's rule broke China's economic model.

head: The BIS list of sanctions
dek: Anyone in business should know who is on the list. Dealing with a listed entity can land you in trouble, and being listed (about 12 Indian entities are) cuts you off from US travel, finance and trade.
more: Anyone in business should know who is on the list. Dealing with a listed entity can land you in trouble, and being listed (about 12 Indian entities are) cuts you off from US travel, finance and trade.
Ajay calls this 'knowledge that you can use' and urges listeners to hang out on the BIS website.

head: The Semiconductor Wars (Episode 358 of The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Abhiram Manchi
dek: It is a long-form deep dive on chips to accompany the book recommendations.
more: It is a long-form deep dive on chips to accompany the book recommendations.
Amit mentions his 'great episode' with the authors of When the Chips Are Down while discussing China's legacy-chip push and India's chip ambitions.

head: The Bipartisan U-Turn on China
dek: Until about 2016, Democrats and Republicans agreed that free trade was good and that America should engage with China.
more: Until about 2016, Democrats and Republicans agreed that free trade was good and that America should engage with China. It felt like an 'end of history' moment. Doubts began inside the Obama administration, including from Jake Sullivan. Trump then won partly through simple, wrong but easy-to-grasp narratives: immigrants and trade are taking your jobs. Biden promised to reverse Trump's policies, but his own team split. Janet Yellen wanted lower tariffs; Katherine Tai wanted higher ones. Biden sided with Sullivan's hawkish view. In eight years the consensus flipped to the opposite pole.

head: The Three-Legged Stool of the Tech War
dek: America's campaign rests on three legs. Industrial policy: heavy subsidies, such as those that drew TSMC to build fabs in Arizona (Amit notes India tried industrial policy in the 1950s–60s).
more: America's campaign rests on three legs. Industrial policy: heavy subsidies, such as those that drew TSMC to build fabs in Arizona (Amit notes India tried industrial policy in the 1950s–60s). Tariffs: rising under both Trump and Biden. Export controls: cutting off the IP, chips and tools China needs to develop indigenously. Chips matter so much because modern science runs on large-scale simulation, which needs high-powered compute.

head: Extraterritorial Export Controls and the FDPR
dek: Ajay says the only comparable precedent is the pre-1989 Western blockade of the USSR, and now Japan, the Netherlands and Germany have joined in.
more: Ajay says the only comparable precedent is the pre-1989 Western blockade of the USSR, and now Japan, the Netherlands and Germany have joined in. ASML's most advanced machines can't go to China or Russia. Neither can the three American software systems all chip design depends on. An Indian firm using American tools to design chips for a Chinese customer gets sanctioned too. US citizens and green-card holders can't work in these Chinese sectors. The Foreign Direct Product Rule goes furthest: goods made abroad with American technology or software count as American even if they never touch US soil. Huawei was its first major target.

head: America's Civilizing Mission in China
dek: Ajay argues that US engagement with China was not just interests and realpolitik but genuine idealism, something Indians struggle to picture.
more: Ajay argues that US engagement with China was not just interests and realpolitik but genuine idealism, something Indians struggle to picture. He says he has seen it face to face. After Nixon's 1972 opening and Deng's rise in 1978, American society and the state signed on to 'the China project'. After 1989, the end-of-history mood held that China would wise up into a free-market liberal democracy if given time. So the West handed over technology, investment and trade, and Bill Clinton championed China's entry into the WTO.

head: Why the West Turned: Misbehaviour Times Size
dek: China largely failed to keep its WTO promises. On top of that came state-backed IP theft and cyber attacks.
more: China largely failed to keep its WTO promises. On top of that came state-backed IP theft and cyber attacks. India has also misbehaved on trade, keeping protectionism while demanding openness, but India was small enough not to matter. China became systemically important. Then Russia invaded Ukraine, arguably funded by European gas purchases and fought with weapons built on German machine tools and Western electronics. Xi Jinping doubled down: he backed Russia, rattled sabres over Taiwan, and acted as a 'revisionist power' that seeks to overturn the international order by force. The West concluded it was arming its own adversaries.

head: The Third Globalization: Conditional Access to the Core
dek: In the second globalization, the advanced-economy core (about 65% of world GDP) gave the periphery unconditional access to capital, technology and markets.
more: In the second globalization, the advanced-economy core (about 65% of world GDP) gave the periphery unconditional access to capital, technology and markets. The only barriers were the periphery's own, such as India's. In the third globalization, access depends on good behaviour in military and foreign affairs. Ajay presents this first as a description of how the world now works, separate from the question of whether it is wise.

head: Economic Warfare Beats Real Warfare (Ajay's Position)
dek: As an economist, Ajay wants world peace and full globalization. But if the trade-off is between killing people and limiting a rogue power's prosperity, he chooses the second.
more: As an economist, Ajay wants world peace and full globalization. But if the trade-off is between killing people and limiting a rogue power's prosperity, he chooses the second. The old saying that two countries with McDonald's never go to war no longer holds. With a hot war under way and Xi refusing to renounce invading Taiwan, he sees the tech war as a reasonable strategy.

head: Economic Warfare Is Economic Warfare (Amit's Position)
dek: Amit argues that freedom and voluntary exchange should be foundational, not contingent.
more: Amit argues that freedom and voluntary exchange should be foundational, not contingent. A selective globalization is no more globalization than crony capitalism is capitalism. Who defines the 'global order' America claims to enforce? Trade is positive-sum, so the Swiss keeping zero tariffs on India is not a favour but in their own interest. Economic warfare hurts ordinary people on both sides while states play games. The answer to cheap Chinese imports or drone dominance is to deregulate your own industry. If local doctors are poor, train them up through competition rather than banning foreign doctors, or the patient dies. He admits he has no answer to IP theft or the Taiwan threat.

head: Did Deng Xiaoping Fail?
dek: Ajay says Deng failed because his project of making China a normal country collapsed under Xi.
more: Ajay says Deng failed because his project of making China a normal country collapsed under Xi. By that standard, he says, he would even call the US Constitution wrong if Trump cancelled democracy. Amit strongly disagrees. Deng lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty and raised the odds of a better political outcome. Blaming him for Xi is like saying Nehru failed had Indira Gandhi not called off the Emergency. The debate is about whether to judge leaders by long-run end states or by the probabilities they improved.

head: Why Self-Reliance Under Sanctions Fails in Authoritarian States
dek: Western export controls helped win the Cold War. Cut off from Western tech, the USSR tried self-reliance and never caught up: it never built competitive computers or got to Unix.
more: Western export controls helped win the Cold War. Cut off from Western tech, the USSR tried self-reliance and never caught up: it never built competitive computers or got to Unix. Part of the reason is that recreating a vast body of knowledge and artifacts is enormously hard. The other part is that authoritarian regimes crush the tiny fraction of maverick geniuses who would have done the catching up.

head: Parallelism as a Sanction-Buster
dek: Ajay notes that a determined person can do a lot without state-of-the-art equipment.
more: Ajay notes that a determined person can do a lot without state-of-the-art equipment. Modern parallel computing strings together many weaker processors, and that capability exists in India, China and Russia. So chip bans mostly add delay and pain. For a defence lab simulating a nuclear explosion, they are not material.

head: Sanctions Work on Races, Not Fixed Targets
dek: Against a fixed goal like a nuclear bomb, export controls are useless: the sanctioned country gets there eventually.
more: Against a fixed goal like a nuclear bomb, export controls are useless: the sanctioned country gets there eventually. In a race, only relative position matters. Examples are the drone war over Ukraine, artillery quality, or winner-takes-all product markets. A one- or two-month lag in DJI's or Russia's drone design could let Ukrainian drones win on the battlefield, and small technology edges can shift global market share. Ajay stresses that the jury is still out on whether this will work against China.

head: Unintended Consequences and Reflexivity
dek: Amit warns that the logic sounds great but the real world reacts. Squeezing China could make it more desperate over Taiwan.
more: Amit warns that the logic sounds great but the real world reacts. Squeezing China could make it more desperate over Taiwan. China is already ramping up legacy chips and could wipe out that business for TSMC, Intel and Samsung, which would also sink India's chip ambitions. He compares this to America's arrogance in arming Afghan guerrillas, including Osama bin Laden. Ajay agrees there will be surprises and adds a nuance: a drone needs mostly simple legacy chips plus one or a few high-end CPUs, so China may come to dominate legacy chips globally.

head: Three Stories, Not One
dek: Ajay separates three overlapping stories. The third globalization: access to the core becoming conditional, with the Trump tariffs of 2016–18 as one big trigger.
more: Ajay separates three overlapping stories. The third globalization: access to the core becoming conditional, with the Trump tariffs of 2016–18 as one big trigger. The tech war: a military-driven escalation from 2022, with the sweeping US export restrictions of 7 October 2022 as the key milestone. And a short-term Chinese macroeconomic problem of overproduction from the last year or two. Mixing them up muddles the debate.

Amit: 'as Donald Trump would say, in all caps, we have the best plans. But the great geopolitical and military strategist Mike Tyson once said that the best plan only survives till you get punched in the face.' Ajay corrects the soundbite to 'everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth', and Amit counter-corrects: 'It's not everybody, it's everyone.'

head: Ajay explains parallel computing by noting that the calculation for Amit is independent of the one for producer Nomsita.
more: Ajay explains parallel computing by noting that the calculation for Amit is independent of the one for producer Nomsita. Amit: 'neither me nor Nomsita understood exactly that parallel whatever you were saying. But you spoke about multiplying our power, so I'm kinda happy with that.'

head: Ajay on India negotiating a free trade agreement with Switzerland
more: Ajay on India negotiating a free trade agreement with Switzerland: 'the humor of this is the Swiss have no tariffs against anything from India. So what are you going to negotiate? The Swiss say we are already at zero.'

head: Francis Fukuyama's
more: Francis Fukuyama's 'end of history', which Amit calls an 'often misinterpreted phrase'. It was the 1990s mood in which the West assumed liberal democracy and free markets were the only game in town.

head: Ajay's sketch of the post-1989 euphoria
more: Ajay's sketch of the post-1989 euphoria: 'This entire nightmare of 2000 years of fighting between Persia and Athens has come to an end, and Athens won.'

head: The old saying that two countries with McDonald's never go to war.
more: The old saying that two countries with McDonald's never go to war. Ajay: 'Well, Russia invaded Ukraine and both countries had McDonald's.'
'Where you stand depends on where you sit': Amit's aside on why Biden's trade chief Katherine Tai pushed for higher tariffs while Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen wanted engagement.

head: The Bureau of Industry and Security, which Ajay calls an obscure agency
more: The Bureau of Industry and Security, which Ajay calls an obscure agency and 'one of the most consequential government organizations in the whole world'. Amit adds that it issued about 100,000 export licences a year at its Cold War peak, around 10,000 in the 1990s, and is back to about 40,000.

head: The pencil thought experiment from the previous episode: if all artifacts vanished
more: The pencil thought experiment from the previous episode: if all artifacts vanished, 'we're just a bunch of seven and a half billion naked people wandering the world. How will we ever build a pencil again?' Ajay uses it to show why a country cut off from global knowledge struggles to catch up.

head: The Bleeding Lip Libertarian
dek: The cold open becomes the frame for the whole episode. India's pension promises are deep cuts with no clotting mechanism, a fiscal haemorrhage that does not heal on its own.
more: On the morning of the shoot, Amit's mind wandered while shaving and he cut his lip. The cut kept bleeding, leaving a trail of blood down to his bare torso. Ajay put on his 'scientific hat', said oxygen makes blood clot, and told him to stand in front of a fan. Amit asked if a hairdryer would do, and so became perhaps the first person in history to aim a hairdryer at his lips. He then drew the metaphor: one superficial cut stops bleeding, but a body with a thousand deep cuts and no clotting mechanism just keeps bleeding.
The cold open becomes the frame for the whole episode. India's pension promises are deep cuts with no clotting mechanism, a fiscal haemorrhage that does not heal on its own.

head: What Kept Jayaprakash Narayan Up at Night
dek: The biggest threats to a country are often invisible to smart, well-read people because they hide behind dull acronyms.
more: In mid-2023 Amit recorded his third episode with the politician Jayaprakash Narayan. JP told him that one thing kept him up at night, something so big he could not think about anything else: India's pensions crisis, as states moved to replace the NPS with the Old Pension Scheme. Amit had never heard of NPS or OPS and wondered what the fuss was about. JP replied, 'No, Amit, we are destroying our future generation.' That sent Amit to Ajay, who turned out to be one of the architects of the NPS.
The biggest threats to a country are often invisible to smart, well-read people because they hide behind dull acronyms. 'Scheme to scheme' turned out to be a question of generational justice.

head: From a Port Workers' Whip-Round to Bismarck's Free Promise
dek: A policy can be easy to announce precisely because its cost is zero today.
more: Pensions began as small acts of grace. At one port, when workers' health broke from lugging cartons, their fellow workers pooled a little money to support them. Bismarck made it a state affair: in 1889 he announced a pension of 50% of last year's income, payable from age 70. There were no antibiotics, doctors were still putting leeches on patients, and few people lived much past 70. The promise sounded generous but cost almost nothing. Over the next century, rising longevity, falling birth rates and political tinkering turned the same idea into a runaway disaster.
A policy can be easy to announce precisely because its cost is zero today. Its price is hidden in mortality tables and demographics that will flip decades later.

head: Project Oasis and the 68% Bombshell
dek: Whoever does the right calculation reframes the debate. People had been alarmed by pension flows that doubled every six years.
more: By the 1990s, pension payouts for the railways, the military and civil servants were surging. In 1998, under the Vajpayee government, Maneka Gandhi was Minister of Social Justice and Anand Bordia was a joint secretary there. Bordia worked with Gautam Bhardwaj, then at the Invest India Economic Foundation, to set up Project Oasis. It was led by Surendra Dave, founding chairman of SEBI, and Ajay sat on its expert committee. Dave's intuition was that equity returns, modern technology and auction-procured index funds could make a cheap, attractive pension system. Bhardwaj and Dave then calculated the present value of the promises made to civil servants: 68% of GDP, for a tiny sliver of the population. The number reached the 'big four' of the NDA cabinet: Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee. All four grasped at once that it had to be fixed.
Whoever does the right calculation reframes the debate. People had been alarmed by pension flows that doubled every six years. Seeing the stock as a share of GDP made the problem existential.

head: Vajpayee's 'Show Me the Calculations'
dek: Good reform is not only technically sound but politically packaged. The 10% sweetener was a statesman's judgement about what people would accept as fair.
more: Ajay was then in the Ministry of Finance. Vajpayee kept sending back variations: suppose we do it like this, show me the numbers. Finally he settled on a formula. Civil servants would get a 10% wage hike, so 100 became 110, and 20 would be deducted into a personal pension account, leaving take-home pay at 90. Vajpayee judged that this was a fair deal for giving up the old defined-benefit promise.
Good reform is not only technically sound but politically packaged. The 10% sweetener was a statesman's judgement about what people would accept as fair.

head: 'Yeh To Karna Hi Hai': The Cabinet Meeting
dek: Reforms with a hundred-year payoff need a leader willing to spend political capital on benefits no current voter will see.
more: Ajay worked directly with Yashwant Sinha, S Narayan and UK Sinha, and they carried the case up to Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee. Ajay was not in the decisive cabinet meeting, but UK Sinha was and told him about it. The big four favoured the reform and many other ministers did not. Vajpayee, who had a way of either appearing to be asleep or actually being asleep in meetings, sat with his eyes almost closed and took in the debate. At the end he ruled: 'Yeh to karna hi hai' ('This simply has to be done'). He signed the file on 12 December 2002, and every new central government employee from 1 January 2004 went into the new system.
Reforms with a hundred-year payoff need a leader willing to spend political capital on benefits no current voter will see. Ajay offers Vajpayee's line as a motto for every reformer.

head: The 2004 Crash That Steadied the Ship
dek: A market panic can discipline politics. Here it helped put a reform-minded team in charge at the moment a fragile reform was handed from one government to the next.
more: In the 2004 campaign, a Congress candidate in Delhi tried to stir up anger that the NDA was taking away defined-benefit pensions, but it got no traction. New recruits were fine with the switch. Then on 17 May 2004 the stock market crashed after some CPM politicians talked about tearing the house down. Ajay makes a causal claim: the crash helped Sonia Gandhi settle on Manmohan Singh, Chidambaram, Montek Ahluwalia and C Rangarajan as the economic team, people who had led the reforms all along. The market calmed down, and the new UPA government re-examined the NPS from scratch rather than scrapping it.
A market panic can discipline politics. Here it helped put a reform-minded team in charge at the moment a fragile reform was handed from one government to the next.

head: Briefing Rahul Gandhi on Pensions
dek: Knowing the right answer does not determine political behaviour. When incentives point the other way, politicians who know better will still pander.
more: While the UPA was re-examining the NPS, Bibek Debroy organised a half-day session at the Rajiv Gandhi Institute. Ajay walked Rahul Gandhi and a group of young Congress MPs through pension reform in detail. Amit later points out the irony: the Congress went on to push for a return to the OPS in state after state, even though its leadership had been personally briefed on why it was a disaster.
Knowing the right answer does not determine political behaviour. When incentives point the other way, politicians who know better will still pander.

head: Surendra Dave vs the Fourteen Insurance CEOs
dek: One well-argued rebuttal at the right table can decide a national policy.
more: The insurance industry rebelled against the NPS, arguing that pensions are insurance and that they, not new index-fund managers, should run them. Chidambaram called a meeting with fourteen insurance company CEOs. Ajay was told he could attend but must not speak. Each CEO argued that they knew the business, could do index funds and could even offer guarantees. Chidambaram then turned to Surendra Dave, who gave what Ajay calls a masterly fifteen-minute rebuttal while Ajay's heart was in his mouth. Nobody said anything after. Chidambaram and Dave went off to talk, and later that day word came: the boss has decided, we're doing NPS.

One well-argued rebuttal at the right table can decide a national policy. Defending against incumbents, who would have turned pensions back into defined-benefit products, mattered as much as the design itself.

head: Chidambaram's Contract Workaround
dek: When legislation is blocked, clever contract design can carry a regulator's load.
more: Chidambaram wanted a law to anchor the NPS and set up the PFRDA as regulator, and UK Sinha led the drafting. But the CPI(M), essential to the UPA-1 coalition, insisted that defined-benefit pensions were 'who we are'. The Congress kept negotiating from 2004 to 2009 and kept going even after 2009 to preserve coalition harmony, finally passing the law in 2013. Meanwhile Chidambaram, whom Ajay calls one of the smartest legal minds in the country, built the regulatory regime out of private contracts. If fund managers or NSDL wanted the business, they had to accept inspections and disclosure. So the NPS ran from 2004, nine years before its law existed.
When legislation is blocked, clever contract design can carry a regulator's load. A brilliant legal mind in government is itself a form of state capacity.

head: 'Your Baradari Is Not Ready': Yashwant Sinha on Inflation Targeting
dek: Even powerful ministers act within the Overton window set by the intellectual community.
more: In 2002 and 2003 Ajay pitched inflation targeting to Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha. Sinha said the idea was too far from conventional Indian economic thinking and that Ajay's community of economists did not yet understand it. Until the broader intellectual consensus shifted, he said, a finance minister could only follow, not lead. Inflation targeting finally arrived in 2015.
Even powerful ministers act within the Overton window set by the intellectual community. Lasting reform comes from shifting what experts broadly accept, not from persuading one official.

head: The Pension Reform Community That Went Home
dek: Passing a reform is the start, not the end. Without a standing community to defend and refine it, the field is left to organised interest groups and pandering politicians.
more: Around 1998 to 2004 India had a real pension reform community, with papers, seminars, op-eds and an intellectual ferment that made the NPS possible. Once the decisions were taken, everyone assumed the job was done and the community dissolved. Pension work also moved from KP Krishnan's DEA to the DFS, and institutional memory was lost. Small flaws went unfixed, equity exposure stayed timid, military pensions drifted into OROP, and nobody redid the implicit-debt calculation. When young civil servants began demanding the OPS, Karnataka once informally asked Ajay to spend a day with its trade unions. That kind of patient engagement should have happened everywhere, but there was no one left to do it.
Passing a reform is the start, not the end. Without a standing community to defend and refine it, the field is left to organised interest groups and pandering politicians.

head: The Project Oasis Report (2000)
by: Project Oasis expert committee, led by Surendra Dave
dek: It is the founding document of Indian pension reform: defined contributions, individual accounts and cheap index funds.
more: It is the founding document of Indian pension reform: defined contributions, individual accounts and cheap index funds.
The 1998 government project whose expert committee, including Ajay, designed what became the New Pension System. Linked in the show notes.

head: Towards Estimating India's Implicit Pension Debt
dek: This number woke up the Vajpayee cabinet. Ajay laments that it was never redone in the two decades since.
more: This number woke up the Vajpayee cabinet. Ajay laments that it was never redone in the two decades since.
The calculation Ajay credits with putting India's civil service pension promises at 68% of GDP.

head: In search of inclusion (2015)
dek: Further reading on pension systems from Renuka Sane, who Amit notes has spent recent years working on this field.
more: Further reading on pension systems from Renuka Sane, who Amit notes has spent recent years working on this field.
Listed in the show notes as pensions research.

head: Simulating Pension Income Scenarios with penCalc (2018)
dek: An example of the pension income simulation work Ajay says India badly needs more of.
more: An example of the pension income simulation work Ajay says India badly needs more of.
Listed in the show notes.

head: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347, The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane
dek: A longer deep dive on the OPS vs NPS story and the bipartisan consensus behind the NPS.
more: A longer deep dive on the OPS vs NPS story and the bipartisan consensus behind the NPS.
The earlier, detailed pensions episode, recorded as the Congress pushed to bring the OPS back.

head: Jayaprakash Narayan Wants to Mend Our Democracy (Episode 334, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It is where Amit first learned the stakes, and the conversation that led to this episode.
more: It is where Amit first learned the stakes, and the conversation that led to this episode.
The episode where JP told Amit the pensions crisis kept him up at night.

head: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls the eight-hour episode an 'absolute masterpiece' on how the state works from the inside, full of amazing stories.
more: Amit calls the eight-hour episode an 'absolute masterpiece' on how the state works from the inside, full of amazing stories.
Recommended after Ajay's behind-the-scenes stories of cabinet meetings and policymaking.

head: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
dek: Reform takes decades and a sustained intellectual community, not whispers in a joint secretary's ear.
more: Reform takes decades and a sustained intellectual community, not whispers in a joint secretary's ear.
Ajay cites it twice: on the 15 years from Project Oasis to the 2013 law, and on the right theory of change.

head: Atomic Habits
dek: It teaches you to turn your mind away from goals and towards habits and processes, the personal version of structural reform.
more: It teaches you to turn your mind away from goals and towards habits and processes, the personal version of structural reform.
Amit's end-of-episode recommendation, following the 'reform thyself' discussion.

head: Defined Benefit vs Defined Contribution
dek: A defined benefit (DB) pension guarantees a payout for life, funded in effect by the young paying the old.
more: A defined benefit (DB) pension guarantees a payout for life, funded in effect by the young paying the old. Every DB payment rests on money coercively taken from someone else, and it pits generations against each other. A defined contribution (DC) pension uses state power only to force you to save into your own account. The money is yours, nobody else can touch it, and nobody pays for anyone else.

head: Why Every DB Pension Blows Up
dek: Three forces break DB schemes everywhere. Longevity rises, so the value of lifelong payments grows.
more: Three forces break DB schemes everywhere. Longevity rises, so the value of lifelong payments grows. Birth rates fall, so fewer young people support more old ones. Democratic politics keeps loosening the parameters, such as the pension percentage and the age at which it starts. Ajay is a 'one-handed economist' on this: every DB programme has reneged, or will renege, on its promises.

head: Nominal vs Inflation-Indexed vs Wage-Indexed: Chalk and Cheese
dek: The three terms sound alike but are completely different creatures. A fixed nominal pension can be funded with sensible planning.
more: The three terms sound alike but are completely different creatures. A fixed nominal pension can be funded with sensible planning. Inflation indexing roughly doubles the present value and can only partly be achieved. Wage indexing, which pays you half of what today's workers earn, is astronomically expensive and impossible to fund. Fairness arguments like OROP ('a general retired 20 years ago should get what a newly retired general gets') blow up the numbers.

head: Conditional Life Expectancy
dek: Life expectancy at birth (about 74 in India) is the wrong number for pensions.
more: Life expectancy at birth (about 74 in India) is the wrong number for pensions. Once you survive to 60 or 70, all the earlier ways you could have died are behind you, so your expected remaining life is longer. Pension costs must also use forward-looking longevity, not backward-looking LIC data. Ajay says a 20-year-old today has a reasonable chance of reaching 120.

head: Pensions as a Test of State Capability
dek: Like waging a war, pension policy is a raw test of whether a state can think.
more: Like waging a war, pension policy is a raw test of whether a state can think. It requires present-value calculations over a hundred years, honest assumptions and the discipline to stay responsible. That is treacherous for a poor country. It ties to defence too: Ajay argues a mighty military is made out of economics, and the first task of Indian military reform is fixing military pensions.

head: Implicit Pension Debt: Stocks vs Flows
dek: Watching this year's pension payouts (the flow) understates the danger.
more: Watching this year's pension payouts (the flow) understates the danger. The real measure is the stock: the present value of all promises already made, equal to the debt you would need to buy annuities for everyone covered. For Indian civil servants that came to 68% of GDP. Ajay says the US figure is 200% of GDP.

head: The NPS: The State Copying Smart Personal Finance
dek: The NPS makes a civil servant do what a sophisticated saver would do anyway: save, hold equities, use cheap index funds and avoid fees. 20% of salary is deducted into a personal account.
more: The NPS makes a civil servant do what a sophisticated saver would do anyway: save, hold equities, use cheap index funds and avoid fees. 20% of salary is deducted into a personal account. A few fund managers chosen by public tender run index funds, where the only test is how little they charge. Choosing by tender is also politically safe, since no one can demand a CBI probe into a manager's performance. An expert committee sets the default mix of equities, corporate bonds and government bonds, but anyone can override it online. NPS Trust holds the money and NSDL keeps the records, and members get an SMS each month as their balance grows.

head: Bought, Not Sold
dek: A toxic saying in finance holds that 'fund management is sold, not bought'.
more: A toxic saying in finance holds that 'fund management is sold, not bought'. It is the logic of celebrity ads, huge commissions and armies of agents pushing tax-saving products on friends and family, which steers money into bad assets. The NPS flips this. Fund managers receive bulk money without even knowing their customers' names, and compete only on price.

head: Keep Insurance Out of Accumulation
dek: From the first job until retirement, a pension is simply asset accumulation.
more: From the first job until retirement, a pension is simply asset accumulation. It is your money, and your heirs inherit it if you die. Insurance enters only at the end, if you choose to convert your savings into a lifelong monthly annuity. Handing the whole system to insurers would have dragged it back towards defined-benefit thinking.

head: Change the Rules at the Point of Recruitment
dek: The NPS did not take back promises made to existing employees, even those hired a month earlier.
more: The NPS did not take back promises made to existing employees, even those hired a month earlier. Only new recruits joined the new system, and job advertisements said so. That made the reform fair and politically defensible. The OPS revival breaks this logic: recruits who knowingly signed up for the NPS now demand the old promises.

head: The Transition Generation Pays Twice
dek: By design, for about 25 years governments pay both the old pensions and the extra 10% salary that funds new NPS accounts.
more: By design, for about 25 years governments pay both the old pensions and the extra 10% salary that funds new NPS accounts. The fiscal gains only show up around 2029. With no researchers modelling this, politicians saw only the extra cost and lost their nerve just before the payoff. The 25-year wait applies to state finances; individuals in a well-run NPS do better than under the OPS.

head: Pension Policy Is for the Pensioner: Diversify Globally
dek: Ajay calls globally diversified equity index funds the closest thing to a free lunch, with global diversification roughly halving risk.
more: Ajay calls globally diversified equity index funds the closest thing to a free lunch, with global diversification roughly halving risk. His one regret about the NPS design is that it was not globally diversified from day one, with perhaps 60 to 80% of the money invested abroad. Pension money should serve only its owners, not prop up the stock market or fund infrastructure. Timid civil servants also kept equity exposure too low.

head: Reforms Decay Without an Intellectual Ecosystem
dek: The OPS revival comes from a small, organised group of civil servants, while the cost falls on everyone.
more: The OPS revival comes from a small, organised group of civil servants, while the cost falls on everyone. Politicians weigh that group against a non-existent intellectual discourse and pander. The only counterweight is a sustained community of researchers, papers, simulations and op-eds, funded and fed with data. India's last implicit-pension-debt calculation dates to Bhardwaj and Dave.

head: Theory of Change: Shift the Overton Window, Don't Whisper in Ears
dek: A popular theory among Indian philanthropists is to place consultants beside a joint secretary and whisper good ideas.
more: A popular theory among Indian philanthropists is to place consultants beside a joint secretary and whisper good ideas. That only produces small changes within what officials already accept. Real reform needs a broad community that changes what is thinkable, as Yashwant Sinha told Ajay about inflation targeting.

head: The UPS Guarantee Is a Put Option
dek: The Unified Pension Scheme keeps a fund but promises to top up any annuity below 50% from a guarantee fund.
more: The Unified Pension Scheme keeps a fund but promises to top up any annuity below 50% from a guarantee fund. In derivatives terms, that is a put option on the portfolio, and put options can be costly. Its partial inflation indexation also assumes a real (inflation-indexed) annuity market that India does not have. No calculations have been published, so it may become a contingent liability for the state.

head: Open-Source Policy Calculations
dek: Decisions involving sums like 50 to 100% of GDP should come with full calculations, every assumption stated, and code anyone can download and rerun.
more: Decisions involving sums like 50 to 100% of GDP should come with full calculations, every assumption stated, and code anyone can download and rerun. Ajay and Renuka Sane did this for OROP. He sees it as the only route to a meaningful democratic debate, and the UPS falls short.

head: Structural vs Parametric Reform
dek: Parametric reform keeps the old structure and adjusts its settings, which politics will keep fiddling with forever.
more: Parametric reform keeps the old structure and adjusts its settings, which politics will keep fiddling with forever. Structural reform builds a new system with no dials to turn. The NPS was structural: your money, your account, no fudge factors. NREGS was promised to be self-liquidating, yet its daily wage keeps rising and it distorts the labour market. Ajay fears a government-designed universal healthcare system would creep upward the same way.

head: Reform Thyself
dek: Amit turns the framework on personal life. Locking yourself away for a weekend to write, or sprinting occasionally while unfit, is a parametric tweak.
more: Amit turns the framework on personal life. Locking yourself away for a weekend to write, or sprinting occasionally while unfit, is a parametric tweak. Building daily habits, or changing what and how you eat, is structural. He asks listeners to pause after the episode and ask what is wrong with their lives, and whether it needs a structural or a parametric fix.

head: Amit on finally caring about his looks
more: Amit on finally caring about his looks: 'I have always thought I have a face for audio, which is why the Seen and the Unseen Audio Podcast. But since I have started doing the show with you, Ajay, especially given how good looking and dashing you are, I thought I have to make some minimal effort.'

head: Amit, bleeding and refusing to cancel
more: Amit, bleeding and refusing to cancel: 'Man, we gotta shoot. I don't care if I die, but we gotta shoot.' And on his blood-streaked torso: 'Had my torso been a little more better developed, it would have been an exceptionally enticing scene, but it wasn't. It was just bloody.'
Amit: 'Just as this nation is regrettably too full of bleeding heart liberals, here you had a bleeding lip libertarian. Though I do not like labels, Pushpa, so we shall not go there.'

head: Harry Truman's plea for a…
more: Harry Truman's plea for a 'one-handed economist', one who wouldn't keep saying 'on the other hand'. Ajay calls himself one on defined-benefit pensions, and Amit explains why that certainty is rare.

head: Amit on wage-indexed pensions
more: Amit on wage-indexed pensions: 'After I retire, I want the state to give me every month half of BeerBiceps' income. And we'll be fine. That's where I want it indexed... As far as money is concerned, I'm not doing his content.'

head: Ajay on the nightmare headline governments fear
more: Ajay on the nightmare headline governments fear: 'Oh, this person was a secretary to government and now she's sitting by the gates of the Bangalore Metro begging for a free idli sambar.'

head: Ajay on pushing cheap index funds in the late 90s against fund-manager machismo (
more: Ajay on pushing cheap index funds in the late 90s against fund-manager machismo ('if you pay peanuts, you will get monkeys'): 'I lost many friends in the financial system.'

head: Amit imagines a pensions web series with Vajpayee gazing at a young Ajay in his…
more: Amit imagines a pensions web series with Vajpayee gazing at a young Ajay in his 'languorous, leisurely way'. Ajay deflates it at once: he never sat with Vajpayee on this question.

head: Ajay on Vajpayee in meetings
more: Ajay on Vajpayee in meetings: 'he had a way of either appearing to be asleep or actually being asleep in meetings. Okay, and you could never tell, but he was a wise man.'

head: Ajay channelling the insurance lobby
more: Ajay channelling the insurance lobby: 'We don't want no stinking pension fund managers, we don't want no stinking index funds.'

head: After Ajay is told to keep quiet in the insurance CEOs' meeting, Amit
more: After Ajay is told to keep quiet in the insurance CEOs' meeting, Amit: 'Gentle reader, this person here who looks like an elder statesman was once a firebrand revolutionary, right? You haven't seen that side of him.'

head: Ajay's dry aside on states trying to grab NPS money
more: Ajay's dry aside on states trying to grab NPS money: 'last I heard it was not yet easy for governments in India to expropriate our private property. I mean I know they can do it, but it is still hard.'

head: Ajay inverts Mark Antony's line from Julius Caesar, 26 years after Project Oasis
more: Ajay inverts Mark Antony's line from Julius Caesar, 26 years after Project Oasis: 'I come to praise the NPS, not bury it.'

head: Amit invokes
more: Amit invokes 'Jefferson's alleged phrase', eternal vigilance, as the lesson for reformers who go home after a policy passes.

head: Ajay quotes Bruce Springsteen on India's missing policy intellectuals
more: Ajay quotes Bruce Springsteen on India's missing policy intellectuals: 'Well man, the poets around here don't write nothing at all. They just stand by and let it all be.'

head: Amit quotes Annie Dillard
more: Amit quotes Annie Dillard, 'How we spend our days is how we spend our lives', to argue for structural reform through daily habits rather than occasional sprints.

head: Amit on his diabetes reversal
more: Amit on his diabetes reversal: 'though at the rate I have fallen off the wagon in terms of food, I might well get it back.'

head: A storm interrupts the outdoor shoot. Amit returns
more: A storm interrupts the outdoor shoot. Amit returns with 'There was a storm. There is a storm', calls the UPS a storm that won't pass easily, and signs off with 'the storm is upon us and we must fight the degradation of the state.' Ajay: 'Does this mean we have to do the next one indoor?'

head: The Day the Cement and Steel Ministries Went Into Mourning
dek: Price controls create shortages, and they also create officials whose importance depends on rationing.
more: A journalist friend of Ajay's covered the cement and steel ministries in the early 1980s, when price controls on both were abolished. Under those controls, anyone doing construction had to fight to get cement and steel, or ended up with substandard cement. Ajay traces a direct line from that bad cement to buildings of the '50s and '60s collapsing later. When the decontrol was announced, the whole government building felt it had suffered a personal catastrophe, because the market would now sort out cement and steel and nobody needed the bureaucrats any more.

Price controls create shortages, and they also create officials whose importance depends on rationing. The grief in that building was about lost power, not about policy. As Ajay puts it, a sensible country doesn't need a ministry of steel or a ministry of cement.

head: The Grocery Store After the Earthquake
dek: In a disaster, the 'price gouger' is sending a signal that pulls in supply and stretches what's left.
more: As a college student, Amit went with paramedic friends in an ambulance for three days through earthquake-hit parts of Maharashtra, including Latur. In one village, one side had collapsed completely and a single grocery store was still standing. Villagers were furious that it was charging so much and said it should be outlawed. Amit, who was reading Marx then, agreed with them. Today he thinks the high prices made it more likely that supplies would flow into the village and that households would economise and share. The government should spend its own money on disaster victims, not interfere with prices.
In a disaster, the 'price gouger' is sending a signal that pulls in supply and stretches what's left. Compassion belongs in direct government spending, not in price caps that empty the shelves.

head: The Friend Who Missed His Flight to an Uber Price Cap
dek: A price cap doesn't hand out scarce goods according to need. It hands them out by luck and queue position, and it switches off the signal that would have brought more supply.
more: Delhi once experimented with capping Uber surge pricing. A friend of Amit's who understands economics well didn't know the cap was in place, so he didn't plan for the shortage it would cause. With prices frozen, the cabs went first come, first served, and he missed his flight. Amit uses this to show what surge pricing does: people with urgent needs, like getting to a hospital or an airport, can outbid casual riders, and the higher fare wakes idle drivers and pulls them onto the road.
A price cap doesn't hand out scarce goods according to need. It hands them out by luck and queue position, and it switches off the signal that would have brought more supply.

head: How Europe Beat Putin's Gas Blackmail Without Price Caps
dek: Prices handled allocation and supply, and fiscal transfers handled fairness.
more: After invading Ukraine, Putin cut gas supplies to Europe, hoping to break the Western coalition. Gas prices shot up and Russian propaganda said Europeans would freeze and come begging. European policymakers did not cap prices. On the demand side, high prices sorted users: some factories shut, some switched to electricity, some paid up and kept running. On the supply side, LNG terminals were built in record time, buyers diverted Qatari tankers bound elsewhere, and American shale gas production and exports surged. To protect the poor, and to deny pro-Putin parties a grievance, governments made large on-budget payments so poor households could afford the expensive gas.

Prices handled allocation and supply, and fiscal transfers handled fairness. Nobody had expected Europe to get past the blackmail, and the high prices were what made it possible. Capping them would have choked off the supply response.

head: Marine Drive's Rs 150 Flats
dek: The decay is exactly what economic theory predicts. For the landlord, rent control is theft, and everyone else in the city pays through higher rents.
more: Walk along Marine Drive in Bombay and you see old, dilapidated buildings. Amit points to rent control, which India started in 1949, as one reason. He hears of tenants paying around Rs 150 a month for flats that would otherwise rent for four or five lakh. Landlords have no reason to maintain the buildings, developers have no reason to build, and the shrinking supply pushes up rents everywhere outside the controlled stock.
The decay is exactly what economic theory predicts. For the landlord, rent control is theft, and everyone else in the city pays through higher rents.

head: The Statist Friend in the Rent-Controlled Flat
dek: Where you stand depends on where you sit. People's views on state control often match what that control does for them personally.
more: A leftist friend whom both Amit and Ajay know, a hardcore statist who thinks the government must control everything, has lived for two generations in a rent-controlled flat near Shivaji Park.
Where you stand depends on where you sit. People's views on state control often match what that control does for them personally.

head: How MSPs Tilted India Toward Carbs
dek: When the state sets prices, farmers grow what the state rewards, not what people need.
more: Amit recalls an example from the show's agriculture episode. In the late 1960s, as he remembers it, the government announced minimum support prices for cereals but not for pulses. That made carbohydrates cheap and plentiful and protein relatively scarce, which Amit links to a worsening of what we now call India's diabetes epidemic.
When the state sets prices, farmers grow what the state rewards, not what people need. Amit calls it a humanitarian crime.

head: From a Rice MSP in Punjab to Smog in Delhi
dek: One distorted price set off a chain: depleted water, burnt fields, poisoned air, and a political deadlock.
more: Punjab is arid and rice needs a lot of water, but an MSP on rice made it worth growing there. Farmers used free farm electricity, which mostly benefits rich farmers, to dig borewells and pump out groundwater. After harvest they are left with rice stubble, and the cheapest way to get rid of it is to burn it. Every year the smoke drifts to Delhi and pollution peaks. Even with the same party ruling both states, nobody can fix it, because the farmers who benefit fight back hard.
One distorted price set off a chain: depleted water, burnt fields, poisoned air, and a political deadlock. A bad equilibrium built by a price intervention is very hard to undo.
printed: Rice in Punjab, smoke in Delhi

head: Azar Nafisi: Liberalism Sounds Truest Where It's Under Threat
dek: People who forget what life without freedom was like stop defending it.
more: At a recent conference on liberalism in Washington, DC, Amit heard Azar Nafisi, author of Reading Lolita in Tehran, say that classical liberal values are expressed most truly by dissenters in Iran, because for them it is an existential fight for basic freedoms. Her implication was that Americans have taken freedom for granted for so long that they can afford luxury beliefs. Amit adds that someone born in 2004 never saw pre-liberalisation India or the Soviet Union.
People who forget what life without freedom was like stop defending it. That generational amnesia is why bad ideas like price controls keep coming back.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: Amit says he still often rereads it to remind himself of its argument.
more: Amit says he still often rereads it to remind himself of its argument. Society is too complex and its knowledge too dispersed for anyone to plan from the top, and prices are the decentralised system that makes coordination possible.
Hayek wrote it in the mid-1940s as a reply to central planners. It anchors the whole episode.

head: The Fatal Conceit
dek: It names the core error behind every price control: thinking you know enough to run society from the top down.
more: It names the core error behind every price control: thinking you know enough to run society from the top down.
Amit uses Hayek's later phrase for the planners' belief that society can be designed from above.

head: I, Pencil
dek: It is short and, in Ajay's word, amazing. It shows millions of people coordinating through prices with no committee in charge, which is the best intuition for what economists call 'the resource allocation'.
more: It is short and, in Ajay's word, amazing. It shows millions of people coordinating through prices with no committee in charge, which is the best intuition for what economists call 'the resource allocation'.
Amit calls it a great essay about how people in many countries cooperate to make a pencil. Ajay tells listeners they must read it.

head: Prices, Fast and Slow
dek: Amit calls it a wonderful piece and asks listeners to read the full thing as a companion to the episode.
more: Amit calls it a wonderful piece and asks listeners to read the full thing as a companion to the episode.
Amit's recommendation in the closing segment. He wanted to discuss it in the episode but it didn't fit the narrative.

head: Alone in the City
dek: It is where Amit first tied the search for a home in the city to the damage rent control does.
more: It is where Amit first tied the search for a home in the city to the damage rent control does.
A piece from Amit's 'Houseful Economics' column that used a song from Gharaonda about being alone in the city and searching for shelter.

head: The Mystery of Capital
dek: It explains why property rights matter, and why an asset whose value the state has drained away stops working as capital.
more: It explains why property rights matter, and why an asset whose value the state has drained away stops working as capital.
Amit's explicit recommendation while arguing that rent control is theft that turns property into 'dead capital'.

head: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
dek: Amit once believed minimum wages were how you pull a country out of poverty.
more: Amit once believed minimum wages were how you pull a country out of poverty. This video sent him into a rabbit hole of books and articles that changed his worldview.
A video Amit cites as the start of his change of mind on minimum wages.

head: Illiberal Reformers
dek: It shows that some celebrated progressive labour legislation of the early 20th century was meant to keep African Americans and women out of the workforce.
more: It shows that some celebrated progressive labour legislation of the early 20th century was meant to keep African Americans and women out of the workforce. The already privileged were protecting themselves.
Cited in the minimum wage chapter. Amit calls it a 'magnificent book'.

head: Snatching decline from the jaws of growth
dek: It proposes a practical wedge: fully deregulate labour law in IT and IT-enabled services, where workers obviously don't need paternalistic protection, then expand to other industries if it works.
more: It proposes a practical wedge: fully deregulate labour law in IT and IT-enabled services, where workers obviously don't need paternalistic protection, then expand to other industries if it works.
A Business Standard column that Ajay found 'rather cool', on how to break India's political deadlock on labour law.

head: How to Do Development (Episode 57 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It argues that every welfare indicator, health included, improves only through economic growth, and growth comes only from economic freedom.
more: It argues that every welfare indicator, health included, improves only through economic growth, and growth comes only from economic freedom.
Amit calls it a great episode on development.

head: Reading Lolita in Tehran
dek: Nafisi's point, that liberal values are voiced most truly by dissenters in Iran, shows what gets lost when free societies take liberty for granted.
more: Nafisi's point, that liberal values are voiced most truly by dissenters in Iran, shows what gets lost when free societies take liberty for granted.
Amit heard the author speak at a liberalism conference in Washington, DC.

head: Slouching Towards Utopia
dek: It gives a better structural understanding of the old economic policy consensus that existed before Trump, Putin, Xi Jinping and the right-wing authoritarians.
more: It gives a better structural understanding of the old economic policy consensus that existed before Trump, Putin, Xi Jinping and the right-wing authoritarians.
One of Ajay's two closing recommendations.

head: Price Theory
dek: Some things were done right by the old masters, and the best way to understand prices is to go back and study them.
more: Some things were done right by the old masters, and the best way to understand prices is to go back and study them.
Ajay's second closing recommendation, 'a beautiful book from my childhood'.

head: Prices: The Original Decentralised Technology
dek: Hayek's answer to the central planners was that society is too complex to plan from the top.
more: Hayek's answer to the central planners was that society is too complex to plan from the top. Millions of people have wants and needs that change minute to minute. The coordinating technology tech bros might hope blockchain will become has existed forever: it's prices. Through them, self-interested strangers end up meeting each other's needs. That is spontaneous order, and no single person or committee could design it.

head: The Resource Allocation
dek: Ajay's term for a full specification of every productive activity in an economy: who cuts which tree, who transports it, which mill processes it.
more: Ajay's term for a full specification of every productive activity in an economy: who cuts which tree, who transports it, which mill processes it. Written down, it would run to millions of pages. Central planning tries to write that document, and Indian finance still does, through tens of thousands of pages of regulations. Markets discover it instead, through millions of autonomous agents pursuing their own interests.

head: Prices Carry Both Information and Incentives
dek: If a fire destroyed 10% of India's timber, you would learn about it through pricier pencils and furniture, without reading any news.
more: If a fire destroyed 10% of India's timber, you would learn about it through pricier pencils and furniture, without reading any news. You would economise, and growers and substitute-makers would be pulled in. The whole economy reshapes itself around those two signals.

head: Price Caps Don't Lower Prices, They Remove Goods
dek: Cap car prices at Rs 10,000 and cars don't become affordable. They vanish into shortages, first-come-first-served queues and black markets.
more: Cap car prices at Rs 10,000 and cars don't become affordable. They vanish into shortages, first-come-first-served queues and black markets. The same happened with air-ticket caps after a natural disaster, Nixon's gasoline cap in the 1970s, Venezuela's controls on essentials, and Soviet bread rationing. In a competitive market, a price is high for a reason, and excess profits attract new competitors anyway.

head: Economic Freedom Is Individual Freedom
dek: A price control is a law that uses state coercion to criminalise a voluntary transaction between consenting adults.
more: A price control is a law that uses state coercion to criminalise a voluntary transaction between consenting adults. Amit notes that some people defend freedom in the bedroom but not the marketplace, and others the reverse. He holds that freedom is indivisible.

head: Surge Pricing as a Miniature Economy
dek: When supply drops from 200 cabs to 100, surge pricing does three things.
more: When supply drops from 200 cabs to 100, surge pricing does three things. Riders who value the ride most, like those heading to a hospital or airport, get one. Idle drivers get pulled onto the road until prices settle. Over the long run, people move between occupations, so an apprentice carpenter might become a driver if that's what society needs more. Capping the surge disables all three.

head: Don't Touch the Furnace
dek: Ajay describes the post-Berlin Wall political compromise this way. The market economy is a furnace that produces prosperity.
more: Ajay describes the post-Berlin Wall political compromise this way. The market economy is a furnace that produces prosperity. Governments may tax it and help the poor through direct transfers, but they must not interfere with it, and the price system is the furnace. Europe's gas response did exactly this: prices went sky-high and poor households got cash. Bill Clinton and Tony Blair are Ajay's examples of that centrist consensus.

head: Political Maturity Means Stomaching Price Swings
dek: Ajay and Shruti Rajagopalan have discussed what makes a political system sane, and their answer is the ability to tolerate large price fluctuations.
more: Ajay and Shruti Rajagopalan have discussed what makes a political system sane, and their answer is the ability to tolerate large price fluctuations. Wars, droughts, cyclones and changes in taste and technology will always move prices. Those movements are the sound of the economy's resource allocation rebuilding itself. Silence the sound and you stop the rebuilding.

head: Rent Control: Seen Intentions, Unseen Consequences
dek: The tenant's cheap rent is visible.
more: The tenant's cheap rent is visible. The hidden costs are landlords abandoning maintenance, developers refusing to build, scarce housing pushing up rents everywhere else, and property values falling toward nothing, which amounts to theft from owners. Amit stresses that these are not unintended consequences. Economic theory predicts exactly this.

head: The Minimum Wage Prices the Poorest Out of Work
dek: Set a floor of 100 and anyone whose work is worth 90 becomes unemployable.
more: Set a floor of 100 and anyone whose work is worth 90 becomes unemployable. India hits the labour market from both sides. Its minimum wage is about Rs 13,000 against roughly Rs 8,000 in comparable Bangladesh, and mandatory entitlements push the all-in cost to about Rs 17,000, which drives low-wage work to other countries. That same wage feeds into NREGS payments and anchors workers' expectations. The result is one of the world's lowest employment rates, below Bangladesh, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile Bangladesh's labour-intensive boom raises its wages year after year.

head: Labour Reform One Industry at a Time
dek: KP Krishnan's idea, endorsed by Ajay, is to start deregulating where the paternalist case is weakest.
more: KP Krishnan's idea, endorsed by Ajay, is to start deregulating where the paternalist case is weakest. IT and IT-enabled services, India's 'first sixer' industry, employ capable people who would quit at a day's notice if mistreated. A state could scrap labour law for that sector entirely, see how it goes, and extend the approach later toward garments, toys and low-end electronics.

head: What Leftism Actually Means
dek: Amit separates caring about people from leftism. A leftist, in his definition, is someone who wants to use state coercion to refashion society.
more: Amit separates caring about people from leftism. A leftist, in his definition, is someone who wants to use state coercion to refashion society. Real compassion respects individual autonomy and follows good intentions through to their actual outcomes, instead of chasing policies that feel virtuous and win retweets.

head: Varma's Law
dek: Take a tariff of Rs 20 on a Chinese good priced at Rs 90 so that a local Rs 100 product wins.
more: Take a tariff of Rs 20 on a Chinese good priced at Rs 90 so that a local Rs 100 product wins. Every consumer pays Rs 10 more without knowing it, and money that would have created jobs elsewhere goes to an organised lobby. Small costs spread across many poor consumers turn into a large benefit for a few rich producers.

head: Protection Makes Firms Lazy
dek: A protected local firm no longer has to compete with China on price or quality, so it stops improving.
more: A protected local firm no longer has to compete with China on price or quality, so it stops improving. If it were exposed to global competition it would develop better processes and thinking, those gains would spread through the economy, and it might start exporting, setting off a virtuous cycle. Transport costs already give domestic firms a natural cushion.

head: The Sorcerer's Apprentice Problem
dek: Hayek, Friedman and others won the argument, and decades of prosperity followed.
more: Hayek, Friedman and others won the argument, and decades of prosperity followed. People who grew up in that prosperity know that the system works but not why, so they fall back on the instinct that the government should fix things. Ajay's working hypothesis is that every 10 to 30 years interventionist governments must fail visibly, and enough intellectualism must exist to diagnose the failure. Angela Merkel said something similar about Germany's generations with no memory of the war.

head: Amit opens by blaming gravity for the Bengali tendency to slouch and proposes the state simply ban it
more: Amit opens by blaming gravity for the Bengali tendency to slouch and proposes the state simply ban it: 'We should use the coercive power of the state to outlaw gravity... Can you please write an application for me in triplicate?' Ajay replies: 'Or I can write the gorgeous economics book, Floating to Utopia.'

head: Amit on the body roundness index, which Ajay had introduced him to a day or two earlier
more: Amit on the body roundness index, which Ajay had introduced him to a day or two earlier: 'I think only to be able to cast a slur upon me without, you know, sounding rude.'

head: Amit's Bengali reading of De Long's title
more: Amit's Bengali reading of De Long's title: 'the urge for utopia is a disease of the mind. But the slouching is a problem of the body.' He returns to it at the close: 'Slouching Towards Utopia totally embodies all Bengaliness.'
Ajay: 'economists are very bad people because we repurpose ordinary English words and endow them with specialized technical meanings and then they are jargon.'

head: Amit on how surge pricing reaches the idle driver
more: Amit on how surge pricing reaches the idle driver: 'You are sitting at a katta. Maybe if you're Bengali, you're going to have an afternoon nap at that point.'

head: Amit on selective libertarians
more: Amit on selective libertarians: 'There will be one group of people who will be like two consenting adults can do whatever they want in the bedroom, but not in the marketplace. And another group which will say the opposite thing... Freedom is freedom.'

head: Amit's mondegreen: for years he misheard
more: Amit's mondegreen: for years he misheard 'Aabodana' in a song from the 1970s film Gharaonda, about being alone in the city searching for shelter, as 'Sabudana'. He sets it up by asking Ajay whether he loves sabudana khichdi and vada, adding 'Full starch, by the way.'

head: Amit on Indian politics
more: Amit on Indian politics: 'every party is left wing on economics, every party is right wing on society, and they're both anti freedom, therefore they're anti freedom in every margin.'

head: Amit introducing his closing recommendation, Prices, Fast and Slow
more: Amit introducing his closing recommendation, Prices, Fast and Slow: 'It's an article written by a very good friend of mine. I don't know if you're aware of him. But your awareness of him may depend on your level of self awareness. Because this is Ajay Shah I'm talking about.'

head: Amit, signing off an episode about prices
more: Amit, signing off an episode about prices: 'The show is free. We're talking about prices and the show is free. Is it worth it?'

head: Yes Minister, via Amit: the politician's instinct is…
more: Yes Minister, via Amit: the politician's instinct is 'this is a problem, we must do something, this is something, let's do it', and the usual 'something' is a price cap.

head: Escape from New York: Amit mentions this dystopian film while describing how rent-controlled parts of New York looked like a…
more: Escape from New York: Amit mentions this dystopian film while describing how rent-controlled parts of New York looked like a 'bombed out city', the image from his early Seen and the Unseen episode with Alex Tabarrok.
'Where you stand depends on where you sit': the old maxim Amit applies to his statist friend in a rent-controlled flat.

head: Ajay calls IT and IT-enabled services
more: Ajay calls IT and IT-enabled services 'the first time India scored a sixer', the one industry India has clearly mastered.

head: Amit on the 2024 US election: both Kamala Harris, with her rhetoric on price gouging, and Donald Trump are…
more: Amit on the 2024 US election: both Kamala Harris, with her rhetoric on price gouging, and Donald Trump are 'enemies of the price system'.

head: Amit's closing line on generational amnesia
more: Amit's closing line on generational amnesia: 'the price of liberty has to be eternal vigilance.'

head: Bob Dylan, quoted by Amit when launching Life Lessons
more: Bob Dylan, quoted by Amit when launching Life Lessons: 'he not busy being born is busy dying.'

head: Larry White and the World of Competing Currencies
dek: Even the state's monopoly on money, which feels like a law of nature, was a historical choice.
more: Amit opens by describing his recent Seen and the Unseen conversation with Larry White, author of The Clash of Economic Ideas and a leading expert on free banking. White studied periods in different countries where there was no single official currency from a central bank. Instead, several banks issued their own competing currencies. The instinctive reaction is that this would be chaos: who do you trust, and how would the currencies work together? White's papers and books show the system worked very well. Some early crypto pioneers, including people thought to be possible Satoshi Nakamotos, cited his papers.
Even the state's monopoly on money, which feels like a law of nature, was a historical choice. That is Amit's Dylan point: don't assume that how things are is the only way they can be.

head: The Daily Benzene Ship Across the Gulf of Gujarat
dek: This is import parity pricing at work. For any globally traded commodity, the exchange rate reaches into transactions that never leave India, which is why the rupee matters far beyond importers and exporters.
more: Ajay recalls something from his time on a company board. Every day, Reliance sent one ship of benzene from its refinery at Jamnagar to an Indian buyer on the other side of the Gulf of Gujarat. Seller and buyer were both Indian and the trip was short. Even so, the contract price was the Korean price of benzene multiplied by the exchange rate, so it changed every day.

This is import parity pricing at work. For any globally traded commodity, the exchange rate reaches into transactions that never leave India, which is why the rupee matters far beyond importers and exporters.

head: The Oil That Hadn't Left the Middle East Yet
dek: Prices move at the speed of information, not the speed of ships. Oil or steel already in storage carries no label showing what was paid for it, so the moment the world price changes, every unit everywhere is repriced.
more: When Ajay was very young, the Middle Eastern producers, angry at losing the Yom Kippur war, quadrupled crude oil from $2 to $8. He remembers laughing out loud at people asking why prices in India and California had risen immediately, when the ship carrying the expensive oil had not even left the Middle East.

Prices move at the speed of information, not the speed of ships. Oil or steel already in storage carries no label showing what was paid for it, so the moment the world price changes, every unit everywhere is repriced.

head: George Soros Bets Against the Bank of England
dek: A central bank defending an artificial exchange rate is fighting the market, and the market can win.
more: Ajay uses Britain as an example of a country that is now out of the currency business. The Bank of England once tried to distort the currency market. George Soros saw that it could not hold that position and placed a huge bet that the Bank would fail. He is reputed to have made a billion in one day. Amit calls it one man betting against the might of the British state, and winning.
A central bank defending an artificial exchange rate is fighting the market, and the market can win. Lessons like this are partly why advanced economies stopped trying to manage their currencies.

head: The 1966 Devaluation That Paid Off Later
dek: Judge macroeconomic moves over the right time horizon. A policy that looks like it did little in the first couple of years may be what saves you later.
more: In the controlled era, every exchange rate change was a policy decision. The famous one was Indira Gandhi's 1966 depreciation. Ajay says most people misjudge it because they look only at 1967 to 1969. Large exchange rate moves affect imports and exports with a time lag. By the early-seventies oil shock, export and import shifts were under way, and that helped India handle the shock relatively well.
Judge macroeconomic moves over the right time horizon. A policy that looks like it did little in the first couple of years may be what saves you later.

head: Ashok Desai and Each Generation's Young Turk Idea
dek: Reform is a relay. Each generation's radical idea becomes the next generation's common sense, and Ajay places India somewhere in the middle of that long journey.
more: Ashok Desai was Manmohan Singh's chief economic advisor in 1991 and drafted the July 1991 budget speech. He once told Ajay that his own generation's big idea was openness to international trade, and they mocked their predecessors for believing in trade barriers. He said Ajay's generation's idea was exchange rate flexibility and an open capital account. He added that when he talked about controls on the exchange rate, he could see Ajay's generation looking at him and wondering what was wrong with him.
Reform is a relay. Each generation's radical idea becomes the next generation's common sense, and Ajay places India somewhere in the middle of that long journey.

head: When India Tasted a Floating Rupee
dek: India's choice is not between theory and the untested. It has already run a floating rupee for several years and then chose to retreat.
more: Under RBI Governor Subbarao, roughly from 2007 to 2012-13, India had a lot of exchange rate flexibility. For long stretches the RBI did no trading on the currency market at all, even though many restrictions on market participants remained. When Raghuram Rajan became governor that period ended, and India went back to a heavily managed exchange rate.
India's choice is not between theory and the untested. It has already run a floating rupee for several years and then chose to retreat.

head: 'Desh Badalna Hai': The Origin of the Show
dek: Changing a country's ideas can begin with patient public explanation that reaches the next generation, rather than with policy levers.
more: Months earlier, Amit found Ajay by the seaside and asked about his plan. Ajay said 'Desh badalna hai' (the country must change), with full stops and an exclamation mark in his voice. Amit told him the country won't change, and Ajay repeated himself. After some back and forth, Amit's answer was: don't worry, let's do YouTube. That, he says, is how Everything is Everything began.
Changing a country's ideas can begin with patient public explanation that reaches the next generation, rather than with policy levers.

head: Larry White and the First Principles of Money (Episode 397 of The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Lawrence H White
dek: It made Amit rethink his instinctive objections to banks issuing competing currencies, and it questions the assumption that only the state can issue money.
more: It made Amit rethink his instinctive objections to banks issuing competing currencies, and it questions the assumption that only the state can issue money.
Amit opens the episode with this recent conversation about free banking.

head: The Clash of Economic Ideas
dek: Amit calls it a great book, written by his friend and a world expert on free banking.
more: Amit calls it a great book, written by his friend and a world expert on free banking.
Mentioned while introducing Larry White as his guest.

head: Free Banking in Britain: Theory, Experience and Debate 1800-1845
dek: It is the historical case study behind the claim that competing private currencies worked well in practice.
more: It is the historical case study behind the claim that competing private currencies worked well in practice.
Listed in the show notes alongside Amit's discussion of White's work on historical free banking.

head: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Amit loves it and says Ajay delivered a masterclass on finance in it.
more: Amit loves it and says Ajay delivered a masterclass on finance in it.
Recommended right after Ajay argues that finance, not trade, drives the currency market.

head: Josh Felman Tries to Make Sense of the World (Episode 321 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls Felman a great thinker, and he coined the episode's central idea.
more: Amit calls Felman a great thinker, and he coined the episode's central idea.
Recommended after Ajay quotes Felman's line that the exchange rate is the most important price of all.

head: The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates (in Essays in Positive Economics)
dek: Friedman worked all of this out back in 1953. Ajay wants listeners to read it and admire the person who figured it out first.
more: Friedman worked all of this out back in 1953. Ajay wants listeners to read it and admire the person who figured it out first.
Ajay's only recommendation of the episode. He also credits Friedman earlier as the first to understand that exchange rates don't need government.

head: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It runs 9 hours 53 minutes and is the year's most popular episode. People watch it more than once, take notes, and email Amit about it every day.
more: It runs 9 hours 53 minutes and is the year's most popular episode. People watch it more than once, take notes, and email Amit about it every day.
Mentioned in the same stretch about India's economic history.
