dek: Amit picked it to educate Ajay about cinema and passes it on to listeners.
more: Amit picked it to educate Ajay about cinema and passes it on to listeners. Ajay still hasn't watched it.
One of the films Amit assigned Ajay under their one-film-a-month deal, made months earlier.

head: Anatomy of a Fall
dek: Amit calls it brilliant and notes that it was released in India too.
more: Amit calls it brilliant and notes that it was released in India too.
The other film Amit assigned Ajay under the same deal.

head: Paris, Texas
dek: It is his favourite Wenders film of all time and 'such a masterpiece'.
more: It is his favourite Wenders film of all time and 'such a masterpiece'. He is excited to watch it again after many years.
Amit thought of it while recommending Perfect Days.

head: The Exchange Rate Is the Most Important Price
dek: The rupee-dollar rate touches importers and exporters, every domestic deal in globally traded goods, and the huge financial flows in and out of India.
more: The rupee-dollar rate touches importers and exporters, every domestic deal in globally traded goods, and the huge financial flows in and out of India. No other single price reaches so far into the economy.

head: 'Strong' and 'Weak' Rupee Are Meaningless
dek: The level of the exchange rate is just a unit. Japan trades at around 130 yen to the dollar and is one of the world's most successful countries.
more: The level of the exchange rate is just a unit. Japan trades at around 130 yen to the dollar and is one of the world's most successful countries. If India swapped every old rupee for ten new ones, the rate would jump from 80 to 800 and nothing real would change. Nationalist talk about rupee levels is innumeracy.

head: Every Price Cuts Both Ways
dek: A depreciation from 80 to 90 makes a Rs 600 Tiruppur shirt cheaper for foreigners, so exporters gain.
more: A depreciation from 80 to 90 makes a Rs 600 Tiruppur shirt cheaper for foreigners, so exporters gain. An appreciation from 80 to 70 makes a $100 imported phone and a trip to Greece cheaper, so consumers gain. There is no single 'good' direction; different people win and lose, as with any price.

head: Import Parity Pricing
dek: Steel has one global market and one price, set on the London Metal Exchange.
more: Steel has one global market and one price, set on the London Metal Exchange. The Indian price is the LME price times the exchange rate. Tata Steel uses Indian ore, coal, power and labour, so when the rupee depreciates its costs stay the same while its rupee revenue rises, and the extra goes straight to operating profit. An appreciation does the reverse.

head: Goods Arbitrage Holds the World Together
dek: No planner or law sets a single world price. Traders watch steel prices in Singapore, Dubai, Visakhapatnam and Bombay, and ship goods whenever a gap opens, which closes the gap.
more: No planner or law sets a single world price. Traders watch steel prices in Singapore, Dubai, Visakhapatnam and Bombay, and ship goods whenever a gap opens, which closes the gap. Most people never check prices this way; a few profit-seeking arbitrageurs keep the world on one price for everyone, and Ajay notes there is an 'I, Pencil' story here.

head: Finance Dwarfs Trade
dek: Many economists who don't know finance think the exchange rate is mainly about trade.
more: Many economists who don't know finance think the exchange rate is mainly about trade. That stopped being true decades ago. Capital flows such as FDI and portfolio investment now dominate the currency market, and trade is the smaller partner.

head: From Gold to Fiat: The Exchange Rate Became a Market Price
dek: Money was first gold, then paper backed by gold. Later the US fixed $35 to an ounce of gold and other currencies were pegged to the dollar, an arrangement Keynes backed after the currency chaos of the Depression.
more: Money was first gold, then paper backed by gold. Later the US fixed $35 to an ounce of gold and other currencies were pegged to the dollar, an arrangement Keynes backed after the currency chaos of the Depression. Ajay thinks that design was unwise. It ended when Nixon took the US off gold and Bretton Woods collapsed. Currencies are now money by state decree, with no common anchor, so exchange rates are set by supply and demand. Milton Friedman was the first to see that governments don't need to be in this business.
printed: Nothing in it but the state

head: Three Rooms in the House
dek: Ajay sorts currency regimes into three types. In the first, like North Korea, the state is the counterparty to every currency transaction.
more: Ajay sorts currency regimes into three types. In the first, like North Korea, the state is the counterparty to every currency transaction. In the second, like India, private transactions are allowed but tightly controlled and channelled through banks that earn a protected spread, while the central bank trades heavily to manage the rate. In the third, the advanced economies, the state stays out: Ajay believes the US Fed hasn't traded currencies since about 1994, and Japan and, recently, Switzerland are the exceptions. Knowing a country's regime explains a lot about the country.

head: Floating Exchange Rates Are a Shock Absorber
dek: In bad times such as floods, demonetisation or a breakdown of law and order, exports suffer and foreign investors pull money out, so the rupee depreciates.
more: In bad times such as floods, demonetisation or a breakdown of law and order, exports suffer and foreign investors pull money out, so the rupee depreciates. That makes exports more competitive, raises profits for import-parity producers, and makes imports dearer so demand shifts to Indian goods. In booms, the rupee appreciates and cools things down. The price system delivers stability with no official needed.

head: The Closet Bureaucrat and the Elite's Love of Stability
dek: Indian elites accept fluctuating prices for steel, cement and nickel but want the rupee to stand still.
more: Indian elites accept fluctuating prices for steel, cement and nickel but want the rupee to stand still. The general rule still applies: prices are information wrapped in an incentive, and their movement is how the economy reallocates resources. Ajay argues policymakers fix the rupee to win the elite's applause, so the real audience to persuade is the elite.

head: Currency Controls Are Theft That Turns Citizens Into Criminals
dek: Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off. Controls that block or slow such exchanges destroy value that we never get to see.
more: Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off. Controls that block or slow such exchanges destroy value that we never get to see. They also force ordinary people to break the law just to do things with their own money.

head: FERA, FEMA and the Inverted Default
dek: FERA, passed in the 1970s, made foreign exchange dealings a crime; being caught with dollar bills could get you into trouble.
more: FERA, passed in the 1970s, made foreign exchange dealings a crime; being caught with dollar bills could get you into trouble. Ajay says economic offences need only civil fines, such as three times the ill-gotten gain. FEMA replaced FERA in 1999, but criminal clauses returned in 2015. FEMA starts by banning all cross-border activity and then lists what is permitted. It is enforced by an Enforcement Directorate whose law gives it raid powers without proper rule of law. The result is a maze of circulars that keeps lawyers and accountants busy.
printed: A law that starts with no

head: The Blind Spot of the 1991 Reformers
dek: The 1991 generation understood economics but not law, public administration or public choice theory.
more: The 1991 generation understood economics but not law, public administration or public choice theory. They gave bodies like the RBI wide arbitrary powers, assuming good people like themselves would always run them. Amit compares this to Nehru's generation writing a constitution that protects the state from the people rather than the other way round.

head: Controls Only Bind the Little Guy
dek: Restrictions always create a black market. The legal route needs expensive lawyers, so only the top 0.1% can buy a Nasdaq ETF or a flat in London.
more: Restrictions always create a black market. The legal route needs expensive lawyers, so only the top 0.1% can buy a Nasdaq ETF or a flat in London. Firms move money through misinvoicing: billing a 100 export at 110 brings 10 into India on the quiet. These hidden flows dwarf the formal ones.

head: Internationalisation Is the Engine of Growth
dek: Trade, FDI and foreign capital arrive as a package of knowledge that raises a country's productivity and capabilities.
more: Trade, FDI and foreign capital arrive as a package of knowledge that raises a country's productivity and capabilities. Every friction placed on cross-border engagement therefore slows growth itself.

head: Cross the River by Feeling the Stones
dek: Ajay is conservative about reform method. Central planning is dismantled one regulation at a time, by persuading people that each rule makes no sense.
more: Ajay is conservative about reform method. Central planning is dismantled one regulation at a time, by persuading people that each rule makes no sense. That needs full-time teams who study data, talk to practitioners and write publicly. India once had such a community for currency reform but no longer does, so nothing is moving.

head: Inflation Targeting Is the Poured Foundation
dek: One piece is in good shape. The RBI is now accountable for an inflation target, not for delivering a particular exchange rate or exchange rate stability.
more: One piece is in good shape. The RBI is now accountable for an inflation target, not for delivering a particular exchange rate or exchange rate stability. That makes the right reform possible: a clean law where all transactions are legal with a few exceptions, real current account convertibility, and few capital account controls.

head: Amit's Arc of India's Economic Journey
dek: Nehru built democratic institutions but distrusted markets, and his mistakes were reversible.
more: Nehru built democratic institutions but distrusted markets, and his mistakes were reversible. Indira's economic policies, including FERA, bank nationalisation, labour laws and a 97% peak income tax rate, were in Amit's view crimes on humanity. Then came the quiet reformers, 1991, and twenty golden years with consensus across parties that lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Since roughly 2011-12, Amit says, India has gone backwards.

head: Ajay pitches his redenomination thought experiment
more: Ajay pitches his redenomination thought experiment as 'better than demonetization', and Amit shoots back: 'That was the worst possible thing. Everything is better.'

head: After Ajay compares the rupee-level obsession to measuring height in millimetres instead of inches, Amit
more: After Ajay compares the rupee-level obsession to measuring height in millimetres instead of inches, Amit says: 'People who live in a country called millimeter must be feeling damn jealous of people who live in a country called Inch.'

head: Ajay pictures the business elite of Bengal
more: Ajay pictures the business elite of Bengal, 'the blood relatives of Rabindranath Tagore', engaged in 'the highly intellectual activity' of watching steel prices in Singapore and Dubai. Later, when Ajay imagines a 'skeptical Bengali' who trusts markets everywhere except exchange rates, Amit replies: 'I'm not that kind of Bengali. In everything markets are good.'

head: Ajay on economists
more: Ajay on economists: 'Trade is some minor thing that real people do. The really big thing in the world is called finance.'

head: Amit, defending wonkish economics episodes
more: Amit, defending wonkish economics episodes: 'No man, this shit has humanitarian consequences.'

head: Ajay keeps invoking
more: Ajay keeps invoking 'every dentist and grandmother in Connecticut or Kyoto' rushing into or out of Indian assets. Amit: 'If you happen to be a grandmother and a dentist at the same time and live dual lives in Connecticut and Kyoto, come to our arms.'

head: Ajay calls FEMA
more: Ajay calls FEMA 'an employment guarantee program for lawyers and accountants', and mocks its absurd detail: 'If you are a foreign investor who is a dentist investing in nanotechnology, then we will permit you to do ECB and you have to fill form number 74, EE1.'

head: Amit, who says his are…
more: Amit, who says his are 'the best show notes in the world... Never a mistake', reveals the one error ever made in them. Ajay sent his favourite papers at the last minute and listed the co-author of his misinvoicing paper as Abhijit Banerjee instead of Abhijit Sen Gupta. Amit pasted it in at 2:30 AM. In this episode Ajay pointedly says: 'Abhijit Sengupta. Not Abhijit Banerjee.'

head: Amit reveals that Ajay has a cat named FEMA. Ajay's cover story is that the cat fell from a third-floor house as a kitten and broke its femur.
more: Amit reveals that Ajay has a cat named FEMA. Ajay's cover story is that the cat fell from a third-floor house as a kitten and broke its femur. Amit: 'Oh, so it's not FEMA, it's femur. Is that what you're claiming?' The verdict: Ajay is a one-track mind, and all he thinks about is exchange rates.

Amit: 'Ajay has watched twenty films in the last twenty years. Eleven of them are the Matrix.' Amit, Vaishnav and Nomsita got him to agree to one film a month from each of them. He thought they would vote and agree on one, and months later he still hasn't watched either of Amit's picks. His defence: 'It's a big life change, okay? I have to implement it.'

head: Bob Dylan's line
more: Bob Dylan's line 'he not busy being born is busy dying', which Amit uses to open the episode as a warning against taking how things are for granted. He uses it again in the Life Lessons pitch.

head: Nehru once told JRD Tata
more: Nehru once told JRD Tata: 'Do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.' Amit cites it as the spirit of top-down Nehruvian economics.

head: Keynes backing a fixed, gold-linked post-war currency order, Nixon taking the US off gold, and the…
more: Keynes backing a fixed, gold-linked post-war currency order, Nixon taking the US off gold, and the 'collapse of Bretton Woods' that started the era of fiat money and floating rates. Ajay says governments are still 'going through their stages of grief' about it.

head: Germany's Reparations, Hyperinflation and the Birth of GDP
dek: Hyperinflation is a political catastrophe as much as an economic one.
more: After the First World War, the winning nations demanded reparations so high that Germany had no option but to print huge amounts of money. Prices ran so far out of control that what could buy a house one week would buy only a loaf of bread the next. The chaos fed the right-wing extremism that produced Adolf Hitler. Keynes, in The Economic Consequences of the Peace, argued that part of the problem was that nobody knew how wealthy a nation actually was, so the victors could make absurd demands. That gap created the demand for something like GDP, which did not yet exist.

Hyperinflation is a political catastrophe as much as an economic one. The story also shows that measurement is policy infrastructure: GDP was born because the world had made a disastrous demand of an economy it could not see.

head: Checking Whether India's CPI Can Be Trusted
dek: Before building anything on a statistic, verify its foundations yourself.
more: Ajay argues that weak state capability affects everything, statistics included, so all government data deserves great skepticism, and India's GDP data is the most famous case. Years ago he and Ila Patnaik tested the CPI independently. They used the CMIE household survey to derive consumption weights and compared them with the government's CPI weights. They then compared private-sector price data with the government's prices. Both broadly matched, so the CPI can be used with reasonable confidence.

Before building anything on a statistic, verify its foundations yourself. Distrust is the sensible default for government data, but the exceptions can be found empirically, and you should not simply assume them.

head: RBI's Early Decades and a Reform Found, Then Lost
dek: Institutional progress is not linear. Good ideas can be understood inside an institution and then abandoned, and reform sometimes has to be carried by people outside it until the moment is right.
more: Ajay says that in the bad old days the RBI was not a real central bank. It was a central planning agency and a handmaiden of the government, grabbing money from the formal financial system and repressing it. In the early 1990s C. Rangarajan and deputy governor Tarapore rethought the RBI from scratch. By the time Ajay met them, they knew India needed an open capital account, a floating exchange rate and an inflation target. Then the RBI slid into a long socialist period of detailed micro-control, exchange-rate control, closed accounts and no accountability for inflation. During that period the intellectual leadership moved to academia and the Ministry of Finance.
Institutional progress is not linear. Good ideas can be understood inside an institution and then abandoned, and reform sometimes has to be carried by people outside it until the moment is right.

head: The 2002 Conversation with Yashwant Sinha
dek: A reform usually has to win the argument in public debate long before it can win in government.
more: In 2002 Ajay was already talking with Yashwant Sinha about inflation targeting. Sinha's view was that these ideas were far ahead of what India's intelligentsia was discussing. They would need to become normal in Indian intellectual debate before some future finance minister could act on them. Ajay accepted the point. The reform finally became law in 2016.
A reform usually has to win the argument in public debate long before it can win in government. Years of persuasion are part of how policy change actually happens.

head: How the 2007 Boom Discredited the Old RBI
dek: Trying to control the exchange rate means giving up control of inflation.
more: In the mid-2000s boom, foreign capital poured into India, as it does in good times. The rupee should have appreciated, but the RBI tried to fix the exchange rate by buying up dollars. It paid for those dollars in rupees, flooding the domestic economy with money. The result was expansionary monetary policy at exactly the wrong moment, followed by a big inflation crisis. Ajay says this convinced most economists that the old RBI could no longer be accepted.
Trying to control the exchange rate means giving up control of inflation. A central bank chasing several targets ends up failing at the one that matters most.

head: FSLRC and the Draft Indian Financial Code
dek: Government commissions rarely have real technical capacity behind them.
more: The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission was set up in 2011 under Justice Srikrishna. Ajay was hired to lead its research team: 35 people at NIPFP, led jointly with Ila Patnaik. The mandate was to start from zero and replace some sixty messy old laws with one clean law built on consistent definitions. The result, the draft Indian Financial Code, was released in 2013 and included chapters on inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee. P. Chidambaram said it was too big to pass at the end of his government's term, especially without a Rajya Sabha majority.

Government commissions rarely have real technical capacity behind them. Pairing a commission with a serious research team made it possible to redesign financial law from first principles instead of patching the existing mess.

head: Borrowing the Ways and Means Trick
dek: When the legislative route is blocked, a public, signed commitment between the two parties can deliver the reform first, and the law can follow later.
more: With the law stuck, Ajay and KP Krishnan exchanged emails at about four an hour while Ajay was travelling abroad. They recalled a precedent from the 1990s. Parliament then could not pass a law to stop the RBI from automatically printing money to fund government deficits. So the Ministry of Finance and the RBI signed a public contract instead, the Ways and Means Agreement, with Montek Ahluwalia and C. Rangarajan signing at a public ceremony. Amit adds that it probably helped to have those two particular people in office. Ajay and Krishnan proposed the same approach for inflation targeting: a Monetary Policy Framework Agreement in which the RBI commits to an inflation target and the government commits not to push it in other directions.

When the legislative route is blocked, a public, signed commitment between the two parties can deliver the reform first, and the law can follow later. It works best when enlightened people happen to hold the key posts.

head: Chidambaram: 'I Leave This to My Successor'
dek: Statesmanship can mean declining to take credit for a reform you believe in, so that it carries proper legitimacy when it happens.
more: By late 2013 or early 2014, the draft Monetary Policy Framework Agreement had been worked over by KP Krishnan and P. Chidambaram and discussed with Montek Ahluwalia and Manmohan Singh. Chidambaram wrote on the file that it was one of the most important milestones in India's history. He said it should not be done lightly by a lame-duck government and left the decision to the next finance minister, correctly predicting that this would not be him.
Statesmanship can mean declining to take credit for a reform you believe in, so that it carries proper legitimacy when it happens.

head: Arun Jaitley's Overnight Yes
dek: Trust across party lines is a form of institutional capital, and it can disappear quietly.
more: Amit retells a story from his episode with KP Krishnan. Krishnan handed the file to the new Finance Minister, Arun Jaitley, and the next morning Jaitley said, 'Let's do it.' Krishnan was alarmed: this was far-reaching, so had Jaitley actually read it? Slightly irritated, Jaitley replied that if the country's finest economic mind and finest legal mind had said it must be done, who was he to argue? He meant Manmohan Singh and P. Chidambaram. Amit calls this grace across party lines and says it never happened again.
Trust across party lines is a form of institutional capital, and it can disappear quietly. Years of reform work cleared its final hurdle because one politician deferred to his opponents' expertise.

head: Erasing 'Temporary Measure' from the RBI Act
dek: A preamble states an institution's purpose. For more than eighty years the RBI had none; it was a placeholder.
more: Rajiv Mehrishi and Raghuram Rajan signed the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement on 20 February 2015. Ajay regrets it was not done as a public ceremony. In 2016 the RBI Act was amended to include inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee. The 1934 Act's preamble had said that, given the disorganised international monetary system, India's monetary arrangements could not yet be decided, so the RBI was being created 'as a temporary measure.' The 2016 amendment removed those words and replaced them with 'in order to deliver price stability.'
A preamble states an institution's purpose. For more than eighty years the RBI had none; it was a placeholder. Inflation targeting finally gave it one.

head: Never normalize anything or take the world for granted
dek: Inflation targeting is a rare, elegant piece of good legislation, and gains like that are always under threat.
more: Inflation targeting is a rare, elegant piece of good legislation, and gains like that are always under threat. Keep questioning and protect the little good that has been achieved.
Amit's first, non-media recommendation at the end of the episode.

head: Blue
dek: Mitchell is a great singer-songwriter and a masterful guitarist and pianist who was ahead of her time.
more: Mitchell is a great singer-songwriter and a masterful guitarist and pianist who was ahead of her time. Folk, rock and jazz musicians drew on her work, and she collaborated with Mingus and Pastorius. Blue is his favourite of her albums. Listen on headphones, on a quiet day, alone.
Amit's music recommendation to close the episode.

head: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
dek: Keynes argued that the reparations demands were so extreme partly because nobody knew national wealth.
more: Keynes argued that the reparations demands were so extreme partly because nobody knew national wealth. That insight helped create the demand for something like GDP.
Amit cites the pamphlet while telling the story of Germany's post-WWI hyperinflation; it is linked in the show notes.

head: The Role of Monetary Policy
dek: It is the origin of the insight that inflation adds noise to price signals, so firms can't tell real changes from monetary ones and make wrong adjustments.
more: It is the origin of the insight that inflation adds noise to price signals, so firms can't tell real changes from monetary ones and make wrong adjustments.
Ajay credits 'Milton Friedman's 1968 paper' as the source of the episode's central argument about inflation; it is linked in the show notes.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: It is the foundation for seeing prices as the carriers of society's decentralised knowledge, which is why putting noise into prices is so damaging.
more: It is the foundation for seeing prices as the carriers of society's decentralised knowledge, which is why putting noise into prices is so damaging.
Ajay echoes the essay's title while agreeing with Amit's summary of how markets work; it is linked in the show notes.

head: How to Do Development (Episode 57 of Everything is Everything)

more: It sets out in detail why growth is the only way out of poverty, which is the deeper reason low and stable inflation matters.
Amit calls it a 'magnificent episode' when explaining why growth is the highest god.

head: CMIE Household Survey
dek: It surveys about 190,000 households three times a year on some 90 consumption items, detailed enough to independently check the government's CPI weights.
more: It surveys about 190,000 households three times a year on some 90 consumption items, detailed enough to independently check the government's CPI weights.
Ajay describes it while explaining how consumption baskets are measured; it is linked in the show notes.

head: Inflation Is a Monetary Phenomenon
dek: A single price rising, such as apples after a maggot infestation, is just supply and demand at work.
more: A single price rising, such as apples after a maggot infestation, is just supply and demand at work. Inflation means nearly everything rising at once. That happens when the amount of money changes relative to the goods and services available: print 20% more money, keep goods the same, and prices go up. The state has a monopoly on money. Today the central bank controls its supply through interest rates, so inflation is directly in the central bank's control.

head: Inflation Is a Tax on the Poor
dek: Governments can print money to fund popular spending, which works politically, but everyone pays through higher prices.
more: Governments can print money to fund popular spending, which works politically, but everyone pays through higher prices. New money is not handed out in proportion to what people already hold, so the poor suffer most. High inflation is something to hold the government accountable for.
printed: Too much money, too few goods

head: Inflation Is the Rising Cost of a Basket
dek: Your personal inflation rate is the cost of what you buy (quantities times prices) tracked month after month.
more: Your personal inflation rate is the cost of what you buy (quantities times prices) tracked month after month. Some items rise and some fall, but that noise averages out. The CPI does this for the whole country. Large household surveys produce average consumption weights, which stay fixed for a couple of years, and each month's prices are plugged in. Nobody's own inflation matches it exactly, but it reflects what is happening to the average household.

head: The WPI: Not Wholesale, Not Meaningful, Still Useful
dek: There is nothing wholesale about the Wholesale Price Index. As an index it is meaningless because its weights reflect nobody's consumption basket.
more: There is nothing wholesale about the Wholesale Price Index. As an index it is meaningless because its weights reflect nobody's consumption basket. Hence nickel sits in it, though nobody eats nickel. Its one good use is as a long-term database of individual component prices. Measure inflation with the CPI.

head: Inflation Corrupts the Signals Firms Rely On
dek: The world keeps changing, and the market's decentralised information processing is how firms read those changes through prices and adapt.
more: The world keeps changing, and the market's decentralised information processing is how firms read those changes through prices and adapt. Inflation changes prices for reasons unrelated to the real economy. A firm cannot tell whether apples are dearer because they are scarce, because people want more of them, or just because of inflation. High inflation is also variable inflation, with more noise in prices across the economy. Firms get misled into wrong adjustments. Inflation is not the price of growth; low and stable inflation is what makes good growth possible.

head: Finite Adjustment Muscle and the Acid on Contracts
dek: Adapting is exhausting, and every firm has a limited budget of effort for it.
more: Adapting is exhausting, and every firm has a limited budget of effort for it. Firms bind themselves to one another through carefully negotiated contracts written in rupees. When inflation changes what a rupee is worth, those contracts have to be renegotiated even though nothing real has changed. That uses up effort that should have gone into responding to real shifts in tastes and technology. It is a depreciation of contracts.

head: Inflation Shrinks the Planning Horizon
dek: Long-term projects, like a highway tolled for 20 years, depend on assumptions about future interest rates and contracts.
more: Long-term projects, like a highway tolled for 20 years, depend on assumptions about future interest rates and contracts. High and variable inflation destroys those assumptions, so people stop planning beyond a couple of years. Growth comes from complex multi-year projects, so the country loses out.

head: Growth Is the Highest God
dek: The whole case for inflation control serves one end: higher GDP growth, because only growth gets a nation out of poverty.
more: The whole case for inflation control serves one end: higher GDP growth, because only growth gets a nation out of poverty. The central bank is one player in that larger effort, and its only part is delivering low and stable inflation.

head: A Central Bank Should Have One Job
dek: The best thing a central bank can do for society is deliver low and stable inflation.
more: The best thing a central bank can do for society is deliver low and stable inflation. Chasing other goals, or having broad discretion that exposes it to other pressures, always comes at the cost of that core job. Keynes's line about economists being humble like dentists is often applied to central bankers: narrow, technical and accountable.

head: Power Must Be Matched by Accountability: New Zealand, 1987
dek: Parliament gives the central bank power to create fiat money. A basic rule of public administration is that every grant of power comes with checks.
more: Parliament gives the central bank power to create fiat money. A basic rule of public administration is that every grant of power comes with checks. Central banks have a long history of failure, and New Zealand's fix in 1987 was an inflation target written into law. It even paid senior central bank staff a bonus for hitting it. This is a simple principal-agent arrangement with parliament as the principal. Today all advanced economies target inflation, and central banks that miss suffer reputational damage.

head: Inflation Targeting Avoids Two Failure Modes
dek: A central bank controlled by the government produces an election business cycle: rates are held low before polls to create a feel-good mood, and the inflation arrives later.
more: A central bank controlled by the government produces an election business cycle: rates are held low before polls to create a feel-good mood, and the inflation arrives later. A fully independent central bank invites economists' self-image as good guys who are beyond public choice theory. An inflation target sits between the two. The legislature defines the job and leaves the bank free to do it, but holds it accountable for the result.

head: One Lever, Long Lags
dek: Good central banks set only the short-term interest rate and leave long-term rates, the exchange rate and equity prices to the market.
more: Good central banks set only the short-term interest rate and leave long-term rates, the exchange rate and equity prices to the market. We are all Wicksellian now. Rate changes take a long time to work, like a car that turns long after you move the wheel, so central banks must forecast inflation rather than react to it. In a boom they raise rates and loans get dearer. In a crisis they cut, as the RBI rightly did when the COVID lockdown hit.

head: Why India Targets 4% ± 2, Not 2%
dek: Zero inflation risks deflationary spirals. A 2% target leaves very little room to cut rates in a slump, because rates can't usefully go below zero.
more: Zero inflation risks deflationary spirals. A 2% target leaves very little room to cut rates in a slump, because rates can't usefully go below zero. India's broken financial system weakens the effect of rate changes, so larger moves are needed, which requires more headroom. Weak transmission also makes hitting an exact number unrealistic, hence the 2-6% band. Two consecutive quarters outside the band require a public letter from the RBI explaining what went wrong and what it will do. The plan was to narrow the band as the financial system improved.

head: Ajay builds Amit's personal inflation basket
more: Ajay builds Amit's personal inflation basket: 'Vast amounts of bacon, tiny amounts of bread… Amit Bhai is a good devout non vegetarian and he eats bacon as a matter of principle.' When the CMIE survey comes up, Amit asks, 'But no bacon?' Ajay: 'They have some generic categories called meat and fish and so on, but not the subtlety of bacon.'

head: Ajay suggests a self-employed doctor can simply charge more when prices rise.
more: Ajay suggests a self-employed doctor can simply charge more when prices rise. Ajay, already reaching for the research on inflation shocks and infant mortality: 'Don't even get me started.'

more: Amit's one-line summary of the case for central bank discipline: 'buggers, we gave you the monopoly on money, you had one job, keep it stable, don't mess with it too much.'

more: Ajay ties the price system to 'either Hindu or Buddhist philosophy of a world that is ever changing.' The economy's job is to keep understanding that change and reallocating resources accordingly.

head: Keynes on humility: Ajay first quotes it as central bankers being
more: Keynes on humility: Ajay first quotes it as central bankers being 'humble like dentists,' then corrects it to economists, noting it always gets applied to central bankers. He extends it: 'we'll treat you like a dentist. If you did a root canal surgery and the tooth works out fine, then we'll give you a bonus.' On advanced economies that skip New Zealand's bonuses: 'Some of them are too polite or too cheap to offer a bonus.'

head: How Humans Invented the Sun God
dek: Storytelling is our first tool for making sense of a complex world. Every story simplifies, but without that instinct we would be paralysed.
more: Amit asks you to picture a prehistoric human with no clothes, phones or internet, watching a bright orange object rise and fall in the sky every day without understanding it. The natural response is to make up a story about it. That gives you sun gods, and with them the beginnings of religion.

Storytelling is our first tool for making sense of a complex world. Every story simplifies, but without that instinct we would be paralysed. Over time some stories get good enough to actually match reality.

head: How Christopher Booker Spotted the Pattern
dek: Booker's taxonomy came from noticing that works with completely different settings and characters share the same underlying structure.
more: Booker was reading and watching several works at once, including Macbeth, Lolita and Truffaut's film Jules et Jim, and saw the same arc in all of them. An unfulfilled hero finds a focus for his desires and enjoys dreamlike success: Macbeth becomes king, Humbert begins his affair, Icarus discovers he can fly, Faust gets the devil's magic. Then the mood darkens and the dream turns into a nightmare that ends in violent self-destruction. Amit notes the same arc runs through Romeo and Juliet and Madame Bovary.
Booker's taxonomy came from noticing that works with completely different settings and characters share the same underlying structure.

head: Stallone Refuses to Sell Rocky
dek: Rocky is a rags-to-riches film, and Stallone's refusal of the safe deal made his own life one too.
more: Sylvester Stallone wrote Rocky and wanted to star in it. The studio offered him a lot of money for the script on the condition that someone else would act. He refused and insisted on playing the role himself.
Rocky is a rags-to-riches film, and Stallone's refusal of the safe deal made his own life one too.

head: His Father's Rags-to-Riches Life
dek: The rags-to-riches archetype is not just fairy tale. It describes real lives shaped by Partition-era South Asia.
more: Ajay's father started out in Hyderabad, Sindh, in what is now Pakistan, where there was nothing around. He went on to become one of the country's prominent economists and founded CMIE, all in a lifespan of fifty-eight years. Amit then teases Ajay that his own arc might turn out to be a tragedy, riches to rags.
The rags-to-riches archetype is not just fairy tale. It describes real lives shaped by Partition-era South Asia.

head: The Battle of Kyiv as 'Overcoming the Monster'
dek: Real history follows archetypal arcs, but which archetype applies depends on how the story ends.
more: Ajay recalls the Battle of Kyiv, which they covered in their 'stories that should be films' episodes. Life in Ukraine was normal until a monster invaded from the north. The world, Ajay included, assumed the only question was when Ukraine would fall. Then the scrappy Ukrainians, armed with artillery and Javelin missiles, stopped the invader. Amit maps it onto Booker's five acts (call, initial success, confrontation, final ordeal, miraculous escape) and adds that because this is real life, the ending is still unwritten: it could yet become a tragedy.
Real history follows archetypal arcs, but which archetype applies depends on how the story ends. A live war is a plot whose genre has not been settled.

head: The CIA's Call to the Climbers of Nanda Devi
dek: The call to adventure often looks like an irresistible offer, and the catch comes in the small print.
more: Discussing 'the call' that opens a quest, Ajay recalls the story of the plutonium-powered device meant to be placed atop Nanda Devi, a mission that went terribly wrong. The paragraph that stayed with him describes the CIA quietly approaching the world's elite climbers one by one with an all-expenses-paid Nanda Devi expedition, plus a minor detail: they would have to do some work for the agency.
The call to adventure often looks like an irresistible offer, and the catch comes in the small print.

head: The Evening Invitation to Climb Kokankada
dek: In real life the call to a quest is rarely dramatic. Often it is one person quietly asking another whether they are in.
more: Ajay was part of a project to climb Kokankada in the Sahyadris. He vividly remembers the first moment, when the project leader, Girish Sant, took him aside one evening and asked whether he wanted to join.
In real life the call to a quest is rarely dramatic. Often it is one person quietly asking another whether they are in.

head: Ajay's Return to India as a Quest
dek: A life can be read through several archetypes at once. Seeing your own choices as a quest gives them shape and meaning.
more: Amit points out that Ajay's own life fits the quest archetype. After IIT and an economics PhD in the US, he chose to come back to India at a time when kids of his generation saw getting out as escaping. His quest, to make India a better place, is still ongoing, with elements of tragedy and rebirth along the way.
A life can be read through several archetypes at once. Seeing your own choices as a quest gives them shape and meaning.

head: Two Interwoven Quests: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Mukulika Banerjee
dek: A quest can end in both victory and heartbreak. Mukulika's own quest was driven by a puzzle: how a people stereotyped as violent led the greatest non-violent movement in history.
more: In an earlier 'stories that should be films' episode, Amit told two stories in parallel. In one, Mukulika Banerjee travels to the Pathan areas of Pakistan to find surviving Khudai Khidmatgars. Her call came when her PhD advisor told her to do a PhD only if something kept her awake at night. In the other, decades earlier, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan sets out to defeat the British Empire and then to build the new nation. He succeeds in the first quest and fails in the second.
A quest can end in both victory and heartbreak. Mukulika's own quest was driven by a puzzle: how a people stereotyped as violent led the greatest non-violent movement in history.
printed: A quest that kept her awake

head: DDLJ's Real Rebirth Belongs to Amrish Puri
dek: In a rebirth story, the person who truly transforms may not be the romantic lead.
more: Ajay remembers DDLJ, one of the few films he has seen, for its last scene: the slow train at an obscure station. Amit uses the film twice. First as voyage and return, then for rebirth: in the 'Ja Simran, jee le apni zindagi' moment, the stern father played by Amrish Puri becomes a fundamentally different person. Amit compares him to Scrooge in A Christmas Carol.
In a rebirth story, the person who truly transforms may not be the romantic lead. One film can also hold several archetypes at once.

head: Retelling Sholay from Gabbar's Side
dek: Once a villain gets a backstory, black and white turn into shades of grey, which is much closer to how the real world works.
more: One exercise in Amit's writing course asks students to retell a well-known story from a different character's point of view. Participants have rewritten Sholay from Gabbar Singh's perspective and Harry Potter from Voldemort's. Some built rich backstories in which the villain is a victim of circumstance. Ajay suggests the Mahabharata from Draupadi's point of view.
Once a villain gets a backstory, black and white turn into shades of grey, which is much closer to how the real world works.

head: The Seven Basic Plots
dek: Amit calls it excellent. It explains why Beowulf, Jaws, James Bond and Sholay are the same story underneath, and he presents it as a lens for writers rather than a rulebook.
more: Amit calls it excellent. It explains why Beowulf, Jaws, James Bond and Sholay are the same story underneath, and he presents it as a lens for writers rather than a rulebook.
The book the whole episode is built on. Amit read it many years ago and walks through all seven archetypes and their five-act structures.

head: The Soul of a New Machine
dek: A journalist embedded inside Data General as a team built a single CPU.
more: A journalist embedded inside Data General as a team built a single CPU. The book takes you into the minds of the engineers and their leader Tom West, including the emptiness they felt once the quest was over.
Ajay's example of a real-world quest during the Quest chapter.

head: The Pathan Unarmed
dek: Amit tells listeners to read it. It investigates how Pathans, stereotyped as violent, built and led the greatest non-violent movement of all time.
more: Amit tells listeners to read it. It investigates how Pathans, stereotyped as violent, built and led the greatest non-violent movement of all time.
Mentioned while retelling the Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Khudai Khidmatgar quest.

head: Three Hundred Ramayanas
dek: It shows how each retelling adapted the epic to its own time and place, with tribal versions being completely different.
more: It shows how each retelling adapted the epic to its own time and place, with tribal versions being completely different. Each version reflects the society that told it.
Invoked to argue that there is not one Ramayana but thousands of competing retellings.

head: Laughable Loves
dek: He calls it 'a great book' and 'magnificent'.
more: He calls it 'a great book' and 'magnificent'.
Amit invokes a Kundera book about love and laughter while explaining that the two have drifted apart in modern comedy.

head: Storytelling Is Our First Instinct
dek: Faced with a deeply complex world, humans make sense of it by telling stories, from sun gods to modern theories.
more: Faced with a deeply complex world, humans make sense of it by telling stories, from sun gods to modern theories. Every story is a simplification, but a necessary one. Ajay adds that science and entertainment are both forms of storytelling. They differ only in how closely they stick to reality.

head: The Seven Basic Plots
dek: Christopher Booker argues that all stories recycle seven archetypes: Overcoming the Monster (Beowulf, Jaws, Sholay), Rags to Riches (Cinderella, Rocky, Rockstar), the Quest (the Odyssey, Raiders of the Lost Ark), Voyage and Return (Alice in Wonderland, DDLJ, Dil Chahta Hai), Comedy, Tragedy, and Rebirth (A Christmas Carol).
more: Christopher Booker argues that all stories recycle seven archetypes: Overcoming the Monster (Beowulf, Jaws, Sholay), Rags to Riches (Cinderella, Rocky, Rockstar), the Quest (the Odyssey, Raiders of the Lost Ark), Voyage and Return (Alice in Wonderland, DDLJ, Dil Chahta Hai), Comedy, Tragedy, and Rebirth (A Christmas Carol). The types blend into one another. Lord of the Rings and the Mahabharata contain all seven, and an ongoing story like the Ukraine war could still turn out to be either a triumph or a tragedy.

head: Each Archetype Has a Five-Act Skeleton
dek: Overcoming the Monster: call, initial success, confrontation, final ordeal, miraculous escape.
more: Overcoming the Monster: call, initial success, confrontation, final ordeal, miraculous escape. Rags to Riches: wretchedness at home, initial success out in the world, central crisis, final ordeal leading to independence, final union. Quest: call, journey, arrival and frustration, final ordeal, the goal. Voyage and Return: anticipation, initial fascination, frustration, nightmare, escape and return. Tragedy: anticipation, dream stage, frustration, nightmare, destruction or death. All of them move from calm, through upheaval, back to calm.

head: Structure Is Not a Constraint
dek: Amit says he is not being prescriptive. Mediocre writers and formula-driven studio executives use templates as crutches, and Sturgeon's Law says 95% of everything is crap.
more: Amit says he is not being prescriptive. Mediocre writers and formula-driven studio executives use templates as crutches, and Sturgeon's Law says 95% of everything is crap. Abandoning structure is not the way out of mediocrity. The way out is to do creative, surprising things within the structure.

head: Ragas as Normative Constraints
dek: Ajay contrasts Booker's descriptive claim (stories happen to fall into seven types) with Indian classical music's normative one.
more: Ajay contrasts Booker's descriptive claim (stories happen to fall into seven types) with Indian classical music's normative one. A raga is a set of rules, and the tradition claims that working within those rules produces more beautiful music than unconstrained imagination.

head: Why These Plots? Because of How We Are Wired
dek: Why does one raga make you sad and another make you happy? Amit argues it comes down to how human brains are wired, and the same is true of stories.
more: Why does one raga make you sad and another make you happy? Amit argues it comes down to how human brains are wired, and the same is true of stories. Archetypes persist because they speak to deep urges: escape, love, adventure. We do not yet understand human nature well enough to map this fully.

head: Comedy Is a Structure, Not a Laugh Track
dek: In Booker's sense, comedy means a small world clouded by confusion, a nightmarish tangle, and then revelation and joyful reunion.
more: In Booker's sense, comedy means a small world clouded by confusion, a nightmarish tangle, and then revelation and joyful reunion. Characters stuck in anger or jealousy must change or be exposed, true identities are revealed, people find their other halves, and whatever was lost is restored. That is why Jane Austen's novels count as comedies. In the 20th century, love and laughter split apart: rom-coms are not always funny, and slapstick like Housefull keeps romance on the margins.

head: Tragedy: The Noble One's Fall
dek: Tragedy follows a noble protagonist lured into ignoble acts, ending in destruction or death.
more: Tragedy follows a noble protagonist lured into ignoble acts, ending in destruction or death. In Julius Caesar the tragedy belongs to Brutus, not Caesar. Amit adds a dark twist: life itself fits the template.

head: Change the Point of View and the Genre Changes
dek: Which archetype a story belongs to depends on whose eyes you see it through.
more: Which archetype a story belongs to depends on whose eyes you see it through. Give Goliath a backstory, trapped in his image of strength and never finding love, and David and Goliath becomes a tragedy.

head: Voyage and Return: The Journey Outside Is a Journey Inside
dek: These stories appeal to people who feel stuck, living what Thoreau called lives of quiet desperation, and who dream that going somewhere will change them.
more: These stories appeal to people who feel stuck, living what Thoreau called lives of quiet desperation, and who dream that going somewhere will change them. Ajay quotes Pirsig: the Zen you find at the top of the mountain is the Zen you take with you. A journey brings out what was already there. Ajay also separates The Hobbit (a finite trip and return) from Lord of the Rings (the quest).

head: Rebirth: Transformation as the Whole Point
dek: Change happens in every archetype, but in Rebirth it is the core of the story: someone becomes a fundamentally different person.
more: Change happens in every archetype, but in Rebirth it is the core of the story: someone becomes a fundamentally different person. Examples include Scrooge, Beauty and the Beast, Sleeping Beauty and Snow White, and DDLJ's Amrish Puri character. Coming-of-age stories work much the same way.

head: The Open-Source Epic
dek: Thousands of stories competed, and the Mahabharata, Ramayana, Iliad and Odyssey survived, which Amit credits to magnificent storytelling more than religion.
more: Thousands of stories competed, and the Mahabharata, Ramayana, Iliad and Odyssey survived, which Amit credits to magnificent storytelling more than religion. The Ramayana is not one text but many retellings, each adapted to its region and era like a Rorschach test of that society's mores. Ajay calls this decentralised, with no single master book, and Amit jokes that India had an open-source epic thousands of years before open-source software.

head: The Line Through Every Heart
dek: Amit closes with Solzhenitsyn's passage from The Gulag Archipelago, which Booker uses to open the Rebirth chapter.
more: Amit closes with Solzhenitsyn's passage from The Gulag Archipelago, which Booker uses to open the Rebirth chapter. Stories must simplify into black and white, but the line between good and evil runs through every person and moves over time. His plea is to avoid rushing to judgment, to recognise the hero and villain in all of us, and to tell stories that embrace that complexity.

head: Amit introduces the first archetype
more: Amit introduces the first archetype as 'overcoming the Indian state', then admits he is kidding. Later he says every monster gets beaten in the end, 'Unless that monster is a Indian state. I don't think that film has been written yet.'

head: Ajay proposes using LLM prompts to mass-produce fiction from the seven templates, then classifying a hundred Malayalam films by type to compute
more: Ajay proposes using LLM prompts to mass-produce fiction from the seven templates, then classifying a hundred Malayalam films by type to compute 'means and variances' of what works. He's the suit, though you're not wearing a suit, but it's close enough.'

head: After Ajay neatly casts the Battle of Kyiv as Overcoming the Monster, Amit
more: After Ajay neatly casts the Battle of Kyiv as Overcoming the Monster, Amit says: 'I am going to buy a kurta and a patiala for you because there is an artist in you.'

head: Amit on the Rags to Riches archetype
more: Amit on the Rags to Riches archetype: 'My life sadly only rags. I hope you've got into riches or will at some point.' On Ajay's father's story: 'your story, will it be tragedy? Are you gonna let him down?', which gets the comeback 'Riches to rags.'

head: Amit on spotting Oppenheimer as a tragedy
more: Amit on spotting Oppenheimer as a tragedy: 'I'm very good at identifying tragedy, you see... The world is filled with tragedy, and also I think my gaze is filled with tragedy, but it is what it is.'

head: Amit says every book from…
