more: Kittens yowl during the tragedy chapter. Amit hopes sound man Gaurav Chintamani won't clean it up, 'because better soundtrack when we talk about tragedy.'

head: Amit lists Devdas as a tragedy
more: Amit lists Devdas as a tragedy: 'Though if it is the... Sanjay Leela Bhansali Devdas, I think the film itself was a tragedy, but we shall uh leave that aside.'

head: Asked whether he has ever been reborn or changed fundamentally, Ajay answers like an engineer
more: Asked whether he has ever been reborn or changed fundamentally, Ajay answers like an engineer: 'lots of implementation detail has happened, but the foundations were the same.'

head: Amit on screenwriting
more: Amit on screenwriting: 'if any of our viewers live in Versova, then no doubt they have tried writing screenplays', so they will know Syd Field's three-act structure.

head: Rain interrupts the Solzhenitsyn finale and the hosts rush indoors (
more: Rain interrupts the Solzhenitsyn finale and the hosts rush indoors ('We are not in a studio with green screen'). The show notes title this chapter 'A Tragic Ending to the Episode.'

head: Sturgeon's Law
more: Sturgeon's Law, '95% of everything is crap', invoked to explain why so much formula writing is mediocre.

head: Thoreau's
more: Thoreau's 'lives of quiet desperation', used to explain why Voyage and Return stories appeal to people who feel stuck. Ajay attributes to Robert McNamara the line that we go on the journey and only on returning understand where we had been.

head: Robert Pirsig, quoted by Ajay
more: Robert Pirsig, quoted by Ajay: 'The zen you find at the top of the mountain is the zen that you take with yourself.'

head: Ajay doubts that comedy survived in 20th-century literature because
more: Ajay doubts that comedy survived in 20th-century literature because 'we don't take P. G. Wodehouse as serious literature'. Amit calls Wodehouse one of the finest examples of the form and notes that Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility and Emma are comedies in structure.

head: Solzhenitsyn's The Gulag Archipelago
more: Solzhenitsyn's The Gulag Archipelago: 'It was on rotting prison straw that I felt the first stirrings of good in myself', which Booker quotes at the start of his Rebirth chapter.

head: The chess.com 2900 that awed Ajay
dek: It is a familiar, everyday version of the adaptive testing Ajay proposes for India's entrance exams, where question difficulty adjusts to how you are doing.
more: Amit recalls solving chess puzzles on chess.com while Ajay sat beside him. The site gives you harder puzzles as your rating rises and easier ones when you slip. Amit reached a 2900 puzzle rating in front of Ajay, who asked in awe whether that made him a 2900 player in the real world. Amit says no: his actual rating is around 1900 to 2000, and puzzle ratings are heavily inflated. Ajay insisted 2900 was still super cool. Amit replied that with that much inflation, it's not that cool.

It is a familiar, everyday version of the adaptive testing Ajay proposes for India's entrance exams, where question difficulty adjusts to how you are doing. It also shows that a score only means something relative to what it actually measures.

head: The NTS interview and the 10th-grader who hacked circuits
dek: India once had a high-stakes selection process that treated a teenager as a whole person rather than a marks-producing machine.
more: Ajay remembers the old National Talent Search exam. As he recalls it, a third of the weight went to an IQ test, a third to subject domains and a third to an interview. In that interview, as a 10th-standard student, he was asked what he did in his spare time. He said he hacked electronic circuitry, and the panel asked him to tell them about it.

India once had a high-stakes selection process that treated a teenager as a whole person rather than a marks-producing machine. Ajay uses it to argue that IIT admissions could also go beyond a single test.

head: Building NSE's on-demand certification exam
dek: The reform he proposes has already been built and run in India. The obstacle is not technical know-how but the habit of holding one giant state-run exam on one day.
more: Years ago Ajay helped NSE build a certification exam for derivatives traders. Test centres were set up across the country and a question bank was built once. Each candidate saw a random subset of questions and booked an appointment to take the test whenever they liked. He offers it as proof that his first reform, computerised testing that runs all year, is nothing new. The SAT and GRE already run this way through ETS.
The reform he proposes has already been built and run in India. The obstacle is not technical know-how but the habit of holding one giant state-run exam on one day.
printed: Book a slot, sit the test

head: Deepak VS's swimming-test thought experiment
dek: Thought experiments like this make the status quo look strange. The lesson is that any single high-stakes filter guarding a scarce prize gets gamed by an industry.
more: On The Seen and the Unseen, Deepak VS once suggested replacing the IIT entrance exam with a swimming test. In Amit's words, you would at least be selecting for desire, and India has a long coastline and could build pools. Amit's twist is that by year two or three the swimming test gets gamed too, with coaching classes and IIT coaches in Speedos on billboards.

Thought experiments like this make the status quo look strange. The lesson is that any single high-stakes filter guarding a scarce prize gets gamed by an industry. The disease is the scarcity, not the particular test.
printed: Sink or swim into the IITs

head: Robert Sapolsky's biology lectures on YouTube
dek: Sapolsky's classroom lectures are free online and, in Amit's words, absolutely masterful.
more: Sapolsky's classroom lectures are free online and, in Amit's words, absolutely masterful. Amit had never been interested in biology before, and says Sapolsky opens your mind in different ways. It is proof that great teaching is freely available.
Amit's main recommendation. It follows his suggestion that every college should put its classes online.

head: Behave
dek: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky's masterpieces and a brilliant book.
more: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky's masterpieces and a brilliant book.
Mentioned while introducing Sapolsky as one of the great thinkers on biology.

head: Determined
dek: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky's masterpieces and a brilliant book.
more: Amit calls it one of Sapolsky's masterpieces and a brilliant book.
Mentioned alongside Behave while introducing Sapolsky.

head: Educational Outreach, IIT Bombay (CDEEP)
by: D. B. Phatak and others at IIT Bombay
dek: It records IIT Bombay's engineering teaching on video and takes it to hundreds of thousands of students across India.
more: It records IIT Bombay's engineering teaching on video and takes it to hundreds of thousands of students across India. For Ajay this separates the knowledge from the credential.
Ajay builds on Amit's idea of putting classes online. He mentions IIT Bombay's legendary mechanics teacher Dipan Ghosh, saying the whole of India needs no second mechanics teacher.

head: E-Yantra
dek: It replaces exam questions with creative challenges like 'build me a robot that does X'.
more: It replaces exam questions with creative challenges like 'build me a robot that does X'. Cheap sourced parts let students all over India take part. There are no marks or certificates, so the only reason to do it is the pleasure of doing it and the thirst for knowledge.
An initiative Ajay's friend Kavi Arya of IIT Bombay's computer science department is part of. It challenges young people to build robots.

head: Varma's Question: Where is the coercion?
dek: Amit's lens for any policy problem: start by asking who is being coerced, because that is usually where the root cause lies.
more: Amit's lens for any policy problem: start by asking who is being coerced, because that is usually where the root cause lies. Kids going to coaching classes involves no coercion; it is a voluntary market response to a broken system. The real coercion is the state blocking private entrepreneurs from creating more seats in higher education.

head: The meritocracy myth
dek: The system's moral legitimacy rests on the claim that higher JEE marks mean more intelligence and knowledge.
more: The system's moral legitimacy rests on the claim that higher JEE marks mean more intelligence and knowledge. Ajay no longer believes it. A high-stakes exam has a finite set of question types, so coaching shrinks it to pattern recognition: see this type, jump to that solution. That is like a computer doing table lookup without understanding anything. The only trait it rewards is conscientiousness, meaning obedience and drilling from morning to night, rather than curiosity, creativity or flexible general intelligence. Given credentialism, playing along is rational for each family, but society misallocates its scarce seats.

head: Coaching classes are the symptom, not the disease
dek: Ajay mock-proposes copying Xi Jinping's shutdown of China's test-prep industry, and Amit calls banning coaching absurd.
more: Ajay mock-proposes copying Xi Jinping's shutdown of China's test-prep industry, and Amit calls banning coaching absurd. If you have a fever of 103 every day, you don't ban paracetamol; you find the cause of the fever. Banning a victimless activity, as with liquor, drugs or prostitution, only creates an unregulated black market that is costlier and more dangerous, like hooch deaths under prohibition.

head: An exam is a statistical estimator
dek: Seeing an exam as an estimator means thinking about its bias and error variance, and trying to reduce both.
more: Seeing an exam as an estimator means thinking about its bias and error variance, and trying to reduce both. Item response theory makes the test adaptive. Easy questions separate candidates from zero to the 75th percentile, and harder ones separate the top tail, which matters most when only about 1% get seats. Questions are reused and checked one by one. If strong candidates don't get a question right more often than weak ones, the question is faulty. Ajay adds that UPSC papers are nonsense as predictors of good civil servants.

head: Run testing as a continuous operation, not an annual event
dek: States get better only by doing things repeatedly, with feedback loops.
more: States get better only by doing things repeatedly, with feedback loops. Ajay's fixes within the current system: randomised computer tests generated at runtime from a large question bank, running about 250 days a year. That turns 2.5 million kids on one day into roughly 10,000 a day. Candidates get two or three attempts and their best score counts, which cuts stress from heat waves, bad air quality or simply feeling unwell. Private firms should run the exams, as ETS does for the SAT and GRE, because governments are poor at efficient operations.

head: Free the colleges to choose their own students
dek: Universities only get better when they have autonomy and a sense of mission.
more: Universities only get better when they have autonomy and a sense of mission. UC Berkeley and UCLA both sit in the state-run UC system, yet run fully separate admissions. A motivated university can calibrate CBSE against ICSE marks, or compare applicants from every country's school system, by itself. Colleges should compete on how well they select students, whether for a liberal-arts or a business-school bent. They should also look at the whole person: the IIMs use group discussions and interviews, and economics PhD admissions now include video interviews. Amit's caveat is that interviews favour privileged kids who grew up speaking English, so they work best as one factor among several.

head: The Pai-Shah eligibility-plus-lottery proposal
dek: Stage one is an all-India conceptual exam at about age 17 that cannot be gamed by test prep.
more: Stage one is an all-India conceptual exam at about age 17 that cannot be gamed by test prep. The target is the top one lakh rather than the top thousand, at roughly an OECD PISA level of 650. Stage two allocates the 20,000 IIT seats by lottery among those one lakh. Ajay sees three benefits. IIT batches become more varied in background. Professors can no longer coast and must improve their teaching. And the other 80,000 strong students spread across colleges all over India, lifting those classrooms. A normal school education plus football, reading and curiosity would be enough to qualify.

head: An excellent technocratic design of a bad solution
dek: Amit's rebuttal of the lottery. It compares the messy real-world system with an idealised alternative.
more: Amit's rebuttal of the lottery. It compares the messy real-world system with an idealised alternative. It doesn't reward desire or hard work, because making the top one lakh would be a breeze for some. It also creates an allocation problem: a kid desperate to do mechanical engineering can lose the seat to someone who would rather write poems, leaving both miserable. Similar lotteries for medicine in the Netherlands and New Zealand have drawn criticism. Above all, it rations the scarcity instead of attacking it.

head: Scarce education is a policy choice
dek: The root cause is that the state suppresses the supply of higher education.
more: The root cause is that the state suppresses the supply of higher education. It does this through licences and years of bureaucracy, land and infrastructure mandates, rules that faculty must have PhDs, and forcing colleges to admit through a central test. As a result, only politicians start universities in India, often for the wrong reasons. Ajay is encouraged by new private universities like Ashoka, FLAME and Nayanta, but asks why so few are allowed. He adds that India simply does not have enough medical colleges.

head: Profit is the best kind of philanthropy
dek: Higher education in India cannot legally be run for profit. That pushes founders into workaround trusts, adding friction and cost.
more: Higher education in India cannot legally be run for profit. That pushes founders into workaround trusts, adding friction and cost. Amit argues that in a free market you profit only by making someone better off, so a ban on profit in education is a ban on the very motive that would create more seats.

head: Separate knowledge from credentials: put every class online
dek: Amit's 'jugaadu hack', a workaround rather than a fix: every college should put a camera in its classrooms and post the lectures.
more: Amit's 'jugaadu hack', a workaround rather than a fix: every college should put a camera in its classrooms and post the lectures. Teachers become more accountable, and students who were filtered out still get the knowledge, if not the network or the degree. Ajay points to IIT Bombay's video outreach as the same idea already working.

head: It's okay to opt out of the rat race
dek: Ajay's advice to parents and students is to ignore the hype around brand names like IIT and MIT.
more: Ajay's advice to parents and students is to ignore the hype around brand names like IIT and MIT. Look at the actual person in the mirror, or your child, and nurture their intellectual and emotional growth. He would rather a child grow up excited and happy, perhaps into organic chemistry or the electric guitar, and aware of the world.

head: The cold open
more: The cold open: Amit says he picked his co-host through an entrance exam with one multiple-choice question. The options were all the money in the world; all the fame with groupies ('Even the thought could get you canceled'); a private jet and a house in the Bahamas; becoming the world's biggest Instagram influencer; or 'none of these, but freedom for everyone.' 'And Ajay Shah chose freedom for everyone, and that's why we're here today. Well done, you aced the entrance test.' Later Amit warns Ajay not to say anything against freedom, or he'll have to hold another entrance exam, 'and now everybody will game it because they know the answer.'

head: Ajay baits Amit with a mock big-state pitch
more: Ajay baits Amit with a mock big-state pitch: 'our dear friend Xi Jinping' shut down China's whole test-prep industry in one fell swoop, 'like free markets and all that is good. But in this one case, you've really got to give it because of the plight of the children. Like come on, where will the children go?' Amit: 'You're trying to needle needle needle me.'

head: Amit catches a slight smile on Ajay's face as he
more: Amit catches a slight smile on Ajay's face as he says 'IIT entrance exams', remembering that he too cleared it, and asks editor Nomsita MS Haritashya to replay the clip: 'I did not miss that.'

head: Ajay on the self-image of IITians as the…
more: Ajay on the self-image of IITians as the 'creme of the country': 'When I was in IIT we used to be called the whipped creme.'

head: Ajay on the coached JEE topper
more: Ajay on the coached JEE topper: 'you will be the fastest gun in the West when you are rapidly solving through. Not because you're so smart, but because you've seen them before.'

head: Amit hypes the next segment
more: Amit hypes the next segment: 'you want Masala, get your popcorn, we are gonna fight here.' He then delivers the verdict on the Pai-Shah lottery: 'I have great fondness for both you and Nitin and great respect. But in this matter, you are both wrong.'

Ajay: 'Okay, I gave up Amit. I'm gonna make you the dictator.' Amit: 'The moment you say I will make you a dictator, solution becomes impossible there, right? You need a liberal democracy with free markets for good solutions to come about.'

head: A quick one-two on centralised education policy.
more: A quick one-two on centralised education policy. Amit: 'Never trust a joint secretary.' Ajay: 'Education is too important to be left to education bureaucrats.'

head: Amit passes on a friend's jibe about Ashoka University students and asks if it's true. Ajay warns that many Ashoka students are the show's audience
more: Amit passes on a friend's jibe about Ashoka University students and asks if it's true. Ajay warns that many Ashoka students are the show's audience, 'so you better be nice to them,' and Amit immediately withdraws his statement.

head: Plugging the old education episode, Amit mentions
more: Plugging the old education episode, Amit mentions 'thirty years of writing on it... much longer than that,' then catches himself: 'sorry, I gave your age away.'

head: Kota, the coaching-class hub where kids are sent from 8th standard
more: Kota, the coaching-class hub where kids are sent from 8th standard, 'Every year you hear about suicides in Kota, it has become an industry.' Also mentioned: Irodov and Resnick and Halliday, the physics books every JEE aspirant grinds through.
'You don't throw the baby out with the bathwater, as it were, old German saying' — Amit, arguing against banning coaching classes.

head: The committee that chose every bank's disk controller
dek: This is the clearest picture of RBI as 'the central planning shop of the financial sector'.
more: When computers arrived in the early 1990s, RBI decided banks needed computerisation, and the Rangarajan Committee wrote down exactly what every bank had to do. It named the CPU and the SMD disk controller, for Uniplus Unix machines running Motorola 68K processors. Every bank in India took the report as its IT strategy. Nobody was embarrassed, because prescribing every product, process and technology was seen as RBI's job.

This is the clearest picture of RBI as 'the central planning shop of the financial sector'. When officials pick technological winners, a whole industry freezes on one choice. Amit later argues that a single state-backed payment system under DPI repeats the same mindset.

head: The Rs 5,500 crore hole that woke up RBI
dek: A visible blow-up can start a reform, but a regulator that sees itself as the system's protective parent will keep hiding bad news instead of exposing it.
more: By the early 1990s RBI had realised that 'banking regulation' existed and that it knew nothing about it. In 1995 a Rs 5,500 crore NPA hole was found inside Indian Bank, and that crisis started RBI thinking about prudential regulation. Two camps formed inside RBI: one wanted to build regulatory capability, the other was happy to keep doing central planning. Ajay says this battle for RBI's soul has had largely poor outcomes, and banking regulation still barely works today.
A visible blow-up can start a reform, but a regulator that sees itself as the system's protective parent will keep hiding bad news instead of exposing it.

head: One payphone per village
dek: Telecom is the counterfactual for banking. A bureaucratic monopoly serves only the elite, while competition reaches the whole country.
more: Telecom used to be a tidy government monopoly: DoT, MTNL, BSNL and VSNL, defended on national-security grounds. The rich got phones after a ten-year wait or a bribe, and most of India got none. The official dream was a village telephone scheme with one payphone per village, where you dropped in a coin and could not call long distance. Then Sudhindra Kulkarni and Arun Shourie, working in the Vajpayee government, opened the sector to private and foreign players. Mobile calls that once cost sixteen rupees a minute became a 'janta product', and India now has about 1.1 billion phones for 1.4 billion people. Amit adds that crediting Sam Pitroda for this is 'rubbish': markets did it.

Telecom is the counterfactual for banking. A bureaucratic monopoly serves only the elite, while competition reaches the whole country. Indian banking stayed a bureaucracy, and it stayed as 'dead' as telecom once was.

head: Why Infosys needed a stock market
dek: Equity markets can finance what collateral-hungry banks cannot see, such as ideas, people and intangible capital.
more: Banks would not lend to the early software industry. They called it too risky, and they practised asset-based lending, which meant pledging a factory as collateral. Software companies have low capital intensity and nothing much to pledge. Ajay draws a straight line from the Infosys IPO of 1994 to NSE and SEBI, which opened funding paths for India's new-age capitalism. He ranks the equity market alongside the telecom reforms and Major General Khanduri's National Highways Authority as heroes of the reform era.
Equity markets can finance what collateral-hungry banks cannot see, such as ideas, people and intangible capital. A working stock market is part of the infrastructure for new industries.

head: Truckloads of share certificates (1993)
dek: The weakness of the pre-reform market was physical, not abstract: paper choking on small inflows.
more: In August and September 1993 the first surge of foreign investment reached India, at what now looks like a tiny $100 million a month. The old BSE settlement system choked and collapsed. Trucks carried paper share certificates around the streets of Bombay, and the exchange could not complete settlement. Foreign investors could not work in such a system, which strengthened the case for NSE, the Depositories Act and NSDL.
The weakness of the pre-reform market was physical, not abstract: paper choking on small inflows. A concrete failure like this is often what makes a reform unstoppable.

head: Five minutes that took years: the birth of NSDL
dek: Big institutional change looks tiny on the day it arrives. Behind it are years of drafting, persuasion and political deal-making by a small group of committed people.
more: The depository needed an enabling law, the Depositories Act, drafted by PJ Nayak and M Sahu. The government of the day lacked a majority to pass it. The British Chancellor of the Exchequer raised it with Manmohan Singh as a real choke point, and Manmohan Singh pressed the Congress establishment to get it through 'by hook or by crook'. At the inauguration at Nehru Centre on 6 November 1996, Bimal Jalan, DR Mehta, CB Bhave and P Chidambaram were on stage. Someone pressed one carriage return to stand in for the first transaction, Chidambaram hugged Bhave, and the ceremony was over in five minutes. Ajay calls it one of the happiest days of his life.
Big institutional change looks tiny on the day it arrives. Behind it are years of drafting, persuasion and political deal-making by a small group of committed people.
printed: Five minutes, years in the making

head: Naidu's price: the insurance regulator goes to Hyderabad
dek: Finance runs on tacit knowledge and dense human networks, and in India those live in Bombay.
more: Under the United Front government, with Chidambaram as finance minister, the law creating an insurance regulator and opening the sector could not get through Parliament. Chandrababu Naidu offered his support on one condition: the IRDA had to be based in Hyderabad. Ajay calls the result a lukewarm experience. LIC stayed huge, private entry was slow, foreign investment limits stayed, and toxic consumer practices flourished. He tells people to be very sceptical of any insurance product sold to them.

Finance runs on tacit knowledge and dense human networks, and in India those live in Bombay. Moving regulators away for political reasons, whether IRDA to Hyderabad or GIFT City to Ahmedabad, weakens them, much as an SEC outside New York would make little sense.

head: Thatcher destroyed the green line
dek: Reforms should be designed so they are hard to reverse. India kept its control apparatus when it replaced FERA with FEMA, and the criminal clauses came back in 2015.
more: When Margaret Thatcher's Britain opened its current and capital accounts, some people proposed freeing everything but keeping reporting requirements: fill in a form, then take an automatic 'green line'. The reformers refused. They argued that if the reporting system stayed, a future government could easily shut the gate again. So in the early 1980s Britain removed the reporting requirements too, so that no future 'lefty' could bring capital controls back.
Reforms should be designed so they are hard to reverse. India kept its control apparatus when it replaced FERA with FEMA, and the criminal clauses came back in 2015.
printed: Thatcher rubs out the green line

head: The economist who hadn't read the law
dek: A press release is not a reform. The real outcome lives in the legal text and in implementation, which is the territory of public administration and public choice.
more: In 1993 India announced 'current account convertibility', and young Ajay cheered that India was growing up. Years later he began reading the actual laws and found it did not exist. FEMA (1999), celebrated for dropping FERA's criminal clauses, begins by banning all transactions and then grants freedoms case by case. In practice, people who can afford lawyers and accountants get capital-account openness, and everyone else is blocked.
A press release is not a reform. The real outcome lives in the legal text and in implementation, which is the territory of public administration and public choice.

head: The European telecom bankruptcies nobody noticed
dek: Good bankruptcy is invisible. When it is fast and predictable, the losses fall on investors while the firm's organisational capital (people, processes, tacit knowledge) survives.
more: European telecom firms bid ridiculous sums in spectrum auctions, the expected revenue never came, and the firms went bankrupt. Customers in France or Germany noticed nothing: phones kept working, numbers stayed and calls didn't drop. Higher up, old shareholders and bondholders took the losses, and new owners bought the firms as going concerns.

Good bankruptcy is invisible. When it is fast and predictable, the losses fall on investors while the firm's organisational capital (people, processes, tacit knowledge) survives. In India, slow processes mean firms have usually decayed past saving by the time anything happens.

head: HDFC had never repossessed a house
dek: Something as basic as a lender being able to claim collateral was missing for decades.
more: In the late 1990s Deepak Parekh, head of HDFC, India's biggest home-loan company, told Ajay that HDFC had never repossessed a house in its entire history. Lenders had no real power to seize pledged collateral. That changed only with SARFAESI in 2002, drafted in Yashwant Sinha's time, which let lenders take the asset when borrowers defaulted.
Something as basic as a lender being able to claim collateral was missing for decades. Secured lending means little without it.

head: From a budget-speech paragraph to a bankruptcy code
dek: Big laws can start with one well-timed nudge, but passing the law is the easy part.
more: FSLRC had drafted a resolution-corporation law for financial firms such as banks and insurers, whose millions of depositors or policyholders cannot negotiate in one room. After FSLRC, KP Krishnan took a section of the 2015 budget speech to Arun Jaitley and suggested expanding it into a full bankruptcy code. TK Viswanathan then led the Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee, with Ajay and Susan as members and Susan leading the drafting team. The result has been lukewarm. RBI has nudged banks away from the code toward quiet restructuring, there were implementation failures at the Ministry of Company Affairs, IBBI and NCLT, and the reform community dispersed.
Big laws can start with one well-timed nudge, but passing the law is the easy part. Without a community looking after it, implementation decays.

head: A loan offer at the movies
dek: Household credit is one of Indian finance's real successes, driven by credit bureaus, which changed borrowers' incentives by recording defaults, and by private NBFCs.
more: At an Indian Express event with KV Kamath and Mukesh Ambani on stage, Shekhar Gupta asked Ambani what he had seen change over the reform years. Ambani said that in the old days his driver came to him when he needed a loan, because there was nowhere else to go. Recently, going to a movie at Metro, a teenager plucked his sleeve and asked if he wanted a loan.

Household credit is one of Indian finance's real successes, driven by credit bureaus, which changed borrowers' incentives by recording defaults, and by private NBFCs. Credit went from a favour you asked of a rich employer to a product sold to everyone.

head: The Journey of Indian Finance
dek: Amit calls it close to a magisterial account of Indian finance from 1947 to now and the definitive work on the subject; the episode is only a condensed recap.
more: Amit calls it close to a magisterial account of Indian finance from 1947 to now and the definitive work on the subject; the episode is only a condensed recap. Ajay points readers to Table 2, a one-page chronology of milestones across every sector.
Ajay's chapter for The Cambridge Economic History of Modern South Asia, which this episode is built on; Amit's recommendation at the end.

head: The Cambridge Economic History of Modern South Asia
by: Edited by Latika Chaudhary, Tirthankar Roy and Anand Swamy
dek: He has seen the table of contents and calls it 'drool'. The best people have been brought together, and he expects a gorgeous book.
more: He has seen the table of contents and calls it 'drool'. The best people have been brought together, and he expects a gorgeous book.
The volume Ajay wrote his finance chapter for, and the first in the series to include a chapter on finance.

head: Capital Ideas
dek: A lovely book about how the early ideas of finance emerged, and 'just great fun'.
more: A lovely book about how the early ideas of finance emerged, and 'just great fun'.
Ajay's second recommendation at the end of the episode.

head: The Long Road to Change (Ep 36, Everything is Everything)
dek: It explains how policy change really works: data, research, and an intellectual community arguing over decades.
more: It explains how policy change really works: data, research, and an intellectual community arguing over decades. It also explains why a reform that isn't looked after will fade away.
Pointed to at the start and again in the chapter on the policy process.

head: The Beauty of Finance (Ep 21, Everything is Everything)
dek: A masterclass on why finance exists and why it matters to the real economy, rather than being 'a bunch of rich people playing in an online casino'.
more: A masterclass on why finance exists and why it matters to the real economy, rather than being 'a bunch of rich people playing in an online casino'.
Recommended as background before the banking chapter.

head: Why Freedom Matters (Ep 10, Everything is Everything)
dek: Ajay calls it an economic history of India. It covers the boom after 1869, when the Suez Canal, the telegraph, the Companies Act and the Contract Act arrived.
more: Ajay calls it an economic history of India. It covers the boom after 1869, when the Suez Canal, the telegraph, the Companies Act and the Contract Act arrived.
The equity markets chapter, on India having Asia's first stock market in 1874.

head: Ajay Shah & Bhargavi Zaveri's article on current account convertibility
dek: A careful reading of the actual rules and laws shows India still has no convertibility on the current account.
more: A careful reading of the actual rules and laws shows India still has no convertibility on the current account.
On the 1993 claim that India had achieved current account convertibility.

head: The Constitution of Liberty
dek: The book Thatcher used to declare her government's creed. Amit calls her one of the towering figures of the twentieth century.
more: The book Thatcher used to declare her government's creed. Amit calls her one of the towering figures of the twentieth century.
Amit's favourite Thatcher story: at her first cabinet meeting she threw a copy on the table and said 'This is what we believe in.'

head: The Hollow Man
dek: A 1935 crime novel voted the greatest locked-room murder mystery of all time.
more: A 1935 crime novel voted the greatest locked-room murder mystery of all time. It walks through the solutions to other locked-room mysteries, including the classic melting ice cube.
A mid-episode recommendation prompted by Ajay's 'melting ice cube' metaphor for distressed firms.

head: The Sun Also Rises
dek: Its exchange on going bankrupt, 'slowly at first and then suddenly', is the classic description of how distress plays out.
more: Its exchange on going bankrupt, 'slowly at first and then suddenly', is the classic description of how distress plays out.
Ajay notes that everyone in the bankruptcy field quotes it.

head: The Good Lion
dek: A Hemingway story Amit loves, about a lion who badly wants a Hindu trader sandwich.
more: A Hemingway story Amit loves, about a lion who badly wants a Hindu trader sandwich. He calls it 'a lovely formulation'.
Amit's follow-up to Ajay's Hemingway quote.

head: What Really Happened?
dek: It supports Amit's view that 2008, usually called a market failure, was mostly state overreach.
more: It supports Amit's view that 2008, usually called a market failure, was mostly state overreach.
Amit's argument about the 2008 crisis.

head: Not What They Had in Mind
dek: Kling's work on the crisis supports the reading that state overreach, not free markets, drove it.
more: Kling's work on the crisis supports the reading that state overreach, not free markets, drove it.
Cited with Larry White's essay on the 2008 crisis.

head: Unchecked and Unbalanced
dek: More of Kling's sceptical analysis, which backs Amit's worry that reactive state intervention makes the next crisis worse.
more: More of Kling's sceptical analysis, which backs Amit's worry that reactive state intervention makes the next crisis worse.
Linked in the show notes alongside Amit's mention of Kling's writing on 2008.

head: Central planning means officials designing products and processes
dek: Ajay's working definition: if the government decides products and processes, it is central planning.
more: Ajay's working definition: if the government decides products and processes, it is central planning. After independence, banking became one extended planning system. Delhi licensed the steel mill and Bombay's bureaucracy then supplied the credit. Each gap was filled with a new monopoly PSU (IDBI, ICICI, HDFC) instead of letting a hundred business models compete and ninety-five go bust. RBI became the central planning shop of finance, echoing the 1848 Communist Manifesto's call for credit centralised in a state monopoly bank.

head: Nationalised banking as hidden taxation that fails the bottom 90%
dek: Officials openly called it 'resource mobilization': take households' money and give it to chosen ones.
more: Officials openly called it 'resource mobilization': take households' money and give it to chosen ones. A bureaucratic, one-size-fits-all bank serves only the top income decile, so reaching ten deciles needs many competing business models. Since 1992 about 5% of one year's GDP has gone from the government to public sector banks, effectively underpriced credit paid for by taxpayers and transferred to bank mismanagers. Amit's framing: the intention is seen, the outcome is unseen, and the result destroys wealth rather than just moving it.

head: Banking regulation at heart: honest valuation and enough equity
dek: Ajay reduces bank regulation to two things. First, mark loans to market: if a loan of 100 would fetch 80 at auction today, book the 20 loss now instead of waiting for it to become an NPA.
more: Ajay reduces bank regulation to two things. First, mark loans to market: if a loan of 100 would fetch 80 at auction today, book the 20 loss now instead of waiting for it to become an NPA. Regulators could force banks to auction random samples of assets to check their internal valuations. Second, hold enough equity capital. Indian banks run roughly 5 of equity against 95 of deposits, which is too thin for India's volatile macroeconomy and weak supervision. That ratio also explains why most family-run Indian banks failed: putting in 5 and lending 100 makes bribery pay.

head: If you can't run air traffic control, fly fewer planes
dek: In Ajay's friendly but heart-breaking disagreement with Harsh Vardhan, Harsh says a strong banking system is fundamental to capitalism.
more: In Ajay's friendly but heart-breaking disagreement with Harsh Vardhan, Harsh says a strong banking system is fundamental to capitalism. Ajay replies that after 25 to 35 years of failing to learn bank regulation and bank resolution, India shouldn't bet on a large banking system. He would grow finance through other routes: bond markets, NBFCs, debt venture funds, and foreign banks regulated and resolved by foreign authorities. His project-proposal title sums up the stance: 'Financial Regulation as if State Capacity Mattered'.

head: Why Marx feels more natural than Hayek
dek: Amit argues that ideas like those in the Communist Manifesto will always appeal more than Hayek's or Friedman's, because they flatter our evolved instincts.
more: Amit argues that ideas like those in the Communist Manifesto will always appeal more than Hayek's or Friedman's, because they flatter our evolved instincts. Those instincts include top-down planning, zero-sum thinking and wanting a strongman for the tribe. Liberty is software that has to override that hardware. So every generation that values freedom has to fight for it again.

head: Four pillars: market failure, central planning, rule of law, state capability
dek: Ajay's single diagnosis across all the sectors: the Indian elite failed intellectually to build knowledge and community around four ideas.
more: Ajay's single diagnosis across all the sectors: the Indian elite failed intellectually to build knowledge and community around four ideas. Without them, India kept doing central planning, neglected the rule of law, ignored public choice theory, and gave regulators wide powers with no checks, balances or transparency. The fix is to avoid central planning, address real market failures, and build checks so state agencies deliver instead of becoming unaccountable power.

head: The BSE's missing Coasian bargain
dek: A puzzle that still troubles Ajay. The 300 to 400 brokers who ran the old Bombay Stock Exchange could have agreed among themselves to modernise settlement, open up to all of India and police market manipulation.
more: A puzzle that still troubles Ajay. The 300 to 400 brokers who ran the old Bombay Stock Exchange could have agreed among themselves to modernise settlement, open up to all of India and police market manipulation. That would have made a great private exchange. But some members colluded with manipulators and the club wouldn't enforce rules on itself, so the state stepped in with SEBI, NSE and NSDL. A single fraudster has a private incentive to cheat; a whole community failing to fix its shared institution is the harder question.

head: Risk sharing and the global free lunch
dek: Capital is the biggest cost in a ton of steel, bigger than iron ore or coal, so firms should be able to raise it wherever it is cheapest.
more: Capital is the biggest cost in a ton of steel, bigger than iron ore or coal, so firms should be able to raise it wherever it is cheapest. Spreading investments globally is a free lunch that lowers risk. Your landlord should not face the same local shocks you do. Capital controls, which India started under the British in 1939 and made criminal under Indira Gandhi's 1973 FERA amendment, block all of this.

head: Capital controls hurt everyone except the rich
dek: Ajay treats freedom to move your wealth as a human right: being free to leave, as a Jewish refugee leaving Germany was, means little if your wealth is trapped.
more: Ajay treats freedom to move your wealth as a human right: being free to leave, as a Jewish refugee leaving Germany was, means little if your wealth is trapped. In practice India's controls don't close the economy, because de facto openness keeps rising. They just make openness cost lawyers and accountants, an employment guarantee scheme for intermediaries that shuts out everyone who isn't rich.

head: Capitalism without failure is socialism for the rich
dek: Firms, financial firms and banks must be able to fail, or there isn't real competition or Schumpeterian energy.
more: Firms, financial firms and banks must be able to fail, or there isn't real competition or Schumpeterian energy. The question is whether failure happens badly, as a power struggle where 'the person with the most gundas grabs assets', or through a predictable institutional script that everyone signs up to in advance.

head: Bankruptcy's magic pair: the loss is sunk, and the firm is a melting ice cube
dek: First, when a firm fails the loss has already happened. If a firm with 100 of capital is now worth 40, the only question is who gets the 40, so blame and attempts to undo the loss are a sunk-cost trap.
more: First, when a firm fails the loss has already happened. If a firm with 100 of capital is now worth 40, the only question is who gets the 40, so blame and attempts to undo the loss are a sunk-cost trap. Second, a distressed firm melts. Unpaid vendors, unmaintained machines and unpaid staff drain away its organisational capital and tacit knowledge. Speed decides whether it can be sold as a going concern or only buried.

head: Regulators always fight the last war
dek: Finance should innovate, and bureaucracies will always fall behind. Silicon Valley Bank showed a new kind of bank run, where electronic payments let the money flee over a weekend while the bank was closed.
more: Finance should innovate, and bureaucracies will always fall behind. Silicon Valley Bank showed a new kind of bank run, where electronic payments let the money flee over a weekend while the bank was closed. As in the Lucas critique, clever people optimise around every rule. Ajay concludes that some financial crises are a permanent cost of a sophisticated system, worth paying for the GDP growth that finance brings.

head: India makes its own systemic crises
dek: A systemic crisis is when a chunk of the financial system breaks down badly enough to hurt the real economy.
more: A systemic crisis is when a chunk of the financial system breaks down badly enough to hurt the real economy. Ajay's view shifted from blaming global shocks (1997, LTCM, 2008) to seeing homegrown ones. They come from three interacting failures: monetary policy that isn't inflation targeting, weak prudential regulation, and no way to close failed firms. His paper counts six systemic crises from 1992 to 2018, including Andhra Pradesh's 2010 microfinance ban, and the Covid lockdowns brought another wave.

head: The bailout debate: moral hazard vs. growth
dek: The hosts disagree. Ajay says finance is essential to a poor country's growth, crises will happen, and attacks on bailouts ignore the GDP that finance delivers.
more: The hosts disagree. Ajay says finance is essential to a poor country's growth, crises will happen, and attacks on bailouts ignore the GDP that finance delivers. Amit says bailouts privatise profits, socialise losses and tax the poor, so the state should never bail anyone out. Ajay partly concedes: in many cases the answer is to let go and take moral hazard seriously, instead of trusting better bureaucracies as his younger self did.

head: Indian regulators fuse all three powers of the state
dek: Since the seventeenth century, liberal democracies have split power among legislature, executive and judiciary.
more: Since the seventeenth century, liberal democracies have split power among legislature, executive and judiciary. Regulators everywhere already combine rule-writing and enforcement. Ajay says India is the only country where regulators also judge, which he believes violates the Constitution's basic structure. The result, combined with central planning, is a climate of fear in which businesses never criticise agencies in public. Amit compares it to the chilling effect in free speech, which also dampens investment.

head: Finance is the brain of the economy; computers are plumbing
dek: Finance is about risk and time: taking risky bets, building portfolios and moving cash flows across years.
more: Finance is about risk and time: taking risky bets, building portfolios and moving cash flows across years. At heart it is information processing, which decides how capital is used across the economy. That is why the best minds belong there, and choosing finance over particle physics is not a waste. Computerisation and payments matter but are plumbing. Amit warns that DPI repeats the Rangarajan Committee's mistake by fixing one payment system and crowding out future competition.

head: Knowledge and community are the theory of change
dek: The equity market reform worked because of a team spanning the Ministry of Finance, SEBI, NSE and academic institutions that argued in blogs, op-eds and seminars.
more: The equity market reform worked because of a team spanning the Ministry of Finance, SEBI, NSE and academic institutions that argued in blogs, op-eds and seminars. When that community was broken up, the reforms were rolled back. Pensions withered from neglect and inflation targeting is under attack. Ajay says reforms must be looked after constantly or they fade, and the next 25 years must be spent rebuilding that community.

head: Isomorphic mimicry and the three phases of Indian finance
dek: Ajay sees three phases: explicit socialism (1947 to 1991), a period of real knowledge-building mixed with exaggerated labels (1991 to around 2016), and today's muddle.
more: Ajay sees three phases: explicit socialism (1947 to 1991), a period of real knowledge-building mixed with exaggerated labels (1991 to around 2016), and today's muddle. Throughout, India builds institutions that look right from outside, like a sign saying 'central bank' or a bond market with screens, but lack the substance. Open entry, speculation and derivatives are missing, and officials effectively set interest rates.

head: Loaded words protect bad policy
dek: Ajay is wary of terms like 'money laundering' and 'terrorist financing' because nobody can be seen to oppose them.
more: Ajay is wary of terms like 'money laundering' and 'terrorist financing' because nobody can be seen to oppose them. Under them, pushed by the US Treasury and welcomed by Indian bureaucrats, India built a financial surveillance system that tracks every transaction and drags households through endless KYC. The rich have staff to deal with compliance; ordinary households get pushed out of formal finance.

head: Amit reports that listeners complained the 10.5-hour Life and Times episode with Ajay was too short and missed topics
more: Amit reports that listeners complained the 10.5-hour Life and Times episode with Ajay was too short and missed topics: 'hey, how much can you do in ten hours'.

head: Ajay, deadpan, on the 1848 Communist Manifesto
more: Ajay, deadpan, on the 1848 Communist Manifesto as 'a radical pamphlet... full of scurrilous ideas', including state-monopoly credit, which independent India went on to adopt: 'Some academic scribbler in the years gone by shapes the madman in frenzy.'

head: Ajay on why RBI hides banking trouble
more: Ajay on why RBI hides banking trouble: 'In a central planning system, RBI is mother. Mother cannot allow bad news to be told to the public.'

head: After Ajay calls the five-minute NSDL launch, one keystroke and a hug, one of the happiest days of his life, Amit
more: After Ajay calls the five-minute NSDL launch, one keystroke and a hug, one of the happiest days of his life, Amit replies: 'It's so easy to make you happy.'

head: Amit's code from a DC meetup: whenever he
more: Amit's code from a DC meetup: whenever he says 'low level equilibrium', he really means a beeped-out expletive followed by 'situation'. Ajay agrees in his own way, saying he uses the phrase 'like a great South American novelist, where everybody is good and pure and pursuing their self-interest, but the outcomes are just terrible.'

head: After the IRDA-in-Hyderabad story, Amit invents an…
more: After the IRDA-in-Hyderabad story, Amit invents an 'Indian Podcasting Regulatory Association': 'What if there's a market failure in podcasting? And there surely is.' Ajay joins in: 'What if a podcaster is taking positions on the shares that she is pushing?'

head: On FERA being replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, Ajay
more: On FERA being replaced by the Foreign Exchange Management Act, Ajay says: 'I don't know which word is more offensive.' Amit wants a Foreign Exchange Freedom Act.

head: Amit complains that Ajay gave away his address in their Seen and the Unseen episode (editor Gaurav Chintamani cut it), and today mentioned
more: Amit complains that Ajay gave away his address in their Seen and the Unseen episode (editor Gaurav Chintamani cut it), and today mentioned 'a tower in Varsova'. He jokes that the exact tower he lives in is now on screen.

head: Amit introduces the bankruptcy chapter
more: Amit introduces the bankruptcy chapter: 'One of your great achievements, your and Susan's great achievements is bankruptcy. By which I don't mean that you guys went bankrupt.'

head: Amit on the shared metaphor: in locked-room mysteries the melting ice cube is the solution; in bankruptcy
more: Amit on the shared metaphor: in locked-room mysteries the melting ice cube is the solution; in bankruptcy 'a melting ice cube which is a solution there is actually a problem here.'

head: Ajay turns the…
more: Ajay turns the 'punch bowl' metaphor around: a bad central bank is 'pouring LSD in the punch when the party gets going'. Amit says he has 'full faith in the ability of the state to pour LSD into punch'.

head: Right after Ajay
more: Right after Ajay says 'I'm not a lefty', Amit tells him: 'You see, Ajay Shah, to me, you are a lefty', because Ajay tolerates bailouts. Ajay replies: 'You are a man after my own heart.'

head: On Ajay and Harsh Vardhan breaking each other's hearts over banking, Amit
more: On Ajay and Harsh Vardhan breaking each other's hearts over banking, Amit says: 'both of you have a good heart, so they should not be broken.'

Amit: 'Once upon a time you were the young Turk of Finance. Now you're just a middle aged Indian sitting on a lawn.' Then: 'Now I'm just a YouTuber.' 'Now you're just a YouTuber, even worse.' Amit's closing recommendation keeps it going, praising a man 'greatly respected by all as an economist, till he turned a YouTuber and started doing content. His name is Ajay Shah.'

head: Nehru to JRD Tata, quoted by Amit to set the post-1947 mood
more: Nehru to JRD Tata, quoted by Amit to set the post-1947 mood: 'do not speak to me of profit, it is a dirty word.'

head: Ajay quotes Merton Miller: banking was…
more: Ajay quotes Merton Miller: banking was 'a disaster prone 19th century industry', where banks kept blowing up, in India too.

head: Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest (1895): Miss Prism tells Cecily
more: Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest (1895): Miss Prism tells Cecily, 'you will read your political economy in my absence. The chapter on the fall of the rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational. Even these metallic problems have their melodramatic side.' Indian monetary policy had made it into a Wilde play.

head: Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, the line everyone in bankruptcy quotes: asked how he went bankrupt, the character answers
more: Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, the line everyone in bankruptcy quotes: asked how he went bankrupt, the character answers, 'slowly at first and then suddenly.'

head: Margaret Thatcher at her first cabinet meeting, throwing Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty on the table
more: Margaret Thatcher at her first cabinet meeting, throwing Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty on the table: 'This is what we believe in.'

head: Amit rejects the popular story that Sam Pitroda caused India's telecom revolution
more: Amit rejects the popular story that Sam Pitroda caused India's telecom revolution: 'This is rubbish.' He says markets and the Vajpayee-era reforms did it.

head: How Ten-Hour Podcasts Changed the Interviewer
dek: A change in length is a change in kind. Long conversations force you to listen to understand rather than to respond, and that changes the person doing the listening.
more: Amit started The Seen and the Unseen assuming people have short attention spans, that you must hook them early, and that episodes can't run past 10-15 minutes. All of it proved wrong. The show grew from 15-20 minute single-subject episodes to three-hour deep dives, then to eight-hour-plus oral histories, and recently a ten-and-a-half-hour episode. In his essay 'A Meditation on Form' he worked out that this wasn't the same thing made longer. A five-minute show can be shallow. A long one demands reading all the guest's books, knowing their field and life, and above all listening without interrupting.
A change in length is a change in kind. Long conversations force you to listen to understand rather than to respond, and that changes the person doing the listening.

head: Bernie Krause Hears a Drought
dek: Sound has a visible structure. Ears and audio charts can pick up changes that eyes miss, whether in an ecosystem or in an edit.
more: Bioacoustician Bernie Krause recorded the soundscape of the same spot in California repeatedly between 2004 and 2015, a period that included a drought. To the eye, people couldn't tell how many species had died off or vanished. The sound recording showed it clearly, because each species occupies its own band of frequencies. Amit adds that his editor Gaurav Chintamani says he can do a first cut of an episode just by looking at the waveforms, then listens at double speed.
Sound has a visible structure. Ears and audio charts can pick up changes that eyes miss, whether in an ecosystem or in an edit.

head: CBGB's: Mess as an Acoustic Feature
dek: Musical scenes partly grow out of the acoustics of the rooms they were born in.
more: If Amit could visit one place at one time, he'd pick CBGB's in New York in 1975, birthplace of American punk and alternative rock, where Television, Patti Smith, the Police and Talking Heads played. Following David Byrne, he explains that the club's crowding, furniture and chatter absorbed sound and killed reverberation. That allowed harmonically complex music and a big return of percussion. His own cluttered home studio, full of bookshelves, works the same way and is easier to record in.
Musical scenes partly grow out of the acoustics of the rooms they were born in. Something that looks like a flaw, such as a messy, crowded room, can be exactly what lets a style work.

head: In Defence of Angus Young
dek: Judge a style by the conditions it was built for, not by abstract complexity.
more: In a Rick Beato interview (the show notes link Beato's conversation with Nuno Bettencourt), the guitarist was asked about AC/DC's Angus Young. People mock Young for working with one kind of sound and three or four chords. The guitarist's answer was to consider the circumstances: AC/DC played huge arenas, where you need a wall of sound, and for that his style is perfect. Amit adds that funk never works in a big arena, while metal does.
Judge a style by the conditions it was built for, not by abstract complexity. Different genres are adapted to different settings, and each produces great musicians.

head: Why the Beatles Quit the Stage
dek: The Beatles' move from live act to studio band was also a change of form.
more: Ajay asked why the Beatles stopped touring. Amit's answer came in two parts. First, their months of club gigs in Hamburg around 1962 gave them what Gladwell calls their 10,000 hours and made them a tight unit. Second, after the early hits, audiences got too noisy to play to, and the band wanted to make more evolved music. Ajay added that the best amplification of the time couldn't overcome screaming fans, and that the band was heading towards 'A Day in the Life', which no screaming crowd could take in.
The Beatles' move from live act to studio band was also a change of form. Their later records were made for headphones and home speakers, not stadiums.

head: Jazz Was Shaped by Necessity
dek: Features we now treat as the essence of a genre often started as workarounds for practical limits.
more: Jazz uses the instruments it does because early jazz was played in venues without amplification, so loud instruments won. The trumpet rose, and the banjo was preferred to the acoustic guitar until amplification brought the guitar back. Improvisation had a practical origin too. Bands played for paying dancers, and when the written music ran out the dancers still wanted to dance, so the band stretched out with solos.
Features we now treat as the essence of a genre often started as workarounds for practical limits.

head: Why a CD Holds 74 Minutes
dek: Standards that feel natural often have arbitrary origins. A whole medium's capacity was set by one executive's favourite symphony.
more: When Philips and Sony developed the compact disc, the Sony president was shown a 60-minute disc that could hold more, and he asked for 74 minutes. Amit asked Ajay to guess why, and Ajay got it right: Beethoven's Ninth. The Sony president was a Beethoven fan, and the Ninth Symphony runs 74 minutes.
Standards that feel natural often have arbitrary origins. A whole medium's capacity was set by one executive's favourite symphony.

head: Dark Side of the Moon Fit FM Radio
dek: Commercial success often comes from fitting the format of the day, and that pressure towards conformity explains why so few artists experiment with form.
more: Ajay pointed out how few musicians challenged the LP format, with exceptions like Pink Floyd's 'Echoes', which takes up the whole of side two of Meddle. He had read that in early FM radio, Dark Side of the Moon fit the medium perfectly. Stations could run ads, play the entire album as one block, run more ads, and fill exactly one hour.
Commercial success often comes from fitting the format of the day, and that pressure towards conformity explains why so few artists experiment with form.
printed: One album, one hour of FM

head: Sleepify, 30-Second Beatles and the TikTok Hook
dek: Every new platform creates new constraints and new loopholes. Amit's argument is that these constraints are much looser than the old ones.
more: Spotify pays a band once a track has played for 30 seconds, and nothing extra after that. Vulfpeck released Sleepify, an album of 30-second songs, and asked fans to loop it while they slept. The band made a fair bit of money until Spotify caught on. The Pocket Gods released 100BeatlesX30, a large batch of 30-second Beatles covers. TikTok has its own accidental rule: liking a video counts as liking its audio, so the algorithm pushes that sound further. Labels now tell musicians to be as indulgent as they like for the rest of the song, as long as they deliver a viral 15-second hook.
Every new platform creates new constraints and new loopholes. Amit's argument is that these constraints are much looser than the old ones.

head: The 200,000 Words on Jane Jacobs That Were Cut
dek: The physical limits of a printed book have decided what got published.
more: Robert Caro delivered The Power Broker to his publisher Robert Gottlieb at one million words. Gottlieb asked his printers what they could do. They said 800,000 words was the most they could bind without the book falling apart. So a 200,000-word section on Jane Jacobs, 'a hero to both you and me' as Amit told Ajay, was dropped. Today it would be put online or published as a separate book. Back then it was simply lost.
The physical limits of a printed book have decided what got published. Every book also has a floor and a ceiling on length, usually 100 to 300 pages.

head: Delhi's 19th-Century Poetry Newsletters
dek: A new medium layered on an old one can speed up learning dramatically.
more: Drawing on Swapna Liddle's history of Delhi from about 1801 to 1857, Amit describes newspapers that regularly printed poetry. Readers bought papers partly for the shayari, and Emperor Zafar's verses appeared alongside other poets'. Ajay found it unimaginable that an emperor would write poetry at all. One entrepreneur, criticised in his time as too commercial, began publishing newsletters of the poems recited at mushairas, with an essay on the form at the start. Learning poetry stopped being a matter of chance encounters and became fast and systematic. (From a separate Rahul Matthan episode: 19th-century English newspapers were already full of smut and gossip.)
A new medium layered on an old one can speed up learning dramatically. Amit compares the poetry newsletters to what the internet did for his generation.

head: Blogging Freed Him from the 800-Word Op-Ed
dek: When a form stops dictating length, timing and approval, both the amount and the variety of what you write can grow sharply.
more: As a young would-be writer in the 1990s, Amit saw only two options: 800-word op-eds sent to Times of India or Indian Express, or a book of around 200 pages. Blogging in the early 2000s removed those limits. He could write 80 words or 8,000, ignore the news cycle, skip gatekeepers, pick his own style and post whenever he liked. He averaged five posts a day for five years, about 8,000 posts, many just a line and a link, and calls it great writing practice. Social media later split blogging's functions apart, and newsletters revived it by letting writers keep their readers.
When a form stops dictating length, timing and approval, both the amount and the variety of what you write can grow sharply.

head: Learning One Format at a Time
dek: Each format is a separate skill that takes sustained immersion to learn.
more: Ajay learned writing formats one after another: research papers, then op-eds, then blog posts, then books. Each meant a couple of years fully immersed in that one format. Now he can switch between all of them whenever he wants. Amit pointed out that Ajay had modestly left out his newest form, YouTube.
Each format is a separate skill that takes sustained immersion to learn. Once learned, the skills accumulate and stay available.

head: A Ten-Hour 'Video' with 50,000 Views
dek: Audiences will commit to very long content when the form suits it. This is part of why Amit says his longest episodes are his most popular.
more: Amit recorded an episode of almost ten hours (9 hours 53 minutes) with Rajeshwari Sengupta, 'The Life and Times of the Indian Economy'. YouTube brings in only a small share of his audience, and the 'video' is just a thumbnail over ten hours of two people talking. Even so, it had passed 50,000 views at the time of recording. He also argues that one ten-hour conversation has a different rhythm from ten one-hour episodes.
Audiences will commit to very long content when the form suits it. This is part of why Amit says his longest episodes are his most popular.

head: Miss Excel
dek: Without gatekeepers, unusual combinations of skills can find a paying audience.
more: Miss Excel is an Instagram creator who teaches Excel while dancing to music she loves. Amit says a traditional gatekeeper would have laughed her out of the room, yet she became a star. He vaguely recalls an article saying she earned around $100,000 a week, mainly from courses sold on the side. He notes that he and Ajay have adopted the same approach: build credibility in one place, then sell a separate product.
Without gatekeepers, unusual combinations of skills can find a paying audience.

head: Shah Rukh Khan to One Person at the Airport
dek: Fame in the creator economy is concentrated in small circles of strong devotion rather than spread across the mainstream.
more: Amit is often stopped at airports by someone who thanks him for his work. The people around them have no idea who he is and wonder who this man is. To the person who stopped him, he is a star.
Fame in the creator economy is concentrated in small circles of strong devotion rather than spread across the mainstream.
printed: Famous in a crowd of one

head: The CRPF Man Who Spotted a YouTuber
dek: 'YouTuber' has become a familiar category in everyday Indian life, recognisable even to a security officer.
more: Ajay went through airport security with a backpack full of gear, including a tripod. The CRPF officer asked whether he did YouTube, and Ajay said yes. Ajay didn't even have the full Everything is Everything kit with him, but the officer guessed he was a creator anyway.
'YouTuber' has become a familiar category in everyday Indian life, recognisable even to a security officer.

head: The Art of Podcasting (Episode 49 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Ajay says it's about more than podcasting: it explains how the modern media and creative economies work.
more: Ajay says it's about more than podcasting: it explains how the modern media and creative economies work.
In the intro, Ajay urges listeners to watch it. Amit says it already holds all his podcasting lessons, so he won't repeat them here.

head: A Meditation on Form
dek: Where he first worked out that long-form podcasting is a different activity from short-form, not just a longer version.
more: Where he first worked out that long-form podcasting is a different activity from short-form, not just a longer version. It is the starting point for this episode.
Written when his episodes had reached four and five hours.

head: How Music Works
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece and gives it to everyone he meets. It shows how venues and technology, from cathedrals to CBGB's, shaped the music played in them.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece and gives it to everyone he meets. It shows how venues and technology, from cathedrals to CBGB's, shaped the music played in them.
The main source for the music chapter, and repeated in the closing recommendations.

head: Nuno Bettencourt interviewed by Rick Beato
dek: Makes the case that AC/DC's simple wall of sound is ideal for arenas, a reminder to judge music against its circumstances.
more: Makes the case that AC/DC's simple wall of sound is ideal for arenas, a reminder to judge music against its circumstances.
The Rick Beato interview the show notes link for the defence of Angus Young.

head: 100BeatlesX30
dek: A large batch of 30-second Beatles covers, another response to the same streaming rule.
more: A large batch of 30-second Beatles covers, another response to the same streaming rule.
Shown on screen right after Sleepify.

head: Der Edelstein
dek: A visual starting point for the story of how printing and distribution shaped writing.
more: A visual starting point for the story of how printing and distribution shaped writing.
Shown on screen as an example of what an early printed book looked like.

head: The Power Broker
dek: A masterful biography of Robert Moses, a portrait of New York City, and a study of how power corrupts.
more: A masterful biography of Robert Moses, a portrait of New York City, and a study of how power corrupts. It also shows how the limits of print cut out a 200,000-word section on Jane Jacobs.
Amit calls it one of his favourite books, then tells the story of its million-word manuscript.

head: The Broken Script
dek: One of Amit's favourite history books. It covers a period of transition when newspapers, newsletters and printed poetry took off.
more: One of Amit's favourite history books. It covers a period of transition when newspapers, newsletters and printed poetry took off.
Liddle's history of Delhi from about 1801 to 1857.

head: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Although the YouTube version is just a thumbnail and ten hours of talk, it has passed 50,000 views, which Amit takes as evidence that the content suits the form.
more: Although the YouTube version is just a thumbnail and ten hours of talk, it has passed 50,000 views, which Amit takes as evidence that the content suits the form.
An episode of almost ten hours with Rajeshwari Sengupta.

dek: Argues that creators don't need to scale: a thousand fans paying $100 a year is a living.
more: Argues that creators don't need to scale: a thousand fans paying $100 a year is a living. It sounded unrealistic when written, and Amit says it is now happening.
Introduced as 'an important concept' for listeners.

head: The Free Press
dek: Evidence that one person starting a newsletter can build a very large business without a mass-media gatekeeper.
more: Evidence that one person starting a newsletter can build a very large business without a mass-media gatekeeper.
Weiss left the New York Times and started a Substack publication that Amit recently read is valued at $100 million.

head: Rick Beato's YouTube channel
dek: A great music channel that Amit enjoys a lot and loves, though he says it isn't much about thinking on form.
more: A great music channel that Amit enjoys a lot and loves, though he says it isn't much about thinking on form.
Closing recommendations.

head: The Design of Everyday Things
dek: A masterpiece. It shows that everything around us looks and works the way it does for particular reasons we have stopped noticing.
more: A masterpiece. It shows that everything around us looks and works the way it does for particular reasons we have stopped noticing.
His main closing recommendation.

head: Ten Years Gone
dek: Since the episode talked so much about music, he chose a song of the day.
more: Since the episode talked so much about music, he chose a song of the day.
Ajay's closing pick.

head: Form Shapes Content, Content Shapes Character
dek: The format you work in decides what content is possible, and producing that content changes you.
more: The format you work in decides what content is possible, and producing that content changes you. A five-minute show can only be rapid-fire, while a ten-hour one requires deep preparation and listening without ego, which makes you a different kind of person. Some content also suits only one form, so pick the form to fit what you want to say.

head: Birdsong Is Shaped by Habitat
dek: Different birds sound different because of their environments. In dense rainforest, repeated calls in a narrow frequency band get through.
more: Different birds sound different because of their environments. In dense rainforest, repeated calls in a narrow frequency band get through. Birds near the forest floor call at lower pitches that are absorbed less. Water birds have calls that carry across water, and long-distance callers use buzzing sounds that cut through. What seems instinctive is the product of natural selection by surroundings.

head: Music Takes the Shape of Its Venue
dek: Outdoor music tends to be percussive because rhythm carries over distance, as in tribal drumming or Ganpati processions.
more: Outdoor music tends to be percussive because rhythm carries over distance, as in tribal drumming or Ganpati processions. Gothic cathedrals echo for more than four seconds, so their music became modal, slow and harmonically simple. Bach often played a pipe organ in smaller churches, larger halls produced Mahler, low-echo clubs supported complex rock, and arenas favour metal.

head: There Is No Hierarchy of Forms
dek: Western classical music is not 'more evolved' than drumming, and a book is not the highest form of writing.
more: Western classical music is not 'more evolved' than drumming, and a book is not the highest form of writing. Each genre and format is an adaptation to its circumstances, and each has its great practitioners. So follow what moves you, without judgment or hesitation.

head: Storage Technology Created Our Formats
dek: The three-minute pop song came from the 78 RPM record's capacity, and it also suited radio.
more: The three-minute pop song came from the 78 RPM record's capacity, and it also suited radio. The 40-minute album came from Columbia's 1948 LP, about 20 minutes per side, and the CD's 74 minutes came from Beethoven's Ninth. Listeners then came to expect these formats, so the conventions outlasted the limits that created them. Nostalgia for the concept album is really nostalgia for a storage constraint.

head: Why Few Artists Break Convention
dek: Ajay observes that few artists experimented with form even when they could, because of strong pressure to conform.
more: Ajay observes that few artists experimented with form even when they could, because of strong pressure to conform. Amit adds a selection effect: an eight-minute song doesn't get radio play unless you're already Pink Floyd, so formats get flattened. He also notes that great work is still possible inside a constraint.

head: Writing Expands Thinking
dek: Adam Smith could not have had his ideas before books existed. Long-form writing lets a thinker build layers of thought on earlier layers, so it is part of how the thinking happens, not just a record of it.
more: Adam Smith could not have had his ideas before books existed. Long-form writing lets a thinker build layers of thought on earlier layers, so it is part of how the thinking happens, not just a record of it.

head: A Film Is a Short Story, a Streaming Series Is a Novel
dek: A 90-minute feature has one main narrative arc and one central tension, like a short story.
more: A 90-minute feature has one main narrative arc and one central tension, like a short story. Streaming platforms made novel-like screen storytelling possible, with many characters and storylines unfolding over seasons. People binge eight hours at a stretch, which undercuts the short-attention-span argument.

head: Closer Media Allow More Intimacy
dek: In cinema the camera is about as far from the actor as the screen is from the viewer, which suits westerns and car chases.
more: In cinema the camera is about as far from the actor as the screen is from the viewer, which suits westerns and car chases. Television is a couple of metres away, which suits sitcoms. YouTube is in your hand, with close-up faces. Microphones made crooning possible, while stage actors without amplification had to project. Radio is shaped by commercial pressure to be like five people in a car, broad and mainstream. A podcast feels intimate enough to go deep and niche.

head: Five Ways the World Changed for Creators
dek: Creators now have the means of production, no gatekeepers in the way, no constraint of form, direct reach to audiences and direct monetisation.
more: Creators now have the means of production, no gatekeepers in the way, no constraint of form, direct reach to audiences and direct monetisation. The old model, where a newspaper gathered readers' attention, sold it to advertisers and paid the writer a small share, was clumsy and existed because micropayments involved too much friction. Your attention is not free either, since time is money.

head: True Fans Instead of Scale
dek: In the past only the very top artists earned anything, while a mediocre engineer or lawyer lived comfortably.
more: In the past only the very top artists earned anything, while a mediocre engineer or lawyer lived comfortably. That pressure to reach a mass audience shaped what artists made. Kevin Kelly's 1,000 fans paying $100 a year, or Li Jin's 100 fans paying $1,000, frees creators from needing scale.

head: Better to Be Loved by a Few Than Liked by Many
dek: Amit's adopted motto from Paul Graham, originally said about startups.
more: Amit's adopted motto from Paul Graham, originally said about startups. People who love your work will pay, support you and stay with you. People who merely like it engage shallowly and like plenty of other things too.

head: The Creator Economy Is Not Survivor Bias
dek: Ajay asked whether this is like rock bands, where a handful break through and most earn nothing.
more: Ajay asked whether this is like rock bands, where a handful break through and most earn nothing. Amit says no: over a lakh Indian creators earn between one and ten lakh rupees a month, and many would never have reached the mainstream. More people alive, more leisure, cheap tools and a far wider range of influences mean there should be more active creators today than in all earlier history combined. Many are known only within their niches.

head: Bias for Action
dek: Amit learns a subject by jumping in, experimenting, and only later working out the first principles.
more: Amit learns a subject by jumping in, experimenting, and only later working out the first principles. His apparent expertise is assembled afterwards from a lot of trial and error.

head: Ajay opens by calling Amit
more: Ajay opens by calling Amit 'more than just an atom in a kinetic theory of gases' since he also contemplates the theory. Amit: 'If I was sexy, I would be an atom bomb.' When Ajay pushes the metaphor, Amit says the answer to why atoms bounce around is 'we have no idea. Life is probably meaningless, we're all gonna die.'

head: On the ten-and-a-half-hour episode.
more: On the ten-and-a-half-hour episode. Ajay: 'I'm still waiting for my gold medal.' Amit: 'until the podcast comes to an end, you can't get the gold medal. You are the provisional gold at the moment.'

head: Pointing out the birdsong in the background
more: Pointing out the birdsong in the background: 'The twittering of birds, not twitter... or perhaps we should call the Xing of birds.'

head: On rainforest birds that repeat the same narrow-frequency call so something gets through
more: On rainforest birds that repeat the same narrow-frequency call so something gets through: 'Like so many columnists, in fact.'

head: Amit's off-colour aside about the author of Der Edelstein
