more: Amit's off-colour aside about the author of Der Edelstein: 'Apparently his wife used to say that every morning I wake up and I find that Boner has a boner. But leaving that aside...'

head: On early crooners singing softly into the mic
more: On early crooners singing softly into the mic: 'much as some podcasters can do with their dynamic microphones.'

head: Amit calls the mushaira newsletters exposure to…
more: Amit calls the mushaira newsletters exposure to 'a large LLM, as it were', using AI vocabulary for a 19th-century reader's sample size.

head: On binge-watching
more: On binge-watching: 'For those of us who have office, we miss office the next day. I don't have to.'

head: Amit says the mediocre artist is…
more: Amit says the mediocre artist is 'starving in an attic as the cliche goes.' Ajay: 'therefore it's called having a girlfriend with a job.'

Ajay: 'owing to the shortage of followers, the production of leaders has been discontinued.' Amit objects that not everyone is a creator, and Ajay does the maths: about 10^8 potential followers and 10^5 creators, 'so there's still like an average of thousand each.'

head: Winston Churchill, quoted by Ajay
more: Winston Churchill, quoted by Ajay: 'we make our buildings and then our buildings make us.'

head: Stephen Covey
more: Stephen Covey: 'we listen to respond, we don't listen to understand.' Amit uses it to describe the listening long conversations require.

head: Stewart Brand, quoted by Ajay
more: Stewart Brand, quoted by Ajay: 'We are as gods and we might as well learn to live like that.'
'It ain't over till the fat lady sings', used to explain why opera singers had to project before the microphone.

head: Sturgeon's Law
more: Sturgeon's Law, 'ninety five percent of everything is crap', which Amit cites while arguing that great art is still being made in Instagram reels and TikTok.

head: Amit calls Bari Weiss
more: Amit calls Bari Weiss 'a fellow winner of the Bastiat Prize.'

head: The Peter Cat Recording Company, loved by Amit and crew Nomsita and Vaishnav
more: The Peter Cat Recording Company, loved by Amit and crew Nomsita and Vaishnav: 'never gonna be the Beatles in terms of scale', but the Beatles to their devoted fans.

head: The Matunga Racket
dek: Outlawing a victimless act gives the state a ready-made lever of shame, and someone will use it to make money.
more: Around 2007-08, before dating apps, gay men in Bombay found partners through classified websites. Vikram Doctor told Amit about a scheme the police were running. A cop would pose as someone looking for love and suggest meeting at Matunga station for coffee. When the man arrived, the cops grabbed him and extorted money by threatening to tell his parents or wife. Sometimes they took him into an ATM and emptied his account. Amit wrote about it in a Mint column.

Outlawing a victimless act gives the state a ready-made lever of shame, and someone will use it to make money. Amit's point is that this is not a few bad cops but incentives at work. Once the law went, the racket became impossible.
printed: Coffee at Matunga, cash at the ATM

head: The German Cannibal
dek: With documented consent on both sides, the case breaks a simple 'were rights infringed?' test.
more: In 2003 Amit read about Armin Meiwes, a 42-year-old man in Rotenburg, Germany. His neighbours called him normal, but he had fantasised about eating a human being since he was eight. He advertised for a well-built young man who wanted to be eaten. Bernd Brandes answered, saying he had always fantasised about being eaten. Brandes consented at every stage, mostly on camera. He took twenty sleeping pills and some schnapps, and his penis was cut off and cooked. Meiwes read a Star Trek novel while Brandes bathed. Meiwes then killed him with a cleaver, froze the body and ate it over many days with olive oil and garlic. Cannibalism is not a crime in Germany; murder is.

With documented consent on both sides, the case breaks a simple 'were rights infringed?' test. It raises hard questions: does consenting to be killed and eaten prove mental illness, and if so, is the killer insane too? Sanity is a continuum, so who gets to draw the line?

head: How the Sugar Lobby Rewrote America's Diet
dek: State guidance can be captured by lobbies and built on bad science, and because everyone follows it, the damage scales.
more: Retelling the history from the show's diabetes episode, Amit says the sugar lobby spent heavily on researchers from Harvard and elsewhere. Their influential studies used bad methodology, mistook correlation for causation, blamed fat and cleared sugar. In 1977 the top US dietary body issued guidelines saying sugar was fine and fat was evil. Charts of the obesity epidemic show it exploding from then, as people followed the guidelines into processed-sugar junk food.

State guidance can be captured by lobbies and built on bad science, and because everyone follows it, the damage scales. Amit does not conclude that sugar should be banned. He concludes the state should stay out, since its knowledge is never good enough.

head: Drinking in Gujarat and Lahore
dek: Two prohibition regimes, and the same outcome as everywhere else: demand doesn't disappear, it goes underground.
more: Amit has had alcohol in Gujarat, which has prohibition. He has also had it in Lahore while visiting Pakistan, which has prohibition too, and found a flourishing black market for alcohol and drugs there.
Two prohibition regimes, and the same outcome as everywhere else: demand doesn't disappear, it goes underground.

head: Five Years at the Poker Table
dek: If even loved ones can't talk someone out of an addiction, a blunt state ban won't do better; social problems have to be solved by society.
more: Amit played poker professionally for five years and spent a lot of time in casinos. In all that time he never once played against the house; he has never put a single rupee on a roulette table, because it is a losing proposition. He also watched gambling addiction destroy lives. When people close to him got hooked, he tried to intervene and failed.

If even loved ones can't talk someone out of an addiction, a blunt state ban won't do better; social problems have to be solved by society. His refusal to bet against the house also shows his wider point that gambling is just weighing probabilities.

head: Telling an MP Why Hate-Speech Laws Backfire
dek: Intent doesn't decide how a law is used; whoever holds power does. Vague laws like 295A and 153A mean anyone can be locked up depending on how they are interpreted.
more: At a recent literary festival, Amit shared a stage with an MP who had brought a bill against hate speech on platforms. He told the MP the intent was beautiful. But after twenty-five years of writing about free speech, he warned that such laws always end up being used to attack dissenters.
Intent doesn't decide how a law is used; whoever holds power does. Vague laws like 295A and 153A mean anyone can be locked up depending on how they are interpreted.

head: We Are All Gamblers (2010)
dek: It argues that every life choice, from marriage to jobs to stocks, is a bet weighed on probabilities, so singling out gambling for stigma makes little sense.
more: It argues that every life choice, from marriage to jobs to stocks, is a bet weighed on probabilities, so singling out gambling for stigma makes little sense.
Linked in the show notes; Amit makes the same argument in the gambling chapter.

head: The Matunga Racket (2007)
dek: A concrete case of a victimless 'crime' becoming a tool for police extortion.
more: A concrete case of a victimless 'crime' becoming a tool for police extortion.
Amit's Mint column on Bombay police extorting gay men, based on a tip from Vikram Doctor.

head: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
dek: Three scholars propose innovative, intuitive metrics for women's empowerment.
more: Three scholars propose innovative, intuitive metrics for women's empowerment. Amit's own opening metric was rising divorce rates.
Amit brings it up after Ajay's point about no-fault divorce.

head: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Anyone who cares about women in India should sign on to the economic growth project instead of 'bleeding heart things' that achieve nothing.
more: Anyone who cares about women in India should sign on to the economic growth project instead of 'bleeding heart things' that achieve nothing.
Ajay points listeners to it after arguing that 8% GDP growth is the greatest instrument for women's emancipation.

head: How to Do Development (Episode 57 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It explains how economic development actually happens, which Ajay sees as the real path to empowering the disempowered.
more: It explains how economic development actually happens, which Ajay sees as the real path to empowering the disempowered.
Recommended together with Why Freedom Matters.

head: A crime needs a victim
dek: Being illegal is not the same as being wrong. For Amit, a crime is infringing someone's rights, such as murdering them or stealing their property.
more: Being illegal is not the same as being wrong. For Amit, a crime is infringing someone's rights, such as murdering them or stealing their property. The state's job is to stop such infringements, not to engineer society to its liking. So-called 'victimless crimes' are not crimes at all, just acts the state has chosen to outlaw.

head: Three objections to banning victimless crimes
dek: 1. Moral: consenting adults should be free to deal with each other however they like, in the bedroom, the marketplace or the public square. 2.
more: 1. Moral: consenting adults should be free to deal with each other however they like, in the bedroom, the marketplace or the public square. 2. Practical: a ban doesn't end demand, it brings in an underworld with coercion and fraud, and still fails to deliver the intended outcome. 3. Power: the state's monopoly on coercion should be limited, because whoever holds it will remake society according to their own values.

head: Baptists and Bootleggers
dek: Bruce Yandle's idea: every prohibition has a moraliser (the Baptist) demanding the ban on ethical grounds, and a bootlegger who profits by selling lower-quality, unregulated supply on the black market.
more: Bruce Yandle's idea: every prohibition has a moraliser (the Baptist) demanding the ban on ethical grounds, and a bootlegger who profits by selling lower-quality, unregulated supply on the black market. Hooch tragedies follow. The two look like enemies but want the same thing.

head: The black-market price paradox
dek: Economists judge how well a ban is enforced by the black-market price premium.
more: Economists judge how well a ban is enforced by the black-market price premium. But a high premium also signals huge profits to criminals and draws them in. So winning in the short run builds a bigger, better-organised underworld in the long run.

head: Bans build criminal firms
dek: A lone criminal can only do so much. Prohibitions give crime the scale to build firms with large teams and complex operations.
more: A lone criminal can only do so much. Prohibitions give crime the scale to build firms with large teams and complex operations. India's import barriers created smuggling, smuggling became a giant business, and Haji Mastan's gangs grew out of it. Amit adds that import duties are themselves a victimless crime. Where the state bans things, its low-paid police also collect hafta from the underworld and from ordinary offenders.

head: Sunlight is the best disinfectant
dek: Legal activity is visible, so it can be regulated. Amit argues match-fixing happens because betting is illegal: the underworld runs it, its money flows go unwatched, and corruption follows.
more: Legal activity is visible, so it can be regulated. Amit argues match-fixing happens because betting is illegal: the underworld runs it, its money flows go unwatched, and corruption follows. Imagine instead betting through a bank account at HDFC or IDFC, the way you hold a demat account for shares, with only light-touch regulation against fraud. The same logic applies to brothels, worker rights and health care in sex work.

head: We are all gamblers
dek: Every decision is a bet based on an intuitive sense of probabilities: talking to someone in a bar, marrying, picking a job, buying a house, investing in stocks.
more: Every decision is a bet based on an intuitive sense of probabilities: talking to someone in a bar, marrying, picking a job, buying a house, investing in stocks. If gambling means weighing probabilities and betting on your best judgment, then everything is gambling, and singling out some forms for stigma is incoherent.
printed: All of life is a bet

head: Drugs as a public-health issue, not a crime
dek: Marijuana is less harmful than alcohol or cigarettes and far less harmful than sugar.
more: Marijuana is less harmful than alcohol or cigarettes and far less harmful than sugar. Yet America's war on drugs soaked up police resources, built a vast underworld, hit African Americans hardest and did not stop drug use. Parts of Europe that allow drugs have seen no ill effects. Ajay says the conversation belongs between parents and children, or in public health, with the state staying out.

head: Sex work is a choice of the best available option
dek: A sex worker sells her services just as writers, economists, carpenters and plumbers sell theirs.
more: A sex worker sells her services just as writers, economists, carpenters and plumbers sell theirs. If someone chose it, it was the best option they had. Amit says India's Immoral Traffic Prevention Act defines prostitution as 'sexual exploitation or abuse,' which leaves consent out and confuses prostitution with trafficking. Coercion must be outlawed, but the way to prevent it is to keep the trade above ground.

head: Self-ownership and the right to end one's life
dek: For Locke, the core right is self-ownership, and all other rights flow from it.
more: For Locke, the core right is self-ownership, and all other rights flow from it. If I own myself, I also have the right to end my life. Suicide is a serious social problem, and friends should help someone out of that dark place, but the state shouldn't criminalise it. Euthanasia raises a separate caution: where state capacity is low, as in India, people could misuse it to kill elders for their property.

head: Free speech has only one limit: direct incitement
dek: Speech becomes criminal only when it directly incites harm. Saying 'Jaake Amit ko maaro' is wrong because the beating itself is a crime.
more: Speech becomes criminal only when it directly incites harm. Saying 'Jaake Amit ko maaro' is wrong because the beating itself is a crime. Otherwise even hate speech should stay legal. Laws like 295A and 153A sound well-meant, but they can be interpreted to lock up anyone.

head: Icky problems: moral instinct versus reason
dek: Two thought experiments. Someone has sex with a chicken they bought and are about to kill and eat.
more: Two thought experiments. Someone has sex with a chicken they bought and are about to kill and eat. Two adult siblings have sex and won't have children. Instinct says both are wrong, but reason finds no victim and no answer to 'why?'. Our moral instincts come from prehistoric programming we don't understand. So when the powerful want to outlaw something because it 'feels wrong,' that is a reason for more suspicion, not less.

head: Even the best states execute innocent people
dek: Roughly 5% of people executed in advanced economies are later believed to have been innocent, despite the highest standards of evidence and the strongest state capability anywhere.
more: Roughly 5% of people executed in advanced economies are later believed to have been innocent, despite the highest standards of evidence and the strongest state capability anywhere. India's failure rate must be far worse, so convictions deserve scepticism. Using such a flawed tool against people's private choices invites disaster.

head: State capability is a finite budget
dek: Drawing on Kelkar and Shah: India has very little state capability, and it grows slowly.
more: Drawing on Kelkar and Shah: India has very little state capability, and it grows slowly. Rich countries like Sweden or the UK can afford to spend it widely; India must focus on a few basics such as defence, monetary policy, criminal justice, financial regulation and tax. Ajay estimates that is 50 to 100 years of work. Amit adds that victimless crimes shouldn't be on the list anyway, and the state should first make the rule of law real.

head: Means and ends: give people the power to walk away
dek: If you care about wives beaten by drunk husbands, banning alcohol won't help.
more: If you care about wives beaten by drunk husbands, banning alcohol won't help. What helps is no-fault divorce: easy, frictionless, codified, with jointly created wealth split equally. That gives the abused spouse the power to leave and changes the husband's incentives. For the same reason Amit treats rising divorce rates as a sign of women's empowerment, and notes that America's no-fault divorce, which he credits to Reagan, was very good for women.

head: Growth is the greatest emancipator
dek: Ajay argues that the biggest driver of women's status in India is 8% GDP growth, so anyone who cares about women should back the growth project.
more: Ajay argues that the biggest driver of women's status in India is 8% GDP growth, so anyone who cares about women should back the growth project. Amit extends this to every marginalised group. Financial ability is what lets people walk away from bad situations.

head: Blow oxygen on the spark of doubt
dek: Decriminalising homosexuality and allowing no-fault divorce show mainstream thinking was once completely wrong, and that removing the state worked well.
more: Decriminalising homosexuality and allowing no-fault divorce show mainstream thinking was once completely wrong, and that removing the state worked well. Once you accept that, you should question other accepted uses of state power, such as drug laws.

head: Amit on India's old law against suicide
more: Amit on India's old law against suicide: 'It was the one crime for which you got punished if you failed to commit it.'

head: Amit's only time smoking up, circa 1995, in the back seat of a car with a friend
more: Amit's only time smoking up, circa 1995, in the back seat of a car with a friend and 'a great world famous guitarist I won't name because it'll seem like too much of a humble brag.' The punchline: 'I felt nothing.'

head: Amit explains…
more: Amit explains 'we are all gamblers' using Pi, who had just been on Ajay's lap. Putting him there was a bet: the chance he disrupts the shoot weighed against the joy and 'the oxytocin flooding through you.'

head: After Amit says he
more: After Amit says he 'entirely supports' the black market for alcohol and drugs in Lahore, teetotaller Ajay replies: 'I will defend unto death your right to say certain things and do certain things.'

head: Amit on import duties
more: Amit on import duties: 'I buy something in America, I bring it here, and I sell it to a friend. And immediately it is a crime because I haven't paid the hafta to the state.'

head: Telling the cannibal story, Amit notes the body was eaten with olive oil and garlic
more: Telling the cannibal story, Amit notes the body was eaten with olive oil and garlic: 'I don't know why there was no salt, perhaps a human flesh has natural salt like bacon does.'

head: Arguing for legal, regulated brothels run by proper organisations, Amit adds…
more: Arguing for legal, regulated brothels run by proper organisations, Amit adds: 'I don't think HDFC or IDFC will do it, but you get what I'm saying.'
Amit on 'whore' as an insult: 'Like which of us is not a whore in some way or the other if you use the term in that manner.'

head: Amit read a Twitter rant listing five things Ronald Reagan got wrong
more: Amit read a Twitter rant listing five things Ronald Reagan got wrong, 'and as I was reading through them I realized that he got all of them right.' One of them was no-fault divorce.

head: Ajay's description of India's state capability
more: Ajay's description of India's state capability: 'we have a teensy-weensy amount of state capability.'

head: Thoreau's
more: Thoreau's 'lives of quiet desperation,' used for people who had to hide their sexuality while it was criminalised.

head: Definitions compared: the Oxford dictionary calls prostitution
more: Definitions compared: the Oxford dictionary calls prostitution 'engaging in sexual activity with someone for payment,' while India's Immoral Traffic Prevention Act calls it 'the sexual exploitation or abuse of persons for commercial purposes.'

head: Alzheimer's being called…
more: Alzheimer's being called 'type three diabetes' by some, mentioned by Amit to show how many harms are traced back to sugar.

head: Lal Bihari Mritak: the man who had to prove he was alive
dek: This is the opening frame for the KYC problem. Once the state's paper version of you separates from the real you, the paper wins.
more: Lal Bihari was born in 1951 in Azamgarh, Uttar Pradesh. In 1976 his cousins wanted his land, so they paid bribes, produced a death certificate and had him declared officially dead. At 25 he set out to become alive again on paper. He staged his own funeral and claimed compensation for his 'widow'. He threw stones at a police station hoping to be arrested, since an arrest would prove he existed, but the bribed police simply ignored him. He kidnapped a 10-year-old cousin, expecting the family to come and settle things. Nobody came, so after ten days he bought the boy ice cream and sent him home. He contested elections against VP Singh in Allahabad in 1988 and against Rajiv Gandhi in Amethi in 1989, on the logic that a candidate on the rolls must be alive. He renamed himself Lal Bihari Mritak ('mritak' means dead) and founded the Uttar Pradesh Mritak Sangh, which grew to 20,000 members who had all been declared dead. He was finally declared alive in 1994. Of those 20,000 members, only four ever made it back.

This is the opening frame for the KYC problem. Once the state's paper version of you separates from the real you, the paper wins. Reversing a bureaucratic record is close to impossible: four out of twenty thousand. Amit also points out that behind every independent candidate who loses a deposit there may be a story like this one.

head: Even a top banker couldn't get his KYC done
dek: If someone with direct access to bank leadership finds KYC painful, the system is not failing only at the edges.
more: Harsh Vardhan is a very senior banking figure. He sits on boards, people respect his judgment, and he knows the people who run the banks. On The Seen and the Unseen he told Amit what a nightmare it had been to get his own KYC sorted out: endless phone calls to one place and then another.

If someone with direct access to bank leadership finds KYC painful, the system is not failing only at the edges. Privilege makes the pain smaller but does not remove it. Both hosts stress that it is far worse for people without such connections.

head: A smart friend and an ageing father, defeated by paperwork
dek: KYC is an annual test of whether you can navigate a bureaucracy, and it hits the elderly hardest.
more: A very smart friend of Amit's, in her 40s, had a supplementary credit card linked to her husband's. She had completed KYC the year before. This year she could not get through the maze of paperwork in time and lost the card, while her husband kept his. Amit also remembers his father in his last years, fumbling and quite unable to cope with these demands.
KYC is an annual test of whether you can navigate a bureaucracy, and it hits the elderly hardest. Amit calls it plain cruelty to make people of advancing years prove themselves again and again.

head: Al Capone's laundromats and the birth of 'money laundering'
dek: Every time the Enforcement Directorate is in the news, Ajay says, we are living with the consequences of states trying to block this gangster trick.
more: In 1930s America, the gangster Al Capone ran criminal cash through cash-income businesses, namely laundromats, the shops where you load your clothes into a machine and collect them washed. The illicit money was shown as the laundromat's income, and that is where the term 'money laundering' comes from.
Every time the Enforcement Directorate is in the news, Ajay says, we are living with the consequences of states trying to block this gangster trick. A worldwide surveillance system grew out of it.

head: 1933: Swiss bank secrecy as a defence against the Nazis
dek: Ajay turns the familiar populist story about Swiss banks and tax havens on its head.
more: Banks had always kept their customers' affairs private as an informal norm. When Hitler came to power in 1933, Nazi Germany passed a law requiring every German citizen to disclose their overseas assets, something states had never done before. Switzerland was then the banking capital of the world, and it worried that informal codes would not protect its foreign customers. So it passed the first laws stating that no bank would divulge customer information except on the order of a Swiss judge prosecuting a crime under Swiss law. Foreign prosecutors were turned away.

Ajay turns the familiar populist story about Swiss banks and tax havens on its head. In the 20th century, people fled governments, and places like Switzerland were how ordinary people protected their wealth and private lives from authoritarian states. He also notes that the Nazi practice of demanding disclosure of overseas assets is now routine everywhere.

head: Russians amazed that the US Treasury taught them surveillance
dek: The post-9/11 anti-money-laundering push, led by the US, ended up handing authoritarian governments the know-how to watch their own citizens.
more: A friend of Ajay's, an Indian official, had quiet private conversations with Russian counterparts. They told him, with real wonder, that the American Treasury was teaching them how to build a mass surveillance system in finance. They had not known how to build one themselves.
The post-9/11 anti-money-laundering push, led by the US, ended up handing authoritarian governments the know-how to watch their own citizens. Ajay calls this a blot on America's conscience.

head: Ajay's mea culpa on Aadhaar as the KYC fix
dek: It is unusual and useful to hear an expert say plainly that he was wrong, and the mistake carries a general lesson: you cannot accept bad institutions and paper over them with technology.
more: Ajay admits that he was among the finance people who thought Aadhaar would get around the KYC mess. Aadhaar arrived, the first number was issued in 2009, and in 2024 banks still demand fresh KYC every year while the AML-CFT burden continues.
It is unusual and useful to hear an expert say plainly that he was wrong, and the mistake carries a general lesson: you cannot accept bad institutions and paper over them with technology.

head: Every Breath You Take
dek: Its refrain, 'I'll be watching you', fits a state that watches every transaction.
more: Its refrain, 'I'll be watching you', fits a state that watches every transaction. Ajay suggests listeners email it to the civil servants in their lives.
Amit's song of the day for an episode about surveillance.

head: The Lives of Others
dek: A debut film about surveillance across East and West Germany, about watching and being watched, and how that can change both sides.
more: A debut film about surveillance across East and West Germany, about watching and being watched, and how that can change both sides. Amit calls it a masterpiece and one of the greatest debut films he has seen.
Amit's film pick. He thinks he may have recommended it before but says it fits this episode too well to skip.

head: "Black and grey" lists
dek: Shows the pressure behind FATF. Ajay explains that countries were offered a choice: join the financial surveillance regime or face more friction in the world.
more: Shows the pressure behind FATF. Ajay explains that countries were offered a choice: join the financial surveillance regime or face more friction in the world.
From Ajay's reading list in the show notes.

head: Financial privacy is personal privacy
dek: A spy following you learns what you say, do and buy. A complete view of your finances reveals just as much.
more: A spy following you learns what you say, do and buy. A complete view of your finances reveals just as much. If surveillance of daily life is unacceptable in a liberal democracy, so is surveillance of financial life. The answer 'if you have nothing to hide' misses the point. Once you know you are watched you are in the panopticon, and you start bending your behaviour to suit the watcher. For Ajay, freedom is the world of not being observed. Amit adds a challenge: let anyone who uses that argument make their Google searches and incognito browsing public.

head: Firms deserve financial privacy too
dek: Modern populism grants individuals some privacy but treats companies as fair game for unlimited disclosure.
more: Modern populism grants individuals some privacy but treats companies as fair game for unlimited disclosure. Ajay disagrees. A firm's list of customers and vendors, handed to competitors or to powerful hostile people, can destroy the business, and financial statements alone reveal who a firm deals with. Treating a firm as having no privacy because it is 'some capitalist' is a mistake.

head: Financial privacy protects freedom of association
dek: The right to form clubs, NGOs, parties and companies is basic to liberal democracy, and Ajay sees free speech and the rest as flowing from it.
more: The right to form clubs, NGOs, parties and companies is basic to liberal democracy, and Ajay sees free speech and the rest as flowing from it. If the state can see who funds an organisation, powerful people can go after its funders. Detailed reporting requirements therefore undermine association itself. Amit's version: a ruling party can see who donates to the opposition and send the tax people after them.

head: Bring the wiretap model to finance
dek: In liberal democracies privacy is the default.
more: In liberal democracies privacy is the default. A police officer who wants a wiretap must convince a judge with prima facie evidence, the tap lasts only a fixed time, and it works only going forward because phone companies don't store past calls and SMS. There is no mass surveillance of everyone's phone. Ajay wants the same in finance. Customers should be able to tell their bank to delete transactions after three days, or even a millisecond. Police should need a warrant from something like a US FISA court to watch a proven suspect for a fixed period, say 90 days. Mass surveillance in finance should be shut down through constitutional law and the courts, building on the Puttaswamy ruling.

head: Walls made the interior life possible
dek: Amit, drawing on Rahul Matthan, says privacy is a historical achievement.
more: Amit, drawing on Rahul Matthan, says privacy is a historical achievement. In hunter-gatherer bands everyone could see and hear everyone else. Early settlements had thin walls, and only later came thick walls, separate houses and separate bedrooms. Being alone and unobserved gave people a rich interior life, the space to think, try new things and challenge convention. Much of human progress depends on that solitude.

head: How financial surveillance crept in, one step at a time
dek: Ajay traces the history. In 1933 Nazi Germany first required citizens to disclose overseas assets.
more: Ajay traces the history. In 1933 Nazi Germany first required citizens to disclose overseas assets. In the 1970s the US IRS required banks to report transactions above $10,000, and nobody objected because it was 'only for tax evaders'. Nixon's war on drugs created the crime of money laundering, built on a 'predicate offence', and the FATF club grew up around it. Countries outside the club face extra friction, and India was the last country admitted. After 9/11 the US Treasury pushed AML-CFT on the whole world. The laws carry Orwellian names; Ajay says the US 'Banking Privacy Act' is really the destruction of privacy in banking.

head: Following the money doesn't catch terrorists
dek: After 9/11 the idea was that you could catch plots by tracing the $100,000 sent to Mohammed Atta.
more: After 9/11 the idea was that you could catch plots by tracing the $100,000 sent to Mohammed Atta. Ajay's counterexample is a 555 cigarette box packed with diamonds: it holds about $100,000 and passes X-ray machines. Monitor seven billion people and terrorists simply switch to other channels. He says it is now well known that this system has not disrupted terrorism. It has fouled up finance worldwide and given governments more information about their subjects.

head: Security theatre vs. the legibility grab
dek: Amit describes the state's reflex after a crisis with Yes Minister's line: 'we must do something, this is something, let's do it'.
more: Amit describes the state's reflex after a crisis with Yes Minister's line: 'we must do something, this is something, let's do it'. He uses Bruce Schneier's term 'security theatre' for checks that only look like security, such as mall guards who check your car boot but never open the suitcase, or metal detectors that beep with no follow-up. A determined attacker will always find another way. He adds that the state often caused the problem in the first place, since Al Qaeda grew out of America arming guerrillas against the Russians in Afghanistan. Ajay separates the two cases. Airport checks are theatre, but financial surveillance is a public-choice grab: the state stokes fear of terrorists and takes legibility (James C. Scott's term) and power over citizens. Amit wants it the other way round: the state should be transparent to citizens, not citizens to the state.

head: Security vs. freedom is a false trade-off
dek: The debate is usually framed as giving up some freedom to get security.
more: The debate is usually framed as giving up some freedom to get security. Amit points out that surrendering freedom to the state also removes your security against the state, and nobody protects you from the state. So you lose both.

head: Why India's KYC is the world's worst: each layer covers itself
dek: Ajay dislikes FATF rules, but in London, Zurich or Washington opening an account is fairly painless; it is like a stupid but tolerable airport check.
more: Ajay dislikes FATF rules, but in London, Zurich or Washington opening an account is fairly painless; it is like a stupid but tolerable airport check. In India the FATF rules get their harshest reading in the national rules. The RBI then makes them worse, the bank makes them worse again, and the frontline employee applies them in the worst possible way. No one at any step answers for the welfare of citizens. Poor people and small firms give up and fall back on cash, gold and real estate. The result is financial exclusion and a country where it gets harder to run a firm of five or forty people.

head: CPUs are never the answer
dek: Ajay's general law: technology cannot fix a malfunctioning state. Aadhaar was meant to end the KYC nightmare, but banks still demand fresh KYC every year.
more: Ajay's general law: technology cannot fix a malfunctioning state. Aadhaar was meant to end the KYC nightmare, but banks still demand fresh KYC every year. Amit argues for not letting the perfect be the enemy of the good: why not a simple central order that Aadhaar is enough? Ajay replies with public choice. Officials who want to protect themselves will keep adding rules, so hoping good sense will prevail is the mistake. The real work is fixing institutions, which he calls the hard work of the humanities and liberal arts.

head: Be skeptical of 'global best practice'
dek: Drawing on Lant Pritchett and on Kelkar and Shah, Ajay argues that policies which seem to work in the US depend on invisible supports there: liberal democracy, checks and balances, courts, communities and norms.
more: Drawing on Lant Pritchett and on Kelkar and Shah, Ajay argues that policies which seem to work in the US depend on invisible supports there: liberal democracy, checks and balances, courts, communities and norms. Copy the policy without those supports and it does far worse. He calls it wrong, dangerous and evil of the US Treasury to push financial surveillance on the world, and stupid of India to accept it.

head: The cold open is a KYC check on the co-host.
more: The cold open is a KYC check on the co-host. Amit: "I'm not sure if this is my good friend Ajay. Bearded economists look alike to me. Are you Ajay Shah? Prove to me that you're Ajay Shah. Kaagaz dikhaao!" Ajay: "I don't have papers. Will you recognize my face? FRT, face recognition technology." Amit: "Biometrics. Take off your glasses, I'll scan your eyes." Amit then introduces himself as "Amit allegedly".

head: Amit on the police facing Lal Bihari's stones
more: Amit on the police facing Lal Bihari's stones: "the police, for the first time in recorded Indian history, take a Gandhian view of the situation and ignore the stones."

head: On Lal Bihari's failed kidnapping
more: On Lal Bihari's failed kidnapping: "India's population is awesome. There are many kids in that family, no one gives a shit." After ten days he gives the boy ice cream and sends him home.

A running gag casts the episode's cameraman Vaishnav Vyas as Lal Bihari in the film version. Amit says behind every independent candidate who loses a deposit there is a story "rich in life, rich in drama, rich in pathos. Rich in cinematic potential. Are you listening, Vaishnav Vyas?"

head: Ajay on why his bank wants yearly re-KYC
more: Ajay on why his bank wants yearly re-KYC: "Like proofs have the depreciation and they vanish with time, so it has to be re-upped."

head: Amit on the…
more: Amit on the 'nothing to hide' argument: he dares its defenders to make their Google search results public. "What do you do in the Chrome incognito window? Everybody has a private life, boss."

head: Amit on a reported plot to hide bombs in breast implants
more: Amit on a reported plot to hide bombs in breast implants: "You're not gonna say take out your breast implants and put them on the security tray."

head: Ajay sings The Police
more: Ajay sings The Police: "Every vow you break, every claim you stake, I'll be watching you. This has been traditionally thought of as a creepy male stalker song, but gentle readers, please email this to all the civil servants in your life." Amit: "The state is a creepy male stalker. And much worse."

head: Amit, after saying The Lives of Others shows how watching can change both watcher and watched
more: Amit, after saying The Lives of Others shows how watching can change both watcher and watched: "So I don't think the Indian state is really going to get reformed because they're watching us."

head: Yes Minister's political logic, quoted by Amit as the state's reflex after a terror attack
more: Yes Minister's political logic, quoted by Amit as the state's reflex after a terror attack: "we must do something, this is something, let's do it."

head: Ajay quotes…
more: Ajay quotes "the great man" on liberty and safety, with the terms swapped: "those who will sacrifice security in exchange for freedom will end up with neither security nor freedom."
"That old saw of power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely", invoked by Amit to explain what a state does with surveillance power: crack down on dissent and political opponents.

head: The Doctors Who Never Stop Reading
dek: In a fast-moving field, what you learned in school goes stale unless reading is a daily habit.
more: Amit recalls that two doctors he interviewed on The Seen and the Unseen, Lancelot Pinto and Abby Philips, both observed that most doctors learn their craft in college and then stop updating. Both make time every day to read new papers. Amit uses this to open the episode's question: what should generalists, who have no professional obligation to keep up, do about reading papers?

In a fast-moving field, what you learned in school goes stale unless reading is a daily habit. For generalists the choice is between waiting for good ideas to filter up into books and reading at the cutting edge yourself.

head: Arguing With James C Scott, Page After Page
dek: The books that change you are the ones you argue with, not the ones you memorise.
more: Ajay says one of the wildest reading experiences of his life was Seeing Like a State. On nearly every page he was arguing with the author: sometimes disagreeing, sometimes unhappy because Scott was heading somewhere opposed to what Ajay then believed, sometimes proposing alternative explanations. He stresses the book isn't perfect. It simply reached him when he was primed for it. Amit adds that Scott cured him of 'the fatal disease of seeing like an engineer.'
The books that change you are the ones you argue with, not the ones you memorise. Timing matters too: the right book at the right moment can rewire a worldview.

head: Charles Booth's 17-Year Portrait of London
dek: Before disciplines split apart, social inquiry used every method available.
more: Biju Rao's paper opens with Charles Booth's late-19th-century multi-volume study of London, which took about 17 years to compile. It combined data, household surveys, interviews and observation, and it ran continuously rather than as a one-off survey. It covered employment, but also harder things like illness, infirmity and family size, and habits like drinking and thrift. The result was a magisterial picture of rich, poor and changing neighbourhoods.
Before disciplines split apart, social inquiry used every method available. Booth's work was part of a 'dying breed' that 20th-century academic incentives pushed aside.

head: Biju Rao and the Women Who Stopped Lying
dek: Detached surveys would have missed the real story entirely. Without the fieldwork, Rao says, they would never have thought to study domestic violence.
more: In 1992 Biju Rao was with researchers in a village, interviewing a room full of women about household income. A husband walked in, grabbed his wife by the hair and dragged her out. Her offence was talking to Biju. For about a week the women blamed the state for bad schools and water. Once trust was built, one said they felt like they were in jail: their husbands beat them, spent the family money on alcohol, and no one helped. Tracking this over time, combining qualitative and quantitative data, linked the violence to power within the family, female sterilisation (which raised the risk of being accused of infidelity), alcoholism and dowry demands. Violence was often a rational way to extract money from the wife's family. No economics journal would publish the mixed-methods version, so the work came out years later as two papers: one in a public health journal and one in an economics journal.

Detached surveys would have missed the real story entirely. Without the fieldwork, Rao says, they would never have thought to study domestic violence. The story also shows reflexivity: the researcher's presence changes the situation. And journal incentives split one rich study into two partial ones.

head: The Questionnaire the Tribals Wrote
dek: Who defines the categories shapes what you find. Treat people as participants rather than subjects and you discover how much of the standard instrument was the researcher's frame, not theirs.
more: In 2014, Biju Rao and a World Bank team gathered tribal communities in South Indian villages. Instead of asking standard poverty questions about jobs, income and seasonality, they asked what mattered to the people themselves, and built their tracking metrics from the answers. Behaviour that had seemed puzzling began to make sense. The final questionnaire shared only 17% of its questions with the National Sample Survey, which Amit suggests was possibly designed in Delhi by bureaucrats.
Who defines the categories shapes what you find. Treat people as participants rather than subjects and you discover how much of the standard instrument was the researcher's frame, not theirs.

head: Too Loyal to India to Be Objective
dek: Honest scholarship means treating your own attachments as biases to guard against.
more: Ajay admits he worries that his love for India interferes with his objectivity: he is rooting for the country. He suspects he would be a cleaner scholar if he studied Cambodia. Cultural pride and respect for one's forefathers can slide into propaganda. When he gets close to mass deprivation in India, the blood rushes to his head, so he 'runs away' and takes refuge in data. Later he adds that he and Susan know they cannot stay remote, and that is one reason they hide in the data.
Honest scholarship means treating your own attachments as biases to guard against. Sometimes choosing data is not coldness but self-knowledge about how easily emotion bends judgement.

head: A Life Designed Around Talking to People
dek: Conversations on the ground give you common sense and hypotheses. You then go back and test them with clean data.
more: Ajay never builds field conversations into his formal research, which he calls 'set piece battles'. But he has designed his life around them. He calls Bombay one of the best places to study the Indian economy because it holds both financial and non-financial firms, and everyday conversations with practitioners are full of insight. Over many years of building trust, people stop giving him press releases and tell him how they actually see their constraints. He also talks to officials and politicians and takes every factory or field visit he can. One peak learning experience was a four-hour walk through a mall in which a firm's head of marketing explained his business to him. He cautions, via Milton Friedman's billiards player, that what people say about their reasons is not necessarily the true explanation.

Conversations on the ground give you common sense and hypotheses. You then go back and test them with clean data. Trust takes years, and what people tell you is 'the truth as they know it,' not the final truth.

head: Can Economics Become More Reflexive?
dek: Its core thesis is the show's thesis: everything is everything.
more: Its core thesis is the show's thesis: everything is everything. It argues that economics, anthropology and sociology drifted into silos, and sets out four things economists can learn from ethnographers: cognitive empathy, taking words seriously, studying process, and making people participants. Amit says it shows no sign of rigor mortis and could be a book by itself.
The paper at the centre of the episode, by World Bank economist Biju Rao.

head: Life and labour of the people in London
dek: A 17-year, multi-volume study that mixed surveys, interviews and observation so freely that you can't assign it to any one discipline.
more: A 17-year, multi-volume study that mixed surveys, interviews and observation so freely that you can't assign it to any one discipline. It is a model of the integrated social science the episode mourns.
Cited at the start of Biju Rao's paper; Amit describes it at length.

head: The Extended Case Method
dek: It contrasts the positivist approach (detachment, standardised data, representative samples) with the reflexive one (engagement, embedding yourself in a community).
more: It contrasts the positivist approach (detachment, standardised data, representative samples) with the reflexive one (engagement, embedding yourself in a community). Burawoy treats them as separate; Rao argues they can be combined.
Amit cites this 1998 work as the clearest statement of the trade-off Biju Rao addresses.

head: Seeing Like a State
dek: It provoked a running dialogue on almost every page and challenged what he then believed.
more: It provoked a running dialogue on almost every page and challenged what he then believed. It reached him at exactly the right moment.
Ajay's example of reading as an argument with the author.

head: Free to Choose (1980 and 1990 series)
dek: It is lasting work that forms a body of knowledge others build on, unlike the constant 'flow' of tweets and columns.
more: It is lasting work that forms a body of knowledge others build on, unlike the constant 'flow' of tweets and columns.
Amit's example of 'stock' in his stock-and-flow framework for creators.

head: The Story of Art
dek: It explains the context and stories behind works of art, so even people who only respond to art viscerally can understand it.
more: It explains the context and stories behind works of art, so even people who only respond to art viscerally can understand it. Amit says it is also the story of thinking, of the human mind, and of stories.
Amit's end-of-episode recommendation; a book he dips into regularly.

head: Civilisation
dek: A foundational book for him when he was young.
more: A foundational book for him when he was young.
Ajay's recommendation, building on Amit's Gombrich pick.

head: Seven Bridges Road
dek: He thinks both versions are wonderful. Amit reveals Ajay has sung his own cover.
more: He thinks both versions are wonderful. Amit reveals Ajay has sung his own cover.
Ajay's song recommendation. He first knew the Eagles' live version and later found Steve Young's original.

head: Google Scholar
dek: It is his first stop for any search, ahead of Google. Spending time with original papers, even ones you can't fully follow, teaches you their rhythm.
more: It is his first stop for any search, ahead of Google. Spending time with original papers, even ones you can't fully follow, teaches you their rhythm. He credits this habit for being able to read papers across many disciplines.
Ajay's practical advice on how non-specialists should approach research.

head: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It is the predecessor to this one, which turns to papers closer to the present.
more: It is the predecessor to this one, which turns to papers closer to the present.
Mentioned as a popular earlier episode on great papers in economic history.

head: How to Write a Paper (Episode 62 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It explains the IMRD structure (Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion), which is the key to extracting value from papers outside your field.
more: It explains the IMRD structure (Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion), which is the key to extracting value from papers outside your field.
Amit mentions it as popular, and Ajay points back to it when explaining how to read papers.

head: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Episode 72 of Everything is Everything)
dek: That episode showed how the venue shapes the music: percussion in open air, none in echoing gothic churches, alternative rock in CBGB's crowded room.
more: That episode showed how the venue shapes the music: percussion in open air, none in echoing gothic churches, alternative rock in CBGB's crowded room. Methods shape the questions in the same way.
Amit draws on it to explain Rao's line that methods lead the questions.

head: Read Books for Ideas, Papers for Techniques
dek: Ajay cites economist Ed Glaeser's line to describe a supply chain of ideas.
more: Ajay cites economist Ed Glaeser's line to describe a supply chain of ideas. In chasing persuasiveness, social-science papers have become narrow and involuted; the pursuit of rigor has induced 'rigor mortis.' Big ideas, speculation and world-building now live in books, blogs, podcasts and YouTube. The ideal is big thinkers who plant a flag around a complex argument, followed by an array of detailed work. Everyone needs both kinds of reading.

head: Learning Has Increasing Returns to Scale
dek: A common excuse for not reading is 'I won't remember it.' Ajay's answer is that the more you know, the more new knowledge sticks, because you have context to attach it to.
more: A common excuse for not reading is 'I won't remember it.' Ajay's answer is that the more you know, the more new knowledge sticks, because you have context to attach it to. The cycle feeds on itself. As health spans stretch toward 95 or 105, he imagines people with a depth of knowledge and perspective never seen before in history.

head: Read as an Argument With the Author
dek: Ajay's method is to read every paper as a conversation, building disagreements or alternative explanations every paragraph or two.
more: Ajay's method is to read every paper as a conversation, building disagreements or alternative explanations every paragraph or two. He contrasts this with passive reading and India's rote-memorisation exam culture, and says it is far more powerful.

head: Stock and Flow for Creators
dek: Amit borrows these economics terms for creative work. Flow is the constant output (tweets, columns, episodes, papers) that keeps you in dialogue with the world and improves your work through feedback.
more: Amit borrows these economics terms for creative work. Flow is the constant output (tweets, columns, episodes, papers) that keeps you in dialogue with the world and improves your work through feedback. Stock is the lasting body of knowledge others build on, such as books or Free to Choose. The best papers are both.

head: The Methods Lead the Questions
dek: Economics, anthropology and sociology once shared one quest: understanding people and society.
more: Economics, anthropology and sociology once shared one quest: understanding people and society. Over the 20th century, incentives pushed each into a silo: quantitative economics, cultural anthropology, qualitative sociology. Once a field is loyal to a method, it can only ask the questions that method can answer. Incentives then lock the methods in place.

head: Scale vs Depth: Positivist vs Reflexive
dek: Following Michael Burawoy, there are two approaches. The positivist economist stays detached, uses survey intermediaries, standardises data and gets scale, but sees people at a social distance.
more: Following Michael Burawoy, there are two approaches. The positivist economist stays detached, uses survey intermediaries, standardises data and gets scale, but sees people at a social distance. The reflexive ethnographer embeds in one community and gets nuance and people's own self-understanding, but can't generalise and may miss the forest for the trees. The ethnographer also changes what she observes. Burawoy sees the two as necessarily separate; Biju Rao argues economists can learn from ethnographers.

head: Ethnography: From Hunter-Gatherer to Cultivator
dek: Anthropologist Bhrigupati Singh, quoted in Rao's paper, describes fieldwork in two phases.
more: Anthropologist Bhrigupati Singh, quoted in Rao's paper, describes fieldwork in two phases. First you hunt and gather scattered impressions, which alone look like anecdotes. Then you settle and cultivate: you organise impressions around concepts so they grow into thoughts. Done properly it is a long game of deep immersion, not a handful of stories.

head: Cognitive Empathy
dek: Mario Small's phrase and Rao's first lesson. It is not imagining how you would feel in someone's shoes.
more: Mario Small's phrase and Rao's first lesson. It is not imagining how you would feel in someone's shoes. It is understanding how they see themselves, which may be very different from how you see them. That takes talking to people and staying with them, not sending a survey team and dispensing advice from a distance.

head: Take Words Seriously
dek: Rao's second lesson. Numbers give a static picture, while the narratives people tell about themselves, followed over time, reveal far more.
more: Rao's second lesson. Numbers give a static picture, while the narratives people tell about themselves, followed over time, reveal far more. This must be done rigorously, not by generalising from a few quotes. Amit expects machine learning to help parse thousands of interviews, catching patterns humans miss or invent.

head: Watch the Process, Not Just the Snapshots
dek: Rao's third lesson. Since the credibility revolution, empirical economics measures outcomes and leaves mechanisms to theory or speculation.
more: Rao's third lesson. Since the credibility revolution, empirical economics measures outcomes and leaves mechanisms to theory or speculation. Two snapshots of a place miss how change actually happens. Ethnographers stay on the ground and watch it unfold. Amit invokes Heraclitus's river and Deng Xiaoping's 'crossing the river by feeling the stones.'

head: Participants, Not Subjects
dek: Rao's fourth lesson. Calling people 'subjects' already implies distance.
more: Rao's fourth lesson. Calling people 'subjects' already implies distance. Ethnographers invite people to define what matters to them and to help shape the metrics, as in the 2014 tribal study whose questionnaire overlapped only 17% with the National Sample Survey.

head: Journals as Clubhouses, Fads as Gatekeepers
dek: Universities created departments, and promotion came to depend on publishing in each discipline's journals, its 'little clubhouse.' In economics, a fad (RCTs, instrumental variables, experimental economics, DSGE models) wins, takes over the journals, and through them controls hiring and promotion.
more: Universities created departments, and promotion came to depend on publishing in each discipline's journals, its 'little clubhouse.' In economics, a fad (RCTs, instrumental variables, experimental economics, DSGE models) wins, takes over the journals, and through them controls hiring and promotion. Everyone either conforms or exits, and diverse views go unpublished. Ajay calls insisting on methodological purity 'childish.' The right approach is to start from the question and assemble whatever toolkit fits it.

head: See the Tears, but Don't Cry
dek: Ajay quotes the line 'statistics are human beings with the tears washed away' and admits he prefers cold data to protect his objectivity.
more: Ajay quotes the line 'statistics are human beings with the tears washed away' and admits he prefers cold data to protect his objectivity. Amit's reply is that a researcher should get close enough to see people's tears and understand where they come from, while keeping their own emotions out of the analysis.

head: Internal vs External Validity
dek: Internal validity asks whether your claims about the one village you studied are true.
more: Internal validity asks whether your claims about the one village you studied are true. External validity asks whether they hold for other villages or the whole country. They are different questions and should be kept separate.

head: The Intervention in All That Context
dek: Reading a paper crediting e-filing with certain results, Ajay objected that reforms are always surrounded by hundreds of details of law, public administration, invisible infrastructure, culture and norms.
more: Reading a paper crediting e-filing with certain results, Ajay objected that reforms are always surrounded by hundreds of details of law, public administration, invisible infrastructure, culture and norms. Economists make a reductionist mistake: data alone hides that context, and studying a single village normalises it. His preferred remedy is longitudinal (panel) data, observing the same firms and households across the country over time to make credible average claims about India.

head: Labels Help and Hurt, So Resurrect 'Philosopher'
dek: Amit notes that Plato and Aristotle studied everything, and subjects later split off into sciences, which left philosophy with only the leftover problems.
more: Amit notes that Plato and Aristotle studied everything, and subjects later split off into sciences, which left philosophy with only the leftover problems. Naming a field clarifies it but also cuts it off from everything else, and he laments the loss of the Renaissance person. Ajay wants to reclaim 'philosopher' for anyone eclectic enough to study the world from many angles, and to deny philosophy departments a monopoly on the word.

head: Climb the Gradient Toward Breadth
dek: Asked about breadth versus depth, Ajay says formal knowledge production has over-emphasised specialisation, so as a first approximation almost everyone would gain from more breadth.
more: Asked about breadth versus depth, Ajay says formal knowledge production has over-emphasised specialisation, so as a first approximation almost everyone would gain from more breadth. This is a claim about direction given where we are now, not a claim that pure breadth is always best.

head: Distrust Grandiose Titles
dek: If a paper studies Tamil Nadu but leaves Tamil Nadu out of its title, the author is reaching for fame and you should be more skeptical.
more: If a paper studies Tamil Nadu but leaves Tamil Nadu out of its title, the author is reaching for fame and you should be more skeptical. Ajay says this is common in advanced economies, where papers about America don't mention America. Every locale is different, and a modest title and abstract reflect well on the author.

head: How a Non-Specialist Should Read Papers
dek: When entering a new field, first build the big picture through broad, integrating reading, then move to narrow papers.
more: When entering a new field, first build the big picture through broad, integrating reading, then move to narrow papers. Make Google Scholar your first search engine. Even without technical training, learn the IMRD structure: read the abstract and introduction, get the gist of the methodology, skim the results, read the discussion. Ajay likens the paper to a thumri, an art form whose rhythm you pick up with exposure.

head: After Ajay calls learning
more: After Ajay calls learning 'a bloody vicious cycle,' Amit gently corrects him: 'At one point... you said vicious cycle. I would say virtuous cycle, which is surely what you meant.'

head: Amit, riffing on the title of Seeing Like a State
more: Amit, riffing on the title of Seeing Like a State: 'James C. Scott cured you of the fatal disease of seeing like an engineer, which you no longer do.'

head: Ajay's pun on academic papers
more: Ajay's pun on academic papers: 'the very pursuit for rigor has induced rigor mortis.'

head: Ajay on what young academics are told
more: Ajay on what young academics are told: 'shut up and read papers, shut up and write papers, be narrow, don't think more, like just be a galley slave like everybody else.'

head: Ajay proposes a new name for the firm Amit has never set up
more: Ajay proposes a new name for the firm Amit has never set up: 'Amit Bhai Philosophy Private Limited,' replacing his earlier 'Amit Bhai Media Private Limited.' Amit replies: 'Your earlier suggestion was a low level equilibrium suggestion, and this one is even lower level, Ajay Bhai, so what to do.'

head: Amit asks what to do about…
more: Amit asks what to do about 'too much breadth' and, as Ajay ponders, pounces: 'No no, you're thinking seriously, don't think seriously. Ah, you're thinking of Ozempic.'

head: Ajay on authors who give narrow studies universal-sounding titles
more: Ajay on authors who give narrow studies universal-sounding titles: 'they're just like frat boys running for tenure.'

head: Two papers were promised, but only one was discussed
more: Two papers were promised, but only one was discussed: 'time has gone by, we have to go for lunch. We'll talk about the other papers some other time.'

head: Amit introduces Gombrich
more: Amit introduces Gombrich: 'my recommendation is nothing to do with the subject of the episode, but everything to do with the subject of this episode, because everything is everything.'

head: Amit reveals that Ajay has sung his own cover of Seven Bridges Road
more: Amit reveals that Ajay has sung his own cover of Seven Bridges Road: 'we'll have to negotiate whether we can put a little bit of that video here. We'll get a copyright strike for fuck's sake.'

head: Heraclitus's
more: Heraclitus's 'no man steps in the same river twice' is Amit's image for why snapshots miss change: both the man and the river have changed.

head: Amit quotes…
more: Amit quotes 'your favorite Chinese personality,' Deng Xiaoping, to Ajay: 'crossing the river by feeling the stones,' as the ethnographer's way of following change step by step.

head: Sanskrit's Borrowed Tongue-Curl
dek: Even the 'purest' sacred language is a mixture. Language evolves through spontaneous order, and the mothers quietly reshaped the newcomers' tongue.
more: Amit has Ajay say two words so he can feel the difference between dental sounds, where the tongue touches the upper teeth, and retroflex sounds, where the tongue curls back towards the roof of the mouth. Dental sounds run through Sanskrit's whole language family. Retroflex sounds do not, but they appear in all the Dravidian languages. Madhav Deshpande's 1976 essay, which Peggy Mohan cites, showed that even the Rig Veda's language had picked these sounds up from languages already spoken here. That stunned people who saw Sanskrit as pure. Peggy's explanation is that the migrants were mostly men who married local women, and the children spent their first years with mothers who spoke a different tongue. Amit adds that he was taught in school that all Indian languages come from Sanskrit, which is untrue. Tamil may well be older, and Tony Joseph suggests the Indus Valley language evolved into the Dravidian languages.

Even the 'purest' sacred language is a mixture. Language evolves through spontaneous order, and the mothers quietly reshaped the newcomers' tongue. One small fact about sounds undoes both the 'pure origin' story and the 'Sanskrit is the mother of all Indian languages' story.

head: How Local Gods Joined the Family
dek: Hinduism's unity was built by accommodation rather than conquest. Rivals were absorbed into the family tree instead of being erased.
more: As the Vedic Brahmins fanned out across the subcontinent, they lacked the political power to impose their beliefs. So they absorbed local beliefs and told stories about them, and these stories became the Puranas. In Andhra, instead of calling the Chenchu tribe savages, a myth had Vishnu consort with a Chenchu woman, and their child becomes the Chenchu god. In Tamil country, Ayyanar became Shiva's son by a beguiling female form of Vishnu. In 12th-century Maharashtra, Vitthal was declared a form of Vishnu even as some locals protested that he belonged to the Jain tradition. The rough rule was that Shaivites expanded Shiva's family, while Vaishnavites made the local god an avatar. Manu Pillai calls the Puranas 'works of genius' because they tied the local to the pan-Indian.
Hinduism's unity was built by accommodation rather than conquest. Rivals were absorbed into the family tree instead of being erased.

head: The Lakshman Rekha Isn't in Valmiki
dek: The epics are 'open source', more like rivers than fixed texts. Some of today's most 'traditional' ideas are later regional additions, and this multiplicity is a feature, not a flaw.
more: Drawing on AK Ramanujan's essay '300 Ramayanas', Amit shows how the epic kept being rewritten across regions and centuries. Surpanakha is ugly in Valmiki but beautiful in Kamban. In the Telugu version, Urmila sleeps for fourteen years: half for herself and half for Lakshman, so he can stay awake. The Lakshman Rekha, now a universal metaphor for a line one must not cross, first appears in Krittivasa's 15th-century Bengali version. Krittivasa also invents a particular washerman who starts the gossip about Sita. Versions disagree about who built the bridge to Lanka, and in some, Lav and Kush are one person rather than two.
The epics are 'open source', more like rivers than fixed texts. Some of today's most 'traditional' ideas are later regional additions, and this multiplicity is a feature, not a flaw.

head: Islam Came First as a Trader
dek: A clean Hindu-versus-Muslim binary flattens centuries of trade, intermarriage and shared worship, even as a sense of 'us versus an other' slowly began to form.
more: The first Muslims in India were not invaders but peaceful traders on the Kerala coast; some say this happened within Muhammad's lifetime. Amit suggests this may be one reason communal feeling can seem lower in the south. The raiders came from the north, and they did destroy temples. But once rule settled, syncretism followed. In Sindh, Ali was adopted as an avatar of Vishnu, and in Maharashtra one god was also worshipped by some Muslims. In classic battles between a Mughal emperor and a Hindu rebel, half the emperor's generals were Hindu, and Amit recalls Turkish mercenaries fighting for Shivaji.
A clean Hindu-versus-Muslim binary flattens centuries of trade, intermarriage and shared worship, even as a sense of 'us versus an other' slowly began to form.

head: The Ox-God and the Kidnapping Syndicates
dek: Who pays for knowledge shapes what that knowledge says. A fundraising incentive turned reports on India into tabloid fiction, and Europe's great thinkers built their picture of India on it.
more: Missionaries were not always paid by the merchants and had to raise funds back home. Like a modern NGO, they played up the most extreme version of events. One Italian missionary invented a half-man, half-ox god who demanded the blood of 400 virgins. In this story, Indian parents gave up children to be beheaded, much as Christian parents gave children to the church. Others sent home erotic fantasies. In one, lonely widows at the shrine of Akbar's grandson took their pick of male pilgrims. In another, powerful women ran gangs that kidnapped men off the street for a night. These accounts shaped Europe's view of India. Voltaire read them and called it a barbarous nation, and James Mill wrote a history of India without ever visiting.
Who pays for knowledge shapes what that knowledge says. A fundraising incentive turned reports on India into tabloid fiction, and Europe's great thinkers built their picture of India on it.
printed: The ox-god was made in Italy

head: Ten Thousand Satis That Were Thirty-Eight
dek: Even a real social evil got distorted by exaggeration and projection. Reasoning about incentives, when built on wrong assumptions, produces confident nonsense.
more: One report claimed ten thousand satis in a single year; when Manu Pillai checked, the real figure was 38. The accounts also explained sati with a strange incentive story. Indian women were supposedly lecherous and unfaithful, so men feared their wives would kill them to be with other lovers, and ensured that widows would burn with them. Amit notes that this mirrors medieval Europe, where in some places unfaithful wives were burnt at the stake. The outsiders were projecting their own evils onto India.
Even a real social evil got distorted by exaggeration and projection. Reasoning about incentives, when built on wrong assumptions, produces confident nonsense.

head: The Missionary Who Was Told to Back Off
dek: Real engagement tends to dissolve contempt, but institutions punish those who report it.
more: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg arrived with the usual missionary impulse to convert. But the more he engaged, the more he found, including much wisdom in the later Vedas. He wrote to his superiors that they had got it wrong: there was nothing to teach these people, because the best of their own learning was already mirrored in Indian teachings. His superiors slapped him down. Amit says Manu documents many such respectful dialogues and debates, but they were a small minority within a shrill discourse.
Real engagement tends to dissolve contempt, but institutions punish those who report it. Thoughtful conversation has always been a narrow band, then as now.

head: The Industrial Revolution's Freelance Missionaries
dek: A change the hosts celebrate for spreading prosperity also had a hidden side effect.
more: Ajay asks when missionaries became politically important, given that the Portuguese first came to Calicut for pepper. Amit says missionaries never dominated the merchants until the Industrial Revolution. Earlier missionaries were professionals in formal orders such as the Jesuits. Now anyone could become one; Manu writes about a shoemaker who came out. These freelancers competed for attention, and the journals printing their accounts sold in the hundreds of thousands. At the end of the 18th century, the British were still telling missionaries to hold back. Within twenty years that had flipped, and missionary zeal fed into governance, increasing both religious oppression and the reaction to it.
A change the hosts celebrate for spreading prosperity also had a hidden side effect. It lowered the barrier to entry for missionary work and turned it into a competitive media market.

head: How 'Sanskari' Prudishness Came from the Victorians
dek: Much of what is defended today as traditional Indian modesty is a colonial import.
more: Once the British began governing, they imposed their own laws and Victorian morality rather than adapting to local custom. In the original Shakuntala, the heroine is sweaty and sultry, and William Jones's translation drains away that sensuality. In The Ivory Throne, Manu Pillai wrote that it was once common for women in Kerala to be bare-breasted, until the British came and couldn't deal with it. The irony is that the same Europe sending home erotic fantasies about India was imposing prudery on it.
Much of what is defended today as traditional Indian modesty is a colonial import.

head: Ram Mohan Roy: From Seeker to Columnist
dek: A reformer arguing for an audience's approval ends up shaping the religion to fit that audience.
more: Raja Ram Mohan Roy wrote his first book, Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin, in Persian, the language of the elites. It held radical views on religion and was a genuine quest to understand the world. Later, writing in Bengali, he became more like a modern columnist trying to persuade people. He was anglicised, comfortable with the British, and even went to London as the Mughal emperor's emissary. He drew on the Upanishads and later Vedas to argue that Hinduism resembled Western philosophy rather than being polytheistic. His aims were to modernise the faith and to win British respect. The Brahmo Samaj he founded was the version the British liked, since 'these people make for good babus'. Its line runs to Tagore, with Vivekananda in a similar vein.
A reformer arguing for an audience's approval ends up shaping the religion to fit that audience. The result is respectable, but elite.

head: Dayanand Saraswati, the Mouse and the Corpse
dek: A single falsifying observation can launch a movement. And the elite rival taught him the mass-marketing tools that would help his movement outlast theirs.
more: One night at a Shiva temple, Dayanand Saraswati watched a mouse eat the prasad left for the idol. He expected the god to strike it dead, but nothing happened, and he began to question. He travelled and spent a few years with a hermit. Once, on the banks of the Ganga, he cut open a corpse to check whether the body matched its description in the scriptures; it didn't. He cared nothing for the British and was disgusted by the Puranic melange. He sought a purer faith rooted in the early Vedas and founded the Arya Samaj. At the Brahmo Samaj in Kolkata he learned that he had to speak the people's language, so he began writing in Hindi. He also learned pamphleteering, publicity, marketing and brand building from them.
A single falsifying observation can launch a movement. And the elite rival taught him the mass-marketing tools that would help his movement outlast theirs.
printed: Of mice and the Arya Samaj

head: Tilak Takes Religion to the Streets
dek: Political identity is built through ritual and mass mobilisation before it is built through theory.
more: Amit finds Bal Gangadhar Tilak odious in many of his views; he opposed girls being educated, for instance. But Tilak was a deeply astute political strategist who saw that a movement couldn't be built in elite drawing rooms. He did two big things. First, he revived Shivaji as a brand, as one of the earliest articulators of Hindu-versus-the-other. Second, he took Ganapati, a local festival not then celebrated at scale, and made it a grand public celebration that brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets. That common identity could then be used for other purposes. What he never did was define what Hinduism is.
Political identity is built through ritual and mass mobilisation before it is built through theory. Backward views and strategic brilliance can live in the same person.

head: The Two Savarkars
dek: An ideology can carry the imprint of one man's trauma. Had Savarkar died in 1910, he would be remembered entirely differently.
more: Having read nearly all of Savarkar's biographies, Amit sees two Savarkars. Until 1910 he is a Bhagat Singh-like revolutionary who organises revolutionary acts. His book was praised by Nehru, he shared a London stage with Gandhi, and he insisted that Hindus and Muslims must throw off the yoke together. Then he was jailed in the Andamans as a terrorist rather than a political prisoner, far from the genteel imprisonment Nehru got. Between the British jailers and the prisoners stood a layer of mostly Pathan guards who brutalised the inmates, and there are rumours of worse than torture. He came out around 1920 radicalised and hating Muslims, and wrote Essentials of Hindutva. Amit first found the book lousy and incoherent, before seeing its political genius.
An ideology can carry the imprint of one man's trauma. Had Savarkar died in 1910, he would be remembered entirely differently.

head: Ambedkar and Adam Smith
dek: Diagnosis and remedy can come from different traditions. Pairing the great critic of caste with the economist of markets dissolves a false choice.
more: The Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad told Amit on The Seen and the Unseen that his heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith. Amit finds this utterly resonant. He points to the growth after 1991 that lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, including hundreds of millions of Dalits.
Diagnosis and remedy can come from different traditions. Pairing the great critic of caste with the economist of markets dissolves a false choice.

dek: Its introductory essay, 'A Brief History of Hinduism', synthesises the Puranic period so beautifully that he urges everyone to go out and buy the book.
more: Its introductory essay, 'A Brief History of Hinduism', synthesises the Puranic period so beautifully that he urges everyone to go out and buy the book. It is also the source of much of the colonial-era material: the missionaries, the sati figures and the reformers.
