head: The Name May Be New, but the River Was Always There
dek: Amit rejects two simple narratives. The first is the nationalist one: a glorious Hindu past was interrupted by invaders and must now be revived as a Hindu rashtra.
more: Amit rejects two simple narratives. The first is the nationalist one: a glorious Hindu past was interrupted by invaders and must now be revived as a Hindu rashtra. The second is the academic one, which he held until recently. It says Hinduism is a recent construction: the word was coined by a Britisher in the late 18th century, Brahmin interlocutors sold the British a Vedic version, and the British fed that version back to Indians. Both are top-down simplifications. Following Manu Pillai, the truth is a continuous, plural tradition that only later acquired a name and borders.

head: We Are Layered Migrants, and Genetics Settled the Aryan Debate
dek: Homo sapiens fossils appear in Africa about 300,000 years ago. The successful dispersal out of Africa came about 70,000 years ago; earlier migrants left no genetic trace.
more: Homo sapiens fossils appear in Africa about 300,000 years ago. The successful dispersal out of Africa came about 70,000 years ago; earlier migrants left no genetic trace. Humans reached the subcontinent around 65,000 to 60,000 years ago, travelling along the coast from near Basra into Kutch (Ajay, citing Tony Joseph). About 7,000 years ago, pastoralists from Iran settled at Mehrgarh, mixed with the earlier Indians, and this mixing led to the Harappan civilisation. Around 2100 BCE, migrants from the steppes arrived; they were mostly men, and they mixed with the locals. The 'Aryan invasion' became toxic partly because the Nazis loved the story, and partly because of the feeling that 'we are the original people'. Archaeology couldn't settle the question, but genetics can date the arrivals. Reich adds a caveat: the Germanic invasion of Rome would leave no archaeological trace either.

head: Ahimsa as Trading, Not Raiding
dek: Devdutt Pattanaik argues that Harappan city design reveals a society that prioritised traders over raiders.
more: Devdutt Pattanaik argues that Harappan city design reveals a society that prioritised traders over raiders. On this reading, ahimsa is more than non-violence: its fullest expression is voluntary exchange between consenting adults, which is exactly how one would describe free trade. Amit closes the episode on the same note. The great lesson of the modern world is cooperation and mutual benefit, and that is compatible with Hinduism.

head: Three Reasons Religion Exists
dek: The first is consolation. Facing death, those who tell themselves sustaining stories may pass on their genes better, so we are wired for belief.
more: The first is consolation. Facing death, those who tell themselves sustaining stories may pass on their genes better, so we are wired for belief. The second is explanation. In a bewildering world, myth fills the gaps in our knowledge (the 'God of the gaps'), which is why the earliest gods were nature gods; science has steadily taken over those gaps. The third is codification. A society's natural ways of behaving get written into its religion, not just the other way round. Ajay adds an evolutionary layer: in bands of about 150 hunter-gatherers, religiosity produced coherence, and the more coherent bands won wars, so genes predisposing people to belief were favoured.

head: Religion as Spontaneous Order
dek: In the Puranic period, Hinduism was curated from the bottom up, through people's lives and rituals, rather than decreed from above.
more: In the Puranic period, Hinduism was curated from the bottom up, through people's lives and rituals, rather than decreed from above. Beliefs shifted gradually across space; Ajay compares this to language changing every hundred kilometres. Kings found Brahmin narratives useful for legitimacy, and Brahmins edged towards influence without pushing hard enough to tear the fabric. Meanwhile, Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists feuded and satirised each other. Brahmins themselves varied hugely: some were vegetarian and some not, some cremated their dead and some buried them. The simplistic narratives are top-down; the reality was emergent.

head: Writing Things Down Ossifies Them
dek: Ajay asks whether Hinduism stayed malleable because it was vast, oral and pre-printing press.
more: Ajay asks whether Hinduism stayed malleable because it was vast, oral and pre-printing press. In religions with a single, error-corrected written book, the book becomes a boundary that blocks organic evolution. Amit agrees and extends the point. When the British census made everyone record their caste, it arguably froze caste in place.

head: Worship Was Practice, Not Identity
dek: Manu Devadevan argues that worshipping Shiva or Vishnu once conferred no identity.
more: Manu Devadevan argues that worshipping Shiva or Vishnu once conferred no identity. Wearing cotton never made anyone a 'cotton wearer', and living in a thatched hut never made anyone a 'hut dweller'. Amit's analogy is liking black clothes versus white: a preference, not a tribe. Religious labels hardened later, with colonial definitions.

head: Roving Bandits vs Stationary Bandits
dek: This is Mancur Olson's frame. A roving bandit grabs everything and leaves, so he has no reason to preserve anything.
more: This is Mancur Olson's frame. A roving bandit grabs everything and leaves, so he has no reason to preserve anything. A stationary bandit stays, wants a steady flow of revenue, governs, fits in, and eventually becomes 'of the people', as the Mughals did by marrying Rajput princesses. Applied to Islamic rule in India, destruction happened mainly at the expanding edges; once rule was settled came coexistence, court life and intermarriage (Richard Eaton has written about this). Ajay adds a caution: the medieval world was horrific everywhere and had no good guys, so singling out some cruelties and judging them by today's standards misleads.

head: A Common Enemy Forges a Common Identity
dek: Before the invasions, the people later called Hindus were at loggerheads, with worshippers of Shiva and Vishnu fighting each other.
more: Before the invasions, the people later called Hindus were at loggerheads, with worshippers of Shiva and Vishnu fighting each other. A common enemy made them start seeing themselves as politically unified, though the word 'Hindu' came later. Colonialism sharpened this, as in Manu Pillai's image of four squabbling brown-skinned men who discover their shared brownness only when a white man attacks them all. The earlier Brahmins had assimilated others, but the colonisers wanted to rule, so assimilation was no longer an option and a counter-story had to be built.

head: Cognitive Closure and Colonial Simplification
dek: When something is too complex to grasp, the mind craves closure and invents a story, possibly a false one.
more: When something is too complex to grasp, the mind craves closure and invents a story, possibly a false one. Europeans facing an open-source religion they couldn't grok simplified it in several ways. They adopted a Brahminical, caste-based view, ran a census in which everyone ticked a box, and pushed these narratives through education. This reshaped how Indians saw themselves. As Sudipta Kaviraj puts it, giving itself a history is a community's most fundamental act of self-identification.

head: Savarkar's Homeland-and-Holy-Land Test
dek: Savarkar's political masterstroke was to make Hindutva the umbrella term, with Hinduism as only one part of it.
more: Savarkar's political masterstroke was to make Hindutva the umbrella term, with Hinduism as only one part of it. To belong, two conditions must both hold: India must be your homeland, and India must be your holy land. This excludes the British, and also Muslims, who turn to Mecca, while bringing in Buddhists, Jains, Shaivites, Vaishnavites and Dalits. Nobody asked why the line should be drawn there; it simply worked politically. Amit sees this as a radical departure: a tradition defined by absorbing the multitudes was now built on hard othering.

head: Caste Will Erode from the Bottom Up, Through Markets
dek: Amit calls caste a deep problem; he often calls it Hinduism's original sin, though he notes it isn't original as such.
more: Amit calls caste a deep problem; he often calls it Hinduism's original sin, though he notes it isn't original as such. It is a social evil, like sati, and it has to go. Top-down fixes disappoint. Savarkar insisted Dalits belonged, and repeatedly held inter-caste feasts in Ratnagiri that angered Brahmins. Modern Hindutva claims to have united the Hindu vote, but in practice the BJP worked existing fault lines like every party does. In UP it courted non-Jatav Dalits against Mayawati's Jatav base; in Maharashtra, non-Maratha OBCs. Amit's hope lies in markets and growth, which change incentives: there is less casteism in cities, and those who discriminate pay a price in a free market. Change will be slow, because 'paradigms change one funeral at a time'.

head: Secularisation Comes with Prosperity
dek: Ajay's observation is that the very poor are not especially oriented towards religion.
more: Ajay's observation is that the very poor are not especially oriented towards religion. Religiosity peaks in the middle, and secularisation arrives once societies become rich, educated and connected to the world. India's 1991 reforms created a middle class that began asserting its identity, which puts India at the religious peak of the middle stage. In time, secularisation will come for India too.

head: Why the Genteel Elite Vision Lost
dek: Ajay notes that the humanist Hinduism of Ram Mohan Roy, Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru seemed settled to his parents' generation, but the last twenty years have shown another face of the country.
more: Ajay notes that the humanist Hinduism of Ram Mohan Roy, Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru seemed settled to his parents' generation, but the last twenty years have shown another face of the country. Amit says that vision was bound to fail, because its champions were Westernised elites who were sometimes condescending to the masses. History had already signalled this. When Dayanand died, the elites expected the Brahmo Samaj to thrive and the Arya Samaj to fade, and the reverse happened. Real reform comes from below. Dayanand and Tilak took it in a direction Amit dislikes, but other directions are possible.

head: Hinduism Is Compatible with a Liberal Life
dek: Amit, a non-believer, argues that Hinduism holds values compatible with classical liberalism: respect for women, no divisions in society, consent.
more: Amit, a non-believer, argues that Hinduism holds values compatible with classical liberalism: respect for women, no divisions in society, consent. It is still a khichdi. Practising Hindus still visit dargahs and eat biryani on Eid; we may hate 'the other' in the abstract, but in the concrete we mingle. His own values, he says, are not foreign values; they are 'in the air around us'.

head: Description, Not Prescription
dek: Amit addresses English-speaking urban elites who have never engaged with Hinduism.
more: Amit addresses English-speaking urban elites who have never engaged with Hinduism. He asks them not to be condescending, because this is not infra-dig stuff. To understand yourself you must understand your society, and to understand your society you must understand the deep past. Read history to understand how things came to be, while keeping your own values intact.

head: After noting that the Lakshman Rekha first appears in Krittivasa's Bengali Ramayana, Amit
more: After noting that the Lakshman Rekha first appears in Krittivasa's Bengali Ramayana, Amit says: 'See, Bengali is being normative again, we know best, we'll tell you what to do.'

One of the missionaries' invented tales was about women who ran gangs that kidnapped men off the street for a night. In it, a woman has a man kidnapped 'only to find out it is her own lawfully wedded husband.'

head: Judging by the stories missionaries sent home, Amit concludes
more: Judging by the stories missionaries sent home, Amit concludes that 'Europe at this point must have been deeply sexually repressed', and calls these tales 'a mad fantasy of some bored, frustrated missionary somewhere.'

head: Ziegenbalg's superiors respond to his praise of Indian wisdom with, in effect
more: Ziegenbalg's superiors respond to his praise of Indian wisdom with, in effect, 'fuck off, what are you doing?' Amit says they were accusing him of Stockholm syndrome, 'though of course the term didn't exist then.'

head: On how small the space for civil discourse was in colonial times
more: On how small the space for civil discourse was in colonial times: 'somewhere that age also has an Amit Varma and Ajay Shah and they're chatting with the British interlocutors and everything is civil. But that's a small part of it.'

head: On how invasion united feuding sects
more: On how invasion united feuding sects: 'a common enemy comes who says, Stop this show, you're all going to jail. Right? And instantly we unite against that common enemy.'

head: Amit raises his own line
more: Amit raises his own line: 'I used to think there are as many Hinduisms as there are Hindus. I actually think there are more Hinduisms than there are Hindus.'

head: Amit opens with Dilip Chitre's poem
more: Amit opens with Dilip Chitre's poem 'Father Returning Home'. In it, a tired father gets off the train 'like a word dropped from a long sentence' and falls asleep 'thinking of nomads entering a subcontinent through a narrow pass.'

head: Game of Thrones: Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists destroying each other's places of worship is…
more: Game of Thrones: Shaivites, Vaishnavites, Jains and Buddhists destroying each other's places of worship is 'actually like Game of Thrones, that people are just going mad.'

head: Harry Potter: the Vedas are not
more: Harry Potter: the Vedas are not 'one series like the Harry Potter series'. They were composed over ages, and the early and later Vedas are startlingly different.

head: MG Ranade said that in the Puranic period Hinduism
more: MG Ranade said that in the Puranic period Hinduism 'was conquered by the multitudes', meaning it not only contains multitudes but was made by them.

head: Dilip Menon, on Puranic syncretism
more: Dilip Menon, on Puranic syncretism: 'deceased ancestors, local heroes and heroines, gods of the Vedic pantheon and nature gods all rubbed shoulders in a seamless fabric of worship.'

head: Purushottam Agrawal on colonial law
more: Purushottam Agrawal on colonial law: 'instead of cutting the cloth to fit the body, they cut the body to fit the cloth.'

head: Shruti Kapila: Hindutva is…
more: Shruti Kapila: Hindutva is 'a theory of violence in search of a history'. Savarkar supplied the history.

head: Richard Eaton
more: Richard Eaton 'has written wonderfully well' about how, once the Mughal empire settled, violence was confined to its expanding edges.

head: Amit's heroes among the Congress moderates are Ranade, Gokhale and Agarkar
more: Amit's heroes among the Congress moderates are Ranade, Gokhale and Agarkar, 'men who follow liberal ends through conservative means' and who didn't want to burn everything down. They were set against extremists like Tilak.

head: Jyotirao Phule, with his formidable wife, questioned both caste and the confinement of women at a time when other
more: Jyotirao Phule, with his formidable wife, questioned both caste and the confinement of women at a time when other 'reformers' didn't. Amit calls their work 'a great movement worth studying in great depth'.

head: On syncretic food, Amit nods to an earlier Everything is Everything episode on…
more: On syncretic food, Amit nods to an earlier Everything is Everything episode on 'how all the food that you think is Indian actually came from somewhere else.'

head: Sara Rai: 'We Had Nothing Else to Do, So We Looked at Things'
dek: Deep observation and rich memory grow out of unfilled time.
more: While recording a Seen and the Unseen episode with the writer Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand's granddaughter, Amit was struck by how precise and evocative her childhood memories were. They sounded like crafted fiction. He asked how she remembered so much. Her answer was that there was nothing else to do, so they looked at things. Amit links this to growing up in the 70s and 80s: books, music and films were scarce, but time was plentiful, and he daydreamed a great deal.

Deep observation and rich memory grow out of unfilled time. When the scroll-and-swipe treadmill fills every gap, the attention that once went to the world around us gets spent elsewhere, and paying close attention becomes something we have to choose deliberately.

head: The Mixtapes Made for a Future Wife
dek: A gift that costs real time and effort says 'this is who I am, and I want you to like it' in a way that a one-minute Spotify playlist can't.
more: Amit pulls out a TDK and a Sony cassette. He made these mixtapes at nineteen for the seventeen-year-old girl he was wooing, whom he later married. Making one was hard work. Foreign music was hard to find. You recorded in real time on a double-deck player, coordinated the two tapes, and worked out how many minutes of songs would fit on each side. He says that with the people he was wooing, mixtapes had a hundred percent strike rate.

A gift that costs real time and effort says 'this is who I am, and I want you to like it' in a way that a one-minute Spotify playlist can't. Choosing what to include also forces you to work out what you love and why, so making the tape shapes the maker as well as the receiver.

head: Posting Letters to a Classmate Two Buildings Away
dek: Letters were worth writing even when you saw the person every day, because the form itself asks for care.
more: In Class 8, Ajay and his friend Manisha Purohit sat one desk apart at school and lived two buildings apart in Bandra East. They still began a ritual of writing letters to each other: writing at home, dropping the letter in a post box, and waiting for a physical reply.

Letters were worth writing even when you saw the person every day, because the form itself asks for care. You write carefully and you read carefully, and that is a different kind of exchange from conversation.

head: How CMIE Was Born from a Stack of Inland Letters
dek: A major institution was started with an evening of handwritten requests to a trusted network.
more: On 13 April 1976, Ajay's father came home and said he had been sacked. Asked what he would do, he said he would start a new organisation called CMIE. That same evening he wrote a pile of inland letters to friends all over India. Each explained what had happened, described the new venture, and asked for specific help.

A major institution was started with an evening of handwritten requests to a trusted network. Each letter carried a story and a specific ask. Ajay's lesson for today is that email can carry the same care and seriousness if we choose to write it that way.

head: The Locked Godrej Almirah and Dad's 1967 Playboys
dek: Scarcity changes the imaginative life. One locked cupboard held enormous value when there was nothing else available.
more: Every Godrej steel almirah in Amit's childhood home was left unlocked except the one in his father's study. Young Amit found the hidden key. Among video cassettes and books inside were stacks of Playboy and Mayfair. He shows two issues, May and November 1967, from when his father was about twenty-five or twenty-six. He reflects on how little information men of that era had about sex: there was no Debonair yet, Bollywood offered warped ideas of romance, and there was no internet. Then he turns the old joke around. He really did read Playboy for the stories. A Playboy fiction anthology he bought around 1998 or 1999 is where he first read Haruki Murakami ('The Second Bakery Attack'), alongside Updike, Cheever and Nabokov. In the 1980s, he says, the two prestigious places to publish a short story were The New Yorker and Playboy.

Scarcity changes the imaginative life. One locked cupboard held enormous value when there was nothing else available. The story also shows that serious literature and erotica shared the same pages: Playboy was a home for great fiction and long-form journalism.

head: The Empty 1986 Diary and 'Tantalising Tantrums'
dek: For Amit the empty diary stands for all the writing he never did. It also points to a hidden privilege.
more: Amit's father, a government servant, received stacks of official diaries every year. Knowing his son wanted to be a writer, he would hand them over and say 'Beta, likho' (son, write). In the 1986 diary, twelve-year-old Amit began a novel called 'Tales of Saint Johns'. Part one, chapter one was titled 'Tantalising Tantrums', which at least alliterates. He wrote a couple of chapters in handwriting far neater than today's, then stopped. The rest of the diary is empty.

For Amit the empty diary stands for all the writing he never did. It also points to a hidden privilege. Getting good at writing takes volume, enough pages that you can afford to throw some away, and many children never have that much paper.

head: A Mother's Last Gift: Handwritten Recipes
dek: Handwritten recipes record how people lived inside.
more: Amit's mother died of pancreatic cancer in 2008. Knowing she was dying, she carefully wrote down recipes for all the dishes he loved, including a liver dish that is a particular favourite, and gave them to him. When he cleared out his late father's house, he also found a recipe book his maternal grandmother had written in the 1960s. It is in beautiful English and mixes Western and Indian recipes.

Handwritten recipes record how people lived inside. For a woman of his grandmother's generation, limited in many ways by her circumstances, cooking and collecting recipes was probably a rich part of her inner world rather than mere drudgery. Free YouTube recipes can't hold that kind of meaning.

head: A Recipe Book Compiled by Code
dek: The same urge that drove handwritten family recipe books lives on in a programmer's household.
more: As a PhD student who had to cook, Ajay and Susan invented a fixed text-file format for writing down recipes. They wrote an AWK program that converted those files into LaTeX, which produced a PDF that became their recipe book. Amit's response was a mock 'sashtang pranam' (a full bow).
The same urge that drove handwritten family recipe books lives on in a programmer's household. The tools have changed, but the habit of keeping a personal, organised record of what you cook has not.

head: 'Creative Animal' and 'Manic Beast': Amit's MTV Visiting Cards
dek: Even a dull corporate formality can be a chance to be yourself. Refusing the template costs nothing and says something about who you are.
more: Amit was never the corporate or networking type. At MTV, his third job, they insisted he have a visiting card and asked for his designation. 'Writer' seemed too boring, so he asked for 'Creative Animal' and got it. Years later, after a promotion, they offered him something like 'senior supervising whatever'. He asked what a promotion from Creative Animal would be, and his new card said 'Manic Beast'.
Even a dull corporate formality can be a chance to be yourself. Refusing the template costs nothing and says something about who you are.

head: Narendra Shenoy's Half-Hour on Michael Porter
dek: When a call was rare and expensive, it felt like a performance with a script you had to fill.
more: Amit retells a story his friend Narendra Shenoy told on The Seen and the Unseen. Narendra had an arranged marriage with Sheila. Her twin sister had been matched with a smooth conversationalist, and Narendra was not one. Sheila once asked him whether he had anything to talk about. When he later called her long-distance while studying for an MBA in another city, he felt pressure to be interesting, so he spent half an hour explaining Michael Porter's business philosophy.
When a call was rare and expensive, it felt like a performance with a script you had to fill. Young men often had no idea what to say, and this is a gentle, funny example of that.

head: The Badminton Partner Who Needed an 'Urgent' Phone Call
dek: Before mobiles, the household landline could be an excuse for courtship.
more: Amit came to Fergusson College's junior college straight from a boys' school and couldn't read signals from girls. A girl he played badminton with turned up at his house one day with a friend and asked to use his phone for an urgent call. She made the call and left. It took Amit years to realise this was probably a sign of interest, since nobody walks into a random person's house just to use the phone.
Before mobiles, the household landline could be an excuse for courtship. People missed the signals as easily then as they do now.

head: The Calcutta Crossed Line
dek: It's a reminder of how badly basic infrastructure used to work, and of how a broken system could produce a moment stranger than fiction.
more: Ajay recalls a woman from Calcutta describing the city's barely working phone system. Sometimes you got no dial tone, and sometimes you picked up the receiver and heard someone else's conversation. Once she picked up the phone, found herself connected into a call between two strangers, and realised they were talking about her.
It's a reminder of how badly basic infrastructure used to work, and of how a broken system could produce a moment stranger than fiction.

head: One Payphone for an Entire IIT Hostel
dek: Receiving a phone call used to be a public event. Shared infrastructure had its own social rituals, and those disappeared along with the device.
more: At IIT Bombay, Ajay's whole hostel shared one coin payphone, with a queue to make outgoing calls. For incoming calls, the watchman answered, heard something like 'I want to speak with Ajay Shah of 262', and shouted the room number across the hostel until the person ran down to take the call. Ajay also recalls that payphones in New York or Singapore were later turned into Wi-Fi points before every phone had internet.
Receiving a phone call used to be a public event. Shared infrastructure had its own social rituals, and those disappeared along with the device.
printed: One call a week, make it count

head: The Three-Metre Map of India on the Family Wall
dek: A huge paper map on the wall makes geography part of everyday family life, something everyone looks at together.
more: Ajay's father bought the four-sheet map of India sold by the Survey of India, built a wooden board of the right size, and pasted the sheets into a map about three metres by three metres that covered a wall of their home. Whenever a place or river came up, the children would scamper up to the map to find it. Ajay has tried for years to build a wall-sized map of the Himalayas and hasn't managed it. He believes a German company makes a good six-sheet set, and he asks listeners for leads.
A huge paper map on the wall makes geography part of everyday family life, something everyone looks at together. That is hard to recreate with a phone, and surprisingly hard to buy today.

head: Glimpses of World History
dek: Ajay ranks it among the great intellectual creations, proof of what careful, sustained letter-writing can produce.
more: Ajay ranks it among the great intellectual creations, proof of what careful, sustained letter-writing can produce.
Ajay's example of letters becoming literature: Nehru's letters to his daughter added up to a book.

head: The Hobbit
dek: Another case of a person writing to family and ending up with a book the world treasures.
more: Another case of a person writing to family and ending up with a book the world treasures.
Paired with Nehru's book. Ajay says Tolkien's letters to his kids turned into The Hobbit.

head: The Second Bakery Attack
dek: The example Amit names of the high-quality fiction Playboy carried.
more: The example Amit names of the high-quality fiction Playboy carried.
A short story that first appeared in Playboy and was Amit's first encounter with Murakami.

head: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
dek: The source of the idea that our brains can keep track of about 150 people, with around five close friends and a wider circle of about twenty.
more: The source of the idea that our brains can keep track of about 150 people, with around five close friends and a wider circle of about twenty.
Mentioned while Amit explains Dunbar's number using an old address book.

head: On Exactitude in Science
dek: Borges's point that a perfectly accurate map would have to be as big as the territory, which Amit uses as a quip about Ajay's search.
more: Borges's point that a perfectly accurate map would have to be as big as the territory, which Amit uses as a quip about Ajay's search.
Amit invokes Borges when Ajay complains he can't find a good wall map of the Himalayas.

head: Let It Be
dek: Amit calls it the best album named Let It Be, ahead of the Beatles. It's where the song Answering Machine comes from.
more: Amit calls it the best album named Let It Be, ahead of the Beatles. It's where the song Answering Machine comes from.
Mentioned in the segment on answering machines.

head: Answering Machine
dek: Amit calls it a great song with an immortal line, 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?', whose sadness is lost on people who never used one.
more: Amit calls it a great song with an immortal line, 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?', whose sadness is lost on people who never used one.
Brought up after Ajay mentions answering machines.

head: After the Gold Rush
dek: Included in the episode's show notes. The hosts don't say why on air.
more: Included in the episode's show notes. The hosts don't say why on air.
Listed among the resources in the show notes. It isn't discussed on air.

head: We Shape Our Objects, Then Our Objects Shape Us
dek: Ajay's framing for the episode. An object's importance goes beyond its function, because a whole culture of habits and rituals grows around it.
more: Ajay's framing for the episode. An object's importance goes beyond its function, because a whole culture of habits and rituals grows around it. When the object disappears, that world goes with it. So the point isn't nostalgia. It's to notice what those habits did to us.

head: The Last Time You Did X
dek: Objects drop out of our lives one at a time, and we rarely notice the moment it happens.
more: Objects drop out of our lives one at a time, and we rarely notice the moment it happens. Ajay suggests trying to be aware, as it happens, that you may be using something for the last time.

head: Scarce Stuff, Abundant Time
dek: In the 70s and 80s, books, music and films were scarce, but time was not.
more: In the 70s and 80s, books, music and films were scarce, but time was not. That spare time went into daydreaming and close observation. Today, constant scrolling and swiping leave little room for either, and Amit says this is a lament about himself, not a complaint about young people. Deep attention now takes deliberate effort.

head: Effort Is the Message
dek: Mixtapes, handwritten letters and trips to the post office took hours, and that cost told the receiver you cared.
more: Mixtapes, handwritten letters and trips to the post office took hours, and that cost told the receiver you cared. Ajay argues that tasks demanding focus put the mind's full power to work and created beauty. An endless supply of frictionless content makes that level of focus harder to reach.

head: Writing Shapes the Writer
dek: Amit, citing Joan Didion's 'I don't know what I think until I write it down', argues that writing doesn't just express what you already think.
more: Amit, citing Joan Didion's 'I don't know what I think until I write it down', argues that writing doesn't just express what you already think. It helps you discover yourself and produces new ideas, which is why he urges private daily journaling. Handwriting goes further, because it is slower, physical, and hard to edit. Ajay adds that this raises the level of thought that goes into it, and Amit wonders whether today's leaders, who no longer write long letters the way Nehru and Patel did, are lesser for it.

head: Turn Email Back into Letters
dek: The tool doesn't force short, careless writing; we choose it. Ajay points out that Gmail keeps drafts, so you can edit one email for days until it's an essay.
more: The tool doesn't force short, careless writing; we choose it. Ajay points out that Gmail keeps drafts, so you can edit one email for days until it's an essay. He and Lant Pritchett exchange 3,000-word emails that can take a month to answer, as a conversation meant to last years. Putting 'long form' in the subject line tells the reader this isn't an everyday email.

head: The Address Book as 'Dunbar Plus'
dek: Dunbar's number says our brains evolved to track about 150 people, roughly a tribe, with about five close friends and a wider circle of about twenty.
more: Dunbar's number says our brains evolved to track about 150 people, roughly a tribe, with about five close friends and a wider circle of about twenty. The old household address book held all of them, plus the grocer, electrician and plumber, in one physical place. Every time you opened it, you were reminded who was in your life. Without that reminder, friendships fade unless we tend them on purpose.
printed: Everyone you know, in one book

head: One-Way Journeys and Religion as a Mirror of Its Times
dek: Ajay shares a friend's idea. For most of history, when someone left, you didn't know whether they would arrive safely or ever return.
more: Ajay shares a friend's idea. For most of history, when someone left, you didn't know whether they would arrive safely or ever return. Video calls and safe air travel have ended that. Amit adds that religious rules often reflect the conditions of their time. The old Hindu ban on overseas travel can be read as elders' fear of losing the young for good, and the pork taboo as protection against disease.

head: Paper as Privilege
dek: You only get good at writing through volume, enough iterations that you can throw pages away.
more: You only get good at writing through volume, enough iterations that you can throw pages away. Many families could afford only the school notebooks they had to buy, so simply having paper to write in was a privilege. Scarcity has two effects. A child given his only diary will value every page, but that same scarcity can paralyse, letting perfection become the enemy of production.

head: Asynchronous Messaging Is a New Mode of Being
dek: Communication used to be either nothing or synchronous, like a planned call from an STD booth that had to be worth the trip.
more: Communication used to be either nothing or synchronous, like a planned call from an STD booth that had to be worth the trip. Now messages are asynchronous and always possible, so contact feels less urgent and often becomes trivial. Ajay's example is the 'did you take your meds today' message. It's a different frame of mind, not just a faster version of the old one.

head: Creative Destruction: Job Loss Usually Isn't the Catastrophe It Seems
dek: When mobile roaming arrived, more than a million STD booths employing millions of people vanished almost overnight.
more: When mobile roaming arrived, more than a million STD booths employing millions of people vanished almost overnight. Ajay argues that in India's dynamic market economy, people move on to other jobs, so the gloom about technology destroying jobs is mostly misplaced.

head: Paper Maps Give a Strategic View
dek: Ajay argues that well-made paper maps, like old Bartholomew or National Geographic maps, show the world in ways designed for a wall, giving a big-picture sense that Google Maps doesn't.
more: Ajay argues that well-made paper maps, like old Bartholomew or National Geographic maps, show the world in ways designed for a wall, giving a big-picture sense that Google Maps doesn't. He has even tried putting Google Maps on a large screen, but its labelling isn't designed for that. Children today can neither read nor fold a paper map.

head: Cash Is Freedom
dek: Ajay argues that cash's universal acceptance and anonymity are underrated, and that we only notice them once they're gone.
more: Ajay argues that cash's universal acceptance and anonymity are underrated, and that we only notice them once they're gone. In places like China, where the infrastructure for accepting cash has broken down, every transaction can be traced and you live in a panopticon. He calls using cash a social responsibility, drawing on what Vitalik Buterin told the hosts in Madras.

head: The Modern Visiting Card
dek: Ajay's practical tip: instead of a paper card, share a QR code linking to your contact file (a VCF).
more: Ajay's practical tip: instead of a paper card, share a QR code linking to your contact file (a VCF). Google Contacts checks that link periodically, so any change to your details updates automatically in everyone's address book.

head: Ajay arrives hoarse and asks why Amit has a bag.
more: Ajay arrives hoarse and asks why Amit has a bag. Amit replies: 'I have a new voice for you in my bag, so in case your voice goes.'

head: Amit on mixtapes as a wooing device
more: Amit on mixtapes as a wooing device: 'as far as people you are wooing is concerned, hundred percent strike rate.'

head: Amit proposes a new Everything is Everything newsletter in which the two hosts write each other long letters. Ajay declines
more: Amit proposes a new Everything is Everything newsletter in which the two hosts write each other long letters. Ajay declines: 'But we talk too much. You also need a little starvation of connection.'

head: Amit turns around the old joke
more: Amit turns around the old joke 'I read Playboy for the stories': 'No, the thing is I actually did.'

head: Editor Nomsita was browsing a long Playboy article on psychedelic drugs, and Ajay asks if she's underage for them.
more: Editor Nomsita was browsing a long Playboy article on psychedelic drugs, and Ajay asks if she's underage for them. Amit: 'Nobody nobody is underage for psychedelic drugs. So I've never had any. I'm just saying random things.'

head: Ajay on first meeting Playboys in his IIT hostel
more: Ajay on first meeting Playboys in his IIT hostel: 'I mean in the wing it was common property.'

head: Joan Didion's
more: Joan Didion's 'I don't know what I think until I write it down', which Amit cites to argue that writing shapes the writer.

head: Angela Merkel's Fukushima Question
dek: Even scientifically literate leaders can be moved by who an accident happened to rather than by base rates.
more: After Chernobyl, many people could explain the disaster away as Soviet stupidity: an oppressive system where people feared being sent to Siberia kept making wrong decisions, and a liberal democracy would do better. Fukushima in 2011 ended that comfort. Angela Merkel, who has a PhD in chemistry and could reason about probabilities, called a meeting around one sentence: the Japanese are as good as us, so if it happened there, can it happen here? Germans saw themselves as better engineers than the Soviets but not better than the Japanese. Germany then decided to shut down all its nuclear power, which Ajay says looks like a poor decision from where we sit in 2024.

Even scientifically literate leaders can be moved by who an accident happened to rather than by base rates. Germany's U-turn came from a shaken sense of 'it could be us', not from new data about nuclear safety.

head: Beating the U-boats with Assembly-Line Ships
dek: Scale and the learning curve beat craftsmanship. Ajay uses this story to explain why nuclear power can become cheap: build small reactors on assembly lines instead of one-off giant plants.
more: In 1941 German U-boats were sinking the transport ships that carried food and military supplies from America to Britain, and hundreds of ships were lost. Ships had always been artisanal products, each one built piece by piece and each slightly different. The Americans took a mediocre British design of about 10,000 tons, nicknamed the 'ugly duckling', and mass-produced it Henry Ford style at 18 shipyards. As the yards learned, the time to commission a ship fell from 270 days to 35. About 2,700 ships were built and the price fell sharply. Germany could not sink ships as fast as American manufacturing could make them.
Scale and the learning curve beat craftsmanship. Ajay uses this story to explain why nuclear power can become cheap: build small reactors on assembly lines instead of one-off giant plants.
printed: You sink them, we’ll build more

head: Tiger Tanks vs Sherman Tanks
dek: Constant tinkering by experts is the enemy of cost reduction. A standardised, good-enough design that can be produced at volume wins wars, and markets.
more: The German Tiger tank was a great tank, but it was built by master craftsmen, and the design changed after every eleven tanks. That pushed costs up. The Americans mass-produced Sherman tanks on assembly lines, taught the Soviets to do the same with the T-34, and together they outproduced German manufacturing by about ten times.
Constant tinkering by experts is the enemy of cost reduction. A standardised, good-enough design that can be produced at volume wins wars, and markets.

head: India's 1974 Nuclear Test, Built from Scratch
dek: Being good at a strategic science project is different from being good at efficient, scaled industry.
more: Most nuclear powers got there through leaks. The Soviets stole secrets from the Manhattan Project, the Soviets passed knowledge to China, and China passed it to North Korea and Pakistan. India went from scratch to a nuclear test in 1974 entirely on its own. Ajay credits Homi Bhabha, Raja Ramanna, Sethna and their colleagues. He then separates that achievement from the problem of cheap nuclear electricity, which is an ordinary industrial problem closer to Bharat Heavy Electricals and a poor fit for the Indian state.

Being good at a strategic science project is different from being good at efficient, scaled industry. Treating civilian power as an extension of the bomb programme is why India's nuclear energy share has stayed tiny.

head: The Numbers That Didn't Add Up at the Finance Ministry
dek: The problem with Indian nuclear power was never only fear of accidents.
more: When Ajay was at the Ministry of Finance, he ran early calculations on India's government-run nuclear plants. The conclusion was that, once costs were measured properly, they could never play a meaningful role in India's energy mix. Top-of-the-line French and American reactors were far more cost-efficient than what was being built in India.
The problem with Indian nuclear power was never only fear of accidents. The state-monopoly model simply could not deliver competitive economics.
printed: A reactor that failed the sums

head: When Fear Itself Kills: Fukushima and 9/11
dek: Refusing a technology does not mean choosing zero risk. It means accepting the risks of whatever replaces it.
more: Amit recalls Ajay's point, made before recording, that after Fukushima the reactors were shut down and Japan shifted to coal, and that switch caused deaths. He adds a fact he half-remembers: after 9/11, tighter security and fear led people to fly less and drive more. Car accidents kill far more people than plane crashes, so mortality went up.
Refusing a technology does not mean choosing zero risk. It means accepting the risks of whatever replaces it. Not using nuclear power has a body count too.

Ajay's end-of-episode pick, which he says has nothing to do with nuclear power.

more: Amit calls it a masterpiece.
The name 'Paul' reminds Amit of Paul Young's cover of this song.

head: Nuclear Is the Safest Form of Energy
dek: Three Mile Island killed no one. At Fukushima, people died from the tsunami and the rushed evacuation, not from radiation.
more: Three Mile Island killed no one. At Fukushima, people died from the tsunami and the rushed evacuation, not from radiation. Chernobyl did kill people, though the numbers are disputed. Even on the worst estimates, sixty years of nuclear power have killed fewer people than one month of coal-related accidents. France gets 71% of its power from nuclear, has had no safety issues and has low carbon emissions. Sixty years of nuclear waste would fit in an underground bunker the size of a Walmart.

head: Ideological Packages and the Environmentalist's Dissonance
dek: Nuclear power and nuclear bombs are separate things. Twenty-four countries run nuclear power and have never built a bomb.
more: Nuclear power and nuclear bombs are separate things. Twenty-four countries run nuclear power and have never built a bomb. The two got fused in the 1970s peace and environmental movements. Tribes adopt a bundle of dogmas and defend the whole bundle even when the facts change. The result is environmentalists who call climate change one of the great problems of our time but welcome solar and wind while banning nuclear.

head: The Three Distinct Sources of Nuclear Risk
dek: Ajay's first-principles breakdown has three parts. First, radioactive material behaves unlike anything in daily life: it travels thousands of kilometres, falls as radioactive rain and causes birth defects.
more: Ajay's first-principles breakdown has three parts. First, radioactive material behaves unlike anything in daily life: it travels thousands of kilometres, falls as radioactive rain and causes birth defects. Second, a runaway chain reaction can melt deep into the ground and contaminate groundwater. Third, a reactor is a complex system with nonlinear interactions, where small human errors can grow into catastrophes.

head: Renormalise Risk: Deaths per Megawatt-Hour
dek: The real choice is to add some nuclear risk and remove some coal risk.
more: The real choice is to add some nuclear risk and remove some coal risk. Coal is the dirtiest source on pollution, carbon dioxide and deaths, before you even count climate change. Measured by deaths per megawatt-hour, nuclear wins. Our intuition gets this wrong for the same reason it gets planes and cars wrong: flying from Bombay to Delhi is far safer than driving, but plane crashes make headlines and car crashes don't.

head: Safety Is an Engineering Problem, Not a Fixed Fact
dek: Ralph Nader's 'Unsafe at Any Speed' did not end cars; it set off huge gains in car safety.
more: Ralph Nader's 'Unsafe at Any Speed' did not end cars; it set off huge gains in car safety. The three famous accidents all involved first-generation designs from when humanity was just starting out. Newer reactors shut themselves down when something goes wrong, with forces like gravity pulling the fissile material apart so no runaway reaction is possible. There is already proof that this works: the nuclear reactors on aircraft carriers and submarines have run for decades without incident in advanced economies.

head: Authoritarianism, Not Physics, Caused Chernobyl
dek: Chernobyl was a failure of decision-making inside an oppressive system where people were afraid to object.
more: Chernobyl was a failure of decision-making inside an oppressive system where people were afraid to object. Societies with free speech, dissent and criticism notice when things go wrong and correct them. That is also why the Soviets never mastered aircraft carriers or submarines while advanced democracies did. Nuclear safety depends heavily on institutions.

head: Industrialise the Reactor: Small Modular Reactors
dek: A 4,000 MW plant takes about twenty years to build and will only ever be made in a handful, so it never gets cheaper.
more: A 4,000 MW plant takes about twenty years to build and will only ever be made in a handful, so it never gets cheaper. A 50–100 MW small modular reactor, roughly the size of a big truck, could be made by the thousand on an assembly line. It would arrive in a crate and be switched on like a factory's diesel generator. By Ajay's rough maths, 50 MW serves about 25,000 households or runs a large factory. Solar's huge cost collapse came the same way, from two simple, scaled manufacturing steps: polysilicon made in about ten factories worldwide, then simple semiconductor processing. This is no longer just theory: Meta and Google have placed big SMR orders.

head: Nuclear Power Is a Business, Not a Department
dek: Separate weapons from energy, the way steel for artillery shells is a defence matter while steel for everything else is ordinary trade.
more: Separate weapons from energy, the way steel for artillery shells is a defence matter while steel for everything else is ordinary trade. India assumed everything nuclear belongs to the Department of Atomic Energy, and nuclear's share of India's energy has stayed minuscule and has not grown. Building reactors (L&T), running power plants (Tata Power, Reliance Energy) and buying captive power (Hindalco) should all be private business decisions, with competing imports, the way imported equipment competes with BHEL.

head: The Evening Peak: Storage vs Nuclear as a Private Bet
dek: Solar is unbeatable while the sun shines, but it sets just as people get home and switch on ACs, TVs and fridges.
more: Solar is unbeatable while the sun shines, but it sets just as people get home and switch on ACs, TVs and fridges. Once coal is gone, every evening brings a supply crunch and a price spike. Investors who think storage technology can handle it should build storage. Those who doubt it should build nuclear, which keeps running into the evening. Ajay says these should be speculative bets by private players, with no central planning.

head: The Five Conditions for Nuclear Freedom in India
dek: (1) Private Indians must be free to import nuclear plants.
more: (1) Private Indians must be free to import nuclear plants. A 50 MW unit costs about $200–300 million, which India's top hundred companies can afford. (2) Plant owners must be free to sell power directly to industrial and commercial buyers, bypassing reluctant DISCOMs, as offshore wind developers can. (3) Security on the airport model: the CISF guards uranium and waste at private plants under clear protocols, paid for by the operator. (4) India must sign and comply with IAEA standards on fuel and waste so the world will sell it reactors and fuel. (5) Civil nuclear liability law must be fixed.

head: Operator-First Nuclear Liability
dek: Indian law makes the reactor vendor liable forever for any safety problem, so no global vendor will sell to India.
more: Indian law makes the reactor vendor liable forever for any safety problem, so no global vendor will sell to India. The international doctrine works like a car: after the handover date, the operator is responsible. Victims sue only the operator, and the operator alone can sue the vendor if a design defect caused the accident.

head: An Argument for Freedom, Not for Action
dek: The hosts are not telling companies to invest in nuclear or telling the state to build it.
more: The hosts are not telling companies to invest in nuclear or telling the state to build it. They are asking only that the state stop blocking the choice. Amit adds a twist: if the government truly regulated for safety, it would mandate nuclear, and they don't want that either. Under freedom, private players will weigh solar, wind, storage and nuclear on their own business logic.

head: Invisible Infrastructure and the Homeostasis of Debate
dek: Amit worries that India lacks the invisible infrastructure, such as rule of law and mature processes, that makes this model work in the West.
more: Amit worries that India lacks the invisible infrastructure, such as rule of law and mature processes, that makes this model work in the West. The state might hand the sector to a crony, botch security, or turn any small role into rent-seeking. Ajay admits the path will be difficult. His answer is a lively intellectual ecosystem of researchers, writers and critics that pulls a fumbling state back whenever it overshoots in either direction.

head: The Collector of Bills
dek: Amit makes a petty rent-seeker sympathetic, a small human version of the 'hafta' state.
more: The pitch began with a dream. The show's cinematographer, Vaishnav Vyas, dreamt that Ajay was stealing everyone's paperwork, and Amit turned that into a quiet love story. The hero is a geeky, unmarried man in his early fifties. He lives in a messy flat full of wires, storage boxes and Maggi packets, in an oldish building that could be in Bandra East. He picks up his neighbours' electricity bills from their doorsteps. Residents with no bill in hand forget to pay, and his friend in the electricity department cuts their power. Then the helpful 'Ajay Bhai' gets it reconnected for the bill amount, a late fee and a bribe, and the two split the money. The habit grew out of a hoarder's compulsion: he sees paper and can't help collecting it. A woman in her forties moves in alone, and her bill vanishes too, but she never comes to him because she is too ill to get out of bed. He is moved, gets her power back and offers to make her dal chawal. He botches it and gets it from somewhere else, and as she eats she quietly realises he couldn't have cooked it. She cooks for him in return, and we see her obsessive-compulsive neatness. At his place she tries to shut a bathroom cupboard that keeps springing open and finds his hoard of bills, including her own. She storms out threatening to call the police, but never reports him. In the end she sees he meant no real harm, since the money funded his electronics hobby, and he apologises clumsily. The final shot: doorbells ring across the building, doors open in split-screen, every bill is there, and the residents dance over the credits.

Amit makes a petty rent-seeker sympathetic, a small human version of the 'hafta' state. He also shows the screenwriter's craft: the wires, the Maggi, the dip-dip tea and her tidiness are each planted early so they pay off later, without a line of explanation.
printed: Love in the time of late fees

head: The Khalsa Bridge: Bota Singh and Garja Singh, 1739
dek: This is a story of alienation in the vein of Beckett and Stoppard. Two young men don't know what they want, so they die trying to prove something to others and to themselves.
more: Amit takes this from Sarbpreet Singh's history of the Sikhs, and the date is 27 July 1739. Zakaria Khan governs Punjab for the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah, and he has crushed a Sikh revolt so thoroughly that the Sikhs are in hiding. Two young Sikhs, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, are hiding in the fields when they overhear a farmer sneer that they aren't lions ('singh') but jackals, because real lions don't run and hide. Stung, they 'conquer' an empty wooden bridge beside a sarai on the Delhi–Lahore road. They then levy a 'Khalsa regime tax' of one paisa per donkey and six per cart. Every traveller simply pays. Garja is happy with the money, but Bota says they came to be warriors, not traders. Wanting a real fight, Bota sends Zakaria Khan a taunting verse letter that addresses him as 'sister-in-law'. With no war on, the governor is bored and rides out himself with a hundred horses. In the Sikh accounts, the two beat back wave after wave until the Mughals use guns and shoot them in the legs. With one working leg between them, they lock arms, face opposite directions and fight on until they die. Amit invents only their inner lives: Bota as his family's black sheep, Garja as a rejected suitor, both desperate for respect.

This is a story of alienation in the vein of Beckett and Stoppard. Two young men don't know what they want, so they die trying to prove something to others and to themselves. Amit turns it into a question for all of us about the futile battles we fight.
printed: Two men, one leg, no retreat

head: Two Chess Stories: Sultan Khan Meets Mr. B
dek: Here chess is a means of finding out who you are. The real contest is the one inside each player's head, and seeing that clearly can mean letting go of the win.
more: Amit combines Stefan Zweig's novella The Royal Game with the real life of Sultan Khan. In Zweig's story, the mysterious Mr. B is held by the Nazis in solitary confinement with nothing but a chess book. He memorises its games, creates an alter ego and plays against himself again and again. Later, on a ship, he takes on a brilliant but uncultured world champion. Sultan Khan was born in 1903. He first became the best player of Indian chess, which has slightly different rules, and then learned European chess. He never read chess books or discussed the game with other players, yet he won the British Chess Championship in 1928 and won it three times in all. Then he returned to India and never played again. In Amit's fiction, Sultan's father is the family's black sheep, and the boy's wins over his father and then over the head of the household restore the father's standing. From then on every game becomes a fight for respect: his own, his family's, his nation's. Mr. B is a calculator who sees concrete lines far ahead. Sultan is an intuitive positional player who can picture the endgame pawn structure on move eight. The fictional Sultan becomes world champion and faces Mr. B in a reversed version of Zweig's match. He chooses to let Mr. B win.
Here chess is a means of finding out who you are. The real contest is the one inside each player's head, and seeing that clearly can mean letting go of the win.

head: The Time Amit 'Beat a Grandmaster'
dek: A funny example of how a technically true claim can mislead by what it leaves out.
more: Amit admits he likes to boast that he once beat a grandmaster. The fine print: he was 17, and his opponent was Abhijit Kunte, then a 14-year-old prodigy at a chess club on Karve Road in Pune and not yet a grandmaster. Kunte later became a grandmaster, Indian champion and British champion. Amit won one blitz game with a queen sacrifice, and the boy said, 'My God, I didn't know you could play like this.' They must have played dozens of blitz games, and Amit says he surely lost all the others.
A funny example of how a technically true claim can mislead by what it leaves out. It also captures how sweet it is to win just once against someone much better.

head: The Postal Boy
dek: An absurd quirk of a real institution can reveal how much a society trusts strangers.
more: In the 19th century the US post office built a public good: universal parcel delivery anywhere in the country at modest prices. People mailed potatoes and sacks of wheat. Then, almost as a joke, someone asked to post a child. The clerks played along. They weighed the child, charged the parcel rate and pasted the address on his shirt. The child was routed from one clearing centre to the next like any parcel and delivered, Ajay thinks, to his grandparents. It was talked about everywhere, and posting children became a normal thing, with postal employees feeding them along the way. Amit adds the human drama. A drunk father posts his surly, unloved son on a pub bet. A storm strands the boy for days in a sorting office, where a lonely old man, abandoned by his own grown children, bonds with the 'parcel' before it has to be sent on its way.
An absurd quirk of a real institution can reveal how much a society trusts strangers. Reality really can be stranger than fiction.

head: Chekhov's Gun
dek: Amit explains Anton Chekhov's principle that nothing in a story should be there without a reason.
more: Amit explains Anton Chekhov's principle that nothing in a story should be there without a reason. He then shows it at work in his own pitch. The hero's tangle of wires sets up his geeky hoarding, his Maggi-and-dip-dip-tea kitchen sets up the failed dal chawal, and her obsessive neatness sets up the cupboard door she can't leave half-open.

head: Show, Don't Spell Out the Why
dek: Ajay suggests grounding the bill collector in the Marxist idea of alienation.
more: Ajay suggests grounding the bill collector in the Marxist idea of alienation. Amit pushes back: the 'why' should come through in how characters live and act, not be stated outright. In his pitch the hero's isolation is told through the messy flat, and the woman realises he didn't cook the dal through a shared look.

head: Rent-Seeking: 'Crooks or Government'
dek: Both of Amit's first two stories are small studies of rent-seeking. The bill collector creates a problem and then charges to solve it, which Amit calls a mirror of the Indian state.
more: Both of Amit's first two stories are small studies of rent-seeking. The bill collector creates a problem and then charges to solve it, which Amit calls a mirror of the Indian state. On the bridge, Bota tells Garja they aren't traders, because nobody pays them voluntarily. They are 'like crooks or government', which to Bota mean the same thing. Amit notes that rent-seeking usually needs the state's connivance, but here travellers' apathy was enough: nobody asked who these two were, and the toll simply became normal.

head: History From the Loser's Side
dek: History is usually written by the winners. Yet the only surviving accounts of the Khalsa Bridge come from the side that lost, in Sikh texts that treat the two men's deaths as martyrdom and a moral victory.
more: History is usually written by the winners. Yet the only surviving accounts of the Khalsa Bridge come from the side that lost, in Sikh texts that treat the two men's deaths as martyrdom and a moral victory. That is why the fight reads like a superhero film. Narrative battles are old too: after an earlier clash, the Mughals and the Sikhs each claimed to have won.

head: Calculation vs Pattern Recognition
dek: Adriaan de Groot found that strong and weak players look about equally far ahead.
more: Adriaan de Groot found that strong and weak players look about equally far ahead. Expertise is mostly pattern recognition, though some players also calculate unusually well. Amit's two players stand for the two routes to mastery. Mr. B, trained by endlessly playing himself in a cell, calculates almost like an engine. Sultan Khan, self-taught and without a chess school, works by intuition about space, initiative and pawn structure.

head: Futile Battles for Respect
dek: This thread runs through Amit's stories. Bota and Garja die proving they aren't jackals.
more: This thread runs through Amit's stories. Bota and Garja die proving they aren't jackals. Sultan Khan has to win every game because his father's, his family's and his nation's pride depend on it. Amit asks how much of life is spent proving things to others and to ourselves, and whether the battle we are really fighting is the one in front of us at all.

head: Trust Capital
dek: Ajay's takeaway from children being posted in America. Parents, postal workers and the children themselves all trusted strangers to behave well, enough to send a child across the country as a parcel.
more: Ajay's takeaway from children being posted in America. Parents, postal workers and the children themselves all trusted strangers to behave well, enough to send a child across the country as a parcel. That level of social trust is a form of capital, and seen with today's eyes it is astonishing. Ajay also flags, and leaves for another day, why universal delivery was a public good rather than something markets supplied.

head: Two Ways to Pitch a Story
dek: Ajay describes his approach as the opposite of Amit's. He looks for a striking real situation, sets out its rules, and leaves the human drama to someone else.
more: Ajay describes his approach as the opposite of Amit's. He looks for a striking real situation, sets out its rules, and leaves the human drama to someone else. Amit starts from inner lives: backstory, motive, glances and props. The postal-boy segment shows both, with Ajay's historical premise and Amit's improvised lonely old man.

head: Ajay's response to the premise of a man stealing his neighbours' bills
more: Ajay's response to the premise of a man stealing his neighbours' bills: 'If I would scoop up the bills of people, the only earthly reason would be to create a data set about electricity consumption.'

head: On casting: Vaishnav offered to play the Ajay-like hero, but Amit told him
more: On casting: Vaishnav offered to play the Ajay-like hero, but Amit told him 'you're too young and handsome. Which is not to say you are not handsome, but you are not young.'

head: The cupboard door the obsessive-compulsive neighbour can't get shut
more: The cupboard door the obsessive-compulsive neighbour can't get shut 'springs back out like an adamant economist,' and when pushed again, 'springs back out further like a recalcitrant communist.'

head: Amit on male haplessness. Having offered to cook, the hero
more: Amit on male haplessness. Having offered to cook, the hero 'remembers that like all men he has overpromised.' When caught with the bills, he says 'I can explain': 'Have you ever been in a fight with a woman, Ajay Shah, where you have said something like I can explain, knowing that you can't? You have. An essential part of the human experience.'

head: Asked how he opens a wine bottle, Ajay
more: Asked how he opens a wine bottle, Ajay says: 'Oh, there have been many disasters because there is no cork opener in my house.'

head: Amit refuses to reveal how the bill story resolves, saying audiences are suckers
more: Amit refuses to reveal how the bill story resolves, saying audiences are suckers 'for good storytelling, not just good stories', and admitting it is 'partly because I haven't thought of them yet.'

head: Garja Singh's nickname was Mota Singh
more: Garja Singh's nickname was Mota Singh: 'So I presume that in appearance at least he might have looked a little bit like me.'

head: Why a governor who has faced fifty thousand horses rides out against two men on a bridge
more: Why a governor who has faced fifty thousand horses rides out against two men on a bridge: 'There are no ongoing wars. Number two, there is no television, no internet, no mobile phone, no OTTs to watch. So Zakaria Khan is bored.' On his hundred horses: 'I am guessing that they were humans with those horses.'

head: Bota Singh's letter to Zakaria Khan, in Sarbpreet Singh's translation
more: Bota Singh's letter to Zakaria Khan, in Sarbpreet Singh's translation: 'Staff in hand on the road I stand, a penny an ass, sixpence a cart, this is a toll that I command. My sister-in-law, my dear Khan, a response does Bota Singh demand.' Amit admits he doesn't quite understand why 'sister-in-law' was the insult.

head: Ajay on chess matches with a psychological edge
more: Ajay on chess matches with a psychological edge: 'In Fischer–Spassky there is a psychological aspect, in Gukesh–Ding. Some matches are more normal than others, but these matches stick out.'

Indians could still play the British Chess Championship after independence. As Amit remembers it, after RB Ramesh and then Abhijit Kunte won it around 2002, the organisers decided: 'Fuck it, these Indians are winning it, no more Indians.' Today, he says, the top ten would all be Indian.

head: Amit's posted boy, stranded in a sorting office by a storm
more: Amit's posted boy, stranded in a sorting office by a storm: 'there is no protocol of who feeds a parcel because you know, you don't normally need to feed parcels.'

head: Amit's modern postal-boy story
more: Amit's modern postal-boy story: a friend in Bangalore who couldn't get an Uber booked a Dunzo parcel delivery from his office. When the rider arrived, he said 'I am the parcel' and rode to his destination on the back of the scooter.

head: Offending a committee with the word 'zombie'
dek: Being uncomfortable with blunt words for failure is itself part of the sentimentality Ajay argues against.
more: Years ago Ajay sat on the Percy Mistry committee on making Bombay an international financial centre. He and Percy kept using the term 'zombie bank' freely, and some committee members were offended because they thought it was a disrespectful word. Ajay's point is that 'zombie firm' and 'zombie bank' are technical terms that came out of the research on Japan.
Being uncomfortable with blunt words for failure is itself part of the sentimentality Ajay argues against. You cannot deal with dead-men-walking institutions if you will not call them that.

head: The bankruptcy code that was promised but never written
dek: A promise made in a ministry is not law on paper. A real bankruptcy code is a negotiation mechanism for creditors, which is very different from winding-up clauses.
more: Montek Singh Ahluwalia, then deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, told the Ministry of Company Affairs that the new Companies Act of 2013 should contain a full bankruptcy code, with collective negotiation among creditors. He was assured it would be done. It wasn't. When Ajay later raised the issue, Montek asked whether he was sure it wasn't in the Act. Ajay had read the statute: it had only trivial winding-up provisions and no bankruptcy process.

A promise made in a ministry is not law on paper. A real bankruptcy code is a negotiation mechanism for creditors, which is very different from winding-up clauses. It took a long time, and someone who actually read the law, for that basic point to land.

head: How one budget paragraph grew into the IBC
dek: Big reform needs an ambitious ask and a believable answer to 'can we actually do this?'.
more: Ajay retells a story KP Krishnan told on The Seen and the Unseen. The 2015 budget speech carried a paragraph from the small and medium enterprises ministry promising a bankruptcy code for small companies. Krishnan went to Jaitley and asked whether they could aim higher, with a full bankruptcy code. Jaitley asked whether they had the ability and the teams. Krishnan pointed to the FSLRC, which had shown India could run large research teams and draft complex laws to a world-class standard. That led to the BLRC, chaired by TK Viswanathan, with Ajay and Susan Thomas as members. The committee started with a narrow plan to amend winding-up provisions. Rajiv Mehrishi, then secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs, backed the more radical goal of a full code. Susan led the team that wrote the first draft, which became the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code in 2016.

Big reform needs an ambitious ask and a believable answer to 'can we actually do this?'. Here that answer came from capability the FSLRC had built earlier. Even so, the narrow vision had to be overcome before the real project began.
printed: The paragraph that grew a code

head: Japan's thirty lost years
dek: Keeping dead firms alive is not kindness. It drains the profits that healthy firms need in order to invest, and the bill can run for decades.
more: After 1986, Japan's Ministry of Finance and MITI ran an industrial policy that kept bad firms alive through bad banks. These zombie firms kept competing with healthy ones and destroyed their profitability across the economy. Ajay says this cost Japan thirty years of economic dynamism.
Keeping dead firms alive is not kindness. It drains the profits that healthy firms need in order to invest, and the bill can run for decades.

head: 140 sections deleted, 8 pasted in
dek: Institutional quality is decided in dull drafting details. One shortcut can lock a new regulator into an old regulator's flaws.
more: The original draft of the bankruptcy law set out how to build the new regulator, the IBBI, in about 140 sections covering checks and balances, separation of powers and governance, at FSLRC-level quality. All of it was deleted. Someone instead copied about eight sections from the SEBI Act, which brought SEBI's malfunctions into the IBBI. The regulator then hit state-capability limits from day one, along with the usual pull toward grabbing more power for itself.
Institutional quality is decided in dull drafting details. One shortcut can lock a new regulator into an old regulator's flaws.

head: Edited volume of papers on the Indian bankruptcy reform
dek: A collection of serious research on how the reform was designed and how it has worked, which is the kind of knowledge ecosystem he says the field needs.
more: A collection of serious research on how the reform was designed and how it has worked, which is the kind of knowledge ecosystem he says the field needs.
Ajay's first recommendation at the end of the episode.

head: An annotated reading list on the Indian bankruptcy reform (2018)
dek: A guided route into the literature for anyone who wants to go deeper than this episode.
more: A guided route into the literature for anyone who wants to go deeper than this episode.

head: State-of-the-art reviews of the Indian bankruptcy reform (2016, 2017, 2018)
dek: Year-by-year snapshots of how the reform was progressing: the kind of ongoing public criticism Ajay says keeps policymakers honest.
more: Year-by-year snapshots of how the reform was progressing: the kind of ongoing public criticism Ajay says keeps policymakers honest.
Listed in Ajay's recommended readings in the show notes as a review of the state of the art.

head: Code 2.0
dek: The first book he thinks of on the power of law and how every word matters.
more: The first book he thinks of on the power of law and how every word matters. Lessig argues that law works like code and shapes how the rest of the machinery runs, which fits the episode's theme of living 'in the shadow of the law'.
Amit's pick in the recommendations segment.

head: Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid
dek: A light pick after an hour on banks and creditors. The recording cuts off before he says more.
more: A light pick after an hour on banks and creditors. The recording cuts off before he says more.
Ajay's closing recommendation, which he describes as 'a movie of bank robbers'.
