dek: On how family firms can and should evolve, where 'the obvious answers may be wrong'.
more: On how family firms can and should evolve, where 'the obvious answers may be wrong'.
Part of the earlier episodes on firms that Amit lists.

head: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Ep 37, Everything is Everything)
dek: On different kinds of firms and when to centralise versus decentralise.
more: On different kinds of firms and when to centralise versus decentralise.
Part of the earlier episodes on firms that Amit lists.

head: Four Papers That Changed the World (Ep 41, Everything is Everything)
dek: It covers both the paper on firms and Hayek's paper on how prices let markets meet each other's needs from the bottom up.
more: It covers both the paper on firms and Hayek's paper on how prices let markets meet each other's needs from the bottom up.
Amit brings it up while explaining why complexity and constant change rule out central planning.

head: The Nature of the Firm
dek: The starting point for asking what a firm is, which you need before thinking about when a firm should die.
more: The starting point for asking what a firm is, which you need before thinking about when a firm should die.
The 'paper talking about firms' from the Four Papers episode; linked in the show notes.

head: The Importance of Finance (Ep 125, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Background on why finance matters, recommended alongside the zombie-banks episode.
more: Background on why finance matters, recommended alongside the zombie-banks episode.
Mentioned with Ep 118 as the next episode, which was about finance in general.

head: Creative destruction needs Shiva as well as Vishnu
dek: Schumpeter's account of progress: innovators take risks and earn a temporary monopoly rent on a new idea, and the prospect of that rent drives research and business-model innovation.
more: Schumpeter's account of progress: innovators take risks and earn a temporary monopoly rent on a new idea, and the prospect of that rent drives research and business-model innovation. Old firms that cannot keep up go bankrupt. Their labour and capital are not lost; they flow back to other firms, the way the atoms in our bodies return to other forms of life. Ajay maps this onto the Hindu ideas of creation, preservation and destruction: interfere with any one of them and the balance breaks.

head: A complex, changing world: adapt or make way
dek: Amit's two axioms are that the world is complex and that it is constantly changing, so needs cannot be met by central planning.
more: Amit's two axioms are that the world is complex and that it is constantly changing, so needs cannot be met by central planning. Firms that meet needs earn profits. Those that stop adapting, meaning they stop learning how to keep serving others, should go out of business so their resources can be used elsewhere. Ajay adds that a firm's way of organising labour and capital is like an organism's DNA: we get attached to it, but the recipe can be bad or the world can move on. Some firms do transform; Tata Steel of 2024 is unrecognisable from Jamsetji Tata's. Many won't.

head: Default hands the firm to the creditors
dek: As the company was conceived in 15th–16th century Europe, shareholders run the firm only while they service their debts, and creditors have no say.
more: As the company was conceived in 15th–16th century Europe, shareholders run the firm only while they service their debts, and creditors have no say. On default, the only questions before a judge should be whether there was credit and whether there was a default. Shareholders are then thrown out and usually wiped out, and the firm is rebuilt on a new balance sheet controlled by the creditors. Suppliers owed money are creditors just as much as lenders, and should not be treated as second-class.

head: Cold reasoning, no stigma
dek: Indian thinking tends to get emotional about a company and its founding family.
more: Indian thinking tends to get emotional about a company and its founding family. Ajay insists that equity and debt are cold relationships. Business failure is normal: people and firms should take risks, firms should go bankrupt, and bankruptcy should carry no stigma. What matters is a well-defined script for what happens after a default.

head: Zombie firms and zombie banks
dek: A failing firm propped up with more debt, because badly regulated banks won't admit the problem or the government leans on them, keeps competing with healthy firms and eats their margins.
more: A failing firm propped up with more debt, because badly regulated banks won't admit the problem or the government leans on them, keeps competing with healthy firms and eats their margins. Without profits, healthy firms don't invest, and dynamism drains from the whole economy. Ajay's example: a kept-alive Air India or Jet Airways sells cheap tickets and harms quality airlines like Vistara.

head: The melting ice cube: speed is everything
dek: Once a firm is in trouble, insiders know first. Key employees leave, suppliers hold back goods, and maintenance is skipped.
more: Once a firm is in trouble, insiders know first. Key employees leave, suppliers hold back goods, and maintenance is skipped. A promoter family that knows more than outsiders may start quietly taking cash out. Every delay destroys value and gives the family more time to extract cash. A healthy system needs an objective early warning that triggers the bankruptcy process quickly.

head: Going concern vs liquidation is a business call
dek: A firm is more than its factory and offices. Its people, processes, IT systems, culture and outside relationships add up to intangible capital that is often worth a lot.
more: A firm is more than its factory and offices. Its people, processes, IT systems, culture and outside relationships add up to intangible capital that is often worth a lot. Caught early, the firm may fetch more sold as a running business than broken up. Caught late, only liquidation is left. Creditors must compare the two (say 40 from liquidation against 70 from a sale as a going concern) as a commercial judgment, not a humanitarian one.

head: The committee of creditors as a bargaining table
dek: Creditors' interests clash. A secured creditor holding a key factory can threaten to wreck a going-concern plan unless paid first.
more: Creditors' interests clash. A secured creditor holding a key factory can threaten to wreck a going-concern plan unless paid first. Decisions need a supermajority, not just 51%. Many good bids are not all-cash; they are promises to repay over years, which forces a judgment about whether to trust the bidder. India's instinct is to turn this into rule-bound, procurement-style bid opening, because its financial firms are bureaucracies. That is a central bottleneck.

head: The loss has already happened, and banks want to hide it
dek: By the time of bankruptcy the loss is real; the only question is who bears it.
more: By the time of bankruptcy the loss is real; the only question is who bears it. Indian banks, especially public-sector ones, keep the loan on their books at full value and delay recognising the loss, including through evergreening (lending the borrower fresh money to repay the old loan). They also fear future CBI investigations, so they act to look good later rather than to recover the most money. Ajay's unorthodox second-best fix: until banking regulation improves, cut banks' voting power in the committee of creditors, since mutual funds, foreign institutional investors, NBFCs and insurers are more commercial.

head: Promoters, poison pills and secret deals
dek: India bars promoters from bidding for their own bankrupt firm. Ajay thinks this is a mistake in principle: promoters know the business best and would likely bid higher.
more: India bars promoters from bidding for their own bankrupt firm. Ajay thinks this is a mistake in principle: promoters know the business best and would likely bid higher. But he accepts the counter-argument. A promoter who expects to return could plant hidden traps that only they can defuse, scaring off other bidders, and weak rule of law means this goes unpunished. The result is two bad extremes: promoters are shut out of formal bankruptcy, while banks quietly restructure loans with them in secret.
printed: A rat trap under the chair

head: Market practice vs waiting for the regulator
dek: In the UK, bankruptcy practice grew for centuries out of common law and the way business was actually done, and was written into law only late.
more: In the UK, bankruptcy practice grew for centuries out of common law and the way business was actually done, and was written into law only late. India expects every step to be written down in law and regulation, so banks won't act without a rule, and outcomes depend on the regulator's quality and its one-size-fits-all rules. Ajay sees this as losing sight of how a market economy works, where creditors negotiate and write contracts that suit them.

head: Judge a reform by outcomes: life in the shadow of the law
dek: Inputs are the law, the NCLT and the committees. Outputs are the bankruptcy cases and how much creditors recover.
more: Inputs are the law, the NCLT and the committees. Outputs are the bankruptcy cases and how much creditors recover. The outcome that matters is a better credit market: borrowers keen to repay, lenders willing to lend, and more borrowing overall. In advanced economies, most disputes never reach court because everyone negotiates privately, knowing what the law would do.

head: No good law in a vacuum
dek: Amit argues that 'the law' is more than the written statute.
more: Amit argues that 'the law' is more than the written statute. It includes the invisible infrastructure of state capability and people's reasonable expectations that the law will be enforced, and when that is broken, the whole commercial culture suffers. Ajay frames the choice as a trade-off. Pass a strong law that underperforms today and improves as the environment catches up, or settle for a weaker compromise suited to current conditions.

head: Reform needs a knowledge ecosystem
dek: Policy improves through a pipeline: data sets, researchers, working papers, blogs, competing proposals and op-eds criticising the status quo.
more: Policy improves through a pipeline: data sets, researchers, working papers, blogs, competing proposals and op-eds criticising the status quo. Ministers and secretaries cannot generate this knowledge themselves. Policy-support organisations that place fluent young staff with officials are a staffing arrangement, not intellectual leadership. India briefly had a bankruptcy research community, but it scattered. Ajay estimates about two papers a year appear where twenty are needed, and without criticism nothing gets fixed.

head: Parallel reforms reinforce each other
dek: Ajay attributes the 1991–2011 successes to many reforms moving at once (capital controls, the equity market, software, telecom), each strengthening the others.
more: Ajay attributes the 1991–2011 successes to many reforms moving at once (capital controls, the equity market, software, telecom), each strengthening the others. Bankruptcy reform suffered because the parallel fix to banking regulation never happened, so badly regulated banks became weak players inside the new process.

head: Zero-base the state
dek: Reform capacity, research talent and philanthropic money are very scarce, so priorities matter.
more: Reform capacity, research talent and philanthropic money are very scarce, so priorities matter. Ajay and Vijay Kelkar start by listing what civilisation and a market economy cannot do without: foreign policy, the military, fiat money, criminal justice, police and courts, a tax system to pay for them, and commercial law and financial regulation. These come first, ahead of causes that feel more urgent on humanitarian grounds, such as health.

head: Amit's opening
more: Amit's opening: 'Firms are awesome, firms are amazing, firms are edifying, firms are illuminating, and when firms are sexually aroused, firms are firm.'

head: Amit told a creator friend who wanted to start a vlog to…
more: Amit told a creator friend who wanted to start a vlog to 'throw things at the wall'. 'Five minutes later he calls back and says the camera broke. So this is not always great advice.'

head: Amit on Japan: it
more: Amit on Japan: it 'not only had zombie firms and zombie banks, she also made a lot of great zombie movies'. He wonders whether to rewatch them for deeper metaphor beyond the surface: 'dead man walking, axe in hand, hand chopped off.'

head: Ajay, on checking whether the Companies Act 2013 had a bankruptcy code
more: Ajay, on checking whether the Companies Act 2013 had a bankruptcy code: 'I have done my fair share of bedtime reading of the Companies Act.'

more: Ajay on whether lenders keep getting fooled by misbehaving promoters: 'The credit markets in India are medium foolish. They are not deeply foolish.'

more: Amit worries that bankers on a committee won't know the first thing about biscuits. Ajay: 'They gave you hundred crore rupees... At that time, they're bloody well going to understand your industry.'

more: After Ajay grades his own creation a 'C grade' bankruptcy process, Amit protests that the work of Ajay, Susan and Bhargavi is 'being dismissed by some random uncle as third rate.'

head: Hindu trinity: Ajay maps creation, preservation and destruction onto the life cycle of firms, with bankruptcy as Shiva's work.
more: Hindu trinity: Ajay maps creation, preservation and destruction onto the life cycle of firms, with bankruptcy as Shiva's work. 'If you'd interfere with any one of them, the great balance of the universe would be disrupted.'

head: Tata Steel: Ajay's proof that old dogs can learn new tricks.
more: Tata Steel: Ajay's proof that old dogs can learn new tricks. 'Tata Steel of 2024 is unrecognizably different from the original Tata Steel of Jamsetji Tata.'

head: SARFAESI Act, 2002: India's first milestone, giving secured creditors rights over collateral. In Ajay's example, if Amit pledges
more: SARFAESI Act, 2002: India's first milestone, giving secured creditors rights over collateral. In Ajay's example, if Amit pledges 'that pretty microphone' and defaults, the lender can seize it. With no forum for creditors to negotiate collectively, it pushed everything toward liquidation.
'Sunlight is the best disinfectant': the quip that follows Ajay's point that banks prefer to negotiate in darkness, one creditor at a time.
'Turtles all the way down': Amit's phrase for how a law broken at its foundations, in enforcement and state capability, damages the whole commercial culture built on top of it.

head: The hosts riff
more: The hosts riff that 'internationalization' should really be said 'I eighteen N'.

head: Ding's Last Blunder: 55. Rf2
dek: The blunder was not a calculation failure. It was a failure to notice that the world had changed.
more: In Game 14 of the World Championship, Ding was a pawn down in a rook-and-bishop endgame that is a theoretical draw unless both rooks and both bishops come off. At move 52 a bishop trade was impossible: the white bishop could step away, and Gukesh's king was two squares too far to support his bishop. By move 54 both conditions had quietly changed. The white bishop was on a8 with only one diagonal open, and Gukesh's king had moved up. Ding, already thinking ahead to the rapid tiebreak where he was the favourite, played 55. Rf2, allowing a rook trade followed by a forced bishop trade. Gukesh did not see it either at first. He said he was about to play Rb3. Then he spotted it, and only after watching Gukesh's reaction did Ding realise what he had done.

The blunder was not a calculation failure. It was a failure to notice that the world had changed. Two elite grandmasters were both stuck in the old equilibrium, just as people get stuck with fixed views of their careers or their partners.

head: Gukesh's Plan: Make Every Game Long
dek: At the top, raw skill is roughly equal. What decides outcomes is preparation, fitness and attitude, the game outside the game.
more: Ding came in poorly prepared in two ways. He had a small team, so he was often surprised in the opening and burned an hour or more recovering. He was also not physically fit. Amit recalls a factoid from his junior days: in a five-hour classical game, a player burns as many calories as a boxer does in a round. Anand did yoga, and Carlsen and Gukesh play sports. Gukesh noticed Ding looked tired and deliberately dragged every game out. In Game 6, Ding was slightly better and offered a draw by threefold repetition, and Gukesh, in the worse position, declined it to keep playing. Fatigue finally showed at the end of Game 14.
At the top, raw skill is roughly equal. What decides outcomes is preparation, fitness and attitude, the game outside the game.

head: Gukesh's Global Team and the Teenager Who Joined Anyway
dek: A great attitude can override narrow rivalry logic. Keymer chose learning over guarding territory, and the team as a whole was built for the job rather than for comfort.
more: On Anand's suggestion, Gukesh made Grzegorz Gajewski, Anand's former second, his head of team. Jan-Krzysztof Duda played more than 300 practice games with him. Radosław Wojtaszek and Harikrishna also joined, which Amit calls 'a slight Polish band.' The seconds worked from Spain on a time-zone schedule so they could prepare while Gukesh slept. Gukesh did not invite Indian peers like Arjun, Pragg or Nihal, who are natural rivals. Yet a 16- or 17-year-old German talent, Vincent Keymer, trained by Peter Leko and himself a potential future rival, joined for the learning. Amit credits two of the match's most spectacular opening ideas to Keymer.
A great attitude can override narrow rivalry logic. Keymer chose learning over guarding territory, and the team as a whole was built for the job rather than for comfort.

head: The Boy Trained Without Computers
dek: How you are trained leaves fingerprints. Forcing yourself to work things out without a crutch can build unusual depth, at the price of gaps elsewhere.
more: Gukesh's early coach Vishnu Prasanna proposed an experiment to his parents: train the boy without chess engines. Until Gukesh became a grandmaster, he reportedly used no computers at all. Today his calculation in complex middlegames is unmatched; Carlsen has said Gukesh finds lines in post-mortems that never crossed his mind. The flip side, critics such as Carlsen say, is odd positional intuition. Amit suspects this may also be because Gukesh skipped the online blitz grind of 2020-21, when other Indians filled the top spots at Titled Tuesday. His rapid and blitz ratings sit 100-150 points below the elite.
How you are trained leaves fingerprints. Forcing yourself to work things out without a crutch can build unusual depth, at the price of gaps elsewhere.

head: How Arjun Erigaisi Became a 'Madman'
dek: Arjun didn't choose his style. A structural constraint forced it on him, and it made him unique.
more: Players who cross 2700 usually get invited to elite round-robins. There you press with White, settle for draws with Black, and 6/10 is a decent score. Arjun got few invites because India already had Pragg, Vidit, Nihal and Harikrishna in that circuit, and organisers won't invite four Indians to a ten-player event planned a year ahead. So he played Swiss-system opens against 2600-2650 grandmasters. Every draw there cost him rating points, so he had to try to win every game. He developed a wild, risk-taking style that Carlsen called that of a madman, and rose from about 2700 to a live peak of 2809, world number two. Amit compares the dominance to Bobby Fischer's 6-0 wins over Taimanov and Larsen.
Arjun didn't choose his style. A structural constraint forced it on him, and it made him unique.

head: Srinath's Board-Three Gambit at the Olympiad
dek: Smart strategy puts people where their specific edge pays off most, not where hierarchy says they belong.
more: At the 2024 Olympiad, Arjun was India's top-rated player, but team coach Srinath Narayanan put him on board three rather than board one. His logic was that Arjun is brilliant at beating 2600s and board three is where he would face them. If everyone else just drew, India would still win. Arjun dominated, and Gukesh scored around 10/11 on top board. That included a miraculous endgame win against Wei Yi, then the top Chinese player with the world's best performance rating, which even Hikaru Nakamura praised. Both the open and women's teams won gold.
Smart strategy puts people where their specific edge pays off most, not where hierarchy says they belong.

head: 'But Don't Come for Class Anymore' (The Disciple)
dek: The choice is not about an activity. It is about identity.
more: In Chaitanya Tamhane's film, Sharad Nerulkar is a purist Hindustani classical singer and teacher. A student's mother says her son wants to join a college fusion band, with one singer doing Western rock and her son doing classical. The boy won't join without his guru's permission, and the mother clearly wants him to. Nerulkar tells the boy he can join. After a silence, he adds that the boy should stop coming to class.
The choice is not about an activity. It is about identity. Doing something repeatedly changes the kind of person you become.
printed: Join the band, leave the class

head: Why Magnus Walked Away From the Crown
dek: Carlsen gave up guaranteed dominance in exchange for the joy of the game, choosing renewal over mastery.
more: Carlsen did not quit the classical World Championship out of petulance. Before each title match, against Caruana, Karjakin and Nepomniachtchi, he and his team spent six months in prep camps memorising engine lines. If an opponent steered into a line he hadn't memorised, he could lose. He concluded his quality of life had gone to bits and that it wasn't really chess anymore. He moved to rapid and blitz, and now to 'freestyle' (Fischer Random, or Chess960), which Bobby Fischer devised in the 1970s out of the same frustration. Carlsen has already lost two Chess960 world titles, to Wesley So and Hikaru Nakamura, but plays anyway.
Carlsen gave up guaranteed dominance in exchange for the joy of the game, choosing renewal over mastery.

head: The Niemann Accusation
dek: Because the accuser was Magnus, the burden of proof quietly shifted onto the accused, which is exactly backwards.
more: At the 2022 Sinquefield Cup, Carlsen lost to American GM Hans Niemann, withdrew, and called him a cheat. Niemann had admitted to cheating online on Chess.com as a 14- or 15-year-old but said that was in the past. Amit first gave Carlsen the benefit of the doubt, but stopped within a few months. Nobody ever offered a plausible mechanism for cheating over the board: broadcasts run on a delay, and players are checked for devices. The 'vibrating anal beads' theory, which Elon Musk retweeted, was never serious. Carlsen never apologised. At the recent World Blitz quarterfinal, Niemann won game two against him, and Carlsen's hands visibly shook in game three before he won games three and four.
Because the accuser was Magnus, the burden of proof quietly shifted onto the accused, which is exactly backwards.

head: Jeansgate
dek: Amit doubts the tantrum would have happened if Carlsen had been winning.
more: At the World Rapid in New York, Carlsen scored only 2.5/5 on day one and turned up on day two in jeans, which breaks the dress code every player signs. Ian Nepomniachtchi had already been asked to change out of sneakers and did. Carlsen's hotel was three minutes away, and he was given until round nine to change. He refused 'on principle,' so FIDE would not pair him. He withdrew from both the Rapid and the Blitz and swore at FIDE on Take Take Take. He then went over the heads of CEO Emil Sutovsky and vice-president Vishy Anand to FIDE president Arkady Dvorkovich and was let back into the Blitz in jeans. He said there were 'no grown-ups in FIDE' and that Anand was not up to his job.
Amit doubts the tantrum would have happened if Carlsen had been winning. A bad mood plus star power turned a dress code into an ego war.

head: The Shared Blitz Title and the 'Short Draws' Clip
dek: Hundreds of players travelled to New York for a tournament that should have a winner.
more: In the World Blitz final, Carlsen won the first two games against Nepomniachtchi, and Nepo came back with a brilliancy to level it. Three sudden-death games were drawn. Carlsen then proposed splitting the title, Nepo agreed, and the arbiter went to consult FIDE. Dvorkovich allowed it. A ChessBase India video of the waiting period later caught Carlsen telling Nepo that if FIDE refused, they should just play one short draw after another. Sutovsky called out the behaviour, and Carlsen said he had been joking.
Hundreds of players travelled to New York for a tournament that should have a winner. Once a system has bent for one powerful person, everyone becomes afraid to say no.

head: Havel on Free Speech (via Salil Tripathi)
dek: A principled person holds the same line when it is diplomatically awkward.
more: At a press conference, journalist Salil Tripathi asked Václav Havel, then Czechoslovakia's head of state, about the argument that feeding people matters more than free speech. Havel said free speech is the most important right, then asked who argues otherwise. Salil replied that it was Lee Kuan Yew, whom Havel was meeting that afternoon. After a silence, Havel said he would make sure to tell him he was wrong.
A principled person holds the same line when it is diplomatically awkward.

head: 'Prisoner Mandela' vs 'President Mandela' (via Salil Tripathi)
dek: Amit calls the answer glib and disgusting. It is a vivid example of how power changes people who once claimed principles.
more: During President Nelson Mandela's tour of Asian countries, while Aung San Suu Kyi was still imprisoned, Salil Tripathi asked whether he would protest her treatment. Mandela conferred with aides and said no. Salil pressed him: when Mandela was in prison, people like Salil had spoken up for him, so why not speak for her? Mandela's reply was that this was a different Mandela now.
Amit calls the answer glib and disgusting. It is a vivid example of how power changes people who once claimed principles.

head: The Blunder Seen Through the Engine
dek: Technology meant to illuminate can stop you from actually experiencing and understanding the game.
more: Amit watched 55. Rf2 on Sagar Shah's stream. The moment it was played, the engine evaluation swung and everyone stood up. Only Tania Sachdev, he says, worked it out from the board, and even Sagar glanced at the computer to confirm. On David Howell's broadcast, which had no engine evaluation, Howell took about as long as Gukesh to see the blunder because he was thinking for himself. Amit also bristles at audiences who clap whenever a player finds the engine's top move.
Technology meant to illuminate can stop you from actually experiencing and understanding the game.

head: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal, the Long Game
dek: Amit would give them the second 'Bharat Ratna for chess' after Anand. Building something for love, without overthinking the market, can shape a whole ecosystem.
more: Sagar Shah, an International Master who never made GM, and his wife Amruta Mokal ran ChessBase India for years as a labour of love. Sagar filmed on his mobile phone, went to under-11 and district events, interviewed small kids and women players without hesitation, and saw little growth for three to five years. During Covid, with comedian Samay Raina's help, the channel exploded and now has millions of subscribers. A clip shows an 11-year-old Gukesh telling Sagar he wants to be the youngest world champion. Another shows Sagar explaining positions to kids sitting on the floor, Gukesh among them. The morning after the 2024 title, Sagar and Amruta flew to Singapore, and Gukesh hugged both of them.
Amit would give them the second 'Bharat Ratna for chess' after Anand. Building something for love, without overthinking the market, can shape a whole ecosystem.
printed: A mobile phone and a long game

head: ChessBase India
dek: Amit calls it outstanding and a pioneer in using computers to educate and illuminate.
more: Amit calls it outstanding and a pioneer in using computers to educate and illuminate. He would give its founders a second 'Bharat Ratna for chess.'
Praised in the chapters on coverage and on Sagar and Amruta.

head: The World Is Not Static
dek: Ding's blunder came from a frozen mental model, not from bad calculation.
more: Ding's blunder came from a frozen mental model, not from bad calculation. The same thing happens in life. Your specialty gets automated while you aren't watching, or a couple stops noticing how each other has changed and becomes 'strangers in the same house.' You can't update your priors every minute, but you should watch for the moment the king has moved two squares.

head: Overestimate the Short Term, Underestimate the Long Term
dek: Ajay's framing of status quo bias. We wave away novel developments as overblown, which makes big shifts feel sudden when they finally land.
more: Ajay's framing of status quo bias. We wave away novel developments as overblown, which makes big shifts feel sudden when they finally land. Waking up and changing course is one of life's great skills.

head: Danger Zone: Almost Home
dek: The worst hiking accidents happen near the end. Tom Vanderbilt finds the same for traffic accidents close to home.
more: The worst hiking accidents happen near the end. Tom Vanderbilt finds the same for traffic accidents close to home. Ding's mind had already moved on to the tiebreak. The sharpness you bring at move 10 fades by move 50, and that is exactly when you're most vulnerable.

head: The Game Outside the Game
dek: Excellence alone entitles you to nothing. Preparation, team, physical fitness and a fighting attitude decided the World Championship more than the moves did.
more: Excellence alone entitles you to nothing. Preparation, team, physical fitness and a fighting attitude decided the World Championship more than the moves did.

head: Hire for the Job, Not the Tribe
dek: An all-Indian team with the comfort of familiar relationships would have been easy.
more: An all-Indian team with the comfort of familiar relationships would have been easy. Gukesh's team was almost entirely foreign, chosen to fix specific weaknesses; Duda, for instance, is a top rapid player. Ajay's lesson for Indian firms: assemble global talent around the task.

head: Intergenerational Transfer
dek: Anand made Gukesh possible. He passed on knowledge and culture, and even suggested Gajewski as head of the team.
more: Anand made Gukesh possible. He passed on knowledge and culture, and even suggested Gajewski as head of the team. Each generation is helped, and also limited, by the one before it, and then hands down something better.

head: What You Do Shapes Who You Are
dek: Gukesh's computer-free training and Arjun's forced diet of opens shaped them into very different players.
more: Gukesh's computer-free training and Arjun's forced diet of opens shaped them into very different players. The same holds for the rest of us. Our company, our habits, and whether we spend time scrolling or reading and watching good cinema all shape our character. Each choice is really about who we want to be.

head: Know the Oddities of Your Origin Story
dek: Everyone's path leaves them with particular strengths and blind spots.
more: Everyone's path leaves them with particular strengths and blind spots. Without whining or beating yourself up, map them. Then decide whether to compensate for weaknesses (longer lives make us more malleable) or to make big bets on your strengths.

head: How Engines Turned Classical Chess Into Memorisation
dek: Engine evaluations assume perfect play from both sides, and humans never play perfectly.
more: Engine evaluations assume perfect play from both sides, and humans never play perfectly. So elite preparation has become a hunt for deliberately suboptimal deviations that only a computer could refute, which pushes opponents out of their memorised lines. Theory has grown exponentially, and every newcomer faces a mountain of it before getting to actually play.

head: Mastery Is Good, Renewal Is Better
dek: People master one form and then run on autopilot, like a brain surgeon who stops reading new papers.
more: People master one form and then run on autopilot, like a brain surgeon who stops reading new papers. Carlsen chose the joy of fresh play over guaranteed dominance. Ajay adds that longer lifespans make spending a lifetime in one unchanging trade far drearier.

head: Familiarity vs Novelty for Spectators
dek: Ajay worries that Chess960 strips away the familiar board that lets casual fans follow along.
more: Ajay worries that Chess960 strips away the familiar board that lets casual fans follow along. Amit replies that casual fans never really read classical positions either. Strong commentators like David Howell, Peter Svidler and Tania Sachdev are the bridge in either format.

head: Power Corrodes Character
dek: Carlsen's dominance, status and business clout preceded his worst behaviour.
more: Carlsen's dominance, status and business clout preceded his worst behaviour. Amit warns he risks becoming Kramnik, a great champion now an embittered accuser of Nakamura, Naroditsky and Gukesh. Much of success is luck. The model for handling power is Anand: powerful, but soft-spoken and working behind the scenes.

head: Judge the Act, Not the Name
dek: Borrowing a line from Hans Niemann: strip away the speaker's identity and evaluate what was said or done.
more: Borrowing a line from Hans Niemann: strip away the speaker's identity and evaluate what was said or done. Forget that it's the world number one and ask whether the behaviour is acceptable from anyone.

head: A Tool, Not a Crutch
dek: Engine bars teach viewers to react to numbers instead of understanding positions.
more: Engine bars teach viewers to react to numbers instead of understanding positions. AI can be used the same way. Use ChatGPT for ideas and polish, but do the writing yourself so your brain keeps working.

head: Love and a Bias for Action
dek: Sagar and Amruta never asked whether there was a market or whether they were good enough.
more: Sagar and Amruta never asked whether there was a market or whether they were good enough. They kept showing up for years out of love for chess. People overthink new ventures. Amit's prescription is to act.

head: Community Organisers Matter
dek: Ajay's addendum: movements need more than the direct doers like Anand and WestBridge.
more: Ajay's addendum: movements need more than the direct doers like Anand and WestBridge. They also need people who tend the community and keep morale and enthusiasm alive. It takes a village.

head: A wink at their own course name: Amit on calling everything
more: A wink at their own course name: Amit on calling everything 'life lessons': 'Well I mean, why not? We haven't trademarked it because like who cares?'

head: Ajay introducing a familiar maxim with a straight face
more: Ajay introducing a familiar maxim with a straight face: 'The great philosopher Bill Gates says...'

head: On Gukesh's seconds Gajewski, Duda and Wojtaszek
more: On Gukesh's seconds Gajewski, Duda and Wojtaszek: 'Slight Polish band kind of happening here.'

head: Ajay on the cosier alternative of an all-Indian team
more: Ajay on the cosier alternative of an all-Indian team: 'the comfort of the relationships and sharing biryani at night.'

head: Amit on outwitting your opponent at chess
more: Amit on outwitting your opponent at chess, 'the way I outwit you the one time we played chess, Ajay, and is there on record as well.'

head: Amit on audiences clapping when Gukesh found the engine's top move
more: Amit on audiences clapping when Gukesh found the engine's top move: 'Are you guys morons? There are probably four or five moves which are fine here.'

head: Carlsen, per Amit, went on Take Take Take and
more: Carlsen, per Amit, went on Take Take Take and said 'Fuck you' to FIDE 'in exactly these many words', and later complained there are 'no grown-ups in FIDE.'
The 'vibrating anal beads' theory of how Niemann might have cheated, retweeted by Elon Musk. Amit: 'shit like that was never serious.'

head: Peter Leko, Keymer's coach, once led Kramnik 6-5 in a World Championship match. Kramnik won the last game to tie, and as the incumbent kept the title
more: Peter Leko, Keymer's coach, once led Kramnik 6-5 in a World Championship match. Kramnik won the last game to tie, and as the incumbent kept the title, 'bit of a tragedy.'
'Power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely', which Amit widens from governments to anyone with power and success.

head: Where the light bulb went off: French healthcare
dek: A successful institution is the visible top of a large stack of supporting systems.
more: Ajay says the French healthcare system is where the idea clicked for him. France runs an unusually good mix of public and private healthcare, while the US spends about three times as much as other OECD countries and gets worse outcomes. A health enthusiast naturally studies France and asks why India can't adopt it. But the French system rests on about a hundred other French subsystems: budgeting, rule of law, product and medical liability, government HR and contracting, and how the public and private sectors behave. Health specialists, swapping ideas between the NHS and the French system, never look at those parts.

A successful institution is the visible top of a large stack of supporting systems. The specialist's depth is exactly what keeps that stack out of view, so the expert is often the one most likely to propose a transplant that fails.

head: The fruit of the poisonous tree
dek: Privacy was protected in the West long before computers existed, through rules that change police incentives.
more: Ajay describes a US doctrine he believes was set by judges around 1938. Suppose a cop taps your phone without a warrant and finds proof you are the murderer. The court throws all that evidence out, because evidence obtained illegally is inadmissible. Without this bright-line rule, cops would never bother with warrants: if they found something, the ends would justify the means, and if they didn't, they would still have blackmail material. Amit adds a second safeguard: investigation and prosecution are separate departments, and prosecutors are judged on successful prosecutions, so weak cases get filtered out before they reach court. Ajay notes that India has neither protection.

Privacy was protected in the West long before computers existed, through rules that change police incentives. When modern Western debates take state restraint for granted, it is because this invisible infrastructure was built generations ago.

head: Lant Pritchett's New York taxi driver
dek: Running a system and designing one are different kinds of knowledge. Practitioners know the 'how'; the 'why' is about incentives, and only the 'why' carries over to a new country.
more: Ajay passes on Lant Pritchett's analogy. Someone with twenty years inside the Norwegian military, the New York Fed or the Bank of England knows as much about policy design as a New York taxi driver knows about how cars work. The driver can steer, brake and read the lights, but knows nothing about why the car was built as it was or what trade-offs shaped its brakes. Practitioners likewise take for granted centuries of institution-building, such as the fact that something like India's Armed Forces Special Powers Act is unimaginable in Norway. Yet Indians often defer to them because they have 'worked twenty years at the Bank of England.'
Running a system and designing one are different kinds of knowledge. Practitioners know the 'how'; the 'why' is about incentives, and only the 'why' carries over to a new country.

head: Sowmya Dhanaraj's bottom-up understanding
dek: Good policy instinct comes from being rooted in a place, not from credentials.
more: Amit names his episode with Sowmya Dhanaraj as one of his top ten on The Seen and the Unseen. She studied under Susan at IGIDR. Her parents worked in a factory, and her mother ran a tea stall on the Coimbatore Highway for many years. Her education was the same as anyone else's, but her thinking rests on lived knowledge of how India actually works, not on frameworks imported from abroad.

Good policy instinct comes from being rooted in a place, not from credentials. Ajay connects this to 'authenticity': if you want to transplant something into Haryana, you need to know whether a truck carrying expensive goods can safely drive at night on a given road there.

head: Swachh Bharat toilets with no drainage
dek: Every intervention depends on supporting systems. Leave them out and the fix can make the original problem worse.
more: Amit recalls a point Shruti Rajagopalan made on The Seen and the Unseen. Swachh Bharat built toilets in villages everywhere, but often with no drainage. Higher-caste households would not handle their own waste, so they had lower-caste people do it, which worsened caste practices. Ajay objects that drainage is visible infrastructure: what kind of water and sanitation expert builds a toilet without thinking about water coming in and sewage going out? Amit replies that things like drainage, water and electricity become invisible because we assume they exist.
Every intervention depends on supporting systems. Leave them out and the fix can make the original problem worse.
printed: A toilet with nowhere to go

head: Air conditioners for Latur
dek: Someone looking from far away, whether a rich donor or an Ivy League policy elite, assumes the infrastructure they live with exists everywhere.
more: After the Latur earthquake, Amit recalls, Japan sent about four hundred air conditioners as relief. Most of the affected places had no electricity, and the survivors didn't need air conditioners anyway.
Someone looking from far away, whether a rich donor or an Ivy League policy elite, assumes the infrastructure they live with exists everywhere. Then the 'API call' fails without anyone noticing.

head: How the show got its name
dek: The name states the episode's argument: no field can be understood on its own terms alone.
more: When Amit and Ajay were choosing a name, they took two candidates from favourite songs: John Lennon's 'Watching the Wheels' and the phrase 'everything is everything' from Bruce Springsteen's 'You're Missing'. Amit picked the second, and Ajay said the song meant a lot to him too. Once they set the songs aside, the phrase still fit because it describes how they try to think about the world.
The name states the episode's argument: no field can be understood on its own terms alone.

head: Premature Imitation and India's Flailing State
dek: It makes essentially the same argument as this episode: India copies the forms of advanced-economy policy too early and ends up with a flailing state.
more: It makes essentially the same argument as this episode: India copies the forms of advanced-economy policy too early and ends up with a flailing state. It also links to Lant Pritchett's work and the idea of isomorphic mimicry.
Brought up right after Ajay stated the transplantation problem; Amit calls it 'this great paper' (and almost mangles the title).

head: Watching the Wheels
dek: A song both hosts love; it was the runner-up name for the podcast.
more: A song both hosts love; it was the runner-up name for the podcast.
One of two favourite songs they considered when naming the show.

head: You're Missing
dek: The source of the show's name and its worldview.
more: The source of the show's name and its worldview.
Amit took the phrase 'everything is everything' from this 'great' Springsteen song, and Ajay said it resonates with him too.

head: Johan Norberg's books and videos
dek: Norberg shows that Scandinavia grew rich through free markets and entrepreneurship first and added the welfare state only after becoming advanced economies.
more: Norberg shows that Scandinavia grew rich through free markets and entrepreneurship first and added the welfare state only after becoming advanced economies. That order matters for anyone who wants to copy Sweden.
Amit says he learned about Sweden and Scandinavia from Norberg and tells listeners to 'please check them out.'

head: Invisible infrastructure
dek: A policy or institution that works in one country depends on many surrounding capabilities: courts, rule of law, liability regimes, government HR and contracting, anti-corruption norms.
more: A policy or institution that works in one country depends on many surrounding capabilities: courts, rule of law, liability regimes, government HR and contracting, anti-corruption norms. You can't copy the visible part (a Norwegian military doctrine, a French health design, a TSMC) and expect it to work where those supports are missing. The supports are not literally hidden. They are invisible because modern specialists don't look at them.

head: Isomorphic mimicry vs. invisible-infrastructure failure
dek: Amit brings in the biological term isomorphic mimicry, and Ajay separates it from the invisible-infrastructure problem.
more: Amit brings in the biological term isomorphic mimicry, and Ajay separates it from the invisible-infrastructure problem. In mimicry, a harmless moth wears a poisonous insect's colours: India sets up a 'central bank' or 'food safety regulator' with all the pomp, staff and conference rooms, but no real people, processes, checks or incentives inside. In the invisible-infrastructure failure, the effort is genuine and the inside is staffed, but the institution still doesn't work because what it depends on is missing. Amit suggests the two sit on a continuum.

head: Every institution makes 'API calls' to the rest of the economy
dek: Ajay uses a software analogy. Each institution calls on capabilities it doesn't own.
more: Ajay uses a software analogy. Each institution calls on capabilities it doesn't own. A military calls 'pensions'; a hospital calls 'product liability' and 'courts'. In rich countries those calls return reliably. Underdevelopment means the capability is missing or unreliable. India's military reforms stalled because military pensions were never fixed as part of an economy-wide pension reform. Courts work the same way: the key measure of a legal system is the chance a case is decided correctly. Ajay guesses about 80% for a UK malpractice case and near a coin toss in India, and that difference changes how the whole healthcare system behaves.

head: Incentives and checks and balances usually come from outside the institution
dek: Ajay's second and third lenses. People inside an institution are self-interested, and their incentives are shaped by the surrounding culture.
more: Ajay's second and third lenses. People inside an institution are self-interested, and their incentives are shaped by the surrounding culture. A canteen vendor in the Norwegian military can't even imagine corruption in food procurement, but Indian conditions are different, and that changes how the whole organisation behaves. Many checks are also inherited rather than designed. The US Inspector General system, built over a hundred years, gives every federal agency a reasonably independent corruption investigator, and new agencies simply assume they will have one.

head: Public choice theory as a superpower for seeing what's hidden
dek: Don't assume the Norwegian general or the French doctor is a good person.
more: Don't assume the Norwegian general or the French doctor is a good person. Ask awkward questions. Why won't the doctor overprescribe for a kickback from the X-ray clinic? Why won't the general take a cut on procurement? Why will a soldier stand and fight instead of running? Ajay says the honest answers almost always lead to the invisible infrastructure.

head: India's privacy fight is against the state, not Google
dek: After WWII, Germany and other OECD countries built checks so that even an elected Hitler could not harm citizens.
more: After WWII, Germany and other OECD countries built checks so that even an elected Hitler could not harm citizens. Add the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine and the separation of powers, and Western privacy debates can assume the state is restrained, which is why they focus on Google and targeted ads. Indian policy people who learned privacy from Western blogs and the GDPR carried that focus into India and sent the debate in the wrong direction. In India the danger is a state that can see everything about citizens without checks.

head: Be wary of specialisation: breadth is the harder, more useful skill
dek: The modern world rewards narrow expertise, because expertise earns respect.
more: The modern world rewards narrow expertise, because expertise earns respect. Ajay argues narrow depth makes you less useful and is the easier path. Build broad understanding, plus the ability to go deep on anything within a couple of weeks when needed. Amit generalises C.L.R. James: 'what do they know of X who only X know'. He adds that more than mastery, people need renewal, because narrow masters stop learning.

head: STEM is easy, humanities is hard
dek: Ajay says he and a colleague once silently agreed on this. Technical knowledge comes from a finite set of books, can be taught, and can be examined; an LLM can quiz you on matrix differentiation.
more: Ajay says he and a colleague once silently agreed on this. Technical knowledge comes from a finite set of books, can be taught, and can be examined; an LLM can quiz you on matrix differentiation. Understanding the world has no syllabus or exam. Amit adds that by 'humanities' they mean learning about the human condition through books, world cinema, music and engaging with life, not today's university departments.

head: Technician vs. thinker (execution vs. strategy)
dek: Narrow depth makes you a technician, a useful part of a machine that people get work out of.
more: Narrow depth makes you a technician, a useful part of a machine that people get work out of. Thinking at a larger scale, including strategy and entrepreneurship, takes breadth. Organisations prefer people who 'shut up and execute' and use strong narrow incentives to keep them that way. That suits the principal, not necessarily the agent. Amit adds that the over-specialised risk being replaced by AI. Like Henry Ford imagining cars when others wanted faster horses, the aim is to think one level above your specialty.

head: Think locally: authenticity
dek: Before transplanting the French healthcare system into Haryana, you have to understand Haryana well, down to whether a truck carrying expensive goods can safely travel a certain road at night.
more: Before transplanting the French healthcare system into Haryana, you have to understand Haryana well, down to whether a truck carrying expensive goods can safely travel a certain road at night. That kind of common-sense knowledge comes only from being embedded in a place. Ajay also warns Indians who want to export Indian successes to Morocco or Mozambique, whose invisible infrastructure is different again.

head: Sometimes the wise move is to do nothing
dek: Ajay admires Sweden ('I confess I'm a soft pinko'), but Indian state capability is a finite muscle.
more: Ajay admires Sweden ('I confess I'm a soft pinko'), but Indian state capability is a finite muscle. It should go to a few problems, and the state should walk away from problems that are too hard or impossible in Indian conditions. His example is that India should not attempt defined-benefit pensions at all; the invisible infrastructure is hostile to them. Amit adds that a market failure is necessary for state intervention but not sufficient. The state should act on things like famines, humanitarian crises and pollution, not on small matters, because India tends to do many things badly instead of a few things well, and every intervention has an opportunity cost.

head: Growth first, welfare state later: the order of operations
dek: Drawing on Johan Norberg, Amit says Scandinavian countries got rich through free markets and entrepreneurship and built welfare states only afterwards, while keeping business easy.
more: Drawing on Johan Norberg, Amit says Scandinavian countries got rich through free markets and entrepreneurship and built welfare states only afterwards, while keeping business easy. Lant Pritchett's paper shows a 99% correlation between human welfare indicators and per capita GDP. Indians who want a Swedish welfare state now are skipping the growth and the invisible infrastructure that made it affordable.

head: Design the state for the worst person in power
dek: Amit says the test of state design is how little damage the worst possible ruler could do, and a constitution is central to that.
more: Amit says the test of state design is how little damage the worst possible ruler could do, and a constitution is central to that. In his view India's constitution fails this test because it centralises too much power, so even good people behave badly with it. Ajay links this back to the episode's theme: the constitution sits at the bottom of every failure of invisible infrastructure.

head: Rocket and payload: fix the foundations
dek: From the Kelkar and Shah book. Take the central statistical organisation.
more: From the Kelkar and Shah book. Take the central statistical organisation. The 'payload' is the domain work: GDP measurement, double deflation. The 'rocket' is most of the organisation: budgeting, public financial management, contracting, HR. If the rocket fails, domain expertise is useless. So more people should work on foundations that cut across sectors, such as rule of law, checks on coercive power, government HR and contracting, and agency governance, because fixing them improves every sector at once.

head: Economic development means more API calls that work
dek: To build a TSMC in India, list its external interfaces: the public goods it needs from government and the private firms it must contract with.
more: To build a TSMC in India, list its external interfaces: the public goods it needs from government and the private firms it must contract with. Firms like Infosys work in India because their particular calls return reliably. In this view, development is the steady growth of a country's public-goods capabilities, its private contracting capabilities and its legal system's contract enforcement, which lets more complex firms take root.

head: Amit's opening
more: Amit's opening: 'Welcome to Everything Is Everything and welcome to the Seen and the Unseen. And no, this is not a crossover episode,' since the episode is all about unseen things.

head: Amit naming Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok's paper
more: Amit naming Shruti Rajagopalan and Alex Tabarrok's paper: 'They did this great paper called Premature uh I was about to say ejaculation. That's not the name of the… Premature Imitation and the Flailing State.'

head: Ajay inverts the old economist joke
more: Ajay inverts the old economist joke: 'An economist is someone who, when something works in practice, wonders whether it works in theory. So here you have something that doesn't work in practice, and so we should understand why it doesn't work in theory.'

head: Amit uses American cop shows to explain the fruit of the poisonous tree
more: Amit uses American cop shows to explain the fruit of the poisonous tree: 'anyone who's watched like a Chicago PD or a law and order would know that… if you get evidence from an illegal search and seizure, it's not admissible.'

head: Post-1945 Germany: Ajay describes the effort, across the OECD and most of all in Germany, to protect individuals
more: Post-1945 Germany: Ajay describes the effort, across the OECD and most of all in Germany, to protect individuals 'even if a Hitler would win a future election a la 1933.'

head: Ajay quotes…
more: Ajay quotes 'the great man Karl Marx' (the tombstone line about philosophers and changing the world). Amit quickly tells listeners it's tongue-in-cheek and that both think Marx's ideas were devastating: 'Groucho Marx is great, but you've got to be careful.'

head: Ajay names his action plan after Lenin's manifesto
more: Ajay names his action plan after Lenin's manifesto 'What is to be done'. Amit replies: 'with hindsight we know is what is not to be done.'

head: C.L.R. James's
more: C.L.R. James's 'What do they know of cricket, who only cricket know', which Amit notes was itself a riff on Rudyard Kipling's 'what do they know of Britain who only Britain know.' Amit ends with his own twist: 'what do they know of depth only depth know.'

head: Amit on Henry Ford and Elon Musk: transport people wanted a faster horse until Ford dreamed of cars
more: Amit on Henry Ford and Elon Musk: transport people wanted a faster horse until Ford dreamed of cars, and 'it takes an Elon Musk to think of Mars. Now, however outlandish, and literally outlandish in this case, you think that is…'

head: Amit teasing Ajay
more: Amit teasing Ajay: 'I know you have depth in eight subjects you are happy to talk about and eight more you will not reveal to the public.'

head: Amit on specialists
more: Amit on specialists: 'they'll get work done out of you for a while. After that, they'll get it done from AI.'

head: Ajay on the Swedish state
more: Ajay on the Swedish state: 'I mean you need to be a real ideologue to be irritated at Sweden. I confess I'm a soft pinko. I love Sweden.'

head: Ajay's second item under
more: Ajay's second item under 'what is to be done': 'there is an obscure YouTube show by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah which is called Everything Is Everything.' The episode ends on the same joke, with Amit adding 'the YouTube shows that expand the discourse, how could you forget that?' and Ajay agreeing: 'to get to those three things, you need great YouTube shows.'

head: Ajay attacks the Swachh Bharat planners
more: Ajay attacks the Swachh Bharat planners: 'What kind of water and sanitation person are you if you think that there'll be toilet but you haven't thought through how the water will come and how the sewage will go out?' Amit, defensively: 'This was not my decision.'

head: Amit plugging their 10.5-hour Seen and the Unseen episode
more: Amit plugging their 10.5-hour Seen and the Unseen episode: 'so if you haven't seen that yet, gentle readers, [it] is a lot for you to gently read.'

head: Outgrowing a Teenage 'Spirituality'
dek: Disbelief can be something you reason your way into slowly rather than a single act of rebellion.
more: Amit says he was always an atheist, but as an 'immature' teen he briefly held a vague belief that spirituality is different from religion and that some vast, unknowable presence governs us all. Life and rationality soon cured him of it. He grants that many people turn to atheism as a rebellion against convention, and that this may have been part of his story too. He only began thinking about atheism seriously as an adult, and his definition of it took shape over a long time.
Disbelief can be something you reason your way into slowly rather than a single act of rebellion. The 'spiritual but not religious' stage is often a halfway house.

head: The Stamp-Collector's Letter to The Economist
dek: Atheists are not a rival tribe chasing influence. They are simply people who don't do a particular thing, and what they ask of the state is neutrality.
more: Around 2007, when Amit wrote his first columns on atheism, The Economist had described atheism as a kind of new religion. Chad English of Ottawa wrote in to object, and Amit reads the letter in full on the show. The letter argues that atheism is a religion only in the sense that not collecting stamps is a hobby, which is why atheists don't congregate or seek power as a group. What atheists want is for officials to keep their religion out of governing, just as a 'philatelist government' that favoured stamp collectors would be a bad government. It signs off: 'See you at the next non-meeting.'
Atheists are not a rival tribe chasing influence. They are simply people who don't do a particular thing, and what they ask of the state is neutrality.

head: Grief Without God: Writing After His Mother's Death
dek: Intellectual honesty sometimes costs you comfort. Amit openly gives up this one piece of ground to religion rather than pretend that reason solves everything.
more: Amit's mother died in 2007. In 2008 he wrote a column for Mail Today called 'What's Consolation for an Atheist?' that took on the one function of religion he admits he cannot replace: comfort in the face of death. He concluded that he couldn't start believing a fiction just to console himself. Grief is grief and has to be dealt with. He adds that he doubts religion consoles much either.
Intellectual honesty sometimes costs you comfort. Amit openly gives up this one piece of ground to religion rather than pretend that reason solves everything.

head: Pastafarianism and 'Don't Insult Pasta'
dek: Gentle satire can expose how arbitrary demands for religious privilege and 'hurt sentiments' are, without any hostility.
more: In 2005 the Kansas School Board was trying to teach creationism. Bobby Henderson wrote to them demanding equal treatment for his own faith, Pastafarianism, whose god is the Flying Spaghetti Monster, and insisting that his beliefs must not be offended either. Around 2007 Amit borrowed the idea for a free-speech column called 'Don't Insult Pasta', declaring himself a proud Pastafarian and demanding that nobody offend his god.
Gentle satire can expose how arbitrary demands for religious privilege and 'hurt sentiments' are, without any hostility. Amit says he prefers this benign way of protesting religion.

head: Ashok Desai on Why Some God-Stories Survive
dek: Myths spread by something like natural selection among stories. What survives is whatever fits human cognition best, which need not be what is true.
more: Ajay passes on an insight from Ashok Desai. Oral traditions were a competition in which people invented and mutated countless stories, and only the ones that were cute and clicked with the human mind got remembered. So the human mind came first, and the sun god and wind god were the hits that survived. Ajay compares it to the many subreddits about JFK's murder, of which only a few become prominent.
Myths spread by something like natural selection among stories. What survives is whatever fits human cognition best, which need not be what is true.

head: His Father's Exit From Hinduism and a Family That Never Went Back
dek: This is a personal example of Ajay's larger thesis: religious belief that isn't instilled in childhood rarely returns, so leaving religion is a one-way door for families.
more: Ajay's father grew up deeply committed to Hinduism and knew it well, then became an atheist as an adult. His atheism was relaxed: he fit in easily among religious people, as Ajay does today. After that switch, religion simply vanished from the family. Ajay and his sisters have none, and neither do their children.
This is a personal example of Ajay's larger thesis: religious belief that isn't instilled in childhood rarely returns, so leaving religion is a one-way door for families.

head: The Moral Animal
dek: Of the many books on natural selection, this is the one Amit picks because it deals specifically with morality.
more: Of the many books on natural selection, this is the one Amit picks because it deals specifically with morality. He read it 20 to 25 years ago and it stayed with him. It shows how evolution produced our better instincts, and it taught him the term 'reciprocal altruism'.
Amit's answer to the claim that morality needs religion, made while explaining how our moral instincts are hardwired.

head: The Selfish Gene
dek: He uses it to correct a common misreading. 'Selfish gene' does not mean humans are hardwired to be selfish.
more: He uses it to correct a common misreading. 'Selfish gene' does not mean humans are hardwired to be selfish. Love, care and altruism are what selfish genes produce.
Amit mentions he cited it in a recent Seen and the Unseen episode on altruism, where he felt his guest misunderstood it.

head: The God Delusion
dek: Amit thinks the New Atheists make many great points about organised religion and dogma that deserve to be taken seriously, even though his own atheism is gentler.
more: Amit thinks the New Atheists make many great points about organised religion and dogma that deserve to be taken seriously, even though his own atheism is gentler.
Introduced as 'the great book' by Dawkins, one of the Four Horsemen of New Atheism.

head: The End of Faith
dek: One of the founding New Atheist books whose critiques of organised religion Amit says you have to take seriously.
more: One of the founding New Atheist books whose critiques of organised religion Amit says you have to take seriously.
Named as Sam Harris's contribution to New Atheism.

head: Sam Harris's conversation podcast
dek: Amit calls it a great conversation podcast and says he learned a lot about the craft of podcasting from it, though Harris has since moved in different directions.
more: Amit calls it a great conversation podcast and says he learned a lot about the craft of podcasting from it, though Harris has since moved in different directions.
Mentioned while noting that the New Atheist movement has run its course.

head: Christopher Hitchens's writing
dek: Amit says he adored Hitchens and misses him. He calls his writing amazing and incredible.
more: Amit says he adored Hitchens and misses him. He calls his writing amazing and incredible. He admires how Hitchens, once a communist, turned away from 'that religion' and became a fearless voice against all kinds of conventional thinking.
Hitchens is named as one of the Four Horsemen of New Atheism.

head: What's Consolation for an Atheist?
dek: It is where he takes on the one function of religion he can't replace, consolation in grief, and decides he won't adopt a comforting fiction.
more: It is where he takes on the one function of religion he can't replace, consolation in grief, and decides he won't adopt a comforting fiction.
Amit's 2008 Mail Today column, written after his mother died in 2007.

head: Don't Insult Pasta
dek: It is a playful satire on demands not to offend religious sentiment: if you don't want me to offend your god, don't offend mine.
more: It is a playful satire on demands not to offend religious sentiment: if you don't want me to offend your god, don't offend mine.
Amit's 2007 free-speech column, inspired by Pastafarianism.

head: Flying Spaghetti Monster
dek: Amit's favourite example of the benign, tongue-in-cheek way to protest religion, by showing how absurd it is to demand special treatment for beliefs.
more: Amit's favourite example of the benign, tongue-in-cheek way to protest religion, by showing how absurd it is to demand special treatment for beliefs.
Bobby Henderson's 2005 letter to the Kansas School Board, which was trying to teach creationism.

head: Falsifiability
dek: He finds it a lovely organising principle. A theory deserves consideration when it makes predictions that could be proven wrong, and that helps us sort our beliefs by how much confidence they deserve.
more: He finds it a lovely organising principle. A theory deserves consideration when it makes predictions that could be proven wrong, and that helps us sort our beliefs by how much confidence they deserve.
Ajay brings up Popper while discussing agnosticism and how strongly to hold our claims.

head: The Euthyphro Dilemma
dek: It shows that even if God exists, morality cannot simply come from divine command.
more: It shows that even if God exists, morality cannot simply come from divine command.
Amit's first example of reasoning about morality without religion.

head: The Categorical Imperative
dek: He finds the formulation 'treat people as ends in themselves, not as means to an end' incredibly deep and beautiful.
more: He finds the formulation 'treat people as ends in themselves, not as means to an end' incredibly deep and beautiful. He says it enriches how we engage with others and has nothing to do with religion.
Amit's second example of morality derived from pure reason.

head: Utilitarianism
by: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill
dek: He thinks it is sound on the whole and worth knowing, but critiques it with Hayek's knowledge problem: the world is too complex to know the consequences of our actions.
more: He thinks it is sound on the whole and worth knowing, but critiques it with Hayek's knowledge problem: the world is too complex to know the consequences of our actions.
Amit's third secular moral framework: the greatest good for the greatest number.

head: Virtue Ethics
dek: It appeals to him because it identifies ways of behaving that make everybody better off and lead to human prosperity, without needing religion.
more: It appeals to him because it identifies ways of behaving that make everybody better off and lead to human prosperity, without needing religion.
Amit's fourth secular moral framework.

head: Atheism Is an Absence of Belief, Not a Belief
dek: The '-ism' misleads people into treating atheism as a belief system. 'I believe there is no God' claims a certainty nobody can have, because you can't prove a negative.
more: The '-ism' misleads people into treating atheism as a belief system. 'I believe there is no God' claims a certainty nobody can have, because you can't prove a negative. 'I don't believe there is a God' just withholds belief from something unproven, the same way you'd withhold belief in pink fairies. The burden of proof lies with whoever asserts the claim. A rationalist atheist would become a believer if God's existence were ever actually proven.

head: Atheist and Agnostic Are Different Axes, Not Points on One Line
dek: People picture a line running believer, agnostic, atheist, with the agnostic as the undecided middle.
more: People picture a line running believer, agnostic, atheist, with the agnostic as the undecided middle. In fact the two words answer different questions. Atheism is about belief. Agnosticism, from 'gnosis', is about knowledge: the view that the truth about God cannot be known. So you can be a believer and an agnostic, or, like Amit, an atheist and an agnostic.

head: Sorting Your Beliefs Into Bins
dek: Ajay builds on Popper's falsifiability to sort beliefs into four bins.
more: Ajay builds on Popper's falsifiability to sort beliefs into four bins. The first is fanciful nonsense that will never produce a testable claim, like Chariots of the Gods. The second is beliefs held because of social programming, peer pressure or political convenience, which everyone has and should be aware of. The third is working bets you expect future evidence to settle. The fourth is hard knowledge built on falsifiable propositions that have held up, like evolutionary biology. Knowing which bin a belief sits in tells you how strongly to hold it.

head: The Four Jobs Religion Does, and Which Ones Reason Can Take Over
dek: Amit lists four functions religion has served: explanation, meaning, morality and consolation.
more: Amit lists four functions religion has served: explanation, meaning, morality and consolation. Science has largely replaced explanation. Meaning has to come from reality rather than invented stories. Morality can be derived without God. Consolation in the face of death is the one function he concedes he has no convincing answer for.

head: The God of the Gaps
dek: Early humans filled whatever they couldn't explain with gods: a sun god, a wind god.
more: Early humans filled whatever they couldn't explain with gods: a sun god, a wind god. As knowledge filled the gaps, these gods gradually disappeared. Some questions may never be answered, but an unanswered question is not evidence for God.

head: Morality Comes First, Religion Writes It Down Later
dek: Amit's sequence starts with evolution, which hardwires moral instincts like compassion and caring for kin.
more: Amit's sequence starts with evolution, which hardwires moral instincts like compassion and caring for kin. Living together then produces norms such as not stealing, not killing, and treating others as you'd want to be treated. These norms vary with local conditions: polygamy where war has left too few men, a ban on pork where pigs spread disease. Religion arrives last, codifies those norms, and sometimes hardens them into dogma. Reason sits on top and lets humans correct their own hardwiring.

head: Reciprocal Altruism: The Selfish Gene Makes Us Loving
dek: Feelings like compassion and family love are genuine, not hypocrisy. They evolved because they helped our genes spread, so the ultimate cause differs from the felt, proximate one.
more: Feelings like compassion and family love are genuine, not hypocrisy. They evolved because they helped our genes spread, so the ultimate cause differs from the felt, proximate one. The common misreading is that a selfish gene makes us selfish. In fact it wires us to care, especially for kin. Favouring kin is the bias that reason later has to correct.

head: The Euthyphro Dilemma
dek: Plato asks whether something is good because God wills it, or whether God wills it because it is good.
more: Plato asks whether something is good because God wills it, or whether God wills it because it is good. If the first, morality is arbitrary and we have no agency. If the second, goodness exists independently of God and before God, so God is merely a broker passing it on. Either way, morality does not depend on religion.

head: Ethics From Reason Alone
dek: Several philosophical traditions reach morality without God. Kant's categorical imperative says to treat people as ends, never merely as means.
more: Several philosophical traditions reach morality without God. Kant's categorical imperative says to treat people as ends, never merely as means. Bentham's and Mill's utilitarianism seeks the greatest good for the greatest number, though Amit's critique is Hayek's knowledge problem: we can't know the consequences of our actions. Aristotle's virtue ethics looks for the dispositions that lead to human flourishing. These schools disagree with each other, and that is fine.

head: The Religion Gene as a Military Advantage
dek: Ajay sets out the standard evolutionary story. Hunter-gatherer bands averaged about 150 people.
more: Ajay sets out the standard evolutionary story. Hunter-gatherer bands averaged about 150 people. Mutations that enabled religious behaviour let much larger groups cooperate as fanatics for an invisible cause. The resulting bigger armies beat smaller secular ones, so the trait spread. There may even be a 'God gene' because believing helped us survive.

head: New Atheism: Every Believer Is Already an Atheist
dek: About two decades ago, the 'Four Horsemen' (Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris, Daniel Dennett and Christopher Hitchens) launched a more assertive atheism.
more: About two decades ago, the 'Four Horsemen' (Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris, Daniel Dennett and Christopher Hitchens) launched a more assertive atheism. They argued that religion causes real harm through irrationality and dogma, and must be spoken against. Ironically, their assertiveness made atheism look like just another competing 'ism'. Amit thinks the movement has played itself out. Ajay counters that the rise of right-wing religious nationalism may justify calling out harmful old beliefs more firmly today.

head: Why Religiosity's Decline Is a One-Way Door
dek: Surveys show religiosity falling worldwide. It fell first in post-war Western Europe, where after Auschwitz faith in a benign, all-powerful God became hard to sustain.
more: Surveys show religiosity falling worldwide. It fell first in post-war Western Europe, where after Auschwitz faith in a benign, all-powerful God became hard to sustain. It held up in the US for a while, then collapsed there too over the last 25 years. Ajay offers two mechanisms. First, faith that isn't instilled in childhood seems as strange as another religion's beliefs, so families that leave never return, and the process only runs one way. Second, conformity: when 70 to 80 percent are religious, people go along, but once belief falls below a critical mass people say openly that they don't care, and the decline accelerates.

head: The Banality of Evil, and Prosperity as the Best Safeguard
dek: Following Hannah Arendt, Amit warns that ordinary people can suddenly commit terrible cruelty, and that neither religion nor rationality prevents it.
more: Following Hannah Arendt, Amit warns that ordinary people can suddenly commit terrible cruelty, and that neither religion nor rationality prevents it. His tentative answer is prosperity, because people with good lives have an incentive to keep the peace, while scarcity and turmoil wear morality down. Ajay pushes back with Nazi Germany, 'the land of Albert Einstein and Beethoven'. Amit replies that Hitler rose out of the ruin and torment that followed World War One.

head: Beware the New Secular Religions
dek: Organised religion is declining, but the urge to adopt a belief system remains.
more: Organised religion is declining, but the urge to adopt a belief system remains. It reappears in ideologies such as Marxism and, today, wokeism, each with its own dogma and excommunications. Amit compares how cancellation spreads (defend someone who has been cast out and you are cast out too) to Pakistan's blasphemy law. His test for whether someone is thinking independently: do they accept an ideological tribe's whole package?

head: Keep the Tradition, Drop the Dogma
dek: Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater. Festivals and rituals give comfort and community, and they evolved for a reason.
more: Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater. Festivals and rituals give comfort and community, and they evolved for a reason. Refusing to celebrate Diwali because you don't believe in Hinduism makes no sense when family gathers and there is light everywhere. Reject the regressive, misogynistic customs and embrace the life-affirming ones, without ever coercing anyone.
printed: Keep the lamps, drop the dogma

head: The Greatest Religion: Treat People as Ends
dek: Amit's final exhortation is that whether you are religious or an atheist, you should not impose your beliefs on others.
more: Amit's final exhortation is that whether you are religious or an atheist, you should not impose your beliefs on others. Atheists who mock believers are behaving badly too. Many of Amit's friends are religious, and neither side tries to dictate to the other.

head: Amit isn't impressed by talk of a future woman US president, since Hillary Clinton already won the popular vote in 2016. His real benchmark
more: Amit isn't impressed by talk of a future woman US president, since Hillary Clinton already won the popular vote in 2016. His real benchmark: 'what I would love to see is, say, a gay atheist in the White House. You know, that'll be the day when I'll say society has really progressed.'

head: Mid-Pastafarianism, Amit swerves into diet advice
more: Mid-Pastafarianism, Amit swerves into diet advice: 'pasta is carbs. Gentle readers, please have a lot of meat, some fat, not much carb, pasta is evil... But except once in a while. But I'm not gonna be dogmatic about this because hey, atheists are not dogmatic, good ones.'

head: Ajay on Kant
