more: Ajay on Kant: 'hear no evil, see no evil, do no evil, and you will never write a bestseller... never use another human being as an instrument and you probably won't gain a lot of power.' Amit: 'Shame shame, how can you say such a thing?'

head: Douglas Adams on natural selection, quoted by Amit
more: Douglas Adams on natural selection, quoted by Amit: 'I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.'

head: Austin Cline, quoted by Amit: a person who truly enjoys their life will do so regardless of whether any afterlife exists
more: Austin Cline, quoted by Amit: a person who truly enjoys their life will do so regardless of whether any afterlife exists, and 'won't depend upon the existence of such a heaven in order for their lives to have meaning or purpose.'

head: Ajay invokes
more: Ajay invokes 'the famous quote' 'After Auschwitz, there can be no art' to explain why, after the war, Western Europeans found it hard to believe in a benign, all-powerful God.

head: Ajay's childhood read, Erich von Däniken's Chariots of the Gods, which he calls…
more: Ajay's childhood read, Erich von Däniken's Chariots of the Gods, which he calls 'obscure nonsense': a fanciful story of beings from outer space starting life on Earth that 'just doesn't make a single testable proposition'.

head: Amit compares wokeism's cancellations to Pakistan's blasphemy law, under which defending the accused makes you a blasphemer too
more: Amit compares wokeism's cancellations to Pakistan's blasphemy law, under which defending the accused makes you a blasphemer too: 'And turtles all the way down.' He cites what happened to J.K. Rowling.

head: Amit sets the scene for why religion arose by describing the pre-scientific world
more: Amit sets the scene for why religion arose by describing the pre-scientific world as 'nature red in tooth and claw', where 'life is nasty, brutish, and short'.

head: The Code That Sabotaged Iran's Centrifuges
dek: This is the cleanest example of an attack that stays below the detection threshold.
more: Israel, long keen to disrupt Iran's nuclear programme, got into the operating system of the industrial controllers running Iran's uranium centrifuges. The code knew the frequencies the centrifuges needed. Whenever scientists told a centrifuge to do the right thing, the code made it do the wrong thing, so machines fell apart and the uranium purification failed. For a long time the Iranians thought they simply had unsolved engineering problems. Even after the sabotage was discovered, they still faced hard questions: who did it, which powers were involved, and how could they respond?

This is the cleanest example of an attack that stays below the detection threshold. The victim pays the full cost while believing it is bad luck, and by the time it learns the truth, attribution and retaliation are still hard.

head: The Anchor Dragged Across the Baltic Seabed
dek: An ordinary object becomes a weapon when its use can be denied. Deniability only breaks when someone physically seizes the perpetrator and starts asking questions.
more: Russia runs a 'shadow fleet' of tankers that carry its crude oil to friendly buyers, including China and India. A Chinese tanker in this fleet dragged its anchor along the floor of the Baltic Sea and tore through gas pipelines, oil pipelines and fibre-optic lines. A crew can simply call this an accident. This time, though, the Finnish Navy boarded the ship and detained the crew for interrogation. Ajay compares this to India capturing Kasab alive in 2008. He sees the incident as a major escalation, with Russia now using Chinese ships to harm the Baltic nations.
An ordinary object becomes a weapon when its use can be denied. Deniability only breaks when someone physically seizes the perpetrator and starts asking questions.

head: The Day Paris Lost Its Fibre
dek: Every small hybrid attack carries a veiled threat: 'if I could do this, what else could I do?' That fear changes the victim's behaviour, and it is how a weak power gets the peacemakers on the other side to argue for appeasement.
more: Russia is believed to have run a test in which about fourteen fibre-optic cables carrying internet connectivity into Paris were all cut at the same moment. It was a highly professional job by people who understood the city's entire network. In peacetime it was 'only' a nuisance that disrupted business for days. The unstated message was that the same could perhaps be done to twenty European cities.

Every small hybrid attack carries a veiled threat: 'if I could do this, what else could I do?' That fear changes the victim's behaviour, and it is how a weak power gets the peacemakers on the other side to argue for appeasement.

head: Crimea and the 'Little Green Men'
dek: Deniability does not need to fool anyone forever. It only needs to delay attribution until the facts on the ground can no longer be reversed.
more: Putin sent men in plain clothes to take over Crimea. They were nicknamed the Little Green Men because they claimed to be a local militia, not Russian soldiers, and the operation was kept tightly secret. The Obama team was fooled for a while and treated it as an internal rebellion that the US should stay out of. By the time it was clear that this was a Putin operation, the Russian army controlled Crimea.
Deniability does not need to fool anyone forever. It only needs to delay attribution until the facts on the ground can no longer be reversed. Slow attribution meant no response.

head: Publishing Putin's Invasion Plan in Advance
dek: Intelligence is usually hoarded, but spending it publicly can defeat a lie before it is told.
more: Before Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the Biden team decided to release its intelligence publicly: the invasion plan, the dates, which tanks would move where. When the invasion came, nobody could plausibly claim it was a local uprising. Ajay calls this the triumph of Western intelligence, in contrast to its failures over Crimea and Iraq.
Intelligence is usually hoarded, but spending it publicly can defeat a lie before it is told. Early, credible attribution leaves the propagandist nothing to work with.

head: Tukaram Omble and the One Terrorist Taken Alive
dek: In deniable warfare, attribution can depend on a single thread. One constable's sacrifice turned an anonymous terror strike into a documented state-backed operation.
more: During the 2008 Mumbai attack, constable Tukaram Omble grappled with Ajmal Kasab on Marine Drive as he tried to get away. Omble kept him from escaping so he could be taken alive, and was shot and killed doing it. Because Kasab survived, India could get the full story of his origins and training and show that this was proxy warfare by Pakistan. Had every attacker died, Pakistan would have kept complete plausible deniability.
In deniable warfare, attribution can depend on a single thread. One constable's sacrifice turned an anonymous terror strike into a documented state-backed operation.
printed: The man who would not let go

head: 1965: Guerrillas Named After Invaders
dek: Proxy war is an old Indian experience: 1948, 1965, 2008. It is the weaker side's tool, and it fails when the population you hope to stir up does not see the proxies as its own.
more: Drawing on Probal Dasgupta's book, Amit says a CIA simulation around 1964 predicted that Pakistan, then booming under Ayub Khan, would attack India in 1966 using proxies. Guerrilla teams would stir a popular uprising in Kashmir while China entered through Sikkim. Pakistan brought the plan forward to August 1965 and sent seven guerrilla teams into Kashmir. It named them after invaders such as Ghaznavi and Babur. The locals saw the infiltrators as foreigners, the uprising never happened, and India pushed them back.
Proxy war is an old Indian experience: 1948, 1965, 2008. It is the weaker side's tool, and it fails when the population you hope to stir up does not see the proxies as its own.

head: Sagat Singh Refuses to Withdraw at Nathu La
dek: Good strategy starts with asking what the adversary actually wants. Sagat Singh's disobedience rested on a better reading of Chinese intentions than his orders did, and its payoff came years later.
more: In 1965 the Indian Army expected China to push through the Sikkim passes, Jelep La and Nathu La, deep into Sikkim. It ordered a pullback so the passes could be defended from wider positions. The general at Jelep La complied. Sagat Singh at Nathu La refused. He reasoned that China might simply want to occupy the high ground, which gives a small force dominance over a larger one below. The Chinese, puzzled that only one pass had been vacated, held off. When fighting came in 1967 at Nathu La and Cho La, they were repelled. Amit argues that a Chinese hold on Nathu La could have cut India off from East Pakistan in 1971.
Good strategy starts with asking what the adversary actually wants. Sagat Singh's disobedience rested on a better reading of Chinese intentions than his orders did, and its payoff came years later.

head: Shuddh Hindi Propaganda Blasted at Jat Soldiers
dek: Even in 1967 armies knew information shapes morale. But information warfare is only as good as its model of the audience.
more: At Nathu La in 1967, the Chinese army translated its propaganda into Shuddh Hindi and played it over loudspeakers at Indian troops. Shuddh Hindi is an artificial register that grew out of the 19th-century political split of Hindustani. Nobody speaks it, and the soldiers were Jats who had no idea what was being said. Assuming the broadcasts were working, the Chinese went from four loudspeakers to twelve. The Indians set up their own loudspeakers and somehow shouted counter-propaganda back in Chinese. Amit calls it 'almost like a comic book thing.'

Even in 1967 armies knew information shapes morale. But information warfare is only as good as its model of the audience. Get the language wrong and you can scale up a useless operation with total confidence.

head: A Real Colorado Rally Organised from St Petersburg
dek: Online influence operations can produce real crowds in real streets, and the aim is less to win an argument than to set citizens against each other.
more: Ajay says there is blow-by-blow evidence that the Internet Research Agency, Yevgeny Prigozhin's outfit in St Petersburg, built up grievance and anger among Americans with targeted messaging. It escalated this all the way to organising a physical Republican protest on the streets of Colorado. He adds that the FBI charged Prigozhin and the IRA over 2016 election interference. Amit accepts that the attempt happened but argues its impact on the election was vastly overstated.

Online influence operations can produce real crowds in real streets, and the aim is less to win an argument than to set citizens against each other. How much such operations actually change outcomes is still debatable.

head: Russia's Campaign Against India's AstraZeneca Vaccine
dek: Information warfare often shows up as an apparently non-political health scare.
more: The AstraZeneca vaccine was developed by AstraZeneca and Oxford, manufactured at scale by the Serum Institute in India with Gates Foundation help, and protected much of the subcontinent from COVID. Meta documented that in 2021 Russian intelligence ran an influence operation in India to cast doubt on it. The goal was to stop Western institutions from earning Indian goodwill. Amit replies that he had three shots of it and is glad he did.
Information warfare often shows up as an apparently non-political health scare. Some of the strange things trending on the Indian internet are run by foreign powers chasing geopolitical goals.

head: Why Everyone Believed Saddam Had WMD
dek: In authoritarian systems the regime lies to itself first, so reading its internal documents means reading its lies.
more: Amit noted that every intelligence agency, including France's, which opposed the invasion, believed Iraq had weapons of mass destruction. Ajay explains what went wrong. Under a tyrant who would destroy anyone reporting failure, Iraqi civil servants wrote fictional progress reports. Those documents leaked to Western agencies, which trusted the paper. Saddam refused inspections, and only an invading army found that the labs were empty.

In authoritarian systems the regime lies to itself first, so reading its internal documents means reading its lies. Good intelligence needs a sociological understanding of how a state actually works. Ajay compares it to Swachh Bharat toilet counts, where fake numbers flow up a bureaucracy until the top believes them.
printed: The weapons that lived on paper

head: The Hamas Short Position That Wasn't
dek: Terror and private profit can in principle mix, which makes attribution harder still.
more: Ajay billed this as 'the world's best story' for researchers. Soon after the October 7 attack, an American research paper claimed someone had taken a vast short position on Israeli markets just before it. The implication was that the plotters made about half a billion dollars from their own atrocity. Amit said the evil of the attack dwarfs any trading profit anyway. The punchline: the paper had programming errors and the result was wrong.

Terror and private profit can in principle mix, which makes attribution harder still. But a sensational finding deserves suspicion until its code has been checked, a lesson Ajay aims squarely at researchers.

head: Concerns About Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI): An Indian Perspective
by: University of Navarra and XKDR Forum
dek: It collects global evidence and fragments of hard information about foreign actors around Indian elections.
more: It collects global evidence and fragments of hard information about foreign actors around Indian elections. Ajay's point is that India cannot assume hybrid warfare only happens elsewhere.
Ajay mentions it as his organisation's working paper on foreign interference in elections.

head: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
dek: It shows that the communal strain has run through Indian society all along.
more: It shows that the communal strain has run through Indian society all along. Secular liberals were the fringe, and politics simply caught up with society.
Listed in the show notes after Amit cited his conversation with Mukul to push back on blaming India's Hindu-Muslim tensions on foreign interference.

head: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It is the long-form version of his argument that foreign powers can only add to divisions that already exist.
more: It is the long-form version of his argument that foreign powers can only add to divisions that already exist.
Amit calls it 'a great episode' while arguing that India's fault lines are homegrown.

head: The Lost Decade
dek: It details how post-2008 economic policy, including retrospective taxation, set the economy sliding from 2011.
more: It details how post-2008 economic policy, including retrospective taxation, set the economy sliding from 2011. Amit uses it to argue that no foreign plotter could have foreseen or planned that chain of events.
Amit cites it while discussing how 26/11 led to Chidambaram's move to the Home Ministry and Pranab Mukherjee's return to Finance.

head: The Grey Zone: Detection, Attribution, Response
dek: War is no longer simply on or off. Between explicit war (Russia and Ukraine) and explicit peace (Japan and the US) lies a grey zone of hostile acts.
more: War is no longer simply on or off. Between explicit war (Russia and Ukraine) and explicit peace (Japan and the US) lies a grey zone of hostile acts. Hybrid warfare is the craft of harming a rival while staying below the threshold of detection (the victim doesn't know it was attacked) or attribution (it can't tell who did it). Either way, a response becomes hard. There is also a time dimension: detection and attribution usually arrive eventually, so short-term players get their punch in, and the bill comes later.

head: Hybrid Warfare Is the Strategy of the Weak
dek: A country that cannot fight frontally turns to sneaky, deniable tactics.
more: A country that cannot fight frontally turns to sneaky, deniable tactics. Russia, with an economy Ajay puts at the size of Italy's, gets outsized returns from cheap hybrid operations. Each small attack, like the Paris cable cuts, carries a veiled threat of bigger ones. That fear strengthens the 'let's just make peace' faction in the target country, as seen in Germany's long softness on Putin.

head: The Hybrid Toolkit
dek: Ajay lists four main tools. (1) Cyber attacks, for example on power grids, routed through friendly countries' IP addresses. (2) Proxies: Wagner, Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed for the ISI, Hamas and Hezbollah for Iran, Russian soldiers posing as Donetsk rebels, and private cyber gangs deliberately grown by Russia and China so governments can blame 'criminals'. (3) Information warfare, where propaganda is old but social media's rabbit holes are the new turning point. (4) Economic coercion and violent acts that stay below the threshold, such as the Baltic anchor drag.
more: Ajay lists four main tools. (1) Cyber attacks, for example on power grids, routed through friendly countries' IP addresses. (2) Proxies: Wagner, Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed for the ISI, Hamas and Hezbollah for Iran, Russian soldiers posing as Donetsk rebels, and private cyber gangs deliberately grown by Russia and China so governments can blame 'criminals'. (3) Information warfare, where propaganda is old but social media's rabbit holes are the new turning point. (4) Economic coercion and violent acts that stay below the threshold, such as the Baltic anchor drag.

head: APT: Advanced Persistent Threat
dek: This is a cyber-security term for attackers who are both highly skilled and sustained over time.
more: This is a cyber-security term for attackers who are both highly skilled and sustained over time. Teenage 'script kiddies' lack the skill, and private criminals lose interest after one crime. Only states can buy the brainpower and keep at it, so an attack that is both advanced and persistent points to a state, even one hiding behind contracted private gangs.

head: The Authoritarian Asymmetry
dek: Authoritarian states can keep secrets and act without legislatures, freedom-of-information laws or lawyers, so dirty tricks come easily to them.
more: Authoritarian states can keep secrets and act without legislatures, freedom-of-information laws or lawyers, so dirty tricks come easily to them. The CIA, by contrast, is tied down by law at every step. Meanwhile the openness of democracies, now distorted by social media, gives attackers an easy surface to exploit. Attack capability sits with autocracies and the exposure sits with democracies.

head: Pouring Oxygen on Existing Fires
dek: Amit pushed back that India's Hindu-Muslim tensions are homegrown, citing the Gita Press history.
more: Amit pushed back that India's Hindu-Muslim tensions are homegrown, citing the Gita Press history. Ajay agreed completely: the raw material cannot be invented. Information warfare looks for a society's weak spots and inflames them, such as the Tea Party and Trumpists in America or communal fault lines in India. Hybrid warfare in general works by finding the point of greatest pain, whether that is the Taj and Oberoi in Mumbai or the long, open Baltic seabed.

head: Division as a Weapon Against Foreign Policy
dek: Through the Cold War, Democrats and Republicans differed in degree but agreed the communist bloc had to be confronted.
more: Through the Cold War, Democrats and Republicans differed in degree but agreed the communist bloc had to be confronted. Ajay argues that today pro-Russian views are mainstream in America, which he calls one of Putin's greatest achievements. A country at war with itself cannot mount a coherent response abroad. Amit counters that Putin invaded no one during Trump's first term, and that the Russia-Trump case needs extraordinary evidence.

head: The Hindsight Teleology Trap
dek: Amit warns against reading history backwards, as in '26/11 happened, Chidambaram was moved, the economy tanked, so the ISI planned it.' Foreign interference serves narrow, immediate aims.
more: Amit warns against reading history backwards, as in '26/11 happened, Chidambaram was moved, the economy tanked, so the ISI planned it.' Foreign interference serves narrow, immediate aims. What follows is a chain of unintended consequences that nobody can foresee. Ajay agrees and cites Karl Popper's argument that complex conspiracy theories are implausible because no small cabal can plan that much. As his example he asks who could have predicted that October 7 would lead to the fall of the Assad regime.

head: Tactical Wins, Strategic Losses: The Rogue-Nation Bill
dek: Hawks in the ISI might score 26/11 as a success.
more: Hawks in the ISI might score 26/11 as a success. But it destroyed global trust in Pakistan: Fortune 500 boards backed away, foreign governments made hundreds of small decisions against it, and its economy suffered from isolation. Hybrid warfare suits leaders who manage headlines rather than countries. At the 'high table' of well-run nations (Norway would never do this to France), such behaviour is off-limits. That is where Ajay says India should aspire to be, which is why he does not see hybrid warfare as optimal for India.

head: Intelligence Is the First Line of Defence
dek: Early detection and attribution weaken an information campaign, because once people know a foreign power is behind it, they discount it.
more: Early detection and attribution weaken an information campaign, because once people know a foreign power is behind it, they discount it. Intelligence has to be sociologically deep, as the Iraq WMD failure shows, and timely, as Crimea shows. The Ukraine 2022 disclosures show what it can achieve. Its scope must also widen beyond traditional war to cover cyber, proxies and influence operations, while accepting that mistakes will still happen.

head: India Is Already a Battlefield
dek: The danger lies in reading about the Baltic or Australian elections and assuming nothing is happening in India.
more: The danger lies in reading about the Baltic or Australian elections and assuming nothing is happening in India. Ajay says that by one estimate about 43% of Russia's Ukraine-war influence campaign targeted India. He also cites Russia's anti-AstraZeneca operation, the 2022 attacks on India's power system believed to have come from China, and the AIIMS hack, believed to be Chinese, which exposed the medical records of powerful Indians. His advice is to wake up, without branding every dissident a 'foreign hand.'

head: India as the Cyber Attackers' Test Range
dek: India calls itself an IT superpower, yet Ajay says global attack groups now use it as a training ground.
more: India calls itself an IT superpower, yet Ajay says global attack groups now use it as a training ground. There are plenty of misconfigured systems, and Indian companies tend to hush up breaches instead of reporting them to vendors, so holes stay unpatched. Attackers debug new zero-day exploits on Indian targets before using them on the West. The fix is to raise standards across public and private systems, starting with India's 'abysmal' government software.

head: Misinformation Is the Larger Sea
dek: Amit argues that foreign state information warfare is a small part of the wider misinformation problem, most of which he guesses is generated at home.
more: Amit argues that foreign state information warfare is a small part of the wider misinformation problem, most of which he guesses is generated at home. Since attribution is often impossible, the sensible policy is to fight misinformation wherever it comes from, whether China, Russia or 'some guy sitting in UP.' Hybrid warfare thrives because it can blend into that existing sea.

head: Protect the Marketplace of Ideas
dek: Amit says most pro-Russian opinion in America is sincerely held, not bought, and a democracy is healthier for having it.
more: Amit says most pro-Russian opinion in America is sincerely held, not bought, and a democracy is healthier for having it. Dismissing opposing views as foreign-sponsored is like the Indian government calling dissidents 'anti-national.' His example of the opposite danger is the Hunter Biden laptop affair, where, he argues, mainstream media and Twitter suppressed a true story as 'Russian propaganda.' Covert foreign manipulation is a real but separate problem, and the two should not be conflated.

head: Epistemic Institutions Are the Real Defence
dek: Ajay matches responses to threats: kinetic capability against proxies and terror ('get guns there faster'), better-engineered systems against cyber attacks.
more: Ajay matches responses to threats: kinetic capability against proxies and terror ('get guns there faster'), better-engineered systems against cyber attacks. For information warfare, the only real defence is a society's ability to establish what is true. That means good data and statistics, universities, researchers, trusted media and believable government bodies. Fact-checkers are only a thin layer on top. Where these institutions are weak, as Ajay says they are in India, every manipulator has a field day. The US came through Cold War propaganda because trusted people spoke up and were believed.

head: Amit's opening
more: Amit's opening: 'we are both men of peace. Shanti Shanti Shanti' who want everyone to love everyone else, 'not in an amorous way, don't get naughty thoughts, but in a platonic way.'

head: On the Finnish Navy boarding the Chinese tanker, Amit imagines the captain asking
more: On the Finnish Navy boarding the Chinese tanker, Amit imagines the captain asking 'Who are you and what do you want?' and getting the reply 'We are Finnish, you are finished.' Ajay helpfully notes that his own version of the punchline was 'and you are finished.' Amit protests: 'Always elaborating on jokes... This man, I gotta tell you, freaking analyze the jokes... Can you improve the copywriting?'

head: Ajay on the Nathu La loudspeaker battle
more: Ajay on the Nathu La loudspeaker battle: 'And pre-Google Translate. Spare a thought for the plight of the Indian soldiers trying to create propaganda shouting in Chinese.'

head: When Ajay announces
more: When Ajay announces 'the world's best story,' Amit says he is 'so excited now' because this sounds like his own habit: 'I'm going to tell the world's best story, South Asia's best anecdote.' Ajay replies: 'We are a linear combination of our influences. So you are reshaping my standards of telling stories.'

head: After the AstraZeneca story, Amit tells Ajay that without the vaccine
more: After the AstraZeneca story, Amit tells Ajay that without the vaccine 'You could have been talking to an empty chair. With sadness in your eyes.' Ajay: 'There would have been no Everything is Everything... Everything is nothing.'

head: Amit's sign-off: the episode was…
more: Amit's sign-off: the episode was 'a primer, a wake up call, and a confession,' because Ajay has been waging hybrid warfare on him with fruit, biryani and sweets. 'You're killing me softly with your sugar.' Now wise to the tactic, Amit vows to resist, though Ajay 'may give me coffee and cheese.'
'Uber for artillery': Amit's name for the bottom-up way Ukrainian forces organise artillery and ammunition, alongside drones striking trenches far behind the front lines.

head: Ajay invokes the…
more: Ajay invokes the 'end of history' mood, a period when the West thought 'everything is going to be hunky-dory' and ignored China's misbehaviour.

'It is Swachh Bharat all over again': Ajay on bureaucracies where fake numbers flow upward until leaders believe them, as in Saddam's Iraq. 'Because a document says we built so many toilets, it doesn't mean you should start cheering.'

head: Karl Popper's case against complex conspiracy theories, invoked by Ajay: nobody can plan that much
more: Karl Popper's case against complex conspiracy theories, invoked by Ajay: nobody can plan that much, 'least of all a secret small cabal of conspirators.'

head: Sarajevo: Ajay says no ISI officer can claim, like the man who…
more: Sarajevo: Ajay says no ISI officer can claim, like the man who 'committed one murder in Sarajevo and then the whole world went aflame,' credit for every domino that fell after 26/11.

head: Ajay asks…
more: Ajay asks 'Who could have predicted that the October 7 attack would lead to the fall of the Assad regime?' as an illustration of the law of unintended consequences.

head: Crying at a beautiful sentence
dek: This is his case for letting men cry. Men who bottle up emotion hide their true selves from others and also from themselves, and that missing self-knowledge does harm.
more: Amit admits he cries not only when he is sad but when something is beautiful. The title story of Ken Liu's The Paper Menagerie made him weep, and across the whole collection he would tear up at random sentences purely for their elegance and rhythm. On Episode 200 of The Seen and the Unseen with Shruti Rajagopalan, he planned to read out a favourite Dilip Chitre poem, knew he would break down, and started sobbing. She ended up reading it instead.

This is his case for letting men cry. Men who bottle up emotion hide their true selves from others and also from themselves, and that missing self-knowledge does harm. Ajay adds that the macho script is a leftover of agricultural patriarchy, and a post-industrial world can drop it.

head: Josh Felman's two-word cure for gossip
dek: One respected person refusing to play along can set the culture of a whole room.
more: In Ajay's professional circle, his good friend Josh Felman was an older figure who commanded respect. Whenever a conversation slid toward who was sleeping with whom, Josh would put his hands down and say, 'It's not important.' Ajay ties this to the maxim that little minds discuss people, medium minds discuss news, and great minds discuss ideas.

One respected person refusing to play along can set the culture of a whole room. Ajay's broader advice is to guard your hours: spend them on big ideas and understanding the world, because the rest is petty bickering you should have outgrown after school.

head: Why stop before Kanyakumari?
dek: Deep into a long walk, the trip stops being a project with an endpoint.
more: Ajay logs about twenty trail days a year, roughly ten in the Sahyadris and ten in the Himalayas. He and Ayush Patnaik were walking a north-south route through the Sahyadris in Maharashtra. By day eight or nine they looked at each other and realised they could simply keep going, ten to thirty kilometres a day, all the way to Kanyakumari.
Deep into a long walk, the trip stops being a project with an endpoint. The question shifts from 'when do we finish?' to 'why would we ever stop?' That state is the core of Ajay's love for hiking.

head: Who would you take on your last hike?
dek: It is a small, warm picture of the kind of friendship the hosts describe elsewhere in the episode: deep, respectful, and expressed through quiet gestures rather than declarations.
more: Amit is not a hiker. The day before the shoot, the crew asked Ajay who he would take with him if he were going on a last hike, and Ajay answered, 'Amit, will you come?' Amit says it made everyone tear up a bit, and he only realised later how much it meant. He then deflects with a joke that he has no expertise to add, since Ajay doesn't like people talking without expertise.
It is a small, warm picture of the kind of friendship the hosts describe elsewhere in the episode: deep, respectful, and expressed through quiet gestures rather than declarations.

head: Dad's three-at-a-time comics ration
dek: It is a fond memory of a father and son playing game theory with each other.
more: In early-1980s Chandigarh, foreign comics were nearly impossible to find beyond the likes of Phantom and Indrajal. Amit's father found a supplier in Delhi and brought back batches of Marvel and DC comics from his trips. He handed them over only three at a time, claiming that was all he had. Amit knew there were more and schemed to get them faster, and his father knew Amit was playing the game. Amit calls it an early game of poker. Through these comics he fell for Marvel's characters, who were shades of grey rather than caricatures.

It is a fond memory of a father and son playing game theory with each other. It also explains Amit's split verdict on Marvel: the comics' morally complex universe, created by Stan Lee and his collaborators, is underrated, while the Marvel Cinematic Universe is a cynical franchise exploitation.

head: The one awkward hug
dek: Most people never see their parents as real humans; they see the job description of 'father' or 'mother', and everyone is winging it.
more: Amit's mother died in 2008. In his last years, his father in Chandigarh seemed to be trying to reach out. Once, as Amit was getting into his Uber after a visit, his father opened his arms, something he had never done because they had never really hugged. Amit gave him a very awkward hug. He had also once sat his father down with a recorder for a couple of hours to preserve his life story, but it was a one-off, and much remained unsaid.

Most people never see their parents as real humans; they see the job description of 'father' or 'mother', and everyone is winging it. Amit's exercise: estimate your age, their life expectancy and how often you meet, then count how many visits you have left. The number will be small enough that you should call them right after the show.

head: The accidental best prawns ever
dek: Culinary experimentation is underrated. Amit hates pineapple on pizza but defends people's right to try it, and he likes chowmein dosa, because all food evolved from something else.
more: During his one-meal-a-day phase (eating between 5 and 7 pm, ten kilos lighter), Amit cooked three-course meals for himself. He once marinated prawns in gochugaru, olive oil and gin, then cooked them in olive oil with lots of butter and bird's-eye chilli. His mind was blown twice over: it was the best prawn he had ever eaten, and he had made it. He then jokingly turned Ajay's Musk argument on himself, calling it 'the Elon Musk of my food', a survivorship-bias fluke.

Culinary experimentation is underrated. Amit hates pineapple on pizza but defends people's right to try it, and he likes chowmein dosa, because all food evolved from something else. Ajay adds his honey-in-bread logic: that is how we keep inventing stuff.

head: 'Look closely. They are all the same.'
dek: Behind the delightful rant is a real point: cosmetic procedures sand away human variety.
more: Over tea while recording a Seen and the Unseen episode, a friend, 'a distinguished gentleman who also happens to be gay', mentioned that young celebrities in their twenties had done Botox. When Amit was shocked, the friend said that was nothing: they had boob jobs too. Then he leaned forward and told Amit to go out and look closely at the breasts of young women today, because they are all the same. In his time there was variety and diversity, and this was a scandal. Amit says he did not follow the instructions.

Behind the delightful rant is a real point: cosmetic procedures sand away human variety. Amit's stance is to be comfortable in your own body, with exceptions for genuine health issues or accident reconstruction, and to treat anyone who judges your looks as toxic. Ajay links it to fashion: these are superficial props, and the real journey is building character.

head: How Amit became an Asian poker champion
dek: When a game is new, first-principles thinkers beat people relying on inherited heuristics.
more: Amit was a professional poker player for five years, until 2015. A friend who owned the Haryana Hawks in an IPL-style league for match poker brought him out of retirement. Match poker changes the rules so the usual heuristics no longer work. Amit worked the new game out from first principles, nobody else did, and the Hawks won twice. He then played for India and won the Asian championship. At the world championship in Greece the team got slaughtered, partly because three teammates couldn't get visas and replacements had to be taught the strategy on the fly. He had a similar run in chess.com variants, briefly reaching number one in Atomic and Fog of War before getting bored.

When a game is new, first-principles thinkers beat people relying on inherited heuristics. The story also gives his limited, tongue-in-cheek defence of 'playing for the country': in some sports, such as Olympic disciplines, the national team is the only stage available.

head: Running in the rain is talent
dek: Talent alone is overrated. What gets called talent is mostly attitude, love for the thing, and constant iteration.
more: About twenty-five years ago Amit read an interview with an athlete whose name he can no longer recall. The athlete redefined talent this way: you're due to run at 5 am, you were up late, you're hungover with a cold, your next event is six months away, and it's raining. You still go running. That, the athlete said, is talent.
Talent alone is overrated. What gets called talent is mostly attitude, love for the thing, and constant iteration. Widen the definition to include showing up on bad days.

head: Modafinil and the 100-point chess bump
dek: His rule is that pharmacology should be a tool, not a crutch. It is not a substitute for sleep, exercise and good habits, and you should check the research and FDA approval rather than follow fashion.
more: Amit has sleep apnea, which he says leads to narcolepsy, so modafinil is legitimate for him. He takes it on recording days to stay lucid through eight-hour podcasts, after reading the scientific studies on its side effects. He plays bullet chess like an addict, with no desire to improve. He has noticed that his chess.com rating goes up about a hundred points when he is on keto or modafinil and drops back when he stops, so he treats it as a rough gauge of mental sharpness.

His rule is that pharmacology should be a tool, not a crutch. It is not a substitute for sleep, exercise and good habits, and you should check the research and FDA approval rather than follow fashion. Ajay pushes back: he prefers no props at all, not even caffeine, as part of building character.

head: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
dek: It is the essay behind Amit's podcast name, and Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson was directly based on it.
more: It is the essay behind Amit's podcast name, and Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson was directly based on it.
Mentioned as the source of the title of Amit's podcast, The Seen and the Unseen.

head: Economics in One Lesson
dek: Amit calls it a great book that carries Bastiat's economic thinking forward.
more: Amit calls it a great book that carries Bastiat's economic thinking forward.
Cited as a book shaped by Bastiat's seen-and-unseen essay.

head: The Blank Slate
dek: It examines many aspects of human society and life through the lens of our evolutionary hardwiring.
more: It examines many aspects of human society and life through the lens of our evolutionary hardwiring. Amit says, with admitted hyperbole, that he divides his life into before and after reading it, because it was his gateway into natural selection and evolutionary theory.
A mid-episode recommendation during the discussion of evolution and 'know thyself'.

head: Bob Dylan's own recordings (e.g. Lay Lady Lay)
dek: Dylan's voice is authentic to his music, and some songs only he can sing; Amit and the crew sang Lay Lady Lay to prove it needs his nasal twang.
more: Dylan's voice is authentic to his music, and some songs only he can sing; Amit and the crew sang Lay Lady Lay to prove it needs his nasal twang. Amit also loves the covers, such as Springsteen's Chimes of Freedom and The Byrds' versions. He wrote a piece defending Dylan's Nobel as rightly given, though he warns against America-England-centric 'greatest ever' hyperbole.
Amit's rebuttal to Ajay calling Dylan a bad singer who should have left the singing to others.

head: A Country Is Not a Company (Everything is Everything episode)
dek: Ajay says it should be recommended viewing for Mr Musk, given the 'great man syndrome' of rich people opining on everything, including how to run a government.
more: Ajay says it should be recommended viewing for Mr Musk, given the 'great man syndrome' of rich people opining on everything, including how to run a government.
Ajay's argument that Elon Musk is overrated.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: Hayek understood the complexity of the world and wrote about it lucidly.
more: Hayek understood the complexity of the world and wrote about it lucidly. Amit feels people like him and Ajay have a duty to keep these ideas alive and push people to go to the source and read the man.
Part of Amit's 'Hayek: underrated' verdict. The hosts discussed it in their Four Papers That Changed the World episode.

head: India Moving
dek: An excellent book that makes an eye-opening point: most internal migration in India happens when women marry and move to their husband's home, uprooting their friends and their way of life.
more: An excellent book that makes an eye-opening point: most internal migration in India happens when women marry and move to their husband's home, uprooting their friends and their way of life.
Amit's correction that the hosts were taking a privileged male view of marriage.

head: El Amor de Mi Vida
dek: Lines like 'I only wish it had been us, but I'm happy for your happiness' show true love as wanting the other person to be happy, not owning them.
more: Lines like 'I only wish it had been us, but I'm happy for your happiness' show true love as wanting the other person to be happy, not owning them. Amit finds them deeply moving.
Read out during the marriage discussion to illustrate love without possession.

head: The Wind
dek: Amit calls it a great album. Zevon made it after a terminal diagnosis, knowing he would die, surrounded by friends who played with him.
more: Amit calls it a great album. Zevon made it after a terminal diagnosis, knowing he would die, surrounded by friends who played with him.
The album containing El Amor de Mi Vida.

head: The Cats
dek: It is a delightful portrait of creatures who find glory in a dehydrated pea and find themselves 'so remarkable all the day long'.
more: It is a delightful portrait of creatures who find glory in a dehydrated pea and find themselves 'so remarkable all the day long'. Ajay called it an aspirational statement; Amit called cats sociopaths.
Read aloud as 'the ultimate navel gazing poem', which Amit had sent the crew on WhatsApp the day before.

head: Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat
dek: It teaches you to think in four elements, how they act and combine. That makes it a great way to cook organically and go with the flow without always geeking out.
more: It teaches you to think in four elements, how they act and combine. That makes it a great way to cook organically and go with the flow without always geeking out.
A mid-episode recommendation during the pineapple-on-pizza and food experimentation segment.

head: A Poetry Handbook
dek: It covers the mechanics of language, not just of poetry. Amit says you will fall in love with language all over again, and he turns to poetry in his moments of deepest emotion.
more: It covers the mechanics of language, not just of poetry. Amit says you will fall in love with language all over again, and he turns to poetry in his moments of deepest emotion.
A mid-episode recommendation when poetry came up.

head: The Broken Script
dek: It is a great history of Delhi from 1803 to 1857.
more: It is a great history of Delhi from 1803 to 1857. It shows that poetry was popular culture then, with newspapers routinely publishing poems even before Bahadur Shah Zafar's reign, so the trend can't be explained by poets currying favour with the emperor.
Cited in response to Ajay's observations about poetry and language in India. Amit had done an episode with Liddle.

head: Why We Sleep
dek: Amit says this book taught him how underrated sleep is. Without good sleep you cannot be the best version of yourself.
more: Amit says this book taught him how underrated sleep is. Without good sleep you cannot be the best version of yourself.
The sleep segment.

head: Matthew Walker's episode on the Huberman Lab podcast
dek: In it, Walker explains the importance of sleep.
more: In it, Walker explains the importance of sleep.
Recommended right after Why We Sleep.

head: Inverting the Pyramid
dek: It is a great book on football tactics. It helps you watch sport with deeper attention, as the chess game underneath, instead of in a shallow, tribal 'my team is winning' way.
more: It is a great book on football tactics. It helps you watch sport with deeper attention, as the chess game underneath, instead of in a shallow, tribal 'my team is winning' way.
A mid-episode recommendation in the sports segment, after Amit watched Manchester City with Vaishnav.

head: The Blue Book, The Yellow Book and The Green Book
dek: The books are journals combining writing and drawing, and they model the daily writing habit Amit says will shape you into a richer, deeper person.
more: The books are journals combining writing and drawing, and they model the daily writing habit Amit says will shape you into a richer, deeper person.
Amit's plea to journal, in the writing segment. He has done three episodes with Kumar about writing.

head: People are brains, not stomachs: why cities are underrated
dek: Population density is a strength, not a problem. Cities bring diverse people together, which enlarges your worldview and your exposure to art, culture and ideas.
more: Population density is a strength, not a problem. Cities bring diverse people together, which enlarges your worldview and your exposure to art, culture and ideas. Bigger economic networks also let people specialise more deeply and rise to prosperity, and people keep voting with their feet by moving there despite griping about traffic. Ajay adds that villages are hotbeds of ignorance, superstition and unfreedom (Amit cites Ambedkar's 'dens of ignorance'), so moving to the city is the beginning of freedom.

head: Curiosity as extended juvenility
dek: Mainstream culture treats curiosity as cute and childish. Ajay argues that staying childlike in your curiosity is what greatness is made of.
more: Mainstream culture treats curiosity as cute and childish. Ajay argues that staying childlike in your curiosity is what greatness is made of. Amit adds that most adults lose it, settle into a groove, stop reading and watching, and constrict their world. So when a friend complains about losing three hours in a rabbit hole irrelevant to his life, Amit's response is: fantastic, that is what you should do.

head: Evolution as a universal lens, and 'know thyself' without the is-ought trap
dek: Ajay notes that evolutionary thinking applies far beyond biology: jihadist groups in Iraq, business models and software all evolve under selection pressure.
more: Ajay notes that evolutionary thinking applies far beyond biology: jihadist groups in Iraq, business models and software all evolve under selection pressure. Amit argues you cannot know yourself without evolutionary biology and psychology, because we are not blank slates. Explaining why we feel something doesn't make the feeling right, though: deriving an 'ought' from an 'is' is a fallacy, and our instincts often contradict each other. Rationality lets us choose which hardwiring to dampen and which to amplify.

head: Do things you can undo: the case against the death penalty
dek: Amit has moral qualms about killing, but his deeper objection is that even in advanced economies the state is a fumbling beast.
more: Amit has moral qualms about killing, but his deeper objection is that even in advanced economies the state is a fumbling beast. Innocent people have been executed and later exonerated by DNA evidence, and execution is irreversible. Ajay cites a public-policy principle, 'do things that you can undo', whose author footnotes it as a reason to oppose capital punishment. Ajay adds a second argument: whoever holds the sword of the death sentence over you, whether policeman, prosecutor or judge, gains absolute power, so harsh penalties corrode state capability.

head: Dictatorship is a lottery, and 'he'll only crush my neighbours' is a fallacy
dek: Ajay argues that without democracy's checks, debate and epistemic institutions, outcomes depend on the luck of the draw.
more: Ajay argues that without democracy's checks, debate and epistemic institutions, outcomes depend on the luck of the draw. Some dictators will turn out well by chance, just as some monkeys will pick good portfolios, but that doesn't make the system good. He also diagnoses middle-class fondness for strongmen: people assume the dictator will crush their annoying neighbours but leave their own freedoms intact, which ignores five thousand years of history. Amit adds that the state exists to serve us, and that dictatorships always end badly.

head: Survivorship bias versus the need for moonshots (the Musk debate)
dek: Ajay sees Musk as the visible winner among many dice-rollers, the same trap as venerating a 'great fund manager'.
more: Ajay sees Musk as the visible winner among many dice-rollers, the same trap as venerating a 'great fund manager'. He also argues that a rough idea to reform the state (like reforming the RBI) is very different from the lifetime of skill needed to actually do it. Amit counters that few people even attempt such audacious, contrarian bets in electric cars, batteries and space. Even if only one in a hundred succeeds, we need all hundred, because that one changes the world. On DOGE, Amit says Musk's real argument is not 'I ran a company' but that the state is too large and oppressive.

head: Failure is underrated: wish young people failure
dek: Amit credits whatever is good in him to failing all his life. It stripped away his hubris and sense of entitlement, made him humble about learning, and turned him from a whiner into a doer.
more: Amit credits whatever is good in him to failing all his life. It stripped away his hubris and sense of entitlement, made him humble about learning, and turned him from a whiner into a doer. Early success, by contrast, can go to people's heads. Ajay adds that mass culture worships billionaires despite how much luck is involved, and mentions an old Marwari culture in which a man's worth is measured by the number of failed businesses he has run.

head: Heretics versus reverence for knowledge
dek: This was the episode's sharpest disagreement. Amit argues that flat-earth theory is nonsense, but heretical thinking is how humanity progresses.
more: This was the episode's sharpest disagreement. Amit argues that flat-earth theory is nonsense, but heretical thinking is how humanity progresses. Heliocentrism was once heresy, and 'sugar is fine, fat is the problem' was once settled consensus, enshrined in 1977 US dietary guidelines just before the obesity epidemic. Outsiders like Mendel and Semmelweis were ignored. Ajay argues that experts define what is open for debate (intermittent fasting is, flat earth isn't), and a teenager deciding on Reddit whether a COVID vaccine works is the post-truth crisis. They partly converge: an ordinary person can default to the conventional view, while genuine heretics should still publish. They still split on whether social media is a net positive (Amit, who built his career on it) or a net negative (Ajay).

head: Whiners and doers
dek: At a party, their friend Bhargavi asked guests to complete the sentence 'There are two kinds of people in the world.' Amit's answer: whiners and doers.
more: At a party, their friend Bhargavi asked guests to complete the sentence 'There are two kinds of people in the world.' Amit's answer: whiners and doers. Doers create a virtuous cycle of encouragement and positivity in which good things happen. Whiners create a vicious cycle of cribbing, resentment and bitterness that drags everyone down. So choose friends who make you a better version of yourself, and watch for toxic negativity in your circle.

head: Frugality buys freedom
dek: Ajay frames it in financial terms: the lower the fixed commitments of your life, its operational leverage, the freer you are.
more: Ajay frames it in financial terms: the lower the fixed commitments of your life, its operational leverage, the freer you are. Amit adds that clearing out the inessential frees up cognitive space. He could live out of a suitcase, because the real value is already in the cloud and in his relationships, and gadgets are replaceable. He refuses to be dogmatic, though: small indulgences like books, good food and comfortable travel are fine if you can afford them. Just don't buy private jets.

head: Amit's 'Bengali' theory of happiness
dek: In a dark moment, Amit realised that ending his life was an option that never expires, so there was no hurry.
more: In a dark moment, Amit realised that ending his life was an option that never expires, so there was no hurry. In classic Bengali-procrastination style it could always wait, while something in this very moment could lift his mood. He stresses that anyone with suicidal thoughts should get help. From this came his theory of happiness: real happiness is mostly unselfconscious and noticed in hindsight, and narrating it (posting it on Instagram) can kill it, like Schrödinger's cat. Even so, at any instant you can make the next moment happier with a small act: a song, a call to a friend, some bacon.

head: The consent argument against having children
dek: In a deliberately provocative, tongue-in-cheek column, Amit argued it is immoral to have children.
more: In a deliberately provocative, tongue-in-cheek column, Amit argued it is immoral to have children. This is not the usual consequentialist 'the world is going to hell' case but a moral one built from three propositions most people accept. A child cannot consent to being born, will feel pain and will die. He then shrugs that we do many 'sinful' things, like the white lies that sustain friendships, so go ahead if you want kids. Ajay rates parenthood underrated: parent-child journeys are among life's great ones, once you strip away resource-intensive, helicopter, performative and competitive parenting.

head: Breadth over specialisation, and why STEM gets the prestige
dek: Understanding the world needs breadth: art, literature, cinema and music, which narrow IIT-IIM tracks often skip.
more: Understanding the world needs breadth: art, literature, cinema and music, which narrow IIT-IIM tracks often skip. Ajay argues breadth takes years of deliberate investment and most people fail at it. He also explains why STEM enjoys outsized prestige: it is easy to teach and test. You can prove Pythagoras in an exam, then be thrown Apollonius' theorem and prove that too. Testability isn't everything, though. Amit's twist: humanities departments are overrated and disconnected from reality, so get your humanities education from life itself.

head: Legacy is vanity
dek: Amit thinks validation is overrated in life and irrelevant after it. What matters is leaving the world a little better and helping the people around you become their best selves, not being remembered.
more: Amit thinks validation is overrated in life and irrelevant after it. What matters is leaving the world a little better and helping the people around you become their best selves, not being remembered. Ajay gives the materialist version: you are a temporary arrangement of atoms, and there is nothing after.

head: Marriage as an unbundleable package
dek: In a frame Amit credits to Ajay, marriage bundles love, sex, romance, companionship, parenthood and friendship.
more: In a frame Amit credits to Ajay, marriage bundles love, sex, romance, companionship, parenthood and friendship. We rarely unbundle it in our heads, so when one strand fails, everything seems to collapse. Ajay sees the institution as an artefact of the agricultural world of religion and patriarchy, mismatched with a post-industrial age that resembles the hunter-gatherer one. The 20th century also loaded a single person with being your everything. Amit adds that for most Indian women outside privileged elites, marriage is closer to imprisonment; per Chinmay Tumbe, it is the largest driver of internal migration.

head: Surrounded by miracles we take for granted
dek: Ajay notes that his and Amit's generation grew up amid the bounty of the scientific revolution.
more: Ajay notes that his and Amit's generation grew up amid the bounty of the scientific revolution. A studio mic would have seemed impossible a century ago, and at XKDR Forum they rent a GPU for eight dollars an hour, which buys unimaginable capability. At their incomes, gadgets have become trivial, which is exactly why chasing business jets seems pointless. Meanwhile, mass poverty means India still faces a hundred-year journey before everyone has such access.

head: Social media: race to the bottom, or the best minds on tap
dek: Amit accepts the harms.
more: Amit accepts the harms. Haidt's research links social media to teenage depression, especially among girls who compare their real selves with friends' projected selves on Instagram, unlike the feared effects of video games on boys, which never materialised. He also says Facebook reportedly suppressed its own study. Engagement incentives feed tribalism: you gain status by attacking the other side and policing your own side's purity. But curate your 'following' feed and you get something that would have been magical in the 1980s, and for outsiders like him it put the means of production in their hands.

head: Introspection versus navel gazing
dek: Self-reflection that recursively spirals into the self, which Amit calls the Bengali way, is self-indulgent.
more: Self-reflection that recursively spirals into the self, which Amit calls the Bengali way, is self-indulgent. Ajay suggests indulging in the world instead, which ends up enhancing yourself. Genuine self-examination is underrated: Amit reckons 99% of people never do it, and he didn't for much of his life. Ajay pins down the difference in what the two English words convey.

head: State and society, with markets and NGOs as tools of society
dek: Raghuram Rajan and Rohini Nilekani frame the world as three pillars: state, markets and society.
more: Raghuram Rajan and Rohini Nilekani frame the world as three pillars: state, markets and society. Amit disputes this, as he did with Nilekani on his show. He sees only state and society. Markets and NGOs are both mechanisms through which people voluntarily meet each other's needs. NGOs fill real gaps, but fall into a common trap: founders end up fundraising instead of doing the work, and they chase donors' wishes. They are also incentivised to exaggerate how bad the problem is. Ajay values work outside markets and coercion, but calls humanitarianism a band-aid on a gigantic wound that economic growth would heal at the root.

head: Happiness is remembered; life is a collection of peak experiences
dek: Ajay defends nostalgia: as you age, you realise life is about accumulating amazing moments and stories, and recalling them is the point, not pointless mourning.
more: Ajay defends nostalgia: as you age, you realise life is about accumulating amazing moments and stories, and recalling them is the point, not pointless mourning. Amit adds that memories are how the dead stay with us in grief. He also warns that most people live too much in the past or the future, and the deepest work happens when you live in the present.

head: Tool, not crutch, versus no props at all
dek: Amit's test for any technology or drug is whether it makes you a better version of yourself.
more: Amit's test for any technology or drug is whether it makes you a better version of yourself. Modafinil, coffee (practically health food at a cup a day) and eventually Ozempic are fine on top of sleep, exercise and good habits, but never instead of them. Research them and stick to FDA-approved, evidence-backed options rather than alternative medicine. Ajay holds the old-fashioned opposite view: he wants to face each day with no aids, not even caffeine, apart from his metformin for diabetes. To him, the discipline and the straitjacket are how character is built.

head: Country, state and people are not the same thing
dek: Ajay objects to 'playing for the country'. The people of India, the Indian state and an individual like Gukesh are distinct, and conflating them lets the state and the crowd claim credit for individual achievement.
more: Ajay objects to 'playing for the country'. The people of India, the Indian state and an individual like Gukesh are distinct, and conflating them lets the state and the crowd claim credit for individual achievement. Say who you mean: Indian society, the Indian economy, the Indian state, or a bunch of guys playing football. Amit adds Orwell's view of sport as war minus the shooting, and how tribal sport emotions are a step backwards in building character.

head: Respect elders, but neither reflexively nor dismissively
dek: Amit refused to touch elders' feet as a child and still thinks deference should be earned.
more: Amit refused to touch elders' feet as a child and still thinks deference should be earned. But he now sees default disrespect as equally shallow. The world evolved in particular ways for particular reasons, change comes slowly ('one funeral at a time'), and youthful certainty is often wrong. Phrases like 'okay boomer' or 'sit down, uncle' are a lazy way of claiming you know more and are more virtuous. Ajay frames the whole episode as a set of offsets to a mass culture that simply goes along with society.

head: Solitude is not loneliness
dek: Ajay says we spend too much time in low-grade chatter, and the good life means being alone to think, read and write.
more: Ajay says we spend too much time in low-grade chatter, and the good life means being alone to think, read and write. Amit separates the two states. Loneliness is feeling the absence of others, while solitude gives you room for self-reflection and self-awareness and is worth nurturing.

head: Life is not a spectator sport
dek: Ajay worries about the balance between doing and watching. He would rather go on his own modest hike than watch YouTube videos of other people hiking, and he urges everyone to get off their butts and do things.
more: Ajay worries about the balance between doing and watching. He would rather go on his own modest hike than watch YouTube videos of other people hiking, and he urges everyone to get off their butts and do things. Amit agrees but defends watching with deeper attention: every sport has a chess game underneath, and decoding its tactics is real intellectual fun. Ajay still won't rank it alongside humanity's knowledge.

head: Listen to understand, not to respond
dek: Amit says long-form podcasting made him a better listener. He quotes Stephen Covey, and draws on the idea of cognitive empathy that Biju Rao introduced him to.
more: Amit says long-form podcasting made him a better listener. He quotes Stephen Covey, and draws on the idea of cognitive empathy that Biju Rao introduced him to. Most people listen with their ego, waiting to retort or crack a joke. Interruption is a tell, because the more someone interrupts, the less they are learning. He also notes a gendered pattern: men constantly interrupt women, for example on conference panels, often without realising it. Ajay adds that speaking beautifully is an art worth cultivating.

head: Travel versus tourism, and read before you go
dek: Tourism ticks boxes for social media: a photo at Angkor Wat, a tally of countries.
more: Tourism ticks boxes for social media: a photo at Angkor Wat, a tally of countries. Travel means immersing yourself without a bucket list. Ajay's rules of thumb are to stay more than two days and to know the place deeply beforehand. Because he has read about Poland for years, Warsaw meant something to him on his first visit, while Prague, which he knows little about, would mean less.

head: Talent is path-dependent validation
dek: Ajay argues that what we call a child's 'talent' is usually accident.
more: Ajay argues that what we call a child's 'talent' is usually accident. A young person hungry for approval gets praised for something, practises it more and becomes good at it, often in areas that reflect what their parents know and do. Amit extends this: a girl praised for being demure and a good cook may bury her rebellious side to keep the validation coming. So parents should think carefully about what their words reward.

head: Mental health: see it in your family, but judge actions, not people
dek: Mental illness is far more common than we admit. Three of Amit's guests spoke of mothers with schizophrenia, and his own mother had similar issues, so recognising it within families is a first step toward healing.
more: Mental illness is far more common than we admit. Three of Amit's guests spoke of mothers with schizophrenia, and his own mother had similar issues, so recognising it within families is a first step toward healing. He also worries about over-pathologising, such as therapy as fashion or turning poor concentration into a victim narrative. Rationality is a continuum: everyone carries chemical imbalances and baggage. Ajay adds the strong research linking social media to mental-health damage in people under 25.

head: The crew opened with a spoof of the show's intro
more: The crew opened with a spoof of the show's intro: 'Welcome to Nothing Is Nothing... We will make you waste your time perfectly. And you will lead a life filled with regrets.' Amit played along, declaring that 'jealousy is my best friend' and 'everything is everything is overrated', and calling Bruce Springsteen, whom both hosts love, 'one of the most terrible artists to live in our age'.

head: Amit, rhapsodising about cities
more: Amit, rhapsodising about cities: 'There is nothing like going to a mall at ten AM as it is opening. The smell of fresh commerce in the morning.'

head: To prove Dylan is irreplaceable, Amit and the crew sang
more: To prove Dylan is irreplaceable, Amit and the crew sang 'Lay Lady Lay' in full nasal twang ('So now you can't cover this'), then warned: 'Dylan fans in the house, Ajay, you're gonna get beaten up after this.'

head: Amit on Indian menswear
more: Amit on Indian menswear: 'There are no slim fit men in India... They're complete freaking outliers.' Then he thanked H&M for stocking every fit: 'H&M, if you're watching this, either H or M, hats off to you.'

head: Amit's anti-gossip pledge
more: Amit's anti-gossip pledge: 'I would never speak bad things about any of you behind your back, but I have to your face very often.' Later, his example of 'caring' gossip roasted himself: 'this Amit has no discipline at all, fifty years gone by, not written a book.'

head: Amit defending white lies
more: Amit defending white lies: 'every time I ask you, Ajay, am I looking fat? You say no, no, no. Now you're clearly lying, but it is for a good reason, and I appreciate that.'

head: Amit needling Ajay on having babies
more: Amit needling Ajay on having babies: 'since you are so concerned about climate change, even that I wonder, because your babies are going to cause climate change.'

head: After the long flat-earth fight over expertise, Amit declined to opine on hiking
more: After the long flat-earth fight over expertise, Amit declined to opine on hiking: 'I have no expertise to add on that. As you know, he doesn't like people talking without expertise.'

head: Ajay on the Marvel Cinematic Universe
more: Ajay on the Marvel Cinematic Universe: 'Is it at the sufficiently low level that the entire movie can be made by an LLM?' Amit: 'Iron Man 38 can of course be made by LLM.'

head: Amit's retail-therapy logic after a gruelling shoot
more: Amit's retail-therapy logic after a gruelling shoot: 'if I don't buy something, I'll probably eat the largest pizza I can find. So it is healthier to just buy something.'

head: After Amit's ode to Bengali melancholy, Ajay's entire rebuttal
more: After Amit's ode to Bengali melancholy, Ajay's entire rebuttal: 'Ice cream is better.' Amit stayed 'on the fence about ice cream' because of the sugar.

head: Amit on navel gazing: if you sit by the seaside looking out to sea
more: Amit on navel gazing: if you sit by the seaside looking out to sea 'and there are ships, it's also naval gazing.' Ajay: 'Yes, that is very funny. But more substantively...'

head: After the cats poem, Ajay said he wished he could find himself that remarkable. Amit's verdict
more: After the cats poem, Ajay said he wished he could find himself that remarkable. Amit's verdict: 'Cats are fucking sociopaths.'

head: The vegetable Maggi incident: Ajay offered the crew Maggi, the kids eagerly chose his…
more: The vegetable Maggi incident: Ajay offered the crew Maggi, the kids eagerly chose his 'vegetable' version, and then cauliflowers started being chopped. Amit, who had wisely chosen plain: 'Maggi is Maggi, bruh. Why do you want to mess with something perfect?'

head: Amit called his accidental perfect prawns
more: Amit called his accidental perfect prawns 'the Elon Musk of my food. It's survivorship bias. This is a one in a million that happened to be good. Though you said it about Elon Musk, I don't.'

head: Amit owns about twenty shower gels, one for every mood: Bath and Body Works' Ocean for seaside moods, Teakwood or Noir for sophisticated ones.
more: Amit owns about twenty shower gels, one for every mood: Bath and Body Works' Ocean for seaside moods, Teakwood or Noir for sophisticated ones. 'This is not even a life of the body, it's a life of the skin.' Ajay: 'The great gods of advertising will be very sad to know that I have not paid attention to any of their attempts.'

head: Ajay on sleep
more: Ajay on sleep: 'If you're not sleeping well, you're getting a twenty percent discount on your IQ.' Amit: 'T-shirt lines from Ajay.'

head: Amit on his childhood refusal to touch elders' feet
more: Amit on his childhood refusal to touch elders' feet: 'I would say they have to earn it, and no one earned it.'

head: Amit, half-joking
more: Amit, half-joking: 'I'm just waiting for Ozempic to come to India, frankly,' because the Bengali in him doesn't want to exercise. Ajay: 'Ozempic will be launched by Novo Nordisk in India this year. So your wish is about to become reality.'

head: Bob Dylan's line
more: Bob Dylan's line 'He not busy being born is busy dying', quoted by Amit on why adults who stop being curious essentially die. Later Ajay quoted another Dylan line on failure: 'There's no success like failure, and failure's no success at all.'
'Freedom's just another word for nothing left to lose', the line Ajay borrowed to open his case that frugality buys freedom.

head: George Orwell's description of sport
more: George Orwell's description of sport as 'war minus the shooting', cited by Amit on the tribal emotions that 'playing for the country' unleashes.

head: Stephen Covey
more: Stephen Covey: 'we listen to respond when we should listen to understand', Amit's anchor for the talking-and-listening segment.

head: The Eagles'
more: The Eagles' 'Life in the Fast Lane', quoted by Ajay against cosmetic and pharmacological props: 'they knew all the right people, they took all the right pills, they threw outrageous parties, they paid heavenly bills.'
'Little minds discuss people, medium minds discuss news, great minds discuss ideas', Ajay's maxim against gossip.
'Paradigm change one funeral at a time', which Amit invoked as a reason for youthful rebels to have some humility toward elders.

head: Dunbar's number: Amit on nurturing your inner circles of…
more: Dunbar's number: Amit on nurturing your inner circles of 'your five, your fifteen, or your one fifty', crediting Ajay for often raising it.

head: Amit's counterpoint to Ajay dating the…
more: Amit's counterpoint to Ajay dating the 'assault on truth' to social media: mainstream media and Twitter's censorship of the Hunter Biden laptop story, including blocking the New York Post's account.

head: The heart attack he never noticed
dek: Our picture of catastrophe comes from cinema, but real danger often arrives without a soundtrack.
more: After digging through dusty old letters for the 'Objects From Our Past' episode and attending a conference in early December, Amit fell ill with something COVID-like. Then came what he took for food poisoning: acidity, bad bouts of vomiting at night, and a tightening in the chest whenever he exerted himself. He assumed it was a lingering lung or viral issue. Lancelot Pinto found his lungs performing at 103–106% of normal for his age and sent him to a cardiologist. An HS troponin test showed he had already had a minor heart attack without noticing. A CT scan found an 80–90% block in the right coronary artery, and by the time of the angioplasty it was 100%. A stent requires lifelong aspirin and he was allergic to it, so he first spent a day or two in ICU being 'desensitized' to aspirin, and then got a drug-eluting stent. Because the procedure carried a 1–2% mortality risk, he wrote 'if I die' emails, briefed Gaurav Chintamani on the two Seen and the Unseen episodes in the bank, and got the next EIE episode ready for Nomsita to publish.

Our picture of catastrophe comes from cinema, but real danger often arrives without a soundtrack. The faint, persistent signals are the warning. The trap is explaining them away with the most convenient story: dust, COVID, bad food.

head: Venomous snake bites are not cinematic
dek: The deadliest events can feel like nothing at the moment they happen. Calibrating your alarm to drama rather than to consequences is how you get killed.
more: Ajay offers an analogy for the silent heart attack. As a city child he imagined a cobra bite as a cataclysm: fangs gripping your calf, and you drop dead moments later. In reality venomous snakes do a high-speed bite, pump in venom like a hypodermic syringe and get away immediately, so the victim feels very little. You may only see two puncture marks, and the drama unfolds over minutes and hours. With common krait bites, people are bitten in their sleep, never wake up, and are found dead in the morning.
The deadliest events can feel like nothing at the moment they happen. Calibrating your alarm to drama rather than to consequences is how you get killed.

head: His father's heart attack, forty years earlier
dek: Almost the same event, four decades apart, ended in death in 1984 and in a one-hour procedure in 2025.
more: When Sudhir Sarnobat called during Amit's procedure, Ajay was at peak anxiety, because heart attacks are personal for him. In 1982 his father had a small heart attack that was only recognised as one a month later. None of today's tools existed; he was prescribed nitroglycerin as a blood thinner. In 1984 he had a second heart attack and died, aged 58.
Almost the same event, four decades apart, ended in death in 1984 and in a one-hour procedure in 2025. That gap is what the 'miracles of modern science' actually mean in a single family's life.

head: Werner Forssmann puts a catheter into his own heart (1929)
dek: A procedure that is routine in 2025 began with one rebel betting his own body against the consensus.
more: In 1929 Berlin, catheters existed and early angiography of other organs had begun, but the dogma said never go near the heart. Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doctor, believed a catheter could safely reach it, and his superior forbade the experiment. His devoted nurse refused to let someone so important risk himself and insisted he experiment on her. He strapped her down and gave her local anaesthetic. Then, while she waited, he inserted the catheter into his own arm and guided it up using a mirror. He walked to the X-ray lab and, with a fluoroscope, guided it into his right atrium. He repeated it nine more times on himself and lost his job. His next boss, Ferdinand Sauerbruch, sneered at such circus experiments, and by 1932 Forssmann had left for urology. He joined the Nazi party and spent five years imprisoned after the war, but his work was rediscovered and he won a Nobel Prize in the 1950s. He died in 1979, at 75, of a heart attack. Narendra Shenoy told Amit this story while he was in hospital.
A procedure that is routine in 2025 began with one rebel betting his own body against the consensus. Amit separates art from artist: Forssmann's Nazi membership doesn't erase what he contributed.
printed: A man after his own heart

head: Barry Marshall swallows the ulcer bacterium
dek: When a whole field has put a problem in the wrong category, incremental work inside that frame can't help.
more: Stomach ulcers were treated as a degenerative, non-communicable disease of old age, like cholesterol. The only advice was bland food and avoiding stress, and people died horrible deaths. In Australia, Barry Marshall argued it was a simple infectious disease, and nobody believed him. To satisfy Koch's postulates he experimented on himself. He scoped his own healthy stomach, drank water containing Helicobacter pylori, and scoped again to show full-blown ulcers. He then took a simple course of antibiotics and scoped a third time to show they were gone. He won the 2005 Nobel Prize for Medicine.
When a whole field has put a problem in the wrong category, incremental work inside that frame can't help. Sometimes one heretic has to become the experiment.

head: Charles Dotter borrows a salesman's blowtorch
dek: Dotter was a thinker, not just a technician. He questioned the principles and then built the thing with his own hands.
more: Charles Dotter pioneered angioplasty in other parts of the body from the 1960s. He was openly rebellious and a lifelong tinkerer who reasoned from first principles that the heart is ultimately a physical object. His favourite 'conceptual trademark' was a sketch of a crossed pipe and wrench, and he assembled catheters in his own kitchen. At an early-1960s conference, travelling salesman Bill Cook noticed a short, bald man with darting eyes sitting on a box behind his stall, which made him nervous. At closing time the stranger asked to borrow his blowtorch and some Teflon tubing to practise making catheters in his hotel room. Cook thought he had 'a real space cadet' on his hands, but agreed. Next morning Dotter returned with ten beautifully made catheters, which Cook sold that day for ten dollars each. Cook called him his 'first production employee', and went on to found the company that led the angioplasty-equipment market.
Dotter was a thinker, not just a technician. He questioned the principles and then built the thing with his own hands.

head: Andreas Gruentzig and the first coronary angioplasty (1977)
dek: Each stage, first the balloon and then the stent, had to defeat conventional wisdom all over again.
more: Andreas Gruentzig was much younger than Dotter and thought the same way, but had the opposite temperament: he played the system. Bypass surgery had been common since the 1960s, and he asked why the chest needed to be opened when a catheter could carry a balloon to the blockage. Textbooks and top surgeons said it would trigger ventricular fibrillation and kill patients within minutes.
