In 1977 he did it anyway, on around six patients, and when he presented the results he got a standing ovation. Early on, 30–40% of patients still needed a bypass, but they would have needed one anyway. Stent pioneers then faced the same resistance, because a stent can't be removed from the heart once it's in. Stents arrived in the 1980s and were routine by the mid-1990s. In 2025 Amit was conscious through the whole procedure and was told he now had the heart of a twenty-year-old.
Each stage, first the balloon and then the stent, had to defeat conventional wisdom all over again. It took both the outsider who says 'fuck you' and the insider who persuades.

head: Sri Lanka's 1996 World Cup heresy
dek: When you're outgunned, strategy derived from the rules can beat talent.
more: Suggested to Amit by Pranay Kotasthane. The conventional ODI template was that openers build, the middle order consolidates, and everyone slogs in the last ten overs. Mark Greatbatch had hit early in 1992, but it didn't catch on; India tried Kapil Dev as an opener for one match and gave up. Underdog Sri Lanka, much like India in 1983, reasoned that they were weaker in every other department and needed a tactical edge. Since field restrictions made boundaries more profitable early, they promoted two lower-order batsmen, Romesh Kaluwitharana and Sanath Jayasuriya, to open and attack from ball one. The shock and awe worked, and with Muralitharan and a young Chaminda Vaas also in the side, they won the World Cup.
When you're outgunned, strategy derived from the rules can beat talent. Underdogs also have the least to lose from heresy.
printed: Bang bang bang from ball one

head: Always bet on the team batting second
dek: When a whole league shares the same wrong conventional wisdom, the error shows up as a systematic, exploitable edge.
more: Around 2016, a poker friend who bet on cricket asked Amit for an IPL strategy. Amit had played professional poker from 2010 to 2015 but doesn't bet on cricket himself. His advice was to wait for the toss and always back the team batting second. After fourteen games, thirteen had been won by the chasing side. Knowing the target should give at most a 55-45 or 60-40 edge. The real cause was that teams batting first underestimated the par score and didn't go hard enough. That season RCB lost four in a row batting first, and captain Virat Kohli said the batsmen had done their job and the bowlers couldn't defend. Amit found that excuse pathetic: the batsmen had followed the wrong brief.
When a whole league shares the same wrong conventional wisdom, the error shows up as a systematic, exploitable edge.

head: Netflix disrupts Blockbuster, then disrupts itself
dek: Kodak saw digital photography coming but protected its market. BlackBerry was sure people wanted physical keyboards, and Nokia was disrupted too.
more: In the late 1990s Blockbuster dominated American home video. You had to visit a store with a limited collection, and pay late fees if you didn't return the rental on time. From 1997 Netflix mailed DVDs with no late fees, soon on a monthly subscription, with a near-unlimited catalogue browsable on the web. Blockbuster dismissed it as a niche until Netflix had 4.2 million subscribers by 2004, and copied it too late. In 2007, when internet speeds and screens made streaming seem absurd, Netflix moved into streaming anyway, reasoning that someone else would otherwise kill their business. Five or six years later came original shows like House of Cards and Orange Is the New Black, dropped a whole season at once against the appointment-viewing model, and binge-watching became the norm.

Kodak saw digital photography coming but protected its market. BlackBerry was sure people wanted physical keyboards, and Nokia was disrupted too. Netflix kept attacking its own business before anyone else could. Amit, who often criticises Netflix's conduct in India, credits it fully for this.

head: Govind Nihalani's missing copy of Party
dek: Even a great director couldn't get an independent film funded. Netflix's 'unlimited catalogue' held a film its own maker couldn't find in his own country.
more: Around 2010, director Govind Nihalani wanted to film Amit's 2009 novel. Amit naively tried to talk him out of it, then helped write a treatment. Despite Nihalani having made Ardh Satya and Tamas, nobody would fund it. Nihalani suggested the Marathi industry, which he said was like Hindi cinema of the 1980s for independent film, so Amit wrote a Pune-based treatment. Then he lost touch and was too embarrassed to reconnect, and the film was never made. Nihalani once told him his one regret was not having a copy of his own iconic film Party, which wasn't available in India. Amit's New York friend Ved Sharma found it on Netflix, rented it, paid the lost-disc charge, and mailed the DVD. By then Amit had lost touch and inertia had set in, so it never reached Nihalani. Amit believes he got a copy from elsewhere.
Even a great director couldn't get an independent film funded. Netflix's 'unlimited catalogue' held a film its own maker couldn't find in his own country.

head: Sonictown: iTunes and MySpace from Bombay, in 2000
dek: Being early is indistinguishable from being wrong. Amit says he had the wrong time and the wrong place (Bombay, not Silicon Valley or New York).
more: In 1999, in his early twenties, Amit was shown the godown of Magnasound, Shashi Gopal's label behind Daler Mehndi, Alisha Chinai and Baba Sehgal. Thousands of CDs from foreign collaborators sat there, and Gopal told him to take what he wanted. Amit told him that in ten years they would all be worthless, because all music would be digital and sold online. He convinced Gopal and marketing head Sunil Mengrajani, and the three became equal partners in Sonictown, which got a double spread in Business World. This was the Napster era, when labels wanted to crush digital. Even so, Sunil secured rights to 80,000 tracks from US labels. In a New York room of investors in early 2000, Amit pitched online song sales plus pages where musicians could connect with each other and update fans. The room was excited, and then the Nasdaq crashed. A second venture later left him deeply in debt.

Being early is indistinguishable from being wrong. Amit says he had the wrong time and the wrong place (Bombay, not Silicon Valley or New York). Many others probably had the same idea, which is survivorship bias in action. The answer is persistence and a bias for action, not giving up on bold ideas.

head: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
dek: It names the 'aggressively conventional minded', who experience a challenge to convention as a personal affront and stand in the way of every disruptor in the episode.
more: It names the 'aggressively conventional minded', who experience a challenge to convention as a personal affront and stand in the way of every disruptor in the episode.
Amit invokes this essay, which he loves, while framing the episode's theme.

head: Morgan Brown's tweet on DeepSeek
dek: Its line, 'Incumbents optimize existing processes while disruptors rethink the fundamental approach', is the episode's thesis in one sentence.
more: Its line, 'Incumbents optimize existing processes while disruptors rethink the fundamental approach', is the episode's thesis in one sentence.
Amit read this thread from his hospital bed, and it seeded the entire episode.

dek: It has his strategic arguments in much more detail than this episode.
more: It has his strategic arguments in much more detail than this episode.
Amit refers to it for his fuller thinking on cricket strategy and teams' failure to adapt to T20.

dek: It explains why the conventional thinking about short attention spans is completely wrong.
more: It explains why the conventional thinking about short attention spans is completely wrong.
Essentially Amit's podcasting course in video form.

more: It sets up Amit's own story of early failure with Sonictown.
The previous episode, where both hosts rated 'failure' as underrated.

more: The surviving trace of a venture that otherwise left no mark on the internet.

more: It's the fuller case for persistence and bias for action as the way to give luck more chances to find you.
Amit urges listeners to check it out after the Sonictown story.

more: It addresses the institutional soil that disruptive thinkers need.
Paired with the education episode in Ajay's social-and-cultural pillar.

head: Dwarkesh Patel's tweet on why LLMs haven't made discoveries
dek: Amit calls it a great question, one Dwarkesh said nobody had answered satisfactorily, and it sharpens the human-vs-AI novelty debate.
more: Amit calls it a great question, one Dwarkesh said nobody had answered satisfactorily, and it sharpens the human-vs-AI novelty debate.
A question Dwarkesh posed to Dario Amodei: LLMs have memorised the whole corpus of human knowledge, yet haven't made a single new connection that led to a discovery.

head: Michael's response to Dwarkesh Patel
dek: It argues that to an LLM a novel discovery is indistinguishable from an error.
more: It argues that to an LLM a novel discovery is indistinguishable from an error. Amit thinks this holds a grain of truth, though AI isn't only LLMs.
The answer to Dwarkesh's question that Amit found most interesting.

head: Google Gemini (paid)
dek: It gave five good suggestions 'like what a master editor would do', and he signed up for $20 a month that day.
more: It gave five good suggestions 'like what a master editor would do', and he signed up for $20 a month that day. He treats LLMs as good language processors, not AGI.
Ajay prompted it to find ambiguous sentences, grammar flaws and typesetting errors in a Business Standard column he had just submitted.

head: Perplexity (Pro)
dek: A 'mind blowing' learning tool: it answers better than search or Wikipedia and nudges you towards the right questions and down rewarding rabbit holes.
more: A 'mind blowing' learning tool: it answers better than search or Wikipedia and nudges you towards the right questions and down rewarding rabbit holes.
His main research source before his procedure, using models including ChatGPT and DeepSeek.

head: Incumbents optimize; disruptors rethink the fundamentals
dek: Taken from Morgan Brown's line on DeepSeek. Conventional players polish the existing process, while progress comes from those who ask whether the whole approach is wrong, and who are usually maligned as heretics for it.
more: Taken from Morgan Brown's line on DeepSeek. Conventional players polish the existing process, while progress comes from those who ask whether the whole approach is wrong, and who are usually maligned as heretics for it. Amit makes this the episode's spine, across medicine, cricket and business.

head: The aggressively conventional minded
dek: From Paul Graham's Four Quadrants of Conformism.
more: From Paul Graham's Four Quadrants of Conformism. The real enemies of progress aren't merely conventional people, but those who defend convention aggressively, because a challenge to it feels like an attack on their worldview. Sauerbruch's sneer at Forssmann is the archetype.

head: Thinkers vs technicians
dek: A distinction Ajay once made, which Amit applies to medicine. Technicians master trained procedures and can be superb surgeons.
more: A distinction Ajay once made, which Amit applies to medicine. Technicians master trained procedures and can be superb surgeons. Thinkers like Charles Dotter step back, go to first principles ('the heart is a physical object'; what a plumber does to pipes can be done to blood vessels) and question how things are done. The best do both.

head: Strategy lags rule changes by years or decades
dek: When a game's format changes, the optimal strategy changes too, but players keep the old rhythm.
more: When a game's format changes, the optimal strategy changes too, but players keep the old rhythm. Gavaskar batted through a 60-over match for 36 not out in 1975 as if it were Test cricket. Sri Lanka's 1996 heresy and England's later ODI revolution came decades after one-day cricket began. Even after a heretic is proven right, adoption is slow.

head: The expected value of aggression in T20
dek: Think like an economist about scarce resources. With the same eleven batsmen but only twenty overs, each dot ball costs more and each wicket costs less.
more: Think like an economist about scarce resources. With the same eleven batsmen but only twenty overs, each dot ball costs more and each wicket costs less. So you front-load: send hitters early, keep hitting whatever falls, and hold the anchor back for emergencies. West Indies won a T20 World Cup doing this, and England applied the logic back to ODIs, making 300-plus scores common worldwide.

head: A slow scorer's runs can be a liability
dek: In T20, runs alone mislead; what matters is scoring rate relative to the par score.
more: In T20, runs alone mislead; what matters is scoring rate relative to the par score. A batsman scoring below the par rate burdens his teammates in proportion to how long he bats. So a 900-run season at a sub-par rate isn't a triumph.

head: Disrupt yourself before someone else does
dek: Kodak saw digital photography coming but protected its film business. BlackBerry assumed people wanted physical keyboards, and Nokia was disrupted too.
more: Kodak saw digital photography coming but protected its film business. BlackBerry assumed people wanted physical keyboards, and Nokia was disrupted too. Netflix kept cannibalising itself: mail-order DVDs to streaming before the technology was ready, then original content and whole-season drops. Incumbents fail because the safe move inside a big company is to protect the present.

head: Outside-the-box thinking is necessary but not sufficient
dek: Amit's Sonictown pitch was essentially iTunes and MySpace, years early, from Bombay.
more: Amit's Sonictown pitch was essentially iTunes and MySpace, years early, from Bombay. Right ideas fail at the wrong time and place, and many others likely had the same idea. The answer isn't to stop trying but to persist and keep throwing things at the world so luck has more chances to find you.

head: Disruption needs a culture of irreverence
dek: Ajay's first pillar. Societies that regiment children, push them into competitive exams and punish deviation produce conformists, and their talent ends up as bankers.
more: Ajay's first pillar. Societies that regiment children, push them into competitive exams and punish deviation produce conformists, and their talent ends up as bankers. A more easygoing culture tolerates heretics, dropouts and failures; most will go nowhere, but a few become remarkable. Amit adds that Silicon Valley works partly because the culture makes it okay to fail and to be a maverick.

head: From hippie culture to Unix
dek: Ajay argues there was no path to Unix except through the American counterculture.
more: Ajay argues there was no path to Unix except through the American counterculture. That cultural difference helps answer the great question of the twentieth century: why the Soviet Union never got to computers, CPUs, Unix and the internet. Amit notes, in passing, that China's DeepSeek is open source while OpenAI and Gemini are not.

head: Gatekeepers decide whether a society progresses
dek: Ajay's second pillar. The 'commanding heights' of a society are held by allocators: venture capitalists, research funders, journal editors, patent offices and licensing bureaucracies.
more: Ajay's second pillar. The 'commanding heights' of a society are held by allocators: venture capitalists, research funders, journal editors, patent offices and licensing bureaucracies. In India, all too often, everything is banned unless explicitly permitted. If allocators reward conformity, researchers stop thinking and just 'polish the apple'. Shruti Rajagopalan's Emergent Ventures India is the counter-model.

head: Embrace survivorship bias: honour failure, don't worship winners
dek: Ajay's third pillar. Success is drawn from a large pool of risk-takers, many of whose lives get chewed up, as with Amit's Nasdaq-crashed startup and his debt-laden second venture.
more: Ajay's third pillar. Success is drawn from a large pool of risk-takers, many of whose lives get chewed up, as with Amit's Nasdaq-crashed startup and his debt-laden second venture. You throw a hundred darts and two work out. Marwari-Gujarati business culture and startup culture get this; much of Indian society doesn't.

head: Disruptors are often not nice people
dek: Ajay's fourth pillar. Maverick dissidents come as a package with their rough edges.
more: Ajay's fourth pillar. Maverick dissidents come as a package with their rough edges. Solzhenitsyn, up close, was not a good human being, and the only way to be a dissident in the Soviet Union was to be a weirdo. Newton's writings would look cringeworthy on social media. Modern polite conformity, amplified by social media, is harmful, and we should support 'the nutcases amongst us'. Ajay's own counterpoint: he keeps everyday life orderly and habitual so his brain is saved for creative work.

head: Expanding the Overton window of the possible
dek: Amit offers Elon Musk as a repeat disruptor, not a survivorship-bias fluke.
more: Amit offers Elon Musk as a repeat disruptor, not a survivorship-bias fluke. Musk made electric cars objects of lust, rethought their interface, vertical integration and direct sales, and challenged thinking on reusable rockets and private spaceflight. Even a wild goal like Mars matters, because it widens what people believe can be attempted.

head: To an LLM, a novel discovery looks like an error
dek: Dwarkesh Patel asked why LLMs, with all human knowledge memorised, haven't made a single new connection that led to a discovery.
more: Dwarkesh Patel asked why LLMs, with all human knowledge memorised, haven't made a single new connection that led to a discovery. Michael's answer: anything outside the training data resembles a hallucination. Amit sees some truth in it, but thinks AI isn't only LLMs and will eventually discover things. The enduring human edge is diving into the new without assuming that what hasn't been said must be crap.

head: Ajay's law: if an LLM can write it, it's not worth writing
dek: Ajay uses LLMs as a novelty test. If a one-paragraph prompt yields the full paper, the paper is trivial and you should publish the prompt instead.
more: Ajay uses LLMs as a novelty test. If a one-paragraph prompt yields the full paper, the paper is trivial and you should publish the prompt instead. Amit pushes back: by Sturgeon's law most training data is mediocre, so first-pass output will be too, but with careful prompting LLMs are mind-blowing research and learning tools. At most the test should apply to what an LLM can do at the first pass.

head: Ajay introduces the show as a dialectic between
more: Ajay introduces the show as a dialectic between 'the irresistible force, Amit Varma' and 'the immovable object, me, the time traveller'. Amit replies that it's an apt metaphor, 'because I have felt like a movable object recently. But thankfully I haven't been moved.'

head: Why the full-sleeve shirt? Amit says he got feedback he was showing too much skin
more: Why the full-sleeve shirt? Amit says he got feedback he was showing too much skin: 'I didn't want virality to be achieved by raw sex appeal, but by the power of our ideas.' The real reason is that half his arm is shaved from the procedure.

head: Lancelot Pinto's verdict on Amit's lungs
more: Lancelot Pinto's verdict on Amit's lungs: 'These might even be the best lungs in South Asia, Ajay Shah. Not his words, mine.'

head: Having been desensitized to aspirin, Amit notes that Ajay is…
more: Having been desensitized to aspirin, Amit notes that Ajay is 'allergic to communists. But that matter can be solved. Some communists can be good people'. Ajay proposes a 'communism desensitization program', and Amit signs him up for it, 'though it won't work on me.'

head: Sudhir Sarnobat called Ajay to say the procedure went well and reported back that Ajay is…
more: Sudhir Sarnobat called Ajay to say the procedure went well and reported back that Ajay is 'an extremely expressionless man. I said I'm Sudhir speaking and he just said okay.' Amit had imagined Ajay seeing Sudhir's name flash on the caller ID and concluding Amit was dead.

head: Riffing on Ajay's point about silent snake bites, Amit imagines the Shah–Thomas bedroom at night: Ajay wakes and asks…
more: Riffing on Ajay's point about silent snake bites, Amit imagines the Shah–Thomas bedroom at night: Ajay wakes and asks, 'Susan, did you bite me just now?', she tells him to fuck off and goes back to sleep, 'at which point you realize the horrible truth.'

head: Amit on his hospital bill
more: Amit on his hospital bill: 'this can be a perpetual heart attack machine'. You have a heart attack, get the procedure, see the bill, have another heart attack, and so on, with the game-theoretic catch that the surgeon must keep you alive long enough to pay the next bill. Ajay diagnoses 'Zeno-phobia', 'the irrational fear of convergent sequences', after Zeno's paradox. Amit: 'This is the finest analysis of a bad joke I have ever seen. Sashtang pranam.'

head: When Ajay credits the thousands of innovations that brought medicine to…
more: When Ajay credits the thousands of innovations that brought medicine to 'the state of healing Amit Varma', Amit replies: 'All the amazing people that brought me here in front of you are really my parents and their parents before them and so on down the line all the way to a woman in Africa and even she had parents.'

head: Contrasting the two angioplasty pioneers: Dotter
more: Contrasting the two angioplasty pioneers: Dotter 'is happy to say fuck you to everyone, kinda like me', while Gruentzig knows 'you gotta be polite to everyone. Kinda like you.'

head: On Gukesh's heart rate of 62 in a crucial position
more: On Gukesh's heart rate of 62 in a crucial position: 'Sixty two, like I don't even have sixty two when I'm doing nothing.'

head: Blockbuster's late fees were…
more: Blockbuster's late fees were 'punishing the Bengali procrastinator, which is not a good thing'. When Amit admits the Netflix DVD of Party never reached Nihalani, Ajay worries that 'DVDs became obsolete and there were no DVD players left in the world' in the time Amit took.

head: Ajay on cultural permissiveness
more: Ajay on cultural permissiveness: 'Very many people will go off to the beaches of Goa and get doped out, but a small fraction of them will become amazing people.'

head: After Ajay says disruptors require
more: After Ajay says disruptors require 'being a little less Amit Varma', Amit notes he has been implied to be 'A, not a nice guy, B a weirdo, and C one of the nut cases among us'. He accepts all of it, and observes that Ajay has agreed with everything this episode because 'poor guy, his heart. I just won't mess with it.'

head: Praising Emergent Ventures: conventional allocators are…
more: Praising Emergent Ventures: conventional allocators are 'missing the freaks, we are missing the nutcases, we are missing the Amit Varmas.' Amit closes the AI argument on theme: 'And you are restating fundamental thinking. I am challenging them, Ajay Shah.'

head: Ferdinand Sauerbruch's dismissal of Forssmann, Amit's emblem of the aggressively conventional minded
more: Ferdinand Sauerbruch's dismissal of Forssmann, Amit's emblem of the aggressively conventional minded: 'With such experiments you might habilitate in a circus, but these have no place in a decent German hospital.'

head: Amit describes his own angioplasty as a video game
more: Amit describes his own angioplasty as a video game: three screens beside him like a day trader's setup, a doctor with what is practically a game controller, and, 'like in a game of Pac-Man', manoeuvring through the arteries zapping clots.

head: Ajay quotes a friend's pithy line
more: Ajay quotes a friend's pithy line, 'the heart is a solved problem'. Amit's answer: biologically yes ('cardiac is solved, cancer is the next target'), 'but metaphorically the heart is, no one can solve the heart.'

head: Sturgeon's law
more: Sturgeon's law, '95 percent of everything is crap', which Amit uses to explain why default LLM writing is mediocre: the data it learns from mostly is.

head: Larry Summers: from a car phone to a river in Africa
dek: When a technology rides a falling price curve, democratisation is measured in months, not generations.
more: Ajay retells what Larry Summers calls the most dramatic technical change of his life. Ajay places it around the 1992 US elections, when Summers was advising Michael Dukakis at a Democratic convention that Ajay thinks was in Chicago. A car sent to pick Summers up had a phone in it. He had never seen one before, so he picked it up and called his wife to tell her he was calling from a car. A scant year and a half later he was crossing a river in Africa when someone handed him a GSM phone and said, 'This call is for you.'
When a technology rides a falling price curve, democratisation is measured in months, not generations. The exotic toy of the rich becomes ordinary kit in the remotest places almost immediately.

head: A whole university on one T1 line
dek: Bandwidth is one of the 'Moore's Laws' of price. What was once a whole institution's prized resource is now an unnoticed household utility, and that is the kind of change we tend to normalise and forget.
more: When Ajay was a PhD student in America, the entire University of Southern California ran on a single T1 line of about 1.5 megabits a second, and that was considered the height of cool. Today an ordinary home connection gives something like 300 megabits a second, at a price lower than what was paid for that T1 line.

Bandwidth is one of the 'Moore's Laws' of price. What was once a whole institution's prized resource is now an unnoticed household utility, and that is the kind of change we tend to normalise and forget.

head: The startup killed by its own success
dek: The same metric can bankrupt you or make you, depending on where you sit on the cost curve.
more: In 2000, after the Nasdaq crash scared off the investors in his first startup, and while Kaun Banega Crorepati was becoming a hit, Amit built Crow Master. It was a gamified online quiz with a quizmaster called Babu Moshai, running on thousands of questions written by paid quizzer friends, and it was part of a site called Mindfever.com. Because the game was interactive, he hosted it on VSNL to keep the server close to users, and VSNL charged by traffic. The game went viral, and for one month it was the number two site in India, between Rediff and Cricinfo. A buyout interest from Star's Bangalore digital arm fell through when that arm shut down. The traffic bill put him heavily into debt, and the site closed after about three months.

The same metric can bankrupt you or make you, depending on where you sit on the cost curve. In 2000, success in user acquisition was ruinous. Today no startup fears traffic, because nobody pays for it that way anymore.
printed: Second in India, first in debt

head: One perfect pot vs ten pots a day
dek: This is Wright's Law for creators: excellence comes from cumulative doing, not from agonising over one artefact.
more: Amit cites an experiment whose details he admits he has forgotten. One group was told to spend a month crafting a single perfect pot. The other was told to make ten pots a day, and their best would be judged. The perfectionists' pot came out mediocre, while the volume group quickly passed that standard and went on to make really good pots.
This is Wright's Law for creators: excellence comes from cumulative doing, not from agonising over one artefact. It is why Amit keeps urging creators to have a bias for action.

head: The Ritz-Carlton's $2,000 discretion
dek: Incentives and trust turn employees who would otherwise go through the motions into owners who show initiative.
more: Drawing on a Twitter thread by Ben Wolff, Amit describes how Horst Schulze, leading the Ritz-Carlton in 1983, let every employee from top to bottom spend up to $2,000 of the hotel's money on a guest without asking anyone. His reasoning was that a regular guest was worth $200,000 over a lifetime. Amit gives four examples. An employee flew from Atlanta to Hawaii himself to deliver a laptop a guest had left behind. Staff returned a child's forgotten Thomas the Tank Engine along with photos of Thomas enjoying spa treatment. When a couple lost their wedding ring on a Cancun beach the day before the wedding, an employee bought four metal detectors and had staff search all night until it was found. A server who overheard diners planning a conference at another hotel comped their $600 dinner, and they moved the conference to the Ritz, where it was held every year after that.
Incentives and trust turn employees who would otherwise go through the motions into owners who show initiative. The payoff is hard to measure but very real.
printed: A ring, a laptop, a tank engine

head: An upgrade on the day his mother died
dek: One small act of discretion by a frontline employee can create lifelong loyalty, which is the human side of the argument for empowering staff.
more: In 2008, when Amit's mother died, the family was flying back. At the airport counter one of them happened to mention it, and the woman at the counter, who had no need to do anything, gave them a free upgrade to business class. Amit thinks the airline was Jet, which no longer exists.
One small act of discretion by a frontline employee can create lifelong loyalty, which is the human side of the argument for empowering staff.

head: ASML's decade-early bet on extreme ultraviolet
dek: A shared belief in the curve gives firms the closest thing to an assurance that a huge, risky, long-horizon investment will find a market.
more: ASML in Holland makes what Ajay calls arguably the most complex machines on earth. Projecting along Moore's Law ten years ahead, it saw that conventional lithography would max out and that chipmaking would need extreme ultraviolet light, at around 13.5 nanometres. Nobody knew how to do it, and there were severe physics problems. Other firms that tried failed. ASML kept investing for years ahead of demand and got through.
A shared belief in the curve gives firms the closest thing to an assurance that a huge, risky, long-horizon investment will find a market. That is how Moore's Law keeps fulfilling itself.

head: The Ehrlich–Simon wager
dek: Population growth adds innovators, not just consumers. Prices fell because people kept innovating, which is the core of the 'people are brains, not stomachs' view.
more: Paul Ehrlich made Malthusian predictions: Britain would be extinct by 2000, and half of India would starve by the end of the decade. Economist Julian Simon thought these claims were ridiculous. In 1980 they bet on the prices of five materials chosen by Ehrlich over ten years. Malthusian logic said a rising population would push prices up. Instead all five fell, and Simon won.
Population growth adds innovators, not just consumers. Prices fell because people kept innovating, which is the core of the 'people are brains, not stomachs' view.

head: The fiber-optic glut that wasn't a waste
dek: Overbuilt capacity is not necessarily waste. Once a constraint is lifted, human ingenuity fills the space, and the losses are part of healthy creative destruction.
more: Around 2000, big companies sank more than $100 billion into laying fiber-optic cable across America, expecting the boom to continue. The dot-com bust left about 90% of that capacity unused. Companies went under and people called it a waste. But because the capacity physically existed, innovators built on it: broadband, mobile telephony and cloud computing. Today 80 to 90% of it is in use.
Overbuilt capacity is not necessarily waste. Once a constraint is lifted, human ingenuity fills the space, and the losses are part of healthy creative destruction.

head: Missing the curve on digital cameras and batteries
dek: Even enthusiasts underestimate exponential improvement. Today's gap is the wrong thing to stare at; the slope is what matters.
more: At the dawn of digital photography Ajay was a hardcore analog photographer, shooting Kodachrome and Ektachrome on Nikons and loving his slides. The engineer in him loved the idea of files, but early digital gear looked hopelessly shabby. Good images seemed to need about 12 megapixels, and the human fovea resolves something like 10,000 dots per inch. The gap seemed insuperable. He made the same mistake with lithium-ion batteries: although he and Ayush Patnaik spent many evenings dreaming about batteries, he didn't see the straight line in the semi-log graph, and today's battery miracles surprised him.
Even enthusiasts underestimate exponential improvement. Today's gap is the wrong thing to stare at; the slope is what matters.
printed: From whale oil to the cloud

head: Astral Weeks, the accidental masterpiece
dek: Sometimes the best work comes from losing control and letting other people's improvisation in.
more: Van Morrison went to record Astral Weeks with a couple of musicians of his own, but the producer quickly sacked them and brought in his own crew, including the bassist Richard Davis. Morrison sang and played guitar while jazz musicians he didn't know improvised around him. He wasn't happy at first because it didn't match the picture in his head, but over time he came to see it as a masterpiece. Amit recalls that about thirty years later Morrison toured with Davis and wanted him to play the parts exactly as on the album. Davis refused, saying he was a jazz player and would do something different each time.
Sometimes the best work comes from losing control and letting other people's improvisation in. The creator is not always the best judge of his own work in the moment.

head: Astral Weeks
dek: He calls it simply a masterpiece of deeply moving songs. It was born when the producer replaced Morrison's musicians with jazz players, including bassist Richard Davis, who improvised around him.
more: He calls it simply a masterpiece of deeply moving songs. It was born when the producer replaced Morrison's musicians with jazz players, including bassist Richard Davis, who improvised around him.
Amit's main recommendation for the episode, reached via the 'transistor radio' line in Brown Eyed Girl.

head: Moondance
dek: It is the counterpoint to Astral Weeks: Morrison with his own band, doing R&B the traditional way, exactly as he wanted.
more: It is the counterpoint to Astral Weeks: Morrison with his own band, doing R&B the traditional way, exactly as he wanted. Amit says every song is great and he could talk about it for another hour.
His second album recommendation, from around 1970.

head: Brown Eyed Girl
dek: It is a playful bridge from transistors on chips to the transistor radio.
more: It is a playful bridge from transistors on chips to the transistor radio. Amit himself calls it a cheesy early pop song and points listeners to the two albums instead.
Linked in the show notes. Amit brings it up after asking whether Ajay's wife Susan has brown eyes, because it has the line about going down to the old mine with a transistor radio.

head: Madame George
dek: It is the centrepiece of the album he considers a masterpiece.
more: It is the centrepiece of the album he considers a masterpiece.
Linked in the show notes as the iconic song of Astral Weeks.

head: Madame George (Luka Bloom's version)
dek: He calls it another great version of the song.
more: He calls it another great version of the song.
The second cover version Amit linked.

head: Even Cowgirls Get the Blues
dek: He calls its line about routine flights beautiful. It captures how stagnation is a mindset: only those who think they are on routine flights are on them.
more: He calls its line about routine flights beautiful. It captures how stagnation is a mindset: only those who think they are on routine flights are on them.
Ajay quotes it while describing firms that stagnate despite rising volume.

head: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It is one of the 'other interesting subjects' Ajay has steered the show towards.
more: It is one of the 'other interesting subjects' Ajay has steered the show towards.
Linked alongside the firm episodes for the opening tease about Ajay's favourite subjects.

head: A CPU at heart: fetch, add, branch
dek: The Intel 4004 was the world's first CPU on a single chip, and it did the whole job with about 2,300 transistors, where earlier CPUs were room-sized.
more: The Intel 4004 was the world's first CPU on a single chip, and it did the whole job with about 2,300 transistors, where earlier CPUs were room-sized. At heart a CPU is a Turing machine that needs only three things: fetch a memory cell into a register, add, and branch on an 'if'. Today we casually spend billions of transistors.

head: Moore's Law is an economic law, not a law of physics
dek: Gordon Moore's 1965 paper used just seven data points to observe that the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every 18 months.
more: Gordon Moore's 1965 paper used just seven data points to observe that the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every 18 months. The industry itself was pushed into being by NASA's hunger for compact equipment on satellites. Nothing in nature guarantees the doubling. It holds because people keep piling on innovation and capital. Plotted on a semi-log graph (linear time, log y-axis), it is a straight line, which means a tenfold rise every few years.
printed: Seven dots and a straight line

head: Moore's Laws (plural): put price on the y-axis
dek: Billions of transistors would be an exotic curiosity if each chip cost a million dollars.
more: Billions of transistors would be an exotic curiosity if each chip cost a million dollars. Ajay argues the more important version, perhaps five times more important, puts price or performance-per-price on the y-axis. That also gives straight semi-log lines, in solar panels, bandwidth, lithium-ion batteries, DNA sequencing and launch costs, where people now predict about $10 per kg to near-earth orbit. Our eyes should learn to spot these lines.

head: From mechanical cleverness to trivial software
dek: Cruise control and automatic transmission were once peaks of mechanical engineering that needed very clever people.
more: Cruise control and automatic transmission were once peaks of mechanical engineering that needed very clever people. With cheap CPUs they become a few lines of code: nudge the speed up or down around a target, or pick a gear from elevation and velocity. Ubiquitous cheap computation turns hard engineering problems into easy ones.

head: Steady grinding vs discontinuous jumps
dek: Lighting went from candles to gas lamps, tungsten, fluorescent and LEDs, rising from roughly 9% to 90% efficiency.
more: Lighting went from candles to gas lamps, tungsten, fluorescent and LEDs, rising from roughly 9% to 90% efficiency. That happened through discontinuous jumps separated by stagnation, and now the journey is essentially over. Moore's Law is different: relentless improvement every year. Amit maps this onto learning, which can be continuous accumulation or a quantum leap followed by refinement and then another leap.

head: More transistors doesn't mean faster CPUs
dek: CPUs were built around the single-threaded PDP-11 model, which chokes because the chip mostly waits on memory fetches.
more: CPUs were built around the single-threaded PDP-11 model, which chokes because the chip mostly waits on memory fetches. Tricks like speculative branch prediction, which computes both sides of an 'if', squeezed out about 10x and then maxed out. The resolution was the GPU: a thousand small parallel processors on one chip, with humans left to learn how to use them.

head: Three rival laws of progress: time, lifetime volume, annual scale
dek: Moore's Law puts time on the x-axis.
more: Moore's Law puts time on the x-axis. Wright's Law (1936, from a man who was not one of the Wright brothers) puts cumulative lifetime output there, with roughly a 20% productivity gain for every doubling, also called the learning or experience curve. Goddard's Law puts annual production there, which is plain economies of scale. Across 62 industries, Nagy et al. found Wright's Law the best predictor. So think of a person or firm by lifetime output: the cobbler who has repaired 53,000 shoes, or the Indian doctor who has seen huge numbers of patients.

head: Bias for action: perfection is the enemy of production
dek: For creators, Wright's Law means volume beats polishing. Many get stuck trying to make the perfect blog or episode.
more: For creators, Wright's Law means volume beats polishing. Many get stuck trying to make the perfect blog or episode. Amit's case is that doing over and over raises your baseline until excellence emerges.

head: Deliberate practice
dek: Amit adds the qualifier from Anders Ericsson, popularised by Malcolm Gladwell: volume alone is not enough.
more: Amit adds the qualifier from Anders Ericsson, popularised by Malcolm Gladwell: volume alone is not enough. A boy at the cricket nets can mindlessly hit balls for half an hour, or he can work on footwork, elbow position, balance and a still head, internalising one quality at a time.

head: Wright's Law is earned, not given
dek: The learning curve is a frontier, not a guarantee. Gains come from purposive 'manufacturing excellence'.
more: The learning curve is a frontier, not a guarantee. Gains come from purposive 'manufacturing excellence'. Ajay sees this on the Britannia board, where the company squeezes out energy savings and lower wastage every year. His test for any firm is to plot productivity against cumulative volume on a log scale. If there is no straight line, something is wrong with the organisation.

head: Why bad firms add volume but don't learn
dek: Ajay names three failure modes. Workers operate consultant-chosen machines like helpless peasants and wait for the next upgrade instead of improving the process.
more: Ajay names three failure modes. Workers operate consultant-chosen machines like helpless peasants and wait for the next upgrade instead of improving the process. Teams churn, so tacit knowledge walks out the door. And firms are cut to the bone, with a pure 'shut up and execute' culture that leaves no slack for thinking, debate, experiments or mistakes. Lean looks efficient in the short run but kills the journey to quality.

head: I, CPU: Moore's Law as a coordination mechanism
dek: Making a chip involves ASML's machines in Holland, three American firms' chip-design software, tens of thousands of engineers in Bangalore, and ARM, Apple, Intel and hundreds of others.
more: Making a chip involves ASML's machines in Holland, three American firms' chip-design software, tens of thousands of engineers in Bangalore, and ARM, Apple, Intel and hundreds of others. That is a huge coordination problem, and Mahalanobis-style thinking says only a coercive government could solve it. Yet no government does. The shared, near-religious belief in the 18-month doubling lets firms invest ahead of each other in sync, making the law self-fulfilling. Amit's addition: articulating the law matters as much as the law itself, because the shared dream is what makes action look coordinated.

head: Build for tomorrow's cost curve, not today's
dek: Today's AI spending is outrageous and unprofitable. At about fifty paise per Gemini API call, most Indian app ideas don't pay.
more: Today's AI spending is outrageous and unprofitable. At about fifty paise per Gemini API call, most Indian app ideas don't pay. Ajay says innovators must imagine the world when that falls to 0.05 paise and build for it, like a science-fiction writer. Amit says the same to entrepreneurs, citing Netflix betting on streaming in 2007 before bandwidth and displays were ready.

head: Humans are bad at exponential thinking
dek: Having misjudged digital cameras and batteries himself, Ajay warns that we all underrate straight lines on semi-log graphs.
more: Having misjudged digital cameras and batteries himself, Ajay warns that we all underrate straight lines on semi-log graphs. The habit to build is to keep scanning industries for Wright's-law curves and ask what you would do with them, since they are happening all around us and ignoring them is dangerous.

head: Technology as the great equalizer
dek: Against the claim that new technology widens inequality, Amit asks for evidence.
more: Against the claim that new technology widens inequality, Amit asks for evidence. Technology starts with governments or the rich, as GPS went from military and space use to luxury cars, and then reaches everyone. AI is usable by anyone today, and falling prices are what make this democratisation happen.

head: People are brains, not stomachs
dek: Each time an energy source looked exhausted, scarcity raised prices and triggered innovation.
more: Each time an energy source looked exhausted, scarcity raised prices and triggered innovation. As forests thinned, wood gave way to coal. Whale oil, with its race for better ships, extraction and storage, gave way to fossil fuels. Nuclear and renewables now promise a way beyond those. Amit argues the deepest fact about humans is endless innovation, and the Ehrlich–Simon bet is evidence for it.

head: Lift the constraints and humans fill the space
dek: Capacity built for one purpose gets repurposed by human imagination. Overbuilt fiber became the backbone of broadband and the cloud.
more: Capacity built for one purpose gets repurposed by human imagination. Overbuilt fiber became the backbone of broadband and the cloud. GPS, made for the military, now gets your food delivered. Memory-foam pillows made for spacecraft are now in homes. Technology is downstream of human creativity.

head: The cold open is a…
more: The cold open is a 'test of Ajay's math skills': the sum of the squares of the first four primes. Ajay adds 4, 9, 25 and 49 aloud and lands on 87, so Amit says 'Welcome to episode eighty seven.'

head: Amit refuses to let Ajay simply announce another topic
more: Amit refuses to let Ajay simply announce another topic: 'God knows how many episodes on firms you've gotten away with and other interesting subjects like bankruptcy regulation.' Ajay is interviewed like a job applicant. 'Applicant's name.' 'Moore's Laws.' 'Is your name Moore's Laws?' 'My father was Mr. Laws.' Age fifty-nine, occupation YouTuber. His pitch begins: 'There's a great wild west wind tearing through this modern world and it is called CPUs.' It ends with the question of whether the form must be submitted in triplicate: 'Yes, why not... in physical copies.'

head: After the chessboard parable, Ajay works out the rice in kilograms against the mass of the earth and concludes it is…
more: After the chessboard parable, Ajay works out the rice in kilograms against the mass of the earth and concludes it is 'well beyond the resources of any king.' Amit shrugs: 'Doesn't matter. It's a lot of grain.'

Ajay: 'for all ye callow gentle readers that are used to squandering like billions of transistors in the CPUs on your phones, I will have you know... the Intel 4004 had something like 2300 transistors.'

Amit: 'I am the best driver in Bombay partly because automatic transmission allows me to take my mind off' gear-shifting and onto 'optimal lane shifting'. He calls manual vs automatic 'a deeply ideological question, akin to the Oxford comma and the semicolon.'

head: On dial-up days, Amit recalls having
more: On dial-up days, Amit recalls having 'half a picture of Samantha Fox' when the connection drops and the screen says buffering, while the edit plays the modem sound: 'Just as you are seeing now, gentle reader, we are so smart.' Ajay tops it: 'I could listen to the negotiation of the modem and I would know which protocol it got through.'

head: Amit applies Wright's Law to the show
more: Amit applies Wright's Law to the show: 'when we make episode one seventy four will be twenty percent better than we are now.' Ajay agrees, and notes the bulk of the gains came early and 'now the learning rate has gone down.'

head: Asked by Van Morrison decades later to replay his Astral Weeks bass lines exactly, Richard Davis replies, as Amit tells it
more: Asked by Van Morrison decades later to replay his Astral Weeks bass lines exactly, Richard Davis replies, as Amit tells it: 'No, you fucker, I'm a jazz player, I'll do something different each time.'

head: Priyanka Chopra Flopped, the Aghori Baba Went Viral
dek: Creators and politicians both follow the numbers. Ideological labels are often pinned on someone because of who appears on their show, not because of anything they believe.
more: Amit relays what their friend Roshan Abbas told them at a party at Ajay's house. One week Ranveer Allahbadia (BeerBiceps) released a Priyanka Chopra interview he expected to go viral, and nothing happened. Another episode, with an Aghori Baba, got about two million views in six hours, so he leaned into tantra and Aghori content. Later, ahead of the elections, government ministers including Jaishankar and Piyush Goyal skipped the smaller right-wing podcasts and went on his show for its reach. The left promptly branded him a right-winger. Amit says he was no kind of winger, just a curious host with no ideology who let big names come on.
Creators and politicians both follow the numbers. Ideological labels are often pinned on someone because of who appears on their show, not because of anything they believe.

head: Defending the Guy Nobody Will Defend
dek: Free speech is tested by the people nobody wants to defend. Once a crackdown is normalised against a disliked target, the same tools can be used on everyone else.
more: On Samay's subscription-only show India's Got Latent, Ranveer asked a crude question about parents and incest. Amit points out it wasn't even original: it had been an old Reddit question for twenty years, and a much bigger Indian comedian used it in a show seven years earlier. A clip went viral, the right piled on, and then the state stepped in. Police cases were filed in several places including Assam. The Supreme Court process left him with his passport taken away and an order to produce no more content. Around forty people connected to the show faced cases, including the editor. Amit, who has never watched a full episode of Ranveer's show, tweeted that he was a well-intentioned kid who had apologised gracefully, and that anyone who disliked the content shouldn't watch it. Both left and right attacked Amit for it. His worry is that a hated target lets the state sneak in a broadcast bill through the back door, or simply normalise treating creators this way.
Free speech is tested by the people nobody wants to defend. Once a crackdown is normalised against a disliked target, the same tools can be used on everyone else.
printed: Stand by the man you can’t stand

head: Section 295A: Beef, Weddings and a Joke Book
dek: Vague speech laws do their damage through the legal process itself, whatever the verdict.
more: Amit recalls a column he wrote around 2007 on how Section 295A (deliberately outraging religious feelings) was being used. Cases were filed against Ravi Shastri for saying on air, during a series in South Africa, that he likes eating beef. Another was filed over Elizabeth Hurley's marriage to Arun Nayar because not all Hindu rituals were performed. Another targeted the publisher of a Santa-Banta joke book. Since such a case can be filed anywhere, the accused may have to keep turning up at a court in, say, Tripura.
Vague speech laws do their damage through the legal process itself, whatever the verdict. Anyone can be dragged across the country over almost anything.

head: How Nehru Amended His Way Past the Courts
dek: Even a celebrated liberal, convinced that 'people like me' will use power wisely, will build tools his rivals later inherit.
more: In the early 1950s Nehru was cracking down on speech, from the RSS magazine The Organiser to Romesh Thapar's communist magazine Crossroads. The Supreme Court overturned the Crossroads ban, and the sedition law (124A) was struck down. Nehru responded with the First Amendment, adding caveats such as public order and relations with friendly countries. Those caveats later let sedition return. He argued that when the courts block the legislature on basic social matters, the legislature should amend the Constitution. He was opposed by Acharya Kripalani, Jayaprakash Narayan and Syama Prasad Mookerjee, and Naziruddin Ahmad, an MP from Bengal, warned that sedition would come back. Amit admits he once wrongly said the First Amendment itself revived sedition and got corrected, but says it was true in spirit because the amendment laid the grounds.
Even a celebrated liberal, convinced that 'people like me' will use power wisely, will build tools his rivals later inherit. Today the boot is on the other foot, and every party uses these laws.

head: Why Films Get Censored but Books Don't
dek: Censorship rests on a paternalistic view that ordinary people are too impressionable to be trusted.
more: In 1968 K.A. Abbas made A Tale of Four Cities, a documentary set in Mumbai's red-light districts. The challenge to it went to the Supreme Court, which ruled that cinema needs closer scrutiny than books because a moving image stirs people more deeply. That reasoning underpins film censorship, where a board of bureaucrats decides what Indian society is fit to see.
Censorship rests on a paternalistic view that ordinary people are too impressionable to be trusted. Society has normalised that assumption so fully that it goes unquestioned.

head: 295A Is Bad, Except Against My Enemies
dek: Many self-declared free speech defenders only defend speech they agree with.
more: A prominent figure on the left told Amit that 295A and 153A are bad laws. In the same breath, she told a colleague that a 295A case should be filed against a right-wing politician for something he said.
Many self-declared free speech defenders only defend speech they agree with. A principle that switches off for your opponents isn't a principle.

head: Satanic Verses Yes, Danish Cartoons No?
dek: Free speech can't depend on whether you rate the work as art or as provocation.
more: Around 2007-08, during the violence over the Danish cartoons, a man Amit calls perhaps the most sensible MP in India today wrote a column. He said he supported Salman Rushdie and The Satanic Verses but not the Danish cartoonists, because the novel was art and the cartoons were mere provocation. Amit rejects the distinction.
Free speech can't depend on whether you rate the work as art or as provocation. The right belongs equally to the masterpiece and to the obnoxious.

head: 'Uplift the Consciousness of the Masses'
dek: Infantilising the public is an elite habit that runs across parties. In a democracy, the duty to understand and persuade lies with the leaders, not the voters.
more: Amit was recently on a podcast co-hosted by a former guest of The Seen and the Unseen who is close to the Congress party. She said 'we need to uplift the consciousness of the masses.' Amit pushed back: elites should ask whether they are wrong, or why they can't communicate what they think is good, instead of blaming voters as racist or misogynist.
Infantilising the public is an elite habit that runs across parties. In a democracy, the duty to understand and persuade lies with the leaders, not the voters.

head: Sixteen Stormy Days
dek: Amit calls it brilliant and says everyone should read it. It is the definitive account of the episode that hobbled free speech in India's constitution.
more: Amit calls it brilliant and says everyone should read it. It is the definitive account of the episode that hobbled free speech in India's constitution.
Brought up while telling how Nehru pushed through the First Amendment after the courts struck down his speech restrictions.

head: The First Assault on Our Constitution (Episode 194 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A conversational way into the First Amendment story at the heart of this episode.
more: A conversational way into the First Amendment story at the heart of this episode.
Amit mentions that Tripurdaman has done an episode with him on Sixteen Stormy Days.

head: Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back
dek: It argues that constitutions are products of their circumstances.
more: It argues that constitutions are products of their circumstances. America's came from a fight for individual freedom; India's was drafted amid turmoil and fragmentation, so it centralised power and paid only lip service to freedom.
Amit calls it an excellent book while explaining why India's Constitution centralised power.

head: Subhashish Bhadra on Our Dysfunctional State (Episode 333 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: The longer conversation behind the argument that India inherited a state built to rule rather than serve.
more: The longer conversation behind the argument that India inherited a state built to rule rather than serve.
Amit says Bhadra elaborated on the point about circumstantial constitutions in his episode.

head: When Ideas Have Sex
dek: It captures why ideas must collide and recombine freely for the best ones to emerge and for society to progress.
more: It captures why ideas must collide and recombine freely for the best ones to emerge and for society to progress.
Amit uses Ridley's 'great phrase' to explain the marketplace-of-ideas argument; the talk is linked in the show notes.

head: Open on Facts, Firm on Values
dek: Amit says that after years of thinking, he is all shades of grey on facts, because the world is too complex to understand fully, but black and white on certain values.
more: Amit says that after years of thinking, he is all shades of grey on facts, because the world is too complex to understand fully, but black and white on certain values. Free speech is one of those values. Ajay doesn't accept a clean facts/values split. He prefers calibrated, Bayesian confidence: some beliefs need a very big fact to topple them, others only a modest dose.

head: Free Speech Absolutism: One Bright Line
dek: Amit's absolutism follows the US standard. All speech is allowed, including hate speech.
more: Amit's absolutism follows the US standard. All speech is allowed, including hate speech. The only line is direct incitement to violence, which is already illegal. So 'Gujarati economists shouldn't speak' is protected, while 'here is his address, go lynch him' is not. The deeper reason to be absolute is the question of who decides what is offensive: any gatekeeper you empower today may be your enemy tomorrow.

head: Three Arguments for Free Speech
dek: (1) First principles, following John Locke: a newborn owns itself, not the king or the state, and every right flows from self-ownership.
more: (1) First principles, following John Locke: a newborn owns itself, not the king or the state, and every right flows from self-ownership. Silencing someone denies their personhood and agency. (2) The marketplace of ideas: ideas should compete and recombine (Matt Ridley's 'when ideas have sex'), and an official view can be wrong, so progress usually comes from heretics. (3) Democracy is a contest of ideas about how to run a country. When the state controls information or punishes speech, the result is information asymmetry and a chilling effect, because tomorrow I will think twice before saying the same thing. That is electoral manipulation without touching a ballot box.

head: Rights Framed from a Police Constable's Point of View
dek: India's Constitution was drafted amid chaos, with more than 500 princely states and real fear that things would fall apart, so it centralised power.
more: India's Constitution was drafted amid chaos, with more than 500 princely states and real fear that things would fall apart, so it centralised power. Article 19(1)(a) grants free speech, but 19(2) immediately allows 'reasonable restrictions' on vague grounds like public order, decency and morality, which a police constable gets to interpret. India took over the colonial state, built to rule subjects rather than serve citizens, more or less wholesale: in Amit's words, white-skinned rulers were exchanged for brown-skinned ones. That is why colonial-era laws like 295A, 153A and sedition (124A) survive in India though they no longer exist in Britain, and why challenging them as unconstitutional doesn't work. Ajay adds that the constituent assembly had India's best minds but lacked a theory of the state: the problem was seen simply as getting rid of the white rulers.

head: Power Corrupts Character, Not Just Wallets
dek: Amit says the founding generation, in government and opposition, were the best and brightest, and men like Nehru were never corrupt for money.
more: Amit says the founding generation, in government and opposition, were the best and brightest, and men like Nehru were never corrupt for money. But proximity to power breeds arrogance and the belief that you know better than everyone else. The result: a Constitution amended so often that, as Amit recounts, Ambedkar said in the early 1950s he would gladly burn it himself. Amit adds that no party in India is squeaky clean; whoever is in power uses these laws against their enemies.

head: Two Failings of the Elites: Infantilisation and Hypocrisy
dek: Infantilisation means treating citizens as incapable of making their own decisions.
more: Infantilisation means treating citizens as incapable of making their own decisions. Film censorship and talk of 'uplifting the consciousness of the masses' both come from it. Hypocrisy means opposing speech laws when they are used against your side and cheering when they hit your enemies. Amit's prescription for any free speech controversy: don't personalise it ('we don't like him') and don't politicise it. Either way it will come back to hurt society, and creators especially.
printed: The masses are not the problem

head: Punish the Act, Not the Speech
dek: Amit answers the standard objections. Falsely shouting fire in a crowded theatre is already punishable as trespass on the owner's property and as harm or attempted harm to others, so no speech exception is needed.
more: Amit answers the standard objections. Falsely shouting fire in a crowded theatre is already punishable as trespass on the owner's property and as harm or attempted harm to others, so no speech exception is needed. Hurt feelings are subjective and could cover anything; adults should not invoke the coercive power of the state over offence. Ajay adds that India's 'snowflakes problem' reflects insecurity and low self-esteem: why listen to, or read, what you dislike? If hate speech leads to violence, punish the violence, and treat the speaker as an accessory only if there was direct incitement. Libel is for civil courts and damages, not criminal law; India is unusual in treating it as criminal. Fraud, like Ajay's example of a medicine claiming 100mg of salicylic acid that contains 50mg, is fraud, not a speech issue.
printed: Punish the act, not the word

head: Let Judges Draw the Line
dek: Ajay's response to people who think incitement must be defined in black-and-white law: in the common law, judges exist to read subtle situations and decide whether something was humour or a genuine incitement to violence.
more: Ajay's response to people who think incitement must be defined in black-and-white law: in the common law, judges exist to read subtle situations and decide whether something was humour or a genuine incitement to violence. A workable principle doesn't need a mechanical rule.

head: Free Speech Is a Battle Against the State
dek: Blocking someone on Twitter, or a platform enforcing terms you agreed to, is not censorship.
more: Blocking someone on Twitter, or a platform enforcing terms you agreed to, is not censorship. The state holds a monopoly on violence, and when it silences you, you are silenced everywhere. A private person merely declines to give you space in their home or timeline. Your rights end where they infringe on someone else's property and rules, and no one is entitled to anyone else's attention.

head: Weak State Capacity Means India Needs More Free Speech, Not Less
dek: Ajay flips the usual argument that if the UK or Germany has restriction X, India should too.
more: Ajay flips the usual argument that if the UK or Germany has restriction X, India should too. In India, filing a criminal or civil case and going through the courts is itself the punishment, and police, prosecutors and judges don't function well. So until India learns how to make these institutions work, which he puts at the next hundred years, the bar for free speech should be higher than in the West. Amit adds that claiming Indians are too sensitive for free speech insults a society that has managed more diversity than any other, for centuries.

head: Truth Is Too High a Bar: Finance as a Marketplace of Ideas
dek: Ajay worries about rules that protect only true statements. Most of the world is a fog of war, and if you could speak only with documentary proof, you would hardly speak at all.
more: Ajay worries about rules that protect only true statements. Most of the world is a fog of war, and if you could speak only with documentary proof, you would hardly speak at all. Securities and derivatives markets are pure marketplaces of opinion. Treating speculators as unable to sift claims for themselves is infantilisation. Short sellers who take a position and then publish damaging findings about a company are healthy, almost investigative journalism, and they deserve more respect because they put money behind their views. Forcing companies to monitor and rebut every social-media rumour is 'just dumb' and pulls them away from running their business.

head: Every Propaganda Medium Has a Learning Curve
dek: Ajay credits this idea to their friend Suyash Rai. Each new medium, from Mussolini's radio to film, television, WhatsApp and now LLMs, sets off a moral panic.
more: Ajay credits this idea to their friend Suyash Rai. Each new medium, from Mussolini's radio to film, television, WhatsApp and now LLMs, sets off a moral panic. In 2012-13, WhatsApp felt like an alien spaceship: messages seemed to come from family, and people believed everything. Today nobody believes WhatsApp forwards. For now, a perfectly typeset, grammatical text earns trust, and LLMs are being used to push propaganda that way, but people will learn. Ajay says he is less optimistic about the masses than Amit, yet the remedy is still to let it play out rather than reach for state power.

The 'black and white' opener: Amit notes that below the waist both hosts are in black, so Ajay is actually black and white while 'I am black alone.' Later: 'when it comes to shirts, I know you are firmly a white man and I am firmly black.'

head: Amit acts out Ranveer's interview trick of repeating your last line back as a question: you say
more: Amit acts out Ranveer's interview trick of repeating your last line back as a question: you say 'free speech is important for a democracy,' and he goes, eyes wide, 'Oh, free speech is important for a democracy?' Then you elaborate for another two minutes.

head: On the election-season podcast rush: the right-wing podcasters must have thought
more: On the election-season podcast rush: the right-wing podcasters must have thought 'Modi hamare paas aayenge' (Modi will come to us). 'Modiji completely ignored those guys, just went for the numbers.'

head: On the India's Got Latent editor being booked
more: On the India's Got Latent editor being booked: 'as young Nomsita would know, an editor's job is to cut things out, and this editor did not cut out the anap-shanap, as it were. Except that if you try to cut out everything that people will find objectionable from a comedy show, you'll basically have nothing left.' (Nomsita edits this show.)

head: Amit's hate-speech example
more: Amit's hate-speech example: saying 'Gujarati economists should not be allowed to speak up' is protected hate speech, as is what Ajay has said about Bengali economists ('all of that, which I agree with, by the way'). The line is crossed only at 'here is Ajay Shah's address, go and lynch him.'

head: Ajay's test case for incitement: a tweet ordering Amit's 100,000 followers to…
more: Ajay's test case for incitement: a tweet ordering Amit's 100,000 followers to 'get a glass of cold water and dunk it on Nomsita's head.' His followers, being wise and sensible, know it's humour and no water lands on her head. Deciding such cases is what judges are for.

head: Introducing the history chapter
more: Introducing the history chapter: 'When life used to be short, nasty, and brutish, the folks endowed with the biceps would hurl a punch at the folks endowed with a silver tongue.'

head: The cartoon Amit recalls from the early Republic: someone at the parliament bookstore asks for a copy of the Constitution, and the clerk
more: The cartoon Amit recalls from the early Republic: someone at the parliament bookstore asks for a copy of the Constitution, and the clerk replies, 'I'm afraid we don't stock periodicals.'

On 'decency and morality' as grounds for restriction: if Amit opened another couple of shirt buttons, 'it offends decency and morality. I mean, I might say it myself, actually, frankly, because I know what my chest looks like.'

head: Amit on hurt feelings
more: Amit on hurt feelings: 'We are adults. It's not like we are kindergarten children or Oh teacher, teacher, Ajay hurt my feelings, take away his tiffin box.'

head: Amit, as Ajay rails against India's snowflakes
more: Amit, as Ajay rails against India's snowflakes: 'Oh, is your God so weak that mere words from someone like me can hurt your God?' Ajay adds: 'what kind of omniscient, omnipotent creature can be affected by mere words.'

head: Sign-off: if you disagree
more: Sign-off: if you disagree, 'tell us why in the comments, because you have free speech.'

head: The closing line twists the old slogan
more: The closing line twists the old slogan 'the revolution will not be televised': 'even if the revolution has all the tools of propaganda at its disposal, the counter-revolution will also be televised.'

head: Hanlon's razor (
more: Hanlon's razor ('never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity'), which Amit applies to Ranveer as perhaps ignorance: 'I don't want to call him stupid.'

head: Ambedkar's early-1950s lament, as recounted by Amit: he had been proud of the Constitution, but seeing what was being done to it
more: Ambedkar's early-1950s lament, as recounted by Amit: he had been proud of the Constitution, but seeing what was being done to it, 'I would gladly burn it myself.'

head: Wright's Law, in Ajay's rant about being forced to rebut social-media rumours: a company should be busy getting
more: Wright's Law, in Ajay's rant about being forced to rebut social-media rumours: a company should be busy getting 'twenty percent gains for each doubling of output', not policing chat groups.

head: The Fan Who Wanted Them to Plan India's Economy
dek: Being good at one thing does not qualify you to steer a society. The flattering wish to put 'smart people on top' is the same top-down instinct that produces industrial policy.
more: A fan sent Amit a gushing email that ended with two lines he found deeply disturbing: 'you guys are so smart, I wish you were running the country. You should plan our economy.' Amit replied with three objections. First, you can't run a country like a YouTube show, a play on their episode 'Don't Run a Country Like a Company'. Second, power corrupts, and whatever humility the two of them have comes from setbacks, not success. Third, the word 'plan' itself: you can plan your day or a shoot schedule, but planning a nation is the hubris Hayek called the fatal conceit.
Being good at one thing does not qualify you to steer a society. The flattering wish to put 'smart people on top' is the same top-down instinct that produces industrial policy.

head: A Callow 35-Year-Old Meets the Finance Ministry
dek: From outside, government looks like a list of easy fixes. From inside, the hard problems are hard for real reasons.
more: As a young economist, Ajay assumed the policy world was full of stupid mistakes he could easily improve on. At 35 he joined the Ministry of Finance, hired by Yashwant Sinha, whom he admires enormously and calls one of the great people of the country. He worked intensively with Sinha, and within days he realised that being finance minister is extremely hard. There were no obvious mistakes and no low-hanging fruit.

From outside, government looks like a list of easy fixes. From inside, the hard problems are hard for real reasons. That humility is the starting point for the whole case against planners who think they know best.

head: Who Exports: India, or Indians?
dek: The abstraction 'India' hides who actually acts. Firms export, not the state.
more: At a Ministry of Finance meeting run by Ashok Lahiri, then chief economic advisor, the routine business included the Ministry of Commerce setting an export target for India. Ajay, the junior-most person in the room, asked what the Ministry of Commerce, or any of them, had to do with what India exports. Individual firms make export decisions, and the state's job is only to create enabling conditions. Even the word 'target' is semi-offensive, because missing it triggers urgent mid-year meetings about 'policy measures to boost exports'.
The abstraction 'India' hides who actually acts. Firms export, not the state. Treating the nation as one agent with targets is the root of the control mindset behind industrial policy.

head: Nanotech and Poultry: The RBI's Chosen Industries
dek: This is what 'picking winners' looks like in practice: an arbitrary list that hands some sectors a privilege while denying it to others, and nobody could defend the choices on economic grounds.
more: The RBI has long imposed capital controls on foreign borrowing, and Ajay says he has never seen an economic reason for them. One day a rule restricted external commercial borrowing to just nine industries, so the chosen ones would get access to cheaper foreign credit and the rest would not. Ajay, 'bloody minded and masochistic' enough to actually read such documents, found that the chosen industries included nanotechnology and poultry farms.
This is what 'picking winners' looks like in practice: an arbitrary list that hands some sectors a privilege while denying it to others, and nobody could defend the choices on economic grounds.

head: UPI by Decree, GPS by Choice
dek: A good technology wins adoption without force. Reaching for coercion first is a distinctly Indian habit, and it shuts down the competition through which better options emerge.
more: Their friend Suyash observed that the government picked UPI as the technology and then used income tax law to back it: income tax inspectors can fine any shop that does not accept UPI. Amit called this a TIL and argued that even though UPI is outstanding technology, every shopkeeper should be free to choose how to accept payment. Ajay contrasted it with the US. He recalls that around 1993 Bill Clinton signed off on releasing high-resolution GPS data to the whole world. People rushed to adopt it, yet the government never mandated it. Phone makers themselves aspired to put GPS in every phone.
A good technology wins adoption without force. Reaching for coercion first is a distinctly Indian habit, and it shuts down the competition through which better options emerge.
printed: Pay by UPI, or pay a fine

head: Seven-Year Waits for a Telephone
dek: The cost of a state monopoly is easy to forget once it is gone. The same test applies to every sector that is still closed: what would competition do there?
more: Amit grew up in a privileged household, with a father in the civil service. Even so, in the 1980s you waited seven or eight years for a telephone from the MTNL monopoly. Air fares were about 8,000 rupees, roughly what they cost now but a huge sum then, so even an officer's family rarely flew. He still remembers the excitement of his first flight. After 1991, when these sectors opened up, competitors flooded in and prices fell. MTNL and BSNL were never shut down; they simply became irrelevant. Many TV channels arrived too, and nobody had to watch Doordarshan anymore. He retells this often because about 70% of Indians were born after liberalisation.
The cost of a state monopoly is easy to forget once it is gone. The same test applies to every sector that is still closed: what would competition do there?

head: Air India's Long, Expensive Detour
dek: Privatisation recovers only part of the loss. The real cost is the decades of competition, service and growth that never happened.
more: Air India began as a private company owned by the Tatas. The government expropriated it and made it a monopoly. When the airline industry was later opened to competition, Air India turned into a zombie firm that, at its peak, Ajay believes was bleeding about 35,000 crore rupees a year in taxpayer subsidy. The BJP government eventually privatised it back to the Tatas, which Ajay calls a great achievement. He asks what would have happened if it had never been nationalised, and why Lufthansa doesn't fly Bombay–Delhi.
Privatisation recovers only part of the loss. The real cost is the decades of competition, service and growth that never happened.
printed: Tata to state and back again

head: SEEPZ: The Radio Plan That Birthed Diamonds and Software
dek: Ajay calls it one of the greatest industrial-policy successes in history, but it worked because it added freedom, not because anyone picked the right industry.
more: In the 1970s, bureaucrats saw East Asia exporting radios and electronic parts and asked why India couldn't do the same. They diagnosed the problem as customs duty: paying 150% on imported transistors made Indian-made radios impossible to export. So in the boondocks of North Bombay they walled off land as the Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ). Every truck through its gate was inspected. Components came in from the airport under guard, Ajay imagines with a shotgun rider, so nothing leaked into the Indian market, and finished goods went straight back out to planes. Given this pocket of freedom to import and export, entrepreneurs discovered things nobody planned. One was polishing rough diamonds brought from South Africa and Antwerp; India today polishes about 55% of the world's diamonds by number. The other was importing computers so Indian programmers could build and export software, making SEEPZ one of the early sites of the Indian software industry.

Ajay calls it one of the greatest industrial-policy successes in history, but it worked because it added freedom, not because anyone picked the right industry. The two big winners were ones no planner foresaw.

head: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism
dek: Hayek's phrase names the core error of the whole episode: a nation is too complex for anyone to plan from the top.
more: Hayek's phrase names the core error of the whole episode: a nation is too complex for anyone to plan from the top.
Amit invoked 'our hero' Hayek while explaining why he dislikes the word 'plan' applied to a country.

head: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
