dek: It sets out the public policy process: gather data, do research, hold public debate, write committee reports and draft laws.
more: It sets out the public policy process: gather data, do research, hold public debate, write committee reports and draft laws. Not six weeks, maybe six months, surely six years.
Ajay's answer to 'how hard is it to fix the indirect tax system instead of doing PLI?'

head: Eat a Peach
dek: Amit singles out two tracks, 'Little Martha' and 'Blue Sky', both featuring Duane Allman: 'Absolutely love his guitaring, great feel, great vibe, just incredible.'
more: Amit singles out two tracks, 'Little Martha' and 'Blue Sky', both featuring Duane Allman: 'Absolutely love his guitaring, great feel, great vibe, just incredible.'
Slipped in after the Derek Trucks pun, because viewers had complained they don't give enough recommendations.

head: The Fatal Conceit: Nations Can't Be Planned
dek: You can plan your own day, but a nation is too complex for anyone to plan from the top.
more: You can plan your own day, but a nation is too complex for anyone to plan from the top. Top-down thinking leads to ruin again and again, however enlightened the planners believe their approach is. Amit holds that industrial policy should not be done better; it should not be done at all.

head: Industrial Policy Means Picking Winners, Using Four Levers
dek: When the government decides which industry, technology, firm or location is good or bad, that is industrial policy.
more: When the government decides which industry, technology, firm or location is good or bad, that is industrial policy. It works through four levers: subsidies (public money, tax breaks), coercive power (for example, fining shops that don't take UPI), ethno-nationalism (favour Indian firms, keep foreigners out), and outright government monopolies. In the first, the state plays venture capitalist; in the last, it plays entrepreneur.

head: Clusters Emerge, They Can't Be Willed
dek: Silicon Valley, Tirupur's garments and Gujarat's chemicals grew organically.
more: Silicon Valley, Tirupur's garments and Gujarat's chemicals grew organically. Skills, vendors and labour markets accumulated and created network effects. Governments see this and try to declare clusters, and the decisions get contaminated by 'equity' (every state deserves one, so a drug cluster in Himachal Pradesh) or by a powerful politician's constituency.

head: Economic Development Is a Story of Firms
dek: By simple arithmetic, GDP is the sum of the value added by all firms. A rich country is full of high-productivity firms and a poor one is full of low-productivity firms.
more: By simple arithmetic, GDP is the sum of the value added by all firms. A rich country is full of high-productivity firms and a poor one is full of low-productivity firms. People are the same everywhere; Sundar Pichai and Satya Nadella are Indians. The difference lies in the incentives created by the firms' operating environment.

head: Coercion Has No Budget Constraint
dek: Spending is limited by taxes, deficits and competing claims, because the budget has to add up.
more: Spending is limited by taxes, deficits and competing claims, because the budget has to add up. Coercive power has no such limit, so the state can keep adding restrictions every day at no budget cost. That is why coercion spreads so easily through industrial policy.

head: Finance Works Through Failure
dek: If an industry has good prospects, investors will fund it with equity or debt, because looking for the next good opportunity is what finance does all day.
more: If an industry has good prospects, investors will fund it with equity or debt, because looking for the next good opportunity is what finance does all day. The system works by placing many bets on long shots, most of which fail. A government instead backs one national champion through thick and thin. If the financial system is weak, the fix is to repair it and let foreign financial firms in, not to replace it with the state.

head: The Marginal Cost of Public Funds Is About Three
dek: Public money is taken from people by force. People reorganise their lives and firms to avoid tax, which lowers productivity, and the economy also bears the overhead of compliance, lawyers and enforcement.
more: Public money is taken from people by force. People reorganise their lives and firms to avoid tax, which lowers productivity, and the economy also bears the overhead of compliance, lawyers and enforcement. Each rupee the government spends therefore costs the economy about three. Only public goods and real market failures, such as defence, foreign policy or a vaccination campaign, return enough to justify that. Subsidising poultry or textiles does not.

head: Intervention Redistributes From the Poor to the Rich
dek: Socialists believe interventions move wealth from rich to poor. Amit argues the reverse happens: costs are spread thinly and invisibly across everyone, while the benefits go to concentrated interests.
more: Socialists believe interventions move wealth from rich to poor. Amit argues the reverse happens: costs are spread thinly and invisibly across everyone, while the benefits go to concentrated interests. The poor pay most, often by staying poor longer than they otherwise would.

head: Milton Friedman's Spending Matrix
dek: Spending your own money on yourself, you economise and seek value. Your money on others: you economise but care less about value.
more: Spending your own money on yourself, you economise and seek value. Your money on others: you economise but care less about value. Others' money on yourself: you seek value but don't economise. Government spends other people's money on other people, so it does neither.

head: Public Choice and the Power Paradox
dek: Officials are not selfless, all-knowing welfare maximisers; they are ordinary people pursuing their own careers and goals.
more: Officials are not selfless, all-knowing welfare maximisers; they are ordinary people pursuing their own careers and goals. Investors have skin in the game and are judged on results, so they pay for information and research. Bureaucrats have little incentive to learn, and everyone who visits them flatters them ('Sir, you are so great... just one small thing, your subsidy scheme should work well for my industry'). Power cuts them off from honest information, which leads to more confidence, more control and even worse information. Ajay calls this the socialist trap.

head: A Country Is Not a Company: The Double Error
dek: Engineers and businesspeople who are convinced about, say, lithium-ion batteries leap to wanting state power behind them.
more: Engineers and businesspeople who are convinced about, say, lithium-ion batteries leap to wanting state power behind them. Government is a different arena, with its own rules: political economy, public administration, checks and balances, rule of law. Their reasoning also contains two errors: assuming they know what's right for the world, and assuming they'd be the joint secretary making the call.

head: The Rent-Seeking Mentality of a Protected Economy
dek: For decades India had a protected economy run by a powerful state. Firms got ahead by working the state rather than by serving customers better than global rivals, and that habit has become a mindset.
more: For decades India had a protected economy run by a powerful state. Firms got ahead by working the state rather than by serving customers better than global rivals, and that habit has become a mindset. An American entrepreneur asks how to create enough value to get rich; too often an Indian one asks how to influence a joint secretary to beat local competitors.

head: PLI Patches Tax Mistakes Deal by Deal
dek: The average Indian non-financial firm makes about 6% profit after tax on sales, so a 1–3% indirect-tax error can swing the return on equity by 50–100%.
more: The average Indian non-financial firm makes about 6% profit after tax on sales, so a 1–3% indirect-tax error can swing the return on equity by 50–100%. Ajay credits Ila Patnaik with teaching him this. Good countries refund indirect taxes on exports because you don't tax foreigners. India doesn't, so Apple is right to demand compensation, and PLI provides it. But PLI only reaches giants that can afford roughly a $10 million policy operation in Delhi to negotiate and actually get paid. Fixing the tax system at the root would attract the thousands of firms that won't bother.

head: Real Disabilities vs. Whining (the Negative Disability)
dek: Tax mistakes are genuine disabilities created by the state and should be fixed.
more: Tax mistakes are genuine disabilities created by the state and should be fixed. Expensive transport, unreliable electricity and unskilled workers are ordinary features of producing anywhere, and no government should compensate firms for them. India's very low wages are a huge advantage in the firm's pocket. Ajay credits Rahul Ahluwalia with the point that the real surprise is how little India exports, given labour costs that low.

head: Engineer's Technology vs. Economist's Technology
dek: States force particular technologies on the economy believing productivity lives in the machine.
more: States force particular technologies on the economy believing productivity lives in the machine. It mostly lives in tacit knowledge, process and management, which are learned by doing (Wright's Law). Giving an army great tanks doesn't make it world-class. Know-how spreads through people, such as Hindustan Lever alumni who carried Unilever's knowledge into new consumer goods companies. Ajay also argues that multiple rival standards competing for supremacy are healthy.

head: Foreign Firms Are India's Best Teachers
dek: The global state of the art lives inside foreign firms, so their presence spreads productivity across India.
more: The global state of the art lives inside foreign firms, so their presence spreads productivity across India. 'Indian firm' is a slippery idea anyway: ICICI Bank is 90% foreign-owned and Microsoft has an Indian CEO. Apple's presence could push Indian vendors from hundred-micron to one-micron tolerances, much as Texas Instruments helped seed Indian IT.

head: The Two Unseen Effects of Protectionism
dek: Suppose a tariff protects Indian firm A from a better Italian firm X. The visible effect is that A prospers.
more: Suppose a tariff protects Indian firm A from a better Italian firm X. The visible effect is that A prospers. The first unseen effect is that consumers lose lower prices or better value, which is a dispersed transfer to a concentrated beneficiary. The second is that A no longer has to match the global best, so it stays stuck in a low-productivity equilibrium.
printed: The firm that never grows up

head: Wall Off National Security; GDP Is the Real Defence
dek: The army has real reasons to avoid Chinese gear that may contain backdoors, given the border tensions at Doklam and Galwan.
more: The army has real reasons to avoid Chinese gear that may contain backdoors, given the border tensions at Doklam and Galwan. It should solve that for itself, through trusted supply chains and partnerships with like-minded actors. Ajay cites Europe working on drones without Chinese backdoors and Ukraine, now one of the world's largest drone producers, avoiding Chinese parts. That is no reason to be anti-foreign across the whole economy. Strategic strength comes from growth: Russia's GDP is Italy-sized, which is why Europe can absorb the threat.

head: The China Question: Don't Cherry-Pick
dek: Chinese EVs and solar panels are real successes, but they are picked out from a long list of failures.
more: Chinese EVs and solar panels are real successes, but they are picked out from a long list of failures. Taken as a whole, Chinese state control and industrial policy produced about 1.5 apartments per household, a shrinking population and lost dynamism under Xi Jinping. China's per capita GDP remains far below that of advanced economies.

head: Enable Winners, Don't Pick Them
dek: Unknown geniuses are hidden in the private sector, and the state's job is to create conditions in which some of them win.
more: Unknown geniuses are hidden in the private sector, and the state's job is to create conditions in which some of them win. Ajay's list: industry-neutral R&D contracts and grants that push the limits of knowledge, whose spillovers nobody can predict; fierce competition from startup to bankruptcy, so firms keep striving; deep internationalisation with free imports and exports, Indian multinationals and unrestricted foreign firms; and open immigration of talent. Amit adds a caution: limit the state to rule of law, because most monopolies exist only with the state's collusion.

Amit's version of the classic $500-bill joke. A Bengali economist who believes in rational markets walks past a 500-rupee note, reasoning that if it were real someone would have picked it up already. Then a Gujarati YouTuber ('hint hint, wink wink') spots it and says not 'money' but 'content', and sets up his selfie stick to film himself discovering it. Meanwhile Amit Varma walks up from behind and pockets it. 'The story doesn't end well for either of our two protagonists.'

head: After Ajay says he publicly declared his official occupation as YouTuber, Amit
more: After Ajay says he publicly declared his official occupation as YouTuber, Amit: 'So you are henceforth not an economist. You're a card carrying YouTuber.'

head: On the RBI letting poultry farms borrow abroad
more: On the RBI letting poultry farms borrow abroad: 'Amit, you're not eating enough chicken. Chicken needs cheap credit.' Amit's comeback: 'Picking chickens in nanotechnology and resulting in really tiny chickens... we have nano chickens.'

head: Ajay claims YouTube says most viewers are engineers.
more: Ajay claims YouTube says most viewers are engineers. Amit: 'Wait a minute, what analytics are you examining? This is nowhere in the analytics.' Ajay: 'Young males and almost all young males in India are engineers.' Amit: 'No, many creative women watch our show, I mean partly mainly because of me.' After Ajay's rant against engineers jumping to industrial policy, Amit adds: 'Gentle readers, Ajay Shah is an engineer.'

head: Ajay's tribute to the show's own camera crew
more: Ajay's tribute to the show's own camera crew: 'If any idiot had a Sony Alpha DSLR, they do not become Nomsita.'

head: Amit on Ajay's coinage
more: Amit on Ajay's coinage 'negative disability': 'At some point someday, Ajay Shah, people are gonna come and hit on you and they'll say things like Ajay, you have so many negative disabilities.' Ajay can't find a snappy reply, and Amit tells him to bring one next episode.

head: Amit's riddle
more: Amit's riddle: a dear leader appoints a secretary for each system of organs, a digestion secretary for the stomach and a respiration secretary for the lungs. What do you call the one in charge of his elbows, knees and ankles? Ajay gets it (the joint secretary, the bureaucratic rank mocked all episode), and Amit says: 'Well done. I'm so proud of you.'

head: After Ajay calls Russia
more: After Ajay calls Russia 'an Italy-sized GDP', Amit says many, many Italian viewers are at this point deeply disappointed.

head: Amit on how fast technology moves
more: Amit on how fast technology moves: 'Today's cutting edge is passe by midnight and obsolete by noon tomorrow.'

head: Ajay's ideal industry-neutral research agenda includes landing a craft on Venus (
more: Ajay's ideal industry-neutral research agenda includes landing a craft on Venus ('a nonsensical objective') and grants on how to double the size of an egg: 'We want Wright's law of eggs.'

head: Amit's SEEPZ pun: the Allman Brothers Band came to perform there, everyone was let in, but one member was examined. Who? Derek Trucks
more: Amit's SEEPZ pun: the Allman Brothers Band came to perform there, everyone was let in, but one member was examined. Who? Derek Trucks, 'because we were examining all the trucks.'

head: The recommendations heist. Amit complains that every episode he proposes a recommendations chapter, the crew
more: The recommendations heist. Amit complains that every episode he proposes a recommendations chapter, the crew 'break their silence and say yes, yes, yes,' and Ajay says 'forget it, next time.' Then Ajay answers Amit's Duane Allman quiz with 'Layla' and declares it 'my recommendation for today'. Amit: 'You cannot fucking do this. I had already named the song. This was gonna be my recommendation.' Ajay: 'I promise next episode, I will have five recommendations.'

head: Amit quotes the famous maxim
more: Amit quotes the famous maxim 'Power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely' and adds that, more than anything, it corrupts character.

head: Oliver Cromwell, cited by Ajay against governments sure of their technology bets
more: Oliver Cromwell, cited by Ajay against governments sure of their technology bets: 'in the bowels of Christ, consider it possible you may be mistaken.'

head: Ajay's twist on the opening line of Tolstoy's Anna Karenina
more: Ajay's twist on the opening line of Tolstoy's Anna Karenina: 'All successful advanced economies look alike. All unhappy, poor countries are unhappy in their own way.'

head: Joni Mitchell, Polio, and Fifty Alternative Tunings
dek: Because she couldn't play the guitar the normal way, she came to know it more closely than conventionally trained players did.
more: At nine, Joni Mitchell got polio, which left her left hand much weaker for a long time. Instead of dropping the guitar, she invented about fifty alternative tunings. When she heard a chord in her head that she could not finger the standard way, she kept retuning the strings until the guitar produced it. David Crosby said her experiments blew his mind. She called the odd chords she found 'chords of inquiry,' and heard a whole orchestra in six strings, with the top three acting like a horn section. She later said polio gave her an inner life and made her an artist.

Because she couldn't play the guitar the normal way, she came to know it more closely than conventionally trained players did. Her distinct sound, which is hard to file under folk, blues or jazz, follows from that handicap. The constraint was no blessing for her, but it was a blessing for music.
printed: Fifty ways to tune a guitar

head: Shivani Wrote in the Middle of Family Dinner
dek: You don't have to remove your constraints before you start the work. Shivani worked in the scraps of time her life allowed.
more: Mrinal Pande told Amit how her mother, the Hindi writer Shivani, worked. She cooked, served the whole family, and then sat down and wrote while everyone ate and the children squabbled around her. She never waited for a vacation, a quiet retreat or an early-morning hour. The family simply learned not to disturb her. Amit tells this story to his writing students, especially women carrying a double load, when they say they have no time.
You don't have to remove your constraints before you start the work. Shivani worked in the scraps of time her life allowed. 'I'm too busy' is usually a story we tell ourselves.

head: Frida Kahlo Painting From Her Bed With a Mirror
dek: Her signature subject, herself, came partly from a bed, a mirror and forced solitude.
more: Frida Kahlo had polio at six, which left one leg weaker and kept her out of school for months. At eighteen, on her way to becoming a doctor, she was in a wooden bus that collided with a rail car. A metal railing went through her pelvis and damaged her spine. She faced some thirty-two surgeries and long spells in bed. Her parents rigged an easel over her bed and placed a mirror so she could see herself, and her famous self-portraits followed. She also painted her plaster corsets and medical equipment. 'The Broken Column' (1944) came after a spinal surgery went wrong.

Her signature subject, herself, came partly from a bed, a mirror and forced solitude. She turned the tools of her confinement into her material and still lived a full life, including a stormy marriage to Diego Rivera.

head: One Tennis Ball Among Twenty Kids
dek: Scarcity makes the imagination work, and abundance can turn play into a treadmill of novelty.
more: Ajay compares today's upper-class Indian children with his own childhood. Today's kids get rooms full of toys, tire of each one in three days and move on to the next. In his time, twenty children might share a single tennis ball and had to invent a whole day of fun using stones, trees and shrubs.
Scarcity makes the imagination work, and abundance can turn play into a treadmill of novelty.

head: Gavaskar's Ground Strokes Were Built by Windows
dek: A technique that looks like pure talent can be the trace of local rules from childhood play.
more: Amit says, from memory, that Sunil Gavaskar's habit of keeping the ball along the ground came from gully cricket. If you broke a window, your ball or bat was confiscated and the game ended. Gavaskar rarely lofted the ball, a notable exception being his hundred against New Zealand in the 1987 World Cup.
A technique that looks like pure talent can be the trace of local rules from childhood play. The constraint coached him before any coach did.

head: Dr Seuss and the Fifty-Word Bet
dek: An arbitrary limit from outside produced a beloved classic. Amit uses the story to tell his writing students that a small vocabulary need not hold them back.
more: Bennett Cerf, a co-founder of Random House and Dr Seuss's publisher, challenged Theodor Geisel to write a whole book using only fifty different words. The book could be any length, but its vocabulary had to stay within fifty words. Geisel reportedly kept a chart to track his words and pulled it off with Green Eggs and Ham. Amit read passages aloud ('I do not like green eggs and ham, I do not like them, Sam I am') to show how delightful the result is.
An arbitrary limit from outside produced a beloved classic. Amit uses the story to tell his writing students that a small vocabulary need not hold them back.

head: Agatha Christie's Struggle With Words Became Her Style
dek: A limitation, worked with honestly, can become the defining strength of a body of work.
more: Agatha Christie had dysgraphia and possibly dyslexia. She didn't give up writing. She developed a clear, concise prose style and very tight, intricate plotting that left no room for confusion.
A limitation, worked with honestly, can become the defining strength of a body of work.

head: Hemingway's Iceberg Came Out of the Newsroom
dek: Deadline pressure taught him economy, and economy became his style. Saying less leaves room for the reader to do some of the work.
more: Hemingway's spare prose came partly from journalism, where he filed dispatches on deadline with no time for padding or polished sentences. From that economy grew his 'iceberg' approach. Only about an eighth of what is going on needs to appear on the page, and the rest lies underneath for the reader to infer. Amit adds that the famous six-word story 'For sale, baby shoes, never worn' is wrongly credited to Hemingway, who was six when it was first published.
Deadline pressure taught him economy, and economy became his style. Saying less leaves room for the reader to do some of the work.

head: Dick Fosbury Couldn't Do the Straddle
dek: Fosbury didn't reason his way to the flop from aerodynamics. He couldn't do the accepted method, so he found another one.
more: In high school Dick Fosbury was bad at the standard high-jump technique, the straddle, in which you face the bar and cross it one leg at a time. He didn't have the coordination for it, so he experimented and was mocked like any heretic. Headlines said 'Fosbury flops,' likening him to a fish flopping into a boat. In 1968 he won Olympic gold with the Fosbury flop, which became the standard technique. Its spread also depended on deep foam landing mats replacing sand and shallow padding, which had made back-first landings dangerous. Amit admits he tried the high jump in school, failed and gave up.

Fosbury didn't reason his way to the flop from aerodynamics. He couldn't do the accepted method, so he found another one. And it took a second change, the removal of the hard-landing constraint, for his idea to succeed.

head: Sachin's Double Hundred Without the Off Side
dek: Amit grants this isn't an innovation story like the others. It is about the best batsman in the world refusing to sit out, removing his favourite shot and still dominating.
more: Sachin Tendulkar's tennis elbow, which he never fully disclosed, got so bad that, according to a close mutual friend, he couldn't lift a cup of tea. With a Test against Australia in Sydney ahead and no cover drive available to him, he chose to give up driving through the off side altogether. He made a double hundred without driving through the off side once.
Amit grants this isn't an innovation story like the others. It is about the best batsman in the world refusing to sit out, removing his favourite shot and still dominating.

head: Hacking Digger With a Broken Right Arm
dek: Shut out of playing the game, he went one level up and rewrote it. Amit calls it cheating.
more: At IIT, the big obsession among students was the keyboard game Digger, whose high scores were stored encrypted on a floppy disk and decided bragging rights. Ajay suffered multiple compound fractures of his right arm and couldn't play. With time on his hands, he disassembled the game's binary and studied it for hours. He found where each level's floor plan was stored and wrote an editor to design his own levels. He then built a level where the monsters died on their own, left the machine running overnight, and came back with 300,000 points against champions' 10,000 to 20,000.

Shut out of playing the game, he went one level up and rewrote it. Amit calls it cheating. Ajay notes it was the only time in his life he read binary, which he did only because the constraint left him nothing else to do.
printed: Can’t play the game? Rewrite it

head: Night Hikes in Rubber Chappals
dek: Constraints you choose can turn something merely doable into something that fully engages your mind, much like playing chess blindfold.
more: In his IIT days, Ajay and his friends made hikes deliberately harder. They wore rubber chappals instead of shoes, carried very heavy loads, hiked at night, and eventually did all three at once.
Constraints you choose can turn something merely doable into something that fully engages your mind, much like playing chess blindfold.

head: A Failed Super-Glue Became the Post-it Note
dek: A failure judged against the original goal can be a success against a different one.
more: Spencer Silver at 3M set out to create the strongest adhesive possible and failed. One attempt produced a notably weak adhesive, and using it gave him the idea that became the Post-it note. Post-its are now so common in offices that software imitates them with virtual versions.
A failure judged against the original goal can be a success against a different one.

head: Coco Chanel and Underwear Jersey
dek: A personal budget constraint started something that later became common in fashion.
more: Coco Chanel came from a modest family and couldn't afford the silks and brocades of high fashion. So she experimented with cheaper fabrics such as jersey, then used for men's underwear, and made classy women's clothes from them. This also made her garments cheaper and more accessible.
A personal budget constraint started something that later became common in fashion. Lacking expensive materials pushed her toward a new kind of elegance that more people could afford.

head: Keith Haring's Subway Chalk Drawings
dek: Having to hurry acted as a design brief. The conditions of illicit, fast public drawing produced a visual vocabulary that later became iconic.
more: In the early 1980s Keith Haring was an art student in New York who preferred painting in public to selling elitist gallery pieces. Expired subway advertisements were covered with black canvas, which made a ready-made surface. He had to work fast before the transit police arrived, so he used chalk. That speed, the medium and the knowledge that the work would soon disappear shaped a style of quick, iconic motifs, such as his barking dog. He later became famous and was commissioned for permanent murals, but the style stayed.
Having to hurry acted as a design brief. The conditions of illicit, fast public drawing produced a visual vocabulary that later became iconic.
printed: Chalk it up to the transit police

head: Blue
dek: Her unusual polio-driven approach to the guitar gives her a sound that fits no single genre.
more: Her unusual polio-driven approach to the guitar gives her a sound that fits no single genre. He says to listen to everything she made, starting with Blue, and singles out 'All I Want', 'Little Green', 'River' and 'A Case of You', which he also loves for her piano.
Amit's opening story about Joni Mitchell. He first recommended the album in the Inflation Targeting episode.

head: Green Eggs and Ham
dek: It shows a tight constraint producing something joyful, and it supports his advice that writers don't need a big vocabulary.
more: It shows a tight constraint producing something joyful, and it supports his advice that writers don't need a big vocabulary.
Amit read passages aloud as a quiz for Ajay, then told the story of Bennett Cerf's fifty-word challenge.

head: Life's Grandeur: The Spread of Excellence From Plato to Darwin
dek: He calls it brilliant on how baseball keeps adjusting its rules to keep the game balanced.
more: He calls it brilliant on how baseball keeps adjusting its rules to keep the game balanced. That is a kind of central planning that works only because a game, unlike the real world, has bounded complexity.
While explaining that a sport's rules are its constraints, Amit recalled a book he read some thirty years ago but couldn't name. The show notes identify it.

head: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Episode 72, Everything is Everything)
dek: It is the companion episode on how form shapes content, the larger frame this episode's constraint stories fit into.
more: It is the companion episode on how form shapes content, the larger frame this episode's constraint stories fit into.
Cited when Amit noted that every instrument and form is a constraint. Ajay linked this to Amit's general theory of form.

head: We Are Stupid, Therefore Creative
dek: The brain can't take in the world's full complexity. So we tell stories that are simpler than reality, never entirely true, but useful, and our creativity grows out of that limit.
more: The brain can't take in the world's full complexity. So we tell stories that are simpler than reality, never entirely true, but useful, and our creativity grows out of that limit. Ajay points out that a storyteller's 'story' and a scientist's 'model' are the same thing, as in George Box's line that all models are wrong but some are useful.

head: Constraints as a Creative Force
dek: This is the episode's thesis. A disability, poverty, a deadline, a word limit or a publisher's challenge doesn't only reduce what you can do.
more: This is the episode's thesis. A disability, poverty, a deadline, a word limit or a publisher's challenge doesn't only reduce what you can do. It sends effort in directions an unconstrained person would never try, as with Joni Mitchell's tunings, Frida Kahlo's self-portraits, the Fosbury flop and Chanel's jersey. Amit stresses that the constraint isn't good in itself, polio least of all. The value lies in how people respond to it.

head: Imposed vs Chosen Constraints
dek: Ajay separates constraints the world forces on you, such as polio or a broken arm, from constraints you choose, such as blindfold chess, hiking at night in chappals, writing without adverbs, or Apple setting thinness and weight targets for the MacBook Air that existing technology couldn't meet.
more: Ajay separates constraints the world forces on you, such as polio or a broken arm, from constraints you choose, such as blindfold chess, hiking at night in chappals, writing without adverbs, or Apple setting thinness and weight targets for the MacBook Air that existing technology couldn't meet. Chosen constraints can be just a game, but often they wake the mind up and push invention.

head: Everything Is Constrained, Everything Is Boundless
dek: Every form is a constraint, whether a guitar, a keyboard, an 800-word column, a 280-character tweet, a 60–90 minute show or the rules of a sport.
more: Every form is a constraint, whether a guitar, a keyboard, an 800-word column, a 280-character tweet, a 60–90 minute show or the rules of a sport. Fielding restrictions in one-day cricket and the offside rule in football change incentives and so change the game. Someone who loves a form, like Eddie Van Halen with the guitar, sees possibilities rather than limits.

head: Your Vocabulary Is Enough
dek: Writers worry that their vocabulary is too small. Amit argues that a writer never needs more words than the readers know, since the goal is to be understood.
more: Writers worry that their vocabulary is too small. Amit argues that a writer never needs more words than the readers know, since the goal is to be understood. Reading widely will expand your vocabulary, but what limits good writing is care, not word count.
printed: Just the tip of the iceberg

head: Show Enough and No More
dek: Hemingway's iceberg idea says to put only a fraction of what is happening on the page and let the reader infer the rest from small cues, like an impatient look or a tapping finger.
more: Hemingway's iceberg idea says to put only a fraction of what is happening on the page and let the reader infer the rest from small cues, like an impatient look or a tapping finger. Economy here means trusting the reader, not leaving things out.

head: Artificial Constraints Sharpen Craft
dek: Amit used to complain about 800-word column limits, write 1,200 words, and then find that what he cut wasn't needed.
more: Amit used to complain about 800-word column limits, write 1,200 words, and then find that what he cut wasn't needed. Deadlines force work to get finished. Haiku (5-7-5 syllables) and his no-adverb, no-adjective, no-long-word exercise make writers look closely at language. Great lyricists like Sahir Ludhianvi, Gulzar and Javed Akhtar always wrote to meter and music.

head: A Constraint Triggers an Innovation; Removing One Lets It Spread
dek: Fosbury invented the flop because he couldn't do the straddle. The flop took over only because deep foam mats made landing on your back safe.
more: Fosbury invented the flop because he couldn't do the straddle. The flop took over only because deep foam mats made landing on your back safe. New ideas often need something pushing them into being and an old barrier being lifted.

head: The Maths of Constrained Optimisation
dek: Ajay notes that mathematically, adding constraints to an optimisation problem can at best match the unconstrained optimum and usually does worse.
more: Ajay notes that mathematically, adding constraints to an optimisation problem can at best match the unconstrained optimum and usually does worse. The stories in this episode go the other way because humans don't accept the problem as given. They rethink the objective and the framing, which a solver cannot do.

head: Selection Bias in Inspiring Stories
dek: Ajay cautions that millions of people got polio and for most it made life worse.
more: Ajay cautions that millions of people got polio and for most it made life worse. We remember the few who broke through. Be inspired by them, but don't mistake the exceptions for the typical outcome.

head: Skeuomorphic Design
dek: New technology borrows the look of what it replaces so people feel at home: an e-book app drawn as a bookshelf, a floppy-disk save icon, folder icons, virtual Post-its.
more: New technology borrows the look of what it replaces so people feel at home: an e-book app drawn as a bookshelf, a floppy-disk save icon, folder icons, virtual Post-its. Ajay adds that a phone camera's 'pro' mode shows aperture and exposure controls, but it is all image processing and nothing physical changes. The shutter click is a fake sound too. The approach helps early adoption but can outlast its usefulness.

head: The Lost Constraint of Having Nothing to Do
dek: Amit and Ajay grew up without the internet or mobile phones and had to spend time with themselves.
more: Amit and Ajay grew up without the internet or mobile phones and had to spend time with themselves. That is how Frida Kahlo's solitude and Sara Rai's richly observed childhood came about. Amit wonders whether losing boredom has turned us into creatures that hop from one stimulus to the next and rarely spend time with ourselves.

head: Ajay opens offended at being called stupid, saying that in any decent age he would have slapped Amit with a glove and fought a duel at fifty paces
more: Ajay opens offended at being called stupid, saying that in any decent age he would have slapped Amit with a glove and fought a duel at fifty paces 'with rusty guns that barely aim accurately.' Amit, the libertarian, replies: 'So much talk about the coercion of the state, monopoly on violence. Are you the state that you can threaten me with violence?'

head: Amit refuses to…
more: Amit refuses to 'tell us about models': 'None of the people I'm talking about today is a model per se in the fashion model sense, but they are all models for us to aspire to.'

head: Amit accuses Ajay of hijacking his recommendation of Derek and the Dominos'
more: Amit accuses Ajay of hijacking his recommendation of Derek and the Dominos' 'Layla' the previous week: 'quite creative, anything but stupid, but deeply devious.' He also notes that Vaishnav Vyas calls the Inflation Targeting episode 'the inflammation targeting episode.'

head: On Frida Kahlo's supportive parents
more: On Frida Kahlo's supportive parents: 'God bless their souls, though we don't believe in God, but flying spaghetti monster should bless their souls.'

Showing viewers a Dr Seuss page that Ajay can't see, Amit compares it to a chess broadcast, where everyone sees the engine evaluation except the two players: 'So they are the two chutiyas who don't know the right move. Everybody else does.'

head: Amit on cricket
more: Amit on cricket: 'every good Indian by the definition of that for the purpose of this chapter is someone who follows cricket,' which rules out Ajay, who doesn't.

head: On the Digger saga, Amit first asks of the…
more: On the Digger saga, Amit first asks of the 'most important male objective' at IIT: 'What kind of male objective is that? Shame on you.' When Ajay mentions breaking his right hand, Amit adds a family-show aside that 'it's much better for a male engineer to injure his right hand than his left hand.' Then: 'At one level this might be called adapting to constraints. Fancy term. This is cheating.' Finally: 'Nomsita, leave this in... let the world see what a shameless man this is... at one level I just lost respect for you, but at another level I gained respect for you.'

head: Amit calls Everything is Everything a work of art made within a 60–90 minute limit
more: Amit calls Everything is Everything a work of art made within a 60–90 minute limit: 'Aren't you still watching? If you're still watching, you can't diss.'

head: Picking up Ajay's phrase
more: Picking up Ajay's phrase 'black and white fact,' Amit says, 'It should be noted that I am right now a black and white fact.' He then reminds Ajay that he promised five recommendations for this episode. When Ajay tries to defer, Amit threatens to demand ten, and they settle on six for the next episode.

head: George Box's line
more: George Box's line 'All models are wrong, some models are useful,' quoted by Ajay to argue that stories and scientific models are the same thing.

head: Douglas Adams
more: Douglas Adams: 'I love deadlines, especially the sound they make as they go whooshing by,' quoted by Amit on deadlines as a constraint of time.

head: Frida Kahlo
more: Frida Kahlo: 'Feet, what do I need you for when I have wings to fly.' Amit says it would sound cheesy if you didn't know who said it.

head: Joni Mitchell called herself
more: Joni Mitchell called herself 'a painter derailed by circumstance,' though she painted all her own album covers. Amit notes that 'Both Sides Now' is one of Ajay's favourite songs.

head: The six-word story
more: The six-word story 'For sale, baby shoes, never worn,' wrongly attributed to Hemingway, who was six years old when it was first published.

head: Examples of great writing under constraint: Shakespeare, Lincoln's Gettysburg Address (
more: Examples of great writing under constraint: Shakespeare, Lincoln's Gettysburg Address ('in one sixty seven words or something'), and Hindi film lyricists Sahir Ludhianvi, Gulzar and Javed Akhtar writing to meter and music.

head: Gavaskar's 1987 World Cup hundred against New Zealand
more: Gavaskar's 1987 World Cup hundred against New Zealand, 'hitting even Chatfield all over the park,' the rare time he lofted the ball.

head: From Aurangzeb to a knife at King John's throat
dek: Limits on power were not gifted by rulers. They were extracted, and each step built on people watching the previous one work.
more: Ajay traces how humanity learned to shrink the king. Under monarchy, the ruler's word was total: Aurangzeb could order a beheading, and the Pope crowned Napoleon to bless absolute authority. Rome ran the first experiment with a republic, where about fifty families took power from the monarch and set up judges, until it was 'destroyed by the great man Julius Caesar.' The story restarted in England in 1215. King John was demanding crazy taxes and loans, so a group of merchants and finance people seized him, put a knife to his throat and forced him to sign the Magna Carta. Its language looks archaic and flimsy today, but it was the first clear statement that a king's power has limits. That journey ran through Parliament to Cromwell and the beheading of Charles I. It then reached Montesquieu's proposal to cut the state into three pieces, and finally Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution.

Limits on power were not gifted by rulers. They were extracted, and each step built on people watching the previous one work. Separation of powers is the mature form of a centuries-old project to make sure no one has a king's authority.
printed: A knife at King John’s throat

head: Ambedkar's case against American-style separation
dek: India's executive-heavy state was not an accident. Its most respected framer chose it deliberately and gave reasons.
more: In the Constituent Assembly, Professor K.T. Shah moved a resolution, Article 40A, to write a clear separation of powers into the Constitution. Ajay reads Ambedkar's reply. Ambedkar accepted that the executive must be separate from the judiciary. He argued against separating the executive from the legislature as the US does, saying many Americans disliked that rigidity. He also said Parliament's work was so vast and complicated that MPs needed direct guidance from executive members sitting in Parliament. So India began with no meaningful separation of powers. Amit adds that the choice should be judged in its context: the country was falling apart and today's map did not yet exist. The point is to learn from it, not to judge personalities.
India's executive-heavy state was not an accident. Its most respected framer chose it deliberately and gave reasons. It shows how a reasonable-sounding design choice can shape a country for decades.

head: Nehru, Shastri and the Babri idol
dek: Democracy inside a party is itself a check on power. When it disappeared and the anti-defection law came in, a ruling party could control both the executive and the legislature from the top.
more: When the Ram idol was placed inside the Babri Masjid, Nehru in Delhi ordered it removed within a couple of days, before things got out of hand. But the UP chief minister was Govind Ballabh Pant and his deputy was Lal Bahadur Shastri. Shastri, who would have had to carry out the order, refused. Amit wishes that in this case they had obeyed Nehru. His broader point is that the Congress of the 1950s and 60s was a 'grand tent': local politicians could defy the centre, and the local party chose its own chief minister. In the 1970s Indira Gandhi centralised power, and the high command began appointing chief ministers.
Democracy inside a party is itself a check on power. When it disappeared and the anti-defection law came in, a ruling party could control both the executive and the legislature from the top.

head: Standing committees: a great institution that lived only in norms
dek: This is the core lesson of public choice theory. A check that exists only as a custom can vanish quietly.
more: People saw that a joint secretary writing the laws was a farce. So, starting with Shivraj Patil, a norm grew of sending important bills to parliamentary standing committees. When Ajay was in the Ministry of Finance, the Speaker would refer a bill to a committee if it drew significant criticism. The committees had both ruling and opposition MPs and were chaired by opposition members. They debated the bill, summoned expert witnesses and questioned the civil servants who drafted it. Ajay appeared before many as an expert. He counts this among the good things behind India's 1991–2011 growth episode. But it was never written into the rules, and today, he says, there is really no check and balance around these things.
This is the core lesson of public choice theory. A check that exists only as a custom can vanish quietly. If it isn't written into law or the Constitution, it isn't real.
printed: A good habit, never written down

head: SEBI: where the judge, prosecutor and investigator have lunch together
dek: Without separation of powers, a regulator quietly becomes a miniature state.
more: SEBI was created in 1992 by founders Ajay deeply respects, including Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain. It copied practices from RBI and ended up with all three branches of the state under one roof. It drafts regulations, which are laws written by unelected officials; Ajay says the original Act had 'excessive delegation.' It investigates and prosecutes, with those two roles mixed up. And a SEBI employee plays judge while a colleague prosecutes. Appeals originally went to the Secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), who sat on SEBI's board. Early orders simply declared someone guilty and imposed a fine of, say, ₹10 crore, with no reasoning at all. Other countries do it differently. At the US SEC, the administrative law judge sits in a courtroom inside the building but belongs to the judiciary. In Britain's FCA model and Australia's twin-peaks model, the regulator builds a case and takes it to a court or tribunal. Ajay reckons India is about 30% of the way to fixing this.

Without separation of powers, a regulator quietly becomes a miniature state. The clean model is that the regulator stops at investigating and deciding whether to prosecute, and then hands the case to a real judge.

head: The 1992 bet against the Bombay High Court
dek: Every institutional design reflects the constraints of its time. When those constraints change, the trade-offs should be re-examined rather than kept by default.
more: SEBI's founders put a judge inside the regulator because, in 1992, they thought the Bombay High Court was so bad that nothing would ever get done. Ajay cites recent quantitative work from XKDR Forum. It shows the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now reasonably effective and efficient, and improving. The gap between adjudication at SEBI and at these courts is no longer large.
Every institutional design reflects the constraints of its time. When those constraints change, the trade-offs should be re-examined rather than kept by default.

head: America pushes back on its administrative state
dek: Even the model constitutional democracy has to keep fighting against power drifting to unelected officials.
more: Under Roosevelt, the US federal government built agency upon agency. Nervous Republicans pushed through the Administrative Procedure Act in 1946. Later, court orders in a case involving the oil company Chevron created 'Chevron deference.' Under it, if an agency expert had applied her mind and drafted a regulation, judges could review only the process, not the substance. Many saw this as letting legislative power seep into the administrative state. In 2024 the US Supreme Court largely struck it down. In a second development, someone argued that the SEC's in-house administrative law judge denied him his constitutional right to a jury trial. The Supreme Court struck down that SEC arrangement as unconstitutional. Ajay calls the field 'red hot', and the Emerging Markets Conference held a whole session on it.
Even the model constitutional democracy has to keep fighting against power drifting to unelected officials. Settled arrangements can be reopened, and they can move in a good direction.

head: The Machinery of Freedom
dek: Amit calls it a magnificent and very libertarian book. He was delighted that Ajay, whom he teases as a 'secret statist', cited it.
more: Amit calls it a magnificent and very libertarian book. He was delighted that Ajay, whom he teases as a 'secret statist', cited it.

Ajay borrowed Friedman's phrase 'the machinery of freedom' for the practical machinery of liberty: decentralisation, separation of powers, keeping investigator and prosecutor apart. Amit made it a mid-episode recommendation.

head: The Anti-Defection Law (Episode 13, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A deeper look at how a well-meant law to stop horse-trading turned MPs into votes that follow the whip.
more: A deeper look at how a well-meant law to stop horse-trading turned MPs into votes that follow the whip.
Cited while explaining how the anti-defection law ended debate in Parliament.

head: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A long conversation with MR Madhavan, whom both hosts admire. He talks at length about how the anti-defection law changed Parliament.
more: A long conversation with MR Madhavan, whom both hosts admire. He talks at length about how the anti-defection law changed Parliament.
The second of the two episodes Amit cites on the anti-defection law and Parliament's decline.

head: Emerging Markets Conference
dek: He calls the field red hot, full of interesting developments and good intellectual debates.
more: He calls the field red hot, full of interesting developments and good intellectual debates.
Ajay recalls that last year's conference, which Amit attended, had an entire session on recent developments in the US administrative state.

head: XKDR Forum's paper on Indian courts
dek: It weakens the 1992 argument for giving SEBI its own in-house judging.
more: It weakens the 1992 argument for giving SEBI its own in-house judging. Ajay suggests the trade-offs have changed and the arrangement should be rethought.
Cited as quantitative evidence that the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now reasonably effective and efficient.

head: Chocolate by Manam
dek: A Hyderabad company making expensive, really good chocolate. Not sponsored, just something they love.
more: A Hyderabad company making expensive, really good chocolate. Not sponsored, just something they love.
The first of his promised recommendations, 'for some fun and silliness.'

head: Introduction to Modern Climate Change
dek: Ajay sees climate change as one of the great crises of the modern world, alongside populism.
more: Ajay sees climate change as one of the great crises of the modern world, alongside populism. This slim, sensible book of about 200 pages covers climate science, mitigation and adaptation. He thinks everybody should read it.
The 2022 third edition.

head: IPCC reports
dek: Ajay usually finds reports by international bodies such as the World Bank and IMF bland, because they are written by committee.
more: Ajay usually finds reports by international bodies such as the World Bank and IMF bland, because they are written by committee. IPCC reports are different. They are written by committees of scientists with real processes for debate, they give state-of-the-art thinking, and they show where experts disagree by setting out the range of models. He says just looking at the graphics will make you think about the world in new ways.
A pick Ajay himself calls 'a little bit geeky.'

head: Fateful Choices
dek: It shows how Churchill and Roosevelt worked to bring America into the Second World War on the Allied side.
more: It shows how Churchill and Roosevelt worked to bring America into the Second World War on the Allied side. It was a close call: as late as August 1941, about half the House of Representatives still opposed it. Ajay finds it timely for understanding America today.
Ajay keeps thinking about the collapse of the Atlantic Alliance, which takes him back to 1940–41.

head: Ten Years Gone
dek: Ajay thinks it is the greatest Led Zeppelin song that is not widely known.
more: Ajay thinks it is the greatest Led Zeppelin song that is not widely known.
The first of three lesser-known Led Zeppelin songs.

head: I'm Gonna Crawl
dek: Ajay considers it one of the great things Plant, Page, John Paul Jones and Bonzo ever did, made at the peak of their powers just before the band ended.
more: Ajay considers it one of the great things Plant, Page, John Paul Jones and Bonzo ever did, made at the peak of their powers just before the band ended.
From In Through the Out Door, the last Led Zeppelin album. John Bonham died shortly after it.

head: The Planner and the Doer
dek: This is Ajay's personal version of separation of powers. The Planner sits down and sets priorities, probabilities and a calendar.
more: This is Ajay's personal version of separation of powers. The Planner sits down and sets priorities, probabilities and a calendar. Then the Doer takes over and simply executes, without re-planning or worrying about the fifty other demands on his time. You trust the choice you already made, give the one task everything, and accept missing other deadlines. When the task is done, the Doer is kicked out and the Planner decides what comes next.

head: Democracy is dispersion of power, not voting
dek: Elections only choose who plays the legislative role. If voting just picked a king, he would be almost impossible to remove, because how could anyone organise an opposition against a king?
more: Elections only choose who plays the legislative role. If voting just picked a king, he would be almost impossible to remove, because how could anyone organise an opposition against a king? Democracy really means checks and balances. One way to spread power is decentralisation: under the subsidiarity principle, each function goes to the lowest level of government that can handle it. The other is separation of powers.

head: Separation of powers, explained through a speech crime
dek: Ajay uses a speech offence under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) to show how the three branches work.
more: Ajay uses a speech offence under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) to show how the three branches work. The legislature alone decides whether something, say defamation or sedition, is a crime, and it has to win elections to earn that power. The police only investigate against the written law and file a charge sheet. They cannot decide what is offensive or who deserves punishment. The judge alone decides on punishment after hearing both sides, and cannot go after anyone on her own initiative. Ajay calls this a mind-blowing achievement in political philosophy. He admits that as an economist, trained to treat government as one big monolith, it took him years to see how important it is.

head: The state should be a game of conflict
dek: The three branches are meant to be co-equal, unafraid of each other, and in constant tension.
more: The three branches are meant to be co-equal, unafraid of each other, and in constant tension. Amit adds that friction, normally seen as bad, is good when it comes to the state. A slow process guards against hasty action. A formal separation also makes any power grab visible: Indira Gandhi's Emergency could not pass as normal democracy.

head: The fear test for arbitrary power
dek: Ajay offers a simple test of whether checks and balances are working: is anyone in your country someone you are afraid of?
more: Ajay offers a simple test of whether checks and balances are working: is anyone in your country someone you are afraid of? Turning that ideal into practice takes concrete design: decentralisation, separate branches, and an investigator and prosecutor who are separate people and argue with each other. Borrowing David Friedman's phrase, this is 'the machinery of freedom.'

head: The administrative state
dek: This is an American term that Ajay recommends, partly because it opens the door to a large body of writing on the subject.
more: This is an American term that Ajay recommends, partly because it opens the door to a large body of writing on the subject. The trend began with FDR's expansion of government. Ajay says no country has it worse than India: joint secretaries write the laws, district collectors double as district magistrates (a British legacy from when courts were scarce), and civil servants routinely play judge. Its Indian roots are a Constitution with no real separation of powers, the anti-defection law, and the peculiar way Indian parties work.

head: The anti-defection law: good intentions, bad outcome
dek: The anti-defection law of the late 1980s was meant to stop MPs switching sides for favours.
more: The anti-defection law of the late 1980s was meant to stop MPs switching sides for favours. Instead it forced every MP to vote as the party whip says, which ended genuine debate. MPs stopped reading bills, the bureaucracy ended up drafting the laws, and power within parties had already been centralised under Indira Gandhi. Together, these let the ruling party run both the executive and the legislature from the top.

head: Rules and norms: both matter, but only rules survive pressure
dek: Every society runs on a mix of formal rules and informal norms. James Buchanan's public choice view is that lines written into law and the Constitution change incentives in a lasting way.
more: Every society runs on a mix of formal rules and informal norms. James Buchanan's public choice view is that lines written into law and the Constitution change incentives in a lasting way. Norms, like the standing-committee practice, can be swept away quickly. Yet norms still do real work. A judge who writes a bad ruling loses standing among her peers.

head: Separation of powers entered India through the basic structure doctrine
dek: The Supreme Court built a core of the Constitution that Parliament cannot amend.
more: The Supreme Court built a core of the Constitution that Parliament cannot amend. It reasoned that Parliament is not a constituent assembly and is more open to majority impulses. The doctrine then grew in two ways. First, it became a test for all new laws, not just constitutional amendments. Second, it kept expanding as courts reread rights such as the right to life. Separation of powers came in this way. A plain reading of the text, or an LLM fed the Constitution, would say it isn't there. That is why Ajay is optimistic.

head: Regulators must not become mini-states
dek: A regulator that drafts rules, investigates, prosecutes and adjudicates combines all three branches.
more: A regulator that drafts rules, investigates, prosecutes and adjudicates combines all three branches. Parliament may hand narrow law-making power to officials, but it must be tightly controlled; doing too much of it is called 'excessive delegation.' The clean design is that the regulator investigates and decides whether to prosecute, and a real court or tribunal judges.

head: One rulebook for every agency
dek: The US Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 applies the same rules on transparency and checks and balances to all federal agencies.
more: The US Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 applies the same rules on transparency and checks and balances to all federal agencies. India's draft Indian Financial Code, which Ajay worked on, took the same approach: about 140 sections governing every financial agency, whether RBI, SEBI or a debt management agency. The idea is that these basic rules of good conduct should not change depending on what an agency regulates.

head: Who checks the judges? Their peers
dek: Ajay cites Tarunabh Khaitan, a law academic in the UK: ministers, bureaucrats and parliamentarians should not have power over judges.
more: Ajay cites Tarunabh Khaitan, a law academic in the UK: ministers, bureaucrats and parliamentarians should not have power over judges. The real check is reputation, meaning the respect of other judges, lawyers, law bloggers and academic journals. This makes a strong legal culture of critique a pillar of the rule of law.

head: Atrophy is the default; every generation must fight again
dek: Amit worries that, given human nature and power, well-designed systems tend to decay.
more: Amit worries that, given human nature and power, well-designed systems tend to decay. A party in power for long enough can fill every institution with its own people. Hence 'eternal vigilance', in words attributed to Jefferson. Ajay agrees that freedom has to be re-earned. He cites Angela Merkel saying Germany's true soul will be known only when the last people who lived through the Second World War have died, and notes that 20% of Germans now vote for the AfD.

head: Politics is downstream of culture
dek: Amit cautions against treating any constitution, including the deeply flawed Indian one, like a holy book.
more: Amit cautions against treating any constitution, including the deeply flawed Indian one, like a holy book. A constitution is shaped by the circumstances in which it was written, and good design on paper is only the start. He quotes Andrew Breitbart's line that politics is downstream of culture. Liberty lasts only when citizens instinctively object every time freedom is infringed. Ajay agrees that in India the instinct is still to look for a strongman.

head: Amit on Ajay's planner-doer framework
more: Amit on Ajay's planner-doer framework: 'Amit the planner rocks… but Amit the doer is a frickin' nikamma.' Then he adds a third self: 'there's Amit the regretter… I could have been a contender.'

head: Ajay on absolute monarchy
more: Ajay on absolute monarchy: 'If Aurangzeb said that off with his head, then Mr. Beer Biceps would have no choice.'

head: Ajay's dry jab at strongman worship: Rome's republic, the world's first
more: Ajay's dry jab at strongman worship: Rome's republic, the world's first, 'was destroyed by the great man Julius Caesar.'

head: Ajay on how economists picture government
more: Ajay on how economists picture government: 'you don't have some Aurangzeb and you're supposed to go whisper in Aurangzeb's ears that dude, we should do inflation targeting.' Amit promises viewers an on-screen cartoon of exactly that: 'What even are these images you are putting in my head?'

head: Amit, overjoyed that Ajay cited David Friedman: a very libertarian book
more: Amit, overjoyed that Ajay cited David Friedman: a very libertarian book 'which I did not expect from the secret statist… I've finally found a kindred soul.' Ajay replies: 'my heart sees the machinery of freedom, but my head has worked out all the compromises.'

head: Amit on what the anti-defection law did to Parliament
more: Amit on what the anti-defection law did to Parliament: 'you could run parliament from an Excel sheet. You don't even need people to show up. Frankly, you don't even need to elect individual legislators.'

head: Before the chapter on regulators, Amit reminds Ajay
more: Before the chapter on regulators, Amit reminds Ajay 'explicitly for the camera' to be kind. Ajay's first verdict is that the original SEBI Act 'was just like a really bad piece of work.'

head: Amit predicts Perplexity would produce Ajay's whole basic-structure outline. Later, explaining the US Administrative Procedure Act, Ajay jabs back at…
more: Amit predicts Perplexity would produce Ajay's whole basic-structure outline. Later, explaining the US Administrative Procedure Act, Ajay jabs back at 'the inability of perplexity to read one law and parse it' without the thousands of court rulings that interpret it.

head: Ajay on the climate change textbook
more: Ajay on the climate change textbook: 'Nomsita will stay up at night with edge of the seat excitement around the Dessler book.'

head: Amit, after being promised six recommendations and getting seven (
more: Amit, after being promised six recommendations and getting seven ('a big bonus'), says Ajay's pitch for IPCC reports (a clutch of models, look at all the pictures, it will change how you see the world) applies equally to a teenager discovering the Sports Illustrated swimsuit edition. 'But you've been a different kind of teenager, I guess.'

head: Max Weber's definition of the state, via Ajay
more: Max Weber's definition of the state, via Ajay: 'a community that creates and maintains a monopoly of violence.'

head: Andrew Breitbart's
more: Andrew Breitbart's 'politics is downstream of culture', which Amit uses to argue that the deeper battle for liberty is cultural.

head: From Rebel Without Restraints to Rebel With Rules
dek: This is the episode's thesis turned inward. A constitution constrains the state, not the people.
more: Amit opens and closes the episode with a self-portrait. At fifteen to seventeen he was 'a rebel without a cause', or, to alliterate, a rebel without restraints: he stayed up late, worked three days straight, drank beer with friends whenever he liked, skipped exercise and ate anything. Today he tries to be a rebel with rules: at least eight hours of sleep with enough REM and deep sleep, predictable meal times, a careful diet (especially after a recent health episode), and more exercise, though he admits that last one is still 'do as I say, don't do as I do.' He compares these rules to the countless algorithms that let an Elon Musk rocket be caught when it comes back.

This is the episode's thesis turned inward. A constitution constrains the state, not the people. In the same way, personal rules constrain your bad habits, not your freedom. They are the scaffolding from which bold, independent work can take off.
printed: The rebel goes to bed early

head: Drunk With Happiness Over a 1977 Paper
dek: Foundational ideas reward rereading. Going back to a classic decades later can do more than refresh your memory.
more: While preparing for this episode, Ajay had an anxiety attack: had he forgotten something about Kydland and Prescott? So early that morning he reread the 1977 paper he first met in his first-year PhD coursework, when he was 'a happy, giddy child' studying macro and micro. He found he still knew all of it. But rereading it brought back the feeling of discovering these ideas for the first time. Amit had set up the moment by teasing that Ajay reads papers all night the way other people binge.

Foundational ideas reward rereading. Going back to a classic decades later can do more than refresh your memory. It can rekindle the original thrill of discovery, and that thrill is part of what keeps a lifetime of learning going.

head: The Hypothetical Irish Tax Grab
dek: Opportunism looks like a free win, but it destroys the credibility that made the original policy work.
more: Ireland powered its growth with a very low corporate tax rate that drew global firms to build factories and offices there. Ajay would recommend low, ideally zero, corporate tax for India too. Now imagine a downturn or an earthquake, and a 'clever' policymaker who reasons that the factories are already built, so the firms are hostages, and raises the 5% rate for just two or three years. The move is popular, the press praises it, and it might even win an election. But firms plan on 5-, 10- and 25-year horizons, and turning an expected 8% dollar return on equity into 6% wrecks their calculations. Worse, once a firm has been socked, it assumes it can be socked again. So every future plan builds in a higher assumed tax rate or a higher risk premium, and the low-tax policy loses its pulling power for years.

Opportunism looks like a free win, but it destroys the credibility that made the original policy work. Economists treated this kind of clever exploitation as normal until the 1970s. The modern view is that a state that tries to be clever ends up weaker.

head: The Four-Bet That Stopped Meaning Aces
dek: People respond to your actions, so the world doesn't stand still while you exploit it.
more: Most poker is exploitative: you spot a mistake the table keeps making, such as folding too much or bluffing too much, and adjust to profit from it. The trap is assuming the table won't adjust back. In the 2000s Amit read a canonical poker book which said that a four-bet (re-raising a re-raise) almost always means aces. By the time he was a professional, a four-bet was often nothing at all, because players were exploiting the people who had learned that rule. Ajay's quip: 'Everybody read the book and said, Oh, I can exploit this.'

People respond to your actions, so the world doesn't stand still while you exploit it. Amit applies the same logic to taxes. Assuming a higher tax rate brings in proportionally more revenue ignores how people adjust, and India's roughly 97% top tax rate in the 1970s did not produce a booming economy.

head: Julius Caesar and the Invention of Rule by Law
dek: Even a strongman, purely to stay in control, sees that rules beat discretion for everyone below him.
more: Ajay says Julius Caesar was no democrat: he destroyed the Roman Republic just as Rome was learning to disperse power. Ajay also counts him among the greatest human beings and thinkers who ever lived. Running a vast empire, Caesar did not want minions everywhere deciding for themselves how to use his coercive power, each one becoming a local tyrant. So he began writing laws and process manuals, so that everyone beneath him would act predictably under his authority. Caesar himself stayed unbound.

Even a strongman, purely to stay in control, sees that rules beat discretion for everyone below him. Amit points out that this is 'rule by law', which is quite different from 'rule of law', where the ruler too is subject to the law.

head: The 1970s Oil Shock and Unhinged Expectations
dek: Discretion in the name of compassion can unhinge expectations, and rebuilding them takes decades.
more: When a central bank credibly promises stable inflation (India's RBI Act holds it to 4%), firms stop overreacting to one-off cost shocks and bond markets can price 25-year debt with confidence. During the 1970s oil shock, American policymakers were already watching people pay more for petrol and unemployment rise. They felt that raising rates would add to the misery of ordinary people, so they let inflation run 'for some time'. Firms and bond markets learned that inflation was no longer guaranteed, behaviour changed across the economy, and growth suffered.

Discretion in the name of compassion can unhinge expectations, and rebuilding them takes decades. That is why modern thinking says a central bank must hit its inflation target whatever is happening, whether an election, a crisis or a drought.
printed: Four per cent, no matter what

head: Pranab Mukherjee and Retrospective Taxation
dek: Trust is asymmetric: it takes decades to build and an instant to lose.
more: Amit traces how India's 1991–2011 growth episode went bust. After the terror attacks in Bombay, the home minister had to be moved, and Manmohan Singh put his most capable man, P. Chidambaram, into the home ministry. Sonia Gandhi then gave finance to Pranab Mukherjee, whom Amit calls a 'wild evil courtier' with no knowledge of economics, and Manmohan Singh, who had health issues, did not take the portfolio himself. Mukherjee produced one disastrous measure after another. The worst was retrospective taxation: telling companies that new tax rules applied to the past too, so they owed back dues.

Trust is asymmetric: it takes decades to build and an instant to lose. Retrospective tax is the ultimate discretionary ambush, and it especially hurts foreign investors, whom India needs. Amit adds that good policy isn't a party matter. Between 1991 and 2011, different parties governed with the nation's interests at heart.

head: General Sagat Singh's Disobedience
dek: Rules versus discretion is not an either/or choice. Good institutions decide which layer gets which discretion.
more: Amit draws on his episode with military historian Probal DasGupta. At Nathu La and Cho La, a local commander, General Sagat Singh, disobeyed an order from high command because he understood conditions on the ground, and this later helped India enormously. Yet an army only works if orders are followed. Amit's tentative answer is to build complexity into the rules so the rules themselves say when discretion applies. Ajay agrees: great militaries separate strategy, operations and tactics, and each level fully owns its own sphere.

Rules versus discretion is not an either/or choice. Good institutions decide which layer gets which discretion. Ajay's caveat for governments: what matters in the Kydland-Prescott sense is that the state's rules, however long, are known to the people.
printed: Orders, and when to break them

head: Kodak's Straitjacket, Google's Passion Projects
dek: Rules can fossilise firms, so smart firms design rules that leave room to disrupt themselves.
more: Citing Clayton Christensen's innovator's dilemma, Amit notes that Kodak had the know-how to move into digital photography, but its rules, processes and incentives kept it stuck. Google, at least in the early 2000s, let employees spend part of their time on passion projects inside the company. Ajay agrees that firms need occasional big strategy pivots. Government, he says, is different: a city like Liverpool has wanted the same things for centuries, namely streets, parks, solid waste management, water and sanitation. The exception is war. The Russia-Ukraine war has set off an innovation spiral in drones and precision-guided munitions, and armies that keep fighting the last war get left behind.
Rules can fossilise firms, so smart firms design rules that leave room to disrupt themselves. Governments mostly deliver basics that don't change, and there predictability is the whole point.

head: Big Firms Bullying Small Vendors
dek: Dealing with vendors is a repeated game, and the price you get in an auction reflects your reputation.
more: Many large Indian firms buying some humble part believe a hundred small suppliers are desperate to sell to them. So they drive brutal bargains, extract working-capital credit from small firms (which is backwards, since big firms have the cheaper capital), and practise gundagiri by opportunistically breaking the contract. The executives take pride in this machismo. But small firms build the treatment into their expectations and shade their bids upward. The bully ends up paying more than firms that behave well. Ajay would instead promise vendors swift payment and get better prices in return.
Dealing with vendors is a repeated game, and the price you get in an auction reflects your reputation. Opportunism that wins one procurement quietly loses you every future one.

head: The Parent Who Can't Bring Himself to Punish
dek: Kydland and Prescott apply at home. Predictable, gradually evolving rules (not micromanagement) give children clearer boundaries than loving but erratic discretion.
more: A parent says, 'If you do X, I will punish you.' No parent actually wants to punish a child, so when the moment comes it is very tempting to let it go. But that is exactly how the parent loses credibility. A household run on mood, yes today and no tomorrow, leaves children confused, and they start working out how to game the parent instead of learning the guardrails.
Kydland and Prescott apply at home. Predictable, gradually evolving rules (not micromanagement) give children clearer boundaries than loving but erratic discretion.

head: Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans
by: Finn E. Kydland and Edward C. Prescott
dek: It is a landmark of the rational expectations revolution and, Ajay notes, part of the work behind both authors' Nobel Prizes.
more: It is a landmark of the rational expectations revolution and, Ajay notes, part of the work behind both authors' Nobel Prizes. It made economists take credibility and commitment seriously and showed that a state which ties its own hands becomes more effective.
The 1977 Journal of Political Economy paper at the centre of the episode. Ajay first studied it in his PhD coursework and reread it the morning he prepared for this episode.

head: The Equity Premium: A Puzzle
dek: Ajay calls it an 'amazing paper', co-written by a friend of the show with one of the authors of the episode's key paper.
more: Ajay calls it an 'amazing paper', co-written by a friend of the show with one of the authors of the episode's key paper.
Mentioned while introducing Prescott, via Ajay's friend Rajnish Mehra.

head: Designing the Monetary Policy Committee
dek: It sets out a concrete commitment device.
more: It sets out a concrete commitment device. The government-appointed governor is the channel for political pressure, so put the governor alongside four independent private economists, with five votes in total, so that only one vote is exposed to that pressure.
Ajay's blog post, cited while discussing how to stop politicians from manipulating interest rates.

head: The Calculus of Consent
dek: Amit says it speaks directly to the episode's theme. He calls it a masterpiece: not an easy read, but a foundational book everyone who wants to understand the field should read.
more: Amit says it speaks directly to the episode's theme. He calls it a masterpiece: not an easy read, but a foundational book everyone who wants to understand the field should read.
Amit's end-of-episode recommendation.

head: A rowing machine (the Concept2 is the most common)
dek: If you are lazy and will commit to only one exercise, make it rowing. It is cardio and works something like 80–85% of the body's muscles.
more: If you are lazy and will commit to only one exercise, make it rowing. It is cardio and works something like 80–85% of the body's muscles.
Ajay's end-of-episode recommendation, after Amit made him show off his biceps on camera.

head: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
dek: It makes the argument that growth is the only way out of poverty, which this episode connects to rules and credibility.
more: It makes the argument that growth is the only way out of poverty, which this episode connects to rules and credibility.
Invoked when Amit asks how rules-not-discretion connects to ending India's poverty.

head: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37)
dek: It maps how Indian firms moved from regional satraps in the 1980s, to top-down 'imperial' firms with uniform best practices in the 1990s, to 'adaptive' firms that pair rules with local flexibility.
more: It maps how Indian firms moved from regional satraps in the 1980s, to top-down 'imperial' firms with uniform best practices in the 1990s, to 'adaptive' firms that pair rules with local flexibility.
