Amit's starting point for asking how rules and local discretion coexist inside organisations.

head: The Innovator's Dilemma
dek: It explains how dominant companies like Kodak can have the know-how to adapt yet fail, trapped by their own processes, priorities and incentives.
more: It explains how dominant companies like Kodak can have the know-how to adapt yet fail, trapped by their own processes, priorities and incentives.
Raised when Amit asks whether rules can become a straitjacket for firms.

head: The Heart of Disruption (Episode 86)
dek: It is the companion discussion on why big companies crumble when they can't adapt, and how some escape that fate.
more: It is the companion discussion on why big companies crumble when they can't adapt, and how some escape that fate.
Referenced for Netflix as the 'honorable example' of a company that adapted.

head: The journey of Indian finance (Episode 71)
dek: It covers a 25-year stretch in which the Ministry of Finance, NSE, SEBI and academics worked together and got a lot done, and how things went wrong one by one after that group scattered.
more: It covers a 25-year stretch in which the Ministry of Finance, NSE, SEBI and academics worked together and got a lot done, and how things went wrong one by one after that group scattered.
A second example of policy held together by an intellectual community.

head: Three Arguments Against the Strongman
dek: Ajay lays out three escalating arguments.
more: Ajay lays out three escalating arguments. First, public choice theory: the strongman is an ordinary person with wants, needs and flaws, so absolute power in his hands is a nightmare, and the answer is checks and balances, rule of law and dispersed power. Second, public administration: every strongman's minions become little tyrants, so even an autocrat wants rules to bind them. Third, the economists' contribution: the state itself becomes more effective when it gives up discretion. That third point clashes with the macho instinct of most civil servants, who enjoy granting favours to supplicants.

head: What a 'Weak Leader' Really Means
dek: Our attraction to strongmen is hardwired from prehistoric tribes of about 150 people, where top-down, zero-sum thinking worked, and we have to consciously fight it.
more: Our attraction to strongmen is hardwired from prehistoric tribes of about 150 people, where top-down, zero-sum thinking worked, and we have to consciously fight it. 'Weak' here doesn't mean weak in character or intellect. It means a leader whose ability to act on whims is boxed in by laws and institutions. Amit cites James Buchanan's design test: build a system so robust that even if the worst person imaginable, whether Hitler or anyone, rises to the top, they can't do much damage.

head: Rule by Law vs Rule of Law
dek: Under rule by law, the ruler writes laws that everyone else must obey but stays above them himself, which is the Caesar model.
more: Under rule by law, the ruler writes laws that everyone else must obey but stays above them himself, which is the Caesar model. Under rule of law, the ruler is also subject to the law and cannot override it. The first makes a strongman more efficient. Only the second actually restrains him.

head: You Are Not Wood, You Are Not Stones: Rational Expectations
dek: Until the 1960s, economists modelled a smart, optimising state ruling over passive, credulous people.
more: Until the 1960s, economists modelled a smart, optimising state ruling over passive, credulous people. The rational expectations revolution of the late 60s and 70s assumed instead that people look ahead, watch the policymaker and adjust. Ajay disowns the word 'rational', because people aren't perfect Bayesian computers. The real point is that they aren't fools either. So any surprise the state springs changes how people behave afterwards, through things like higher risk premia and padded tax assumptions.

head: Anchored Inflation as a Public Good
dek: Once everyone believes inflation will be 4%, firms stop panicking over one-off cost shocks and price strategically.
more: Once everyone believes inflation will be 4%, firms stop panicking over one-off cost shocks and price strategically. Bond markets can also price 25-year debt, because long-term interest rates are essentially a bet on inflation. India's RBI Act holds the RBI accountable for 4%. But with a short track record and middling performance, Ajay says it will take decades to anchor the minds of firms, savers and pension planners.

head: Policymaking Is Rule Design, Not Day-to-Day Decisions
dek: The primitive model of governance is a person who looks at each situation and decides.
more: The primitive model of governance is a person who looks at each situation and decides. In a rules-based world, the real intellectual work is designing the rule ('if state X arises, we do Y'). After that, officials simply carry out a publicly stated manual. A good country puts its best and brightest into imagining incentive-compatible rules, as with the Constituent Assembly, the NPS and inflation targeting.

head: Credibility and Commitment Are the State's Real Power
dek: A government that flips back and forth, with a tariff one day and none the next, gets discounted by everyone, and private uncertainty rises.
more: A government that flips back and forth, with a tariff one day and none the next, gets discounted by everyone, and private uncertainty rises. Power comes from announcing something and then doing it, again and again, with no gap between words and deeds. Populist regimes believe their propaganda can float free of their actions, which is why people say 'watch not what they say, but watch what they do'. That decoupling doesn't last, because people are smart.

head: Handcuffs as Commitment Devices
dek: This is the opposite of strongman logic: you gain power by deliberately giving it up.
more: This is the opposite of strongman logic: you gain power by deliberately giving it up. The state lacks credibility, so it builds mechanisms that make breaking its own rules costly. Ajay's examples: a monetary policy committee where four independent economists outvote the politically exposed governor; New Zealand-style bonuses for central bankers who hit the target and money lost when they miss, all announced by press release; and a public mea culpa letter that diagnoses what went wrong (data, models, analysis or transmission). These devices work because leaders care most about the respect of their peers.

head: Communication Is Part of Governance, Not Advertising
dek: We usually treat government communication as propaganda wrapped around the real work.
more: We usually treat government communication as propaganda wrapped around the real work. Amit argues that consistent communication matched by action is itself governance, because it builds the trust that drives economic behaviour. Where rules can't spell everything out, leaders must explain their philosophy and their view of the world in speeches, so people can predict how they'll act in situations nobody foresaw. Ajay notes that such speeches have nearly died out in India. Done badly, the process runs backwards: a slogan comes first and drives the policy.

head: Rules Can Be Complex, Just Not Surprising
dek: Rules-based doesn't mean simplistic; Ajay says a rule needn't be 160 bytes and can run to 16,000 pages.
more: Rules-based doesn't mean simplistic; Ajay says a rule needn't be 160 bytes and can run to 16,000 pages. You could issue a government bond that, by its own terms, pays zero interest in any year real GDP growth is negative. That is fine because it was promised upfront. What is not fine is skipping interest payments after the fact because 'we had a bad year'. The test is whether the rule was known in advance, not how long it is: a world of rules, not deals.

head: India Needs Rules More, Not Less
dek: It's tempting to treat Kydland-Prescott as a luxury for rich countries.
more: It's tempting to treat Kydland-Prescott as a luxury for rich countries. Ajay argues the reverse. If German firms and bondholders are skeptical of the Bundesbank, Indians, after a long history of bad state behaviour, are ten times more so. So Indian policymakers need tighter handcuffs, louder communication, and daily press conferences and unscripted town halls where they face hard questions.

head: Rules Are the Machinery of Growth
dek: Growth comes from high-productivity firms controlling large amounts of labour and capital.
more: Growth comes from high-productivity firms controlling large amounts of labour and capital. Such firms are built over decades by people who commit their money, passion, time and even their children to them. Whether anyone makes that bet depends on the state. Every expropriation, every sudden rule change, every monopoly PSU or rigged game favouring a national champion teaches investors, Indian and foreign, to hold back, diversify abroad and wait and see. The result is low GDP growth.

head: Layering Discretion: Strategy, Operations, Tactics and Subsidiarity
dek: Rules and discretion can be divided between levels. Militaries give strategy to the top, operations to the middle and tactics to the field.
more: Rules and discretion can be divided between levels. Militaries give strategy to the top, operations to the middle and tactics to the field. Amit adapts the subsidiarity principle: decide the 'why' at the top, the 'what' a level below, and the 'how' locally, where the best information is. Ajay grounds it in India's diversity. Local priorities and costs differ: a teacher costs something different in Bihar than in Kerala, and a malarial city faces problems a desert town doesn't. So monetary policy belongs with the Union, a few things with the states, and most things with cities.

head: Policy Is an Incomplete Contract: Communities Pour the Concrete
dek: No law truly pre-commits the state. Inflation targeting is an ordinary act of parliament that could be amended tomorrow.
more: No law truly pre-commits the state. Inflation targeting is an ordinary act of parliament that could be amended tomorrow. Ajay mocks the caricature of economists whispering into the ear of a ruler like Aurangzeb, because the next whisperer can undo it. What actually makes policy last is a broad intellectual community of owners and guardians who watch the space, write and criticise. The NPS and Indian financial reform both thrived while their communities existed and unravelled once those communities dispersed. The bipartisan US foreign-policy consensus held for the same reason.

head: Opportunism Is Never Free: Contracts, Sentencing, Treaties
dek: The same logic applies far beyond economics. Between firms, renegotiating a contract opportunistically just leads counterparties to price in the risk.
more: The same logic applies far beyond economics. Between firms, renegotiating a contract opportunistically just leads counterparties to price in the risk. In criminal law, broad judicial discretion over sentences opens a Pandora's box of doubts about fair play and invites criminals to bet on leniency, so Ajay favours sentencing guidelines. In international relations, where no court can enforce anything, a strongman who walks out of a treaty gets cheered at home, but every other treaty partner learns not to trust his country. In each case the short-term win is paid for over the long run.

head: Quiet Life, Explosive Ideas
dek: Ajay's one-line summary of the personal version of rules over discretion.
more: Ajay's one-line summary of the personal version of rules over discretion. Steady routines in sleep, food and exercise free up energy and attention for bold, creative thinking. Discipline is what makes the rebellion effective.

head: Amit's self-diagnosis riffing on…
more: Amit's self-diagnosis riffing on 'Rebel Without a Cause': as a teenager he was a rebel without a cause, 'or if we wish to alliterate, a rebel without restraints', and today he is 'a rebel with rules.'

head: A sly dig at dynasties
more: A sly dig at dynasties: 'we instinctively prefer strong men, or even strong women sometimes, especially if they're from a family of an earlier strong man.'

head: Ajay describing the policymaker who wants to squeeze trapped foreign firms
more: Ajay describing the policymaker who wants to squeeze trapped foreign firms: 'the clever policy maker, okay, it's Indian IAS level of IQ.'

head: Amit to listeners
more: Amit to listeners: 'Ajay Shah reads papers the way other adolescent boys watch porn.' You start one paper at 9 PM and suddenly it's 4 AM and you've gone through forty.

head: Ajay's caricature of how many economists think policy happens: they
more: Ajay's caricature of how many economists think policy happens: they 'whisper in the ears of Aurangzeb and miraculously some policy will happen', until Aurangzeb 'wakes up from the wrong side of the bed' or someone else whispers in his ear.

head: Ajay offers the aphorism
more: Ajay offers the aphorism 'Be quiet and predictable in your life, so that you can be explosive and creative in your ideas', and Amit deadpans: 'Have you ever considered Twitter?'

head: Amit makes Ajay roll up his sleeve and flex for the camera (
more: Amit makes Ajay roll up his sleeve and flex for the camera ('Nomsita, can we zoom, please?'), then points out that the biceps came from a rules-based regime, not from doing whatever exercise he felt like.

head: Ajay pitches rowing to anyone who is…
more: Ajay pitches rowing to anyone who is 'a lazy bum' or 'a sleepy Bengali'. Amit hits back with a Hindi pun: his Bengali melodrama makes him want to weep copiously and become a 'rona' (crying) machine. He adds that Bengal gave India Rabindra Sangeet and Satyajit Ray, while Gujarat gave 'a diet that is guaranteed to produce diabetes. Well done.'

head: Amit on the final recommendations
more: Amit on the final recommendations: 'I am recommending a geeky scholarly book and he is recommending a rowing machine… This is a man of action. So I guess the second half of your life will be more action than thought.'

head: Mark Antony's speech over Caesar's corpse in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar (
more: Mark Antony's speech over Caesar's corpse in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar ('You are not wood, you are not stones, but men'), which Ajay adapts into his personal economics slogan: '…and being men, you will optimize.'

head: Ram Rajya and the mai-baap state: Ajay says we grow up imagining the strongman will be a Ram, a ruler who grants wishes
more: Ram Rajya and the mai-baap state: Ajay says we grow up imagining the strongman will be a Ram, a ruler who grants wishes 'straight out of Hindu mythology', and that a good country is one where he can grant very few.

head: From an earlier decentralisation discussion: Japan has about thirty varieties of Kit Kat, while India has
more: From an earlier decentralisation discussion: Japan has about thirty varieties of Kit Kat, while India has 'only one Maggi, one Kit Kat'. Amit uses it to show how uniform rules can ignore local tastes.

head: Ajay's pitch for a future episode
more: Ajay's pitch for a future episode, 'Legitimacy: Why and How', on legitimacy as the subtle state in which 'the people are in harmony with the project of the state.'

head: The Good Gyan folder he never opens
dek: What you save says as much about you as about the people who wrote it.
more: Twitter lets you sort bookmarks into folders, and Amit keeps one called 'Good Gyan' for tweets that strike him as wise. He saves them meaning to come back and be enlightened, then admits he never does. This episode was his way of finally putting the folder to use: he reads the tweets to Ajay, who has not seen them, and Ajay reacts on the spot.

What you save says as much about you as about the people who wrote it. Amit expects the folder to expose his own foibles, and Ajay sums it up: 'The reader makes the tweet as much as the writer.' Turning a private hoard into a conversation is one way to make bookmarking worth something.

head: Aanchal Malhotra, Partition, and Chinese whispers in the brain
dek: Memory is rebuilt every time we use it, and it is shaped by who we are from the first impression onward.
more: While preparing for his episode with Aanchal Malhotra, who collected memories of Partition in a book, Amit learned that memory is not a file stored once and pulled up unchanged. Each time you remember something, you are recalling your last act of remembering it. That is why two people who shared a moment can later describe it in completely different ways.
Memory is rebuilt every time we use it, and it is shaped by who we are from the first impression onward. This was Amit's gloss on Anais Nin's line, and the lesson he draws is to be slow to judge.

head: Drifting toward Hawaii off Santa Cruz
dek: Ajay told this in response to Faulkner's line about losing sight of the shore, and Amit teased him for taking the metaphor literally.
more: A friend who teaches at UC Santa Cruz took Ajay and Ila out sailing. The wind began pushing the boat away from Santa Cruz, and Ajay realised that if they did nothing at all, the wind would carry them to Hawaii. His friend confirmed it. Ajay found it eerie that the boat could simply keep going forever on the wind.

Ajay told this in response to Faulkner's line about losing sight of the shore, and Amit teased him for taking the metaphor literally. The story still makes the metaphor felt: leaving the shore is unsettling because open water has no natural stopping point, and that is exactly why it takes courage.

head: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan and the all-vegetarian weekend
dek: What goes in shapes what comes out. You cannot starve an artist of what feeds him and expect magic.
more: A Raja invited Bade Ghulam Ali Khan to give a Sunday concert. The singer arrived on Friday and was treated lavishly, except that every meal was vegetarian: Friday, Saturday and Sunday. After the concert the Raja told him that his performances elsewhere had been so magical the oceans seemed ready to part, but today's, though good, lacked that flavour. The maestro answered with a rhyming one-liner tying the quality of his singing to the food he had been given.
What goes in shapes what comes out. You cannot starve an artist of what feeds him and expect magic. Amit, a committed carnivore like Ajay, told it right after Ajay's 'restaurant, not a meadow' joke.
printed: Three days of cabbage, one concert

head: The WhatsApp group that ran on bitching
dek: Groups of complainers keep sinking, and anyone who leaves becomes the next target.
more: Amit was once in a WhatsApp group of people both he and Ajay know, where about ninety percent of the conversation was bitching about others, mutual friends included. He left. He later heard that they then bitched about him, which did not surprise him.

Groups of complainers keep sinking, and anyone who leaves becomes the next target. Amit's conclusion is to cut such people out as brutally as you can and spend your time with people who help you build ideas instead of tearing them down.

head: A father's death and the missing medical data
dek: Personal grief led him to a systems problem. Consolidated records let a doctor, with consent, see the whole picture.
more: Amit's father died in 2021 during the second COVID wave. He got talking with a friend who had just sold his company and had also lost his father. Amit concluded that the real failure was data: no one had a patient's full information in one place, and someone should build a startup to fix that. He has since heard of several people working on parts of the problem.

Personal grief led him to a systems problem. Consolidated records let a doctor, with consent, see the whole picture. Anonymised data across a whole population lets AI spot local disease patterns, such as something unusual in Sholapur, that no single doctor ever could. That is a public health gain, beyond individual care.

head: From twenty-minute episodes to ten-hour ones
dek: This is Faulkner's 'lose sight of the shore' in practice. Many of the rules we follow are inherited rather than tested, and good work often needs you to ignore them and trust yourself.
more: Amit started The Seen and the Unseen with twenty-minute episodes because the standard advice was that attention spans are short. He has since recorded oral-history-style episodes of eight, nine and even ten hours.
This is Faulkner's 'lose sight of the shore' in practice. Many of the rules we follow are inherited rather than tested, and good work often needs you to ignore them and trust yourself.

head: How Ajay writes his Business Standard column
dek: A practical version of Amit's point about learning: load the question into your head, stop pushing, and let sleep connect the pieces.
more: Ajay has written a fortnightly Business Standard column since the mid-1990s, due on Sunday afternoon. When it goes well, he settles on the idea by Saturday evening, often after texting friends for suggestions. He then reads around the topic without taking notes or planning the argument, looking at data and graphs, and goes to sleep. On Sunday, between about ten and noon, he writes it with far more clarity.

A practical version of Amit's point about learning: load the question into your head, stop pushing, and let sleep connect the pieces. Amit, who wrote weekly columns for fifteen years, agrees that once the brain accepts a deadline, it finds a way.

head: The industrial policy paper that missed the point
dek: This illustrates Shahab Bakhtiari's 'five meters away' rule.
more: Ajay recently came across an article on industrial policy for developing countries and was excited by it. He found it had been written by a narrow economist who had read only development economics papers and knew nothing of state capability or public choice theory. Yet the one distinctive thing about industrial policy in a poor country is that the state is far more likely to be out of control and to make mistakes.

This illustrates Shahab Bakhtiari's 'five meters away' rule. Specialists who never read outside their own corner write papers that miss the central issue, here the principal-agent problem between citizens and a weak state.

head: Underrated, Overrated, Complicated (Episode 85 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Round one of the debate this episode continues: Ajay sees Twitter as a cesspool, and Amit agrees but says a well-curated feed is a gift.
more: Round one of the debate this episode continues: Ajay sees Twitter as a cesspool, and Amit agrees but says a well-curated feed is a gift.
Mentioned in the intro as the episode where they first argued about social media.

dek: A reminder that we are part of whatever we perceive, so we should take a step back before judging.
more: A reminder that we are part of whatever we perceive, so we should take a step back before judging. It set off the episode's first argument, with Ajay pushing back in defence of objective truth.
Good Gyan 1, on perception.

more: A sharp diagnosis of envy, more relevant than ever now that social media pits our real lives against other people's curated ones.

dek: It diagnoses tribal thinking on questions that really are complex. Ajay objected that some debates, such as nationalism and militarism, are closed for him.
more: It diagnoses tribal thinking on questions that really are complex. Ajay objected that some debates, such as nationalism and militarism, are closed for him.

more: It sharpens the case for using AI as a tool rather than a crutch.

Amit's sign-off recommendation, with his essays page linked in the show notes.

head: Twitter rewards curation
dek: Amit agrees that social media went bad when retweets and likes began amplifying tribalism and the hunger for validation.
more: Amit agrees that social media went bad when retweets and likes began amplifying tribalism and the hunger for validation. But a well-curated feed lets you listen to the world's best minds think aloud every morning, sometimes even in dialogue with each other. Bookmark folders turn that stream into a personal library.

head: Perception is never objective
dek: Anais Nin's line is about perception rather than reality. Chairs are real, but how we read people, relationships and complex events depends on who we are.
more: Anais Nin's line is about perception rather than reality. Chairs are real, but how we read people, relationships and complex events depends on who we are. Memory adds another layer of distortion because it is rebuilt each time it is recalled. The practical lesson is humility: on anything too complex to fully grasp, keep open the possibility that you are wrong.

head: Attach a degree of confidence to everything you believe
dek: Ajay objects to the post-truth idea that everyone has their own truth, which opens the door to every conspiracy theory.
more: Ajay objects to the post-truth idea that everyone has their own truth, which opens the door to every conspiracy theory. Some knowledge is certain, like Planck's formula for black body radiation, which is correct to the last decimal. How social media changed the world is much fuzzier. The real skill is calibrating how sure you are about each belief while continuing the uphill search for truth, which is what separates us from cats.

head: Learn a field in the order it developed
dek: Old work matters even when it is obsolete. Learning the sequence of puzzle, crisis and solution builds deep understanding.
more: Old work matters even when it is obsolete. Learning the sequence of puzzle, crisis and solution builds deep understanding. Philosophy has barely moved since Plato, and even a physicist gains from going back to Newton. Old engineering was often done under brutal constraints, such as Apollo's 64 KB of RAM, which forced deep insight. Without this history, fields like computer science keep reinventing the same things badly.

head: Breadth makes you deeper
dek: Interdisciplinary work is more than a hunt for unclaimed ground at the edges of fields.
more: Interdisciplinary work is more than a hunt for unclaimed ground at the edges of fields. Understanding the world takes history, geography and neighbouring disciplines, and breadth makes your work matter to more people. Max Weber's 'I am not a donkey, I don't have a field' sums up the case against silos.

head: Solitude for reflection, company for sparks
dek: Amit sees too little self-reflection in the world, and even our time alone is swallowed by screens.
more: Amit sees too little self-reflection in the world, and even our time alone is swallowed by screens. Solitary hobbies give that reflection room. Ajay values long, quiet mountain walks, but says his research has always needed other people to argue with, persuade and fail to persuade, in a setting where it is safe to make mistakes.

head: Gardening versus architecture
dek: Gurpriya Sidhu suggests being a coach or comrade at work and a gardener with the people you love.
more: Gurpriya Sidhu suggests being a coach or comrade at work and a gardener with the people you love. The metaphor also fits novel-writing: architects plan every room before building, while gardeners start with overgrowth and prune until a shape emerges, which Amit thinks is how most great novelists work. It fits firms too: one view runs a firm like cooking, mixing ingredients from the top down, while the other creates conditions where many attempts can bloom or fail.

head: Envy, and the healthy selfishness that cures it
dek: Montesquieu says happiness is easy but being happier than others is hard, because we overestimate how happy they are.
more: Montesquieu says happiness is easy but being happier than others is hard, because we overestimate how happy they are. Social media makes this worse by pitting our real lives against other people's curated ones. Ajay's cure is to stay absorbed in your own work of writing, making and building, which leaves no room for envy. Amit adds Naval Ravikant's test: before envying someone, ask whether you would take their whole life as a package, not just the part you admire.

head: Learning happens in the downtime
dek: Focused study uses a small working memory that holds about four chunks, so forcing it leads to frustration.
more: Focused study uses a small working memory that holds about four chunks, so forcing it leads to frustration. Insight comes later, while you relax or sleep and different parts of the brain make connections. So schedule free time deliberately instead of packing your calendar, and do what Ajay does with his column: fill your head with the question, then sleep on it.

head: Don't whine, and back ideas when they are new
dek: Gurwinder Bhogal's rule is to fix the problem, ask for help, or stop complaining, because complaining only spreads bitterness.
more: Gurwinder Bhogal's rule is to fix the problem, ask for help, or stop complaining, because complaining only spreads bitterness. Ajay adds the positive side: when someone shares a new idea, support it first and save the fifteen criticisms for later, because we are shaped by how others respond to our ideas. Amit notes that harsh feedback lands differently on different people. He has often seen men take it as a personal insult and women turn it on themselves through impostor syndrome, so it pays to think about how you deliver it.

head: Don't shrink an issue to fit your mind
dek: If people have argued about something for ages and you find the answer obvious, you have probably reduced it to a tribal script.
more: If people have argued about something for ages and you find the answer obvious, you have probably reduced it to a tribal script. Choosing the tribal line on a genuinely complex question shows you care more about your side than about the truth. Ajay notes that some questions, such as nationalism and militarism, he personally regards as settled, even though many people still champion them.

head: Purpose is powerful, but don't cling to outcomes
dek: Nietzsche's 'why' makes almost any 'how' bearable. Practical problems can be solved, but the fire has to come from you.
more: Nietzsche's 'why' makes almost any 'how' bearable. Practical problems can be solved, but the fire has to come from you. Amit asks whether purpose actually brings happiness. Ajay answers with the Bhagavad Gita: you are obliged to try, but you do not control outcomes. If you measure a big purpose only by its results, you set yourself up for pain, because the world owes you nothing.

head: Wisdom means knowing what to ignore
dek: Schopenhauer's art of not reading and Rousseau's definition of wisdom make the same point.
more: Schopenhauer's art of not reading and Rousseau's definition of wisdom make the same point. Real wisdom is sorting things into necessary, less necessary and completely unnecessary to know, and skipping whatever the crowd is excited about this week. Pico Iyer adds that you cannot do this without putting your phone away.

head: Use AI as a tool, not a crutch
dek: Bhogal warns that outsourcing our thinking makes us more machine-like.
more: Bhogal warns that outsourcing our thinking makes us more machine-like. Ajay is not worried, because he believes creativity comes from deep inside the human mind and AI will just take over tasks. Amit, an AI optimist, gives the same caveat he would give for any technology: use it to extend your own thinking, not to replace it.

head: Informed patients, and AI to make up for doctor shortages
dek: Patients who research their conditions are allies. Ajay's worry is that most Indian doctors do not read the medical literature.
more: Patients who research their conditions are allies. Ajay's worry is that most Indian doctors do not read the medical literature. Amit adds that in fields like nutrition, old training can be not just outdated but harmful. Ajay's hope is a new model: nurses spend hours compiling a complete patient history, and that file goes to an AI. Research suggests that, given a full formal history, AI beats almost all doctors, which could be India's way to solve both the quantity and quality of doctors.

head: Preparation beats planning
dek: Plans assume order and break at the first punch. Preparation assumes chaos and becomes second nature through years of practice.
more: Plans assume order and break at the first punch. Preparation assumes chaos and becomes second nature through years of practice. Ajay says good military planning is valuable because it rehearses many scenarios, logistics and the fact that the opponent also gets a say, which readies the mind even after the plan itself fails.

head: Want it badly enough, or don't do it
dek: From Lynk's crackhead tweet: people who really want something find a way.
more: From Lynk's crackhead tweet: people who really want something find a way. When aspiring writers ask Amit whether they should write a book, his answer is no, because anyone who truly wanted to would already be writing. Wanting can be cultivated, and remembering that your time is limited is one way to do it.

head: Let go of the shore
dek: Faulkner's line is about clearing conventional thinking out of the way, the way Amit's podcast grew from twenty minutes to ten hours.
more: Faulkner's line is about clearing conventional thinking out of the way, the way Amit's podcast grew from twenty minutes to ten hours. Ajay adds his own: 'A headful of fears has no space for dreams.' Asked which oceans he has fallen in love with, Ajay says he never stayed stuck in one field and always moved to the next adjacent one.

head: Ajay opens the episode by throwing down the gauntlet
more: Ajay opens the episode by throwing down the gauntlet: 'Amit, you have once claimed to me that Twitter is more than the cesspool of the global mind. Prove it.'

head: Ajay on why we should keep pursuing truth: otherwise
more: Ajay on why we should keep pursuing truth: otherwise 'you might as well, you know, be a cat. So cats have no upward journey of figuring out the spectrum of black body radiation.'

head: Amit ends the perception argument by insisting on agreement
more: Amit ends the perception argument by insisting on agreement: 'Of course I agree with you, and of course you agree with me, right? Right? Right, Ajay? You agree with me, right? Don't mess with me, just agree with me.'
Ajay: 'But I mean novelists don't start with a spreadsheet of all the characters and their characteristics.' Amit: 'Oh my God, this is what you would do, isn't it? Please remain an economist.'

head: Ajay on his love of mountain walks
more: Ajay on his love of mountain walks: 'I'm so out of breath that mostly I can't talk,' so the walks turn into long, quiet meditation by default.

After the Weber tweet, Ajay recalls the film Ninotchka. A humourless Russian communist in a Paris restaurant orders boiled cabbage and beet, and the waiter replies: 'Ma'am, this is a restaurant, not a meadow.'

head: Ajay brings back a one-liner from when Facebook's market cap overtook Google's
more: Ajay brings back a one-liner from when Facebook's market cap overtook Google's: 'knowing everyone is worth more than knowing everything.' Amit: 'This is brilliant, but on Facebook you don't know everyone, and Google you don't know everything.'

head: Ajay's AI summary of Schopenhauer's art of not reading
more: Ajay's AI summary of Schopenhauer's art of not reading: 'Don't follow anybody on Twitter.' Amit, in the middle of a Twitter-sourced episode: 'All these are from Twitter. Don't mess with me, man.'

head: Amit on pulmonologist Lancelot Pinto's book in progress: it will still be read fifty years from now
more: Amit on pulmonologist Lancelot Pinto's book in progress: it will still be read fifty years from now, 'but the fucker has to write it first.'

head: Ajay's six tiers of medical literacy
more: Ajay's six tiers of medical literacy: 'Doctor that uses Google Scholar. Doctor that uses Google, doctor that uses nothing, patient that uses Google Scholar, patient that uses Google, patient that uses nothing.'

head: As daylight fades during the shoot, Amit falls back on their own earlier episode
more: As daylight fades during the shoot, Amit falls back on their own earlier episode: 'Ajay, you know the light is going. We've done an episode on constraints. Great things happen despite constraints.'

head: After Amit's
more: After Amit's 'think like a dope head who wants crack', Ajay offers 'a useless tweet' in reply: 'cocaine is nature's way of saying you have too much money.'

head: After the Pico Iyer line about putting your phone away, Amit points at Ajay, who…
more: After the Pico Iyer line about putting your phone away, Amit points at Ajay, who 'is laughing because he's fucking guilty', having spent half an hour before the shoot taking calls about the markets and America. Amit then improvises a Beatles-style lyric: 'Hey, you gotta hide that phone away.'

head: Amit on Ajay's erratic recommendation habits, which swing between zero and seven
more: Amit on Ajay's erratic recommendation habits, which swing between zero and seven: 'luckily there's no scope for you giving minus seven recommendations. You take away seven things from the readers' heads.'

head: Amit, explaining working memory, takes a dig at…
more: Amit, explaining working memory, takes a dig at 'the Monty Hall problem which you are still refusing to grok.'

head: Ajay uses the line
more: Ajay uses the line 'If you prick us, do we not bleed?' to argue that some realities are shared by all seven billion people and are not matters of opinion.

head: Ajay's one-liner capturing the zero-sum mindset
more: Ajay's one-liner capturing the zero-sum mindset: 'It is not enough to win, others have to lose.' He follows it with: 'Resentment is like taking poison and hoping the other person dies.'

head: Ajay offers the prayer he attributes to…
more: Ajay offers the prayer he attributes to 'maybe some Christian sources': strength to change what I can, serenity to accept what I can't, and the wisdom to know the difference.

head: On planning: Mike Tyson's
more: On planning: Mike Tyson's 'Everybody has a plan until they are punched in the mouth', plus 'Once the shooting starts, the plan is useless, but the planning is everything' (Ajay admits 'I forget who' said it). Amit imagines Tyson's plan for Lennox Lewis falling apart after the first punch.

head: Amit recalls a 1980s Japanese saying from the days of expensive Kodak film and manual cameras
more: Amit recalls a 1980s Japanese saying from the days of expensive Kodak film and manual cameras: 'if you want to make a man a pauper, give him a camera.'

head: A father's gift and three lifetime regrets
dek: Deep curiosity is often inherited as a disposition rather than chosen as a goal.
more: Asked what he would have pursued no matter what, Ajay says he can't picture himself outside the path his father set. His father gave him an interest in the world and died when Ajay was seventeen. With that interest in place, Ajay says, he never needed money, books or universities. He would have powered through anyway. He then names three great lifetime regrets: never learning a musical instrument, never seriously knowing maths, and not knowing more biology.

Deep curiosity is often inherited as a disposition rather than chosen as a goal. Even a restless polymath carries a short list of roads not taken. Later in the episode, Nomsita turns the first regret into a recommendation for viewers.

head: The introvert who hated his face on camera
dek: Comfort in your own skin comes from doing the uncomfortable thing again and again.
more: Amit calls himself an extreme introvert who doesn't find it easy to put himself out there, yet he started his audio podcast anyway. When EIE moved to YouTube, neither host knew anything about the medium. Amit hated how he looked in the early episodes and wished the camera sat higher to hide his double chin. He kept going. Now, nearing episode 100, Ajay says he is 'astonished and happy beyond my wildest dreams' that YouTube's democratisation lets them make timeless material without needing a BBC commission.
Comfort in your own skin comes from doing the uncomfortable thing again and again. It is not something you need before you start.

head: The early-morning panic before 'Rules, Not Discretion'
dek: Even on your home turf, keep a live sense of what you might not know. That nervousness is what stops expertise from turning into smug confidence.
more: Before recording the EIE episode on rules versus discretion, Ajay woke up in a panic. The paper behind that episode had been one of the great highs of his life as a PhD student, a long time ago. What if he had missed something essential in the years since? He hadn't, but he values having had the panic.
Even on your home turf, keep a live sense of what you might not know. That nervousness is what stops expertise from turning into smug confidence.

head: The one-book question
dek: A forced-choice question can quickly reveal what matters most to you. Acting on the answer is the hard part.
more: A friend was torn between several book ideas. Amit asked him one question: if you had only one book in you, and you would die once it was done, which book would you write? The friend named something deeply personal. Amit told him that was the book to write. The friend went on to write something else.
A forced-choice question can quickly reveal what matters most to you. Acting on the answer is the hard part.

head: The poker grinders who wouldn't get up to pee
dek: Hard work matters, but treating self-punishing grind as the only route to excellence is a distortion.
more: Nomsita asked how young people should read pop culture's image of greatness as sleepless, protein-bar-fuelled grind. In reply, Amit recalls his professional poker days. Some players multi-tabled fifteen tables at once and kept a bottle beside them so they never had to leave the screen to use the bathroom.
Hard work matters, but treating self-punishing grind as the only route to excellence is a distortion. Ideas also need slow, quiet time to marinate.

head: Newton and the moon that didn't add up
dek: Greatness looks less like a frantic sprint and more like extreme concentration plus a perfectionist's refusal to accept a near-miss.
more: Newton already had pretty much all the right ideas when he did a rough calculation of the moon's period. It came out ten to fifteen percent off. He concluded he was wrong and sat quietly with it. Months and years later, better constants reached him, the pieces clicked, and he realised he had been right all along.
Greatness looks less like a frantic sprint and more like extreme concentration plus a perfectionist's refusal to accept a near-miss. Hence Ajay's line: don't fetishise the sprint.

head: The walk he couldn't take
dek: This is Brene Brown's point made personal: we chase the extraordinary, then beg for a normal moment once it's gone.
more: On an earlier shoot at the same location, Amit skipped the crew's usual ten-to-fifteen-minute neighbourhood walk. His chest felt constricted and something seemed wrong. This was before the heart attack discussed in 'The Heart of Disruption'. Now he can do the walk again. He adds that even a blocked nostril during a cold makes him realise he should have been grateful for every day he could breathe freely.
This is Brene Brown's point made personal: we chase the extraordinary, then beg for a normal moment once it's gone. Ordinary health is worth noticing while you have it.

head: Gukesh's world-championship team had no Indian quota
dek: The same logic applies to Indian firms. Not all the knowledge is in India, and a culturally homogeneous workplace is an impediment, because diverse teams have better debates.
more: Responding to Paul Graham's point that most of the world's best people are born abroad, Ajay cites Gukesh's world-championship campaign. Anand helped him bring in a Polish helper and a bunch of others, building an unabashedly international team with just one Indian. To win a world championship, you need a team at the top of world capabilities.
The same logic applies to Indian firms. Not all the knowledge is in India, and a culturally homogeneous workplace is an impediment, because diverse teams have better debates.

head: Being turned into someone's bug tester
dek: Promise doesn't show in the absence of errors. It shows in a thirst for excellence: shipping your genuine best, and asking after each correction what deeper rule you missed.
more: With young colleagues, Ajay is happy to point out a type of mistake once, twice, even three times. When the same error comes back a fifth or sixth time, he realises the person is only fixing whatever he flags, like a typist correcting a typo. They never extract the general principle. The skilled senior has been reduced to a clerical bug tester.
Promise doesn't show in the absence of errors. It shows in a thirst for excellence: shipping your genuine best, and asking after each correction what deeper rule you missed.

head: The king of typos and his reader copy-editors
dek: Shipping and letting the world help you fix things beats endless private polishing.
more: Across hundreds of columns and many thousands of blog posts, Amit has accepted that he will never catch every typo. His system now is to write, read it over once, read it over twice, and publish. A typo always slips through. Within a couple of days, readers write in to point it out, and the page is clean.
Shipping and letting the world help you fix things beats endless private polishing. It is a working example of 'perfection is the enemy of production'.

head: FU money, FO money, and the danger of comfort
dek: Complacency is a side effect of prosperity. Once you're comfortable, the hunger that drove you can quietly fade unless you keep pushing yourself.
more: Amit recalls asking Roshan Abbas on The Seen and the Unseen about FU money and FO money. Roshan said he had FU money but not FO money, and gave figures for both that Amit found insane. Amit says he is far from both, but he is comfortable, and that comfort worries him.
Complacency is a side effect of prosperity. Once you're comfortable, the hunger that drove you can quietly fade unless you keep pushing yourself.

head: Slow Productivity
dek: It argues you don't need a constant mad sprint. You can live a quiet life and let ideas marinate, and creativity emerges from that over time.
more: It argues you don't need a constant mad sprint. You can live a quiet life and let ideas marinate, and creativity emerges from that over time. A counterweight to hustle culture.
Came up in Amit's answer to Nomsita's question about pop culture equating greatness with sleepless grind. Amit read it on a flight; it is Newport's book after Deep Work.

head: Life Lessons (Scorsese's segment of New York Stories)
dek: Amit calls Scorsese's short a masterpiece whose scenes still play in his head.
more: Amit calls Scorsese's short a masterpiece whose scenes still play in his head. It inspired the name of their course. It is also where he first heard Procol Harum's 'A Whiter Shade of Pale', over a slow-motion shot of a falling cigarette: 'the magic of film editing'. Even many Scorsese fans have missed it.

Part of the late-1980s anthology New York Stories, with shorts by Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola and Woody Allen. Amit first saw it when his father was administrative director of the film institute in Pune.

head: The Last Waltz
dek: In the late 1970s The Band, often Dylan's backing band on tour, decided to retire after one last concert and invited friends to perform, including Dylan and Van Morrison (Amit's favourite).
more: In the late 1970s The Band, often Dylan's backing band on tour, decided to retire after one last concert and invited friends to perform, including Dylan and Van Morrison (Amit's favourite). Scorsese filmed it. Amit calls it 'absolutely stirring stuff'.
Recommended after Nomsita's Scorsese pick reminded him of it.

head: Red Dead Redemption 2
dek: It is a slow, peaceful game with a thick story, history it gets right, thick characters, well-written dialogue and strong acting.
more: It is a slow, peaceful game with a thick story, history it gets right, thick characters, well-written dialogue and strong acting. It puts you among some twenty people running from the law and makes you decide what's right and wrong. Vaishnav cried at the end and learned from it.
Vaishnav's third pick, a video game, after Amit insisted he give the why.

head: Rolling Thunder Review
dek: It captures the hunger the hosts keep describing: to get to something, to do something, and to do it with the people you love.
more: It captures the hunger the hosts keep describing: to get to something, to do something, and to do it with the people you love.
A film about Bob Dylan and friends on tour.

head: Pick up a musical instrument
dek: If you have even two percent of the willpower, do it. It changes your life and your mind, and can give you the concentration and meditation that are otherwise hard to find.
more: If you have even two percent of the willpower, do it. It changes your life and your mind, and can give you the concentration and meditation that are otherwise hard to find.
Nomsita turns Ajay's lifetime regret into a recommendation.

head: John Coltrane on desire
dek: Amit's answer to people who say they lack the gear or resources to pursue what they love.
more: Amit's answer to people who say they lack the gear or resources to pursue what they love.
The opening Good Gyan, found on the Twitter account Melodies and Masterpieces: 'You can play a shoestring if you're sincere.'

head: Polina Pompliano quoting Brene Brown on normalcy
dek: Amit finds it beautiful and lives it: a blocked nostril, or a walk he couldn't take before his heart attack, reminds him to value normalcy.
more: Amit finds it beautiful and lives it: a blocked nostril, or a walk he couldn't take before his heart attack, reminds him to value normalcy.
The quote: we chase extraordinary moments instead of being grateful for ordinary ones, until hard things happen and all we beg for is a normal moment.

head: John Collison on passion
dek: It blew Amit's mind. Almost everything good around us exists because someone tenaciously made it happen.
more: It blew Amit's mind. Almost everything good around us exists because someone tenaciously made it happen. He urges viewers to follow such accounts.
A screenshot of the Stripe co-founder's tweet, found via the Banger Archive account: 'The world is a museum of passion projects.'

head: Paul Graham on talent
dek: A sharp answer to today's xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment.
more: A sharp answer to today's xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment.
Graham's 'very simple math' tweet: with five percent of world population and evenly distributed ability, 95% of the best at anything are born abroad.

head: Dharmesh on imperfectionism
dek: Amit calls it almost the mantra of his life, the same thing he tells his writing students.
more: Amit calls it almost the mantra of his life, the same thing he tells his writing students.
The tweet: imperfectionists hit publish, ship product and iterate publicly; they dream big but iterate small.

head: Sahil Bloom on making it
dek: It resonated as a warning against the complacency that prosperity breeds.
more: It resonated as a warning against the complacency that prosperity breeds.
A mini-essay titled 'There is no such thing as making it', built on the gazelle-and-lion parable.

head: The Heart of Disruption (Episode 86, EIE)
dek: Background to his newfound gratitude for ordinary moments.
more: Background to his newfound gratitude for ordinary moments.
The episode where Amit's heart attack was discussed, referenced in his story about the walk he couldn't take.

head: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309, The Seen and the Unseen)
by: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye & Roshan Abbas
dek: The source of the anecdote behind Amit's worry about comfort and complacency.
more: The source of the anecdote behind Amit's worry about comfort and complacency.
The episode where Roshan Abbas distinguished FU money from FO money.

head: You can play a shoestring if you're sincere
dek: Coltrane's line, used by Amit against the 'I lack resources' excuse: no Fender, no iPhone, no studio.
more: Coltrane's line, used by Amit against the 'I lack resources' excuse: no Fender, no iPhone, no studio. Shakespeare found a quill. Ajay adds that you don't need an invitation to a Rockefeller castle in Italy or a hundred-dollar pen. You can read and think on the floor of an Indian second-class train.

head: Index every belief on a zero-to-one scale
dek: Ajay tags everything he believes with how sure he is, and with whether it came from authorities or from his own first-principles reasoning.
more: Ajay tags everything he believes with how sure he is, and with whether it came from authorities or from his own first-principles reasoning. With this habit, entering a new field feels natural: everything starts near zero and you're used to operating amid ambiguity. It also guards against getting 'drunk on that smug nature of confidence'.

head: Be comfortable with physical discomfort
dek: Ajay argues that people wedded to a minimum level of luxury end up pushing away great experiences.
more: Ajay argues that people wedded to a minimum level of luxury end up pushing away great experiences. Laugh at creature comforts, and accept dingy hotels, hard travel and bad food. Amit's caveat: real financial precarity imposes a cognitive burden, so learn to live frugally but don't romanticise worrying about rent.

head: Deep foundations make old fields portable
dek: Ajay is a self-confessed novelty seeker who recklessly starts new fields.
more: Ajay is a self-confessed novelty seeker who recklessly starts new fields. He isn't torn about leaving old ones, because once you deeply know a field's basic machinery, staying reasonably current is cheap. He hasn't tracked financial regulation for seven or eight years, including the post-SVB work on bank fragility under electronic payments, but a couple of papers would bring him up to speed.

head: Age trades horsepower for judgment
dek: Ajay cites research suggesting memory, intelligence, problem-solving and even creativity peak in youth and middle age.
more: Ajay cites research suggesting memory, intelligence, problem-solving and even creativity peak in youth and middle age. Age brings judgment and integration: the spidey sense that a pawn storm is coming on the board. So play the violin, solve maths problems and play chess when young, and invest in breadth and strategy when older.

head: Greatness is visible only in hindsight; track your energy instead
dek: Amit wonders whether greatness is a false target that may not coexist with happiness, and may arrive only by the way as you live (Annie Dillard).
more: Amit wonders whether greatness is a false target that may not coexist with happiness, and may arrive only by the way as you live (Annie Dillard). Ajay's practical answer: you can't see greatness while you're in the flow. The only observable signal is whether you are bringing full energy, interest and concentration to the work.

head: Don't fetishise the sprint: you need both din and thehrav
dek: You need the din of the world to collect dots, and stillness (thehrav, sukoon) to let them soak in.
more: You need the din of the world to collect dots, and stillness (thehrav, sukoon) to let them soak in. This echoes Cal Newport's Slow Productivity. Ajay adds that startup culture's adrenaline-laced sprint is not the model: Newton's and Einstein's were lives of quiet, extreme concentration and perfectionism.

head: Genius is a skin over the basics
dek: A crew member asked whether imitating a Messi or a Coltrane makes sense.
more: A crew member asked whether imitating a Messi or a Coltrane makes sense. Amit's answer: you can't copy the style. Messi starts with love for the game, and love can also be an act of intentionality. Then he drills the basics daily, and his genius sits on top like a skin. Coltrane knew music theory inside out before the Coltrane style emerged.

head: Productivity is more than tasks
dek: Tiago Forte splits productivity into task (efficiency), intellectual (learning), emotional (well-being) and social (relationships), and warns against neglecting the last three.
more: Tiago Forte splits productivity into task (efficiency), intellectual (learning), emotional (well-being) and social (relationships), and warns against neglecting the last three. Ajay resists the word altogether: we are here to create things that didn't exist. Amit prefers 'intentionality'. We are intentional about tasks but rarely about what matters.

head: Notice the ordinary: the 'last time' exercise
dek: Brene Brown observes that we chase extraordinary moments until hardship makes us beg for a normal one.
more: Brene Brown observes that we chase extraordinary moments until hardship makes us beg for a normal one. Ajay felt this when a broken ankle kept him in bed. A friend's exercise brings it alive: pause and imagine this is the last time you'll be with this person, or drink this hot chocolate. The moment changes colour.

head: Be intentional, not calculating, in relationships
dek: Ajay worries that intentionality in friendships sounds calculating. Amit's distinction is that caring effort isn't transactional.
more: Ajay worries that intentionality in friendships sounds calculating. Amit's distinction is that caring effort isn't transactional. A friend of theirs has two practices: meeting a new person every week and spending real time with them, and calling a loved one every single day. You can even calendarise care.

head: The world is a museum of passion projects
dek: John Collison notes that every hotel, park and railway exists because someone tenaciously made it happen.
more: John Collison notes that every hotel, park and railway exists because someone tenaciously made it happen. Ajay adds a Turkish proverb: a forest takes a hundred years to grow and one night to burn. Frontier economies like the US or Switzerland are centuries-old Rube Goldberg machines, so he shares the conservative instinct to avoid wrecking balls.

head: Talent is mostly born abroad, and migration is positive-sum
dek: Paul Graham's math means the best teams must be international. Ajay says Indian firms should hire explicitly multinational workforces, as Gukesh did and as university rankings reward through foreign faculty and students.
more: Paul Graham's math means the best teams must be international. Ajay says Indian firms should hire explicitly multinational workforces, as Gukesh did and as university rankings reward through foreign faculty and students. Amit adds that low-skilled migrants do jobs locals won't, and that slums are a city's entry point. High-skilled immigration builds clusters that attract more talent.

head: A culture of mavericks fattens the upper tail
dek: With 1.4 billion people, India has huge numbers of exceptional people, and so wastes many Ramanujans; that is why growth matters ('people are brains, not stomachs').
more: With 1.4 billion people, India has huge numbers of exceptional people, and so wastes many Ramanujans; that is why growth matters ('people are brains, not stomachs'). Ajay argues that variance is cultural as well as biological. A society that embraces dissidents and nonconformists widens its distribution and gets more outliers at the top, where all good things come from. An obedient, straight-laced culture gets a tight distribution.

head: Imperfectionism, done right
dek: Amit's mantra, echoing Dharmesh: you suck at anything when you start, so keep a bias for action, ship and iterate.
more: Amit's mantra, echoing Dharmesh: you suck at anything when you start, so keep a bias for action, ship and iterate. Yet perfection and production aren't opposites. Ajay's caveat: put in the volume, but ship your genuine best each time and pull the general principle out of every piece of feedback.

head: A tool, not a crutch: think above the API
dek: Amit's advice to writers asking about Grammarly, Hemingway or ChatGPT applies to mentors too.
more: Amit's advice to writers asking about Grammarly, Hemingway or ChatGPT applies to mentors too. People who mechanically apply corrections without asking why aren't doing higher-order thinking. They are exactly the people AI will replace, which may spur everyone to get more out of themselves.

head: Two stages of procrastination
dek: Ajay's stage one is really marination: he mulls a problem until the pieces click, then writes in a torrent.
more: Ajay's stage one is really marination: he mulls a problem until the pieces click, then writes in a torrent. Stage two is perfectionist terror of the idea that arrives too late. His fix borrows software's bug curve: plot new ideas per day after finishing, and ship once the count has held at zero for a couple of days.

head: Thin desires vs thick desires
dek: Via Luke Burgis and René Girard: thin desires are mimetic, like wanting a Mercedes because someone else has one, wanting to be Arnold, or wanting book prizes and lit-fest stages.
more: Via Luke Burgis and René Girard: thin desires are mimetic, like wanting a Mercedes because someone else has one, wanting to be Arnold, or wanting book prizes and lit-fest stages. Thick desires are intrinsic: loving the dull ache of lifting, or the work of filling a blank page. Ronnie Coleman's line captures the gap. A gym membership you never use is a thin desire.

head: Outwit the guy in your head, or find a purpose
dek: Bourdain's life was a series of stratagems to outwit the lazy guy in his head, and Amit's lazy guy is so big he dwarfs him (online chess, YouTube rabbit holes).
more: Bourdain's life was a series of stratagems to outwit the lazy guy in his head, and Amit's lazy guy is so big he dwarfs him (online chess, YouTube rabbit holes). Ajay has never felt that conflict: he calls himself a junkie who wakes up thirsting for more. His only problem is triage among too many wonderful things.

head: There's no 'making it', but the real enemy is short-termism
dek: Sahil Bloom's lion and gazelle must run every day, and Apple must keep making iPhones.
more: Sahil Bloom's lion and gazelle must run every day, and Apple must keep making iPhones. Amit warns that good times can get too good and breed complacency. Ajay finds that view too bleak. Most of us have space; the real choke points are playing short-term versus long-term, and chasing likes instead of genuine thought. Workaholics need more risk, not more grind.

head: Your future is constantly shrinking
dek: Gurwinder Bhogal's call to action, alongside Burkeman's Four Thousand Weeks.
more: Gurwinder Bhogal's call to action, alongside Burkeman's Four Thousand Weeks. Amit suggests an exercise for people in their thirties living away from their parents: optimistically estimate their remaining years and how often you'll visit each year. The total is startlingly small.

head: You only control you
dek: When people voice vague angst about the world, Ajay asks: so what are you going to do?
more: When people voice vague angst about the world, Ajay asks: so what are you going to do? Be selfish. You have tomorrow: what will you read, write, do, and who will you meet? Becoming a very good you creates positive externalities for everyone around you. Amit: nothing stands between you and your best version except your actions.

head: Zoom out, then act
dek: Frog's father promises that spring is around the corner. Sahil Bloom's zoom-out chart shows that daily noise becomes a rising line over decades.
more: Frog's father promises that spring is around the corner. Sahil Bloom's zoom-out chart shows that daily noise becomes a rising line over decades. Amit adds the catch: things only get better when you do things. Ajay agrees: whether you're crushed under an authoritarian regime in Russia or invaded in Ukraine, you still have to wake up and do things.

head: Ajay mocking writers who can't write a great book because they haven't been invited to…
more: Ajay mocking writers who can't write a great book because they haven't been invited to 'a Rockefeller Foundation castle in Italy' or don't own a hundred-dollar pen. You can sit on the floor of an Indian second-class train and think.

head: After Ajay says chess is for the young mind, Amit
more: After Ajay says chess is for the young mind, Amit: 'This is a comment on my chess addiction. I am deeply disappointed, Ajay Shah.' He then extends the old line: youth is wasted on the young, and 'wisdom is wasted on the old because what are we gonna do with it?'
Ajay's 'last time' exercise includes 'the last time I will drink hot chocolate with seven hundred grams of sugar'. Amit: 'This could be the last episode we record. Who knows? I mean I hope not.'

more: On Ajay's broken promise to watch one film a month: 'I'll watch movies thoroughly when you turn cartwheels on the floor.' Amit: 'Bro, if I try to turn cartwheels on the floor, I could get another heart attack. You can watch movies without any danger to your health. Kindly consider.'

more: Ajay recalls Roger Waters in The Final Cut looking back at his younger self: 'Does anybody love you? Or is it just a crazy dream?'

head: Five Biryanis Within Five Kilometres of Mangalore
dek: Globalisation shows up on a single street, not only in abstract trade statistics.
more: Amit and about fifteen friends went on a food trip through Mysore and Mangalore by bus. They planned their stops on an Excel sheet and ate around eight meals a day. In one area within roughly five kilometres of Mangalore, they found five different kinds of biryani. Each had arisen in its own way, and each was authentic to the place.

Globalisation shows up on a single street, not only in abstract trade statistics. What we call 'authentic' local food is the layered result of exchange, which is why Amit thinks the cultural case for trade may be the strongest one of all.
printed: Eight meals and a lesson in trade

head: Islam First Came to India Through Trade, Not Conquest
dek: The popular story of how a faith arrived can hide an older and gentler one.
more: Most people assume Islam arrived in India with invaders a few hundred years ago. Amit points out that well before that, during the Prophet Muhammad's own lifetime, Muslims came to the south of India, to Kerala as he recalls it, as traders. He uses this to show that trade routes carry religions and ideas along with goods.
The popular story of how a faith arrived can hide an older and gentler one. Trade has always carried ideas, and most cultural mixing has happened through voluntary exchange rather than force.

head: How India Missed the Bus That the East Asian Tigers Caught
dek: Comparative advantage only pays off if policy lets you use it. Starting with more advantages counts for little if you shut the door that lets you scale them.
more: Around 1950, India was doing well next to South Korea and Taiwan. It had democracy and many other advantages. India kept its markets closed, while the East Asian Tigers opened theirs, reached economies of scale, raised their standards by competing globally, and took off. Through the 1960s and 70s, India could have used its cheap labour to build mass manufacturing. Terrible labour and industrial laws held it back. Bangladesh is winning today because it embraced that path. India later found a niche in services mostly because many of its people were educated in English.
Comparative advantage only pays off if policy lets you use it. Starting with more advantages counts for little if you shut the door that lets you scale them.

head: The Rent-Seeking Entrepreneurs of Amit's Youth
dek: A closed economy does more than slow growth. It shapes how a whole generation thinks about making money.
more: Jagdish Bhagwati once observed that people's mentality in China is profit-seeking while in India it is rent-seeking. Amit says he and a former colleague of Ajay's once planned to write a piece on this. In his younger years, Amit was often shocked that people who wanted to start a business thought in exploitative terms. Their plan was to get rich through the state, either by becoming part of it or by becoming its crony, using tariffs on competitors or entry barriers.

A closed economy does more than slow growth. It shapes how a whole generation thinks about making money. When the path to prosperity runs through the state, ambitious people learn to capture the state instead of serving customers.

head: It Wasn't the Crash. It Was the Tariffs.
dek: The policy response, not the original shock, turned a downturn into a decade-long catastrophe.
more: Popular memory dates the Great Depression to the October 1929 stock market crash. Drawing on Thomas Sowell, Amit tells it differently. Unemployment peaked at 9% a couple of months after the crash and then fell to 6.3% by June 1930. President Hoover then tried to lift employment by protecting domestic manufacturers with the Smoot-Hawley tariffs. Other countries retaliated and a trade war followed. Within five months US unemployment was back above 10%, and it stayed in double digits for the rest of the 1930s. Sowell, now 94, recently gave an interview saying Trump's tariffs are the same thing happening again.
The policy response, not the original shock, turned a downturn into a decade-long catastrophe. The tariff logic of the 1930s is the same zero-sum logic driving tariff talk today.

head: The Line From Smoot-Hawley to the Second World War
dek: Trade is more than a route to prosperity. It is the peaceful alternative to taking things by force.
more: Ajay recalls that global trade fell by about 66% after Smoot-Hawley. He traces two routes from there to war. First, economic hardship hollows out the political centre and boosts extremists, whether national socialist or communist. Second, if you cannot buy what you need, such as rare earths from Africa, you start thinking about marching in and taking it. After 1930 came the Japanese invasion of 1931, Italy's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935, and Germany's push for Lebensraum. Mein Kampf predates the tariffs, but Smoot-Hawley strengthened the German belief that the global trading system was British-controlled, especially after the British blockade in World War I, and that Germany must conquer land to prosper.
Trade is more than a route to prosperity. It is the peaceful alternative to taking things by force. Shut down voluntary exchange and you push nations back toward conquest.
printed: From tariff wall to world war

head: The 1909 Book That Declared War Impossible
dek: Being right about the benefits of trade is not the same as those benefits being secure.
more: The first wave of globalisation in the 19th century, built on the ideas of Smith and Ricardo, felt so settled that Norman Angell argued in The Great Illusion (1909) that war was now impossible because nations were too intertwined by trade. The next decade brought World War I. Keynes later described the lost world in The Economic Consequences of the Peace: in 1914 a Londoner could order goods from across the earth by telephone over his morning tea. The war left people cynical and led to disastrous decades that followed.
Being right about the benefits of trade is not the same as those benefits being secure. Amit admits that he and Ajay also 'drank the Kool-Aid' of believing the globalised order was a done deal.

head: Basic Economics
dek: A fantastic book for learning the basic concepts in simple language. Amit calls Sowell a towering thinker of the 20th century and says you should read all his books.
more: A fantastic book for learning the basic concepts in simple language. Amit calls Sowell a towering thinker of the 20th century and says you should read all his books.
First of Amit's closing recommendations, offered so the episode works as a long-term resource.

more: Part of Amit's advice to read everything Sowell has written.

more: One of Amit's core picks for building first-principles economic intuition.

dek: His single go-to book on the subject. Bhagwati's work also underlies the episode's elite-conflict and rent-seeking arguments.
more: His single go-to book on the subject. Bhagwati's work also underlies the episode's elite-conflict and rent-seeking arguments.
Ajay's pick when Amit hands over to him at the end: 'The globalization book by Jagdish Bhagwati. That's the one.'

dek: Ajay says Smith is to economics what Darwin is to biology. The first grand ideas and deep intuitions of economics are all here, and it is 'eerie' how much Smith got right.
more: Ajay says Smith is to economics what Darwin is to biology. The first grand ideas and deep intuitions of economics are all here, and it is 'eerie' how much Smith got right.

more: A way into Smith's moral philosophy for anyone who wants more than his economics.
Amit mentions he has an episode on The Theory of Moral Sentiments with Russ Roberts.

head: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
dek: A vivid record of how globalised the pre-WWI world was, and of what war destroyed.
more: A vivid record of how globalised the pre-WWI world was, and of what war destroyed.
Amit calls it Keynes's 'great book' and reads its famous passage about the 1914 Londoner ordering the world's goods over morning tea.

head: The Great Illusion
dek: Worth knowing as a cautionary tale. Trade's incentives are real, but treating them as a guarantee is a mistake.
more: Worth knowing as a cautionary tale. Trade's incentives are real, but treating them as a guarantee is a mistake.
Cited as the 1909 book arguing that trade had made war impossible, a decade before World War I.

dek: Sowell, who wrote about Smoot-Hawley decades ago, says today's tariffs are the same thing happening again.
more: Sowell, who wrote about Smoot-Hawley decades ago, says today's tariffs are the same thing happening again.
Amit notes that Sowell, now 94, recently gave an interview about Trump's tariffs.

head: I, Pencil
dek: Told in the first person by a pencil, it shows how people in many countries cooperate to make a simple product, coordinated only by prices and not by any central planner.
more: Told in the first person by a pencil, it shows how people in many countries cooperate to make a simple product, coordinated only by prices and not by any central planner.

dek: Harford runs a permanent trade deficit with his babysitter and both are better off, which shows why the word 'deficit' misleads.
more: Harford runs a permanent trade deficit with his babysitter and both are better off, which shows why the word 'deficit' misleads.

dek: It tells the story of India opening up to freedom and economic success, which is closely tied to opening up to globalisation.
more: It tells the story of India opening up to freedom and economic success, which is closely tied to opening up to globalisation.
Ajay points listeners to it after the growth discussion.

head: How to Do Development (Episode 57, Everything is Everything)
dek: Covers Pritchett's finding that per capita GDP drives every human welfare indicator, which is the moral case for growth.
more: Covers Pritchett's finding that per capita GDP drives every human welfare indicator, which is the moral case for growth.
Amit's 'great episode on development', where they discuss Lant Pritchett's paper.

head: Nothing is Indian! Everything is Indian! (Episode 12, Everything is Everything)
dek: Argues that everything we consider quintessentially Indian, from clothes to food to languages, came from elsewhere and blended together.
more: Argues that everything we consider quintessentially Indian, from clothes to food to languages, came from elsewhere and blended together.
Cited in the cultural argument for globalisation.

head: The Indianness of Indian Food (Episode 95, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Another deep dive into how Indian cuisine is built from imported ingredients such as the potato, the chilli and the guava.
more: Another deep dive into how Indian cuisine is built from imported ingredients such as the potato, the chilli and the guava.
Mentioned alongside the Pushpesh Pant episode.

head: The Freedom Argument: Who Is the State to Stop a Voluntary Exchange?
dek: The first reason trade is good is moral, not economic.
more: The first reason trade is good is moral, not economic. If two people want to trade voluntarily and no one else's rights are infringed, nobody has any business stopping them, and it shouldn't matter whether one is in India and the other in Washington, DC. Amit notes that ideologies are inconsistent here: some defend freedom in the bedroom but not the marketplace, others the reverse. Ajay says calling Pune or Mozambique to make a deal is the same act, and this point should be made first.

head: Trade Is Positive-Sum: The Double Thank You Moment
dek: When you buy coffee, you value the coffee more than the money and the seller values the money more than the coffee, so both say thank you.
more: When you buy coffee, you value the coffee more than the money and the seller values the money more than the coffee, so both say thank you. Tennis is zero-sum, but voluntary exchange is not, whether between individuals, firms or countries. The key word is voluntary, so colonial extraction does not count as free trade. Every trade that is blocked destroys value that would otherwise have existed.
printed: Who is the state to stop us?

head: Comparative Advantage: Ratios, Not Being the Best
dek: David Ricardo's example: even if Portugal is better than England at making both cloth and wine, both countries end up with more of each if each specialises and trades.
more: David Ricardo's example: even if Portugal is better than England at making both cloth and wine, both countries end up with more of each if each specialises and trades. Amit's version: even if Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma were the best drivers in Bombay, they should hire a chauffeur and spend their minds on cricket and acting. Ajay's takeaway for India is that being poor or not world-class at anything is no barrier to gaining from trade, because what matters is the ratio of relative superiority.

head: The Self-Sufficiency Fallacy
dek: Imagine growing, cooking and cleaning everything for yourself. Anyone who truly tries to be self-sufficient is instantly poor.
more: Imagine growing, cooking and cleaning everything for yourself. Anyone who truly tries to be self-sufficient is instantly poor. We prosper by specialising and buying everything else: Amit podcasts and buys his cauliflower. The same applies to nations, so 'our country should make everything' rhetoric gets prosperity backwards. A country's advantage often comes from its endowments, such as cheap labour or an English-educated workforce.

head: Scale and Hyper-Specialisation
dek: A market of ten shirt buyers doesn't justify a machine. A global market justifies investment that raises quality and lowers cost.
more: A market of ten shirt buyers doesn't justify a machine. A global market justifies investment that raises quality and lowers cost. A phone can be designed in Silicon Valley, use African rare earths, Taiwanese chips and Chinese assembly, much like Leonard Read's pencil, coordinated only by prices. The world effectively outsources aircraft to two competitors, Boeing and Airbus. Ajay adds the firm's view: you max out in one country, and the world is the next ladder, which is why the biggest corporations are multinationals.

head: Growth Is Contagious, and Poverty Is Not Inequality
dek: In a globalised world, one country's rising middle class becomes another's export market: China buys German machines and Australian minerals.
more: In a globalised world, one country's rising middle class becomes another's export market: China buys German machines and Australian minerals.
