A World Bank study found free trade cut poverty and reduced global inequality. Global extreme poverty fell from 35% to 10% between 1988 and 2013. Within India after 1991, inequality rose but poverty fell. Amit's test question: would you rather be poor in Bangladesh or the USA? People pick the USA, which has more inequality but less poverty.

head: Economic Growth Is the Whole Game
dek: Lant Pritchett's paper, discussed in an earlier episode, shows that per capita GDP is the key factor behind every human welfare indicator, from health onwards.
more: Lant Pritchett's paper, discussed in an earlier episode, shows that per capita GDP is the key factor behind every human welfare indicator, from health onwards. Amit puts it as roughly 99% versus 1% for welfare redistribution. Their friend Nitin Pai estimated that each 1% of GDP growth lifts a million people out of poverty, a figure he later revised to two million. For Amit this makes growth a moral matter, not something for elites to debate abstractly.

head: Every Culture Is a Khichri
dek: Nothing we treasure as 'ours' is purely home-grown. The Silk Road carried religions and ideas along with goods.
more: Nothing we treasure as 'ours' is purely home-grown. The Silk Road carried religions and ideas along with goods. The Columbian Exchange brought India the potato, the chilli and the guava. Stitched clothing came from outside. Globalisation is the source of culture, not a threat to it. Ajay's alternative picture is a shallow North Korea behind a high wall.

head: Openness Reduces Elite Conflict
dek: Ajay builds on Bhagwati, Srinivasan and Krueger. In a closed economy, elites see a fixed pie and fight wastefully over slices, which raises conflict in the country.
more: Ajay builds on Bhagwati, Srinivasan and Krueger. In a closed economy, elites see a fixed pie and fight wastefully over slices, which raises conflict in the country. Once the arena becomes the world market, elites find common ground in policies that make the country strong and competitive, so conflict falls and better policy gets done.

head: Profit-Seeking vs Rent-Seeking
dek: Profit-seeking means making money by giving others value in a double-thank-you exchange.
more: Profit-seeking means making money by giving others value in a double-thank-you exchange. Rent-seeking means extracting money, for example through state monopolies, cronyism, tariffs on competitors or entry barriers. Bhagwati saw China as profit-seeking and India as rent-seeking. Amit argues that decades of a closed economy produced this, because the levers of prosperity sat with the state.

head: Mercantilism vs 'The Real Fun Is in Importing'
dek: From the 16th to the 18th century, kings saw trade as zero-sum: exports bring in gold, imports send it out, so aim for a surplus.
more: From the 16th to the 18th century, kings saw trade as zero-sum: exports bring in gold, imports send it out, so aim for a surplus. Alexander Hamilton's 'infant industry' tariffs came from the same thinking, and Trump's balance-sheet view of trade echoes it. Smith and Ricardo flipped the frame. We export only to earn the means to import the world's goods. Ajay's 1,100-rupee Casio watch exists only because he can buy from overseas. The export obsession serves governments, not citizens.

head: Trade Is the Peaceful Alternative to War
dek: War is negative-sum and trade is positive-sum. When trade breaks down, two things follow.
more: War is negative-sum and trade is positive-sum. When trade breaks down, two things follow. Hardship erodes the political centre and feeds extremists, and nations that cannot buy what they need start thinking about seizing it. Ajay's rare-earths example: if trade fails, someone decides to 'bloody march into Africa' and take them. Defending trade also means defending peace.

head: Your Own Consumers Pay the Tariff, Twice
dek: A 100-rupee import with a 10% tariff sells for 110, and the domestic buyer pays the difference, not the foreign exporter.
more: A 100-rupee import with a 10% tariff sells for 110, and the domestic buyer pays the difference, not the foreign exporter. It goes further: if a 500-rupee foreign shirt becomes 550, Indian shirt-makers raise their prices to 550 as well. Consumers pay more for foreign and domestic goods alike.

head: Varma's Law
dek: Amit's half-joking law: every interference in free markets moves wealth from the poor to the rich.
more: Amit's half-joking law: every interference in free markets moves wealth from the poor to the rich. Suppose a Chinese widget costs 100 rupees and the Indian one 110. A 20-rupee tariff forces buyers onto the 110-rupee local version. That extra 10 rupees, taken from many consumers, would otherwise have funded other double-thank-you transactions and jobs. Instead it goes to one protected interest group. Tariffs are always a tax on your own poor.

head: Reciprocal Tariffs Are Self-Harm
dek: Since a tariff taxes your own citizens, 'retaliating' against another country's tariffs just hurts your own people a second time.
more: Since a tariff taxes your own citizens, 'retaliating' against another country's tariffs just hurts your own people a second time. Joan Robinson put it this way: other countries putting rocks in their harbours is no reason to put rocks in ours. Amit's position is that India should cut tariffs to zero on everything, whatever others do.

head: A Trade Deficit Is Accounting, Not a Loss
dek: In any market, the quantity bought equals the quantity sold after the fact.
more: In any market, the quantity bought equals the quantity sold after the fact. That holds for tomatoes and it holds for dollars. Capital flows (foreigners buying Indian shares, Indians buying London homes) and trade flows (importing microphones or Diet Coke) must sum to zero. An investment boom that brings capital in therefore requires a trade deficit. Amit adds that individuals trade, not countries, and Tim Harford runs a happy permanent deficit with his babysitter. Saying 'we made a loss trading with China' is a basic failure of economics.
printed: In the red with the babysitter

head: Tariffs Hurt the Industries They Claim to Protect
dek: Around half of US imports are inputs that local manufacturers use, so tariffs make domestic products more expensive too.
more: Around half of US imports are inputs that local manufacturers use, so tariffs make domestic products more expensive too. Sheltered firms compete for influence with the government instead of competing to serve customers, and they stagnate. Ajay's example is decades of the Ambassador and the Premier Padmini behind trade barriers, which did not produce a great Indian car industry.

head: The Goods-vs-Services Fetish
dek: Many people have an 'almost mystical attachment' to goods and manufacturing because you can touch a car.
more: Many people have an 'almost mystical attachment' to goods and manufacturing because you can touch a car. Trade figures often leave out services, and the current account is the right measure. Before fibre-optic cables, services couldn't be traded. Today they can, so barriers should go both ways: global law firms should be able to operate in India and Indian firms abroad. Growth is about productivity, whatever form the output takes.

head: 1991–2011: India's Best Era Was an Openness Story, Not a Party Story
dek: Ajay calls the fourfold GDP gain from 1991 to 2011 India's greatest economic achievement, and links it causally to trade barriers and capital controls steadily falling from 1991 to 2008.
more: Ajay calls the fourfold GDP gain from 1991 to 2011 India's greatest economic achievement, and links it causally to trade barriers and capital controls steadily falling from 1991 to 2008. Amit stresses that this cuts across parties. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh began it, the Vajpayee government advanced it, and later governments of both parties got many things wrong. He also says the import-substitution thinking of the Nehru era and today's self-reliance rhetoric share the same bad economics.

head: Amit takes over the comparative-advantage example from Ajay (
more: Amit takes over the comparative-advantage example from Ajay ('Let me break this down because you will find a way to mess it up'), then asks us to assume Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma are the best drivers in Bombay: 'Actually they're not. I am.'

head: Amit on camera craft
more: Amit on camera craft: 'You should look at the camera and say, Amit said, or you should look at me and say as you said, which would suitably flatter me that I'm being quoted to myself.'
Amit: 'bookmark this episode, but watch it now. Don't bookmark it and never watch it... Ajay, you do that a lot, don't you? You've bookmarked Perfect Days.'

head: Ajay on the claim that exporters pay tariffs
more: Ajay on the claim that exporters pay tariffs: 'I've never heard this idea in my whole life until one low IQ American president said it.'

head: Amit acting out the local manufacturer asking for protection
more: Amit acting out the local manufacturer asking for protection: 'See, I'm crying, I'm an infant, protect me.'

head: After Ajay argues goods and services are equal, Amit worries Trump might conclude
more: After Ajay argues goods and services are equal, Amit worries Trump might conclude: 'Why should I put tariffs only on goods? I will also put tariffs on services. And it will be your fault, Ajay.'

head: Amit on India's protectionism: what Nehru-ji did and Modi-ji is doing are much the same
more: Amit on India's protectionism: what Nehru-ji did and Modi-ji is doing are much the same, 'like one is a successor of the other in terms of bad economic thinking. In other ways they are very, very, very different.'

head: Amit's jab at critics of growth
more: Amit's jab at critics of growth: 'It is okay for elites to sit in their air conditioned rooms sipping their single malt to talk about neoliberal values', while growth is what puts food on people's plates.

head: The Economist was founded in 1843 to defend free trade and, as Amit notes…
more: The Economist was founded in 1843 to defend free trade and, as Amit notes, 'still calls itself a newspaper, by the way, for some reason.'

head: Ajay applies
more: Ajay applies 'An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind' to tit-for-tat trade wars.
Ajay: 'Adam Smith is to economics, what Charles Darwin is to biology.' Amit, who doesn't believe in the great man theory of history, makes an exception for Smith.

head: Counter-currents to free trade: Alexander Hamilton, the mercantilist who popularised
more: Counter-currents to free trade: Alexander Hamilton, the mercantilist who popularised 'infant industry' protection (against Jefferson, 'more of a freedom guy'), and Friedrich List's German economic nationalism.

head: Marx and Engels, in Amit's view, got the description right and the analysis wrong
more: Marx and Engels, in Amit's view, got the description right and the analysis wrong: 'national one-sidedness and narrow-mindedness become more and more impossible.'

head: From Peter Vanham's WEF piece on the Columbian Exchange
more: From Peter Vanham's WEF piece on the Columbian Exchange: 'Imagine Italian cuisine without tomatoes, which came from the new world, or Irish history without the potato.'

head: How Hoover's Tariff Blunder Handed Trump His Power
dek: An institution built to undo one tariff disaster became the lever for the next one.
more: Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley tariffs into law in 1930 even though thousands of economists and academics urged him not to. The US raised tariffs on the rich countries, they retaliated, and world trade fell 66%. Hoover lost the election. Roosevelt then asked Congress for presidential authority on trade, through the RTAA of 1934, so the president could negotiate reciprocal tariff cuts. That authority still exists today.

An institution built to undo one tariff disaster became the lever for the next one. Trump can impose sweeping tariffs on his own because of a power Congress handed the president to bring tariffs down. Amit adds that the trade war cut world trade by as much as you would expect from a world war.

head: Pakistan's Outrage Over India Being Its 'Most Favoured Nation'
dek: Technical jargon read through a nationalist lens can turn into political outrage.
more: In trade treaties, 'most favoured nation' (MFN) means that a tariff cut negotiated with one country is extended to every country. Ajay recalls amused commentary in the Pakistani press about hawks who were outraged that Pakistan treats India as its 'most favoured nation'. They read a piece of trade plumbing as a statement of friendship.
Technical jargon read through a nationalist lens can turn into political outrage. In trade, MFN is not a compliment. It is a non-discrimination rule that pushes every country's tariffs down.

head: Leopard Tanks to Ukraine, Machine Tools to Russia
dek: Trade and war are not two separate worlds. Once a real conflict exists, the free-trade logic of 'sell to whoever pays' collides with the logic of not arming your enemy.
more: Germany was sending Leopard 2 tanks to Ukraine. At the same time the question arose whether Germany should keep selling Russia the precision machine tools used to make the T-90 tanks on the other side. That contradiction made pure free-trade positions hard to hold and pushed governments toward export controls on military and dual-use goods.

Trade and war are not two separate worlds. Once a real conflict exists, the free-trade logic of 'sell to whoever pays' collides with the logic of not arming your enemy. Dual-use technology makes the line very messy.
printed: Tanks to Ukraine, tools to Russia

head: India's Pharma Industry and the Chinese API Lever
dek: Specialisation is the source of gains from trade, but a chokepoint held by a hostile state becomes a weapon.
more: India makes good-quality generic drugs for the world, but many of the raw ingredients (APIs) are imported from China. About 80% of the world's API capacity sits in China. Ideally an Indian firm like Dr. Reddy's buying from a Chinese supplier is a private-to-private deal. But Chinese firms are indirectly controlled by the Communist Party, so Ajay imagines a negotiation over Ladakh in which China threatens in private to cut off API exports. Ajay, Vijay Kelkar and co-authors have worked on how India could reduce this vulnerability with minimal, uncorrupt state intervention. He says the daft way would be to hand one company at a time a big contract.

Specialisation is the source of gains from trade, but a chokepoint held by a hostile state becomes a weapon. For every threat that is carried out publicly, there are likely many more made behind closed doors.

head: Rare Earths: A Monopoly Built on Tolerating Pollution
dek: A monopoly can come from being willing to absorb a cost that others refuse, not from innovation.
more: Rare-earth deposits are not unique to China; they exist everywhere. Producing them is painful and polluting, and China's lax pollution regulation let it become a global monopoly. China blocked rare-earth sales to Japan around 2011. Days before this recording it announced a blockage of sales, which Ajay also describes as aimed at the United States. The processing is not inherently hard, but the knowledge would take years to rebuild elsewhere.
A monopoly can come from being willing to absorb a cost that others refuse, not from innovation. Once the know-how is gone from the rest of the world, the holder gains leverage that lasts for years.

head: The Grapes of Nashik and Europe's Pesticide Rules
dek: A strict standard is not automatically a trade barrier. If French and Indian growers face the same rule, it is a level playing field, and a democracy has the right to choose its own safety standards.
more: On a visit to Sahyadri Farms, a farmer-connected organisation in Nashik, Ajay and Amit learned that grapes exported to Europe face strict phytosanitary rules. For example, no pesticides can be used for two months before harvest. Indian exporters have had to build entire supply chains around such practices.
A strict standard is not automatically a trade barrier. If French and Indian growers face the same rule, it is a level playing field, and a democracy has the right to choose its own safety standards.
printed: Not every rule is a wall

head: Apple's iPhone Airlift Out of Madras
dek: It is a vivid picture of the uncertainty shock. Supply chains optimised over decades get rewired overnight, and large companies spend effort routing around policy whims instead of producing.
more: As the Trump tariffs on China landed, newspapers reported that Apple was filling planes 'to the gills' with iPhones and flying them from Madras to America. Shipping from China to America no longer made sense under the new tariffs.
It is a vivid picture of the uncertainty shock. Supply chains optimised over decades get rewired overnight, and large companies spend effort routing around policy whims instead of producing.
printed: Packed to the gills in Madras

head: India's Olive Branch: Dropping the Google Tax
dek: A smart negotiating move is to give up your own bad policies as concessions.
more: When the tariff trouble began, the Indian government on its own initiative removed the 6% 'equalisation levy', popularly called the Google tax. In effect it was saying it understood that such measures are not considered good behaviour in the new world of trade.
A smart negotiating move is to give up your own bad policies as concessions. They cost the country nothing it should value, and they build goodwill.

head: When a Used Car Cost More Than a New One
dek: People normalise the costs of protectionism and stop seeing them. Recalling how absurd the licence-raj world was shows how much hidden cost today's tariffs still impose.
more: Amit recalls 1980s India, when a second-hand car cost more than a new one because a new car took seven years to be delivered. A telephone connection also meant a seven-year wait, and everything was expensive even for the elite. The 1991 opening-up ended that world. He argues that removing today's tariffs and non-tariff barriers would make cars about 30% cheaper: the car he bought for ten lakhs would have cost seven.
People normalise the costs of protectionism and stop seeing them. Recalling how absurd the licence-raj world was shows how much hidden cost today's tariffs still impose.

head: Weeping Over Adolescence in Business Class
dek: Great craft in a mainstream, hugely popular show can still overwhelm you.
more: Flying back from Spain on Etihad business class, Amit watched Adolescence on his iPad. He first suspected the one-take-per-episode format was a gimmick, but within minutes decided it was essential, because with no cuts, your attention never cuts either. By the first half of the fourth episode he was weeping on the flight, while nearby passengers looked at him as if to ask how one of the luckiest people around could be crying.
Great craft in a mainstream, hugely popular show can still overwhelm you. Amit uses this as evidence against the idea that popular culture is in decline.

head: Kemi Badenoch Grilled for Not Watching Netflix
dek: A work of art turns into a political litmus test, wielded by people who have not engaged with it.
more: Through a tweet by Andrew Doyle, Amit found a British breakfast-TV interview in which two anchors harangued opposition leader Kemi Badenoch for not having watched Adolescence. She said she had been travelling the country talking to parents and children, and that understanding what is wrong with hospitals does not require watching Casualty. The female anchor called the show 'a great documentary', though it is fiction, which suggested the anchors had not watched it either.
A work of art turns into a political litmus test, wielded by people who have not engaged with it. Amit argues the show is about the human condition, not any political agenda.

head: Andrew Doyle's tweet on Kemi Badenoch's grilling
dek: Amit likes Doyle a lot and calls him a great free-speech thinker. The clip shows how a show gets turned into a political cudgel.
more: Amit likes Doyle a lot and calls him a great free-speech thinker. The clip shows how a show gets turned into a political cudgel.
The tweet through which Amit discovered the breakfast-TV interview in which Kemi Badenoch was harangued for not watching Adolescence.

head: How to Do Development (Episode 57 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It develops the idea that development is learning by doing, not following a manual.
more: It develops the idea that development is learning by doing, not following a manual.
Invoked by Ajay ('like we say in the development episode') when explaining why lost manufacturing know-how is hard to rebuild.

head: The Shopkeeper vs the Warrior
dek: Ajay frames the trade debate as a choice between two outlooks. The martial outlook grabs land; the shopkeeper's outlook trades its way to whatever it wants.
more: Ajay frames the trade debate as a choice between two outlooks. The martial outlook grabs land; the shopkeeper's outlook trades its way to whatever it wants. When countries are shut out of trade, as after Smoot-Hawley, they turn to armies and territory, from Japan's 1931 invasion to Italy's conquest of Ethiopia and German Lebensraum. Amit adds that this is not a binary: the positive-sum world of trade will always coexist with, and be shaped by, the negative-sum world of war.

head: Reciprocity Plus the MFN Kicker
dek: Britain grew rich by cutting tariffs unilaterally, which is pure Ricardian logic.
more: Britain grew rich by cutting tariffs unilaterally, which is pure Ricardian logic. The US political bargain of 1934 was different: the president could cut tariffs when other countries cut theirs too. Built into that law was most-favoured-nation treatment, meaning a cut negotiated with one country applies to all. That avoids a messy patchwork of country-specific rates and goods being routed through third countries, and it creates a steady bias toward lower tariffs everywhere. Amit's gloss is that you treat everyone the way you treat your best friend.

head: Why the GATT Worked, and Why It Stopped Working
dek: The GATT succeeded because its designers left out agriculture to avoid fights with small but lethal farm lobbies, trade in 1945 meant manufactured goods, global corporations lobbied for liberalisation, and the West used military and aid leverage to bring spoilers like India along.
more: The GATT succeeded because its designers left out agriculture to avoid fights with small but lethal farm lobbies, trade in 1945 meant manufactured goods, global corporations lobbied for liberalisation, and the West used military and aid leverage to bring spoilers like India along. Each piece later broke down. Services are now about 67% of GDP in the median country (71.5% for the OECD) and barely covered by trade rules. Corporations lost interest once their goods agenda was done. Elites assumed the battle was won. After the Cold War the West cut its military, foreign-policy and aid budgets, losing leverage in a WTO where any 'dinky country' can veto. Ajay would even trade away some manufacturing for sweeping free trade in services.
printed: A club that ran out of steam

head: The Gain From Trade Is the Imports
dek: The benefit of trade is being able to buy cheap things from abroad, not exporting.
more: The benefit of trade is being able to buy cheap things from abroad, not exporting. India sells software and uses the money to buy cheap solar panels; if the Chinese state subsidises those panels, that is a gift to Indian consumers. Amit pushes this through Smith and Ricardo: when cheap goods close local factories, consumers save money, and that money creates economic activity and jobs elsewhere. If someone subsidises us, we should take the subsidy with open arms.

head: Four Reasons Even a Free Trader Worries
dek: Ajay's four doubts about free trade are these. (1) Military conflict: selling capabilities to an enemy, and losing your own industrial base. (2) Economic statecraft: specialisation creates chokepoints, such as APIs and rare earths, that a hostile state can squeeze. (3) Hidden subsidies plus economies of scale: cheap directed credit, expropriated land and subsidised inputs let Chinese firms dominate products like polysilicon and solar panels and set them up for monopoly pricing later. (4) Macroeconomic dumping: a large economy that answers its own debt overhang by flooding the world with cheap goods exports its unemployment.
more: Ajay's four doubts about free trade are these. (1) Military conflict: selling capabilities to an enemy, and losing your own industrial base. (2) Economic statecraft: specialisation creates chokepoints, such as APIs and rare earths, that a hostile state can squeeze. (3) Hidden subsidies plus economies of scale: cheap directed credit, expropriated land and subsidised inputs let Chinese firms dominate products like polysilicon and solar panels and set them up for monopoly pricing later. (4) Macroeconomic dumping: a large economy that answers its own debt overhang by flooding the world with cheap goods exports its unemployment. He also sets himself a rule: anyone raising such worries must spell out concrete scenarios of harm.

head: Military Strength Lives in the Civilian Economy
dek: Modern defence economics stresses the military industrial base. A country with a commercial shipbuilding industry can repurpose it to build warships; one without it cannot.
more: Modern defence economics stresses the military industrial base. A country with a commercial shipbuilding industry can repurpose it to build warships; one without it cannot. In World War II the US was 'the arsenal of democracy' because it was the world's greatest manufacturer, but that capability now sits in China. Requiring 'Made in India' for military procurement does not work if the wider private economy lacks the skills.

head: Status-Quo Powers vs Revisionist Powers
dek: Free trade assumes partners who will not turn dependence into a weapon.
more: Free trade assumes partners who will not turn dependence into a weapon. Depending on Britain for APIs would be fine, because Britain is a status-quo power with a good relationship with India. China is a one-party state, a 'party that has a country', with a century-of-humiliation grievance and wolf-warrior diplomacy. Ajay names China and Russia as revisionist powers that are hostile to the liberal order. The ideal is a system of alliances in which countries credibly promise never to do such things to each other, so that trade can work as Ricardo described.

head: Manufacturing Know-How Is Hard to Rebuild
dek: Complex manufacturing is not a book you can copy. Ajay calls this learning by doing that takes years to build.
more: Complex manufacturing is not a book you can copy. Ajay calls this learning by doing that takes years to build. When subsidised Chinese firms hollow out production elsewhere, the knowledge disappears, and a supply cutoff becomes very disruptive. He also calls this a breach of faith: China was admitted to the WTO on the understanding it would play by the rules, and its hidden subsidies have drained political support for free trade among lawmakers and academics.

head: Monopoly Recoupment vs Contestability
dek: Textbooks say a firm cuts prices to kill rivals and then raises them once it has a monopoly.
more: Textbooks say a firm cuts prices to kill rivals and then raises them once it has a monopoly. Amit calls this rubbish: Amazon, Jio and cell-phone firms never did it, and it only happens with state coercion. Ajay reframes the question as how contestable the industry is, not whether a monopoly exists. If Amazon overcharged for hand towels, Myntra would step in. Rebuilding a complex manufacturing supply chain would take five to ten years. He adds that a $19-trillion single-party state with no checks and balances is a new situation. The two did not resolve this and suggested a future episode on monopolies.

head: Not Every Regulation Is a Trade Barrier
dek: Lighthizer counts strict standards, low taxes and weak regulation as unfair trade practices.
more: Lighthizer counts strict standards, low taxes and weak regulation as unfair trade practices. Ajay separates the two cases. Rules that apply equally to local and foreign firms, like GDPR or Europe's rules for grapes, are a democracy's birthright. Each country also chooses its own trade-off on local pollution, labour rules and taxation, so India's lower standards are not a subsidy. Carbon dioxide is the exception, because it is a global pollutant. Real non-tariff barriers do exist, such as India's data-localisation rules, which keep out good foreign cloud providers and raise costs for Indians. Some of the critique holds up, and some is mumbo jumbo.

head: Bilateral Trade Deficits Mean Nothing
dek: Trump treats a country's bilateral trade deficit as a measure of its non-tariff barriers, and his team even derived tariff rates from it.
more: Trump treats a country's bilateral trade deficit as a measure of its non-tariff barriers, and his team even derived tariff rates from it. The idea Ajay attributes to Amit makes the point: you run a deficit with your egg seller because you buy his eggs and he never buys your podcasting services. Specialisation naturally produces bilateral imbalances.

head: Uncertainty Destroys Capital
dek: The bigger harm is unpredictability, not any single tariff. If the US can do this, firms wonder what it might do next.
more: The bigger harm is unpredictability, not any single tariff. If the US can do this, firms wonder what it might do next. Every firm planning its next factory faces a headache, and the supply chains built over decades, with a factory in Madras, another in China, another in Argentina and distribution in America, are thrown into disarray. Amit adds that uncertainty distorts investment, planning and expansion.

head: Deep Integration: A WTO 2.0 With Open Architecture
dek: The way forward is a group of willing countries negotiating deep liberalisation that covers subsidies, directed banking, currency manipulation, IP theft, carbon and treatment of foreign firms, so tightly that cheating is hard.
more: The way forward is a group of willing countries negotiating deep liberalisation that covers subsidies, directed banking, currency manipulation, IP theft, carbon and treatment of foreign firms, so tightly that cheating is hard. The Trans-Pacific Partnership was conceived this way. Because the Chinese Communist Party is a concern and the US has lost capability, Ajay would leave both out and build the core from the rest of the OECD plus India. Others like Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or Pakistan could join later on take-it-or-leave-it terms.

head: India's Opportunity in the Tariff Crisis
dek: Ajay sees a deep India-US free trade agreement as feasible and urgent.
more: Ajay sees a deep India-US free trade agreement as feasible and urgent. Trump could claim he opened fifteen closed doors, India could say it secured a deal with a key partner, and similar deals could follow with the UK, EU and Japan. He praises the Union government's thinking here. Amit goes further and wants India to remove all tariffs unilaterally, for all countries. Ajay adds that non-tariff barriers must go too. The payoff would be cars about 30% cheaper and better, cheaper goods across the board.

head: Two Kinds of Industrialist
dek: Business can respond to liberalisation in two ways. It can ask for protection and rule a small, fixed pond, as the Bombay Club did when it backed state control of the Indian economy.
more: Business can respond to liberalisation in two ways. It can ask for protection and rule a small, fixed pond, as the Bombay Club did when it backed state control of the Indian economy. Or it can demand a global market and grow into great companies by competing, as firms in the developed world did when they lobbied for the GATT.

head: Progress Must Be Won Anew Each Generation
dek: Elites repeatedly assumed the argument was settled: the 1909 book that said trade had made war obsolete, Fukuyama's End of History, and the Washington Consensus formula for development.
more: Elites repeatedly assumed the argument was settled: the 1909 book that said trade had made war obsolete, Fukuyama's End of History, and the Washington Consensus formula for development. Popular opposition never went away. The case for open trade has to be argued again by every generation, and some generations did not try hard enough.

head: Steelmanning
dek: Steelmanning is the opposite of a straw man: you state your opponent's argument so well that they could have said it themselves, and only then disagree.
more: Steelmanning is the opposite of a straw man: you state your opponent's argument so well that they could have said it themselves, and only then disagree. Amit demonstrates it by restating Ajay's case about China before setting out his own dissent from Smith and Ricardo.

head: Engage With Culture Before Dismissing It
dek: Amit argues we are in a golden age of cinema and culture. Masterpieces like Adolescence are hugely popular, and films like Anora now win the Oscar.
more: Amit argues we are in a golden age of cinema and culture. Masterpieces like Adolescence are hugely popular, and films like Anora now win the Oscar. He challenges Ajay, who often says popular culture is dumbing down, to engage with it first, because culture is part of the humanities Ajay always urges people to study.

head: Amit on his bad hair day
more: Amit on his bad hair day: 'When I started The Seen and the Unseen... they would ask me why an audio podcast and I would say I have a face for audio. I have realized today... I also have a head for audio.' He also describes washing his hair and then working to make it look 'naturally uncombed'.

head: Amit on the tariff formula: one of the officials who published the math had an Indian name, and someone on Twitter joked
more: Amit on the tariff formula: one of the officials who published the math had an Indian name, and someone on Twitter joked, 'just imagine they hired the one Indian who doesn't know math.' Amit adds: 'If you're watching this, learn some math, bro. While you're working for Trump.'

head: Ajay, recalling Amit's favourite illustration of why bilateral deficits are meaningless
more: Ajay, recalling Amit's favourite illustration of why bilateral deficits are meaningless: 'I have a bilateral trade deficit with my local shop that sells me eggs because I only buy eggs from him and he never buys the services of a prominent podcaster.'

head: Ajay on the tariff rollout
more: Ajay on the tariff rollout: 'Into this came a stable genius called Donald Trump.' After Trump started exempting phones and CPUs, he says: 'this is everything but a stable genius.'

head: Ajay on the poor preparation behind the tariffs
more: Ajay on the poor preparation behind the tariffs: 'there is no tariff on Russia, and there are tariffs on countries that have no people.'

head: Ajay points out the irony: he had worried about the Chinese Communist Party cutting off goods to the world
more: Ajay points out the irony: he had worried about the Chinese Communist Party cutting off goods to the world, 'Well, here you've got the Republican Party blocking the sale of those Chinese things into America.'

head: After Ajay describes…
more: After Ajay describes 'cost complexity fear that is going to turn into an adverse global macroeconomic shock', Amit translates: 'You used a lot of jargon there. What you actually meant to say is that the shit has hit the fan.'

head: When Ajay calls 1989
more: When Ajay calls 1989 'one of the great achievements of human history', Amit quickly clarifies: 'You mean to say the collapse was one of the great achievements, in case anyone misunderstands not the USSR.' Ajay says it was one of the happiest moments of his life.

head: Amit on Indian politics
more: Amit on Indian politics: 'All parties are... left wing on economics, right wing on society, which is exactly the opposite of what it should be, because they're both anti-freedom.' He adds that Trump and Bernie Sanders are similar in their anti-free-trade thinking. Ajay says the whole left-right vocabulary has 'become a khichdi'.

head: Ajay on Japan's farm lobby: rice farmers are…
more: Ajay on Japan's farm lobby: rice farmers are 'a lethal lobby', about two percent of the population, in 'the country that is making semiconductors. But why pick fights?'

head: Amit weeping at Adolescence in business class while nearby passengers seemed to wonder how
more: Amit weeping at Adolescence in business class while nearby passengers seemed to wonder how 'one of the luckiest people ever' could be crying, adding: 'you can have all the champagne you want, though of course I never drink.'

head: Amit says Ajay agreed to watch an episode of Adolescence on his iPad after the shoot
more: Amit says Ajay agreed to watch an episode of Adolescence on his iPad after the shoot 'and then found a way to wriggle out', and demands 'a public commitment, Ajay Shah, that before the airing of this episode you will watch Adolescence.' Ajay commits only to episode one, and Amit concedes that four hours 'is a huge commitment.'

head: When Ajay says Keynes would be dreaming of a deep, open trade agreement, Amit quips…
more: When Ajay says Keynes would be dreaming of a deep, open trade agreement, Amit quips, 'In the long run, Keynes is right,' a twist on Keynes's own 'in the long run' line. Ajay sighs: 'Sadly, we don't have a John Maynard Keynes today.'

'Make love, not war': Ajay borrows the slogan for the shopkeeper's outlook. He contrasts it with Britain, the 'nation of shopkeepers' that built navies and a trading system, and says 'Britannia ruled the waves' because it unilaterally cut tariffs.
'The arsenal of democracy': the World War II phrase for America's manufacturing might, which Ajay says now sits in China.

head: Wolf-warrior diplomacy and China's
more: Wolf-warrior diplomacy and China's 'century of humiliation': Ajay's shorthand for the grievances that make China a revisionist power.

head: Joan Robinson's metaphor, invoked by Amit for unilateral free trade
more: Joan Robinson's metaphor, invoked by Amit for unilateral free trade: 'we've put rocks on our own coastline, remove the rocks.'

head: Martin Amis, as recalled by Amit
more: Martin Amis, as recalled by Amit: 'the worst kind of criticism is when you criticize an author for not writing the book you want.' Amit uses it against critics who fault Adolescence for centring the accused boy rather than the victim.

head: Self-teaching art history with ChatGPT Deep Research
dek: Preparing the context beforehand turns sightseeing into an education. Once you know an artist's journey, each work becomes a readable point on that path, and AI tools now make this kind of self-directed preparation easy.
more: On a 15-day vacation in Spain, walking about eight kilometres a day, Amit set out to give himself an art education. Before each museum (the Prado, the Reina Sofía and the Thyssen in Madrid, plus the Miró and Picasso museums in Barcelona and the Dali museum in Figueres), he asked ChatGPT Deep Research for a narrative art-history lesson. Each lesson included biographies, a guide to the paintings actually on display, and the order to see them in. He arrived with full context, skipped the audio guide, and by the end could roughly guess the year of a Velázquez painting from where it sat in the artist's evolution.

Preparing the context beforehand turns sightseeing into an education. Once you know an artist's journey, each work becomes a readable point on that path, and AI tools now make this kind of self-directed preparation easy.

head: Velázquez: few influences, one royal break
dek: Great careers are shaped by the economics of the time (patronage) and by deliberately seeking out influences (Rubens, Italy).
more: Velázquez was born in 1599 in a world with no cinema, few books and no way to see most of the art made before him. His teacher Pacheco was a mediocre realist who trained him in the classics. Even so, he painted Old Woman Frying Eggs at 19 and The Waterseller of Seville at 20, and came across Caravaggio's frail, flawed humans somewhere along the way. Artists then lived on royal patronage, not a market. In 1624 Philip IV summoned him, loved his portrait and decreed that only Velázquez would paint him, making him court painter at about 25. In 1628 he spent time with Rubens, and in 1629 he got leave to travel Italy for a year and a half, and those influences flowed into his work.
Great careers are shaped by the economics of the time (patronage) and by deliberately seeking out influences (Rubens, Italy). Reaching the top at 25 was only the start of his growth.

head: A dignified dwarf and a Pope who found his portrait 'too real'
dek: A painter is not a crude photographer. Mastery includes the nerve to show a deeper truth, even about the most powerful person in the room, rather than the flattering version the patron expects.
more: Court tradition painted the royal buffoons and dwarfs as caricatures. Velázquez instead painted one dwarf as a learned, thoughtful man. At 51, in 1650, he painted Pope Innocent, who hated the portrait because it was 'too real'. He also painted Aesop and Menippus as beggars, with faces so full of story that you can stand before them and imagine their lives.
A painter is not a crude photographer. Mastery includes the nerve to show a deeper truth, even about the most powerful person in the room, rather than the flattering version the patron expects.

head: Standing in front of Las Meninas
dek: This was Amit's first sign of the episode's thesis: a work that could not have been made at 20 or 25.
more: Velázquez painted Las Meninas in 1656, at 57. It is a huge canvas full of depth: a little girl and her attendants, an open door in the back, motivated lighting from the right, chiaroscuro, Velázquez painting himself at work, and a distant mirror showing the royal couple, who may be standing where the viewer stands. Amit calls it more enigmatic than the Mona Lisa. It went on to obsess Goya, who said Velázquez was the only artist worth imitating, and Picasso, who sat at the Prado copying Velázquez and Goya.
This was Amit's first sign of the episode's thesis: a work that could not have been made at 20 or 25. Here the technique has become second nature and the artist is playing at another level.

head: The Black Paintings: Goya's art for no one
dek: With no audience and no need for validation, Goya made work that anticipated Impressionism and Surrealism by decades.
more: Goya's war etchings, The Disasters of War (with plates like 'Bury them and stay silent'), stayed hidden for decades. In his late seventies, struggling with mortality, he painted fourteen very dark murals on the walls of a house called the Abode of the Deaf, named for its deaf previous owner. He never told anyone about them. They were found after his death, taken off the plaster with a newly invented technique, and now fill one room at the Prado. Amit spent half an hour there, nearly left the building, and went back. His favourite is the unexplained The Dog, and the famous Saturn Devouring His Son moved him least.

With no audience and no need for validation, Goya made work that anticipated Impressionism and Surrealism by decades. That is why he is called the last of the old masters and the first of the moderns.

head: Picasso's restless search for a new language
dek: Breakthrough work often looks like a joke to the best people of the previous wave.
more: At 15 and 16 Picasso was already a master of classical painting. As a teenager he hung out at Els Quatre Gats café in Barcelona, even designing its menu, and soon left for Paris and post-Impressionism. A close friend's suicide in 1901 sent him into the Blue Period, followed by the Rose Period. Then he and his café circle got tired of realism and every 'ism' that followed, with the camera now able to record what's in front of you. African tribal art led him to Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (c. 1907). Matisse, whom he admired, thought it was a prank. Braque understood it, and the two built Cubism together without rivalry, moving from analytic to synthetic Cubism. After World War One, Picasso returned to neoclassicism.
Breakthrough work often looks like a joke to the best people of the previous wave. Picasso would have been a legend if he had stopped here, but he refused to stay in the style that made him famous.

head: Picasso paints Las Meninas 58 times at 75
dek: An old master reinterpreting another old master's late masterpiece, in a spirit of play.
more: In 1957, at 75, Picasso went back to Las Meninas, which had overwhelmed him as a young man, and painted 58 versions of it. They hang in one room of the Picasso Museum in Barcelona, ordered by date. Large canvases are dated a day apart, and four on one wall were all made on the same day. Amit watched visitors rush past in the wrong direction, missing the progression entirely.
An old master reinterpreting another old master's late masterpiece, in a spirit of play. He wasn't trying to get it right, because there is no right; the work itself was his diary of growth.

head: Dylan, pericarditis and 'Not Dark Yet'
dek: A brush with mortality, survived, can produce work no younger version of the artist could have made.
more: At 56, Bob Dylan was hospitalised with pericarditis and thought he was dying. He survived and that year made Time Out of Mind, Amit's favourite Dylan album, which includes 'Not Dark Yet': 'Sometimes my burden is more than I can bear. It's not dark yet, but it's getting there.' It is a period, Amit notes, that the Dylan biopic won't show.
A brush with mortality, survived, can produce work no younger version of the artist could have made.

head: Henry Ford and the one-dollar bolt
dek: Mastery is mostly invisible. The simple gesture an old master makes contains decades of accumulated judgment.
more: Ford's factory broke down and his best engineers couldn't fix it, so he called in the foremost expert in the field, a man of about seventy. The expert walked around, put his ear to the machinery, tapped a bit, asked for a screwdriver, took out a bolt, adjusted something inside and put it back. Everything worked. His invoice (Amit puts it at around $80,000) itemised one dollar for the bolt and the rest for seventy years of learning what to look for. Amit tells it alongside Miró's line about a brushstroke that took a moment but years of reflection.
Mastery is mostly invisible. The simple gesture an old master makes contains decades of accumulated judgment.

head: Miró strips it down and paints for the future
dek: Late mastery means the confidence to strip things down and ignore the critics of the day, playing like a child while keeping full command of the craft.
more: Miró wanted to get past the clichés of depiction toward the essential, thinking in terms of poetry and music. After phases of Surrealism and symbols, late in life he returned to stark minimalism. Blue I, II and III, painted at 65, are a few marks on vast fields of colour, and one room at the Fundació Joan Miró holds canvases that are just a single line or a single blotch. Peers and critics said it was easy to parody. At 85 he answered that he was painting for the young of the future, and he kept working into his late eighties.
Late mastery means the confidence to strip things down and ignore the critics of the day, playing like a child while keeping full command of the craft.

head: Beethoven composing in silence
dek: Losing the noise of the outside world can turn an artist inward. If you can quieten the din inside too, what's left may be your deepest voice.
more: Beethoven went deaf at around the same time as Goya. His famous string quartets came near the end of his life, after he had been deaf for ten years or more, while Goya was producing his finest work.
Losing the noise of the outside world can turn an artist inward. If you can quieten the din inside too, what's left may be your deepest voice.

head: ChatGPT Deep Research
dek: It produced a narrative art-history lesson for each museum, with artist biographies, a guide to the actual paintings on display and an order to see them in.
more: It produced a narrative art-history lesson for each museum, with artist biographies, a guide to the actual paintings on display and an order to see them in. He arrived with full context and didn't need the audio guide.
Amit's method for preparing before each museum visit in Madrid and Barcelona.

head: The Black Paintings (especially The Dog)
dek: Amit calls the half hour he spent there an emotionally moving experience and went back for more.
more: Amit calls the half hour he spent there an emotionally moving experience and went back for more. The Dog, untitled and unexplained, gives a sense of profound desolation.
Fourteen murals Goya painted secretly on his walls in his late seventies, now in one room at the Prado.

head: Los Caprichos (especially The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters)
dek: They are dark, socially piercing work, and The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters is perhaps Amit's favourite single Goya work.
more: They are dark, socially piercing work, and The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters is perhaps Amit's favourite single Goya work.
Goya's satirical etchings, made a few years after he went deaf.

head: Picasso's Las Meninas series
dek: Seen in chronological order, they show an old master playing and growing day by day.
more: Seen in chronological order, they show an old master playing and growing day by day. Amit advises walking them in date order, unlike the visitors he saw rushing past backwards.
58 variations painted at 75, hung by date at the Picasso Museum in Barcelona.

head: Massacre in Korea
dek: Critics don't rate it, but Amit calls it a masterpiece. You can see Goya's influence 'stolen' and made Picasso's own.
more: Critics don't rate it, but Amit calls it a masterpiece. You can see Goya's influence 'stolen' and made Picasso's own.
Picasso's 1951 war painting, shown beside Goya's 1808 execution scene and Guernica.

head: Self Portrait Facing Death
dek: Amit finds it 'genius' and 'masterful', proof that Picasso's late work deserved more respect than the critics of the time gave it.
more: Amit finds it 'genius' and 'masterful', proof that Picasso's late work deserved more respect than the critics of the time gave it.
Shown at the end of the Picasso chapter as an example of his late work.

head: Salvador Dali's later work
dek: His later work 'hit me really hard', with an assurance that blew Amit away.
more: His later work 'hit me really hard', with an assurance that blew Amit away.
Dali didn't get a full chapter because the light was fading, so Amit urged viewers to explore him on their own.

head: The Push Man and Other Stories
dek: An example of a modern artist working in the same dark vein that Goya opened up centuries earlier.
more: An example of a modern artist working in the same dark vein that Goya opened up centuries earlier.
Goya's Disasters of War reminded Amit of Tatsumi, the Japanese founder of gekiga, whom he has recommended on the show before.

head: Time Out of Mind
dek: It is Amit's favourite Dylan album and a prime example of late-career mastery that the Dylan biopic skips.
more: It is Amit's favourite Dylan album and a prime example of late-career mastery that the Dylan biopic skips.
Made at 56, after Dylan thought he was dying of pericarditis.

head: Not Dark Yet
dek: 'It's not dark yet, but it's getting there' is an ageing artist facing mortality and turning it into art.
more: 'It's not dark yet, but it's getting there' is an ageing artist facing mortality and turning it into art.
The track from Time Out of Mind that 'blows me away'.

head: The Gate of Angels
dek: It is proof that great fiction can come very late in life.
more: It is proof that great fiction can come very late in life.
Amit's favourite novel by one of his favourite novelists, written in her mid-seventies.

head: Penelope Fitzgerald's novels
dek: She wrote her first novel after 60, so 'there is time for you to be a novelist'.
more: She wrote her first novel after 60, so 'there is time for you to be a novelist'.
Cited as an example of someone who started late rather than peaking young.

head: The Story of Art
dek: It goes painting by painting and gives you a sense of the whole world.
more: It goes painting by painting and gives you a sense of the whole world. Amit suggests reading 'a page a day' and says it 'will expand your brain'. A total must-read.
The first of four classic art books in the recommendations chapter.

head: The Spirit of Indian Painting
dek: It does for Indian art what Gombrich does for art in general. A classic and a masterpiece.
more: It does for Indian art what Gombrich does for art in general. A classic and a masterpiece.
The second must-read in the recommendations chapter.

head: Ways of Seeing
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece.
Recommended for a deeper dive.

head: The Shock of the New
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece too.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece too.
Recommended for a deeper dive, alongside Berger.

head: The light in winter: late mastery
dek: Velázquez, Goya, Picasso, Miró and Dali were all famous national icons by their twenties and thirties.
more: Velázquez, Goya, Picasso, Miró and Dali were all famous national icons by their twenties and thirties. Most people who peak like that coast on past glory and never risk annoying their fans. These five kept reinventing themselves, and the work that moved Amit most was made in their fifties to eighties. In Dylan's words, they stayed busy being born.

head: Craft comes first, art comes later
dek: A 20-year-old prodigy, like a teenage guitarist playing Eddie Van Halen licks, can have perfect craft.
more: A 20-year-old prodigy, like a teenage guitarist playing Eddie Van Halen licks, can have perfect craft. The art, though, arrives only once technique has become second nature and the artist can play at another level. Amit associates this with thehraav, a settledness that comes with age.

head: Context multiplies appreciation
dek: Nomsita asked why context matters if art should stand on its own. Amit's answer is that it should, but knowing the artist's journey and the ferment of the times greatly deepens what you see.
more: Nomsita asked why context matters if art should stand on its own. Amit's answer is that it should, but knowing the artist's journey and the ferment of the times greatly deepens what you see.

head: Good artists borrow, great artists steal
dek: Influence runs in a chain. Goya copied Velázquez, and Picasso sat in the Prado copying both.
more: Influence runs in a chain. Goya copied Velázquez, and Picasso sat in the Prado copying both. Goya's 1808 execution scene, with faceless soldiers, a lantern on the doomed man and a sense of movement, resurfaces in Guernica and Massacre in Korea. Stealing in art is not dishonourable; it means absorbing an influence until it is wholly yours.

head: Goya as a bridge between worlds
dek: Ajay recalls Keynes on Newton as both first of the scientists and last of the magicians.
more: Ajay recalls Keynes on Newton as both first of the scientists and last of the magicians. Amit sees Goya the same way: the last of the old masters and the first of the moderns, a hundred years ahead of his time. Like Istanbul straddling Asia and Europe, he connected two eras, and he gave later artists permission to think differently.

head: Freedom from validation
dek: Much late mastery was made with no audience in mind. Goya hid the Black Paintings, much of Picasso's late work was shown only after he died, and Miró painted 'for the young of the future'.
more: Much late mastery was made with no audience in mind. Goya hid the Black Paintings, much of Picasso's late work was shown only after he died, and Miró painted 'for the young of the future'. Once the need for approval is gone, the work becomes its own reason, and Amit finds that as moving as the art.

head: It takes a long time to grow young
dek: Amit reads Picasso's late quotes as a philosophy of ageing. You master technique early, and spend a lifetime learning to drop it and play freely like a child.
more: Amit reads Picasso's late quotes as a philosophy of ageing. You master technique early, and spend a lifetime learning to drop it and play freely like a child. Picasso said youth arrives at sixty and is 'too late', but with longer lifespans Amit says it no longer is.

head: The work as a diary: there is no 'right'
dek: Picasso saw his work as a diary and said he was always doing what he couldn't yet do in order to learn it.
more: Picasso saw his work as a diary and said he was always doing what he couldn't yet do in order to learn it. His 58 Las Meninas were an exploration of something with no single correct answer, which even Velázquez would have accepted.

head: The tyranny of the hit
dek: Once a song gets famous, the audience wants you frozen in it, and you spend the rest of your career covering your younger self.
more: Once a song gets famous, the audience wants you frozen in it, and you spend the rest of your career covering your younger self. When Dylan went electric, fans called him Judas because they had come for an old image of him, not for Dylan. Reinterpretation, like U2's re-recordings or Picasso's Las Meninas, is a way of resisting this.

head: Always work against yourself
dek: Miró's rule for staying alive as an artist is to keep tearing down your own past achievements rather than repeating them.
more: Miró's rule for staying alive as an artist is to keep tearing down your own past achievements rather than repeating them. It applies to any career in which success tempts you to coast.

head: Stop demanding explanations from art
dek: Miró thought in terms of music and poetry. A musician can't explain why a sequence of notes makes you cry, and you can't either.
more: Miró thought in terms of music and poetry. A musician can't explain why a sequence of notes makes you cry, and you can't either. Sometimes the right response is a visceral reaction, not an interpretation.

head: The stroke takes a moment, the idea takes years
dek: Miró's single lines and patches of colour look simple, but they rest on years of reflection, the same point as the Ford bolt story.
more: Miró's single lines and patches of colour look simple, but they rest on years of reflection, the same point as the Ford bolt story. Minimalism pays off when the essentials have been earned: in Miró's words, 'the slightest noise in silence becomes enormous.'

head: Success buys the time to keep producing
dek: Picasso is thought to have made more paintings than any other painter, partly because success let him keep painting.
more: Picasso is thought to have made more paintings than any other painter, partly because success let him keep painting. Unsuccessful painters eventually quit to do something else. The remarkable thing is that he used this privilege to keep changing rather than to stay comfortable.

head: It's never too late (could vs can)
dek: Some people master their craft young and keep going. Others, like Penelope Fitzgerald, who wrote her first novel after 60, start late.
more: Some people master their craft young and keep going. Others, like Penelope Fitzgerald, who wrote her first novel after 60, start late. Amit's message to a 45-year-old banker who could have been a writer or musician is that he still can, especially with longer lifespans.

head: Peak age depends on the field, and it is rising
dek: Ajay notes that finite, pattern-recognition fields like chess, mathematics and theoretical physics peak in the twenties to forties.
more: Ajay notes that finite, pattern-recognition fields like chess, mathematics and theoretical physics peak in the twenties to forties. Amit adds that chess, like a language, has to be learned young. Fields that need a complex understanding of the world peak later: economics in the forties to sixties, CEOs in their fifties, and the ideal startup founder at about 50. Fifty years of evidence shows all these peak ages rising.

head: Two forces behind later peaks: healthspan and broken institutions
dek: Ajay's first force is good news: longer healthspans let people keep accumulating knowledge across fields for longer.
more: Ajay's first force is good news: longer healthspans let people keep accumulating knowledge across fields for longer. His second is bad news: science has become a business of PhDs, publishing, journal politics and grants, and the age of a researcher's first grant, the point at which they become free, keeps rising while research produces less innovation per dollar. His ideal is to give brilliant young people autonomy early and also give them long healthspans.

head: What older minds are best at: integration
dek: The young do sharp, clean, black-and-white work like 'cute code'. With age comes interdisciplinarity: seeing the big picture, thinking strategically and intuiting how a complex world fits together.
more: The young do sharp, clean, black-and-white work like 'cute code'. With age comes interdisciplinarity: seeing the big picture, thinking strategically and intuiting how a complex world fits together. Ajay argues people should change the nature of their work as they age rather than compete at a young person's game.

head: Amit on the 27 Club fantasy
more: Amit on the 27 Club fantasy: 'when I was twenty one, I would fantasize that I will die when I'm twenty seven after achieving something great. I achieved nothing great, so I postponed it.'

head: Ajay's version: he and Susan had a plan to do cool things by 29 and then give up, with no life beyond 29.
more: Ajay's version: he and Susan had a plan to do cool things by 29 and then give up, with no life beyond 29. 'And twenty nine came along and like we settled into a marathon.' Amit, deadpan: 'You settled into a marathon.'

head: Kurt Cobain's
more: Kurt Cobain's 'it's better to burn out than to fade away', and the rock stars who died at 27 (Janis Joplin, Jimi Hendrix, Jim Morrison), with 33 as 'another age' alongside Jesus Christ. Amit uses them as the myth of youthful genius that the episode argues against.

head: Bob Dylan's line
more: Bob Dylan's line 'he not busy being born is busy dying' frames the whole episode: the Spanish masters 'were busy being born' into old age.

head: Dylan going electric and being branded Judas, used as the classic case of fans who come to see
more: Dylan going electric and being branded Judas, used as the classic case of fans who come to see 'the photograph that Dylan left of himself' rather than the man himself.

head: Amit says Las Meninas is…
more: Amit says Las Meninas is 'much more enigmatic than that famous enigmatic Mona Lisa'. He also borrows the film term 'motivated lighting', where light comes from a logical source, together with chiaroscuro to explain Velázquez's and Goya's use of light.

head: On Matisse taking Les Demoiselles d'Avignon for a prank: if he'd had a Garmin watch
more: On Matisse taking Les Demoiselles d'Avignon for a prank: if he'd had a Garmin watch, 'he would probably check it' to see whether it was April 1.

head: After telling how a friend of Picasso shot himself after trying to shoot the woman who spurned him
more: After telling how a friend of Picasso shot himself after trying to shoot the woman who spurned him: 'And Picasso later sleeps with the woman, I think, but leave that aside later, later, not then.'

head: On the Paris café circles
more: On the Paris café circles: 'Imagine at your local BKC Starbucks, the greatest minds of the age gathering together. But you don't know they're the greatest minds now. You'll find out much later.'

head: Seeing Guernica in person is like…
more: Seeing Guernica in person is like 'Lionel Messi is taking a penalty in a World Cup final', with a mass of people crowded in front of the giant canvas.

head: Ajay recalls John Maynard Keynes on Newton
more: Ajay recalls John Maynard Keynes on Newton: 'Newton was not just the first of the scientists, he was the last of the magicians.' Amit's own image for Goya as a bridge between worlds: 'Oh my fucking God he's Istanbul.'

head: Amit's rant at the critic who sneered at late Picasso
more: Amit's rant at the critic who sneered at late Picasso: 'Are you fucking crazy? You're a fucking art critic who went to a university and learned something from some academic fool. This is fucking Picasso. Respect what he is doing.'

head: On why late bloomers inspire him
more: On why late bloomers inspire him: 'this feeds into my Bengali procrastination. Because now I can think it I have wasted all my life so far, but I can waste twenty more years of it. Best work will happen at 70, 80.'

head: Dylan, hospitalised with pericarditis and sure he was dying
more: Dylan, hospitalised with pericarditis and sure he was dying: 'I think I'm going to see Elvis soon.'

head: The fading-light running gag in an episode called The Light in Winter. The Dali chapter is dropped
more: The fading-light running gag in an episode called The Light in Winter. The Dali chapter is dropped 'because I think we'll run out of light'. On cutting the Miró chapter short: 'Miró would not have approved. Miró would have said I have captured the fucking light.' And the sign-off: 'The light has gone. I don't even know if I'm visible anymore... Are we audible? We are audible.'
Ajay: 'Take us to Dali.' Amit: 'But when I was doing my notes on Dali, my laptop melted.'

head: After Ajay's riff on what older minds are good for, Amit
more: After Ajay's riff on what older minds are good for, Amit says: 'the wisdom that you just shared in the last five minutes could not have been given by the twenty-year-old Ajay Shah. Am I correct?' Ajay: 'Absolutely.'

head: Bhagwati, Yashwant Sinha and the Bharatanatyam Dancer
dek: A government earns legitimacy partly by visibly assembling competent teams.
more: Soon after Yashwant Sinha became Finance Minister, he shared a conference panel with Jagdish Bhagwati. Bhagwati told him that expertise really matters and that he should bring the best people in the country in as advisors. Sinha named a couple of people who were working with him. Bhagwati replied that if they were economists, then he was a Bharatanatyam dancer.

A government earns legitimacy partly by visibly assembling competent teams. Citizens and experts judge a regime by who it chooses to listen to, and advisors who are experts only in name drain its credibility.

head: The Policeman Beating the Beggar
dek: Our instincts quietly grant the state's agents a moral license we would never give a private person.
more: Amit retells a two-part thought experiment from Jason Brennan's book. If a random man on the street starts hitting a beggar, your first instinct is to step in. If the man doing the beating is a policeman with a lathi, most people stay away. The act and the victim are the same; only the uniform has changed. Amit says he does not want to take a position on what we should do.

Our instincts quietly grant the state's agents a moral license we would never give a private person. The uniform does real ethical work in our heads, which shows that legitimacy is a belief people hold, not just a legal status.

head: The Dictator Nehru Chose Not to Be
dek: Self-restraint is itself a source of power. Leaders who respect norms when they could break them earn a legitimacy that raw power cannot buy.
more: Ajay offers Jawaharlal Nehru as India's closest example of charismatic legitimacy: a loved and respected figure whose authority was moral and intellectual, not just electoral. Ajay points out that the young Indian state was limited and Nehru could have gone down the path of becoming one more third-world dictator. He did not, because there were norms and things that simply were not done.
Self-restraint is itself a source of power. Leaders who respect norms when they could break them earn a legitimacy that raw power cannot buy.

head: Politics as a Vocation
dek: Ajay calls it one of the great books of the world and says everybody should read it.
more: Ajay calls it one of the great books of the world and says everybody should read it.
Ajay's one recommendation for the episode. The whole discussion is built on Weber's definition of the state as a monopoly of violence and his three sources of legitimacy.

head: When All Else Fails: The Ethics of Resistance to State Injustice
dek: It poses the policeman-versus-stranger thought experiment, which forces you to ask why we grant state agents moral cover.
more: It poses the policeman-versus-stranger thought experiment, which forces you to ask why we grant state agents moral cover. Amit was blown away by the clarity of Brennan's thinking and says the book will make you think about state legitimacy and morality.
Amit's pick for the episode. Their mutual friend Abhinav Singh urged him to read it and to invite Brennan on The Seen and the Unseen.

head: Is India a Flailing State?
dek: It describes India as a state with a world-class brain of senior officials but with the nerves to the fingers cut, so nothing changes on the ground.
more: It describes India as a state with a world-class brain of senior officials but with the nerves to the fingers cut, so nothing changes on the ground. Ajay sees cynical, eye-rolling functionaries as one cause of that flailing.
Ajay cites it while explaining that legitimacy also has to exist in the minds of civil servants.

head: The Logic of Collective Action
dek: Olson's thinking shows why even a purely self-interested ruler gains from letting people prosper and from trying to be a legitimate bandit.
more: Olson's thinking shows why even a purely self-interested ruler gains from letting people prosper and from trying to be a legitimate bandit.
Linked in the show notes when Amit brings up Mancur Olson's roving and stationary bandits.

head: India Grows at Night
dek: Amit calls the title great because it captures how Indians live and thrive despite a dysfunctional, extractive state, which makes the question of its legitimacy almost beside the point.
more: Amit calls the title great because it captures how Indians live and thrive despite a dysfunctional, extractive state, which makes the question of its legitimacy almost beside the point.
Amit cites the title while arguing that most Indians are apathetic about the state.

head: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It explains that the state may intervene only in a limited set of circumstances, and that those conditions are necessary but not sufficient.
more: It explains that the state may intervene only in a limited set of circumstances, and that those conditions are necessary but not sufficient.
Listed in the intro as part of the show's framework for thinking about the Indian state.

head: Legitimacy: The Belief That the State Has a Right to Rule
dek: Weber defines the state by its monopoly of violence. Legitimacy is the partner idea: the belief among people that this monopoly has a right to rule over them.
more: Weber defines the state by its monopoly of violence. Legitimacy is the partner idea: the belief among people that this monopoly has a right to rule over them. Where it exists, citizens give the state the benefit of the doubt, and its laws turn into social norms that enforce themselves. Without it, the state has to reach into every home by force, which is ruinously expensive. Ajay adds that every large organization, companies included, runs on this soft currency of respect and not only on fear.

head: Legitimacy Lives Inside the State Too
dek: Soldiers, police and civil servants also have to believe in the state.
more: Soldiers, police and civil servants also have to believe in the state. In an illegitimate state they become cynical. They roll their eyes at each new edict, look for ways to turn new laws into protection rackets, favour kith and kin (Fukuyama's point), and quietly help buddies bypass new systems. Ajay links this to Lant Pritchett's 'flailing state', where a brilliant brain at the top is cut off from the fingers on the ground. State capability is built on legitimacy.

head: Legality and Power Are Not Legitimacy
dek: Amit frames this as the gap between political authority and political legitimacy.
more: Amit frames this as the gap between political authority and political legitimacy. Stalin's Russia ran on laws, yet everybody hated the regime and broke the law with pleasure whenever they could. Holding the monopoly of violence, so that police can always break down a door without facing return fire, is only Weber's first level. Legitimacy is what comes after that.

head: Four Sources of Legitimacy
dek: Weber named three. Tradition: Aurangzeb inherited the respect owed to a centuries-old empire, and patriarchy gets respect for free.
more: Weber named three. Tradition: Aurangzeb inherited the respect owed to a centuries-old empire, and patriarchy gets respect for free. Charisma: Napoleon rose after the Revolution destroyed the old dynasty, and Nehru held moral and intellectual authority. Legal-bureaucratic procedure with rule of law: a known passport process instead of phoning a friend in government. Later scholars added a fourth, performance. The Chinese Communist Party earned respect by delivering a 10x rise in per capita GDP. Twelve-hour daily power cuts in rural Maharashtra, where the hosts were recording, are the opposite.

head: Winning Elections Is Not Legitimacy
dek: The media covers elections like cricket matches and treats a big seat count as a mandate.
more: The media covers elections like cricket matches and treats a big seat count as a mandate. But Putin also holds elections and wins about 85% of the vote. Legitimacy lies in whether citizens and officials trust and go along with the state. Populist regimes that chase only their base can keep winning elections and still have a legitimacy gap.

head: What Breaks Without Legitimacy
dek: Ajay traces a chain of harms. Spending on policing and surveillance balloons, which is pure deadweight loss.
more: Ajay traces a chain of harms. Spending on policing and surveillance balloons, which is pure deadweight loss. Interpersonal violence rises, and that includes violence by the police and the hangman. Information stops flowing because people lie to the state, so it can no longer 'see like a state'. Brain drain and capital flight follow. Small sparks, like a Jat agitation in Haryana, snowball because nobody gives the state the benefit of the doubt. In the end the regime itself becomes unstable.

head: The Selfish Case for Legitimacy (Public Choice)
dek: Assume rulers care only about themselves. Legitimacy still pays.
more: Assume rulers care only about themselves. Legitimacy still pays. Coercion is costly and tiring. A legitimate government collects more tax because people comply, whereas India's GST pushed whole industries into cash to avoid it. Legitimate regimes are also stable, while illegitimate ones look adored until they collapse, as East Germany's Communist Party did. A smart ruler who wants more for himself should cultivate legitimacy.

head: Roving vs Stationary Bandits
dek: Amit brings in Mancur Olson's idea. A roving bandit destroys a village because he has no stake in its future.
more: Amit brings in Mancur Olson's idea. A roving bandit destroys a village because he has no stake in its future. A stationary bandit must let it prosper so there is something left to rob. Ajay extends it: under a legitimate bandit, villagers improve land, open shops and build homes. Under an arbitrary one, they dig holes in the ground and hide their gold.

head: Even Ideologues Need Legitimacy
dek: Now take a ruler who wants neither money nor arbitrary power but a cultural or nationalist programme.
more: Now take a ruler who wants neither money nor arbitrary power but a cultural or nationalist programme. That ruler still needs a state that works, and an illegitimate state is a blunt tool that cynical civil servants only pretend to obey. Forcing an agenda on people makes them resent it more each day. A legitimate authority, by contrast, can move people 10% its way and slowly shift social norms. It grows the nation rather than shrinking it.

head: A Toolkit for Earning Legitimacy
dek: Ajay's checklist for politicians and civil servants: - Transparency: expert reports, publicly debated draft laws. - Accountability: grievance redressal, audit, low corruption. - Procedural fairness: laws that are known in advance, enforced equally, with fair hearings. - Consultation: open consultations and town halls, though not plebiscites. - Decentralization: push power to cities. - Performance: the 1991-2011 growth gave the Indian state a halo. - Visible expertise: show the reasoning, not commandments handed down from a mountain. - Respect for norms. - Telling the truth: propaganda corrodes trust once people find out.
more:
Ajay's checklist for politicians and civil servants:
- Transparency: expert reports, publicly debated draft laws.
- Accountability: grievance redressal, audit, low corruption.
- Procedural fairness: laws that are known in advance, enforced equally, with fair hearings.
- Consultation: open consultations and town halls, though not plebiscites.
- Decentralization: push power to cities.
- Performance: the 1991-2011 growth gave the Indian state a halo.
- Visible expertise: show the reasoning, not commandments handed down from a mountain.
- Respect for norms.
- Telling the truth: propaganda corrodes trust once people find out.

head: Compliance Is Not Consent
dek: Amit warns against reading obedience, or the absence of dissent, as legitimacy.
more: Amit warns against reading obedience, or the absence of dissent, as legitimacy. He personally considers no government legitimate, just as he rejects the 'social contract', because a contract needs voluntary consent. He obeys the law carefully, but for practical reasons, to stay out of jail, not ethical ones. The only norms he follows on ethical grounds are ones he has chosen or agrees with.

head: Broken Accountability Breeds Apathy
dek: For most Indians, Amit argues, rule of law does not exist and the state is parasitic, so they thrive despite it rather than judging its legitimacy.
more: For most Indians, Amit argues, rule of law does not exist and the state is parasitic, so they thrive despite it rather than judging its legitimacy. The deeper cause is centralization: power and accountability have come apart. Voting then becomes tribal loyalty, like supporting Manchester United or Liverpool, with little effect on one's life.

head: The Fracture at the Heart of the Republic
dek: India's Constitution was more liberal than the society shaped by caste and misogyny that it governed.
more: India's Constitution was more liberal than the society shaped by caste and misogyny that it governed. That gift brought things like early universal adult franchise. But Ambedkar himself saw it as mere topsoil and called villages dens of ignorance. The missed task was to spread liberal values bottom-up through the culture. Now politics has caught up with society. Amit argues that the English-speaking elite cannot declare a government illegitimate just because they dislike its values, and that the real fight is in the marketplace of ideas.

head: Legitimacy Requires Freedom
dek: If legitimacy must come from people broadly agreeing on values, there has to be an open contest of ideas.
more: If legitimacy must come from people broadly agreeing on values, there has to be an open contest of ideas. Amit argues India lacks free speech, free markets and truly free and fair elections.
