Even if the voting itself is clean, freezing opposition bank accounts and blocking campaigns tilts the field. Liberals must first win society over, and that requires freedom.

head: Amit's opening: they are sitting in the summer sun to discuss a subject that is…
more: Amit's opening: they are sitting in the summer sun to discuss a subject that is 'like the sun. You know, it is ubiquitous. We experience it every day, and yet we kind of take it for granted, which is the Indian state.' Ajay widens the scope: 'Not just the Indian state. So this is of great interest to our viewers ranging from Germany to Mozambique.'

head: Ajay reads his legitimacy checklist from notes…
more: Ajay reads his legitimacy checklist from notes 'because I'm 59 years old, my memory is starting to fade.' Amit tells the 'gentle listener' that Ajay normally does the whole show from memory while Amit glances at his phone, so 'he's finally showing that he's human in some ways.'

head: Ajay's made-up obscure regulation to illustrate procedural unfairness
more: Ajay's made-up obscure regulation to illustrate procedural unfairness: 'Did you know that on camera you cannot be consuming Diet Coke? It has to be Diet Pepsi.'

head: After Ajay explains why even ideologues should seek legitimacy, Amit
more: After Ajay explains why even ideologues should seek legitimacy, Amit says: 'Ajay Shah, you're teaching demagogues how to think rationally, this will not do. You will be held responsible for this, you mad Gujarati.'

head: On why governments must show their reasoning, Ajay says edicts can't just come down
more: On why governments must show their reasoning, Ajay says edicts can't just come down 'from the top of a mountain that you know Moses went and met God and these are the ten commandments. Okay, that earns no respect.'

head: Jagdish Bhagwati, hearing which advisors the new Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha had chosen
more: Jagdish Bhagwati, hearing which advisors the new Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha had chosen: 'if they are economists, then I'm a Bharatanatyam dancer.'

head: James C. Scott's
more: James C. Scott's 'Seeing Like a State': Ajay uses it to show how an illegitimate state goes blind when citizens stop giving it truthful information.

head: East Germany
more: East Germany: 'everybody in East Germany loved the Communist Party until the day the communist party fell, and then suddenly you realized that the Communist Party had absolutely no friends.'

head: Ambedkar called villages
more: Ambedkar called villages 'dens of ignorance' and 'sinks of localism' and saw the Constitution as mere topsoil. Amit contrasts this with Gandhi's dream of village republics, which khap panchayats undercut.

head: Amit says Indian voting is like supporting Manchester United or Liverpool
more: Amit says Indian voting is like supporting Manchester United or Liverpool: 'that kind of tribal loyalty without actually a consequential impact on my life.'

head: TCS-run Passport Seva as Ajay's everyday example of legal-bureaucratic legitimacy: a clear procedure accepting set forms of ID, about which…
more: TCS-run Passport Seva as Ajay's everyday example of legal-bureaucratic legitimacy: a clear procedure accepting set forms of ID, about which 'we tell tales to each other' that it works really well.

head: A Prediction Comes True: The India-UK Trade Deal
dek: A credible, pre-announced glide path forces firms to take a hard look at themselves: raise productivity or go out of business.
more: At the end of the second globalisation episode, Ajay predicted that good things were in store for India's trade policy. He based this on reading newspapers and 'understanding the chessboard', not on inside information. At recording time (May 8), the first piece had arrived: a free trade agreement with the UK. The newspaper reports describe tariff cuts on 90% of products and a 10-year glide path (he would have preferred five). By the end of the ten years, 80% of products reach zero tariff. UK companies will also be able to bid in Indian government procurement. He cautions that he has only read news reports, that you should always read the legal documents, and that the devil is in the details.

A credible, pre-announced glide path forces firms to take a hard look at themselves: raise productivity or go out of business. Cheaper imported raw materials make other Indian firms more competitive. Opening procurement means taxpayers' money buys steel for a police station at the lowest price. And zero tariffs with one country weaken the case for tariffs with everyone else, so one deal can cascade.

head: The Bank That Wanted Its ATM to Dispense a Five Star
dek: This is intrusive central planning in miniature. A product decision that should be the firm's own business judgment became a permission slip.
more: Many years ago, a bank wanted to coax customers away from branch counters and towards ATMs. Its idea was to stock Cadbury Five Star bars inside the ATM, so that any withdrawal above Rs 5,000 would also spit out a chocolate. Sad story number one: the bank had to seek the regulator's approval. Sad story number two: approval was denied, because handing out candy along with cash was 'undignified'. Ajay notes it may not work this way today.

This is intrusive central planning in miniature. A product decision that should be the firm's own business judgment became a permission slip. When everything is banned by default, innovation depends on a regulator's taste.

head: How a 2012 Paper Woke Up a 'Clueless Economist'
dek: This was a comprehensive intellectual failure. Philosophers, legal experts, political scientists and economists all missed a danger understood since the 17th century.
more: Ajay personally knows many of the people who laid the foundations of RBI and SEBI. He calls them wonderful people who meant well. But they lacked the knowledge, and they recklessly fused legislative, executive and judicial powers into single agencies. The first person to see the problem was Dr. Sahu, who had worked in the Ministry of Finance, SEBI and the Competition Commission, and became the first chairman of the bankruptcy regulator. In 2012 he wrote a paper and started giving talks pointing out that this violated separation of powers.

This was a comprehensive intellectual failure. Philosophers, legal experts, political scientists and economists all missed a danger understood since the 17th century. Good intentions without knowledge produce bad institutions, which is why Ajay says a country can only be as good as its thinkers.

head: Dr. Sahu Puts Checks on Himself at IBBI
dek: When you can't fix the law, a reformer who holds power can still fix the practice by binding himself.
more: The team that drafted the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code had imported FSLRC's 140 sections on how a regulator should work. Inside the government, those sections were deleted and replaced by 'the bad 15 sections from the SEBI Act'. When Dr. Sahu became the first chairman of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, the law imposed no checks on him. He knew that would go badly, so he created checks himself. He split IBBI internally into legislative, executive and judicial departments. Around 2016 or 2017, the IBBI board enacted a regulation governing how IBBI makes regulations, importing a subset of the FSLRC procedure. This mirrored the semi-legal agreements between the Finance Ministry and RBI that came before proper law.
When you can't fix the law, a reformer who holds power can still fix the practice by binding himself. That voluntary practice can later become a template for others.
printed: A chairman ties his own hands

head: FSLRC: The Unenacted Law That Seeded Reforms
dek: By one measure the project failed. Ajay argues that this measure is wrong: democracies don't progress through one cathedral project.
more: In 2011, finance minister Pranab Mukherjee kicked off the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission. It was begun by KP Krishnan in the Department of Economic Affairs and chaired by Justice Srikrishna. Ajay faced 'the only job interview of my entire life', conducted by Justice Srikrishna, and went on to co-lead the technical team with Ila Patnaik. The commission produced a clean modern law to replace sixty bad financial laws, including 140 sections of general regulatory theory. It processed about 800 public comments over a four-year project (2011–2015). The law-drafting team was trained by one of the world's top law drafters. Ten years later the law has not been enacted. But ideas incubated inside it, such as inflation targeting and a monetary policy committee, later became a separate law.

By one measure the project failed. Ajay argues that this measure is wrong: democracies don't progress through one cathedral project. Progress comes from building intellectual products and persuading, until ideas creep into practice one by one.
printed: The cathedral that was never built

head: Mango Season: RBI Agrees to Rules on Making Rules
dek: A journey that began in the 2000s has reached a milestone in 2025. Nobody in good faith can now claim that a regulator should have unchecked power to make regulations.
more: IBBI's self-imposed rule-making procedure sat alone for years. Then SEBI issued its own regulation on how it makes regulations, importing the same bag of ideas. On the morning of recording, Ajay got an SMS that RBI had done the same. Three regulators now have board-approved regulations governing their own regulation-making. Ajay stresses this is not the end. A board binding its own staff is weaker than Parliament binding the agency. And it will take another decade to build the state capability needed, such as civil servants who understand market failure and cost-benefit analysis.

A journey that began in the 2000s has reached a milestone in 2025. Nobody in good faith can now claim that a regulator should have unchecked power to make regulations. It shows the hosts' theory of change in action.

head: David Stockman's Despair in Reagan's Washington
dek: Demosclerosis is structural, not partisan. Once interest groups and regulations pile up, they defeat even reformers at the very top, from either party.
more: In Government's End, Jonathan Rauch recalls arriving in Washington in the mid-1980s and chatting with David Stockman, Reagan's man. Reagan's rhetoric promised to make government small and lean. Yet Stockman was depressed and bitter: they had come with such good intentions, and it was so hard to get anything done. Later, Bill Clinton and Newt Gingrich each tried in their own ways to do the same thing, and both failed.
Demosclerosis is structural, not partisan. Once interest groups and regulations pile up, they defeat even reformers at the very top, from either party.

head: Raees Got the Economics Backwards
dek: This is Bruce Yandle's Bootleggers and Baptists in pop culture. The moral crusader and the profiteer are natural allies.
more: When the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees came out, Amit wrote that it got basic economics wrong. In the film, a politician tours town campaigning for prohibition, and Shah Rukh's bootlegger character tries to stop him. But a bootlegger's business only exists because of prohibition.
This is Bruce Yandle's Bootleggers and Baptists in pop culture. The moral crusader and the profiteer are natural allies. When you see a campaign for a ban, ask who profits from it.
printed: The gangster who got it backwards

head: Regulation: A Primer
dek: Amit calls it a wonderful book. It is mostly about how regulation works in America, but the first and last chapters cover the general theory of regulation.
more: Amit calls it a wonderful book. It is mostly about how regulation works in America, but the first and last chapters cover the general theory of regulation. It overlaps with what Ajay covered, though 'nowhere near as comprehensively'.
At the end, Ajay asked Amit for a great book on regulation. Ajay then revealed it is Amit's loo reading.

head: The Theory of Economic Regulation
dek: A famous 1971 essay with three axioms. The state has coercive power; private parties benefit from steering it; so every private party has a rational self-interest in trying to.
more: A famous 1971 essay with three axioms. The state has coercive power; private parties benefit from steering it; so every private party has a rational self-interest in trying to. It explains why lobbying is inevitable and why you must be super careful.
Amit tracing how thinking moved beyond public-interest theory and capture theory.

head: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC) Report, Volume 1
dek: A crisp summary of 20 years of Indian research on regulation and regulatory theory.
more: A crisp summary of 20 years of Indian research on regulation and regulatory theory. It is written as elegant, compact chapters, each ending in a box of drafting instructions for the law-drafting team.
Ajay explicitly recommends it to everybody while describing FSLRC. Amit says he will read it.

head: FSLRC Volume 2: The Indian Financial Code (draft law)
dek: Ajay calls it the cleanest, best-drafted modern law-drafting project in Indian history and a role model for how laws should be drafted.
more: Ajay calls it the cleanest, best-drafted modern law-drafting project in Indian history and a role model for how laws should be drafted. It also incubated ideas like inflation targeting.
The draft law that came out of FSLRC.

head: Rethinking Regulation in India (talk and slides)
dek: A fuller presentation of the regulatory-theory argument Ajay makes in this episode.
more: A fuller presentation of the regulatory-theory argument Ajay makes in this episode.
Show-notes link to Ajay's talk and slideshow on Indian regulatory theory.

head: The Administrative Procedures Act (1946)
dek: 'A brilliant piece of law' ('Don't you envy these countries?'). It applies to all US federal agencies rather than one at a time.
more: 'A brilliant piece of law' ('Don't you envy these countries?'). It applies to all US federal agencies rather than one at a time. It came as a Republican pushback against the Democrats creating too many federal agencies. Court challenges under it built up a body of jurisprudence constraining regulators.
Ajay's model of a general law that disciplines all regulators at once.

head: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Amit calls it Ajay's 'great masterclass' on the four kinds of market failure and when the state may intervene.
more: Amit calls it Ajay's 'great masterclass' on the four kinds of market failure and when the state may intervene.
Referenced as the basis for the market-failure discussion.

head: Separation of Powers (Episode 91 of Everything is Everything)
dek: The foundation for seeing why regulators fusing legislative, executive and judicial powers is so dangerous.
more: The foundation for seeing why regulators fusing legislative, executive and judicial powers is so dangerous.
Referenced twice: on separation of powers, and on recent US developments around the SEC and Chevron Doctrine.

head: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Progress is a story of intellectual persuasion, not one big cathedral project.
more: Progress is a story of intellectual persuasion, not one big cathedral project.
Invoked as 'our theory of change episode' when explaining why FSLRC's unenacted law still mattered.

head: Rule of Law First; Competition Is the Best Regulation
dek: The liberal paradox: we give the state a monopoly on violence, surrendering some rights so it can protect the rest through the rule of law.
more: The liberal paradox: we give the state a monopoly on violence, surrendering some rights so it can protect the rest through the rule of law. That means everyone knows the law, it applies equally, there is due process, the prosecutor isn't the judge, and the law is predictable. The rule of law also protects us from our protectors. Under it, sellers competing for a customer's money keep each other honest. Amit insists that rule of law and regulation are different things. The answer to 'evil capitalists' is a strong rule of law, after which, as Hayek argued, little regulation is needed.

head: Default Skepticism: Three Questions for Any Regulation
dek: A market failure is necessary but not sufficient for intervention. Most of the time doing nothing is better, though some cases, like pollution beyond a point, do justify action.
more: A market failure is necessary but not sufficient for intervention. Most of the time doing nothing is better, though some cases, like pollution beyond a point, do justify action. Amit's stance is to meet every proposed or existing regulation with extreme skepticism and ask three questions.

head: Only Some Market Failures Call for Regulation
dek: Ajay's sorting: public goods call for the government to make or buy the good, not regulate.
more: Ajay's sorting: public goods call for the government to make or buy the good, not regulate. Positive externalities, like building an R&D system, call for voucher-type solutions. Negative externalities, asymmetric information and market power may justify coercing firms. Counting positive and negative externalities as halves gives his tally of 'one and a half' versus 'two and a half'.

head: Regulation vs Regulators vs Regulatory Theory
dek: Regulation is state coercion aimed at firms, rarely individuals. Regulators are specialised arms of the state that do regulation, but a government department can regulate too.
more: Regulation is state coercion aimed at firms, rarely individuals. Regulators are specialised arms of the state that do regulation, but a government department can regulate too. Regulatory theory is the general technology that applies across airports, banks and drugs alike. Domain knowledge should be built on top of it.

head: Stigler's Axioms and Concentrated Benefits, Diffuse Costs
dek: Stigler's three axioms: the state has coercive power, whoever steers it benefits, so every private party will rationally try.
more: Stigler's three axioms: the state has coercive power, whoever steers it benefits, so every private party will rationally try. Public choice explains why this works. A tax or entry barrier that costs each citizen a rupee goes unnoticed, while the beneficiary collects a fortune and can share it with politicians. Each of us loses many such rupees without ever knowing.

head: Demosclerosis
dek: Jonathan Rauch's term for what happened in Washington. Interest groups and regulations multiply until they become almost impossible to reverse, and they crowd out the space for other policymaking.
more: Jonathan Rauch's term for what happened in Washington. Interest groups and regulations multiply until they become almost impossible to reverse, and they crowd out the space for other policymaking. Presidents, Reagan's own man, Clinton and Gingrich all failed to roll it back.

head: Bootleggers and Baptists
dek: Bruce Yandle's insight. A moral crusader (the Baptist) lobbies for prohibition, and the bootlegger, who profits from the ban, is his natural ally and sometimes his funder.
more: Bruce Yandle's insight. A moral crusader (the Baptist) lobbies for prohibition, and the bootlegger, who profits from the ban, is his natural ally and sometimes his funder. Related modern examples Amit gives: tobacco companies supporting FDA pre-approval rules for new cigarettes because they create entry barriers, and the sugar lobby funding studies that blamed fat.

head: Government Failure Is Ubiquitous, and Often Unseen
dek: Public choice holds that bureaucrats want bigger budgets and departments, politicians want re-election, and nobody is omniscient.
more: Public choice holds that bureaucrats want bigger budgets and departments, politicians want re-election, and nobody is omniscient. The FDA shows the seen and the unseen. The seen: approved drugs are safe. The unseen: rigid procedures delay approvals by seven or eight years and cost lives. In Graboyes' terms, regulated healthcare is a walled fortress, while tech is an open frontier.
printed: A rupee here, a fortune there

head: The Interventionist Spiral
dek: From Hayek and Mises: each regulation creates downstream problems that invite more regulation.
more: From Hayek and Mises: each regulation creates downstream problems that invite more regulation. Rent controls cause housing shortages, which lead to housing subsidies, which lead to zoning laws, until everything 'starts to go to hell'.

head: Separation of Powers: Only a Judge Should Be Able to Harm You
dek: Since the 17th century, liberal democracy has worked by dispersing power.
more: Since the 17th century, liberal democracy has worked by dispersing power. It is split between union, state and city, and between legislature (writes the law), executive (investigates and prosecutes) and judiciary (alone can punish). A citizen should be completely unafraid of civil servants and legislators.

head: The Regulator Bargain: Parliament and Police in One Agency, Surgically
dek: Globally, regulators exist for two reasons. One is specialisation, unlike generalist ministries that rotate staff every five years.
more: Globally, regulators exist for two reasons. One is specialisation, unlike generalist ministries that rotate staff every five years. Ajay would prefer rotation across regulators over India's cradle-to-grave employment in one agency. The other is a deliberate breach of separation of powers: fusing law-writing with enforcement, as with the US SEC born in the 1930s. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority writes rules, polices and investigates, then takes cases to a tribunal. The bargain only works if Parliament delegates narrowly, one market failure at a time. The airport regulator should regulate monopoly returns, not be 'feudal lord of airports' deciding the colour of the mirrors in the loo.

head: India's Three-Power Monster and the Silence of the Graveyard
dek: Indian regulators like RBI and SEBI also took the judicial power to punish, on top of low rule of law.
more: Indian regulators like RBI and SEBI also took the judicial power to punish, on top of low rule of law. They have sweeping delegated law-making, licensing that can't be appealed, and opaque punishments. Regulated firms, whose survival depends on the regulator, stop speaking. They praise the regulator and lobby it to block rivals, killing competition, entry and innovation.

head: 1991 Did Not End Central Planning
dek: Liberalisation is believed to have killed central planning.
more: Liberalisation is believed to have killed central planning. Instead, about 75% of the economy came under regulators, whose staff control products and internal processes more intrusively than the old, distant state ever did. A headline saying a regulator 'introduced' a product should make you see red. Ajay calls this one of the most important elements of how India lost the growth dynamic of 1991–2011.

head: The Fix Lives in the Founding Law
dek: There are three steps. First, narrow each delegation of law-making power into a precise section with an objective and balancing considerations.
more: There are three steps. First, narrow each delegation of law-making power into a precise section with an objective and balancing considerations. Second, wrap law-making and licensing in due process, including appeals against denials. Third, move the power to punish out to High Courts, as in the UK and Australia. XKDR Forum research suggests the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are improving. This is generic technology, so India could have a general law like America's Administrative Procedures Act.

head: Earning Democratic Legitimacy for Unelected Rule-Makers
dek: FSLRC's procedure for making a regulation runs as follows. A board with a majority of independent, non-civil-servant directors starts and ends the process.
more: FSLRC's procedure for making a regulation runs as follows. A board with a majority of independent, non-civil-servant directors starts and ends the process. Staff write down the objective and demonstrate a market failure. They weigh six alternatives with cost-benefit analysis and pick the lowest-cost option that works. The draft goes out for 90 days of public comment, and the board revises it in light of the criticism.

head: Theory of Change: Persuasion, Not Cathedrals
dek: Reform rarely comes from one grand project being enacted.
more: Reform rarely comes from one grand project being enacted. It comes from building intellectual products and persuading repeatedly until ideas creep into practice, as inflation targeting and regulators' rule-making procedures did. Foreign models can't be transplanted mechanically. You have to be rooted here and spend twenty years researching Indian conditions.

head: A Country Is Only as Good as Its Thinkers
dek: India's 'doctor engineer' obsession starved law, philosophy, political science and public administration.
more: India's 'doctor engineer' obsession starved law, philosophy, political science and public administration. What humanities exist often became a simplistic social-justice project rather than the study of how advanced economies became advanced. Law schools teach how to litigate a section, not how to design one. Designing law takes political philosophy, public administration, public economics and history: you need to know about the rise of Nazi Germany to think about surveillance. Lawyers should be the coders, with thinkers upstream.

head: Research and Reform Communities Need Expertise and Staying Power
dek: Reforms survive when a community of experts stays engaged for years. They write publicly and stay five, ten or twenty years ahead of officials, ready when problems become pressing.
more: Reforms survive when a community of experts stays engaged for years. They write publicly and stay five, ten or twenty years ahead of officials, ready when problems become pressing. The pension reform shows what happens otherwise: the core group dispersed and nobody was left to defend it. Ajay rejects merely staffing today's officials, and tells young people that without mastery they have no business in public policy.

head: Amit's opening
more: Amit's opening: 'we have two pieces of good news for you, which are that I'm Amit and he's Ajay. No no no. We have two actual pieces of good news for you.'

head: Amit's blockbuster pitch for the India-UK FTA
more: Amit's blockbuster pitch for the India-UK FTA, 'Return to Zero': 'India invented zero, and now these tariffs are gonna go back to zero now. Now the foreigners are bringing zero back to India.'

head: Amit needles Ajay that decades of economists couldn't liberalise trade
more: Amit needles Ajay that decades of economists couldn't liberalise trade: 'Who got it done? Donald Trump got it done.' Ajay: 'Amitbhai, you and I should nominate Donald Trump for the Bharat Ratna.' Amit, hastily: 'He is joking... people are gonna like clip this and put this on Twitter and say he's a Trump bhakt.'

head: After Ajay's careful definitions, Amit
more: After Ajay's careful definitions, Amit says: 'I love the way you say regulation and regulator. I could listen to you all day.' Ajay apologises: 'forgive me, this is a lifetime of angst.'

head: Ajay on what surgical delegation should prevent: a regulator acting
more: Ajay on what surgical delegation should prevent: a regulator acting as 'feudal lord of airports', deciding 'what shall be the color of the mirrors in the loo'.

head: Amit's humblebrag while recommending Graboyes: he won the Bastiat Prize in 2014
more: Amit's humblebrag while recommending Graboyes: he won the Bastiat Prize in 2014, 'the year before I won it for the second time.'

head: Amit to Ajay
more: Amit to Ajay: 'You were a clueless economist in your words. I'm not calling you names.'

head: Amit on incremental reform
more: Amit on incremental reform: 'One baby step at a time, the infant crawls away from the precipice, but it can still hear the labored breathing of the monster.'

head: Amit, after hearing about the 25-year journey, on the show's own prospects
more: Amit, after hearing about the 25-year journey, on the show's own prospects: 'twenty-three years later Everything is Everything will have its first viral video. That is my hope.'

head: Behind-the-scenes clip on recommendations perpetually deferred to…
more: Behind-the-scenes clip on recommendations perpetually deferred to 'next episode': 'Every episode he does this. The sevens are multiplying. Compound interest.'

head: Amit on his book pick
more: Amit on his book pick: 'this episode is actually the recommendation. So please watch this episode, but if you are watching this, you already have. So please watch it again.'

head: Ajay reveals Regulation: A Primer
more: Ajay reveals Regulation: A Primer 'is sitting in his loo. It is his loo time reading.' Amit: 'you must have sneaked into my loo... at my home in Andheri... Please do not reveal any of the other books you saw there.'

head: Amit reaches for the classic maxim after Ajay's account of regulators' fused powers
more: Amit reaches for the classic maxim after Ajay's account of regulators' fused powers: 'power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely.'

head: Recent US developments recalled from the Separation of Powers episode
more: Recent US developments recalled from the Separation of Powers episode: the right to a jury trial being used to knock out trials run inside the SEC, and developments around Chevron Doctrine. Courts are now 'all over the working of these regulatory agencies'.

head: The CXO who has nothing to talk about
dek: Seniority and success don't make people interesting; self-reflection and curiosity do.
more: A friend of Amit's, a CXO at a big company, complains that evenings with fellow C-suite executives are deadly dull. None of them read books, watch world cinema, or care about world affairs or history, so conversation loops through cricket, Bollywood and office gossip. Amit reckons about ninety-five percent of people live in a groove like this.
Seniority and success don't make people interesting; self-reflection and curiosity do. Without them, people stop growing. As Amit puts it via Dylan, they are busy dying.

head: Six classes in three years: the self-taught polymath
dek: Formal credentials aren't the gate. Once a field's first principles click (scarcity, incentives, natural selection), the rest of the field opens up, and you can carry the tools elsewhere.
more: Amit's degree is a BA in English Literature from Fergusson College, Pune. He picked it because he knew he wouldn't have to study, and says he attended about six classes across three years. His real education was obsessive reading. Steven Pinker's The Blank Slate opened up natural selection for him, and he went on to read all of Dawkins, Daniel Dennett and Robert Wright. Hazlitt, Bastiat and popular economics books did the same for economics. Five years of professional poker taught him probabilistic thinking.

Formal credentials aren't the gate. Once a field's first principles click (scarcity, incentives, natural selection), the rest of the field opens up, and you can carry the tools elsewhere. Amit has used economic thinking to break down cricket strategy.

head: Walking away from being a company man
dek: The choice didn't always look like good fortune. It bought him the key input for a learning life: control over his time, so he can read what he wants, when he wants, without being pushed down a corporate track.
more: Around 2006–07 Amit was managing editor of Cricinfo. He decided he would never hold a job again, moved to a contributing-editor consulting role for a couple of years, then left entirely. Since then he has written a book, played professional poker for five years, and edited the policy magazine Pragati for the Takshashila Institution, remotely and part-time.

The choice didn't always look like good fortune. It bought him the key input for a learning life: control over his time, so he can read what he wants, when he wants, without being pushed down a corporate track.

head: A life lived through one global drama after another
dek: Broad building blocks across science, statistics, economics and history work as entry gates.
more:
Ajay never accepted the narrow specialise-and-publish track. As a PhD student he read biology on the side for the pleasure of it. Looking back, his life has been a series of deep dives into world crises:
- the Asian crisis
- 9/11, Islamic extremism and the Afghanistan wars
- the 2008 financial crisis
- the pandemic
- the rise of modern populism

Reading about the Great Depression, he says, is different from living through a crisis yourself: watching the data, knowing who said what on which date, and being surprised when the VIX crossed 68.
Broad building blocks across science, statistics, economics and history work as entry gates. With them, each unfolding world event becomes a live seminar rather than a headline.

head: Mohit Satyanand's unbroken Sundays
dek: A fixed, non-negotiable cadence turns 'someday' into a habit. A friend's nudge at the right moment can launch years of consistent work.
more: While staying with his friend Mohit Satyanand in Delhi, Amit gave him his usual lecture: start a newsletter, be bloody-minded, have a bias for action. Mohit started, and in roughly three years he hasn't missed a single Sunday.
A fixed, non-negotiable cadence turns 'someday' into a habit. A friend's nudge at the right moment can launch years of consistent work.

head: A boat that never sailed and a pact to write books
dek: Pacts among friends create accountability, but they only pay off for whoever actually does the work.
more: At a conference in Kochi two years ago, Amit, Lancelot Pinto and Vasant Dhar were put on a boat for a ride. A storm started and the boat never left. Standing on board and talking about the books they each wanted to write, the three promised that all of them would have written one by the next year's conference. Amit had earlier pushed Vasant to start a newsletter in a personal tone, and then to write a book in that voice. Two years on, Vasant has just sent his final manuscript to his publisher. Amit and Lancelot, whenever they meet, marvel at Vasant and hope to be inspired by him.

Pacts among friends create accountability, but they only pay off for whoever actually does the work. Amit casts himself as the cautionary half of the story: a prolific weekly producer who keeps postponing the deep projects he cares about most.
printed: The boat stayed, one book sailed

head: From books by strangers to a shelf of signed copies
dek: An intellectual life matures when the books on your shelf stop coming from a distant priesthood and start coming from people you know.
more: When Ajay was a child, the great books in the house were written by strange, mysterious people far away. Recently, at lunch with Akshay Jaitly, who is finishing what Ajay calls an absolutely grand book, the two marvelled that they now live among friends and family who write books. Both plan a shelf of nothing but signed copies.
An intellectual life matures when the books on your shelf stop coming from a distant priesthood and start coming from people you know. Being part of such a community is a blessing in itself.

head: Touring Spain with ChatGPT Deep Research
dek: The AI's output is only as deep as your prompts, and your prompts are only as deep as your curiosity and prior knowledge.
more: Travelling through Spain, Amit had ChatGPT Deep Research write reports of around twenty thousand words before each museum: the Picasso Museum, the Prado, the Reina Sofia. Each covered the artists' lives and phases, the key works in each room, and the order in which to walk through the rooms. Before a train from Barcelona to Madrid with a huge bag, he asked where to stow it. The AI asked which train, then told him which coach to board and where the luggage racks were at the start and end of the coach, with a photograph.

The AI's output is only as deep as your prompts, and your prompts are only as deep as your curiosity and prior knowledge. Amit treats it as a complete Google replacement but still checks the cited sources himself.

head: The widows who bloom
dek: An institution's cost can be invisible to the people inside it.
more: Amit has recently seen several real cases of an elderly woman whose husband dies and who suddenly becomes a new person: free, learning an instrument, travelling solo. These women may never have thought of their marriages as confining, because marriage was the structure they flowed into, it was normalised, and no alternative ever seemed to exist.

An institution's cost can be invisible to the people inside it. Amit ties this to Chinmay Tumbe's finding that marriage drives the largest internal migration in India: women are uprooted from their villages and their friends, and sometimes even lose their names.

head: Why We Sleep
dek: He calls it an excellent book. It shows that roughly thirty percent of people are night owls whose natural rhythm is simply different, which explains 'the tyranny of the larks.'
more: He calls it an excellent book. It shows that roughly thirty percent of people are night owls whose natural rhythm is simply different, which explains 'the tyranny of the larks.'
Cited when a listener asked for an episode shot at dawn, to explain why that's impossible for him.

head: Superforecasting
dek: Tetlock shows that TV experts are often wrong, while the people who get things right are constantly doing Bayesian thinking and updating their priors.
more: Tetlock shows that TV experts are often wrong, while the people who get things right are constantly doing Bayesian thinking and updating their priors. Amit wants that idea to spread more widely in society.
His deliberate 'book recommendation middle of the episode,' made while discussing academics and pundits who perform certainty.

head: The Blank Slate
dek: It gave him the first principles of human nature and evolution. After it, the whole field opened up and reshaped his view of the world.
more: It gave him the first principles of human nature and evolution. After it, the whole field opened up and reshaped his view of the world.
Named as his gateway into natural selection.

head: Richard Dawkins's books, including The Selfish Gene and The Blind Watchmaker
dek: He read 'the whole shebang.' Understanding natural selection deeply changed how he sees human nature.
more: He read 'the whole shebang.' Understanding natural selection deeply changed how he sees human nature.
Part of the evolution rabbit hole he went down after Pinker, along with Daniel Dennett and Robert Wright.

head: Economics in One Lesson
dek: A first-principles entry into economic thinking. You don't need regressions, just the fundamentals of scarcity and incentives.
more: A first-principles entry into economic thinking. You don't need regressions, just the fundamentals of scarcity and incentives.
Mentioned as an early economics book. Lant Pritchett told Amit on The Seen and the Unseen that it was one of his own formative books.

head: The Logic of Life
dek: Popular economics that shows how economic reasoning explains everyday life.
more: Popular economics that shows how economic reasoning explains everyday life. Once you absorb such fundamentals, everything else starts to make sense.
Singled out among 'Tim Harford's great books' as a particularly good one.

head: The Language Instinct
dek: He calls it a great book on how the structures of language are built into the brain.
more: He calls it a great book on how the structures of language are built into the brain. Even so, a child who never hears words won't speak.
Cited in his thought experiment about a child raised without hearing language.

head: Brave New World
dek: Mentioned warmly as the show of a very dear friend whose work Amit backs.
more: Mentioned warmly as the show of a very dear friend whose work Amit backs.
Vasant's podcast. Amit used to produce it; Gaurav Chintamani produces it now.

head: Charlie Munger's wisdom
dek: Munger has always been a source of great wisdom on how to think.
more: Munger has always been a source of great wisdom on how to think.
Raised in the same question about mental models.

head: Just (song and music video)
dek: There's so much more to Radiohead than Creep. 'Just' is also awesome, and its video is a masterpiece.
more: There's so much more to Radiohead than Creep. 'Just' is also awesome, and its video is a masterpiece.
A listener asked about people playing Radiohead's Creep on loop. Amit admitted he did the same in the early 90s.

head: The Art of Clear Writing
dek: His writing course, built on the philosophy of writing something good rather than chasing an audience.
more: His writing course, built on the philosophy of writing something good rather than chasing an audience.
A listener asked how to build an audience on Substack. The last cohort ran the previous October, and the waiting list is long.

head: Episode 50: Ask Me ANYTHING!
dek: The companion to this episode, recorded at the halfway mark.
more: The companion to this episode, recorded at the halfway mark.
Linked in the show notes as the show's earlier AMA.

head: Speculate, but with transparency
dek: Ajay worried about straying beyond his expertise. Amit's view of the show is to bring frames from one field to bear on another without pretending to be certain.
more: Ajay worried about straying beyond his expertise. Amit's view of the show is to bring frames from one field to bear on another without pretending to be certain. You can talk usefully about things you're still learning, as long as you're open that you're speculating and exploring.

head: Self-reflection is what sets thoughtful people apart
dek: Most people, especially men, never reflect on why they do what they do or want what they want.
more: Most people, especially men, never reflect on why they do what they do or want what they want. Those who do enter a virtuous cycle: they improve themselves and seek out other reflective people who reinforce the habit. Yet we contain multitudes. Amit is thoughtful about ideas but on autopilot about his finances and his health.

head: Politicians are the entrepreneurs of the state
dek: From Vijay Kelkar, Ajay learned that officials are trained into conservatism while politicians take risks.
more: From Vijay Kelkar, Ajay learned that officials are trained into conservatism while politicians take risks. Politicians walk thousands of kilometres meeting real people and know far more about farm distress or jobs than their slogans suggest. Amit pushes back that politics is downstream of culture, so populist demand shapes populist supply. Ajay's answer is that great leadership means doing more than following the polls.

head: Judging expert debates you can't follow technically
dek: Amit's checklist for weighing economists you can't fully follow: - Apply the frameworks you do understand.
more:
Amit's checklist for weighing economists you can't fully follow:
- Apply the frameworks you do understand. Anyone treating inequality and poverty as the same thing is thinking in zero-sum terms.
- Be suspicious of people who toe a whole tribal package of positions.
- Notice incoherence, such as backing free markets while opposing personal freedom.
- Focus on arguments, not personalities. Ideas last; people die.
- Remember you don't have to hold an opinion at all.

head: Read constrained speech as the party line
dek: People have different degrees of freedom to speak, depending on their institution.
more: People have different degrees of freedom to speak, depending on their institution. A Federal Reserve official, a party member, or anyone at a regulated financial firm is under pressure to conform. Their public statements reflect a negotiated consensus, so don't judge them by the standards of sharp logic. The person is often much better than their writing suggests.

head: Pride vs self-respect depends on where you start
dek: Ajay calls pride a negative emotion that slides into hubris once you start inhaling your own press releases.
more: Ajay calls pride a negative emotion that slides into hubris once you start inhaling your own press releases. Amit calls that 'a thinking male answer.' Citing Shrayana Bhattacharya, he notes that men tend toward unwarranted self-confidence and women toward unwarranted self-doubt. Men should watch their pride; many women need more of it.

head: Think in probabilities; life is managing luck
dek: Poker taught Amit to think in a Bayesian way, which made him less certain, less judgmental of others, and less proud of his own successes.
more: Poker taught Amit to think in a Bayesian way, which made him less certain, less judgmental of others, and less proud of his own successes. People who perform certainty are either simplifying or are charlatans. The best forecasters keep updating their priors.

head: High-powered incentives broke academic research
dek: Publication bias rewards sensational results. Behavioural findings fail to replicate at the magnitudes originally claimed.
more: Publication bias rewards sensational results. Behavioural findings fail to replicate at the magnitudes originally claimed. Careers revolve around raising money and schmoozing editors. From 1900 to 1925, with almost no funding, field after field was revolutionised; million-fold increases in spending since then have disappointed. Ajay calls this a sobering lesson for economists: people chase exactly what you reward.

head: First principles plus rabbit holes
dek: You don't need technical training in a field. What matters is that its fundamentals (scarcity, incentives, natural selection) become part of how you think.
more: You don't need technical training in a field. What matters is that its fundamentals (scarcity, incentives, natural selection) become part of how you think. The way to get there is to dive into whatever fascinates you, without asking what productive thing will come of it.

head: Memory comes from volume and connections
dek: Amit's retention is low, but he reads so much that what sticks still adds up to a lot, and Roam catches the rest.
more: Amit's retention is low, but he reads so much that what sticks still adds up to a lot, and Roam catches the rest. Ajay adds the idea of adjacencies. We remember knowledge that connects richly to what we already know; topology is far easier after calculus and real analysis. And every use of a memory refreshes it, like a static RAM cell.
printed: Read a lot, forget a lot

head: Knowledge is a social project; solitude is for reflection
dek: Ajay increasingly finds his work comes from arguing with people and being corrected by them, much like the early-20th-century physicists at Göttingen who argued about matter and energy while hiking together.
more: Ajay increasingly finds his work comes from arguing with people and being corrected by them, much like the early-20th-century physicists at Göttingen who argued about matter and energy while hiking together. Amit agrees you need people both to grow and to be happy. You also need solitude, as long as it goes into healthy self-reflection rather than wallowing.

head: Do the work; don't chase validation
dek: Asking 'how do I build an audience?' first is a trap. Beginners are bad and get no audience; if validation matters to them, they quit and never get good.
more: Asking 'how do I build an audience?' first is a trap. Beginners are bad and get no audience; if validation matters to them, they quit and never get good. A good product is the best marketing. The same goes for fearing irrelevance or controversy, since both depend on how the world responds to you. The hosts committed to 104 episodes before judging the show, and Amit keeps putting episodes out despite having 'a face for audio.'

head: Reading is collecting dots
dek: We understand the world by joining dots, and personal experience can only supply so many.
more: We understand the world by joining dots, and personal experience can only supply so many. Each book lets you live another life, so your picture of the world becomes higher-definition, and so does your picture of yourself.

head: Stock and flow
dek: Flow is blogs and columns. It is valuable as thinking aloud and as a writing gym; Amit wrote about eight thousand blog posts from 2003 to 2008, though he considers none worth preserving.
more: Flow is blogs and columns. It is valuable as thinking aloud and as a writing gym; Amit wrote about eight thousand blog posts from 2003 to 2008, though he considers none worth preserving. Stock is books, and he admits he hasn't produced enough of it. Ajay writes his columns and LEAP blog posts with a researcher's push for novelty, so they become reusable. A book then weaves those small inventions into one large tapestry.

head: Money is blood; time is the real scarcity
dek: Ajay: you need money to live, but it isn't how you keep score in the video game or the thing to maximise.
more: Ajay: you need money to live, but it isn't how you keep score in the video game or the thing to maximise. Amit: when you're young, money feels like the binding constraint, but over a whole life, time is what you will definitely run out of.

head: There is no self apart from your influences
dek: Amit's thought experiment: a child who hears no language for its first years won't speak at all.
more: Amit's thought experiment: a child who hears no language for its first years won't speak at all. A child who hears only its parents gets a limited vocabulary and personality. Add television, playmates and books, and the self widens. Phineas Gage shows how fragile the self is. Even if free will is doubtful, you still choose your company, your reading and your influences, and those shape you.

head: Climate change is a coordination problem, not a technology problem
dek: Ajay says the energy revolution in solar, wind, nuclear and storage has worked, so with adequate carbon taxes the world can keep growing while decarbonising.
more: Ajay says the energy revolution in solar, wind, nuclear and storage has worked, so with adequate carbon taxes the world can keep growing while decarbonising. The hard part is getting countries to cooperate on a global public good when each has an incentive to renege. Amit adds that France shows nuclear works, and warns that NGOs have a fundraising incentive to exaggerate the danger.

head: Unknown unknowns are a source of hope
dek: Amit won't call anything about India's future inevitable. The world of 2040 can't be pictured today, and rapid change could undo the things he dislikes now.
more: Amit won't call anything about India's future inevitable. The world of 2040 can't be pictured today, and rapid change could undo the things he dislikes now. Ajay names two high-probability problems: a dramatic fall in fertility that will bring rapid ageing, and global warming that is already baked in.

head: Conventional marriage is misaligned with modernity
dek: Amit's answer to which non-economic part of Indian life clashes with modernity.
more: Amit's answer to which non-economic part of Indian life clashes with modernity. Women move to the husband's village, sometimes change their names, lose their childhood friends, and live in service of the husband. He grants that tradition offers reassurance and admits modern dating is complicated too.

head: The religion of the state
dek: Ajay is optimistic that the statism born of the 1914–1945 crisis era is fading as India globalises and grows comfortable with markets.
more: Ajay is optimistic that the statism born of the 1914–1945 crisis era is fading as India globalises and grows comfortable with markets. Amit, who meets more young people, thinks most still treat the state as mai-baap, expected to solve every problem and ban whatever offends. Because zero-sum, top-down intuitions are hardwired, each generation has to fight this battle again.

head: Communities of choice over communities of circumstance
dek: Both hosts grew up making friends with whoever lived nearby; the internet let them form communities by choice.
more: Both hosts grew up making friends with whoever lived nearby; the internet let them form communities by choice. Amit wonders whether nation-states will matter less to identity, even though they keep their coercive power. India has been a nation-state for only about seventy-eight years, and maps keep changing. Ajay notes that borders have softened over fifty years and calls state interference in voluntary cross-border deals a dumb idea.

head: Mortality puts every other problem in perspective
dek: Asked how he stays funny, Amit says death is the fundamental tragedy, and as atheists the hosts take it seriously.
more: Asked how he stays funny, Amit says death is the fundamental tragedy, and as atheists the hosts take it seriously. Next to it every other tragedy shrinks, so stressing over an article becomes laughable. Ajay's version: since the end is certain, live fully and delight in being here.

head: Play the hand you're dealt; reject victimhood
dek: Ajay: everyone gets a random hand of cards, whether pretty or ugly, rich or poor, with or without books at home.
more: Ajay: everyone gets a random hand of cards, whether pretty or ugly, rich or poor, with or without books at home. The only interesting question is what you do next, not complaining about structural injustice. Amit: the worst thing you can do is wrap yourself in a narrative of victimhood, because your circumstances of birth don't define you.

head: As an X, contribute by doing X well
dek: A software engineer asked how to contribute to the world. Ajay's advice: practise the craft, write good code, join open-source projects, and fuel others' passion.
more: A software engineer asked how to contribute to the world. Ajay's advice: practise the craft, write good code, join open-source projects, and fuel others' passion. Amit generalises it: if people pay you for your work, you are adding value to their lives, and that is a respectable contribution. You don't need to go and feed the hungry.

head: Labour unions as market power
dek: Ajay sees a union as market power: a group saying take it or leave it.
more: Ajay sees a union as market power: a group saying take it or leave it. An open labour market with free entry and exit produces a Pareto-superior outcome. Amit defends the right to form unions, but says the 'evil capitalist versus poor worker' story often hurts workers more than it helps them.

head: The 70/30 rule for creative careers
dek: Amit spent his early years as a copywriter, an MTV scriptwriter and a journalist, which felt like a waiting room for creative greatness.
more:
Amit spent his early years as a copywriter, an MTV scriptwriter and a journalist, which felt like a waiting room for creative greatness. His advice:
- If seventy percent of your work is drudgery and thirty percent satisfies you, you're lucky.
- Be bloody-minded about protecting that thirty percent.
- Bring care to the drudgery too, because that's where you learn the craft.
- As you succeed, don't let the ratio drift to 100/0 and lose the spark.

head: With closed-minded family, pick your battles
dek: Share your views without preaching and gift good books. But with elders who won't budge, step back: love them for everything else and keep the relationship intact.
more: Share your views without preaching and gift good books. But with elders who won't budge, step back: love them for everything else and keep the relationship intact. Keep the humility to accept that you might be wrong. Among the friends you choose, bigotry and sexism are firm red lines.

head: A country can't be better than its elite
dek: Ajay admires the generation that led the Congress through the freedom movement.
more: Ajay admires the generation that led the Congress through the freedom movement. Even so, he thinks India is building critical mass in intellectual capacity for the first time in a century, helped by the internet, across science, business, the humanities and policy. That is why he is optimistic. His advice to young people: find your people and the pleasure of thinking and building.

head: Judge AI by its trajectory, not today's snapshot
dek: Amit thinks it is very early days for AI. Tools like Deep Research are already superb tutors and research aids, but they amplify your curiosity rather than replacing your thinking.
more: Amit thinks it is very early days for AI. Tools like Deep Research are already superb tutors and research aids, but they amplify your curiosity rather than replacing your thinking. Always go back to the sources.

head: Ajay's apology after a hundred episodes outside his expertise
more: Ajay's apology after a hundred episodes outside his expertise: 'I apologise to you, gentle reader. If I have on occasion misrepresented my standard errors.'

head: Ajay gushes about growing mushrooms (
more: Ajay gushes about growing mushrooms ('my stomach is bursting with anticipation'), then admits, 'This is all theoretical. I haven't done it yet.' Amit: 'You must be a fungi.' Later Ajay says Arvind Modi's excitement about tax policy after forty years matches his own about mushrooms, 'and I haven't even grown any mushrooms.' Amit: 'Which is why you're excited.'

head: The running taxation-is-theft dig at Ajay's upcoming tax book. Amit starts
more: The running taxation-is-theft dig at Ajay's upcoming tax book. Amit starts, 'it is not a book about taxation alone, it is a book about theft, because taxation is', and Ajay cuts him off. Later, on friends with wrong opinions: 'people will say taxation is not theft. Or even write books about it.'

head: Amit the night owl accuses Ajay, a morning lark, of complicity in…
more: Amit the night owl accuses Ajay, a morning lark, of complicity in 'the tyranny of the larks' against 'my people, the unfortunate night owls': 'Waking up in the morning is just like animal cruelty at this point.'

head: After Ajay calls himself a child of the Asian crisis, 9/11, 2008 and the pandemic, Amit
more: After Ajay calls himself a child of the Asian crisis, 9/11, 2008 and the pandemic, Amit says: 'There's an old Chinese curse, may you live in interesting times. For you it seems a blessing which can only mean you're a sociopath.'

Asked whether a show like this was inevitable in modern India, Amit rejects the Marxian view in favour of the great man theory. The tides of history, he says, wouldn't produce two other people like them, because 'There are no people like us.'

head: Amit on moving from an audio show to video
more: Amit on moving from an audio show to video: 'I have a face for audio.'

head: Amit admits he keeps repeating Dylan's
more: Amit admits he keeps repeating Dylan's 'he not busy being born is busy dying'. When that happens he curses himself for not reading enough, for not having 'enough new things coming into my LLM.'

head: Asked for hair-care advice, Amit plugs a daily
more: Asked for hair-care advice, Amit plugs a daily 'quotidian' shampoo from Bath and Body Works, then adds: 'I should be the last fucking influencer you look at for hair.' Ajay claims the scene where Amit ruffled his hair 'made waves.' Amit: 'No, it has not made waves. I also know how to look at the analytics.'

head: Asked whether he'd keep a seagull as a pet after once declaring
more: Asked whether he'd keep a seagull as a pet after once declaring 'seagulls are bastards', Amit replies: 'If a seagull is a bastard, why would I keep a seagull as a pet?' He'd keep Steven Seagal as a pet instead.

head: Amit credits a good friend with the line
more: Amit credits a good friend with the line 'life is not a spectator sport.' 'His name is Ajay Shah.' Yet the crew brought a football to the farm, and Ajay, who always says 'play football, don't watch football,' refuses to play.

head: Ajay introduces a question from…
more: Ajay introduces a question from 'an obscure viewer called Nomsita.' Amit: 'There's only one Nomsita in India. She's sitting behind the camera here. Hello, camera.'

head: Amit's farewell
more: Amit's farewell: 'The show will go on not because we like the show. The show will go on because we like the company.' Then, to Ajay: 'I'm not talking about you, Ajay Shah, don't be so happy.'

head: After the hosts agree that mortality makes everything else funny, Ajay twists the show's title
more: After the hosts agree that mortality makes everything else funny, Ajay twists the show's title: 'Everything is everything and everything will die.'

head: On solitude, Amit says it's fine as long as it involves healthy self-reflection
more: On solitude, Amit says it's fine as long as it involves healthy self-reflection, 'not just basking in the melodrama of your perceived miseries as Bengalis tend to do.'

head: Ajay opens with an Indianised riff on the song from Shakespeare's As You Like It
more: Ajay opens with an Indianised riff on the song from Shakespeare's As You Like It: 'Under the Banyan Tree, who loves to play with me, here shall she find no enemy, but summer and rough weather.'

head: Bob Dylan, Amit's favourite line about thoughtless lives
more: Bob Dylan, Amit's favourite line about thoughtless lives: 'if you're not busy being born, you're busy dying.'

head: Thomas Watson, president of IBM, who famously
more: Thomas Watson, president of IBM, who famously said 'I think there's a world market for three computers.' Amit cites it as a warning against judging AI by its current state.
'As Thomas Jefferson allegedly said, the price of liberty is eternal vigilance.' Amit's coda on why each generation must fight statism anew.

head: Ajay quotes John Lennon's
more: Ajay quotes John Lennon's 'Imagine' while arguing that borders are softening: 'imagine there's no country it's easy if you try.'

head: Ajay on the freedom-movement generation: Gandhi as a…
more: Ajay on the freedom-movement generation: Gandhi as a 'black swan,' and 'the idea of Nehru sitting in a jail writing letter to his daughter, okay, it's out of the world.'

head: Ajay's heroes of Indian economics are the people of the sixties who challenged the establishment: Jagdish Bhagwati, T.N. Srinivasan, Anne Krueger (
more: Ajay's heroes of Indian economics are the people of the sixties who challenged the establishment: Jagdish Bhagwati, T.N. Srinivasan, Anne Krueger ('Professor Krueger, for this purpose I treat you as an Indian economist'), Arun Shourie, Manmohan Singh, Montek Singh Ahluwalia and Vijay Kelkar. Amit adds Padma Desai and Isher Ahluwalia, then: 'You forgot one man. Narottam Shah.' Ajay replies that his father started CMIE, 'a grand project.'

head: Dan Ariely, cited by Amit as an academic who…
more: Dan Ariely, cited by Amit as an academic who 'got into a lot of trouble' over his studies, while discussing replication problems in behavioural research.

head: Landings in Burma vs. Landings in China
dek: We already make fast, calibrated 'easy vs. hard' judgments in some domains.
more: To open the toolkit, Ajay asks us to imagine a hypothetical Indian expeditionary force weighing amphibious landings in Burma against landings in China. We see at once that both are very hard. But a sufficiently complex naval operation could manage Burma, while China is practically impossible. He then asks whether we could make the same quick call about demands like manipulating the exchange rate, stabilising inflation, building an atom bomb, or polio vaccination.

We already make fast, calibrated 'easy vs. hard' judgments in some domains. The goal is to make that same move routine for policy proposals, so they are weighed on feasibility and not just desirability.

head: The Op-ed Behind 'Monetary Policy is Easy, Financial Regulation is Hard'
dek: Two activities that look alike to outsiders sit at opposite ends of the difficulty spectrum once you take them apart.
more: Ajay calls the day he figured this out one of the happy days of his life. We tend to see central banking as one blur. But a modern monetary policy committee has five members, which he says should be the RBI governor plus four independent private economists. They meet six times a year to hit a 4% inflation target and each writes a public rationale. That makes it low on transactions, discretion, stakes and opacity. Financial regulation is the opposite. It means about a thousand firms and roughly 2,000 touch points a year, judgment calls on whether a loan is an NPA, billions of dollars that can make or break business models, and supervision done in secrecy. That is four on four.

Two activities that look alike to outsiders sit at opposite ends of the difficulty spectrum once you take them apart. A country like India can build an inflation-targeting system fairly easily. Banking regulation will always be hard, and even the United States suffers doing it.

head: The Railway Ticket Clerk Who Could Lie
dek: The real reform value of an IT system is not glamour. It is that it removes discretion from the frontline civil servant and so turns a hard component into an easy one.
more: In the old days, the booking status of every seat on every train lived in a paper register inside the railway office. The clerk at the ticket window therefore had complete discretion and could simply claim there were no seats. Once the data moved into a database that the whole world can see, ideally through an open API, that discretion vanished: seat 2A is either taken or not. Ajay adds that the government needn't even run IRCTC. It only needs to open an API, and ClearTrip and MakeMyTrip will do the rest.
The real reform value of an IT system is not glamour. It is that it removes discretion from the frontline civil servant and so turns a hard component into an easy one.

head: What Nehru Should Have Heard in 1947
dek: The essentials of statecraft are not modest chores you finish before the exciting projects.
more: After reading Adam Smith's line on peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice, Ajay imagines someone saying this to Jawaharlal Nehru in 1947. Nehru brushes it off: that's all good, but we also need land reform. The right answer, Ajay argues, would have been to take fright at how hard each of the three is and refuse everything else.

The essentials of statecraft are not modest chores you finish before the exciting projects. They are among the hardest problems there are, and taking on extra goals early robs them of scarce capability.

head: The Drunk Under the Lamppost
dek: Measurable, attributable problems tempt us because they let us feel productive, while the consequential problems stay fuzzy and in the dark.
more: A good policeman in a rule-of-law country finds a drunk man searching under a lamppost and helps him look for his key. Finding nothing, he asks where the key was dropped. 'Over there in the bushes where it's very dark.' Then why look here? 'Because this is where the light is.' Amit uses the parable against RCTs in development economics, which he used to open his Seen and the Unseen episode with Lant Pritchett. He later found Yuen Yuen Ang used the same metaphor, almost simultaneously, in her paper 'Adaptive Political Economy', and wrote to her about it.

Measurable, attributable problems tempt us because they let us feel productive, while the consequential problems stay fuzzy and in the dark. It is worth asking whether you are working on something because it matters or because it is well-lit.
printed: The key is in the dark

head: Solutions When the Solution is the Problem: Arraying the Disarray in Development
dek: Ajay loves it because the question it asks, whether an intervention is easy or hard to implement, was itself a breakthrough.
more: Ajay loves it because the question it asks, whether an intervention is easy or hard to implement, was itself a breakthrough. Indian policy debate rarely asks it.
The 2004 paper that first proposed two of the metrics, number of transactions and discretion. Ajay and Vijay Kelkar later built on it.
