head: Why State Intervention Goes Wrong
dek: Ajay gives four quick reasons for his and Amit's scepticism of the Indian state. (1) Information: society is too complex, so the true facts are unknowable to planners. (2) Public choice: the incentives of state personnel clash with the state's objectives. (3) Political economy: special interest groups push government behaviour around. (4) State capability: even well-meant projects get badly implemented.
more: Ajay gives four quick reasons for his and Amit's scepticism of the Indian state. (1) Information: society is too complex, so the true facts are unknowable to planners. (2) Public choice: the incentives of state personnel clash with the state's objectives. (3) Political economy: special interest groups push government behaviour around. (4) State capability: even well-meant projects get badly implemented. Hence their 'environment of diffidence' whenever someone says the government should do one more thing.

head: Ask 'Is It Possible?', Not Just 'Is It Justified?'
dek: Whether the state should intervene depends on whether it can succeed, not only on whether the goal is worthy.
more: Whether the state should intervene depends on whether it can succeed, not only on whether the goal is worthy. Implementation constraints belong at the start of any policy discussion. Mainstream Indian debate 'blithely runs forward' from values to action. If you first judge which goals are easy and which are hard, you can ration money and management effort, letting some lovely objectives go and taking on the ones you can actually win.
printed: First ask: can it be done?

head: The Four Metrics for Intervention
dek: A proposed intervention gets harder the higher it scores on four tests. (1) Transactions: 500 research grants a year vs. polio drops for 500 million people. (2) Discretion of frontline workers: people use discretion in favour of friends, kin and self-interest. (3) Stakes: a policeman who can jail you vs. a vaccinator with nothing to gain. (4) Opacity: body cams, the CAG, RTI and published statistics let journalists, researchers and opposition parties criticise, while secrecy hands over raw arbitrary power.
more: A proposed intervention gets harder the higher it scores on four tests. (1) Transactions: 500 research grants a year vs. polio drops for 500 million people. (2) Discretion of frontline workers: people use discretion in favour of friends, kin and self-interest. (3) Stakes: a policeman who can jail you vs. a vaccinator with nothing to gain. (4) Opacity: body cams, the CAG, RTI and published statistics let journalists, researchers and opposition parties criticise, while secrecy hands over raw arbitrary power. Pritchett and Woolcock proposed the first two, and Kelkar and Shah added stakes and opacity. Amit notes that all four probe the same gap between the state's objectives and its employees' incentives.

head: Scoring Real Interventions
dek: Ajay fills an imaginary table on the fly.
more: Ajay fills an imaginary table on the fly. Elementary schools score high on transactions and discretion (the teacher decides whether to teach, make eye contact, or try harder), but stakes are low (a modest salary) and opacity can be fixed: two out of four. HPV or polio vaccination involves high transactions but a fixed protocol, no stakes and full transparency, so it is easy. The judiciary has ultimate discretion and stakes, plus closed-door bench deliberations: three and a half out of four. Taxation has huge numbers of transactions, high officer discretion, stakes of thousands of crores and full opacity: four on four.

head: The Hacking Mindset: Redesign a Hard Problem into an Easy One
dek: Difficulty is often a product of institutional design. Monetary policy was once an opaque, high-discretion domain ruled by a powerful governor.
more: Difficulty is often a product of institutional design. Monetary policy was once an opaque, high-discretion domain ruled by a powerful governor. An inflation target, a committee dominated by private economists, and full transparency 'hacked the components' to make it easy. IT can do the same: computerisation tames high transaction volumes, and open databases strip frontline discretion, as with railway reservations. Facing a bad row in the table, ask which metric you can flip by redesign.

head: Metrics Guard Against Vulgar Familiarity
dek: A finance person may find banking regulation easy because it is familiar, and monetary policy mysterious because it is alien.
more: A finance person may find banking regulation easy because it is familiar, and monetary policy mysterious because it is alien. Neither feeling says anything about real difficulty; unfamiliarity only means you need the right expertise. A shared, explicit framework removes this bias and gives people a common language to argue in. Amit adds that even imperfect measurement sharpens thinking: 'Not everything is precisely measurable, but the more you attempt to measure something, the more clarity you gain in thinking about it.'

head: Adam Smith's Essentials Are the Hardest Problems
dek: Smith said little else is needed for opulence but peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice.
more: Smith said little else is needed for opulence but peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice. Run these through the four metrics. Peace (military, police, criminal justice), taxes and courts are all brutally hard. So the minimal state is not an easy state. Capability has a budget constraint: money, civil servant headcount, and above all the attention of leaders, researchers and reform teams. A chief minister's calendar decides what gets done. This is why mission creep is so costly: every extra project drains the core, which may take 50 to 100 years to get right.

head: Hard Is Not the Same as Unimportant
dek: The four metrics measure difficulty, not importance. Smith's three essentials are both necessary and practically sufficient, so they must be done however hard they are.
more: The four metrics measure difficulty, not importance. Smith's three essentials are both necessary and practically sufficient, so they must be done however hard they are. The danger is drifting toward easy, inconsequential problems that don't move the needle, as in the lamppost parable.

head: Scope vs. Strength
dek: Amit borrows Francis Fukuyama's distinction. Scope is how many things a state does, and strength is how well it does them.
more: Amit borrows Francis Fukuyama's distinction. Scope is how many things a state does, and strength is how well it does them. The Indian state is high on scope and low on strength. The four metrics explain why the fix is hard: the few things a state must do well are exactly the hardest ones, so the state has to narrow its scope to build strength.

head: The Two Exit Ramps from Hard Work
dek: Ajay's classification of how policymakers dodge the hard core. The first is welfareism: humanitarian projects that bring the satisfaction of having fed some children lunch without touching the hard problems.
more: Ajay's classification of how policymakers dodge the hard core. The first is welfareism: humanitarian projects that bring the satisfaction of having fed some children lunch without touching the hard problems. The second is the engineer's ramp: build an app or website, hold an inauguration, celebrate, and achieve nothing. In their book, Kelkar and Shah title a section 'Everybody Loves a Good IT System', riffing on P. Sainath.

head: Amit opens in the dark (
more: Amit opens in the dark ('I don't know if you can see us') and turns it into a parable: 'We are shrouded in darkness today. The light of freedom has gone out of our lives. Everyone thought intervention will show us a way... but instead it burnt everything to the ground and there is no power anymore.'

head: After Ajay says Lant Pritchett would agree that their extended version is better, Amit plugs his Seen and the Unseen episodes. Ajay now has fourteen
more: After Ajay says Lant Pritchett would agree that their extended version is better, Amit plugs his Seen and the Unseen episodes. Ajay now has fourteen, 'tied with our good friend Pranay Kotasthane... it's a good battle who's gonna win.'

head: Ajay says this kind of feasibility conversation is…
more: Ajay says this kind of feasibility conversation is 'conspicuously absent' in Indian public affairs. Amit: 'Actually, it is conspicuously absent only now that we have brought it to people's attention. Before this it was unconspicuously absent because nobody knew it was missing. Words matter.'

head: Amit uses the writing-workshop rule on Ajay to ask for examples
more: Amit uses the writing-workshop rule on Ajay to ask for examples: 'I'm gonna do the writer thing and tell you now. Don't tell me, show me, show, don't tell.'

head: Ajay's teacher-discretion example asks…
more: Ajay's teacher-discretion example asks 'Do I teach to the genius Amit Varma in my front row...?' Amit protests: 'I was always a backbencher... I never sat on a front bench.'

head: Amit, delighted with the difficulty table
more: Amit, delighted with the difficulty table: 'I want you to build tables like this for me in every area of my life, so all my decision making becomes easy.'

head: In the lamppost parable Amit stresses this is…
more: In the lamppost parable Amit stresses this is 'a good policeman in a country with rule of law' who helps 'with great humility and a sense of service'. He also declares that the tough, fuzzy problems are 'what a real man tries to solve and Lant Pritchett is a real man.'

head: Ajay on government IT launches
more: Ajay on government IT launches: 'you celebrate, you'll inaugurate it, nothing will get done... No one was saved. Eleanor Rigby.' Amit signs off: 'We've got a Beatles song about IT systems.'

head: Adam Smith, which Ajay calls one of the greatest quotes in economics
more: Adam Smith, which Ajay calls one of the greatest quotes in economics: 'little else is requisite to carry a state to the highest degree of opulence from the lowest barbarism, but peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice. All the rest being brought about by the natural course of things.'

head: P. Sainath's book
more: P. Sainath's book 'Everybody Loves a Good Drought', which Kelkar and Shah riff on in a section titled 'Everybody Loves a Good IT System'.

head: Yuen Yuen Ang's
more: Yuen Yuen Ang's 'Adaptive Political Economy' uses the same drunk-under-the-lamppost metaphor that Amit used to open his Lant Pritchett episode. Amit says she will be on The Seen and the Unseen once she finishes a very important book she is writing.

head: Brian Chesky Turns Up With the Camera
dek: When you have only a few customers, serve each one personally and build exactly what they ask for.
more: In Airbnb's early days, Brian Chesky visited individual hosts to see their places and what they were advertising. He noticed that the photos hosts took themselves looked bad, so he asked one host whether a button that sends a photographer to shoot the place would help. The host said yes. Chesky later called to say the button was live. The host clicked it, and the next day the doorbell rang. It was Chesky himself, holding a camera.

When you have only a few customers, serve each one personally and build exactly what they ask for. A hundred people who love the product make it good enough to spread on its own, and then scaling is easy.

head: Jan Koum's One-Dollar Speed Brake
dek: Slowing your own growth on purpose can be the right call. Delight the users you have before chasing the next stage.
more: In an interview, which Amit thinks was with Sam Altman, Jan Koum explained that early WhatsApp charged users a dollar because the team didn't want it to grow too fast. They wanted a user base they could handle and please: faster servers, more responsive customer service. They planned to expand only after getting things right for the users they already had.
Slowing your own growth on purpose can be the right call. Delight the users you have before chasing the next stage.

head: The Focus Group That Hated Seinfeld
dek: Focus groups and market surveys judge new things against what already exists, so they often reject the genuinely new.
more: In 1989 the Seinfeld pilot was shown to a test audience. One piece of feedback said no segment of the audience wanted to see the show again. Another said they didn't like Jerry's supporting ensemble, the cast that went on to become legendary. If the marketing people had won the argument, the show would never have been made.
Focus groups and market surveys judge new things against what already exists, so they often reject the genuinely new. The better the idea, the more people will tell you it can't work.

head: The Red Flag Law: Three Men per Car
dek: Transformative technologies look absurd at first. Before the car, the telephone was imagined as a tool for telegraph operators and the internet as a curiosity.
more: Early cars kept stalling after a few minutes, so each needed a 'stoker' to restart the engine. Cars were seen as toys for the rich, who also hired drivers. Britain then passed a law requiring three people per car: a stoker, a driver, and a man walking sixty metres ahead waving a red flag so horses and carriages wouldn't get into trouble. Amit adds that if Henry Ford had surveyed customers, people in transport would have asked for better-bred, faster horses.

Transformative technologies look absurd at first. Before the car, the telephone was imagined as a tool for telegraph operators and the internet as a curiosity. Naysayers judge the new by the old world's logic.
printed: Three men and a motor car

head: Forty-Minute Sessions on The Seen and the Unseen
dek: A small audience that engages deeply is worth more than a huge, shallow one, both in meaning and in what it can sustain commercially.
more: Amit used to say he would rather have a hundred thousand people download an episode than ten million watch a YouTube show, where average view times can be fifteen or twenty seconds. When he checked, the average session on The Seen and the Unseen was forty minutes, and people listened across multiple sessions. That kind of deep engagement is also why their courses can charge a premium and get it.
A small audience that engages deeply is worth more than a huge, shallow one, both in meaning and in what it can sustain commercially.

head: Google Began as a Puzzle, Not a Company
dek: You don't need a grand business vision at the start. Solve a problem that grips you and the business can emerge later.
more: Amit lists great companies that started as projects or hobbies. Yahoo began as a web directory for Stanford. Page and Brin started with PageRank, an intellectual challenge about how to do search better, and tried to sell it to other search engines like Excite. Jobs and Wozniak built computers as a hobby, and Facebook started in a dorm room.
You don't need a grand business vision at the start. Solve a problem that grips you and the business can emerge later.

head: A-B-C vs D-E-F: Advice to a Celebrity Friend
dek: Time is scarce, and longevity isn't immortality. Spend it on work that is uniquely yours, not on things others could do just as well.
more: Chatting with a very famous friend from the creator economy (unnamed), Amit broke down everything the friend does. Some of it, A-B-C, anyone could do. Some of it, D-E-F, only he could do, like a film he wrote: a love story set in Lucknow that is 'so much him'. Amit applies the same test to himself. He's glad the business show a channel offered him and Ajay didn't work out, because it wasn't something only they could do.
Time is scarce, and longevity isn't immortality. Spend it on work that is uniquely yours, not on things others could do just as well.

head: Buffett's Empty Calendar
dek: Saying no to things you don't want is easy. The real discipline is protecting your attention so it goes to the few things that matter.
more: Bill Gates and Warren Buffett, interviewed together, both named focus as their most important quality. Gates said one thing he learned from Buffett was how to say no. When Gates once asked Buffett to set up an event, Buffett opened his calendar and it was almost blank. Gates asked how he managed it.
Saying no to things you don't want is easy. The real discipline is protecting your attention so it goes to the few things that matter.

head: Andy Grove's Lesson Saves Dropbox's Focus
dek: Focus sometimes means abandoning good products you've already invested in, so you can get one thing right.
more: Drew Houston said Dropbox reached an inflection point where it was doing both video sharing and file sharing and was all over the place. He then read Andy Grove's 'Only the Paranoid Survive'. Grove describes how early Intel, struggling in the crowded memory-chip market with an opening in microprocessors, decided to go all in on one thing. Dropbox dropped the video side, including companies Amit recalls it had acquired, to focus.
Focus sometimes means abandoning good products you've already invested in, so you can get one thing right.
printed: All the chips in one basket

head: Seeing Like a State
dek: He cites Scott's line that 'the most powerful fertilizer is the tender gaze of an owner' to show how ownership brings out energy and competence that working to someone else's KRAs doesn't.
more: He cites Scott's line that 'the most powerful fertilizer is the tender gaze of an owner' to show how ownership brings out energy and competence that working to someone else's KRAs doesn't.
Ajay's first reason to start a business: you work at a higher level when you work for yourself.

head: The Nature of the Firm
dek: It explains how transaction costs made firms inevitable. Amit thinks Coase himself would recognise that this logic is now shifting toward gig work and webs of small startups.
more: It explains how transaction costs made firms inevitable. Amit thinks Coase himself would recognise that this logic is now shifting toward gig work and webs of small startups.
The paper discussed in the Four Papers episode.

head: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21 of EIE)
dek: That episode discussed the Middle Ages trading voyages, where entrepreneurs bet everything on one big voyage, the analogy Graham uses.
more: That episode discussed the Middle Ages trading voyages, where entrepreneurs bet everything on one big voyage, the analogy Graham uses.
Explaining Paul Graham's idea of a startup as compressing your working life.

head: Mark Zuckerberg on Peter Thiel's advice
dek: Zuckerberg names Thiel's line as the best advice he got: in a rapidly changing world, the biggest risk is not changing.
more: Zuckerberg names Thiel's line as the best advice he got: in a rapidly changing world, the biggest risk is not changing. That matters more than ever in an age of AI and automation.
Amit's second reason to start a business: the world is changing fast.

head: Naval Ravikant: 'The future will be almost all startups'
dek: Naval predicts most companies will be small startups of four or ten people that can scale to a billion dollars, a future that rewards nimble, entrepreneurial people.
more: Naval predicts most companies will be small startups of four or ten people that can scale to a billion dollars, a future that rewards nimble, entrepreneurial people.
On how work and firms will look in the future.

head: Paul Graham on compressing your working life
dek: Graham's frame: instead of working at low intensity for forty years, work at high intensity for four and give it everything.
more: Graham's frame: instead of working at low intensity for forty years, work at high intensity for four and give it everything.
On the intensity a business demands.

head: Brian Chesky on Graham's advice
dek: Chesky took Graham's words to heart at early Airbnb, including personally photographing a host's home.
more: Chesky took Graham's words to heart at early Airbnb, including personally photographing a host's home.
Illustrating 'better to be loved by a few than liked by many'.

head: Jerry Seinfeld on early naysayers
dek: The source of the story about the brutal focus-group feedback on the 1989 Seinfeld pilot.
more: The source of the story about the brutal focus-group feedback on the 1989 Seinfeld pilot.
Chapter on not listening to naysayers.

head: Steve Jobs hates consultants
dek: Jobs's rule was to hire the best people and ignore consultants, who have no skin in the game.
more: Jobs's rule was to hire the best people and ignore consultants, who have no skin in the game.
On whose advice to ignore.

head: Peter Thiel says trends are overrated
dek: Thiel treats buzzwords in a pitch as a red flag. A genuinely new idea doesn't need a buzzword, and often no buzzword fits it.
more: Thiel treats buzzwords in a pitch as a red flag. A genuinely new idea doesn't need a buzzword, and often no buzzword fits it.
Chapter on being internally driven rather than chasing market gaps.

head: Paul Graham says, Just Learn
dek: Start by learning and gaining domain expertise, and projects worth building will emerge from it.
more: Start by learning and gaining domain expertise, and projects worth building will emerge from it.
Advice for would-be founders.

head: Peter Thiel on working on problems that wouldn't get solved without you
dek: Amit reads it as a filter for scarce time: do what wouldn't exist if you didn't do it, at any scale, not just Mars missions.
more: Amit reads it as a filter for scarce time: do what wouldn't exist if you didn't do it, at any scale, not just Mars missions.
Using Musk and SpaceX as the example.

head: Sam Altman on focus
dek: 'Focus is a force multiplier on work': working on the right thing matters more than working many hours, and Altman has yet to meet a slow-moving person who is very successful.
more: 'Focus is a force multiplier on work': working on the right thing matters more than working many hours, and Altman has yet to meet a slow-moving person who is very successful.
Amit reads the quote in full.

head: Bill Gates and Warren Buffet on the best advice they got
dek: Both name focus as their most important quality. It's the source of the story of Buffett's nearly blank calendar.
more: Both name focus as their most important quality. It's the source of the story of Buffett's nearly blank calendar.
On focus.

head: Drew Houston on focus
dek: Houston describes how Dropbox dropped its video-sharing work to focus on one thing.
more: Houston describes how Dropbox dropped its video-sharing work to focus on one thing.
On focus.

head: Only the Paranoid Survive
dek: Grove describes Intel's move from a crowded memory-chip market to going all in, which is why it's useful for anyone torn between too many product lines.
more: Grove describes Intel's move from a crowded memory-chip market to going all in, which is why it's useful for anyone torn between too many product lines.
The book Drew Houston read at Dropbox's inflection point.

head: 'Action produces information' — Brian Armstrong
dek: Every action teaches you something. Armstrong's foggy-mountain image: wait for the fog to clear and you stay at the bottom forever.
more: Every action teaches you something. Armstrong's foggy-mountain image: wait for the fog to clear and you stay at the bottom forever.
Chapter on having a bias for action.

head: Testaments Betrayed
dek: Amit loves Kundera's image of a man in a fog who makes his road step by step; looking back, observers see the road but not the fog.
more: Amit loves Kundera's image of a man in a fog who makes his road step by step; looking back, observers see the road but not the fog.
Closing the episode.

head: The Art of Clear Writing
dek: An earlier example of charging a premium to a smaller, more committed audience.
more: An earlier example of charging a premium to a smaller, more committed audience.
Mentioned alongside Life Lessons.

head: The Tender Gaze of an Owner
dek: Ajay's first reason to start something: you work at a different level when it's yours.
more: Ajay's first reason to start something: you work at a different level when it's yours. Quality, clarity, precision, deadlines and competence all rise when you own the outcome instead of chasing someone else's KRAs.

head: Running a Business Makes You a Better Employee
dek: Even if you plan to stay an employee, running a business, even a side gig, teaches you what it's like to be the boss and owner.
more: Even if you plan to stay an employee, running a business, even a side gig, teaches you what it's like to be the boss and owner. You become less entitled and more empathetic when you return to a job.

head: Business as Hypothesis Testing
dek: Every business is a bundle of beliefs about the world, like 'buy this atta and Italian tomatoes and I can sell pizza at a profit'.
more: Every business is a bundle of beliefs about the world, like 'buy this atta and Italian tomatoes and I can sell pizza at a profit'. Trying it exposes the many things that go wrong and forces feedback loops, so you learn how the world actually works.

head: Change Before You Have To
dek: Amit's reasons to start a business. First, the default script of education, one career, CEO, retirement leaves you ossified, so that when the world changes nobody wants the one thing you can do.
more: Amit's reasons to start a business. First, the default script of education, one career, CEO, retirement leaves you ossified, so that when the world changes nobody wants the one thing you can do. Second, in an AI-driven, fast-changing world, Thiel's warning applies: not changing is the biggest risk. Coase's logic of the firm is weakening, so the future may belong to small startups and gig work, which reward nimble, entrepreneurial people.

head: Compress Your Working Life
dek: Paul Graham's view of a startup as a medieval trading voyage, where you bet everything on one big trip.
more: Paul Graham's view of a startup as a medieval trading voyage, where you bet everything on one big trip. Instead of working at low intensity for forty years, work at high intensity for four. Any successful business, big or small, demands intensity, passion and focus.

head: Detachment vs Full Commitment (the Hosts' Disagreement)
dek: Ajay sees business as a spectrum, from a side gig on Urban Company to a VC-funded IPO-bound firm.
more: Ajay sees business as a spectrum, from a side gig on Urban Company to a VC-funded IPO-bound firm. He favours side gigs run with detachment: low stakes, comfort with failure, many experiments. He notes that traders who love money most do worse because hunger clouds their thinking. Amit agrees detachment is a fine life philosophy, but argues traders earned it by first plunging in with full passion. He also thinks believing your detached 30% can beat someone else's all-in 100% is arrogant. Ajay replies that he assumes your 30% already reflects full mastery. Amit adds that Ajay's other reasons (becoming a better employee, learning about the world) are byproducts, not reasons to start a business.

head: Loved by a Few Beats Liked by Many
dek: Don't think about scale too early. Paul Graham: a hundred people who love your product beat a million who like it.
more: Don't think about scale too early. Paul Graham: a hundred people who love your product beat a million who like it. Talk to each early customer, build what they want, and the product gets good enough to spread. Deep engagement, like forty-minute podcast sessions, beats shallow reach and is what people will pay a premium for.

head: Ignore Naysayers and Advice Without Skin in the Game
dek: Our instinct when we hear something new is 'no, but', and Amit consciously checks this in himself.
more: Our instinct when we hear something new is 'no, but', and Amit consciously checks this in himself. Focus groups, the media, consultants and many VCs judge the new by old templates. The telephone, the internet and the car were all dismissed at first. Founders who live with an idea should take their own conviction more seriously than outside advice from people with no skin in the game.

head: Be Internally Driven: Start From Inside, Not From the Market
dek: Hunting for gaps in the market pushes you where everyone else is rushing, which leads to mediocrity, and buzzwords are a warning sign.
more: Hunting for gaps in the market pushes you where everyone else is rushing, which leads to mediocrity, and buzzwords are a warning sign. Instead, follow Graham's 'just learn': build domain expertise, follow your curiosity, and let a project emerge. Most great companies started as hobbies or intellectual puzzles.

head: Work on What Wouldn't Happen Without You
dek: Thiel's rule, which Amit reads in two ways. Doing what only you can do carries some hubris.
more: Thiel's rule, which Amit reads in two ways. Doing what only you can do carries some hubris. Doing what wouldn't exist if you didn't do it works at any scale, like The Seen and the Unseen. Ajay adds nuance: without Einstein, people would still have reached relativity bit by bit, but at a given moment one person or group with a creative fire makes the difference. Since time is scarce, spend it on what is uniquely yours.

head: Triage Your Ideas and Your Time
dek: Ajay borrows triage from emergency medicine. After a bomb blast, first responders sort victims into green (will survive anyway), black (will die) and red (where effort makes the most difference).
more: Ajay borrows triage from emergency medicine. After a bomb blast, first responders sort victims into green (will survive anyway), black (will die) and red (where effort makes the most difference). With a laptop full of half-page idea scribbles, he picks battles the same way: a few big, high-impact things only he can do. If you're doing work many others could do, you probably aren't delegating enough.

head: Focus Means Saying No to Things You Love
dek: Altman calls focus a force multiplier, and Gates and Buffett both name it as their key quality.
more: Altman calls focus a force multiplier, and Gates and Buffett both name it as their key quality. Saying no to things you dislike is easy. The hard part, as Jobs told Ive, is refusing things you love that don't fit your chosen priority. Grove's Intel and Houston's Dropbox both went all in on one thing.

head: Bias for Action: The Man in the Fog
dek: Life is a trade-off between getting it done and getting it right, and too many people never stop planning.
more: Life is a trade-off between getting it done and getting it right, and too many people never stop planning. Action produces information: launch, learn and refine until a hundred people love it. Kundera's man in the fog makes his road step by step. People who see past journeys as clearly mapped are falling for hindsight bias; everyone looking ahead is in fog, and the only way through is to move forward.
printed: A road made step by step

head: The cold open: Amit translates Bruce Springsteen lyrics into Hindi for Ajay to identify, including Brilliant Disguise, a song from The River (
more: The cold open: Amit translates Bruce Springsteen lyrics into Hindi for Ajay to identify, including Brilliant Disguise, a song from The River ('Great double album') and If I Should Fall Behind, then Thunder Road at Ajay's request. Before one lyric (the intro chapter is titled 'Eh, Chhoti Ladki!'), he warns: 'This is kinda creepy actually when you think about these lyrics, it could get you cancelled.' Ajay's verdict on another: 'It's gorgeous in Hindi.' Amit afterwards: 'So now we are done with the tough part of the show.'

head: Amit on quoting Bob Dylan's
more: Amit on quoting Bob Dylan's 'he not busy being born is busy dying' so often that 'even Dylan must be fed up', before announcing he'll find new quotes by looking 'down into my iPad unabashedly.'

head: Amit's summary of the standard life script
more: Amit's summary of the standard life script: 'we become vice president, we become CEO, hopefully, and then we retire, and then we get dementia and then we die.'

head: Amit, after asking Ajay if he's watched Seinfeld
more: Amit, after asking Ajay if he's watched Seinfeld: 'between us, I want to assure you, we have watched Seinfeld an average number of times because I've probably watched it twice as much as the normal person.'

head: On the business-channel show they didn't do because it wasn't uniquely theirs
more: On the business-channel show they didn't do because it wasn't uniquely theirs: 'Though if somebody comes with a shit ton of money, we are still open to it, but a shit ton of money only.'

head: Amit's twist on Lincoln's
more: Amit's twist on Lincoln's 'Give me six hours to chop a tree and I'll spend the first four sharpening the axe': 'Too many of us spend the first four thousand hours sharpening the axe.'

head: Peter Thiel's buzzword detector, via Amit: anything trendy
more: Peter Thiel's buzzword detector, via Amit: anything trendy 'is generally full of shit'. Big data, cloud computing, blockchain or AI/machine learning in a pitch means 'chances are it's full of shit.'

head: The show notes' sign-off
more: The show notes' sign-off: 'If you don't start a business after this, you are doomed! Start! Now!' Amit adds that if you start one before the next episode, 'I will be so happy.'

head: Amit's anti-comfort-zone quotes: Benjamin Franklin's
more: Amit's anti-comfort-zone quotes: Benjamin Franklin's 'When you're finished changing, you're finished', Neale Donald Walsch's 'Life begins at the end of your comfort zone', and John A. Shedd ('with the double D'): 'A ship in harbor is safe, but that is not what ships are for.' Amit notes that Ajay is a fan of ships, not of harbours and safety.

head: Jack Welch
more: Jack Welch: 'Change before you have to.'

head: Henry Ford and the faster horses: had Ford surveyed customers, people in transportation would have asked for…
more: Henry Ford and the faster horses: had Ford surveyed customers, people in transportation would have asked for 'better bred horses, faster horses', not a car.

head: Amit wonders whether Brian Armstrong's foggy-mountain metaphor came from Milan Kundera's
more: Amit wonders whether Brian Armstrong's foggy-mountain metaphor came from Milan Kundera's 'man in a fog' passage in Testaments Betrayed.

head: Musk Prices a Battery From Scratch
dek: Conventional wisdom is often a stale snapshot. Either it took a limited view, or it was right once and the world moved on.
more: Experts said batteries couldn't get much cheaper. Market forces and the best scientists had already done their work, so only small gains were left. Musk broke a battery down into its material constituents. He worked out how much of each went into a pack, what each cost on the spot markets and what assembly cost. By the time of the interview he had cut costs from $600 to $80 per kilowatt hour. Amit contrasts this with Ajay's advice, in an earlier episode, to respect experts in complicated fields.

Conventional wisdom is often a stale snapshot. Either it took a limited view, or it was right once and the world moved on. Rebuilding a problem from its raw ingredients is how you catch that lag, and Amit argues all progress comes from doing so.

head: Larry Page Demos PageRank to Excite
dek: When users struggle, saying 'you're using it wrong' is the founder's Kool-Aid talking.
more: Aravind Srinivas recalls a Larry Page interview. Page tried to sell his PageRank technology to Excite, then one of the big search engines. In the demo, searching 'university' with his tech brought up Harvard and Stanford, while Excite returned random junk. The Excite executive said nobody types 'university'; a proper user would ask for the best Ivy League university in America. Page said that was blaming the user. Years later, Srinivas's mother complained that Perplexity wasn't giving her what she wanted. He was about to tell her to fix the grammar of her question, then stopped himself.
When users struggle, saying 'you're using it wrong' is the founder's Kool-Aid talking. The customer's confusion is feedback on the product, not a flaw in the customer.

head: Phil Knight and the Guy Under the Lamp Post
dek: 'Just Do It' is about doing, not winning. A brand that stands beside your perseverance is selling a story about who you are, not sneakers.
more: Simon Sinek recalls a conference where Phil Knight asked everyone who runs to stand. He then asked people to sit down in stages: first those who don't run weekly, then those who don't run twice a week. Finally only those who run three times a week, rain or shine, whether they feel good or bad, were left standing, just a handful. Knight told them that the next time they are out before dawn, wet and miserable and still running, the guy under the lamp post cheering them on is Nike.
'Just Do It' is about doing, not winning. A brand that stands beside your perseverance is selling a story about who you are, not sneakers.
printed: Just do it, in the dark

head: Bill Gates Pulled the Radio Out of His Car
dek: Obsession in practice means designing distractions out of your life. Amit borrows Apoorva Mehta's definition: the company is the last thing you think about at night and the first thing in the morning.
more: Mike Moritz was being driven to the airport by Bill Gates, probably in the early eighties by Amit's guess. He noticed the slot where the car radio should be was empty and asked if it had been stolen. Gates said he had taken it out himself. Amit pairs this with Jensen Huang, who doesn't wear a watch because 'now is the most important time.'

Obsession in practice means designing distractions out of your life. Amit borrows Apoorva Mehta's definition: the company is the last thing you think about at night and the first thing in the morning.

head: BillDesk's Three Founders in One Room
dek: Founder structure can follow temperament rather than template. Humility plus genuine interest in the argument can make shared leadership work where ego would break it.
more: Ajay's friend Ajay Kaushal co-founded BillDesk, a very successful Indian firm. Its big exit got snarled up by Indian government delays; otherwise it would have been one of the biggest exits in Indian history. Its three co-founders sit in one room and argue over every important decision together, and none of them wants to be sole CEO. They did this with zero employees and still do it with ten thousand. Ajay credits Kaushal's quiet, unassuming, idea-first character. Amit calls it an outlier, but a lesson to think for yourself rather than follow 'have one CEO' as a hard rule.
Founder structure can follow temperament rather than template. Humility plus genuine interest in the argument can make shared leadership work where ego would break it.

head: Nonstop Dan's Phantom Vegan Meal on Air India
dek: This is Bezos's 'optimise for truth-telling' in miniature.
more: Nonstop Dan pays his own way to review business and first class, and Amit has twice picked an airline on his advice. Dan praised Air India's new business class: higher walls, more privacy, a door you can close. But his pre-ordered special meal (vegan, Amit thinks) was never loaded. The crew insisted the regular menu dish, with cheese in it, was his vegan meal. A superior came over and seemed just as lost, and the same thing happened at the second meal. Amit's right answer: apologise, admit the meal was forgotten, offer options from other cabins, and make it up to him afterwards.

This is Bezos's 'optimise for truth-telling' in miniature. The reflex to cover up rather than admit ignorance can be dangerous in service, and Amit sees the same habit in people who give street directions they don't actually know.

head: Stripe Turned a Seven-Day Integration Into Five Minutes
dek: Simplicity is subtraction. A grand mission becomes concrete through the ruthless removal of friction for the user.
more: When e-commerce was taking off, integrating PayPal into a website took about seven days and a hundred-page manual, sometimes with a dedicated team. Stripe, chasing its mission to 'increase the GDP of the internet', stripped out every unnecessary feature and process. You paste a snippet of embed code, test it once, and you're done. Amit has seen this himself while setting up payments for his courses.
Simplicity is subtraction. A grand mission becomes concrete through the ruthless removal of friction for the user.

head: Bezos's 30-Page Plan He Knew Was BS
dek: The plan is worthless but the planning is not. Writing at length about the future forces long-term, clarified thinking.
more: Bezos wrote a 30-page business plan for Amazon to show investors. He knew it would fall apart on contact with reality, and so did the VCs. Amit pairs it with Mike Tyson's line about everyone having a plan until they get punched in the face.
The plan is worthless but the planning is not. Writing at length about the future forces long-term, clarified thinking. The same logic underlies Eric Schmidt's case for five-year plans inside firms.

head: The Founder Who Turned His Hires Into Co-Founders
dek: The people worth hiring are those who already act like owners. They question the task, suggest better ways, and tell the founder when he's wrong.
more: A friend of the hosts started a company in Bangalore as more or less a solopreneur. He then hired a CTO and one other person. He was so impressed by their commitment, insight and passion that he gave them equal shares and made them co-founders. Amit notes you don't have to go that far, since there are other ways to reward early employees.
The people worth hiring are those who already act like owners. They question the task, suggest better ways, and tell the founder when he's wrong.

head: Amit Discovers He Works Like a Lion
dek: Seeing a 'flaw' as evolved hardware removes the moral shame and points to practical workarounds.
more: In Eisenhower's matrix, Amit has long lamented living in two quadrants: 'not important, not urgent' or 'important and urgent' (deadlines, shoots, releases). He rarely reaches 'important, not urgent', where reading and learning happen. Tim Urban wrote about the same dilemma. Naval Ravikant's 'work like a lion' reframed it for him. A lion sleeps most of the day and then sprints for the kill, and humans shaped in the hunter-gatherer age are similar. Focus burns calories, so distraction conserves energy for the hunt. His fix is to accept the wiring and use hacks like calendarising to turn important-not-urgent tasks into urgent ones.
Seeing a 'flaw' as evolved hardware removes the moral shame and points to practical workarounds. This is the Life Lessons idea of amplifying good wiring and mitigating bad wiring.

head: Paul Graham's essays
dek: Graham takes months over each essay and gathers feedback from friends.
more: Graham takes months over each essay and gathers feedback from friends. The essays are models of simple, elegant, clear writing, and offer frameworks for life and humanity, not just business.
Amit's closing recommendation, given before and repeated here.

head: Specialist for the Project, Generalist for the Company
dek: Following Sam Altman, Amit says a project can be driven by deep specialism, as Page and Brin's PageRank was.
more: Following Sam Altman, Amit says a project can be driven by deep specialism, as Page and Brin's PageRank was. Once it becomes a company, the founder must step back and think broadly. Ajay adds that missions like 'organise the world's information' open you to adjacencies, and warns that VCs often try to keep founders tied to the last pitch deck. Amit recalls Vinod Khosla's claim that most VCs add negative value, which puts the burden on founders to do their own learning.

head: Leadership Is Strategy, Not Execution
dek: Ajay argues that the highest-level work in any firm is strategy: who are we, what are our capabilities, what amazing things can we do that the world will like?
more: Ajay argues that the highest-level work in any firm is strategy: who are we, what are our capabilities, what amazing things can we do that the world will like? Execution orders flow down from that. Leaders must keep re-evaluating and changing their minds, so thinking like a founder makes even employees better.
printed: What do they know of X?

head: First-Principles Thinking
dek: Don't inherit assumptions; rebuild the problem from its fundamentals. Conventional thinking lags reality.
more: Don't inherit assumptions; rebuild the problem from its fundamentals. Conventional thinking lags reality. Sometimes it took a limited view, sometimes it was right once and the world changed.

head: Obsess Over Customers, Not Competitors, and Act Small
dek: Start inward-driven, but once the business exists the customer is everything.
more: Start inward-driven, but once the business exists the customer is everything. Bezos ignored competitors and focused on what won't change: people will always want lower prices, better value and faster delivery. Never blame the user for your product's failures. Garry Tan adds: when you're small, act small. Don't mimic big-company polish; use your size to talk to every customer.

head: Product Over Marketing
dek: A great product spreads by word of mouth, and your tribe will find you.
more: A great product spreads by word of mouth, and your tribe will find you. Amit admits there may be an optimum of 5–10% marketing, but he won't spend bandwidth finding it. The real danger is that a marketing mindset takes over your thinking and pulls you toward the lowest common denominator and short-term gratification. Naval applies the same logic to people: networking is personal marketing, so do great work instead.
printed: The tax on a dull product

head: A Mission Bigger Than Yourself
dek: Examples include Sony ('make Japan known for quality again'), Google ('organise the world's information'), Stripe ('increase the GDP of the internet'), Nike (be with people when they do, not only when they win) and NVIDIA (grow the pond instead of fighting in it).
more: Examples include Sony ('make Japan known for quality again'), Google ('organise the world's information'), Stripe ('increase the GDP of the internet'), Nike (be with people when they do, not only when they win) and NVIDIA (grow the pond instead of fighting in it). A big mission keeps you energised. Ajay adds that it also shapes recruitment: narrow bean-counter firms attract average people, while audacious ones attract remarkable people, as Apple's love of beauty attracted the best designers.

head: Long-Term Commitment as the Last Arbitrage
dek: When everyone optimises for the next quarter, thinking in decades is your edge, and it attracts a different calibre of people.
more: When everyone optimises for the next quarter, thinking in decades is your edge, and it attracts a different calibre of people. Hold the vision firmly but change tactics daily as reality pushes back. Plans, whether Bezos's 30 pages or Schmidt's five years, matter for the thinking they force, not the document.

head: Incentives Beat Exhortations: Rethink HR
dek: Ajay notes that bosses preach long-term thinking while HR pays bonuses on narrow, one-quarter KPIs, which teaches people to shut up and execute.
more: Ajay notes that bosses preach long-term thinking while HR pays bonuses on narrow, one-quarter KPIs, which teaches people to shut up and execute. He calls short-termism the bane of India. His fix is to speak in compounding numbers that excite people, like 5x in five years or 10x in ten. That pushes managers to ask what a ten-times bigger firm needs and to invest in the foundations of growth, instead of squeezing a bit more profit from existing capabilities.

head: The Glory of Capitalism Is in Large Firms
dek: Ajay argues that the top twenty thousand non-financial firms essentially are the Indian economy.
more: Ajay argues that the top twenty thousand non-financial firms essentially are the Indian economy. Scale buys the resources for subtle refinements of product, process and productivity. The puzzle is keeping a small firm's hunger, imagination and strategic thinking once you have ten thousand people. Amit counters with Naval's vision of tiny teams doing what giant firms do. Ajay replies that this will hold in a few industries, but operations like Britannia's will always be vast and complex.

head: Choosing Co-Founders
dek: You'll spend more time with your co-founder than your spouse, so closeness is an asset.
more: You'll spend more time with your co-founder than your spouse, so closeness is an asset. Look for intelligence, energy and above all integrity. Preserve the relationship over winning arguments. Prefer a single CEO so decisions don't stall, but treat even that as a default to reason about, not a law.

head: Disagreement as Joint Model-Building
dek: Ajay's addition: the best partnerships bring different knowledge and viewpoints, and both people update on each other's evidence (Bayesian updating).
more: Ajay's addition: the best partnerships bring different knowledge and viewpoints, and both people update on each other's evidence (Bayesian updating). The point of arguing isn't the single decision but jointly building a better theory of the world and of the firm, so later decisions keep improving. People too sure of themselves to update have a serious character flaw.

head: Hire A-Players for Values, Not Credentials
dek: Hire for values first, aptitude second, skill third. A-list people pick what excites them over the best salary, and they attract more A-list people.
more: Hire for values first, aptitude second, skill third. A-list people pick what excites them over the best salary, and they attract more A-list people. Hire people who think like co-founders, and don't fear hiring people smarter than you. Ajay's caution: 'best' means knowledge, character and connection with the world, not IIT or IIM badges.

head: Hard Work Is Non-Negotiable
dek: Mandated 70-hour weeks are wrong, but there's no route to excellence without hard work you choose.
more: Mandated 70-hour weeks are wrong, but there's no route to excellence without hard work you choose. Momentum energises; Amit thinks burnout comes more from worrying, procrastinating and overthinking. Aim for work-life harmony and go where the energy is. Huang's distinction is that work won't always bring joy, but love for the mission sustains it.

head: Optimise for Truth-Telling
dek: We evolved as social animals to get along, and in a tribe a truth-teller could be clubbed to death.
more: We evolved as social animals to get along, and in a tribe a truth-teller could be clubbed to death. So by default organisations drift toward deference up the hierarchy and politeness among peers. Firms must build mechanisms against this, like Bezos's 'disagree and commit'. Amit links failures like Kodak, which sat on digital photography, partly to truth not travelling upward.

head: The Imperial Firm's Information Problem
dek: Ajay calls information the central crisis of firms. Knowledge about customers in each locale and the best way to produce there exists inside the firm, but in large 'imperial' firms it doesn't bubble up.
more: Ajay calls information the central crisis of firms. Knowledge about customers in each locale and the best way to produce there exists inside the firm, but in large 'imperial' firms it doesn't bubble up. A top team convinced it has the one right answer for the whole world pushes orders down and stops listening, and productivity suffers.

head: Simplicity and Beauty
dek: Examples include Robinhood's one screen, one button, one action and Stripe's five-minute integration.
more: Examples include Robinhood's one screen, one button, one action and Stripe's five-minute integration. SpaceX's Raptor 3 looked like a toy next to the 'Christmas tree' Raptor 1, yet was lighter and more powerful. A pen design has gone unchanged since 1955, and Picasso's bulls were distilled to a few lines. Beauty travels with simplicity: Amit, once an Apple sceptic, now concedes the value of its aesthetic.

head: Professional Pride in the Unseen 99%
dek: Following Bezos, most of your work will never be seen by anyone, so take pride in it anyway.
more: Following Bezos, most of your work will never be seen by anyone, so take pride in it anyway. Excellence is a habit that builds up from small things into big ones; there is no separate moment when you do 'big things'. Ajay's coda: be humble and self-effacing as a person, but put everything into your work and stand by it.

head: The Inner Scorecard
dek: Buffett's father's lesson: judge yourself by your own values, not by money, success or what people write about you.
more: Buffett's father's lesson: judge yourself by your own values, not by money, success or what people write about you. Ask whether you were true to your values, told friends the truth when they needed it, and walked your own path. This applies to life and to the company you build.

head: Business as a Home for Great Thinkers
dek: Amit, a literature student who once would have been surprised to hear himself say this, argues that many of today's finest thinkers come from business, such as Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant and Peter Thiel.
more: Amit, a literature student who once would have been surprised to hear himself say this, argues that many of today's finest thinkers come from business, such as Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant and Peter Thiel. Business is now a route to both making money and changing the world, because a business can only succeed by creating value for people and, at scale, for society.

head: Mike Tyson's
more: Mike Tyson's 'Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face', which Ajay supplies when Amit fumbles it, used to frame Bezos's admittedly BS business plan.

head: On Eric Schmidt's advice to make five-year plans
more: On Eric Schmidt's advice to make five-year plans: 'Now you and I, Ajay Shah, are not quite fans of five year plans in an Indian economy context.' Amit's distinction: economies can't be centrally planned, but companies can.

head: Amit quizzes Ajay on his favourite Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song, fishing for…
more: Amit quizzes Ajay on his favourite Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young song, fishing for 'Teach Your Children' to segue into choosing co-founders. Ajay offers 'Helpless' and 'Southern Cross' and calls 'Teach Your Children' 'okay, little cliched'. Amit: 'See, we don't script anything.'
