head: After Ajay's story about BillDesk's Ajay Kaushal
more: After Ajay's story about BillDesk's Ajay Kaushal: 'Ajays are awesome. I'm not so sure about Shahs or Amits for that matter.'

head: Amit on credentials
more: Amit on credentials: 'I of course have no credentials, which is despite that Ajay came with me, so he's living the dream. But Ajay has credentials. He is IIT, he has foreign PhD.'

head: Defending startup founders from Ajay's
more: Defending startup founders from Ajay's 'dollar signs' jab: 'You use terms like tech bro disparagingly. Yes, of course, in every community, most people are assholes, that's Sturgeon's law.'

head: Amit to Ajay, a Britannia board member
more: Amit to Ajay, a Britannia board member: 'Are biscuits healthy?' Ajay, diplomatically: 'Some Britannia biscuits are worth eating.'

head: Narayana Murthy's 70-hour work week. Amit: mandatory, he completely disapproves; voluntary
more: Narayana Murthy's 70-hour work week. Amit: mandatory, he completely disapproves; voluntary, 'Every hour of my week when I'm not sleeping could be towards that because that is how obsessive I am.'

head: Brian Armstrong's
more: Brian Armstrong's 'Action produces information', carried over from the last episode to link a fixed vision with flexible tactics.

head: On the Indian habit of pretending to know
more: On the Indian habit of pretending to know: ask someone for directions and even if they don't know, they'll confidently point you right, then left, to some paanwala. Amit's coda: 'Not the last part.'

head: Amit's carve-out from radical truth-telling
more: Amit's carve-out from radical truth-telling: 'If your lady love says, Am I looking fat in this dress? Ajay Shah, there is only one answer.'

head: Professional pride, applied: Amit boasts that the bacon and sourdough he made for the crew the night before
more: Professional pride, applied: Amit boasts that the bacon and sourdough he made for the crew the night before 'was the best bacon and sourdough ever made in these climes in which we record.'

head: The marketing-hater's sign-off
more: The marketing-hater's sign-off: 'send them to all your friends, like, subscribe, and whatever else you're supposed to say. Did I just say I will never do marketing? I will never do marketing, don't bother.'

head: The Baroda Pipe Network
dek: This is what manufacturing looks like at its best: specialised firms sitting close together and feeding each other.
more: In the Baroda region, Ajay saw a chemical industry complex where several private factories run pipes directly to each other. One factory's output flows through a pipe into the next factory. A meter measures how much has flowed, and the supplier invoices on that basis. No trucks, no handling, no friction.

This is what manufacturing looks like at its best: specialised firms sitting close together and feeding each other. Albert Hirschman called these 'linkages'. They are also why manufacturing is fragile in India. If even a few links in such a network fail, the whole ecosystem loses its advantage.

head: Ten Power Cuts a Day, 70 km From Bombay
dek: India's electricity problem shows up close to its richest city, not just in remote corners.
more: The episode was recorded in rural Maharashtra, about 70 km from Bombay, where the power trips around ten times a day. Ajay asks how a factory could run like that. It can't, so every manufacturer buys a generator. That raises capital costs, and running a factory on diesel is ruinously expensive. Power from the grid is overpriced too, because commercial and industrial users subsidise farmers, households and electricity thieves.

India's electricity problem shows up close to its richest city, not just in remote corners. Each outage becomes a hidden tax on manufacturing: generators to buy, diesel to burn, and a cross-subsidy built into every grid bill.

head: Infosys, the Import Licence and the Outdated Disk Drive
dek: The licence raj was not just ideologically mistaken. It could not work in practice in industries where technology changes faster than files move through ministries.
more: Amit reads an anecdote from Montek Singh Ahluwalia's memoir 'Backstage'. In 1983 Infosys wanted to import a Data General MV 8000 computer with three 200 MB disk drives. Getting the import licence took several trips to New Delhi. By the time it came through, a 300 MB drive had come out that was 30% cheaper. The licence named the exact model number, so Infosys had to make more trips to Delhi just to amend it.

The licence raj was not just ideologically mistaken. It could not work in practice in industries where technology changes faster than files move through ministries. For exporters racing to deliver on time, these delays were fatal.

head: How India Fell From 25% to 2% of World Manufacturing
dek: The usual villain-only story misses the role of technological obsolescence.
more: In 1750 India produced about 20-25% of the world's manufacturing output, all of it artisanal. By 1900 that share was about 2%. One narrative, voiced by Dadabhai Naoroji in the British Parliament, blames colonialism: cheap machine-made Manchester textiles destroyed Indian weavers. Historians such as Tirthankar Roy point to a bigger cause. The Industrial Revolution wiped out handloom workers even in countries that were never colonised. Some industrialisation did begin from the 1850s: textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad, jute mills in Bengal, and Tata Iron and Steel in 1907. Manufacturing's share of output roughly doubled from 3.8% in 1913 to 7.5% at Independence. Even so, only about 2.5 million of India's 350 million people worked in it.

The usual villain-only story misses the role of technological obsolescence. India's deeper bad luck was industrialising late. That left a thin manufacturing base for the new state to build on, and it then made things worse.
printed: From a quarter of the world to 2%

head: How Frameworks (howframeworks.com)
dek: It offers frameworks to grow a business, turn it around or take it to the next level.
more: It offers frameworks to grow a business, turn it around or take it to the next level. Amit says these come from a lifetime of experience in Indian conditions, not consultant talk or bookish theory. Amit doesn't run a business and still spent hours going down the rabbit hole, because the frameworks also apply to how individuals live. The code 'seen unseen' gets listeners a discount; Amit takes no commission.

Amit's recommendation at the end of the episode. It is a new venture by Sudhir Sarnobat, a guest on Episode 419 of The Seen and the Unseen, set up with a partner whom Amit calls a legend among Maharashtra's entrepreneurs.

head: Modern Times
dek: The film captures the mental image most people carry when they hear 'economic development'.
more: The film captures the mental image most people carry when they hear 'economic development'. The episode then examines and questions that image.
Ajay uses it to describe the popular dream of manufacturing: vast factories with tens of thousands of workers sitting obediently on an assembly line.

head: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
dek: Friedman explains the core point clearly: a minimum wage does not raise a low-productivity worker's pay to the legal floor.
more: Friedman explains the core point clearly: a minimum wage does not raise a low-productivity worker's pay to the legal floor. It makes their job illegal, so their wage drops to zero.
Amit shows the video on screen while explaining why minimum wage laws backfire.

head: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Episode 55, Everything is Everything)
dek: That episode showed that big infrastructure gains brought no comparable rise in FDI, manufacturing exports or manufacturing jobs.
more: That episode showed that big infrastructure gains brought no comparable rise in FDI, manufacturing exports or manufacturing jobs. Ajay therefore argues infrastructure is no longer the binding constraint.
Cited when Ajay reaches infrastructure on his list of twelve problems.

head: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21, Everything is Everything)
dek: Manufacturing needs a lot of capital for land, machines and working capital.
more: Manufacturing needs a lot of capital for land, machines and working capital. Understanding finance is a prerequisite for seeing why the cost of capital matters so much.
Mentioned in the finance section of Ajay's twelve problems.

head: The Journey of Indian Finance (Episode 71, Everything is Everything)
dek: It tells the story of which Indian financial reforms got done and which didn't.
more: It tells the story of which Indian financial reforms got done and which didn't. Ajay says there is no hard political reason not to finish them, and cheaper capital would transform manufacturing.
Ajay says this episode matters 'more importantly' than the Beauty of Finance one for the manufacturing question.

head: The Journey of Indian Finance
dek: The written roadmap of the unfinished financial-reform agenda.
more: The written roadmap of the unfinished financial-reform agenda.
Ajay notes the paper is available on the XKDR Forum website.

head: Bimal Patel's talk at the Emerging Markets Conference
dek: Patel lays out one unifying theme for urban planning: around 40% of land should go to streets and parks, with a mechanism for money to flow back into urban infrastructure.
more: Patel lays out one unifying theme for urban planning: around 40% of land should go to streets and parks, with a mechanism for money to flow back into urban infrastructure. Ajay wants manufacturing built into that kind of planning.
Ajay calls it 'this great talk' while arguing that factories must be part of urban planning.

head: Three Numbers That Show Indian Manufacturing Is Broken
dek: First, manufacturing has been stuck at 15-20% of GDP for 30 years. Countries in the middle stage of development typically reach 40-50%.
more: First, manufacturing has been stuck at 15-20% of GDP for 30 years. Countries in the middle stage of development typically reach 40-50%. Second, manufacturing's share of employment is small and not rising. Third, and most starkly, goods exports grew from $319 billion to $442 billion in a decade. That is 38% in nominal dollars, or roughly 0.5% a year in real terms. Services exports grew from $151 billion to $341 billion over the same period, a 126% rise.

head: Why Services Escaped and Manufacturing Didn't
dek: Amit's simple answer: IT services were new, and the state was caught off guard.
more: Amit's simple answer: IT services were new, and the state was caught off guard. No decades-old regulations were waiting for them. Manufacturing inherited a long legacy of oppressive rules. Ajay's checklist adds the structural reasons. Factories are visible, while services hide in office buildings. Manufacturing depends on dense local networks of suppliers, while services connect over fibre. Manufacturing needs land, machines and working capital, while services rent. Factories need reliable electricity. They must move physical goods, while services move electrons. They pay back over 5-7 years rather than 1-2. And they depend on a dense web of enforceable contracts.

head: State Legibility: Factories Are Sitting Ducks
dek: Ajay borrows James C. Scott's idea of 'legibility' from Seeing Like a State.
more: Ajay borrows James C. Scott's idea of 'legibility' from Seeing Like a State. A factory is big and visible, so everyone can find it. Local goons demand protection money for trucks to pass, neighbours demand funding for pujas or schools, and every kind of inspector turns up to extort. A services firm sits on one floor of a building that looks like every other, among many firms, with no single visible owner. In a weak rule-of-law environment, being visible is a liability.

head: When Linkages Become a Disability
dek: Albert Hirschman argued that manufacturing's strength lies in linkages: specialised firms buying from and selling to each other nearby.
more: Albert Hirschman argued that manufacturing's strength lies in linkages: specialised firms buying from and selling to each other nearby. Ajay imagines twenty friends planning interlinked factories within 10 km of each other near Nashik. In India, something trips up five of the ten: a labour-law problem, a bank, a local politician. The network never comes together. Services avoid this because they connect over fibre and are indifferent to location.

head: The Cathedral of Complexity Needs Contract Enforcement
dek: Global manufacturing runs on just-in-time supply. If a supplier fails to deliver 5,000 ball bearings on the agreed day, the whole assembly line stops.
more: Global manufacturing runs on just-in-time supply. If a supplier fails to deliver 5,000 ball bearings on the agreed day, the whole assembly line stops. The common-law remedy is for courts to quickly calculate liquidated damages and impose them. That lets the manufacturer recover the penalties foreign buyers impose on it. It also deters sloppiness, so suppliers move heaven and earth to deliver, even getting trucks through a political bandh. Without enforcement, firms hoard inventory or deal only with family and trusted contacts, and their competitiveness erodes.

head: Manufacturing Is High-Skill, Not Low-Skill
dek: Ajay rejects the idea that manufacturing is a dumb, unskilled activity.
more: Ajay rejects the idea that manufacturing is a dumb, unskilled activity. A world-class export operation might hire 10,000 workers at 8,000 rupees a month. It also needs 1,000 more capable people, 100 super-capable ones and 20 global geniuses, and much of that talent doesn't exist in India yet. Sri Lanka, for example, is ahead in garment-making expertise. So India must make it effortless for companies to hire foreigners.

head: Nehru's Forgivable Mistakes, Indira's Unforgivable Ones
dek: Nehru followed the fashion of the times. The Soviet Union then looked like a success, though Amit says it was mainly a public relations one.
more: Nehru followed the fashion of the times. The Soviet Union then looked like a success, though Amit says it was mainly a public relations one. His two big mistakes were import substitution, which cut India's share of world trade from about 2% in 1947 to 0.5% by 1990, and Mahalanobis's belief that competition is wasteful. Meanwhile Hong Kong's export income in the 1960s equalled India's entire income. By 1965 the model was visibly failing, yet India went further down the same road. Amit lists the licence raj, the MRTP Act against large firms, small-scale industry reservations, FERA criminalising foreign capital, and the Industrial Disputes Act. The 1970s, when India's cheap labour could have made it a manufacturing superpower, were lost.

head: Why India's MSMEs Are Mostly Micro
dek: Under the Industrial Disputes Act, a firm with 100 or more workers needed government permission to fire anyone, and in practice permission was impossible to get.
more: Under the Industrial Disputes Act, a firm with 100 or more workers needed government permission to fire anyone, and in practice permission was impossible to get. Other rules kicked in at 10 and 20 workers. Firms responded by staying at 9, 19 or 99 employees and splitting into separate units to grow. The threshold was recently raised to 300, which Amit still calls absurd. The 'small' and 'medium' in MSME barely exist. Laws meant to protect workers end up hurting them. Amit adds that big companies aren't bad: large profits mean a firm serves many people well at scale.

head: Minimum Wages and Unions Hurt the Poor
dek: Take a worker whose labour is worth 8,000 rupees. A 13,000-rupee minimum wage doesn't raise his pay.
more: Take a worker whose labour is worth 8,000 rupees. A 13,000-rupee minimum wage doesn't raise his pay. It makes his job illegal, so he earns zero. The job he took was his best available option, and in a competitive market a rival employer would pay more if his work were worth more. Ajay describes it as the state using its monopoly of violence to block a voluntary deal between consenting adults. One result is capital-intensive garment factories in a country with mass unemployment. Ajay also notes that unions are a form of market power, a market failure the state should counteract rather than entrench.

head: Factories Are an Urban-Planning Problem
dek: A village of 150 households has about 750 people, perhaps 300 of working age, and at most about 100 would go to one factory.
more: A village of 150 households has about 750 people, perhaps 300 of working age, and at most about 100 would go to one factory. A globally competitive plant needs well over 2,000 workers. A factory with 10,000 machines also needs maintenance vendors and managers, and those people need offices, homes and schools for their children. So factories belong near cities, built into planning with higher FSI for multi-storey plants and matching road and rail links. Ajay finds the Chinese dormitory model deeply dissatisfying. He also notes that land prices look like a China-style bubble.

head: Electricity's Double Whammy
dek: Commercial and industrial users are overcharged for grid power to subsidise agriculture, free household units and outright theft.
more: Commercial and industrial users are overcharged for grid power to subsidise agriculture, free household units and outright theft. Supply is also unreliable. Then Europe, the UK and others are introducing carbon border taxes. An Indian exporter pays for some of the world's most expensive and intermittent electricity, and then pays again at the border because that power is carbon-intensive. Exporters also cannot buy certifiable, auditable 100% renewable power. Ajay says Gujarat works reasonably well, and other states do badly.

head: Raw Materials at Global Prices
dek: Any friction at the border makes imported inputs dearer and Indian manufacturers less competitive.
more: Any friction at the border makes imported inputs dearer and Indian manufacturers less competitive. Ajay's example: the yarn that goes into artificial (non-cotton) fabric is the world's most important, and India puts a 10% duty on it. That makes all synthetic fabric in India 10% dearer than in Bangladesh or Vietnam, which hurts the entire garment industry.

head: The Bankruptcy Code as the Fix for Late Payments
dek: Big Indian companies routinely squeeze small suppliers on payments. Ajay calls this short-sighted, since big firms have access to cheaper capital and would get better procurement by paying promptly.
more: Big Indian companies routinely squeeze small suppliers on payments. Ajay calls this short-sighted, since big firms have access to cheaper capital and would get better procurement by paying promptly. The fix is not a government invoice portal. It is strict enforcement of whatever payment terms were freely agreed, through a bankruptcy code that empowers operational creditors. The current code was shaped by big companies, which won protections against such creditors. Push ten important big companies into bankruptcy over unpaid suppliers, Ajay says, and everyone else will get the message.

head: Punitive Court Interest Rates
dek: Shubho Roy, a law academic at Shiv Nadar University and a friend of the hosts, has long campaigned on this.
more: Shubho Roy, a law academic at Shiv Nadar University and a friend of the hosts, has long campaigned on this. If you owe 100 rupees, stall for 10 years in court, and are then ordered to pay 100 rupees at 5% interest, you have got a cheap loan. Courts should apply punitive interest rates so that defaulting on a contract costs more than honouring it.

head: Don't Tax Non-Residents
dek: When goods are exported, every bit of indirect tax paid along the way should be refunded.
more: When goods are exported, every bit of indirect tax paid along the way should be refunded. Elsewhere in the world, VAT is fully refunded at the point of export. India's GST and RoDTEP refund only part of it. Several taxes are never refunded, and delays in refunds tie up working capital. Indian exporters therefore carry tax that their competitors don't.

head: Scale and Wright's Law
dek: Wright's Law: each doubling of a firm's cumulative lifetime output brings about a 20% gain in productivity.
more: Wright's Law: each doubling of a firm's cumulative lifetime output brings about a 20% gain in productivity. In a factory with 10,000 machines, even a 0.1% efficiency gain per machine adds up to serious money, so complex optimisations pay off. Small factories can't justify them. India celebrates 2,000-worker factories, but successful low-cost manufacturers run 10,000 to 100,000 workers, and India's system trips up anything that grows big.
printed: Pay up, scale up, fly out

head: The Indian State as an Autarky
dek: Global manufacturing means constant travel, cross-border contracts, foreign bank accounts and arbitration abroad.
more: Global manufacturing means constant travel, cross-border contracts, foreign bank accounts and arbitration abroad. The Indian state distrusts all of it. A tax officer who finds a foreign bank account suspects hawala. Ajay suggests a simple fix: the UK lets people hold two passports, so one can be away getting a visa while you travel on the other. India makes this hard, which slows down how often executives can travel.

head: Twelve Problems: Five for the Union, Seven for the States
dek: Ajay's checklist of what holds manufacturing back: labour law and minimum wages; infrastructure (no longer the binding constraint); land; locating the workforce; electricity; trade barriers; finance; an anti-globalisation state; hostility to size; dispute resolution; tax refunds on exports; and the skilled-labour gap.
more: Ajay's checklist of what holds manufacturing back: labour law and minimum wages; infrastructure (no longer the binding constraint); land; locating the workforce; electricity; trade barriers; finance; an anti-globalisation state; hostility to size; dispute resolution; tax refunds on exports; and the skilled-labour gap. Five of the twelve are in the union government's hands and seven are with the states. That explains why Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have pulled ahead. Every state should run its own growth strategy on its seven.

head: Amit on Ajay praising his MSME episode: it's like a novice songwriter taking his song to Bob Dylan and Dylan
more: Amit on Ajay praising his MSME episode: it's like a novice songwriter taking his song to Bob Dylan and Dylan saying 'Wow, this is such a great song.' For Amit to do a manufacturing episode and have Ajay call it good 'is exactly the same thing.'

head: Ajay says everyone should put the checklist of manufacturing problems up in their bathroom
more: Ajay says everyone should put the checklist of manufacturing problems up in their bathroom and 'worship every day'. Amit replies: 'You are the kind of economist who actually has lists in his bathroom about how to make Indian manufacturing better… Actually I don't have any lists, so there's nothing embarrassing there. There are shower gels and shampoos, but let's not go there again.'

head: Before recording, while going through pointers on industrial policy and labour laws, Ajay declared he was having so much fun.
more: Before recording, while going through pointers on industrial policy and labour laws, Ajay declared he was having so much fun. Amit: 'Bhai, you are having fun. I'm trying to memorize phrases, you are having fun.'

head: Ajay boasts that services exports grew 126% in a decade
more: Ajay boasts that services exports grew 126% in a decade, 'nothing to sneeze at'. Amit: 'That happened to my weight, but continue.'

Ajay's 'North Korea-South Korea comparison': 'a communist country called West Bengal, where the minimum wage is 13,000 rupees, and a capitalist country called East Bengal' with a minimum wage of 7,000-8,000. Guess which one built the successful garment export industry.

head: Ajay grants that Maharashtra has reined in wildcat unions, then adds…
more: Ajay grants that Maharashtra has reined in wildcat unions, then adds: 'I will point out that there are many states in India that are not called Maharashtra.'

head: Ajay says a 2,000-worker factory
more: Ajay says a 2,000-worker factory 'ain't much' globally. Amit jokes: 'Some would dream of a factory with 1.7 billion people… Manufacturing national pride.'

head: Amit on the Nehru era: the world didn't yet know the Soviet Union was…
more: Amit on the Nehru era: the world didn't yet know the Soviet Union was 'a complete and utter failure. It was really a public relations success.'

head: Amit after Ajay's twelve-point diagnosis
more: Amit after Ajay's twelve-point diagnosis: 'I will watch this episode again and again and again and maybe get our editor to do a version of it that doesn't have me and only you.'

head: Frédéric Bastiat's
more: Frédéric Bastiat's 'the seen and the unseen', the phrase Amit named his podcast after. He invokes it for the vast unseen costs of FERA-style capital controls.

head: P.C. Mahalanobis's mid-1950s claim that competition is wasteful (
more: P.C. Mahalanobis's mid-1950s claim that competition is wasteful ('Why should two companies make cars, one is enough'). Amit notes it still underlies laws today: 'Why should ten people make potato chips?'

head: The 'Naadaan Baalak' at the Export-Target Meeting
dek: The central-planner reflex runs so deep that the state sets targets for activity it does not perform and waves away the obvious objection as immaturity.
more: Soon after joining the Ministry of Finance, Ajay attended the annual meeting where officials set India's export target. He asked who in the room actually did any exporting. Exporting is done by private people, he said, so the government's real target should be which rules it removed so those people could export. The senior officials treated him like a 'naadaan baalak' (naive child) and told him he would understand the importance of targets once he grew up and became a real policymaker.

The central-planner reflex runs so deep that the state sets targets for activity it does not perform and waves away the obvious objection as immaturity. The useful question for government is what it got out of the way, not what number it announced.

head: Jaswant Singh's 25-Year Dream: Bombay Must Challenge London
dek: A single good question from a politician can launch a decades-long reform programme, and such programmes can just as easily stall.
more: When Jaswant Singh was Finance Minister, he sat with Rakesh Mohan and Ajay and asked whether they had thought about Bombay as a global producer of financial services. He said it would take 25 years but that Bombay had to challenge London. Ajay says the idea came from the minister, not from them. It led to Percy Mistry's government committee report 'Bombay as an International Financial Centre' (2007), which ultimately led to FSLRC and a draft law. The report argued that Bombay already has the raw material, including derivatives traders everywhere, deals struck in coffee shops and global banks like JP Morgan with perhaps 60,000 staff in India. What it needed was correct financial regulation and a livable, expat-friendly city that could attract 100,000 top global professionals, down to police stations that can deal with them in English. Then everything got derailed.

A single good question from a politician can launch a decades-long reform programme, and such programmes can just as easily stall. Becoming a financial centre is a long institutional and urban project, and Ajay says the next generation has to pick up the pieces.

head: Percy Mistry Punctures a Young Technologist's Pride
dek: Technology is not the moat in financial services. Institutions are.
more: As a young man, Ajay was proud that NSE had the best computer technology in the world and thought it could serve global customers. Percy Mistry told him that was nowhere near enough. Someone holding a two-month dollar-yen futures position in Chicago sleeps soundly because of a whole machinery of private institutions, regulators and law that guarantees the promise. A microphone is different: once made and tested, nobody cares where it came from. Ajay notes NSE once had a real technology edge, but the West has since caught up.
Technology is not the moat in financial services. Institutions are. A financial product is a promise that lasts over time, so buying it means trusting the country that stands behind it.

head: The 2019 NSE Payment Delay
dek: Trust in financial infrastructure takes decades to build and one bad day to lose.
more: In 2019, a dispute between NSE and SEBI led to a payment delay to foreign participants on NSE. Jayanth Varma wrote a blog post about it. Reading it, Ajay remembered Percy's lesson. The reason for the failure does not matter. On that day the foreigner concludes that payments from a third-world exchange cannot be trusted, and rebuilding that goodwill can take 25 years.
Trust in financial infrastructure takes decades to build and one bad day to lose. An institution must have the competence to make sure 'the show goes on' no matter what the internal dispute is.

head: Sharad Joshi's Couplet on the APMC Squeeze
dek: A state-granted middleman monopoly does not trade off the farmer against the consumer.
more: Amit recalled the farmer leader Sharad Joshi, one of the few post-independence politicians he truly admires because Joshi cared about freedom. Joshi attacked the APMCs, which had a state-granted monopoly to buy from the farmer at one rupee and sell to the consumer at twenty, leaving neither side any choice. He summed it up in a sher: 'Marte hum bhi hain, marte tum bhi ho. Hum sasta bech ke marte hain, tum mehenga khareed ke marte ho.'
A state-granted middleman monopoly does not trade off the farmer against the consumer. It hurts both at once, and a single couplet captures what pages of policy analysis argue.
printed: Cheap to sell, dear to buy

head: The books of Albert O. Hirschman
dek: Hirschman wasn't wrong about linkages; they simply moved beyond national borders.
more: Hirschman wasn't wrong about linkages; they simply moved beyond national borders. Thinkers aren't obliged to be precisely correct fifty years later, and Ajay calls him 'one of the great people' whose books and biography everyone should read.
Ajay's closing recommendation, right after spending the episode critiquing Hirschman's linkages argument.

head: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
dek: It is the only Hirschman book Amit has read, and he would love to recommend it.
more: It is the only Hirschman book Amit has read, and he would love to recommend it. Ajay's enthusiasm convinced Amit to go read Hirschman's other work, and he urges listeners to do the same.
Amit's recommendation, prompted by Ajay's praise of Hirschman.

head: The Journey of Indian Finance (Ep 71, Everything is Everything)
dek: It tells how Indian financial reform got badly stuck, which is the backstory to why the Bombay-as-financial-centre dream remains unfinished.
more: It tells how Indian financial reform got badly stuck, which is the backstory to why the Bombay-as-financial-centre dream remains unfinished.
Cited when explaining how the Bombay financial-centre project stalled after FSLRC.

head: The Four Pillars of the Old Manufacturing Dogma
dek: Ajay rebuilds the development economics of the 1960s to 1980s from four ideas. (1) Nicholas Kaldor saw that manufacturing growth was correlated with GDP growth. (2) Wright's Law, the experience curve, was claimed to apply only to manufacturing: make 10^8 ball bearings and you get far more productive. (3) Albert Hirschman's linkages: one factory sparks many others, so the state should deliberately induce 'unbalanced growth' and light a few candles to start the chain. (4) Hollis Chenery's World Bank data showed a 'structural transformation' in which successful countries pass through a phase of 20 to 50 percent of GDP in manufacturing before becoming services economies.
more: Ajay rebuilds the development economics of the 1960s to 1980s from four ideas. (1) Nicholas Kaldor saw that manufacturing growth was correlated with GDP growth. (2) Wright's Law, the experience curve, was claimed to apply only to manufacturing: make 10^8 ball bearings and you get far more productive. (3) Albert Hirschman's linkages: one factory sparks many others, so the state should deliberately induce 'unbalanced growth' and light a few candles to start the chain. (4) Hollis Chenery's World Bank data showed a 'structural transformation' in which successful countries pass through a phase of 20 to 50 percent of GDP in manufacturing before becoming services economies. Together these became a dogma that manufacturing is a mandatory stage, and many economists were willing to use state power to fake it.

head: Hirschman Was Right About Linkages, but Linkages Went Global
dek: Linkages are real, but they no longer stop at national borders. A 'German' car has seats from the Czech Republic, wiring from Romania and operating-system software from KPIT in Pune.
more: Linkages are real, but they no longer stop at national borders. A 'German' car has seats from the Czech Republic, wiring from Romania and operating-system software from KPIT in Pune. In a world of global value chains, the right policy is not to seed domestic factories. It is to remove every friction against deep global integration: passports, visas, PMLA, the Enforcement Directorate, cross-border payments, and current and capital account restrictions.

head: Correlations Are Not Exploitable
dek: A recurring Everything is Everything theme. Rich countries have universal schooling, good infrastructure, computerised governments and, historically, manufacturing booms.
more: A recurring Everything is Everything theme. Rich countries have universal schooling, good infrastructure, computerised governments and, historically, manufacturing booms. Sloppy thinking turns these correlations into theories of change and mobilises huge resources around them. Nehru saw lots of schooling in England and pushed schooling first. Ajay argues that what drives growth is peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice. Then private firms build complex, high-productivity businesses over a hundred-year journey, and the correlates follow.

head: Subsidised Output Is Fake Output
dek: Subsidise anything and it will grow, but that isn't growth. A rigged exchange rate makes the most incompetent manufacturer look globally competitive, which amounts to a transfer from poor people to exporters.
more: Subsidise anything and it will grow, but that isn't growth. A rigged exchange rate makes the most incompetent manufacturer look globally competitive, which amounts to a transfer from poor people to exporters. Real manufacturing has to emerge organically, from self-interested people choosing it because it is optimal for them, not because the state tipped the scales.

head: Don't Pick Winners Among Sectors: Lay Foundations and Stay Neutral
dek: The state should fix everything that hobbles manufacturing, agriculture and services alike, then stay neutral.
more: The state should fix everything that hobbles manufacturing, agriculture and services alike, then stay neutral. Ranking sectors (manufacturing good, agriculture bad, services unimportant) is central planning, and it keeps poor countries poor for longer. Amit stresses the point is not anti-manufacturing. It is anti-coercion: the trouble starts when the state declares one path to growth and uses force to favour it. The state's job is peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice.

head: Modern Manufacturing Is a High-Skill Game
dek: The image of vast factories absorbing unskilled villagers is gone. Modern manufacturing means automation, capital intensity and CNC lathes programmed by English speakers who read manuals and watch YouTube guides.
more: The image of vast factories absorbing unskilled villagers is gone. Modern manufacturing means automation, capital intensity and CNC lathes programmed by English speakers who read manuals and watch YouTube guides. It also needs industrial discipline: showing up at 9 a.m. and working correctly for eight hours, because hundreds of people share an assembly line. Ajay flags a real problem with young Indian men here, a culture of machismo, alcohol, violence and late nights.

head: The Line Between Manufacturing and Services Has Dissolved
dek: Rolls-Royce doesn't sell engines; it bills by the engine-hour and handles maintenance, remote diagnostics, finance and insurance.
more: Rolls-Royce doesn't sell engines; it bills by the engine-hour and handles maintenance, remote diagnostics, finance and insurance. A John Deere tractor downloads firmware, probes the soil and sends telemetry to a Hyderabad call centre, which phones the farmer about an infestation. In Ajay's words it is a 'sensor platform', an agricultural productivity service. Kirit Parikh, Ajay's mentor, explained the rise of services long ago: once basic needs are met, people pay for skill and design.

head: Services Are Now More Tradable Than Goods, and India Proves It
dek: Manufacturing was once special because it was tradable. Ajay's father told him haircuts aren't tradable, while widgets are.
more: Manufacturing was once special because it was tradable. Ajay's father told him haircuts aren't tradable, while widgets are. Fibre-optic cables changed that: a Chicago exchange takes orders from the whole world, and the remaining barriers, such as restrictions on foreign lawyers and accountants, are only in our minds. Over ten years, India's goods exports grew 38% in nominal dollars, roughly half a percent a year after US inflation, while services exports grew 126%. Ajay calls India 'ground zero' where the old theory is being destroyed. Services exports, about $300 billion a year from a small educated elite, are what separate India from Pakistan and Bangladesh.

head: A Financial Product Is Only as Good as Its Institutions
dek: Percy Mistry's lesson. Once a microphone is made and tested, where it came from no longer matters.
more: Percy Mistry's lesson. Once a microphone is made and tested, where it came from no longer matters. A two-month dollar-yen futures position leaves you exposed, for those two months, to how the whole system around it works: checks and balances, conflict resolution, regulators and law. Exporting financial services therefore means exporting trustworthy institutions, which is far harder than having good technology.

head: Umpires, Not Stadiums
dek: Build the world's finest stadiums, Wankhede or Brabourne, and top teams still won't come if the umpires are shady.
more: Build the world's finest stadiums, Wankhede or Brabourne, and top teams still won't come if the umpires are shady. Ajay credits Britain's success at Wimbledon, where foreigners always win, to the same idea. Britain built the rules of the game and won the world's trust that British common law will deliver and that the unwritten constitution prevents the excesses of state power. Getting to the top in services is an institutional challenge, not a matter of machines.

head: Norms: The Layer Beneath the Law
dek: Good behaviour by umpires and judges isn't produced by statute alone. An umpire should feel embarrassed when friends ask what on earth he was doing.
more: Good behaviour by umpires and judges isn't produced by statute alone. An umpire should feel embarrassed when friends ask what on earth he was doing. Judges behave better when researchers write blog posts criticising their orders. Building institutions requires a culture of respect, scrutiny and constant striving to do better.

head: Agriculture Is a Frontier of Productivity, Not a Backwater
dek: The Netherlands, roughly the size of Haryana or Kerala, is the world's third-largest food exporter at about $140 billion a year.
more: The Netherlands, roughly the size of Haryana or Kerala, is the world's third-largest food exporter at about $140 billion a year. Modern agriculture means indoor farming, agri-robots and genetic engineering, run by skilled people rather than unskilled peasants. Ajay says the world economy pays for complexity: getting lychees from Bihar to Tokyo is complex, and private people worked that trade out, not the government. India's food exports (about $43 billion) already exceed its textile and apparel exports (about $34 billion).

head: The East Asian Miracle Is Not a Model
dek: Many people are 'taken by', and in Ajay's view 'taken in by', the East Asian miracle.
more: Many people are 'taken by', and in Ajay's view 'taken in by', the East Asian miracle. A rare kind of developmental dictatorship pushed manufacturing and got growth, but Ajay 'wouldn't wish it on my worst enemies'. Those countries are not admirable examples to emulate, and the world has changed since then anyway.

head: The Intellectual Map Lags the Territory
dek: Amit's framing of why manufacturing dogma survives. The world changes faster than the people who think about it, and conventional wisdom catches up slowly.
more: Amit's framing of why manufacturing dogma survives. The world changes faster than the people who think about it, and conventional wisdom catches up slowly. Ajay's two lessons for young economists: be very cautious about correlation versus causation, and distrust any leadership role for the state in choosing society's path.

head: Amit on Ajay's cooling temper between the off-camera rant and the recording
more: Amit on Ajay's cooling temper between the off-camera rant and the recording: 'Ten minutes ago, before we started the shoot, he was using words like rage and fury. He was then a volcano. He is now a flickering candle. But it doesn't matter because you will still get the light and insight.'

head: Ajay's opening salvo
more: Ajay's opening salvo: 'Development economists are a bit of a creepy bunch. They are statist control people, and they have long had this smug comfort and superiority complex that they get to control the world.'

head: Right after Ajay's lyrical riff on John Deere tractors as sensor platforms, Amit tries a groaner pun
more: Right after Ajay's lyrical riff on John Deere tractors as sensor platforms, Amit tries a groaner pun: 'If you are a man who gets turned on by farm vehicles, what would those vehicles be called?' Ajay's verdict: 'Brilliant.'

head: Ajay's test for a real financial centre
more: Ajay's test for a real financial centre: 'You throw a stone at any residential building in Bombay, and you will hit some derivatives trader.' He then ribs Amit: 'I know you hang out with the people who do conversations about poker, but I hang out with the people who do conversations about derivatives trading.'

head: Amit on the roller coaster of Ajay's example: being invited to imagine a thousand-crore dollar-yen futures position felt great, since
more: Amit on the roller coaster of Ajay's example: being invited to imagine a thousand-crore dollar-yen futures position felt great, since 'I have never traded in futures or options, and I have much closer to a thousand rupees than a thousand crores. But much, much closer.' Then the poker jibe brought him crashing down.

head: Amit's hasty disclaimer after the…
more: Amit's hasty disclaimer after the 'shady umpires' analogy: 'When he talks about umpires, he is not implying that Indian umpires are bad. Indian umpires are the best umpires.'

Prompted by the Netherlands being the size of Haryana, Amit recalls Iceland drawing 1-1 with Argentina at the 2018 World Cup. He calculated from his study that Iceland's population is the size of Versova: 'Not Bombay, not Andheri, not even Andheri West, because Andheri is vast and contains multitudes. But freaking Versova. So from this we can come to the conclusion that football and food have more in common than you think.' Ajay adds: 'Iceland is three hundred thousand fishermen.'

head: Amit reveals Ajay's
more: Amit reveals Ajay's 'metric for goodness': the fraction of Everything is Everything episodes you've watched. 'At noon every Friday, even if you were hundred percent good at eleven fifty-nine, you get a little less good because a new episode is out,' but watching at 3x speed lets you catch up fast. 'So my question for you, dear listeners, is: are you good?'

head: Nicholas Kaldor's
more: Nicholas Kaldor's 'laws of growth': his 1950s observation that manufacturing growth tracks GDP growth, the first pillar of the manufacturing dogma.

head: Japan's MITI
more: Japan's MITI: 'For every one Japanese MITI that did some good things, I can show you 50 other examples where industrial policy went wrong.'

head: Wimbledon
more: Wimbledon: 'The British organized Wimbledon and foreigners always win at Wimbledon. That's the glory of Britain,' credited to rule of law and the world's trust in British common law.

head: The Great Tragedy: Losing Faith in Interstellar Travel
dek: Technological progress is not a law of nature. Some frontiers stay closed because of physics, not because of effort.
more: Ajay was born in 1966 and grew up after men walked on the moon in 1969, expecting boundless progress to follow. As a young man he treated physics as malleable: surely there would be ways past the speed of light, surely wormholes. But Alpha Centauri is four and a half light years away, and he sees no way to get the trip below a thousand years. That leaves robotic probes, or humans in a fully self-sustaining ecosystem. The hundred years before his birth, which gave us quantum electrodynamics, changed how we saw the world every decade. His own lifetime, he says, produced no comparable breakthrough in the standard paradigm.

Technological progress is not a law of nature. Some frontiers stay closed because of physics, not because of effort. Scientific revolutions also come in bursts, and one generation's sparkle can be followed by another's long plateau.

head: Montek Ahluwalia Went to Study by Boat
dek: Living memory still reaches back to an era when going abroad meant weeks at sea.
more: Ajay recalls Montek Ahluwalia telling him that when he went to study in the UK, he was among the last cohorts to travel by sea. He went from Delhi to Bombay and caught a boat that sailed up the Red Sea to Britain. By the late 1980s, when Ajay left for his PhD, flying was standard.
Living memory still reaches back to an era when going abroad meant weeks at sea. A single generation can hold a complete change in how the world is connected.

head: The Geek Who Had Never Touched a CD
dek: The story measures how far India has come. Then, travelling abroad made India feel backward.
more: In the late 1980s Ajay flew to Los Angeles to do a PhD. His middle-class family were early adopters of every new gadget, yet America was full of firsts for him. He saw his first CD player and his first CD; India then had only LPs and cassettes. He knew everything about CD technology from reading IEEE Spectrum, but had never held one. He saw dahi sold in boxes in shops, when Indians always set their own at home. He saw protected-access highways with speeds of 100 kph, and LAX felt like a science fiction city.

The story measures how far India has come. Then, travelling abroad made India feel backward. Today his mic, lenses, iPad, clothes and watch are the global state of the art, so the old gap in personal consumption has closed.
printed: All the theory, none of the CDs

head: Queueing at the STD Booth in Pune
dek: This is Clarke's third law in everyday life. Things that would have seemed utopian in 1990, like never getting lost (GPS) or free video calls, have become so normal that we no longer notice they are magic.
more: As a student in the late 1980s, Amit lined up at an STD booth outside the Fergusson College hostel in Pune to call his parents long distance. Before that, as he reminds Ajay, people booked trunk calls that an operator connected. Today he can video-call any loved one anywhere in the world at a moment's notice, and those loved ones are now spread across the world.

This is Clarke's third law in everyday life. Things that would have seemed utopian in 1990, like never getting lost (GPS) or free video calls, have become so normal that we no longer notice they are magic.

head: How AI Made Chess Richer, Not Deader
dek: This is Amit's model for the future: machines can intensify human engagement instead of replacing it.
more: When engines became stronger than the world champion, everyone expected chess to be 'solved' and to die, or to turn into rote memorisation of computer lines with everyone playing alike. The opposite happened. Before AI, most players followed the Soviet school's shared heuristics. Engines exposed concrete exceptions to those general principles. Many players also learned straight from AI instead of from the same books and circuits. The result is players like Wesley So, Nakamura and Giri with sharply different individual styles. Games now combine deeper preparation with machines and more original play over the board, as players steer opponents into second- and third-best lines they haven't prepared.

This is Amit's model for the future: machines can intensify human engagement instead of replacing it. He uses it to argue that human relationships will deepen once machines handle the instrumental parts.

head: The First Beethoven's Ninth in India
dek: In an age when any recording is freely available, live performance is valued for the people and the occasion, not for technical perfection.
more: Ajay was in the audience in Bombay when Beethoven's Ninth was performed in India for the first time, by players from the Bombay Symphony Orchestra along with some musicians from abroad. He could hear flaws in the performance, but that wasn't the point. What moved him was that a local community had reached the critical mass needed to stage it at all. He then raises a worry: if live art matters only for this human reason, the economics may collapse into something like a school show of friends and family applauding each other.

In an age when any recording is freely available, live performance is valued for the people and the occasion, not for technical perfection. Whether that value can pay the artists is still an open question.

head: When Bill Gates Said Voice Recognition Was Coming
dek: Problems that look intractable often fall when they are important enough and the tools arrive from an unexpected direction.
more: Ajay remembers an interview, long ago, in which Bill Gates predicted that voice recognition was coming. Ajay was sceptical because the problem seemed so hard. Gates could not have known which AI was in the pipeline; he simply believed an important problem would get solved. Today voice recognition is astonishingly good, and Ajay expects it to work perfectly even in noisy rooms with thick accents. He uses this to justify his confidence about brain-machine interfaces.
Problems that look intractable often fall when they are important enough and the tools arrive from an unexpected direction. That is useful humility for anyone dismissing a forecast as impossible.

head: The Symphonies Trapped in Amit's Head
dek: Brain-machine interfaces could do more than raise productivity. They could release creativity that is now locked behind years of physical practice.
more: Amit's mother was a musician. Since he was seven or eight he has composed whole songs and symphonies in his head, hearing every instrument. He never became a musician because he was too lazy to learn an instrument, and learning one remains one of his resolutions. A brain-machine interface that played a tune exactly as he imagined it, and let him tweak it, would finally get that music out.
Brain-machine interfaces could do more than raise productivity. They could release creativity that is now locked behind years of physical practice.

head: Tolstoy's Chicken
dek: Our moral comfort with meat depends on not seeing where it comes from.
more: By the time this happened, Tolstoy was a vegetarian. His aunt announced that when she came to dinner she would eat chicken and nothing else. When she sat down in the dining room she found a live chicken on her chair, and Tolstoy told her to kill it, cook it and eat it. Amit once wrote an essay called 'Tolstoy's Chicken' about this; it no longer exists. Amit loves meat and thinks it is necessary for health, but hates the idea of being responsible for killing animals. For him, lab-grown meat would settle that dilemma.
Our moral comfort with meat depends on not seeing where it comes from. Lab-grown meat appeals because it removes the cruelty without asking people to give up meat.

head: Ukraine's Drone Strike on Russia's Strategic Bombers
dek: This is a new template for asymmetric warfare: a few million dollars destroying billions in assets that cannot be replaced.
more: Ukraine smuggled 117 drones carrying 3-5 kg explosive payloads into Russia, probably across the Chinese or Kazakh border, where checks are lax. They were assembled in a safe house reportedly next to an FSB building and loaded into containers on trucks whose tops could retract. Unwitting Russian drivers were told to drive to specific GPS coordinates and step out. The roofs opened 5-10 km from several airbases. The drones flew at about 50 kph, the peak speed of birds, which makes them hard to tell apart from birds on detection. They used the ordinary 4G network over a VPN, and the operators were safely back inside Ukraine. Ukraine claims 41 strategic bombers and AWACS planes worth about $7 billion were destroyed; independent estimates confirm 21. Russia can no longer build these aircraft. Ajay estimates the drones cost about two lakh dollars and the whole operation about $2 million.

This is a new template for asymmetric warfare: a few million dollars destroying billions in assets that cannot be replaced. Amit notes that such an attack was unimaginable three years ago and was born of necessity in an existential war. As with 9/11, once it has been done, others will copy it.
printed: The day the truck roofs opened

head: When the World Fixed the Ozone Layer
dek: This shows that global coordination on a shared atmosphere has worked before.
more: Scientists found that CFCs such as Freon, used in every fridge and air conditioner, were leaking into the upper atmosphere and destroying the ozone layer, which would mean more ultraviolet light and more skin cancer. The advanced economies put together a global agreement and CFCs were phased out. India did not demand 20 more years of Freon on the grounds that rich countries had developed using it. India signed on, and the problem was largely stopped.

This shows that global coordination on a shared atmosphere has worked before. Ajay's grim conclusion is that the conditions that made it work, chiefly American leadership, no longer exist, which is why he is pessimistic about CO2.

head: The Experience Machine
dek: Nozick is one of Amit's favourite thinkers, but here Amit disagrees with him.
more: Nozick is one of Amit's favourite thinkers, but here Amit disagrees with him. The thought experiment is the clearest way into the question of whether machine-made feelings are worth less than real ones.

Raised in Amit's prediction that technology will give us feelings on demand. Nozick imagined a machine plugged into your brain that could make you feel anything, and argued that we would still choose the real world, so pleasure cannot be everything.

head: The Moral Animal
dek: He calls it a great book on how marriage evolved, including the circumstances in which monogamy or polygamy arises.
more: He calls it a great book on how marriage evolved, including the circumstances in which monogamy or polygamy arises.
Mentioned as Amit argues that marriage evolved as an equilibrium for how men and women relate, and is now an outdated artifact.

head: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit calls it a great episode, and says Shrayana's book also covers this.
more: Amit calls it a great episode, and says Shrayana's book also covers this. Both document what conventional marriage does to many Indian women.
Cited for Amit's claim that for Indian women outside the privileged elite, marriage can be a terrible prison that uproots them.

head: Sell the Tiger to Save It (2006)
dek: It argues that legalising tiger hunting and trade in China would give people a reason to breed tigers and so save them from extinction.
more: It argues that legalising tiger hunting and trade in China would give people a reason to breed tigers and so save them from extinction. The same logic suggests animals that lose their economic purpose could disappear.
Amit cites his friend Barun Mitra's New York Times piece while warning that lab-grown meat might push cows and goats toward extinction.

head: Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren (1930)
dek: One of the smartest people in history tried hard to predict future productivity, and much of it didn't work out.
more: One of the smartest people in history tried hard to predict future productivity, and much of it didn't work out. That makes it a useful lesson in how hard forecasting is. Amit adds that putting yourself out like this takes intellectual bravery.
Ajay's recommendation for the episode.

head: Ex Machina
dek: The film asks whether AI beings are real and have moral standing. If an AGI is conscious by every definition we use, why should bits rather than organic matter deny it a moral personality?
more: The film asks whether AI beings are real and have moral standing. If an AGI is conscious by every definition we use, why should bits rather than organic matter deny it a moral personality?
Part of Amit's recommendation that listeners take science fiction seriously.

head: The Tesseract
dek: The Beach is Garland's more famous novel, but Amit prefers The Tesseract and calls it fantastic.
more: The Beach is Garland's more famous novel, but Amit prefers The Tesseract and calls it fantastic.
Mentioned alongside Ex Machina as another work by Garland, whom Amit calls an excellent writer.

head: Overestimate the Short Term, Underestimate the Long Term
dek: Forecasts tend to expect too much soon and too little later. Amit sets this caveat up front, since 25 years may be 'short term' for some predictions.
more: Forecasts tend to expect too much soon and too little later. Amit sets this caveat up front, since 25 years may be 'short term' for some predictions. The hosts look back at 1990 to show how little of today anyone foresaw, and promise a mea culpa episode in 2050. Ajay's Keynes recommendation makes the same point: even a genius gets much of the future wrong.

head: Communities of Choice vs Communities of Circumstance
dek: Before the internet, your friends came from geography: school, college, workplace.
more: Before the internet, your friends came from geography: school, college, workplace. You could never find the million people who shared your interests or values. Now people form communities by choice. This matters most for people who don't fit the mainstream. Most of Amit's dear friends are people he could not have met otherwise, and he and Ajay would never have crossed paths despite both living in Bombay.

head: Post-Scarcity in Bits, Not Yet in Atoms
dek: Making a mixtape, or tracking down a Van Morrison album after hearing one song, used to be hard work.
more: Making a mixtape, or tracking down a Van Morrison album after hearing one song, used to be hard work. Today any song, book or film is instantly available, so arts and entertainment are effectively post-scarcity. Amit believes productivity gains will eventually do the same for physical goods and end poverty, but he won't predict that for 2050.

head: We Have Normalized Magic
dek: Clarke's third law says sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
more: Clarke's third law says sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. Never being lost thanks to GPS, and video-calling anyone anywhere, would have looked utopian in 1990. Ajay adds that the computer revolution is still underrated: the phone in your hand is more powerful than the world's most powerful supercomputer of twenty years ago.

head: India Caught Up on Private Goods, Not Public Goods
dek: Ajay argues that the Indian elite now consume at the global state of the art: mics, lenses, iPads, LLMs, clothes, watches.
more: Ajay argues that the Indian elite now consume at the global state of the art: mics, lenses, iPads, LLMs, clothes, watches. The gap that remains is in public goods. The West has cleaner air, better criminal justice, less dangerous income tax and more safety. What India still lacks is what states provide, not what markets sell.

head: Don't Judge AI by Today's AI
dek: Judging AI by today's ChatGPT is like judging computing by the room-sized machines of 1950, the era when IBM's Thomas Watson saw a world market for three computers at most.
more: Judging AI by today's ChatGPT is like judging computing by the room-sized machines of 1950, the era when IBM's Thomas Watson saw a world market for three computers at most. AI also means more than generative AI and LLMs; machine learning is advancing on many fronts. Amit thinks AGI is about five years away, partly because we overestimate human intelligence.

head: The Algorithm Will Become the Creator
dek: Technology first helped art scale, which produced a homogenised mainstream: Hollywood, Bollywood, Tollywood.
more: Technology first helped art scale, which produced a homogenised mainstream: Hollywood, Bollywood, Tollywood. In its second phase it fragments culture into niches. Amit predicts the end point will be AI generating songs, shows and books to fit each person's tastes and moods. Ajay pushes back: perhaps the billions of existing items already cover every taste, and platforms only need to find yours. He quotes Netflix: 'we're competing with sleep'. Amit insists that the content he wants doesn't exist yet.

head: The World Is a Technology for Making Us Feel
dek: Amit argues that songs, meditation and drugs are all technologies for putting the brain into particular states, and current ones are blunt tools.
more: Amit argues that songs, meditation and drugs are all technologies for putting the brain into particular states, and current ones are blunt tools. As AI comes to understand the brain, even as a black box, we will be able to produce peace, focus or happiness directly. That could treat chronic depression or ADHD. Unlike Nozick, Amit sees no reason to prefer the slower route through the world.

head: You Can Do What You Want, But You Can't Want What You Want
dek: Ajay's response to feelings on demand. Today our preferences feel fixed and given, and freedom means acting on them.
more: Ajay's response to feelings on demand. Today our preferences feel fixed and given, and freedom means acting on them. If we can press a button to change how we feel, we have to decide what we would like to feel, which reopens questions about the meaning of life, culture and philosophy. Ajay admits he would be bewildered.

head: Machines Handle the Instrumental, Humans Get the Real
dek: Amit predicts deeper bonds with both machines and people. If sex dolls and AI companions meet instrumental needs, human relationships no longer have to rest on them, and conversations can become more honest.
more: Amit predicts deeper bonds with both machines and people. If sex dolls and AI companions meet instrumental needs, human relationships no longer have to rest on them, and conversations can become more honest. He respects lust more than love because lust is honest, while love may be a rationalisation. In art, AI may take away the validation artists get, but not the joy of creating or of live connection. Live shows and stand-up will become more valuable, and ticket prices will rise.

head: The Great Unbundling of Marriage
dek: Two hundred years ago marriage bundled sex, companionship, romance, parenthood and friendship together.
more: Two hundred years ago marriage bundled sex, companionship, romance, parenthood and friendship together. Recent decades have pulled these apart. Amit thinks the sexual revolution suited people wired for promiscuity better than those wired for stability, and suited men better than women. His utopia is 'non-uniform civil codes': the state just enforces private contracts, so people can set their own rules, three-person marriages included. In the meantime he supports a uniform civil code, because the law should treat everyone equally. Ajay agrees with the direction but expects facts on the ground to change long before institutions do.

head: Truly Global Cities (or Walled Citadels)
dek: Amit predicts cities that compete by being open: you come if you have a job, with no interview or visa.
more: Amit predicts cities that compete by being open: you come if you have a job, with no interview or visa. Labour, like migrants from Bihar and UP who drive Mumbai's taxis, makes everyone better off. Dubai, Singapore and Hong Kong are his examples, with low taxes and no nationalism. He also expects a global currency, a successor to the 'proto-something' that is Bitcoin. Ajay adds two things. One is a darker vision of cosmopolitan city walls with barbarians at the gates, held off by drone warfare. The other is the pandemic-era digital nomad visas of Estonia and Portugal, which accept any stable remote income, not just a job. He doubts Dubai will win, since remote workers choose for life, people, weather and culture, not a hot desert.

head: Crypto: Theorems Instead of Frail Institutions
dek: Ajay says fiat money began around 1100-1200 and central banks then failed for centuries, producing hyperinflation and Nazi Germany.
more: Ajay says fiat money began around 1100-1200 and central banks then failed for centuries, producing hyperinflation and Nazi Germany. They only found the recipe of inflation targeting in the late 1980s (he cites New Zealand, 1987), after some 700 years. Amit adds the moral objection that a monopoly on money is wrong in principle. Ajay's practical case: if a Trump administration can pack the Fed with MAGA appointees, world GDP is too big to rest on one country's fragile institutions. Crypto is now full of grifters like Trump coin, but he expects 25 years of real innovation.
printed: A job is the only visa

head: The Staggering Consequences of the Word Zero
dek: Nuclear power was once sold as 'too cheap to meter', but its capital costs are high.
more: Nuclear power was once sold as 'too cheap to meter', but its capital costs are high. The real revolution is solar, wind and batteries moving down Wright's-law experience curves, through small steps such as an undergraduate's maths that improves windmill blades by 1-2%. India's best wind sites are offshore beyond Tamil Nadu and in a ring around Sri Lanka. Ajay predicts sunny hours when India's grid price of electricity is zero, and asks what we would build if power were free for part of every day. Desalinating seawater along the coast is one simple answer. He also says no sensible person in India should be building fossil-fuel capacity.

head: Editing the Genes of Living Adults
dek: Each of us carries billions of letters of genetic code, and mistakes in it cause disease.
more: Each of us carries billions of letters of genetic code, and mistakes in it cause disease. Ajay predicts targeted edits not just to embryos but to grown adults, building on early single-patient experiments such as a liver being fixed. His example is type 2 diabetes. A friendly virus could edit the mitochondria in muscle cells so they handle insulin correctly, curing the disease for life. Asked whether this will also make us happy, Ajay says certainly not.

head: Brain-Machine Interfaces for Everyday Thinking
dek: Ajay's hopes are modest and concrete.
more: Ajay's hopes are modest and concrete. He wants to run compound-interest calculations, regressions and maximum likelihood in his head, and to search ('grep') his own archive of millions of written words so that he never forgets. Amit wants the music he imagines played back. Neuralink has already shown a paralysed person playing chess by thought. Ajay considers his own wishes more achievable than Amit's.

head: Mine the Asteroids Where They Are
dek: Ajay argues it is wrong to picture towing asteroids home, because hauling rock is like hauling all the waste out of a coal mine.
more: Ajay argues it is wrong to picture towing asteroids home, because hauling rock is like hauling all the waste out of a coal mine. Instead, robotic factories in the asteroid belt would refine metals like yttrium and tantalum into clean blocks and ship them back, ending resource shortages. Taken to its limit this becomes the von Neumann probe: a spacecraft that lands somewhere, builds a hundred copies of itself and spreads through the galaxy over billions of years.

head: Robot Wars Cost Machines, Not Blood
dek: Unmanned boats have already sunk a large share of Russia's Black Sea fleet.
more: Unmanned boats have already sunk a large share of Russia's Black Sea fleet. Ajay predicts fully robotic warfare, with humans far from the border writing better code. His insight is that once a war like Putin's has cost tens of thousands of lives, the blood already spilled makes it politically impossible to back down. If only machines are destroyed, battlefield facts become clear to both sides and stopping the war becomes easier.

head: The Future of War Is the Future of Terror
dek: Amit's concrete worry for 2026, not 2050, is cheap drone swarms launched from a few miles outside Mumbai at a concert ground or at Parliament.
more: Amit's concrete worry for 2026, not 2050, is cheap drone swarms launched from a few miles outside Mumbai at a concert ground or at Parliament. High-value targets can be protected with jammers, but random crowds cannot be protected without advance intelligence. Since an attack may be impossible to attribute (Pakistan, China, or a domestic lunatic), he asks what scapegoat the state will reach for. Ajay connects this to the hybrid-warfare idea of operating below the thresholds of detection and attribution.

head: Lab-Grown Meat Ends Animal Farming, and Maybe the Animals
dek: Re-engineered bacteria or algae will produce muscle and blood cells that taste exactly like meat.
more: Re-engineered bacteria or algae will produce muscle and blood cells that taste exactly like meat. That is far cheaper than feeding a goat for years, so by 2050 Ajay expects industrial animal farming to collapse. It will be a huge economic shock and also a moral triumph. Lab-grown milk would end the cruelty of keeping animals pregnant for years. Amit warns of an irony that follows Barun Mitra's incentive logic: once cows and goats lose their economic purpose, they may die out, because few people want such large pets.

head: Autonomous Vehicles End the Waste of Idle Cars
dek: A private car sits idle most of the day, wasting capital and urban land, which is the scarcest resource.
more: A private car sits idle most of the day, wasting capital and urban land, which is the scarcest resource. That is why mass transit is efficient. A self-driving car that moves all day matches a metro's efficiency and also takes you door to door, needing only roads, which grow wherever people live. Ajay imagines platoons riding in each other's slipstream and paying one rupee to cars that let you pass. Amit imagines networked cars at 200 kph with no traffic lights, but fears the state will force the transition before the technology is ready.

head: Three Pillars of Fertility
dek: Patterns from the past make poor forecasts. Kerala's fertility rate (1.25) is already below that of Germany and France.
more: Patterns from the past make poor forecasts. Kerala's fertility rate (1.25) is already below that of Germany and France. From first principles, three things shape a woman's decision to have a child. First, social acceptance of childbirth outside marriage: conservative rich East Asia lags the West. Second, good childcare and women's work, where France has excelled. Third, reproductive technology, from surrogacy (which India bans) to whole pregnancies inside machines, which Ajay thinks is feasible by 2050. Countries strong on all three, such as France, Germany and Scandinavia, may end up with more children than India.

head: Keep the State Out of Reproduction
dek: Amit's counterpoint. Once people panicked about too many people, and now they panic about too few.
more: Amit's counterpoint. Once people panicked about too many people, and now they panic about too few. In both cases the next step is usually state social engineering. For him the level that matters is individual agency, and whether to have children belongs to each person. No one should influence that choice, whether coercively, subtly or otherwise.

head: Warming Is Already Baked In
dek: Ajay says CO2 stays in the air for about a thousand years, so what matters is the accumulated stock, not just today's emissions.
more: Ajay says CO2 stays in the air for about a thousand years, so what matters is the accumulated stock, not just today's emissions. We are at about 1.5°C above pre-industrial temperatures, roughly as the models predicted. The oceans absorb heat for 20-40 years, so the full effect shows up late. Today's stock and today's emissions are both unacceptable. CO2 is a negative externality that needs a matching tax, and with no global coordination he expects 2050 to be grim.

head: Alarmism Follows Funding Incentives
dek: Amit accepts that climate change is real and caused by humans, but thinks it is less severe than claimed and will be solved.
more: Amit accepts that climate change is real and caused by humans, but thinks it is less severe than claimed and will be solved. Climate NGOs are funded for predicting dystopia, so they exaggerate, and decades of alarmist forecasts have failed. The fix is already visible: France is 71% nuclear and emits a tenth of the world average CO2 per kilowatt hour. Coercive state interventions often do more harm than good.

head: Science Fiction Is About the Present
dek: People dismiss science fiction as genre entertainment. Amit argues the best of it takes on the biggest philosophical questions, such as the moral status of AI and the nature of memory, before philosophers do.
more: People dismiss science fiction as genre entertainment. Amit argues the best of it takes on the biggest philosophical questions, such as the moral status of AI and the nature of memory, before philosophers do. Reading it is a way of thinking hard about today.

head: After lamenting that Alpha Centauri is out of reach and the sun won't last forever, Ajay adds…
more: After lamenting that Alpha Centauri is out of reach and the sun won't last forever, Ajay adds: 'only fifty-two billion episodes from now, this show will have to come to an end.'

head: Amit deflates the interstellar gloom
more: Amit deflates the interstellar gloom: 'Bro, you are a big, big thinker. Most days my worry if I leave my home is how do I get to Bandra from Andheri.'

head: Ajay boasts that his pants, shirt and watch match anything in the West.
more: Ajay boasts that his pants, shirt and watch match anything in the West. Amit: 'Not just your pants, not just your shirt, not just your watch, your personality is world class.'

head: On algorithms finding your kink
more: On algorithms finding your kink: 'whatever my kinks are, and I will not tell you about my kinks'. Moments later, after imagining a film with only decapitation: 'I don't know why I got to decapitation, it's not my kink.'

head: Amit wants an AI version of Ajay for when the real one is busy, one that can tell him what advice Ajay would give
more: Amit wants an AI version of Ajay for when the real one is busy, one that can tell him what advice Ajay would give 'so I can conveniently ignore it.'

more: Ajay compares the future economics of live art to a school show, with parents dragged in to applaud and 'really the world's worst hours that any parent has had to spend.' head: The Bengali running gag: Ajay calls Amit
more: The Bengali running gag: Ajay calls Amit 'a deep Bengali philosopher'. Amit lists 'melancholy as Bengalis like to feel' among feelings on demand. Ajay says voice recognition will cope with 'a thick Tamilian accent or even worse, a thick Bengali accent' (Amit: 'Unnecessary'). Amit says brain-machine interfaces are 'great for the Bengali in me' because he won't have to physically move.

more: Amit on gene editing: 'I edited my genes in 1992.' He was eighteen, 'fully grunge and Nirvana Pearl Jam', and wanted torn jeans, so he ripped them himself. 'I ripped the code. So I've been there done that.'

head: Amit lists what gene editing might solve: cancer, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, living to 120
more: Amit lists what gene editing might solve: cancer, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, living to 120, 'Are we going to be happy?' Ajay: 'Certainly we're not going to be happy.'

more: After Ajay dreams of running grep on his own brain, Amit says: 'the first thing I'm going to Google from my head? I'm going to Google the word grep.' Ajay explains it as a Unix command for searching text files, e.g. 'let me grep in this restaurant menu for all the steaks.'

more: On humans writing code far from the front while robots fight: 'So the macho IIT-ian gets his fantasies fulfilled without putting himself in danger.' Ajay: 'Correct.'

more: Ajay pictures a quadcopter taxi waiting at Amit's 21st-floor window. Amit: 'And I will miss and I will fall down.'

more: After praising Dubai's ambitions to be a global hub: 'If you run Dubai, get in touch with me, I have ideas.'

more: Ajay finds babies grown in machines 'truly glorious'. Amit points listeners to his old piece on why it is immoral to have children 'inside or outside bodies, if I now have to add that caveat.'

head: Rebutting Ajay on climate, Amit uses Ajay's own arguments, citing
more: Rebutting Ajay on climate, Amit uses Ajay's own arguments, citing 'one of my closest friends and men I admire the most, the great economist Ajay Shah' and his episodes on cheap energy.

head: Arthur C. Clarke's third law
more: Arthur C. Clarke's third law, 'any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic', applied to GPS, video calls and Neuralink.

head: IBM chief Thomas Watson's famous line, quoted by Amit
more: IBM chief Thomas Watson's famous line, quoted by Amit as 'I think there's a world market for three computers at most', as a warning against judging a technology by its early form.
