more: Netflix executives' remark that 'we're competing with sleep', cited by Ajay to describe tech companies chasing 100% of our attention.

Matt Ridley's argument, in a book Amit can't recall, that eating meat made human brains grow and let Homo sapiens outlast Neanderthals, and his speculation that we ate them. Amit: 'it feels like a form of cannibalism. I wonder if you can also make human meat in a lab.'

head: Al Gore's documentary, cited by Amit as a forecast whose ten-year predictions
more: Al Gore's documentary, cited by Amit as a forecast whose ten-year predictions 'turned out to be completely wrong'.

head: Trump coin, Ajay's example of the…
more: Trump coin, Ajay's example of the 'scams and monsters' typical of crypto's early stage.

head: Mao's War on Sparrows
dek: This is Amit's standard example of Adam Smith's 'man of system', who moves one piece on society's chessboard and forgets that every piece moves on its own.
more: In 1958, farmers complained to the Chinese state that sparrows were a nuisance. Chairman Mao ordered them killed, and sparrows were hunted down all over China. But sparrows ate locusts. Once the sparrows were gone, the locusts multiplied and destroyed China's crops. The famine that followed killed about forty-five million people, in what became known as the Great Leap Forward.

This is Amit's standard example of Adam Smith's 'man of system', who moves one piece on society's chessboard and forgets that every piece moves on its own. Complex systems punish top-down tinkering, and the costs can run into millions of lives. It is the conservative warning to respect complexity, shown at its most extreme.

head: Ambedkar Keeps 'Socialist' Out of the Preamble
dek: A founder of the Constitution warned that writing an ideology into it would take away the people's freedom to choose a better arrangement later.
more: In 1948, K.T. Shah moved to add three words to the Preamble. Ambedkar rejected two of them, 'secular' and 'socialist'. On secularism, he said it was already written into the Constitution's articles, so stating it was unnecessary. On socialism, he said a constitution is only a mechanism for regulating the organs of the state. How society is organised must be left to the people to decide according to time and circumstances. Indira Gandhi added both words in the mid-1970s. Today every political party registering in India must pledge allegiance to socialism. That means Amit and Ajay could not start a party without betraying their beliefs. S.V. Raju of the Swatantra Party fought this rule in court for years and lost.

A founder of the Constitution warned that writing an ideology into it would take away the people's freedom to choose a better arrangement later. The later amendment that overrode him still decides who is allowed to enter Indian politics.

head: The Wrong Preamble at the CAA Protests
dek: People can hold up a document as a symbol without knowing its history.
more: Amit opposed the CAA and was delighted to see young people across India marching with the Preamble. But many of them carried the amended version with the word 'socialist' in it, not Ambedkar's original. He wanted to ask whether they knew what the word means. In his view, socialism kept India poor for decades longer than necessary.

People can hold up a document as a symbol without knowing its history. The protesters treated 'socialist' as a common noun meaning 'good for society', when it is a proper noun for a specific program that Ambedkar himself kept out.

head: Burke and Robespierre Exchange Postcards
dek: Ends and means are separate questions. Good intentions pursued by tearing everything down tend to destroy the people who pursue them.
more: In 1790 Edmund Burke wrote Reflections on the Revolution in France. He did not object to the revolution's ideals. He warned that its means were disastrous. For the 'History of Ideas' webinar in their Life Lessons course, Amit invented postcards between the two men, built from real quotes. Robespierre tells Burke, roughly, to shut up, calls him an old fogey and asks what he is even trying to conserve. Burke replies, 'Bro, I warned you, I hope you're around to read this.' By then Robespierre had himself been purged, after doing a fair amount of purging.

Ends and means are separate questions. Good intentions pursued by tearing everything down tend to destroy the people who pursue them. Burke's case was that institutions and norms have survived a kind of natural selection, so they exist for a reason.

head: Extreme in Their Moderation
dek: Amit says the moderates were liberal in their ends and conservative in their means.
more: Amit's real heroes of the freedom struggle come before Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and Ambedkar. They are the moderates of the late 19th and early 20th century: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar and Ranade. The usual story sets them against extremists like Tilak. But the Scottish statesman James Keir Hardie observed that the two camps were not far apart. Then Gandhi arrived, a 'black swan' who broke with everything before him.

Amit says the moderates were liberal in their ends and conservative in their means. They wanted a freer and more empowered India, but they worked step by step instead of through random violence. He uses this as a template for reform anywhere.

head: Tiki-Taka Began as an Insult
dek: Amit offers this as a parallel to 'liberal' and 'conservative', both of which began as cuss words thrown at people who never chose them.
more: 'Tiki-taka' is now the name for Pep Guardiola's possession football, which descends from Johan Cruyff's Total Football. But Guardiola did not coin the term and hates it. The broadcaster Andrés Montes coined it during the 2006 World Cup, before Guardiola was a coach, to mock Spain's pointless passing. Athletic Bilbao's coach Javier Clemente used it the same dismissive way. The insult later got attached to Barcelona's style.

Amit offers this as a parallel to 'liberal' and 'conservative', both of which began as cuss words thrown at people who never chose them. A label's origin can be the opposite of how it ends up being worn.

head: From Acres to Infosys
dek: This shows why 'liberal' and 'conservative' became opposites. From Adam Smith to Marx, thinkers saw capitalism and globalisation as a 'wild west wind' that would tear up the feudal order.
more: In 1907 or 1947, land carried deep emotional weight in India, especially in old North Indian machismo, because owning land meant wealth and income. A man with fifty thousand acres outranked a man with ten thousand. Today India's wealth comes from building businesses like Infosys and Reliance. Land is nice to have but neither necessary nor sufficient for success. The old landed classes did not want this change.

This shows why 'liberal' and 'conservative' became opposites. From Adam Smith to Marx, thinkers saw capitalism and globalisation as a 'wild west wind' that would tear up the feudal order. The people who benefited from aristocracy, land, religion and family hierarchy fought to keep it, and that defence became one meaning of conservatism.

head: Mary Wollstonecraft Reads Locke
dek: Modern feminism grew directly out of classical liberalism's idea of individual rights.
more: John Locke argued that we are born owning ourselves, and that the rights to life, free speech and property follow from that. At the end of the 18th century Mary Wollstonecraft read Locke and drew the next conclusion: if everyone has these inalienable rights, women have them too. In a world where 'he' and 'him' were the default for all people, this was a radical idea, and modern feminism grew out of it.
Modern feminism grew directly out of classical liberalism's idea of individual rights. A principle stated in general terms tends to be extended to people its author never had in mind.

head: Carrying Das Kapital to College
dek: Total theories are seductive to the young because they seem to explain everything, and they come with a flattering self-image.
more: At eighteen, Amit carried Das Kapital around in his college bag for a few days, feeling cool and intellectual. He had actually read Marx and Engels when young. He jokes that, thankfully, it did not completely destroy his brain.

Total theories are seductive to the young because they seem to explain everything, and they come with a flattering self-image. Amit's later views came from being 'mugged by reality': watching outcomes rather than intentions.

head: The Guest Who Couldn't Define 'Neoliberal'
dek: If someone cannot define a label they use as an insult, the label is doing their thinking for them.
more: At the end of an otherwise excellent episode of The Seen and the Unseen, a guest used 'neoliberal' as a slur. Amit asked her to define it, and she could not. He won't link the episode, but he now stops taking people seriously when they use the word.
If someone cannot define a label they use as an insult, the label is doing their thinking for them. A useful habit in any debate is to ask the other person to define their terms.

head: The Friend Who Dropped 'Proud Right Winger'
dek: You can stay exactly where you are while the label you wear moves. Tribes you do not control can change what your self-description means.
more: A dear friend of both hosts used to describe himself on Twitter as 'a proud right winger', meaning he supported free markets. About eleven or twelve years ago he removed it, because the word's connotations had changed and now covered much more than economics.
You can stay exactly where you are while the label you wear moves. Tribes you do not control can change what your self-description means.

head: The Professor Who Ranted Only Off the Record
dek: Amit cites this as a sign that even the left has started to recoil from wokeism, while privately disagreeing still feels unsafe in public.
more: Amit once had an openly left-wing American academic on his show. When the subject of wokeism came up, the guest asked him not to raise it on air. He said he would rant and rave about it privately, but as a professor at a US university there were things he could not say on the record.

Amit cites this as a sign that even the left has started to recoil from wokeism, while privately disagreeing still feels unsafe in public. It is a small view of how an ideological climate can silence its own sympathisers.

head: The Three Languages of Politics
dek: Explains why political discourse is broken: progressives argue from equality, libertarians from freedom and conservatives from tradition, so they talk past each other.
more: Explains why political discourse is broken: progressives argue from equality, libertarians from freedom and conservatives from tradition, so they talk past each other. The book teaches you to grant the other side's first principles and argue on their terms, which is how minds actually change.
First book on the closing reading list.

head: Communism
dek: A slim volume on what actually happened under communism, linking ideas to actions to consequences.
more: A slim volume on what actually happened under communism, linking ideas to actions to consequences. Amit suggests it as a way into Pipes's other books and into historians like Robert Conquest.

dek: Boaz is one of Amit's modern heroes, a great thinker who died recently.
more: Boaz is one of Amit's modern heroes, a great thinker who died recently. The book is a clear statement of the case for freedom.

dek: Amit calls it Ambedkar's 'great masterpiece of a book'. It is an early challenge to class-only thinking that puts caste at the centre.

dek: The founding text for the idea that means matter. Burke accepts the revolutionaries' ideals but warns that you cannot burn institutions to the ground and expect good outcomes.
more: The founding text for the idea that means matter. Burke accepts the revolutionaries' ideals but warns that you cannot burn institutions to the ground and expect good outcomes.

more: Source of Popper's diagnosis that nationalism appeals to tribal instinct and lets people escape the strain of individual responsibility.

more: A serious scholarly case for nationalism. Amit disagrees, and reading it alongside his review gives both sides. The review ends by arguing that those who divide us are the true anti-nationals.

head: Episode on Mary Wollstonecraft
dek: Wollstonecraft is one of Amit's great heroes. The episode covers how she extended Locke's rights to women and so began modern feminism.
more: Wollstonecraft is one of Amit's great heroes. The episode covers how she extended Locke's rights to women and so began modern feminism.

head: Common Noun vs Proper Noun
dek: A political label has a dictionary meaning and a separate meaning as a tribal brand.
more: A political label has a dictionary meaning and a separate meaning as a tribal brand. Quoting the dictionary to defend 'liberal' or 'socialist' misses that the label has picked up its own, often contradictory, baggage. Labels also change over time and between places, so a clear conversation needs both sides to say which meaning they intend.

head: Varma's Fifth Law
dek: Any label that confers prestige attracts people who want the prestige without the beliefs.
more: Any label that confers prestige attracts people who want the prestige without the beliefs. Once those people outnumber the believers, the label comes to mean its opposite. Amit says grifters took 'liberal' and are now taking 'libertarian'. This is part of why he now refuses all labels.

head: Cause, Movement, Racket — and Ideas Aren't Guilty by Association
dek: Ajay notes that every great idea starts as a cause, becomes a movement and ends up a racket as political formations grow around it.
more: Ajay notes that every great idea starts as a cause, becomes a movement and ends up a racket as political formations grow around it. He separates the idea from its followers: if Trump believes X, that says nothing about whether X is true. Ideas should be judged on their merits, not by who holds them.

head: Tribalism vs the Minor Matter of Being Correct
dek: People who join an ideological tribe take on all its dogmas and follow it wherever it drifts.
more: People who join an ideological tribe take on all its dogmas and follow it wherever it drifts. Amit's example is how so many conservatives and libertarians lined up behind Trump once he took over the Republican Party. He sees the same pattern in India. Ajay's remedy is to care about being right: forecasting what an intervention will actually do and judging it after ten, fifty or a hundred years.

head: The Hosts' Four First Principles
dek: Amit lays out their shared priors before defining anything. (1) The world is positive-sum, so poverty and inequality call for different, even opposite, policies. (2) Top-down design that worked in small hunter-gatherer tribes fails at the scale of a society. (3) Judge actions by outcomes, not intentions, since every ideology has fine intentions. (4) Freedom is good in itself and also produces the best outcomes, so think in terms of individuals, not groups.
more: Amit lays out their shared priors before defining anything. (1) The world is positive-sum, so poverty and inequality call for different, even opposite, policies. (2) Top-down design that worked in small hunter-gatherer tribes fails at the scale of a society. (3) Judge actions by outcomes, not intentions, since every ideology has fine intentions. (4) Freedom is good in itself and also produces the best outcomes, so think in terms of individuals, not groups. Ajay's illustration of point three is Hitler: no one did more damage to the 'Germanic peoples' than the man who championed them most fiercely.

head: Self-Ownership, Negative Rights and Positive Rights
dek: Locke's foundational right is self-ownership. The rights to life, free speech and property follow from it.
more: Locke's foundational right is self-ownership. The rights to life, free speech and property follow from it. Isaiah Berlin later called these 'negative' rights because they only require others not to do something to you. 'Positive rights' such as a right to food or free broadband require someone else to provide them, which means taxing others and so infringing their negative rights. Amit's point is not that the state should never feed people, for example in a famine. It is that calling entitlements 'rights' muddles every debate.

head: The Great Liberal Paradox
dek: Rights mean nothing unless someone enforces them, so we need a state. Thomas Paine called government a 'necessary evil'.
more: Rights mean nothing unless someone enforces them, so we need a state. Thomas Paine called government a 'necessary evil'. It is evil because it holds a monopoly on violence and lives on coerced taxes, so to protect our rights we must give some of them up. Amit concludes that every ideology is really an argument about how much state violence is justified. Adam Smith's version of the minimal state is 'peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice'.

head: How 'Liberal' Flipped in America — and Why 'Libertarian' Was Born
dek: Smith probably first used 'liberal' politically, writing of a 'liberal system of free exportation and free importation'.
more: Smith probably first used 'liberal' politically, writing of a 'liberal system of free exportation and free importation'. In the 20th century, American liberals took up positive rights and an expanding welfare state to fix inequality, while Europe kept the older meaning. Asked by Ajay, Amit agrees that small-state thinkers then adopted 'libertarian' for themselves. In effect, 'classical liberal' and 'libertarian' describe the same old-school liberalism.

head: Two Conservatisms
dek: Amit separates two impulses in the word. One defends an established order, whether religion, family, social hierarchy or oligarchy, often because its defenders benefit from it.
more: Amit separates two impulses in the word. One defends an established order, whether religion, family, social hierarchy or oligarchy, often because its defenders benefit from it. The other is a more sophisticated stance: the world is too complex for grand coercive schemes, and means matter. Amit rejects the first, because the world needs radical change, and fully accepts the second.

head: Liberal Ends, Conservative Means
dek: Burke's central lesson separates ends from means. Change the world, by all means, but remember that institutions and norms have survived for reasons and cannot be burnt down without consequences.
more: Burke's central lesson separates ends from means. Change the world, by all means, but remember that institutions and norms have survived for reasons and cannot be burnt down without consequences. Amit argues that India has little of this Burkean conservatism. What gets called conservatism here is either preserving the past for its own sake or a radical, divisive tribalism that goes against India's assimilative traditions.

head: Marxism as Theory, Socialism as Path, Communism as Destination
dek: Marxism, from the Communist Manifesto (1848) and Das Kapital (1867), divides the world into a bourgeoisie that oppresses and exploits a proletariat.
more: Marxism, from the Communist Manifesto (1848) and Das Kapital (1867), divides the world into a bourgeoisie that oppresses and exploits a proletariat. The predicted revolution passes through a 'dictatorship of the proletariat'. Amit lists the criticisms: it reduces everything to class (Weber, Popper); its predicted collapse of capitalism never came (Popper, Fukuyama); it ignores race, gender and caste (Foucault, intersectional thinkers); it goes against human nature (Isaiah Berlin, and E.O. Wilson's 'Great idea, wrong species'); and it can only be reached through mass violence (Arendt, Aron). Communism's destination is no private property and 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'. Amit says this amounts to equality of poverty, and that it was markets, not communism, that made China rich.

head: Why Total Theories Seduce
dek: A successful ideology offers a frame into which every event can be fitted, so it seems to explain everything.
more: A successful ideology offers a frame into which every event can be fitted, so it seems to explain everything. That is what makes it so attractive to the young, and it is also a warning sign. A theory that can absorb any evidence is not really being tested by any.

head: Growth Dwarfs the Business Cycle
dek: Marx predicted that capitalism's booms and busts would grow worse, and the Great Depression seemed to confirm it.
more: Marx predicted that capitalism's booms and busts would grow worse, and the Great Depression seemed to confirm it. Amit adds that it is now understood to have been caused by state action, as Thomas Sowell has written. Ajay notes that no shock since has been as large, and that 2008 was relatively small. Booms and busts are a normal part of how capitalism works. As Robert Lucas observed, they are trivial next to the steady compounding of growth. Natural experiments like North versus South Korea and East versus West Germany settle the question.

head: Individuals, Not Groups
dek: Liberalism takes the individual as its unit. Marxism, and any ideology built on group averages, essentialises people who contain multitudes.
more: Liberalism takes the individual as its unit. Marxism, and any ideology built on group averages, essentialises people who contain multitudes. Amit cites Ayn Rand: the smallest minority is the individual. Ajay adds that people are heterogeneous, and averages like 'men are taller than women' flatten that richness.

head: Socialism Is a Program, Not a Synonym for 'Good for Society'
dek: In political theory, socialism has four features: public ownership of resources, redistribution towards equal outcomes, a centrally planned economy, and attractive stated intentions that it fails to deliver.
more: In political theory, socialism has four features: public ownership of resources, redistribution towards equal outcomes, a centrally planned economy, and attractive stated intentions that it fails to deliver. Indians tend to read it as the Hindi 'samajwad', meaning broadly 'on the side of society', which Amit happily accepts. As a proper noun, though, it describes the Fabian-style planning that kept India poor. Ajay adds that socialism can only be built by crushing individual rights, so it cannot coexist with constitutional liberal democracy.

head: From Revolutionary Violence to One-Party Rule
dek: Ajay asks why state ownership of everything always ends in one-party dictatorship.
more: Ajay asks why state ownership of everything always ends in one-party dictatorship. Amit, thinking aloud, says a movement that accepts coercion as a way to take power will use it to keep power. Once you have built a state strong enough to jail every opponent, you have no reason to give it up.

head: Statism and Smith's 'Man of System'
dek: Statism is not a separate ideology. It is an attitude many ideologies share: the belief that society can be run from the top down.
more: Statism is not a separate ideology. It is an attitude many ideologies share: the belief that society can be run from the top down. Adam Smith's 'man of system' falls in love with his ideal plan and arranges people like pieces on a chessboard. Real people have their own motives, and when those clash with the plan, society falls into disorder.

head: Libertarianism: Treat People as Adults
dek: Libertarians come in two kinds. Anarchists think norms are enough and no state is needed.
more: Libertarians come in two kinds. Anarchists think norms are enough and no state is needed. Minarchists, which includes Amit, accept a limited night-watchman state. Amit quotes David Boaz: conservatives want to be your daddy, liberals want to be your mommy, and libertarians want to treat you as an adult. Amit's test is that two consenting adults who harm no one should be left alone, both in the bedroom and in the marketplace.

head: Left and Right: Seating Chart Turned Shorthand
dek: The terms come from the French National Assembly. Those seated on the left opposed the monarchy and the feudal order, and those on the right defended them.
more: The terms come from the French National Assembly. Those seated on the left opposed the monarchy and the feudal order, and those on the right defended them. Amit describes today's left as using the state as the instrument of change, with coercion and zero-sum thinking built in, though it is often right about social freedoms. Today's right combines both kinds of conservatism with support for free markets. Ajay once mapped left and right onto inequality versus growth. He now notes Lant Pritchett's 'anti-growth coalition' in every country, and that anti-growth policies increasingly come from the right. In India, Amit says, the label makes no sense, because every party is against freedom in both domains.

head: Patriotism vs Nationalism
dek: Patriotism is loving your country. Nationalism defines the nation by 'othering' some people and plays on hardwired tribal instincts.
more: Patriotism is loving your country. Nationalism defines the nation by 'othering' some people and plays on hardwired tribal instincts. Tagore called nationalism a great menace. Popper said it appeals to passion and prejudice and lets people escape the strain of individual responsibility. Ramachandra Guha, quoted by Amit, says a patriot works to make his country less violent, less poor and less exploitative, while a nationalist wants to bomb everybody else. Amit proposes Varma's Sixth Law: anyone who calls others anti-national is the true anti-national.

head: Hindutva as Othering by Definition
dek: In 'What is Hindutva' (1925), Savarkar defined a Hindu as someone whose homeland and land of worship are both India.
more: In 'What is Hindutva' (1925), Savarkar defined a Hindu as someone whose homeland and land of worship are both India. Amit calls the definition masterful but toxic, because it neatly includes Jains and Buddhists while excluding Muslims and Christians, and no one questions the premise. Aakar Patel's test, which Amit puts to listeners, is that for most ideologies you can say what they are for, but for Hindutva you can only say what it is against.

head: Nationalism Is Born of Insecurity
dek: Ajay observes that intensely nationalistic people are often privately anxious about India's weaknesses and about the success of advanced economies.
more: Ajay observes that intensely nationalistic people are often privately anxious about India's weaknesses and about the success of advanced economies. Confident people relax and engage with others as equals. He contrasts this with how Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru combined being Indian with openness to the world. Gandhi, for instance, was deeply influenced by Tolstoy and read the New Testament closely.

head: Wokeism Begins Where Liberalism Ends
dek: 'Woke' originally meant being awake to social injustice, a meaning Amit embraces.
more: 'Woke' originally meant being awake to social injustice, a meaning Amit embraces. As an ideology, he argues, it succeeds Marxism. It keeps the oppressor/oppressed frame and multiplies the categories through intersectionality. People are fixed by their identity at birth as victim or oppressor, which leads to an 'Olympics of victimhood'. Liberalism respects the individual's complexity, while wokeism essentialises it. Amit thinks peak woke is behind us.

head: Argue From the Other Side's First Principles
dek: Following Arnold Kling, Amit argues that progressives (equality), libertarians (freedom) and conservatives (tradition) talk past each other by repeating their own values.
more: Following Arnold Kling, Amit argues that progressives (equality), libertarians (freedom) and conservatives (tradition) talk past each other by repeating their own values. If you care about freedom and the other person cares about equality, start by agreeing on the goal, such as reducing poverty, and then argue from history and evidence about what will achieve it. That is how Bayesian updating actually happens.

head: After Ajay promises listeners a…
more: After Ajay promises listeners a 'beautiful storyline', Amit replies: 'there is one way in which you are like a socialist. Which is that you promise a lot. And I'm worried if [I] can deliver.'

head: Introducing Varma's Fifth Law, Amit asks Ajay
more: Introducing Varma's Fifth Law, Amit asks Ajay: 'Do you know the first four laws?' Ajay: 'No, not even one.' Amit: 'Neither do I.' He promises to 'figure out three more in between later'.

head: Amit imagines the biologist E.O. Wilson telling Karl Marx, who died long before Wilson was born
more: Amit imagines the biologist E.O. Wilson telling Karl Marx, who died long before Wilson was born: 'dude, great freaking theory, man, but sell it to the ants.' Then he adds that ants are already like that, so you don't need to sell them anything.

head: Ajay's Soviet joke: they justified the destruction by saying you have to break eggs to make an omelette, and then someone asks…
more: Ajay's Soviet joke: they justified the destruction by saying you have to break eggs to make an omelette, and then someone asks, 'We broke a lot of eggs. Where's the omelette?'

Ajay: 'He who has not been a Marxist as a child has no heart. And he who is a Marxist as an adult has no brain.' Amit scolds him for using 'left' before they have defined it, telling him not to use words they haven't explained yet, 'which basically would mean don't say anything'.

head: Ajay on human inequality
more: Ajay on human inequality: 'Everybody is not born with an Elo of 2830... My Elo sucks and you just got to accept this. We're all different. I'm not Magnus.' Later Amit says that when they play chess the plan may work 'even if you're not 2830'.

head: Amit on communism: he'd presumably be allowed to keep his iPad, though the state could take it any time
more: Amit on communism: he'd presumably be allowed to keep his iPad, though the state could take it any time, 'Except that there would be no iPad because I would not be rich enough in a communist society to buy an iPad unless I was kind of running the show.'

head: On being unable to register a party without pledging to socialism
more: On being unable to register a party without pledging to socialism: 'which of course we never will, because we are thinkers and not doers. No, we are doers but in a different way.'

head: Amit on why he dropped the libertarian label
more: Amit on why he dropped the libertarian label: 'I don't like labels, and I also don't like other libertarians because they're not libertarian.'

head: On Bill Clinton's sensible pro-market presidency
more: On Bill Clinton's sensible pro-market presidency: 'One could say his personal failing was he was too liberal with his affections, but leaving that aside.' This calls back to the episode's opening point about 'liberal with her affections' as a common-noun usage.

head: Amit on doing a full episode about wokeism someday
more: Amit on doing a full episode about wokeism someday: 'after which I will get lynched and the show will end. So maybe that's well into the future.'

head: After the tiki-taka story
more: After the tiki-taka story: 'Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman, Pep Guardiola, these are all geniuses, and we should respect and venerate them.'

head: Etymology
more: Etymology: 'liberal' comes from the Latin liber/liberalis, meaning generous and befitting a free person. That is the source of everyday phrases like 'liberal with her affections' or 'liberal with his wealth'.

head: Hobbes's
more: Hobbes's 'nasty, brutish and short' and Thomas Paine's description of government as 'a necessary evil' in Common Sense. Amit says Paine's is where the phrase first comes from.

head: Adam Smith probably first used
more: Adam Smith probably first used 'liberal' in a political sense in The Wealth of Nations, writing of 'the liberal system of free exportation and free importation'. Amit adds: 'So globalization Zindabad.'

head: Ajay criticises Subhas Chandra Bose, whom he describes as an ICS topper who…
more: Ajay criticises Subhas Chandra Bose, whom he describes as an ICS topper who 'wanted to pick up guns and change the order'. He argues that anti-colonial movements fought with guns left a legacy of violence that ripped up their societies.

head: Nehru was…
more: Nehru was 'under the sway' of the Fabian Society, which he encountered in England, and so became a Fabian socialist, which led to India's five-year plans.

head: Mark Carney: From the Bank of England to Prime Minister of Canada, via Donald Trump
dek: Manmohan Singh was appointed at every step. Carney won fair and square through the constitution, and that gives him a different level of authority.
more: In 2012, after scandals in the UK, Britain's appointment process chose a Canadian, Mark Carney, to run its central bank. This worked because both countries have mature statistics, sound models and strong research teams, so inflation targeting in Canada is much like inflation targeting in the UK. Carney later went home and entered party politics. Then two 'miracles' happened. Trudeau's popularity collapsed, which opened space for a right-wing nationalist. Then Trump threatened to annex Canada as the next US state, and angry Canadians voted for any plausible candidate who was not a right-wing conservative. That candidate turned out to be Carney.

Manmohan Singh was appointed at every step. Carney won fair and square through the constitution, and that gives him a different level of authority. But a technocrat with little knowledge of party machines may have been lifted by a one-off moment. Whether he can win again once Trump matters less is an open question.

head: Nehru's Congress: When Chief Ministers Could Say No
dek: A prime minister being refused by his own party's state leaders was a sign of institutional health.
more: In the late 1940s, a Ram idol was placed inside the Babri Masjid. An aghast Nehru asked UP chief minister Govind Ballabh Pant to remove it ('isko hatao'). Pant refused, and so did UP's home minister at the time, Lal Bahadur Shastri. In Nehru's era, state legislators elected their own chief minister and party politics ran bottom-up. Amit argues that Indira Gandhi later hollowed out the Congress by removing and appointing chief ministers at will.
A prime minister being refused by his own party's state leaders was a sign of institutional health. A party that becomes an extension of one leader's will turns into a toothless shell.

head: Havel's Notebook: 'Questions I Cannot Answer'
dek: Blocked from the formal path, Havel educated himself anyway. The notebook title captures what Amit admires most: deep curiosity paired with deep humility.
more: The communists branded Havel's well-to-do family class enemies, so he was barred from studying philosophy at university. He took a job as a lab technician there just to be near it. Michael Zantovsky's biography describes him arriving in overalls, pockets stuffed with Kafka, Camus, Heidegger and Nietzsche, and writing alone in a battered journal during breaks while co-workers joked that he was a professor. Amit also recalls, from memory and without being able to find it online, a friend's story: Havel was scribbling furiously in a notebook, and as he closed it the friend saw its title, 'Questions I Cannot Answer'.
Blocked from the formal path, Havel educated himself anyway. The notebook title captures what Amit admires most: deep curiosity paired with deep humility.

head: Charter 77: 'You Have Already Taken a Side'
dek: Neutrality under oppression is an illusion. Staying silent is itself a choice that favours the oppressor, so a citizen's duty goes beyond not doing evil to actually speaking up.
more: In 1977 Havel co-authored Charter 77 and wanted many Czechoslovaks to sign it. One fellow traveller said she agreed with it but felt signing was dangerous and wasn't sure she should take a side. Havel told her she had already taken one, just not the one she thought. She signed. Decades later, campaigning in 2008 for the Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo to get the Nobel Prize, Havel said the crimes of the twentieth century began when good men stayed silent.
Neutrality under oppression is an illusion. Staying silent is itself a choice that favours the oppressor, so a citizen's duty goes beyond not doing evil to actually speaking up.
printed: The side she had already taken

head: Havel, the President Who Refused to Become a Politician
dek: Authenticity in office means refusing to let the role turn you into its uniform.
more: Havel spent four continuous years in prison (1979–83). After the Velvet Revolution he formed the Civic Forum, a motley crew of civil-society figures; one fellow dissident said they had 'no plan, no money, no weapons. Only Havel's calm voice and his moral authority.' As president he would not move into the presidential palace and stayed in his humble flat. Amit contrasts this with Arvind Kejriwal, who made noises about refusing an official bungalow and then had a palatial house refurbished. Havel also refused to wear a tie. When a reporter asked why the president had dishevelled hair and a messy jacket, Havel said he represented the people, and the people were like that. And instead of filling his calendar with summits, he invited Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones to perform.
Authenticity in office means refusing to let the role turn you into its uniform. Amit draws the Indian parallel of the white kurta-pyjama, worn by many only because it is what politicians wear.

head: Havel vs Lee Kuan Yew: 'Then I Shall Tell Him He Is Wrong'
dek: Meetings between heads of state are usually choreographed and diplomatic.
more: Salil Tripathi, telling the story on The Seen and the Unseen, was at a press conference with Havel, who was due to meet Lee Kuan Yew that afternoon. Salil asked Havel about the view that free speech matters less than feeding a hungry person. Havel said he disagreed: without free speech, how would a hungry person say they are hungry? Then he asked who held that view. Salil replied that it was the person he was meeting that afternoon. The room went silent. Havel said he would make sure to tell Lee he was wrong.
Meetings between heads of state are usually choreographed and diplomatic. Havel's way of doing things was to stay true to himself, even when holding power.

head: Katyn: Why Tyrants Hunt Thinkers
dek: Occupiers understand that a country's thinking elite is the source of its long-term strength.
more: When the Soviet army invaded Poland in 1939 and met the German army, splitting the country roughly in half, the Soviets came with a list of Polish intellectuals, leaders, thinkers and scientists. These people were seized, taken to a camp called Katyn in the USSR, and killed one by one.

Occupiers understand that a country's thinking elite is the source of its long-term strength. Destroy that class and the country stays weak, which makes it easier to dominate. That is why people like Havel matter so disproportionately.

head: Nehru's 'Chanakya' Letter Against Himself
dek: Ajay calls it his favourite Nehru story. A sitting leader publicly sounding the alarm about his own power is the opposite of a politician's instinct, and it shows a man genuinely worried about concentrated power.
more: While Nehru was prime minister, a letter signed 'Chanakya' appeared in the Hindustan Times. It warned that Nehru was becoming a Julius Caesar: power had concentrated in him, he was surrounded by sycophants, he dismissed people with a wave of his hand, and readers should get together and dethrone him. Years later it emerged that Nehru himself had written it.

Ajay calls it his favourite Nehru story. A sitting leader publicly sounding the alarm about his own power is the opposite of a politician's instinct, and it shows a man genuinely worried about concentrated power.

head: Nehru the Writer: Jail Notebooks and a Speech on Tissue Paper
dek: Tryst with Destiny has become a cliché, but read with fresh eyes it shows a thinker, dreamer and idealist rather than a normal politician.
more: Nehru spent nine years in British jails. There was no heating or air conditioning, but he had books and notebooks and was not beaten, a decency the British did not extend to Savarkar. He used the time to read and write, producing Glimpses of World History as letters to his daughter, and The Discovery of India. Tryst with Destiny, which Salman Rushdie made chapter one of his anthology of Indian writing, was scribbled on a random piece of tissue paper about fifteen minutes before the speech.
Tryst with Destiny has become a cliché, but read with fresh eyes it shows a thinker, dreamer and idealist rather than a normal politician. Nehru turned prison into a workshop for ideas.

head: The Chain of Accidents That Made Nehru Prime Minister
dek: Even a towering 'natural' leader was an accident of history. Decent people choosing decent people, rather than realpolitik, put him there.
more: Nehru was a highly educated, English-speaking returnee from the UK with no obvious political career ahead of him. Without the First World War, the Great Depression, the Second World War and the Atlantic Charter, Ajay argues, the British would not have left in 1947, and if they had stayed twenty more years it would not have been Nehru's time. Gandhi then picked him out of a galaxy of great people as the dreamer and philosopher he wanted. Amit adds that Gandhi's main reason for choosing him over the free-market-loving Rajaji was that Nehru was much younger, yet Rajaji outlived him. Nehru then won genuine mass popularity: people trekked for a week to catch a glimpse of him, with no big screens and barely any loudspeakers.
Even a towering 'natural' leader was an accident of history. Decent people choosing decent people, rather than realpolitik, put him there.

head: Manmohan Singh's PhD: Indians Can Export
dek: The quiet technocrat began as an iconoclast. Fatalistic beliefs about a nation's 'nature' often turn out to be the result of bad policy.
more: In the 1960s, Indian economists broadly agreed that India, being India, was incapable of exporting. In his PhD thesis, Manmohan Singh was one of the first to challenge this. He argued that export success depends on incentives such as prices, customs duties and exchange rates, so with the right policies there was no reason India could not export.
The quiet technocrat began as an iconoclast. Fatalistic beliefs about a nation's 'nature' often turn out to be the result of bad policy.
printed: When India was a dinky country

head: Percy Mistry's Million-Pound Cheque
dek: Ajay offers it as an example of a bigger-scale generation, people who personally underwrote public-spirited projects when institutions failed.
more: Manmohan Singh was to head the South-South Commission in Geneva when Ronald Reagan cut off UN funding, leaving him with no money to function or build the institution. Percy Mistry wrote a personal cheque for a million pounds as a loan to the commission, which got it started. When funding later resumed, the money was repaid.
Ajay offers it as an example of a bigger-scale generation, people who personally underwrote public-spirited projects when institutions failed.

head: 1991: When Nobody Gave a Damn About India
dek: The reform that launched India 'into a different orbit' rested on unglamorous groundwork, built-up documentation and a quiet man doing the legwork when India counted for little.
more: By the late-1980s balance of payments crisis, policy confusion between the RBI and the Finance Ministry had run India into a wall. Imports had stalled, life-saving drugs and raw materials couldn't come in, and factories were closing. Reform ideas had been developed under Chandra Shekhar with Yashwant Sinha as finance minister, but that government was short-lived. India was friendless after the USSR's fall, and Manmohan Singh quietly trekked between the India ED's office, the US Treasury and the IMF to get programmes moving. Percy Mistry worked his networks to speed up the money. A young Urjit Patel was negotiating on the IMF's side of the table, and Ashok Desai was chief economic adviser. Then came the July 1991 budget speech.
The reform that launched India 'into a different orbit' rested on unglamorous groundwork, built-up documentation and a quiet man doing the legwork when India counted for little.

head: Manmohan Singh in the Back Row, and at the Book Launch
dek: Ajay sees this quiet decency as Manmohan Singh's method. He spent decades learning India's institutions, built coalitions gently, and moved a climate of opinion.
more: Between his stints in power, Manmohan Singh was a private citizen in Delhi. Ajay, then a young researcher from Bombay giving talks, kept noticing him slip into the back seats, listen, and almost never speak or throw his weight around. In 2019, Vijay Kelkar invited him to release the first edition of Kelkar and Ajay's book In Service of the Republic. Manmohan Singh declined to be announced as chief guest because he was unwell and didn't want to derail the launch if he couldn't come. Then, without any announcement, he showed up, sat in the front row, shook Ajay's hand and told him it was a very important book.

Ajay sees this quiet decency as Manmohan Singh's method. He spent decades learning India's institutions, built coalitions gently, and moved a climate of opinion. Ajay calls that how a paradigm shifts, and he compares Manmohan Singh to Vajpayee in this respect.
printed: From the back row to the front

head: Manmohan Singh Puts His Foot Down on the Nuclear Deal
dek: Amit uses it to show that accidental politicians can show real rectitude and courage once they are in the game.
more: In UPA-1, the Left parties supporting the government from outside threatened to pull out over the nuclear deal with the US. That was an existential risk to the government. Manmohan Singh refused to back down and got the deal through.
Amit uses it to show that accidental politicians can show real rectitude and courage once they are in the game.

head: Putin's Misreadings Before the Ukraine Invasion
dek: Strongman thinking mistakes the restraint and rule-following of liberal democracies, and talent in unfamiliar packaging, for weakness.
more: Ajay argues Putin, a strongman 'deeply grounded in maleness', underestimated three things. He saw Zelenskyy as just a TV comedian. He looked at Western Europe's female defence ministers and thought 'they're women, what will they do?' And he read America's chaotic Afghanistan withdrawal as weakness: the US kept to a deal with the Taliban rather than staying longer for a managed exit. (Amit points out the withdrawal was botched under Biden; Ajay notes the dates were set by Trump.)

Strongman thinking mistakes the restraint and rule-following of liberal democracies, and talent in unfamiliar packaging, for weakness. Ajay sees these misjudgements as steps toward the mistake of February 2022.

head: Zelenskyy: 'I Need Ammunition, Not a Ride'
dek: His choice to stay showed Western countries that Ukraine would fight, and that is what made them willing to send military kit.
more: Zelenskyy, a successful comedian, had played a president in a TV series. He then won 73% of the vote with an internet-heavy campaign as a clean outsider. When Russia invaded, Ajay expected the armoured thrust from Belarus to take Kyiv and Zelenskyy to flee to Lviv or run a government in exile from Poland. It is believed three separate assassination teams came for his house on the first night, with his wife and two small children there. Offered a way out, he said his place was here and he needed ammunition, not a ride.
His choice to stay showed Western countries that Ukraine would fight, and that is what made them willing to send military kit. Ajay says Zelenskyy made the right call every step of the way.
printed: The comedian who would not leave

head: Roosevelt's Dying Envoy to Stalin
dek: Before allies commit resources, they need to know the leader has the stomach for a fight.
more: After Germany launched Operation Barbarossa in 1941, Roosevelt sent one of his most trusted advisers, who was dying of cancer, on a long route through Britain, North Africa and Iran to Moscow. His single task was to judge whether Stalin would stand and fight. The adviser met Stalin and sent back a short message: yes.
Before allies commit resources, they need to know the leader has the stomach for a fight. The West made the same judgement about Zelenskyy.

head: Demonetisation and the Paan Shop
dek: Leaders cut off from ordinary transactions miss the texture of the economy.
more: Amit wrote a series of pieces against demonetisation, and one in the Times of India went viral: Rahul Gandhi and Kejriwal tweeted it, and an IT cell abused him for it. In it he took apart each of Modi's reasons. A key one was that Modi had been out of touch with daily life for decades. When Indira Gandhi demonetised in 1978, a thousand-rupee note was worth about twelve thousand rupees in 2016 terms. The 500-rupee note scrapped in 2016 was an everyday transaction note, and the cash-based informal economy was devastated.
Leaders cut off from ordinary transactions miss the texture of the economy. Amit argues an outsider with real-world experience would never have assumed poor people don't use 500-rupee notes.
printed: Out of touch, out of notes

head: George H.W. Bush Meets a Barcode Scanner
dek: Elite life cuts leaders off from the ordinary world. Ajay's broader point is that real knowledge flows to leaders through conversations with people who aren't reverential toward them.
more: While running for election, Bush did a staged photo op at a supermarket checkout. When the cashier scanned an item and the price appeared instantly on the terminal, astonishment showed on his face, with the TV cameras rolling.
Elite life cuts leaders off from the ordinary world. Ajay's broader point is that real knowledge flows to leaders through conversations with people who aren't reverential toward them.

head: The Garden Party and Other Plays
dek: He says they are hilarious, available in English and worth reading in full.
more: He says they are hilarious, available in English and worth reading in full. The plays dramatise Havel's conviction that language shapes reality.

Amit summarised The Garden Party, in which a young man rises to head a liquidation office by mastering content-free bureaucratic language until his own parents can't recognise him. He also discussed The Memorandum, built around an invented language designed for obfuscation.

head: Letters to Olga
dek: Amit calls it beautiful and quotes a line that sends a chill up his spine: 'If I am to be punished, let it be for who I am.
more: Amit calls it beautiful and quotes a line that sends a chill up his spine: 'If I am to be punished, let it be for who I am. If I am to be free, let it be as myself, not someone else's puppet.'
Havel's letters to his wife during his years in prison.

head: The Power of the Powerless
dek: He calls it a wonderful extended essay and notes the latest edition has an introduction by Timothy Snyder, also worth reading.
more: He calls it a wonderful extended essay and notes the latest edition has an introduction by Timothy Snyder, also worth reading.
Amit's end-of-episode recommendation, alongside all of Havel's plays.

head: To the Castle and Back
dek: Amit calls it a wonderful book.
more: Amit calls it a wonderful book.
Havel's memoir, recommended at the end.

head: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It is a close-to-home example of how everyday grammar robs women of agency.
more: It is a close-to-home example of how everyday grammar robs women of agency.
Amit recalled Shrayana pointing out that men describe marriage as something they do, while women describe it as something that happens to them.

head: Glimpses of World History
dek: It gave Ajay the feeling of a father telling stories to a daughter, exactly how his own father talked to him.
more: It gave Ajay the feeling of a father telling stories to a daughter, exactly how his own father talked to him. He calls it a phenomenal book.
Written as letters from jail to his daughter. It was one of the earliest books Ajay read, as a child.

head: The Discovery of India
dek: Ajay considers it one of the most important theoretical books about India.
more: Ajay considers it one of the most important theoretical books about India. It salvages an idea of India grounded in history and free of hatred, and sets up a modern synthesis comfortable with science and liberal democracy.
Discussed as part of Nehru's jail-time output.

head: A Tryst With Destiny
dek: Ajay urges listeners to step out of the cliché and read it with fresh eyes, as transcendental writing.
more: Ajay urges listeners to step out of the cliché and read it with fresh eyes, as transcendental writing.
Scribbled on tissue paper about fifteen minutes before it was delivered.

head: The Light Has Gone Out of Our Lives
dek: He says that raspy voice still does something to you across all these years.
more: He says that raspy voice still does something to you across all these years.
Ajay asked for Nehru's recording to be linked alongside Tryst with Destiny.

head: Letters to Chief Ministers
dek: They show a prime minister who wrote copiously and clearly. For Amit, that habit made Nehru a better thinker, and no modern politician of any party does it.
more: They show a prime minister who wrote copiously and clearly. For Amit, that habit made Nehru a better thinker, and no modern politician of any party does it.
Amit had been reading these before recording. He added them to Ajay's list of Nehru's books and later recommended all of Nehru's books.

head: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
dek: He uses them to argue that India's founding leaders were great thinkers partly because they were prolific writers.
more: He uses them to argue that India's founding leaders were great thinkers partly because they were prolific writers.
Amit mentioned that Gandhi's 99 volumes are online.

head: The Collected Writings and Speeches of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar
dek: Same argument: prolific writing went hand in hand with great thinking.
more: Same argument: prolific writing went hand in hand with great thinking.
Mentioned alongside Gandhi's volumes. Ambedkar's 60-plus volumes are online.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: It is the book Manmohan Singh personally endorsed, written by two people who worked inside India's policy process.
more: It is the book Manmohan Singh personally endorsed, written by two people who worked inside India's policy process.
Manmohan Singh came unannounced to its 2019 launch and told Ajay it was a very important book. A second-edition paperback is now out.

head: Servant of the People
dek: It is the improbable starting point of the most unlikely accidental-politician story.
more: It is the improbable starting point of the most unlikely accidental-politician story.
The TV series in which Zelenskyy, then a comedian, played a president before becoming one.

head: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It is the source of his framework of electoral politics, intra-party/legislative politics, and governance.
more: It is the source of his framework of electoral politics, intra-party/legislative politics, and governance.
The episode where Amit put to MR Madhavan the idea that politicians play three different games.

head: Yes Prime Minister
dek: Ajay calls both of them masterpieces.
more: Ajay calls both of them masterpieces.
Recommended together with Yes Minister.

head: Mature Institutions Make Expertise Portable, and Importable
dek: A Canadian could run the Bank of England because advanced economies have sound measurement, good models, strong research teams and invisible checks and balances.
more: A Canadian could run the Bank of England because advanced economies have sound measurement, good models, strong research teams and invisible checks and balances. Knowledge then travels across borders, in a kind of post-nationalism. India is different: the measurement is bad, the models barely exist and the RBI sits in a political mess, so expertise has to be rebuilt locally. Ajay applies the same logic to countries. East Germany 'cheated' by simply grabbing West German institutions. Poland imported some twenty thousand pages of EU rules on how to be a European country. Ukraine got no such machinery and inherited only the arbitrary violence of the USSR.

head: Political Parties Need to Be Depersonalised
dek: India has paid too little attention to the political party as an institution.
more: India has paid too little attention to the political party as an institution. Like firms, parties need internal rules, norms, culture and a deep talent pool that outlasts individuals. The US has access points into politics at every level, from city to state to federal. Amit adds that Nehru's Congress worked this way, with chief ministers elected by legislators and able to refuse the PM, until Indira Gandhi hollowed it out.

head: Language Shapes Reality
dek: Havel's plays show people losing their individuality by adopting empty bureaucratic language, and he told his actors that language shapes reality.
more: Havel's plays show people losing their individuality by adopting empty bureaucratic language, and he told his actors that language shapes reality. Vague language hides what is happening and makes everything seem banal. Jackson Katz shows how the passive voice in 'violence against women' leaves out who is doing it. Shrayana Bhattacharya noted that women speak of marriage as something that happens to them, which robs them of agency.

head: Silence Is Taking a Side
dek: Havel's lesson from Charter 77 and the Liu Xiaobo campaign echoes the line attributed to Edmund Burke.
more: Havel's lesson from Charter 77 and the Liu Xiaobo campaign echoes the line attributed to Edmund Burke. A citizen's duty is not only to refuse to cooperate with evil but also to speak up, because neutrality favours the powerful.

head: The Appetite for Decency
dek: After the violence and lies of communism, or after Watergate, societies briefly crave a safe, ethical leader.
more: After the violence and lies of communism, or after Watergate, societies briefly crave a safe, ethical leader. That is when a poet like Havel, a Lech Walesa or a Jimmy Carter becomes possible. Soft moral power was also the only option against the USSR, just as fighting the British Empire needed a Gandhi rather than guns. Once the window closes, normal machine politics of polling booths and party organisation returns.

head: A Country Cannot Be Better Than Its Thinkers
dek: A nation's thinkers set its production possibility frontier. A country can fall far below that frontier but cannot go beyond it.
more: A nation's thinkers set its production possibility frontier. A country can fall far below that frontier but cannot go beyond it. Post-communist Eastern Europe had its Havels and Walesas, and post-1947 India had Nehru, Gandhi and Ambedkar. Building a country from scratch, including choices like letting Slovakia go peacefully, depends on that intellectual and moral capability. Tyrants know this, which is why the Soviets killed Poland's thinkers at Katyn.

head: Incentives and High Activation Energy Selected the Freedom Generation
dek: Amit's answer to why India's first generation of leaders was so outstanding is incentives.
more: Amit's answer to why India's first generation of leaders was so outstanding is incentives. They were crusaders for principles, not careerists, whereas today politics is rival mafias fighting for a monopoly on violence and it attracts that kind of person. Ajay adds a selection effect: taking on the British Empire was so costly that only the best jumped in, and then they found and argued with each other, as Gandhi did with Tagore.

head: The Means Matter
dek: Postcolonial countries whose liberation movements took up guns tend to fall into repeated cycles of violence.
more: Postcolonial countries whose liberation movements took up guns tend to fall into repeated cycles of violence. India was lucky that its freedom movement sidelined the violent figures, Savarkar and Bose among them, and that Gandhi would call off a nationwide movement over violence at one police station. After 1947, Nehru's era firmly separated civilian rule from the military, so the army was never invited into power.

head: The Strongman Pose Masks Inner Weakness
dek: Nehru, even after nine years in jail, stayed a happy man who smiled, told jokes and made fun of himself.
more: Nehru, even after nine years in jail, stayed a happy man who smiled, told jokes and made fun of himself. Ajay sees that comfort with oneself as a mark of great leaders. A secure person has nothing to prove, while the swagger of modern strongmen signals insecurity.

head: Writing Is a Way of Thinking
dek: Nehru wrote long letters to chief ministers, and Gandhi and Ambedkar left dozens of volumes.
more: Nehru wrote long letters to chief ministers, and Gandhi and Ambedkar left dozens of volumes. They were great thinkers partly because they were prolific writers. Writing, even in private, is how you engage with the world, understand yourself and shape your character. Amit laments that no modern Indian politician does this.

head: Hybrid Warfare: Turning a Country Against Itself
dek: After 94% of Ukrainians voted for independence in 1991, Russia kept interfering.
more: After 94% of Ukrainians voted for independence in 1991, Russia kept interfering. It backed and armed a pro-Russian party and fomented polarisation, conflict and anger so the country stayed weak.

head: The Three Games of Politics
dek: From Amit's conversation with MR Madhavan: a politician in government plays three separate games.
more: From Amit's conversation with MR Madhavan: a politician in government plays three separate games. The first is electoral politics, reading the public pulse and winning votes, a skill Amit says we shouldn't disdain. The second is politics within the party and the legislature. The third is governance, running ministries, bureaucracies and institutions. Skill in one predicts little about the others, and Churchill, a war winner booted out in peace, is the reminder. So Amit's answer on whether Zelenskyy can win a post-war election is that we simply don't know.

head: Outsiders Are Generalists
dek: A career politician, especially in India, may never have had a paying job and doesn't know the outside world.
more: A career politician, especially in India, may never have had a paying job and doesn't know the outside world. Bankers, lawyers and businesspeople bring domain knowledge and respect for enterprise. Someone who chooses to leave a successful career for politics also tends to have wider interests than their peers.

head: Skin in the Game, and Unreverential Friends
dek: Outsiders have lived in the real world and may have been on the receiving end of bad policy, while insulated careerists produce errors like demonetisation.
more: Outsiders have lived in the real world and may have been on the receiving end of bad policy, while insulated careerists produce errors like demonetisation. Ajay adds that knowledge reaches leaders mainly through conversations. A Havel or a Zelenskyy arrives with a large network of real people who aren't reverential toward a new head of state and will tell it straight.

head: Independent Directors as Funnels of Information
dek: Companies need a majority of independent directors because inside the firm the CEO's power breeds groupthink and kills dissent.
more: Companies need a majority of independent directors because inside the firm the CEO's power breeds groupthink and kills dissent. Each independent director brings in the blunt opinions of dozens of outsiders. Ajay argues every government organisation should have a majority of independent directors who are genuinely private people, not retired civil servants, because the state tends to have a very narrow view of the world.

head: Low Stakes Make Better Politics
dek: An outsider with a career to fall back on can be more equanimous and less brutal, since losing power won't destroy them.
more: An outsider with a career to fall back on can be more equanimous and less brutal, since losing power won't destroy them. Ajay extends this to whole systems: if losing an election means jail, people fight elections far more dirtily. Vijay Kelkar's ideal is power dispersed so that it is never winner-takes-all.

head: The Money–Power Repeated Game Corrupts
dek: Contesting elections in India costs crores even at corporator level.
more: Contesting elections in India costs crores even at corporator level. Funders expect a return on investment through contracts, protection from competition such as FDI in retail, and roads that grow potholes again so the repair contract comes back. Career politicians are locked into this repeated game. Outsiders haven't played it as long, so they have slightly more room to stay clean, and Ajay adds that a lifetime of forged character makes it hard to become a mere deal-maker.

head: Technocrat Plus Politician: The Manmohan–Narasimha Rao Partnership
dek: Outsiders struggle to navigate politics and bureaucracy.
more: Outsiders struggle to navigate politics and bureaucracy. In 1991 Manmohan Singh knew exactly what to do economically and had a team in place, while Narasimha Rao, an insider for decades, handled the manoeuvres, compromises and negotiations. Amit thinks Manmohan was right as finance minister but might have been wrong as prime minister at that moment. Ajay recalls the UK Labour insider who said that on coming to power after a long spell out, 'we pressed the levers of power and nothing happened.'

head: Outsiders and Parties Want Different Levels of Risk
dek: Career politicians face elections again and again over decades, so they lean toward the status quo and avoid high-variance bets.
more: Career politicians face elections again and again over decades, so they lean toward the status quo and avoid high-variance bets. An outsider whose legacy is already made may want a bold gamble for a grand success. These subtly misaligned incentives make it hard for an outsider to carry a party over the long run.

head: Amit asks whether Ajay would accept absolute power, given
more: Amit asks whether Ajay would accept absolute power, given that 'power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely.' Ajay: 'Power corrupts, but absolute power is pretty cool… get a better constitution of India. What better use of absolute power?'

head: Ajay borrows the lyric
more: Ajay borrows the lyric 'imagine there's no country, it's easy if you try' to describe the post-nationalist world that let a Canadian run the Bank of England.

head: Ajay on Watergate as the scandal that led to Jimmy Carter
more: Ajay on Watergate as the scandal that led to Jimmy Carter: 'Oh how helpless we were in those days, we thought that those are dreadful things. Standards of crime have changed.'

head: Ajay on rebuilding post-communist Europe
more: Ajay on rebuilding post-communist Europe: 'East Germany is cheating because it just grabbed West German institutions.'

head: Amit on Havel inviting Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones instead of summitry
more: Amit on Havel inviting Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones instead of summitry: 'I can have important conferences and World Economic Forum and this forum and that forum and that committee and G eighteen and B fifty nine, I'm just making shit up… but it's Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones.'

head: Amit voices Havel's tie refusal in Hindi (
more: Amit voices Havel's tie refusal in Hindi ('Tie nahi pehnunga… chalis saal se… kyun change karu?'), then adds: 'of course not in Hindi, because while he was a very learned man, he was not aware of this particular language.'

head: Amit on Gandhi choosing Nehru over the free-market-loving Rajaji because Nehru was much younger
more: Amit on Gandhi choosing Nehru over the free-market-loving Rajaji because Nehru was much younger: 'So it's ironic that Rajaji actually outlived Nehru.'

head: Ajay on Nehru's nine years in British jails, kept in decent conditions
more: Ajay on Nehru's nine years in British jails, kept in decent conditions: 'It was pretty...' Amit finishes: 'luxurious jail.'

head: Amit praising Manmohan Singh's nuclear deal
more: Amit praising Manmohan Singh's nuclear deal: 'I also admire the economist who will go unnamed, who sent a memo to the Prime Minister's office outlining why such a nuclear deal should happen, after which it happened.' This is a dig at Ajay, whose memos Amit had earlier said he 'can't speak about in public.'

Ajay: 'O ye Namsita and Vaishnav, O ye little bit players of Bollywood, can you imagine that a comedian in Indian tinsel town can stand up and achieve such character.' Amit: 'They are future superstars of world cinema. So kindly hold your horses. Do you have any horses? Acquire horses and hold them there.'

head: Amit on Zelenskyy's unmatched credential
more: Amit on Zelenskyy's unmatched credential: 'Churchill cannot compare. Nehruji cannot compare. Havel for all his skills in theatre cannot compare. Zelenskyy played the piano with his dick.' He adds that making a fool of yourself on stage night after night also takes courage.

head: Ajay on Zelenskyy rallying his people, citing the line about Churchill
more: Ajay on Zelenskyy rallying his people, citing the line about Churchill that 'he picked up the words of the English language and hurled them into battle.'

head: Amit on outsiders
more: Amit on outsiders: 'You could be a chaiwala, as long as you're an actual chaiwala selling chai at a train station.'

head: Amit on election costs
more: Amit on election costs: 'I was gonna say shit ton of money. It's fine, I can say it, it's my show.'

head: Amit's limerick on politics, from his days as the Times of India's weekly limerick writer (
more: Amit's limerick on politics, from his days as the Times of India's weekly limerick writer ('the world's only paid limerick writer, I think'): 'A neta who loves currency notes / told me what his line of work denotes. / It is kind of funny, we steal people's money / and use some of it to buy their votes.'

head: Amit quotes the line attributed to Edmund Burke
more: Amit quotes the line attributed to Edmund Burke, 'The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to stand by and do nothing,' as a mirror of Havel's Charter 77 retort.

head: Amit adapts Kipling and C.L.R.
more: Amit adapts Kipling and C.L.R. James: 'What do they know of politics who only politics know?'

head: Mitt Romney, the 2012 Republican candidate, is Amit's example of the US norm of business people entering politics
more: Mitt Romney, the 2012 Republican candidate, is Amit's example of the US norm of business people entering politics: 'those were the days you had good candidates from both parties. Look at today, it's just a joke.'

head: Ajay on the freedom fighters taking on the British Empire
more: Ajay on the freedom fighters taking on the British Empire: 'you and whose army?' They had to be crazy people. And when such people argue, as Gandhi did with Tagore, 'you're going to build something great out of it.'

head: Ajay recalls a Labour insider after the party returned to power in the UK
more: Ajay recalls a Labour insider after the party returned to power in the UK: 'we pressed the levers of power and nothing happened.'

head: Amit's sign-off after asking viewers to like and subscribe
more: Amit's sign-off after asking viewers to like and subscribe: 'You know they don't listen to me. This is why I could never win as a politician. No one would vote for me. They might like me, but they won't vote for me.' Ajay repeats the request; Amit: 'Let's hope you're better at this than I am.'

head: The Economist Who Puked on a Forest
dek: A warm, self-deprecating opener that sets the show's tone. Ajay shrugs it off by noting that anyone who paraglides seriously deals with motion sickness.
more: During a few days in Bir, Ajay spent time with trail runner Sanat Sachdev, who got him thinking about running in the mountains. He also took a two-hour tandem paragliding ride. At the highest point the air turned rocky, and his pilot calmly taught him how to stick his head out and throw up onto the forest below. Amit wondered whether he was the first economist ever to do so.
A warm, self-deprecating opener that sets the show's tone. Ajay shrugs it off by noting that anyone who paraglides seriously deals with motion sickness. Discomfort is simply part of the adventure.

head: When You Could Rent a Bombay Flat in Fifteen Minutes
dek: Rent control's deepest damage is invisible to anyone born after it arrives.
more: Around 1976, when Ajay was about ten, his father told the family over dinner what Bombay was like when he arrived in 1942, the year Gandhiji launched the Quit India movement. Back then you could walk the streets and rent a flat within fifteen minutes. By the 1970s, rent control and the pagdi system had made renting nearly impossible, so the children listened wide-eyed to what sounded like a fairy tale.

Rent control's deepest damage is invisible to anyone born after it arrives. A whole generation grew up thinking a broken housing market was normal, when a free rental market had once worked effortlessly in the same city.

head: Hitler's Autobahns and the Great Depression Exception
dek: Economic rules come with context. Ajay sees debt-financed stimulus as defensible only when the financial system has collapsed, and argues that modern policy would never repeat the mistakes that caused that collapse.
more: Ajay broadly agrees with Hazlitt on make-work spending but offers one exception: the Great Depression. Monetary mistakes collapsed the money supply and roughly a quarter of banks failed. Because banks held unique information about their borrowers, firms that lost their bank could not easily start over with a new one. Hitler then borrowed to fund rearmament and the autobahns, which he actually wanted, and the resulting jobs and re-spending pulled Germany out of the Depression. Roosevelt's Tennessee Valley Authority had similar effects. Amit pushed back, pointing to contrary accounts by Amity Shlaes and Thomas Sowell.

Economic rules come with context. Ajay sees debt-financed stimulus as defensible only when the financial system has collapsed, and argues that modern policy would never repeat the mistakes that caused that collapse. Hosts who agree on fundamentals still disagree on edge cases.

head: The Bureaucrat Who Wanted to Save Jute
dek: This is Hazlitt's 'Saving the X Industry' in real life. Any subsidy to one industry is taken from others whose lost jobs and welfare go unseen.
more: Amit once asked a senior West Bengal bureaucrat who looked after the jute industry what the thinking was. The answer: jute is struggling, it is an indigenous industry, it is 'our thing', so the government must keep it alive with subsidies, price controls and land grants. Amit asked why the government had any role at all, and argued that supply and demand should decide. Ajay later added a twist: jute today is doing extremely well, because global technological forces made the world want more of it, and this has nothing to do with the government.

This is Hazlitt's 'Saving the X Industry' in real life. Any subsidy to one industry is taken from others whose lost jobs and welfare go unseen. The punchline is that the industry thrived without being 'saved'.

head: Tribals, Google Earth, and Toilets
dek: Ownership changes incentives overnight. People do not invest in land they could lose, and once it is theirs, they build.
more: About twenty years ago, Barun Mitra was part of a movement to win property rights for tribals in Gujarat. Using historical Google Earth satellite imagery, they proved how long the tribals had lived on the land and where its boundaries lay, and the tribals got their titles. The first thing the tribals did was build pakka houses and toilets, which they had never done while they could be evicted at any time. The story is told in the documentary India Awakes.
Ownership changes incentives overnight. People do not invest in land they could lose, and once it is theirs, they build. This is Hernando de Soto's 'dead capital' coming back to life.
printed: From Google Earth to pakka homes

head: The Leftist Friend Surprised That Amit Cared
dek: Disagreement about policy is often mistaken for disagreement about values.
more: A few years ago an ardent leftist friend told Amit, mid-conversation, that he hadn't realised Amit cared so much, because he assumed libertarians don't care about people. Amit recalled this on reading a Daniel Hannan tweet arguing that the left's defining trait is not compassion but the conviction that compassion belongs only to their side.

Disagreement about policy is often mistaken for disagreement about values. Critics of rent control or price controls usually care about the same people, and they ask whether the policy actually helps them.

head: The Painting Made in Excel
dek: Tools spread slowly, and in the right hands they are used in ways no one planned.
more: After invoking Arthur C. Clarke on technology and magic, Amit showed Ajay a painting by the artist Tatsuo Horiuchi and quizzed him on the medium. Ajay had no idea. It was made in Microsoft Excel, the same spreadsheet technology Ajay had just described as still not fully adopted across Indian business, decades after it arrived.
Tools spread slowly, and in the right hands they are used in ways no one planned. A spreadsheet becomes a paintbrush.

head: Economics in One Lesson
dek: It is a 1946 'collection of light bulbs' on economic fallacies that are still committed today.
more: It is a 1946 'collection of light bulbs' on economic fallacies that are still committed today. Hazlitt never changed a word of the original text in later editions because the principles still held. Lant Pritchett told Amit it turned him onto economics, and one of Ajay's mentees says the same. Ajay urges listeners to read the book itself rather than treat the episode as a substitute.
The book this whole episode breaks down. It is the first in a new series where every five episodes or so the hosts pick a book that shaped them.

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: There are very few primers on public policy, and fewer still that place it in the Indian context.
more: There are very few primers on public policy, and fewer still that place it in the Indian context. This book does both, which is why it matters so much to Amit.
Cited as an example of a rare foundational primer in a field that lacks one.

head: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Ep 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A deep conversation on why growth, not redistribution, drives human welfare.
more: A deep conversation on why growth, not redistribution, drives human welfare.
Mentioned twice: Pritchett said Hazlitt turned him onto economics, and they discussed growth versus redistribution.

head: Economic growth is enough and only economic growth is enough
dek: Pritchett finds that a wide range of human welfare indicators, from health onwards, correlate at around 99% with per capita GDP.
more: Pritchett finds that a wide range of human welfare indicators, from health onwards, correlate at around 99% with per capita GDP. That leaves redistribution and welfarism a sliver of the story.
Cited in the growth-versus-redistribution discussion.

head: Four Papers That Changed the World (Ep 41 of Everything is Everything)
