dek: It includes Hayek's essay on prices, which gave Amit his light-bulb moment about how prices work.
more: It includes Hayek's essay on prices, which gave Amit his light-bulb moment about how prices work.
Recalled while describing the light-bulb moments that retrain intuition.

head: The Use of Knowledge in Society
dek: Understanding how prices carry knowledge made the folly and hubris of legislating prices impossible to unsee.
more: Understanding how prices carry knowledge made the folly and hubris of legislating prices impossible to unsee.
Named as one of Amit's own light bulbs.

head: The Evolution of Everything
dek: It made Amit see spontaneous order running through natural selection, the evolution of language, prices and all of society.
more: It made Amit see spontaneous order running through natural selection, the evolution of language, prices and all of society. He calls it 'so miraculous'.
Cited for showing spontaneous order everywhere.

head: The Evolution of Everything (Ep 96 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: A companion to the book on how bottom-up order shapes the world.
more: A companion to the book on how bottom-up order shapes the world.
Amit's conversation with Ridley about the book.

head: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
dek: Its parable of the broken window is the cleanest illustration of looking past the visible effect to the unseen opportunity cost.
more: Its parable of the broken window is the cleanest illustration of looking past the visible effect to the unseen opportunity cost.
The mid-19th-century essay that inspired both Hazlitt's book and the name of Amit's podcast.

head: The Mystery of Capital
dek: Amit calls it essential reading and a masterpiece. It explains 'dead capital': without property rights, slum dwellers and tribals cannot borrow against or invest in what they effectively own.
more: Amit calls it essential reading and a masterpiece. It explains 'dead capital': without property rights, slum dwellers and tribals cannot borrow against or invest in what they effectively own.
Introduced as a 'great concept' during the rent control discussion.

head: Seeing Like a State
dek: Ajay calls it an amazing book that the hosts have discussed many times.
more: Ajay calls it an amazing book that the hosts have discussed many times. It contains his favourite line on ownership: 'the greatest fertilizer of all is the tender gaze of an owner'.
Quoted on why property rights drive land improvement. Amit says a full episode on it is coming.

head: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
dek: A great video on how minimum wages hurt the poor they are meant to help.
more: A great video on how minimum wages hurt the poor they are meant to help.
Suggested alongside Hazlitt's chapter on the minimum wage.

head: India Awakes
dek: It tells Barun Mitra's story of using satellite imagery to win land rights for tribals.
more: It tells Barun Mitra's story of using satellite imagery to win land rights for tribals.
A documentary presented by Johan Norberg, produced via the Free to Choose network.

head: The One Lesson: Look at Longer Effects and All Groups
dek: Hazlitt's whole book in a sentence. The bad economist sees only the immediate, direct effect on one visible group.
more: Hazlitt's whole book in a sentence. The bad economist sees only the immediate, direct effect on one visible group. The good economist traces the longer, indirect effects on everyone. Policies that look compassionate at first glance often turn out to harm the very people they purport to help.

head: The Broken Window and Opportunity Cost
dek: From Bastiat's parable: a broken shop window looks like stimulus because the glazier gets paid.
more: From Bastiat's parable: a broken shop window looks like stimulus because the glazier gets paid. What goes unseen is the suit the shopkeeper would have bought with the same money, and the tailor who would have spent it. The same logic demolishes the claim that war, or rebuilding destroyed cities, is good for the economy.

head: Light-Bulb Moments Retrain Intuition
dek: Our default intuitions are zero-sum and top-down. Ideas like how prices work or spontaneous order switch on a light that can't be switched off, and they become our new intuition.
more: Our default intuitions are zero-sum and top-down. Ideas like how prices work or spontaneous order switch on a light that can't be switched off, and they become our new intuition. Ajay says the price system and general equilibrium are now his 3 a.m. default, while market imperfections must be layered on consciously.

head: Growth Over Redistribution
dek: Sustained growth transforms everyone's life. Redistribution is the seen benefit with unseen costs: coercion, distorted incentives and slower growth.
more: Sustained growth transforms everyone's life. Redistribution is the seen benefit with unseen costs: coercion, distorted incentives and slower growth. Lant Pritchett's work finds that welfare indicators correlate around 99% with per capita GDP. Ajay sees redistribution politics as divide-and-conquer.

head: Public Works Mean Taxes
dek: Make-work projects show you the visible workers on the bridge but hide the private jobs that the taxes destroyed.
more: Make-work projects show you the visible workers on the bridge but hide the private jobs that the taxes destroyed. Once employment becomes the goal, governments stop asking where bridges must be built and start asking where they can be built. Amit sees NREGS as a modern example with crowding-out effects.

head: Taxes Discourage Production, and Taxes as Time
dek: Taxing Ajay to give to Amit is not a neutral transfer. It blunts Ajay's incentive to produce, expand and take risks.
more: Taxing Ajay to give to Amit is not a neutral transfer. It blunts Ajay's incentive to produce, expand and take risks. Translate tax into months worked for the state and it becomes visceral. Everyone pays tax, including the beggar buying salt and the domestic help buying soap, and inflation is a tax on the poor. Indira Gandhi's peak personal rate of roughly 95 to 97% pushed people to leave the country or hoard black money. Amit applies the same opportunity-cost lens to India's space program.

head: Bureaucrats Make Bad Bankers
dek: Finance means processing information, forecasting and taking risks, and it requires tolerating failures.
more: Finance means processing information, forecasting and taking risks, and it requires tolerating failures. Bureaucrats have no incentive to do this hard work, and government finance invites political capture. That capture takes the form of financial repression to fund the state, directed lending to agriculture, and pressure to favour particular borrowers.

head: The 'Curse of Machinery' Fallacy
dek: Every era fears that technology will kill jobs, from the Luddites to the anti-automation voices of the 1960s to today's AI worriers.
more: Every era fears that technology will kill jobs, from the Luddites to the anti-automation voices of the 1960s to today's AI worriers. Hazlitt uses Adam Smith's pin makers to show that, by this logic, machinery should have caused near-total unemployment. Instead productivity gains spill into the economy and create jobs. If saving labour were bad, freight should be carried on men's backs.

head: Production Equals Consumption, and Diffusion Is Slow
dek: Ajay's two-part rebuttal to technology panic. First, a society can only consume what it produces, so productivity gains are gains in per capita consumption.
more: Ajay's two-part rebuttal to technology panic. First, a society can only consume what it produces, so productivity gains are gains in per capita consumption. Second, adoption takes time: steam, electricity and spreadsheets all spread slowly, which leaves room to adjust. Driverless cars will replace India's drivers 'with probability one', but over perhaps 25 years, not overnight.

head: Trade Is a Technology
dek: You can build an electric vehicle in Mahindra's Igatpuri factory, or you can raise chickens on Maharashtra's poultry farms, ship frozen chicken out of JNPT, and get EVs back.
more: You can build an electric vehicle in Mahindra's Igatpuri factory, or you can raise chickens on Maharashtra's poultry farms, ship frozen chicken out of JNPT, and get EVs back. Both are technologies that turn inputs into outputs. Tariffs are therefore industrial policy that picks a winner between them. To stop progress you would have to shut down trade as well as science.

head: Culture Decides Whether Change Becomes Conflict
dek: Technological change always hurts some firms, creditors and workers. In a culture of populism and class warfare, each shift detonates anger and 'gives you the next Donald Trump'.
more: Technological change always hurts some firms, creditors and workers. In a culture of populism and class warfare, each shift detonates anger and 'gives you the next Donald Trump'. Ajay argues great societies are 'more Gandhiji and less Karl Marx': they absorb change together.

head: Saving the X Industry and the Truth About Tariffs
dek: Propping up a favoured industry, whether jute, local producers or anything 'ours', is paid for by other industries whose losses go unseen.
more: Propping up a favoured industry, whether jute, local producers or anything 'ours', is paid for by other industries whose losses go unseen. Tariffs protect a small group of producers at the expense of your own people, a transfer from poor consumers to rich interest groups. Ajay notes that China runs the same industrial-policy playbook as India, 'just done 5x more extreme'.

head: What Rent Control Really Does
dek: Price controls always cause scarcity, and rent is no exception. Landlords stop maintaining buildings, which is why Marine Drive has sprawling flats renting for a few hundred rupees in dilapidated buildings.
more: Price controls always cause scarcity, and rent is no exception. Landlords stop maintaining buildings, which is why Marine Drive has sprawling flats renting for a few hundred rupees in dilapidated buildings. Developers stop building, and tenants stop economising on space. It sounds compassionate, but it shrinks the supply of affordable housing for those who need it most. Amit sees this as the danger in Zohran Mamdani's New York platform.

head: Dead Capital and Property Rights
dek: From Hernando de Soto: without formal title, land that people effectively own cannot be borrowed against or confidently improved, so it is 'dead capital'.
more: From Hernando de Soto: without formal title, land that people effectively own cannot be borrowed against or confidently improved, so it is 'dead capital'. Giving slum dwellers and long-settled tribals property rights unlocks investment. Rent control does the reverse, killing capital that was alive.

head: Real Compassion Requires Rigour
dek: Schemes like rent control and price controls let people project virtue.
more: Schemes like rent control and price controls let people project virtue. Without the intellectual rigour to trace outcomes, they hurt the poor. Compassion is measured by results, not intentions.

head: Reframe the Claim From the Other Side
dek: Bad policy hides in good-sounding words. Hazlitt pairs them: more credit means more debt.
more: Bad policy hides in good-sounding words. Hazlitt pairs them: more credit means more debt. Higher farm prices mean dearer food for city workers. Subsidies mean higher taxes. More exports ultimately means more imports. Higher wage rates mean higher costs of production. Restating a claim from the opposite side reveals what is really being proposed.

head: Think in Individuals, Not Abstractions
dek: Talk of 'the nation' or 'the good of society' can hide who actually gains and who loses.
more: Talk of 'the nation' or 'the good of society' can hide who actually gains and who loses. Ask what happens to real people.

head: The Hidden Immorality of Cost-Benefit Analysis
dek: Via Suyash Rai: aggregate cost-benefit sums hide that one group bears real costs now while another enjoys benefits that are often imagined and in the future.
more: Via Suyash Rai: aggregate cost-benefit sums hide that one group bears real costs now while another enjoys benefits that are often imagined and in the future. Demonetisation, in Amit's view, had costs and no benefits at all.

head: The Hazlitt Toolkit
dek: Five lenses for judging any policy. First, opportunity cost: what is the unseen alternative, and whose money is being taken?
more: Five lenses for judging any policy. First, opportunity cost: what is the unseen alternative, and whose money is being taken? Second, general welfare over interest-group welfare. Third, incentives and distortions. Fourth, the price system as sacred information. Fifth, how capital formation and savings work.

head: Private Prudence, Public Folly
dek: Hazlitt quotes Adam Smith: what is prudence in a family can scarcely be folly in a kingdom.
more: Hazlitt quotes Adam Smith: what is prudence in a family can scarcely be folly in a kingdom. Amit extends it. In personal life decent people are libertarian: we don't force friends what to eat or steal to pay for our meal. Yet one level of abstraction up, at the level of the state, coercion and social engineering suddenly seem fine. The task is to reconcile our personal values with how we think about the state.

head: When Amit mentions a secret project, Ajay warns him
more: When Amit mentions a secret project, Ajay warns him: 'the FSB, they scrape YouTube, they will hear the words. Secret project. And now they will start tapping your phone.' Then he helpfully explains that the FSB is the new name of the KGB.

head: After Ajay's paragliding confession, Amit asks…
more: After Ajay's paragliding confession, Amit asks: 'Are you the first economist to puke on a forest?' Then he follows up: 'If you puke on a forest but nobody sees it, did you puke?'

head: Amit reads Hazlitt's swipe at an unnamed
more: Amit reads Hazlitt's swipe at an unnamed 'brilliant economist' whose flippant line was 'In the long run we are all dead', and asks Ajay to guess which of his heroes it is. Ajay: 'I love John Maynard Keynes dearly and one of his crimes was that he was wise, witty, and wonderful.' Amit: 'That was the only thing that was not a crime.' Amit then twists the line: in the long run, 'we are wrong'.

head: Amit explains that intuition tells us the world must be controlled from the top down, then notices Ajay smiling
more: Amit explains that intuition tells us the world must be controlled from the top down, then notices Ajay smiling: 'Because you are the man on the top controlling.'

head: Amit says the show is…
more: Amit says the show is 'constantly throwing light bulbs at the screen', not literally. Ajay then pitches Everything is Everything merch: a cannon beside the TV that fires defunct tungsten bulbs at the viewer, with Amit controlling the timing from inside the show.

head: The running Bengali-economist gag. In Bastiat's parable, the man who says the broken window is good for the economy is…
more: The running Bengali-economist gag. In Bastiat's parable, the man who says the broken window is good for the economy is 'no doubt a wise Bengali economist'. Amit later explains: 'I am a Bengali. The name doesn't indicate it... he doesn't like Bengali economists in particular, and I don't like Bengali economists either.' He then adds that 'a certain Gujarati hubris' also comes into play sometimes.

head: Ajay on India paying a foreign company to launch an Indian astronaut
more: Ajay on India paying a foreign company to launch an Indian astronaut: it's cheaper than doing it through ISRO, with the same propaganda value. Taken to its logical conclusion, 'what you need is an AI video'.

head: Amit on conspiracy theories that the moon landings happened in Nevada
more: Amit on conspiracy theories that the moon landings happened in Nevada: 'which of course they did not, they happened on the moon. We are fairly certain of that.'

head: In the jute story, Amit slips in a Hindi pun on jute
more: In the jute story, Amit slips in a Hindi pun on jute and 'jhoot' (lie), the 'Jute ka Jhoot' of the chapter title, and refuses to explain it. Ajay gets it 'forty-five milliseconds later'. Amit then says the jute fixation gets his goat, adding: 'I should be careful about what I say because I don't have a goat.'

head: Amit's T-shirt line for the show's merch
more: Amit's T-shirt line for the show's merch: 'Make trade not war.' He follows up by asking whether Ajay prefers making trade or making love. The answer: 'Unprintable.'

head: Amit stumbles over Arthur C. Clarke's line
more: Amit stumbles over Arthur C. Clarke's line, 'any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic'. He calls 'indistinguishable' 'as difficult a word as internationalization' and says it as 'internationalization from magic'. He decides that if you turned a chicken into an EV in front of Clarke, 'he would say why this is magic.'

head: Ajay defends Zohran Mamdani with the old saw
more: Ajay defends Zohran Mamdani with the old saw: 'He who is not a communist when he is young has no heart. He who is a communist as an adult has no brain. So give him a break.' Amit: 'Thirty-four is old enough.'

head: Amit says Ajay's mentee is…
more: Amit says Ajay's mentee is 'turning into an Ajay, which is rather alarming', and asks how Ajay feels about young Ajays running around the world. Ajay: they'll soon get over the delusion that 'there is anything here which is somehow special.' Amit: 'Oh my god, such modesty.'

Gunnar Myrdal, the Nobel-winning economist who argued that machinery was good for the West but not for India because demand for labour might fall. Amit's verdict: 'Dude wins the Nobel Prize for talking this shit.'

head: George Santayana, The Life of Reason (1905), quoted in Hazlitt's book too
more: George Santayana, The Life of Reason (1905), quoted in Hazlitt's book too: 'Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.' Amit invokes it against every new wave of technophobia, from the Luddites to AI.

head: Ajay recalls the old line about bank robbers in the American West
more: Ajay recalls the old line about bank robbers in the American West, 'Why do you rob banks? Because that's where the money is', to explain why governments everywhere raid the financial system.

head: Margaret Thatcher's
more: Margaret Thatcher's 'don't speak to me of society, there are individuals', invoked by Amit along with 'the smallest minority is the individual'.

head: James C. Scott in Seeing Like a State, quoted by Ajay
more: James C. Scott in Seeing Like a State, quoted by Ajay: 'The greatest fertilizer of all is the tender gaze of an owner.'

Zohran Mamdani, winner of New York's Democratic mayoral primary and son of filmmaker Mira Nair and academic Mahmood Mamdani. Amit finds him charming and condemns the racist attacks on him, but calls his policies, such as government grocery stores, free buses and rent control, 'a throwback to the worst excesses of the twentieth century'. Amit is a big Mira Nair fan and won't tolerate 'any nonsense' about her.

head: The Question That Made a Calm Man Violent
dek: A badly framed question is still worth taking seriously when many people are asking it.
more: A friend of Amit's asked him to put one question to Ajay Shah: how much wealth do you need to retire? Amit describes Ajay as a picture of calm, yet each time he raised the question, 'violence resulted.' He asked again the next day, and then a third time. Finally Ajay agreed to do a whole episode on it, because it is a stupid question but an important one, since so many people are thinking about it.
A badly framed question is still worth taking seriously when many people are asking it. The useful answer is to explain why the question is wrong, not to hand over a number.

head: Burning Money in a Savings Account
dek: The 'safe' cultural default can quietly destroy wealth. Real safety means letting your money work for you rather than relying only on your ability to earn.
more: Amit admits that for the longest time he kept his money in a savings account, following the Indian middle-class script: get an education, build a career, put the salary in the bank or in fixed deposits to be safe. It took him years to see that high inflation made this a losing proposition. In that same script, the words 'stock market' trigger fears of losing everything. He says Ajay's personal finance module could have changed his life twenty years ago, though he doubts he would have been receptive to it then.
The 'safe' cultural default can quietly destroy wealth. Real safety means letting your money work for you rather than relying only on your ability to earn.

head: 'Without Equity, Financial Planning Is Not Possible'
dek: Equity investing is not an optional extra for coping with long lifespans.
more: Ajay recounts how someone who had been running spreadsheet calculations (not named in the episode) shocked him by turning the usual advice upside down. The usual line is that holding globally diversified equity index funds is wise. Her point was stronger: without access to the equity premium, the numbers cannot be made to work for any normal affluent person, and you will be miserable in old age.
Equity investing is not an optional extra for coping with long lifespans. It is the one thing without which lifetime financial planning does not add up.

head: Japan's Dead Decades and the Escape Hatch
dek: Even a rich, free country's stock market can fail you for decades. Owning the index is recipe one; owning the indexes of many democracies is recipe two, and recipe two is what survives a national catastrophe.
more: Japan's macroeconomy was in a giant mess through the 70s and 80s, ending in a crash that began in 1986. For roughly twenty years afterward its equity market simply did not deliver, so a Japanese investor holding only domestic index funds got abysmal returns. But Japan was an advanced democracy without capital controls. Its citizens were free to spread their money around the world, and global diversification rescued them.

Even a rich, free country's stock market can fail you for decades. Owning the index is recipe one; owning the indexes of many democracies is recipe two, and recipe two is what survives a national catastrophe.
printed: Twenty dead years, one way out

head: STD Booths and the Unknowable Future
dek: The future arrives through unknown unknowns. That makes it foolish to extrapolate today's world into a spreadsheet and call it a retirement plan.
more: Ajay asks whether a 20-year-old Amit could have described a good life at 52. Amit says no: at 20 he could not have imagined smartphones, AI that turns images into video, or holding the means of production to make shows and films. His example is that before mobile telephony India had a million STD booths, and today it has none. Those jobs vanished, but the economy and productivity grew and new jobs appeared in ways no one could have predicted. He adds that the bad surprises tend to come from politics and geopolitics: war, hyperinflation, institutional failure.
The future arrives through unknown unknowns. That makes it foolish to extrapolate today's world into a spreadsheet and call it a retirement plan.

head: Japan's Minister for Loneliness
dek: Longer lives and weaker family support networks turn old age into a social problem.
more: Amit came across a piece of trivia: Japan has had a minister for loneliness for a few years. The post exists mainly for the elderly in an ageing society, and the job involves things like organising scrabble and carrom tournaments to keep old people occupied. Amit calls it a very first-world problem and notes that Indian problems would look very different.
Longer lives and weaker family support networks turn old age into a social problem. It is a vivid example of how unprepared traditional arrangements are for long lifespans.

head: Stocks for the Long Run
dek: It builds the basic intuition from two hundred years of equity index investing, which is the foundation of the episode's whole argument.
more: It builds the basic intuition from two hundred years of equity index investing, which is the foundation of the episode's whole argument. He says everybody should read it and take the message in deeply.
Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode.

head: Freedom House Index
dek: It gives a simple rule: take the top 20 democracies on the list, buy their equity index funds, and put about 5% in each.
more: It gives a simple rule: take the top 20 democracies on the list, buy their equity index funds, and put about 5% in each.
Ajay's concrete actionable for global diversification.

head: The World in 2050 (Ep 106 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Imagining just 25 years ahead already sounds like science fiction, and Ajay insists the hosts meant every claim seriously.
more: Imagining just 25 years ahead already sounds like science fiction, and Ajay insists the hosts meant every claim seriously. Fifty- or seventy-five-year retirement spreadsheets are therefore an illusion.
Cited to show how hard long-horizon forecasting is.

head: The China Model is Broken (Ep 16 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It is the wider story behind China's failed equity market, its capital controls, and its real-estate overbuilding.
more: It is the wider story behind China's failed equity market, its capital controls, and its real-estate overbuilding.
Ajay tells listeners to watch it while explaining why Chinese households cannot do lifetime financial planning.

head: The Journey of Indian Finance (Ep 71 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It tells how the Indian equity market made remarkable progress from about 1991 to 2009–10, and how a big early push later petered out.
more: It tells how the Indian equity market made remarkable progress from about 1991 to 2009–10, and how a big early push later petered out.
Mentioned while discussing India's equity market and what the government still needs to fix.

head: The journey of Indian finance
dek: It is the written, detailed account of the reforms that built India's equity market, the precondition for index-fund investing.
more: It is the written, detailed account of the reforms that built India's equity market, the precondition for index-fund investing.
Ajay mentions he has a paper by the same name as the episode.

head: Longevity Breaks Our Traditional Operating System
dek: Hunter-gatherers lived thirty or forty years. In the agricultural age people died by fifty or sixty.
more: Hunter-gatherers lived thirty or forty years. In the agricultural age people died by fifty or sixty. A healthy, affluent person today has to plan for a radically longer lifespan; Ajay suggests a 21-year-old should realistically expect to reach 121. Traditional culture, including the old-age support that came from having children nearby, was built for medium lifespans. And the family as an institution is declining.

head: The Equity Premium: The Counterweight to Longevity
dek: The equity premium is the extra average return you get for holding diversified equities.
more: The equity premium is the extra average return you get for holding diversified equities. You are paid for bearing systematic risk that diversification cannot remove, not for reckless concentrated bets. Long lifespans also make compounding more powerful. A rough real doubling every ten years gives 4x in 20 years, 8x in 30, 16x in 40 and 32x in 50, and over decades the ups and downs tend to cancel out. Because small differences in the expected return get magnified over long periods, the size of the premium matters enormously.
printed: Paid to wait, not to gamble

head: Global Diversification Is a Free Lunch
dek: Diversification runs from one company to many, from one industry to twenty, and most importantly from one country to many.
more: Diversification runs from one company to many, from one industry to twenty, and most importantly from one country to many. Ajay's rule is to hold equity index funds of the top 20 democracies on the Freedom House list, about 5% each. Average returns stay roughly intact while risk falls, which roughly doubles the risk-adjusted return compared with being in India, or any single country, alone. The shorter your time horizon, the more crucial this becomes.

head: Equity Culture Drives Wealth Inequality Across Generations
dek: Ajay cites US papers showing that households that get into equity investment over multi-generational horizons compound their wealth generation after generation.
more: Ajay cites US papers showing that households that get into equity investment over multi-generational horizons compound their wealth generation after generation. Households that don't get stuck, and the gap shows up as wealth inequality. He suggests this is a major factor behind the rising gulf between Gujarati and Bengali wealth in India. The fix has to happen family by family, by changing attitudes to risk.

head: Three Strikes Against the Retirement Spreadsheet
dek: A retirement spreadsheet assumes three things you cannot know. First, your returns: plugging in a historical average such as 13% nominal for the Nifty ignores the risk that earns you the premium.
more: A retirement spreadsheet assumes three things you cannot know. First, your returns: plugging in a historical average such as 13% nominal for the Nifty ignores the risk that earns you the premium. Second, the future cost of your consumption basket, which will shift and which you will keep re-optimising. Third, your own future preferences, values and ideas of what is enough. Over many decades all three become fog, so the numbers give only an illusion of control.

head: Baumol's Cost Disease Will Reshape Your Old-Age Budget
dek: Anything machines can make will become dramatically cheaper: a ₹20,000 phone's capability will cost ₹1,000, and cars become driverless robots.
more: Anything machines can make will become dramatically cheaper: a ₹20,000 phone's capability will cost ₹1,000, and cars become driverless robots. Anything that needs human effort keeps getting pricier, because GDP growth pushes wages up. A doctor's consultation will cost ever more steel as steel gets cheaper to make. Some personal services, like the bathing robots being built in Japan, may still be automated. Ajay's point is not that old age will be expensive but that nobody knows, and people will adjust their consumption as relative prices move.

head: Process Over Destination; Calm Over Control
dek: Amit warns against treating life as a destination where you hit a number and sail into the sunset.
more: Amit warns against treating life as a destination where you hit a number and sail into the sunset. Ajay argues that wanting a locked-down plan comes from insecurity. Someone who calculates 'X money', gets it, and sets off to travel the world will feel betrayed and entitled when the world changes. The alternative is to do the hygiene (a high savings rate and globally diversified index funds), accept radical uncertainty, and deal with the future as it comes.
printed: Your heart isn’t in the sheet

head: Retirement Is an Industrial-Age Idea
dek: The word 'retirement' comes from a world where you stopped working at 55 and died by 60.
more: The word 'retirement' comes from a world where you stopped working at 55 and died by 60. The data show that people who drop into true retirement suffer rapid health collapse, while those who stay engaged with work and people do better. You can change course, for example quitting the nine-to-five or moving to a village in Himachal Pradesh, but keep working and stay connected. Amit adds that everyone has something others value, so 'really no one retires till they die.'

head: Personal Finance Is Hygiene, Like Health
dek: You don't need to pick stocks or become a finance buff, just as staying healthy doesn't require being a fitness freak.
more: You don't need to pick stocks or become a finance buff, just as staying healthy doesn't require being a fitness freak. Pay the one-time cost of learning the basics: avoid the traditional traps of bank deposits and real estate, use equity index funds and global diversification, and learn to operate the accounts. After that, about 15 minutes a month is enough. Ajay adds that cutting back on restaurant meals and alcohol to raise savings can transform a life.

head: Women Must Own Their Financial Planning
dek: Women live longer, so their lifespan problem is sharper. Traditional culture also tells them money is 'not a girl thing', which leads even educated women, CAs and MBAs included, to hand everything to men.
more: Women live longer, so their lifespan problem is sharper. Traditional culture also tells them money is 'not a girl thing', which leads even educated women, CAs and MBAs included, to hand everything to men. Ajay says every woman should know her savings rate, what an index fund is, which countries top the Freedom House list, who her service provider is, and the password to her own account. Without that knowledge, confidence erodes into insecurity and fear.

head: Two $500 Bills Lying on the Ground for Firms
dek: Ajay says firms are ignoring two big pools of talent. One is women with children who want flexibility and time at home on their own terms.
more: Ajay says firms are ignoring two big pools of talent. One is women with children who want flexibility and time at home on their own terms. The other is older people who no longer want to show up at 9 a.m. but still have knowledge, expertise and energy. Firms that redesign how they work to use these people stand to gain enormously.

head: What Citizens Should Demand From the State
dek: Fifty-year planning needs five things from government. First, inflation reliably held at 4%, since India's inflation targeting dates only from 20 February 2015.
more: Fifty-year planning needs five things from government. First, inflation reliably held at 4%, since India's inflation targeting dates only from 20 February 2015. Second, no fiscal crisis, which in India's case means roughly halving a debt-to-GDP ratio about twice what it should be. Third, law and order, because violence is equally bad whether it comes from a gangster or a government employee. Fourth, a well-functioning system of firms and financial markets. Fifth, no capital controls. The goal is that ordinary people can free-ride on all that institutional work.

head: Capital Controls Are Immoral
dek: Ajay notes that capital controls began with Hitler in 1933 and were gone from rich countries by the late 1970s.
more: Ajay notes that capital controls began with Hitler in 1933 and were gone from rich countries by the late 1970s. He treats your freedom to move your own money as a basic, Magna Carta–style right. Forcing citizens to accept a worse risk-reward trade-off is like banning an imported dengue vaccine. India's controls are irksome but solvable: with a lawyer, a bank and an advisor you can get your money out, and you should.
printed: Pour concrete on four per cent

head: China: Growth Without Gains for Households
dek: China grew fast, yet unusually its equity index never performed. Ajay suggests the reason may be fake GDP data, the state grabbing the wealth created, or both.
more: China grew fast, yet unusually its equity index never performed. Ajay suggests the reason may be fake GDP data, the state grabbing the wealth created, or both. Capital controls also trap people's money at home. Unable to plan for long lives, households pile into real estate, producing massive overbuilding and what Ajay calls the worst real-estate market in the world. He calls this the hole in the heart of the China model: it looks successful from the state's view but not from the people's.

head: Amit's intro hype for Ajay's personal finance module
more: Amit's intro hype for Ajay's personal finance module: 'People could have written songs about it, made films on it, written poetry on it, but they haven't because it is too legendary even for that.'

head: Amit introduces Ajay as a picture of calm
more: Amit introduces Ajay as a picture of calm, 'absolute shanti', yet asking him the retirement question three times produced 'violence'. Ajay's eventual reply: 'I am a man of peace. Make episodes not war.'

head: Ajay on longevity, pointing to the 21-year-old crew member Nomsita: she has to realistically plan to be…
more: Ajay on longevity, pointing to the 21-year-old crew member Nomsita: she has to realistically plan to be 'an active little old lady doing paragliding at one twenty one.'

head: Ajay catches himself mid-argument about rising wages
more: Ajay catches himself mid-argument about rising wages: 'the price you will pay for a cook, for a driver, oops, driverless cars. Scratch that.'

head: Ajay on how easy investing has become
more: Ajay on how easy investing has become: 'It is like 3x harder to use Zerodha than it is to use Zepto.'

head: When Ajay suggests redirecting restaurant and alcohol spending into savings, Amit protests
more: When Ajay suggests redirecting restaurant and alcohol spending into savings, Amit protests: 'Alcohol, though I don't have, but Swiggy is surviving in India because of me. Why do you want to mess with that?' The answer is to make boiled vegetables, and Amit mourns: 'Very sad. Very sad.'

head: Amit's offer to Chinese viewers trapped by capital controls
more: Amit's offer to Chinese viewers trapped by capital controls: 'You send an apartment my way or a full house, the country villa, perhaps, and I will share the password of my Zerodha account.'

head: Amit's grammar grievance
more: Amit's grammar grievance: 'societal' is just a fancy academic word for 'social', so 'it broke my heart, Ajay Shah, to see you fall under the sway of that.'

head: A callback to Ajay's line that CDs will become
more: A callback to Ajay's line that CDs will become 'museum pieces': Amit recommends Led Zeppelin, noting the CD beside Ajay is 'worthless, but the music remains with you and it has shaped you.'

head: Magna Carta: Ajay calls the freedom to use your money as you like…
more: Magna Carta: Ajay calls the freedom to use your money as you like 'a magna carta right.'

head: Corning Glass Gets Turned Away
dek: Ajay's first encounter with FDI was watching it get refused. A foreign businessman found India's hostility to his investment simply incomprehensible.
more: In the early 1980s (his father died in 1984), Ajay was at home when an American from Corning Glass came to meet his father. Corning wanted to set up a factory in India to make glass, expecting demand for things like television picture tubes. His father told him it wouldn't happen, because the Indian state banned this and banned that. The visitor was baffled that a government would want to stop a company from building factories in its country.

Ajay's first encounter with FDI was watching it get refused. A foreign businessman found India's hostility to his investment simply incomprehensible. Amit reframes the episode's subject on the spot: what Ajay really loves is not FDI but freedom.

head: Nokia Packs Up and Leaves Tamil Nadu
dek: Welcoming foreign investors is not enough. If the state does not wall foreign firms off from the treatment it normally inflicts on Indian companies, even a marquee investment walks out.
more: Nokia built a manufacturing facility in Tamil Nadu, exactly the kind of foreign factory India says it wants. The Indian state then went after the company with income-tax demands and asset freezes, and eventually Nokia packed up and left.

Welcoming foreign investors is not enough. If the state does not wall foreign firms off from the treatment it normally inflicts on Indian companies, even a marquee investment walks out. Ajay sees this as a failure of intellectual clarity about why FDI works in the first place.

head: How Bangladesh Learned the Garment Business
dek: The real prize of FDI is not the foreign factory but the knowledge it leaves behind.
more: Taiwanese and South Korean companies were the first to set up garment operations in Bangladesh. Local people who worked there learned the business, then stepped out and started garment firms of their own, and the industry spread from there.

The real prize of FDI is not the foreign factory but the knowledge it leaves behind. That knowledge sits with workers, not with the foreign firm, and it spreads as they switch jobs and start companies.

head: From George Fernandes to Xi Jinping: The Same Mistake Twice
dek: Countries keep relearning that FDI dies when the state can't resist meddling.
more: Ajay recalls that George Fernandes drove IBM (which supported the IBM mainframes used in India) and Coca-Cola out of India by imposing conditions: forced technology transfer, a forced IPO in India, a forced joint venture. Decades later, he says, the same kinds of rules crept back into Xi Jinping's China, undoing Deng Xiaoping's promise to leave foreign firms alone. FDI into China collapsed.

Countries keep relearning that FDI dies when the state can't resist meddling. China's FDI miracle was not a permanent feature of China. It rested on a political commitment, and it ended when that commitment did.
printed: From Fernandes to Xi, a rerun

head: The China Model is Broken (Episode 16 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Background on how China moved from Deng Xiaoping's clarity to Xi Jinping-era interference, which this episode links to the collapse of FDI into China.
more: Background on how China moved from Deng Xiaoping's clarity to Xi Jinping-era interference, which this episode links to the collapse of FDI into China.
Cited by Ajay alongside the development episode as an example of how the China model failed.

head: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Episode 104 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It explains the structural drag of expensive raw materials. For example, duties on imported inputs for artificial fabric raise the cost of Indian yarn and cloth, which makes Indian shirts uncompetitive.
more: It explains the structural drag of expensive raw materials. For example, duties on imported inputs for artificial fabric raise the cost of Indian yarn and cloth, which makes Indian shirts uncompetitive. This is why trade barriers sabotage export-oriented FDI.
Ajay invokes it in the tariff-jumping FDI chapter.

head: What Counts as FDI
dek: FDI means a foreigner holding a substantial, long-term stake in an Indian production arrangement.
more: FDI means a foreigner holding a substantial, long-term stake in an Indian production arrangement. The OECD and IMF line is 10% equity: 9% is portfolio investment, 10% is FDI. Several things also count: a foreign parent's loan to its Indian subsidiary, a foreign private equity fund's 11% stake in a fully Indian company, and profits that a foreign-owned Indian operation reinvests instead of repatriating (booked as fresh FDI that year). 'FDI in India' and 'FDI by India' are separate flows.

head: The Seven FDI Numbers and the Propagandist's Menu
dek: The balance of payments produces seven FDI numbers: gross inflow, repatriation and net for FDI in India; gross outflow, money coming back and net for FDI by India; and 'net net' overall.
more: The balance of payments produces seven FDI numbers: gross inflow, repatriation and net for FDI in India; gross outflow, money coming back and net for FDI by India; and 'net net' overall. Propagandists of every stripe cherry-pick whichever one flatters their story. Ajay's tell for propaganda is a chart or table labelled simply 'FDI' without saying which series it is.

head: The Dream of FDI: An Honest Enclave
dek: FDI's magic comes from a country admitting its institutions are bad and building an escape valve.
more: FDI's magic comes from a country admitting its institutions are bad and building an escape valve. It sets aside, say, one square kilometre where there is no local labour law, no tax harassment, no visa trouble and no customs duties on goods in or out. A bonded warehouse is the cleanest version of this. In return, the state collects only income tax on workers' wages and GST on their spending, and the workers get jobs. Deng Xiaoping's insight was that fixing China's company law and taxes would take a century, so China built a trusted, predictable interface for foreigners in the meantime. Ajay says India never said these paragraphs to itself clearly.

head: Knowledge Diffusion Is FDI's Ultimate Prize
dek: If knowledge is what drives a society forward, foreign firms are where much of it gets made.
more: If knowledge is what drives a society forward, foreign firms are where much of it gets made. Workers learn the global productivity frontier and how globalised production works. That knowledge stays with them rather than with the company, and it spreads when they move to other jobs or start firms.

head: It's Unfair to Indian Firms, and That's the Point
dek: Treating foreign firms exactly like Indian ones, with the same regulators, capital controls and visa problems, removes the point of FDI.
more: Treating foreign firms exactly like Indian ones, with the same regulators, capital controls and visa problems, removes the point of FDI. The bargain only works if foreigners get better treatment than domestic businesses. Amit adds that this is no argument against fixing India's institutions, a fight that continues. Meanwhile, 'little islands of freedom' are worth having, and the perfect shouldn't be the enemy of the good.

head: 'Hot Money' Fear Is Insecurity, Not Analysis
dek: Indian policy circles call FDI the good guy and portfolio investment dangerous 'hot money'.
more: Indian policy circles call FDI the good guy and portfolio investment dangerous 'hot money'. Ajay rejects this on three counts. Foreigners already know India's weaknesses, and those are priced in as lower security prices. Foreign investors are not a monolithic bloc: every day sees large gross buying and selling with a tiny net, all absorbed by the market. And India has never had a big crisis from foreign portfolio exit; in shocks like the COVID lockdown, Indians and foreigners sold alike.

head: Portfolio Investment Needs Better Institutions Than FDI
dek: FDI can work with a short rulebook and a state that backs off. Portfolio investment has no way around local institutions.
more: FDI can work with a short rulebook and a state that backs off. Portfolio investment has no way around local institutions. It needs trustworthy accounting, audit, a stock market and a depository, so an investor in Tokyo can trust that a piece of paper really means they own shares. That is why China never got portfolio investment going while India, with about 150 years of accounting tradition, can. Ajay also treats FDI and FPI as different technologies: governments should build institutions, not decree which flows are good.

head: Who in India Wants Which Foreign Money
dek: India's elite reacts differently to the two kinds of foreign money. FDI means competition: a foreign carmaker hurts Premier Padmini, and Indian retail resents Amazon and Walmart.
more: India's elite reacts differently to the two kinds of foreign money. FDI means competition: a foreign carmaker hurts Premier Padmini, and Indian retail resents Amazon and Walmart. Portfolio investment means more buyers for Indian firms' shares and bonds, and a lower cost of capital. So the incumbent business community welcomes FPI and resists FDI. The insight is credited to Ila Patnaik. Ajay thinks a pure export enclave would be politically harmless and has failed only for lack of intellectual clarity.

head: Tariff-Jumping FDI
dek: This is Jagdish Bhagwati's term, which he raised in the early 1990s when the first FDI surge reached India.
more: This is Jagdish Bhagwati's term, which he raised in the early 1990s when the first FDI surge reached India. Erect trade barriers and foreigners will set up minimal plants inside them, assembling semi-knocked-down cars and selling into the protected market. It looks like FDI but is really arbitrage around policy, and much of India's auto industry fits this pattern. Trade liberalisation comes first: either run a duty-free enclave, or allow mainline FDI with no trade barriers.

head: Bilateral Investment Treaties as Insurance and a Self-Slap
dek: Foreigners don't trust a state that did Vodafone-style retrospective taxation.
more: Foreigners don't trust a state that did Vodafone-style retrospective taxation. Bilateral investment treaties bridge that gap: India promises to compensate foreign investors when any level of the Indian state expropriates them. Paying out $1 billion a year to stabilise $100 billion of FDI is a cheap insurance premium, and the slap disciplines the state. But officials took lost cases personally, a 'sovereign right to expropriate' machismo set in, and the 2016 model BIT abandoned many good ideas. India is now increasingly hostile to such treaties.

head: The Anti-Foreigner Streak and the Cult of Third-Worldism
dek: India's distrust of foreign capital comes from a deep anti-Western streak and a third-worldism that casts multinationals as exploiters of helpless workers.
more: India's distrust of foreign capital comes from a deep anti-Western streak and a third-worldism that casts multinationals as exploiters of helpless workers. A newer arrogance adds that India is so important foreigners must come anyway. Ajay argues that success lies in embracing the global frontier. Amit adds that all trade and human connection is positive-sum.

head: The HMY Ladder and Its Indian Software Inversion
dek: The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple model ranks firms by productivity: the weakest stay domestic, better ones export, the best do FDI abroad.
more: The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple model ranks firms by productivity: the weakest stay domestic, better ones export, the best do FDI abroad. That gives a simple test of an Indian firm: domestic, exporter, or multinational? Hundreds of Indian firms are now multinationals. Indian software reverses the ladder. Firms that sit in India while foreign business comes to them are the most productive. Those that do outbound FDI by 'body shopping' staff into the UK and Germany are weaker.

head: 2025 as India's Window
dek: The breakdown of the China model and America's tariff turmoil have reshaped the world economy, and Ajay sees a rare opening for India.
more: The breakdown of the China model and America's tariff turmoil have reshaped the world economy, and Ajay sees a rare opening for India. A surge in FDI or goods exports does not yet show up in the data, but he believes the conditions for change are now in place.

head: Amit opens by insisting
more: Amit opens by insisting 'this episode is not about money, this episode is about love'. Ajay has confided five great loves: firm productivity, capital account openness, inflation targeting and, above all, FDI. When Ajay says 'inflation targeting', Amit cracks, 'Oh my God, you almost came as you said that.' He then asks, mock-romantically, 'Tell me about the first time you guys met. You and FDI.'

head: Ajay on the Chinese model
more: Ajay on the Chinese model: 'Deng Xiaoping's dream was there will be no Xi Jinping. We will fix China one day.'

head: After Ajay declares anyone who labels a chart just
more: After Ajay declares anyone who labels a chart just 'FDI' a propagandist, Amit says: 'You have terrified me. I'm never gonna say FDI in front of you again. Straight away it will be like net inflow, gross inflow.'

head: Ajay explains market churn with a foreign seller matched by…
more: Ajay explains market churn with a foreign seller matched by 'a Bengali who is buying'. Amit quips: 'Some foreign portfolio investors are Bengali. We are everywhere.'

head: Ajay applies a love maxim to capital flows
more: Ajay applies a love maxim to capital flows: 'If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it is yours. If it doesn't, it never was. That is the right approach to apply to all the great loves of your life, whether FDI or FPI.' He later mocks the anti-FPI economists as asking, 'will you love me next week?'

head: Amit sums up the FDI-versus-FPI debate
more: Amit sums up the FDI-versus-FPI debate: 'On one side of the debate you have securities. On the other side you have insecurities.'

head: Amit recalls his first reaction to SEZs
more: Amit recalls his first reaction to SEZs: 'my purest libertarian mind reacted by saying, Why do we need SEZ? A whole country should be an SEZ. Into that heaven of freedom, my father, let my country awake.' He caps it with a famous line of verse.

head: Amit asks why there can't be world-class Indian firms
more: Amit asks why there can't be world-class Indian firms 'when There are world class Indian YouTube shows'. Ajay declares the show 'an exporting show' with a 30% overseas audience: 'You have graduated.' Amit panics that this will invite an income-tax raid: 'My head is spinning, bro.'

head: Amit, closing the love metaphor
more: Amit, closing the love metaphor: 'the good thing is that FDI is liberal with her affections. We do not have to compete. We can both get FDI.'

head: Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (dir. Aziz Mirza) gives the chapter its title and metaphor
more: Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (dir. Aziz Mirza) gives the chapter its title and metaphor: 'Raju Wants to be gentlemen. Indian firms want to be global firms.'

head: Cafe Coffee Day in Vienna, Ajay's example of…
more: Cafe Coffee Day in Vienna, Ajay's example of 'FDI by India'. He says he has a photograph to prove it.

head: Black Death Pogroms and the 1933 Nazi Vote
dek: Culture is sticky over centuries. A shock from nearly six hundred years ago can still show up in the data, so a city's present can be read as the residue of its deep past.
more: Ajay opens with research on Germany. Cities where Jews were attacked in pogroms during the fourteenth-century Black Death, after being accused of bringing the plague, had a statistically higher Nazi vote share in the 1933 election. The finding came back to him on a recent trip to Pune.
Culture is sticky over centuries. A shock from nearly six hundred years ago can still show up in the data, so a city's present can be read as the residue of its deep past.

head: Pune's Endowment, and Twenty Pages of Criticism
dek: Being a capital is an initial endowment that keeps compounding: resources draw thinking, research and educational institutions for centuries.
more: Pune feels like a mid-sized second-tier city today, but a scant two hundred years ago the Peshwas ran India's biggest empire from it, with finance ministers, military strategists and logistics experts. On a two-day visit Ajay met what he calls the height of Pune's intelligentsia. Among them were the Prayas Energy Group, co-founded by his late friend Girish Sant, and about ten manufacturing CEOs gathered by Prashant Girbane of the Maratha Chamber of Commerce. That meeting was devoted entirely to criticising EIE's two manufacturing episodes. Ajay sat and listened.

Being a capital is an initial endowment that keeps compounding: resources draw thinking, research and educational institutions for centuries. And the right response to informed criticism is delight, not defensiveness.

head: The 15% Margin Problem in Manufacturing
dek: Manufacturing is harder than services for a structural reason, not just a policy one.
more: The best feedback came from his IIT wingmate Ajay Bhagavat. Global competition makes it very hard for manufacturing to earn an operating profit margin above 15%. Early software and services firms earned 50 to 70%, and that margin paid for their learning curve. Manufacturing instead demands a 5, 10 or 15-year journey of learning its intricate complexity without making cash hand over fist.

Manufacturing is harder than services for a structural reason, not just a policy one. Thin margins mean there is no cushion for learning, so it takes an ethos of patience and a willingness to commit to 10 to 20-year journeys of excellence.

head: Fergusson College, 'That Hotbed of Atheism'
dek: A genuine culture of ideas breeds radicalism in several directions at once.
more: Amit traces Pune's ferment to education as well as to the Peshwas. Gokhale and his colleagues founded the Deccan Education Society, which includes Amit's alma mater Fergusson College, and Gandhi first met Gokhale on its grounds in 1894. Gopal Ganesh Agarkar once asked a biology class what God would look like if donkeys had a God, then gestured to show it would be a donkey. In B.R. Nanda's biography of Gokhale, an Englishwoman hears that Gokhale teaches at Fergusson and exclaims about the place. Amit adds that Pune produced great liberals but also a deep RSS base, and Godse.
A genuine culture of ideas breeds radicalism in several directions at once. Nineteenth-century Pune was more irreverent than many places would tolerate today.

head: How a Country With No Navy Won the Black Sea
dek: The decisive weapon was a culture of engineering under fire. That means rejecting the 'third world' assumption that equipment is fixed for the duration of a war.
more:
Early in the war, Ukraine's navy was one ship, which it scuttled so Russia couldn't capture it. Russia's fleet sat in Sevastopol, a great natural port and Russian base since the Crimean War of the mid-nineteenth century. Ukraine used three innovations:
1. Constant NATO-quality and drone surveillance, so every Russian ship's latitude and longitude was known in real time.
2. Shore-based anti-ship missiles skimming two metres above the waves, hidden in sea clutter on ship radar, which sank the Moskva.
3. Drone boats carrying a thousand kg of explosive, some steered via Starlink dishes. When Russian helicopters hunted them, the boats were redesigned to fire anti-air missiles back.
Russia stopped using Sevastopol, and Ukrainian commercial ships ply the Black Sea again.

The decisive weapon was a culture of engineering under fire. That means rejecting the 'third world' assumption that equipment is fixed for the duration of a war. Amit adds the incentive lens: for Ukraine the war is existential, so it must innovate.

head: The Hellscape of the Ukraine Front
dek: Pervasive sensing plus cheap precision strike has made the battlefield itself uninhabitable.
more: Two exhausted armies face each other across something new in history. It is not a line of trenches one or two kilometres apart, as in the First World War, but a 10 to 30 km no-man's-land under relentless drone surveillance and precision-guided munitions. Anything that moves is seen. Massing 500 men and 50 tanks gets spotted and destroyed. Russia, nearly out of Soviet equipment, has resorted to golf carts. Soldiers huddle and hide, managing only small, dinky actions day after day.
Pervasive sensing plus cheap precision strike has made the battlefield itself uninhabitable. Amit notes that because technology drives the expansion, the hellscape could keep growing.

head: Operation Spider Web
dek: Commercial off-the-shelf technology now lets the weak strike deep inside the strong at an absurd cost ratio.
more: Over 18 months, Ukrainian special forces smuggled materials into safe houses inside Russia, one right next to an FSB building, and assembled 117 attack drones with 3D printers. The drones went into shipping containers on trucks driven by unwitting commercial drivers, told to wait at a Google Maps pin 5 to 10 km from five air bases. By the time the trucks moved, every Ukrainian had left Russia. From Ukraine, a button opened the container roofs and the drones flew out. They ran on ordinary Russian mobile-data SIMs, reportedly streamed video over Telegram, and may have used onboard AI with a table of Russia's costliest planes. About 20 aircraft, central to the nightly bombing of Ukraine and worth an estimated $2 to 3 billion, were destroyed for about $0.5 million. Amit adds that the containers had false ceilings, so an inspecting cop would find nothing.
Commercial off-the-shelf technology now lets the weak strike deep inside the strong at an absurd cost ratio. A country's own interior is no longer safe ground.
printed: Russia caught in a Spider Web

head: Operation Rising Lion
dek: Spider Web is a template, not a one-off: covert inside-out drone strikes combined with a conventional outside-in attack.
more: Mossad operatives built a safe house inside Iran, shipped in parts and 3D-printed drones. In a synchronised assault, those drones rose from inside Iran and knocked out much of its air defence just before Israeli planes arrived to hit targets across the country. Whether the nuclear programme was stopped is unknown; perhaps 400 kg of 60% enriched uranium remains. But Ajay says Iran's conventional power was set back five or ten years. Iran retaliated with probably 1,000 missiles and drones, and only about 50 got through.
Spider Web is a template, not a one-off: covert inside-out drone strikes combined with a conventional outside-in attack. Missile defence has also reached a new level.
printed: The lion that rose from within

head: The India-Pakistan Skirmish Fought From Home Airspace
dek: The dogfight imagery of 1965 and 1971 is obsolete. Air combat now means beyond-visual-range exchanges in which neither side crosses the border.
more: Ajay first insists on terminology: by international standard a war needs 1,000 deaths, so this was a skirmish or conflict, not a war. In the four days, planes on both sides stayed high over their own territory and fired standoff weapons at each other. To fire deep into Pakistan, Indian planes had to climb, which made them visible to ground radars and exposed them to ground-to-air and air-to-air missiles.
The dogfight imagery of 1965 and 1971 is obsolete. Air combat now means beyond-visual-range exchanges in which neither side crosses the border.

head: The First Hour of a War on Taiwan
dek: Open, trade-heavy societies are especially exposed to the inside-out attack model, so defence planning has to start at home.
more: Half the world's military experts study Ukraine; the other half war-game a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, which Xi Jinping has openly talked about. China is deeply infiltrated in Taiwan, with operatives inside and connections to the Taiwanese underworld, and containers flow constantly through this trading nation. Reading about Spider Web, Ajay feared the war's first hour would be fought from inside. Drones and operatives would take out political and military leadership and air defences, creating chaos before a conventional second wave.
Open, trade-heavy societies are especially exposed to the inside-out attack model, so defence planning has to start at home.

head: The Strange Sand of the Sinai
dek: Winning militaries fold scientists and problem-solvers into live operations.
more: In the 1973 Yom Kippur War, Israeli equipment in the Sinai malfunctioned because the sand had characteristics never seen before. Tank treads, tyres and, he believes, bridging gear were affected. Scientists from the Weizmann Institute came to the battlefield and experimented with the sand while the war was going on. They went home and redesigned the bridging gear, which Ajay credits for Israel's success in the Sinai. Amit's verdict: 'Human software.'
Winning militaries fold scientists and problem-solvers into live operations. This is the case for the brainy soldier over the brawny one.

head: Vasili Arkhipov, the Man Who Said 'Hold On'
dek: Amit uses this story to frame his first fear. Future wars will move at bewildering speed, and the incentive to delegate decisions to AI could erase the calm human checkpoint that saved the world in 1962.
more: In October 1962, during the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Soviet submarine B-59, carrying nuclear torpedoes, came under attack off Cuba. Its captain believed the two countries were at war and wanted to fire. Launching required three sign-offs: the captain, the political officer and the first officer. The first officer, Vasili Arkhipov, warned that if they were wrong, a nuclear first strike could trigger world war. He used his veto, and the torpedo was never fired.

Amit uses this story to frame his first fear. Future wars will move at bewildering speed, and the incentive to delegate decisions to AI could erase the calm human checkpoint that saved the world in 1962.

head: Conflict
dek: A book on the recent history and evolution of warfare that Amit enjoyed a few months ago and found full of things he didn't know.
more: A book on the recent history and evolution of warfare that Amit enjoyed a few months ago and found full of things he didn't know. He had wanted to use it as the base for a 'history of war' episode before Ajay steered them to the future.
Amit's recommendation at the end of the episode. He describes the authors as 'one a great historian, one a general and a very fine thinker' and expects Ajay would recommend it too.

head: The World in 2050 (Ep 106 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It had a section on the future of war, including Operation Spider Web's false-ceiling containers and the scenario of terrorists launching swarms of cheap drones.
more: It had a section on the future of war, including Operation Spider Web's false-ceiling containers and the scenario of terrorists launching swarms of cheap drones.
Amit calls it an episode he really loves and tells listeners to go watch it if they haven't.

head: The UNIX Episode (Ep 32 of Everything is Everything)
dek: War is increasingly a software problem, so their software episode is unexpectedly relevant.
more: War is increasingly a software problem, so their software episode is unexpectedly relevant.
Amit realises it belongs to this episode's cluster after Ajay argues that equipment upgrades now happen in software.

head: The India-Pakistan Conflict (Ep 111 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: It is the second episode supporting the view that the nuclear shadow doesn't make conventional war go away.
more: It is the second episode supporting the view that the nuclear shadow doesn't make conventional war go away.
Amit's older episode with Srinath Raghavan on India-Pakistan relations, cited in the same discussion.

head: You Can't Understand the State Without Understanding War
dek: Early states really did one thing: wage war. Creating internal peace was relatively cheap.
more: Early states really did one thing: wage war. Creating internal peace was relatively cheap. War is what forced states to build fiscal systems to raise money and to learn public procurement. War has repeatedly driven science and technology, and it shaped the very boundaries of states. Abhorring violence doesn't make war go away; you have to understand the world in order to play it well.

head: The Sword and the Shield: War Advances in Discontinuous Jumps
dek: Military history is an endless dance between attack and defence, punctuated by technologies that suddenly make old force designs obsolete.
more: Military history is an endless dance between attack and defence, punctuated by technologies that suddenly make old force designs obsolete. Aircraft carriers made the Royal Navy's battleship fleet look wrong-footed when Japan destroyed British ships near Singapore. German tanks with Stuka dive-bomber support stunned Poland and France. Ajay argues the last five years are another such break, bigger than the Gulf War's 'first triumph of silicon over steel'.

head: Principles Before Action
dek: Asked how he would revamp India's military, Ajay refuses to jump to a to-do list.
more: Asked how he would revamp India's military, Ajay refuses to jump to a to-do list. He first lays out nine principles, then derives strategy from them.

head: The Intelligence Revolution Kills Surprise, Mass and the Safe Rear
dek: Satellite imagery, drone imagery and open-source intelligence mean the enemy sees everything.
more: Satellite imagery, drone imagery and open-source intelligence mean the enemy sees everything. If you mass forces for a breakthrough in the Second World War or Soviet deep-battle style, they are spotted and destroyed by precision weapons. Every major campaign in Ukraine has been fully known to the other side. Logistics suffers too: ammunition dumps and supply trucks are visible targets, and a logistics truck is now more prized than a tank.

head: Strategic War Is a War of Economies, and Burn Rates Have Exploded
dek: Long wars are decided by production, innovation and the defence industrial base, because stored stocks run out.
more: Long wars are decided by production, innovation and the defence industrial base, because stored stocks run out. The intelligence revolution makes this worse. Israel's military has a system that fuses all its sensors into targeting data, producing targets at an unprecedented rate, so munitions are burned far faster than any peacetime factory supplies. Ajay's answer is to design surge capacity in advance. Private producers should run one shift in peacetime but be contractually ready to scale 3x to 5x on demand.

head: The Tactical-Strategic Inversion
dek: At short range, defence now dominates: any attacking force is seen and destroyed before it can break through.
more: At short range, defence now dominates: any attacking force is seen and destroyed before it can break through. At long range, attack dominates. Ukraine flies drones 1,000 to 2,000 km into Russia and destroys factories nightly, because ground-based air defences can be overwhelmed by volume. A factory in Dehradun was once safe during a war on the China border; now targets thousands of kilometres inside India are exposed.

head: The Soldier as Sensor, and the Algorithmic Fog of War
dek: Modern soldiers spend much of their time reporting position, ammunition left and sightings into software.
more: Modern soldiers spend much of their time reporting position, ammunition left and sightings into software. That data feeds situational-awareness systems which allocate scarce resources, like an 'Uber for artillery' matching a target to the best-placed gun. But too much data brings its own confusion, which Ajay calls the 'algorithmic fog of war', or death by data.

head: The Software-Defined Military
dek: Upgrades once meant swapping hardware, stepping out of a Tiger tank into a King Tiger.
more: Upgrades once meant swapping hardware, stepping out of a Tiger tank into a King Tiger. Now every piece of equipment reduces to mobility, a sensor and a gun, and everything else is software. A new revision pushed over the air to a million devices at the front is an instant force upgrade. So wartime R&D that diagnoses problems day by day becomes a core combat capability.

head: Brains Over Brawn
dek: The soldier of the future is less about machismo and fitness and more about intelligence and problem-solving on the fly.
more: The soldier of the future is less about machismo and fitness and more about intelligence and problem-solving on the fly. Ajay wants recruits who resemble teams inside India's technologically advanced private companies more than traditional junior-level military recruitment.

head: A Second World War-Speed Moment: Don't Fight the Last War
dek: Between 1939 and Hiroshima, dogma was overturned every few months. Ajay believes we are in such a period now.
more: Between 1939 and Hiroshima, dogma was overturned every few months. Ajay believes we are in such a period now. Most militaries have only just digested 1967, 1973, Iraq and Afghanistan. The Russians, Chinese and Americans are all unprepared for what the last five years revealed, so experimentation and risk-taking are essential.

head: Ukraine Is Today's Spanish Civil War
dek: Hitler perfected the Blitzkrieg in the Spanish Civil War of 1936, and the wise move for others was to be there and learn before Poland in 1939.
more: Hitler perfected the Blitzkrieg in the Spanish Civil War of 1936, and the wise move for others was to be there and learn before Poland in 1939. Ukraine is today's live lab for conventional war between peers. Every sensible country should send teams there, which will likely mean helping Ukraine in return. Ukraine has also become a world-leading vendor of many weapons systems.

head: Nuclear Weapons Haven't Made Conventional War Obsolete
dek: India, China and Pakistan once seemed locked in a nuclear standoff in which conventional war was a sideshow.
more: India, China and Pakistan once seemed locked in a nuclear standoff in which conventional war was a sideshow. Ajay argues conventional capability must go back to the drawing board. Amit notes his Seen and the Unseen guests made the counterintuitive case that nuclear weapons make conventional war more important.

head: Small, Cheap and Civilian Beats Exquisite Platforms
dek: Ajay's prescriptions for procurement: - Use commercial off-the-shelf technology wherever possible.
more:
Ajay's prescriptions for procurement:
- Use commercial off-the-shelf technology wherever possible. Starlink, a mass-market product, has huge military value, and a battlefield 3D printer should be an ordinary civilian one.
- Question big showpiece platforms. Shore-based missiles on Great Nicobar could dominate the Straits of Malacca, which raises the question of whether carriers are needed there.
- Rebuild procurement for speed. Ukraine fields a new generation of drones every four months, so aim for three revisions a year rather than one every five years.

head: All Roads Lead to Scale, and Hence to Partnership
dek: Military production follows Wright's Law: costs fall only with volume.
more: Military production follows Wright's Law: costs fall only with volume. Only the US and China have budgets large enough to reach scale alone; everyone else going it alone ends up subscale, expensive and short on R&D. The way out is deep international collaboration, with five to ten countries buying the same gear. Ajay points to two 'vortexes': a post-Trump European defence industrial base, and a Poland-Ukraine-South Korea partnership aiming for lower price points. India could manufacture for the latter, since a factory in Tamil Nadu is far from any front. Ajay cites India's Israel partnership since Narasimha Rao's time, which upgraded old Soviet equipment cheaply, as proof this works.

head: Freedom as a Force Multiplier
dek: Ukraine's flood of innovation reflects incentives, since it is fighting for its life, but also freedom.
more: Ukraine's flood of innovation reflects incentives, since it is fighting for its life, but also freedom. Free citizens bring their whole selves to the effort, while subjects of authoritarian states merely obey and become shadows of themselves. Amit frames it as citizen versus subject: citizens have skin in the game.

head: Speed, Autonomy and the Need for New Doctrine
dek: Edge AI lets drones pick and strike targets without a human in the loop.
more: Edge AI lets drones pick and strike targets without a human in the loop. Ajay calls this ethically fraught but inevitable, since countries like Russia and China won't sign treaties against it. Amit fears that the incentive for speed will push decisions to machines, and mistakes at scale could be catastrophic. Ajay's response is to do for conventional war what von Neumann, Nash and Schelling did for nuclear weapons after 1945: build game-theoretic deterrence doctrines that make for stable, peaceful behaviour.

head: The New Fog of War: Are We at War, and With Whom?
dek: Amit's second fear is ambiguity on two fronts. A power outage, a GST or Aadhaar backend failure, or contaminated water could be an accident, terrorism or a deliberate act of war.
more: Amit's second fear is ambiguity on two fronts. A power outage, a GST or Aadhaar backend failure, or contaminated water could be an accident, terrorism or a deliberate act of war. Cheap drones mean the attacker could be Pakistan, China, a dissident group, internal actors or the state's own false flag. In that fog, societies are liable to panic and make mistakes.

head: Make Trade, Not War: Be Citizens, Not Subjects
dek: Geopolitics often runs on a zero-sum, mercantilist instinct that makes war seem natural.
more: Geopolitics often runs on a zero-sum, mercantilist instinct that makes war seem natural. But human flourishing has always come through trade and peaceful cooperation. India should trade with China and Pakistan, and musicians on both sides should keep jamming. Amit's exhortation is to act as citizens: demand a state ready for future war, but one that actively makes peace rather than mongering war. Ajay agrees, adding that there is evil in the world, so the state still needs capabilities.

head: Amit says Ajay's pitch for a future-of-war episode felt like…
more: Amit says Ajay's pitch for a future-of-war episode felt like 'a glitch in the matrix, in other words, Deja Vu', since they'd already covered hybrid warfare and the world in 2050. He adds: 'We are not like other YouTube channels that we will recycle our old material and repeat ourselves as you know, men with egos tend to do. Shameful. Absolutely shameful.'

head: Amit on why Ukraine innovates so furiously
more: Amit on why Ukraine innovates so furiously: 'when you have a breakfast of bacon and eggs, what is the difference between the chicken and the pig? And the answer is that the chicken is interested, but the pig is committed. And in that sense, Ukraine is a pig.'

head: A riddle on incentives
more: A riddle on incentives: 'Who runs faster, the fox or the hare?' The punchline: 'The fox is only running for his lunch. The hare is running for his life.'

head: Ajay on a Russian helicopter hunting a Ukrainian drone boat
more: Ajay on a Russian helicopter hunting a Ukrainian drone boat: 'Just think of the arrogance and the confidence of a helicopter. You feel you are the god of the sky, and you're looking down at a dumb boat... and the boat says, Oops, and it just puts up its hand and a missile flies out of the boat and shoots down a helicopter.'

head: Ajay describes the relative calm of a First World War trench
more: Ajay describes the relative calm of a First World War trench: 'You're talking to your buddies. You're drinking water.' Amit chips in: 'You're writing diary entries about masturbation, as Wittgenstein did, the great philosopher.'

head: Ajay's test for listeners
more: Ajay's test for listeners: 'put on your sorting hat and classify yourself that are you a genuine military geek or are you fake? A genuine military geek knows the names of all the operations.' He lists Barbarossa, Citadel and Market Garden, and says Operation Spider Web will join them in history.

head: On the false ceilings that hid the Spider Web drones, Ajay notes you only need about six inches.

head: Amit, having established that Ajay is no expert on Indian mass culture, asks a quiz anyway

more: As Ajay scales drone swarms from ten to a hundred to 10,000, Amit quips: 'You just change the kitty party into a cricket match.'

head: Ajay's friend Ayush Patnaik built a 3D printer that prints everything about itself except one nozzle
more: Ajay's friend Ayush Patnaik built a 3D printer that prints everything about itself except one nozzle: 'you have to buy one nozzle and then you have to give Ayush one milk shake and he will print a three D printer for you.' more: After a long stretch on Tiger and King Tiger tanks, Ajay announces 'I want to digress.' Amit: 'You were talking tiger tanks. We can get you a tigress.'

head: Ajay says the military needs
more: Ajay says the military needs 'wimps like Vaishnav'.
