more: Ajay on his organisation: 'in my organization, XKDR Forum, we are crazy geeks. We in addition to loving FDI and loving our programming, we also love government contracting. We think government contracting is hot.'

head: How this episode came about: Amit emailed
more: How this episode came about: Amit emailed 'history of war', Ajay replied 'future of war', Amit repeated 'history of war', Ajay repeated 'future of war', until Amit realised Ajay had a different idea. Ajay's justification: every child already knows 'everything that happened in the Second World War and Six Day War.'

head: Amit's sign-off
more: Amit's sign-off: 'We hope none of our worst fears come true. And we trade and trade and trade until we can trade no more. Make trade, not war.'

head: The Spanish Civil War of 1936 as the lab
more: The Spanish Civil War of 1936 as the lab 'where Adolf Hitler perfected the Blitzkrieg'. It is Ajay's analogy for why every military should study Ukraine up close.

head: Israel's 1967 war, which people joke was Second World War capability fully realised, and the Gulf War
more: Israel's 1967 war, which people joke was Second World War capability fully realised, and the Gulf War as 'the first triumph of silicon over steel'. Ajay uses them as the last 'recognisable' wars before today's break.

head: Growing Up Among 80 Journalist Households
dek: Indian journalism as a 'noble calling' is not a myth. Within living memory, newspaper editors had the kind of influence over a nation's thinking that France's philosophers had in the 1960s.
more: From age six to seventeen, Ajay lived in a housing complex where about 80 households worked in print media, including Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati papers, before television arrived. His father was the second head of the Economic Times Research Bureau (ETRB), which K.A. Antony, formerly of the RBI, had created. Top economists like Hanan Ezekiel edited the Economic Times, and the Times of India grew up around Shamlal and Girilal Jain, whose dense opinion pieces the whole country read. When Ajay was ten, the Emergency came, and the Indian Express ran empty white space rather than print what the censors wanted. Later, Arun Shourie's full-page front-page investigation into A.R. Antulay's trusts cost the Maharashtra chief minister his job. Journalists were poorly paid and the business made little money, but it had a sense of purpose.

Indian journalism as a 'noble calling' is not a myth. Within living memory, newspaper editors had the kind of influence over a nation's thinking that France's philosophers had in the 1960s. Amit adds a caveat: this is partly selective nostalgia, since not everything was rosy then.

head: When TV Made the Cricket Match Report Obsolete
dek: This is a small version of journalism's whole crisis of relevance. Once information is abundant, the value moves to perspective and sense-making.
more: When Amit started in cricket journalism in the early 2000s, the job had just changed. A match report used to tell readers what happened. Now readers had already watched the game on TV or knew the result. British papers like The Guardian, the Telegraph and The Times led the shift: ball-by-ball description became a free commodity, so writers had to bring perspective and colour instead. The writing got richer as a result.

This is a small version of journalism's whole crisis of relevance. Once information is abundant, the value moves to perspective and sense-making. Outlets that keep selling the commodity turn into artifacts.

head: Yahoo India: The Party Photographer vs. the Award-Winning Originals
dek: This is the economics behind the gutting of serious journalism. There was no malice involved.
more: Around 2009–2010, Prem Panicker ran editorial at Yahoo India (Amit freelanced for him, putting together a columns page). The India team was set a target of 500 million page views a month. Prem built 'Originals', a long-form reporting section with a budget of more than a crore a year; its award-winning pieces drew 40,000–50,000 page views each. Meanwhile a section called OMG, fed by one Bombay photographer paid a one-lakh monthly retainer (12 lakh a year) to shoot Bollywood parties, brought in 450–500 million page views on its own. The higher-ups told Prem his return on investment didn't compare and the money was wasted, and Originals was eventually shut down.
This is the economics behind the gutting of serious journalism. There was no malice involved. A metric that counts every page view the same will always pick party photos over deep reporting.

head: The Editor Whose Job Was to 'Comfort the Comforted'
dek: Amit calls the statement rational. A newspaper is a business with shareholders, employees and pressure from the state, so inverting journalism's dharma is a response to incentives, not just a personal failing.
more: In the 20th century, journalism took on higher purposes: seeking truth, speaking truth to power, and 'afflicting the comfortable, comforting the afflicted'. Yet the editor of a major Indian newspaper told one of the journalists Amit spoke to that he believed their job was to comfort the comforted. He said it seriously.

Amit calls the statement rational. A newspaper is a business with shareholders, employees and pressure from the state, so inverting journalism's dharma is a response to incentives, not just a personal failing. That is why Amit insists the story has no villains, only structures.

head: Refusing Pagination at Cricinfo
dek: An industry 'courtesy' that happens to inflate your own metric is usually a rationalisation.
more: In the page-view era, sites split an 800-word piece into four pages of 200 words so that one reader produced four page views. The official justification was the conventional wisdom 'don't make the reader scroll.' As managing editor of Cricinfo, Amit called it bullshit. Cricinfo didn't paginate and avoided pop-ups and other tricks.
An industry 'courtesy' that happens to inflate your own metric is usually a rationalisation. Real respect for readers means good content and as few clicks as possible.

head: Bennett Coleman's Clickbait Bet That Failed
dek: If anyone could make a mass-market, advertising-led clickbait model work in India, it was Bennett Coleman.
more: For a long time the rough rule in Indian media was that Bennett Coleman made money and everyone else together made roughly zero. Ajay then watched the company go all in on tabloidization, scale, lower paper quality and internet clickbait. It had the DNA, size and market punch to win billions of clicks. Its operating profit has nonetheless declined significantly.

If anyone could make a mass-market, advertising-led clickbait model work in India, it was Bennett Coleman. Its failure is a clean natural experiment showing the circle can't be squared. Amit adds that the long-term game being played could never have been won.

head: 'Is Nevertheless Two Words or Three?'
dek: Nostalgia for a golden age is partly selection bias. Before the internet, readers had no New Yorker or Economist to compare with.
more: Growing up in the 80s and 90s, Amit thought of journalism as the place where people went if they couldn't get into engineering, medicine or the UPSC. Many old-school journalists he worked with couldn't write a proper English sentence. A noted Hindu journalist, a nice man, once sidled up to him at Chinnaswami Stadium during a cricket match and asked whether 'nevertheless' was two words or three. Amit says we remember the legends, like Arun Shourie, Vir Sanghvi's Sunday magazine, and India Today's copy desk under Dilip Bobb, but they were exceptions.
Nostalgia for a golden age is partly selection bias. Before the internet, readers had no New Yorker or Economist to compare with. Low standards fed low expectations, which fed lower standards.

head: The New Yorker Fact-Checks One Paragraph
dek: Quality journalism comes from expensive process and labour, not talent alone.
more: Siddhartha Mukherjee, author of The Emperor of All Maladies, interviewed Ajay over video for a New Yorker article on excess COVID deaths in India; Ajay had one of the first papers on the subject. The magazine's checkers confirmed every sentence attributed to him. That wasn't enough: they asked him to show the paper backing his claims. All this was for one paragraph in a 20,000-word story. T.N. Ninan once told Ajay that quality requires investing in process, meaning enough man-hours at a high enough price per hour. In India, he said, only Bennett Coleman could afford it, and it wouldn't.
Quality journalism comes from expensive process and labour, not talent alone. Indian journalism is chronically under-resourced, produces low quality, and then concludes nobody will pay for it.

head: Why Readers Trust the WSJ Against Trump
dek: A record of rigour lets a paper take on the powerful and keep readers on its side.
more: Trump sued the Wall Street Journal for $10 billion over a recent story. Ajay's reaction was that the WSJ would never make a move like that without being extremely sure of its facts. Trump is famous for suing newspapers, so the paper would have done its hard work before publishing. Readers therefore give it full benefit of the doubt.
A record of rigour lets a paper take on the powerful and keep readers on its side. A media ecosystem without that record has no such reserve of trust to draw on.

head: Long-Form Profiles That Were Really Hit Pieces
dek: Inside a weak ecosystem, awards and prestige reflect that ecosystem's own standards.
more: One Indian magazine known for long-form journalism ran deep profiles that were in fact hit pieces. The writer set out from the start to take the subject down, and most quotes came from unnamed former colleagues. Some of these stories won awards. Amit has read the New Yorker since childhood and found it disgraceful.
Inside a weak ecosystem, awards and prestige reflect that ecosystem's own standards. Readers exposed to a higher benchmark notice the gap at once, and trust erodes.

head: Sacked Editors and Police at the Door
dek: The state's stick is real, used by both parties, and mostly works through quiet pressure rather than law.
more: Amit gave two examples, both from the HT group. When Mint launched, editor Raju Narisetti wrote something that angered P. Chidambaram, who had him sacked; Narisetti left the country. Years later, under the BJP, Bobby Ghosh ran a hate-crime tracker at the Hindustan Times; Arun Jaitley allegedly disliked it and got him sacked. Shephali Bhatt told Amit that after the Financial Times published an exposé of a leading business family, police visited every Indian name on the byline within a day. The foreign lead correspondent went back to her previous posting because of the harassment. Amit also recalled a friend's investigative story, spiked at the last minute, that everyone had admired as explosive. That was exactly why it was spiked.

The state's stick is real, used by both parties, and mostly works through quiet pressure rather than law. It also explains why the small independent outlets, with nothing to lose, are often the ones showing a spine.

head: T.N. Ninan Refuses to Show Columnists Their Views
dek: Feedback loops built on views slowly replace editorial judgment with whatever the crowd clicks.
more: Around 2006, Ajay asked T.N. Ninan whether he should send columnists data on how many views their pieces got. Ninan said absolutely not. What makes a good editorial or op-ed page should come from the editorial team's own aesthetic and intellectual judgment, built out of their minds and philosophy. Ajay now says he was stupid to ask and Ninan was right. Amit runs his own shows the same way and says he hasn't looked at the figures for The Seen and the Unseen in a year and a half.
Feedback loops built on views slowly replace editorial judgment with whatever the crowd clicks. Refusing to look at the numbers can be a way of protecting the work.

head: The Columnist Nobody Liked
dek: Once views become the yardstick, they quietly overrule the editor's own taste and values.
more: About five years ago, a friend who edited the features section of a major publication was carrying a columnist she despised, a misogynist nobody liked. When asked why she kept running him, she said he got more views than everyone else combined.
Once views become the yardstick, they quietly overrule the editor's own taste and values. This is the world Ninan was guarding against.

head: Two YouTubes That Never Overlap
dek: Algorithms don't just bias us; they build separate realities. A newspaper that printed a column for demonetization next to Amit's column against it gave readers a shared world.
more: Amit wanted to see what the kooky right-wing ecosystem on YouTube looked like. He opened an incognito window, logged into a different Gmail account, and followed the recommendations. He now has two YouTube feeds that have never shown a single common video.

Algorithms don't just bias us; they build separate realities. A newspaper that printed a column for demonetization next to Amit's column against it gave readers a shared world. Without one, people from different feeds will each find the other evil, and from inside their own world that is a reasonable conclusion.

head: Three Physical Papers and a Cup of Coffee
dek: A physical paper offers something an algorithm can't: someone else's considered judgment about what matters, built into the layout itself.
more: Ajay takes Business Standard, Indian Express and Mint in print. He leaves home by 8:15–8:30 to beat traffic and reads them at the office with coffee. He does it partly for a broad scan of the news, but mostly to get out of his bubble and see the world through editors he respects even when he disagrees with them. He pays attention to page design, photographs articles to send to friends for discussion, and keeps a Google Gemini audio prompt open to ask questions as he reads. He suggests newspapers print a QR code on every story.

A physical paper offers something an algorithm can't: someone else's considered judgment about what matters, built into the layout itself. Here the newspaper works as a deliberate antidote to the filter bubble.

head: Public Opinion
dek: An early-20th-century classic on the media that Amit calls outstanding and says everyone should read.
more: An early-20th-century classic on the media that Amit calls outstanding and says everyone should read.
The first of three books on the media Amit recommended at the end of the episode. He says he has probably recommended it on the show before.

dek: Amit calls it absolutely worth reading for anyone thinking about how media shapes us.
more: Amit calls it absolutely worth reading for anyone thinking about how media shapes us.
The second of Amit's three closing books on the media. He also pointed to McLuhan's 'The Medium is the Message'.

head: Amusing Ourselves to Death
dek: It completes his reading list on the media, which fits an episode about sensationalism, fragmented attention and media as entertainment.
more: It completes his reading list on the media, which fits an episode about sensationalism, fragmented attention and media as entertainment.
The third of Amit's three closing books on the media.

head: Amused to Death
dek: Ajay says Roger Waters read Neil Postman's book and then wrote the album, so it is a musical companion to Postman's argument.
more: Ajay says Roger Waters read Neil Postman's book and then wrote the album, so it is a musical companion to Postman's argument.

head: The age of the partial outsider
dek: It names a useful stance: being close enough to a field to have influence but outside enough not to be bound by its conventions.
more: It names a useful stance: being close enough to a field to have influence but outside enough not to be bound by its conventions.
A recent FT column whose phrase 'partial outsider' Amit uses to describe his relationship with journalism and every other field he has worked in.

more: Amit says Prem's episodes with him are really good. Prem is a legend in the field and the source of insights like the Yahoo story and 'a mile wide and an inch deep'.

dek: It led to Ajay's first-hand experience of the New Yorker's fact-checking, his main example of what real editorial process involves.
more: It led to Ajay's first-hand experience of the New Yorker's fact-checking, his main example of what real editorial process involves.
The New Yorker piece that quoted Ajay on excess COVID deaths in India.

head: Gell-Mann Amnesia
dek: It explains why readers who spot errors in their own field should stop trusting the rest of a generalist newspaper.
more: It explains why readers who spot errors in their own field should stop trusting the rest of a generalist newspaper.
A phrase Amit says he loves, used to explain the crisis of trust.

more: Ajay uses it as an example of journalism you can trust: a paper wouldn't take on someone famous for suing without doing the hard work.
The recent story over which Trump sued the Wall Street Journal for $10 billion.
