dek: An earlier, more playful attempt at forecasting the future that the hosts enjoyed doing.
more: An earlier, more playful attempt at forecasting the future that the hosts enjoyed doing.
Mentioned while Amit explained why forecasting journalism's future is so hard.

head: Mohak Mangal's YouTube channel
dek: Amit says he works hard and does a pretty good job of the sense-making function.
more: Amit says he works hard and does a pretty good job of the sense-making function.
Cited as a young solo creator doing explanatory news.

head: Eric Topol's writing on medicine
dek: To understand cutting-edge medicine, Amit would read Topol on Twitter, in his articles or in his books rather than the Times of India.
more: To understand cutting-edge medicine, Amit would read Topol on Twitter, in his articles or in his books rather than the Times of India.
Amit's example of going straight to a specialist instead of reading a newspaper.

head: The Crisis of Relevance: Information Is No Longer Scarce
dek: Journalism is older than newspapers: town criers and oral poets met the needs to know what was happening, to preserve it, and to debate it.
more: Journalism is older than newspapers: town criers and oral poets met the needs to know what was happening, to preserve it, and to debate it. Over time it added truth-seeking, sense-making and, in the 20th century, a watchdog role. Its founding reason was that information was scarce, and that is no longer true. Information is abundant, and better sense-makers, often specialists, are everywhere, while the old institutions linger like artifacts. People scrolling Instagram aren't to blame; their needs are being met elsewhere. Ajay pushes back that truth is still scarce, because the information firehose is full of lies from companies, governments and tribes. Amit agrees a good paper should be 'a filter to the truth', but says mainstream media has given up that role.

head: The Partial Outsider
dek: Janan Ganesh's phrase describes someone who is an outsider to a field but still connected to it.
more: Janan Ganesh's phrase describes someone who is an outsider to a field but still connected to it. Such a person has influence but isn't bound by the field's conventions, and can apply frameworks from elsewhere. Amit says this position, which he has held in every field he has worked in including journalism, is one of his greatest advantages in understanding the world.

head: Dharma vs. Business: The Newsroom as Cost Center
dek: Every profession has a kind of dharma.
more: Every profession has a kind of dharma. Journalism's higher purposes, such as truth-seeking and speaking truth to power, only took shape in the 20th century, while it has always been a business with shareholders and payrolls. Individuals can choose purpose over profit, but a firm has fiduciary duties. Shephali Bhatt's first newsroom treated journalists as a cost centre. Amit treats this as a value-free description of how things are, not an accusation.

head: Page-View Inflation
dek: In the 2000s, advertising was the only way to make money online and the page view was the unit being sold.
more: In the 2000s, advertising was the only way to make money online and the page view was the unit being sold. As sites multiplied, page views multiplied, and each became worth less, just as printing money devalues a currency. That pushed publishers into ever more desperate tactics such as clickbait, SEO headlines and pagination, and into a race to the bottom. The metric was also widely gamed.

head: Platforms Ate the Ad Money, and AI Broke Google's Bargain
dek: Samarth describes a wave of digital-native outlets from 2010 to 2020, such as Vox, Vice and BuzzFeed.
more: Samarth describes a wave of digital-native outlets from 2010 to 2020, such as Vox, Vice and BuzzFeed. They were promised traffic in exchange for original content, but the advertising money went to Facebook, YouTube and Instagram. Ajay adds a newer blow: Google used to send traffic in return for crawling content, but it now puts a Gemini AI answer at the top of search results, and click-throughs to media sites have collapsed.

head: Advertising Is Dying; Monetize the Community Directly
dek: Advertising has always been wasteful. John Wanamaker said half of it is wasted, and Ambi Paramaeswaran says far more than half, and that online ads are a scandal.
more: Advertising has always been wasteful. John Wanamaker said half of it is wasted, and Ambi Paramaeswaran says far more than half, and that online ads are a scandal. In the old model a writer sold a piece to a newspaper, which gathered eyeballs, sold them to advertisers and passed the writer a sliver. Readers always valued writers with their time and attention, but writers had no way to capture that value directly. Now they do, through subscriptions, courses and communities, and Amit thinks that for media, advertising is dead.

head: Shallow vs. Deep Engagement
dek: Advertisers treat every page view the same, but a 10-second glance at Bollywood gossip is worth almost nothing, while a 40-minute podcast session is deeply immersive and a host's recommendation carries real credibility.
more: Advertisers treat every page view the same, but a 10-second glance at Bollywood gossip is worth almost nothing, while a 40-minute podcast session is deeply immersive and a host's recommendation carries real credibility. Amit thinks advertisers haven't caught on to this because nobody looks below the surface metric. Every metric can be gamed, but the quality of attention is what actually matters.

head: Attributability Shrinks the Imagination
dek: Digital commerce lets you count exactly which click led to which sale and pay only for that.
more: Digital commerce lets you count exactly which click led to which sale and pay only for that. Ajay first found this appealing, but now thinks it narrows thinking. Building a brand, its visibility and an environment of trust around a business involves much more than whatever can be traced to a click.

head: Civic Purpose and the Vanishing Beats
dek: Samarth's term 'civic purpose' covers beats like the municipality, the RBI, a dusty flyover site or a water problem in one lane.
more: Samarth's term 'civic purpose' covers beats like the municipality, the RBI, a dusty flyover site or a water problem in one lane. Nobody demands or pays for this coverage, but it records local history. When journalists are treated as cost centres, these beats are cut first and specialists become generalists who file three stories a day. Quality and readership fall, and the cycle feeds itself. Amit doesn't know who will produce this record in the new world, because individual passion can't replace an institution.

head: The Chronic Under-Investment Trap
dek: Quality comes from process: many well-paid hours behind each well-checked story, as T.N.
more: Quality comes from process: many well-paid hours behind each well-checked story, as T.N. Ninan told Ajay. Indian journalism is under-resourced and underpaid, so it produces low quality, and the industry then concludes nobody will pay for journalism. Samarth also describes 'invisible quitting': talented people leave one at a time, so it never makes the news. Samarth adds that India's media ecosystem is so shallow that a few failed subscription experiments get read as proof that Indian readers won't pay. Ajay hopes patient investors with hundreds or thousands of crores will fund five years of quality first; Amit is sceptical.
printed: A mile wide, an inch deep

head: Gell-Mann Amnesia and the Rise of Specialists
dek: Michael Crichton named this effect after the physicist Murray Gell-Mann.
more: Michael Crichton named this effect after the physicist Murray Gell-Mann. You read a newspaper story on a subject you know well and see that it's rubbish, then turn the page and trust the rest of the paper. India's generalist journalism makes this especially costly. Since the 2000s, specialists have had their own means of production in blogs and Twitter: Tyler Cowen on economics, Eric Topol on medicine. Readers can see the gap in quality, and they leave.

head: Steel-Man the Other Side
dek: Amit's advice to opinion writers is to state the opposing view so well that an opponent would say 'that's exactly how I would have put it', and only then argue against it.
more: Amit's advice to opinion writers is to state the opposing view so well that an opponent would say 'that's exactly how I would have put it', and only then argue against it. It sharpens your own thinking and shows readers you aren't a partisan hack. Amit says mainstream media rarely does this, as outlets get drawn into narrative battles because outrage brings clicks.

head: The State's Stick and Carrot, and the Inverted Hedge
dek: In the 1970s and 80s, owners used media to stand up to the state. Ramnath Goenka hired Arun Shourie and spoke truth to power, and the Singhanias started the Indian Post as a hedge during their battle with the Wadias.
more: In the 1970s and 80s, owners used media to stand up to the state. Ramnath Goenka hired Arun Shourie and spoke truth to power, and the Singhanias started the Indian Post as a hedge during their battle with the Wadias. Today, corporate barons buy media houses to do the government a favour. The stick is pressure on owners' other businesses (an ED raid on a chemical factory, for example), sackings of editors, and police visits. The carrot is government, PSU and party advertising, which can be withdrawn at any time. Small outlets with nothing to lose hold out longest.

head: Proximity to Government Cheapens the Product
dek: Ajay points to two more channels of state influence. Media companies earn from conferences, and corporate sponsors come because ministers attend, which gives the government a veto over that income.
more: Ajay points to two more channels of state influence. Media companies earn from conferences, and corporate sponsors come because ministers attend, which gives the government a veto over that income. Newspapers also hand opinion space to sitting civil servants and politicians. The government already has Doordarshan, the PIB and press conferences, so its propaganda is free. Printing it undermines the reason anyone would pay for a newspaper.

head: Price Controls Made TV News Shout
dek: Ashok Malik's argument, relayed by Amit: in the West, a large share of channel revenue comes from subscriptions, which pays for expensive niche content like National Geographic.
more: Ashok Malik's argument, relayed by Amit: in the West, a large share of channel revenue comes from subscriptions, which pays for expensive niche content like National Geographic. In India, channels pay huge licence fees and then face government caps on what they can charge subscribers, so they depend on advertising and race to the bottom. FM radio is similar: high licence fees and a ban on news and politics push every station into mainstream Bollywood, unlike the varied niche stations in New York. The behaviour that looks like private companies failing has regulation at its root.

head: Embedded Journalism Comes Home
dek: Embedded journalism started with reporters travelling with the US Department of Defense in Iraq: the reporter gets access, and coverage tends to go easy on the host.
more: Embedded journalism started with reporters travelling with the US Department of Defense in Iraq: the reporter gets access, and coverage tends to go easy on the host. Ajay, citing a friend, says the same arrangement now applies in Kashmir, Naxal-affected districts and parts of the Northeast. The state often blocks independent reporting there, so embedding is the only way in, and the resulting coverage ends up close to PIB and Doordarshan messaging.

head: Social Media Selects for Anger
dek: Journalists want to go viral, and strong polarised views go viral while plain news doesn't.
more: Journalists want to go viral, and strong polarised views go viral while plain news doesn't. That erodes the classic separation of news and opinion, and young reporters slip some virtue signalling into news stories. Ajay says that even if no individual chases outrage, the system selects for it. Social media amplifies anger and emotion, views are tallied (he believes Fox News has a live views screen in its newsroom), and so calm reporters lose out while emotional ones get the bonuses.

head: Fragmented Attention and Algorithmic Worlds
dek: Mornings used to start with a newspaper; now they start with phones, scrolling and swiping.
more: Mornings used to start with a newspaper; now they start with phones, scrolling and swiping. Algorithms feed you more of whatever you clicked. A 15-year-old who clicks one misogynistic, rabble-rousing piece can end up inside a world of that content and take it for reality. A newspaper puts opposing columns on the same page; an algorithm narrows your world to one sliver that may not even be true.

head: The Mainstream Is Crumbling, but Nothing Has Replaced It
dek: The conditions that produced journalism and its values no longer exist, and the mainstream is collapsing in media, entertainment and elsewhere, but institutions lag behind.
more: The conditions that produced journalism and its values no longer exist, and the mainstream is collapsing in media, entertainment and elsewhere, but institutions lag behind. Solo creators on Substack and YouTube take on parts of the job, especially sense-making. But a reporter covering a city beat can't be expected to also master video, marketing and thumbnails, and once independent, they will start chasing clicks. Ajay says the answer is firms, meaning teams with a business model. So far, the convincing successes globally are old media that reinvented themselves: the FT, the WSJ, the New York Times and The Economist.

head: Societies Build Immunity to New Media
dek: This is Suyash Rai's more optimistic account, relayed by Ajay. Every new medium causes damage at first.
more: This is Suyash Rai's more optimistic account, relayed by Ajay. Every new medium causes damage at first. Radio was a weapon for Mussolini and Hitler: a crackling box urging people to burn the Jews was hugely persuasive. Over time, cultures absorbed radio and normalised it. Today almost nobody takes WhatsApp forwards seriously. Algorithms and social media may follow the same path, but only if culture adapts and people meet each link with scepticism.

head: Amit refuses to name the famous journalists' housing enclave where Ajay grew up
more: Amit refuses to name the famous journalists' housing enclave where Ajay grew up: 'We won't take the name because we don't want admiring nubile young women to land up at your house if we accidentally give the address away.'

head: When Amit described himself as a perpetual outsider, Ajay called him
more: When Amit described himself as a perpetual outsider, Ajay called him 'The mighty podcaster who will not join any club that will have him.' Amit replied: 'I'm really glad, really glad for once that you quoted the right Marx. This of course is Groucho Marx, right? So well done.'

head: Amit's growing-up view of journalism
more: Amit's growing-up view of journalism: it was where society's rejects went, the people who couldn't get into engineering, medicine or the UPSC. One noted Hindu journalist sidled up to him in the Chinnaswami press box and asked, 'Amit, tell me something, is nevertheless two words or three words?'

head: On the irony of censorship: a friend's investigative story was spiked at the last minute even though everyone said it was explosive (
more: On the irony of censorship: a friend's investigative story was spiked at the last minute even though everyone said it was explosive ('dhamaka'). As Amit put it, 'But that is the very reason it was sort of spiked.'

head: After Ajay called the episode plan bleak and asked for something hopeful, Amit
more: After Ajay called the episode plan bleak and asked for something hopeful, Amit says: 'I said we'll do it in the last chapter. I lied.'

head: Amit on phones
more: Amit on phones: 'I'm not saying everything we do on our phones is wrong. It's only about 99.8% is wrong.' He then goes off on a 'like and subscribe' tangent ('Ajay looks at the numbers. So let's see if my saying this moves the needle... If it does, we'll say it in every episode. No, we won't'), loses his thread, and admits: 'My attention went to hell. See what just happened, these are bad habits.'

head: After Ajay's ode to reading print with coffee
more: After Ajay's ode to reading print with coffee 'like a civilized person', Amit notes that newspapers 'are also useful when you run out of water in the morning and you're stuck in the loo', and predicts the editor will cut it.

head: Amit interrupts Ajay's vision of media firms full of specialists
more: Amit interrupts Ajay's vision of media firms full of specialists: 'I just want to interrupt and say no one knows how to make thumbnails. Everybody's winging it.'

head: Asked how The Seen and the Unseen is doing after going fortnightly, Amit says he hasn't checked the numbers in a year and a half
more: Asked how The Seen and the Unseen is doing after going fortnightly, Amit says he hasn't checked the numbers in a year and a half: 'I do the work I do. I'm not a circus monkey.'

head: When Ajay recommends Roger Waters' Amused to Death, Amit says he's
more: When Ajay recommends Roger Waters' Amused to Death, Amit says he's 'just piggybacking on words.' Ajay explains that Waters read the Postman book before writing it. Asked if he made that up, he says: 'No no seriously I'm not just an LLM.'

head: L.K. Advani on the press during the Emergency
more: L.K. Advani on the press during the Emergency: 'they were asked to bend, they chose to crawl', set against Ramnath Goenka's blank page in the Indian Express.

'If you ain't got nothing, you got nothing to lose', quoted by Amit, who wasn't sure whether it came from Dylan, Joan Baez or Kris Kristofferson, to explain why small independent outlets are the ones showing a spine.

head: Hanan Ezekiel
more: Hanan Ezekiel, 'brother of the much more famous Nissim Ezekiel, but really one of the best economists of India', once edited the Economic Times. Ajay compares that era's editors to France's 1960s philosophers.

head: Prem Panicker's verdict, quoted by Amit: the Indian media is…
more: Prem Panicker's verdict, quoted by Amit: the Indian media is 'a mile wide and an inch deep'.

head: The classic journalistic motto
more: The classic journalistic motto 'afflict the comfortable, comfort the afflicted', and journalism as 'the first draft of history', which Amit extends to 'often the only draft of history'.

head: Build for episode 100, not episode 1
dek: Content compounds. A body of work that stays relevant becomes a library people binge, and each new piece links into the rest.
more: A friend starting a podcast asked Amit for advice because The Seen and the Unseen had done so well. He told her not to worry about what listeners find in episode one, but about what they will find to binge on by episode hundred. He also told her to make episodes that travel across time as well as geography, so they still make sense thirty years later. He frames this episode the same way: timely about the tariffs, but meant as a 'first draft of history' of a pivotal moment.
Content compounds. A body of work that stays relevant becomes a library people binge, and each new piece links into the rest. Amit calls this 'one long conversation', not a set of separate episodes.

head: Hyundai knew more about cars than Tata Motors, and that's fine
dek: The real payload of FDI is knowledge, and it walks out of the factory gate with the people who learned it.
more: When Hyundai built a car factory in India, the Indians who learned to make Hyundai cars picked up a new level of automobile technology and management. They then moved to Tata Motors, started ancillary firms and launched the next generation of EV projects. Hyundai later decided that all the small cars it sells worldwide would be made in India, which Ajay reads as proof of Indian manufacturing capability. He contrasts this with the Meiji Restoration, when Japan sent only a couple of thousand young people West. India sent far more abroad, and they learned mostly on the job before coming back.
The real payload of FDI is knowledge, and it walks out of the factory gate with the people who learned it. Ego about who is 'better' only gets in the way of that diffusion.

head: Twelve branches a year for all foreign banks combined
dek: Economic nationalism mostly hurts Indians. Here it is Indian bank customers who lose out when foreign branches are rationed.
more: All foreign banks in India put together were allowed to open only twelve branches a year. In what was billed as a great liberalisation, the limit was raised to eighteen. Ajay asks why the state should come between an Indian customer who wants to bank with Citibank and Citibank. He calls this one of innumerable normalised pieces of Indian economic nationalism.
Economic nationalism mostly hurts Indians. Here it is Indian bank customers who lose out when foreign branches are rationed. Such rules also give Western populists ammunition against India.

head: The map with no tankers in the Red Sea
dek: The open trading system rested on a security guarantee nobody noticed.
more: A friend, Ashima Sharma, showed Ajay a world map with every one of the roughly 700 LNG tankers plotted as a dot. Not one was in the Red Sea. The Houthis are choking the route, and some ships pay them ransom to pass. Since 1945 the US Navy has run freedom of navigation operations as a global public good, but this time it has stepped back. For India this is huge, because the Suez route is the short way to Europe compared with going around the Cape of Good Hope.
The open trading system rested on a security guarantee nobody noticed. When the guarantee lapses, India's natural route to its natural market closes.

head: The 85-year-old and the 12-year-old
dek: Resilience and autarky are opposite answers to a risky world. Ajay argues India's urge to hide behind high fences comes from insecurity.
more: At a conference Ajay and Ila Patnaik organised at NIPFP, a Chilean economist explained capital account convertibility with an analogy. You can be an 85-year-old who never leaves the house or eats out because you're scared of falling sick. Or you can be a 12-year-old who flies out the door, tumbles on the ground, plays with frogs and eats panipuri on the roadside. The child falls sick all the time but bounces back.

Resilience and autarky are opposite answers to a risky world. Ajay argues India's urge to hide behind high fences comes from insecurity. India has already rolled with the 1991 crisis, nuclear tests, Y2K, the Asian crisis and 2008.

head: Arguing with Nitin Pai about kowtowing to Trump
dek: The test for a leader is national welfare, not national ego. Pride is a cost paid by citizens, and Ajay's 'prosperity over pride' argument makes the same point.
more: Amit had lunch with Nitin Pai, Narendra Shenoy and Sudhir Sarnobat just after the first 25% tariff. The inside dope was that Trump would not have imposed it if Modi had simply agreed that Trump helped the India-Pakistan peace process. Pakistan had played along and nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. Amit argued Modi should kowtow if needed, since the tariff hurts both Indians and Americans. Nitin was completely against it. They remain friends.
The test for a leader is national welfare, not national ego. Pride is a cost paid by citizens, and Ajay's 'prosperity over pride' argument makes the same point.
printed: A bow too far for Nitin Pai

head: Reforms by stealth: 'You come back and sell them for me'
dek: Reform needs public salesmanship, and insiders often can't do it. That makes it the job of citizens and outside voices.
more: In the early 1990s, Gurcharan Das wrote to Manmohan Singh asking why he was doing reforms by stealth. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh were selling the reforms as a better socialism that Nehru and Indira would have liked, when they were really a repudiation of socialism. Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher, by contrast, sold their reforms openly. Manmohan replied that Gurcharan should come back and sell them for him. Separately, Naushad Forbes told Amit that after a meeting with industrialists, Manmohan took him aside and asked him to say everything from the meeting in public.
Reform needs public salesmanship, and insiders often can't do it. That makes it the job of citizens and outside voices. Amit uses this to urge listeners who agree to be vocal.

head: Moving factories under fire
dek: Nimbleness can be a killer app. The assumption that a factory must stay where it was built is a mental block, not a law of nature.
more: In June 1941, Germany invaded the USSR and pushed about a thousand kilometres into its industrial heartland. Under fire, the Soviets dismantled entire factories, moved them to Central Asia, reassembled them and restarted war production. Ajay suggests Indian firms facing a 50% US tariff think the same way: dismantle the factory and take it to a zero-tariff country like Sri Lanka.
Nimbleness can be a killer app. The assumption that a factory must stay where it was built is a mental block, not a law of nature.

head: How Vicks VapoRub became Ayurvedic, and every employee got a house
dek: Indian firms can be remarkably nimble under bad policy. Amit doesn't celebrate jugaad, since firms shouldn't have to do it, but it gives him hope that Indian business can adapt to the tariff shock.
more: Gurcharan Das told Amit this story from his time as CEO of Richardson Vicks, around the early 1980s by Amit's reckoning. A new government levy on certain medicines threatened to make Vicks VapoRub unprofitable. In a crisis meeting, someone quietly pointed out that the formulation was compatible with Ayurveda, and Ayurveda wasn't taxed. Within 24 hours they filed it as an Ayurvedic rub. The bureaucrat saw what they were doing but it was within the letter of the law, so it passed. As an Ayurvedic product it could be sold at about four million outlets, including paanwalas, instead of about 50,000 medical shops. Gurcharan gave stock options to everyone down to the lowest peon, and the company registrar suspected a scam. The company lent money to staff who couldn't afford Rs 20 a share. Amit recalls the share price rising about forty times within a year, and every employee made a down payment on a house.
Indian firms can be remarkably nimble under bad policy. Amit doesn't celebrate jugaad, since firms shouldn't have to do it, but it gives him hope that Indian business can adapt to the tariff shock.
printed: The rub that dodged a tax

head: Recent columns on India's response to the tariffs
by: Sajjid Z Chinoy, Soham Das, TN Ninan, M Govinda Rao, Rajeswari Sengupta, Mihir S Sharma
dek: He respects and values their work as part of 'one communal sense of knowledge' India is building on this question.
more: He respects and values their work as part of 'one communal sense of knowledge' India is building on this question.
Ajay lists people who have written on the subject in recent weeks, including 'my ex-boss' M Govinda Rao and 'our good friend' Rajeswari Sengupta.

head: Is Globalization Doomed? (EIE Ep 96)
dek: It explains how the open order broke down, mainly because China, and to a lesser extent India, didn't play by the rules.
more: It explains how the open order broke down, mainly because China, and to a lesser extent India, didn't play by the rules.
The 'unhappy' companion episode, which took Robert Lighthizer's arguments seriously.

head: How to Do Development (EIE Ep 57)
dek: It shows that human welfare indicators track per capita GDP far more than redistribution, so talking about GDP means talking about the poor.
more: It shows that human welfare indicators track per capita GDP far more than redistribution, so talking about GDP means talking about the poor.
Cited for Lant Pritchett's insight on growth and welfare.

head: Economics in One Lesson (EIE Ep 109)
dek: It is a reminder that downstream adjustments don't make tariffs good. You have to count what would have happened without them.
more: It is a reminder that downstream adjustments don't make tariffs good. You have to count what would have happened without them.
Amit's episode on Henry Hazlitt, cited for the broken window fallacy.

head: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (EIE Ep 8)
dek: It is 'the essence of how we should think about' making cities work as talent clusters.
more: It is 'the essence of how we should think about' making cities work as talent clusters.
Cited when arguing that cities are central to the response.

head: The Beauty of Finance (EIE Ep 21)
dek: Indian firms reorienting to new markets will need a financial system that can fund complex, risky projects.
more: Indian firms reorienting to new markets will need a financial system that can fund complex, risky projects.
Cited for finance as the brain and resource allocator of the economy.

head: Great leaders choose prosperity over pride
dek: The core stance for negotiating with Trump: national interest over ego.
more: The core stance for negotiating with Trump: national interest over ego.
His recent Business Standard column, cited on how to deal with the US and China.

head: The Long Road to Change (EIE Ep 36)
dek: Change comes from shaping ideas and the climate of opinion upstream of policymakers, not from whispering to a joint secretary.
more: Change comes from shaping ideas and the climate of opinion upstream of policymakers, not from whispering to a joint secretary.
Ajay's framework for how the episode's ideas could become policy.

head: Globalisation built India's best twenty years
dek: Ajay calls 1991-2011 the biggest success in 5,000 years of Indian history: GDP grew about fourfold and hundreds of millions escaped poverty.
more: Ajay calls 1991-2011 the biggest success in 5,000 years of Indian history: GDP grew about fourfold and hundreds of millions escaped poverty. The gains came through four channels once the Indian state got out of the way. Technology came in as machine tools, CPUs, operating systems, fibre and the internet. Knowledge came from Indians who studied and, above all, worked abroad and returned, and from foreign firms training Indians at home. Finance came from foreign capital, which backed the new economy before Indian investors did, and 'it was the foreigners that made Infosys great.' Markets came from abroad too: over 90% of Infosys revenue is foreign. Ajay's 'West' means liberal democracies, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan included.

head: There's nothing sovereign about technology
dek: India's tech boom ran on global CPUs, Unix, TCP/IP and foreign database engines.
more: India's tech boom ran on global CPUs, Unix, TCP/IP and foreign database engines. Nobody demanded an Indian CPU or a subsidised chip fab. Ajay applies the same logic to today's calls for an Indian LLM. If Indian geniuses can help build a CPU, great; if not, buy other people's. The goal is progress, not owning the technology stack.

head: Poverty is the default; growth is how people escape it
dek: Amit points out that for most of history almost everyone was poor. Wealth arrived through technology and markets.
more: Amit points out that for most of history almost everyone was poor. Wealth arrived through technology and markets. Citing Lant Pritchett via EIE 57, every human welfare indicator has a 99% correlation with per capita GDP, and less than 1% with welfarism and redistribution. So GDP talk is a conversation about poor people's lives, and getting policy right is a moral imperative.

head: The end of the West's indulgence
dek: India was never a good-faith player in the global system. Its officials spoiled trade talks, its rhetoric stayed anti-colonial, and unfairness to foreign firms was normal.
more: India was never a good-faith player in the global system. Its officials spoiled trade talks, its rhetoric stayed anti-colonial, and unfairness to foreign firms was normal. Advanced democracies tolerated this, pushing deals through anyway and assuming India would grow up, since economic nationalism mostly hurts Indians. Right-wing populism across the West has ended that patience. China caused about 90% of the problem and India about 10%, but the rules have changed for both. Indian misbehaviour now feeds the politicians most hostile to India.

head: The gravity model of trade
dek: Trade between two countries works like Newton's gravity: it rises with the product of their GDPs and falls with the square of the distance between them.
more: Trade between two countries works like Newton's gravity: it rises with the product of their GDPs and falls with the square of the distance between them. The US is huge but fairly inward-looking; India trades more as a share of GDP. It is also the farthest place India can ship goods, while China and Japan are a short hop across the Pacific. India's natural goods market is Europe via the Red Sea and Suez. Services escape gravity: photons on fibre are weightless, so California isn't far. That is why Indian services exports to the US thrive while goods struggle.

head: Tariffs hurt the country that imposes them, and India needs a healthy US
dek: Amit is an anti-tariff absolutist: tariffs always hurt your own people.
more: Amit is an anti-tariff absolutist: tariffs always hurt your own people. Ajay says the US damage is masked by a once-in-a-century AI capex boom, but it shows once you split out the Magnificent 7. He lists the harms: rising prices and unanchored inflation; uncertainty that chokes investment, making the US 'an emerging market'; cost shocks for US exporters who rely on imported inputs; and a fraying dollar safe haven. India should worry more about a faltering US than about the $65 billion hit. It relies on American finance, services demand, technology, GCCs and a Navy that keeps sea lanes open.
printed: A sound US is India’s business

head: Shocks are absorbed by many small adjustments, but the window is still broken
dek: Of about $460bn in Indian goods exports, about $85bn go to the US and about $65bn face the 50% tariff.
more: Of about $460bn in Indian goods exports, about $85bn go to the US and about $65bn face the 50% tariff. That is roughly 15%, while $370bn of services exports are where the dynamism is. A $10 shirt becoming $15 looks like game over, yet the price system responds in several ways. Trade gets redirected: Vietnam takes the US order, and India picks up the German buyer Vietnam used to serve. The rupee depreciates. Firms absorb some margin, and workers move to other employers. Amit adds Hazlitt's broken window caveat: adjustment doesn't make the tariff harmless, because what is unseen is what would have happened without it.

head: Bet on the 66%: rules-based democracies
dek: The US is only about a third of advanced-economy trade. The rest stays open: Western Europe, Canada, Chile, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Israel.
more: The US is only about a third of advanced-economy trade. The rest stays open: Western Europe, Canada, Chile, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Israel. These countries are rich and democratic, so treaties signed with them hold for five, ten or twenty years. Firms need that kind of horizon to invest. Strongmen rule by discretion and change their minds overnight, so businesses just wait and watch.

head: Deep trade agreements and a new globalisation
dek: The WTO failed because countries could cheat.
more: The WTO failed because countries could cheat. A deep trade agreement (DTA) commits members to fair play across regulation, intellectual property, capital flows and foreign firms' right to operate, ruling out economic nationalism. The EU is the classic example. The TPP is another: when Trump walked out, the remaining 11 countries went ahead. Ajay wants India to help found a new coalition of 10-20 like-minded countries. He also wants India to start upgrading the UK FTA into a DTA now, since talks take two or three years, and to bring new imagination to deals with the EU and Japan. That means dropping third-worldism and the '500 red lines'.

head: No red lines, no holy cows
dek: In diplomacy, everything is negotiable at some price. Declaring agriculture off the table, as with the dairy barriers Trump targeted, throws away bargaining power.
more: In diplomacy, everything is negotiable at some price. Declaring agriculture off the table, as with the dairy barriers Trump targeted, throws away bargaining power. The Europeans don't get emotional about Trump; they play hardball and do deals. That makes fixing Indian agriculture at home a precondition for leverage abroad.

head: What deep integration could look like
dek: Ajay offers four concrete possibilities. German carmakers could build components, R&D and software in India.
more: Ajay offers four concrete possibilities. German carmakers could build components, R&D and software in India. Japanese electronics firms, strong in design but now wary of China after it turned nationalist on them, could pair with Indian factories and engineers. South Korean shipbuilders under Chinese price pressure could combine their design skills with Indian production. In defence, Ukraine, Poland and South Korea are building frontier weapons at frugal prices, unlike 'gold plated' F-35s. India's southern cone could host R&D and factories far from Russian, North Korean and Chinese missiles. All of this requires India to drop oddities like curbs on royalties, capital movement and work visas. Along the way Ajay stresses that manufacturing jobs are high-skill, not unskilled assembly-line work.

head: Don't tax foreigners: a clean GST plus a carbon tax
dek: Non-residents are not India's tax base, so exporters should get back every indirect tax paid along the supply chain (zero-rated GST).
more: Non-residents are not India's tax base, so exporters should get back every indirect tax paid along the supply chain (zero-rated GST). India's GST has 'birth defects': missing input tax credits and unrefunded cesses and electricity duties. Ajay sees the world converging on two taxes, a GST and an auditable carbon tax, that 'handshake' at the border. Under the EU's CBAM, carbon tax paid in India would be credited at Europe's border. He, Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi have argued for this design since the GST's early days.

head: Domestic reform is trade policy
dek: Every domestic fix ties back to winning the 66%. India's regulators have become a new central planning system and need fixing at the organisational source.
more: Every domestic fix ties back to winning the 66%. India's regulators have become a new central planning system and need fixing at the organisational source. Courts must work so a manufacturer facing strict penalties from a foreign buyer can pass them on to Indian vendors, and so foreigners can rely on contracts rather than caste and kin. Cities must work, because a 20,000-worker factory running three shifts needs about 60,000 households nearby. Finance must be able to fund $5-10bn complex projects, with players like Goldman Sachs in Bombay. Foreign firms need fair treatment through OECD-style tax treaties and bilateral investment treaties.

head: Resilience, not autarky
dek: Autarky means hiding in a bunker; resilience means taking shocks and bouncing back.
more: Autarky means hiding in a bunker; resilience means taking shocks and bouncing back. Ajay lists what resilience requires. First, fiscal prudence, since the debt-to-GDP ratio and primary deficit are too high. Second, an RBI devoted only to inflation targeting. Third, a genuinely floating rupee that falls instantly on bad news, which helps exporters. Fourth, deep, liquid markets and banks that don't blow up. The correct combination, he says, is an open capital account, inflation targeting and a floating exchange rate.

head: Policy is an incomplete contract
dek: A tariff cut from 100 to 10 can always be reversed, so an announcement alone doesn't stabilise private decisions.
more: A tariff cut from 100 to 10 can always be reversed, so an announcement alone doesn't stabilise private decisions. Credibility comes from a visible team that understands the reform, an explanation of its full logic, and honesty about problems rather than propaganda. When the next crisis hits, the government needs that store of trust, so that people turn to Indian policymakers rather than the New York Times for the truth. A full rationale beats a fatwa handed down like the Ten Commandments.

head: Prosperity over pride
dek: India can't do autarky with the US or China. With Trump, it needs deep expertise on MAGA and right-wing populism, and if flattery works, it should flatter.
more: India can't do autarky with the US or China. With Trump, it needs deep expertise on MAGA and right-wing populism, and if flattery works, it should flatter. With China, 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai' won't do after Doklam, Galwan and Chinese overproduction. Instead India needs a brains trust that can get inside Xi Jinping's mind and work out the carrots and sticks. Twitter one-liners, autarky and 'strategic autonomy' serve moral purity, not the national interest.

head: Trade is never zero-sum
dek: Amit argues that trade games are either positive-sum or negative-sum. Treating them as zero-sum, for example by answering a 50% tariff with 60%, turns them into lose-lose.
more: Amit argues that trade games are either positive-sum or negative-sum. Treating them as zero-sum, for example by answering a 50% tariff with 60%, turns them into lose-lose. This reflex is the first of his three pessimisms. The second is that leaders find narrative battles, like the TikTok ban, easier than hard global work. The third is that the opposition opposes everything, and the small, mediocre elite clings to status-quo thinking.

head: Theory of change: work upstream of the policymaker
dek: Ajay argues that a joint secretary already has her own worldview and can hire KPMG or Bain to implement things, so advice offered downstream adds little.
more: Ajay argues that a joint secretary already has her own worldview and can hire KPMG or Bain to implement things, so advice offered downstream adds little. What shifts policy is new knowledge and a changed climate of opinion. The 1991 reforms came from thinkers who had spent years writing about what was wrong. Amit adds Andrew Breitbart's line that politics is downstream of culture, and says both mass culture and elite culture must change.

head: A playbook for Indian firms
dek: Ajay's advice to firms has four parts.
more: Ajay's advice to firms has four parts. First, treat the US like an emerging market: be opportunistic and don't make long-term plans around it, since tariffs could swing from 50 to 300 and a Senate bill proposes 500% secondary oil tariffs. Second, tariff-hit American exporters may lose ground to Indian firms in markets like Belgium. Third, shift focus to the rest of the OECD. Fourth, be nimble, even to the point of moving a factory.

head: After Ajay explains the gravity model, Amit concludes
more: After Ajay explains the gravity model, Amit concludes that 'the closer Ajay and I get to each other, the more likely we are to hug.' Ajay asks, 'And will there be a hugging black hole?' Amit backs off: 'I'm not going to be getting into very dangerous things.'

head: Ajay offers a free T-shirt to whoever binge-watches the most episodes in one weekend. Amit adds that the winner gets
more: Ajay offers a free T-shirt to whoever binge-watches the most episodes in one weekend. Amit adds that the winner gets 'that shirt which you're wearing now, unwashed.'

head: Amit's detour into nihilism
more: Amit's detour into nihilism: 'No man is an island. Even though it must be said that every man is alone and will die realizing that life was meaningless and any sense of purpose was a mere illusion... Forget about searching for the truth, settle for a good illusion.'

head: When Amit turns pessimistic, Ajay
more: When Amit turns pessimistic, Ajay says, 'You embody the mood of Bengali movies, but we should keep making more movies.' Amit fires back that 'you Gujaratis have a lot of responsibility for the state of the nation today, and I'm of course referring to Gandhi and Patel.'

head: Amit's pun on Ajay's call for nimbleness
more: Amit's pun on Ajay's call for nimbleness: 'if a firm should be nimble, why call it firm?'

head: After recounting his kowtowing argument with Nitin Pai, Amit cuts to a video of Nitin's reaction: he
more: After recounting his kowtowing argument with Nitin Pai, Amit cuts to a video of Nitin's reaction: he 'remains a friend. We survived that grievous incident.'

head: Ajay imagining the West's patience with India
more: Ajay imagining the West's patience with India: 'As knowledge comes about in India, shows like EIE will come to India and the Indian side will gradually change.'

head: Amit's translation of the…
more: Amit's translation of the 'tapestry' of interlinked episodes: 'tapestry is really a fancy way of telling the gentle readers, binge watch, binge watch us.'

head: Ajay corrects himself after a YouTube commenter accused him of always saying electrons: on fibre optic cables
more: Ajay corrects himself after a YouTube commenter accused him of always saying electrons: on fibre optic cables 'it is photons that fly,' and they are weightless.
'We're not in Kansas anymore': Ajay's line for how much the world has changed, and why India must rethink from scratch.

head: The Suez Canal
more: The Suez Canal and 'the glory of 1869': Ajay traces India's natural route to Europe via Gibraltar, the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, versus the long way around the Cape of Good Hope.

head: The F-35: Ajay calls the American jet
more: The F-35: Ajay calls the American jet 'completely gold plated' to explain why frugal Ukrainian, Polish and South Korean defence partners suit India better.

head: The Ten Commandments: Ajay says that coming
more: The Ten Commandments: Ajay says that coming 'down from the mountain with the ten commandments' is worse policy communication than showing the full logic.

head: Andrew Breitbart's
more: Andrew Breitbart's 'politics is downstream of culture', quoted by Amit to explain why think tanks targeting bureaucrats miss the point.
'Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will': the 'great line' Amit says he embodies, pessimistic about the world but still working to improve it.

head: Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher
more: Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher: the leaders Gurcharan Das held up as reformers who sold their ideas openly, unlike India's selling of reform as a better socialism that 'Nehru would have liked'.

head: The Book That Sat on the Shelf for Eight Years
dek: An unread book on your shelf is not a failure. Its physical presence shapes the day you finally pull it out.
more: Seeing Like a State came out in 1998 and Ajay missed it, even though Brad DeLong had written about it on a blog in his RSS feed. Around 2004, after the UPA government came to power, Lant Pritchett moved to Delhi and gave him the book, along with Chester Barnard's The Functions of the Executive, saying it would change the way he thought about the world. It then sat on his shelf until 2012. When he finally read it, every page felt like an attack on what he believed. He cancelled all his meetings and spent a couple of days reading it straight through, arguing back the whole time.
An unread book on your shelf is not a failure. Its physical presence shapes the day you finally pull it out. The books that change you are often the ones you fight with page after page.
printed: The book that waited eight years

head: Newton's 'Shoulders of Giants' Was a Put-Down
dek: Quotes we treat as gracious can come from petty personal feuds. Being a great thinker and being a nice person are separate things.
more: When Amit brings up 'standing on the shoulders of giants', Ajay explains that the line is Newton's, and that Newton was a truly mean and unpleasant man. He had a lifelong rivalry with Robert Hooke, who was a hunchback and who had implied that Newton's ideas were built on his own work. The famous line was Newton's put-down of Hooke.
Quotes we treat as gracious can come from petty personal feuds. Being a great thinker and being a nice person are separate things.

head: The Long Shadow of Soviet Collectivisation
dek: One top-down scheme played out over sixty years. It planted a nation's lasting hostility and left the empire unable to feed itself, which in the end helped bring it down.
more: Stalin could be pragmatic, but on collectivisation he was a 'bloody minded ideologue'. Rich farmers resisted the state taking their land, and he crushed them brutally. In Ukraine he blocked food from coming in and seized the grain, and somewhere between 4% and 10% of the population died in a man-made famine. In 1991, 90% of Ukraine voted to leave. Decades later, by the mid-80s, the Soviet economy survived by exporting crude oil and importing grain. When crude prices fell and grain prices rose, the USSR collapsed.
One top-down scheme played out over sixty years. It planted a nation's lasting hostility and left the empire unable to feed itself, which in the end helped bring it down.

head: Aadhaar Was Built Before the Privacy Law
dek: Once a state legibility system is built, it is very hard to undo, and the promised safeguards may never arrive.
more: Ajay took part in the Aadhaar debates. The first Aadhaar number was issued in 2009, on the understanding that Manmohan Singh's government would bring in a privacy law alongside it. Ajay read Scott only in 2012. Today he says the order was wrong: the privacy law should have come first, strong enough to match the dangers of a single number that can be traced to every person in the country.
Once a state legibility system is built, it is very hard to undo, and the promised safeguards may never arrive. Insist on the checks and balances before the system is built, not after.

head: Mao's War on Sparrows
dek: Ecosystems and societies are webs. Pull one thread on the strength of a simple top-down theory and the effects can be catastrophic.
more: Amit recalls an earlier episode about Mao's high modernism. Mao ordered sparrows to be killed because they were eating crops. But sparrows ate locusts. With the sparrows gone, the locusts multiplied, destroyed the crops, and millions starved.
Ecosystems and societies are webs. Pull one thread on the strength of a simple top-down theory and the effects can be catastrophic.

head: Born in Le Corbusier's Chandigarh
dek: The benefits of a planned city are easy to see. Its costs, the organic city life that never got to grow, are the unseen.
more: Amit admits he was born in Chandigarh, a city designed by Le Corbusier, whom he calls one of the villains of high modernism. On a recent visit with friends, he conceded that the roads are wide, the air is clean and it looks nice. But he knew there was a cost underneath. Ajay added that a great modern living city is not Chandigarh.
The benefits of a planned city are easy to see. Its costs, the organic city life that never got to grow, are the unseen.

head: The Jane Jacobs Chapter Cut from The Power Broker
dek: The two opposing philosophies, Robert Moses's high modernism and Jane Jacobs's respect for organic order, nearly appeared in the same book.
more: Robert Caro's The Power Broker was originally more than a million words. The publisher, looking at how thin the paper would have to be, said the book would fall apart beyond a certain length. So a section of about 100,000 words on Jane Jacobs was removed.
The two opposing philosophies, Robert Moses's high modernism and Jane Jacobs's respect for organic order, nearly appeared in the same book. A physical limit of bookbinding shaped the canon.

head: Tughlaq Was Really About Nehru
dek: Art can criticise the present by dressing it up as history. And admiring Nehru does not prevent you from seeing his follies.
more: At 18 or 19, Amit and a college friend tried to stage Girish Karnad's Tughlaq as a two-man play. The project fell apart through Amit's procrastination. He explains that Tughlaq was a high modernist who shifted his capital and tampered with the currency, and all of it failed. Karnad wrote the play in the mid-sixties, when disillusionment with Nehruvian socialism was setting in, so the play was also about Nehru.
Art can criticise the present by dressing it up as history. And admiring Nehru does not prevent you from seeing his follies.

head: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
dek: It covers political philosophy, sociology, anthropology, urban policy and development studies, and it gives you a toolkit (state legibility, high modernism, metis) that you can apply almost anywhere.
more: It covers political philosophy, sociology, anthropology, urban policy and development studies, and it gives you a toolkit (state legibility, high modernism, metis) that you can apply almost anywhere. Ajay says even every YouTube creator should read it.
The book the whole episode is about. Amit opens by calling it a remarkable book that profoundly changed Ajay's life.

head: The Velvet Underground
dek: The band is a model for James C Scott: little known to the public, but hugely influential on the people who go on to influence everyone else.
more: The band is a model for James C Scott: little known to the public, but hugely influential on the people who go on to influence everyone else.
Amit's opening analogy. It was said that only thirty people bought their albums and all thirty became musicians.

head: The Long Road to Change (Ep 36 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It sets out the theory of change behind the show: the world improves through a long relay of ideas, and you have to see everyone who passed the baton, not just the final runner.
more: It sets out the theory of change behind the show: the world improves through a long relay of ideas, and you have to see everyone who passed the baton, not just the final runner.
Ajay raises it while explaining why a less famous thinker like Scott matters.

head: Forests, Trees, and Intellectual Roots (review of Seeing Like a State)
dek: An economist's engagement with the book, and the place where Ajay could have discovered it first.
more: An economist's engagement with the book, and the place where Ajay could have discovered it first.
Ajay mentions that DeLong wrote about the book on his blog, which was in Ajay's RSS feed, though he missed it at the time. The show notes link the review.

head: The Functions of the Executive
dek: Pritchett offered the two together as books that matter. It appears in the episode as part of how Ajay came to Scott.
more: Pritchett offered the two together as books that matter. It appears in the episode as part of how Ajay came to Scott.
The other book Lant Pritchett gave Ajay in 2004, along with Seeing Like a State.

head: Freedom House country scores
dek: It ranks democracies from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bottom.
more: It ranks democracies from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bottom. Ajay argues that the right level of state legibility should depend on where a country sits on this list.
Ajay's starting point for judging which state legibility mechanisms a country can safely adopt.

head: The Power Broker
dek: A masterpiece that is at once a biography of Robert Moses, a biography of New York, and a study of how power is used, misused and corrupts.
more: A masterpiece that is at once a biography of Robert Moses, a biography of New York, and a study of how power is used, misused and corrupts. Moses designed the city's bridges and parks from the top down.
Amit's first recommendation, prompted by the discussion of high modernism. He has recommended it on the show before.

head: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
dek: Jacobs represents an organic appreciation of spontaneous order and metis, against Moses's high modernism.
more: Jacobs represents an organic appreciation of spontaneous order and metis, against Moses's high modernism. Amit says everyone has to read her.
Paired with The Power Broker as the opposite philosophy. Ajay adds that Scott draws heavily on Jacobs in Seeing Like a State.

head: Order Without Design
dek: It brings solid economic thinking and many disciplines to urban planning, exposes the follies of high modernism, and respects the local knowledge behind why streets and cities work as they do.
more: It brings solid economic thinking and many disciplines to urban planning, exposes the follies of high modernism, and respects the local knowledge behind why streets and cities work as they do. Ajay notes that Bertaud is not an economist.
A book both hosts love, recommended after the Chandigarh discussion.

head: The Hidden Life of Trees
dek: It shows that a natural forest is a communicating system, with roots talking to each other and trees adjusting when one is harmed.
more: It shows that a natural forest is a communicating system, with roots talking to each other and trees adjusting when one is harmed. It made Amit see that planting forty trees together is not an ecosystem, and it challenges the human belief that we have figured everything out.
Prompted by Ajay's account of Prussian scientific forestry and metis.

head: Ideas Move the World Through a Relay
dek: Change does not need a mass-market hit at every step. Ideas emerge, reshape the culture, and eventually change policy.
more: Change does not need a mass-market hit at every step. Ideas emerge, reshape the culture, and eventually change policy. Thinkers like Scott hand the baton to the people who reach the finish line, so judge progress by the whole relay.

head: Why 1998 Was the Right Moment for This Book
dek: After the Berlin Wall fell and the USSR collapsed, many people in democracies felt the ideological battle was over.
more: After the Berlin Wall fell and the USSR collapsed, many people in democracies felt the ideological battle was over. In the middle of the computer and internet revolution, they turned to technocratic social engineering and lost touch with the defence of freedom associated with Friedman and Hayek. Scott's book was a warning against that turn.

head: Brilliant People, Monumental Failures
dek: The book's puzzle is why some of the smartest people led disastrous grand schemes.
more: The book's puzzle is why some of the smartest people led disastrous grand schemes. P C Mahalanobis was a great statistician and was wrong about society. Nehru, whom Ajay loves, was a great artist whose art (his policy) was bad in many ways. Raw intelligence does not protect you from the high-modernist trap.

head: State Legibility: A Bureaucracy Cannot See Like a Human
dek: For a person, seeing is effortless. For a state, seeing means officials recording facts in files that then trigger policy.
more: For a person, seeing is effortless. For a state, seeing means officials recording facts in files that then trigger policy. Every step suffers from discretion, principal-agent problems, bribes and opacity. People also hide from the state, because history shows states using information for taxation, conscription and worse. Assuming that seeing is free is a technocrat's illusion, because in a lab the instruments don't lie.

head: State Legibility Schemes Have Unintended Consequences
dek: Frustrated by complexity, states force people to become easier to read: fixed surnames, ID numbers, single land ownership.
more: Frustrated by complexity, states force people to become easier to read: fixed surnames, ID numbers, single land ownership. This flattening destroys arrangements that evolved for good reasons. In one example, a farmer owns the land, someone else has rights to the Kharif crop, and a third person grazes cattle on it when it lies fallow. Ajay calls this a Burkean point. Clarity helps the state collect taxes, but it does not necessarily serve the people.

head: Legibility Should Flow From the State to the Citizen
dek: Amit turns the question around. The state exists to serve us, not to rule us, so the government should be fully transparent and accountable to citizens.
more: Amit turns the question around. The state exists to serve us, not to rule us, so the government should be fully transparent and accountable to citizens. Normalising citizens being legible to the state turns the proper order upside down.

head: Data Deletion as a Constitutional Default
dek: When you pay a toll, the state learns where your car was. Ajay proposes that such data be deleted within seconds by default.
more: When you pay a toll, the state learns where your car was. Ajay proposes that such data be deleted within seconds by default. If the state wants to keep data, it should have to persuade the people, just as every act of state coercion needs the people's authorisation.

head: High Modernism Is Not Modernity
dek: Modernity is good: secular, individualist, free of superstition and tribe.
more: Modernity is good: secular, individualist, free of superstition and tribe. High modernism is the belief that scientists and engineers know best how society should work and should reshape it through centralised schemes backed by state coercion ('one India, one X'). It fails because planners lack local information, and because people respond to incentives by quietly undermining the scheme. Ajay warns that India is in a second wave of it, driven by tech success and weak political philosophy.

head: Metis: Local, Tacit, Experiential Knowledge
dek: Scott took this Greek word into English. Unlike universal knowledge such as special relativity, most knowledge about society is metis.
more: Scott took this Greek word into English. Unlike universal knowledge such as special relativity, most knowledge about society is metis. It is gained by doing, it cannot be written down and handed over, and it changes if you move a hundred kilometres. Respecting it, with humility, is the opposite of imposing a manual from above.

head: Scientific Forestry: Legibility That Kills the Forest
dek: Scott's central example, which Ajay says applies equally to British forestry in India.
more: Scott's central example, which Ajay says applies equally to British forestry in India. The forest is reduced to a single goal, timber volume: plant the best-yielding species in neat rows and run experiments over decades (as at FRI Dehradun) on how far apart to space the trees. The result is countable and legible, but it is a fragile monoculture. It degrades the soil and can be wiped out by a single insect or fungus. It ignores the web of fungi, insects and plants that make a real forest resilient. Ajay calls this ignorance passed off as science.
printed: The forest as a timber farm

head: Scott's Four Ingredients for Disaster
dek: Things go badly wrong when four elements combine: (1) a high-modernist philosophy, (2) state power used to make society legible, (3) an authoritarian state, and (4) a civil society too weak to push back.
more: Things go badly wrong when four elements combine: (1) a high-modernist philosophy, (2) state power used to make society legible, (3) an authoritarian state, and (4) a civil society too weak to push back. Practical advice: in a country with an authoritarian government and weak civil society, be wary of encouraging high-modernist tendencies or improving state legibility.

head: Cities Can't Be Centrally Planned
dek: Grand new capitals, from the move to Daulatabad to Brasília, fail because people don't respond to central plans.
more: Grand new capitals, from the move to Daulatabad to Brasília, fail because people don't respond to central plans. Ajay cites Bimal Patel's rule: reserve about 40% of land for streets and parks and let people decide the rest, with no master plan and no micromanaging of private land. Bandra Kurla Complex, built as a financial centre, has towers but no room for coffee shops and pavement life.

head: The Green Revolution as High Modernism
dek: India remembers the Green Revolution as the escape from dependence on PL 480 food aid.
more: India remembers the Green Revolution as the escape from dependence on PL 480 food aid. Seen through Scott, it was a top-down package of MSP, fertiliser subsidies, free power for pumps and a few rice and wheat cultivars. Over the longer term it has worked badly: pesticides in groundwater, cancer clusters, a groundwater crisis, struggling farmers in Punjab and Haryana (the Netherlands, about Haryana's size, exports $140 billion of food), and a national diet heavy in starch.

head: Humility, Not Abolition of the State
dek: Scott is not arguing for the state to wither away. We need a monopoly of violence, law and order, and monetary policy.
more: Scott is not arguing for the state to wither away. We need a monopoly of violence, law and order, and monetary policy. But the state wants arbitrary power the way firms want profit, so it must be met with checks and balances. Make small, reversible moves. Scott even has a footnote saying this is one reason he opposes the death penalty.

head: Match State Legibility to a Country's Level of Freedom
dek: Whether a legibility mechanism is safe depends on a country's checks and balances.
more: Whether a legibility mechanism is safe depends on a country's checks and balances. Electronic payments are reasonably safe in Norway but a prison in North Korea. Medical records held by the state are fine in the UK but unwise in India. Ajay points out that biometric IDs exist mainly in poorer, relatively authoritarian countries. He proposes a research programme to work out which mechanisms are safe at which Freedom House rank.

head: Decentralisation and Subsidiarity for India
dek: India covers 3.3 million square km and is made up of a thousand Singapore-sized locales, so one ruler instructing all of it invites trouble.
more: India covers 3.3 million square km and is made up of a thousand Singapore-sized locales, so one ruler instructing all of it invites trouble. Every function should sit at the lowest level of government able to perform it. Bombay's transport needs Bombay expertise, and having built Delhi's metro does not qualify you to dictate to every other city. One currency and one military make sense; most other things should be local and competing. Ajay holds up the EU as a model: goods, people and capital move freely while countries make their own laws.

head: Scott's Toolkit as an Engine for Thinking
dek: State legibility, high modernism and metis apply well beyond governments.
more: State legibility, high modernism and metis apply well beyond governments. Ajay uses them on firms, for example a giant national bank running the whole country through one manual. He challenges listeners to link any EIE episode to Seeing Like a State.

head: Amit's highest praise for Scott: the biggest compliment he can give Lou Reed is that the Velvet Underground is…
more: Amit's highest praise for Scott: the biggest compliment he can give Lou Reed is that the Velvet Underground is 'the James C. Scott of music'.

head: Ajay's EIE T-shirt line: volume one, number one is…
more: Ajay's EIE T-shirt line: volume one, number one is 'Make trade not war', and number two is 'State legibility schemes have unintended consequences'. Amit replies that you could only buy it in triple XL, 'because how will the words fit?'
Amit: 'When I first heard the phrase high modernism, I thought it basically means that you wear shirt pant and you do drugs.'

head: Amit on how confusingly similar
more: Amit on how confusingly similar 'modernity' and 'high modernism' sound: 'It's like popularity and populism... They're almost opposite things.'

head: Ajay on the misuse of…
more: Ajay on the misuse of 'scientific' in policy: 'So I get offended when anybody says scientific. I'm like dude don't pull the science card on me.'

head: Ajay on Nehru
more: Ajay on Nehru: 'I'm very comfortable separating art and artist. So this is a great artist and his art was like pretty bad in some ways.'

head: Amit carries Ajay's challenge over to the cycling episode: what is a formation of cyclists in slipstream
more: Amit carries Ajay's challenge over to the cycling episode: what is a formation of cyclists in slipstream 'if not high modernism'? But near a sprint finish there is a 'washing machine effect, which is much like spontaneous order'.

head: Amit's one acceptable
more: Amit's one acceptable 'one India, one X': 'One India, one YouTube show is an idea I can get behind', since the show is dubbed into other languages. Ajay then complains that when Susan wanted Malayalam dubbing for her stepmother, YouTube offered Hindi but not Malayalam: 'If you keep going like this, you'll have serious problems.'

head: On his failed college staging of Tughlaq
more: On his failed college staging of Tughlaq: 'inevitably one of us was Bengali and hint it wasn't him. And therefore the project went to hell and I procrastinated.'

head: Amit reminds Ajay he once promised seven recommendations and then gave none.
more: Amit reminds Ajay he once promised seven recommendations and then gave none. Ajay: 'In the next episode I will give you nine recommendations.'

head: Amit calls James C Scott
more: Amit calls James C Scott 'the Velvet Underground of ideas', after the line that only thirty people bought the band's albums and all thirty became musicians. He adds that the Velvet Revolution was named after the band.

head: A Unix fortune Ajay quotes as a counterpoint to Newton
more: A Unix fortune Ajay quotes as a counterpoint to Newton: 'in computer science we stand on each other's shoulders.'

head: Ajay on scientific forestry
more: Ajay on scientific forestry: 'explaining a joke is like dissecting a frog. You can understand it, but it kills the frog.' Imposing legibility killed the forest in the same way.

head: The Domesday Book, which Ajay invokes as the state's basic legibility logic
more: The Domesday Book, which Ajay invokes as the state's basic legibility logic: 'if you have the land, I'll tax you and I want clarity on who has the land.'

head: Deng Xiaoping's
more: Deng Xiaoping's 'Cross the River by Feeling the Stones', a chapter title in Kelkar and Shah's book, used as shorthand for Scott's advice to make small, reversible moves.
'Some bloke in Delhi who thought why don't we go to Daulatabad and shift the capital': Ajay's nod to Tughlaq, paired with Brasília as a failed planned capital.

head: Le Corbusier and Chandigarh: Amit was born in a city designed by…
more: Le Corbusier and Chandigarh: Amit was born in a city designed by 'one of the villains of high modernism' and applies his own 'seen and unseen' lens to it.

head: A field born from a satellite's side effect
dek: Whole research fields can grow out of accidental by-products of someone else's project.
more: US government satellites were photographing the Earth at night for unrelated purposes. Analysts noticed that the images were picking up the light over cities, and that a city's light footprint grew as the city prospered. That led to a conjecture: could light seen from space be used to infer economic activity? The early data was crude. Pixels were 3 km by 3 km, bright cities saturated and got top-coded, and readings came once a year. Then in 2011 NASA and NOAA launched the VIIRS sensor package, which photographs the world every night at 1:30 AM with pixels of roughly 700–800 metres.
Whole research fields can grow out of accidental by-products of someone else's project. The data was always there; someone just had to look at it with a different question.

head: The poster on the wall that Ajay refused to use
dek: Rigour sometimes means not using exciting data until you truly understand its innards.
more: At NIPFP, his colleagues Shekhar Hari Kumar and Shubho Roy were passionate about nighttime lights. They made beautiful maps and put up a poster in the office. Ajay held back for years. His CMIE training told him never to use a measure casually. Only when Ayush Patnaik started working intensely inside the VIIRS data did he dive in. He notes that the World Bank publishes a district-level dataset for India, and that many economists simply download it and hope nothing is wrong.
Rigour sometimes means not using exciting data until you truly understand its innards. Being early matters less than being right.

head: Why Bombay seemed to go dark every July
dek: Local ground truth can expose a bias that even great institutions miss.
more: To sanity-check the data, the team looked at places they knew, such as Bandra West versus Bandra East. They found that Bombay's radiance collapsed every July, which made no economic sense. NASA/NOAA classify each night as cloudy or cloud-free, discard the cloudy nights, and average the rest. In July only about three of 31 nights pass. The team reasoned that those 'cloud-free' nights in the monsoon still carry wisps of cloud that dim the signal. By contrast, January yields about 25 good nights out of 31. So the fraction of cloud-free days could serve as a proxy for bias. They built a deliberately conservative correction and checked it on other cities. Dubai, cloud-free all year, barely changed. Monsoon cities like Johannesburg did. The paper and a Julia package are public.
Local ground truth can expose a bias that even great institutions miss. Knowing that Bombay is never really clear in July was the clue that cracked the problem.
printed: Monsoon, with a chance of bias

head: Swedish intelligence beat the academics to it
dek: Don't assume an obvious piece of research is already being done. People who need an answer to act can outrun people who only need it to publish.
more: When the Russia-Ukraine war began, Ajay, Susan Thomas and Ayush Patnaik thought of studying Russia with nighttime lights. They held off because 'there are like 500 labs in the world' that could do it, and surely the Europeans would. They went back to studying households in Karnataka. Years passed and no good paper on the Russian economy appeared, while the idea kept 'waking up every three days'. Then in 2024 Swedish intelligence publicly said nighttime lights over Russia had fallen sharply in 2023. Amit remarked that the intelligence agencies have skin in the game. Ajay's under-resourced team decided to do the work themselves.
Don't assume an obvious piece of research is already being done. People who need an answer to act can outrun people who only need it to publish. If you want something done, do it yourself.

head: Russia breaks every method built for India
dek: Methods that work under one set of conditions can fail badly in another.
more: Studying Russia threw up surprises. The country was too big to load into a computer's memory, so it had to be cut into provinces, and the largest province is still bigger than India. In summer the sun is shining at 1:30 AM in St Petersburg, so the 'night' photo isn't night. Faint moonlight reflecting off the empty vastness of Siberia added up to fake radiance. Their background-noise algorithms had been tuned for the much smaller deserts of Rajasthan. The Aurora Borealis produced a huge amount of light over Ukraine in 2019. Gas flares also had to be filtered out.
Methods that work under one set of conditions can fail badly in another. You only catch these traps by staying close to your data.

head: How WWII was decided by factories, not battles
dek: Long wars are won by production capacity and by understanding your adversary.
more: After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and 'poked the giant', Hitler foolishly declared war on America the very next day. He thought he was obliged to, and did not understand America. Once American production mobilised, it was game over. Japan, an island, depended on raw materials shipped from across East Asia. The US Navy strangled those supply chains. Occupied Europe could not match the US, Britain with its empire, and the Soviet Union combined. Allied bombers flew from Britain to destroy German factories one by one. Germany never built a long-range bomber, so Soviet factories moved deep inland stayed safe.
Long wars are won by production capacity and by understanding your adversary. Battlefield brilliance can't overcome a hopeless economic balance.

head: Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War
by: Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Susan Thomas
dek: It uses carefully corrected nighttime lights to read Russia's economy while official data is withheld.
more: It uses carefully corrected nighttime lights to read Russia's economy while official data is withheld. It finds the economy roughly flat from January 2019 to January 2025, damage along the Ukraine and European borders, and a 245 km eastward shift in the economy's centre of mass.
The xKDR paper at the heart of the episode, which Amit brings up as the work shedding light on 'the greatest question of our age'.

dek: Ajay calls it 'answer one' to the question of whether socialism works.
more: Ajay calls it 'answer one' to the question of whether socialism works. The satellite image of the Korean peninsula is answer two.
Invoked while showing the North Korea vs South Korea night-time image.

head: Both Sides Now
dek: Amit asks Joni Mitchell fans to appreciate the allusion and listen to 'the great song' linked in the show notes.
more: Amit asks Joni Mitchell fans to appreciate the allusion and listen to 'the great song' linked in the show notes.
Prompted by the title of Ajay's methods paper, 'But Clouds Got In My Way'.

head: The Future of War (Episode 112 of Everything is Everything)
dek: It sets out how modern war has changed, including long-range standoff weapons.
more: It sets out how modern war has changed, including long-range standoff weapons. That framing explains why Russian regions far from the Ukrainian border are being damaged.
Ajay links the Russia analysis back to this recent episode.

head: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: In that episode Amit and his guests (Niti Gupta, Hamsini Hariharan and Devika) invented non-traditional measures of women's empowerment on the fly.
more: In that episode Amit and his guests (Niti Gupta, Hamsini Hariharan and Devika) invented non-traditional measures of women's empowerment on the fly. It is the seed of the next episode's theme.
Amit recalls it at the end, after hearing about nighttime lights as unconventional data.

head: Nighttime lights as a measure of prosperity
dek: Every night at 1:30 AM, satellites record how much light comes out of each roughly 700–800 m patch of Earth.
more: Every night at 1:30 AM, satellites record how much light comes out of each roughly 700–800 m patch of Earth. Streetlights, compound walls, cars, all-night petrol pumps and restaurants rise with prosperity, so brightness tracks economic activity. Bandra West shows up brighter than Bandra East. Ships even reveal congestion at ports.

head: Nighttime lights is not GDP
dek: Light rises with income but not in a straight line, and the data has traps.
more: Light rises with income but not in a straight line, and the data has traps. Taller buildings trap light under their roofs. LEDs register about 34% less light at the sensor, so the shift to LEDs understates growth. Faint moonlight summed over a vast area can make Jaisalmer look as bright as Bandra West, whose GDP is ten times bigger. And at rich-country levels, more income doesn't mean more lights, so Switzerland and the US look alike. Ajay thinks economists got over-excited treating it as a straight replacement for GDP data.

head: A statistical system with a twist
dek: NASA, NOAA, the European Space Agency and the Japanese space agency release maintained, regularly updated satellite data free to the world.
