more: NASA, NOAA, the European Space Agency and the Japanese space agency release maintained, regularly updated satellite data free to the world. This is measurement without the institutional complexity of a statistics office walking the country. Because each pixel is small, you can draw any boundary, such as the 300 urban local bodies of Karnataka. You get city-level, monthly signals, whereas GDP comes out once a year with a long lag.

head: Wage war on measurement
dek: Ajay holds that half the battle in economics is measuring something correctly.
more: Ajay holds that half the battle in economics is measuring something correctly. Analysis and theorising come after. Without depth in measurement you get garbage in, garbage out, and waste everyone's time. His advice to economists is to love their data deeply.

head: Sanity-check data against what you know
dek: Before trusting a new dataset, test it on places you understand. Is Bandra West brighter than Bandra East, and Bandra East brighter than Karjat?
more: Before trusting a new dataset, test it on places you understand. Is Bandra West brighter than Bandra East, and Bandra East brighter than Karjat? Local knowledge, like knowing Bombay is never clear in July, is what exposes hidden biases.

head: Deliberate under-correction
dek: When fixing a bias you can be aggressive and risk new errors, or conservative and certain.
more: When fixing a bias you can be aggressive and risk new errors, or conservative and certain. Ajay's team chose to correct only where they were absolutely sure. The aim was a fix so safe that everyone should adopt it, leaving bolder corrections to later researchers.

head: Strategic war is economic war
dek: A long war of attrition is decided by whether the economy can supply guns, butter and soldiers.
more: A long war of attrition is decided by whether the economy can supply guns, butter and soldiers. Ukraine doesn't need to produce much itself, because it is backed by Europe: guns are made in Germany and butter in the UK. Russia is an Italy-sized economy whose only important patron is North Korea.

head: The pressures on Russia's economy
dek: Ajay lists four. One to two million of the most educated and richest people fled.
more: Ajay lists four. One to two million of the most educated and richest people fled. Western sanctions made buying, paying and earning hard. The economy was rejigged toward war production at the expense of civilian output. And Ukrainian standoff weapons are now hitting its industry.

head: No more safe hinterland
dek: In WWII, Soviet factories were safe deep inland because Germany had no long-range bomber.
more: In WWII, Soviet factories were safe deep inland because Germany had no long-range bomber. Ukraine's deep-strike weapons now reach hundreds to 2,000 km into Russia, destroying factories and refineries, and these weapons arrived only in the last six to nine months. Ajay draws an implication: if China invades Taiwan, expect hundreds of kilometres of the Chinese coast to face the same treatment.

head: Reading a wartime economy from space
dek: Russia has, 'as they should', withheld economic data because it is now strategic, so satellites fill the gap.
more:
Russia has, 'as they should', withheld economic data because it is now strategic, so satellites fill the gap. Ajay compares January to January, since Russian Januaries are dark at 1:30 AM and cloud-free. The findings:
- Overall radiance in 2025 is about where it was in 2019: war production up, civilian economy down.
- Regions near Ukraine are hit by strikes.
- Regions near the Baltic states and Europe are hurt by sanctions reversing the gains from trade.
- Eastern borders, where sanctions aren't enforced, are fine.
- The economy's centre of mass has moved east.
For January 2026, Ajay is watching two opposing forces: Trump easing sanctions and Ukraine improving its deep-strike weapons.

head: Unconventional metrics
dek: Beyond GDP-style proxies, creative indicators can reveal how a society actually lives.
more: Beyond GDP-style proxies, creative indicators can reveal how a society actually lives. Examples include rising divorce rates as a sign of women's empowerment, or who orders more from grocery apps. Amit proposes devoting the next episode to such metrics.

head: Amit opens with an acrostic poem
more: Amit opens with an acrostic poem, 'Nighttime Lights', whose first letters spell 'I LOVE FREEDOM'. He explains the phrase made 'the poet in me arose. I was about to say was aroused, but that's not the right word.' After reading it to a dry-eyed Ajay he adds: 'I can see that you aren't tearing up. This is very sad. Maybe we should make AI make you cry.'

head: Ajay on the North Korea vs South Korea night image as the answer to whether socialism works
more: Ajay on the North Korea vs South Korea night image as the answer to whether socialism works: 'you should have tried it on hamsters first.'

head: Ajay explaining why light stops tracking income at the top
more: Ajay explaining why light stops tracking income at the top: 'We have Amit Varma... when your income doubles, is your lighting going to double? No. You're done. You've reached the zenith of human prosperity where there is no possibility of your buying any more lights.' Amit: 'Also double of zero is zero, but continue.'

head: The word
more: The word 'incandescent' sparks a quatrain from Amit: 'I told her she was incandescent when I met her for a lark. She looked at me with twinkling eyes and said I was too dark.'

head: Ajay's passion for measurement inspires another
more: Ajay's passion for measurement inspires another: 'I said to her, I'll treasure you, I love you bit by bit. But first, my love, I'll measure you to make sure that I fit.' When Ajay says he's getting better and better, Amit replies: 'You weren't a good economist at twenty or thirty or forty, it took some time.'
Amit: 'the reason you're my favorite economist friend... Sorry to other economist friends who might be watching this, oh wait, I have none.'

head: Ajay on NASA and NOAA giving away data
more: Ajay on NASA and NOAA giving away data: 'we shouldn't say this too loudly because... if Donald Trump is an enthusiastic watcher of Everything is Everything, he will complain that these are global public goods and the US government is not being compensated.'

head: After Ajay says Hitler didn't understand America, Amit
more: After Ajay says Hitler didn't understand America, Amit: 'I don't think anybody understands America. I don't think America understands America.'

head: Ajay on why January is the month to study Russia, with short days and no clouds
more: Ajay on why January is the month to study Russia, with short days and no clouds: 'January is the time to peek into the Kremlin and look at what Putin [is] doing on his morning walk.'

head: Ajay describes Russia as a…
more: Ajay describes Russia as a 'petroleum producing country which also happens to have nuclear weapons'. On why it flares so much gas: 'Russia is a Communist country, they don't know how to handle the gas.'

head: Amit wonders how
more: Amit wonders how 'many a slip between cup and lip' ever originated: 'There's a cup, there's a lip. Generally there are no slips.' He then spins it into a cricket riff about Vivian Richards, playing India, about to raise his cup to his lip.

head: Amit had asked about…
more: Amit had asked about 'the light' Ajay's paper sheds on the war. When Ajay reveals it is titled 'Shedding Light on the Russia-Ukraine War', the response is: 'lame minds think alike.'

head: Ajay's advice to every economist, in romantic mode
more: Ajay's advice to every economist, in romantic mode: 'please love your data deeply and you know, look deep in her eyes because without that you'll never make progress.'

head: The methods paper's title
more: The methods paper's title, 'But Clouds Got In My Way', nods to Joni Mitchell's 'Both Sides Now', which Amit asks fans to appreciate.

head: The iconic satellite image of North and South Korea at night, shown for 2012 and 2025, which Ajay calls…
more: The iconic satellite image of North and South Korea at night, shown for 2012 and 2025, which Ajay calls 'one of the most influential pictures in the history of the socialism question.'

head: Pearl Harbor, where Japan
more: Pearl Harbor, where Japan 'poked the giant', followed by Hitler declaring war on America the next day. Ajay notes Hitler had no idea that 'a MAGA isolationist problem was alive and well in America at that time.'

head: Luca Cavalli-Sforza's Wild Bet
dek: Visionary science often commits to a kind of evidence decades before the technology exists to collect it.
more: Cavalli-Sforza, a scientist born around 1918, was obsessed with the deep past at a time when the only tools were fossils, ruins and early carbon dating. Scant data from these sources had hardened into conventional wisdom. He first tried reading history through the blood groups of different populations. In the early 1960s he made a bet that seemed insane: human history would be revealed through our genes. The human genome wasn't fully sequenced until 2001. Mitochondrial DNA work in the 1980s showed we all came out of Africa. By around 2009, full-genome studies of the past were a mature science, and his vision had come true.
Visionary science often commits to a kind of evidence decades before the technology exists to collect it. When that evidence finally arrives, it can overturn a century of confident consensus.
printed: The long bet on our DNA

head: India's Four Waves of Migration
dek: The genetic data rules out both politically convenient myths. There was no clean Aryan invasion, and Aryans were not the original people from whom everything came.
more: Drawing on Tony Joseph's Early Indians, Amit traces four major migrations into the subcontinent. The 'first Indians' came out of Africa about 65,000 years ago; tribal communities carry more of their genes today. Agricultural people from Central Asia came next, brought wheat and barley, and formed the Harappan civilisation. They probably spoke a proto-Dravidian language, an early form of Tamil, which is older than Sanskrit. Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman peoples arrived in the north-east. Around 2000 BCE came Indo-European speakers from the steppes, carrying an early form of Sanskrit. Their descendants mixed into 'Ancient North Indians' and 'Ancient South Indians', and every Indian carries both in differing degrees.

The genetic data rules out both politically convenient myths. There was no clean Aryan invasion, and Aryans were not the original people from whom everything came. What happened was migration followed by deep mixing.
printed: Out of Africa, into the mix

head: Why Sanskrit Has Retroflex Sounds
dek: Even a 'sacred' classical language is a hybrid. Languages carry the imprint of who raised the children, not just who held power.
more: From Peggy Mohan's Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: Sanskrit is not a pure Indo-European language. It has retroflex sounds, made with the tongue curled up toward the roof of the mouth. Amit demonstrates these with Hindi word pairs. Persian and other Indo-European neighbours to the west lack these sounds, but the Dravidian languages the migrants met in India have them. The mechanism was intimate. The migrants were mostly men who married local women. Children spent their early years speaking their mother's tongue, and boys later learned the men's language through apprenticeship and hunting. Vedic Sanskrit emerged as a blend, was later frozen as a language of learning for a class and caste, and became a dead language like Latin. Prakrit kept evolving.
Even a 'sacred' classical language is a hybrid. Languages carry the imprint of who raised the children, not just who held power.

head: When the Great Party Ended: Caste Endogamy Around 100 CE
dek: Caste endogamy is real and visible in our DNA, but it is about two thousand years old, while the mixing is about four thousand.
more: For roughly two thousand years after the Indo-Europeans arrived, the genetic evidence shows full intermingling. Nobody was drawing lines between 'our people' and 'not our people'. Around 100 CE a particular ideological strand in the Gangetic belt won out, and severe caste endogamy began. It left a clear signature in the genes. Upper-caste men also proved more successful at spreading their genes than lower-caste men.
Caste endogamy is real and visible in our DNA, but it is about two thousand years old, while the mixing is about four thousand. It was a path India took, not a destiny, and it can be reversed.

head: The Rs 80 Credit Card Standoff
dek: A single traditional metric can badly misjudge a person. Richer behavioural data could build a far more holistic, and fairer, picture of who someone really is.
more: About 25 years ago Amit had a Standard Chartered credit card with no auto-pay. Being, as he puts it, a lazy Bengali, he relied on the bank calling him so he could send someone to collect payment. Once the outstanding was so small, Rs 80, that nobody called. The card was cancelled and his CIBIL score collapsed. With interest the amount grew to Rs 3,000, then Rs 5,000, then Rs 29,000. The bank refused to send a bill and abusive recovery agents made threats. He refused on principle to pay, even though he easily could have. His score is still bad today. He pays vendors immediately or even in advance, and has never had an EMI.
A single traditional metric can badly misjudge a person. Richer behavioural data could build a far more holistic, and fairer, picture of who someone really is.

head: Your Phone Battery as a Credit Score
dek: Nobody starts with a theory that low battery means risk. The algorithm finds the pattern across millions of phones, and the 'why' is left for humans to work out.
more: Smart Finance, a Chinese micro-lender, scores borrowers from their phone data. If your battery regularly falls below 12%, you won't get a loan. So will filling in your birth date too fast, or making a typo and going back to fix it. Lenddo found the opposite extreme also bad: a phone that is always fully charged signals an unreliable borrower, so there is a sweet spot. Amit keeps his phone around 80%. Tala, which operates in Africa and Asia, penalises frequent small recharges and looks at how many of your contacts have repaid loans. A 2018 German study found iPhone users default less than Android users (roughly 1.07% vs 1.7%). It also found that Hotmail or Yahoo addresses, typos in your email, and habitual 2 AM shopping predict higher default.
Nobody starts with a theory that low battery means risk. The algorithm finds the pattern across millions of phones, and the 'why' is left for humans to work out. That makes the system hard to game.

head: COVID Seen Through Location Data
dek: What people actually do, captured passively, can diverge sharply from official declarations.
more: After COVID struck, researchers in India and elsewhere used phone location data. It showed the lockdown largely worked, with the migrant-labour exodus as the exception. It also showed that recovery did not begin when the government said it was safe; people stayed wary for a while. The data could flag likely surges when festivals like Diwali drew crowds, which markets could use to predict demand for drugs or masks. Ajay adds that Google and Facebook released mobility measures for the whole country.
What people actually do, captured passively, can diverge sharply from official declarations. Public release of such data is a public good.

head: The Diamond Brothers and the Walmart Parking Lot
dek: An old shopkeeper's intuition plus new measurement became an industry.
more: In 2009 Tom Diamond visited his brother Alex, who worked at a satellite-imagery firm. Alex had just used imagery to confirm that a factory a client wanted to buy was representing itself honestly. While the brothers were jamming (their hobby was rock versions of Western classical music, including Schubert), they remembered Sam Walton's habit. The Walmart founder judged how a store was doing by counting cars in its parking lot. Why not do that for every store? Alex quit, bought three years of imagery and back-tested it. Parking-lot traffic predicted quarterly results. They founded RS Metrics (RS for remote sensing), and UBS came calling. Ajay's nephew joined later. Early on they got only about twelve expensive pictures a month; the data later became cheap and plentiful, birthing the 'alt data' industry. For Tesla production they once flew their own plane overhead. Two Berkeley professors later used parking data from 67,000 stores and estimated a 4.7% edge over ordinary investors, when traders would die for 0.2%.
An old shopkeeper's intuition plus new measurement became an industry. Satellite pictures of parking lots are really pictures of real people buying real things.
printed: Count the cars, beat the market

head: The Capsized Iron Ore Train
dek: Markets react to headlines. Whoever looks directly at reality, rather than reasoning from the news, holds the edge.
more: A train carrying around 268 wagons of iron ore crashed and capsized. Stock prices fell, iron ore prices rose, and the market priced in the expected loss. Traders who checked satellite images saw the ore was just lying flat and easy to reload. They bet the market would recover faster than expected and made a killing.
Markets react to headlines. Whoever looks directly at reality, rather than reasoning from the news, holds the edge.

head: Reading Oil Tanks From Their Shadows
dek: Simple geometry plus a camera in the sky can reveal private inventories.
more: Many oil storage tanks have a roof that floats on the oil, so it sinks as the tank empties. The sun's position is known. When a tank is full there is no shadow inside it. As it empties, the sunken roof shows a shadow in an overhead satellite image, and the shadow's size tells you how full the tank is.
Simple geometry plus a camera in the sky can reveal private inventories. This is the kind of creative measurement that is reshaping what we can know.

head: The Lipstick Index and Its COVID Exception
dek: Counterintuitive signals hide in everyday spending. Every index also rests on hidden assumptions, here that your face is seen, and it fails when those assumptions break.
more: Amit quizzes Ajay, who guesses right: lipstick sales rise in tough times. Leonard Lauder of Estée Lauder coined the 'lipstick index' after sales rose during the 2001 recession. His logic was that people cut back on $200 handbags but still want to feel good, so they buy the cheapest luxury available, a $20 lipstick. The pattern held in 2008 and in 2011. COVID broke it, because masks made lipstick pointless.
Counterintuitive signals hide in everyday spending. Every index also rests on hidden assumptions, here that your face is seen, and it fails when those assumptions break.

head: The Billion Prices Project Catches Argentina
dek: Independent, large-scale data can expose official statistics that understate the truth.
more: Roberto Rigobon and Alberto Cavallo argued that economies are measured with too little data when far more is available online. So they scraped huge volumes of internet prices to build their own index. They found online prices track offline prices closely. For Argentina between 2007 and 2015, official inflation was about 7-10%, but their data showed 20-30% a year, and the crisis eventually exploded. Ajay has met Rigobon at conferences, knows his work on identification through heteroskedasticity, and says his own team intuitively reinvented part of that idea.
Independent, large-scale data can expose official statistics that understate the truth. The more diverse the sources behind an index, the more you can trust it.

head: Who We Are and How We Got Here: Ancient DNA and the new science of the human past
dek: Explains the science of full-genome studies and how they overturned received wisdom from archaeology.
more: Explains the science of full-genome studies and how they overturned received wisdom from archaeology. Amit says he hasn't stopped thinking about its findings since reading it years ago.
Named as one of 'two books that everyone should read' while introducing the genetics of prehistory.

head: Early Indians: The Story of Our Ancestors and Where We Came From
dek: Applies the genetic evidence to India: first Indians, Harappans, Ancient North and South Indians, and the Aryan migration.
more: Applies the genetic evidence to India: first Indians, Harappans, Ancient North and South Indians, and the Aryan migration. Amit calls its findings 'just stunning'.
The second of the 'two books that everyone should read', and the basis for Amit's account of India's four migrations.

head: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants: The Story of India through Its Languages
dek: Does with language what Reich and Joseph did with genes. It is the source of the retroflex-sound and mothers'-tongue insights that 'blew my mind'.
more: Does with language what Reich and Joseph did with genes. It is the source of the retroflex-sound and mothers'-tongue insights that 'blew my mind'.
Called 'another great book' during the discussion of Sanskrit and the Aryan migration.

head: A History of Hinduism (Ep 76 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Their earlier episode built on Manu Pillai's account of Hinduism as an assimilative, almost 'open source' tradition.
more: Their earlier episode built on Manu Pillai's account of Hinduism as an assimilative, almost 'open source' tradition.
Recalled while explaining how caste and religion followed different paths.

head: The Hindi Heartland
dek: Has a 'great excerpt' on tribals made to tick a 'Hindu' box, and the mass movement now reasserting their earlier identities.
more: Has a 'great excerpt' on tribals made to tick a 'Hindu' box, and the mass movement now reasserting their earlier identities.
Discussed on a recent Seen and the Unseen episode; cited in the census and categorisation discussion.

head: Caste and the Census (Ep 417 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: For anyone wanting the deeper debate on what counting caste could do to society.
more: For anyone wanting the deeper debate on what counting caste could do to society.
Mentioned in the context of debates over a caste census.

head: The Alchemy of Finance
dek: Source of the concept that the narratives imposed on a system change how that system sees and shapes itself.
more: Source of the concept that the narratives imposed on a system change how that system sees and shapes itself.
Where Amit first learned the idea of reflexivity, which he applies to caste.

head: In Praise of Floods
dek: Covers the diversity that existed before the agricultural age. He has some misgivings, but says parts are a masterpiece and promises to discuss it in detail later.
more: Covers the diversity that existed before the agricultural age. He has some misgivings, but says parts are a masterpiece and promises to discuss it in detail later.
Amit had just finished it while discussing how homogenisation destroyed diversity.

head: Against the Grain
dek: To see the havoc the agricultural age brought to humankind. Amit's broader advice: 'you should read everything by James C Scott.'
more: To see the havoc the agricultural age brought to humankind. Amit's broader advice: 'you should read everything by James C Scott.'
Recommended to the 'gentle reader' as Scott's earlier book.

head: Data First, Then Regularities, Then Theory
dek: Ajay's model of how knowledge grows: Kepler measured and found statistical regularities, and only then did Newton build theory.
more: Ajay's model of how knowledge grows: Kepler measured and found statistical regularities, and only then did Newton build theory. Without measurement, debate is just opinion. India badly under-measures itself, and institutions like the CSO and CMIE were long the only game in town.

head: The Measurement Revolution
dek: Over the last twenty years, new data sources have given us 'new eyes': ancient DNA, satellite night-lights, phone footprints, parking-lot imagery.
more: Over the last twenty years, new data sources have given us 'new eyes': ancient DNA, satellite night-lights, phone footprints, parking-lot imagery. These let us see things old statistical systems never could, and they can decisively settle debates that careful archaeology or opinion never resolved.

head: Today's Science Is Tomorrow's Bloodletting
dek: Nineteenth-century medicine relied on bloodletting, had no germ theory, and killed people in hospitals, which is partly why quack remedies thrived.
more: Nineteenth-century medicine relied on bloodletting, had no germ theory, and killed people in hospitals, which is partly why quack remedies thrived. We assume today's knowledge is near-final, but two centuries from now people will see us as equally ignorant. Genetics has just overturned much of what archaeology confidently believed.

head: We Are All a Khichri
dek: The key finding of ancient DNA is that humans are far more mixed than once assumed.
more: The key finding of ancient DNA is that humans are far more mixed than once assumed. All of us descend from 'mitochondrial Eve' in Africa, then mixed endlessly: five major migrations into Europe, four into India, and 3-5% Neanderthal ancestry in many Europeans and Asians. Visible differences exist, but beneath them is one deeply interwoven people.

head: Languages Encode Ways of Thinking
dek: A language is more than a tool for communication; it carries values. Japanese and Korean favour terse minimalism, while Urdu, Punjabi and Bengali are exuberant and expressive.
more: A language is more than a tool for communication; it carries values. Japanese and Korean favour terse minimalism, while Urdu, Punjabi and Bengali are exuberant and expressive. English sits in a utilitarian middle, which is why Tagore loses something in English. Different languages may encourage different kinds of thinking and feeling.

head: Caste: The Deepest Sin, Not the Original Sin
dek: Genetics proves caste endogamy is real, harmful and about two thousand years old, so no spin can erase it.
more: Genetics proves caste endogamy is real, harmful and about two thousand years old, so no spin can erase it. That is the sad story: it runs deep, and markets and urbanisation help but are no magic bullet. Amit argues that the 1991 reforms lifted hundreds of millions of Dalits and that Manmohan Singh did more for them than any twentieth-century thinker, while still crediting Ambedkar. The happy story is that the mixing is twice as old, so caste was a path chosen, not a fate, and it can be reversed.

head: Endogamy Breeds Control of Women
dek: If marriage must stay within the caste, female sexuality has to be policed: no affairs, no children outside the group, no falling in love.
more: If marriage must stay within the caste, female sexuality has to be policed: no affairs, no children outside the group, no falling in love. Amit argues this created a sexually repressive society. Today's prudishness comes partly from this and partly from imported Victorian morality.

head: Legibility and Reflexivity: Measuring Changes the Measured
dek: Amit lays out the theory that British census-takers, guided by Brahmin informants, forced fluid identities into fixed boxes of caste and religion, and that the boxes then shaped how people saw themselves.
more: Amit lays out the theory that British census-takers, guided by Brahmin informants, forced fluid identities into fixed boxes of caste and religion, and that the boxes then shaped how people saw themselves. He calls this reflexivity, a term from Soros, and notes that tribals made to tick 'Hindu' are now pushing back. He holds that both this theory and the genetic evidence of real caste endogamy contain truth. Ajay frames it in terms of Seeing Like a State: state legibility projects have unintended consequences, a kind of Heisenberg effect.

head: Don't Derive the Ought From the Is
dek: Reich and Joseph both stress that genetic differences must never justify racist thinking.
more: Reich and Joseph both stress that genetic differences must never justify racist thinking. Amit invokes G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy and Hume's is-ought problem: that something is natural doesn't make it right. Differences, including those between men and women, deserve celebration, not enshrinement as rules or hierarchies.

head: Homogenisation vs. the Long Tail
dek: Agriculture narrowed diversity: of some 200,000 plant varieties, about twelve dominate our diet, and four animal species dominate the landscape.
more: Agriculture narrowed diversity: of some 200,000 plant varieties, about twelve dominate our diet, and four animal species dominate the landscape. There are three chickens for every human, all industrially farmed. Dialects like Bhojpuri, Maithili and Haryanvi were swallowed by big languages. Yet markets work in two phases: first they chase scale and homogenise, then they empower niches, as Stage.in shows. Diversity can return.

head: Endogamy's Hidden Health Cost (Ajay's Open Question)
dek: Ajay asks whether smaller jatis fall below a minimum viable population, so that endogamy degrades their gene pool.
more: Ajay asks whether smaller jatis fall below a minimum viable population, so that endogamy degrades their gene pool. If so, the spread of modernity and intermarriage would bring a large public-health gain. He also notes from travels in Mauritius and Sri Lanka that coasts and islands show more genetic diversity because sailors and traders mixed there for millennia. He wonders whether India's coasts have been measured this way.

head: Black-Box Metrics Are Hard to Game
dek: Machine-learning credit models find patterns across millions of users without caring why they hold, much as AlphaZero taught chess players that initiative mattered more than they thought.
more: Machine-learning credit models find patterns across millions of users without caring why they hold, much as AlphaZero taught chess players that initiative mattered more than they thought. A known metric, like battery level, can be gamed. Thousands of opaque ones cannot, even by the lender itself. Unlike China's state social credit score, this is voluntary: you trade access to your phone for a loan.

head: Digital Exhaust
dek: Ordinary life (emailing, shopping, buying vada pav) throws off a trail of data that looks like trash.
more: Ordinary life (emailing, shopping, buying vada pav) throws off a trail of data that looks like trash. People are now opening that garbage bin and finding powerful information in it.

head: Privacy's First Enemy Is the State
dek: Private firms using personal data need privacy rules, but those problems are qualitatively easier.
more: Private firms using personal data need privacy rules, but those problems are qualitatively easier. India has it upside down: the government has unlimited access to personal information while restricting private firms. Google can do you little harm; the state can coerce you.

head: Smart Speculators Make Prices a Public Good
dek: Critics call alt-data edges unfair. Ajay replies that finance rewards smart people for producing information, and their trading builds efficient prices that help the whole economy run.
more: Critics call alt-data edges unfair. Ajay replies that finance rewards smart people for producing information, and their trading builds efficient prices that help the whole economy run. Speculation is voluntary and meant to be hard. Those who don't want to compete should buy and hold index funds.
printed: Watch the ore, not the news

head: Weigh Your Data When Updating Beliefs
dek: Comparing several measures of the same thing reveals the strengths and limits of each.
more: Comparing several measures of the same thing reveals the strengths and limits of each. All measurement ultimately serves the updating of priors, and how far you move should depend on how good the data is.

head: Fertility Tracks a Nation's Mood
dek: Amit recalls Ajay's point, from his PhD on fertility, that people have fewer children in bad or authoritarian times, and wonders whether hemlines reflect the same mood.
more: Amit recalls Ajay's point, from his PhD on fertility, that people have fewer children in bad or authoritarian times, and wonders whether hemlines reflect the same mood. Ajay invokes Hannah Arendt's line that authoritarians run out of people to oppress. He cautions that the measure needs high-quality birth data, a privilege of rich countries like South Korea and Japan. He also notes recent claims that China's population is smaller than official figures say.

head: Everyday Behaviour as an Economic Barometer
dek: Quirky indexes read the economy from ordinary choices. Lipstick sales rise in downturns.
more: Quirky indexes read the economy from ordinary choices. Lipstick sales rise in downturns. Men delay buying underwear (Greenspan's index). Hemlines rose in the 1920s and 1960s and fell in the Depression and after the 1973 oil shock. Tie sales fall with layoffs, though that may also reflect work from home. Diaper sales fell while rash-ointment sales rose in 2008. A stripper index (2021-22) tracked fewer high-value customers. The hard part is attribution: knowing what is really driving a signal.

head: Ajay introduces
more: Ajay introduces 'the great Omit Varma' in Bengali style. Amit replies that to Ajay he's Amit, 'just as you are Ajay and not Ajoy. Two can play this game. Kindly control.'

head: Amit, after Ajay's ode to data
more: Amit, after Ajay's ode to data: 'the road to knowledge begins with data, and I would say the road to knowledge ends in despair.'

head: On all 7.5 billion humans descending from mitochondrial Eve
more: On all 7.5 billion humans descending from mitochondrial Eve: 'Why are you laughing? This is a serious subject. But I suspect the lady would also laugh if she knew what she had wrought. All for a few moments of pleasure.'

head: On 3-5% Neanderthal DNA in Europeans and Asians
more: On 3-5% Neanderthal DNA in Europeans and Asians: 'we were having a party with Neanderthals'. So calling someone a Neanderthal who 'won't understand art' is really an insult to part of ourselves.

head: Amit teases Ajay for constantly texting: the crew wonders what he's up to…
more: Amit teases Ajay for constantly texting: the crew wonders what he's up to, 'and you always say while you blush, I am checking the weather. I'm not so sure about that.'

head: Amit blames his credit-card fiasco on being Bengali (
more: Amit blames his credit-card fiasco on being Bengali ('because I'm Bengali I'd be lazy'). He has a credit card again only because, 'and this is a typical Indian story, a friend of mine runs a bank.'

head: Before the 4.7% parking-lot statistic, Amit borrows clickbait style
more: Before the 4.7% parking-lot statistic, Amit borrows clickbait style: 'you won't believe what happened next.'
On saying 'indexes' rather than the British 'indices': it's sexier, 'because we don't talk of the sises, we talk of the sexes.'

head: The lipstick index failed during COVID
more: The lipstick index failed during COVID: 'People are wearing masks so they don't need lipstick. You understand what I'm saying? This is a profound point.'

head: Introducing Greenspan's male underwear index, Amit describes him as an economist who…
more: Introducing Greenspan's male underwear index, Amit describes him as an economist who 'loved low interest rates'. In bad times the gap between underwear purchases gets, pun not intended, 'stretched', until the elastic is falling off completely.

head: An unnamed older friend who played chess across Europe and the Soviet Union in the 1980s turned his underwear inside out when it got dirty
more: An unnamed older friend who played chess across Europe and the Soviet Union in the 1980s turned his underwear inside out when it got dirty, so 'every underwear is effectively like two underwear'. He also once traded his corduroys for sex in Russia. Amit: 'I think I've revealed who it is.'

head: On the hemline index: after the 1973 oil shock maxi skirts came into vogue
more: On the hemline index: after the 1973 oil shock maxi skirts came into vogue, 'see the result of bad economics', which Amit finds 'utterly shocking'. He also tells Ajay he is 'spiritually a child of the sixties'.

head: On the diaper rash index
more: On the diaper rash index: 'You simply have to get your babies all the diapers they need, which is a sentence I never thought I'd say.'

head: The closing
more: The closing 'EIE shirts index' stands at five: Ajay scores 9.5 and black-clad Amit 0.5 ('Black is a state of mind'). When Ajay once asked why Turn Black doesn't make its kurtas in white, he suggested launching 'Turn White'. Asked whether Ajay looks sexy because of the shirt or himself: 'Of course it's a shirt.'

head: James C Scott's Seeing Like a State: Ajay quips its alternative title could be…
more: James C Scott's Seeing Like a State: Ajay quips its alternative title could be 'State Legibility Projects Have Unintended Consequences'. He also calls census-making a Heisenberg effect.
'A language is a dialect with an army', the old line Amit uses to explain why Bhojpuri, Maithili and Haryanvi were swallowed by Hindi.

head: The pro-divorce column and the hunt for odd empowerment metrics
dek: A number that sounds bad, like divorces or women in jail, can be a sign of freedom.
more: Years ago Amit wrote a controversial column arguing that India's rising divorce rates were a good thing. That idea grew into a Seen and the Unseen episode, 'Metrics of Empowerment', where he and three friends looked for unusual data points that show how much agency women have. The ideas included solo travel by women, which Amit notes is rising. Nidhi Gupta suggested counting how many families have a male last child. Hamsini Hariharan suggested counting women in prisons. Another idea was how many men download BigBasket, which Amit then questions: in traditional homes the man may download the app only because he pays, then hands the phone to his wife to pick the groceries.

A number that sounds bad, like divorces or women in jail, can be a sign of freedom. A number that sounds good, like men ordering groceries, can hide the same old patriarchy. What matters is who is actually choosing.

head: Who really decided to order the pizza?
dek: A digital record shows who tapped the button, not who made the decision.
more: Responding to Amit's BigBasket caveat, Ajay recalls an example from their Life Lessons course. Ordering pizza involves a chain of decisions: someone decides 'let's have pizza', someone decides 'let's order Domino's', and someone places the order on the app. If the men make the first two decisions and tell the woman to place the order, her using the app shows nothing about her agency.
A digital record shows who tapped the button, not who made the decision. To measure agency you have to separate out each step of the decision.

head: Office air conditioning was set for men in suits
dek: Everyday infrastructure quietly builds in assumptions about who it serves.
more: Amit proposes a new metric: the default temperature of office air conditioning. When AC became common in offices in the 1950s and 60s, settings were designed for men in suits, and men prefer it colder because of different metabolic rates. This is the source of the familiar marital argument where the wife says she's cold and the husband says put on a sweater. He would like defaults to drift upward until both sexes are comfortable, though he admits he doesn't know how to measure this at scale.
Everyday infrastructure quietly builds in assumptions about who it serves. Watching those defaults change is a way to track social change.

head: A camera on the pavement to count women in public
dek: How many women are out in public, especially after dark, is a simple, continuous measure of how free a society is.
more: Ajay describes a measurement idea he hasn't built yet but thinks is feasible. Point a telephoto camera at a stretch of pavement and use image classification to count passers-by and classify their gender. That gives two things: the share of people in public who are women, and how that share falls as evening comes in. He connects it to his work on crime victimisation surveys, which ask parents what time their teenage daughter should be home. That answer reflects both social norms and how safe parents think the streets are.
How many women are out in public, especially after dark, is a simple, continuous measure of how free a society is. With today's tools it is a small piece of software waiting to be written.

head: Google saw Trump coming
dek: Small details of anonymous behaviour, even the order of words in a search, can reveal what surveys miss.
more: Amit retells findings from Seth Stephens-Davidowitz. Four years before Trump's 2016 rise, Google showed many people searching for a racial slur alongside Obama's victory rather than 'first black president', concentrated in states that later voted a particular way. After the most recent US election, Stephens-Davidowitz wrote in The Economist that searches beat the polls. In states where people searched 'Trump Harris debate', Trump won. Where they searched 'Harris Trump debate', Harris won.
Small details of anonymous behaviour, even the order of words in a search, can reveal what surveys miss. It is the kind of signal humans would never think to look for but machines can find.

head: Comparing Google autocomplete in India and Australia
dek: Basic urges are shared, but culture shapes how they show up. Anyone can examine a country's private preoccupations from home for free.
more: Amit tried the book's experiment himself, using Google autocomplete in an incognito window and switching his VPN between countries. When the book was written, India's top completion for 'my husband wants' was a request to be breastfed. Today it is 'serve his mistress', with breastfeeding at number two. The book reports that porn searches for women breastfeeding men are four times higher in India and Bangladesh than anywhere else, which Amit says he cannot explain. With the VPN set to Australia, the results included 'an open marriage', 'a second wife', 'an open marriage novel' and something far stranger. Ajay asks whether VPNs could compare Indian states, and Amit thinks that could be a research project.
Basic urges are shared, but culture shapes how they show up. Anyone can examine a country's private preoccupations from home for free.

head: Why parents were furious about his anti-children column
dek: Strong backlash can be a sign that an argument touched a private regret.
more: Amit once wrote a column, partly to provoke, arguing that it is immoral to have children, and many parents were angry. Everybody Lies helped him understand why. People are seven times more likely to ask Google whether they will regret not having children than whether they will regret having them. Yet adults with children are 3.6 times more likely to tell Google they regret their choice than adults without children.
Strong backlash can be a sign that an argument touched a private regret. What people say about parenthood in public and what they type alone can be very different.

head: From lonely misfit to friends found online
dek: For people who don't fit in locally, the internet's biggest gift was escaping the limits of geography.
more: Amit describes growing up limited to communities of circumstance: you are born somewhere, go to the local school and work where you work. As someone whose interests nobody around him shared, he was a loner until early adulthood. The internet let him form communities of choice. Most of his friends today are people he met online, and he and Ajay, though both in Bombay, met through the internet (not, he adds, on a dating app).
For people who don't fit in locally, the internet's biggest gift was escaping the limits of geography. Dating apps apply the same shift to romance.

head: The student who wouldn't date anyone from her college
dek: Part of what dating apps offer is an easy exit. Being able to leave without social cost makes people more willing to try, especially women who would otherwise be judged within a small circle.
more: Amit recalls a quote from a dating survey. A young woman explained that she used dating apps instead of dating classmates because if it didn't work out she would see the man every day, possibly with another girl. An app lets her date someone she will never run into again.
Part of what dating apps offer is an easy exit. Being able to leave without social cost makes people more willing to try, especially women who would otherwise be judged within a small circle.

head: A friend's real answer about age preferences
dek: Even app data can reflect appearances. What people choose in public may be the socially safe choice rather than what they actually want.
more: Dating studies say women look for men about their own age, while men of every age look for women in their early twenties (OkCupid found 21). Amit found this doubtful and asked a friend. She said women want to be seen with same-age men because it is socially acceptable, since a date at Starbucks with someone much older or younger looks odd. Personally, though, she prefers men who are either much older or much younger.
Even app data can reflect appearances. What people choose in public may be the socially safe choice rather than what they actually want.

head: Amit's early trip into the manosphere
dek: The manosphere grows out of real resentment among men who get little attention on dating apps.
more: About twenty-five years ago, Amit got absorbed in what is now called the manosphere. He read Neil Strauss's The Game, a bestselling handbook for pickup artists that he calls basically a manual for manipulating women, but one that also showed a real understanding of human nature. That world has since grown into a large social-media industry, with advice books sold on places like Gumroad. Amit says the show Adolescence captured only a small part of it.
The manosphere grows out of real resentment among men who get little attention on dating apps. For many of them dating has become a game to win by any means rather than a search for love.

head: Months in Delhi, weeks in Mumbai, days in Bangalore
dek: Too much choice can undermine relationships. Building one means working through friction, and an app full of alternatives makes giving up easier than staying.
more: In Unboxing Bengaluru, Malini Goyal studied Tinder data from three cities, measuring how long people took to go to each other's homes after matching. It took months in Delhi, weeks in Mumbai and days in Bangalore. Amit lists possible reasons: Delhi is a low-trust society, housing in Mumbai is at a premium, and many singles in Bangalore live alone. When she then interviewed users, she found extreme promiscuity but nobody happy. People became jaded and stopped working through conflicts, because ten other matches were always chatting in real time.
Too much choice can undermine relationships. Building one means working through friction, and an app full of alternatives makes giving up easier than staying.

head: Google Trends
dek: You can save a search as a fixed URL and rerun it to see what the world is paying attention to over time.
more: You can save a search as a fixed URL and rerun it to see what the world is paying attention to over time.
Ajay follows up on Amit's advice to run search experiments yourself.

head: Google Autocomplete experiments (incognito window, optionally with a VPN)
dek: In an incognito window autocomplete isn't biased by your history, and a VPN shows other countries' results.
more: In an incognito window autocomplete isn't biased by your history, and a VPN shows other countries' results. You don't need special access to Google's data to learn something.
Amit urges listeners to try the Everybody Lies experiment themselves.

head: Adolescence
dek: Amit calls it an awesome show that depicts a small part of the manosphere, which grows out of real resentment on dating apps.
more: Amit calls it an awesome show that depicts a small part of the manosphere, which grows out of real resentment on dating apps.
Brought up while discussing incels and the manosphere.

head: The Game
dek: It is a manipulative pickup-artist handbook but shows a real understanding of human nature, and helps explain where today's manosphere came from.
more: It is a manipulative pickup-artist handbook but shows a real understanding of human nature, and helps explain where today's manosphere came from.
Recalled from his time exploring the manosphere 25 years ago.

head: Rob Henderson's tweet on dark triad men and dating apps
dek: Amit calls it fantastic. It explains how a minority of manipulative men can push everyone on dating apps toward mutual mistreatment.
more: Amit calls it fantastic. It explains how a minority of manipulative men can push everyone on dating apps toward mutual mistreatment.
Amit reads it out in full in the dating-apps chapter.

head: The Romantic Recession report
dek: It documents falling trust among singles: women avoiding dating strangers, and men feeling women don't give them a fair chance.
more: It documents falling trust among singles: women avoiding dating strangers, and men feeling women don't give them a fair chance.
A 2024 survey cited in the dating-apps chapter.

head: When Harry Met Sally
dek: Amit loves it and calls it a charming film. Its premise that men and women can't be friends gave the Facebook friendship index its nickname.
more: Amit loves it and calls it a charming film. Its premise that men and women can't be friends gave the Facebook friendship index its nickname.
Introduces the chapter on whether men and women can be friends.

head: Can men and women be just friends?
dek: It explains the Facebook index and proposes naming it after When Harry Met Sally.
more: It explains the Facebook index and proposes naming it after When Harry Met Sally.
Amit calls it a beautiful piece.

head: Parade's End
dek: The passage argues that real intimate conversation needs years of living together.
more: The passage argues that real intimate conversation needs years of living together. Amit's response: 'Beautiful. You have a romantic soul in you.'
Ajay reads a passage from it about whether men and women can talk without becoming lovers.

head: Novels of Georges Simenon
dek: Amit says Simenon's work keeps returning to the idea that no person can fully communicate himself to another, which he sees as one of humanity's great problems.
more: Amit says Simenon's work keeps returning to the idea that no person can fully communicate himself to another, which he sees as one of humanity's great problems.
In his closing argument Amit calls Simenon one of his favourite novelists of all time.

head: Measure agency, not activity
dek: Good empowerment metrics ask who is choosing. Some numbers that sound bad signal freedom: rising divorce, more women in prison, more women travelling alone.
more: Good empowerment metrics ask who is choosing. Some numbers that sound bad signal freedom: rising divorce, more women in prison, more women travelling alone. Some that sound good can hide patriarchy: men downloading grocery apps or women placing pizza orders that men decided on. Office AC temperatures and the share of women on the street at night are other indirect measures.

head: Richer families pull women out of work
dek: Women's labour-force participation in India rose and then fell sharply, even as incomes grew.
more: Women's labour-force participation in India rose and then fell sharply, even as incomes grew. Amit stresses there are many causes. One is that once a family can afford it, a working wife is seen as hurting the family's honour, so women's earnings help raise the family's status and that status then keeps them at home.

head: Search data reveals the secret self
dek: Amit cites Gabriel García Márquez's idea that we have a public self, a private self known to a few intimates, and a secret self known to nobody.
more: Amit cites Gabriel García Márquez's idea that we have a public self, a private self known to a few intimates, and a secret self known to nobody. Stephens-Davidowitz's premise is that anonymous searching is where the secret self shows, because nobody is watching. On Facebook people present their best lives. Search data shows sexless marriages, regret and anxiety.

head: What searches reveal about sex and intimacy
dek: The top complaint about marriage is lack of sex.
more: The top complaint about marriage is lack of sex. Searches for 'sexless marriage' are 3.5 times more common than 'unhappy marriage', and complaints about a spouse not wanting sex are 16 times more common than about one not wanting to talk. The top complaint about boyfriends is that they won't have sex. Only 25% of men and 8% of women admit to searching for porn, yet more men search for porn than for weather. Amit stresses that searches and fantasies are not what people want in real life.

head: Parents' hidden gender bias
dek: Parents are 2.5 times more likely to ask Google whether their son is gifted than their daughter.
more: Parents are 2.5 times more likely to ask Google whether their son is gifted than their daughter. They ask whether their daughter is overweight about twice as often as their son. This contradicts the facts: young girls have larger vocabularies, are more often in gifted programmes, and about 28% of girls versus 25% of boys are overweight. Amit suspects the bias is worse in India.

head: You can't be loved if you hide yourself
dek: Many people never show their true selves to anyone, and some don't admit them even to themselves.
more: Many people never show their true selves to anyone, and some don't admit them even to themselves. Searching is the only place it shows. Amit draws the consequence: people can only love what you let them see.

head: Data shows you the median Indian
dek: Everyone lives in a bubble, and society is too large to know firsthand.
more: Everyone lives in a bubble, and society is too large to know firsthand. Aggregate data shows people unlike yourself. Ajay adds that it reflects the median Indian, who is very different from people like the hosts.

head: From communities of circumstance to communities of choice
dek: Before the internet, geography, school and work decided who you could meet, love or befriend.
more: Before the internet, geography, school and work decided who you could meet, love or befriend. Dating apps remove that limit. You are unlikely ever to meet a single destined soulmate, but your chances of meeting someone good rise sharply. Women can date with more privacy and less judgement, and Amit cites a figure that 60% of recent marriages began online. The gain is biggest for LGBTQ people.

head: The Tinder Gini coefficient
dek: Women swipe right on about 5 to 14% of profiles and men on about 50%, and men are 6.2 times more likely to like a woman than the reverse.
more: Women swipe right on about 5 to 14% of profiles and men on about 50%, and men are 6.2 times more likely to like a woman than the reverse. A few men get most of the attention while the median man gets almost none, and nearly all women get picked. The resulting resentment fuels incels and the manosphere.

head: Same instincts, far more choice
dek: Ajay asks what has changed, since desire hasn't changed in 65,000 years.
more: Ajay asks what has changed, since desire hasn't changed in 65,000 years. Amit's answer: a biologist would say men are wired to seek youth and beauty and women status and affluence, and he stresses that this is a description, not an endorsement. When your choices came from a small social circle, ordinary men found partners. With a million profiles, everyone is extremely selective and goes for people they could never have met before. Amit concludes the instincts haven't changed but the behaviour has. He also notes that culture can soften the uglier parts of human nature.

head: Rob Henderson's defect-defect equilibrium
dek: Men high on the 'dark triad' traits of psychopathy, narcissism and Machiavellianism may be 10 to 20% of dating-app users, and they are good at faking romantic qualities.
more: Men high on the 'dark triad' traits of psychopathy, narcissism and Machiavellianism may be 10 to 20% of dating-app users, and they are good at faking romantic qualities. Women they mistreat protect themselves by turning cold and exploiting ordinary men. Those men then treat ordinary women the same way to get even. The apps' anonymity and superficiality spread this until everyone is cold and calculating.

head: Marriage as a bundle that is coming apart
dek: Marriage arose when people met few others and social norms were enforced.
more: Marriage arose when people met few others and social norms were enforced. It was an uneasy arrangement that left both sexes partly unsatisfied but held together. It combines love, sex, companionship, friendship and parenting. In modern society that arrangement may no longer work, and nobody has figured out how to organise relationships once those parts separate. Amit suspects today's dating apps may one day look primitive.

head: The sex recession
dek: Despite apps promising plenty of options, many people are dropping out.
more: Despite apps promising plenty of options, many people are dropping out. Gen Z has much less sex than millennials, and Amit says some are returning to family values. In one survey, three in ten men and one in four women said they hadn't had sex in a year. The Romantic Recession report describes falling trust: women avoid strangers and men feel shut out.

head: Measurement that changes what it measures
dek: A satellite photographing North Korea at night doesn't change North Korea.
more: A satellite photographing North Korea at night doesn't change North Korea. Dating apps are different. They made romantic behaviour visible in data for the first time, and in doing so they changed that behaviour. When a tool makes something newly measurable, ask whether it is also reshaping it.

head: The When Harry Met Sally index
dek: Facebook mapped closeness across 1.4 trillion connections among 1.8 billion adults to build a cross-gender friendship index.
more: Facebook mapped closeness across 1.4 trillion connections among 1.8 billion adults to build a cross-gender friendship index. Zero means men and women are completely segregated, and one means equal numbers of same-sex and opposite-sex friends. India scores 0.35, higher than Amit expected given how awkward Indian men are with women. Ajay calls the separation of the sexes in India a social crisis and wants researchers to use the district-level data.

head: Apply the economist's toolkit to human nature
dek: Amit's closing argument is that the right policies are already known and won't be implemented, so data-minded people are often working on the wrong problems.
more: Amit's closing argument is that the right policies are already known and won't be implemented, so data-minded people are often working on the wrong problems. The deeper unsolved questions are about society and ourselves. He wants tools from psychology, sociology, anthropology, genetics, data, economics and literature applied to that question, citing Georges Simenon's theme that no one can fully communicate himself to another person.

head: Ajay's opening dig
more: Ajay's opening dig: 'in this team the internal name for Amit Varma is the Energizer Bunny because he goes on and on.' Amit responds with a running gag about Ajay lasting only five seconds, which comes back all episode.

head: Amit, explaining the private self
more: Amit, explaining the private self: 'very few people now know that you only last five seconds. Which was private until now. Now it's public.'

head: Amit's definition of Ajay's term
more: Amit's definition of Ajay's term 'digital exhaust': 'which is basically a phone running out of battery.'

head: After noting that more men search for porn than for weather, Amit tells Ajay he must search a lot for weather
more: After noting that more men search for porn than for weather, Amit tells Ajay he must search a lot for weather: 'But you can't jerk off to clouds. So there's an understandable reason for that.'

head: On the Australian autocomplete results
more: On the Australian autocomplete results 'an open marriage' and 'an open marriage novel': 'from this I can only gather that Australians want to read books about the things that they are bothered about.'

head: Amit's favourite finding from the book, which he says shows two deep truths about men
more: Amit's favourite finding from the book, which he says shows two deep truths about men, 'the self obsession and the stupidity': men search as often for how to perform oral sex on themselves as for how to give women an orgasm.

head: Stephens-Davidowitz on the long list of women's anxieties about how their bodies smell
more: Stephens-Davidowitz on the long list of women's anxieties about how their bodies smell: 'we are all so busy judging our own bodies that there is little energy left over to judge other people.'

head: On parental regret
more: On parental regret: 'So full buyer's remorse happening if you can call parenting buying.'

head: Amit after reading the search data
more: Amit after reading the search data: 'the next time I'm in a bus, I will look around me and I will think, huh, twenty percent of these men want to be breastfed. What the fuck, dude? I'll be like judging every guy out there.'

head: Asked if he has used a dating app, Ajay
more: Asked if he has used a dating app, Ajay says 'For about ten seconds.' Amit: 'So you lasted twice as long as one would expect. Well done. This used to be a family show till this episode.'

head: Amit on meeting Ajay online
more: Amit on meeting Ajay online, 'though not on a dating app': 'Though I would always swipe right on you. But anyway, if swipe right is the correct direction.'

head: On the name
more: On the name 'WHMSI': 'I was calling it the Whimsy Index till I realized that the I at the end of it stands for index. So it would be like calling it When Harry Met Sally Index Index, which we don't want to do.'

head: Ajay defines the Gini coefficient on the spot
more: Ajay defines the Gini coefficient on the spot, 'the area between the forty-five degree line and the cumulative distribution of income', before Amit applies it to Tinder.

head: Gabriel García Márquez's three selves (public, private, secret). Amit adds that the private self is known to a handful of intimates
more: Gabriel García Márquez's three selves (public, private, secret). Amit adds that the private self is known to a handful of intimates, 'Dunbar's smaller number, not one fifty, but five', and the secret self is known to nobody 'except Google Baba'.
'Dance like no one's looking': Amit's description of how we search online, as if nobody is watching.

head: Stephens-Davidowitz's line
more: Stephens-Davidowitz's line: 'Facebook is digital brag-to-my-friends-about-how-good-my-life-is serum,' where everyone seems happily married and on holiday in the Caribbean, while in reality people are ignoring calls from spouses they haven't slept with in years.

head: When Harry Met Sally, written by Nora Ephron, directed by Rob Reiner, starring Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan. Amit calls its restaurant scene
more: When Harry Met Sally, written by Nora Ephron, directed by Rob Reiner, starring Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan. Amit calls its restaurant scene 'the greatest orgasm in movie history', admits a crush on Meg Ryan, and quotes the premise that men and women can't be friends because 'the sex part always gets in the way.'

head: Rob Henderson
more: Rob Henderson, 'a guy who coined the term luxury beliefs', and his dark triad of psychopathy, narcissism and Machiavellianism applied to dating apps.

head: Georges Simenon, whom Amit calls one of his favourite novelists, on the theme running through all his work
more: Georges Simenon, whom Amit calls one of his favourite novelists, on the theme running through all his work: 'it is impossible for any one person to communicate himself to another person.'

head: 1929: How a New York Crash Toppled the World
dek: A crash in one market is too small to shake the world by itself. It needs amplification mechanisms to do that.
more: The Fed had already been doing a poor job through the Roaring Twenties when, for reasons still not fully understood, the New York Stock Exchange crashed in 1929. Shocks triggered further shocks until about 30% of the US banking system went bankrupt. Within months the crash was hurting the Indian economy. Ajay draws a direct line from the Great Depression to Adolf Hitler and the Second World War. He adds a twist: FDR and Hitler ran what we would now call Keynesian policies by improvising, not by reading Keynes.

A crash in one market is too small to shake the world by itself. It needs amplification mechanisms to do that. This is why Ajay says financial crises are 'upstream of wars and revolutions', and why 'the fate of the world is on the line'.
printed: New York falls, the world follows

head: 1991: Anatomy of India's Balance of Payments Crisis
dek: Once a devaluation looks near-certain, ordinary self-interested decisions all bet on it, and together they make it happen.
more: Fiscal deficits ballooned through the late 80s, especially in the political instability after Rajiv Gandhi. That cut domestic savings and raised India's need for foreign capital. Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait then hit remittances. Capital controls meant money could only enter through a few 'patli gallis' (narrow lanes), and these choked. Once everyone was sure the rupee would crash, exporters kept their dollars abroad, importers bought dollars early, and Indians moved assets out of the country.

Once a devaluation looks near-certain, ordinary self-interested decisions all bet on it, and together they make it happen. The lasting lesson is resilience: a country needs many independent channels for capital, not a few narrow ones.

head: Harshad Mehta and the Delayed Payoff of 1991
dek: What makes it a financial crisis is the damage to a function of finance, not the losses of particular firms.
more: In the early 90s, Harshad Mehta extracted money from the banking system and the RBI through a bond and money market scandal. He pumped it into extreme leverage on the Bombay Stock Exchange, which had structural design flaws. The result was a crazy asset bubble and then a crash. This came just as foreign capital was about to flow in after the 1991 reforms. Ajay thinks it delayed the investment boom, which peaked only in 1996-97.

What makes it a financial crisis is the damage to a function of finance, not the losses of particular firms. Prices allocate resources. When they swing wildly, the whole real economy pauses investment.

head: Thailand's Secret Forward Book and the Birth of Macro Hedge Funds
dek: Bad policy got punished, which keeps policymakers honest. 'Contagion' was just thinking people updating their beliefs, not a disease.
more: East Asian governments ran fixed exchange rates. When confidence in Thailand cracked, its central bank secretly sold the baht forward on a huge scale to defend it. One day it emerged that the forward position exceeded the entire reserves, and every speculator in the world shorted the baht. A few people who had studied Thailand through macroeconomics saw it coming and made fortunes. Ajay says this is where the 'macro hedge fund' was born. Speculators then took a hard look at Indonesia, South Korea and others, and the crisis spread from country to country.
Bad policy got punished, which keeps policymakers honest. 'Contagion' was just thinking people updating their beliefs, not a disease.

head: Soros Breaks the Pound
dek: A currency crisis is really a macroeconomics problem. Whoever understands the political and economic trade-off a government faces can predict whether it will hold.
more: George Soros, whom Ajay calls the greatest hero of currency crises, studied the Bank of England's dilemma. Defending the pound would need a sharp rise in interest rates, which would hurt an already weak economy close to an election. So he bet the pound would leave the European exchange rate mechanism and made over a billion dollars in a day. Once a few traders bet against a currency, hundreds more join, because those bets can themselves make the collapse happen. Amit adds that Soros called this 'reflexivity': the world changes through our actions.
A currency crisis is really a macroeconomics problem. Whoever understands the political and economic trade-off a government faces can predict whether it will hold.

head: The UTI / US-64 Crisis of 2000 and a Model Resolution
dek: Good crisis resolution limits moral hazard, gets public money back over time, and uses the crisis to push through overdue reform.
more: Around 2000, problems at the Calcutta Stock Exchange, the BSE and UTI's US-64 scheme fed into each other. Ajay admits that Raj Chitale had warned him US-64 would blow up, and that he hadn't understood it deeply. Yashwant Sinha brought Ajay into the Ministry of Finance, where he was 'a humble staffer'. Bimal Jalan and S. Narayan led the response. Sinha heard all the arguments and split the cost 50-50 between public money and the unit holders. When the assets were later sold, the net cost to the government was zero. UTI was privatised, its act was repealed, and the crisis was used to replace the BSE's Badla system with derivatives and a modern clearing corporation.
Good crisis resolution limits moral hazard, gets public money back over time, and uses the crisis to push through overdue reform. It also helps to admit openly where you were wrong.

head: Bernanke Apologises to Friedman
dek: Ajay calls this 'how great countries are made': learn from past mistakes across generations, then put the thinkers in the hot seat.
more: In a 2002 speech, Ben Bernanke was a Fed governor and not yet its chairman. Milton Friedman was on the stage with him. Bernanke told him, about the Great Depression, that the Fed had caused it. Friedman, Anna Schwartz and the young Bernanke had built the body of knowledge on what went wrong in 1929. Six years later, Bernanke ran the Fed through the 2008 crisis and applied it.
Ajay calls this 'how great countries are made': learn from past mistakes across generations, then put the thinkers in the hot seat. Amit adds that it is a rare case of a thinker becoming a doer.

head: 2008: The Fed Goes 5x
dek: Practical people stop at 10-30% because anything more is unprecedented.
more: The 2008 team was Hank Paulson, an ex-Goldman Sachs man, as Treasury Secretary, and Tim Geithner, a career civil servant, at the New York Fed. Bernanke chaired the Fed, and Larry Summers joined once Obama came in. They let Bear Stearns and Lehman fail but refused to let the functions of finance fail. The Fed's balance sheet grew roughly five-fold, from about $0.9 trillion to $4.5 trillion at its 2014 peak. Inflation stayed under control, and the crisis was largely contained within two or three years, compared with the Great Depression's nearly decade-long slump.
Practical people stop at 10-30% because anything more is unprecedented. Doing whatever it takes requires a theory you trust, in this case one built from studying 1929.
printed: Lend freely, and make them cry

head: Your Friendly Neighbourhood Banker
dek: Financial intermediation contains a large stock of tacit knowledge. When banks die, that knowledge is destroyed, and that is a separate channel through which crises hurt the real economy.
more: Ajay retells Bernanke's insight about pre-digital America. A local bank manager knew his borrowers personally, down to whether they were upstanding members of the community, and kept their repayment history in paper files. When the bank failed because of loans against shares in New York, that knowledge died with it. The borrower goes to a new bank, run by Vaishnav in Ajay's example, and has to start again with a 10-rupee loan. Multiply this across 30% of US banks and small firms everywhere lose working capital just when they need it most.
Financial intermediation contains a large stock of tacit knowledge. When banks die, that knowledge is destroyed, and that is a separate channel through which crises hurt the real economy.

head: Did Taxpayers Really Bail Out the Fat Cats?
dek: Judge a bailout on the whole intervention over its full life, not on one leg at one moment.
more: On UTI, Ajay had argued with M. Damodaran, who headed UTI. He now concedes that the temporary fiscal support turned into a big profit once the shares were sold five years later. In the US, TARP, headed by Neel Kashkari, committed about $0.45 trillion. After the assets were sold, a GAO report found the Treasury's loss was only $31 billion. The Fed's crisis-era asset purchases were very profitable, and those profits flow back to the Treasury as dividends. Ajay concludes that, taken as a whole, the US intervention made money.
Judge a bailout on the whole intervention over its full life, not on one leg at one moment. Amit strongly disagrees, arguing that who pays matters even if the totals come out positive.

head: It Doesn't Rain, It Pours: India 1997-2001
dek: Banks fail together because they share the same regulator's mistakes and the same business cycle.
more: India was hit by one shock after another. First came the August 1997 Asian crisis. In January 1998 the RBI sharply raised interest rates to defend the rupee. In May 1998 the nuclear tests brought problems from all sides. Then came the Y2K and dot-com bust, and then 9/11. Each blow hurt the real economy, and the real economy had borrowed from the banks.
Banks fail together because they share the same regulator's mistakes and the same business cycle. With 20x leverage, bad times in the economy quickly become bad times in the banks.

head: IL&FS 2018: A Leveraged Bet on Indian Infrastructure
dek: Sometimes a financial crisis is the visible part of a deeper failure in the real economy, here the failure of India's infrastructure model.
more: IL&FS defaulted in 2018. It had some bad internal practices, but its basic problem was that it was a leveraged bet on private-led infrastructure in India, and that bet failed. The crisis then spread to Yes Bank, other NBFCs and real estate developers.
Sometimes a financial crisis is the visible part of a deeper failure in the real economy, here the failure of India's infrastructure model.

head: The Beauty of Finance (Ep 21 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Amit calls it foundational to how they think about finance and one of the show's most popular episodes.
more: Amit calls it foundational to how they think about finance and one of the show's most popular episodes. It is the source of the 'finance is the brain of the economy' framing.
Recommended in the opening. Ajay then reuses its definition of finance to frame this episode.

head: The Journey of Indian Finance (Ep 71 of Everything is Everything)
dek: An insider's account of how Indian finance was built, from someone who had skin in the game.
more: An insider's account of how Indian finance was built, from someone who had skin in the game.
Recommended in the intro as a deep dive into a field Ajay helped shape.

head: The journey of Indian finance (paper)
dek: The written, researched companion to Ep 71.
more: The written, researched companion to Ep 71.
Amit mentions the 'great paper' Ajay wrote on how the field was shaped and his part in it.

head: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Ep 355 of The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: An insider account of how India responded to 2008.
more: An insider account of how India responded to 2008.
Amit calls it 'a classic episode' that covers Ajay's 2008 role. Ajay says he worked closely with KP Krishnan when Lehman's collapse hit India within hours.

head: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Ep 67 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Explains why the exchange rate is the economy's most important price and why governments managing it invite currency crises.
more: Explains why the exchange rate is the economy's most important price and why governments managing it invite currency crises.
Cited while explaining the East Asian crisis.

head: Impossible Germany
dek: Amit calls it 'absolutely magnificent', adding: 'Nothing to do with finance, and thank God for that.'
more: Amit calls it 'absolutely magnificent', adding: 'Nothing to do with finance, and thank God for that.'
A mid-episode recommendation prompted by Ajay's talk of the 'Impossible Trinity'. It opens with 'Impossible Germany, unlikely Japan'.

head: The GPT 5 Deep Research Info Dump on Financial Crises
dek: He thought it 'pretty good' for historical background and for summarising how Austrians, Keynesians and monetarists, as well as Minsky and Bernanke individually, read each crisis.
more: He thought it 'pretty good' for historical background and for summarising how Austrians, Keynesians and monetarists, as well as Minsky and Bernanke individually, read each crisis. It helps readers think for themselves.
Linked by Amit in his dissent chapter.

head: Economic Facts and Fallacies
dek: Sowell argues the economy began recovering within months of the 1929 crash, and that government intervention then made things worse.
more: Sowell argues the economy began recovering within months of the 1929 crash, and that government intervention then made things worse.
Cited for an alternative history of the Great Depression.

head: Economics in One Lesson
dek: Teaches you to ask not only what government spending appears to do, but what that money would have done if left with consumers.
more: Teaches you to ask not only what government spending appears to do, but what that money would have done if left with consumers.
Amit uses Hazlitt's warning to challenge the idea that Depression-era spending, including Hitler's, revived economies.

head: Economics in One Lesson (Ep 109 of Everything is Everything)
dek: Applies Hazlitt's seen-versus-unseen lens to government spending.
more: Applies Hazlitt's seen-versus-unseen lens to government spending.
The episode where Amit and Ajay previously argued about Hitler's spending.

head: What Really Happened?
dek: Amit calls it a 'great essay' showing how easy money, bad government incentives and quasi-government entities caused the crisis.
more: Amit calls it a 'great essay' showing how easy money, bad government incentives and quasi-government entities caused the crisis.
Amit's main source for seeing 2008 as a crisis of the state, not of capitalism.

head: Not What They Had in Mind
dek: A whole book making the case that 2008 was a failure of the state.
more: A whole book making the case that 2008 was a failure of the state.
Cited alongside Larry White on 2008.

head: In Praise of Floods
dek: Shows how suppressing every small disaster builds up a much bigger one.
more: Shows how suppressing every small disaster builds up a much bigger one. Amit applies this to bailouts and moral hazard.
Scott's latest book, used for its flood and forest fire analogies.

head: The Clash of Economic Ideas
dek: A good place to start: you see what Keynes, Friedman and others thought, and that 'they were all right in some ways, they were all wrong in some ways.'
more: A good place to start: you see what Keynes, Friedman and others thought, and that 'they were all right in some ways, they were all wrong in some ways.'
Recommended at the end as an overview of competing schools of thought.

head: A Financial Crisis Is When the Brain of the Economy Breaks
dek: Finance makes prices, allocates resources and solves people's financing problems: moving money across time, managing risk and funding big projects.
