more: Finance makes prices, allocates resources and solves people's financing problems: moving money across time, managing risk and funding big projects. A crisis is a sudden, nonlinear breakdown of those functions. One firm failing, or even a whole industry, is not a crisis if the economy can get the same work done through other channels. The hosts care about the functions, not the institutions.

head: Everyone Has Skin in the Game
dek: Financial crises impose costs on firms and people who did nothing wrong.
more: Financial crises impose costs on firms and people who did nothing wrong. Ajay's example is a small firm whose IPO plans are wrecked. Both hosts end on the same note: ordinary citizens should learn the basics of how crises work.

head: Positive Feedback Loops
dek: Market economies usually correct themselves. Finance, more than any other field, produces loops where bad gets worse.
more: Market economies usually correct themselves. Finance, more than any other field, produces loops where bad gets worse. Examples are bank failures worsening the economy, which then causes more bank failures, and falling NAVs triggering redemptions that push NAVs lower still. To understand any crisis, look for the amplification mechanism.

head: The Current Account Deficit Is Investment Minus Savings
dek: The usual story is that the current account deficit comes from trade. The deeper fact is an accounting identity: a country imports the gap between what it invests and what it saves.
more: The usual story is that the current account deficit comes from trade. The deeper fact is an accounting identity: a country imports the gap between what it invests and what it saves. Fiscal deficits reduce national savings, so they push up the need for foreign capital. That is how India's late-80s deficits set up the 1991 crisis.

head: Avoid a Monoculture: Build Many Pathways
dek: A resilient financial system has many institutional ways of doing the same job.
more: A resilient financial system has many institutional ways of doing the same job. If banks fail, non-bank finance carries on. For capital flows, India needs twenty big channels free of government involvement, not a few narrow lanes. Design for resilience from the start.

head: Crises Have Scripts, So Learn the Five Types
dek: Ajay's five types are: banking crises; currency crises; debt crises; securities market malfunctions; and mixed crises where several combine, as in Indonesia.
more: Ajay's five types are: banking crises; currency crises; debt crises; securities market malfunctions; and mixed crises where several combine, as in Indonesia. Each follows a recognisable script, which lets you see one move ahead, the way a doctor reads a cancer. Practitioners learn the script by living through a crisis. Everyone else should learn it from economic history and books, because 'you don't have to be a hen to know about eggs.'

head: Currency Crises Are Macro, and Contagion Is Rational
dek: Pegging an exchange rate eventually requires painful interest rate hikes.
more: Pegging an exchange rate eventually requires painful interest rate hikes. Traders who understand that trade-off can tell when a peg will break, as in Thailand in 1997 and Britain with Soros. Global markets are more powerful than any government, and Ajay thinks that is healthy because it disciplines bad policy. When the crisis spreads to the next country, that is investors updating their beliefs, not an irrational disease.

head: Banks: A Disaster-Prone 19th-Century Industry
dek: Ajay borrows the phrase from Merton Miller. Indian banks run about 20x leverage, so a 5% loss wipes them out.
more: Ajay borrows the phrase from Merton Miller. Indian banks run about 20x leverage, so a 5% loss wipes them out. Their loans are opaque, with no market price, and illiquid, because there is nowhere to sell them. Bank failures are linked because all banks share the same regulator's mistakes and the same business cycle. Banks also attract political looting, for the same reason robbers target them: that's where the money is. India's saving grace is that banks matter less and less for financing large firms.

head: The Friedman-Bernanke Playbook
dek: Friedman and Bernanke identified three Fed failures in the Depression.
more: Friedman and Bernanke identified three Fed failures in the Depression. First, it did not act as lender of last resort, which Bagehot defined as lending freely against good collateral at a penalty rate. Second, it let the money supply contract sharply, causing deflation, which raised the real burden of every debt. Third, as banks died, the knowledge they held about borrowers died too. The remedy is the functional view of finance: let individual firms fail, but protect the functions with whatever it takes.

head: Debt Crises: Interest Rate vs Top-Line Growth
dek: Borrowing from Peter to repay Paul is fine if you are only rolling over principal.
more: Borrowing from Peter to repay Paul is fine if you are only rolling over principal. Borrowing to pay interest puts you on a treadmill. For a government, the test is whether the nominal interest rate exceeds nominal GDP growth. If it does, debt-to-GDP rises nonlinearly until interest payments crowd out everything else. India hides this through financial repression, forcing the financial system to lend to the government cheaply, which Ajay calls violating the Magna Carta.

head: Liquid Securities Markets Are the Inner Sanctum
dek: If finance is at the core of the economy, securities markets are at the core of finance.
more: If finance is at the core of the economy, securities markets are at the core of finance. An illiquid market, like India's corporate bond market, turns a random large sale into falling prices, falling NAVs and more redemptions. The 1990s reformers' answer was deep, liquid markets open to everyone, with clearing corporations that never fail.

head: Why Crises Will Always Happen
dek: Ajay gives four reasons.
more: Ajay gives four reasons. First, human cognition: people shaped by twenty good years between ages 20 and 40 forget that things can go wrong, the most leveraged look like heroes, and statisticians fit models only on recent good years. Second, cleverness: finance is a Spy vs Spy game where well-paid, brilliant staff with lopsided payoffs find the gaps in every rule. Third, state failure: public choice problems and too much regulatory power. Fourth, the fallacy of composition: making each bank safe does not make the system safe, because many moves in the same direction add up to an avalanche. Believing perfect regulation can end crises is an illusion of control.

head: The Crisis Toolkit and the Standing Army
dek: Get the basics right first: regulate each firm properly. Then build a lender of last resort, which India has not yet begun.
more: Get the basics right first: regulate each firm properly. Then build a lender of last resort, which India has not yet begun. Then create a financial resolution framework that lets firms fail while protecting small savers. The Financial Resolution Bill that came out of FSLRC stalled after opposition from bank unions. Finally, keep a standing army of experts, data and authority, for example in the Department of Economic Affairs, modelled on America's post-2008 Office of Financial Research. It exists for the crises nobody designed for.
printed: A standing army for bad days

head: Ajay's Heresy: India Should Have a Small Banking System
dek: Ajay says a good banking system is a first-world achievement. It needs privatisation, a resolution law and a strong regulator, which would take India 25 years at best.
more: Ajay says a good banking system is a first-world achievement. It needs privatisation, a resolution law and a strong regulator, which would take India 25 years at best. Until then, he welcomes the steady shrinking of banks' role. India's future, in his view, lies in internationalised securities markets. Amit warns that this sounds like central planning: 'don't use state coercion to get there.'

head: Rejecting the Three Extremes
dek: Pure laissez-faire has a messy history. Only state-backed money with inflation targeting has worked well, and the world worked out inflation targeting only in 1987, in New Zealand.
more: Pure laissez-faire has a messy history. Only state-backed money with inflation targeting has worked well, and the world worked out inflation targeting only in 1987, in New Zealand. Crypto may mature but is still chaotic. The populist claim that bailouts protect fat cats ignores what the data show over time. Indian-style central planning ('ban it') suffocates innovation. Ajay's middle path is to let sophisticated finance grow, implement FSLRC, and accept that crises will come.

head: Amit's Dissent: The Austrian View
dek: In the Austrian view, crises begin with easy credit from central banks: the Roaring Twenties, and Alan Greenspan's long run of cheap money.
more: In the Austrian view, crises begin with easy credit from central banks: the Roaring Twenties, and Alan Greenspan's long run of cheap money. State intervention then deepens them. Amit cites the Smoot-Hawley tariffs, the Community Reinvestment Act pushing banks to lend to people who weren't creditworthy, Fannie and Freddie, and rating agency incentives. He reads Bernanke's apology as the Fed admitting state failure. He also disputes the claim that Hitler's spending revived Germany, saying the recovery began before Hitler came to power.

head: Moral Hazard and Who Really Pays
dek: Bailouts teach firms they will be rescued, which encourages reckless risk-taking and privatises profits while socialising losses.
more: Bailouts teach firms they will be rescued, which encourages reckless risk-taking and privatises profits while socialising losses. Amit rejects the argument that the bailouts made money later. He uses Suyash Rai's test: a cost-benefit argument fails when one group bears the cost and another gets the benefit. Bailouts are funded by everyone's taxes, including the indirect taxes paid by the poorest.

head: In Praise of Floods: Small Failures Prevent Big Ones
dek: Amit draws on James C. Scott.
more: Amit draws on James C. Scott. Dams and embankments raise a river above the surrounding land until the eventual flood is far worse. Putting out every small forest fire builds up fuel for a fire the size of a state. In the same way, suppressing every small financial failure may store up a bigger crisis. The Austrian response to systemic risk is 'so be it'. Otherwise you are just kicking the can down the road.

head: Be Sceptical, Not Dismissive, of Convention
dek: Amit places Ajay's view slightly to the right of mainstream economics.
more: Amit places Ajay's view slightly to the right of mainstream economics. He reminds listeners that conventional wisdom keeps changing, as accounts of the Great Depression have. Read the Austrians, Keynesians and monetarists, and keep studying economic history.

head: Amit says he is really a…
more: Amit says he is really a 'gentle listener' learning from Ajay, then adds: 'If you don't agree, why are you a regular viewer? It's because of me, isn't it? I'm so hot.'

head: Explaining what a neighbourhood bank manager knows about a regular borrower, Ajay describes himself
more: Explaining what a neighbourhood bank manager knows about a regular borrower, Ajay describes himself: 'when I get drunk in the evening, I'm extremely temperate in my ways. I only have milk in a bar. Okay, I'm that kind of guy.'

Amit's 'Incredible Trinity': he owes Vaishnav 100, Vaishnav owes Namsita 100, Namsita owes Amit 100. He borrows 100 from Ajay and everyone settles up, so total debt falls from 300 to 100, 'and it's actually zero because I'm not gonna fucking pay you back.' Ajay earnestly turns it into a lesson on network effects in crises, then explains: 'I am a one-track mind... when I do finance, I do it seriously.' Amit: 'You've just dissected a frog, but well done.'

head: Ajay on who makes a deep, liquid market
more: Ajay on who makes a deep, liquid market: 'There should be foreigners, there should be Indians, there should be Bengalis, there should be Tamilians, there should be algorithmic traders, there should be astrology traders.'

head: Ajay on complacent practitioners who think execution is all that matters and
more: Ajay on complacent practitioners who think execution is all that matters and that 'watching these verbose males on long-winded shows is completely a waste of time'. Earlier he lists among humanity's failings: 'People fail to watch an EIE episode on financial crisis.'

head: Ajay on the…
more: Ajay on the 'lefties' who say evil capitalists profited from Thailand's collapse: 'No, it's called capitalism. This is how it works.'

head: Ajay, defending his small-banking dream
more: Ajay, defending his small-banking dream: 'So I said I hate to pick winners, I hate to pick losers. But I am proposing a loser.' Amit: 'I mean you're free to imagine your dream world, but don't use state coercion to get there.'

head: After Ajay rejects the…
more: After Ajay rejects the 'fat cat' story, Amit starts a pun: 'So Ajay, what do you call the confession of a cat?' Ajay deflects: 'The wordsmithing that is required is what do you call the confession of a fat cat, and we need to find a correct answer. I want to tell you about financial crisis.' Amit: 'No fooling around. Continue.'

head: Spy vs Spy
more: Spy vs Spy: 'you have to be my age to know something called Mad Magazine and a cartoon strip called Spy versus Spy,' says Ajay, to describe the cat-and-mouse game between regulators and bankers. Amit: 'Are you thirteen again? Spy versus spy was amazing.'

head: The bank robber's line
more: The bank robber's line, 'Why do you rob banks? Answer, because that's where the money is.' Ajay uses it to explain why every political economy tries to grab bank money.

head: Ajay's twist on the old adage
more: Ajay's twist on the old adage: 'Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to participate in its repetition.'

head: Ajay opens by noting that we pay attention to aviation safety only when
more: Ajay opens by noting that we pay attention to aviation safety only when 'an Air India plane crashes into a medical college hostel in Amdavad'. Financial crises get the same limited attention span.

head: Walter Bagehot's lender-of-last-resort rule, in Ajay's words
more: Walter Bagehot's lender-of-last-resort rule, in Ajay's words: 'Lend freely against good collateral at a penal rate. So people should cry when they come asking for credit from a central bank.'

head: Ajay treats the flawed pre-2008 securitisation models as a scientific gap, not a moral failure
more: Ajay treats the flawed pre-2008 securitisation models as a scientific gap, not a moral failure: 'You needed to figure out the photoelectric effect in order to play correctly around it.' He credits 'our friend' Viral Acharya with improving understanding of those products.

head: The East Asian crisis, says Ajay
more: The East Asian crisis, says Ajay, 'is where the word macro hedge fund was born', because a few people analysed Thailand through macroeconomics and saw the peg would break.

head: New Zealand, 1987: Ajay says only then did central banking
more: New Zealand, 1987: Ajay says only then did central banking 'get to the basics' with inflation targeting. 'Conventional money took a thousand years before we got to inflation targeting', which is why he is patient but sceptical about crypto.

head: Magna Carta: describing India's financial repression, Ajay
more: Magna Carta: describing India's financial repression, Ajay says 'We basically violate the Magna Carta,' because the state forcibly takes money from the economy to fund its debt.

head: Why a Poker Player Loves Hoodies
dek: Since signals leak, the disciplined move is to shut the channel entirely.
more: Amit's fondness for hoodies dates to his years as a professional poker player (2010–2015). Poker is overwhelmingly math, but live games leak tells: dilating pupils, a pulsing carotid artery. So after betting he would cover his face, avoid eye contact, never smile or react, and keep the exact same posture whether bluffing or not. His own favourite read was to crack a joke and check whether the opponent's smile was genuine (comfortable) or fake (worried). He adds that a fake smile might just mean a great hand and an urgent need for the loo.
Since signals leak, the disciplined move is to shut the channel entirely. And reading people only lets you update your priors a little. It never gives you certainty.

head: The Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
dek: Experience only shows you the present and a narrow slice of it. Spontaneous order, positive-sum exchange and the workings of an economy can't be seen with your own eyes.
more: A friend who knew Narendra Modi when he was Gujarat's chief minister told Amit this story. Modi once recounted, in tears, a childhood night when his mother was ill and hot, and he flicked the fan switch only to find there was no electricity. Her point was that Modi's understanding is purely experiential. He grasps electricity and roads because he lived them, and he made village electrification a priority. But he doesn't go beyond what he has seen. Amit doesn't blame him for not reading, given his humble background. But he says such a leader should then surround himself with experts, and he sees little evidence of that.
Experience only shows you the present and a narrow slice of it. Spontaneous order, positive-sum exchange and the workings of an economy can't be seen with your own eyes. They have to be read.

head: Stalin the Erudite Reader
dek: Reading makes better citizens on average, but it is not a sufficient condition for goodness.
more: Ajay ranks Stalin as history's second-worst monster, after Mao and ahead of Hitler. Yet he was considered extremely sophisticated and erudite. Citing Stephen Kotkin, Ajay says Stalin, language problems aside, could sit for an hour's comfortable conversation with any philosopher in the world. He had a vast library, read intensively and scribbled in his books, so his reactions survive. Amit adds Mao, a foundational thinker on guerrilla warfare. Ajay stresses that Mao actually theorized how a guerrilla force could beat the KMT rather than winging it.
Reading makes better citizens on average, but it is not a sufficient condition for goodness. Some of history's worst monsters were serious readers and theorists.

head: Tolstoy Sobbing Through War and Peace
dek: Fiction works as an empathy engine because it lets you fully inhabit another consciousness.
more: Ajay recalls reading that while Tolstoy was writing War and Peace, he walked around his house sobbing uncontrollably because he was lost in the minds of his characters.
Fiction works as an empathy engine because it lets you fully inhabit another consciousness. The writer feels this at full intensity, and the careful reader gets a share of it.

head: Ambushed by After Virtue
dek: Serendipity and pleasure, not duty, drive a real reading life. Idea books can grip you as hard as stories do, and when one does, you should embrace it.
more: Exhausted and stressed during a six-episode shoot, Amit opened his iPad at bedtime only to keep Harold Bloom's book ready on Kindle. Searching 'Bloom' also surfaced Bloomsbury titles, including Alasdair MacIntyre's After Virtue. Suyash Rai had recommended the book long ago. Pratap Bhanu Mehta had recently praised MacIntyre over lunch, and MacIntyre had died that May. Amit read the first chapter and half the second, woke with the argument running through his head, and skipped his usual seventeen snoozes. He then read it over morning coffee instead of prepping for the episode.
Serendipity and pleasure, not duty, drive a real reading life. Idea books can grip you as hard as stories do, and when one does, you should embrace it.

head: Ila Patnaik's Paperclip Jar
dek: A tiny, visible ritual cost can change behaviour more than any lecture.
more: At NIPFP, Ila Patnaik was irritated that the admin team kept bringing her decisions they could make themselves. Her rule: every time you come to ask me a question, drop a paperclip into this jar. People would walk up, deposit the clip, hang their heads in shame, and then ask. The flow of trivial interruptions fell dramatically and the team became more thoughtful. Amit's verdict: 'Ila is a paperclip minimizer.'

A tiny, visible ritual cost can change behaviour more than any lecture. It makes people pause and ask whether the question is really worth it. It is the same mechanism as gamifying a habit, run in reverse.

head: His Father's Sixty Volumes
dek: Books can be kept out of love rather than use. The Synopticon also shows what thematic, cross-canon reading looks like: one quote leads you straight into another author's volume.
more: Amit's father owned the 60-volume Great Books of the Western World, most of it still wrapped. For about ten years he urged Amit to take it to Bombay, and Amit kept refusing for lack of space in his rented house. After his father died, his library of many thousands of books went to a community library, but Amit kept these sixty as a memory of his dad. The two volumes he actually reads sit on his desk: the Synopticon, Mortimer Adler's essays on themes like love, death, desire and purpose, synthesised across the whole canon.
Books can be kept out of love rather than use. The Synopticon also shows what thematic, cross-canon reading looks like: one quote leads you straight into another author's volume.
printed: Great Books, kept for a father

head: Thirty Books for Two Gandhi Episodes
dek: This is synoptical reading in practice. Each new entry point into one subject makes your understanding richer than any single narrative could.
more: For his two-part Seen and the Unseen series on Gandhi with Ramachandra Guha, Amit read some thirty books: every available biography, essay and analysis. Afterwards Guha recommended Rajmohan Gandhi's The Good Boatman, a set of thematic essays on Gandhi's life, which Amit regards as a synoptical book that synthesises a lot.
This is synoptical reading in practice. Each new entry point into one subject makes your understanding richer than any single narrative could.

head: The 200-Books Pile-On
dek: Reading is not a competition. Speed is just the residue of a long habit.
more: Amit once said, quite honestly, that he had read two hundred books in a year, and a Twitter storm followed, with people abusing him for showing off. He has never mentioned a number since, and says his count is now a fraction of that. He credits his speed to a reading habit begun at age three or four, which means forty-five years of practice.
Reading is not a competition. Speed is just the residue of a long habit. What matters is the time spent in a contemplative state, not the score.

head: The World's Slowest Reader
dek: Depth can beat volume. There is no single right reading speed, and making peace with your own mode beats chasing someone else's numbers.
more: Ajay confesses he reads pages slowly and has only one mode. He would like to read three times the papers and ten times the books he does. But he plays with every sentence, word and argument as he goes, and needs extreme attention and long chunks of time. He has stopped fighting it, because everything that has happened to him has come out of reading this way.
Depth can beat volume. There is no single right reading speed, and making peace with your own mode beats chasing someone else's numbers.

head: The DC Friend and the AI Summaries
dek: A book's value is not information transfer. It teaches you how to think, and that process has no shortcut.
more: On a drive in DC, a friend proudly told Amit, expecting approval, that he had AI make 500-word summaries of Amit's eight-hour Seen and the Unseen episodes. He did the same for books, and felt he now knew everything in them. Amit was viscerally angry, not because it was his show but because it is such a stupid way to consume knowledge.
A book's value is not information transfer. It teaches you how to think, and that process has no shortcut.

head: How to Read a Book
by: Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren
dek: Lays out the four levels of reading (elementary, inspectional, analytical, synoptical).
more: Lays out the four levels of reading (elementary, inspectional, analytical, synoptical). It also gives a concrete four-step method for analytical reading: classify the book, state its gist briefly, outline its parts, and define the problem the author is solving.
The first of three classic books Amit drew on for the 'how to read a book' section, mainly as a guide to nonfiction.

head: How to Read and Why
dek: Bloom explains what attitude each genre demands. Slow down for short stories and novels, memorize poems, and read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again.
more: Bloom explains what attitude each genre demands. Slow down for short stories and novels, memorize poems, and read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again.
Recommended explicitly 'for gentle readers' as Amit moves from nonfiction to fiction, poetry and plays.

head: Reading Like a Writer
dek: Teaches you to notice the author's tools, such as why one word and not another, and how sentence length builds rhythm or immersion.
more: Teaches you to notice the author's tools, such as why one word and not another, and how sentence length builds rhythm or immersion. Amit says this enriches reading even if you never write.
The third book recommended in the 'how to read' section.

head: Is Google Making Us Stupid?
dek: Argues that our shallow interaction with the internet keeps us from going deep and makes us stupider, while books pull the other way.
more: Argues that our shallow interaction with the internet keeps us from going deep and makes us stupider, while books pull the other way. Amit thinks things have only gotten worse since.
Carr's famous 2008 essay, which Amit believes was an Atlantic cover story, cited under 'reading is good for the brain'.

head: Jim Heckman's work (The Heckman Equation)
dek: Children aged zero to five who grow up hearing 'ten-letter words', a proxy for complex discourse, gain a layer of intelligence that can't be made up later.
more: Children aged zero to five who grow up hearing 'ten-letter words', a proxy for complex discourse, gain a layer of intelligence that can't be made up later.
A study Amit says he and Ajay often refer to, cited when arguing that complexity of input shapes the brain.

head: Man's Search for Meaning
dek: Frankl records that for concentration-camp inmates, literature, whether held, remembered or discussed, gave solace and a sense that the present moment is not all there is.
more: Frankl records that for concentration-camp inmates, literature, whether held, remembered or discussed, gave solace and a sense that the present moment is not all there is.
Cited as 'his great book' under reading as good for the psyche.

head: Atomic Habits
dek: Source of two ideas used in the episode. Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement.
more: Source of two ideas used in the episode. Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. And small dopamine rewards help habits stick, like the writer who moved a hairpin between jars for every paragraph or the bodybuilder who moved marbles for every set.
Called 'his great book' in the section on building a reading habit.

head: The Paris Review Book for Planes, Trains, Elevators, and Waiting Rooms
dek: Its stories run from elevator-ride length to long-haul-flight length. That makes it ideal when you want fiction but not a novel's full immersion.
more: Its stories run from elevator-ride length to long-haul-flight length. That makes it ideal when you want fiction but not a novel's full immersion.
Mentioned under 'choice architecture': it's fine to read several books across genres at once.

head: The End of History and the Last Man (and the essay 'The End of History?')
dek: A rare case where the book is genuinely great and goes well beyond the essay it grew from.
more: A rare case where the book is genuinely great and goes well beyond the essay it grew from.
Cited during inspectional reading, against the trend of nonfiction books that should have stayed essays.

head: The Good Boatman
dek: Its thematic essays on Gandhi's life synthesise a vast amount of material.
more: Its thematic essays on Gandhi's life synthesise a vast amount of material. Amit holds it up as a model synoptical book.
Recommended to Amit by Ramachandra Guha after the Gandhi episodes. Amit calls it a 'great book'.

head: Great Books of the Western World (especially the Synopticon volumes)
dek: Adler's thematic essays on death, love, desire, purpose and agency draw on the entire canon.
more: Adler's thematic essays on death, love, desire, purpose and agency draw on the entire canon. Amit says they fill him with 'awe' and 'joy', and send him to read the original authors.
His late father's 60-volume set. The two Synopticon volumes sit on Amit's desk.

head: How Should One Read a Book?
dek: Amit calls it a great essay on exactly this episode's question.
more: Amit calls it a great essay on exactly this episode's question.
First on Amit's list of further reading on the subject, offered instead of end-of-show recommendations.

head: Aspects of the Novel
dek: It gives a great insight into a great novelist's mind.
more: It gives a great insight into a great novelist's mind.
Part of Amit's further-reading list. Written in 1927.

head: Why Read the Classics?
dek: Amit calls it an excellent book on the case for the classics.
more: Amit calls it an excellent book on the case for the classics.
Part of Amit's further-reading list.

head: How Fiction Works
dek: Useful for readers, not just writers. It explains voice and how the modern novel evolved, including Flaubert's role.
more: Useful for readers, not just writers. It explains voice and how the modern novel evolved, including Flaubert's role. Amit promises it 'will transform the way you read a book'.
A book Amit says he 'absolutely loves', from his further-reading list.

head: The Pleasures of Reading in an Age of Distraction
dek: A contemporary take on reading well amid the distractions this episode keeps fighting.
more: A contemporary take on reading well amid the distractions this episode keeps fighting.
The recent book that closes Amit's further-reading list.

head: Susan Thomas's book club in Bombay
dek: An in-person reading community in Bombay. Joining one is the ultimate way to design your environment for reading.
more: An in-person reading community in Bombay. Joining one is the ultimate way to design your environment for reading.
Plugged right after the advice to find a community of readers.

head: Being Muslim in India (Ep 216, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Shows chapter-by-chapter note-taking in action. The book also supplies a 'beautiful example of Show Don't Tell' that Amit reads out.
more: Shows chapter-by-chapter note-taking in action. The book also supplies a 'beautiful example of Show Don't Tell' that Amit reads out.
Used in the Roam demo, which shows his notes on Ghazala Wahab's book Born a Muslim.

head: Connect More Dots: Books Give You Many Lives
dek: We paint pictures of the world by connecting dots, and more dots mean a higher-definition picture.
more: We paint pictures of the world by connecting dots, and more dots mean a higher-definition picture. Experience gives you only the present and a narrow slice of it. Spontaneous order, positive-sum exchange and the complexity of an economy can't be seen. Ajay's framing: a practical doer reaches seventy with one life's knowledge, while a reader taps hundreds or thousands of lives.

head: The Quality of Leisure Shapes the Brain
dek: Scrolling and reading can both look like time-pass, but scrolling hops from factoid to factoid without building anything.
more: Scrolling and reading can both look like time-pass, but scrolling hops from factoid to factoid without building anything. Reading forges connections. Citing Nicholas Carr, neuroscientist Maryanne Wolf, and London cabbies whose brains rewired once they stopped memorising routes, Amit argues that the structure of what you engage with changes your brain. A richer vocabulary also means more dots: Wittgenstein held that our understanding is limited by language.

head: Narrative Imagination
dek: Reading, especially fiction, lets you feel pain that would never happen to you, which expands what Martha Nussbaum calls narrative imagination.
more: Reading, especially fiction, lets you feel pain that would never happen to you, which expands what Martha Nussbaum calls narrative imagination. Faced with a curt colleague, you can assume he's an asshole, or imagine he's preoccupied with work. The second reading replaces reptile-brain ego with understanding and deepens relationships. Ajay argues fiction is the prime engine of this; Amit agrees but says good biography does it too. So read both, and don't take a utilitarian, facts-only view of reading.
printed: Eleven reasons to open a book

head: Reading as Solace and Self-Knowledge
dek: In dark times literature works like therapy, as Frankl saw in the camps.
more: In dark times literature works like therapy, as Frankl saw in the camps. It also holds up a mirror. Seeing a character feel what you thought was unique to you exposes your private and even secret self, in the sense of Gabriel García Márquez's public, private and secret selves. That is how reading answers the Greek command to 'know thyself'.

head: Reading Saves Solitude From Loneliness
dek: In a funk we see the world through one prism, and reading, which Schopenhauer called thinking with someone else's head, offers others.
more: In a funk we see the world through one prism, and reading, which Schopenhauer called thinking with someone else's head, offers others. Learning to be alone without being lonely is an essential skill, and books provide that companionship. Harold Bloom: imaginative literature is otherness, and so it alleviates loneliness.

head: Reading as a Civic Good: Necessary, Not Sufficient
dek: Following Tocqueville, democracy needs informed citizens, not just voters, and reading is how people get informed.
more: Following Tocqueville, democracy needs informed citizens, not just voters, and reading is how people get informed. Ajay adds that a reader imposes a positive externality, making the people around them think and debate better. But the hosts flag the limit: Stalin and Mao were serious readers and theorists. Reading is not a guarantee of goodness.

head: Feed Your Internal LLM
dek: Aspiring writers who don't read have a training corpus that is too small.
more: Aspiring writers who don't read have a training corpus that is too small. Creativity works on what you've absorbed. Someone who has heard a million songs writes better songs than someone who has heard a hundred, not by copying but because their subconscious has learned the forms. Even mindless reading teaches by osmosis. Ajay returns to the metaphor at the end: the payoff of reading is that you're training your LLM.

head: A Conversation Across Time
dek: Every species communicates, but only humans carry that conversation across time.
more: Every species communicates, but only humans carry that conversation across time. Through books you can argue with Plato, Adi Shankaracharya or a dead author a continent away, the way Ajay felt James C. Scott berating him in Seeing Like a State. Without books there are no giants' shoulders to stand on.

head: A Latticework of Models: Everything Is Everything
dek: One or two mental models can't explain a reality this complicated. Reading builds Charlie Munger's 'latticework of models': incentives here, anthropology there, natural selection, genetics, the cinema of an era.
more: One or two mental models can't explain a reality this complicated. Reading builds Charlie Munger's 'latticework of models': incentives here, anthropology there, natural selection, genetics, the cinema of an era. The disciplines are silos only in name, since all of them study the human condition. That insight is where the show's name comes from.

head: Habit Over Targets, Identity Over Goals
dek: Don't set targets like 'I'll finish that prize-winner'. Build a habit, which James Clear calls the compound interest of self-improvement.
more: Don't set targets like 'I'll finish that prize-winner'. Build a habit, which James Clear calls the compound interest of self-improvement. Be bloody-minded for about three months, until the loop is hardwired in the basal ganglia and feels automatic. Better still, start from identity. Ask who the best version of you is. If that person reaches for a book instead of a phone, actions flow from that self-image and a missed day doesn't break you.

head: Engineer the Habit: Small, Frequent, Anchored, Designed
dek: Start small: two pages or fifteen minutes. Favour frequency over duration.
more: Start small: two pages or fifteen minutes. Favour frequency over duration. Anchor reading to an existing routine such as morning coffee, the commute or bedtime, because neurons that fire together wire together. Design your environment: keep books everywhere, put Kindle up front and delete social apps, or use a dedicated device. Ajay's version is an old iPad with only a book reader and a throwaway account. Pre-decide what you'll read next to avoid decision fatigue, the way Ajay runs 'the planner code' once each morning and then just executes. Gamify with small rewards. And find a community of readers.

head: Adler's Four Levels of Reading
dek: Elementary reading means understanding the sentences.
more: Elementary reading means understanding the sentences. Inspectional reading is a first date with the book: table of contents, preface, a skim to see whether it's really an essay padded into a book, as many modern nonfiction books are. Analytical reading means chewing: classify the book, state its gist in a line, outline its parts, and name the problem the author is solving. Synoptical reading means reading many books on one subject, say Bernanke, Minsky, Friedman, Keynes and the Austrians on financial crises, until the picture deepens.

head: Go Down the Rabbit Holes
dek: When a subject grabs you, don't stop at one book. Chase the footnotes, look up the people mentioned, ask ChatGPT, check Wikipedia, and buy the next book.
more: When a subject grabs you, don't stop at one book. Chase the footnotes, look up the people mentioned, ask ChatGPT, check Wikipedia, and buy the next book. These detours are not digressions. They are how knowledge gets rich.

head: Read Fiction, Poems and Plays Differently
dek: Following Bloom, never skim fiction. Short stories favour the tacit and make you discern what the writer leaves out (show, don't tell; Hemingway's iceberg).
more: Following Bloom, never skim fiction. Short stories favour the tacit and make you discern what the writer leaves out (show, don't tell; Hemingway's iceberg). A novel becomes a different book for each reader, and it pays to ask whether the characters change and why. Memorize poems, because poetry lives in rhythm. Read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again. Reading like a writer adds attention to form: clipped hard-boiled sentences for action, Saramago's pages-long sentences for immersion.

head: Format Doesn't Matter; the Words Do
dek: Paper, Kindle, phone or audiobook is just packaging. Insisting on physical books shows nostalgia, not love of literature.
more: Paper, Kindle, phone or audiobook is just packaging. Insisting on physical books shows nostalgia, not love of literature. Audiobooks are a somewhat different experience because you can't easily pause and reread, but they let people with no quiet time, like a commuter hanging on a local train, still spend that time with words.

head: Quit Books Freely: Your Lifetime Book Budget
dek: Multiply an optimistic life expectancy by an optimistic books-per-year figure.
more: Multiply an optimistic life expectancy by an optimistic books-per-year figure. That is roughly the most books you'll ever read, a pitiful fraction of what exists. So drop books you aren't enjoying without sunk-cost guilt, even celebrated prize-winners. And don't be a snob: an airport bestseller or an academic paper is fine if it brings enjoyment or enlightenment.

head: Reading Is Not an Olympics
dek: Book counts are meaningless. What matters is time spent in the contemplative, processing state that reading induces.
more: Book counts are meaningless. What matters is time spent in the contemplative, processing state that reading induces. Five books a year is fine, and speed is just the residue of a long habit. Don't even keep score.
printed: Drop the book, not the habit

head: Reading Is a Social Project
dek: Ajay compares it to eating healthy, which is nearly impossible for one person in a household full of junk food.
more: Ajay compares it to eating healthy, which is nearly impossible for one person in a household full of junk food. Modern nutrition thinking changes the whole food environment instead. Likewise, reading thrives in a community of family and friends, a book club, or group viewings of the show that pause at each chapter break to argue. Arguing turns passive consumption into active learning and makes the knowledge your own.

head: Books Are Not Information
dek: A thousand-word AI summary lets you sound sophisticated at a cocktail party, and you'll forget most details of a book within a month anyway.
more: A thousand-word AI summary lets you sound sophisticated at a cocktail party, and you'll forget most details of a book within a month anyway. The point is the ten to twenty hours of intimate conversation with one great mind: grappling, disagreeing, having aha moments. That changes your brain and even your character. Information is trivial and you can look it up.

head: Note-Taking as Mapping the Territory
dek: Amit's Roam workflow starts by making the book's chapters top-level entries, then nesting every point and quote beneath them.
more: Amit's Roam workflow starts by making the book's chapters top-level entries, then nesting every point and quote beneath them. Bracketed tags create bidirectional links that gather related quotes across sources. When material has no structure, like Mahima Vashisht's hundred-plus newsletter posts, he builds his own themes layer: controlling female sexuality, stereotypes, a world designed by men. The result isn't just notes but a framework for the whole subject.

head: Amit opens an episode on reading by parsing his own sentence
more: Amit opens an episode on reading by parsing his own sentence: 'What does it mean to say I'm a huge fan of hoodies? It means two things. One, I'm huge, and two, I'm a fan of hoodies... So you see, a careful reading will reward you with additional meaning and layers.'

head: Amit, announcing his eleven reasons
more: Amit, announcing his eleven reasons: 'I'm not scared of taking a number because Ajay can't count, but Amit can.'

head: After Ajay explains that Mao theorized his way into guerrilla warfare, Amit
more: After Ajay explains that Mao theorized his way into guerrilla warfare, Amit says: 'Kinda like you, Ajay Shah, right? You theorize about the world and then you do a YouTube show.' Ajay: 'Those who can do, the others become podcasters.'

head: Amit on communication between species
more: Amit on communication between species: 'Dogs will bark to each other, cats will meow to each other, especially while confessing, you'll have meowpas.'

head: Amit, voicing a viewer
more: Amit, voicing a viewer: 'Ajay Shah recommended Seeing Like a State on that very cool YouTube show, and so far I've been watching it for his sex appeal and his shirts and Amit's deep, dulcet tones.'

head: On abandoned reading goals
more: On abandoned reading goals: 'fifth day you're like, I'm not a books kind of person, I'm a Netflix kind of person, or a Netflix and chill kind of person if you're adequately gregarious.'
Amit says 'Frequency matters more than duration', and Ajay laughs. Amit: 'You thought of sex again.' Ajay: 'Bro. Frequency matters more than duration. What else can I think of?'

head: On removing competition to reading
more: On removing competition to reading: 'If you're living with other people, start living alone. I'm kidding. You know, why are you nodding?'

head: On James Clear's bodybuilder who moved a marble between jars for every set
more: On James Clear's bodybuilder who moved a marble between jars for every set: 'one sincerely hopes he never dropped his weights on his head because then he might have lost his marbles... I keep making this joke. People keep laughing, I don't know why.'

head: Amit on Ila Patnaik's jar
more: Amit on Ila Patnaik's jar: 'in AI they run this famous thought experiment about the paperclip maximizer. It turns out that Ila is a paperclip minimizer.'

head: Introducing Reading Like a Writer
more: Introducing Reading Like a Writer: 'the third book I want to recommend for you is by Francine Prose, aptly named.'

head: Amit demonstrates immersive long sentences with one of his own, ending
more: Amit demonstrates immersive long sentences with one of his own, ending '...and you are them and they are you, and see what a long sentence this was.'

head: On viewers pausing the show to argue, Amit worries they might be…
more: On viewers pausing the show to argue, Amit worries they might be saying 'Ajay is so sexy, why is Amit on the show. How would the show look with two Ajays talking to each other?'

head: In the Roam demo, Amit lets a secret out: listeners of The Seen and the Unseen are impressed that Amit has all the quotes at his fingertips.
more: In the Roam demo, Amit lets a secret out: listeners of The Seen and the Unseen are impressed that Amit has all the quotes at his fingertips. 'No, bro. I'm kind of reading them out from this.'

head: Ajay quotes a hard-boiled fiction line
more: Ajay quotes a hard-boiled fiction line, 'She had a smile that never reached her eyes'. Amit can't place which of 'those hard-boiled fiction boys' wrote it, and later names Dashiell Hammett and Raymond Chandler as masters of terse action prose. Ajay adds the craft trick: a run of short sentences makes one elaborate sentence come alive.

head: Montaigne
more: Montaigne: 'I have no more made my book than my book has made me', used for reading as self-discovery.

head: Harold Bloom
more: Harold Bloom: 'Information is readily available. Where is wisdom to be found?' Also: 'Imaginative literature is otherness and as such alleviates loneliness.'

head: Hemingway's iceberg theory
more: Hemingway's iceberg theory and 'show, don't tell', illustrated by Amit's image of himself at a window as the light fades and his tea goes cold, undrunk. Ghazala Wahab's grandfather offers another: he shelled pine nuts all day to reward the grandkids with fistfuls in the evening, rather than her writing 'he loved us'.
'Neurons that fire together, wire together', which is why a song can bring back the memory of a first kiss, or a first slap, and why anchoring reading to existing routines works.

head: The 400-Rupee Shirt That Paid 100 Rupees in Tax
dek: A headline tax rate can hide the real burden. What matters is whether tax piles on top of tax.
more: Ajay follows one shirt through four stages under a 'mild' 10% tax on every sale. A farmer sells cotton for 100, a spinner sells yarn for 200, the cloth is sold to a tailor for 300, and the tailor sells the shirt for 400. Each invoice carries 10%, so the government collects 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 = 100 rupees on a shirt priced at 400, an effective 25%. He then runs the same chain as a VAT. Each seller deducts the tax already paid upstream (input tax credit), so each stage remits only 10 and the total tax on the shirt is exactly 40, a true 10%.
A headline tax rate can hide the real burden. What matters is whether tax piles on top of tax. The same 10% can mean 25% or 10% depending purely on the design.
printed: Ten per cent, four times over

head: Why It's Called 'GST' and Not 'VAT'
dek: The GST began as a fix for India's fiscal problem, not a tax-collection scheme.
more: In 2003, Vijay Kelkar led a committee appointed by Jaswant Singh on implementing the FRBM Act. Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay concluded that India's fiscal problem could not be solved without a proper VAT. But the word 'VAT' was already taken by CENVAT, a 'central VAT' that wasn't really a VAT: it didn't handle input tax credit or services correctly. To avoid confusion, they coined a new name, 'Goods and Services Tax'.
The GST began as a fix for India's fiscal problem, not a tax-collection scheme. Its name was a deliberate move to separate a clean idea from a flawed one that already carried the label.
printed: A VAT by any other name

head: The Long Road From the 2003 Report to a Flawed GST
dek: A good idea can be adopted in name and still lose its core. Political economy can shrink a reform until little more than the label survives.
more: The authors proposed a way forward that did not need all states on board: the Centre could build an integrated tax on goods and services for itself, and states could join later. In 2004, Finance Minister Chidambaram chose not to pursue it. He cited a lack of support from state governments, and the BJP refused to take part in tax reform. The idea sat idle through ten years of Congress rule. Arun Jaitley revived it after 2014, it was announced in 2016, and it launched in 2017. By then it broke all three principles of a good VAT: many high rates and cesses, and whole sectors left out (electricity, petroleum, real estate). Input tax credit has since been increasingly blocked.
A good idea can be adopted in name and still lose its core. Political economy can shrink a reform until little more than the label survives.
printed: From excise to a leaky GST

head: Demonetization vs GST, and a Prediction That Came True
dek: It helps to separate a policy's concept from its execution. A sound idea can still be ruined in the doing, and informed observers can often see the failures coming.
more: In the early days of The Seen and the Unseen, Amit did short episodes on one policy at a time, including demonetization and the GST. He judged demonetization wrong in concept and in every other way. The GST, by contrast, was great in concept and terrible in implementation. His first GST guest, Devangshu Datta, predicted everything that would go wrong before the GST was even announced. A later episode with Shruti Rajagopalan covered it in full.
It helps to separate a policy's concept from its execution. A sound idea can still be ruined in the doing, and informed observers can often see the failures coming.

head: Three Engines of High-Productivity Firms, and the Tax System's Duty to Stay Out of Their Way
dek: Growth comes from high-productivity firms, which rest on three pillars.
more: Growth comes from high-productivity firms, which rest on three pillars. The first is specialization (Adam Smith's pin idea). The second is learning by doing: Wright's Law and cost experience curves say your lifetime output determines your cost efficiency. The third is globalization: removing barriers to capital, labour, goods, services and enterprise. A good tax system is neutral to all three and never tilts firms away from them.

head: GDP First, Tax-GDP Ratio Second
dek: Taxing 15 on a GDP of 200 is far better than taxing 15 on a GDP of 100, even though the tax-GDP ratio is lower.
more: Taxing 15 on a GDP of 200 is far better than taxing 15 on a GDP of 100, even though the tax-GDP ratio is lower. Many tax experts and development economists instinctively prefer the higher ratio, which confuses the means with the end. Amit links this to a mindset that treats the state as ruler rather than servant. That mindset presumes citizens guilty until proven innocent, for example by blocking input tax credit until a firm proves it is owed.

head: A Small State Can Do the Essential Job
dek: The state's core tasks are peace, easy taxes, a tolerable administration of justice and a few basics, and these don't need much money.
more: The state's core tasks are peace, easy taxes, a tolerable administration of justice and a few basics, and these don't need much money. Ajay thinks the Indian state is oversized: it should tax and spend less. He also doubts it spends well; India would probably be better off if it had half the money it has today.

head: Bad Taxes: Why Cascading Taxes Are a Monster
dek: Among economists, 'bad tax' is not a mild phrase. A tax on production at every stage taxes tax on tax, so a mild-looking rate becomes a large real burden.
more: Among economists, 'bad tax' is not a mild phrase. A tax on production at every stage taxes tax on tax, so a mild-looking rate becomes a large real burden. It attacks specialization by rewarding giant vertically integrated firms that run from petrochemicals to fabric. It hurts exporters competing with countries that have clean VATs. And it makes imports look cheap, which leads domestic firms to lobby for tariffs.

head: The VAT and the Travel of Input Tax Credit
dek: Invented by French economist Maurice Lauré in 1954, the VAT taxes only the value added at each stage.
more: Invented by French economist Maurice Lauré in 1954, the VAT taxes only the value added at each stage. Each firm deducts the tax already paid upstream (input tax credit, or ITC), so the total tax is the same however production is split up. That makes it neutral to specialization. The flow of ITC is what makes it a VAT; without it, you are back to a production tax.

head: Zero-Rating of Exports
dek: Exports carry no domestic VAT, and exporters get a refund of all their accumulated input tax credit.
more: Exports carry no domestic VAT, and exporters get a refund of all their accumulated input tax credit. Goods therefore compete on world markets at tax-free prices, whatever each country's VAT rate. They then pay the importing country's VAT at its border, just as local goods do. This gives full neutrality between imports and domestic production and makes the VAT compatible with globalization.

head: Low Rate, Single Rate, Comprehensive Base
dek: A good VAT has a low rate (Ajay prefers 8%, at most 9% for India), no exemptions, and one rate for everything.
more: A good VAT has a low rate (Ajay prefers 8%, at most 9% for India), no exemptions, and one rate for everything. A broad base is the path to a low rate, because a narrow base makes the ever-thirsty government push the rate up. Multiple rates invite lobbying, corruption and classification fights, such as paratha at 18% versus roti at 5%. They also overload a low-capability state. High rates encourage evasion, because economic distortion rises roughly with the square of the tax rate: doubling the rate quadruples the damage.

head: Blocked ITC: How India Partly Lost Its VAT
dek: India's biggest GST failure is the growing blockage of input tax credit.
more: India's biggest GST failure is the growing blockage of input tax credit. Final-stage goods producers are not given proper credit on services and capital goods, and services firms face blockages too. Several 5% rates come with ITC blocked, so the real burden is far higher than the headline rate. Even delayed credit is a tax, because firms pay interest on the working capital the government holds. Across a large part of the economy, the GST has slid back into old-style excise and service tax. That disadvantages Indian producers against imports and denies exporters zero-rating.

head: Tax Policy Should Be Designed by Economists, Not Tax Collectors
dek: In advanced countries, economists design tax policy and administrators implement it.
more: In advanced countries, economists design tax policy and administrators implement it. In Indian terms, the Department of Economic Affairs should write the law and the Department of Revenue should administer it. In India, power has shifted to the Department of Revenue. Practical officials charged with raising money now decide to block ITC for a little extra revenue, without counting the cost to GDP.

head: Change Happens Upstream of Policymakers
dek: Lasting reform comes from the climate of opinion: ideas, papers, books, blogs, seminars and public debate.
more: Lasting reform comes from the climate of opinion: ideas, papers, books, blogs, seminars and public debate. Civil servants are busy firefighting, and the consultants they hire implement requests rather than supply principles. Without a strong ecosystem of ideas outside government, policy drifts away from first principles. Amit sums it up by saying policy, like politics, is downstream of culture.

head: The Fix Is the Original Prescription
dek: The first step, and the most urgent, is to remove every blockage of input tax credit and restore seamless end-to-end credit.
more: The first step, and the most urgent, is to remove every blockage of input tax credit and restore seamless end-to-end credit. After that comes a single low rate on a comprehensive base that brings every sector into the GST. Twenty years on, the cure is unchanged.

Amit on the Business Standard column, which he admits he didn't read in print because he doesn't subscribe to any paper: policymakers across the country 'squealed in delight, unless they were part of government, where they squealed in embarrassment because all their follies were revealed to the world.'

head: Ajay on the…
more: Ajay on the 'easy' recipe for growth: 'You just have to get NVIDIA and Google emerge out of the Indian soil.' After listing the three pillars, he adds: 'It's very easy, yeah. You should try it one of these days.'

head: After Ajay explains that economists divide taxes into good and bad, Amit
more: After Ajay explains that economists divide taxes into good and bad, Amit says: 'I feel like starting a hashtag not all taxes.'

head: On the vertically integrated petrochemicals-to-fabric giant that cascading taxes reward
more: On the vertically integrated petrochemicals-to-fabric giant that cascading taxes reward: 'And I have a suggested brand name for that cloth. It's called Vimal.'
Ajay: 'Every God fearing economist should stand up and put up a dharna.' Amit: 'Our economists don't fear God. They fear government. Government fearing economists should be the new term.'

head: Ajay's running gag about the neighbour that got its tax system right
more: Ajay's running gag about the neighbour that got its tax system right: 'a country with brilliant Bengali economists who have constructed a superior tax system? It's called Bangladesh... Because Bangladesh has only Bengali economists.'

head: On a low 5% GST rate that comes with blocked input tax credit
more: On a low 5% GST rate that comes with blocked input tax credit: 'the taxman giveth and the taxman taketh away.'

head: Explaining the destination VAT
more: Explaining the destination VAT: 'you know the French are very socialist, so they have a 20% VAT.'

head: Listing where real change comes from (ideas, papers, books, blog articles), Ajay adds…
more: Listing where real change comes from (ideas, papers, books, blog articles), Ajay adds: 'and you know what? It is in certain remarkable YouTube channels.' Amit later says the episode was 'edge of the seat indeed, and thankfully I haven't fallen off my chair yet.'

head: Maurice Lauré, the French economist who invented the VAT in 1954. Ajay uses him to rebut the idea of economics as a…
more: Maurice Lauré, the French economist who invented the VAT in 1954. Ajay uses him to rebut the idea of economics as a 'dismal science' or 'the boring game of sitting in an office and writing R programs.'

Adam Smith's pin example (specialization), Wright's Law and cost experience curves, and the show's Moore's Law episode, invoked as the foundations of firm productivity. Ajay also borrows Amit's phrase 'put in volume': 'If you've made 10,000 pins, you ain't seen nothing yet.'

head: The GST classification disputes: Amit's
more: The GST classification disputes: Amit's 'is KitKat a chocolate or a biscuit?' and Ajay's paratha taxed at 18% versus roti at 5%, as examples of the mess multiple rates create.

head: PricewaterhouseCoopers as shorthand for consultants who implement rather than think
more: PricewaterhouseCoopers as shorthand for consultants who implement rather than think: 'a Price Waterhouse is not going to give them economic principles... You want to get X done, we'll get X done.'

head: The India-Pakistan cricket match that sparked this episode
dek: A single sporting moment showed how quickly a whole country can be roused to hate people it has never met.
more: The day after India played Pakistan in a recent tournament, Amit scrolled through Twitter and was deeply disturbed. Indian players had refused to shake hands with the Pakistani team. The captain and politicians made belligerent noises at press conferences, and social media erupted after India won. India had the far stronger team, and any knockout game has an element of lottery. Indian and Pakistani cricketers have historically been friendly, and Pakistani commentators like Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis and Ramiz Raja are hugely popular in India. Vaishnav, the show's cinematographer, told Amit he couldn't sleep properly after seeing it.

A single sporting moment showed how quickly a whole country can be roused to hate people it has never met. It also showed how easily people confuse the citizens of Pakistan with the Pakistani state, whose interests run opposite to theirs.

head: The Wars of the Roses and the birth of 'Englishness'
dek: Nations are not primordial. A sense of nationhood can emerge as an accidental side effect of war, once the old local loyalties collapse and something larger fills the gap.
more: Some historians date English national consciousness to the 15th-century Wars of the Roses. The dynastic civil war wiped out many feudal overlords, and with them went the local loyalty that people had owed those lords. Both sides also put commoners and royals into battle together. That created a new shared feeling: I'm a commoner, you're a royal, but we are the same people.
Nations are not primordial. A sense of nationhood can emerge as an accidental side effect of war, once the old local loyalties collapse and something larger fills the gap.

head: Mussolini's 'trenchocracy' and the ghost of Rome
dek: Nationalist strongmen often don't need coercion at first. A narrative of lost glory makes people walk into disaster willingly.
more: Mussolini rose to power in the early 1920s, just after World War One. He rallied Italians by promising rule by the 'trenchocracy', the common men who had fought in the war. He also exploited Italy's link to the Roman Empire: look how glorious we were, look how far we have fallen, let us rise again. He used pomp, grandeur, and talk of Roman military valour and discipline. Through his disastrous reign he stayed supremely popular.
Nationalist strongmen often don't need coercion at first. A narrative of lost glory makes people walk into disaster willingly.
printed: All roads lead to the trenchocracy

head: Stalin, Pushkin, and Russia's unbroken nationalist thread
dek: Ideologies that claim to transcend the nation, like class-war communism, slide back into nationalism, because both work the same way: build an in-group and paint everyone else as the enemy.
more: The Tsars used Russification and Russian nationalism to bolster their legitimacy. The communists initially railed against nationalism: 'workers of the world unite', not workers of Russia. After Lenin, though, Stalin brought Russification back. At a 1937 celebration of the Soviet Union's great poets, the poet celebrated most was the Russian, Pushkin. The same strain now runs through Putin's imperial project.
Ideologies that claim to transcend the nation, like class-war communism, slide back into nationalism, because both work the same way: build an in-group and paint everyone else as the enemy.

head: How Gandhi's Khilafat gambit turned Jinnah
dek: Borders and nationalisms that look eternal can come from accidents of history: a promise to a dying mentor, an opportunistic alliance, one man's bitterness.
more: Gandhi returned from South Africa around 1914. His hero Gokhale told him to spend a year travelling India without doing active politics, then died a month later. Gandhi kept the promise, and travelled barefoot as a tribute ('I don't know what the logic of that is'). At Congress gatherings around 1917-18 nobody took him seriously. His breakthrough came when he joined the Ali brothers' Khilafat movement, which wanted the caliphate revived after its abolition at the end of WWI. An Indian independence movement had no coherent reason to ally with a pan-Islamic one, but the tactical masterstroke let Gandhi take over the Congress around 1920-21. Jinnah, then the last great moderate and expecting to lead Congress, couldn't make sense of it. Embittered, he abandoned moderation and became the biggest champion of a Muslim nation.
Borders and nationalisms that look eternal can come from accidents of history: a promise to a dying mentor, an opportunistic alliance, one man's bitterness.

head: Acing Hindi exams by stringing together Shudh Hindi
dek: The Sanskritised, de-Persianised 'pure' Hindi taught in schools is a political construction rather than the living language.
more: In both 10th and 12th standard Amit scored more in Hindi than in English, despite being 'lazy as fuck' and not studying. His hack was to memorise lots of Shudh Hindi words (dwar instead of darwaza, mitra instead of dost) and string them together. Teachers rewarded it because nobody actually speaks that way.

The Sanskritised, de-Persianised 'pure' Hindi taught in schools is a political construction rather than the living language. The education system rewards the artificial register over the Hindustani people actually speak.

head: Neeraj Chopra's mother: 'Arshad is our son too'
dek: This is the antidote to state-manufactured enmity: people who actually know the 'other side' see them as family.
more: When Neeraj Chopra won javelin gold two Olympics ago, he praised Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem, a close friend he had always encouraged, almost like a mentor. At the last Olympics Arshad won gold with an outlier throw of over 92 metres, and a disappointed Neeraj didn't. A TV crew asked Neeraj's mother how she felt. She said Arshad was her son too.

This is the antidote to state-manufactured enmity: people who actually know the 'other side' see them as family. Amit's point is that Indians and Pakistanis are 'the same damn people' with the same culture.

head: The 1969 Soccer War
dek: Sport doesn't cause these conflicts; nationalism does. Sport is just an easy trigger and amplifier for passions already stoked.
more: In 1969 Honduras and El Salvador played a series of World Cup qualifiers marked by so much sloganeering and fighting that a war followed. Amit recalls it lasting about 100 days, with around six thousand dead. It is commonly called the Soccer War.
Sport doesn't cause these conflicts; nationalism does. Sport is just an easy trigger and amplifier for passions already stoked.

head: Shubha Mudgal's sigh about renamed ragas
dek: Nationalist re-coding reaches even art forms whose lineage is plainly multicultural.
more: On The Seen and the Unseen, Amit suggested to Shubha Mudgal that nationalism surely couldn't touch music, since Hindustani classical music owes so much to great Muslim performers. She sighed and told him he'd be surprised: there is revisionist history in music too, including attempts by some people to rename ragas.
Nationalist re-coding reaches even art forms whose lineage is plainly multicultural.

head: The friend who wouldn't let his sister wear salwar kameez
dek: Clothes have no religion, but identity politics assigns them one. Those labels are arbitrary, and they can flip within a generation.
more: A Kashmiri Pandit, once a close friend of Amit's, told him he didn't let his sister wear salwar kameez because he saw it as something Muslims wear. When Amit grew up in the 70s and 80s, salwar kameez on women was widely frowned upon as 'Muslim'; today it is completely normal. The pathani suit Amit wears on the show would still be read by many as Eid-wear or a sign that you're Muslim.
Clothes have no religion, but identity politics assigns them one. Those labels are arbitrary, and they can flip within a generation.

head: Imagined Communities
dek: Possibly his favourite book on nationalism. It supplies the episode's core definition (a nation is an 'imagined political community', necessarily limited and sovereign) and the three paradoxes of nationhood.
more: Possibly his favourite book on nationalism. It supplies the episode's core definition (a nation is an 'imagined political community', necessarily limited and sovereign) and the three paradoxes of nationhood.
Amit's opening answer to Ajay's request to define nationalism.

head: History of European Morals
dek: Source of the 'expanding circle': the idea that the circle of people we grant moral consideration widens over time, from family to tribe to village and beyond.
more: Source of the 'expanding circle': the idea that the circle of people we grant moral consideration widens over time, from family to tribe to village and beyond.
Explaining how our tribal instincts gradually widened into loyalty to larger communities.

head: The Expanding Circle
dek: Singer argued the circle would one day include animals. Amit's wry note: 'Alas, it hasn't even expanded to include all human beings.'
more: Singer argued the circle would one day include animals. Amit's wry note: 'Alas, it hasn't even expanded to include all human beings.'
Follows from Lecky's idea.

head: The Mahatma and the Poet
dek: A 'beautiful book' laying out the Gandhi-Tagore debate: Gandhi as a soft nationalist, Tagore holding the view Amit and Ajay hold today, that nationalism is simply bad.
more: A 'beautiful book' laying out the Gandhi-Tagore debate: Gandhi as a soft nationalist, Tagore holding the view Amit and Ajay hold today, that nationalism is simply bad.
Discussing whether anti-colonial nationalism is a force for good.

head: Essays on Nationalism
dek: Amit calls it 'awesome' and urges listeners to read Tagore's full arguments.
more: Amit calls it 'awesome' and urges listeners to read Tagore's full arguments. He applauds Tagore's prescience a century ago, from a man who supported Indian independence yet saw nationalism as toxic whoever wielded it.
Tagore's lectures from 1917, which Amit quotes at length in the Tagore chapter.

head: The End of History?
dek: Captures the brief hope that liberalism had won before nationalism's revival.
more: Captures the brief hope that liberalism had won before nationalism's revival. Amit points out the question mark at the end of the original essay's title.
Describing the late-80s/early-90s moment when it seemed the world was entering a better age.

head: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
dek: Amit calls it a masterpiece that shows how deeply Hindu nationalist ideas were embedded in Indian society.
more: Amit calls it a masterpiece that shows how deeply Hindu nationalist ideas were embedded in Indian society.
Arguing that the secular idea of India was imposed top-down while society held different ideas.

head: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: Amit's 'great episode' with Mukul, a conversational route into the same argument.
more: Amit's 'great episode' with Mukul, a conversational route into the same argument.
Mentioned alongside Mukul's book.

head: The Sporting Spirit
dek: The 'great essay' that called sport 'war minus the shooting', drawing on an ugly football match involving a Moscow team and a riot in Spain.
more: The 'great essay' that called sport 'war minus the shooting', drawing on an ugly football match involving a Moscow team and a riot in Spain. It frames the India-Pakistan cricket episode.
The chapter on how nationalism invades everyday life, starting with sport.

head: Vaishnav Vyas's football Substack
dek: Amit and Vaishnav bond over the thinkers of the game (like Guardiola turning 'anti-Guardiola').
more: Amit and Vaishnav bond over the thinkers of the game (like Guardiola turning 'anti-Guardiola'). The newsletter models loving sport for ideas rather than flags.
Explaining that he supports football teams for their playing philosophy, not tribal loyalty.

head: The Life and Music of Shubha Mudgal (Episode 426, The Seen and the Unseen)
dek: 'My great episode with her', in which Mudgal reveals revisionist history and attempts to rename ragas in Hindustani classical music.
more: 'My great episode with her', in which Mudgal reveals revisionist history and attempts to rename ragas in Hindustani classical music.
Discussing nationalism creeping into music.

head: The Peter Cat Recording Company
dek: The band has a cult following that forms its own community. Amit tells Ajay 'we will introduce you to some good music.'
more: The band has a cult following that forms its own community. Amit tells Ajay 'we will introduce you to some good music.'
Example of communities forming around shared tastes rather than national identity.

head: Nationalism is not patriotism or the national interest
dek: Three things often get conflated. The national interest is what is good for your country.
more: Three things often get conflated. The national interest is what is good for your country. Patriotism is love for your country. Nationalism is an ideology, and Amit regards it as toxic. His thesis: nationalism is bad for the nation, any nationalism, any nation.

head: Two Pakistans: the people vs the state
dek: Pakistan's civil society is distinct from what Pranay Kotasthane calls its military-jihadi complex.
more: Pakistan's civil society is distinct from what Pranay Kotasthane calls its military-jihadi complex. The Pakistani state draws legitimacy from painting India as the enemy and uses that to oppress its own people. Hostility toward ordinary Pakistanis therefore serves the very state that oppresses them.

head: Tribal instincts and the expanding circle
dek: Nationalism is modern but rides on primordial instincts. We evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes where solidarity with your group and suspicion of outsiders was selected for.
more: Nationalism is modern but rides on primordial instincts. We evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes where solidarity with your group and suspicion of outsiders was selected for. Lecky's 'expanding circle' describes how moral concern widens over time from kin to tribe to village to larger communities. The nation is one stage of that widening, and it can freeze there.

head: A nation is an imagined political community
dek: In Benedict Anderson's definition, a nation is necessarily imagined. Unlike a Dunbar-sized tribe of about 150, you never meet most members or know their preferences, yet you picture them as one homogeneous 'we'.
more: In Benedict Anderson's definition, a nation is necessarily imagined. Unlike a Dunbar-sized tribe of about 150, you never meet most members or know their preferences, yet you picture them as one homogeneous 'we'. That makes the nation fictional at its heart, and it flattens real complexity: Hinduism, for instance, was an amorphous, almost open-source religion. Anderson adds that a nation must be limited (bounded) and sovereign to make sense.

head: Anderson's three paradoxes of nationhood
dek: First, objective modernity vs subjective antiquity: nation-states are a few centuries old, yet each claims a glorious ancient past, which has to be invented (Hobsbawm's 'invention of tradition'; Kapila's 'a theory of violence in search of a history').
more: First, objective modernity vs subjective antiquity: nation-states are a few centuries old, yet each claims a glorious ancient past, which has to be invented (Hobsbawm's 'invention of tradition'; Kapila's 'a theory of violence in search of a history'). Second, universal vs particular: everyone supposedly has a nationality, yet each one is unique and potentially hostile to the others. Third, nationalism is a huge political force but philosophically nebulous.

head: Nationalism has no serious thinkers, only rationalisations
dek: Liberalism has Locke and Smith; socialism has Marx. Ajay pushes back that Mussolini had theory, and we just refuse to take him seriously.
more: Liberalism has Locke and Smith; socialism has Marx. Ajay pushes back that Mussolini had theory, and we just refuse to take him seriously. Amit's reply: Mussolini, Hitler and Savarkar (with his 'motherland and holy land' test) offer assertions, not first-principles reasoning. They are men of action, and their worldview is a rationalisation for what they are doing.

head: What made nationalism possible, and what revives it
dek: In medieval Europe loyalties were local, and without maps or printing people barely conceived of a wider world.
more: In medieval Europe loyalties were local, and without maps or printing people barely conceived of a wider world. Several things changed that. Revived vernaculars (French, German) gave people a shared marker. The printing press scaled narratives. Locke and Rousseau's 'will of the people' needed a 'people' to attach to. The Romantic movement, reacting against the Enlightenment's cold rationality, supplied folk songs and fairy tales to rally around. The American and French Revolutions fused these. By the end of the 19th century nationalism ruled the world, and imperialism was nationalism projected outward, with anti-colonial nationalisms rising in response. Social media is today's printing press.

head: Land-rooted vs cosmopolitan worldviews
dek: Ajay contrasts landed, culturally conservative people with the commercial, cosmopolitan people of capitalism, like Gujarati traders who sailed off to work across East Africa.
more: Ajay contrasts landed, culturally conservative people with the commercial, cosmopolitan people of capitalism, like Gujarati traders who sailed off to work across East Africa. Amit thinks nationalism is more about people than land. Ajay locates the overlap in obsession over territory: the cosmopolitan sees the Louisiana or Alaska Purchase as sensible deals, while the nationalist would excoriate any transaction involving land.

head: The yin and yang of nationalism
dek: Each claimed good has a matching harm. Liberation vs oppression: nationalism unites the colonised, but every oppressor uses it, and Carl Schmitt said politics needs an other.
more: Each claimed good has a matching harm. Liberation vs oppression: nationalism unites the colonised, but every oppressor uses it, and Carl Schmitt said politics needs an other. Cohesion vs exclusion: it bonds people, but every 'we' others a 'them'. Cultural pride vs cultural suppression: it can revive a culture, but declaring A to be 'ours' implies X, Y and Z aren't. Amit's verdict is that the goods can come from elsewhere (liberal self-governance, cities, shared tastes), while the harms are built in.

head: Love, don't be proud
dek: Pride belongs to things you actually did, or helped shape. You can love Kishori Amonkar, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and Van Morrison without any narrative of nationhood.
more: Pride belongs to things you actually did, or helped shape. You can love Kishori Amonkar, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and Van Morrison without any narrative of nationhood. 'Taking pride' in your nation's accomplishments is taking credit for what you had nothing to do with.

head: Nationalism essentialises, and so dehumanises
dek: Amit's deepest objection. Nationalism, like other identity ideologies, ties you to an accident of birth or location and declares it the most important thing about you.
