more: Amit's deepest objection. Nationalism, like other identity ideologies, ties you to an accident of birth or location and declares it the most important thing about you. That makes you forever a victim, forever an oppressor, or forever bound to the tribe's dictates. It denies agency and the multitudes every individual contains.

head: The magic trick: how the state turns citizens into subjects
dek: In Ajay's public-choice view the people are the principal and the state is their hired agent, there to produce public goods and get kicked around when it underperforms.
more: In Ajay's public-choice view the people are the principal and the state is their hired agent, there to produce public goods and get kicked around when it underperforms. Nationalism inverts this by blurring 'Italy' the football team, 'Italy' the people, and 'Italy' the state that monopolises violence. The state then claims to be the nation, and dissent becomes 'anti-national'. Mussolini said it outright: 'It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people.'

head: Nationalists pour their own people into war
dek: Whatever the route, the nationalism of Mussolini, Hitler and Putin ended in mobilising their own people for violence.
more: Whatever the route, the nationalism of Mussolini, Hitler and Putin ended in mobilising their own people for violence. Ajay notes that something like ten to thirty percent of these countries' men were killed in war. Amit adds that our hardwiring makes this a battle each generation must fight again.

head: India's top-down 'idea of India' was bound to fail
dek: Three nationalisms competed under the British: Hindutva (homogenising, aimed at Muslims more than the British), Muslim nationalism (which became Pakistan), and the elite secular nationalism of Nehru, Gandhi and Patel.
more: Three nationalisms competed under the British: Hindutva (homogenising, aimed at Muslims more than the British), Muslim nationalism (which became Pakistan), and the elite secular nationalism of Nehru, Gandhi and Patel. Amit argues all three are equally imagined, and that every nationalism is imposed through coercion. The secular one won formally but was imposed from the top, while society held other ideas (see the Gita Press). Ambedkar called the constitution a mere topsoil, and Gandhi insisted change must come bottom-up. A smug westernised elite didn't take that seriously, and 'politics has caught up with society.'

head: Hindustani: a spontaneous order split by politics
dek: North India's language grew bottom-up as a khichdi of Persian, Sanskrit, Prakrit and many tongues now dismissed as dialects ('a language is a dialect with an army').
more: North India's language grew bottom-up as a khichdi of Persian, Sanskrit, Prakrit and many tongues now dismissed as dialects ('a language is a dialect with an army'). Then politics intervened: post-1857 British divide-and-rule plus movements within both religions. Urdu was painted as Muslim, and a de-Persianised Hindi was consciously constructed and promoted. Yet the two remain mutually intelligible, and many great writers saw themselves as both Hindi and Urdu writers.

head: Support playing philosophies, not flags
dek: Sport is inherently tribal. Indians who've never been to England pick Manchester United or Liverpool, often whichever team was winning when they were 12 or 13.
more: Sport is inherently tribal. Indians who've never been to England pick Manchester United or Liverpool, often whichever team was winning when they were 12 or 13. Any team is a Ship of Theseus whose players keep being bought and sold, so loyalty to the badge makes little sense. Amit's alternative is to follow the thinkers of the game and back teams whose style of play you admire.

head: Economic nationalism is protectionism wearing a flag
dek: Every voluntary trade is positive-sum, a 'double thank you', whether with Pune or Poland.
more: Every voluntary trade is positive-sum, a 'double thank you', whether with Pune or Poland. 'Indian company' barely means anything: ICICI Bank is about 90% foreign-owned, and Infosys has mostly foreign shareholders and customers. Data-localisation rules force data centres into India's heat, unreliable power, thin pool of top-end engineers and tariff-inflated equipment, when Greenland would be cheaper and greener. 'Data is the new crude oil' is just cover for firms that want to avoid competition. The legitimate exception is defence, and even there the fix is foreign policy (e.g. sourcing components from countries like Ukraine), not costly self-reliance.

head: Nationalism diminishes us in three ways
dek: Amit's closing case rests on consequences, not first principles. Economically: protectionism makes only us poorer.
more: Amit's closing case rests on consequences, not first principles. Economically: protectionism makes only us poorer. Culturally and intellectually: we should let all the world's rivers flow into our ocean, and build our own cocktail of Indic and Enlightenment values rather than choosing sides. In character: sorting people into 'ours' and 'foreign' cuts us off from the richness of the world's people, music and languages.

head: The 'America Stack' counterfactual
dek: Ajay asks: what if the pioneers of Unix and the Internet had branded them 'America Stack'?
more: Ajay asks: what if the pioneers of Unix and the Internet had branded them 'America Stack'? Would the world have adopted those ideas as readily? Ideas spread best when they don't carry a national flag.

head: Amit, mid-explanation of how nations invent a glorious past, notices Ajay grinning and asks…
more: Amit, mid-explanation of how nations invent a glorious past, notices Ajay grinning and asks 'Why are you smiling?' Ajay: 'Under communism, the future was always certain. It's the past that keeps changing.'

head: Amit dates English consciousness to the Wars of the Roses, then deadpans that The War of the Roses
more: Amit dates English consciousness to the Wars of the Roses, then deadpans that The War of the Roses 'of course, was a 1989 film recently made into a film called The Roses, but that is completely different. Popular culture lovers may not know that it is a tongue in cheek reference to something else that happened.'

head: On Shudh Hindi sounding like nobody: imagine English speakers using only Latinate words, so that instead of…
more: On Shudh Hindi sounding like nobody: imagine English speakers using only Latinate words, so that instead of 'we shall fight them in the streets', Winston Churchill had said 'we shall combat them in the boulevards'.

head: Amit imagines Tagore with modern tech
more: Amit imagines Tagore with modern tech: 'he could have done a YouTube show. Called, and I think he would have called it Everything is Everything. Shob kichu shob kichu.' He also tells Ajay that whatever he says against Bengali economists, 'among Bengali philosophers, Robi-da stands alone.'

head: After saying it's
more: After saying it's 'not the ideas of Tagore but those of Putin which will thrive', Amit adds: 'I never thought I'll have those two names in the same sentence.'

head: Ajay dismantling the word
more: Ajay dismantling the word 'Italy': 'Is Italy a football team? That's fine. It's 11 guys that are playing football. Or is Italy the people of Italy? ... Or is it the Italian state? Fine. It is the community that achieves and maintains a monopoly of physical violence on the territory that is Italy.'

head: Ajay's fix for nationalism in sport
more: Ajay's fix for nationalism in sport: 'form teams based on purely random imagined communities, put a little bit of old fashioned capitalism into it, have buying and selling of players. And you're done.' Amit: in theory every Manchester United player could be playing for Liverpool five years later, 'though it is actually practically impossible because none of them would get into that side.'

head: On fans picking whichever team was winning when they were 12 or 13
more: On fans picking whichever team was winning when they were 12 or 13: 'Which is why there are chutiyas my age supporting Manchester United. Well, good luck, brother.'

head: On biryani being treated as anti-national (the
more: On biryani being treated as anti-national (the 'Ajmal Kasab was given biryani' rhetoric): 'Biryani is not anti national. You're right, it is somewhat unhealthy, but it is deeply, deeply tasty, especially when made well. I am never going to give up biryani.'

head: Ajay on data-localisation rhetoric
more: Ajay on data-localisation rhetoric: 'somebody will say data is a new crude oil, which is like supposed to be a checkmate.'

head: Amit on America's turn to economic nationalism
more: Amit on America's turn to economic nationalism: 'Like we're in a bad video game simulation and there's a bug in the system and something weird just happened.'

head: Amit on Gandhi walking India barefoot as a tribute to Gokhale
more: Amit on Gandhi walking India barefoot as a tribute to Gokhale: 'I don't know what the logic of that is, but he does that.'

head: Doug Stanhope on nationalism
more: Doug Stanhope on nationalism: 'hating people you have never met and taking pride in accomplishments you had nothing to do with'.

head: George Orwell's description of sport
more: George Orwell's description of sport as 'war minus the shooting', from 'The Sporting Spirit', applied to the India-Pakistan matches.

head: Ernest Gellner
more: Ernest Gellner: 'nationalism is not the awakening of nations to self-consciousness. It invents nations where they do not exist.' Paired with Eric Hobsbawm's 'invention of tradition'.

head: Walt Whitman's
more: Walt Whitman's 'we contain multitudes', which Amit extends: 'Individuals contain multitudes and multitudes of individuals contain further multitudes.'

head: Carl Schmitt
more: Carl Schmitt: 'politics needs an other'. Nationalism supplies one automatically.

head: Mussolini, read out by Amit
more: Mussolini, read out by Amit: 'It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people', and 'The fascist conception of the state is all embracing. Outside it no human or spiritual values can exist.'
Ajay: 'if only Vladimir Putin could sign on for Rabindranath Tagore as his spiritual guide instead of Alexander Dugin, then millions of Russians would be alive today.'

head: Tagore on nationalism
more: Tagore on nationalism: 'a cruel epidemic of evil eating into humanity's moral vitality' and 'the nation, with its flags and pious hymns, cannot hide the fact that the nation is the greatest evil for the earth'. Amit also cites Tagore's view that World War One was caused by the toxic concept of the nation.

head: Ambedkar calling the Constitution
more: Ambedkar calling the Constitution 'a mere topsoil' over a deeper Indian society.
'A language is a dialect with an army', Amit's aside on the many north Indian tongues now dismissed as dialects.
Ajay: 'What you want is the press conferences of Gukesh and Ding'. The gracious world chess championship rivals are the model of sporting conduct.

head: Amit, arguing that clothes have no religion
more: Amit, arguing that clothes have no religion: 'you didn't think I was gonna quote Dylan here, right? As Bob Dylan once said, even the president of the United States must someday stand naked.'

head: Ajay recalls, attributing it to Tagore, the wish for…
more: Ajay recalls, attributing it to Tagore, the wish for 'the winds from the seven continents to blow through my nation'.

head: The 1991 Reforms Were Twenty Years in the Making
dek: A crisis looks like the cause of reform, but it only opened a window. The reform itself came from decades of patient, mostly invisible work by people who made sure the ideas were ready.
more: Amit used to believe the 1991 reforms happened only because the balance of payments crisis left India no choice. Through his conversations on The Seen and the Unseen and Everything is Everything, he learned the story began much earlier. From the late 1960s Manmohan Singh was quietly building a community. He asked Vijay Kelkar to return to India in the early 1970s and Montek to return in the late 1970s. From then on, people inside and outside government worked out reform ideas, picked their battles, and avoided fights that could cost them their place. In 1990 Montek wrote the famous 'M document', which held much of what was done a year later. Ajay compared this to a relay race: we only watch the last runner cross the line, but the baton passed through many earlier hands.
A crisis looks like the cause of reform, but it only opened a window. The reform itself came from decades of patient, mostly invisible work by people who made sure the ideas were ready.
printed: The baton was passed long before

head: Two Failed Harvests and the Green Revolution
dek: This is the best case for crisis-driven reform, and Ajay offers it as the steelman.
more: In the 1950s and 60s India's population grew fast while the food system stayed broken, even though many people knew what needed fixing. Then the kharif crops of 1965 and 1966 failed back to back, and India came close to mass starvation. The United States bailed India out through the PL 480 program, which gave concessional aid in the form of food grain. That humiliation concentrated minds. Indira Gandhi and C. Subramaniam pushed high-yielding varieties, fertilisers and irrigation, and the result was the Green Revolution.
This is the best case for crisis-driven reform, and Ajay offers it as the steelman. It shows a crisis can break a long deadlock when everyone already knew what the fixes were.

head: The Insider Who Couldn't See the House Was on Fire
dek: The people running a system when it breaks are the people least able to diagnose it.
more: Ajay remembers a well-known Indian economics bureaucrat who had been very good to him personally and who was part of the fiscal mess and balance of payments collapse of the late 1980s. In the run-up to 1991, this man stubbornly could not see that the system was broken. He was protecting his legacy and defending his own past decisions.

The people running a system when it breaks are the people least able to diagnose it. Fresh thinking in a crisis has to come from outside the establishment, so gathering establishment figures together in a crisis produces more of the same.

head: How the Nirbhaya Moment Was Wasted
dek: Public outrage and political will are not enough. If the ideas have not been developed in peacetime, the window closes with nothing to show for it.
more: The horrific 2012 Nirbhaya rape case in Delhi brought the problem and the politics together. Ajay says Manmohan Singh and Montek wanted to use the moment to reform the criminal justice system. The policy groundwork did not exist. Nobody had spent twenty years building people, documents, books, seminars and an interconnected picture of how the system's parts fit together. The crisis produced only some activist-style lawmaking that didn't move the needle.
Public outrage and political will are not enough. If the ideas have not been developed in peacetime, the window closes with nothing to show for it.

head: GST: Thirteen Years From Report to Reality
dek: Be suspicious of a 'we want action by the day after tomorrow' mindset.
more: Vijay Kelkar, Arvind Modi and Ajay wrote the first fully worked-out proposal for a GST in 2003. The first real move towards a complete GST came in 2016, thirteen years later. Ajay thinks that is perfectly normal. Serious ideas need knowledge, philosophy, papers, books and endless debate before a country is ready for them.
Be suspicious of a 'we want action by the day after tomorrow' mindset. It produces trivial changes. Deep reform runs on a timescale of decades.

head: The Road to the Emergency
dek: This is the Indian version of Carl Schmitt's 'true ruler', someone who uses a crisis as cover to suspend the rule of law.
more: Ajay treats the 1975 Emergency, which followed the Justice Sinha ruling, as the end point of a longer slide. The 1971 war created a huge fiscal problem. By 1974 inflation hit 16%, the highest in India's history. Society came apart: the JP Narayan movement, buses being burned, things falling apart. In that atmosphere Indira Gandhi suspended the rule of law.

This is the Indian version of Carl Schmitt's 'true ruler', someone who uses a crisis as cover to suspend the rule of law. The lesson is to fear crises in a country whose checks and balances are already weak.

head: The Authoritarian Wish List That Waited for 9/11
dek: This is the 1991 story with the sign flipped. Bad ideas can also be waiting in the policy pipeline, and a crisis lets them through just as easily as good ones.
more: A hawkish part of the US national security establishment had long been developing authoritarian tools: the Patriot Act, countering the financing of terror, anti-money laundering rules, and FATF, which in India shows up as the PMLA and the Enforcement Directorate. In normal times, principled lawmakers would have debated these and blocked them. After 9/11 they all passed within weeks. Ajay considers almost every piece a bad idea, and argues that tracing money flows has never disrupted a terrorist plot. What it did build was mass surveillance of finance.
This is the 1991 story with the sign flipped. Bad ideas can also be waiting in the policy pipeline, and a crisis lets them through just as easily as good ones.

head: Jim Comey's Dash to the Hospital
dek: Checks and balances are not only written rules. They depend on individuals who will physically race across a city to defend the rule of law.
more: Ajay retells a story Jim Comey tells about a mass surveillance program. Comey, at the top of the US national security establishment, urgently rushed by car to a hospital to brief a desperately ill official before something bad was done about that program. Ajay contrasts this with weak democracies, where most people would just bow their heads and go along.

Checks and balances are not only written rules. They depend on individuals who will physically race across a city to defend the rule of law. That is why crises do less damage in mature democracies than in fledgling ones.

head: An Eight-Year-Old Versus Indira Gandhi on Inflation
dek: When governments mismanage the economy, they look for a villain. Blaming hoarders shifts attention from bad policy to an 'other'.
more: In 1974 young Ajay watched Indira Gandhi blame the high inflation on hoarders and speculators. He was eight that year, and he already knew prices are set by supply and demand, not by villains. He was genuinely baffled that someone raised on 'all those beautiful letters', Glimpses of World History, could be so clueless. As an adult he understood it was not cluelessness. It was populism: making the elites the enemy so no one blames monetary policy, and building that into the Garibi Hatao ideology and attacks on things like privy purses.
When governments mismanage the economy, they look for a villain. Blaming hoarders shifts attention from bad policy to an 'other'.

head: 74 Regulations in 50 Days, 1,324 Press Releases
dek: A crisis does not need a villain to go wrong. A weak state reacting incoherently in a panic can do great damage by itself.
more: After demonetisation, with no prior planning, the RBI issued 74 regulations in 50 days, working things out on the fly and making a bad situation worse. During COVID the Ministry of Health issued 1,324 press releases. Ajay says this is what Lant Pritchett calls premature load bearing: an institution given more than it can carry collapses into organisational rout. He also cites the 2013 taper tantrum, set off by Ben Bernanke's remarks to a journalist. There, he says, the RBI and the Ministry of Finance misread the situation and turned a medium problem into a much bigger one.
A crisis does not need a villain to go wrong. A weak state reacting incoherently in a panic can do great damage by itself.

head: Amit's Two Attempts to Move the Overton Window
dek: A position at the extreme makes moderate versions of the same idea sound reasonable.
more: Amit has tried to widen two Overton windows. The first is freedom. He calls himself a tariff absolutist (all tariffs should be zero) and a free speech absolutist, and says these are sincere beliefs, not tactics. This is a long game whose result is unknown. The second is podcast length, where he says he has won. When he started The Seen and the Unseen, people thought an hour was too long. After his ten-hour, twelve-hour and several eight-hour episodes, an hour no longer counts as a deep dive, and others in India now do three- and four-hour shows.
A position at the extreme makes moderate versions of the same idea sound reasonable. Amit's own career shows the window can move.

head: A Heart Scare, Diabetes, and the Lesson for Nations
dek: Celebrating a crisis that forced reform skips the real question, which is why the crisis was allowed to happen.
more: Amit applies the argument to himself. A heart scare earlier this year (he got a stent) and, earlier, a diabetes diagnosis both pushed him into lifestyle 'reforms', and he reversed the diabetes through diet. But he could have died, and he knew all along what a healthy life looked like. He lacked the discipline to exercise, do resistance training, avoid sugar and sleep well. If he had, neither crisis would have happened. Likewise, if India had done the right things in the 1980s, there would have been no 1991 crisis. He then notes where the metaphor breaks: an individual can respond to a crisis far more coherently than a state, which is full of conflicting incentives and stakeholders. Ajay agreed with both halves of the point.

Celebrating a crisis that forced reform skips the real question, which is why the crisis was allowed to happen. Do the dull disciplined work in good times, and expect states to be much worse than individuals at improvising in an emergency.
printed: The patient who knew the cure

head: In Service of the Republic
dek: Amit calls it Ajay's 'fine book' with Vijay Kelkar. It is where Ajay first set out the idea that crises are ladders for the wrong people.
more: Amit calls it Ajay's 'fine book' with Vijay Kelkar. It is where Ajay first set out the idea that crises are ladders for the wrong people.
Amit introduces the 'Chaos is a Ladder' chapter by noting that Ajay wrote the line in this book before learning it also appears in Game of Thrones.

head: The Long Road to Change (Everything is Everything episode)
dek: It is the hosts' fullest statement of their theory of change, which this episode builds on.
more: It is the hosts' fullest statement of their theory of change, which this episode builds on.
Ajay refers to it as the place where the hosts set out the policy pipeline, and where he first told the Nirbhaya story.

head: Activism and wonkery are the yin and yang
dek: It argues that street and social-media activism is useful but useless without careful conceptual work about how a complex system actually fits together.
more: It argues that street and social-media activism is useful but useless without careful conceptual work about how a complex system actually fits together.
A blog post Ajay wrote at the time of the 2012 Nirbhaya case.

head: Crises Are Dangerous, Not Golden Opportunities
dek: Many Indians believe sweeping reform only happens in a crisis because 1991 worked that way.
more: Many Indians believe sweeping reform only happens in a crisis because 1991 worked that way. Amit says this confuses correlation with causation and suffers from selection bias, because it looks at one crisis that ended well and ignores the many that ended badly. Ajay's view is that the default reaction to a crisis should be fear, especially in a young democracy with weak checks and balances.

head: Why Crises Seem to Work, and Why the Overton Window Cuts Both Ways
dek: Here is the case for crises. Prospect theory says people treat the status quo as their reference point and, because of loss aversion, avoid rocking the boat.
more: Here is the case for crises. Prospect theory says people treat the status quo as their reference point and, because of loss aversion, avoid rocking the boat. Special interests lock policy in place. When it seems the world is going to hell anyway, people become open to new ideas. Ajay frames this using the Overton window, the range of ideas acceptable in public discussion. A crisis widens it, which can make good ideas that were heresy become doable. It also normalises terrible ideas, and in poor countries that is more dangerous than in mature democracies.

head: The Real Problems Are Upstream of Policymakers
dek: Ajay argues that helping a policymaker carry out what they already want, as consulting firms do, is not what matters.
more: Ajay argues that helping a policymaker carry out what they already want, as consulting firms do, is not what matters. If you implemented everything a thousand good Indian policymakers want today, he doubts India would improve much. What matters is changing ideas and imagination, and building a group of independent thinkers who work on political economy and philosophy, not consulting. Without them a crisis brings no new ideas, only the same establishment voices.

head: Kingdon's Three Streams
dek: John Kingdon says change happens when three streams come together: a recognised problem, ready policy ideas, and favourable politics.
more: John Kingdon says change happens when three streams come together: a recognised problem, ready policy ideas, and favourable politics. In 1991 all three lined up. In the Nirbhaya case the problem and the politics lined up, but the policy ideas did not exist, so nothing came of it. A crisis can only bring the first and third. The second has to be built in advance.

head: Activism Needs Wonkery
dek: Shouting in the streets or on social media has its place, but real systems have many moving parts.
more: Shouting in the streets or on social media has its place, but real systems have many moving parts. You need people who have modelled the whole system in their heads. They know that changing one part forces changes elsewhere, which side effects to expect, and what order to do things in. Social media has produced many more activists, but not more of these people.

head: Carl Schmitt's 'True Ruler'
dek: Ajay describes Carl Schmitt as a philosopher who helped give rise to the Nazis and to authoritarian thinking.
more: Ajay describes Carl Schmitt as a philosopher who helped give rise to the Nazis and to authoritarian thinking. Schmitt held that the true ruler is the one who can suspend the rule of law in a crisis. Ajay says this is exactly what to be afraid of. Examples: Indira Gandhi's Emergency after the 1974 inflation crisis, and Hitler using the Reichstag fire to suspend Weimar Germany's constitution. A crisis weakens the usual checks on power, and opportunists take advantage.

head: Inventing an 'Other' to Exploit or Create a Crisis
dek: Amit adds another idea from Schmitt: politics requires an 'other'.
more: Amit adds another idea from Schmitt: politics requires an 'other'. In a crisis, the easy political move is to name an enemy, such as another community or 'the elites', present things as black and white, and play the victim even from a position of strength. Authoritarians use crises to gain power, and they also use this rhetoric to manufacture crises that justify taking more. Indira Gandhi blaming hoarders and speculators for inflation is Ajay's example.

head: Inflation Breaks Societies
dek: Ajay ties political disasters to monetary mistakes. Weimar Germany's hyperinflation came before Hitler, and India's 16% inflation in 1974 came before the Emergency.
more: Ajay ties political disasters to monetary mistakes. Weimar Germany's hyperinflation came before Hitler, and India's 16% inflation in 1974 came before the Emergency. Hyperinflation destroys polite society and the basis of ordinary lives. Ajay says monetary economists deserve credit for the good since inflation targeting and blame for disasters like these. Amit adds that the blame also belongs to leaders who overrule monetary economists.

head: Three Ways a Crisis Goes Wrong
dek: Ajay's summary. First, if no ideas were prepared, the crisis is simply wasted.
more: Ajay's summary. First, if no ideas were prepared, the crisis is simply wasted. Second, in a fragile state, malice: would-be autocrats suspend the rule of law, with Hitler as the extreme case. Third, in a state with low capability, incompetence: officials react with a flood of uncoordinated measures, as with demonetisation, COVID and the 2013 taper tantrum. Amit's use of Hanlon's razor ('never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity') introduced the third path.

head: Premature Load Bearing and Coherence
dek: Ajay uses Lant Pritchett's term. When a weak institution is suddenly given a heavy load, it does not rise to it.
more: Ajay uses Lant Pritchett's term. When a weak institution is suddenly given a heavy load, it does not rise to it. It collapses into organisational rout. The result is incoherence: practical people meeting each problem with a quick fix, with no shared strategy, so their actions work against each other. Coherence comes from thinking, which means understanding the world first and then applying one strategy to many problems.

head: Utopian vs Incremental Social Engineering (Popper)
dek: Karl Popper distinguished utopian social engineering, meaning grand plans such as collectivising every farm in the USSR, which usually end badly, from incremental engineering.
more: Karl Popper distinguished utopian social engineering, meaning grand plans such as collectivising every farm in the USSR, which usually end badly, from incremental engineering. Ajay compares two histories. The French Revolution tore society down and set France back for many years. Britain moved from monarchy to liberal democracy step by step, through gradual growth in Parliament's power, with Cromwell's execution of Charles I as the only dramatic moment, and became the most successful country in the world. Indian equity market reform from 1992 to 2007 is a local example of steady, data-driven progress.

head: Liberal in Ends, Conservative in Means
dek: The hosts call themselves conservative in Edmund Burke's sense. That does not mean opposing change.
more: The hosts call themselves conservative in Edmund Burke's sense. That does not mean opposing change. It means being humble about how complex the world is. Every change has unintended consequences and knock-on effects nobody controls, so move one step at a time. If you move too fast, you break things without understanding what happened.

head: Fix the Roof While the Sun Is Shining
dek: Ajay's prescription for reformers: don't wait for a crisis and don't try to engineer one.
more: Ajay's prescription for reformers: don't wait for a crisis and don't try to engineer one. Make progress every day in calm times by building people, ideas and communities one brick at a time. He asks for humility twice. Once because none of us understands the world well enough for grand plans, and again because we must admit when the evidence shows a step failed, then change course. A great country makes progress without needing a crisis.

head: Ajay asks who was key on the IMF side of the 1991 program. Amit answers Urjit Patel (
more: Ajay asks who was key on the IMF side of the 1991 program. Amit answers Urjit Patel ('See, my GK is in place') and then mentions A.N. Varma, 'not related to me', who was also critical: 'So you get good things done with Varmas in the mix.'

head: On their weak YouTube numbers, Amit
more: On their weak YouTube numbers, Amit says: 'Do the right thing, don't worry about the fruits of your action. The Bhagavad Gita meets Spike Lee.'

head: Amit says Ajay wrote
more: Amit says Ajay wrote 'Chaos is a ladder' in In Service of the Republic on his own, only to find out later it is also in Game of Thrones. Amit voices Ajay's disappointment: 'it's such a great line I came up with it, but you know, if shit happens, man.'

head: Amit checks that Ajay's eighth birthday was 7 August 1974, the year of record inflation.
more: Amit checks that Ajay's eighth birthday was 7 August 1974, the year of record inflation. Ajay: 'So I was like fully in the know by that time. Like supply and demand was something, you know, that every child knew. So why was Indira Gandhi so clueless?'

head: Playing on the letters collected as Glimpses of World History, Amit suggests a title for Ajay's next book
more: Playing on the letters collected as Glimpses of World History, Amit suggests a title for Ajay's next book: 'Glimpses of Good Economics.' Ajay agrees and promises to write letters of his own.

head: Amit introduces Hanlon's razor
more: Amit introduces Hanlon's razor: 'Ajay, I love your beard, but I want to give to you a razor.'

head: Rain stops the outdoor recording. Ajay vows to carry on…
more: Rain stops the outdoor recording. Ajay vows to carry on 'without an organisational rout', a callback to Lant Pritchett. Indoors, Amit says 'as our good friend Obelix would say, the sky fell on our heads.' He mentions his comfort bear Freddy, named after Bastiat and Hayek, is relieved Ajay 'did not throw a tantrum', and uses that to segue into the 2013 taper tantrum.

head: While reading the Weber quote, Ajay changes a…
more: While reading the Weber quote, Ajay changes a 'he' to 'she' by habit. Amit points out that both hosts use the feminine pronoun by default, and says of Weber's time: 'That is the age where men were men.'
'A crisis is a terrible thing to waste' is attributed to Rahm Emanuel, Barack Obama's chief of staff. Ajay notes it plays on 'the mind is a terrible thing to waste.'

head: Ajay invokes
more: Ajay invokes 'the beautiful poem The Center Does Not Hold' for Weimar Germany, where communists and extremists crushed the centre. He sees 'more than a passing resemblance' in today's world, with 'crazy on both sides'.

head: Kirit Parikh and the Three 'Selfs' of NREGS
dek: The best welfare design lets people's own choices do the targeting and scaling, with no official deciding who gets help.
more: Ajay traces workfare in India. It is welfare with a catch: you must turn up in the hot sun and break stones. Studies through the 1980s found real gains among the very poor from workfare programmes in places like Maharashtra, and the UPA government later made the idea national as NREGS. Professor Kirit Parikh used to tell Ajay that NREGS has three virtues. It is self-targeting, because only people down on their luck would do that work. It is self-adjusting, because in a good harvest people simply stay away. In the early 90s Parikh added that it is self-liquidating: once India is rich, nobody will work for 100 rupees a day, so the programme shuts itself down. That last part never happened, because governments kept raising NREGS wages, which Ajay says also distorted the labour market.

The best welfare design lets people's own choices do the targeting and scaling, with no official deciding who gets help. Once politicians start fiddling with the price, the programme loses the property that would have let it end.
printed: The scheme that should have quit

head: The Naka and the Taxi Stand
dek: The 'scary new' gig economy is a very old Indian arrangement made digital.
more: For centuries, Indian towns have had a naka or chowk. Labourers gather there in the morning, people who need workers for a construction job show up, they haggle a price out loud, and someone gets a day's work. There is no tenure, no provident fund, no labour law and no HR department, just a pure spot market. The taxi stand was the same: five or ten cabs waiting in one place for customers. Gig platforms are this old institution with an electronic layer on top.
The 'scary new' gig economy is a very old Indian arrangement made digital. What is new is not the contract but the technology underneath, which changes where the boundary of the firm sits.
printed: Haggling at the chowk, now by app

head: Amazon Mechanical Turk and India's 40%
dek: A whole global labour market for tiny cognitive jobs appeared almost unnoticed, and India took a large share of it.
more: Ajay explains how Amazon invented the microtask business. Workers log in, read a task description, take a short training course, pass a small exam, and then do the task again and again for a piece rate, maybe one rupee or ten rupees each. On the other side, a firm writes up a task it wants done by a hundred or a million people, sets the qualifying exam, uploads the data, and Amazon farms the work out and returns the answers. Ajay recalls reading that about 40% of the world's microtasks are done by Indian workers.

A whole global labour market for tiny cognitive jobs appeared almost unnoticed, and India took a large share of it. This is also the raw material behind the 'AI built on cheap Indian labour' criticism the hosts take on later.

head: Why Slums Are an Entry Ticket
dek: Judge a rough-looking institution by the real next-best option of the person using it, not by your own ideal.
more: When well-off urban Indians complain that slums are an eyesore and should be cleared, Amit reminds them of two things. First, their domestic help and most of the people they rely on live in slums. Second, at this stage of India's economy, slums are an entry point into the city. A villager who arrives can't afford to live anywhere else. Amit says gig work plays the same role: it is the first rung for someone trying to reach a better life.
Judge a rough-looking institution by the real next-best option of the person using it, not by your own ideal. Remove the bottom rung of the ladder and you don't lift anyone up; you lock them out.
printed: The slum as a first address

head: Swiggy Doesn't Care About Your Caste
dek: The impersonal platform, often criticised as dehumanising, quietly becomes a force for inclusion in a society full of social fault lines.
more: In India, caste networks, appearance, language and accent keep many people out of many jobs. A Dalit, for example, may find certain kinds of work very hard to get. Gig platforms don't ask, and the customer waiting for dinner only cares that it arrives on time. Amit admits that some buildings discriminate, for instance against a Muslim delivery person. He notes that delivery workers sometimes cleverly use a nom de plume at the door, though they shouldn't have to. By and large, he argues, your caste or religion no longer stops you from getting a gig.
The impersonal platform, often criticised as dehumanising, quietly becomes a force for inclusion in a society full of social fault lines.

head: The Nature of the Firm
dek: Coase asked what a firm does inside its boundary, with managers and long-term employees, and what it buys through arm's-length contracts.
more: Coase asked what a firm does inside its boundary, with managers and long-term employees, and what it buys through arm's-length contracts. Gig work reopens that question. Algorithms replace managers and push employees outside the firm, which is why Ajay calls it a milestone in the history of the firm.
Ajay points back to the EIE episode on four papers to explain why gig work is more than a convenience app.

head: The Market for 'Lemons'
dek: Akerlof showed that when buyers can't judge quality, prices fall. A platform that watches workers closely removes that information gap, so the logic says such monitoring should push workers' pay up, not down.
more: Akerlof showed that when buyers can't judge quality, prices fall. A platform that watches workers closely removes that information gap, so the logic says such monitoring should push workers' pay up, not down.
Ajay's reply to the complaint that algorithmic bosses spy on gig workers. Amit then explains the paper for listeners.

head: Why Gig Work Matters
dek: It argues that gig work is a ready-made urban safety net that needs no government, and an answer to recurring populist demands for an NREGS in the cities.
more: It argues that gig work is a ready-made urban safety net that needs no government, and an answer to recurring populist demands for an NREGS in the cities.
Ajay's co-authored piece, the basis of the closing chapter, 'Gig Work is the Urban NREGS'.

head: Gig Work Defined, in Three Kinds
dek: Gig work is a two-sided market where buyers and sellers of labour trade small tasks without complicated contracts.
more: Gig work is a two-sided market where buyers and sellers of labour trade small tasks without complicated contracts. Ajay sorts it into three kinds. (1) Capital-intensive gigs, where the worker owns the asset: the Uber driver's car, the Airbnb host's house, the photographer's expensive equipment. (2) Skill-intensive gigs, where the worker brings know-how to your home, like an Urban Company plumber or hairdresser. (3) Microtasks, such as labelling a photograph or picking the biggest of three numbers, sent by firms to workers worldwide over platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk.

head: Gig Work Is a Milestone in the Theory of the Firm
dek: Coase asked why some work happens inside a firm, with managers and long-term employees, while other work is bought through arm's-length contracts.
more: Coase asked why some work happens inside a firm, with managers and long-term employees, while other work is bought through arm's-length contracts. GPS, rating systems and the 'digital exhaust' workers generate now let an algorithm do what a supervisor of ten taxi drivers used to do. Two things follow. The manager is no longer needed, and the person who would have been an employee becomes an outside contractor. Ajay sees this as more efficiency, higher productivity and higher GDP in a country fighting mass poverty.

head: Freedom and Consent Come First
dek: Ajay's first response to every criticism: nobody forces a firm to post tasks or a worker to take them.
more: Ajay's first response to every criticism: nobody forces a firm to post tasks or a worker to take them. These are consenting adults, like buyers and sellers in a potato market. He would accept limits only for minors, who can't consent. Without coercion there is no market failure and no case for intervention. He also rejects the worry about 'atomised' workers. Why start from a collectivist view when each person can think for themselves? Leaving is healthy, and with many platforms to choose from, platforms have little power over workers.

head: Ask 'Better Than What?'
dek: Amit's version of the consent argument, focused on outcomes. People pick gig work because every other option they have is worse.
more: Amit's version of the consent argument, focused on outcomes. People pick gig work because every other option they have is worse. It may look demeaning from an air-conditioned middle-class room, but the alternative is not an office job with benefits. It is unemployment, begging or harder work. This is the same case the hosts made for sweatshops.

head: The Algorithmic Boss Is Better Than It Sounds
dek: Human bosses can be moody and tyrannical. An algorithm at least behaves predictably every day.
more: Human bosses can be moody and tyrannical. An algorithm at least behaves predictably every day. Akerlof's lemons logic says that the more fully a platform can see a worker's quality, the smaller the information gap and the higher the price that worker can command. Amit adds that ratings create a meritocracy: careful, hardworking people get rewarded, and companies waste less. The surveillance worth fearing is the state using its coercive power, not a platform workers choose to join.
printed: A fair hearing for the critics

head: Competition Is the Best Regulation
dek: Worried that platforms will exploit workers? There is no single giant buyer of gig labour, no monopsony.
more: Worried that platforms will exploit workers? There is no single giant buyer of gig labour, no monopsony. Swiggy has to treat its workers well or they move to Zomato, and Zomato loses them to Urban Company. Platforms competing for the same workers deliver the protection critics want regulation to provide.

head: Workers Have Always Trained Their Replacements
dek: Is it wrong that gig workers train the AI that will replace them? Ajay says this is how industrial capitalism has always worked.
more: Is it wrong that gig workers train the AI that will replace them? Ajay says this is how industrial capitalism has always worked. In the Industrial Revolution, engineers studied skilled workers and built their know-how into better machine tools. Programmers follow the same rule. Amit adds that the value created spills over into new jobs, as happened when India's IT services boom built whole ecosystems around it.

head: Sand and Silicon
dek: Is it unfair that trillion-dollar AI firms rest on low piece rates paid in India?
more: Is it unfair that trillion-dollar AI firms rest on low piece rates paid in India? By that logic, says Ajay, the whole Indian services boom was unfair too: JP Morgan's and American Express's market value would be 'built on' underpaid Gurgaon call-centre staff. The firm that turns sand into ultra-pure polycrystalline silicon doesn't owe the sand seller more because its product is valuable. Each price should come from supply and demand in its own market. Comparing a worker's wage with a company's market value is the wrong comparison.

head: Ten Reasons Gig Work Is Awesome
dek: Amit's case for gig work.
more: Amit's case for gig work. Economic reasons: an easy entry point into the city and into work, freedom to switch between platforms, work that is still there when the economy turns down (as it was during COVID), rewards through ratings, and borrowing a platform's ready-made customer network, so a village plumber doesn't need his own brand on day one. Social reasons: openness across caste and religion, setting your own work-life balance, and the ability to move cities or work remotely. Ethical reasons: the dignity of having work at all, and control over whom you work for each day.

head: India's Real Problem Is Too Few Jobs
dek: Only about 440 million people work in a country of 1.4 to 1.5 billion.
more: Only about 440 million people work in a country of 1.4 to 1.5 billion. Women's labour force participation is around 10%. About half of college graduates aren't working. Only about 10% of the population has the protected formal-sector jobs that critics treat as normal. For everyone else, those protections are a luxury they have never had, which is why gig work, now about 10 million workers, is a breakthrough. It also works as an on-ramp to moving: learn the Uber app in Patna, and it carries you to Bhopal or Amdavad.

head: Indian Labour Law Protects an Aristocracy
dek: Ajay says nearly everyone agrees India's formal-sector labour law is deeply broken.
more: Ajay says nearly everyone agrees India's formal-sector labour law is deeply broken. It helps explain why so few work in the organised sector, why growth falters and why large firms don't form. Employers don't want to deal with that law, and workers don't want to be unemployed, so both move to gig arrangements. That makes the case for algorithmic, outside-the-firm work even stronger in India than elsewhere. Amit calls the labour laws the core reason India missed its manufacturing revolution.
printed: Too few jobs, too much law

head: Flexibility Brings Women Into Work
dek: Indian women carry most of the housework and childcare, and that keeps them out of paid work.
more: Indian women carry most of the housework and childcare, and that keeps them out of paid work. Gig work lets a woman choose how much to work, even a few minutes, around those duties. Ajay calls this a real breakthrough and says the people making such work available to women deserve admiration.

head: Gig Work Is the Urban NREGS
dek: Apply Kirit Parikh's test to gig work. It is self-targeting, since only people down on their luck take on delivery work.
more: Apply Kirit Parikh's test to gig work. It is self-targeting, since only people down on their luck take on delivery work. It is self-adjusting, because supply, demand and surge pricing set the price. Unlike NREGS it is not self-liquidating, and it shouldn't be: it is a permanent safety net under the urban economy, and the first place people turned during COVID. It also makes a populist urban NREGS unnecessary. The private sector built it purely for profit, yet it delivers what a state safety net is supposed to.

head: Make Gig-Work Skills Universal
dek: Ajay's suggestion for anyone running programmes to help people: make sure everyone has the basic skills to get gig work.
more: Ajay's suggestion for anyone running programmes to help people: make sure everyone has the basic skills to get gig work. That means a smartphone, UPI payments in and out, reading English on a screen, and knowing at least two apps, whether for Swiggy deliveries or Amazon Mechanical Turk. Then everyone has the security of knowing there is always work to fall back on. Amit's gloss: public goods through voluntary private action.

head: Amit's made-up origin story for the show. Sipping a bourbon, he decided he needed a co-host and built a gig app called…
more: Amit's made-up origin story for the show. Sipping a bourbon, he decided he needed a co-host and built a gig app called 'Bourbon Company' to find a new one every week. Week one, only Ajay applied. Amit hoped pretty women or Bengali economists might apply next, but weeks two and three it was Ajay again. 'So the gig economy is a strange and curious thing. What should have been a one-night stand became an affair.' He then asks Ajay to respond to his 'magnificent soliloquy.'

head: Ajay ends his case
more: Ajay ends his case with 'The person who invented gig work should get a Bharat Ratna.' Amit, the libertarian, objects at once: 'The notion of gig work came out of spontaneous order. It was not one central planner who invented it.'

head: Ajay's dig at other cities while describing the old taxi stand
more: Ajay's dig at other cities while describing the old taxi stand: 'Perhaps if you're in a bad city other than Bombay, you would negotiate a price.'

head: Amit, a freelancer for over 15 years
more: Amit, a freelancer for over 15 years: 'I only do gigs for myself and I don't pay very well. At least I don't pay myself very well.'

head: Amit on setting your own work-life balance
more: Amit on setting your own work-life balance: 'If I am a Bengali who wants an afternoon nap, I will nap in the afternoon. Mera Uber app bandh hai, and then I will go out and drive in the evening.'

head: Ajay suggests that do-gooders
more: Ajay suggests that do-gooders 'round up every urban teenager, boys and girls, and take them into camps and teach them the basics of how to get gig work.' Amit steps in: 'No, you didn't literally mean this. No one should go and take young people... Because young people, out of their own incentives, will figure it out.'

head: The closing callback to the Bourbon Company bit, aimed at Ajay's co-author Maitreesh Ghatak
more: The closing callback to the Bourbon Company bit, aimed at Ajay's co-author Maitreesh Ghatak: 'And you co-wrote that article with a Bengali economist, didn't you? That too. You like Bengalis.'

head: Amit describes a gig worker hopping platforms (
more: Amit describes a gig worker hopping platforms ('Today is Swiggy, tomorrow's Zomato') with a Cliff Richard song he places in the 1960s: 'Goodbye Sam, Hello Samantha... Goodbye Lou, Hello Louise.' He adds: 'I don't think Cliff Richard was talking about the gig economy.'

head: From Carrying Marx to Class to Discovering Spontaneous Order
dek: Markets and evolution are one idea showing up in two domains: complex order that emerges bottom-up, with no central planner and no grand designer.
more: In college Amit was fairly left-leaning and carried Marx to classes, and Marxism seemed to explain everything. That changed once he looked at the world more closely and read Friedman, Hayek and Bastiat. His second awakening came later, in adulthood. Steven Pinker's The Blank Slate opened up evolutionary psychology for him, and he went on to read everything by Dawkins, Dennett and Robert Wright. He had never believed in God, but understanding natural selection made his atheism settle into a 'comfort zone'.
Markets and evolution are one idea showing up in two domains: complex order that emerges bottom-up, with no central planner and no grand designer. Once you grasp one, the other clicks into place.

head: The Scientific American Article That Hooked an Economist
dek: Economics and evolutionary biology share a mode of thought: simple competitive forces shaping a system over time.
more: While Ajay was an economics PhD student, he grew more and more interested in biology. The turning point was Paul Ewald's Scientific American article on the evolution of virulence. He saw deep commonalities between how economists and evolutionary biologists think about the forces that shape a system, and he 'geeked out' on books and papers. Evolution has stayed with him as a way of looking at the world ever since.
Economics and evolutionary biology share a mode of thought: simple competitive forces shaping a system over time. A single article from a neighbouring field can permanently rewire how you see things.

head: How Newton Made Room for God
dek: Science need not evict faith. It moves the designer's role from tinkering with every detail to setting the laws or initial conditions.
more: People once believed God personally chose the exact location and orbit of Jupiter. Newton's reconciliation was that God made universal laws like F = GMm/r², set the system going and let it whirl along, and humans find joy in deciphering that machine. Ajay offers a parallel for biology. All you need is to reach self-replicating molecules. After that, sexual reproduction, sexual selection and ever-escalating complexity are more or less inevitable, so a believer could place God at that initialization, or all the way back at the Big Bang.
Science need not evict faith. It moves the designer's role from tinkering with every detail to setting the laws or initial conditions. Natural selection, like gravity, then runs on its own.

head: A Friend Who Thought Gym Gains Are Heritable
dek: Folk Lamarckism still feels intuitive. Behaviour you adopt in your lifetime doesn't rewrite the DNA you pass on.
more: A friend told Amit that if he worked out well and lived a disciplined life, his kid could inherit those properties. Amit replied that the child can pick up the habits by watching him, but they won't be in his DNA. The belief is Lamarckism: the idea that changes you make in your lifetime, like a blacksmith's strong arms, pass on through your genes. It was common in the 19th century, before genetics was understood, and we now know there is nothing to it.

Folk Lamarckism still feels intuitive. Behaviour you adopt in your lifetime doesn't rewrite the DNA you pass on. What your children get from your discipline travels through example, which means culture.

head: Dara Singh's Daughter and a Father's Lesson in Biology
dek: What looks like inherited talent is genes plus a correlated upbringing, never the parent's acquired gains.
more: When Ajay was growing up, his sister had a classmate who was the daughter of the wrestler Dara Singh, and she was very strong. Ajay's father used her to teach his children about Lamarckism. Some nature was transmitted, but it was not the bodybuilding Dara Singh had done. His strength was in his genes at birth. On top of that, she grew up in a household that prized physicality and probably exercised a lot.
What looks like inherited talent is genes plus a correlated upbringing, never the parent's acquired gains. A good childhood example can become lifelong intellectual scaffolding.

head: Kapil Dev on How to Get Another Kapil Dev
dek: A deadpan reminder that exceptional talent can't be manufactured on demand.
more: Near the end of his career, Kapil Dev was asked mournfully by a reporter at a press conference: 'Sir, you will retire soon, how can we get another Kapil Dev?' Kapil replied that his father was dead and his mother was too old. Amit recalled it right after the discussion of what is and isn't inherited.
A deadpan reminder that exceptional talent can't be manufactured on demand. Part of what made him came from his parents, and that is not a recipe anyone can repeat.

head: Sickle Cell, Thalassemia and the Malaria Trade-off
dek: An apparent defect can be a defence against a threat you weren't looking at.
more: In sickle cell anemia, red blood cells collapse into a sickle shape when the heart is pushed hard, so a person running from a leopard can abruptly crash. Thalassemia also involves malfunctioning red blood cells. For a long time it seemed these traits should have died out. Scientists later understood that they are selected for where malaria is common. The malaria plasmodium hides inside red blood cells, beyond the reach of the immune system, and multiplies there. Sickling makes the plasmodium's survival much harder. Evolution struck a balance between peak cardiac capability and malaria survival, which is why entire communities in India carry these traits.
An apparent defect can be a defence against a threat you weren't looking at. Evolution doesn't perfect single traits. It trades them off against the real dangers of a particular environment.

head: Lactase Persistence and the Milk Cultures
dek: Biology and culture co-evolve. A mutation unlocks a resource, culture builds itself around exploiting it, and together they produce enormous genetic success that you can still trace on a map.
more: All mammal infants make lactase to digest the lactose in milk, and they lose the ability as they grow up. About 7,000 to 8,000 years ago, a mutation on the border between Bulgaria and Turkey let adults keep making lactase. Milk became high-quality adult nutrition. Whole cow-owning, cow-herding cultures grew around it, and its carriers reproduced well and conquered faraway lands, including northern India. In India, the gene is still far more common in the north, where those invasions happened, than in the south.
Biology and culture co-evolve. A mutation unlocks a resource, culture builds itself around exploiting it, and together they produce enormous genetic success that you can still trace on a map.

head: The Deep-Sea Diving Women of Jeju Island
dek: Natural selection is not only ancient history. A livelihood that applies steady pressure over centuries can visibly shape a population's biology.
more: On Korea's Jeju Island, diving into the deep sea (for pearls, as Ajay puts it) has been the main livelihood for hundreds of years. Women better able to hold their breath, process oxygen and cope with pressure came back with the catch. Those less adapted had accidents and died. Over centuries the population developed remarkable physical adaptations for diving, much as Himalayan Sherpas cope with low oxygen. Amit added that the world's top long-distance runners come from East Africa, with altitude, terrain and culture amplifying the effect.
Natural selection is not only ancient history. A livelihood that applies steady pressure over centuries can visibly shape a population's biology.

head: How the Industrial Revolution Turned Britain's Moths Black
dek: Evolution can play out in front of your eyes when selection pressure is strong.
more: British moths were originally white or off-white. Then poor-quality coal furnaces covered buildings in black soot, and white moths resting on black walls became easy prey for birds. Darker mutants survived better, and within a couple of decades industrial England's moths had turned black. The example played a big role in the earliest debates over evolution. Amit spelled out the mechanism: a few random dark mutants always exist, and the environment decides who survives. The same process explains mosquitoes resistant to insecticides and bacteria resistant to antibiotics. Nothing is being 'learned'; rare resistant mutants simply survive and multiply.
Evolution can play out in front of your eyes when selection pressure is strong. The environment does the choosing among random variations that already exist.

head: DDT Fogging, Antibiotic Courses and Breeding Superbugs
dek: Partial doses are worse than useless because they actively select for resistance.
more: When a single housing colony does DDT fogging, neighbouring buildings get a partial dose. The mosquitoes that survive it are the ones with some resistance, so each round ratchets the population toward complete resistance. Antibiotics fail the same way. A full course drives pathogens down to very low counts so the immune system can finish them off. But people feel better within two or three weeks and stop early, which leaves the most resistant pathogens alive to surge back. Each imperfect cycle breeds antimicrobial resistance. Amit called it evolutionary theory meeting human hubris.

Partial doses are worse than useless because they actively select for resistance. Individual incentives (fog just my colony, stop when I feel fine) erode collective assets, so this has to be handled as a population-scale public health problem.
printed: Half a dose, twice the trouble

head: Cholera in East Bengal vs West Bengal
dek: Public health measures do more than block spread. They change the evolutionary incentives of the pathogen itself, so better sanitation can make a disease less deadly.
more: In the early years after independence, West Bengal improved its drinking water and reduced fecal contamination, while East Bengal did not. Where contaminated water guaranteed transmission, cholera had no reason to keep its host alive. It killed fast, driving diarrhea into the water supply. Where transmission got harder, cholera strains evolved toward lower virulence. Ajay applies the same logic to COVID. In crowded settings like Bombay's suburban trains or the Maha Kumbh, the most rapacious strains win. Masking and distancing push the virus toward mildness.
Public health measures do more than block spread. They change the evolutionary incentives of the pathogen itself, so better sanitation can make a disease less deadly.

head: The 1944 Amsterdam Famine and Its Children
dek: Same DNA, different outcome. Early environment changes how genes are expressed, and that is how nurture physically turns nature's knobs.
more: In 1944, after a rebellion around Amsterdam, the Nazis cut off the roads to starve the city as punishment. The Allies airdropped food, but there was a terrible famine. Years later, scientists studied children who were exposed to the famine in varying degrees between conception and birth, comparing them with those born before and after. Those exposed to starvation in the womb had a much higher propensity to obesity, hoarding food more desperately, and the effect persisted for several generations.
Same DNA, different outcome. Early environment changes how genes are expressed, and that is how nurture physically turns nature's knobs.

head: The Evolution of Virulence
dek: It blew his mind. The idea that how easily a pathogen spreads determines how deadly it evolves to be is a lens you can't unsee.
more: It blew his mind. The idea that how easily a pathogen spreads determines how deadly it evolves to be is a lens you can't unsee.
Ajay names it as the turning point of his PhD years and later lays out its argument, using cholera and COVID as examples. Linked in the show notes.

head: The Evolution of Everything
dek: It shows the same bottom-up process, with no central planner and no grand designer, behind natural selection, languages, society and economies.
more: It shows the same bottom-up process, with no central planner and no grand designer, behind natural selection, languages, society and economies. That bridges Amit's two intellectual awakenings.
Raised when Ajay linked evolution to spontaneous order. It is also on the show notes' further reading list.

head: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Matt Ridley)
dek: The long-form conversation on spontaneous order across biology, culture and markets.
more: The long-form conversation on spontaneous order across biology, culture and markets.
Amit mentions doing an episode with Matt Ridley on the book. Linked in the show notes.

head: I, Pencil
dek: It makes you see how mind-boggling it is to make even a pencil, which is the first step toward understanding that such complexity comes from self-organizing systems, not central planning.
more: It makes you see how mind-boggling it is to make even a pencil, which is the first step toward understanding that such complexity comes from self-organizing systems, not central planning.
Ajay's levels-of-understanding analogy: level one is the person who 'gets I, Pencil'. Linked in the show notes.

head: The Blank Slate
dek: He calls it a masterpiece and his window into evolutionary psychology and natural selection.
more: He calls it a masterpiece and his window into evolutionary psychology and natural selection.
Amit's entry point into natural selection in adulthood. On the further reading list.

head: The Selfish Gene
dek: A landmark book with a 'fantastic metaphor'. Read carefully rather than literally, selfish-gene reasoning ends up explaining why humans are altruistic.
more: A landmark book with a 'fantastic metaphor'. Read carefully rather than literally, selfish-gene reasoning ends up explaining why humans are altruistic.
Discussed in the segment on semantic confusion. On the further reading list.

head: The Blind Watchmaker
dek: One of the books the hosts learned the subject from. It pairs with the episode's point that intricate design can arise without a designer.
more: One of the books the hosts learned the subject from. It pairs with the episode's point that intricate design can arise without a designer.
On the show notes' further reading list. Amit says he read everything by Dawkins, and the episode discusses Paley's watchmaker argument.

head: Darwin's Dangerous Idea
dek: One of the core books the hosts learned evolution from, by the thinker who framed it as an idea that dissolves simple preconceptions.
more: One of the core books the hosts learned evolution from, by the thinker who framed it as an idea that dissolves simple preconceptions.
On the further reading list. Ajay quotes Dennett calling evolutionary theory a 'universal acid', and Amit read everything by Dennett.

head: The Moral Animal
dek: Part of the core reading through which Amit came to understand natural selection and evolutionary psychology.
more: Part of the core reading through which Amit came to understand natural selection and evolutionary psychology.
Robert Wright is among the authors Amit read after The Blank Slate. On the further reading list.

head: The Evolution of Human Sexuality
dek: Formative for Amit's understanding of how and why men and women evolved differently.
more: Formative for Amit's understanding of how and why men and women evolved differently. He says A Billion Wicked Thoughts later confirmed its arguments with data.
Cited for the observation that science expands knowledge but not language, and as part of Amit's early reading. On the further reading list.

head: The Evolution of Cooperation
dek: Uses game theory and natural selection to show why we evolved to cooperate and even sacrifice for the tribe, which makes sense from the gene's point of view.
more: Uses game theory and natural selection to show why we evolved to cooperate and even sacrifice for the tribe, which makes sense from the gene's point of view.
Raised when the hosts explain why selfish-gene logic leads to altruism. On the further reading list.

head: A Billion Wicked Thoughts
dek: He calls it a brilliant book and a masterpiece.
more: He calls it a brilliant book and a masterpiece. It uses hard data on anonymized internet behaviour to show what men and women want, explains why through natural selection, and confirms the arguments of Symons, Buss, Miller and Pinker.

Recommended to Amit by a friend, Aditi, after the alt-data episode (EIE 118). It is the basis for next week's episode on sexual preferences, and Amit reads its passage on taste and culture in this one.

head: The Age of Pandemics
dek: Highlights that past pandemics ended not because we eliminated the strain but because it evolved toward the least virulent form.
more: Highlights that past pandemics ended not because we eliminated the strain but because it evolved toward the least virulent form. That is why Amit was confident COVID would become something we live with.
Mentioned during the discussion of how pathogen virulence evolves. Linked in the show notes.

head: Evolution as the Ultimate Spontaneous Order
dek: Dennett called evolutionary theory a 'universal acid' that strips away simple preconceptions.
more: Dennett called evolutionary theory a 'universal acid' that strips away simple preconceptions. Evolution has no central planner, no teleology and no objective, yet it produces the human eye and the eagle's eye. Ajay's moral: when you marvel at such design and feel the engineer's urge to plan and control, remember that it came from an uncontrolled, self-organizing system. That is an argument against central planning and industrial policy.

head: The Pencil Ladder: Levels of Understanding Complexity
dek: Ajay's four levels. Level zero thinks pencils are easy to make.
more: Ajay's four levels. Level zero thinks pencils are easy to make. Level one 'gets I, Pencil' and is amazed at how much it takes. Level two concludes something this complex needs a central committee directing the aluminium and steel. The highest level understands that self-organizing systems produce pencils without anyone in charge. Faced with nature's complexity, the same trap is to assume a designer.

head: Design Without a Designer (Paley's Watchmaker)
dek: William Paley argued that a watch found on a beach, unlike a stone, implies a watchmaker, and so the intricacy of the human eye implies God.
more: William Paley argued that a watch found on a beach, unlike a stone, implies a watchmaker, and so the intricacy of the human eye implies God. Natural selection shows that random variation plus selection can produce such intricacy bottom-up. That makes the metaphorical watchmaker unnecessary, though not impossible: a believer can say God created the process itself. Natural selection is independent of the question of God and of where morality comes from.

head: The Is-Ought and Naturalistic Fallacies
dek: Hume's is-ought fallacy derives a prescription from a description. G.E.
more: Hume's is-ought fallacy derives a prescription from a description. G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy defines 'good' as 'natural'. Bigots once called homosexuality unnatural and therefore wrong, which committed the fallacy and was also factually false, since homosexuality occurs across many species. Amit sees the right committing it (his objection to Jordan Peterson's arguments about traditional gender roles) and the left too, when it denies any differences between men and women for fear that description implies unequal treatment. Combined with the 'man of system' engineering mindset, these fallacies fed early-20th-century eugenics, on the right and the left alike. Morality is ours to decide through reason; nature can constrain or enable, but it shouldn't dictate.

head: Nature Gives You Knobs, Nurture Turns Them
dek: Nature versus nurture is a false binary. Amit attributes the 'knobs' line to Steven Pinker but admits he has never been able to find the source.
more: Nature versus nurture is a false binary. Amit attributes the 'knobs' line to Steven Pinker but admits he has never been able to find the source. Someone predisposed to anger may live calmly in a peaceful environment, and a placid person can be pushed to fury by a brutal life. Amit calls the Enlightenment project an exercise in deciding how we ought to live, then using culture to mitigate the hardwiring we dislike and amplify what we like.

head: Why We Overstate the Role of Nature
dek: Nature and nurture are correlated. In a hockey-playing family, the kids may inherit explosive strength and also get early coaching, praise and constant hockey talk.
more: Nature and nurture are correlated. In a hockey-playing family, the kids may inherit explosive strength and also get early coaching, praise and constant hockey talk. A talented child in such a home gets every support. Because we don't separate the two, we see 'genes for chess in this family' when a big part of what passes down is environment.

head: Stone-Age Hardware, Modern Operating System
dek: Our nature was tuned for prehistoric problems. Scarce food made us crave high-fat, high-sugar food.
more: Our nature was tuned for prehistoric problems. Scarce food made us crave high-fat, high-sugar food. Lethal threats like a charging lion wired a hair-trigger fight-or-flight response. Life in bands of about 150 made outsiders seem dangerous, which is tribalism. Culture is the operating system on top. It can teach us to eat less sugar, to presume good faith, and to form imagined communities across the world. Amit adds that engagement-maximizing social media has accidentally amplified our tribal instincts.

head: Proximate vs Ultimate Causation
dek: Evolutionary explanations answer why a trait was selected for about a hundred thousand years ago.
more: Evolutionary explanations answer why a trait was selected for about a hundred thousand years ago. They don't describe what you consciously feel today. A man who likes youth in women isn't thinking of childbearing, and a sweet tooth isn't a conscious plan to store scarce calories. Objecting 'but I don't feel that way' confuses the two levels. Ajay adds that the conscious voice in our head is just one evolutionary adaptation among many; much of what drives us, like the circuitry that raises the heart rate, runs below awareness.

head: Language Traps: Metaphor, Anthropomorphism and Teleology
dek: Donald Symons noted that science expands knowledge but not language.
more: Donald Symons noted that science expands knowledge but not language. As with 'public goods' or 'market failure' in economics, biology borrows ordinary words like messenger genes, master and slave genes, and the selfish gene, and lay readers take them literally. Genes don't 'want' anything. Read crudely, 'selfish gene' suggests people are selfish; done rigorously, the same reasoning explains human altruism. The deepest trap is teleology, the belief that evolution is aiming somewhere. It has no purpose at all.

head: The Bare Mechanics of Natural Selection
dek: All you need are things that make copies of themselves (organisms, or even firms), variation in their traits, and finite resources to compete for.
more: All you need are things that make copies of themselves (organisms, or even firms), variation in their traits, and finite resources to compete for. Natural selection then follows inexorably. Better resource-users leave more copies, so their traits spread and get refined to 'fiendish levels of excellence', slowly, generation after generation. There is no equality, no apex and no endpoint, just an endless competition.

head: Sex as a Variation Engine, and Sexual Selection
dek: Asexual reproduction, like an amoeba splitting, yields near-copies with little variation.
more: Asexual reproduction, like an amoeba splitting, yields near-copies with little variation. Sexual reproduction shuffles genes and greatly increases the variation that selection can act on. In complex creatures, mate choice becomes a second engine: traits the opposite sex prefers multiply. The springbok's huge leap when chased signals health and spare energy to mates, but it also lets the lion wait for it to land. The two engines can pull against each other.

head: Epigenetics Is Not Lamarckism
dek: DNA is not a fixed program. Epigenetics studies gene expression, the way environment interacts with the genetic code to produce different outcomes.
more: DNA is not a fixed program. Epigenetics studies gene expression, the way environment interacts with the genetic code to produce different outcomes. In the 1944 Amsterdam famine, exposure to starvation in the womb raised the propensity to obesity. That is not Lamarckism, which holds that behaviour you adopt in your lifetime alters the DNA you pass on. The famine didn't change anyone's DNA. It changed how existing genes were expressed.

head: The Evolution of Virulence
dek: Paul Ewald's idea is that a pathogen's virulence is tuned to how it spreads.
more: Paul Ewald's idea is that a pathogen's virulence is tuned to how it spreads. A pathogen that must wait a long time to jump hosts does best by keeping its host alive. One that spreads easily, through dirty water or crowded air, can be rapacious. So virulence is not random. Sanitation, masking and distancing select for milder strains, and Amit notes past pandemics ended as the strains evolved toward the least virulent.

head: Evolutionary Time Is Measured in Generations
dek: Big mutations are usually birth defects, so change comes in tiny steps accumulated over hundreds or thousands of generations.
more: Big mutations are usually birth defects, so change comes in tiny steps accumulated over hundreds or thousands of generations. Bacteria reproduce roughly every ten minutes and evolve at a frightening pace, which has made the immune system a major evolutionary battleground. Humans manage about one generation every 25 years, so only about 400 in 10,000 years, which barely changes anything. We are mostly the humans of 10,000 years ago living in a modernity that, on that scale, has barely begun.

head: The Brain Is Part of the Body
dek: No one denies that natural selection shaped male and female bodies differently.
more: No one denies that natural selection shaped male and female bodies differently. Yet many insist that behavioural differences are purely cultural. Amit argues the brain is shaped by selection like every other organ. Cultures do magnify the worst parts of our nature, and patriarchy is real, but some differences are hardwired. The goal is to acknowledge them without concluding they justify unequal treatment.
printed: It doesn’t stop at the neck

head: Amit's cold open
more: Amit's cold open: 'Just a few moments ago, Mr. Ajay Shah was telling me about a young female mosquito which got knocked up and came looking for mammalian proteins, but unfortunately collided with my jeans pants. So nothing much is happening there.'

head: After Ajay recites F = GMm/r² and builds his pencil analogy, Amit asks…
more: After Ajay recites F = GMm/r² and builds his pencil analogy, Amit asks: 'How many equations do you know by heart, by the way?'

head: Amit illustrating the anger knob: your life could be nasty, brutish and hard
more: Amit illustrating the anger knob: your life could be nasty, brutish and hard, and 'you keep meeting Bengali economists and you can't help shouting at them.'

head: Ajay, self-aware

head: After the shoot moved indoors because of rain, Amit
more: After the shoot moved indoors because of rain, Amit: 'under the pressure of natural selection, my shirt changed into a hoodie. Isn't it miraculous how these things work?'

head: On the springbok, whose showy leaps for mates let the lion wait for it to land, Amit
more: On the springbok, whose showy leaps for mates let the lion wait for it to land, Amit: 'I guess evolution among the springboks could then be called a race to the top.'
