more: Amit on the Amsterdam famine babies: the famine turned the sweetness knob up full, and 'those kids ended up, you know, eating a lot of laddoos, if laddoos were ever in Amsterdam.'

head: On sickle cell's trade-off between outrunning a leopard and surviving malaria, Amit
more: On sickle cell's trade-off between outrunning a leopard and surviving malaria, Amit: 'I have a title for the short story. The Lion and the Mosquito.' Ajay corrects: 'The Lion or the Mosquito.'

more: Ajay explaining that a too-virulent pathogen can't get copies out to others: 'Not that he's thinking, this is just evolutionary theory.' Amit: 'Not that he's a he.' Ajay: 'in fact, many of them have no gender.'

head: Amit, right after the chapter on semantics
more: Amit, right after the chapter on semantics: 'I'm really glad that we had that chapter where we spoke about the importance of semantics, because here you are talking about the incentives of COVID virus.'

head: On why this became a two-parter
more: On why this became a two-parter: 'this will become like a Seen and the Unseen eight-hour episode if we try to combine it all into one thing.'

head: Amit's closing pun after Ajay's ode to the human and eagle eye
more: Amit's closing pun after Ajay's ode to the human and eagle eye: 'The only kind of eye I don't like, Ajay, is the I in ego.'

head: Douglas Adams, quoted by Amit on natural selection
more: Douglas Adams, quoted by Amit on natural selection: 'The awe it inspired in me made the awe that people talk about in respect of religious experience seem, frankly, silly beside it. I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.'

head: Ghiselin, quoted by Amit on why Darwin's cosmology was so hard to accept
more: Ghiselin, quoted by Amit on why Darwin's cosmology was so hard to accept: 'A world populated by organisms striving to no end, but rather playing ridiculous sexual games. A world in which the brain is itself an extension of the gonads simply cannot be reconciled with the old way of thinking.'

head: Eugenics wasn't only Hitler's project
more: Eugenics wasn't only Hitler's project: Amit notes that H.G. Wells and George Bernard Shaw, both Fabian socialists and both inspirations for Nehru, also believed in it. He sees it as the naturalistic fallacy combined with Adam Smith's 'man of system'.

head: Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam on culture shaping taste
more: Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam on culture shaping taste: 'We can learn to appreciate food that is bitter, like coffee or olives, but no culture enjoys cinnamon sprinkled feces.'

head: Ajay on how recent the rule of law is in evolutionary terms
more: Ajay on how recent the rule of law is in evolutionary terms: 'the Magna Carta is 1215, it's like blink of an eye. It was only the day before yesterday that the Magna Carta happened.'

head: The Life Lessons Meetup in Goa
dek: Price and effort act as filters. A high bar can select for exactly the community you want, and the internet lets us build communities of choice instead of living only within communities of circumstance.
more: After three 2025 cohorts of their course Life Lessons (about 130 participants), Amit and Ajay held an in-person meetup in Goa. They hoped for 20 to 30 people. Between 50 and 60 came, each paying for their own flights and hotel, with last-minute arrivals from Thailand and New York driven by FOMO in the WhatsApp group. At the first lunch, the first seven people to sit with Amit were all on sabbatical. Amit calls himself a socially awkward introvert who dislikes crowds, yet this was the one gathering where he felt at ease with everyone. He credits a selection effect: a premium price and serious content attracted curious people with agency who weren't on the beaten path.

Price and effort act as filters. A high bar can select for exactly the community you want, and the internet lets us build communities of choice instead of living only within communities of circumstance.

head: Kinsey: Punished for Being Right
dek: People who state uncomfortable truths are often punished in their lifetimes and vindicated so completely later that their treatment looks absurd.
more: Alfred Kinsey put 521 questions to thousands of respondents and published books on male (1948) and female (1953) sexuality. He found that about a third of men admitted a homosexual experience, and that many women masturbated, thought about sex, and had partners beyond their husbands. The female volume proved too much even for America. The Rockefeller Foundation dropped his funding, he was ostracised, and he died of pneumonia at 62. Amit compares him to Ignaz Semmelweis, who showed that hand-washing before surgery saves lives, was ignored, and died in a lunatic asylum. Amit also flags Kinsey's limitation: his sample came from elite Westernised society and recorded stated rather than revealed preferences.

People who state uncomfortable truths are often punished in their lifetimes and vindicated so completely later that their treatment looks absurd. The obvious truths of tomorrow are often the taboos of today.

head: Savita Bhabhi's Favourite Blog
dek: A funny snapshot of how things went viral before social media, when bloggers and underground comics fed each other's popularity, told with Amit's self-mocking pride.
more: Around 2006–07, an adult comic called Savita Bhabhi was becoming popular. Amit was then running his hugely popular blog India Uncut, about 8,000 posts in five years, roughly five a day. He blogged about the comic and likes to think he helped it go viral in the pre-Twitter era. One day he opened a new edition and found Savita Bhabhi discussing her favourite blog: India Uncut. Ajay introduced the tale as 'one of the highlights of Amit Varma's life.'
A funny snapshot of how things went viral before social media, when bloggers and underground comics fed each other's popularity, told with Amit's self-mocking pride.

head: Women Who Hunted Osama bin Laden
dek: Our mental image of who suits a job is often shaped by fiction, not by the traits the job actually needs.
more: Amit described the 'Miss Marple's Detective Agency' in women's minds: strong memory, attention to detail, relentless information-gathering. Ajay pointed out that we picture intelligence operatives as men out of John le Carré novels or James Bond films, yet these traits suit intelligence work perfectly. Critical people in the CIA's hunt for Osama bin Laden were women who could hold vast databases in their heads and spot the one thing that broke the pattern. He suggested India's intelligence services be rebuilt with many more women. Amit stressed that although it sounded glib, they both meant it seriously.
Our mental image of who suits a job is often shaped by fiction, not by the traits the job actually needs. Hiring for the real cognitive demands can reveal talent that stereotypes hide.

head: Ovulation, Lap Dancers and Unconscious Signals
dek: A great deal of mating behaviour runs on signals that neither sender nor receiver consciously perceives.
more: At the Goa meetup Amit joked that he would 'mansplain ovulation'. The finding he shared: during ovulation, women, whether they know it or not, tend to dress more revealingly, behave more sexily and be more open to 'bad boy' types. A study of lap dancers found that ovulating dancers earned by far the highest tips, then dancers who were neither ovulating nor menstruating, then menstruating dancers. It is unclear whether the women behaved differently or the men picked up on something. Even more striking, men became more protective of their partners during ovulation despite having no conscious way to know it was happening. In a separate blind smell test, the men women found sexiest by body odour turned out to be the most dominant and high-status.
A great deal of mating behaviour runs on signals that neither sender nor receiver consciously perceives. Our bodies are negotiating beneath our awareness.

head: A Billion Wicked Thoughts
dek: It moves beyond Kinsey's stated preferences to revealed preferences. Amit underlined nearly every page and says it made things he knew intuitively 'high definition' and showed him phenomena he had never considered.
more: It moves beyond Kinsey's stated preferences to revealed preferences. Amit underlined nearly every page and says it made things he knew intuitively 'high definition' and showed him phenomena he had never considered. He especially loved the chapter on homosexuality. Ajay closed by urging readers to read it, because much of it is uncomfortable and departs from mainstream narratives.

The book the whole episode is built around. Amit calls it an episode about a book, in the tradition of their earlier book episodes. It uses anonymised internet data (porn searches, romance-novel readership) to map what people actually want, then explains it with natural selection, psychology and sociology.

head: The Selfish Gene
dek: Essential background for the 'why' of sexuality. Amit cautions that the 'selfish gene' is a metaphor and should not be read literally.
more: Essential background for the 'why' of sexuality. Amit cautions that the 'selfish gene' is a metaphor and should not be read literally.
Cited as the 1975 landmark that brought natural selection to a mass audience.

head: The Evolution of Human Sexuality
dek: It used natural selection to explain why men and women are wired differently, and it set off a flood of later books on the subject, including A Billion Wicked Thoughts.
more: It used natural selection to explain why men and women are wired differently, and it set off a flood of later books on the subject, including A Billion Wicked Thoughts.
Amit calls this 1979 book the second big milestone in popular evolutionary writing after Dawkins.

head: The Blank Slate
dek: It opened his eyes to how biology shapes us. He also cites Pinker's argument there that art and culture may be male ornamentation.
more: It opened his eyes to how biology shapes us. He also cites Pinker's argument there that art and culture may be male ornamentation.
The book through which Amit first discovered natural selection in the early 2000s.

head: The Mating Mind
dek: Part of the group of books that showed him how biology works on human desire, and on his reading list for this subject.
more: Part of the group of books that showed him how biology works on human desire, and on his reading list for this subject.
One of the books Amit read that continued Symons's work.

head: The Evolution of Desire
dek: It builds the evolutionary account of why men and women want what they want, which forms the shared ground this episode starts from.
more: It builds the evolutionary account of why men and women want what they want, which forms the shared ground this episode starts from.
Another of the post-Symons books Amit read and 'thoroughly enjoyed'.

head: The Moral Animal
dek: Wright shows how the same impulses can produce different equilibria, with both monogamy and polygamy as logical adaptations depending on a society's direction.
more: Wright shows how the same impulses can produce different equilibria, with both monogamy and polygamy as logical adaptations depending on a society's direction. Amit leaves those 'fascinating' explanations for readers to discover.
Cited while discussing romance and jealousy as evolutionary adaptations.

head: Communities of Circumstance vs Communities of Choice
dek: For most of history your friends were set by geography: where you went to school and where you worked.
more: For most of history your friends were set by geography: where you went to school and where you worked. The internet let Amit's 'cusp generation' form communities around shared interests instead. Almost all his close friends now come from such communities, and Life Lessons amplifies that.

head: Why Understanding Sexuality Matters
dek: Amit gives four reasons. (1) Know thyself: otherwise we gaslight ourselves about our own urges.
more: Amit gives four reasons. (1) Know thyself: otherwise we gaslight ourselves about our own urges. You must know yourself before you can be kind to yourself, and be kind to yourself before you can be kind to others. (2) Know others: we wrongly assume others share our instincts and judge them by our own standards. (3) It builds agency and compassion: knowing our wiring lets us override it, as Amit and Ajay did by choosing not to have kids despite the hardwired urge. (4) Mismatch: instincts built for hunter-gatherer scarcity misfire in a world of porn, dating apps and birth control.

head: Is-Ought and the Naturalistic Fallacy
dek: Two guardrails. Hume's is-ought problem: 'men are wired to be promiscuous' does not imply they should be, just as being hardwired for violence doesn't justify violence.
more: Two guardrails. Hume's is-ought problem: 'men are wired to be promiscuous' does not imply they should be, just as being hardwired for violence doesn't justify violence. G. E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy is the reverse error of treating natural as good. Bigots once called homosexuality unnatural and therefore bad, which is wrong on both counts, since it is perfectly natural in our species and many others.

head: Proximate vs Ultimate Causation
dek: We crave sweets because, when calories were unpredictable, people who stocked up survived and passed on their genes.
more: We crave sweets because, when calories were unpredictable, people who stocked up survived and passed on their genes. We dislike bitterness because poisonous plants taste bitter. That is the ultimate cause. The proximate cause is simply 'I like it.' Evolutionary explanations describe why instincts were shaped hundreds of thousands of years ago, not what anyone consciously thinks today.

head: Averages Are Not Identities (The Shoe-Size Analogy)
dek: Ajay's statistical intuition: on average older kids have bigger feet, but not every older child has bigger feet than every younger one, and five-year-olds vary hugely among themselves.
more: Ajay's statistical intuition: on average older kids have bigger feet, but not every older child has bigger feet than every younger one, and five-year-olds vary hugely among themselves. A real correlation has explanatory power while leaving lots of individual variation. Generalisations about men and women work the same way.

head: The Root Asymmetry: Promiscuous Men, Selective Women
dek: In ancestral conditions, spreading genes cost a man almost nothing, while a woman paid with pregnancy and years of child-rearing and got few 'shots'.
more: In ancestral conditions, spreading genes cost a man almost nothing, while a woman paid with pregnancy and years of child-rearing and got few 'shots'. So men evolved to seek quantity, and women to be selective in two ways: good genes (dominant, high-status men whose sons will also spread genes) and a reliable provider who helps the child survive. From this follow men's attraction to youth and beauty (present and future fertility, health) and women's attraction to status and power. Amit says nearly every male–female difference flows from this asymmetry, and it is description, not prescription.

head: Ornamentation: Signals Built for Sexual Selection
dek: Ornaments like the peacock's tail or a springbok's high jump help an animal get mates even if they make it easier for predators to spot, so there is an optimal trade-off between the two pressures.
more: Ornaments like the peacock's tail or a springbok's high jump help an animal get mates even if they make it easier for predators to spot, so there is an optimal trade-off between the two pressures. In humans, beauty works as a health signal. Ideal female faces differ across cultures but are all symmetrical, and symmetry and clear skin both indicate good health.

head: What Men's Searches Reveal: Fertility Cues
dek: Revealed preferences (what men search for, not what they say they want) point to youth and fertility.
more: Revealed preferences (what men search for, not what they say they want) point to youth and fertility. 'Teenage' is the top search term. Searches for 'fat' outnumber 'skinny' three to one, which suggests the skinny ideal comes from women's magazines like Vogue and Cosmopolitan rather than from men. Men prefer a 0.7 waist-to-hip ratio without ever searching for hips. In a British bar experiment, a woman got hit on far more as padding took her from an A cup to a C cup. Big breasts, big butts and small feet form one cluster, because healthy estrogen levels produce gynoid fat and small feet.

head: When the Cue Matters More Than the Woman
dek: Visual triggers can work almost independently of any actual partner. About half of roosters tried to mate with a fake hen's head on a feathered board, and turkeys will try with a rubber ball at the right height.
more: Visual triggers can work almost independently of any actual partner. About half of roosters tried to mate with a fake hen's head on a feathered board, and turkeys will try with a rubber ball at the right height. Hentai exploits the same logic by exaggerating every cue.

head: Visual Men, Narrative Women
dek: The book's headline finding. Men respond to images and women to stories.
more: The book's headline finding. Men respond to images and women to stories. At the time of writing, about 2% of credit-card payments for porn came from women, while about 90% of romance novels are read by women, and romance is by far the largest fiction genre. A brief clip can be enough for a man, while the female equivalent is a whole novel.

head: Miss Marple's Detective Agency
dek: Ogas and Gaddam's metaphor: every woman's mind runs four detectives (social, cultural, emotional and physical) to vet potential mates, while men have only the physical one.
more: Ogas and Gaddam's metaphor: every woman's mind runs four detectives (social, cultural, emotional and physical) to vet potential mates, while men have only the physical one. This helps explain why women tend to remember more, talk and text more, and build networks of 'informants'. The downside is higher rates of anxiety, depression and eating disorders, because the detective work never stops. Amit has learned to seek advice from women close to him when he's stuck on 'male hardware issues'.

head: Physical vs Psychological Arousal
dek: In men, physical and psychological arousal go together. In women they are separate processes in different parts of the brain.
more: In men, physical and psychological arousal go together. In women they are separate processes in different parts of the brain. In one study, women showed physical arousal to almost every image, including gorillas mating, but psychological arousal to only one or two, while men's bodies didn't respond to the gorillas at all. A critical consequence: a woman's body may respond during rape, but that is not consent or secret enjoyment.

head: The Power of Or vs the Power of And
dek: Male arousal works on 'or': any one cue, whether breasts, a butt or simple willingness, can be enough.
more: Male arousal works on 'or': any one cue, whether breasts, a butt or simple willingness, can be enough. Female arousal works on 'and': looks, conversation, attentiveness, status ('is he a chauffeur or a CEO?') and more all have to line up. That is why turning on a man is easy and turning on a woman is hard. Amit rejects the advice books telling women to 'settle'.

head: Romance Novels as Women's Revealed Preferences
dek: Just as porn reveals male preferences, romance novels reveal female ones.
more: Just as porn reveals male preferences, romance novels reveal female ones. Heroes tend to be dominant, even obnoxious, which helps explain why serial killers attract female admirers. The core fantasy is 'taming the wild coconut': a cad who is hard outside and soft inside, whom the heroine alone domesticates, often bringing him to tears. Status matters enormously too.

head: The Two Great Self-Delusions
dek: Each sex has a typical fantasy. The female one is that the exciting bad boy and the steady provider can be found in one man, which romance novels endlessly sell even though few people are both.
more: Each sex has a typical fantasy. The female one is that the exciting bad boy and the steady provider can be found in one man, which romance novels endlessly sell even though few people are both. The male one is that he can reliably give a woman sexual satisfaction, which is often untrue and leads women to fake it to please men.

head: Romance, Jealousy and Their Asymmetry
dek: Romance and jealousy are adaptations that keep parents together long enough to raise children.
more: Romance and jealousy are adaptations that keep parents together long enough to raise children. Male jealousy is sexual because a man doesn't want to raise another man's child. Female jealousy is emotional because a woman needs commitment and provision. Amit says this, alongside patriarchy and social conditioning, partly explains why wives forgive infidelity more often than husbands do.

head: Men Are Smart Because Women Are Selective
dek: In many species, such as dragonflies, females aren't choosy. Human females are, so men must compete, and male intelligence and displays become ornaments.
more: In many species, such as dragonflies, females aren't choosy. Human females are, so men must compete, and male intelligence and displays become ornaments. Pinker suggests in The Blank Slate that art and culture may be male ornamentation.

head: Women Want to Be Lovable, Men Aspire to Greatness
dek: Being lovable secures commitment and is relatively achievable.
more: Being lovable secures commitment and is relatively achievable. Men compete in a winner-take-most game: Amit's rough recollection is that about 80% of women but about 30% of men have descendants, and dating apps make it worse. So men take mad risks (the 'dumb ways to die' accounts are nearly all men) and chase greatness. Amit calls that chase toxic and an obstacle to happiness, a hardwired trait to recognise and resist. Men should also aspire to be lovable.

head: Gay Men Have Male Brains
dek: Gay men's desire works like straight men's: visual, focused on the same body zones, with little interest in story.
more: Gay men's desire works like straight men's: visual, focused on the same body zones, with little interest in story. They often prefer straight porn because they are drawn to macho, actually-straight men. That gave rise to 'straight porn for gay men', which focuses the camera on the man, and women started watching it too because they finally got to look at the man.

head: Madame de Staël's Asymmetry of Desire
dek: Amit's closing line, which he thinks sits at the heart of human sexuality.
more: Amit's closing line, which he thinks sits at the heart of human sexuality. Men's desire points at women, while women's desire is for being desired. He suggests much modern behaviour and social complexity follows from this.

head: Hardwiring Is Not Destiny: The Project of Civilisation
dek: Nature and nurture interact rather than one ruling. Knowing our wiring, rather than denying it, is what lets us choose otherwise and live by values we pick.
more: Nature and nurture interact rather than one ruling. Knowing our wiring, rather than denying it, is what lets us choose otherwise and live by values we pick. Ajay adds that modern social-media culture, in peculiar ways, enforces very old-fashioned sexual inhibitions even more toxically than traditional society did.

head: On presenting the sexuality session at Goa, Amit was…
more: On presenting the sexuality session at Goa, Amit was 'at pains to give the caveat to everyone present that this is not a practical class, but theory, theory.'

head: After Ajay's lesson on averages, Amit's WhatsApp joke
more: After Ajay's lesson on averages, Amit's WhatsApp joke: 'On Life Lessons, everybody reads an average of one paper a day. But what's really happening is 139 of us don't read papers at all, and Ajay Shah reads 140 papers every night.' Ajay corrects him: 'I'm averaging three papers a week.'

head: Amit, tripping over
more: Amit, tripping over 'who they are, who be them': 'Who says who be them? Gentle readers, I'm sorry, we are growing old. Enjoy these episodes while they last, we'll be a babbling mess in a scant few weeks.'

head: Amit, on the comic's visiting tailors
more: Amit, on the comic's visiting tailors: 'I like to tell people I'm a trained ladies tailor, which is not true in the tailoring aspect of it.'

head: Amit's naughty rewrite of…
more: Amit's naughty rewrite of 'My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean' (once covered by the Beatles), in honour of the voluptuous Bengali boudi: 'My Boudi Lies Over the Lotion.'

head: Ajay notes that porn thrived even on weak 640x480 screens and was…
more: Ajay notes that porn thrived even on weak 640x480 screens and was 'always the pioneering app that drove computer usage'. Amit recalls dial-up days when 'Samantha Fox is half done, she's at the neck and you're waiting for the rest to come.'

head: Amit's CEO joke, from their friend Narendra Shenoy
more: Amit's CEO joke, from their friend Narendra Shenoy: a CEO gives each of three girlfriends a million dollars. One beautifies herself, one buys him a Sony FX3 and XM4 headphones, and one invests in diversified index funds 'just as you recommend in our finance webinar' and turns it into three million. 'Who does he choose? He chooses the one with the big boobs.' Ajay: 'I didn't see that coming.' Amit: 'I'm glad it came.'

head: Amit before his Goa talk
more: Amit before his Goa talk: 'ladies, I'm gonna go up there and I'm gonna mansplain to you about ovulation.'

head: Amit, on the rarity of combining cad and provider
more: Amit, on the rarity of combining cad and provider: 'seldom can everyone combine the sexual allure of the younger Ajay Shah and the responsible vibe of the older Ajay Shah. Or would you say you combine both of them now... let's not embarrass you.'

Amit: 'Ajay Shah, you're so lovable. Is this intentional or are you just naturally a little woman?' Ajay: 'I'm fifty-nine years old. I grew up.' Amit: 'Nobody grows up... There are no adults... Adulting is the biggest con job that they tell you.'
Ajay's 'pretty line': 'Men love women, women love children, children love kittens.' Amit: 'There is no reciprocity.'

head: Ogas and Gaddam's opening observation that we understand our sexuality poorly
more: Ogas and Gaddam's opening observation that we understand our sexuality poorly: 'Scientists have an easier time gazing at intergalactic quasars than peeking into someone's bedroom.'
'Know thyself', the inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, together with Socrates's 'the unexamined life is not worth living', as Amit's first reason for studying sexuality.

head: Donald Symons
more: Donald Symons: 'To encounter erotica designed to appeal to the other sex is to gaze into the psychological abyss that separates the sexes.'

head: Neil Strauss's The Game, which Amit calls…
more: Neil Strauss's The Game, which Amit calls 'perhaps the earliest handbook for incels': 'You don't have to be an asshole, but if you have no choice, being an inconsiderate asshole beats being a polite beta every time.'

head: Why Failing All His Life Was a Blessing
dek: Early success that comes from luck can lock in arrogance and end learning.
more: Amit says that as an arrogant young man who knew nothing, the worst thing that could have happened to him was early success. He would have credited it to his own greatness and stopped learning. People sometimes read his line 'I failed all my life' as Bengali self-pity. He insists those years of failure are what made him who he is: humble, more aware of the world's complexity, and more empathetic towards other people.
Early success that comes from luck can lock in arrogance and end learning. Failure forces the humility that growth depends on. This is the personal side of Ajay's 'the world is complex' framework.

head: The Human Heart vs a Quasar
dek: It is a candid look at two kinds of intellectual temperament, one pulled towards people and one towards physics.
more: While Amit was explaining that the mysteries of human nature move him more than science, Ajay burst out laughing. He then asked Amit a question: if a genie offered you a window into the human heart or a window into a quasar fifty million light years away, which would you pick? Amit chose the human heart. Ajay picked the cosmos without hesitating: give him two neutron stars about to collide and a camera pointed at them, and let him build an observatory there.
It is a candid look at two kinds of intellectual temperament, one pulled towards people and one towards physics. The show's chemistry comes from having both.

head: Tigran Petrosian: 'I'm Playing to Play'
dek: If you anchor your effort to outcomes such as winning or reaching goals, the work becomes a means to an end.
more: In the last round of a tournament, the Soviet grandmaster Tigran Petrosian's opponent wanted a draw. He leaned over and whispered, 'Are you playing to win?' Petrosian shook his head. A few moves later he asked, 'Are you playing to draw then?' Again Petrosian said no. The confused opponent asked why he was playing at all, and Petrosian replied, 'I'm playing to play.' Amit made this his life philosophy, wrote a newsletter post about it, and a listener later had the phrase tattooed on his arm.
If you anchor your effort to outcomes such as winning or reaching goals, the work becomes a means to an end. Doing something for its own sake is more joyful and more sustainable.
printed: Not to win, not to draw

head: How René Girard Discovered Mimetic Desire
dek: A big idea came out of a side gig taken for money, and from noticing a pattern across many books.
more: As a young man, the philosopher René Girard agreed to teach a literature course because he needed extra pocket money. He put together a reading list of the classics and noticed that in all of them, the heroes and heroines want things because somebody else wants them, not because the desire is their own. He called this mimetic desire. Luke Burgis's book Wanting later built on it to distinguish thick desires from thin ones.
A big idea came out of a side gig taken for money, and from noticing a pattern across many books. It also prompts a personal question: how many of your own wants are borrowed from other people?

head: The Joy of Reinventing What Others Already Found
dek: This is 'play to play' inside an intellectual career. The deepest satisfaction is seeing something for yourself, even when the world has seen it before.
more: Ajay says the excitement of his research life lies in doing the research. Reading papers is only a means to that end. He often reinvents something from scratch that others have already done, and he is fine with that. If your aim is the joy of doing, you're happy. If your aim is a publication or a patent, you're unhappy.
This is 'play to play' inside an intellectual career. The deepest satisfaction is seeing something for yourself, even when the world has seen it before.

head: Seventeen Years Without a Full-Time Job
dek: If life is just an accumulation of days, then designing a good day matters more than designing an impressive career.
more: Amit explains that he hasn't held a full-time job for seventeen or eighteen years for one reason: he wants to be master of his own time. He wants to wake up looking forward to the day and end it happy with how he spent it, whether that means shooting an episode or doing matargashti with Ajay.
If life is just an accumulation of days, then designing a good day matters more than designing an impressive career. Annie Dillard's line becomes a practical life choice here.

head: 'It Took Me All My Life'
dek: Even seasoned policy thinkers learn slowly about institutions. Admitting past errors is part of practising the humility the episode argues for.
more: Amit asks Ajay whether his deep scepticism of the state, formed after years inside 'the belly of the beast', grew slowly or was always there. Ajay answers that it took him his whole life to understand these things deeply, and he apologises for the mistakes he made along the way.
Even seasoned policy thinkers learn slowly about institutions. Admitting past errors is part of practising the humility the episode argues for.

head: Ajay Actually Lives 'Give Unconditionally'
dek: A philosophy of giving is credible when someone close to the person can vouch for it from experience.
more: After Ajay describes his framework of giving unconditionally, Amit adds a personal testimony. He has known Ajay for many years and has himself benefited from Ajay's generosity. Usually Amit's advice comes with 'do as I say, not as I do', but here he tells listeners to copy Ajay's actions, not only his words.
A philosophy of giving is credible when someone close to the person can vouch for it from experience.

head: The Blank Slate
dek: It opened up natural selection as a lens for understanding human nature and knowing yourself.
more: It opened up natural selection as a lens for understanding human nature and knowing yourself.
The first book Amit names when describing how he came to understand natural selection through popular science rather than biology class.

dek: It gave him a frame for looking at himself and the world, and it solidified his atheism.
more: It gave him a frame for looking at himself and the world, and it solidified his atheism.

dek: Another of the popular-science books that made natural selection his first framework.
more: Another of the popular-science books that made natural selection his first framework.

dek: It helped him apply evolutionary thinking to the mysteries of the mind and human nature.
more: It helped him apply evolutionary thinking to the mysteries of the mind and human nature.

head: Every Grain of Sand
dek: Dylan's image of finding meaning in 'every grain of sand' captures the idea that the answers are distributed all around us.
more: Dylan's image of finding meaning in 'every grain of sand' captures the idea that the answers are distributed all around us.
Amit read the lyrics aloud after Ajay argued that knowledge is scattered across every human being.

dek: It shows spontaneous order at work across natural selection, language, the economy, cultural norms and common law.
more: It shows spontaneous order at work across natural selection, language, the economy, cultural norms and common law. He suggests reading it and then using an AI to dig deep into each example.
Amit's answer to a listener who asked him to explain spontaneous order.

dek: It shows the price system as a language through which strangers a thousand miles apart tell each other what they want and lack.
more: It shows the price system as a language through which strangers a thousand miles apart tell each other what they want and lack. This is spontaneous order in action.
Discussed in their 'Four Papers That Changed the World' episode, which Amit notes is surprisingly one of their most popular.

head: State Building
dek: Fukuyama's split between a state's scope and its strength explains India's problem: it does many things badly when it should do a few things, starting with rule of law, well.
more: Fukuyama's split between a state's scope and its strength explains India's problem: it does many things badly when it should do a few things, starting with rule of law, well.
The source of Amit's 'bonus framework' after Ajay's rule-of-law segment.

head: I Play to Play
dek: It sets out the philosophy he says guides his life and that he gives to every young person he advises.
more: It sets out the philosophy he says guides his life and that he gives to every young person he advises.
His newsletter post on the Petrosian story, which inspired a listener's tattoo.

head: Machines of Loving Grace
dek: Ajay is no 'rah-rah' booster of tech paradises, but he finds this essay sensible and thoughtful about what happens as AI progresses, and says everyone should read it.
more: Ajay is no 'rah-rah' booster of tech paradises, but he finds this essay sensible and thoughtful about what happens as AI progresses, and says everyone should read it.
Ajay's end-of-episode recommendation.

head: First Principles Thinking as a Defence Against Nonsense
dek: Ajay frames the whole episode this way. You can accept an inherited edifice of assumptions and work within it.
more: Ajay frames the whole episode this way. You can accept an inherited edifice of assumptions and work within it. But if you want to reason from first principles, which is your best protection against the world's nonsense, you need a toolkit of basic frameworks. The ten frameworks are that toolkit.

head: Natural Selection as a Tool for Knowing Yourself
dek: Natural selection shouldn't be confined to biology class. Following the Delphic 'know thyself', understanding how evolution wired you lets you decide which tendencies to dampen and which to amplify.
more: Natural selection shouldn't be confined to biology class. Following the Delphic 'know thyself', understanding how evolution wired you lets you decide which tendencies to dampen and which to amplify. For Amit, a literature-loving person, it is the best key to puzzles like why we love, cry and feel lonely. It also solidified an atheism he already held.

head: The World Is Complex
dek: This is the one thing Ajay would tell his 20-year-old self.
more: This is the one thing Ajay would tell his 20-year-old self. He gives three sources of complexity. (1) Randomness: our tidy histories only see the lottery outcome, so analogies to the past mislead. (2) Nonlinearity: small changes cause large ones later, and chaos limits prediction. (3) Dispersed information: even with the right equations, as with weather and Navier-Stokes, nobody has enough data. The implications are humility, firms that push autonomy to the employees who hold local knowledge, and building societies that draw out the knowledge held by every person. Ajay says the opposite arrogance is the delusion behind China-style engineering states.

head: Spontaneous Order
dek: Our hunter-gatherer instincts make us see every problem as an engineering task needing a leader.
more: Our hunter-gatherer instincts make us see every problem as an engineering task needing a leader. Yet much of the world is 'the result of human action, but not human design' (Adam Ferguson). Examples include evolution, common law, cultural norms and language, where dialects shift village by village and no committee decides anything. Above all it is the economy, where prices act as a language that lets strangers meet each other's needs without a central planner.

head: The State Is a Monopoly of Violence Run by Self-Interested People
dek: Indians tend to see the state as a benevolent mother or an NGO. Ajay offers two corrections.
more: Indians tend to see the state as a benevolent mother or an NGO. Ajay offers two corrections. Weber: the state is a community that holds a monopoly on physical violence over a territory. Public choice theory: the people who staff it pursue their own goals, not public welfare. The central puzzle of politics is turning that coercive power into human welfare. Amit adds that you should assume the state is both malign and incompetent. He also argues that every state drifts along Buchanan's path from protective to productive to predatory, and that the predatory state is now so normal that nobody questions it.

head: The Double Thank-You Moment
dek: When you buy coffee, you thank the seller and the seller thanks you, because each values what they receive more than what they give up.
more: When you buy coffee, you thank the seller and the seller thanks you, because each values what they receive more than what they give up. Voluntary exchange is positive-sum, even though our instincts are zero-sum. The explosion of human welfare in the Maddison graph comes partly from markets widening the circle of people we can trade with. Amit adds three points. Profit from voluntary exchange is the greatest philanthropy. Markets are society's own mechanism for meeting needs, not a third pillar set against it. Every state interference in such a moment reduces the welfare of both parties.

head: Rule of Law: Taking Discretion Away from Civil Servants
dek: This is the only defence against coercive power sliding into tyranny.
more: This is the only defence against coercive power sliding into tyranny. It requires separation of powers: the legislature, chosen in free and fair elections, writes the laws; the executive only investigates; only the judiciary sentences. Laws must be compact and knowable, because a 50,000-word law plus selective enforcement means anyone can be jailed. The accused must get the charges and evidence in writing, a hearing before an independent judge, and appeals. At its core, the civil servant should have no discretion over what counts as a crime, whom to investigate, or whom to prosecute.
printed: The only gunda on the block

head: State Scope vs Strength (Fukuyama)
dek: Amit's bonus framework. A state can try to do many things or few things, and it can do them well or badly.
more: Amit's bonus framework. A state can try to do many things or few things, and it can do them well or badly. The Indian state does many things badly. Both hosts want it to do a few things well, beginning with rule of law, from which the rest can follow.

head: I Play to Play
dek: Don't play to win, and don't fix on outcomes or grand goals. Play for the beauty of it.
more: Don't play to win, and don't fix on outcomes or grand goals. Play for the beauty of it. Sisyphus is tragic only if the aim is to get the rock to the top. If the aim is the rolling itself, it is your dharma and you can be happy. Goals can be toxic because of hedonic adaptation: whatever you achieve quickly becomes the new baseline and is taken for granted.

head: Thick vs Thin Desires
dek: This builds on Girard's mimetic desire, as popularised by Luke Burgis.
more: This builds on Girard's mimetic desire, as popularised by Luke Burgis. Thin desires are borrowed from others in search of validation. They can be very intense, like wanting a Mercedes, a vice-president title, or the scripted marriage-and-two-kids life. Thick desires are intrinsic and deep, and often hidden even from yourself. Writing to win prizes is a thin desire. Writing for the magic of filling a blank page is a thick one. Playing to play is how thick desires express themselves.

head: Life Is Not a Spectator Sport
dek: This is Ajay's own slogan about the balance between consuming and making.
more: This is Ajay's own slogan about the balance between consuming and making. Reading others' books and watching others play has its place. Organising your life around your own creations and activities is a hundred times more exciting. Amit defends watching sport as a form of participation, but agrees with the bias for action.

head: How We Spend Our Days Is How We Spend Our Lives
dek: Annie Dillard's line, which Amit quotes so often that people joke about it.
more: Annie Dillard's line, which Amit quotes so often that people joke about it. Chasing greatness turns each day into a waiting room for a future that hedonic adaptation will cheapen anyway. A life is an accumulation of days, so live each one fully. Ajay adds that 'life', set against a complex world, is too big to plan and breeds apathy, while a day is a tangible problem you have agency over.

head: Give Unconditionally: Flourishing over Prospering
dek: Much of life is a hustle of trading favours and tracking IOUs to climb a ladder.
more: Much of life is a hustle of trading favours and tracking IOUs to climb a ladder. Keeping score reflects fear and a scarcity mindset. Giving without keeping accounts reflects abundance. It makes you happier, frees mental bandwidth for truth and beauty, and invites unexpected kindness back. It is in your self-interest.

head: Amit opens
more: Amit opens: 'You come here for enlightenment, but today we will give you intimacy.' The episode was meant to be shot before a live Life Lessons audience in Goa, but 'It rained in Goa in October, who would have thought?'

head: For years Amit heard Ajay say he'd
more: For years Amit heard Ajay say he'd 'just written a BS article' and admired the extreme modesty. Then he realised BS meant Business Standard, where Ajay has had a column for thirty years.

head: When Ajay laughs mid-monologue, Amit asks…
more: When Ajay laughs mid-monologue, Amit asks: 'Am I so deeply attractive that you can't just help burst out with happiness?' After Ajay picks the quasar over the human heart, Amit adds: 'Ladies, this is Ajay Shah. This is why he doesn't ask you questions and listen well. He's thinking of quasars.'

head: Amit's spontaneous-order digression into Gen Z slang: once upon a time it wasn't good to be sick
more: Amit's spontaneous-order digression into Gen Z slang: once upon a time it wasn't good to be sick, but 'Today when someone says Amit, you're so sick, man... I'm like yeah in multiple ways, but how did you know?' Then: 'Why did I digress like this? Because we digress, that's what we do.'

head: Explaining prices as a language through which distant strangers fulfil each other's needs and make each other happy, Amit stops himself
more: Explaining prices as a language through which distant strangers fulfil each other's needs and make each other happy, Amit stops himself: 'This is sounding so sensuous already.'

head: On the listener who had
more: On the listener who had 'I play to play' tattooed on his arm, Amit was 'obviously very moved', but also couldn't help a 'why body mutilation?' reaction, admitting he's 'a little old fashioned that way.'
Amit's 'vociferous demand': since Ajay preaches generosity, 'you also have to be generous with your fucking recommendations.'

head: Heading off at the end, Amit tells Ajay to lead
more: Heading off at the end, Amit tells Ajay to lead 'partly to make sure that any obstacles on the path are encountered by you first and I can craftily avoid them.' Ajay replies: 'I'll clear all the spider webs as we pass.'

head: Douglas Adams on natural selection, read by Amit
more: Douglas Adams on natural selection, read by Amit: 'I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.'

head: Dan Wang's recent book on China's
more: Dan Wang's recent book on China's 'engineer's view of the world', cited by Ajay as the arrogance of believing the world isn't complicated.

head: Adam Ferguson's phrase for spontaneous order
more: Adam Ferguson's phrase for spontaneous order: 'the result of human action, but not human design.'
'A language is a dialect with an army.' Amit uses it to argue that Hindi isn't inherently superior to Bhojpuri or Maithili, and notes how politics split Hindustani into Hindi and Urdu.

head: Max Weber's definition of the state as a community holding a monopoly of physical violence over a territory, which Ajay calls…
more: Max Weber's definition of the state as a community holding a monopoly of physical violence over a territory, which Ajay calls 'the only gunda on the block'.

head: Hanlon's razor (
more: Hanlon's razor ('never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity'), which Amit stretches into: assume the state is both malign and incompetent.

head: Raghuram Rajan and Rohini Nilekani's
more: Raghuram Rajan and Rohini Nilekani's 'state, society, markets' trichotomy, which Amit argued against on his show.

head: Gorbachev, quoted by Ajay
more: Gorbachev, quoted by Ajay: 'markets are not a feature of capitalism, markets are the invention of civilization.'

head: Neil Simon, quoted by Amit
more: Neil Simon, quoted by Amit: 'the world is full of two kinds of people, the watchers and the doers, and the watchers sit around watching the doers do.'

head: Annie Dillard
more: Annie Dillard: 'How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.'
'Matargashti', which Amit calls 'one of the great terms of our times', and doing it with a friend is his idea of a day well spent.

head: Dario Amodei's essay title
more: Dario Amodei's essay title 'Machines of Loving Grace', which Ajay notes is a line from a poem.

head: Running Out of Lifetimes
dek: The best content is a distilled lifetime, and that supply is finite. A creator who admits the well is running dry, instead of padding the schedule, keeps the body of work honest.
more: Ajay's main reason for ending the show is that he has said what he wanted to say. Complete, satisfying episodes come from lifetimes of lived knowledge: a lifetime of hiking yields one episode, a lifetime of cycling another, a lifetime of poker another. Nobody can live extra lives to produce more of them. As the show moved away from that familiar material, each episode got harder to make. On top of that he has a book on taxes with Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi, several research papers, and three conferences in early December. Stopping looked like the optimal call.
The best content is a distilled lifetime, and that supply is finite. A creator who admits the well is running dry, instead of padding the schedule, keeps the body of work honest.
printed: Said what he had to say

head: Friday, 12 O'Clock, No Matter What
dek: A relentless cadence builds trust, but its real cost is mental bandwidth more than logistics.
more: Amit has never missed a scheduled release. The Seen and the Unseen ran weekly for seven years and is now fortnightly. Everything is Everything has dropped every Friday at noon, with one Saturday slip very early on. That held even when Amit was in hospital for a procedure and when Ajay broke his leg. The shooting was easy: three days at a friend's farmhouse every six weeks, two episodes a day. The burden was producing. Nomsita sent Amit a rough cut, he built the detailed list of on-screen inserts, and the two of them talked over the edit every day, week after week.
A relentless cadence builds trust, but its real cost is mental bandwidth more than logistics. Amit stopped so he could reclaim space for writing and 'get some chill back' in his life.

head: Fifty Ideas, One Show
dek: Ideas are cheap and everyone has a folder full of them. What sets a project apart is starting, then improving through iteration.
more: Amit first pitched a joint show to Ajay three or four years earlier, at a conference in Udaipur. He keeps a creative-ideas folder in Roam Research with around fifty YouTube ideas, such as a solo vlog or a show with this or that person. Most of them never happen. This one did because the two of them simply started, knowing the early episodes would be rough. Some early moments still make them cringe.
Ideas are cheap and everyone has a folder full of them. What sets a project apart is starting, then improving through iteration.

head: The Viewer Who Interrupted
dek: Stars used to be larger than life. Today's medium is intimate, which is why being yourself works and performing doesn't.
more: Amit once recorded an episode of The Seen and the Unseen with Abhinandan Sekhri. A viewer later told him the conversation felt so much like sitting with two friends in their living room that at one point they actually interrupted.
Stars used to be larger than life. Today's medium is intimate, which is why being yourself works and performing doesn't.

head: The Two-Year Pact Ajay Broke
dek: Getting from bad to excellent depends on iteration and on being internally driven.
more: At the start, Amit sat Ajay down and proposed a deal: do the show for two years without looking at the numbers. The idea came from Ali Abdaal's advice that a new YouTuber should ignore the numbers for two years. Ajay ignored the deal and kept checking the analytics. Amit's reasoning was that chasing applause makes you dumb yourself down, and applause never comes at the start anyway because everyone is bad at first. He notes that Ajay went from awkward and clumsy to a consummate professional who nails it on camera.
Getting from bad to excellent depends on iteration and on being internally driven. Early validation-seeking interrupts that process.

head: Advice to a Friend Starting a Podcast
dek: A show is a body of work, a repository. The frequent flow of episodes slowly becomes lasting stock.
more: A few years ago, when The Seen and the Unseen was doing well, a dear friend asked Amit for advice before starting her own podcast, which went on to succeed. He told her not to worry about how the audience would receive the first episode. She should picture the hundred-episode catalogue they would one day binge.
A show is a body of work, a repository. The frequent flow of episodes slowly becomes lasting stock.
printed: Plan for the binge, not the debut

head: Why the Show Won't Get a New Co-Host
dek: A brand belongs to the people in it, not just the format. Sometimes keeping its integrity means letting the name end.
more: Ajay urged Amit to resurrect the show in some form, since the ethos, people and audience are all still there. Others suggested Amit continue with a new co-host. Pranay Kotasthane, whom both hosts admire, came to mind first. When Amit talked to him, Pranay's view, which Amit shares, was that Everything is Everything is Amit and Ajay. They may do a separate, fun show someday, with Bollywood and Hindi in it, under a different name on the same channel, which Amit always meant to host several shows.
A brand belongs to the people in it, not just the format. Sometimes keeping its integrity means letting the name end.

Episodes showing that the hosts aren't 'just dry people who are into ideas'.

head: 'Better to be loved by a few than liked by many'
dek: Deep engagement builds trust, real community and better discourse. Chasing mass appeal leads to mediocrity.
more: Deep engagement builds trust, real community and better discourse. Chasing mass appeal leads to mediocrity.

head: The Seen and the Unseen
dek: Long-form conversations ('ten hour conversations with boring economists') that no gatekeeper would have commissioned.
more: Long-form conversations ('ten hour conversations with boring economists') that no gatekeeper would have commissioned.
Amit's other show, weekly for seven years and now fortnightly. It's where many of his creator lessons were first learned. Linked in the show notes.

head: One Consistent Toolkit Against Default Statism
dek: In India, statism is everywhere: by default, more state coercion is the answer to everything.
more: In India, statism is everywhere: by default, more state coercion is the answer to everything. Attempts to reimagine the country have been piecemeal, and a piecemeal reform fails when every other element around it is still distorted by the state. Ajay claims the show's unique contribution is a complete picture. It applies one internally consistent way of thinking across more than a hundred episodes, with people, freedom, consent and agency as the engine of progress. The state is needed, but it is not the essence.

head: Beyond the Solow Model: Why India Is Poor
dek: The crude Solow model says output comes from labour and capital times a productivity number, and early post-independence thinking read it causally.
more: The crude Solow model says output comes from labour and capital times a productivity number, and early post-independence thinking read it causally. Ajay argues every term hides a deeper story. Labour: only about 36-38% of people aged 16-64 work, roughly half China's ratio. The problem isn't a shortage of people but a lack of firm formation. Capital: the world has effectively infinite capital, but India doesn't open its capital account to lower the cost of capital. Productivity: high-capability firms need a thousand institutional checks and balances and creative destruction. The real question is why capital and labour aren't being mobilised into high-quality firms.

head: One Long Conversation: Public Purpose Meets Private Passion
dek: Amit treats his shows as one long conversation with threads you can pull, not a series of separate episodes.
more: Amit treats his shows as one long conversation with threads you can pull, not a series of separate episodes. Here the threads include the state, firms, finance, education and development. The show also fused public purpose with private passion, so reading, chess, cricket, poker and stories that should be films sat alongside policy.

head: Bias for Action (for Creators, Not the State)
dek: For individual creators, starting is everything: you need a place to begin, and you only improve by iterating.
more: For individual creators, starting is everything: you need a place to begin, and you only improve by iterating. Amit flags the phrase as dangerous, because Ajay has often argued that the state should not have a bias for action. Every state act is deeply consequential, so it needs a gradual process with many stakeholders and diverse opinions.

head: Don't Let Perfection Get in the Way of Production
dek: Amit took this line from Vinay Sitapati. Creators constantly face a trade-off between getting it done and getting it right, and getting it done is how you get it right.
more: Amit took this line from Vinay Sitapati. Creators constantly face a trade-off between getting it done and getting it right, and getting it done is how you get it right. Mistakes will happen, like the typo in every written piece or the 'verbal typos' in every episode. Audiences watch in good faith, so let it go.
printed: Done is the road to right

head: Stock and Flow for Creators
dek: Amit borrows the economist's distinction. Stock, like wealth, lasts: books outlive you and add to the shelf of knowledge, so agonise over them.
more: Amit borrows the economist's distinction. Stock, like wealth, lasts: books outlive you and add to the shelf of knowledge, so agonise over them. Flow, like income, keeps coming: columns, blog posts, newsletters and weekly shows. With flow, think aloud and ship it. Putting it out makes you a better thinker, and the feedback exposes holes in your argument. Over time, a body of flow can itself become stock.

head: Loved by a Few Beats Liked by Many
dek: A smaller audience with deep engagement beats mass reach. Those people stop you at Blossom's bookstore in Bangalore, leave thoughtful comments, buy your courses and trust you.
more: A smaller audience with deep engagement beats mass reach. Those people stop you at Blossom's bookstore in Bangalore, leave thoughtful comments, buy your courses and trust you. Chasing whatever is trending puts you in competition with everyone else doing the same thing.

head: Authenticity Is Easy and Rewarding
dek: Pretending is exhausting, and over a long run it produces contrived content that people see through.
more: Pretending is exhausting, and over a long run it produces contrived content that people see through. Being yourself takes no effort, it's what people connect with, and it's the only thing that sets you apart from eight billion others.

head: Community Is the Only Thing You Can Monetise
dek: In the 1990s, a writer sold an 800-word piece to a paper like the Indian Express.
more: In the 1990s, a writer sold an 800-word piece to a paper like the Indian Express. They went through a gatekeeper, fitted a house style, chased the news cycle, and got a tiny slice of the advertising revenue the paper earned by selling eyeballs. Both middlemen, the publisher and the advertiser, are going away. Creators now reach readers directly, and readers already pay with their time and attention. What matters is the community, not ads.

head: The Means of Production Are in Your Hands
dek: No mainstream channel would have commissioned two unglamorous people discussing inflation targeting, or ten-hour conversations with economists.
more: No mainstream channel would have commissioned two unglamorous people discussing inflation targeting, or ten-hour conversations with economists. Creators now have freedom of subject and freedom of form: one hour, two hours, split into two parts. They can discover who they are by experimenting. Amit says 'creative' covers educators and social-sector thinkers as much as writers and filmmakers.

head: Play the Long Game
dek: The moment outside applause matters, you start dumbing yourself down, and early applause never comes anyway.
more: The moment outside applause matters, you start dumbing yourself down, and early applause never comes anyway. Be internally driven, ignore the 'bad lighting' worries, and build a body of work that lasts. Ajay applies the same principle to public policy.

head: Ajay says he has so many research papers to write.
more: Ajay says he has so many research papers to write. Amit: 'When you said so many, I was hoping you're gonna say so many books', a public nudge to write the books Amit keeps pushing on him, like Invisible Infrastructure.

head: Amit, who cringes at his own footage, revives a line from his audio-only days
more: Amit, who cringes at his own footage, revives a line from his audio-only days: 'I have a face for audio.'

head: Amit imagines pitching the show to mainstream media: inflation targeting, the bankruptcy code, two hosts who…
more: Amit imagines pitching the show to mainstream media: inflation targeting, the bankruptcy code, two hosts who 'aren't even like glamorous, amazing people', and 'neither of us is a good-looking woman'. He quickly adds that Ajay's 'good looks and your shirts are legendary'.

head: On how The Seen and the Unseen would have been pitched
more: On how The Seen and the Unseen would have been pitched: 'You're gonna have ten hour conversations with boring economists, like what the hell?'

head: Amit admits every written piece of his has one typo that a reader flags within an hour. Spoken shows are no different
more: Amit admits every written piece of his has one typo that a reader flags within an hour. Spoken shows are no different: 'when we speak, there are always typos, verbal typos will just happen.'
'No man steps in the same river twice', the old line on constant flux, used in the show notes and by Amit as the frame for letting the show go.

head: Ajay's farewell begins with the line
more: Ajay's farewell begins with the line 'Everything that dies, some day it comes back', as he refuses to treat this as the end of Everything is Everything.

head: Vinay Sitapati's advice, recalled from an old Seen and the Unseen episode about how he wrote his book
more: Vinay Sitapati's advice, recalled from an old Seen and the Unseen episode about how he wrote his book: 'Don't let perfection get in the way of production.'
